The solution trained ViT-Large, ConvNeXt-XXLarge, and modified BLIP-2 models to predict prompt embeddings using approximately 10.6 million generated images. LoRA on lower layers, an additional fully connected head for CLIP models, and removing BLIP-2's language model improved the approach. solution_title: 164th Place Solution — NVIDIA Nemotron Reasoning Challenge
solution_summary: The solution warm-started LoRA training for NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Nano from an existing public adapter using Unsloth and curated chain-of-thought data. solution_title: 15th Place Solution - A Beginner Data Scientist's Journey
solution_summary: The final pipeline filled five prediction slots with template-based modeling, two RNAPro configurations, and Protenix 2025, with the last two slots containing identical coordinates. Template selection combined sequence and ligand similarity with chain composition, while structural corrections improved the pure template predictions. Longer sequences were handled through sliding windows and stitching. Validation used the default validation set, USalign TM-score, and an interactive 3D dashboard that exposed structural problems. Protenix fine-tuning was abandoned because of seed variance and catastrophic forgetting.

The final TensorFlow solution ensembled four selected cross-validation models with one model trained on the entire competition training set. Both model variants used Transformer architectures with LayerNorm and float16 quantization; the full-data model additionally used flip augmentation. Optuna tuning, grouped stratified validation and strong label smoothing were useful, while distillation and several geometric or noise augmentations were unsuccessful. solution_title: 20th Place Solution (Private 0.95533) — Ridge Stacking + Weighted Rank-Average

The Ridge meta-model used an alpha of 14.375664881335657, while the rank ensemble doubled the weights of three RealMLP variants. Saving aligned out-of-fold and test predictions and examining rank correlations were central to keeping the ensembles stable. solution_title: Part of the 18th place solution (Iafoss's model)

Five-second training chunks, soft-label focal loss, and audio augmentation supported this pipeline. Shifted-window prediction averaging and class-level post-processing improved inference, and a weighted two-model ensemble achieved public/private scores of 0.7736/0.6605.

solution_title: 118th Place Solution for the Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations Competition draft

Models predicted onset and wakeup probabilities at several temporal tolerances, followed by peak suppression and small timing adjustments. solution_title: 44th Place Solution for the Stanford Ribonanza RNA Folding Competition

solution_title: 35th place: rtklib tweaking and factor graph approach
solution_summary: The final submission combined an RTKLIB solution and a global factor graph solution using a weighted average. RTKLIB benefited from preserving receiver cycle slip flags and weighting measurements by signal strength and pseudorange uncertainty. The factor graph combined pseudorange, motion, Doppler, and time-differenced carrier phase constraints, with outlier handling and acceleration constraints to improve trajectories. Both approaches used Kalman smoothing, while ambiguity resolution and ensembling alternative RTKLIB weighting schemes did not improve results.

The author's individual model combined wavelet-denoised signals, a basic RNN, and engineered peak features. Peak features reduced overfitting and included counts and statistics of peak heights and widths. Feature outliers were converted to missing values and filled with group means based on a correlated attribute. Training ran for 25 epochs with validation-loss checkpoint monitoring, and the final submission ensembled this model with two publicly shared approaches.

The solution retrieved landmark images using EfficientNet-B5/B6/B7 and ResNet152 embeddings trained with ArcFace and progressively larger images. Training expanded from cleaned GLDv2 to a larger subset containing the same landmark classes. solution_title: The 440th solution of the 'Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations' competition

solution_summary: The solution diversified image resizing, augmentation, tokenization, and CNN-transformer or vision-transformer architectures. Features captured standardized motion, repeated daily patterns, heuristic sleep episodes, and temporal lags. Weighted averaging and a confidence-reduction post-processing method produced a component CV of 0.825 and private score of 0.840; the team's final submissions used a teammate's refined post-processing.

The final agent used a three-stage heuristic pipeline that scored long-term ship tasks, assigned coordinated plans, and translated those plans into actions. Distance-decayed scores and conflict handling maintained consistent targets and coordinated base returns. Specialized mining, construction, defense, hunting, and rescue rules were combined with online estimates of opponent behavior and multistep safety checks. Deep reinforcement learning was abandoned after a month of unsuccessful experimentation, while chase detection and rescue logic helped beat a strong benchmark.

solution_title: 21st place solution [LB 0.948] on simplified data only
solution_summary: The solution rendered simplified drawings as 128×128 images with three channels encoding line order, stroke counts, and a constant intensity. Several deep CNN architectures were trained using cosine learning-rate annealing, checkpoint averaging, and gradient accumulation to reach a batch size of 1024. A LightGBM stacker classified candidate classes using the networks' probabilities and class identifiers, improving validation performance over simple averaging. The final LightGBM ensemble achieved a reported public leaderboard score of 0.948.

The solution recovered leaked targets by matching shifted feature sequences across 113 sets of 40 features. Reconstructing row groups enabled manual inspection that added missing leaks and corrected misaligned targets, yielding 7,897 test leaks. Correcting unusual three-step offsets improved an older blend's private score from 0.53679 to 0.52115. The authors also investigated aggregate relationships among feature sets and observed target censoring.

The solution averaged three unmodified nnUNetResEncUNetL models trained with different patch sizes. Sliding-window inference used mirroring augmentation for two models, followed by direct probability averaging. Most gains came from anisotropic diffusion and adaptive hysteresis with connectivity restricted to the z direction. Diffusion improved local validation by about 0.005, and the stronger diffusion setting was retained for stability despite a slightly worse public score.

solution_title: A simple approach and only 2 cell-wise models to get a silver [LB Private 0.436]
solution_summary: The author trained cell-wise EfficientNet-B0 and EfficientNet-B1 models on RGB images from competition and external data. Cell tiles were generated using code similar to a linked sample-balanced tile notebook, and the CNN inputs were 224 × 224 pixels. Models used five folds and were trained for five epochs, but the first-epoch checkpoint was consistently selected because it performed better on the leaderboard. The author also observed a relationship between local loss and leaderboard score and shared training code and an inference notebook.

The solution combined category-specific Longformer-base experts with a publicly available Deberta-large model. A Longformer first learned all PII labels, then separate experts were fine-tuned from that checkpoint while other categories were relabeled as O. Public datasets supplemented competition data, and final inference concatenated predictions from the experts and Deberta. A Deberta-large LoRA experiment performed worse than Longformer-base for individual categories.

solution_summary: The final solution combined six DynEdge and LSTM models using weights optimized for held-out mean angular error. Models directly predicted unnormalized three-dimensional direction vectors and minimized their Euclidean distance from the true unit vector. Random pulse selection and averaging four sampled predictions improved accuracy, while skipping redundant evaluations on small events limited the inference overhead to about 15%. Training used batches 1–100 with batches 601–602 held out, and the best reported individual LSTM and GNN scores on batch 602 were 0.9859 and about 1.001.

solution_summary: The team describes a location matching pipeline with candidate generation, transformer blocking, and GBDT/BERT stacking. The post celebrates the success of a simple public kernel and congratulates the deepflash2 team and other winners. It links to a public deepflash2 ensemble submission. It provides no technical account of the author's own pipeline.

The author used blending for the final submission, with limited pipeline details provided in the post. Raising resolution from 1024 to 2000 increased the public score from 0.24 to 0.46, making resolution the central improvement. Feature augmentation, SIFT fusion, alternative matchers, and multiple resolutions did not provide clear additional gains. Repeated runs varied by as much as 0.04 on the public leaderboard, and increasing geometric-verification trials did not resolve this instability.

solution_title: Congratulations to every participant.....🙌😍😍🙌🙌  Once again my late and newly discovered "Ensemble Technique" paid off in the last minutes.

The solution initialized tree packings from a dense lattice whose basic unit was a pair of trees, then refined them with custom simulated annealing. Initialization varied with tree count, and temporarily freezing core trees substantially improved efficiency for larger packings. Tournament selection concentrated compute on promising configurations, while a final annealing variant compressed valid layouts or relaxed invalid ones. solution_summary: The solution combined template-based RNA modeling with Protenix inference under a two-T4 GPU budget. Templates were aligned using sequence and ViennaRNA secondary-structure information, with independent chain matching solved by linear assignment. Protenix candidates were generated within sequence-length and runtime limits, then used to replace weaker template candidates. Missing-chain filling and averaging of closely aligned structures helped candidate quality, while several alignment and coordinate-refinement experiments failed to improve scores.

Validation used majority-voted competition annotations, and local scores ultimately guided decisions because public leaderboard scores were unstable. The ensemble achieved 0.7605 CV and 0.779 LB.

All models used an 80% training split because alternative folds performed worse, and the author suspected the selected validation fold was unusually favorable. Five-pass test-time augmentation reduced both public and private scores. Both selected ensembles achieved about 0.92 private kappa, while the author also reported training on the previous competition's training and test data.

The final ensemble combined 15 sound-event detection models trained with different losses, with Dense161 performing well. Training used multilabel-stratified folds, audio augmentations, and warmup followed by cosine learning-rate scheduling. Minority oversampling and majority undersampling worsened leaderboard performance, while an example Dense161 model scored 0.95548 publicly and 0.96300 privately.

The post describes a post-processing optimization that assigns camera labels while enforcing image-count constraints. It maximizes the sum of predicted probabilities for binary image-to-class assignments. The constraints exploit nearly equal camera-type proportions, equal counts of manipulated and unaltered images, and a timestamp-based public/private split. solution_title: 17th Place Solution: An Alternative Rectification Workflow
solution_summary: The solution used a single-fold pipeline comprising template alignment, grid rectification, line segmentation, and signal regression. A CNN–Transformer regressor converted predicted line intensity masks into subpixel signal coordinates. Pretraining achieved 30 dB validation SNR with ground-truth masks, while predicted masks limited fine-tuned performance to approximately 25–26 dB.

Original features were supplemented with versions that replaced singleton-frequency values by the median, followed by augmentation and stacking. They reported successive score improvements but noted that they forgot to include their neural network's weight in the stacking or blending models.

solution_title: preliminary LB 16th solution——Self-examination of a violator

solution_title: REPRO: The Scored Attack Surface Collapses to a Single Primitive

A separate confused-deputy approach transferred approximately one-to-one between public and private evaluation, with a best private score of 19.065. solution_title: 26th Place Solution – MITSUI&CO. Commodity Prediction Challenge Writeup

solution_summary: The solution first trained a dilated ResNet-18 classifier on small patches, then removed its classification output to extract dense spatial features. Class-wise 1×1 convolutions mapped those features to normalized Gaussian density fields, and a simplified ResNet-18 converted ten density channels into five count predictions using RMSE loss. An auxiliary VGG-16 binary classifier filtered empty tiles to reduce the burden of the expensive dense network. Density regression alone worked well on synthetic data but suffered from class confusion and body-shape-related density overestimation on sea lions, motivating the final count-regression stage.

The final submission used a single Cascade Mask R-CNN with a ConvNeXt-tiny backbone and multi-scale TTA with NMS. Training proceeded through several stages, using initial models to pseudo-label Dataset 3 and later a Dataset 1-focused model to regenerate high-confidence labels for Datasets 2 and 3. Trusting expert-reviewed Dataset 1 annotations, training only the blood-vessel class, and scaling images were central decisions. Larger models, flip augmentation, weighted boxes fusion, and ensembles with other models did not improve the approach.

It reports that a byte-identical candidate received public scores of 35.635 and 27.970, while leaving the cause unresolved. It advocates richer run identities, evaluator-era metadata, preregistration, and preservation of negative results, but does not disclose an operational competition solution.

The solution fine-tuned official joint-BERT variants in TensorFlow 1.15 using Google Cloud TPUs. Whole-word-masking weights and revised negative sampling were the strongest improvements, with SQuAD pre-tuning contributing to the best single model. Full-development-set validation guided checkpoint selection, thresholds, and three-model probability averaging. Larger inference strides reduced runtime, while yes/no thresholds and increased context coverage improved final development F1 to 67.0.

solution_summary: The author explored several attack families and selected a structured-mapping candidate and a source-free confused-deputy candidate for final submission. solution_summary: The author extended a statistical text-normalization approach with five-word context matching and selective skipping of punctuation and short words. Custom parsers handled dates, simple URLs, and structured numbers, with num2words covering other numeric cases and a dictionary handling endings. Transliteration was the main difficulty: a CMU-based phonetic approach performed poorly, while transliterate plus over 40 manual rules reached 50% training accuracy.

The solution combined competition data with the original dataset and engineered hour, day, and division features. A CatBoost model used a custom focal loss, with predictions averaged across ten stratified folds. Optuna tuned model parameters and the focal-loss gamma parameter over roughly 50 trials.

The submitted solution equally averaged ranked predictions from two logistic regressions, a PyTorch MLP, CatBoost, and two RealMLP variants. The logistic regressions used target-encoded feature pairs or triplets transformed into logits and polynomial features, while the custom MLP embedded categorical values and original-data target statistics. Local cross-validation guided development because public notebooks were overfitting the public leaderboard. The ensemble achieved CV 0.95583 and private score 0.95532; post-competition analysis identified leakage in the second logistic regression, whose removal improved the private score to 0.95534.

solution_summary: The team predicted tournament game outcomes using a random forest with extensive team performance, ranking, schedule, and efficiency features. solution_title: 2nd place solution: Neutrino direction prediction with transformers
solution_summary: The solution treated photon detections as sequences and trained transformers with Fourier-encoded inputs and relative spacetime attention bias, sometimes adding a GraphNet feature extractor. Chunk caching and length-matched sampling made training efficient and supported longer inference sequences. Training first used von Mises–Fisher loss, then optimized the competition metric with a small auxiliary von Mises–Fisher term, alongside stochastic weight averaging. A confidence-aware linear ensemble of six models achieved 0.9602 on the private leaderboard, compared with 0.9618 for the best single model.

solution_summary: The author trained image-to-sequence models on several image sizes and sequence-length settings using both PyTorch and TensorFlow. The author identified the absence of a voting system as a possible limitation.

solution_summary: The solution used a shared DINOv3 ViT-large backbone on left and right image patches, followed by auxiliary heads and FiLM-conditioned biomass regression. It predicted three log-standardized biomass targets and derived the remaining two from additive relationships. Grouping visually similar species improved R² by about 0.03, while FiLM conditioning raised the reported public score from 0.68 to 0.72. Separate three-fold and five-fold ensembles formed the final submissions, with EMA, gradient clipping, and weaker late-stage augmentation supporting training.

solution_summary: The approach aligns receiver inputs by source midpoint, applies a signed logarithm, and adds spatial coordinates before predicting velocity maps with five stacked U-Nets. Symmetry and velocity scaling augmentations improve training, with symmetric averaging also used at inference. Training alternates between OpenFWI and additional data generated by predicting test examples and running forward simulations. Iteratively correcting inputs through forward reconstruction reduced validation MAE to 12.34 and achieved a reported leaderboard score of 12.7.
compute: Single 4080s; training stages took 12, 6, and 3 days; each full-test reconstruction iteration took approximately 1.5 hours.

solution_title: 19th Place Yuchen20 part of write up (a LLM agentic solution)
solution_summary: The author built an evolutionary LLM program-synthesis agent that generated, tested, and shortened Python solutions for ARC-AGI tasks. A database of verified programs supplied diverse priors and pattern-similar examples, while compact prompts included ARC-GEN snippets and code-golf idioms. Removing misleading DSL solutions and pruning context helped the agent reach about 360 solved tasks and an intermediate score near 0.940. Larger models and longer reasoning budgets stopped yielding gains, so manual coding and reusable human-derived templates addressed the remaining opportunities.
compute: Primarily Gemini free-tier API, with occasional OpenRouter experiments.

solution_summary: The solution combines two differently trained YOLOv5l6 detectors with weighted boxes fusion and camera-motion-aware tracking. One detector increases internal feature resolution by reducing a convolution stride, while the other uses 3100-pixel inference. Both use video-based validation and extensive augmentation, with different choices about empty images and label corrections. ORB-based homography improves tracking across camera movement, producing consistent score gains of about 0.01–0.02 across CV and both leaderboard splits.
compute: Second detector: primarily 4 V100 GPUs with 16GB RAM; approximately 2 hours to train.

solution_summary: The solution processed the middle 16 volume slices with depth-invariant 3D feature extractors followed by SegFormer segmentation models. Large crops provided valuable spatial context, and models were trained on all fragments after validation against fragment 1. Nine models were combined with rotation augmentation and overlapping-window inference, which also improved calibration around a 0.5 threshold. Small connected components were removed from the final masks; the best individual model scored 0.82 publicly and 0.67 privately.

The solution used 3D ResNet-18 and ResNet-34 encoders with a simple CNN decoder, which outperformed the other decoder designs tested. Six models combined fragment-held-out training with random image-block validation and different training strides. Training used 224-pixel patches, extensive augmentation, binary cross-entropy, AdamW, and a warmup scheduler. Inference combined rotations and flips with a 0.5 threshold, achieving public and private scores of 0.786897 and 0.652892.

solution_title: 14th Place Solution - Binary Classification on cropped frequency x time
solution_summary: The solution exploited consistent frequency ranges and event durations for each species and song type to extract targeted spectrogram crops. A single B0 binary classifier detected species presence in these crops, followed by pseudo-label generation and retraining. Recording-level predictions averaged the three highest crop probabilities for each species. Pseudo-labeling and blending improved the reported private score from 0.927 to 0.948.

The team trained XGBoost on 171 features for device-to-handle matching, aggregating cookies belonging to the same handle. Candidate generation required a shared IP with restrictions on cellular IPs, reducing the dataset to approximately seven million samples while retaining about 97.5% of positives. Most features described shared-IP activity, supplemented by categorical conditional probabilities and a property-vector similarity measure. Cookie-cookie and device-device models brought little success, while removing cookies with unknown handles reportedly improved predictions after the competition.

The author provides a simplified version of their coupon purchase prediction solution. The final submission averaged this approach with another XGBoost solution. Local validation used the last four weeks. The simplified version scored 0.008776 on the private leaderboard, compared with 0.008905 for the submitted ensemble.
compute: Around 5 hours on a 4-core CPU with 16GB RAM.

solution_summary: The solution combines deep audio models with shallow learners built on statistical features. Neural models explore raw waveforms, log Mel spectrograms and MFCC inputs, including three-channel representations with delta and delta-delta features, and use Mixup augmentation. ResNeXt was the strongest single CNN, achieving private mAP@3 of 0.942. A meta-learning ensemble exploiting model diversity increased private mAP@3 to 0.951.

The solution extracted class counts from colored annotation dots and trained a patch-based, five-output count regressor. The full model used ImageNet-pretrained VGG16 on 300×300 patches, with multiple training scales and geometric and color augmentation. Scale variation across images remained difficult, so the final inference scale and class-count adjustments were chosen using leaderboard feedback. Final predictions increased juvenile counts by 50%, subtracted the same amount from adult females, and increased pups by 20%.

solution_title: 11th solution - very basic but may different methods
solution_summary: The solution combined extensive passband statistics and fitted light-curve parameters with separate LightGBM models for galactic and extragalactic objects. Each group blended a custom sample-weighted objective with the built-in objective, producing four models overall. SALT2 parameters, removal of unsuitable features, and conservative tree settings helped reduce the validation-to-leaderboard gap. Reported scores were 0.411 on cross-validation, 0.794 on the public leaderboard, and 0.822 on the private leaderboard; a Gaussian-process, wavelet, and PCA pipeline failed.

The author developed a sequential tabular classification workflow, progressing from simple classifiers to a tuned Balanced Random Forest and finally XGBoost. Health-indicator interactions helped the random-forest pipeline, while class imbalance and cross-validation guided subsequent tuning. The final submission used XGBoost with early stopping and achieved 0.94986 publicly and 0.95028 privately. Trusting cross-validation over small public-score changes was a central lesson.

The pipeline generates bitmap images with a diffusion model and converts them to SVG. Improving bitmap-to-SVG conversion mattered most, including relative paths and grouping elements by color to compress output. Two independent VQA questions evaluated shape and color, and batches contained three candidate images. Threshold-based early stopping carried unused time into subsequent predictions.
compute: Assumed a 63-second increment per prediction, with unused time carried forward.

solution_title: Winning Solution in 7 lines of code!
solution_summary: The author presents a rule-based predictor that uses only test-set antivirus signature versions and no training data. Predictions default to 0.5 and become zero for a specified version range, producing a private leaderboard score of 0.681. Further investigation found that detections taper toward zero over the last five days because of detection lag, and a revised approach scored 0.696.

solution_title: 2428 by the numbers - no VRP, no TSP, no MIP
solution_summary: The author first used LKH3 to reach 2440, then identified a simpler construction based on the trajectory structure of classic superpermutations. They chose 76 as the Santa sequence and reorganized trajectories around permutations beginning with it. Splitting the trajectories into three groups and adding complementary mandatory permutations explains the 2440 construction. The post describes the structural insight on the way to 2428 but leaves the wildcard improvements largely unexplained.

The solution used a small feature set consisting of categorical count encoding, arithmetic interactions, and target encoding of selected pairs. The author trained gradient-boosted trees and some neural networks, while also using out-of-fold predictions from public neural-network notebooks. Hill-climbing ensembling performed best among the tested ensemble methods, followed by a final blend with another participant's ensemble. The final blend achieved public and private scores of 0.95471 and 0.95490, respectively.

The pipeline generated zero-shot text features for both questions and misconception descriptions, then retrieved candidates using cached GTE embeddings and shallow MLP adapters. A Qwen 72B reranker evaluated the top 25 candidates using guided choice-token probabilities. Validation held out misconception identities, and an affine score adjustment favored unseen labels. The ensemble achieved 0.537 CV, 0.559 public, and 0.495 private scores, with adapter training taking only minutes.
compute: Five-fold adapter training takes a few minutes; test reranking takes approximately 2 hours.

solution_title: Learnings & my solutions in this competition
solution_summary: The author solved multiple CTF challenges through trial and error, community hints, brute-force searches, and challenge-specific inspection. Successful approaches included black-box iterative adversarial attacks using the original wolf image, simple flag-seeking prompts, and exploiting imperfect OCR. Other challenges used column frequency counts, pixel-count experiments, semantic word searches, simple code functions, and image contrast adjustments. Several challenges remained unsolved, and the author could not confidently explain why the Count MNIST attempt succeeded.

solution_title: Simple approach that scores 0.51734 in private
solution_summary: The author inferred five snapshot times in the test data and constructed matching training subsets, then split each by call type to train 15 XGBoost regressors. Features described observed trip endpoints, coordinate differences, distance, timing, weekday, and call-specific origin identifiers. Cross-validation guided boosting rounds and showed that origin identifiers helped while dummy-coded taxi IDs did not. The approach scored 0.50228 publicly and 0.51734 privately, with the R code running in about ten minutes. The team later judged selecting two highly correlated submissions by public score to have been a poor decision.

solution_summary: The team ensembled four neural text classifiers built around recurrent and convolutional layers. They combined GloVe and fastText word vectors, used a maximum sequence length of 57, and adopted preprocessing from public kernels. The architectures varied pooling, convolution, and attention components, and a rerun reportedly improved on the submitted result.

The solution combined vanilla EfficientNet B6 and B8 with stride-1 EfficientNet B1, B2, and B3 models. Per-image channel standardization reduced the discrepancy between cross-validation and leaderboard results, while retaining full spatial resolution longer substantially improved detection of local manipulation traces. Models trained for 40 epochs with AdamW, cosine decay, mixed precision, and mostly flip and transpose augmentation. The final equal-weight blend of the vanilla and stride-1 model groups achieved 0.937 on the public leaderboard and 0.928 on the private leaderboard.

The team pretrained EfficientNet models on the 2015 competition data and fine-tuned them on the current dataset, sometimes after joint training on both datasets. The final ensemble used EfficientNet-B4 and B5 models with varied retinal preprocessing and augmentations. Mixed precision enabled larger batches, while regression and ordinal regression outperformed classification. A public-leaderboard-weighted average achieved 0.823 on the private leaderboard.

solution_summary: The team used 20-fold cross-validation stratified by Alpha with 20 bags and explored increasingly complex LightGBM-based pipelines. Their selected submissions used stacking with LightGBM and SVM, with the second adding a third stacking stage, EJ-specific models, disease-specific models, and CatBoost. These approaches improved cross-validation and public scores but generalized poorly to the private set. solution_title: My brief summary of this competition[0.795]
solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned pretrained image classifiers with expanded classification heads and combined models across architectures and image sizes. solution_title: Bronze medal border solution (finally in 92th place)
solution_summary: The team modified a public rule-based bot with coordinated discovery responses, more active exploration, and sap attacks. Newly discovered relics or rewards drew all units toward the discovering unit, while otherwise idle units explored unknown nodes during the first three games. Sap attacks were restricted to harvesting units with spare energy and enemies within Manhattan distance eight. An imitation-learning attempt was abandoned after state-management problems caused units to move in only one direction.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution - Span MLM + T5 Augmentations
solution_summary: The solution classified discourse spans using transformer backbones with LSTM and attention layers, explicit discourse markers, and essay prompts. Domain adaptation with high-rate contiguous-span masking delivered the largest reported gain, supported by synthetic essays generated with T5. Fine-tuning combined adversarial training, masking, multi-sample dropout, and span mean pooling. LSTM and LightGBM meta-models combined out-of-fold probabilities, with additional essay and linguistic features for LightGBM.

The post asks for clarification about competition winners' obligations, including conference participation and solution delivery. It quotes the host's requirement for a short video summarizing the solution. The author says a solution writeup is being prepared but provides no technical approach.

The final approach forked a public XGBoost notebook and added 30 to its Tg predictions. The author selected one submission with this mild shift and another with no shift because confidence in larger adjustments was limited. A small TabTransformer improved over its initial configuration but remained insufficiently competitive with boosted trees. LAMMPS-based augmentation was also explored without enough time to develop it.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution for the UBC-OCEAN UBC Ovarian Cancer Subtype Classification and Outlier Detection (UBC-OCEAN)
solution_summary: The pipeline filtered tissue tiles from whole-slide images, extracted features with pretrained Lunit-DINO, and trained an adapted attention-based CLAM classifier. Additional public histopathology data and synthetic tissue microarrays were central to reducing overfitting. The author modified instance-level supervision for the Other class and used PyVips with asynchronous PyTorch loading to process large images within resource limits. Patient-grouped cross-validation initially gave inflated results, so holding out the Hamarneh Lab dataset provided more reliable validation.

solution_summary: The post proposes using cloud cover as a shortcut for image chronology. It claims that cloudy images always occupy the third position. Clouds can be identified manually or by comparing counts of pixels above a whiteness threshold across the five images.

The solution combined source-specific preprocessing with three stages for global alignment, nonlinear rectification, and signal segmentation. A source classifier selected image corrections, while keypoints and grid predictions supported geometric unwarping. The main reported improvement came from smoothing segmentation probabilities and interpolating low-confidence gaps instead of filling them with the isoelectric baseline. Final signal processing also enforced Einthoven's law and applied a Savitzky-Golay filter, although no numerical SNR improvement was provided.

The solution trained separate binary segmentation models for each defect, primarily using full-resolution images and FPN decoders with ImageNet-pretrained SE-ResNeXt-50 or EfficientNet-B3 encoders. Three-fold validation guided model choices, and the main submission omitted defect2 while a second selected submission included a conservative detector. The ensemble used varied augmentations, BCE plus Lovasz hinge loss, validation-tuned mask thresholds, and a defect1 classifier to reduce false positives. Confidence-filtered pseudo-labeling mainly improved defect3 and raised the public score from about 0.917 to 0.919.

solution_summary: The final ensemble combined default pretrained Dr.fold2 and Protenix with two Protenix variants fine-tuned on different RNA sequence sets. It generated 15 candidate structures and selected five using a physics-based energy score. solution_title: Paired-Orphan Division Rescue for 3D Embryonic Cell Tracking
solution_summary: The author based their work on an open-access high-public-score notebook. solution_title: 1st place solution: Summing the power with GPU
solution_summary: The solution used physics-based weighted power summation without machine learning or external data. It searched Doppler-corrected signal templates over frequency and slope, taking the maximum accumulated power after noise normalization. A finer sinc-kernel pass around promising lines improved the public score from 0.825 to 0.848. Coherent wave summation and an additional noise-dependent prediction adjustment did not succeed.

solution_summary: The solution used DenseNet201 transfer learning with three separate models and five-fold cross-validation. Training began with a one-cycle schedule, then unfroze layers and retrained with layer-specific learning rates. Images were resized to 256×256 and augmented using brightness, contrast, gamma, and jitter transformations. Final predictions averaged the five folds' probabilities, and the author emphasized trusting local CV despite unhelpful public leaderboard feedback.

The solution combined CBAM-equipped EfficientNet-B6 and EfficientNet-B5 models using 350×350 images. It addressed class imbalance and overfitting with SMOTE oversampling, extensive augmentation, and categorical cross-entropy with label smoothing. Evaluation used five folds and four-way test-time augmentation, with the authors emphasizing cross-validation over leaderboard feedback. Ensembling with another model improved the reported public score from 0.979 to 0.981 and private score from 0.975 to 0.976, while SENet blocks and CBLoss did not help.

solution_title: 11th Solution: A threshold oriented Competition is not good
solution_summary: The post describes prediction postprocessing without specifying the underlying model. For nine question targets, it sets a tuned fraction of the smallest predictions to zero. The reported PB/LB scores rose from 0.386/0.409 without this step to 0.424/0.450 with it. Later experimentation increased the reported LB score to 0.465 but harmed PB performance.

The solution extracted audio-style features from normalized waveform segments and trained two models using feature sets with and without chroma features. Validation stratified the continuous target using five K-means clusters. Training used LogCosh loss, AdamW, cosine warm restarts, and five random seeds. The final predictions were a simple average of the two model results.

solution_summary: The pipeline first detected helmets with EfficientDet-d5 and then classified impacts using two ResNet18 models. Each classifier used nine frames centered on a helmet, represented either as 27 stacked image channels or a short video for 3D convolutions. Synchronized temporal augmentation, horizontal flip inference, and ensembling supported the final predictions. Temporal duplicate suppression and removal of video boundary frames produced a private score of 0.59.

The author trained separate LightGBM models for each store using walk-forward validation. The approach emphasized lagged rolling statistics, target encodings, stock availability signals, and price and release features. Features generally used the full history from 2011, while encoding features started in 2013, and identified outliers were corrected. The author avoided prediction multipliers and relied on feature engineering and hyperparameter tuning, although a late rebuild limited feature evaluation.

solution_title: Replicating 1st Place Dynamics: KNN Cross-Sectional Features & Adaptive Ensemble
solution_summary: The author implemented an end-to-end volatility prediction pipeline with cross-sectional nearest-neighbor features to represent relationships between assets. Inverse-target sample weights were used to align training with RMSPE. Ridge stacking and adaptive Nelder-Mead weight optimization were compared, but the post does not identify the final ensemble choice or report a score.

solution_title: Lessons learned and experiments. DeBERTaV3-base solutions + extra features.
solution_summary: The author trained DeBERTa-v3-base models with a maximum sequence length of 512 using several training frameworks and text variants. Their predictions were combined with public features, language-quality scores, readability estimates, and text similarities for AutoGluon tabular prediction. The final predictor was a three-level ensemble of roughly 100 models, with the first target prediction also supplied when training the next target. Pseudo-labeling improved experimental scores, while a custom per-target checkpoint ensemble was excluded from the final solution.

solution_summary: The post shares a link to the Visipedia iNaturalist competition repository README. It is presented as an informational reference. The post itself contains no solution description, methods, or results.

The final competition submission combined ten YOLOv5L6 folds trained and inferred at image size 3072, using positive training frames and subsequence-based validation. Weighted Boxes Fusion combined detections, followed by an explicit output confidence threshold of 0.1. This filtering increased private LB from 0.609 to 0.684, with final CV 0.732 and public LB 0.591. The submitted solution omitted tracking and TTA; post-competition experiments improved results with TTA or a YOLOv5M6/YOLOv5L6 ensemble.

solution_summary: The pipeline combined molecular descriptors, fingerprints, and custom chemical features, then selected a separate feature set for each polymer target. Selection used variance filtering, XGBoost SHAP importance, correlation filtering, and Boruta with a random forest. Separate XGBoost regressors used available labels for each target and individually tuned hyperparameters. An 80/20 holdout produced a competition metric of 0.0469, with FFV performing best and sparse Rg data remaining a limitation.

The solution used an end-to-end video model combining EfficientNet, temporal shift modules, and a 1D U-Net event head. Ball-detection pretraining, Gaussian event targets, balanced sampling, and class-weighted focal loss helped stabilize learning. Longer-sequence fine-tuning and inference that retained only central frames improved temporal predictions before non-maximum suppression. A six-model ensemble varying image size, backbone, and sequence length improved the reported score from 0.768 to 0.827.

solution_title: Top 100 Solution - Fast RAPIDS TF-IDF RAG - 2xT4 GPU Acceleration!
solution_summary: The author ensembled diverse Wikipedia retrieval pipelines and scored their retrieved contexts with DeBERTa-v3-large, combining the resulting logits. Retrieval diversity contributed more than adding additional reader models. GPU retrieval, half-precision inference, and splitting samples across two T4 GPUs enabled seven retrieval pipelines within six hours, with memory exhaustion limiting further expansion. Question dropout produced the best individual reader, while choice permutation and pruning unlikely choices provided further accuracy or speed improvements.

solution_title: My bit of the 7th place solution (team ABC)
solution_summary: The author describes the team's earlier pipeline before a merger, after which many methods were replaced by a teammate's ideas. It used earthquake-wise cross-validation, overlapping signal segments, segment mean subtraction, and extensive statistical and spectral features. Feature selection combined iterative adversarial validation with a genetic search using ExtraTrees and validation MAE. A LightGBM model and an MLP used squared-error loss, with a square-root target transformation and small heuristic prediction adjustments.

The solution predicted corrections to baseline coordinates using speed-derived STFT images and IMU features. EfficientNet B3 regressed coordinate noise, while a U-Net++ model predicted STFT noise and supplied speed estimates for masking and interpolation. LightGBM added IMU-based corrections, followed by public trajectory post-processing and downtown nearest-neighbor refinement against training ground truth. The complete pipeline achieved a private score of 2.61693.

The solution used three training stages to recover missing bird labels and correct noisy chunk labels using out-of-fold predictions. Sound event detection models combined attention and max pooling, with long audio crops and waveform augmentation. Later stages used three-channel audio representations and ResNeSt50 or EfficientNet-B0 encoders. The final ensemble combined 11 EMA models trained on the original and extended datasets, with individual models reaching about 0.61 on the public leaderboard.

The author built 60 recursive LightGBM forecasting models with Tweedie loss, varying seeds, iteration counts, and item encoding. Rolling sales statistics, price changes, calendar events, and zero-demand features supported the forecasts. Each model received store-level supersmoother trend correction and forecast-proportion hierarchical reconciliation before trimean aggregation. The approach was reported to be stable across four validation periods and the private leaderboard.

solution_summary: The author trained an image-level classifier and applied it to augmented images of individually extracted cells during inference. This converted the weakly supervised problem into a conventional classification setup and enabled reuse of an HPA2018 solution. A separate MMDetection model trained using cropped segmentation images improved boundary-cell segmentation despite using official segmenter outputs as labels. Faster segmentation also enabled more ensembling.

solution_title: 41st place Solution (7th Public LB) YOLO-Z Inspired Model with Tracking
solution_summary: The solution widened YOLOv5s6 and YOLOv5m6 while retaining their layer counts, initializing them from the next larger model. Training progressed through underwater imagery, synthetic crown-of-thorns images, competition sequences, and a final low-learning-rate fine-tune. Sequence-grouped validation, high-resolution inference, test-time augmentation, and Norfair tracking supported the pipeline. The best reported notebook scored 0.673 public and 0.706 private, while more aggressive resolution tuning overfit the public leaderboard.

This team contribution centered on quadratic-programming trajectory smoothing that jointly used all smartphones from the same drive. Carrier-smoothed GNSS positions and Doppler-derived velocity estimates supplied observations, with velocity estimation improving the public score by about one meter. Map matching was applied specifically to SJC/downtown, while direction-dependent bias correction helped local validation and the public score but not the private score. Parameters were tuned and validated locally with limited reliance on public submissions.

The author reused a Bayesian logistic regression approach from a previous competition. Predictions between 0.23 and 0.77 were randomly partitioned and replaced with complementary probabilities of 0.36 and 0.64 in two submissions. Historical simulations and a threshold grid search supported these settings, while showing substantial variability in outcomes. The strategy depended heavily on tournament luck and the asymmetry of log loss.

solution_title: 27th Place Solution: How to use prompts?
solution_summary: The solution stacked diverse first-stage language models, mostly DeBERTa-v3-large, using gradient-boosted second-stage models. Diversity came from different inputs, pooling methods, and prediction heads, including prompt-aware variants. First-stage predictions were combined with public notebook features, FB3 labels, and metadata such as grade. The selected submission achieved CV 0.486, public score 0.425, and private score 0.464; feature selection and extensive tuning improved CV but hurt leaderboard performance.

The author built multiple feature subsets using iterative LightGBM feature-removal experiments evaluated across random seeds. Subsets targeted lower RMSE, lower fold-score variability, or a balance of both. Optuna tuned model parameters before longer training with a lower learning rate and early stopping. The final ensemble combined XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost predictions across feature subsets and ten random seeds.

The writeup provides instructions for running a whale recognition training and prediction pipeline using neon 1.1.4. Its script prepares the data, trains models, and produces submission predictions. A localizer uses a heuristic stopping rule that can warn when a satisfactory optimum is not detected. The complete steps reportedly take about six hours with eight processors and a Titan X GPU.
compute: About 6 hours on a system with 8 processors and an NVIDIA Titan X GPU; tested only on Ubuntu.

solution_summary: The team combined two distinct approaches, both using weighted ensembles of XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost. They excluded the original data from training and rounded the training data while leaving the test data unchanged. The author's approach generated pairwise arithmetic and comparison features, then selected features using permutation importance with an extremely randomized forest. A variant that modeled two k-means subgroups separately improved cross-validation but was omitted because it did not improve the public leaderboard; the author later reported that it would have been their best notebook.

The team used segmentation-assisted, three-stage teacher–student classification training, with segmentation masks supplying annotations for otherwise unannotated images. They iteratively pseudo-labeled NIH Chest X-rays and MIMIC-CXR, filtered out images without catheters, and kept pseudo labels separate by fold to avoid leakage. The final classifier ensemble contained 40 models across four architectures, two external-data configurations, and five folds, with ensemble coefficients fitted by logistic regression. Final inference omitted segmentation and test-time augmentation, achieving a private leaderboard score of 0.97624.
compute: 8 NVIDIA V100 GPUs with 32GB each; about 4 hours per 15 epochs, about 15 GPU-days for five-fold resnet200d multi-stage training, and 7–8 hours for Kaggle inference.

solution_summary: The solution jointly trained image segmentation, differentiable signal extraction, and a residual 1D UNet to recover ECG signals. Standardized images and scheduled segmentation and signal losses enabled end-to-end optimization. Horizontal flips provided a reported 0.6 dB gain, while EfficientNet encoders and deeper signal refinement also helped. The final prediction combined six models with performance-based weights and averaged three resampling methods to reduce artifacts.

The final approach predicted normalized progress through an earthquake cycle and converted it to time to failure using an estimated length-weighted median cycle duration. LightGBM and neural networks consumed 4,040 FFT and quantile features extracted at full-chunk and subchunk scales, and their predictions were averaged. Two submissions differed in whether they used the last six complete earthquake cycles or all complete cycles. Gap-based test ordering and recurrent representation learning were investigated but did not enter the final solution.

The solution trained diverse neural networks and TabNet on multiple feature sets built with feature selection, quantile transformation, and PCA. Some networks transferred learning from non-scored targets, while separate models used feature dropout augmentation. Ten-fold multilabel stratification supported 16 initial models and another 10 models trained with stacked prediction features. Averaging all 26 models achieved a private score of 0.01608, and a small adjustment to blending weights produced 0.01604.

The solution relied on corpus lookups and accession-prefix rules rather than a learned model. It used DOIs from MDC corpus v3 and accession IDs from the Europe PMC source of MDC v4, falling back to known-prefix matching for absent articles. Prediction rules removed one unidentified accession, whitelisted another prefix, and classified all SAMN accessions as primary. The author reported that extensive modeling attempts did not outperform probing, and removing the problematic accession improved both leaderboard scores by 0.08.

The post reflects on the author's first full Kaggle competition and congratulates the winners. It emphasizes trusting cross-validation over leaderboard feedback. It links a kernel but provides no technical description of the solution.

The team designed day-based validation to resemble the private test distribution, then retrained selected configurations using shuffled KFold for submission. PCA, selected raw features, and metadata aggregation features supported ensembles of neural networks and GPU-based pyBoost models. Multiome neural networks predicted all targets directly, while pyBoost used 64 PCA target components. Training multiome models only on day 7 improved local validation by about 0.02 and yielded their best private submission despite reducing the public score.
compute: GPU-only pyBoost training; Saturn cloud was available.

solution_summary: The solution first trained XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost on four transformed versions of the target. Their predictions became additional features for a second stage using XGBoost and CatBoost. A separate PyTorch neural network was combined with these second-stage predictions through a weighted sum. Predictions were combined directly without rank conversion or classifier-based efs predictions.

solution_title: Pixelated - bad OCR? Generate an adversarial image instead!
solution_summary: The author solved the Pixelated challenge by generating an adversarial image using Hugging Face TrOCR. The resulting image transferred successfully to the server's OCR, which decoded the intended string and returned the flag. Experiments with images targeting an empty decoded string also revealed that the XML text element could not be empty.

solution_title: single silver models (hard voting, mixup, SEResNet)
solution_summary: The author described two models that contributed to the final ensemble: a bidirectional GRU with attention and mixup, and an adapted SE-ResNet-50 for signal inputs. Both used majority voting over cross-validation model classifications at a fixed 0.5 threshold. The CNN consumed three-phase summary features extracted with a window of 40 and stride of 20, using an initial 2D convolution followed by 1D blocks. Mixup improved private performance while hurting public performance, and raw-signal or smaller-window CNN experiments ran out of memory.

The team blended several LightGBM and XGBoost models with an FM-FTRL model, using different training subsets and boosting algorithms to increase diversity. Their features emphasized grouped frequencies, click timing, and historical target statistics, with validation often matching the test set's hours. Negative sampling reduced training costs for several models, while another LightGBM used all training data. Nearly equal blending weights performed about as well as the alternatives they tested.
compute: Access to separate machines with substantial RAM and GPU power, but no machine with both; specifications unstated.

solution_title: [46th Pvt LB] 18th Public LB - Very simple solution
solution_summary: The solution blended public submissions using RidgeCV coefficients fitted against leaked validation targets. Learned coefficients included negative weights and worked better than simple averaging for the enhanced models. Leak replacement improved the reported public score from roughly 1.04 to 0.939. A later update added a second blending level that included the first blend alongside public submissions.

solution_title: 8th Place: How I Made Ender for <$200
solution_summary: Ender uses separate transformer policies for two-player and four-player games, trained with PPO through self-play and leagues of past checkpoints. Its factorized action space builds a turn through successive launches, using incoming-fleet summaries and projected future ownership and garrisons. KL regularization toward conservative launch priors and extra early-game environments substantially improved training. Final submissions used different combinations of sampled policy actions and test-time planning, with a JAX environment providing training throughput on limited hardware.
compute: Own RTX 3080 10GB and 11 rented RTX 4090 days, approximately $170 plus electricity; final two-player run took 3.4 days on RTX 4090; four-player training used RTX 3080.

solution_summary: The post announces a meetup and Zoom discussion for sharing competition solutions and lessons. The intended meeting time is January 23 at 10 AM Pacific, and a meetup link is provided. It also links a recording of an earlier competition discussion to illustrate the format.

The team presented two solutions that both scored 0.812 publicly and 0.815 privately: a single SAINT++ transformer and an ensemble of a transformer, modified SAKT, and LightGBM. SAINT++ used 512 interactions, content-attempt counts, second-level lag encoding, and smart random training windows. Its recursive inference fed rounded predictions back into the model within unanswered bundles, improving scores by about 0.0025. Memory and inference engineering were essential to fit the nine-hour runtime budget.
compute: 9-hour runtime limit, 13GB RAM and 16GB GPU memory; about 30% of effort spent on optimization.

solution_summary: The solution used mostly raw tracking inputs with a few simple features, an RNN encoder, and a spatial-temporal encoder. Its decoder predicted frame-to-frame coordinate changes and accumulated them into trajectories. Temporal Huber loss, flip augmentation, and EMA supported training, which included 2021 and 2023 data. Validation used the last five weeks, and adding more models to the ensemble consistently produced small improvements.

The author blended six models, including a stacking model, and identified blending as the key to the solution. The complete workflow was implemented in a single Kaggle notebook without a local environment. The provided text does not specify the individual architectures, blend weights, validation procedure, or numerical scores.
compute: Entire workflow implemented in one Kaggle notebook, without a local environment.

solution_summary: The final predictor combined LightGBM and a feedforward neural network with equal weights. Time-ID aggregations exploiting the competition leak were a major contributor, alongside features derived from reordered time IDs. Linear trend summaries of 100-second feature windows improved CV and leaderboard scores by about 0.001. The author also used stock-level aggregations over nearby time IDs and BorutaShap feature selection with XGBRegressor.
compute: BorutaShap feature selection ran overnight on a Kaggle kernel.

solution_summary: The author presents an audio classification pipeline using mel-spectrogram inputs and a Cornell-pretrained ResNeSt-50 adapted to 24 classes. Weighted binary cross-entropy and inverse-frequency sampling address species imbalance, while pseudo-labels expand training annotations. Augmentation includes external Cornell bird audio, waveform perturbations, click noise, and spectrogram masking. The author recommends matching validation to test-time chunk aggregation, reports slightly better results with five-second crops, and finds model averaging beneficial.

solution_title: 14th place solution / Single model with different random_states Voting + blending
solution_summary: The central approach ensembled copies of the same model with identical hyperparameters and different random seeds using VotingClassifier. This improved both LightGBM and CatBoost scores over their single-model baselines. Weighted averaging and blending incorporated those predictions, a public stacking submission, and a modified LightGBM notebook. The final reported score was 0.81868, with 0.81752 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Some notebooks executed on a local PC.

solution_summary: The solution trained separate regularized linear models for each label using a modified Java Liblinear implementation that accepted sparse matrices. Encog neural networks trained on 2,000 SVD components added joint multilabel modeling, and a custom sparse multilabel random forest contributed despite slow training and a score around 0.60. ExtraTrees and random forests combined the models into the final blend. Labels were assigned by always selecting the highest-scoring class and adding other classes above a cross-validated threshold.
compute: Custom Java multilabel random forest took about one week to run.

solution_summary: The solution made a few changes to the public GAMMY notebook. The author removed CCI and expanded holiday processing. The two final submissions compared versions with and without CCI.

The author formulated the permutation-string problem as a restricted mixed-integer linear program with explicit mandatory duplicates and implicit 7-edges. MTZ-style constraints, an objective cutoff, and graph coloring controlled paths and assigned nodes to three strings. Structural restrictions inferred from earlier solutions made the otherwise difficult model tractable. The final model solved in about five minutes, producing strings of length 2160 that became valid length-2440 strings after appending missing mandatory permutations.
compute: Unrestricted coloring model found no solution after a day; the structurally restricted final model solved in about five minutes.

solution_summary: The writeup compares eight CNN architectures using NVIDIA DIGITS with a Caffe backend. It reports both training from scratch and fine-tuning ImageNet-trained models, evaluated with an 80/20 train-test split. Fine-tuning improved accuracy across all listed architectures, with GoogLeNet reaching 99.58%. Training times ranged from 35 minutes for AlexNet to one day and 20 hours for ResNet-101.
compute: GeForce GTX 1070; Intel Core 2 Duo E8500 at 3.16GHz. Reported training times range from 35 minutes to 1 day 20 hours.

solution_summary: The team used an MLP with five input branches for categorical, distance and speed, angle, and aggregate features. Their strongest gains came from relative player angles, projected future positions and speeds, mirroring plays to standardize rusher direction, and correcting physically impossible yard predictions. They used five-fold validation grouped by week and restricted validation and early stopping to seasons after 2017. Rescaling 2017 speed and acceleration to 2018 statistics slightly improved the public score, while replacing speed with distance times ten was discarded.

The solution developed modular multimodal neural networks for IMU and ToF signals, using residual temporal CNNs, bidirectional GRUs, and attention pooling. Separate fusion streams supported fine-grained classification and auxiliary gesture detection, with modality dropout for robustness. The author combined multiple five-fold models, adopted EMA models after fixing buffer handling, and added post-processing whose complete details are absent from the truncated text. Correcting the validation metric revealed stronger IMU performance, and a reported intermediate ensemble with post-processing reached 0.871 on the leaderboard.
compute: One owned GPU; sought additional GPU capacity through lighting AI.

solution_summary: The team trained EfficientNet U-Net models to distinguish healthy and unhealthy glomeruli, combining competition data with carefully corrected external annotations. Manual labeling and pseudo-labeling expanded both classes across several data sources. Treating unhealthy glomeruli as a separate class reduced ambiguity, while fixing predictions for an anomalously annotated public leaderboard image made leaderboard feedback more consistent with cross-validation. Their submitted two-model ensemble achieved 0.9439 CV and 0.950 on the private leaderboard.
external_data: ["Mendeley dataset k7nvtgn2x6/3", "Zenodo dataset 4299694", "Two additional HuBMAP portal images"]

solution_summary: The author trained XGBoost only on week 9 rows using twelve features generated with Apache Spark. Features captured average demand across clients, products, cities, and client-product pairs, plus five weekly demand lags. Two FTRL linear-regression predictions supplied additional features based on hashed identifiers, product-pair history, and fourth-order identifier interactions.

The solution used EfficientNet-B5 to extract image features, followed by bidirectional LSTM and shallow BERT sequence models for study-level predictions. Positive-image oversampling and losses aligned with the competition metric were central to training. Predictions were averaged across sequence models and three folds. Chunked image processing and half-precision inference reduced memory enough to fit the ensemble, while several late submissions failed consistency checks.
compute: Initially an AWS V100 with 320×320 images and MacBook CPU prototyping; a single 40GB A100 for 512×512 images during the last three weeks. Image training took about 5 minutes per epoch for approximately 15 epochs.

solution_summary: The author trained a single MedNeXt Large 3D U-Net for 1,400 epochs with a sigmoid segmentation head. The loss combined connected-component Dice and weighted BCE, emphasizing an erosion-derived skeleton. Inference averaged flip-augmented logits and smoothed probabilities with a Gaussian filter to reduce porous predictions. Tangent-plane filling improved the public score slightly but did not help privately, and model ensembling did not improve cross-validation.
compute: Submission inference: 2.5 hours, two processes on 2 T4 GPUs.

solution_summary: The decisive step was recovering the meaning of anonymized variables and recognizing repeated claims as customer-contract time series. Persistent labels within those sequences made lagged and future target values highly predictive, allowing the team to omit the customer identifier and its mean target encoding. Their best single XGBoost model scored 0.42347 publicly and 0.42193 privately, with stacking providing a secondary contribution. The authors explicitly acknowledged that future-target features made the resulting model unsuitable for operational use.
compute: Best single XGBoost model trained in approximately half an hour on a 12-thread CPU.

solution_summary: The author selected two submissions: a hill-climbing ensemble and a Ridge model. The ensemble combined multiple tree models with out-of-fold predictions from AutoGluon and TabNet. It achieved a CV score of 0.058893 and a public score of 0.05876, while Ridge achieved 0.05895 and 0.05877 respectively. Submission selection was difficult because stronger public scores often translated into worse private results.

The solution used a three-layer MLP on 216 engineered features selected through null importance from roughly 1100 candidates. It predicted both accuracy group and a transformed accuracy target, then averaged the outputs of nine models trained with different seeds and epoch counts. Five-fold grouped validation guided evaluation and repeated threshold optimization converted continuous predictions into classes. Including the competition's private data in training yielded a private score of 0.559, compared with 0.552 using the original training data alone.
compute: Submission execution took six hours.

solution_title: 21st Place Solution - Ensemble of 3 Saint++ Models
solution_summary: The solution used a modified SAINT+ Transformer with lecture embeddings, summed tag embeddings, and 12 aggregate features in the decoder. Sampling training examples by row and retrieving the user's preceding history was particularly important, while aggregate features added about 0.002 public AUC. Validation simulated autoregressive inference, and inference fed predicted answers back into subsequent predictions. An ensemble of three models with different dimensions and history windows improved public AUC from 0.808 to 0.810 and achieved a final score of 0.813.
compute: Three machines, each with one Tesla V100 GPU with 16 GB VRAM.

solution_title: 24th Place Solution for the Bengali.AI Speech Recognition Competition
solution_summary: The team further fine-tuned a Bengali wav2vec2 model using roughly 20,000 normalized Common Voice examples, holding out about 700 for validation. A corrected language-model terminator, a six-gram language model, and transformer-based punctuation restoration produced substantial improvements. They combined three models at the logit level and tuned shallow-fusion decoder parameters with Optuna on out-of-distribution example data. Background-noise and other audio augmentations, denoising models, and a larger language model did not help.
