solution_title: 5th Place Solution! 149 Models -> 6 Meta Models -> 3 Blends
solution_summary: The author built a diverse pool of 199 base models spanning boosted trees, tabular neural networks, linear models, and other learners. Predictions were combined using Ridge, BayesianRidge, hill climbing, and an optimized blend of those combinations. RealMLP achieved the strongest reported base-model CV score of 0.91941. The submitted Ridge solution scored 0.91845, while the unselected BayesianRidge configuration achieved 0.91846.

The author adapted a public notebook and tuned models, epoch counts, and data augmentation using cross-validation. The final submission averaged eight submissions selected by CV scores. Averaging substantially different neural network types did not help, so those alternatives were abandoned. A scaled-down submission was also left unselected because the author lacked a convincing rationale for it.

The team developed LightGBM and multiple neural networks, including a Transformer–LSTM model with the strongest validation performance on takoi's side. Kurupical improved a SAKT baseline by using complete user histories, concatenated embeddings, additional timing and repetition features, and a deeper encoder, reaching 0.809 CV for a single transformer. Takoi's models used user and question aggregates, lag features, and content embeddings. Several architectural and optimizer alternatives failed to improve the baseline.

solution_title: 25th place solution (Trained DeepSort + Hyperparameter Sweep + Gmmreg + Hungarian Algorithm)
solution_summary: The pipeline detected helmets with five YOLOv5x6 models, fused their boxes with WBF, tracked helmets with DeepSort, and assigned tracking labels to video detections. DeepSort was trained on cropped competition boxes as a classification problem with over a thousand classes. Label averaging across tracks and Hungarian assignment were the most important assignment components, with gmmreg handling registration. WandB sweeps tuned tracking and assignment parameters, while PointNet, ProbReg, and direct image classification were unsuccessful or inferior.
compute: Five YOLOv5x6 models trained for 10 epochs, approximately 1 hour per epoch at full image resolution.

solution_summary: The post contains only a competition writeup title. It provides no approach, implementation details, or results. There is no solution content to extract.

The team ensembled ten models, primarily DeBERTa-large and RoBERTa-large, including two models trained with 25-fold cross-validation. Increasing fold counts modestly improved performance by allowing more of the small dataset to be used for training. A key improvement was training with BCEWithLogitsLoss on sigmoid-transformed, median-centered targets and restoring the target median during prediction. The two selected submissions achieved private scores of 0.451 and 0.448.
compute: 3 Google Colab Pro instances; AWS p3.8xlarge and 4 GCP V100s for unsuccessful DeBERTa-xlarge experiments.

solution_summary: The solution selected structures from existing Proteinx, DRfold2, and Boltz predictions without fine-tuning. DRfold2 candidates were clustered, with low-energy representatives and structurally diverse alternatives retained using TM-scores. Boltz and Proteinx candidates were selected by confidence scores, with Boltz also run using two seeds. Candidate selection and diversity were the central considerations under limited inference resources.

solution_title: Dinov3 + DoRA + Tweedie Loss + Ballanced R2
solution_summary: The approach fine-tuned a model inspired by a DINOv3 baseline using DoRA. Five-fold validation stratified by state and grouped by sampling date, with seed selection based on training and validation Dry_Total means. Tweedie loss addressed zero-inflated, right-skewed biomass targets. A custom metric penalized variation in category-specific R² to encourage balanced predictions across green, clover, and dead biomass.

The author used exploratory analysis to identify relationships between author and geometry and between D_e and D_h. Those patterns informed preprocessing, alongside missing-value filling with an Unknown category, modes, and means. Categorical variables were label encoded before modeling with mljar and AutoGluon. The post gives no numerical model results or validation details.

solution_title: Silver medal solution: ViT, ConvNext, kNN-regression with BLIP-2 captions
solution_summary: The solution combined direct image-to-prompt-embedding prediction with retrieval-based kNN regression. ViT and ConvNeXt models first learned projection heads on filtered LAION pairs and were then fine-tuned on aggressively filtered diffusion image-prompt data using angular-distance loss. The retrieval branch used deduplicated reference embeddings, distance reweighting, memory mapping, and twenty diverse BLIP-2 captions per test image. Combining both branches achieved 0.61004 public and 0.60787 private scores.
compute: Optimized retrieval inference took one hour.
external_data: ["LAION", "DiffusionDB 14M", "xiaozhouwang GPT2 and Hardcoded datasets", "jeinsong ChatGPT dataset", "motono0223 dataset", "Open Prompts Discord images", "tanreinama 900k dataset images"]

solution_summary: The solution used a single CatBoost model with minimal preprocessing. All features were converted to categorical dtype because most were already object-valued, and this representation worked well for the dataset. The author made only two baseline notebook submissions and did not have time for additional preprocessing or tuning.

The team combined XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost and site-specific feed-forward networks, emphasizing manual noise removal and prediction post-processing. Models trained at several site, building and building-type granularities used fewer than 30 features in the best single model. Predictions were scaled down, usually by 0.8–0.85, to counter the upward bias introduced by removing low target values. Month-based cross-validation, leaked data and leaderboard feedback guided tuning and ensemble weights, with leaked values also inserted into test predictions.

solution_title: 97th place solution for Google - Fast or Slow? Predict AI Model Runtime
solution_summary: The solution used separate models for tile and layout data: a modified BERT with graph attention for tiles and residual graph neural networks for layouts. Four layout models covered the dataset subtypes, while the tile pipeline used five-fold cross-validation and combined fold predictions. Memory requirements drove the switch from BERT to TF-GNN for layouts, reducing reported memory use from over 300 GB to under 30 GB. Checkpointed training and concurrent tile inference helped fit limited computing resources, with a three-thread pool reducing tile inference from about 1.81 hours to 58 minutes.
compute: 4-core CPUs for resource-limited execution; layout training on TPUs. Layout memory under 30 GB versus over 300 GB for BERT. One xla-random epoch took about one CPU hour; GPUs gave little or no speedup. Three-thread tile inference took 3,448 seconds versus 6,532 seconds sequentially.

solution_title: 9th Place Solution, 9 Models in the Ensemble
solution_summary: The author combined nine neural, linear, and tree models using optimized ensemble weights. Feature engineering included M-estimate encoding, reciprocal features, polynomial expansions, and random forest embeddings. Ridge helped identify models to exclude before Optuna optimized the final weights. Ensemble diversity and validation that kept original-source data out of the validation split were emphasized.

The author grouped variables by their shared var number and used simple classifiers to identify promising groups. They engineered binary indicators, zero counts, interactions, and PCA features, then selected features with extra trees and manual greedy adjustments. Three XGBoost models with depths 5, 9, and 12 were combined using weights of 0.6, 0.3, and 0.1. The reported private AUC was 0.825816.

The solution combined four boosting models and three neural models, repeating the ensemble across six training seeds. Agent-swap augmentation with corresponding feature and target transformations produced the main performance gain, while readability scores and rule-based grouping supported feature preparation and five-split validation. OLS fitted ensemble weights, including negative neural-model weights, and predictions were repeatedly clipped and rescaled. A final submission also fitted negative-weight adjustments directly to the public leaderboard, improving the private score from 0.42324 to 0.41996. The author noted that shared game rulesets across public and private test data may have favored these adjustments.

The author removed highly collinear features and selected a smaller feature set. Optuna tuned hyperparameters for five XGBoost models trained on five different targets. Treelite accelerated inference, allowing predictions within 2 minutes 40 seconds.
compute: Inference completed within 2 minutes 40 seconds.

solution_title: [1st place solution] pretrained CNNs -> xgboost -> F1 optimization
solution_summary: The author fine-tuned multiple pretrained image architectures using fastai and PyTorch, switching early from Adam to SGD with the one-cycle policy. Suspected distribution differences motivated cross-validation training on the provided validation set. Per-label XGBoost models combined predictions across labels, and a final optimization pipeline blended raw and stacked outputs while tuning label thresholds for micro F1. Attention-equipped darknet50 and separate per-label neural training were unsuccessful or inefficient.
compute: Single 1080 Ti for training; optimization heuristics took 7 minutes. XGBoost cross-validation took about 1 hour 15 minutes on AWS c5.18xlarge.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution (And How to Score .55571 on Private LB)
solution_summary: The final approach adapted a public ensemble kernel using the union of features selected for a separate stacked ensemble of gradient boosting, random forest, and support vector regression. An adaptive feature learner sampled feature subsets and adjusted their sampling probabilities according to cross-validation performance. Categorical dummy variables worked better than factorized representations, and dimensionality-reduction features did not improve the best score. Targets were clipped at 155, and shuffled five-fold validation guided selection; the submitted solution scored 0.55498 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: 9th place solution - with video visualization - Team Arm Breakers
solution_summary: The team initialized a pixel tour with LKH v3 and refined it using a custom Python Lin–Kernighan-style solver. Penalties encoded arm feasibility constraints, while moves through 5-opt and repeated perturbation helped escape local optima. Shared tours, LKH optimization of sub-tours, and manual repairs produced further improvements. A separate configuration search converted the feasible tour into arm movements using compact candidate sets and adaptive backtracking.
compute: Approximately 30 remote solver instances.

solution_summary: The author reports unsuccessful experiments for biomass prediction rather than a successful final pipeline. Depth-derived height features, physically motivated target decompositions, and spatial feature-map prediction all failed to improve results. Synthetic dead vegetation images worsened training and exposed poor generalization in existing models. A PlantCLEF2024 backbone and segmentation-guided crop training also provided no gains.

The approach estimated vehicle velocity from Doppler measurements and smoothed it with a 1D CNN. Reliable baseline position groups supplied anchors for velocity-based interpolation, while orientation-aware snapping aligned SJC trajectories with ground-truth-derived grids. Iterative optimization smoothed the resulting positions, followed by averaging across grouping conditions and phones in the same collection. Reported scores were 2.331 on training, 3.758 public, and 2.597 private.

The solution used a UNet-CNN pipeline with 768-pixel images and large backbones. A UNet trained on competition annotations supplied spatial supervision through catheter segmentation masks, improving robustness and agreement between validation and leaderboard performance. Pseudo-labeled NIH and MIMIC images trained student models with different feature extractors, followed by fine-tuning on competition data. Conventional single-stage pseudo-labeling was abandoned because convergence was slow.

The author improved a digit classifier through mean normalization, feature scaling, float32 conversion, and LeakyReLU activations. RMSprop, image augmentation, learning rate reduction, and early stopping helped raise the public score from about 0.96 to 0.98. Further gains came from tuning training and augmentation hyperparameters. Averaging model predictions and adding Dig-MNIST training data did not help.

The solution used a U-Net with ASPP and se50 and se101 backbones on 1024 by 1024 images. An auxiliary two-class pneumothorax classifier was trained jointly with segmentation using a weighted sum of binary cross-entropy losses and Adam. Mean-teacher semi-supervision with the NIH dataset improved the reported score from 0.874 to 0.880. The author reported stage scores of 0.8821 and 0.8643.

The pipeline classified chart type and located the plot area, ran OCR, detected chart elements, and associated them with axis ticks. A three-fold U-Net ensemble handled plot segmentation and chart classification, while fine-tuned text detection and pretrained recognition used Paddle ppOCRv3. Mask R-CNN detected bars, scatter points, and dots, and an EfficientNet-B5 U-Net++ segmented lines. OCR geometry fixes and confidence-based rotation selection improved text handling, and rules converted pixel positions into axis-relative values.
compute: Kaggle and Google Colab Pro computing resources.

solution_summary: The solution used a 2.5D pipeline that sampled CT sequences, cropped slices to valid image content, and resized them to 256×384. An InternImage Base backbone and UnetPlusPlus neck supported organ-aware classification with segmentation-mask supervision. A query-based masked-attention head handled organs, while a separate extravasation head used image-level supervision. Predictions were averaged across patient series and ensembled across sequence lengths and data folds.

The author built a fully rule-based agent organized into persistent projects that allocate ships and budgets to hunting, defense, mining, escorting, and expansion. Frequent shipyard conversion shortened risky deposit trips and established internal hunting zones, with the best agent favoring diagonal shipyard placement. Handcrafted action values and priority-ordered movement coordinated ships and avoided collisions. Local evaluation rotated player seats, while deterministic replay reproduction supported debugging.

The solution trained diverse audio backbones on five-second mel spectrograms using independent rounds of soft pseudo-labeling. Soundscape validation, soft teacher targets, and backbone diversity drove the largest gains, with individual five-fold models improving from roughly 0.900–0.915 to 0.945–0.950. Shared-spectrogram OpenVINO graphs reduced ensemble inference time, allowing more models within the runtime budget. Equal-weight rank blending with a public Perch branch produced a final private score of 0.95762.
compute: Each custom ensemble ran in approximately 40–45 minutes; shared-spectrogram export saved 7–8 minutes.

solution_summary: The solution combined LightGBM, CatBoost, and neural networks using weights of 0.5, 0.2, and 0.3. Features captured title-sequence embeddings, historical activity, decayed counts, activity density, previous assessments, and out-of-fold meta targets; word2vec and meta features were especially important. Feature selection retained 300 features, and evaluation used five stratified group folds with one validation sample per user and five random seeds. Thresholds were optimized for cross-validation quadratic weighted kappa, and the selected model scored 0.563 on both public and private evaluations.

The team combined large IMU-only and full-sensor ensembles through weighted logit sums, with additional orientation models and subject-structure post-processing. Their pipelines normalized handedness, handled missing sensor values, filtered problematic sequences or subjects, and engineered motion and distance features. Diverse CNN, recurrent, attention, and TOF-specific models contributed complementary predictions. Subject-grouped validation, temporal augmentation, mixup, and model-selection tricks supported generalization.

The solution used an AWQ-quantized DeepSeek-R1-distilled Qwen 14B model with self-consistency and tool-integrated reasoning. A customized vLLM stopped generation when answers converged, became too diverse, or accumulated too many invalid responses, conserving time for additional generations. Prompts encouraged Python exhaustive search and efficient computation. Repeated evaluation on the 100 most recent AIME problems produced scores around 75–79, compared with about 63–68 for the referenced public notebook.

The solution first classified whether a user would return and purchase, then used regression to predict the purchase amount. Feature engineering followed a public starter notebook. Validation reproduced the prediction windows one year earlier, and the author considered this validation strategy critical because the public leaderboard was unreliable.

solution_title: [0.901 PB solution] From gold to abyss or history on UnLucky leaf
solution_summary: The team combined ResNeXt, EfficientNet, and ViT models, using CatBoost as the second layer in the selected submission. A simpler linear combination of the same models achieved a reported private score of 0.901, compared with 0.889 for the selected version. The author attributed the difference to ensemble complexity on noisy data and recommended simple ensembling.

The solution built queries as OR combinations of field-specific subqueries, using hyphens to AND tokens without increasing Whoosh's measured token count. Candidate subqueries came from tokens shared by small subsets of target patents. Mixed integer programming selected subqueries to maximize recovered targets against a randomly constructed test index. Multithreaded C++ search and frequency-based token restrictions made candidate generation practical.

The solution used two unidirectional LSTM layers with roughly 35 features, training on sequences of 256 and inferring on sequences of 512. The first layer processed question embeddings and their differences from the current question, while the second incorporated continuous features and question-answer interactions. Answer-choice popularity was an important feature, and GPU-resident histories supported inference. Architecture changes and bagging four models improved scores to 0.813 public and 0.816 private.
compute: History features occupied approximately 6 GB on GPU; other objects were stored in RAM.

solution_summary: The team trained LoRA adapters on large synthetic datasets containing reasoning traces from domain-specific algorithmic solvers. They validated against the full original training set and used public leaderboard probes to isolate domain performance. Improved bit-manipulation templates and a pruned cryptarithmetic search were central, while synthetic examples targeted observed failure patterns. The final selection used two seeds of the approximately 0.25-billion-token adapter, favoring its more reliable domain balance over a larger dataset.
compute: Kaggle and Google Cloud G4 environments; Tinker used for faster late-stage adapter training.

solution_summary: The solution grouped patients by whether medication information was available and calculated separate target trends for those groups and the overall population. A LightGBM binary classifier used visit-month, protein, and peptide information to predict group membership. Predictions above 0.75 or below 0.15 selected the corresponding group trend, while intermediate predictions used the overall trend. Ten-fold cross-validation and seed averaging improved robustness, and the P05060 protein contributed strongly to public-score improvement, although validation and leaderboard scores remained unstable.

The pipeline retrieved DOI and accession citations using regex rules, external metadata, and false-positive filtering. It then assigned dataset types through deterministic heuristics followed by a six-fold DeBERTa-v3 Large classification ensemble for unresolved cases. Gradient clipping and exponential moving averages stabilized training on small, noisy labels, while fine-tuned Qwen models were unstable and less effective. The six model predictions were averaged at inference, and XML was searched only when citations could not be found in parsed PDF text.

Splitting validation into the first six days and remaining 33 days exposed a mismatch between public and private performance, leading the team to stop relying on public scores. The solution used mathematical light-curve modeling to predict a single average transit depth and uncertainty per planet. Uncertainty combined variation over time and wavelength, with conservative fallbacks for anomalous curves or failed phase detection. A 100-configuration ensemble improved the local score from 0.437 to 0.440 without improving leaderboard scores, and wavelength-dependent depth prediction performed worse.

Temporal overlap averaging, player-order swapping, and diverse backbone and sequence-length combinations supplied robustness. Forward selection chose six model configurations, whose five-fold predictions were blended and thresholded. The final submission achieved CV 0.8016, public score 0.7902, and private score 0.7913.

Weight-ratio features and synthetic training samples did not improve performance. Attempts to identify age outliers manually or generate additional old-crab samples also failed. SRGNN improved weighted candidate recall to 0.695 while slightly reducing the average candidate count relative to the co-visitation baseline. Ranking used session, item, temporal interaction, and embedding similarity features with grouped cross-validation and negative downsampling. Sessions with insufficient candidates were supplemented using unrestricted co-visitation and recent popular items.

solution_summary: The final predictor took the median of three ensembles, each formed from a learned linear combination of ten XGBoost fold models. Symmetric-game agent swapping, AdvantageP1 interaction features, and aggressive feature removal supported generalization. Validation grouped games by ruleset and stratified discretized targets, while column subsampling and selected early stopping constrained overfitting. Learned ensemble weights amplified predictions before clipping to the target range, and the selected submission scored 0.425 privately.

solution_summary: The solution first predicts coarse masks with a standard U-Net on 320×480 images, then refines boundaries using 256×256 tiles and a deeper U-Net. Overlapping tiles provide repeated predictions for boundary pixels, reducing tile-edge errors. Augmentation, Dice loss, and batch normalization support training, with batches drawing tiles from multiple images. The single model scored 0.9970 and a fold ensemble reached 0.9971, although some severely incorrect first-stage test masks remained uncorrected.

solution_title: 37th place solution - T0m part [Segment Copy-Paste & Progressive Learning]

Progressive learning increased image size and augmentation strength during training, and inference used TTA and tracking. Article IDs from two Wikipedia datasets were used to collect article text through MediaWiki, producing roughly 22 million subsection texts after filtering. An e5-base-v2 retriever searched a sharded Faiss index and refined the retrieved context at the line level. solution_title: MAP Competition 13th Place Gold Medal Solution

It restricted predictions to question-specific targets, derived answer correctness from training data, and added answer choices to prompts. solution_title: 18th solution: From Deterministic Solvers to Learnable Reasoning Traces
solution_summary: The team generated short, consistent teacher reasoning traces with category-specific deterministic solvers and distilled them into LoRA adapters through supervised fine-tuning. Broader solver search, synthetic problems, and answer-assisted label selection improved other experiments, with the strongest single model reaching 0.880 privately. Training on all available data and relying on the noisy public leaderboard caused poor experiment and submission selection.

solution_summary: This inference-only solution served GPT-OSS 120B through vLLM and ran eight parallel tool-assisted reasoning attempts per problem. The most impactful modification was a stronger prompt emphasizing answer constraints, modular reduction, and independent verification. Final answers were extracted only from boxed integers and selected through voting supplemented by tail-window entropy and median confidence. Dynamic budgeting and early stopping conserved runtime, with 50 problems taking approximately four to five hours on one H100 80GB.

solution_summary: The author constructed the solution mathematically by separating sequences into mandatory sequences, their relatives, and all remaining sequences. A cyclic length-to-coverage argument established a relaxed lower bound of 2400 without wildcards. Carefully assembled base permutations produced three sequences of length 2440, then six wildcard substitutions reduced the objective to 2428. The author argued that each wildcard could save at most six characters within this construction, while acknowledging that this was not a complete proof of global optimality.

The author focused on the efficiency stream and chose LightGBM to balance predictive performance with fast inference. Feature engineering used Polars, Numba, and Joblib to reduce processing time, with Polars reported as faster than Pandas. Important features came from reconstructed essays and aggregates of differences in down_time and event_id between events. The provided text does not preserve numerical scores or execution timings.

The final system combined six lightweight Conv1D models with two transformer variants and test-time augmentation. Landmark normalization, varied body-part inputs, and strong spatial and temporal augmentations mattered more than architectural complexity. Same-label body-part recombination and CutMix improved training, while transformers combined coordinate and motion embeddings. The six-model convolutional ensemble achieved 0.8711 private score before transformers were added; additional WLASL data was tested but excluded.

solution_title: There is a silver solution hidden in public notebooks!
solution_summary: The post compares public RTK baselines and highlights how phone-specific performance explains public and private score differences. The Python RTK baseline performed poorly on Pixel4 devices but strongly on Samsung and Pixel5, which dominated the private paths. The authors also report improving taro's baseline from 3.027 to 2.66, without describing the modifications. They suggest replacing Pixel4 predictions from the Python RTK baseline with another public baseline, estimating a public score near 2.6.

The solution combined gradient-boosted trees with diverse neural models through hill climbing. Keras factorization machines treated every feature as categorical, using rounding to reduce cardinality and bigram interactions to improve their predictions. These models complemented the trees particularly well, raising ensemble CV from about 0.9275 to about 0.928. Several neural models and learned stackers improved CV without improving leaderboard performance, making ensemble overfitting a central difficulty.

solution_title: [47th place solution] Pytorch Lightning Framework + Column-wise Ensemble
solution_summary: The solution used transformer encoders trained with PyTorch Lightning and a 90/10 training-validation split. Rotary positional encoding improved the public score by approximately 0.005, and the best single model scored 0.751 publicly and 0.744 privately. Feature-specific transformations and scaling were combined with an Optuna-tuned ensemble that assigned separate model weights to each target column. KAN embeddings and clamped-label training did not improve standalone converged performance but supplied models for the final ensemble, while alternative output heads increased overfitting.

The solution combined two encoder-decoder Transformers trained on sequences of 500 user interactions, with users held out for validation. Engineered timing and repeated-question features improved convergence and AUROC, while container-aware attention masks prevented answer leakage and allowed appropriate within-container context. A time-aware ensemble skipped inference on the first 20% of the test stream and used both models as much as the remaining runtime allowed. The smaller Transformer outperformed the larger model, and training used distributed execution and mixed precision.

solution_title: [6th] RL + league + search with a custom edge attention transformer
solution_summary: The solution trained separate two-player and four-player transformer policies using self-play, with league play added for four-player games. Training used asynchronous PPO, transferred knowledge from a smaller model, and averaged selected checkpoints. A greedy two-step rollout search improved two-player performance by roughly 30–40 points, while compute limits and weaker four-player opponent coverage remained constraints.

Time-based validation and reduced weighting of 2017 samples improved agreement with the leaderboard. Augmenting plays with projected future positions and averaging their predictions improved cross-validation by almost 0.00010 and produced a public score of 0.01299. Later notebook updates added encoder-decoder attention, squeeze-and-excitation, and better data cleaning.

Lower layers diversified categorical encodings, regression objectives, text representations, and model versions. solution_title: Public 9th/Private 331st Place Solution - A Non-Bioinformatician's Journey in CAFA
solution_summary: The approach combined protein embeddings with sequence properties, species information, and UniProt metadata in diverse MLPs, a 1D CNN, and nearest-neighbor models. The final solution averaged three multilevel ensembles built with 5-, 7-, and 10-fold splits. Conservative blends and averaging across parameter settings helped limit dependence on optimistic stacking CV scores. The final ensemble achieved public and private scores of 0.95462 and 0.95487.

Grapheme probabilities were converted into component scores by averaging across graphemes sharing each component value, reducing frequency bias. FMix, synthetic graphemes, and validation that withheld entire graphemes supported this approach. The final seven-model ensemble used component-specific blending and inverse-frequency consonant weights.

The strongest online-learning gains came from alternating between LLMs and ByT5 rather than training models repeatedly on outputs from the same architecture. Predictions from the resulting online-trained models were ensembled for the final submission.

Stage-two model and loss changes provided an additional boost, while ResNeXt101 and a parallel GRU–LSTM alternative did not help. solution_summary: The solution models sales as a product of country GDP, product trends, store and weekday effects, COVID disruption, annual seasonality, and holiday effects. Product trends are smoothed with low-frequency Fourier filtering. Linear regression estimates seasonal coefficients, while ridge regression estimates amplitudes for shared Gaussian holiday response shapes.

The solution trains a 3D U-Net with a pretrained ResNet200 encoder to predict downsampled Gaussian motor heatmaps. It combines corrected competition annotations and external tomograms with heavy augmentation, deep supervision and a pooled auxiliary loss. Inference slides only along depth with substantial overlap, downweights window edges and combines eight seeded models. Motor presence is decided by ranking tomograms by peak confidence and removing the lowest quantile, which was more stable than a fixed probability threshold. Depth-only sliding was four times faster, and final inference took about ten hours.

solution_title: [5th Solution] - housuke's part - Private 0.572, Public 0.566 with single model
solution_summary: The solution treated discourse effectiveness as token classification using DeBERTa backbones, discourse boundary markers, type embeddings, discourse max pooling, and inverse-length token loss weights. Masked language model pretraining, random token masking, and SiFT perturbations improved training, while soft pseudo-labeling benefited from removing masking and perturbations in the author's experiments. Predictions passed through an LSTM discourse-sequence stack and then an XGBoost stack, with discourse length and type added as features. Using third-stage predictions as pseudo-labels, final five-fold DeBERTa models achieved private scores of 0.574 and 0.572, each reported in 27 minutes.
compute: 27 minutes reported for each final five-fold model; hardware and timing scope unspecified.

solution_title: 988th Place solution (4th on Public) - GNN and domain adaption. 800Kb model.
solution_summary: The author replaced molecular fingerprints and XGBoost with a compact graph attention network using rich atom and bond annotations from RDKit. Precomputed cross-validation folds stored on SSD made single-GPU training practical, and the shared-building-block model was trained on one fold before fine-tuning on the full dataset. For non-shared building blocks, a domain adaptation objective used embedding cosine similarities to generate soft labels, improving the public score from 0.498 to 0.517. Despite those gains, the approach generalized poorly to the private leaderboard.
compute: Single GPU; approximately 12 hours preprocessing per split; 1 TB storage; approximately 800 KB model.

solution_summary: The author trained YOLOv5x detectors at image size 640 using labels grouped by annotator agreement. Weighted boxes fusion merged annotations and detector outputs, while scale and horizontal-flip augmentation improved inference. Final selections combined detectors trained with at least one or two annotators' agreement and a disease-only detector, with one selection also including public notebook predictions. A no-finding score was derived from detection confidence; the selected submissions scored 0.297 and 0.303 privately, while an unselected ensemble including the strictest labels reached 0.306.

The author adapted Stockfish 16's handcrafted evaluation engine to the competition's memory and runtime constraints. A compact three-layer MLP learned the difference between NNUE and handcrafted evaluations from positions sampled during approximately 70,000 games. Adding half of the neural correction improved strength by about 30 Elo, compared with less than 10 Elo for the full correction. Both handcrafted-only and neural-enhanced agents were submitted, while memory reductions and efficient search execution helped control resource usage.
compute: Kaggle GPU environment for training; CPU cores in Kaggle TPU environments for some game-generation notebooks

solution_summary: The submission provides a short reproduction workflow for the DecMeg2014 challenge. It requires placing the challenge data in a data folder and installing the covariance toolbox. The workflow runs a preprocessing script followed by a final submission script in MATLAB, without describing the model or reporting numerical results.

solution_title: 131st Place: The 20.220 Hedge That Beat Our 114.570 Public Winner
solution_summary: The team selected two distinct sandbox attack mechanisms: a high-public marker-exfiltration router and a clean-email confused-deputy specialist. The surviving specialist used short templates, per-model live probing, predicate-specific validation, unique synthetic recipients, and conservative deadline budgeting. Its public and private scores were both 20.220, whereas the marker router scored zero privately. The key decision was preserving mechanism diversity despite the specialist's much lower public score.

solution_title: Ablation study on the 1st place solution: effect of ensemble, tick-size leak and normalization
solution_summary: This ablation writeup examines a final ensemble of five LightGBM models, three 1D CNNs, and three MLPs. Its central feature design combined seven nearest-neighbor searches across timestamps and stocks using recovered real prices, volatility, and trade size. The full ensemble achieved 0.19545 private RMSPE, while a single LightGBM achieved 0.19699. Feature diversity mattered more than model diversity, and removing rank normalization had almost no effect.

solution_title: "I don't even see the top" solution | .776/.733
solution_summary: The pipeline first generated candidates using 15 two-dimensional U-Net models trained on provided positives. These comprised five folds each of ResNet34 models at two patch sizes and a ResNet18 model. Threshold-based false-positive mining supplied examples for a second-stage 2.5D discriminator ensemble containing ten models. GRU discriminators reduced performance and were excluded, while mask-derived voxel spacing estimation was intended to normalize samples to a reference spacing of 13.1.

The team built a diverse ensemble dominated by EfficientNet models trained on multiple image sizes, data-year combinations, and lesion crops. Five-fold validation on 2020 data guided model selection, while surrogate-label pretraining, augmentation, and test-time augmentation supported individual models. They filtered 91 models down to 58 using prediction-correlation discrepancies and adversarial validation. Their strongest submission blended averaged predictions with stacking using metadata and prediction statistics, achieving CV AUC 0.9532 and private leaderboard AUC 0.9459.

solution_title: 21st Place Solution : So close Yet So Far
solution_summary: The final approach combined multi-head classifiers with spatial attention and a four-stage ResNet200d model. Models used ResNet200d, EfficientNet B5, and SE-ResNet152d backbones at image sizes of 640 and 768, with fine-tuning on pseudo-labeled NIH, SIIM, and test images. The final submission blended eight models using weights optimized by Optuna on out-of-fold predictions. Many more elaborate attention, training, preprocessing, and augmentation experiments improved cross-validation without meaningful leaderboard gains, so the team favored simpler models.

The team combined LightGBM, XGBoost, and a neural network, with stacking also used. Merging teammates' feature sets brought a major improvement; features included images, Russian-stemmed TF-IDF, ridge predictions, and aggregates. The neural network processed categorical, numerical, image, and text inputs in separate branches before dense layers, with a CNN on 32-by-32 images providing a significant gain. The three main models each achieved public scores near 0.2185–0.2186, and ridge features were regenerated using consistent folds to avoid leakage.

The author shares a processing framework capable of generating more than 3,000 features across the full dataset without running out of memory. The repository includes three methods for restoring decision dates and multiple preprocessing steps. It also provides memory-efficient LightGBM training with more than 1,000 features and feature-selection approaches including PSI. The best single model scored 0.598 publicly and 0.522 privately.

The final submission ensembled strong submissions from several different approaches, including medical reasoning, cluster engineering, and dimensionality reduction. A CatBoost baseline trained directly on the data without preprocessing or feature engineering was excluded from the final ensemble. The ensemble achieved a private score of 0.502, compared with 0.481 for its best individual component. Adversarial validation indicated that leaderboard movement was likely, but the author did not develop a strategy to avoid it.

The pipeline first estimated issue difficulty and skipped issues whose probability of being easy was below 0.5. A single quantized DeepSeek model handled difficulty estimation, repository search, patch generation, and verification, with a LoRA adapter for difficulty classification. Multiple search and patch candidates were checked through LLM judgment, patch parsing, and dry-run application. Avoiding incorrect submissions was central because the competition heavily penalized wrong answers.

The post provides code for inspecting a secret-sloth image in the frequency domain. It computes a two-dimensional Fourier transform and displays its magnitude with logarithmic color normalization. It provides no broader pipeline or quantitative results.

The solution trained eight different base learners with hyperparameters selected through local cross-validation. Gaussian mixture models supplied additional clustering features, while early stopping controlled LightGBM overfitting. A second LightGBM model combined the predictions and powered out-of-fold predictions. The author's strongest submissions did not use pseudo-labeling.

The author used a stacked ensemble with ridge regression in the second modeling stage. The post emphasizes selecting strong, diverse base models and checking validation performance when adding public predictions. It also discusses regularization and reviewing prediction sources for leakage. Exact base-model membership, preprocessing, and numerical results are not provided.

The pipeline extracted roughly 80 candidates per session and reranked them with XGBoost. Most of its 744 features aggregated candidate-to-session-item similarities using weights based on position, timestamp, and interaction type. Recovering sessions excluded by the original split improved carts and orders, while heavy downsampling enabled GPU training. Clicks used a single model, whereas carts and orders used small XGBoost blends; combining these with teammates' predictions reached a private leaderboard score above 0.603.
compute: 32 GB V100 for batched feature computation; GPU training after heavy downsampling.

solution_title: Rank 172, sharing code for the first time.

solution_title: 26th short solution（Listwise stage2 model to transform stage1 scores)
solution_summary: The solution used a two-stage retrieval and score-transformation pipeline. Stage one learned rankings with in-batch negatives and a hard negative from the same channel, with sentence-pair pretraining that added an LSTM head. Stage two used listwise transformer models, where stage-one scores mattered much more than the content text. The final ensemble combined 17 stage-one models and three stage-two models, reporting an LB score of 667 with 90-minute inference.

solution_title: When the Leaderboard Scores One Axis
solution_summary: The final attack build hedged exfiltration with confused-deputy and additional attack predicates, informed by a local simulator over reconstructed guardrails. Selecting the higher-public-scoring hedge produced 2.595 private points, while another held build would have scored 3.960. The writeup also evaluates reconstructed defenses using the SDK defense track, finding that blocking the deputy channel can deny legitimate email traffic. A population analysis of submission histories supports the conclusion that public-score optimization often harmed private transfer and final selection.

solution_summary: The solution combined feature engineering with LightGBM. The author reported relatively stable public and private scores. Cross-validation was emphasized as especially important for this synthetic-data competition, although specific features and validation settings were not described.

The author restricted inputs to measurements available at test time, using only the initial FVC and percent values. FVC was normalized so its initial value equaled one, and the starting week was shifted to zero. A linear regression of normalized FVC against shifted weeks produced the author's best private leaderboard submission.

The post provides reproduction instructions for the team's submission. The listed pipeline runs three preprocessing scripts, three model-fitting scripts, and a final blending script. solution_title: Artifact Verification and LoRA-Alpha Calibration for a Nemotron Reasoning Adapte
solution_summary: The submission reused a public rank-32 LoRA adapter for NVIDIA Nemotron rather than training new weights. A verification notebook checked archive integrity, required root files, adapter metadata, rank limits, and base-model compatibility. A second notebook reduced lora_alpha from 64 to 62 while preserving all learned weights, lowering the adapter contribution by 3.125%. The writeup presents this as a controlled calibration experiment and does not report a measured performance improvement.

solution_title: Solo silver (302nd): 3-min video of my solution
solution_summary: The final entry expanded a public Raptor and R6 blend with 18 knee-centered ConvNeXt and EfficientNet models. It averaged standardized logits rather than percentile ranks. Ten added models learned from expert-graded OAI knees after translating grades into competition labels. The resulting submission achieved 0.944 private AUC.

The selected approach concatenated NFNet image embeddings with several text representations and perceptual hashes, alongside TF-IDF matching. Concatenating image and text embeddings, SAM optimization, and resize plus center-crop test-time augmentation worked well. The selected model achieved a private score of 0.728, while an unselected CurricularFace variant achieved 0.729. Swin, ViT, RoBERTa, and mode-specific thresholds did not help.

The author inferred essay prompts with a shared prompt classifier and trained DeBERTa-v3-large using five stratified folds. DeBERTa predictions were then stacked with public-notebook features into an ensemble of LightGBM and XGBoost trained using seven-fold prompt-grouped validation. This strategy produced relatively stable agreement between cross-validation and leaderboard results, although the author retained concerns about leakage from DeBERTa. Additional ensembles, threshold tuning, and adding PERSUADE data did not help.

The detailed component used a ResNet34 tile encoder on medium-resolution slides after white-background cropping and artifact cleaning. Tile features were reshaped into a square, passed through a squeeze-and-excitation block, pooled, and trained with classification and regression heads. Slide-level and tile-level augmentation, bounded regression outputs, and staged training from 49 to 81 tiles improved learning; only regression outputs were used for prediction. The final team submission averaged four model components, while the detailed five-fold ResNet34 component achieved 0.911 CV.
compute: Medium-resolution images stored on SSD; tile augmentations performed on GPU.

solution_title: 19th Place - Single Model LB 860 Without Pseudo
solution_summary: The team trained large image backbones on six crop datasets using separate ArcFace heads for species and individual identity. Each model produced six embeddings per image, whose weighted average was optimized on cross-validation for nearest-neighbor matching. An eight-fold validation setup supported threshold tuning, and voting across 96 fold models achieved an LB score of 0.868. Post-competition retraining of two ensemble models with pseudo labels improved the private score by 0.016.

solution_title: 2nd place solution ： Segmentation + 2.5D CNN + GRU Attention
solution_summary: The pipeline first segmented vertebrae with a 2.5D EfficientNetB0 U-Net trained on 87 annotated studies. Predicted masks then defined separate cervical-vertebra crops, each represented by 24 uniformly sampled slices. A CNN, bidirectional GRU, and attention classified these sequences using EfficientNetV2-S and ResNeSt50d backbones. Limited disk capacity led the team to store crop coordinates and DICOM references instead of full cropped volumes.

solution_title: How to win a gold medal with basic DL technics and a simple stacking
solution_summary: The pipeline generated diverse neural-network predictions with varying fold counts, test-time augmentation, and selective pseudo-labeling. Networks trained on Fourier-transformed bands provided a substantial gain, while SVM or logistic regression on CNN features added diversity. A second level used 25 LightGBM and XGBoost ensembles over random subsets of predictions and additional features. Final predictions were averaged, power-calibrated, and clipped, with calibration improving log loss by about 0.003.

The approach used four image models—DINOv2-small, BEiTv2, EfficientNetB0, and EfficientNetB3—without test-time augmentation. Training combined mixed precision, repeated negative downsampling, a one-class formulation, and stepwise cosine annealing. Grouped cross-validation produced out-of-fold predictions and guided checkpoint selection across 20 epochs. The reported CV, LB, and PL scores were 0.182, 0.183, and 0.170, and adding EfficientNetB3 reduced private performance.
compute: 20 epochs per model; approximately 1–5 minutes per epoch.

solution_summary: The solution trained an Xception-based motion predictor using offline-rendered images stored as PNG-compressed TFRecords. Validation splits separated map regions using agent-center y positions to avoid similar maps appearing on both sides. The model predicted four trajectory modes and retained the three with highest confidence, using the official multimode metric as an angle-weighted training loss. Multiplicative Gaussian target noise and random removal of history frames improved robustness, while Colab memory limits prevented use of the full training data.

solution_summary: The solution averaged two XGBoost models built through successive feature-selection stages, with the second model using a stacked predictor from the first. Engineered interactions, grouped cumulative binary sums, recoded categories, and ID supplied the initial feature set. Thirty-fold cross-validation guided training rounds and feature selection, although its mean scores were optimistic. A small set of interactions dominated feature gain, and the final average scored 0.55551 on the private leaderboard.

solution_summary: The final submission combined three 2.5D Unet++ models and three ResidualUNet3D models with nearly equal weights. Case-grouped cross-validation used different splits across model configurations to improve diversity. Auxiliary annotation-presence classification addressed inconsistent slice annotations, while questionable boundary slices were excluded from segmentation loss. The ensemble scored 0.880 on the private leaderboard; omitting the last added model would have scored 0.883.

The solution aggregated extensively engineered session features into user-level predictors. A purchase classifier generated out-of-fold probabilities that became features for a LightGBM revenue regressor, with results averaged across four seeds. Validation used the previous year's matching holiday period, although the author later questioned that seasonal assumption and the use of stratified folds. The reported regression RMSE was 0.320785.

solution_summary: The main solution combined DeBERTa models and SVR with pseudo-labels from FB1 and argumentative-element metadata from FB2 models. The author optimized the weights of 13 models using L-BFGS-B. The efficiency solution distilled this ensemble into deberta-v3-xsmall with a maximum sequence length of 512 and uniform length batching. Validation used four multilabel-stratified folds based on targets and BERTopic topics, followed by training on all available training data.

The author combined models from public notebooks and concentrated on ensemble optimization rather than developing new architectures. The decisive change was a constant +40 adjustment to predicted glass transition temperature, addressing a target-specific distribution shift. A Celsius-to-Fahrenheit transformation was rejected during the competition because it hurt the public score, but later inspection showed substantially better private performance. Postcompetition experiments showed that correcting this single target could match or surpass the final ensemble even with a simple ExtraTrees model.

The author iteratively estimated monthly player strengths using a modified Chessmetrics-style rating procedure, then predicted game outcomes from rating differences and a rating-dependent white advantage. Ratings incorporated time-weighted opponents, artificial opponents, and penalties for limited playing experience. The procedure used later results when estimating earlier strengths and also used game participation information from the missing months to adjust predictions. Parameters were tested using historical cutoffs, but the post leaves parts of the strength-estimation algorithm unexplained and reports no numerical evaluation score.

The solution used iterated local search with restricted k-opt moves and custom kicks to escape local optima. Candidate moves excluded reversals and limited moving subsequence lengths to keep expensive scoring manageable. Problem-specific kicks moved or swapped words between structural groups, helping achieve a score of 28.5 on Problem 5. Multiple starts and exhaustive choices for the final word also improved results on other problems.

solution_summary: The solution used hourglass CenterNet models to predict car locations and poses, with perspective transforms reducing differences in apparent car size and covering outliers. Camera rotation was the most important augmentation for controlling overfitting on the small training set. Six models with different heads and transforms were combined with test-time augmentation and weighted averaging. Metric probing informed extensive post-processing, including global roll prediction, coordinate shifts, selective filtering, and duplicate removal.

solution_summary: The solution relied on online training using test-provided examples and ensembled diverse classification, embedding, and instruction-tuned language models. Hard pseudo-labels from confident ensemble predictions enabled additional BERT and LLM training, with earlier LoRA weights reused to reduce training time. Post-submission analysis showed pseudo-labeling improved the private score from 0.92579 to 0.92734.

solution_title: Draper Satellite Image Chronology: Pure ML Solution | Vicens Gaitan
solution_summary: The pipeline registered satellite images using matched local keypoints and trained XGBoost to predict signed time differences between matching patches. Registration parameters and matching quality supplied additional features, while connected image sets were kept together in cross-validation. Image ordering came from averaging patch predictions and iteratively incorporating evidence from overlapping sets. Local validation scored 0.83 ± 0.05, while public and private scores were 0.76786 and 0.69209; tuning aggregation parameters on public feedback caused some overfitting.

solution_title: Source Code for Bryan Gregory & Miroslaw Horbal
solution_summary: This post announces the release of the team's competition code under the BSD-3 OSI license. It lists repositories for the ensemble and individual models. It also links to documents describing the code and contest approach, without presenting the solution details in the post itself.

The solution enriched tabular inputs with target statistics from the original Heart Disease dataset, periodic and interaction features, and fold-aware encodings. Diverse boosted trees and tabular neural networks were trained with ten-fold stratified validation, with RealMLP providing the strongest individual models. Confident test predictions supplied hard pseudo-labels for teacher-student variants, and ridge models stacked out-of-fold predictions. Hill-climbing blending achieved an OOF ROC-AUC of 0.955805; allowing negative weights slightly improved validation but produced the same private leaderboard score as positive-only blending.

The solution uses a six-member ONNX ensemble for multilabel bioacoustic identification and achieves a private macro-AUC of 0.92041. Shared log-mel inputs, GeM pooling, and an attention-based sound-event head support CNN backbones trained through supervised fine-tuning, Noisy Student self-training, and Perch v2 distillation. Soundscape adaptation and ensemble error diversity mattered more than increasing backbone size. BatchNorm recalibration, probability-space blending, and selective augmentation enabled complete CPU inference within the competition budget.

solution_title: 70th Place Solution — Replay BC and Teacher Selection
solution_summary: The final agent combined a 6.54-million-parameter recurrent entity Transformer with behavior cloning from public replays and a deterministic late-game overlay. Replay reconstruction, exact teacher-version tracking, and progressively selecting stronger teachers with compatible openings mattered more than demonstration volume. Shadow-state accounting maintained legal sequential actions, while greedy decoding avoided damaging sampled mistakes. Paired full-game evaluation supported the tomato and endgame overlay, and the final agent scored 4883.6 privately. PPO and self-play experiments were superseded by the behavior-cloning pipeline.

solution_summary: The solution converted engineered sensor time series into pseudo-images using transposed convolutions, then detected sleep events with Faster R-CNN. It used 79 engineered features plus an hour embedding and a pretrained ConvNeXt V2 backbone. A single model trained on all available data performed inference on overlapping windows, retaining their centers and converting detected boxes to event times. Reported five-fold CV was approximately 0.770, with public and private scores of 0.730 and 0.781.

The final solution averaged probabilities from EfficientNet B5 models at image sizes 512 and 331 and a B6 model at size 512, using noisy-student pretrained weights. External flower datasets helped, while Open Images and iNaturalist reduced accuracy and were removed. The author selected configurations through manual experiments using the validation folder and public leaderboard, then retrained with the validation data and selected models with the lowest training loss. Training used mixed precision, large batches, warmup with exponential learning-rate decay, and only random horizontal flips. The author disclosed that the external datasets had recently been banned, making prize eligibility uncertain.

solution_title: 131st place: an LLM harness that refuses to lie to you
solution_summary: The final pipeline stacked seven drift estimators with cross-fitted positive Ridge, blended in a particle-filter selector, and smoothed the resulting path. A trust-gated typewell correction was applied as a depth-dependent ramp rather than a constant offset. Virtual prediction-start resampling improved training diversity and reduced seed correlation. Strict well-level validation, rolled-null controls, and nested selection supported choosing the submission with 7.159 CV RMSE and 7.860 private RMSE.

The solution fine-tuned language models in two stages: multiple-choice discrimination using semantically similar negatives, followed by Yes/No violation classification with rule keyword signals. Validation excluded overlapping rule-comment pairs and used reliable examples after deduplication and conflict removal. Test-time training helped adapt to unseen rules, while rank normalization and weighted averaging combined architectures and random seeds. The two-stage ensemble achieved local ROC AUC of 0.7610, compared with 0.7515 for single-stage training.

solution_title: Main features of final solution [22 on public]
solution_summary: The approach used power-scaled spectrograms with varied mel-bin counts and hop lengths, including hop lengths adapted to audio duration. Noisy training files were selected according to current-model predictions, prioritizing classes rarely predicted on validation. Training used mixup and validation-derived class weights in binary cross-entropy. The final ensemble combined seven relatively uncorrelated models, with seed runs selected separately for each fold.

solution_title: Secondary labels are effective for bronze medal (76th solution)
solution_summary: The team built on a public bird-identifier training notebook and added secondary-label information. Training targets were 0.995 for primary labels, 0.5 for secondary labels, and 0.0025 for other classes. They selected the prediction threshold using training soundscapes. Noise augmentation, mixup, and test-time augmentation did not help; the reported private and public scores were 0.6109 and 0.6861.

solution_title: 2nd place solution (matching prediction by GAT & LGB)
solution_summary: The pipeline learned image, text, and multimodal embeddings, then classified candidate item pairs using LightGBM and graph attention models. CurricularFace, SAM, graph statistics, query expansion, and label-group sample weighting strengthened the models. Predictions were combined after subtracting locally optimized thresholds, with mutual-edge filtering and graph-based pruning refining matches. Combining the teammates' models produced a large initial gain, and the reported score timeline reached 0.792.

solution_summary: The solution used imitation learning from other players' episodes. The bidding model learned from ry_andy_'s episodes. Factory placement and unit and factory actions learned from flg's episodes.

The solution combined lip-r50 and SE-ResNeXt101 classifiers trained with cosine decay, label smoothing, mixup, and cross-entropy. SE-ResNeXt101 initially used smaller images before fine-tuning at 448 pixels, and inference used 576-pixel images with ten-crop augmentation. The final blend weighted SE-ResNeXt101 at 0.6 and lip-r50 at 0.4. A confidence-based rescoring procedure enforced the test-set limit of ten samples per category.

The author built a neural network with parallel branches using different activation functions to explore feature interactions. Shared layers used Swish, while individual branches used Swish, SELU, and ReLU. The best single model scored 0.99822 privately, and an equal-weight blend with a public notebook submission improved this to 0.99825.

The team trained two custom convolutional networks with eye cropping, channel standardization, and extensive geometric and color augmentation. Training progressed from smaller images to larger networks, with patient-level validation and gradually reduced class balancing. Features aggregated over 50 augmentations were combined across both eyes and passed to small blending networks. The final submission averaged six blend outputs and applied fixed thresholds; validation-optimized thresholds and training large networks from scratch were not retained.

solution_title: 18th place solution: Sound Event Detection (SED) with attention

Parallel attention blocks produced clipwise and framewise predictions, supported by max and average pooling. Label smoothing, lower targets for background species, and a two-way focal loss addressed overlapping calls and class imbalance. Validation used stratified folds with exceptionally rare species retained in training; no numerical competition result was reported.

The author used unsupervised graph methods, primarily clique percolation, to identify social circles. For large or dense graphs, iteratively removing the lowest-ranked node until clique percolation became feasible produced the best training and public scores. Partitioning large graphs performed poorly because dense graphs resisted useful splits and circles could cross partition boundaries. Small graphs were partitioned directly into circles, while feature-based clustering remained an untested idea.

solution_summary: The final approach jointly trained a U-Net to predict a class-agnostic Gaussian heatmap and a six-class segmentation mask. solution_summary: The solution models the geological surface as TVT plus Z and decodes piecewise linear paths with an explicit-duration hidden semi-Markov model. Robust gamma matching, slope regularization, heel-calibrated references, and trajectory-based drift constraints reduce ambiguous marker alignment. Neighbor agreement gates specialist rescues, while diverse decodes and bounded corrections improve robustness. The reported leak-free evaluation reduced pooled RMSE from 10.66 to 7.30 ft across 773 wells, with a public score of 5.21 ft.

solution_title: 88th solution with Topology-Preserving 3D U-Net  and 5-Loss Stack  HybridCon
solution_summary: The solution uses a custom 3D U-Net with anisotropic convolutions, multiscale residual blocks, attention, and full-resolution edge refinement. solution_title: A List of Counter Features and Their Strengths
solution_summary: The author explored many grouped feature combinations and evaluated both overall predictive strength and accuracy on the rows each feature covered. Grouping by month, destination distance, and destination ID achieved a validation score of 0.9044 on covered rows, but coverage was limited and the feature was omitted from the final submission. The strongest reported non-leaky grouping combined hotel country, hotel market, and destination ID, scoring 0.3131 on covered rows and 0.3106 overall. PCA data from the destinations file yielded slightly stronger features, while weak individual features were progressively removed to control the number of combinations.

solution_title: Quick Silver - The Late Joiners' Journey
solution_summary: The solution used small ResNet and EfficientNet encoders with FPN decoders, combined segmentation losses, strong geometric augmentation, and validation-selected thresholds. Models used cosine annealing and the Over9000 optimizer, with different single-fold splits to improve ensemble diversity. Two final ensembles contained either 10 ordinary models or those models plus five trained with ensemble-relabeled training data and hard test pseudo labels, all with eight-way TTA. solution_title: Post-mortem: a sparse, dim private embryo — late ladders on the 1st/4th-place pipelines and what the LB could tell us

solution_summary: The described pipeline combines tabular tracking and helmet features, pretrained player detection and pose features, and 2.5D CNN predictions in XGBoost. Separate CNN inputs and backbones handle player–player and player–ground contacts, with simple averaging across backbones. Geometric features include tracked player boxes, pose measurements, field-to-camera projection errors, and temporal lags. The author reshaped seismic channels into a single image and used a pretrained small vision transformer with rotary positional embeddings for velocity regression. Training combined MAE, progressive image-size increases, synthetic forward-modeled data, and iterative pseudo-labeling using validation and test predictions. A specialized model focused on four difficult data-generation methods, with its predictions replacing the corresponding outputs of the general model. The final ensemble achieved 7.28 CV and 6.9 on both public and private leaderboards, with the full process taking about 15 days on four RTX 5090 GPUs.

solution_summary: The author compared regular-expression extraction with BERT named-entity recognition without dataset-label string matching. The stronger regular-expression approach found capitalized patterns and reused discovered names across documents, reporting scores of 0.5/0.56 versus 0.37/0.52 for BERT NER. The BERT pipeline used short text segments, candidate selection, and three token classes marking dataset-name boundaries. Ensembling and searching known datasets did not improve results.

The solution used pretrained VGG16 and a three-input variant that processed the full image alongside manually selected head and right-hand regions. The modified network reduced overfitting and improved the single-model score by about 0.05. Predictions were smoothed using ten nearest neighbors in pretrained VGG16 pool5 feature space, yielding reported improvements of 0.10–0.12. Category-specific model averaging and confidence-based sharing of predictions within similar test-image groups further exploited correlations between video frames.

The team iteratively improved family assignments using chain-based local search, mixed-integer large neighborhood search, and increasingly exact optimization models. Restricting family choices and occupancy gaps reduced model size, while good incumbent solutions supplied warm starts. An exact three-million-variable formulation, combined with selected days fixed at occupancy 125, found an optimal solution overnight. The full CPLEX model subsequently proved optimality in less than three hours using that solution as its starting point.

solution_summary: The solution combined 50k and FGVC9 data, removed conflicting duplicates, and corrected image orientation. Training masks followed test-set mask statistics, while sub-center ArcFace with dynamic margins handled diverse appearances within each hotel. Models first trained on all categories and then fine-tuned on the 3,116 FGVC9 categories, improving performance by about 0.03. Logits were used for prediction, and the ensemble achieved public and private scores of 0.732 and 0.717.

The author reports an AutoML experiment using their own features that scored 0.563. This model was omitted from the final three submissions. The post links a notebook but provides no feature definitions, validation setup, or model configuration.

The final approach used random forest posterior probabilities as purely supervised features, with feature selection and training restricted to labeled data. Inputs combined features selected by nonzero counts and differences between class means, plus the sum of all features for each example. Five submissions supplied the final features, varying the selected feature count from roughly 600 to 1,400 and using slightly different random forest parameters. This approach outperformed the explored unsupervised and semi-supervised alternatives and achieved a private AUC of 0.9771.

solution_title: 26th solution - 1D Unet with 1D CNN, Hybrid CNN-Transformer and WBF
solution_summary: The solution used 1D U-Nets with CNN or hybrid CNN–Transformer encoders to predict event heatmaps, event offsets, and auxiliary sleep segmentation masks. Two- or four-day input windows provided context, while border regions were excluded from the loss. Heatmap width tuning, auxiliary segmentation, and model EMA were important improvements. Point-based NMS followed by weighted fusion combined model outputs, improving two-model OOF AP from 77.0 to 78.3.

The post sketches training on T and NK cell measurements and adapting the model to Myeloid and B cells through transfer learning. Its illustrative implementation uses a 100-tree random forest to predict one gene's expression from compound and cell information. It shows a random holdout evaluation with mean squared error, but reports no numerical results. Molecular fingerprint construction is suggested without an implementation.

solution_title: Potential #5 solution, but I didn't choose it
solution_summary: The author combined manual preprocessing and feature engineering with AutoGluon tabular modeling. Visible features include indicators for premium models and brands, plus a numeric value extracted from text. This was the author's best private leaderboard solution, although it was not selected for the final submission.

The pipeline identified vertebra numbers with EfficientNetV2-S, localized vertebrae with YOLOv5s, and classified fractures in cropped slices. A clean-label initial classifier generated constrained pseudo-labels, improving both public and private scores by 0.03. A GRU then combined slice embeddings, vertebra probabilities, and fracture logits to predict fractures per vertebra. The final solution ensembled five sequence models and computed the patient probability as one minus the product of vertebra-level non-fracture probabilities. Submission inference took four hours, with shared image loading reducing DICOM I/O overhead.

solution_title: 10th place Solution : Single model public lb 0.8562, private lb 0.8717

The solution used separate pipelines for DOI citations and accession IDs, with Qwen2.5 32B processing candidates from external citation sources. Filtering unsupported identifiers, duplicates, low-confidence predictions, and figshare/hepdata citations improved the merged output. Several alternatives failed, including classifier fine-tuning, regex-only extraction, and other Qwen sizes.

solution_summary: The best final submission used separate linear forecasting models for each horizon, optimized directly for SMAPE without regularization. Counties with month-to-month changes exceeding 25% received last-value forecasts, while ETS forecasts supplied features for the remaining modeling pipeline. Moving-average terms appeared most influential, and validation used the last six months. MARS looked promising in CV but underperformed linear models on the private evaluation, where the reported score was 3.9884.

The solution extended a public graph-convolutional autoencoder model with two recurrent layers and MAE reconstruction loss. Four GRU/LSTM layer combinations were trained with 10-fold CV and uniformly blended, with older models and public notebooks providing a tiny additional gain. RNA-specific edge and node features, augmented samples, and signal-to-noise sample weighting were central to the approach. The main blend scored 0.34388 privately, while the expanded blend reached 0.34385.

The team retrieved context with TF-IDF and combined six DeBERTa models trained on differently sized subsets of a shared 60,000-question dataset. DeBERTa outperformed the other models in their initial experiments without context. Several prompts improved results, while subtracting predictions for wrong answers underperformed expectations. An attempted Shepherd critic failed to produce meaningful results because training resources were insufficient.

The final forecast combined LightGBM, a causal-convolution CNN plus dense network, and a GRU encoder-decoder through weighted averaging. Each model was stabilized by averaging runs with different random seeds. Sales aggregates, historical sales sequences, categorical embeddings, and future promotions supplied complementary information, with a fixed chronological validation period. The author also blended models trained with and without promotion information to compensate for suspected promotion bias, but reported that this adjustment did not help the private score.

solution_title: Implementing a critic free RL in adversarial games from scratch
solution_summary: The author first built a simulation and linear optimization agent, then trained a small transformer to imitate strong replay policies. The policy used simulated planet states, distance features, symmetry augmentation, and eight-view inference averaging. Distributed GRPO training subsequently improved the imitation policy after correcting tie rewards and the composition of four-player training games. The final submissions were the supervised policy and a GRPO checkpoint with a reported +0.14 reward against the frozen supervised policy.

solution_title: 5th place - Dual GRU ensemble using geometry files
solution_summary: The solution combined five recurrent networks, each using two parallel GRU branches followed by temporal averaging and a three-layer MLP. Atomic elements were one-hot encoded alongside coordinates, with lattice vectors prepended and inputs zero padded. Rotating atomic coordinates through seven equidistant angles improved cross-validation and leaderboard scores by about 0.01. Networks used MSE, Adam, and gradient clipping, and a linear regression model weighted their final predictions.

solution_title: Hints on 13th place solution.. and finally Grandmaster!

Product image counts and image indices improved accuracy, and the strongest contributor pooled features across a product's images. solution_title: How I did it: The top three from the 2010 INFORMS Data Mining Contest
solution_summary: This report collects three competitors' approaches rather than presenting the post author's own solution. Cole Harris used price-only inputs, appended time-advanced price features, and selected a small feature set before fitting logistic regression and neural networks. Christopher Hefele moved from single-variable logistic regression to an SVM with additional variables selected through stepwise logistic regression. Nan Zhou used two-stage L1-penalized logistic regression with its penalty tuned by five-fold cross-validation.

The pipeline combined four Qwen2.5-14B retrievers by weighted sum to retrieve 40 misconceptions, then used a Qwen2.5-32B reranker to return 25. Synthetic examples, iterative hard negative mining, and LoRA fine-tuning were central to training. The reranker used Wise-FT adapter merging, AWQ quantization, and vLLM inference with prefix caching. Reported public leaderboard improvements progressed from roughly 0.3 for a retriever to 0.59 after the full set of enhancements, with total running time around six hours.

solution_title: 3rd solution - BERT in chemistry - End to End  is all you need
solution_summary: The team replaced distance-based graph models with a BERT-style transformer operating on embedded molecular coordinates and atom-pair properties. Their main architecture used eight encoder layers, eight attention heads, and separate regression readouts for coupling types. Rotation and translation augmentation, auxiliary prediction of coupling contributions, and linear learning-rate decay supported training. Repeated pseudo-labeling followed by further training on original training data produced eight models whose simple average achieved a final score of -3.19.
