solution_summary: The solution used 2.5D U-Net models that predicted masks for stacks of five or seven consecutive slices. Whole-kidney intensity normalization, kidney-region cropping, and careful high-resolution resizing were central to accuracy. Inference combined three anatomical views, larger inputs than those used in training, and an equal-weight ensemble of three backbones. The ensemble achieved CV 0.913 and private score 0.645, although the strongest individual model had a higher private score.

The solution ensembled OneFormer, EfficientNet, MaxViT, ResNet-RS, and NFNet models trained with binary cross-entropy. Training used averaged annotator labels and, for some models, pseudo labels across multiple time frames. Optuna optimized ensemble weights within cross-validation, while augmentation was limited to random image cropping and inference used no test-time augmentation or mask shift. OneFormer was the strongest individual model, achieving a private leaderboard score of 0.70204; pseudo labels improved EfficientNet more than OneFormer.

solution_title: 86th Place Solution for the NFL Big Data Bowl 2026 - Prediction Competition

Extensive motion, ball-relative, spatial, and temporal features supported the models, but architecture and error diversity mattered more than additional neural-network features. The solution treated toxicity severity as a ranking problem and blended seven transformer models with two LightGBM rankers trained on transformer embeddings. RoBERTa, DeBERTa, and ELECTRA used pointwise and listwise objectives, with an additional RoBERTa model using pairwise logistic loss; listwise training performed best. solution_summary: The final model used Ridge regression with a log-transformed target and carefully engineered seasonal and holiday features. Validation grouped observations by year and prioritized April through December because the public leaderboard did not evaluate the important holidays. Residual analysis guided Fourier coefficient selection, country-specific holiday durations, and the addition of OECD consumer confidence data. The solution combined channel-wise grouped convolutions with cross-channel squeeze-and-excitation blocks, a 3D CNN for ToF sensors, and BiGRU attention pooling. Sensor handedness and mounting corrections, rotation augmentation, and rotation-based test-time averaging addressed orientation variation. Multitask gesture, orientation, and behavior losses used soft labels and label smoothing. The final ensemble mixed roughly four to five model variants, including FFT-feature and simple CNN variants; rotation TTA improved scores by approximately 0.002.

The solution used a public first-stage model with relaxed thresholds to propose 32×32×32 regions for reclassification. Each volume crop was flattened into a three-channel image and classified using an ensemble of seven backbones with three test-time augmentations. Synthetic pretraining helped stabilize fine-tuning, and agreement rules combined the classifiers with U-Net and YOLO predictions. The approach improved the underlying first stage by 0.025, but proposal quality limited its overall effectiveness.

The team combined a relatively strong XGBoost model with two financial heuristics. Engineered features included first and second differences, interactions, and cross-sectionally normalized inputs, with features selected after exploring validation scenarios. solution_summary: The solution forecast log-transformed page views using a mixture of constant medians, nearest-neighbor polynomial autoregression, and a yearly-pattern regression model. Mixing weights depended on traffic volume and yearly-pattern strength, and a separate weekday-median component supplied weekly seasonality. Training examples used random temporal cutoffs, with 10-fold cross-validation, line-search tuning, and a ten-model ensemble varying those cutoffs. Predictions were transformed back to page-view counts and rounded; tuning improved SMAPE by 0.5 points, while neural-network mixing did not improve scores.

The approach extracted co-attention scores from pretrained BERT after preprocessing names and locating mentions closer to the pronoun. It selected attention features starting at layer 9 and used maximum attention when an entity spanned multiple tokens. A small neural network and a tuned LightGBM model were trained with stratified ten-fold validation and blended across folds. The author reported that name-replacement test-time augmentation was accidentally omitted from the final predictions.

The team addressed distribution shift by manually merging feature values with differing train and test frequencies and blending models built on three differently processed datasets. They combined LightGBM with embedding-based Keras networks and checked features against several validation schemes. A version-gap feature relating antivirus signature versions to engine versions improved the private score by 0.02. Feeding LightGBM predictions into a Keras model produced the author's best individual private result, while the final blend diversified preprocessing and validation choices.

solution_summary: The approach divided whole slide images into thousands of patches, extracted patch features, and trained multiple instance learning models. Two pretrained DINO vision transformers supplied the features, with ABMIL, DSMIL, and TransMIL used for slide classification. Two labeled external datasets were also used, but the authors reported no significant benefit from additional external data and the Other class.

The post reports a final MSE/Brier score of 0.1225209. Its approach outline names ensembling and seed matchup adjustments. The supplied text provides no implementation details, model specifications, or explanation of unsuccessful experiments.

The strongest clean result came from a five-seed logistic-regression blend using photometric-redshift, sky-context, and light target-encoding features. The author also explored TabPFN probability blending, a 43-model logistic stacker, residual classification, and targeted row edits. Final selection favored an aggressive public-feedback candidate that achieved 0.97260 public but only 0.97001 private, compared with 0.97021 private for the clean blend. The writeup attributes the deterioration primarily to submission selection and overfitting public feedback.

The author describes the feature engineering component of the team's credit default solution. Current application features included simple differences and ratios, while historical tables supplied aggregate features over all available history and one-, two-, and three-year windows. Previous application and bureau records also contributed first and last application features. The text does not explain model training or report numerical performance.

The final approach extended a public 2.5D segmentation baseline with large backbones and eight input slices starting at slice 28. Depth-scanning experiments guided slice selection, and both U-Net and Linknet architectures were explored. Validation on fragments 1 and 3 guided ensemble selection and percentile thresholds, typically around 94%. An ensemble of six MaxViT models performed best locally and on both leaderboards, while a custom fastai pipeline failed to match the baseline variants.

The submitted performance ensemble combined 44 DeBERTa-v3-large models trained with a maximum sequence length of 512 and varying frozen layers. Instead of including the full prompt text, the author marked summary spans matching prompt n-grams of at least three words, then supplied the marked summary, question, and title. Separate-target and joint-target models contributed diversity, producing ensemble CV of 0.4659 and a private score of 0.465. A late LightGBM residual correction centered residuals within folds and added length and hidden-state correlation features, improving CV to 0.4643 but finishing after the submission deadline.

The solution estimated each planet’s mean_s with the baseline notebook, then trained multiple deep learning models to predict wavelength residuals relative to that baseline. Inputs were transformed using mean_s, smoothed across neighboring values, and augmented with random noise and time-axis flips. Simple BiLSTM and CNN models worked well, with validation split into two groups based on star information. Final uncertainty estimates used the standard deviation across model predictions with scale adjustment, although generalization of sigma to unseen data remained difficult.

The solution joined artist-user features from words.csv with user features from users.csv. It added rating means, maxima, minima, and medians for artist-user pairs and for artists and users separately. Each entry's own rating was excluded from its aggregate features. An R gbm gradient boosting model used these features with manually tuned parameters.

The solution blended a tree ensemble predicting TVT offsets with a CNN predicting local slopes integrated from the last known TVT. A LightGBM model then corrected systematic residual shifts over 600-foot segments. Non-learned geological estimators and neighboring-well information supplied the main features. Five-fold well-level validation included difficulty-specific RMSE checks, and the full pipeline achieved 6.32 CV RMSE and 6.376 private RMSE.

solution_summary: The solution exploited angle-dependent class patterns through sample counts and target statistics, encoded as constant image channels in a small CNN. It aggregated the best 100 validation models from 200 random-seed runs using the median. A second ensemble omitted angle features and used confident test pseudo-labels with rotation augmentation. The submitted blend averaged the two ensembles where the first was uncertain, scoring 0.0940 publicly and 0.0910 privately; a rejected alternative later achieved 0.0873 privately.

solution_summary: The solution combined a user-product pair model with a separate model for predicting no reordered products. Features described users, products, orders, aisles, departments and their interactions. The author expanded training data with the last prior order and blended four predictions, including baseline outputs and models trained with different splits. Final baskets were selected using Faron's F1 optimizer together with the none model.

The final solution used hill climbing to combine diverse tabular and survival models with rank-transformed predictions and signed weights. Models used several survival-target constructions, including Kaplan–Meier, Nelson–Aalen, Breslow–Fleming–Harrington, and Cox-based targets, with classification masks and shifts in selected experiments. Validation used 10 random folds after five race-stratified folds proved unhelpful. The strongest initial model was a pairwise ranking network, while CatBoost and XGBoost received prominent ensemble weights. The final ensemble scored 0.688 CV, 0.693 public, and 0.694 private.

The solution combined a modified public regression notebook with the author's own feature-based regression pipeline. The custom pipeline used essay statistics, count and TF-IDF features, and embeddings from three transformer models, with LGBMRegressor trained using a QWK objective and five-fold validation. The final ensemble assigned 90% weight to the public notebook and 10% to the custom pipeline, guided mainly by local cross-validation scores. Predictions were clipped and converted to integers without custom threshold optimization to limit overfitting.

solution_title: 57th place solution: Conv1d model with aux head
solution_summary: The solution trained a compact Conv1D network with a multilabel gait-event head and an auxiliary binary event head. Accelerometer signals were smoothed, time was discretized, and training used centered windows of 256 timesteps with subject-grouped validation. Larger inference windows improved performance, and the final submission combined five-fold predictions at window sizes 1024 and 1224. That submission scored 0.37 publicly and 0.303 privately, while a tested three-window ensemble achieved 0.311 privately.

solution_title: 685th Place Solution for the Child Mind Institute - Detect Sleep States Competition

solution_summary: This post describes the trip-matching component of a broader driver classifier. Trips were simplified with Ramer–Douglas–Peucker, represented by distances between turns and unsigned turn angles, and compared in both directions. SVD alignment and sub-trip alignment error provided the strongest match scoring, and match counts became classifier features. Dynamic time warping and network-based features offered little improvement, while distributed EC2 computation enabled faster iteration and helped push the reported score above 97%.

solution_summary: The solution retrieved 25 misconception candidates and reranked them with an instruction-tuned Qwen model. Retriever training progressed from pretrained embeddings through Qwen models using contrastive learning and randomly sampled hard negatives. GPT-4o generated additional questions for unseen or rare misconceptions, while reranker training varied the number of candidate options. Predictions from two pipelines were merged by averaging scores for overlapping IDs and retaining unique candidates, improving the score by about 0.02 and yielding 0.553 private and 0.617 public.

The pipeline routes images between separate seen-grapheme and unseen-grapheme models using ArcFace. The seen model uses little augmentation and decomposes its grapheme prediction into three components, while the unseen model uses heavy augmentation and predicts components directly. A minimal pair of EfficientNet-B1 models trained at 128×128 achieved over 0.935 private leaderboard score. Larger EfficientNet backbones, higher resolution, longer training, and more model pairs were described as the route to scores above 0.950.

solution_summary: The solution fitted a projection pursuit regression baseline to log-transformed sales for each item-store pair, then modeled residuals with a lasso linear model in Vowpal Wabbit. Calendar indicators and interactions captured weekday effects, monthly patterns, and Black Friday fluctuations. Predictions were converted back to sales and forced to zero under several historical zero-sales rules. Successive-zero handling provided a small final improvement, while weather features contributed little.

The solution combined ResNeSt50-fast-4s2x40d and EfficientNet models trained with different recipes, selecting two ensembles using CV and public leaderboard scores. Label smoothing, external 2019 data, and test-time augmentation helped, while pseudo-labeling improved CV without improving the reported private score for the compared model. solution_summary: The author used a teammate's candidate set and concentrated on improving item-to-item collaborative filtering features. Counts, time differences, sequence differences, weighted variants, and aggregations produced hundreds of final features. XGBoost and CatBoost formed the modeling stage, with first-stage prediction and pseudo-event features also included. The team initialized tours with LKH and refined them using a custom Rust implementation of Lin–Kernighan search. Nonsequential moves, especially 4-opt, gradual penalty increases and penalty-aware merging of tours were central to improvement. They used random kicks and regional penalty perturbations to escape local optima, distributing search across many cores. A 72-core machine could produce a score in the 15141xy range in a day, while the best kernel scored 1514637 with substantial run-to-run variation.

solution_summary: The solution compares observed horizontal gamma-ray slices with candidate trajectories and uses constrained beam search to recover TVT paths. Candidate scores come from physical similarity measures and lightweight dilated 1D CNNs, with predictions combined across architectures and slice lengths. The final ensemble contains two heuristic models and multiple CNN groups, with inference taking about eight GPU hours. The best reported single CNN achieved 8.2 ft private RMSE, and the author's best private submission omitted the neighboring-well constraint.

solution_summary: The solution combined extensive feature engineering with a diverse ensemble of tree models and neural networks. A LightGBM meta-model stacked first-level predictions, and blending with an earlier submission improved the score by 0.02. Separate galactic and extragalactic LightGBM models used importance-selected features, with microlensing and astrophysics-inspired features particularly valuable. Observation subsampling improved neural-network validation, while pseudo-labeling and modeling hostgal_specz did not work.

The solution addressed severe label imbalance with weighted sampling and binary cross-entropy that emphasized positive labels. At prediction time, it used softmax outputs with a fixed 0.04 threshold across classes to improve generalization under label distribution shifts. Training batches were normalized using statistics calculated from the full training data. The final ensemble contained two models trained from scratch, each taking around two weeks on one P100 GPU.

solution_title: [16th place] A pure self-play reinforcement learning approach to the Santa 2020 challenge
solution_summary: The team trained deep reinforcement learning agents using a GPU-parallel game environment that greatly increased simulation throughput. Their strongest agent used per-bandit event histories and a set-based residual network that combined each bandit's features with the mean features of other bandits. Training used a dense zero-sum reward based on the difference in expected pull rewards, with A2C and AWAC giving the best results. Self-play produced continuing improvements, but internal match results did not reliably predict performance against the broader field.

The dual-head architecture jointly learned cell and image predictions, while the other pipelines averaged predictions across multiple models and inference views. External HPA data, extensive augmentation, and refined cell segmentation supported the approach. The dual-head ensemble alone scored 0.550 on both public and private leaderboards; an antibody ArcFace approach helped publicly but did not transfer well privately.

solution_summary: The agent extended an existing deterministic football script through rules refined by watching replays. Defensive changes restricted blind clearances, improved evasion and tackle timing, and made the last defender track the leading attacker against overhead balls. Offensive changes anticipated first contact to issue repeated quick passes or shots and ignored defenders sufficiently far behind during dribbling. The dribbling adjustment helped substantially, while game randomness and slowly converging leaderboard scores made parameter tuning difficult.

This post describes four waveform augmentations rather than a complete detection pipeline. Zebra mixup interleaved alternating samples from two waveforms and reportedly improved the score by 0.001. Other successful augmentations reversed negative waveforms, replaced individual channels with channels from other negative examples, and swapped the two LIGO channels.

The solution combined five-fold EfficientDet D2 models trained at 1024×1024 with five-fold D4 models trained at 512×512. Heavy augmentation, five-way test-time augmentation, and weighted boxes fusion formed the ensemble pipeline. One round of pseudo-labeling trained for one epoch with training data and doubled pseudo-labeled test data, improving the private score from 0.6956 to 0.7050. Bounding-box cleaning, gradient accumulation, CutMix, Mixup, and several threshold or loss adjustments did not help.

The pipeline used a bi-encoder retriever followed by a multi-option LLM reranker. Retrieval benefited from generated explanations of incorrect answers, filling missing misconceptions, and removing unseen training examples. Both models were adapted with LoRA, and reranker training used out-of-fold retrieval candidates with single-token answer labels. Two overlapping candidate windows were reranked and merged, with the complete pipeline taking 210 minutes.

solution_summary: The pipeline replaced baseline helmet detections with a trained YOLOv5 model and linked detections into tracks for player assignment. A two-head ResNet34 jersey reader supplied high-precision corrections to the geometric mapping. Cluster-level confidence aggregation and framewise linear regression completed the helmet-to-player assignments. A custom tracker performed worse publicly but produced the team's best private submission.

solution_summary: The team modeled 19 product targets with separate models trained on June 2015 and May 2016 data to capture seasonality and recent trends. Features included historical target averages, prior product ownership counts and patterns, encoded raw attributes, and new-product flags. Product-specific ensemble weights were the key improvement, raising the reported score from 0.0303 to 0.0306. Ten-fold cross-validation tracked leaderboard performance, while bagging and parameter tuning offered no improvement; a shared script scored approximately 0.03102 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: 2nd Place and 2nd Place Solution to Kaggle Landmark Recognition and Retrieval Competition 2019
solution_summary: The post announces that the team's solution has been released on arXiv. It links to the paper and a GitHub source-code location. It also thanks the organizers and indicates plans to open the source code, without describing methods or results.

The team built around 100 models, dominated by LightGBM and XGBoost, and organized them into two ensembles using different cross-validation schemes. Categorical dummy variables worked well, while neural networks used scaled and log-transformed numerical inputs and simplified genetic-programming features. A simple neural stacking model improved on a linear blender by about 0.001, and the two ensembles were combined through rank averaging. Extensive validation experiments produced limited private-leaderboard gains, and the authors felt broader model exploration would have been more valuable.

The solution uses a single AWQ four-bit DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B model with vLLM and FlashInfer. Generation uses one prompt without a system message and allocates tokens and sequences equally across problems. Repeated local validation on 50 handpicked math problems guided configuration choices, with throughput favored over public leaderboard tuning. The reported scores were 25/50 public and 29/50 private.

The solution removed the known trajectory contribution from TVT and anchored predictions at the end of each well's known section. A convex blend of sequence and row-wise models supplied the baseline, with a small correction based on nearby wells' geological changes relative to their anchors. Reference wells from the evaluated fold were excluded, and corrections were restricted by proximity to both the query and anchor. Selection emphasized well-level OOF results, spatial robustness, shuffled-information controls, and private-test compatibility. The final correction reduced OOF RMSE from 9.9775 to 9.7080 and achieved a private score of 8.861.

The final ensemble combined nine submodels from NetVLAD, Deep Bag of Frames, Fisher Vector, and recurrent network families. Multilayer knowledge distillation and partial 8-bit weight quantization helped fit strong models within the size constraint. Weight averaging improved smaller models, while inference sampling ensured every frame was represented. A held-out subset guided model selection and random-search optimization of ensemble weights.
compute: Single GPU per model; 1.5–3.5 days per model; approximately 60 GPU-days for all models.

solution_summary: The solution averaged eight diverse audio classifiers trained on standardized mel spectrograms with extensive augmentation. Manually completing and checking recording labels was central, supplemented by hand-labeled external frog recordings and some pseudolabels. Training used five-second samples, recording-level multilabel folds, and different losses for confidently complete versus incomplete labels. Overlapping-window maximum predictions and a species-specific threshold completed inference; the author's best single model scored 0.970 publicly.
external_data: ["Dryad frog recordings, DOI 10.5061/dryad.c0g2t, manually labeled", "Freesound50k", "Cornell Competition species recordings, rejected distractor augmentation"]

solution_summary: The team combined complementary sensor models using an equal-weight ensemble, later replacing probabilities with class ranks before averaging. Both approaches emphasized separate sensor or feature branches, with shallow convolutions and recurrent extractors limiting overfitting. Handcrafted IMU features, mixup, and sensor or channel dropout were important components. Postprocessing improved predictions by enforcing at most two gestures per subject orientation and suppressing unseen orientation–gesture combinations.

solution_title: 4th place sharing and tips about having a good teamwork experience
solution_summary: The team built trend features and trained more than 200 diverse models on feature subsets and the combined feature set. Predictions saved during Bayesian parameter optimization also supplied out-of-fold inputs for stacking. Selecting stacking features before fitting LightGBM improved CV by about 0.0005. A final manual correction adjusted high predictions for revolving loans; stacking achieved CV 0.8055 and private leaderboard score 0.804.

The solution adapted a public DeBERTa-v3-large and LightGBM baseline notebook. The author increased the number of folds from five to six and changed the reported cross-validation splits from 15 to 18. These small changes formed the reported solution, with no additional modeling details or scores provided.

The solution classified cell type before applying specialized instance segmentation models and post-processing for each type. LIVE_CELL pretraining and pseudo labels from semi-supervised images supported staged training with cell-specific data. It combined two-stage detectors for cort cells and merged semantically reranked masks for shsy5y cells, while using one astro model. Classwise filtering, overlap removal, and astro contour reconstruction refined the final masks.

solution_title: 119th Place Solution: Transformer is much much better than GRU!
solution_summary: The author trained landmark-based GRU, bidirectional GRU, and Transformer models with Conv1D components on preprocessed data without normalization. Validation used participant-based splits, and training ran for 100 epochs with Adam and plateau-based learning-rate reduction. The selected submission ensembled the three model types and achieved a private score of 0.82339, while an unselected Transformer scored 0.82484. FP16 TFLite quantization reduced model sizes by about half, and positional embeddings and recurrent attention masks caused overfitting.

solution_title: 18 place write up  (short meditation on results)
solution_summary: The team used a ResNet-101 Mask R-CNN at 1024×1024 resolution and combined predictions from multiple snapshots, retaining the most confident overlapping detections. Image classifiers filtered object predictions using optimized thresholds, while class-specific segmentation networks refined masks and provided the largest gains. Attribute classifiers used separate mask-crop and full-image inputs with outputs grouped by attribute co-occurrence, and their predictions were retained only with strong ensemble agreement and confidence. Attribute modeling improved the score by only about 0.005, which the authors considered a poor use of their limited resources.
compute: Two machines with 2×1080 Ti each and one machine with a GTX 1080; one fold of 1024×1024 ResNet-101 Mask R-CNN took 5 days.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled VoxNet and PointNet variants with XGBoost models using distance and position features. VoxNet processed voxelized atom counts, while PointNet consumed atom-level spatial and chemical descriptors; both incorporated organizer-provided features in their final dense layers. Evaluation used 24-fold cross-validation, and the selected ensemble achieved CV 0.0464 and private score 0.0573. A late PointNet++ addition slightly improved private performance but was not selected.

solution_title: Wow, Removing AdaptableSnail fps=25 Wins 2nd Place!
solution_summary: The author performed a postcompetition experiment removing all predictions for AdaptableSnail test videos recorded at 25 frames per second. This increased the private leaderboard score from 0.523 to 0.535. The post provides submission filtering code and attributes the improvement to reportedly incorrect evaluation targets. The adjustment was not applied to the author's final competition submission.

solution_title: 12 flags only - my solutions and approaches to some of the unsolved
solution_summary: The author solved several capture-the-flag tasks using model-output analysis, brute force, synonym search, and tailored prompts. For Cluster 1, filtering high-confidence false positives within the Tech-support occupation produced a successful subset. Language-model tasks were solved through contextual framing, indirect requests, follow-up questions, and searching responses for flag prefixes. Evolutionary word searches failed on Passphrase because the optimization target was wrong, and similar searches did not solve Semantle Level 2.

The solution first built a meta-model from 18 five-fold models spanning CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost, neural networks, and AutoGluon. AutoFeat and Optuna helped create diverse model conditions, followed by further feature exploration and a hill climbing ensemble that selected six additional models. The final CV score improved from 0.05893 to 0.05885. Public leaderboard results were ignored because of unstable CV correlations, and adding the original dataset to training was rejected after insufficient CV improvement.

The agent searched object names alphabetically early in the game and switched to frequency-based, Huffman-like questioning once the candidate set became small. Its responder used extensive regular-expression rules for spelling and membership questions, falling back to a Llama 3.1 model for other questions. Candidate objects came from caption datasets, Amazon reviews, and WordNet, with Gemini Flash filtering nouns. Guesses prioritized the remaining keyword with the highest word frequency.

solution_title: 12th place solution: UNet with mask scoring head
solution_summary: The solution combined segmentation at image size 896 with classification at size 768, removing masks with low probability. Segmentation used an EfficientNet-B4 U-Net with an auxiliary mask-quality scoring head and a combined segmentation and score-regression loss. Two SE-ResNeXt101 classifiers supplied embeddings, which were concatenated with DICOM metadata for an Optuna-tuned LightGBM classifier. Classification training incorporated CheXpert data after ambiguous labels were removed, and inference used horizontal-flip augmentation.

The team trained modified ResNets on standardized six-channel images with cropping, flips and right-angle rotations, limiting receptive fields to emphasize individual cells and nearby neighbors. ArcFace loss with tuned gamma and Adam with warmup and staged learning-rate reductions supported training, including positive and negative controls from test plates. Post-processing centered embeddings by plate, averaged sites and matched wells to training centers through cosine similarity and leak-constrained label assignment. Filtering out inconsistent test predictions before pseudo-label training improved the ensemble's private score from 0.9957 to 0.9967.

The final submission ensembled six token-classification models and one sequence-classification model using several DeBERTa variants. Successful methods included MLM pretraining, text encoding fixes, masking, adversarial training, recurrent layers, and pseudo-labeling. An LSTM second-stage stacker gave a substantial benefit, followed by a smaller improvement from an XGBoost third-stage stacker. The reported final losses were 0.5609 on CV, 0.555 on the public leaderboard, and 0.560 on the private leaderboard.

The team combined EfficientNet B0–B6, ResNeSt, and ResNeXt models trained at multiple image sizes and aspect ratios. Useful methods included heavy test-time augmentation, CutMix, coarse dropout, stochastic weight averaging, label smoothing, and checkpoint prediction averaging. Their submissions blended PyTorch models with context, TensorFlow models without context, and metadata-only predictions. The combined framework submission scored 0.9470 privately, while a more aggressively postprocessed blend overfit the public leaderboard.

solution_title: Solution for 21st place and a PyTorch kernel
solution_summary: The team skipped the competition training dataset and trained on segment-labeled validation data using temporal average pooling followed by an MLP with a 1,000-class softmax classifier. Hyperopt selected the network widths, and the hidden layers used batch normalization and Swish activations. Combining ten folds improved the public leaderboard score from 0.750 to 0.760, while blending four similar models reached the final score of 0.761. Converting labeled data to NumPy arrays accelerated training, and submission-generation optimizations reduced that step from five hours to five minutes.
compute: Training took less than one minute per epoch; the shared kernel achieved 0.753 public LB in less than one hour including submission generation. Submission generation was reduced from five hours to five minutes.

solution_title: 1790th Place Solution - code details, attempts and insights
solution_summary: The author trained LightGBM to classify awake, sleep, onset, and wakeup states using sensor measurements, a one-step angle lag, and cyclic hour features. Validation used a holdout of 56 series against 221 training series. The final submission extracted peaks from onset and wakeup scores and achieved an AP of 0.004. Adding an enmo lag reduced performance, while detecting valleys in awake and sleep scores produced a score of zero.

solution_title: 21st place - Pseudo Labels, Feature Engineering and stable validation scores
solution_summary: The final ensemble combined two Gemma2-9b-it models with a maximum input length of 4096, selected for complementary features, training data, and tie-versus-winner behavior. The largest improvement came from fold-aware pseudo-labeling and an equal mixture of original labels and soft predictions. One model received rounded text statistics appended to its input, and supplementary preference datasets improved stability. Dynamic padding and length-dependent batch sizes made inference fast enough to run both models, with dynamic batching adding about an 18% speedup.
compute: Full training experiments took about 20+ hours before results could be assessed.

solution_title: 14 th solution (that could have been 6 th )
solution_summary: The team used validation splits that train on three product groups and validate on the remaining two, covering all ten combinations. This addressed differences between training and test measurement modalities and helped avoid leaderboard overfitting. Their ensemble included TabNet, logistic regression, LightGBM, a neural network, XGBoost, CatBoost, and KNN, with TabNet reported as the best single model. After the competition, they discovered that CatBoost class predictions had been used instead of probabilities; correcting this improved the ensemble's private score from 0.59090 to 0.59110.

solution_title: 240 place with simple model, no kfold, no combining networks
solution_summary: The best solution was a single FPN with a pretrained SE-ResNeXt101 encoder, trained without folds or architecture ensembling. It used RAdam, BCE-Dice loss, batch size six, and gradient accumulation over two steps. Resizing and geometric augmentation were followed by class-specific probability thresholds and minimum mask sizes. The model achieved public and private scores of 0.65803 and 0.65038, respectively.

solution_title: [28th Place Solution] Pre Training on Supplemental Data gives 0.01 LB Improvement
solution_summary: The solution extended an open-source CTC pipeline with more model blocks, 256-frame inputs, and 128 selected landmark indices. Retaining frames unless all selected parts were missing and choosing extra face and pose landmarks by variance were important improvements. Training combined CTC with KL-based label smoothing and used supplemental-data pretraining before main-data training. Motion features and 120 main-data epochs brought the public score to 0.782.
compute: Training notebook designed for Google Colab; hardware and elapsed training time unspecified

solution_summary: The team ensembled six DeBERTa-large models and one DeBERTa-xlarge model by weighted token probabilities. Diversity came from tagging schemes, MLM pretraining, random masking, LSTM heads, learning rates, and multitask objectives. A LightGBM classifier filtered candidate discourse spans using token-probability aggregates and length features. Additional span rules completed postprocessing, with LightGBM filtering improving public/private scores from 0.716/0.724 to 0.719/0.727.

The solution averaged three pseudo-labeled LSTM position models, including building-specific modeling, and refined their predictions with dynamic programming. Its path-level objective balanced proximity to regression predictions, sensor-derived relative motion, and neighboring paths from the same device. Device metadata hashes linked paths, with path prefixes used when metadata was unavailable. The candidate grid was expanded with off-grid predictions and intermediate points before exact optimization.

The pipeline first extracted vascular regions with a fast tri-axial 2D nnU-Net, then classified uniformly resized volumes using a 3D nnU-Net with auxiliary vessel and aneurysm segmentation. Cross-attention pooling, modality supervision, improved annotations, and rare-class balancing supported stable learning across diverse scans. Left-right augmentation required corresponding label swaps, and eight-view test-time augmentation was combined with a two-fold ensemble. Encoder-only classification inference kept execution near nine hours on two T4 GPUs, with reported private performance around 0.8673.
compute: Two T4 GPUs; approximately 9 hours for final two-fold ensemble inference.
external_data: ["TopCoW Training Data and External Testsets, excluding LargeIA", "TopBrain annotations"]

solution_title: Public LB 10th Place - NN vs. GBM
solution_summary: The team developed neural-network and LightGBM models in parallel, with the neural network ultimately performing better. Their best neural network scored 0.01265 on the leaderboard, compared with 0.01297 for LightGBM, and runtime constraints prevented combining them. Geometric features, forward simulation of plays, label clipping, and a holdout containing each team's last three games helped both approaches. Bagging substantially improved the neural network, while several preprocessing and augmentation choices transferred poorly between model families.

solution_title: #9 Solution: model with only atom type and distance
solution_summary: The solution represented each molecule as a fully connected graph using only atom types and interatomic distances. A modified message-passing network predicted couplings from propagated atom states through separate output layers for the eight coupling types. Radial basis distance encoding and an edge update network with GRU updates produced substantial improvements. Hyperparameter tuning and an ensemble of ten differently initialized models brought the reported leaderboard score to about -2.98.

solution_title: Solutions of team "liveinparis" with codes (6th place)
solution_summary: The agent learned from scratch through PPO self-play against a growing pool of saved opponents. A hierarchical action space, situation-dependent action masks, and zero-sum reward shaping made exploration more efficient. Player representations used a 1D convolutional architecture selected through learning-curve comparisons. Synchronized distributed training maintained on-policy rollouts, and the final agent achieved a 92% win rate against the hard rule-based AI.
compute: 30 CPU cores (AMD Ryzen Threadripper 2950X), 1 RTX 2080 GPU, 370 hours; approximately 450,000 episodes

solution_summary: The solution combined three DINOv3 ViT-Huge architectures with LocalMamba fusion across four folds. Its main improvement was stabilizing dead biomass prediction through a dead-to-total ratio, auxiliary losses, and a state-specific bias. Training used collection-session grouping and stratification by clover and dead biomass presence. Fold weighting and target-specific postprocessing improved the ensemble's private score to 0.65179, although the ratio-based model alone scored 0.65329.
compute: Ensemble submission with TTA exceeded 9 hours; TTA was omitted.

solution_title: 37th place approach in the G-Research Crypto Forecasting Competition.
solution_summary: The solution focused on asset-specific technical indicators across multiple timeframes, with periods capped at 1,440 minutes to meet inference limits. Predictions came from an ensemble of two XGBoost and two LightGBM models with different seeds and minor configuration differences. Per-asset quantile cutoffs handled extreme values, and manually selected bullish, bearish, and intermediate periods supported validation. The two submissions used the same pipeline trained on different datasets, and Polars with TA-Lib supported efficient feature computation.

The solution combined seven classifiers into three weighted probability ensembles, then selected the modal class across their predictions. Models and ensembles were tuned and evaluated using 10-fold out-of-fold accuracy. The final mode ensemble achieved 0.835124 accuracy with a fold standard deviation of 0.004098, slightly exceeding each individual ensemble. Feature engineering was tested but did not improve performance.

The solution combined fine-tuned DINOv3 ViT-Huge regression with a semantic tabular branch based on SigLIP embeddings. It predicted Green, Dead, and Clover components, deriving aggregate targets through deterministic relationships to enforce consistency. A left-right image split captured spatial variation, while semantic features and GBDT models provided complementary predictions. Weighted ensembling combined four-fold DINO models with the semantic branch, achieving weighted R² of approximately 0.62.

The final submission used a single BERT model with answer-type classification, span boundary heads, and a bilinear head scoring token pairs. Preprocessing retained simplified HTML structure, processed entire documents, and heavily subsampled negative examples. The model was first fine-tuned on SQuAD 2.0 and then trained on Natural Questions, with development data used to set answer thresholds. It scored about 0.71 publicly and 0.69 privately.
compute: TPU; 2 epochs, batch size 64, learning rate 2.5e-5

solution_summary: The solution used linear regression on transit depth and shape features derived from polynomial fits to light curves. Features combined SNR-weighted AIRS measurements, adjacent-frequency windows, and FG1 measurements, with slope and percentile features providing substantial gains. Edge transits received a separate Ridge model, while very poor transits were excluded from training and assigned larger uncertainties at inference. Bootstrap prediction variability was combined with cross-validation uncertainty estimates, producing a private score of 61.2.

solution_title: 87th place private and 1st place public solution
solution_summary: The team reduced 270 engineered signal features to 90 using recursive elimination with LightGBM permutation importance. Six model outputs were combined through nonnegative linear stacking optimized for MAE, although this performed similarly to the strongest individual models. Validation used stratified grouped five-fold splits with overlapping boundary segments removed. Merging two short earthquakes was the decisive change, while adding public test segments labeled through leaderboard probing had limited apparent impact.

The solution combined LightGBM models with neural networks for the Cite and Multi tasks. Centered log-ratio normalization, alternative count transformations, and row-wise standardization were important preprocessing choices. LightGBM out-of-fold predictions were compressed with truncated SVD and supplied as neural-network meta features. Three-layer MLPs and GRU variants used several activation and loss functions, while out-of-day validation checked whether features remained useful under temporal shift.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution: An Open Secret - Gather, Ridge, Repeat
solution_summary: The author collected public out-of-fold predictions and repeatedly expanded a Ridge regression stack, eventually reaching 77 OOF inputs. AutoGluon and hill-climbing ensembles were also explored, and some ensemble OOF predictions became inputs to subsequent stacks. Original data and GAN-generated KaggleX data were tested, with KaggleX helping public scores but not private scores. The selected standalone ensemble scored 62958 privately, while blending it with a public notebook improved the public score but yielded 62977 privately.
compute: AutoGluon experiments used CPUs, P100 GPUs, and T4 GPUs.

solution_title: A top solution note for everyone.
solution_summary: This post collects lessons from other competitors rather than describing the author's own final solution. It emphasizes target-permutation feature selection, temporal and grouped aggregations, and domain-informed credit features. Summarized modeling approaches include convolutional and bidirectional LSTM processing of time series, nested LightGBM predictions, and separate models for data blocks. Additional ideas include interest-rate proxies, neighbor-based target statistics, and encoding combinations; no original experimental results are reported.

The solution used only RoBERTa base, ensembled across five folds. Recovering original labels, cleaning problematic text, and correctly finding all label occurrences were central to the pipeline. Training used custom label smoothing, multi-sample dropout, and random shifts of tokens within padding. Pseudo-labeling, alternative models, layer-specific learning rates, and sampling adjustments did not improve results.

solution_summary: The approach concentrated on filtering existing helmet detections, mapping them to player tracking data, and post-processing assignments. IoU tracking formed helmet clusters that supported confidence filtering and label voting. A two-stage assignment process first matched sufficiently populated frames, inferred camera direction, and then refined matches with fixed labels as constraints. Extending cluster boxes by six frames on either side exploited the evaluation behavior and helped achieve 0.787 on the full training set and 0.790 on the private leaderboard.

The final prediction is a weighted blend of an LSTM, GPT-2, and five BERT variants, with BERT models receiving most of the weight. Training uses identity-aware sample weights and binary cross-entropy objectives for the main target and auxiliary toxicity labels. All models receive contraction mapping and light preprocessing. More than 100 models were trained, while several alternative architectures, embeddings, statistical features, and language-model pretraining attempts did not help.

solution_summary: The solution combined full images with several full-body and back-fin crop variants at image sizes from 512 to 896. TensorFlow and PyTorch models used ArcFace, with DOLG additionally attached to the TensorFlow models, and their embeddings were concatenated into a representation exceeding 20,000 dimensions. Inference compared train and test embeddings and applied species-specific thresholds for new individuals. Repeated pseudo-labeling progressively improved the score, while development relied on leaderboard feedback after training on all available training data.

solution_title: 14th Place - 278 Shared OOF Sets + 36 Own Models, All Judged on a Sealed Fold
solution_summary: The final solution stacked 36 own models and 278 publicly shared prediction sets using regularized logistic regression on standardized ranks and logits. Fixed folds, fold-local preprocessing, prediction integrity checks, and sealed-fold ensemble evaluation governed model admission without using the public leaderboard for decisions. Exact-value representations, screen-time budget features, auxiliary imputations, and independent missingness augmentation strengthened the author's diverse model pool. The final stack achieved nested OOF AUC 0.97038 and private AUC 0.97109, compared with private AUC 0.97063 for the own-model safety submission.
compute: Vast.ai GPUs with Runpod fallback; final changed neural member refit used 3 seeds on 3 GPUs for about $0.39. Wide 400-column stacking jobs used 10–16 GB each.

solution_summary: The author manually constructed three strings covering all permutations while including the required Santa-prefixed permutations in every string. Symmetric cycle structures and overlapping sequence joins produced a length of 2440 without wildcards. Carefully placed wildcards, swapped sequence endings, and distribution across different strings reduced the final length to 2428.

The solution averaged transformer models using DeBERTa v3 Large and RoBERTa Large with different sequence lengths and external training datasets. Four-fold experiments using document ID modulo four guided stable settings, followed by full-data training for the ensemble. All models used focal loss, AdamW, and cosine scheduling, with external examples retained without downsampling. Predictions were aligned to spaCy tokens, averaged, and adjusted using out-of-fold optimized thresholds.

The team blended multilingual XLM-RoBERTa models, language-specific BERT models for all six test languages, and domain-adapted XLM-RoBERTa models. Translated data, OpenSubtitles, fold averaging, and masked-language-model training supplied additional diversity. Label smoothing and translation-based test-time augmentation contributed smaller gains. Heuristic corrections for automated template messages added about 0.001 on the leaderboard, and the final blend scored 0.9523 public and 0.9509 private.
compute: Kaggle-provided TPUs; Kaggle Notebooks used for training and inference.

solution_title: Post-Processing Based on Drug Classification (15th place)
solution_summary: A classifier identifies the eight most frequent drugs with over 99% accuracy and uses their known target profiles to adjust other models' predictions. Its confidence sets lower bounds for positive targets and upper bounds for negative targets, with squared negative-class probabilities providing a further improvement. This post-processing improved CV loss from 0.01564 to 0.01559 and public leaderboard loss from 0.01835 to 0.01831.

The final submission blended LightGBM models trained with different feature sets, achieving private RMSE of 3.600. The best single model used 12 folds and 300 features, with CV RMSE of 3.634 and private RMSE of 3.605. Aggregated one-hot merchant identifiers were useful, with merchants selected using transaction counts and outlier prevalence under RAM constraints. Several alternative models and stacking approaches failed, while transaction-level prediction aggregates were omitted despite a small private-score improvement.
compute: RAM constraints required selecting a subset of merchant identifiers; capacity was not stated.

solution_title: Details in 1D model in 4th place solution (bilzard's part)
solution_summary: This writeup describes the author's raw EEG 1D modeling component of the team solution. A lightweight EfficientNet-inspired CNN used shared left/right encoders, symmetric min/max mappings, and projected cosine similarity features to capture laterality. Channel mixing and a time-dependent Channel Quality Factor helped represent relationships and corrupted EEG channels. Training progressively restricted samples by vote count and used symmetry-preserving augmentations; the final 15-model ensemble had 863K parameters per model and required about one to two minutes for test inference.
compute: 863K parameters per 1D model; test inference took 1–2 minutes with 15 models (3 seeds × 5 folds).

solution_title: 4rd Place Solution for the "ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions"
solution_summary: The pipeline recursively imputed missing features with CatBoost regressors and built additional features from the Greek metadata. These included Epsilon-sorted row positions and cross-validated category probabilities for Alpha, Beta, Gamma, and Delta. An untuned CatBoost classifier produced the final predictions without feature elimination. More elaborate feature generation and imputation did not improve cross-validation and made results less stable.

The final solution averaged three MLP variants, a ResNet, and a TabNet, with weights tuned against the public leaderboard. Diversity came from different preprocessing, engineered features, validation strategies, and seed counts. Features included dimensionality reductions, denoising autoencoder representations, clusters, and summary statistics, while some MLPs also used non-scored targets for training or pretraining. Reported validation log losses ranged from about 0.01464 for MLP3 to 0.01681 for ResNet.

solution_title: 0.975+ Private Solution (72nd) with a dumb way to incorporate GMM cluster membership
solution_summary: The author reconstructed synthetic data generation settings and inferred three clusters per class by matching local validation scores. A six-component Gaussian mixture supplied an integer cluster-membership feature to a QDA classifier. Prediction-based outlier removal and averaging across random seeds improved the submitted model to 0.97426 public and 0.97518 private leaderboard scores.

The final submission combined two different approaches in an ensemble. One disclosed component used only leave-one-out features and achieved a leaderboard score of 0.9923 as a single model. The post provides a script and validation toggle for reproducing that component, but does not describe the second approach or ensemble details.

solution_title: My First Kaggle Competition From Baselines to a 5 Model Ensemble
solution_summary: The author began with Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM baselines before developing a stronger feature set using ideas from public notebooks. The final approach trained five unspecified models with five-fold cross-validation. Averaging their predictions and applying calibration produced a score of approximately 0.65. Feature engineering and ensemble stability were emphasized, but model architectures and detailed preprocessing were not provided.

The team retained a public detection, Transformer association, and ILP tracking pipeline and added a three-frame 3D CNN to recover missing cell divisions. Geometry and association gates controlled graph edits, while jump-aware relinking, smoothing, and frozen-frame coordinate consensus addressed repeated frames. Learned division recovery produced the largest measured public improvement, from 0.954 to 0.964, and one selected variant added a distilled coordinate head that reached 0.966 publicly. Cross-embryo testing evaluated the added classifier, but inherited models were in-sample and the private team score of 0.930 could not be attributed to individual components.

solution_summary: The team built a rule-based Halite agent centered on two minimum-cost-flow assignments: ships to target cells and ships to next-turn cells. Its strategy shifted from early mining and ship production to coordinated midgame attacks, followed by late mining without further ship creation. Cell values accounted for safe travel, mining duration, return trips, and enemy cargo, while movement assignments prevented friendly collisions. Permanent base defenders and territorial base expansion supported the strategy; reinforcement learning did not become part of the final approach.

solution_title: 2nd place solution: too risky (don't try at home!)
solution_summary: The author combined Raddar's existing model with a custom Elo approach to assess team strength. The main intervention was to assign 0.95 win probabilities to the top four teams, resolving their mutual matchups by the strength ordering while retaining a binary choice for Baylor versus Notre Dame. This deliberately aggressive heuristic benefited from several tournament outcomes, including Oregon's win over Mississippi State. The same strategy performed very poorly in the men's tournament.

The team combined 67 models spanning recurrent networks, graph networks, attention architectures, and autoencoder-pretrained transformers. Features included base-pair probability summaries, sampled RNA structures and loop types, and positional entropy. Cluster-based grouped validation and error-weighted MCRMSE guided training. Neural and tree-based stacking followed by optimized blending preserved diversity and performed better on the leaderboard than a simple blend, despite worse cross-validation. Domain-adversarial training did not improve results.

The solution stacked 120 transformer models with a single CatBoostRegressor as the second-level model. Base-model diversity came from several pretrained model families, MSE or BCE objectives, input reversal, padding choices, and pooling layers. The stacker also received lexical similarity and context features, with context providing a substantial benefit. Optuna tuned the stacker, and the author relied on a CV score of 0.8557; the best single model was DeBERTa-v3-large with a public score of 0.8352.

The algorithm searched random helix origin and curvature hypotheses and clustered hits in transformed geometric coordinates using sparse binning. It progressively extracted long tracks, resolved duplicate detector hits, and extended tracks with nearby unassigned hits. Larger searches plateaued around 0.765 on the described training event, while merging long runs with learned track scores improved further. Starting tracks from individual hits added gains but was slow.
compute: Each stage took about 8–10 minutes on Kaggle and about half that time on the author's laptop.

solution_title: 21st Place Solution - Hungarian Algorithm, Frame Filling
solution_summary: Two YOLOv5 detectors produced helmets at 1280-pixel image size, followed by geometric player assignment using rotation, scaling, and the Hungarian algorithm. Boundary-player and rotation searches aligned tracking coordinates with video detections, while modified DeepSORT tracking stabilized player labels. The models were combined by using the second model to fill missing assignments from the first, then missing frames were filled from nearby predictions. Selection relied on two validation sets and complementary metrics, with final scores of 0.805 CV, 0.849 public, and 0.795 private.

The solution used a modified WaveNet trained on cleaned Kalman signal data with batch 8 removed. It combined RFC, lag, rolling-statistic, gradient, and nonlinear signal features with flip, noise, and shift augmentation. Low learning rates, prolonged training, and a combined binary cross-entropy and weighted soft-F1 loss were important. Final predictions used flip test-time augmentation and averaging across five grouped folds.

The approach first identified duplicate instances with conflicting labels and used five XGBoost models to infer their labels by majority vote before reinserting them. It then divided the majority class into 24 partitions and paired each partition with all minority-class instances. Predictions from the 24 balanced-data XGBoost models were averaged, preserving majority-class coverage while addressing imbalance. The shared model scored 0.840336 on the public leaderboard and 0.828114 on the private leaderboard, although the author selected two other submissions.

solution_title: 46th place solution - Simple Image Level Multilabel Classifier
solution_summary: The solution trained image-level multilabel classifiers on competition images plus public HPA data, then applied classification to single-cell masks from HPA-Cell-Segmentation. Its network combined residual blocks, ConvLSTM memory, spatial Transformers, and an auxiliary head predicting future enemy locations under partial observability. Dynamic reward scaling, adaptive entropy, and teacher policy and value losses stabilized learning and preserved previously acquired skills. Inference used greedy actions and coordinate-flip augmentation, with augmentation disabled when the overtime budget became tight. The final model trained for about 1.5 billion environment steps over three to four days, with progress assessed through thousands of matches and controlled public evaluations.

solution_summary: The approach evolved from beam-stacked simulated annealing to a more effective standalone simulated annealing search. Neighbor design was central, emphasizing small changes, broad exploration, and recoverability from poor moves. Taking the maximum of linear and logistic temperature schedules improved search behavior. For sample 5, the author used a stopword section followed by an alphabetical block.

The final structure-from-motion pipeline proposed image pairs using pretrained global descriptors, matched them with ALIKED and LightGlue, and reconstructed scenes with COLMAP. solution_title: 22th Place - Lessons learned from a beginner
solution_summary: The final solution ensembled six-fold segmentation models using ResNet34 and EfficientNet B2/B5 encoders with U-Net, FPN, and LinkNet decoders. Three post-processing thresholds were tuned on validation predictions from all six folds to binarize masks, remove small components, and binarize again. The chosen solution achieved 0.6651 CV and 0.66498 privately, while a discarded approach with a separate model per mask type later proved stronger.

The final approach used separate XGBoost models for men's and women's games, with normalized basketball statistics, seeds and derived features. Weighted averages over the current and previous two seasons helped smooth unusual team performance. Model selection used a held-out final season alongside repeated five-fold cross-validation, and predictions were submitted without post-processing. The solution enriched phrase-pair inputs with other targets sharing the same anchor and CPC context or sector, excluding the current target. Transformer backbones were augmented with bidirectional LSTM heads and linear attention pooling, trained using Pearson loss and adversarial weight perturbation. Validation grouped anchors, stratified scores, and kept overlapping anchor/target words together. The final weighted ensemble combined five-fold and full-data models, with output scaling and stronger weighting for full-data models, reaching a reported private score of 0.8782.

The solution extracted transit spectra using calibrated, spatially selected signals and polynomial curve fitting with wavelength averaging. Derivative-based transition detection and fitting trends over wider wavelength ranges improved transit-depth estimation. Dynamics-dependent spectrum corrections and empirical uncertainty estimates were followed by per-star PCA using five components. Additional Taurex samples improved the private score by 0.005, while PCA reduced training RMSE from 4.3e-5 to 3.3e-5 and added 0.015 to the leaderboard score.

solution_title: [64th Place] A simple low computation model
solution_summary: The author describes constructing forecast-period features by copying the last 28 observed sales days into the next 28 days. Three years of history supported two years of training rows with rolling windows up to 365 days, and training was split across hobbies, household, and foods. Under the author's WRMSSE calculation, repeating 28 days performed better than repeating the last seven days four times.

The team combined diverse LightGBM models built with different feature engineering approaches, using stratified 10-fold validation. Applicant-level transaction aggregates over time, delinquency buckets, and zero-filled missing values improved the author's baseline. Combining teammates' features and adding out-of-fold predictions from individual tables as meta features produced models with local CV around 0.800 and public scores up to 0.809. Percentile-ranking predictions before stacking or blending was essential, and the final results supported trusting local validation.
