solution_summary: The team pretrained on LIVECell with all cells treated as one class, then generated pseudo-labels for the provided semi-supervised data. A Cascade R-CNN with a ResNeXt152 backbone reached 0.338 on the leaderboard after this training. Five-fold ResNet34 classification constrained segmentation outputs to the image's predicted cell class. The final pipeline relied heavily on mask repair, overlap-based mask merging, and category-specific weighted non-maximum weighting.

The final submission combined 15 models trained with four folds, with orthogonal initialization, last-layer reinitialization, and layer-wise learning rate decay across all models. Mean pooling was particularly effective, while weighted loss modestly improved some models and added diversity. SiFT and MIXout helped smaller DeBERTa variants despite failing on the base variant. The ensemble averaged target-wise weights optimized with Optuna on out-of-fold predictions and weights adjusted manually using leaderboard feedback.

The solution combined cloud segmentation with separate classifiers that removed false-positive masks. The classifiers included a multiscale Xception network and a jointly supervised mask-and-label model, reaching 78% classification validation accuracy together. Segmentation used an EfficientNetB2 U-Net with crop augmentation, test-time augmentation, and ensembles across folds and initializations. The final solution achieved 0.663 on both cross-validation and the private leaderboard.

solution_title: Code sharing, 13th place, no external data
solution_summary: The author shared an XGBoost notebook that used no external data. The post also described a stronger single-model variant incorporating Google Trends, state information, and weather, but excluded those sources from the shared model over real-world usability concerns. The script required about 8 GB of RAM and several hours, and the author reported selecting submissions based on public leaderboard scores.
compute: About 8 GB RAM; several hours runtime
external_data: ["Google Trends daily searches for Rossmann in Germany", "State data by dune_dweller", "Weather data per state"]

solution_summary: The team trained separate image and title embedding models, concatenated their vectors, and refined embeddings using nearby matches. Nearest-neighbor retrieval produced candidate pairs that GPU XGBoost models scored using embedding distances, ranks, and TF-IDF similarities. A second model used percentage ranks to reduce sensitivity to dataset size, and probability-based agglomerative clustering formed the final matches. Joint image-text representation learning did not improve validation, and the team's two similar kernels could not be combined within the time limit.
compute: GPU used for second-stage XGBoost.

solution_summary: The author built an Excel model that regressed standardized pre-tournament metrics against historical results scored using the ESPN points scheme. Regression coefficients determined metric weights and produced a power rating for each team using the 2018, 2019, and 2021 tournaments. Features covered efficiency, shooting, pace, rankings, seeds, schedule strength, and win/loss indicators. TeamRankings supplied additional statistics for the final three games before the tournament.

The solution retrieved DOI and accession candidates through article-ID lookups in V4 and external Europe PMC text-mined terms, then checked that candidates appeared in the article. DOI type classification used author information where available and a distilled 7B context classifier otherwise. Accession classification combined distilled 7B and 14B models with identifier-specific rules and majority voting. Two rule variants behaved differently on public and private evaluations, while an additional EPI author-information approach was not selected.

solution_title: 13th Place Solution for the Google - Fast or Slow? Predict AI Model Runtime Competition
solution_summary: The approach used separate multilayer perceptrons for layout and tile configuration ranking. The layout model combined configurable-node features with parent and sibling information, averaged node representations, and added graph and subset descriptors. Pairwise hinge loss, balanced graph batches, careful normalization, and deduplication stabilized training, while three independent runs formed the final ensemble. Compressed TFRecords and strict graph-size limits kept training within 16 GB RAM and 4 GB VRAM.
compute: 16 GB RAM, 4 GB VRAM

solution_title: [86th place solution] How a beginner became a expert !
solution_summary: The solution combines public choice and give9 prompt attacks with a custom give9_python attack. The choice attack repeats the topic in option nine, while the Python variant asks the evaluator to output the answer to code and includes a temperature instruction. Multiple seeds were submitted to select stable attacks because local verification and seed consistency were difficult. The reported selected configuration scored 23.749 publicly and 23.319 privately.

solution_title: Bronze Medal Solution for the Vesuvius Challenge - Surface Detection Competition
solution_summary: The final pipeline generated CT surface probabilities with TransUNet, refined them using a lightweight residual UNet, and extracted ridges through orientation-aware relaxed non-maximum suppression. Anisotropic closing and connected-component filtering then repaired gaps and removed fragments. Replacing skeleton thinning with relaxed NMS delivered the largest reported public-score improvement, from 0.555 to 0.570. The final private score was 0.582.

solution_title: 5th Place Solution: Features are all you need!
solution_summary: The team emphasized features describing reconstructed essay structure, punctuation, cursor behavior, and writing activity. Their final system combined four tabular neural networks, a 1D CNN, and LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost models. Score-stratified validation and five shared seeds helped maintain agreement between cross-validation and leaderboard results. Neural and tree ensembles were weighted separately with Optuna and then combined equally, producing a final CV score of 0.5858 and private score of 0.560.

The post announces that the author is attaching source code and documentation to comply with the competition rules. The supplied text contains no description of the approach. It provides no methods, implementation details, or results to extract.

The author combined XGBoost models trained on different time periods to capture product seasonality and longer-term trends. Historical ownership averages, lag features, and customer tenure features helped, while training was restricted to customers acquiring products to fit limited memory. The final blend averaged multi-output and product-specific predictions, adjusted product odds using leaderboard feedback, and incorporated the teammate's predictions with conditional weights.
compute: Computer with 8 GB RAM

solution_summary: The team adapted shared training code with extensive data augmentation and changed the backbone to EfficientNet V2 B3. They trained 10 models using 10-fold cross-validation and a learning rate of 0.0001, reaching approximately 0.92 CV and 0.71 leaderboard scores. Flip-based test-time augmentation with corresponding output-index remapping added about 0.005 to the leaderboard score. They also built a YOLO-based alternative, although its role in the final submission is unspecified.

The solution used a single TensorFlow 2.0 BERT-large model with separate outputs for short-answer boundaries and long-answer locations. Matching the empty-answer sampling ratio to the full dataset was the main improvement. Custom HTML tokens helped slightly, and SQuAD-finetuned whole-word-masking weights performed best among the tested initializations, reaching about 0.73 on the leaderboard. Final training took a little over two hours on TPUs, excluding tokenization and post-processing.
compute: TPUs; final training a little over 2 hours excluding tokenization and post-processing; local machine had 2 x 1080 TI.

solution_summary: The solution refined a weighted least-squares baseline by repeatedly removing measurements with large residuals. It estimated relative motion from GNSS measurements and a convolutional model using IMU data, then combined those estimates with pseudoranges over a 21-timestamp optimization window. Downtown predictions used nearby ground-truth road points with robust residual scoring and medoid selection. A final convolutional error-correction model and aggregation across stationary periods and phones further improved predictions.

solution_title: 11th Place - GRU, CNN, Transformer - GPU Deep Learning!
solution_summary: The solution combined a CNN–Transformer–GRU model using 80 features with a deep GRU using two features. Training windows always contained one onset and one wakeup, allowing a question-answering-style softmax head to predict event minutes. Producing 30 progressively downweighted guesses per night added approximately 0.050 to CV, while auxiliary models reranked event confidence scores. Non-maximum suppression and weighted box fusion combined the diverse event predictions.

solution_title: 7th place solution - the power of randomness
solution_summary: The solution combined transformer models predicting one score per text with token models predicting multiple targets in a shared anchor-context group. Randomly permuted related targets supplied additional context, and balanced encoding was preferred at inference. Token scores combined simple and prediction-weighted averages, while text models mainly used target-masked attention heads. Final submissions used positive-coefficient linear regression ensembles fitted to out-of-fold predictions, with alternative handling of a model that had produced NaNs.
compute: Only Kaggle resources; many experiments used one fold for one epoch.

solution_title: The code of my best submission
solution_summary: The solution blended gradient boosting models. Categorical variables were represented with binary vectors, while dates were decomposed into year, month, and day using both categorical and scalar representations. The implementation used scikit-learn, and the author shared the code for the best submission.

solution_title: 11th Place Solution: Supervised Contrastive Pretraining + Query and Database expansion
solution_summary: The final retrieval ensemble combined two EfficientNetV2-M models with SE-ResNeXt101 and EfficientNet-B6 models. Class-balanced supervised contrastive pretraining followed by AdaCos fine-tuning improved convergence, while a second training pipeline used GeM pooling and ArcFace. Weighted concatenation of normalized embeddings outperformed combining ranked retrieval lists. Query expansion and class-based database reranking improved the leaderboard score by approximately 0.07, with the concatenation experiment reaching 0.455.
compute: GPU augmentation and Faiss postprocessing; hardware unspecified.
external_data: ["GLDv2 cleaned and full datasets", "Google repository index and test validation data"]

solution_summary: The final pipeline allocated one prediction slot to TBM, two to RNAPro, and two to BPP-Protenix, with plain Protenix handling targets unsuitable for BPP features. BPP-Protenix projected EternaFold base-pair probabilities into the initial pair representation of a pretrained Protenix model and was trained on 619 RNA-only PDBs. A simple linear projection outperformed more elaborate binned and Pairformer-based embeddings. The final ensemble scored 0.504 publicly and 0.492 privately, while local analysis found benefits even for targets containing pseudoknots.

The post develops a hypothesis about how the dataset was generated rather than describing a complete modeling pipeline. The author argues that negative examples include Gaussian noise and that the test set contains both real and shuffled fake samples. They propose computing counts using training data and real test samples, then interpreting those counts together with each value's position in its feature distribution. Distinguishing noise from real observations is presented as the key challenge, while the final classifier and measured results are unspecified.

The post announces that the team's solution is available on Docker Hub. It provides a command to launch the container with nvidia-docker. It gives no details about the modeling pipeline, training, or results.

The repository provides the team's competition solution through three contributor-specific code folders. Reproduction requires following the instructions in each folder. The resulting models are combined using a supplied blending script, but the text gives no model architectures or scores.

The system retrieved 200 candidates per session using tuned co-visitation matrices, then reranked them with LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost. Roughly 500 user, item, and interaction features captured activity counts, time patterns, co-visitation, embedding similarities, and BPR scores. Validation used shared datasets with separately fitted validation and full-data retrieval representations to avoid leakage. CatBoost was the strongest ranker, and Optuna optimized a weighted ensemble against local recall@20.
compute: Ensemble weight evaluation took 700 ms per trial for 60 million cart samples.

solution_summary: The solution decomposed survival prediction into censored and uncensored regressions combined through class probabilities. Race-specific target transformations enabled binary cross-entropy regression, while neural networks used a tuned constant for censored cases. Repeated four-fold validation across many split seeds guided model selection and public/private score estimation. The final ensemble blended regressors and stacked classifiers with logistic regression, reaching a reported private score of 0.69937.

The solution combined six image channels, normalized images by experiment, plate, and channel, and added train and test controls as extra classes. DenseNet121 was the main model, alongside EfficientNet-B1, SE-ResNet101, and DenseNet169, with five-fold validation and models at two image resolutions. Batch-level mixup and cutout were particularly helpful, while training also used pseudo-labels, label smoothing, mixed precision, and learning-rate schedules. Predictions used cosine similarity to experiment-level average training logits, test-time augmentation, plate leakage, and prediction balancing.

The submission generated transferable adversarial examples using a momentum iterative attack. Its update accumulates normalized gradients and applies clipped sign-based perturbations. The attack used an ensemble of eight models, many adversarially trained. The writeup also describes a 1,000-image ImageNet validation subset and a Cleverhans implementation.

The post describes feature engineering for volatility prediction rather than a complete modeling pipeline. It generalizes weighted average price to multiple order-book levels and derives liquidity measures from the minimized price objectives. Alternative WAP features provided little benefit, but trade volume divided by liquidity was highly informative, with a reported log-space correlation of about 0.88 with volatility. Strong features combined trade volume over long windows with recent liquidity and sometimes aggregated across stocks.

The pipeline detected helmets with YOLOv5-l, tracked them using optical flow, and classified motion-corrected video crops with Temporal Shift Module networks. Consistent crop scaling and velocity compensation helped isolate acceleration associated with impacts. Predictions from multiple architectures and four folds were averaged, with fast models filtering most easy negatives first. Tracking-based temporal suppression was applied separately by predicted impact type, yielding a small additional validation improvement.
compute: TSM classification models took an hour to a few hours each to train.

solution_title: 25th Place Solution for DAIGT (Public LB: 0.966 Private LB: 0.927)
solution_summary: The team combined typo correction, trained BPE tokenization, and TF-IDF features with an ensemble of four conventional classifiers. LoRA-tuned Mistral-7B predictions were used for difficult cases, alongside a public transformer model described inconsistently as DistilBert and DistilRoberta. Confident predictions supplied pseudo-labels for an additional semi-supervised component, and the resulting predictions were blended. Typo correction and pseudo-labeling reportedly improved the private score by about 0.01 and 0.02 respectively.

The solution used extensive weighted ensembles of CatBoost, LightGBM, and XGBoost models, including stacks with glmnet. Diversity came from random seeds, training subsets enriched for positive examples, and independently generated synthetic features. Repeated random holdouts guided model and hyperparameter choices, while categorical encoding and numerical standardization prepared the inputs. The best selected submission scored 0.29144, and a related unselected ensemble scored 0.29157 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Multiple Intel Xeon workstations totaling 74 physical cores and 448 GB RAM, running Ubuntu Linux 16.04.

solution_title: 3rd place solution - attack the opponent's second shipyard
solution_summary: The agent extended an existing solution with analytical rules for mining, shipyard construction, defense, and attacks. Its main strength was identifying safe opportunities to capture the opponent's second shipyard using a 25-turn simulator and estimates of available attackers, defenders, and future ship production. It merged allied fleets along attack routes and retained ships through mining decisions to create more attack opportunities. Reinforcement learning was abandoned after limited benefits, while accurate attack decisions contributed strongly to winning matches.
compute: About three weeks preparing reinforcement learning and about one week of learning before abandoning it.

solution_title: Neural networks architectures and training methods
solution_summary: The solution used neural networks over approximately 11,000 sparse features, processing feature types separately through one layer before fusion. This fusion strategy improved log loss by about 0.02, and the best individual network achieved 0.61 log loss. The author averaged that network and eight additional neural architectures with one XGBoost model. Numerous alternatives, including autoencoder pretraining and additional recommendation features, produced no major gains.

The solution combined KeyNet, AffNet, and HardNet with a two-stage AdaLAM matching pipeline. Initial candidate matches guided a second local matching pass over ten nearest neighbors, improving feature-track connections across overlapping images for SfM. OriNet was enabled, the feature count was increased to 8,192, and images were resized to a 1,600-pixel longer edge. Grid grouping produced low scores, while DBSCAN matching offered limited gains and multiscale descriptor concatenation remained incompletely tested.

The solution generated purchase candidates through repurchases, collaborative filtering, and global or segmented popularity, then reranked them with LightGBM LambdaMART. Time-decayed ItemkNN provided the largest gain, while candidate ranks were important reranking features. Negative sampling and positive-sample ratios became increasingly important as candidate volume grew. Processing moved to BigQuery and training to GCP Vertex with high-memory machines; the best model scored 0.03861 locally and 0.03252 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Initially a GPU notebook; later parallel experiments on GCP Vertex high-memory machines with up to 512GB RAM.

solution_summary: The solution used two RetinaNet detectors with ResNet-50 and ResNet-101 backbones to predict pneumonia bounding boxes. Training and validation data came from the Stage 1 training labels, without training on the Stage 2 set. The author manually selected snapshots from several training runs using precision and maximum Youden index.
compute: Dell Precision T5500; 3.07 GHz Intel Xeon X5675 CPU; 12 GB NVIDIA Titan Xp GPU; 16 GB DDR3 RAM; 512 GB HDD

solution_summary: The author detected helmets with YOLOv5 and matched detections to tracking data using a coordinate-regression network. This network paired an EfficientNetB0 encoder with a U-Net decoder and predicted x/y coordinate masks from two-channel 256×256 inputs. Training used L1 loss only where tracking labels existed, with an additional segmentation channel providing guidance. DeepSORT and SiamRPN tracking postprocessing increased CV from about 0.7 to 0.9 and the private score from 0.7 to 0.86.

The solution used a combinatorial geometric tracking algorithm that repeatedly seeded, extended, ranked, and pruned candidate tracks. Idealized helices predicted subsequent hits, with training-derived corrections and nearest-neighbor searches guiding extensions. Tracks were committed in quality order to resolve shared hits, and the process repeated on unused hits. Hyperopt tuned the many heuristic parameters, and the final score was 0.86395 with approximately three minutes of single-threaded processing per event.
compute: Intel Core i7-3667U @ 2GHz notebook; about 3 minutes per event using one thread.

solution_title: How some small changes on the public notebook had gave you a 55th place!
solution_summary: The solution modified a public notebook into a manual ensemble of Multinomial Naive Bayes, an SGD classifier, two LightGBM classifiers, and two CatBoost classifiers. Sequential fitting and probability accumulation reduced memory use and allowed additional models. Lower iteration counts helped reduce overfitting, and changing the training objective to log loss was another important adjustment.

solution_title: Best Single Model: 0.915 (Private LB score) with nearly zero pre-processing
solution_summary: The author describes a compact CNN with fewer than 1.5 million parameters and five folds. Preprocessing consists only of silence removal and audio chunking, while unspecified feature engineering is credited with much of the model's strength. The best single model scored 0.915 on the private leaderboard and 0.921 publicly. Mixup increased the public score to 0.925 but reduced the private score to 0.907, and the author says these results were omitted from the final submission and technical report.

The author summed scores from seven models varying RoBERTa encoders, classification heads, datasets, losses, and seeds. Training used either binary cross-entropy or a custom batchwise ranking loss over adjacent examples sorted by label. Large-batch TPU training used a constant learning rate of 1e-4. Model selection relied on one-fold validation and its voting version, with leaky toxic-data comments removed; including OLID was reported to hurt performance.
compute: 8-core TPU; batch size 384

solution_summary: The pipeline fine-tuned google/matcha-base image-to-text models in two phases: synthetic-data adaptation followed by separate scatter and non-scatter specialization. A diverse collection of 700,000 self-generated plots formed the foundation, supplemented by public synthetic data, corrected pseudo-labels, and ICDAR images. Extracted and other real plots were heavily oversampled during specialization. Structured text outputs encoded chart type, point counts, and coordinates, while training used augmentation, gradient accumulation, EMA, and learning-rate scheduling.
external_data: ["Wikipedia tables via TabEL and TURL", "Wikipedia STEM glossaries", "Self-generated synthetic plots", "Brendan Artley Benetech extra generated data", "Wikimedia Commons plot screenshots", "ICDAR"]

solution_summary: The author developed a WaveNet-plus-LSTM model using carefully cleaned signals and engineered features. The most important feature was target encoding of discretized signal values, kept unscaled while other features were scaled. Preprocessing removed noisy training segments, adaptively filtered mains-frequency noise, and aligned channel peaks across batches using earlier predictions for test data. These changes pushed the reported public score to approximately 0.947, although the supplied writeup ends before the full model details.
compute: Unspecified GPUs and additional Google Colab experiments

solution_summary: The solution emphasized a large engineered feature store and diverse tabular models for irrigation-need classification. XGBoost supplied the strongest single models, supplemented by LightGBM, CatBoost, TabM, RealMLP, and other architectures for diversity. Five-fold shuffled validation fed an ensemble pipeline combining AutoGluon stacking, hill-climbing or logistic blending, and final threshold tuning. Feature quality mattered more than ensemble size, and several ensembles improved CV while worsening leaderboard performance.
compute: 2–3 days invested; L4 and A100 Colab GPUs, A100 80GB, and A6000Ada 48GB across model families.

solution_summary: The approach focused on correcting noisy bounding boxes and removing very small annotations. Pseudo-label training used 1024-pixel images after excluding noisy training images and incorporating test images. A 512-pixel model performed better publicly, while an unselected 1024-pixel submission achieved a reported private score of 67.13.

Whole-slide images were downsampled sixfold and tiled, with background removal and learned tile selection reducing the workload. An ImageNet-initialized EfficientNetB0 feature extractor was trained through iterative clustering-based tile pseudo labels, including a noncritical tile category. Attention-based slide aggregation and maximum tile predictions fed a random forest classifier using the 25 darkest tiles. Tile balance and hue augmentation mattered, while the author reported that robust end-to-end validation remained unresolved.

The post asks whether another participant shared a writeup and encourages them to explain their approach. It specifically expresses interest in a reported CatBoost result using few features. It provides no account of the author's own solution.

The author combined outputs from public kernels and simple ensembles using a weighted mean. One example assigned half the weight to the best public kernel and half to the mean of the source predictions. A subsequent rule replaced predictions above 0.75 with the maximum source prediction and those below 0.25 with the minimum source prediction.

The final solution averaged predictions from 14 EfficientNet-B4 models, with checkpoint weights averaged within each model. Diversity came from input preprocessing, training subsets, loss weighting, hard-example mining, external data, and postprocessing. The augmentation pipeline included cutout, grid masks, and mixup, while CutMix was ineffective. BanglaLekha-Isolated examples added ensemble diversity without clear standalone gains, and late postprocessing improved one submission.
compute: Scoring kernel could process up to 18 models within 2 hours.

solution_title: EV Purchase Prediction: OOF Stacking and Blend Analysis
solution_summary: The author compared stacking strategies using shared OOF and test predictions, with percentile-rank normalization and stratified validation. L1-regularized logistic regression achieved the best experimental OOF ROC AUC of 0.946349, narrowly ahead of other combinations. However, the executed export used only the public blend, so its public score of 0.94650 did not validate the stacking experiments. RealMLP lacked matching OOF predictions, creating an additional validation limitation.

solution_summary: The author adapted an existing 270k-article retrieval notebook without training a model, using a publicly fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3-large model. Retrieved context was ordered by descending similarity, and input length was increased to 4500 tokens. The final probability ensemble assigned weights of 0.5 and 0.4 to two DeBERTa outputs and 0.1 to Longformer. Validation scored 0.897 and the private leaderboard scored 0.902; dense retrieval replacements and added Wikipedia data did not improve performance.

The solution extracted toxicity features from pretrained Detoxify models and target-specific TF-IDF models trained on previous Jigsaw datasets, producing 46 features. After testing several learned combiners, the author chose a simpler rank-mean ensemble with feature selection guided by VAL and RUD performance. One submission used 11 Detoxify features and one TF-IDF feature, while the stronger submission retained only 10 Detoxify features. Accepting slightly lower VAL accuracy improved generalization, with the latter submission achieving a private score of 0.81299.

solution_summary: The author trained a TensorFlow speech recognizer combining residual convolutions and a backward LSTM with a CTC objective to learn characters or phonemes. A single training run achieved a private score of 0.89357, while averaging five fold runs reached 0.89874. No test data was used for training. The approach struggled with false negatives, incomplete recordings, and pronunciation ambiguity, although it could generalize to unseen words.

solution_title: 4rd Place Solution for the Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations
solution_summary: The solution blended Pyboost and a neural network with small contributions from public solutions. RAPIDS SVR supplied pseudo-label features using chemical embeddings and target aggregates, while the neural network used leave-one-out encodings and reduced targets. Choosing a validation strategy consistent with leaderboard behavior was central to development. The final private score was approximately 0.733–0.735, with exact reproduction complicated by saved-version differences.

The pipeline handled scatter plots with two-stage YOLOX detection and MatCha axis-label reading, while DePlot predicted other chart types end to end. Training combined competition charts, ICDAR, a public synthetic dataset, and custom Matplotlib-generated charts. Iterative synthetic-data design targeted observed errors, particularly line alignment, difficult labels, and degraded images. DePlot trained for 50 epochs with source-balanced sampling and achieved an overall private score of 0.69.

The team used several segmentation architectures trained on patches, whole images, or patches followed by whole-region fine-tuning. Very strong color, crop, stain, and organ-size augmentations combined with long training raised scores from below 0.6 to consistently above 0.75. Models included EfficientNet with DeepLabv3+, CoaT, PVT, and Swin Transformer U-Net. Reliable cross-validation was not established, so model assessment relied on the leaderboard, with a lower prediction threshold for lung than for other organs.
models_pretrained: ["EfficientNet B7, B6, V2-L with DeepLabv3+", "CoaT-small and CoaT-small-pl", "Swin Transformer U-Net", "PVT"]

solution_summary: The author expanded impact bounding boxes and manually labeled helmet, shoulder, body, and ground regions to provide more context. Head annotations included both helmets, and detections from two models were compared using overlap. Only cases with at least two detections exceeding an IoU of 0.1 were retained, aiming to suppress isolated false positives. The author reported that the overall attempt did not go well.

The team ensembled three complementary components, with this post detailing a genetic search over grid-transformation programs. Programs combined global DSL operations with cellular automaton rules, and late support for splitting and merging grids substantially improved results. Search used mutation and crossover, scored through overall accuracy, per-output accuracy, and exact color matching. A C++ implementation accelerated the algorithm about 100-fold, and the described component solved 10–12 tasks.

The author trained a ship-wise imitation-learning bot using winning replays from strong players. A convolutional and MLP model combined ship-centered map tensors with global player statistics, with separate models for three game stages. Action weights and modified enemy-base inputs controlled aggression, while ordered action selection avoided friendly collisions. Batched inference across all ships achieved approximately 30 ms per step locally and 0.3 seconds online.
compute: Inference: about 30 ms per step locally and 0.3 seconds per step online.

solution_summary: The team combined public and locally trained CaFormer and ConvNeXt predictions using a weighted median, obtaining a private leaderboard MAE of 24.57. A custom acoustic simulator generated synthetic shot gathers from perturbed velocity maps and diffusion-generated maps, with synthetic mixing reduced during training. Family-weighted L1 loss and removal of an all-zero trace row were additional training changes. Weighted median aggregation outperformed weighted mean by about one MAE, while family-specific pipelines and more elaborate postprocessing did not help.

The author used the source experiment paper and feature distributions to select training cycles resembling the test data. The final approach blended four models built on different cycle subsets, using 11 training cycles in total. Each subset underwent feature selection and transformation to a standard normal distribution before training LightGBM, XGBoost, and a very small neural network. Model weights were chosen manually, and local validation was prioritized after its relationship with the public leaderboard appeared inverted.

The solution used a gradient boosting classifier on engineered EEG features from 75-second windows resampled to 100 Hz. Features described spectral power, entropy, spectral edge power, and cross-channel correlations and eigenvalues in both frequency and time domains. Squared versions of all features were added, and training used all data marked safe. The reported submission achieved 0.79458 on the private leaderboard and 0.79650 on the public leaderboard.

solution_title: GPU Poor, PPO Rich: A Top 2%(72nd) Pure Self-Play Solution
solution_summary: The agent used a compact graph-biased transformer trained with PPO and pure self-play in JAX. Each planet independently chose a full-fleet launch target or no-op, using projected planet timelines and directional route features. A relational MLP action head improved on dot-product scoring, while precomputed geometry increased simulation throughput. The submitted checkpoint came from about 412 million steps and outperformed a later checkpoint selected locally, exposing weaknesses in evaluation and model selection.
compute: Local RTX 3070 Ti with 8 GB; two rented Vast.ai RTX 5070 Ti instances for about USD 25 total, reaching roughly 750M and 350M steps; submitted checkpoint around 412M steps.

solution_summary: The solution used pointwise ranking with dynamically sampled notebook context for each markdown cell. It reserved up to 128 query tokens and distributed the remaining budget evenly across code and other markdown cells. CodeT5-base at length 1024 improved the score by about 0.014 over length 512, and the final submission ensembled two checkpoints from different folds. A 27,000-notebook group holdout tracked leaderboard scores closely, and no additional data were used.

solution_summary: The team combined manual Python code golfing with character mutation fuzzing, arithmetic expression search, and compression optimization. A genetic variable renaming optimizer targeted raw compressed size, while shared web tooling supported rapid collaboration. Fuzzing uncovered a grid rotation trick based on pop(), and contributed more than 100 bytes of savings near the deadline. Task-specific solutions included regular expressions, recursive search, and hash-based hardcoding.
compute: Each compression attempt took a couple of minutes to brute-force optimized variable names.

solution_summary: The solution modeled player trajectories with a dual-path Graph-Transformer and individual-motion architecture using geometric, motion, role, and temporal features. Training combined permitted 2018 tracking data with competition data, first pretraining on a smaller feature set and then fine-tuning with a linear bridge and the full features. Player masking, reordering, spatial transformations, temporal cropping, and auxiliary displacement tasks improved generalization. Game-grouped validation, inference augmentation, and averaging four seeded seven-fold ensembles produced a reported public score of 0.456.

solution_title: VishnuDharma ARC Solver: A Hybrid AI Framework
solution_summary: The team described an offline cascade combining heuristic transformations, optional local LLM supervision, and beam-search program synthesis. Candidate programs composed small transformation functions and were checked against training examples before application to test grids. Identity copying or frequent-color fills provided valid fallback outputs, with two attempts saved per task. The post reported no quantitative evaluation results.

This smartphone-addiction classifier relied on extensive feature engineering and a diverse pool of more than 400 candidate models. A store of over 600 engineered features supported models trained on different subsets, with RealMLP the strongest individual model and TabM close behind. All models used fifteen-fold stratified validation. Logistic regression provided the final blending stage because its CV and leaderboard behavior was stable, while AutoGluon and ridge blends were excluded.
compute: Colab L4 for XGBoost, LightGBM, RealMLP and other models; Colab A100 for CatBoost; RunPod A100 80GB for TabM.

solution_title: 93rd Place Solution for the SenNet + HOA - Hacking the Human Vasculature in 3D
solution_summary: The competition submission equally ensembled two ImageNet-initialized 2D U-Nets with ResNeXt50 backbones trained at crop sizes of 1024 and 512. Training and inference used slices from all three spatial axes, with tiled inference, four-rotation TTA, a fixed probability threshold, and majority voting across projections. Preserving native image resolution and avoiding mask cleanup helped retain tiny vessels, while several postprocessing and multislice experiments failed. After the competition, revised normalization, a boundary/Dice/focal loss, an upscale layer, and stronger resolution-aware augmentation improved the private score to 0.682.
compute: Worked under Kaggle's 30 GPU-hours per week limit.

solution_summary: The solution used a five-layer bidirectional LSTM with concatenated skip connections and engineered breath-level time-series features. Inputs included logarithmic airflow, lagged values, cumulative quantities, and first and second derivatives, with robust scaling fitted on inspiratory rows. Training used a custom MAE emphasizing inspiration, AdamW, and 30 stratified group folds, followed by a referenced post-processing method. The reported single-model scores were CV 0.1302 and LB 0.1147.
compute: Pipeline supports TPU and GPU execution and parallel fold training across Colab sessions; actual hardware and elapsed time are unspecified.

solution_title: 40th Place Solution for the ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions Competition
solution_summary: The solution uses a LightGBM pairwise classifier inspired by contrastive learning to address the small training set. Pair features include absolute feature differences and summary statistics, with sampled pairs providing many training examples. Validation is stratified by Alpha, and AUC determines the training rounds. At inference, each observation is compared with all training observations, and classwise average similarities are normalized into a final probability.

The solution combined full-context TabPFN-3.5 models, generator-aware logistic regression, and nested stacks of tree and neural models. GPT-2 token features, label-free generator statistics, and likelihood-ratio features from distilgpt2 trained on the original dataset supplied the strongest complementary signals. A constrained blend optimized a smoothed pairwise AUC objective using histogram convolution and FFT, improving nested validation over the earlier log-loss combiner. Model selection relied on fixed nested folds and statistical gain gates; the second final submission deliberately relaxed those gates for an expanded refit and achieved 0.94588 private AUC. Experiments fitted directly to public leaderboard scores substantially harmed private performance and were excluded.
compute: TabPFN: about 3.5 minutes per fold on Colab RTX PRO 6000, 21–32 minutes on a local GPU; full-context test fit 3,334–3,696 seconds at 22.97 GB. T4 required int8 KV cache and 4,378–5,405 seconds per fold. Surrogate recipes took about 4.1 hours locally or 21 minutes on RTX PRO 6000.

solution_summary: The solution prioritized bounding-box accuracy, using RTMDet-x as its main experimental model and adding mask supervision to improve detection. EMA with a fixed learning rate was the most important training technique, alongside strong geometric augmentation and mixed batches from dataset1 and dataset2. The final ensemble fused boxes from RTMDet, YOLOX-x, and Mask R-CNN, then generated masks with the Mask R-CNN mask head. It used no test-time augmentation and scored 0.589 on the private leaderboard.

The approach transformed raw anglez, enmo, and hour inputs into a wavegram using a CNN feature extractor. A two-dimensional U-Net produced heatmaps, which a one-dimensional U-Net decoded into sleep, onset, and wakeup probabilities before post-processing. The reported configuration used a downsampling rate of two and a sequence length of 5760, achieving a leaderboard score of 0.714. The author cautioned that subsequent code changes could prevent exact reproduction and described a binary-search acceleration for evaluation.

The solution ensembled EfficientNet-B3, EfficientNet-B4, RepVGG-B2g4, and SE-ResNeXt50 trained on the 2020 data with five folds and 512 by 512 images. Training used bi-tempered loss with label smoothing, AdamW, cosine annealing with warm restarts, and several geometric and mixing augmentations. Test-time augmentation used shifts, scaling, rotations, and flips. The ensemble achieved 0.9050 public and 0.9007 private scores, while noisy-image removal, pseudo-labeling, and concatenated pooling features did not help.

solution_title: A Newbie's Journey from Blind Blending to Trusting the CV (My "solution writeup" for this competition 🤣)
solution_summary: The final pipeline stacked seven base models using a Ridge meta-learner trained exclusively on out-of-fold predictions from 10-fold stratified cross-validation. The ensemble combined four XGBoost feature configurations, two LightGBM configurations, and RealMLP, with three-seed averaging for LightGBM and RealMLP. The original 270-row Cleveland Heart Disease dataset was appended to every training fold. RealMLP received the largest Ridge coefficient, and the final cross-validation AUC was 0.9557448.

solution_title: MIP formulation on Gurobi, CPLEX and CBC+PuLP
solution_summary: The author shared a simplified mixed-integer programming formulation with implementations using Gurobi, CPLEX, and CBC with PuLP. The shared code differs slightly from the competition implementation and is intended as a learning resource. The author also describes adding redundant constraints to strengthen the bound, but provides no numerical results.

The author adjusted matching thresholds according to the number of predicted correct matches. Cross-validation thresholds increased from 0.36 for groups of 1–10 to 0.70 for groups of 31–50. They focused on reducing singleton predictions, which accounted for about 40% of predictions with one model. The full pipeline was linked in notebooks, while model and training details were absent from the supplied text.

The approach used log-mel spectrograms with CNN, CNN-GRU, and CNN-transformer architectures. Training combined signal-filtered random clips, spectrogram mixup, and waveform noise extracted from training audio. Stratified five-fold validation, balanced sampling, and label smoothing supported training. Post-processing lowered a species threshold throughout an audio file when any clip produced a confident detection.

solution_title: 9th place solution: RL with LookAhead, Floodfill, and Rules
solution_summary: The team combined a customized HandyRL policy and value network with alpha-beta minimax lookahead, floodfill space analysis, and hand-crafted survival and aggression rules. Extensive checkpoint evaluation and selective switching between policy and search were central to performance. Imitation agents and imitation/RL ensembles added diversity to the submitted flock. ONNX Runtime reduced inference time to one third, leaving more time for search, and the final agent achieved about 1.379 on their local metric against three public HandyRL bots.
compute: TR3970x CPU (32 cores, 64 threads), 128 GB RAM (64 GB used), 2080 Ti GPU; periodic access to a cloud V100 and 128 vCPUs; two full RL runs of 6 and 9 days.

solution_summary: The solution represented typewell depth and horizontal position as a twelve-channel alignment image and predicted a depth class for every horizontal column. ImageNet-pretrained image models were pretrained on physically consistent synthetic wells and then fine-tuned on real wells with additional augmentation and synthetic batches. A coherent trajectory-bank decoder enforced consistency across each whole well. Three image models were blended with a weaker but complementary 1D candidate-verification pipeline. Selection used grouped cross-validation alone, with final pooled CV RMSE of 5.097 and private score of 6.319.

The solution combined YOLOX-s with a ConvNeXt-base Cascade R-CNN detector. Validation trained on videos 0 and 1 and evaluated on video 2, including background images, while final training used all data. YOLOX-s used high-resolution multiscale inference and weighted boxes fusion for test-time augmentation. Weighted boxes fusion combined the detectors, achieving 0.795 cross-validation and 0.726 private leaderboard scores.

The author handled uncertain RNA structures by encoding BPPS matrices as bond-specific color images and extracting sequence-aligned CNN embeddings. Predictions for the three most likely foldings of each test RNA were averaged according to folding probability. They built 109 model variants from recurrent, graph, and autoencoder-based starter pipelines, removed suspicious predictions, and formed a hierarchical weighted ensemble. Multiplying final predictions by 1.04, selected through public leaderboard probing, also helped the private submission.

The solution combined a metadata encoder, a bidirectional GRU light-curve encoder, and a spectroscopic-redshift predictor. Their outputs fed two fully connected layers for class prediction. The light-curve encoder was pretrained as an autoencoder on test data, while the redshift predictor was pretrained on test objects with available spectroscopic redshifts. Gaussian perturbations and observation dropping augmented training, and the top submission averaged five cross-validation runs of three network variants.

The solution combined five U-Net models with 3D SEResNet101, 3D ResNet34, and SegFormer-b3 backbones. It used spatial and depth augmentations, staged training at larger image sizes, and fragment-based validation. Inference averaged rotated and depth-window predictions while excluding patch edges and invalid regions. Fixed-threshold and percentile-threshold submissions achieved private scores of 0.65 and 0.63 respectively.

solution_summary: The author reports using a simple model on market data. They provide a Kaggle kernel link for the implementation. The post gives no explicit model configuration, feature details, or numerical results, and the author attributes some success to luck.

The author used XLM-RoBERTa SQuAD2 after MuRIL performed poorly on the public leaderboard. Increasing batch size from four to sixteen helped, and fold checkpoints were selected using Jaccard score instead of validation loss. The best current model was further fine-tuned on external datasets available on Kaggle. Shared post-processing and inference code also contributed to the pipeline.

The solution used target-specific scikit-learn MLP regressors with RDKit descriptors and fingerprints, supplemented by external polymer property datasets. Mutual information filtering, hierarchical clustering, and iterative permutation importance reduced 4,778 initial features to small target-specific subsets. Inputs were scaled and mixed with PCA, while targets were log-transformed and robust-scaled, with a temperature offset where needed. Architecture and hyperparameters were selected using a custom R2-and-MAE score, followed by repeated fitting and selection of a single best model. Feature selection improved reported R2 for every target, although MAE increased slightly for Tc and Rg.
compute: Approximately 5 seconds per MLP training fit.

solution_summary: The solution combined ViT and TNT encoders with eight-layer transformer decoders. Selective image patches accelerated training, while salt-and-pepper augmentation and RDKit-generated images improved the training data. Output normalization used a cascade to replace invalid InChIs and an agreement rule across models, with cascading providing a large improvement. Two epochs of pseudo-label training gave a small gain, while splitting the decoder into formula and remainder components failed.

The team combined event and app aggregates, device encodings, and sparse app and label representations in a diverse ensemble. Bagged neural networks were particularly strong, with their best initial network reaching a public score of 2.233. The final pipeline incorporated row-order leakage features and rebuilt the 20 best models, then stacked them using neural network, XGBoost, and Extra Trees meta-models weighted 50%, 37.5%, and 12.5%. Neighbor-sequence features failed, and adding leakage features again at the meta-model stage caused overfitting.

The solution combined BERT, XLNet, and GPT2 models with custom heads and auxiliary tasks. Training used bucketed sequence collation and a custom loss that combined overall binary cross-entropy with subgroup-specific terms. Stochastic weight averaging and checkpoint ensembling were also used. The final ensemble averaged prediction ranks from two XLNet models, two BERT models, and GPT2 medium.

The solution used 120 log-mel filterbanks and a CNN that processed time and frequency differently, preserving temporal resolution until the final pooling step. Windowed peak-volume standardization, time stretching, and vocal tract length perturbation improved performance. A single model achieved 90.9% on the private leaderboard. The author also averaged square roots of probabilities from model variants, though ensembling delivered limited benefit.

solution_title: Data Augmentation Improvement for 6th Place Solution
solution_summary: The author added a custom data augmentation method to another participant's solution. The reported result improved from 0.92827 to 0.92894. The post links to a notebook but does not explain the augmentation procedure or underlying model.

The solution combined bidirectional GRU models with word, trigram, and character representations, including a GRU–CNN model for diversity. The strongest single model used three bidirectional GRU layers, label-aware attention, max pooling, and semantic fusion of word and trigram embeddings, achieving reported public and private scores of 0.9863. Strong dropout and per-class learning-rate decay helped control overfitting, while character models improved ensemble diversity and recognition of obfuscated toxic words. A manually checked whitelist of comments with many unknown tokens reduced false toxic predictions and provided a small final improvement.

Validation used ten stratified folds with target creation isolated from validation data. GNN predictions of event status guided prediction shifts, whose magnitudes were tuned separately for each model.

solution_title: 8th place solution: Two stage & kuzushiji data augmentation
solution_summary: The pipeline detected characters with CenterNet using a ResNet18 and U-Net architecture, then classified crops with MobileNetV3 Large. Detection used multi-scale inference and bounding-box voting, while classification benefited from augmentation and confidence-filtered pseudo-label fine-tuning. Book-level group validation guided hyperparameters and detection/classification thresholds. All models were trained on a single GTX 970, and several imbalance and contextual modeling approaches provided little benefit or failed.

They created a visit_number feature counting actual visits and trained XGBoost using it alongside visit_month. Cross-validation was reported as very good, with the proposed explanation that patients developing Parkinson's disease received more frequent visits and analyses.

solution_title: Result of Late Submission: 2D-CNN + XGB + 1D-CNN (Private LB: 0.78703)
solution_summary: This post reports post-competition improvements to a staged XGBoost and CNN contact-detection pipeline. A five-channel 2D CNN, stricter folds with less player duplication, and lagged and grouped prediction features drove major gains. Sequence-level pruning and a fourth-stage 1D CNN improved leaderboard scores further despite little validation benefit. The best reported experiment reached 0.78703 private, and image caching plus NumPy inputs reduced scoring time to about 45 minutes.
compute: Scoring reduced from 3–4 hours to 45 minutes through 2D CNNs, image caching, and NumPy inputs.

solution_summary: The solution calibrated the observations with adjusted AIRS and FGS binning and refined transit boundaries through signal fitting. It extracted seven transit-depth estimates per wavelength using different wavelength grouping scales. A neural network combined wavelength convolutions with stellar information and residual blocks to predict the spectrum. Linear regression on spectrum variability, white-curve variance, and mean predicted spectrum improved uncertainty estimates.

The pipeline selected SuperPoint/SuperGlue or COLMAP SIFT separately for each scene using mean image memory consumption. Large scenes used SIFT, while other scenes used SuperGlue with images capped at a 2560-pixel longest edge. COLMAP incremental reconstruction selected the model with the most registered images and filled missing poses with scene averages. Reported global mAA was 0.7983, with public and private scores of 0.415 and 0.465.

The author combined XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost with averaging across ten seeds. The pipeline used balanced undersampling, removed EJ, constructed ratios from highly correlated features, and added Epsilon_year without imputing missing values. Validation used ten stratified folds based on Class, EJ, and BN. CV scored 0.1172, compared with 0.19 public and 0.40 private scores, and the author reported poor agreement between validation and leaderboard results.

The bot combined heuristic shipyard conversion, role-based ship behavior, spawning policies, and danger-aware navigation. Its main miner policy assigned ships to targets using rewards for mining, attacking, guarding, depositing, and area control. Genetic optimization tuned policy parameters, while an alternative spawning policy imitated leading teams with a small multilayer perceptron and achieved 98% accuracy. Dijkstra navigation and movement priorities supported collision avoidance and friendly position swaps.

The author describes their contribution using LightGBM and XGBoost with fixed tree counts, Huber or gamma objectives, and sample weights. Around 200 features summarize STFT frequency-band energy and raw-signal statistics, with augmentation based on 30,000-sample chunks. Validation holds out one earthquake, and shifting time-to-failure labels for long earthquakes improved cross-validation. To address distribution shift, the team optimized two evaluation measures under possible test distributions; the submission with the weaker public score performed better privately.

The team ensembled diverse pretrained language models with attention, recurrent, convolutional, and masked-sum heads. Validation used multilabel stratification on anchor and score, and training selected BCEWithLogitsLoss after comparing prediction distributions. Useful inputs included natural-language combinations of anchor, target, and context, plus frequent claim words grouped by context. The two final submissions used ridge-derived coefficients for 14 models and Optuna weight search for 15 models, achieving private scores of 0.8641 and 0.8638.

solution_title: 3rd Place Public - We Should Have Trusted CV - 118th Private
solution_summary: The team built a diverse ensemble of 12 model types, including TabNet, denoising autoencoders, DeepInsight EfficientNet, MX10 transfer learning, and PyTorch neural networks. Each model used about 30 folds, producing 360 trained models for inference, and some DeepInsight models used UMAP image layouts for additional diversity. The submitted predictions were postprocessed by reducing probabilities for common targets and increasing them for rare targets that models could not recognize. This improved public log loss by 0.00011 but worsened private log loss by 0.00008; the unprocessed ensemble selected using the best cross-validation results achieved a reported private score of 0.01603.

solution_title: 4th Place Gold - Single Model RAPIDS cuML SVR!
solution_summary: The final model was a TensorFlow MLP trained only on clinical data, using visit month and ten indicators of whether visits occurred at particular months. Indicators distinguished observed visits, observed absences, and unknown future visits, while training rows were expanded to reproduce the forecast horizons. Visit timing supplied the useful signal; protein and peptide features improved validation no more than random features. The MLP achieved CV 55.0, public score 54.9, and private score 60.1.
compute: RAPIDS cuML enabled dozens of model experiments in minutes.

Training retained samples from 2018 onward with nonmissing Epsilon, using its year both as a feature and for joint stratification with the target. Repeated undersampling and randomized splits produced 20 groups of 30 models, with validation scores generally stable across seeds. Features covered win and loss percentages, score differences, recent performance, and ranking snapshots at several points in the season. LightGBM and XGBoost predictions were combined using four-fold grouped validation. The reported LightGBM cross-validation mean was 0.5590 with a standard deviation of 0.0167.

Each fold mixed the competition data with one external dataset. The reported F5 score was 0.965, with training taking approximately 15 hours on one NVIDIA 4090.

solution_summary: The method used one epoch of initial forgetting followed by eight epochs alternating forget and retain training. Initial forgetting minimized KL divergence toward uniform output labels, while subsequent forget rounds used a contrastive objective assigning equal positive weight to retain samples. Retain rounds restored task performance with cross-entropy training. A retain batch size of 256 and cosine annealing during forget rounds improved public evaluation results.

The author trained multiple models with different image sizes in TensorFlow after initially working in PyTorch. Their PyTorch architecture combined EfficientNet image features with metadata features from a multilayer network. The final submission used weighted power ensembling with ranking, with weights chosen to maximize cross-validation performance. It scored 0.9352 in cross-validation, 0.9479 on the public leaderboard, and 0.9321 on the private leaderboard, below some individual models that achieved about 0.9375 privately.

solution_title: [21st place] - My solution to 2 silver medals in GL 2020
solution_summary: For landmark recognition, the author combined five ResNeSt and ResNet global feature models trained with ArcFace, first on GLDv1 plus GLDv2 clean and then at higher resolution on GLDv2 clean. Local features came from the host's DELG baseline because self-trained local feature models performed worse. Reranking combined global similarity, local similarity, and a custom score derived from ranked ArcFace predictions, with the custom term improving the score by 0.006. The recognition ensemble scored 0.5640 and 0.5354 on the reported evaluations. The post also describes a retrieval ensemble of four EfficientNets whose concatenated features were compressed through a learned fully connected layer.

The final solution averaged three BERT fine-tuning approaches: question answering, SWAG-style multiple choice, and span classification. The QA model used tokens surrounding the pronoun as its question, then converted relevant span logits into class probabilities with logistic regression. Five-fold validation stratified by gender and selective fine-tuning of the last six or twelve BERT Large layers were important choices. Extra handcrafted features and Wikipedia language-model adaptation did not improve the approach.

solution_summary: The author trained a neural network and then adjusted its predictions separately for each test-data chunk. The approach exploited small differences in target-flipping rates between chunks, hypothesizing that noisier chunks benefited from predictions closer to 0.5. Nine leaderboard probes tested chunk-specific shrinkage, and the final submissions used different shrinkage strengths for each chunk. The writeup reports that chunk 6 benefited most, while shrinking chunks 1 and 8 worsened results.

The solution extracted ALIKED features and matched them with LightGlue, using multiple image resolutions and advance rotation selection. Expanding the candidate pair search to min_pair values around 60–70 improved both public and private scores by roughly three points compared with 20. Match and detection thresholds were tuned for leaderboard behavior, with min_pair 60 giving the best private score. Parallel CPU/GPU processing and two-GPU feature extraction and matching reduced runtime.

solution_summary: A segmentation model extracted cervical vertebrae, which were cropped into individual C1–C7 volumes for fracture classification. The classifier combined a 2.5D EfficientNetV2-L with a Transformer encoder and vertebra-specific positional embeddings. Overall fracture probability was calculated by summing and clipping vertebra probabilities. A 3D classifier, segmentation-free joint prediction, and a dedicated overall predictor were unsuccessful.

The author improved a public Wav2Vec2 speech recognition baseline by training a custom n-gram language model. Training transcripts were normalized with two Bengali normalizers, standalone visarga characters were replaced with colons, and punctuation was removed. The language model improved public error from 0.445 to 0.436 and private error from 0.534 to 0.515. Fine-tuning XLS-R and MMS models on 30,000 Common Voice 13 samples did not surpass the baseline.

solution_title: Bronze medal: using RCube to solve large Santa puzzles
solution_summary: The author adapted RCube to solve the competition's larger cube puzzles, where its centre-solving routines were effective. Integration required translating state conventions, loading text states, converting coordinate-system operations into physical moves, and exporting competition-compatible move logs. Public optimizers further shortened solutions because RCube was less effective on corners and edges. On the two 33-layer cubes, move counts fell from 123,431 and 139,629 to 25,747 and 25,621 respectively before the additional optimization gains.

solution_title: Private LB: 0.460. Ensemble Model WIth Ordinal Target Encoding
solution_summary: The author describes a cross-validated ensemble of XGBoost, Random Forest, and LightGBM using descriptive statistics of actigraphy enmo and light measurements. The target is represented by three binary indicators for exceeding successive sii thresholds, preserving its ordinal structure. Class probabilities are reconstructed using product-based formulas, and the class with the highest probability is selected. This notebook achieved the author's highest score but was not selected as a final submission.

The team extended a leading public notebook by adding Hunyuan-7B to its ensemble. They constrained predictions using training-set question-answer pairs, zeroing misconception classes never observed for each pair. Adding further models did not improve performance. Other explored ideas included an auxiliary hierarchy of target supersets and a second-stage text model, while swapping misconceptions across correctness groups remained a proposed augmentation.

The best submissions used single pretrained EfficientNet models on log-mel spectrograms. Training emphasized first or last five-second segments, realistic background noise, mixed multi-bird clips, and an explicit no-call class. Adding external no-call recordings was the largest individual improvement, while masking uncertain secondary labels avoided forcing unreliable targets. A validation mixture of bird and no-call clips tracked leaderboard performance and supported selecting a prediction threshold of 0.7.

Nelder-Mead then tuned class-wise multipliers to maximize balanced accuracy, with all tuning performed on OOF predictions rather than leaderboard feedback. OOF log loss fell from 0.105495 to 0.086310, while balanced accuracy increased from 0.889132 to 0.950737.

The solution splits the data into four periods based on the made column and ensembles models including Random Forest and XGBoost. Repeated stratified cross-validation across seeds, stratified by made, guided decisions and measured performance stability. It removes a small number of IQR outliers, uses few estimators, retains all features except CityCode, and adds original data. Artificial features did not improve cross-validation, and the author emphasizes trusting validation over public leaderboard feedback.

It searched arithmetic feature combinations and selected the union of highly ranked features from three boosting models. A diverse ensemble of boosting, neural, linear, and tree models was optimized for AUC with Optuna. Its predictions were then combined with public notebook predictions using public leaderboard ranks as weights, while runtime limits constrained feature selection.

The approach decomposes survival risk ranking into event probability estimation and conditional ranking among patients with observed events. Censored observations receive Kaplan–Meier-derived weights, while event-time ranks are transformed to normal scores for regression and mapped back afterward. TabM, CatBoost, and XGBoost predictions are combined separately for the two tasks before calculating race-group-aware expected ranks; the linked code also includes a small LightGBM contribution. The reported ensemble scores were 0.69936 private and 0.69724 public, with a total runtime of four hours.

solution_summary: The approach builds four noise-contrastive XGBoost models using the eight original classes plus a ninth noise class. It also trains eight binary XGBoost models. The twelve models are combined through stacking, with no validation setup or numerical results provided.

The solution used a single self-quantized DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B AWQ model served through vLLM with its V1 architecture enabled. A single model-generated prompt was supplied as a user-only message, with five attempts per problem to balance stability and runtime. Prefix caching improved inference speed, and long output budgets were considered important for difficult problems. Most gains come from topology-focused post-processing: component removal, skeleton-based thickening, repeated gap repair, Gaussian smoothing, and diagonal bridging.
