solution_summary: The solution trains ArcFace recognition models on YOLOv5-derived fullbody and backfin crops, using EfficientNet-b7 and ConvNeXt-L backbones. Better crops were especially important, while auxiliary species classification, pseudo-labeling, and teacher-feature distillation supported training. Eight models are ensembled by averaging cosine-similarity matrices, with a fixed new-individual threshold and class-balancing adjustments to top predictions. The best single fullbody model achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.781.
compute: Single A100 GPU; 30 epochs take about 30 hours for a fullbody model and 15 hours for a backfin model.

solution_summary: The author combined manual code golfing with iterative refinement by language models. OpenAI Codex Web was the main tool used for the automated refinement. The post links a GitHub repository but provides no further implementation details or quantitative results.

solution_title: 1st PLACE - WINNER SOLUTION - Gilberto Titericz & Stanislav Semenov
solution_summary: The solution used three levels: diverse base models and engineered features, three second-level learners, and a weighted final blend. Shared five-fold splits generated base-model predictions, while four-fold validation guided second-level selection and blend tuning. XGBoost, neural networks, KNN, and t-SNE features contributed most, with extensive bagging stabilizing predictions. The reported cross-validation score was approximately 0.3962, with public and private scores of 0.38055 and 0.38243.
compute: CPU and GPU used for Lasagne neural networks; hardware specifications and elapsed time were not stated.

solution_summary: The author used spaCy tokenization while retaining all tokens and punctuation. Stemming, lemmatization, and spelling correction helped locate word vectors for tokens. The model included two global max-pooling layers, and checkpoints were ensembled. Reliable local cross-validation guided hyperparameter tuning.

The author started with a rank blend of several public notebook predictions, including CatBoost models. The main improvement exploited repeated feature rows by adding out-of-sample target encodings and training-row occurrence counts. CatBoost and a public ensemble pipeline used these features, with their application restricted to test rows matching training rows.

The pipeline combined YOLOv7-X detection with a ResNet and bidirectional LSTM OCR model. Linear interpolation generated training coordinates for chart data points and converted detected coordinates back into numerical series at inference. Geometric heuristics filtered detections and inferred tick locations from label boxes. Additional OCR data improved accuracy from 84% to 89%, but mismatched prediction counts caused roughly a quarter of predictions to score zero.

The final submission used a single XGBoost model with extensive handcrafted features and confidence-filtered pseudo-labeling. Validation grouped examples by WEEK_NUM, although the team found no strategy that aligned reliably with the leaderboard. Count encoding, rare-category collapsing, and selective recovery of highly missing features improved performance. The most influential final adjustment reconstructed test weeks from a date feature and modified predictions over weeks 92–130 to exploit the competition metric.

solution_title: Jumped from 45th to 42nd place? What happened?
solution_summary: The post asks why the private leaderboard changed after the competition ended. The author observes movement in their own position while noting that gold medal positions appear unchanged. It provides no modeling approach, implementation details, or experiments.

The solution split chart extraction into chart classification, component detection, text-orientation classification, OCR, and chart-specific post-processing. ConvNeXt xlarge classified chart types, while TrOCR read detected axis labels. Scatter detection benefited from jointly detecting ticks and using larger images with predictions fused across four inference sizes. Extensive rules converted coordinates into values and corrected OCR symbols, while submission-time fine-tuning on generated scatter images did not improve the score.
compute: About 8 extra hours available during submission for fine-tuning experiments

solution_title: Feature Engineering and Ensemble Architecture (7th place)
solution_summary: The author describes their contribution as NLP feature extraction, feature selection, and ensemble design. Feature engineering improved the performance of multiple models. The post links to the full technical account and mentions attached R examples for RFE and Boruta, but provides no model configurations or quantitative results.

The solution combined a tree-based pipeline using engineered text and event-log features with language models trained on reconstructed essays. Consecutive runs of anonymized q characters were replaced by their lengths, preserving word-length sequences and punctuation structure for the language models. DeBERTa-v3-base and DeBERTa-xlarge predictions were combined using weights. The author reported a private leaderboard error improvement from 0.568 to 0.565 when adding this approach to the public notebook baseline.
The post announces a presentation about the author's competition solution and experience. It links to slides hosted on SlideShare. No methods or results are described in the supplied text.

solution_title: My 9th place solution to the September Tabular competition
solution_summary: The solution combined missing-value-count features, tuned gradient-boosted trees, and a large stacking pipeline. Linear regression worked well as a meta-model over out-of-fold predictions from 34 base models, while seed replication improved individual LightGBM and XGBoost predictions. Training on all available data with more estimators than cross-validation suggested provided further gains. The final submission blended a first-level stacking prediction, five full-data model predictions, and a shared submission.

The author's models use ResNet50 with ArcFace, experiment-based validation, image augmentation, and cell-type-specific training. Dynamic soft pseudo-labels exploit plate restrictions and one-to-one sirna structure, while feature mean normalization reduces experiment bias and incremental hard pseudo-labeling locks confident assignments. Predictions combine 16 test-time transformations and geometric-mean aggregation across sites, folds, runs, and teammates. Iterative probability-matrix normalization and mixed integer assignment enforce unique sirna predictions. Public-score constraints also enabled leaderboard probing, whose estimated private benefit was at most 0.001.
compute: PyTorch on TPUs; $600 in GCP credits used; Cplex solves each assignment matrix in a couple of seconds.

solution_summary: The agent used hand-written rules for factory placement, production, watering, and robot behavior. Factory placement considered resource proximity, rubble density, and distances to friendly and opposing factories. Heavy and light robots had different task priorities, with collision avoidance favoring heavy robots. Late in the game, light robots targeted opposing lichen, while occasional random movement encouraged exploration.

solution_title: 10th solution & thoughts - Part2. LB 0.61 [ Think out of the box version ]
solution_summary: The solution supplemented a TNT/ViT/CAIT ensemble with molecular OCR and an object detector that reconstructed molecules using chemistry rules. A ResNet34 U-Net enhanced images before MolVec OCR, while EfficientDet-D3 detected atom groups and bonds for a custom molecular builder. Replacement rules compared molecular formulas, edit distances, and agreement between OCR and the builder, with OCR used broadly for large images. Updating 7,679 invalid predictions improved the leaderboard score from 0.71 to 0.61.

The agent combined a replay-derived opening book with daily heuristic replanning rather than machine learning. Simulated annealing and beam search drove planning after the opening. Development began from a public shop-routing notebook and evolved through AI-assisted heuristic improvements and local matches. The final opening book used public replays from M & M & P & Q.
compute: Cloud instances with many CPU cores for batches of agent matches
external_data: ["M & M & P & Q public replays", "DECEM and DSM public replays"]

solution_title: 723rd Place Solutions for the AI Village Capture the Flag @ DEFCON31
solution_summary: The author extended a public notebook by solving two additional capture-the-flag tasks. For cluster1, manual filtering in Excel followed by iterative filter removal identified people aged 19–39 working in tech support as the target subgroup. For cluster2, enumerating integers against the scoring endpoint revealed the answer 4. A t-SNE exploration of cluster3 embeddings did not recover all the text, and the final public and private scores were both 3.

The final prediction averages three greedy hill-climbing ensembles and one Ridge stacking ensemble built from a diverse model pool. Each hill-climbing ensemble contains 21–26 models and permits negative weights to correct correlated errors. All predictions use seven-fold cross-validation, with no final calibration or post-processing. Aggressive optimization improved CV but raised overfitting concerns; final public and private scores were 0.05536 and 0.05564.

The solution created features for each level group and also reused features from previous level groups. It trained LightGBM and XGBoost models separately for each level, tuning XGBoost hyperparameters at that same granularity. CatBoost, probability features for stacking, sample weights, per-level F1 threshold tuning, and Word2Vec event-sequence features did not work for the author. Knowledge-tracing ensembles and per-level LightGBM tuning remained untried.

solution_title: private 20th | public 3rd solution: RAFT-refined GR↔typewell matcher
solution_summary: The solution blends a single-well gamma-ray registration transformer with particle-filter residual models and geometry-only predictors. Its strongest component uses shared encoders, a nonuniform drift grid and RAFT refinement, supported by extensive real and synthetic well augmentation. Distance-dependent blending reduces reliance on neighboring geology for isolated wells, while well-grouped validation guides selection. The two selected ensembles achieved private scores of 6.639 and 6.500, and local validation proved more useful than the noisy public leaderboard.
compute: GPU particle filtering with 64 seeds × 500 particles; GPU model and runtime unspecified

solution_summary: The solution used DeepLabV3+ with ResNet and ResNeXt backbones and group normalization at high image resolutions. Models trained on all images with weighted binary cross-entropy were combined with models trained only on positive images using soft Dice loss. The ensemble used segmentation-derived classification scores to scale positive-only predictions, then averaged them with other segmentation predictions. Horizontal-flip augmentation at inference and removal of small predicted masks improved results, yielding a stage-two private score of 0.8627.

solution_title: How I did it: Jeremy Howard on finishing second
solution_summary: The solution used monthly TrueSkill Through Time inference and adjusted player ratings using opponents' average ratings and uncertainty. Predictions came from a cumulative Gaussian with spread controlled by black's skill. Discarding the earliest 40 months and incorporating test-set match counts brought the reported score to 0.653. The author emphasized substantive modeling changes over fine parameter tuning and reported a strong relationship between public and final submission scores.

solution_title: 12th place solution (mysteriously disqualified) - Single ConvNeXt CascadeRCNN
solution_summary: The author used a single ConvNeXt base Cascade R-CNN detector in MMDetection, validated with video-based splits. Training combined bounding-box-centered multiscale crops with balanced sampling of empty and nonempty images, improving CV by about 3% over full-image training. Inference used 3840×2160 images, validation-based thresholds, and temporal detection-cluster filtering to remove false positives. The reported public and private scores were 0.632 and 0.718.
compute: One week spent on the challenge; training hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution built on an existing Siamese network and exploited prediction diversity across many training variants. Roughly 40 prediction sets from different image sizes, color modes, and training continuations were combined through position-wise hard voting and score averaging. Adding classification and prototype models provided further diversity. The combined voting and averaging approach reached 0.941 on the public leaderboard before the final additions.

solution_title: What is your approach and what is your local CV
solution_summary: The author describes feature experiments with a local ten-fold cross-validation log loss of approximately 0.77. Useful features included topic and sentiment representations of selected text sections, clusters of document embeddings, and reduced character TF-IDF representations of variations. The document embeddings were converted into cluster identifiers and distances rather than used directly. Word2vec inputs to a one-dimensional CNN and experiments with an RNN did not produce good results.

The solution extracted image features from a pretrained Inception network and aggregated them into business-level representations. One branch averaged all images for each business, while another clustered similar images before averaging them. Each branch trained nine binary classifiers, and a neural network combined their predictions to capture label dependencies. Adding softmax-layer features provided a small improvement.

The solution combined competition and original datasets, memory-conscious preprocessing, and factorized interaction features. Its final ensemble contained 24 CatBoost, LightGBM, TensorFlow, XGBoost, and LightGBM-based random forest models trained with different data and feature configurations. Ten-fold evaluation guided model comparisons, and hill climbing optimized a linear blend for ROC-AUC. CatBoost was the strongest individual model, reaching 0.895819 with original data included, and the final blend received additional post-processing.

A single SE-ResNet-101 was trained from scratch on human-labeled Open Images data using all 18,000 labels, then fine-tuned on 1,000 stage 1 tuning images. Fine-tuning addressed the substantial difference between training and test label distributions. The author introduced a multilabel softmax cross-entropy loss and used random crops and horizontal flips during training. Ten-crop inference and leaderboard-tuned prediction thresholds and label-count limits improved results; the model without test-time augmentation scored 0.32601 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Used 1×1080; approximately 10 days training and 1.5 hours for stage 2 predictions. Inference without TTA was 10 times faster.

solution_summary: The solution stacked 29 models using an Optuna-tuned ridge classifier. Its meta-features included class probabilities, predicted classes, and Chris' exact formula. Base learners used multiple feature views, including categorical encodings, feature combinations, numerical bins, digit features, and original-data target encoding, with five-fold validation. Bias tuning improved cross-validation but hurt private leaderboard performance.
compute: Laptop used during the competition.

solution_summary: The team validated models on week 9 and formed the final submission as a weighted average of seven models. Their candidates included XGBoost with more than 100 lag-combination features, LR, and libFM using sparse features. To handle unavailable week-11 lag-one values, they trained some models without those features and others using week-10 predictions as week-11 lag inputs. Their best single XGBoost model scored approximately 0.433x on the public leaderboard.

solution_title: [Working Note] 79th Place Solution and Suggesting a Robust Guardrail Design
solution_summary: The submission induced benign business email actions that triggered the competition's confused-deputy scoring predicate. It locally tested attacks against both target models and several hypothesized private guardrails, then selected between single-email and same-domain multi-recipient templates at startup. Recipient uniqueness and a pool of 2,000 candidates supported novelty and throughput within the evaluation budget. The main submission scored 24.090 publicly and 24.060 privately, whereas high-scoring public exfiltration variants scored zero privately.

The solution detects image panels and text with YOLOv8-m, then finds duplicated regions through classical SIFT matching and affine RANSAC. Synthetic training images and manually corrected text annotations support preprocessing that excludes misleading graphs and captions. Low-threshold keypoint extraction, adaptive matching, and image-type-specific geometric filtering make matching viable on low-texture biological images. Two-stage cluster merging and bidirectional geometric mask refinement were essential for accurate instance segmentation.

The solution uses a modified U-Net with inception blocks, strided convolutions, residual skip connections, batch normalization, and an auxiliary nerve-presence head. It trains with Adam and batch-averaged Dice loss, using image augmentation and augmented-image prediction. Random validation splits replaced an unsuccessful patient-based split, and final predictions combine presence estimates from the classification and segmentation branches. The best single model scored 0.694, while an ensemble of six cross-validation ensembles reached 0.70399.
compute: GeForce 1080 or Titan X; batch sizes 64 and 128 respectively. Titan X: about 6 minutes per epoch, early stopping at 15–30 epochs. Batch size 64 requires 6 GB GPU memory.

solution_summary: The pipeline first localized the brain and Circle of Willis, then extracted slice features with separate 2.5D vessel-segmentation and aneurysm models. Sequence models combined those features across depth, with an ensemble of LSTM, GRU, and BERT variants producing scan-level predictions. Hard-negative mining, OOF self-distillation, EMA, and heavy mixup supported training. Two submissions achieved CV AUCs of 0.8909 and 0.9035, but substantially lower private scores; dual-T4 parallel inference processed 11 aneurysm models and 45 sequence models within 12 hours.
compute: 2x T4; inference of 11 aneurysm models and 45 RNN models within 12 hours
external_data: ["Zenodo CT and MRI subset of TotalSegmentator training data", "CoWSeg"]

solution_title: # 28 Solution | Problem with private LB score
solution_summary: The submitted solution combined eight model families in an Optuna-tuned weighted ensemble trained with ten-fold cross-validation. It reused public feature engineering and added binary hydration, osmo, and calc status features. Outlier removal was a particularly influential component, and the author found public scores unreliable for selecting improvements. An unsubmitted variant removed KNN and GradientBoosting and changed the quantiles used for outlier handling, producing a better private result.

The final submission averaged six EfficientNet B0 models trained on Mel spectrograms from the first five seconds of labeled recordings. Its main improvement came from iterative target-domain pseudo-labeling, mixing unlabeled soundscape segments into training audio with randomized amplitudes and maximum-combined targets. Checkpoint soups and variation in spectrogram settings, input sizes, data subsets, and pseudo-label probabilities supported the ensemble. Neighboring-window smoothing completed inference, and the selected stage-two ensemble achieved public and private AUCs of 0.72528 and 0.69035.
compute: Six-model inference could exceed two hours; a two-model notebook took approximately 1 hour 10 minutes.

solution_title: Bronze: from MuZero to a measured hybrid agent
solution_summary: The final agent extended a strong public V78/V79 script with gated rules for garden labor, sheep management, feed recovery, and rival market behavior. MuZero, PPO, imitation learning, and a scripted-planner hybrid were explored, but compute limits, noisy gradients, and rollout distribution shift prevented them from surpassing strong scripts. Exact simulation, paired seat-swapped comparisons, and pinned ladder replays determined which additions survived. Across 252 replayed rated games, the added layers converted 32 losses to wins without reversing any wins and increased average margin by $571.
compute: 96-core Google Cloud VM for PPO/MuZero; smaller Azure VM; Kaggle TPU sessions with 96-core EPYC and 396 GB memory; local 6-core PC with WSL. CPU throughput was 460,072 environment steps/s versus 2,440 with the network.

solution_summary: The author adapted a public cancer subtype classification pipeline with two modifications. They trained a MaxViT Base model, reporting 0.48 on both public and private testing. At inference, they applied a threshold to the maximum mean softmax probability, although the supplied code omits the threshold and fallback output.

solution_title: Bronze Medal Solution - No ML Model
solution_summary: The author built a simple prediction approach based on a public starter kernel. It aggregated historical game results to estimate the probability that a lower-seeded team defeats a higher-seeded team. The post provides no further implementation details or numerical performance metrics.

The best approach extracted pretrained VGG16 features from 512×512 patches and fed them to five gradient-boosted regression trees, one for each sea-lion type. It scored 23.9 on the private leaderboard. Earlier HOG/SVM and six-class CNN approaches produced too many false positives, while adding nearest-sea-lion distances failed at test time. A two-stage CNN detector and count regressor looked promising visually but scored only slightly better than predicting zeros.

The final ensemble combined 32 models, almost all drawn from public solutions, including two notebooks by the author. A GPU logistic regression stacker reached about 0.9702 out-of-fold balanced accuracy, improving to 0.97032 with additional models. A weighted mean of TabPFN-3 and logistic regression stacker outputs reached 0.97043. The best individual RealMLP and boosting models achieved about 0.9691.
compute: GPU used for logistic regression stacking; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_title: 6th Place - PF, PF, PF, PF, Physics and Row-Level Bagging
solution_summary: The solution generated 91 TVT candidate trajectories using diverse, tuned particle filters and fused them with a neural candidate-curve ensembler. Accuracy depended primarily on complementary GR references, a geometry-based physical prior, and full-interval smoothing. Strict out-of-fold construction of the prior and neighbor pools made validation more reliable than public leaderboard ordering. A small global gain corrected amplitude shrinkage, and the final solution achieved CV 5.4577 and private score 5.984.
compute: RTX 5070: one parameter set over 773 wells took about 4.5 minutes without smoothing and 13 minutes with fixed-lag 192.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution for the LLM 20 Questions Competition
solution_summary: The agent combined alphabetic binary search with an online Llama 3.1 8B strategy using eight-bit quantization and no fine-tuning. Its alphabetic component searched a frequency-ranked 120,000-word vocabulary before using the LLM to propose noun phrases. The online questioner progressed through category, location, size, and candidate-splitting questions, while a running natural-language summary supported guessing and recovery from inconsistent answers. The answerer used explicit spelling comparisons and replaced question subjects with the actual keyword; the alpha component achieved an 89% keyword find rate in private matches.

The solution uses RGB images and external HPA data with a ten-model ensemble of ResNet18, ResNet34, and InceptionV3 at two resolutions. Its custom head concatenates attention-weighted average, maximum, and standard-deviation pooling before two fully connected layers. Channel-specific contrast and geometric transformations provide augmentation. Averaging predictions for detected test duplicates improved LB by 0.004–0.005. Lowering thresholds for the five rarest classes was used in the final submissions but reduced both public and private scores.

solution_title: 1st Place of Jane Street 🏆 ➜ Adapted to Crypto 👌
solution_summary: The post presents a configurable crypto forecasting starter adapted from a Jane Street solution. It combines a supervised bottleneck autoencoder with an MLP, concatenating learned features with original inputs. Training both components together within each validation split addresses leakage from separately pretraining the supervised encoder. Gaussian noise, swish activation, batch normalization, dropout, and hyperparameter tuning support the proposed pipeline.
compute: GPU or TPU supported; actual hardware usage unspecified.

solution_title: [18th place solution] Transformer + bpp conv + relative position bias
solution_summary: The solution used only RNA sequences and the host-provided base-pair probability matrix. A single model combined sequence embeddings, a convolution over the probability matrix, and twelve relative-position Transformer blocks to produce two outputs per position. Training used Ranger, MAE loss, and cosine learning-rate decay over 80 epochs. Other features gave little benefit, and the convolution noticeably slowed learning.

The solution combined ten models selected using local cross-validation and leaderboard performance, with diversity in prediction targets and tile layouts. EfficientNet B0 and B4 models included a two-stage approach that learned tile attention weights, then retrained using the best 9 or 16 tiles. At inference, this allowed selection from 128 candidate tiles, and some nine-tile models exceeded 0.90 local CV. The selected ensemble averaged predictions and rounded them, while validation excluded duplicates and suspicious slides. An unselected solution scored 0.936.

solution_title: 4th Place Solution: Hill climbing through the noise
solution_summary: The solution combined many models to improve predictions on a highly noisy target. Hill climbing selected blending weights and outperformed the tested Lasso and Ridge alternatives. Three feature sets included row statistics and counts of individual values. Model diversity also came from manually chosen and Optuna-tuned hyperparameters, including multiple DecisionTreeRegressor configurations.

solution_title: 22nd Place Solution — Five Engines and a Hard Lesson About Leaderboards
solution_summary: The team combined five complementary engines spanning increment-predicting temporal networks, particle filters, template likelihoods, signed-distance U-Nets, and physical or analog decoders. Particle-filter input channels, fake-anchor augmentation, and sibling-well likelihood tables drove major improvements in the initial neural pipeline. Cached out-of-fold predictions supported a 40–50-member ensemble with strict decode consistency checks and a disagreement-based override. Public scores favored several changes that weakened private performance, while validation across 773 wells correlated strongly with private results. The selected CV-oriented submission scored 6.543 privately, and an unselected candidate achieved 6.386.
compute: GPU particle filtering; cached ensemble recipes re-scored in approximately 2 CPU-minutes.

solution_title: Kaggle's Walmart Recruiting - Store Sales Forecasting
solution_summary: The writeup describes a store sales forecasting solution implemented in R. It generates features and trains a gradient boosting model across stores, exploiting similar weekly sales patterns for the same department despite differences in scale. The model struggled to capture periodic behavior in some departments. The reported private leaderboard WMAE was 2561.94597.

The author submitted two independent single models without postprocessing. The stronger model used CatBoost with features including the difference between teams' Elo ratings estimated at the time of their prospective game. Tournament simulations accounted for the wins teams would need before reaching later rounds. A separate Single Query Transformer trained on regular-season results performed worse in 2021, and historical backtests showed mixed relative performance.

41st Place Solution for the Kaggle - LLM Science Exam
solution_summary: The final system averages seven DeBERTa-v3-large models with variation in seeds, training datasets, and pause-token usage, alongside TF-IDF context retrieval at inference. Training uses the shared 60k and 99k datasets, with a common 200-example validation set. Freezing layers and choosing a maximum input length of 512 improved training behavior, while logarithmic TF-IDF scaling and expanded stopwords improved retrieval. The ensemble scored 0.916 publicly and 0.909 privately.

solution_title: RL PPO Self-play Solution (Digs and Transfers Water, Survives Full Game)
solution_summary: The agent used PPO with a U-net-like actor-critic and spatially encoded observations. Invalid-action masking, a learning-rate warmup and decay schedule, and a gradual transition from resource rewards to game outcomes supported training. Self-play mixed current opponents with historical snapshots. After 20 million steps, the agent could collect ice, return it to factories, and grow lichen, although reproduction runs varied substantially. Pretraining on a smaller map did not match the submitted agent's performance.
compute: 20 million training steps; batch size 1152 on Nvidia A10 and 2304 on Nvidia A100.

solution_summary: The final submission rank-blended seven CatBoost and XGBoost models trained with leave-one-out encoding, with three models also using three-dimensional UMAP features. Incorporating the original dataset substantially improved results. Development explored 2,385 models with ten-fold out-of-fold predictions and multiple stacking configurations. The selected blend achieved private AUC 0.89706, while an unselected single XGBoost model performed slightly better at 0.8981.
The post invites competitors to discuss their solutions after the competition ended. It expresses curiosity about other participants' approaches. It provides no implementation, methods, or results.

The solution used ALBERT xLarge v2 trained on SQuAD 2.0 and fine-tuned on tiny-dev. Training augmentation replaced document words with WordNet synonyms, and removing HTML tags also helped. Answer thresholds were selected from ordered model outputs using the observed prevalence of long and short answers. An xxLarge variant performed poorly when constrained to use a very large document stride.

The solution selected useful predictions from 5,000 supplied models using CatBoost loss-change importance and null importance. LightGBM, neural networks and CatBoost were trained on several selected feature subsets and combined by simple averaging. Five-fold CV and repeated runs with five seeds informed model selection and exposed score variability of about ±0.005. Feature selection and mixing neural networks with boosted trees mattered most, yielding a private score of 0.51892.

The solution scaled synthetic ARC puzzle generation and used the resulting data to improve a Qwen3-based ARChitects pipeline. Synthetic puzzles combined human descriptions, separately generated input and output programs, unit tests, and consistency filtering. Supervised training was followed by puzzle-specific LoRA adaptation, batched depth-first decoding, and augmentation-based candidate scoring. The best competition model scored 27.64%; adding Tiny Recursive Model candidates helped the smaller Qwen3 model but did not improve the reported 4B result.
compute: Synthetic generation: 8x H100, 15k tokens/s; 4B full fine-tuning: 32x H100 for 27 hours; TRM pretraining: 8x H100 for 24 hours; competition TRM inference/adaptation: about 2 hours.

solution_summary: The solution combined a 2D Segformer, a 3D SegResNet, and YOLOv8 using the original training data plus an extra dataset with Gaussian blur. Both segmentation models used exponential moving averages, and the 3D model used deep supervision and patch-based training. Seven-fold validation supported a weighted ensemble of 2D and 3D logits, supplemented by YOLO for selected particle types. DBSCAN with a radius scaled to the particle radius produced the final detections.

The selected submission ensembled four model configurations combining DeBERTa-large or DeBERTa-v3-large with an LSTM or GRU. Each configuration was trained on four folds and four additional times on the full training data. The shared inference notebook scored 0.893 on the public leaderboard and 0.894 on the private leaderboard.

The writeup describes separate techniques for a collection of machine learning capture-the-flag challenges. Successful approaches included cluster visualization, pixel counting, white-box image attacks, OCR-mediated XML injection, speech probing, model inversion, and manual language-model interaction. Several challenges remained unsolved, particularly CIFAR counting, single-pixel attacks, and passphrase recovery. Speech dataset probing helped infer a hidden phrase, which was then synthesized as audio.

solution_summary: The author shares a GitHub link to their competition code and submission notebook. They invite readers to inspect the code and provide constructive feedback. The post contains no description of the modeling approach or training pipeline.

The solution first distilled Perch V2 embeddings into a smaller backbone, then trained it with labeled competition audio and soundscapes. Supervised models used 20-second inputs, LSE pooling, waveform mixup, time shifts, and FilterAug. Seed ensembles of hgnetv2_b0 and hgnetv2_b3 generated pseudo-labels for additional training, improving public scores more than private scores. Adding seresnet models brought the private score to 0.956.

The final solution combined 24 models using AutoGluon to ensemble their out-of-fold predictions. Base models included XGBoost, three LightGBM variants, and two AutoGluon models across pipelines with and without the original dataset. All features were retained without feature engineering, and the two AutoGluon models appeared especially important. The author trusted a CV score of 0.94173 despite weaker public leaderboard performance than other submissions.

solution_title: Will implementation of a top scoring solution in practice harm melanoma patients?
solution_summary: The author critiques treating three skin cancer types as equally important within a binary classification objective. Their experiments used three binary classifiers and explored post-processing their outputs to balance recognition across cancer types. Enforcing equal importance improved their private score by 0.002, producing an intentionally unselected submission scoring 0.169. The post emphasizes the distinction between optimizing the competition metric and prioritizing melanoma detection.

solution_title: 98th Place Bronze Solution (43rd on Public LB)
solution_summary: The final approach combined six diverse language models with manually chosen ensemble weights. Custom models were fine-tuned with rank-64 LoRA on original data plus synthetic misconceptions generated for difficult classes. Training used all available examples without a validation split, and augmentation improved the Qwen math model's leaderboard score. Majority-class splitting, undersampling, and head masking did not improve results.
compute: Google Colab Pro high-memory instance with an A100 GPU

solution_summary: The solution combined extensive customer-level historical-loan statistics with features generated by neural networks and LightGBM models. Diverse LightGBM models were trained on random halves of more than 2,000 features and averaged, then blended with the best single model. A separate stack combined LightGBM, XGBoost, random forests, and linear models, eventually incorporating the blending models' out-of-fold predictions. Averaging the blending and stacking outputs achieved local CV of 0.8047, compared with 0.8021 for the best single model.

solution_title: MLP-ResNet on video level features solution
solution_summary: The author used multilayer perceptrons with a ResNet-like architecture. The final ensemble combined networks with different depths and layer widths. Predictions were combined through weighted averaging, with no numerical results or training details provided.

The text documents how to run version 2.02 of a Python implementation for the cause-effect competition. Training uses the competition's train, SUP1, and SUP2 data, but the model architecture and feature pipeline are not described. Training takes approximately 45 minutes, and a prediction example processes the first nine validation entries in 10 seconds. Sample predictions are supplied without an aggregate performance metric.

solution_summary: The solution combined one DeBERTa-v3-base model and two DeBERTa-v3-large models using a weighted average. Different training methods supplied ensemble diversity, including adversarial weight perturbation, differential learning rates, and last-layer reinitialization. Multilabel-stratified validation correlated reasonably well with leaderboard results, and performance on sparsely represented essay topics was particularly informative. Pseudo-labeling, masked language modeling, and adding essay prompts did not improve the solution.

The author describes a five-fold MuRIL-Large blend trained on chaii, MLQA, and XQuAD as a stronger alternative to the submitted XLM-RoBERTa approach. MuRIL-Large reached a public score of 0.75 before subsequent tweaks reduced it. The XLM-RoBERTa submission had overfit the public leaderboard, while MuRIL-Large performed better outside that leaderboard. The main lesson was to rely more consistently on cross-validation when selecting models.

The author trained a shallow LightGBM regressor on the ddG portion of an external dataset shared by jinyuan. Features described mutation position, amino acid properties, DSSP structural information, neighboring residues, and the number of mutations associated with each wild type. The final weighted ensemble combined LightGBM with Rosetta, Thermonet V2, wild-type SASA, and mutation B-factor differences. No validation or leaderboard scores are reported.

The pipeline generated bitmaps with fine-tuned SDXL Turbo and converted them to SVG using carefully tuned Vtracer settings. OCR hallucination suppression and SVG compression, precision reduction, and pruning improved evaluation compatibility while preserving visual quality. Vector-style prompts and score-driven retries across seeds improved individual outputs within a global time budget. Other diffusion models were less efficient, and direct SVG generation with Gemma did not improve results.

solution_summary: The team trained animal classifiers on official detector crops, finding 224-pixel crops better than 64-pixel crops. Their final ensemble combined six NTS models with EfficientNet, with ensemble weights selected by local-validation grid search. Training used horizontal flips, CLAHE, and inverse-frequency class weights. At inference, they reconstructed image clips and assigned each image the label obtained by averaging probabilities across its clip; the final ensemble scored 0.843 public and 0.848 private.

solution_title: 80th Place. Outrunning the Tide of Public Shares
solution_summary: The author ran Sparrow repeatedly to generate packing layouts, focusing on smaller instance sizes where it was competitive. These layouts were combined with public submissions by retaining useful packings across the 200 instances. A particularly complementary public dataset improved 40 packings and helped reduce the combined score to 70.1484. Overlap handling used small layout inflation or replacement with valid layouts from safer submissions.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled sparse generative classifiers extending Multinomial Naive Bayes. Its base models combined document, label, and hierarchy-level multinomials with hierarchical smoothing and TF-IDF or BM25 preprocessing. Different folds and random-search objectives diversified the models. Feature-weighted linear stacking predicted documents for each label to optimize macro-F-score, with label priors and vote thresholds determining how many documents to assign.

The author built a multilevel stack using 15 LightGBM configurations, each averaged over 20 seeds, plus 32 variants of 15 additional model types. Scaling and feature subsets were selected according to cross-validation performance, with Standard and Robust scalers used most often. Nine first-level meta-models combined the base predictions. Linear Discriminant Analysis served as the final second-level model.

solution_title: [Silver Medal | Rank 50 | Score 0.087] My Approach to NeurIPS – Open Polymer Prediction 2025
solution_summary: The solution converted polymer SMILES into RDKit physicochemical descriptors, Morgan fingerprints, and MACCS keys. Separate models were trained for each property, using CatBoost for Tg, LightGBM for density, Random Forest for Rg, and stacked ensembles with a RidgeCV meta-learner for FFV and Tc. Feature cleaning, stratified validation splits, and prediction blending supported stability. The reported leaderboard score was 0.087.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution | Google - Isolated Sign Language Recognition
solution_summary: The solution combined an EfficientNet-B0 trained on one random fold with BERT and DeBERTa trained on the full competition dataset. Landmark sequences were processed as image-like tensors for the CNN, while transformers also received motion and geometric features. Extensive augmentation and Optuna tuning supported performance, and combining model outputs without softmax added about 0.01 to the score. The final ensemble reached approximately 0.81 on the leaderboard, with manually rewritten Keras models improving inference speed.

solution_summary: The solution engineered demographic, vehicle, popularity, and quote-history features after cleaning transaction data. Customers were split into three folds, and a first set of GBMs predicted whether each coverage option would change at purchase. A second set of multinomial GBMs used the first-stage predictions to choose the final coverage value. For each coverage option, three-model ensembles implemented the change decision and subsequent replacement prediction.

solution_title: [2nd Place Solution] - Robust CV and LGBM
solution_summary: The solution trained five LightGBM models using both the original and supplemental training data. Features combined the 300 original columns with time-level averages of selected target-correlated features and row-wise summary statistics. Purged cross-validation with an embargo and early stopping based on cross-validation correlation helped control overfitting. Autoencoder MLPs, feature neutralization, and PCA did not work.

solution_title: Solution Writeup: Jigsaw - Agile Community Rules Classification
solution_summary: The final system combined DeBERTa, a LoRA-tuned Llama classifier, and Qwen embedding-based nearest neighbors through weighted rank averaging. DeBERTa used URL-derived features, expanded training examples, and a hybrid classification and supervised contrastive loss. Llama used few-shot supervised fine-tuning with pseudo-labeled test samples, while Qwen scored rule-specific neighbors by similarity and signed labels. Two DeBERTa seeds were averaged, and Llama inference ran across two GPUs.
compute: Llama inference in parallel across two GPUs; one epoch of Llama fine-tuning.

solution_summary: The solution combined three frozen OpenCLIP image encoders and trained an embedding head with batch normalization and subcenter ArcFace. Dataset selection was a major contributor, with Food101 added to the final mixture late in the competition. Training only the head for five epochs matched the performance of longer runs and enabled more experiments. PCA, backbone fine-tuning, saliency cropping, horizontal-flip TTA, and autoencoders did not help.

solution_title: 21 place solution: Trust CV & Differential fusion
solution_summary: The team built separate RemBERT and XLM-R ensembles, diversifying models through random seeds and external Hindi and Tamil training data. They trained five folds for each configuration and included models only when their CV exceeded 0.68, prioritizing validation over public leaderboard performance. Adding data did not improve individual models, so diversity across ensemble members became the main strategy. Their best private-score submission achieved 0.760 but was not selected because its public score was lower.

solution_title: 84th Place Solution: SDXL-Turbo -> GPU SVG Conversion + OCR Decoy
solution_summary: The pipeline generated bitmap candidates with SDXL-Turbo, converted them into compact SVGs on GPU, and appended a small OCR decoy. It scored candidates with the competition metric using PaliGemma 10B at 448×448 and selected the best within roughly a minute per prompt. Fast generation and conversion enabled about 12 attempts, while two static scoring questions worked better than cheaper scoring alternatives or generated questions. Alternative image generators produced nicer images but did not improve leaderboard performance.

solution_summary: The solution used a U-Net with a CAFormer encoder and repeatedly refined it using simulated seismic data generated from its own test predictions. Forward modeling converted predicted velocity maps into synthetic seismic–velocity pairs, which were used to continue training the current best model across six cycles. This simulation-based pseudo-labeling was the central improvement, while additions from OpenFWI were considered unnecessary in hindsight. The reported public and private scores were both 16.4.
compute: Forward simulation distributed across multiple CPU instances; hardware counts and total runtime unspecified.

solution_title: Sharing Solution of Rank 23 (0.88625 on Private LB)
solution_summary: A logistic regression model classified NDF versus non-NDF using one-hot encoded session features. Its predictions became inputs to XGBoost alongside raw features, encoded session features, and basic engineered feature combinations. The author kept this two-model pipeline with limited additional ensembling because cross-validation and leaderboard results did not correlate well. The solution ran in about 20–25 minutes on a 4GB MacBook Air.

solution_summary: The solution combined competition data with the original dataset, removed multi-label rows, and engineered three features while dropping selected inputs. Four multiclass boosting models were tuned with Optuna using ten-fold cross-validation and fold-averaged predictions. An out-of-fold ensemble aligned validation splits across three pipelines and optimized weights with Nelder-Mead, followed by blending with public submissions. Pseudo-labeling, XGBoost stacking, and changing the evaluation metric did not work; a separate equal-weight public-notebook ensemble achieved 0.89684 public and 0.88923 private scores but was not selected as the final submission.

The solution ensembles 3D UNets, primarily custom SE-ResNeXt152 encoders with attention decoders, trained to regress signed distance fields. Its central loss combines boundary-weighted L1 regression with a continuous mass-based Dice term. Raw predictions are averaged across checkpoints and flip augmentations, with inference performed on full volumes to avoid sliding-window artifacts. Thresholding and iterative topology-aware tunnel filling refine the segmentation, improving the local topology score by about 0.08. Local validation and public leaderboard results correlated poorly with the private leaderboard.
compute: Two GPUs for sharded inference; TTA reduced for larger models to fit the 9-hour Kaggle runtime.

solution_summary: The solution trained pretrained image networks on cached mel spectrograms and combined six models. Manual removal of long segments without target birds, audio mixing, noise augmentation, contrast changes, and high-frequency attenuation were central choices. Validation used recordings resembling the test data, while background bird labels received reduced targets. Predictions were combined with a root-mean-square rule and adjusted using evidence of a bird elsewhere in the recording; pseudo-labeling slightly reduced quality.
compute: Described PC as weak; cached mel spectrograms to speed training.

solution_summary: The solution used SE-ResNeXt50 with 320×512 images and cross-entropy loss. To address conflicting labels on identical or related images, the team trained five-fold models and blended their out-of-fold predictions with ground-truth labels at a 3:7 ratio to train a new model. Training augmentation included brightness, contrast, blur, flips, shifts, scaling, and rotation. Inference averaged five folds with five test-time augmentations, and the team emphasized trusting cross-validation given the small, imbalanced dataset.

The team generated artificial signals containing Gaussian noise and 50 Hz hum, using Fourier transforms to construct the hum component. Their feature pipeline relied mainly on Gaussian mixture and hidden Markov model outputs, with signal means and standard deviations helping convergence. They aligned each channel's average signal to zero using hidden Markov predictions. They hoped this would improve anomaly detection in small classes, but abandoned using all the data along the way.

solution_title: 21st Place Solution: You don't need cell tiles
solution_summary: The approach trained image-level Puzzle-CAM models using ResNeSt-101 and EfficientNet-B4 with global average pooling and focal loss. Training compared activation maps from full images with maps from four image tiles. At inference, class activation maps were multiplied by individual cell masks and image-level class probabilities, with Swish activation providing a small improvement. Final cell probabilities combined per-image standardization followed by sigmoid with a gradient-boosting mapping learned from single-class training images.

The pipeline localized the cervical spine, generated approximate slice labels from segmentation-derived vertebra ratios, and trained sequential fracture classifiers. A 2.5D CNN and attention-equipped RNN first learned from slice windows, then a new RNN was trained on full studies with the CNN frozen. Study-wide cropping and consistent augmentation reduced irrelevant variation without using fracture bounding boxes. The final ensemble combined six resnest50d and four seresnext50 weight sets, with inference taking about 4.5 hours.
compute: Intermediate model training: approximately 9 hours per fold; final inference: approximately 4.5 hours.

solution_summary: The solution stacked 19 diverse base models trained on four cleaned and engineered datasets. Base learners included deep neural networks with categorical embeddings, LightGBM models trained at different grouping levels, and L1/L2 regression models. Neural networks added valuable diversity, while a regularized Gaussian GLM with five-fold validation and meter information provided the strongest ensemble. The best stack scored 1.245 on the private leaderboard compared with 1.270 for the best blend; more complex meta-learners tended to overfit.

solution_title: Toad Brigade’s Approach - Deep Reinforcement Learning
solution_summary: The team developed a self-play reinforcement learning agent whose single convolutional network jointly controlled all units and city tiles. A fully convolutional ResNet encoded spatial state, discrete embeddings, and global game information, with game-phase features proving especially valuable. IMPALA training combined additional policy and value losses with frozen-teacher regularization, progressing from shaped rewards and a small network to sparse rewards and a 24-block network. Test-time rotation averaging, deterministic action selection, and handwritten coordination rules improved deployment behavior. The agent developed sophisticated resource control and long-term strategies but retained weaknesses in fuel budgeting and recovery from losing positions.
compute: Personal PC with 8 cores/16 threads and two GPUs; training overnight most nights. Inference took 2–2.5 seconds on Kaggle servers with batch size 2.

solution_summary: The final submission used a single LightGBM model without post-processing. Rich location-and-time target encodings and lag statistics supplied much of the predictive signal, and Optuna selected features and training-data filters. Validation used observations exactly one week before the test period, with training restricted to matching day and time combinations. Wide neural networks failed, and the author acknowledged that the encodings lacked out-of-fold protection against leakage.

solution_title: 52nd - Silver Medal - RAPIDS Forest Inference Library!
solution_summary: The solution extracted embeddings from RoBERTa-base and RoBERTa-large trained on previous competition data and used them to train XGBoost. RAPIDS FIL enabled comparisons of every possible pair of test comments, whose probabilities were converted into individual toxicity scores. Final submissions were selected using leak-free cross-validation despite poor public leaderboard results, achieving CV 0.707 and private score 0.804.

The team used two stages of SchNet models with molecular geometry, atom attributes, and bond-related edge features. The second stage incorporated out-of-fold coupling predictions on other edges while excluding the target edge to prevent leakage. Multiple seeds and folds were combined using quantile regression, selected cyclic-learning-rate checkpoints, and median aggregation. The second SchNet stage reached about -2.85 on the leaderboard, while the aggregation changes added roughly 0.01–0.02.

solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned a pretrained wav2vec2 XLS-R 1B model for CTC speech recognition in three training stages. A smaller Bengali model filtered the competition audio to the best-scoring 70%, and training used waveform perturbations plus segment-wise and concatenated speech augmentation. Decoding used a KenLM language model trained on cleaned, deduplicated IndicCorpv1 and IndicCorpv2 text, followed by normalization and dari processing. An update clarified that the final submission used a 7-gram model, which scored the same as the initially reported 6-gram version.

solution_title: 16th place write-up: EEG montages -> 2D image + specs
solution_summary: The solution converted spectrograms and normalized bipolar EEG plots into a single large image for a pretrained TinyViT backbone. Training began with examples having more than seven voters, then used a ten-seed ensemble to pseudo-label the remaining data before retraining. A six-seed ensemble formed the final predictor, with flipping augmentation, EMA, and test-time flipping. Label-quality filtering, globally normalized EEG plots, backbone choice, and large input images mattered most; pseudo-labeling, EMA, and TTA provided smaller gains.

solution_title: [MIT] Solution and evaluation code: The Ladder as the Object of Study
solution_summary: The final agent extended Rozen's public V10 policy with selective lethal search and a guarded Boss's Orders priority. Only two of five tested changes were retained after ladder testing. Repeated submissions of an identical build varied substantially, and match tests did not establish an overall win-rate improvement. The public repository provides experiment records and evaluation code but omits replay-derived inputs and a named-card attachment.

solution_title: Gold Medal Solution with Under $60 of Compute
solution_summary: The final agents used Transformers trained from scratch by behavior cloning on top-game replays, followed by a thin inference rule layer. Exact action conversion, masking invalid requests, and jointly predicting worker actions and ordered market orders were central to making imitation work. Checkpoints were selected through full games rather than validation loss, and reinforcement-learning post-training and weight averaging weakened deployed policies. The wider model won 92–36 against the smaller model on fresh local seeds, but the smaller model performed better on the ladder because it handled other opponents more reliably.

solution_summary: The solution combines six YOLOv5 detectors with a second-stage classifier that rescales detection confidence. Three-fold validation grouped by video guided optimization, and final detectors were trained on all data. Classification predicts seven IoU threshold targets from cropped detections, with strong dropout and stochastic depth improving performance. Temporal confidence boosting raised cross-validation F2 above 0.74, while tracking was excluded despite a small gain.

solution_summary: The model predicts changes in player coordinates from the previous frame rather than absolute positions. RoPE identifies the future frame targeted by each embedding, and training uses Huber loss with Muon optimization. A two-stage pipeline combines 2023 NFL competition data with current competition data, expanding to all players through pseudo-labeling in the second stage. Exponential moving averaging uses a decay of 0.995.

The solution retained a public alignment, grid-rectification, and signal-extraction pipeline while tailoring preprocessing to each image type. Converting detected thin black grid lines to red improved grayscale image types, while stronger bilateral filtering and illumination correction addressed moiré artifacts. Another image type benefited from contrast correction and removal of median blur. Evaluation on 50 training samples showed a mean gain of 0.502, with a reported private leaderboard gain of 0.242.

solution_title: [24th place solution]: Pretrain tasks is the key!
solution_summary: The team adapted DeBERTa models with masked language modeling and whole-word masking, and explored several model architectures and custom heads. Its final ensemble used simple prediction averaging. Post-processing addressed annotation misalignment and tuned thresholds by case and feature, restricting thresholds to 0.45–0.55 after broader tuning hurt leaderboard performance. Post-processing improved both public and private scores by about 0.001, while pseudo-labeling, multisample dropout, and recurrent heads did not work for the team.

The author's best submission combined a graph neural network with predictions from public notebooks. It performed well on the public leaderboard despite a fatal bug later discovered in the graph neural network's training code. The author expected its performance to deteriorate, but the final outcome exceeded that expectation.

The author modified the Chessmetrics rating system with player-specific time decay, rating padding, and joint iterative monthly rating estimation. Each player's decay constant depended on their number of games, while padding blended performance ratings with an opponent-based prior. Monthly ratings were repeatedly updated using previously estimated opponent ratings, including both earlier and later games. The best submission was an early variant that had not looked particularly strong in public scoring or cross-validation.

The solution used only competition data and processed WSI and TMA images separately. WSI images were downscaled and tiled with background-based filtering, and models were trained on six randomly sampled tiles per image. A three-stage procedure introduced prediction-derived auxiliary labels, retrained from scratch, and then fine-tuned with a smaller auxiliary loss weight. EfficientNet and MaxViT models were combined by voting, while auxiliary predictions identified Other cases; this outlier handling improved TMA private performance by 0.06.

The final blend combined public boosting approaches with the author's own models and validation choices. Coordinate-derived distances were important features. The author validated on supplied competition data before adding external data to training, then blended with models validated on the merged data for diversity. A Keras neural network tuned with keras_tuner contributed additional diversity despite a local CV score of only 0.59.

solution_title: 4th Place Solution — Cross-Attention Template Reranker + Protenix + RNAPro
solution_summary: The pipeline allocated three predictions to diverse template-based structures and one each to Protenix and RNAPro. A CUDA implementation of US-align generated roughly 1.42 million structural similarity labels for training a cross-attention template selector. Template choices combined sequence similarity, predicted structural similarity, and cluster diversity, with diversity contributing more than scoring refinements. De novo inference included co-folding and overlap-based processing of long sequences, while coordinate averaging and secondary-structure features offered little benefit.
compute: P100-class GPU; pair labeling reduced from days on CPU to hours on one GPU.

solution_title: 6th Place Solution: Detector-Free SfM & Transparent Scene Trick
solution_summary: The solution used Detector-free Structure from Motion for general scenes and a separate circular-trajectory reconstruction strategy for transparent scenes. General-scene reconstruction combined sparse matching, resolution-dependent dense matching, confidence-guided match merging, COLMAP, and iterative geometric refinement. Transparent scenes were identified through foreground segmentation, then image ordering was recovered from pairwise similarities with a traveling-salesman formulation. The selected ALIKED-based variant scored 0.225 publicly and 0.191 privately, while a tested SIFT variant achieved a better private score of 0.201.

solution_title: Really Curious what worked for people
solution_summary: The author converted audio clips into spectrograms with 37 time samples and 40 frequency bins using a short FFT. Classification used deep belief networks built from stacked restricted Boltzmann machines with 500 logistic units per layer. Training combined greedy pretraining with prolonged dropout training. Random forest model combination did not work well, and increasing feature resolution or model size did not improve performance.

The method first pruned 99% of model parameters using an unstructured L1 criterion and reinitialized weights randomly. It then fine-tuned on retained examples using cross-entropy plus an entropy regularizer that matched the original model through mean squared error. Careful tuning of learning rate, epoch count, and mild class weighting was central to performance. The reported public and private scores were 0.0932121752 and 0.0863052371.

The final submission combined DeBERTa models and LightGBM through weighted averaging. The overview calls the neural models two DeBERTa-v3-large models, although the detailed configuration lists one large and one base model with different text inputs and pooling. Grouped layer-wise learning-rate decay and freezing four layers near the embeddings were the main reported improvements. Validation grouped examples by prompt, and the ensemble achieved CV 0.4777 and private leaderboard score 0.46163.

The solution supervised-fine-tuned a model on deterministic, stepwise reasoning traces generated by problem-specific solvers. Numeric solving used a compact operation set and operation-family-aware guessing, while bit traces used hexadecimal compression to fit additional search within the token budget. Cryptarithms used multiplication-pattern lookup, constraint propagation, and backtracking, solving 24.2% of a local cryptarithm dataset within budget. Category-specific synthetic augmentation supplied substantial training data, and the author described two-stage training to separate memorization from execution; the supplied text ends before the full modeling details.

solution_title: 79st Place solution: A Hotchpotch of EfficientNets
solution_summary: The solution classified detected faces frame by frame using five EfficientNet models with different resolutions, datasets, and training variants. RetinaFace replaced MTCNN for faster, better face detection, and the final classifiers used PyTorch. Predictions from 25 evenly spaced frames per video were combined by a simple mean and clipped to 0.01–0.99. Model diversity was central to generalization, while late adoption of augmentation was identified as a limitation. Very low local validation loss suggested possible unidentified leakage.

The solution trains several convolutional motion-prediction models for one epoch on the full Lyft training set and combines sampled trajectories through a three-component Gaussian mixture model. Updating l5kit and matching training sample eligibility to the test data produced major gains. Cosine learning-rate decay, cutout augmentation, and full-set validation further strengthened the pipeline. The final ensemble achieved public and private scores of 10.272 and 9.475.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution for the Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations
solution_summary: The solution treated gene-expression prediction as multi-target regression using neural networks with categorical embeddings and truncated SVD. A first-stage ensemble generated pseudolabels for all 255 test rows, which were added to training for a second-stage ensemble of 20 model configurations. Optuna optimized model parameters and ensemble weights using custom cell-type validation, while repeated training and median aggregation reduced variance. Final predictions were clipped to per-column bounds, and the code ran in about one hour on a laptop CPU with 8 GB RAM.

solution_summary: The selected submission combined eight GBDT models, eight MLP models, and two Event-masked PRL-NN variants. The tree models used survival target transformations, while the MLPs relied on out-of-fold predictions from a separate set of 14 GBDTs as meta features. The neural models explored several target representations and race-stratified regression or ranking losses, with five-fold validation for the in-house models. Adding another public XGBoost solution improved ensemble CV to 0.68748 but was omitted after a public leaderboard decline. GNNs, SurvivalGAN data, Gaussian-noise test-time augmentation, and DeBERTa experiments were unsuccessful.

The solution used only the competition RSNA data in a three-stage pipeline: slice selection, vertebra localization, and severity classification. Slice selection used an encoder, transformer, and classifier, while localization combined segmentation with a coordinate-prediction fallback. The classifier consumed 128×128 crops from five consecutive slices and paired multiple frozen pretrained encoders with multiple classifiers. Training randomly selected an encoder-classifier pair per batch, and inference averaged every pairing. The author reported better results than separately training and averaging models, while acknowledging possible bias in those tests.

solution_title: [Public 9th Private 25th Solution] Consistent CV and LB Results in a Decrease on the PB.
solution_summary: The team fine-tuned token-labeling models using adversarial weight perturbation and hyperparameter sweeps, then combined models through probability averaging and voting. Post-processing corrected name BIO sequences and address newline labels, while recall-oriented thresholds favored retaining potential PII. Dual T4 inference supported seven-model ensembles with a maximum sequence length of 1024. solution_title: 2nd place model (team Dmitry & Leustagos) is released

The final blend combined EfficientNet B4/B3, ViT base/small, and ResNeXt50 models with different image sizes and crop strategies. Training included removal of roughly 150 suspicious healthy samples, cluster-label pretraining on 2019 images, robust losses, and several augmentations. The team combined pretrained MixNet spectrogram models with raw-EEG CNN–Squeezeformer models. Patient-grouped validation and reconstruction of a compact, high-quality dataset were crucial, alongside signal-specific augmentations and careful normalization. Spectrogram models benefited from separate montage channels and magnification of the central ten seconds, while raw-signal models also used noisy labels with decaying weights. A learned blend of 23 base models plus class-specific logit biases achieved CV/public/private scores of 0.207/0.22/0.27.

solution_title: 10th Place: Single Model Using Snapshot Ensemble w/ code
solution_summary: The solution trained a pretrained SE-ResNeXt50 on all training data, with separate spatial squeeze-and-excitation pooling for each grapheme component. Random erasing, geometric augmentation, and three cosine learning-rate cycles helped generalization without a held-out fold. Averaging snapshot probabilities achieved a private score of 0.9536, improving on the best single snapshot by 0.0037. Later ablations supported random erasing and component-specific pooling, while an additional post-processing experiment reached 0.9653.

solution_summary: The solution used StyleGAN with parameter tuning, improving the public score from 140 to 35. Images were cropped to bounding boxes and randomly flipped horizontally. Resource limits led to reducing the style generator input channels to 256. Truncation, auxiliary classification, and several data-cleaning approaches did not improve results.

The solution averaged DenseNet and Dual Path Network segmentation models with U-Net-style and LinkNet-style decoders. Training used ten folds, cycle learning, deep supervision, Lovasz loss, and DenseNet-generated pseudo-labels for DPN. Horizontal-flip inference augmentation and copying adjacent vertical masks in reconstructed jigsaws completed the pipeline. Pseudo-labeling improved the public score by 0.001.

solution_title: 10th-place solution - Agnostic loss for semi-supervised learning
solution_summary: The author iteratively expanded training labels by selecting highly confident positive and negative frames from ensemble predictions on training and test recordings. Models trained on five-second audio windows with a loss that excluded unknown class labels, allowing both true-positive and false-positive annotations to be used. Three-channel mel-spectrogram inputs and audio augmentations supported ResNeSt models and a ResNeSt-based sound-event detection model. The best submission blended ResNeSt-50, ResNeSt-101, EfficientNet-b1, and the sound-event detection model using performance-based weights.

The solution reconstructed sales from yearly totals and separate country, store, product, and day-of-year ratios. Country ratios came from World Bank GDP per capita and were adjusted with linear regression, while store ratios were held constant. Product ratios were estimated separately for odd and even years and smoothed with FFT. Ridge and Huber regression modeled daily ratios using cyclical features, weekdays, and carefully selected holiday offsets.

The solution used Cascade R-CNN with HRNet backbones and multiscale training and inference. GPU memory constraints required training on 1024×1024 crops, while inference used full images with a maximum size limit. Increasing the training and test scales improved the reported leaderboard score from 0.935 to 0.946. Ensembling HRNet_w32 and HRNet_w48 results raised the score to 0.950.

Predictions were summed across model families for each variable and multiplied across variables, with a PCA-based stack providing small further gains. Base models included LightGBM, XGBoost, two SVRs, kernel ridge regression, a neural network, and a two-layer GRU, followed by LightGBM and neural-network stacking. solution_title: My Bet On What The Private Guardrail Was
solution_summary: The author built fixed attack portfolios for transfer from a public guardrail to an unknown private defense. Online Successive Halving explored attack mechanisms, while a locally reconstructed guardrail grid guided portfolio allocation with a worst-case floor. The stronger final portfolio allocated 68% to payload-free confused-deputy attacks, with exfiltration, destructive actions, and read-action chains as insurance. It scored 9.54 privately versus 6.20 for a more concentrated portfolio, supporting the value of anchoring on a broadly surviving mechanism.

The author's contribution was a two-stage recommender generating roughly 100–200 candidates per session and ranking them with LightGBM using about 100 features. Candidates came from previous actions, weighted co-visitation matrices, Word2Vec, and Node2Vec. Embedding similarity to the last item and recency-dependent co-visitation candidate counts were especially useful, with chronological validation using weeks three and four. Two rankers were combined per target, followed by rank voting with teammates' predictions, producing a final private score of 0.600.

solution_summary: The solution trained bird classifiers on mostly five-to-seven-second clips with reduced weight for secondary labels and modified mixup. Ensemble diversity came from multiple CNN backbones, mel-spectrogram resolutions and powers, and noise augmentation. Custom post-processing combined clip probabilities with audio-wide, day-wide, and geographic information, outperforming learned meta-estimators on validation and the public leaderboard. solution_title: 45th Place: CatBoost Stacker paired with MLP Embeddings
solution_summary: The final solution stacked 53 models using a GPU CatBoost classifier fed 159 prediction features and 32 MLP embedding features. The MLP was trained on the original dataset, and its embeddings supplied context for routing predictions on synthetic competition data. A logistic regression stacker deteriorated when correlated models were added, motivating the nonlinear meta-learner. Validation used 25 seeds and five stratified folds, achieving 0.970422 out-of-fold balanced accuracy and 0.97024 on the private leaderboard.

solution_summary: The solution used spaCy entity recognition to extract candidate dataset names and a hand-written grammar to identify genuine dataset references. A second pass searched publication texts using keywords from the strict matches to recover missed mentions. Training data informed the grammar rather than directly training the predictor. The author sampled ten slices from each of four MRI modalities and averaged each modality into one 2D image. These images were concatenated into four channels and projected to three channels with a 1×1 convolution before EfficientNet predicted MGMT status. Taylor Cross Entropy was chosen to handle possible label noise in the small dataset. Training used a publicly shared PNG version of the competition data.

The solution used a custom expectation-maximization algorithm for a Gaussian mixture model tailored to the discovered data structure. Only 14 variables were retained, and integer variables were power-transformed before Gaussian modeling. The model represented 42 components arranged into seven label groups, with structured covariance blocks and floating-point means fixed to zero or plus/minus one. Encoding these constraints produced the author's best leaderboard score.

solution_title: 9th Place Efficiency Solution for CommonLit-Evaluate Student Summaries
solution_summary: The author built an efficiency-focused pipeline based on engineered text features. The strongest features were logarithms of counts of words, bigrams, and trigrams present in a summary but absent from its prompt. Validation was organized by prompt, and attempts to extract additional features using DistilBERT and TF-IDF did not work. The submission scored 0.45943 on the public leaderboard and 0.51579 on the private leaderboard; the downstream pipeline details appear only in an image.

The pipeline used CLIP similarity to screen scenes and combined gimlightglue with alike_lightglue for initial matching. A second matching pass focused on regions selected by clustering the initial correspondences. Loop-consistency filtering and limiting matches to the top 1,500 improved accuracy and efficiency, with secondary matching raising the reported public score to 41.7. Test-time training, additional classifiers, person masking, and multi-resolution or rotation corrections did not improve public performance.

solution_title: Breaking the SFT Ceiling on Nemotron-3-Nano-30B
solution_summary: The final selections were two Nemotron LoRA adapters: V2 trained on deterministic solver reasoning traces and V8 checkpoint 400 as a structural hedge. Increasing sequence length was a major breakthrough, while subsequent solver extensions, trace audits, and targeted synthetic data did not surpass the original adapter. Models learned log-transformed costs under repeated stratified cross-validation, with original data added to every training fold. TabNet, neural networks, linear base models, and an Optuna ensemble did not improve the selected approach.

The author used a single U-net to segment the left ventricle after rescaling, center cropping, and enhancing local image contrast. Training masks were manually drawn for two frames per training patient. Segmented areas were integrated across slices, then a gradient booster corrected systematic volume errors using patient features. Error variability by heart size was used to generate predictive CDFs, and reported volume MAE was roughly 9 ml.

solution_title: Reverse-Engineering the Evaluator: Source-Grounded Agent-Failure Discovery
solution_summary: The authors analyzed evaluator source code first to identify reachable predicates before spending model queries. Their sentinel-post submission used reasoning-skipping prompt structure and shared-prefix alignment to improve throughput. They also submitted a web-search-to-email chain as a hedge against a different private defense, but it failed to execute reliably under scored replay. Both submissions scored zero privately, highlighting both sentinel fragility and the gap between interactive and replay reliability.

solution_title: My approach to the Santa 2020 challenge
solution_summary: The agent combined exact Bayesian updates from its own pulls with an LSTM estimate of the opponent's posterior beliefs. The LSTM used only binary indicators of each player's pulls and learned distributions with KL-divergence loss. Deception tactics concealed reward information through repeated initial pulls and penalties for actions that revealed the agent's true beliefs. Performance evaluation used expected candy totals converted into estimated win probabilities to reduce outcome noise; the author estimated a 63% win probability against strong opponents.

The solution combined a ridge model with three neural models using different text representations: word counts, shared fastText embeddings, and character n-grams. Preprocessing limited names and descriptions to 60 words and incorporated encoded brands and categories into the name feature. Representation diversity mattered, while an LGB model did not help the combination despite strong standalone performance. Doubling neural-network batch sizes after each epoch improved speed, and the published kernel scored 0.38888 publicly and 0.38948 privately in 2800 seconds.
