solution_title: 14th Place Solution for the Google - Fast or Slow? Predict AI Model Runtime Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined graph compression, engineered graph features, and graph neural networks trained with ranking losses. Layout models processed both a three-hop neighborhood graph and a configurable-node graph, while the tile model used three GraphSAGE layers without graph reduction. Numeric normalization was essential, and validation used the competition's supplied split. Layout predictions were ensembled by min-max normalizing scores within each file and summing them, which outperformed rank averaging and Borda count.

solution_title: 155th place and 19 flags solutions (no medals but a lot of fun!)
solution_summary: The author describes solutions for 19 of the competition's 27 capture-the-flag tasks. LLM challenges were solved through prompt changes involving hypothetical disclosure, sequence completion, generated flag formats, and DNS-record requests. Other tasks used semantic-similarity exploration, pixel counting, clustering, visualization, and executable pickle behavior. For embedded token data, t-SNE and K-means separated the content into four visually interpretable groups.

The final solution combined seven large convolutional networks across four image resolutions using a weighted average of model outputs. CutMix, CoarseDropout, extended training, and some variation in validation splits supported ensemble diversity. Class-frequency-based prediction scaling was especially important for the recall metric and robustness to the final leaderboard change. Their strongest individual network achieved 0.9980 locally and 0.9892 publicly, but its inference cost led them to exclude it from the final ensemble.

solution_title: 20th solution - 2 models, various embeds, mixed loss
solution_summary: The author averaged eight classifiers from two architectures trained over four folds, using different combinations of pretrained word embeddings. One architecture combined LSTM and TextCNN, while the other combined LSTM, GRU, and global pooling. A mixed binary cross-entropy and soft F1 loss improved both cross-validation and public scores and made threshold selection more stable. Models trained for four epochs with a cosine learning-rate schedule, and the classification threshold came from out-of-fold predictions. The final submission scored 0.698 in cross-validation and 0.699 on the public leaderboard.

solution_title: 25th Place Solution - Candidate-Path Ensemble with Residual Correction
solution_summary: The solution generates physically plausible TVT paths and combines learned candidate selection with structural and gamma-ray alignment predictors. A fixed ensemble establishes the absolute level, while discrete cosine transforms fuse reference-path residuals at different along-well scales. Endpoint tapering preserves the base prediction at both boundaries. Well-grouped validation improved from 5.732 to 5.713 RMSE, and the final private RMSE was 6.599.

solution_title: From-scratch 2.5D ConvNeXt detector + ILP tracker — Private 0.939

Its strongest detector combination averaged probability maps from two models with different Gaussian target widths before peak extraction. Validation on both embryos using the official full-pipeline scorer was crucial, as many apparent gains failed to transfer. The best unselected model scored 0.939 privately, whereas the two submissions selected for stronger public scores both scored 0.917.

Small wreath puzzles used bidirectional breadth-first search, while large wildcard wreaths used a specialized ring-correction algorithm with randomized preprocessing. solution_title: Sharing My ARC Prize 2024 Code (31 Points in the final submission)
solution_summary: The author trained custom transformer architectures from scratch and combined them in an ensemble that achieved 31 points. Active inference and reverse augmentation were central improvements over an early version that scored about four private-test points. Specialized grid positional encoding and a compact 19-token vocabulary supported the architecture. A transformer mask modification was disabled in the final submission, while the impact of a progressive head remained uncertain because of bugs.

The final solution used XGBoost with frequency features computed from training data and real test rows, excluding fake test rows from the frequency reference. Counts were normalized by the maximum count and multiplied by the original variables to create interaction features. These features and parameter tuning raised the public score to 0.916. Augmentation reduced performance, and investigations of timestamps and customer IDs were unsuccessful.

The solution used SE-ResNeXt50 with three component prediction heads, an auxiliary 1,292-grapheme head, and an ArcFace loss. A frozen binary mapping connected component logits to grapheme logits, while the grapheme loss received substantially more weight than the other losses. Sample-wise CutMix was the most useful augmentation, supplemented by progressively introduced grid shuffling. Self-training on 300,000 unlabeled Ekush images with soft targets and grapheme-balanced sampling improved generalization, and predictions from four randomly split folds were ensembled.

solution_title: Dato Truly Native? Winner's Interview: 2nd place, mortehu

A memory-efficient custom SVM implementation supported 79 million features, with per-class regularization selected through 10-fold cross-validation. The second model used 30,000 selected substrings, while date-related clues exploited differences in when positive and negative documents were downloaded. Combining six times the SVM predictions with the XGBoost predictions achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.99017, compared with 0.98519 and 0.98856 for the individual models.

The solution first trained image-level CNNs and saved their global average pooling features. It reconstructed CT studies by sorting slices by z-position, then trained study-level bidirectional GRUs on the saved features. Seven CNN models used different training-validation splits, extensive augmentation, and input resolutions between 384 and 512 pixels.

The final solution averaged LightGBM, CatBoost, and CNN predictions, benefiting from their different feature representations. The CNN processed interpolated multiband time series alongside detection-weighted flux and interpolation-distance channels, then combined its representation with metadata from a small MLP. Training used sample deletion, flux-error noise, cyclic shifts, and channel scaling across four folds with learning-rate changes and best-weight averaging. Three neural variants scored 0.857, 0.857, and 0.814 individually, while their average scored 0.791; test-time augmentation degraded leaderboard performance.

The final submission combined CT models, tabular neural networks, and Bayesian ridge regression, with the ensemble selected by cross-validation. The CT pipeline used Concatenate Tile Pooling with ResNeXt50 and ResNet18, first training on masked lungs and then fine-tuning on original scans. It modeled FVC and uncertainty over time with a carefully initialized Laplace log-likelihood objective, while tabular validation controlled leakage and evaluated the last three visits. CT models alone performed modestly, while the final ensemble achieved reported private/public scores of 6.8385/6.8884.

solution_summary: The final prediction blended a pseudo-labeled ensemble of three DeBERTa-v3-base models with a separate 22-model stack. The stack combined trained transformer predictions with regressors fitted to frozen transformer text embeddings. Four-fold out-of-fold predictions fed a Lasso stacker, with log transformation and robust scaling providing a small validation improvement. The stacked model achieved CV 0.4473 and leaderboard score 0.43, while a frozen DeBERTa-v3-large embedding model reached CV 0.4518.

The author trained separate LightGBM quantile models for each forecast horizon and quantile across all aggregation levels. Sales were normalized by their nonzero mean and detrended with horizon-lagged rolling means so forecasts remained independent across horizons. Calendar, price, rolling, and target-encoded features supported the models, with normalized and clipped WSPL training weights. Memory and runtime limits required restricting training dates and weekdays, while validation on only two horizons raised concerns about overfitting.

solution_title: Complete MIP formulation and Python code
solution_summary: The author states that their competition approach used a mixed-integer programming formulation. They shared the formulation and Python implementation in a GitHub repository with explanations and comments. The code requires Gurobi, but the post provides no formulation details or results.

The final submission combined two model sets with a weighted blend. One pipeline used CatBoost with stratified grouped validation, adjusted advantage features, and agent-swap augmentation during both training and inference. The other combined CatBoost, LightGBM, and DeepTables, including text TF-IDF features, grouped validation, stacking, and prediction postprocessing. Agent-swap test-time averaging improved the first pipeline's out-of-fold score from 0.4059 to 0.4030.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution - Track me if you can
solution_summary: The solution combined WiFi localization and three sensor models through discrete trajectory optimization over known and generated waypoints. A custom beam search minimized penalties for WiFi similarity, movement, distance, temporal consistency, and grid preferences. Time and device leaks supported floor prediction and estimates of sensor reliability. Selecting among three waypoint grids improved the score by about 10 cm, and a fixed trajectory holdout tracked private leaderboard performance well.

solution_title: Taylor-made NN for 0.285 PLB (part of solution of 8º)
solution_summary: The author built a Keras neural network that learned separate encodings for categorical and numerical inputs within the reg, car, and ind feature groups. Careful parameter tuning, classifier dropout, embedding regularization, and positive oversampling supported training. Smaller training portions allowed finer stopping decisions because the network overfit very quickly. Predictions were averaged across five folds and up to 20 seeds, and this network was the strongest individual component of the team's ensemble.

solution_title: [2/21 Update] Private 13th, Public 52th Place Solution. My first medal competition.
solution_summary: The final solution combined five-fold EfficientNet, DenseNet, Inception, ViT, and ResNeXt models with class-specific ensemble weights optimized using Optuna. Training mixed several losses and augmentation strategies, including Mixup Without Hesitation, SAM, soft-label training on deduplicated 2019 images, and knowledge distillation. Two stratified validation strategies guided model selection, and resize/center-crop inference improved selected models. The reported ensemble achieved CV 0.9071, public LB 0.905, and private LB 0.901, with the best-CV submission also performing best privately.

solution_title: ProtoSSM + SED Blend & Why Rank-Space Taxonomy Smoothing is a Trap
solution_summary: The final pipeline combined two ProtoSSM stages, ResidualSSM refinement, an SED model, and CatBoost predictions for five difficult classes. Its most consequential choice was applying taxonomy smoothing in probability space before rank-space blending, yielding 0.944 private versus 0.938 with rank-space smoothing. Pseudo-labeled Stage 2 remained in the final submission despite hurting generalization. Removing that stage after the deadline improved the private score to 0.946.

The approach combined gamma-ray dynamic-programming alignment, particle tracking with backward smoothing, transformer predictions, and a multiresolution exact grid smoother. Replacing the reference with the well's own labeled landing log and preserving the measured initial dip were major improvements. Five well-level folds and a separate 77-well holdout guarded against overfitting, although later stacking made cross-validation optimistic. The reported best cross-validation RMSE was 7.57 ft and the final private RMSE was 7.855 ft; the supplied text ends during the detailed dynamics discussion.

The team generated artificial training examples by randomly pairing training instances and predicting the difference between their targets from distance features. At inference, they paired test instances with training instances, added predicted differences to known targets, and averaged repeated estimates. Their cosine-distance experiment scored approximately 0.534 on both leaderboards. Memory constraints prevented experiments with a larger generated dataset.

solution_title: 27th place, +720 place shake up with NN model
solution_summary: The author combined LightGBM predictions and a Transformer neural network in an equal-weight ensemble. The neural model attached EfficientNet to a Transformer and used only 60% of the competition training data because compute was limited. The LightGBM component came from public notebooks. The author attributed the unexpectedly strong private-leaderboard outcome primarily to the neural model.

solution_title: 2nd place solution - Test & Compare ASR algorithms
solution_summary: The solution used a deeper and wider convolutional Transformer encoder with GRU-based CTC and Transformer attention decoders. Standardizing all landmark coordinates, normalizing signer handedness, and extending training to 400 epochs were important improvements. Three seed models were ensembled, with CTC prefix scores enabling joint CTC-attention decoding that improved performance by about 0.007–0.008. The final reported public and private leaderboard scores were 0.82 and 0.81.

solution_title: Dave Slate on Winning the R Challenge
solution_summary: The solution used a custom ensemble recursive binary partitioning algorithm with 43 original and synthesized features. Feature engineering combined package dependencies, user installation histories, maintainer information, and text overlap from CRAN descriptions and package pages. Repeated five-fold cross-validation and leaderboard feedback guided feature selection and parameter tuning. Duplicate-label copying and dependency rules enhanced the initial submission; the described selected submission achieved 0.988157.

solution_title: 1st place - How to win the competition if you know nothing about image processing
solution_summary: The author solved image chronology manually by grouping images by location, matching images captured on the same day, and ordering those groups using visual changes. Google Maps helped identify locations and likely shared flights. Shadows and overlapping image regions were the main cues for matching acquisition dates. Construction progress, mud tracks, sand piles, weather traces, and vehicle patterns then supplied chronological evidence across each location.
compute: About 2 weeks of manual image inspection; no computing hardware stated.

solution_summary: The solution combined correspondences from LoFTR, HardNet, ALIKE, DKM, and SuperPoint with SuperGlue, then estimated geometry using MAGSAC++. Multiple image scales, horizontal-flip inference, confidence filtering, and dataset-dependent settings were central to the approach. Validation used a subsampled competition training set, although the author considered its distribution imperfect. The selected submission scored 0.828 privately; an unselected variant with fine-tuned DKM scored 0.831.

solution_title: Get to 2430 with the Power of Randomization!
solution_summary: The author combined TSP conversion, permutation rebalancing, and MinMax CTSP optimization to construct short strings. Randomized rebalancing helped escape local minima, yielding a non-wildcard solution of length 2440. The final improvement modified selected transition costs, reoptimized tours with LKH, and placed wildcards on favorable transitions. This produced a final score of 2430, while further bridge and joint-optimization experiments did not reach 2428 or 2429.

solution_title: My First Non-Tabular Competition. And Its a Silver!!!! 🥈 (41st place Solution)
solution_summary: The author saved predictions from experiments with BERT variants and input formats, retaining models that improved ensemble correlation. Adding an electra-large backbone raised the public score to 0.8504. The final post-processing multiplied predictions in eight score intervals by factors optimized with Nelder-Mead against Pearson correlation. This raised the public score to 0.8507 and reportedly improved private scores by more than 0.0005.

solution_title: Mask RCNN based solution (Keras and pytorch)
solution_summary: The author's solution was based on Mask R-CNN. They used both Keras and PyTorch implementations and experimented with different backbones. The post links to the solution code but provides no training settings, validation details, or performance measurements.

The solution ensembles four ByT5-base models trained through task-adaptive pretraining, supervised fold training, and additional fine-tuning on aligned sentences. Data preparation combines agent-generated sentence alignment and pseudo-labels with manually aligned, segmented, and filtered external examples. Name replacement augmentation, length-ratio stratification, and minimum Bayes risk decoding support the final pipeline, which also mentions ridge regression and an Onomasticon. Additional fine-tuning improved the reported ensemble scores to 36.9 LB and 37.3 PB, while adding the pseudo-labelled model produced 37.5 PB.
compute: TPU for task-adaptive pretraining, around 10–15 epochs.

solution_summary: The team trained three DenseNet201 models on roughly 7,000 images after removing poor-quality and duplicate images. One model used 448-pixel crops with test-time random cropping and flipping, while two used 512-pixel inputs and modified fully connected layers. Majority voting combined the three models, producing public and private scores of 0.962 and 0.969. Switching from Keras with Theano to PyTorch enabled training within their limited compute budget.
compute: Single Titan X GPU; a DenseNet-like network ran in less than 8 hours.

solution_summary: The solution used rule-based dataset-name extraction without training a predictive model. Keyword-specific extractors examined surrounding tokens using spaCy, and the author refined their rules by inspecting frequent extracted mentions. Document-frequency filtering reduced the candidate list before a second document search. Searching longer names first and masking matched text prevented redundant predictions of shorter names embedded within them.
compute: Notebook runtime: 20–25 minutes.

solution_summary: The team trained football agents with distributed off-policy reinforcement learning, combining self-play with games against a changing mixture of opponents. Supervised learning from top-player replays and early knowledge distillation accelerated training before reinforcement learning took over. The model combined player attention, action-history GRU features, player-interaction CNN features, and separate policy, value, and return heads. Expanded directional pass and shot actions and varied starting states improved play, and the final model reached roughly a 90% win rate against hard built-in AI. A weighted policy ensemble performed best locally but could not be submitted before the deadline.
compute: Small experiments used 96 CPU worker cores plus a 24-core CPU and one NVIDIA T4 learner; large experiments used eight 96-core workers plus a 96-core CPU and four T4s. Approximately 4,000 CPUs and 20 GPUs were used in parallel during the last three days; the final agent trained on approximately 700,000 games.

solution_title: Fast and Simple: Ranker fine-tuning + Embeddings + Classifier
solution_summary: The approach fine-tuned multilingual-e5-base for ranking rule-violating comments, then used its embeddings as classifier inputs. Features combined subreddit, rule, and comment embeddings with a rule-to-comment similarity score. An equal-weight voting ensemble of five conventional classifiers achieved column-averaged AUC of 0.89437. The author emphasized inference efficiency and CPU deployment as practical advantages.
compute: Deployment can run on parallel CPU cores; actual training hardware and time unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution built patent search queries as OR combinations of AND-connected subqueries and optimized their selection with simulated annealing. Candidate subqueries were constructed to retrieve only target patents, allowing the objective to focus on target coverage. Compact query syntax, frequency filtering, and candidate deduplication reduced query and search complexity. GPU-accelerated intersections with CuPy were two to three times faster than Python set intersections and enabled broader field coverage.

The solution fine-tuned gemma2-9b-it-fp16 with QLoRA through several stages of general preference-data training and competition-specific adaptation. A competition-adapted model generated pseudo-labels for additional datasets, which were incorporated into renewed training before final competition fine-tuning. Soft label distributions were crucial because hard labels did not provide satisfactory improvements. Inference used sequence-length-dependent dynamic batching and selective response-swap augmentation for uncertain predictions.

solution_summary: The solution combined three largely out-of-the-box 3D nnUNet models trained with default, aggressive, and no augmentation. Aggressive augmentation benefited substantially from test-time augmentation, but that combination was underused in the final ensemble; a 2.5D model was rejected.

The team used a pure segmentation ensemble of EfficientNet U-Nets with B7, B4, and B0 backbones. Models were trained at 256x384 and fine-tuned at full resolution, with mixup, label smoothing, AdamW, and a Noam scheduler among the successful choices. Class thresholds, a minimum area of 100, and a pixel threshold of 0.3 controlled predictions. A reported alternative class-three threshold achieved public and private scores of 0.92016 and 0.90819.

solution_title: 13 Robust Features: Bridging 15 Years of Manufacturing Experience with Machine L
solution_summary: The approach used LightGBM with a deliberately restricted set of 13 features for a stable and explainable pipeline. Inputs combined coordinates, five photometric bands, redshift, categorical metadata, spherical coordinate transformations, and a logarithmic delta feature. Optuna supplied systematic hyperparameter tuning in Kaggle Notebooks. The post does not report a score or validation results.

Objects can be translated by dragging and rotated with the mouse scroll button, while square distance is displayed. solution_summary: The solution combined Qwen 14B instruction and coder retrievers with a Qwen 32B AWQ reranker. Retrievers first learned from 7,000 GPT-4o-generated examples and then were fine-tuned on competition data using LoRA. The reranker treated the top 25 candidates as multiple-choice options and optimized cross-entropy over their answer characters. Five-fold LoRA fusion was used, while attempted distillation from a 72B model showed no offline improvement.

The author shared a simple public notebook using regression models for the task. The approach was inspired by Chris and the author's recent work on CIBMTR. The notebook was not selected as a final submission, and the post provides no model specifications or numerical results.

The solution ensembles Mask R-CNN models with ResNet-50 and ResNet-101 backbones. It averages masks and combines scores using proximity-based weights. Training stopped after a few epochs despite continued improvement because training, inference, and prediction generation were time-consuming on images exceeding 4K resolution. The ensemble offered less benefit than expected, and the authors believed more training epochs would have been a better use of their time.
compute: Training stopped after a few epochs because training and prediction generation were time-consuming.

solution_summary: The solution used separate U-Net segmentation models for each class, with collage-level white balancing and channel alignment. Positive and negative sampling, class-specific model settings and cross-validation helped address sparse classes. Water was segmented jointly and then divided into lakes and rivers using contour size and proximity rules. Vehicle predictions averaged up to 15 models and were cleaned using other class predictions, while final polygons required topology-preserving simplification.

solution_summary: The solution combined a rotation-resistant matching model with Alike-LightGlue and scene-specific adjustments. Center cropping and filtering nearly stationary keypoint matches helped transparent objects, while detecting keypoints in four image sections targeted finer church details. The final submission used a simple-radial camera model for every scene. End-to-end matchers, matched-point region cropping, and CLAHE were excluded because of runtime limits or poor results.
The post links to a video discussing the author's solution and other leading solutions. It also includes an image. The supplied text contains no technical description of the approach.

The solution combined two CatBoost models, one LightGBM model, and one neural network using weights chosen from cross-validation performance. Feature engineering adapted public code, rescaled date differences into years, and added features inspired by the previous Home Credit competition. Validation mixed week-grouped stratified folds with stratified folds using week-based sample weights. Linear shifting and week-number restoration were tried, but the better private result came without metric hacks.

solution_title: Solution - Single transformer without val dataset
solution_summary: The author used a shallow transformer with modified embedding and fully connected layers, label smoothing, learning-rate warmup, and late dropout. Landmark preprocessing normalized handedness, standardized sequence length, and added motion and hand-joint distance features. Small rotations provided some benefit, while a later two-seed ensemble improved after an inappropriate learning-rate reduction was reversed. The corrected ensemble achieved 0.7683 public and 0.8445 private scores.

The solution combined aggregated time-series features and deep autoencoder representations with feature engineering and LightGBM. Rows without targets were removed, and Optuna optimized the three prediction thresholds. The final submission used models and thresholds obtained in Google Colab with voting across manually varied seeds, although a single model performed better than seed averaging.

solution_title: AIMO3: a collection of delightful side quests
solution_summary: The final solver used a layer-wise distilled clone of Nemotron-Cascade-2-30B-A3B, selectively quantized to FP8. It generated eight parallel Python-assisted rollouts and combined answers with entropy-weighted majority voting, achieving a private score of 41. Validation used 50 hard IMO-AnswerBench problems under a five-hour single-H100 budget with three fixed-seed orderings. Pairwise self-verification did not beat the simpler harness, and substantial speculative-decoding work remained outside the final submission.

solution_summary: The final blend combined two ResNeXt models and two ResNeSt models trained on five-second audio crops. Aggressive noise augmentation, modified mixup with union targets, and additional recordings helped address the mismatch between training and test audio. Post-processing applied a 0.5 threshold, site-specific temporal aggregation, and limits on the number of predicted birds. Validation was unreliable, and the five-fold ResNeXt50 alone ultimately produced their best submission.

solution_title: 38th solution, data driven to find embedding weights
solution_summary: The approach combined three pretrained embeddings with data-driven weights of 0.5 for GloVe, 0.4 for para, and 0.1 for wiki. Learned embedding weights were averaged across five folds, and text was lowercased after case-preserving lookup proved ineffective. The author evaluated blended predictions within each validation fold and examined correlations to assess model diversity. Focal loss achieved 0.712 single-model local CV, but its ensemble validation was not completed.

The author presents neural network outputs estimating ventricular volume at 1 mm intervals along the left ventricle's long axis. The region of interest comes from the intersection of four-chamber and two-chamber views. They manually labeled 200 hearts and bootstrapped from those annotations to hearts 1–700. Illustrated failures include incorrect ventricular localization and insufficient short-axis coverage near the heart's end.

The author trained a U-Net imitation learning policy using 1,100 episodes from three Toad team submissions. Improvements included a city action model, flip and rotation augmentation, wider U-Net channels, and a hybrid stochastic and deterministic action policy. The final submission used separate early-, mid-, and endgame models with different loss weights and stacked current and previous states. Limited compute and time led the author to focus on imitation learning instead of pursuing reinforcement learning.

solution_summary: The author trained a RoBERTa named entity recognition model with concatenated output layers, convolutional layers, and Dice loss. An initial model trained on dataset-containing token crops generated approximately 3,000 candidates for manual review. The final model was retrained using positive and negative examples from those candidates, then filtered using prediction length, confidence, keywords, and duplicate merging. Dataset co-occurrence clusters supported validation and sampling, although validation remained unreliable; the reported public and private scores were 0.497 and 0.347.

The solution combined several ImageNet-initialized CNNs with two additional layers of tree models. CNN top-five predictions and duplicate-image hashes generated candidate classes, turning the large multiclass problem into binary candidate verification. Class-frequency priors, including frequencies among nearby product IDs, exploited a slight dataset leak. Weighted third-layer predictions and averaging two inference pipelines improved the ensemble, while pseudo-labeling hurt downstream stacking despite improving individual models.

The solution searched over a three-stage pipeline that extracted parts from an input, transformed those parts, and recombined them into candidate outputs. Each stage allowed an identity operation, enabling simpler solutions such as cropping or recoloring alone. The large combinatorial search was refined through submission feedback, with unhelpful functions removed because the public and private evaluations were the same.

GPU hill climbing selected a weighted ensemble of seven models from hundreds of diverse candidates. The selected models combined target-encoded and arithmetic-feature XGBoost models, CatBoost with categorical bins and group statistics, and two residual-learning pipelines. Five-fold out-of-fold predictions determined ensemble weights, after which models were retrained on all training data and averaged across seeds. Diversity mattered more than individual model scores, and the final ensemble achieved 0.05880 CV RMSLE and 0.05841 private leaderboard RMSLE.
compute: GPU used for candidate modeling and hill climbing; hardware model and runtime not specified.

solution_summary: The author used EfficientNet-B7 and an ensemble of EfficientNet-B6 and B7, with Ben Graham preprocessing and an image size of 299. EfficientNet performed better than the tested DenseNet and ResNet architectures, while batch size and learning rate tuning were important. Three- and five-fold validation were unreliable, so the author used macro F1 to assess model quality instead of quadratic kappa. Focal loss did not help, external data was excluded after experimentation, and pseudo-labeling remained untested because time ran out.

solution_title: A OK solution without peeking test data --  we are hiring talented:)
solution_summary: The author combines original numeric variables with cumulative target encodings and uses a LightGBM classifier. The encoding sorts each variable's values and computes cumulative target sums divided by cumulative counts, with five stratified folds generating out-of-fold training features. Test features are encoded using training labels, without exploiting the true-versus-fake test split discussed by other teams. The reported score is approximately 0.912, although the model training loop is omitted.

solution_title: Congrats to STRAYA, NCCU and adamaconguli!
solution_summary: The best submission combined GBMs that incorporated time and historical teacher behavior. A particularly useful feature described teachers' own donations, rather than donations they received. Teachers who donated to exciting projects were more likely to post exciting projects themselves. The author believed stronger time decay would have helped and reported choosing the wrong submission.

The solution used a DenseNet121 ArcFace identifier with bounding boxes and landmarks predicted by five cross-validated models. Identity and test representations were formed by taking the centers of multiple embedding vectors and comparing them with cosine similarity. Training included singleton identities, mixed aligned and unaligned images, and treated horizontal flips as separate identities while masking their competing logits. New-whale predictions were calibrated to an expected proportion of 0.276, and the final reported private scores ranged from 0.965 to 0.968.

solution_summary: The solution used XLM-RoBERTa-large models trained with translations of the supplied data and combined them through rank averaging. Translation into the target languages was the main reported training improvement. Language-specific scaling of intermediate ranked predictions, supported by repeated CV split experiments, improved global AUC. The full post-processing routine added roughly 0.004, with a further small benefit from averaging predictions for similar texts.

solution_summary: The solution combined embeddings from six ECA-NFNet-L0 image models with TF-IDF title matching. Image training used ArcFace, GeM pooling, limited augmentation, and validation-driven checkpoint selection with a custom weight-averaging procedure. Titles were cleaned and translated from Indonesian to English before image and text matches were retrieved separately and their unique labels combined. A second TF-IDF pass over predicted label sets helped make matching rows more consistent.

solution_title: Child Mind Institute PIU 3rd Place Solution
solution_summary: The solution used LightGBM with 100 repetitions of stratified five-fold cross-validation to stabilize results on a small, noisy dataset. Features summarized actigraphy measurements, activity streaks, and light exposure, alongside selected public-notebook features and custom instrument features. Training data was augmented through missing-value injection and Gaussian noise after simple imputation. Models predicted PCIAT totals, which were converted to sii classes using thresholds optimized on repeated out-of-fold predictions, then combined by majority vote. The stable approach achieved validation QWK of 0.454–0.456 and optimized QWK near 0.470; later fixed-seed leaderboard tuning worsened private scores.

solution_title: Part of 2nd place solution (only kaggle/colab TPU were used)
solution_summary: The author trained an EfficientNet-B3 regression model on large mosaics assembled from slide tiles. The central improvement was using MSE for Karolinska samples and Huber loss for noisier Radboud samples, limiting overfitting to noisy labels. Training used extensive image augmentation, cosine learning-rate scheduling, and checkpoint selection based primarily on Karolinska validation. The single model achieved 0.891 overall validation QWK and 0.927 private QWK, and contributed to a diverse team ensemble.

solution_summary: The solution combined more than 200 CNN models with clustering and post-processing driven by incidence angle. Incidence-angle patterns separated a consistently iceberg-only group from a second group with mixed labels. Retraining CNNs exclusively on the second group improved ship detection by reducing distracting signal. Cross-validation guided clustering thresholds and conservative probability adjustments to control log-loss risk.

The pipeline converted pathology slides into image tiles and trained five-fold base models to identify noisy training labels from held-out predictions. It then retrained two model families on cleaned data, including a cleaning variant that removed 20% of Radboud labels. Final inference combined EfficientNet-B0 and EfficientNet-B1 models, with only folds 1, 4, and 5 used for the second family. The competition submission achieved public/private scores of 0.904/0.940, and a fixed-seed reproduction achieved 0.894/0.939.

solution_summary: The submission combined GPT-120B, Eagle3 speculative decoding, and an adaptive Tree-of-Thoughts solver with 8–16 parallel attempts. Reinforcement attempts restored earlier conversation and Jupyter state, while quadratic resource scaling and effort-weighted answer selection managed constrained inference. The final model was fine-tuned by freezing the model head and training the last transformer layer on cached hidden states. The final structured-prompt SFT submission scored 36 public and 38.5 private, below the base model's 39–41 public results with a simpler prompt.

Candidate SVG evaluation combined a weighted three-question pseudo-VQA score with an adopted OCR hallucination prevention function, restricting OCR checks to top candidates. Geometric transformations, category-specific pseudo-VQA questions, and score distribution calibration did not help.

The approach constructed three training variants using sliding target windows of 14, 28, and 42 days. Historical visitor and reservation aggregates were grouped by restaurant, weekday, holiday, area, and genre over multiple lookback periods. LightGBM, XGBoost, and neural-network predictions were blended within the approach. Averaging the three target-window variants improved the offline score by 0.002, substantially more than blending model types.

solution_title: My scalable and industrializable solution with Scala+Spark
solution_summary: The post links to an external blog describing the author's competition work. It claims the implementation is ready for industrial use and can scale to massive datasets. The supplied text provides no concrete modeling, preprocessing, or validation details.

The solution reduced instrument noise before estimating transit boundaries and screening unreliable samples with simple polynomial fits. A custom nonlinear limb-darkening model then jointly fitted all wavelength channels using sparse nonlinear least squares. A staged increase in system-polynomial order reduced degeneracy between instrument effects and limb darkening. A four-fold gradient-boosting ensemble predicted uncertainty, followed by wavelength scaling, smoothing, and PCA refinements.

solution_title: From ARC Rules to Tiny ONNX Graphs: Our NeuroGolf Bronze
solution_summary: The team solved individual visual reasoning tasks as compact, exact ONNX programs, optimizing stored parameters plus intermediate-tensor memory. Direct-output operations, quantized arithmetic, algebraic color classifiers, and initializer reuse reduced costs across many tasks. Every replacement underwent runtime, sanitizer, correctness, and stress validation before entering a known-good submission bundle. Accumulating verified improvements raised the reported score from about 5,554.69 to 7,454.84.

The team used online adversarial validation and concluded that training and test data were randomly split. A denoiser trained with no-margin cosine loss cleaned the training data while preserving the validation set, and MSE loss helped handle label noise. Thirteen models were blended or stacked, achieving CV scores of 0.908 and 0.910 but private leaderboard scores of 0.899. Scaling healthy-class predictions by 0.9 improved the private score to 0.901.

The final solution combines six LightGBM models and one neural network in a weighted ensemble, followed by graph-based probability recalibration. The models use shared graph and NLP features, with one LightGBM consuming thousands of features including sparse n-gram vectors. Multiple text representations were especially useful because they captured different kinds of similarity. The single model using the full feature set scored approximately 0.116–0.117 on the leaderboard, while the author highlighted distribution artifacts and noisy labels as limitations.

solution_title: Expert Pruning, Masked TIR and Stream Arbitration
solution_summary: The pipeline pruned GPT-OSS-120B experts using routing frequencies measured on math reasoning traces under the submission prompting setup. Dynamic pruning retained a layer-specific set of experts and was favored over fixed pruning because it preserved quality without additional recovery training. Masked tool-integrated reasoning SFT improved aggressively pruned checkpoints, but its added complexity was not retained in the central approach. At inference, eight parallel tool-assisted reasoning streams were governed by a vote-based stopping policy under a 15-minute per-problem cap.

solution_title: Scaling Inference-Time Compute for Mathematical Reasoning
solution_summary: The final pipeline served GPT-OSS-120B through vLLM and generated eight parallel tool-using reasoning attempts per problem. It aggregated answers using inverse weights from a five-component token-entropy score and stopped early when an answer collected four votes. A short prompt, temperature 1.0, a 65K context window, and FP8 KV cache formed the stable configuration, which scored 41/50 after an earlier version reached 42/50. A post-competition reference run solved 10/10 problems in 31 minutes, while verbose prompts, Bayesian voting, and a mismatched fine-tuned model reduced performance.
compute: Single NVIDIA H100, 4.8-hour competition budget; post-competition H100 80GB SXM reference run took 1869 seconds and cost $5.50.

solution_summary: The team averaged PrecTime and LSTM-Unet models, including multiple five-fold model sets and additional single models. They used 28 input features and predicted central sequence regions from longer overlapping inputs to improve boundary accuracy. PrecTime modifications added transformers and residual connections, while dynamic programming postprocessing handled overlapping event predictions. Selected submissions reported public/private scores of 0.75/0.8 and 0.759/0.803.

The team manually developed and shortened Python programs for individual grid tasks, accumulating many small task-specific improvements. Common constructions included recursive rotation, cellular propagation, bitwise encodings, regular expressions and brute-force expression searches. Compression optimization explored zlib and zopfli settings as well as variable names and deliberately repetitive source forms. LLM assistance was generally unhelpful, so most final progress came from manual reasoning and testing.

The author started from publicly shared pretrained models and used a three-stage training strategy. Training progressed from a classifier for all classes to classifiers for each class, then introduced heavier augmentation. Annotation-based mixcut erased annotated regions and their labels and filled those regions with non-label images. Selectively dropping test-time augmentation kept inference within 8 hours 59 minutes, with reported public and private scores of 0.970 and 0.973.

solution_summary: The author moved from a heavily engineered random forest to a linear stack of approximately 58 pretrained models. A classifier predicting seven target quantile regions supplied probabilities for adjusting the stack's predictions toward regional anchors. The final blend trusted these adjustments more when classifier confidence was high and the base models agreed. This gating step produced the largest reported improvement, while gate and model hyperparameters were left untuned.

The solution combines a squeeze-and-excitation CNN, an attention-based sequence model, gated GRUs, and boosted trees. Physics-informed IMU features and statistical sensor features support both neural and tree models. Ensemble weights adapt to confidence, sensor availability, data quality, and Dirichlet posterior estimates. Subject-aware validation is reported, with individual scores of 0.820–0.835 for the neural components and a target ensemble score of 0.856.

The author shares training and inference notebooks alongside the original Colab implementation. A single-seed model reportedly trained in about 20 minutes and had 17 ms latency. Kaggle TPU-VM training was approximately twice as slow as Colab. A four-seed model often encountered submission scoring errors, and a three-seed alternative was suggested without a confirmed improvement.

solution_title: Making my (not submitted) 5th place solution public

solution_title: Rank 28 approach - diversity and CV prevail!
solution_summary: The author trained more than 70 models with diverse tree algorithms and different amounts of replicated training and original data. Shuffled ten-fold validation guided model selection, with a depth-eight XGBoost model performing best individually. AutoGluon and neural network stackers were combined with single models using a GPU hill-climbing blender. The final blending approach achieved cross-validation scores of approximately 0.382–0.383.

solution_summary: The solution combined agent-swapping data generation, manual and OpenFE-generated features, and CatBoost-centered regression models. Validation grouped games and stratified by target and agent identity, while nested cross-validation supplied leakage-safe predictions for second-stage models. A weighted ensemble achieved the best local validation score, but a separate CatBoost submission adjusted to the public prediction distribution performed better on the private test. That distribution-matched submission achieved 0.417 publicly and 0.422 privately.

solution_summary: The solution combined three Cascade Mask R-CNN models for 275 leaf classes with a separate model for 23 parent classes, expanding predictions through the class hierarchy. Class-dependent oversampling and undersampling addressed severe imbalance, while small validation subsets guided learning-rate changes and checkpoint selection. Multi-scale and flip inference combined detections with NMS and averaged instance masks, followed by mask-level NMS to merge parent predictions from both sources. Increasing the leaf ensemble's detection limit on part of the test set produced final public/private scores of 0.5383/0.4922.

solution_title: 376th → 92nd: the signal was non-monotonic, and one model beat every blend
solution_summary: The final submission used a single FT-Transformer with Periodic–Linear–ReLU numerical embeddings and exact-value target encoding. Diagnostics showed reproducible non-monotonic signal at individual numeric values, explaining why histogram-based trees plateaued and why richer value representations helped. Training used fold-specific transformations, class-weighted cross-entropy, mixed precision, and stratified five-fold validation. The model achieved 0.95057 OOF balanced accuracy and 0.95099 public score, outperforming blends whose small OOF gains did not transfer.

solution_summary: The solution centered on reconstructing multiple user identifiers from D features and card information, combining strict identities with more flexible variants. User-level sequence encoding, target encoding of past records, and aggregate features drove substantial improvements. LightGBM supplied most predictions, with a small Regularized Greedy Forest contribution and diversity from seeds and encoding fold counts. The author solved the CTF tasks with a mix of statistical analysis, model inspection, adversarial inputs, and manual search. K-means and PCA recovered cluster counts and dimensions, while PCA followed by distance sorting decoded hidden tokens. Other tasks used autoregressive character generation, targeted image optimization, input perturbations, and exploitation of scoring logic. Inspecting data and implementation details often mattered more than sophisticated modeling.

The solution generated recommendation candidates and reranked them with one XGBoost ranker per target, without ensembling. Candidates came from session history, co-visitation matrices, Word2Vec similarities, and item popularity. The rankers used 53 features describing ranks, interaction history, co-visitation weights, popularity, and embedding similarity. Separate data constructions controlled leakage, and the approach achieved 0.574 overall validation recall@20 and 0.586 on the public leaderboard.

One used contextual state-space models and MLP probes, while another distilled Perch features into EfficientNet-B0 with an attention-based sound event detection head. A third model used high-confidence pseudo-labels selected per class, with stratified folds incorporating pseudo-label provenance. Perch inference was accelerated from roughly 90 to 23 minutes, while BirdNET+ experiments and improved insect validation scores did not translate into better leaderboard performance.

solution_summary: The solution used three stages: diverse base predictions, two MLP stackers, and a simple average of their outputs. Base learners included LightGBM variants, custom CNNs, a public transformer, and Gaussian naive Bayes, with consistent five-fold out-of-fold predictions. Random architecture search selected two MLPs with hidden sizes 52/94 and 10/20. solution_title: A type of solution I was expecting some to try

An EfficientNet-B5 crop classifier learned embeddings and ISUP probabilities from 512×512 level-0 crops containing cancer. Slide-level embedding statistics, probability statistics, class counts, and probability-weighted embedding sums fed a LightGBM classifier. Mixing embeddings from compatible slides expanded the slide-level training dataset from 10,000 to 200,000 rows. Inference averaged predictions from random embedding subsets, then converted expected ISUP scores into grades using fixed thresholds. The author acknowledged feature leakage from training the crop model on the full training set and considered its effect small because of strong augmentation.

The solution combined single-stage and multi-stage spine classifiers with condition-specific weights applied to logits. DINOv2 supplied global image context, while LSTM layers mixed information across MRI slices. The two-stage pipeline localized key points, projected them across imaging sources, and classified cropped slice stacks using ConvNeXtv2 or DINOv2. CLAHE normalization, SPIDER pretraining, and losses approximating the competition metric supported an ensemble CV score of 0.379.

Predictions from models trained with seeds 0, 21, and 42 were averaged before find_peaks post-processing, producing reported scores around 0.73–0.735. Extending input windows from 8 to 24 hours and adjusting Gaussian labels did not improve results. Tuning peak-finding parameters and removing low-score predictions were also unsuccessful.

The author trained two models using maskrcnn-benchmark without modifying the library or applying test-time augmentation or post-processing. Class imbalance was addressed by selecting a fixed number of training images per class. Class hierarchy was handled through separate datasets and models for root classes and deeper classes, with annotation conversion, removal, and gray masking of selected non-target objects. Each model required about 14 hours on eight V100 GPUs.

solution_title: Some of the 3rd place solution history (Danijel|Matias)
solution_summary: The team combined XGBoost, glmnet, and neural-network models, with a regularized Keras network providing the strongest individual model for devices with events. The final approach applied a matching-based leak only to devices without events; the best individual event-device model scored 2.23452 on the leaderboard.

All features were retained and standardized, with simple missing-value imputation rules distributed equally across the ensemble. Training used cross-entropy, batches of 10, and unweighted early epochs followed by weighted epochs. A signal threshold of 0.5575 was selected using cross-validation and the public leaderboard.

solution_title: Summary of things I've learned in get to my moderate 13th place
solution_summary: The author trained random forest, XGBoost, and k-nearest-neighbor models within geographic grids after abandoning an overlapping place-group strategy. solution_summary: The author used pointwise ranking based on association rules, with user click history and historical relevance for the current query providing the strongest signals. Domain associations were more useful than URL associations, and query trigrams also helped. Validation used 900,000 sessions from Day 26 with randomly sampled test queries. solution_summary: The pipeline used DKM correspondences to locate overlapping image regions, then ensembled matches from LoFTR, SE2-LoFTR, and SuperGlue on those crops. Original-image LoFTR matches compensated for regions missed by cropping. Multithreaded processing, spatial keypoint suppression, and weighted sampling reduced matching and estimation costs. Difficult image pairs triggered SGMNet augmentation or a DKM-only fallback, with these rules guided by custom validation.

solution_title: 2nd Place solution: The Godaddy Microbusiness Data Cleaning Challenge
solution_summary: The solution combined public leaderboard probing, reversion forecasts for anomalous counties, and an XGBoost model for smooth changes. Large jumps in active counts were removed by shifting the historical series, which gave the best cross-validation performance among the cleaning methods tried. The model used lagged signals and demographic, geographic, labor, and neighboring-county features with attention to their historical availability. Recursive one-month forecasts performed better than direct three-month forecasts, and predictions were rounded to integer active counts.

solution_summary: The team combined pretrained EfficientNets with experiment-based validation, experiment-specific image normalization, and strong augmentation. Class co-occurrence constraints and Hungarian assignment substantially improved raw network predictions, while train and test controls were added as extra classes. A second training iteration used soft pseudo labels with balanced experiment splits and added larger EfficientNets, although B6 did not converge well in time. The initial B0/B1/B2 blend achieved a private score of 0.990, and final inference used both imaging sites with eight flip/rotation variants each.

solution_summary: The team trained several CNN backbones and extracted their bottleneck features for product-level image aggregation. Padded groups of up to four image features were processed using LSTM, GRU, dense models, and NetVLAD, then averaged across aggregation models and backbones. This ensemble reached around 0.77, compared with roughly 0.69–0.72 for the baseline CNNs. Off-the-shelf EAST text detection and CRNN OCR supplied character n-gram features, adding about 0.01 without retraining the OCR models or correcting their output with a language model.

The post shares links to reverse-engineering notebooks for difficulty levels 3 and 4. It also links the notebook that produced the final submission. The author thanks another participant for kernels and a difficulty 2 solution, but provides no methodological details in the post itself.

solution_title: 20th place solution based on custom sample_weight and data augmentation
solution_summary: The solution combined store-and-calendar target encodings, weather features, customized sample weights, and imputed monthly statistics. Validation held out the final month and separated its first six days from the remainder to assess public-like and private-like performance. Sample weights combined recentness with annual similarity, while regression ensembles filled missing May statistics. Randomly dropping historical observations before target encoding and averaging the resulting predictions improved robustness to differing store observation histories.

The team used a frozen DINOv3 Large backbone with four overlapping image patches, Local Mamba fusion, and patch attention. Validation grouped sampling dates and stratified states across four folds. Color augmentation, artifact inpainting, state conditioning, multiscale instances, and state-specific expert heads addressed domain differences. Backbone unfreezing and TTA hurt performance, while WA-based dead-biomass scaling improved public results but performed worse privately than omitting it.

The solution relied on stacking approximately 40 out-of-fold prediction sets. Combining many predictions was the central strategy described. The author credited shared notebooks and community contributions but provided no base-model or training details.

solution_title: SegFormer  + Depth Pro -> DinoV3Base w/Lora -> Learned Fusion module
solution_summary: This approach fuses DINOv3 image representations with 18 auxiliary features derived from segmentation, depth, and texture. Separate heads predict green, dead, and clover biomass, with total biomass computed as their sum. Training combines LoRA adaptation, increased weighting for high-biomass samples, and component-specific losses. Inference uses horizontal-flip augmentation and differential-evolution-tuned component corrections, including adjustments for occlusion and saturation.

solution_summary: The approach averaged lightweight 3D segmentation models and converted predicted masks into particle centroids using CC3D. Customized particle mask radii, segmentation losses, balanced crop sampling, and augmentation were central to training, while InstanceNorm3d and PReLU improved stability in several architectures. Public leaderboard scores guided ensemble selection, with selected submissions scoring 0.78283 and 0.78381 on the private leaderboard. The author built a largely automated pipeline using cross-validated models from multiple neural network architectures with basic augmentation. The implementation included test-time augmentation, threshold search, several ensemble approaches, and multiple loss functions. Single models scored about 0.55–0.57 on the public leaderboard, while the large ensemble reached 0.601. The solution combined five CNN architectures trained with five-fold multilabel iterative stratification. Training used binary cross-entropy followed by three to five epochs of F2 loss, with only the last two layers and classifier trained. Aggressive learning-rate reduction and logits drawn from the last two layers helped improve performance while keeping training efficient. A weighted model average reached 0.658 on the public leaderboard; test-time augmentation and gradient accumulation did not help.

The author shared useful components of a solution built largely on @mrkmakr's public kernel. Features included trigonometric speed components, distances, and an exponentially weighted measure of defender proximity to the rusher. Simulating player positions one second ahead provided additional derived features. Symmetry flips and coordinate noise improved training, while validation grouped samples by week.

The solution handled accession identifiers with keyword rules filtered by embedding similarity, while DOIs followed a multistage zero-shot Qwen extraction and classification pipeline. Corpus lookup and repository-specific rules supplemented the DOI predictions. Postprocessing capped certain accession predictions and removed identifiers appearing in textual ranges. The author used XGBoost tuned with 10-fold cross-validation and generated predictions from each fold. solution_title: [Working Note] Two transfer failures: instruction complexity & a wasted signal
solution_summary: The final strategy emphasized simple single-action email.send candidates in the competition sandbox because that mechanism transferred to the private guardrail better than marker-based attacks. Packing eight actions into each candidate worked on the local 8B proxy but produced empty or malformed outputs on the real 26B target. The most transferable submission scored 3.720 privately versus 3.900 publicly. solution_summary: The solution separately predicted the probability of no event and the normalized rank of event time, then combined these outputs with a tuned nonlinear function. The solution applies a 30 Hz high-pass filter and normalizes each observation by its absolute mean. Training augmentation includes temporal rolls, amplitude scaling, and sign inversion. All three models share a WaveNet frontend, followed by EfficientNet B3, WaveNet with GRU, or WaveNet modeling. Implemented in TensorFlow and trained on TPU, the models report CV scores ranging from 87.79 to 88.07.
compute: Trained on TPU

solution_summary: The team combined complementary LightGBM solutions, using different models and blends for Investment and OwnerOccupier properties. Extensive cleaning, suspicious-price removal, area-normalized features, and price-per-square-meter modeling improved robustness. Time-period normalization, validation, and leaderboard probing informed prediction scaling. Comparing model disagreements exposed incorrect property locations, and targeted address corrections contributed about 0.004 to the public score.

The solution used out-of-the-box Distance Weighted Discriminant classification without feature selection. The penalization parameter C was tuned using 10-fold cross-validation and ROC area. Performance saturated around C=300, which was used for the submission.

The author used an eight-layer BERT token model for joint regression of RNA reactivity targets. Pretraining predicted four per-token summaries of base-pair probabilities using the combined competition training and test sequences. Fine-tuning added a two-layer probing head over concatenated backbone layers and used filtered competition labels together with external targets. The final ensemble averaged 16 fine-tuning runs, used stochastic weight averaging for some models, and clipped predictions below one.
external_data: ["External RNA dataset from a discussion post (unspecified)"]

solution_summary: The solution engineered workflow-aware batch features from exact and approximate duplicates, including duplicate counts and within-batch ID ranks. A two-level stack combined XGBoost models trained on different feature subsets and station groups, then trained second-level models only on the identified batches. The final predictions averaged XGBoost, random forest, ExtraTrees, and Keras outputs. Batch-grouped validation and a conservative MCC-based threshold selection emphasized robustness, with performance ordering consistent across validation and both leaderboards.

The solution combines an attention-based MLP with a smaller logistic regression contribution using extensive play-level and player-level features. Bounded Voronoi geometry, relative player positions, and projected future movement were important engineered inputs. Grouped and temporal validation were considered together, while coordinate-flip TTA improved predictions. Final submissions used four-seed MLP averaging, with one submission also blending five-fold logistic regression predictions.

solution_title: Looking back at my approach 1284 pos [0.8952 private leaderboard and 0.8950 public leaderboard]
solution_summary: The solution combined ImageNet-initialized ResNeXt50-style and EfficientNet-B4 models trained on the full training set after five-fold stratified model selection. Strong image augmentation, particularly CutMix, improved the difficult classes, while plain cross entropy worked as well as its weighted variant. Training used SGD with cosine annealing, and inference averaged ten randomly augmented predictions per image. A 0.6/0.4 soft-voting ensemble achieved approximately 0.8952 accuracy on both public and private leaderboards.

Images were tiled into 512×512 RGB patches, with 16 instances selected per image. The central improvement was pretraining an ImageNet-initialized ResNet152 on competition images labeled Unknown or Other before learning CE/LAA classification. Training used binary cross entropy with balanced class weights. The selected submission ensembled this model with EfficientNetB0 and Xception, although the single pretrained ResNet achieved the author's best private score of 0.65726.

The solution trained four image-text models using Swin or EfficientNet image backbones and BERT-family text backbones with ArcFace. Each model produced joint, image, and text embeddings, and predictions combined 24 votes across models, embedding types, and distance measures. Validation used five folds grouped by product label, with submission thresholds adjusted from CV settings. Forcing singleton predictions to contain two items improved CV and leaderboard scores by 0.01, while removing matches with inconsistent units further refined results.

solution_title: Do not trust the LB,  trust your CV.  (5th/8th in public/private LB)
solution_summary: The team combined ship-presence classifiers with several segmentation models. ResNet34 and SE-ResNeXt50 classifiers trained on all images, while U-Net and Mask R-CNN variants trained on ship-containing images. A further U-Net variant used deep supervision and all images, and the final submission combined these model families. The author emphasized trusting cross-validation and reported that pseudo-labeling worked, with a single-model private score described as 853.

The solution combined neural networks, ODST variants, and gradient boosting models trained on survival targets. CNN and dense neural models fitted both a CoxPHFitter-derived target and a custom target designed to separate event and censored cases. ODST improvements included replacing unseen categories with training modes, adding public notebook features, and weighting fold predictions. Two classification trees provided post-processing.

The solution combined three DINOv3 Huge pipelines with weights of 50% for subspace-alignment test-time adaptation, 30% for species-aware prediction, and 20% for DINOv3–SigLIP feature fusion. Scaling the pretrained backbone and carefully stabilizing fine-tuning mattered more than increasing image resolution. Target reformulation, predicted species probabilities, and a deeper MLP head improved the biomass models. Validation used five stratified folds based on biomass bins and species after date-grouped validation proved unhelpful. The final ensemble scored 0.760 publicly and 0.652 privately.
compute: A100 GPU; memory constraints influenced backbone and image-size choices.

solution_summary: Fully connected networks processed descriptors and fingerprints for individual building blocks, with some models also using tokenized SMILES embeddings. Binding sites were capped to distinguish and align them, and swapping the second and third building blocks provided augmentation. Training retained all binding molecules and sampled one fifth of nonbinding molecules. Scaffold-based validation guided binary model selection for the ensemble, followed by a rule that zeroed predictions for unsupported building-block combinations.

solution_title: 4th place solution. Boundary DoU Loss is all you need!
solution_summary: The main pipeline equally averaged a multiview 2D EfficientNet-B5 UNet++ model and a 3D DynUNet model, with D4 test-time augmentation. It used percentile-based stack normalization, sparsity-aware sampling, external pseudo-labels, and BoundaryDOULoss. A vessel ROI derived from 2D predictions suppressed false positives in the 3D output, while Canny-based kidney masking improved public results but severely damaged private performance. The main ensemble scored 0.712 privately, although the author reports that their best private submission was a simpler mixture of 2D and 2.5D models.
compute: 2D training: 30 epochs. 3D training: 500 epochs with 2000 samples per epoch.

solution_title: 24th place solution - 2 stage Autogluon and XGB, no post-processing
solution_summary: The solution combined molecular fingerprints, descriptors, graph features, and ChemBERT embeddings with target-specific AutoGluon and XGBoost models. Initial AutoGluon runs used all features and then importance-selected subsets, while a second stage learned pseudo-labels and incorporated predictions for other targets. The final submission selected different models for each target using leaderboard scores, including an average for Density. It scored 0.66 publicly and 0.86 privately; a more conservative median ensemble performed worse privately.
compute: GPU notebooks with a 12-hour budget for AutoGluon runs and feature selection.

solution_summary: The final solution combined six DeBERTa models, comprising two base and four large variants, with a LightGBM regressor on top of each model and a late-fusion ensemble. Variants differed in whether prompt text and questions were included and whether external Feedback Prize data was used for pretraining. Handcrafted prompt-text features in LightGBM substantially improved models that omitted prompt inputs. The ensemble achieved approximately 0.4734 cross-validation MCRMSE and 0.468 private leaderboard MCRMSE.

solution_title: 554 Place Solution for the ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined XGBoost and LightGBM models trained with cross-validation. Preprocessing distinguished categorical columns from other features and applied no normalization. GridSearchCV tuned the models using balanced log loss. The final submission averaged the two models' predicted probabilities equally.

solution_title: 516th solution with the one which is supposed to win Copper medal in private score
solution_summary: The author modified two public notebook approaches by changing the datasets they used. Two variants of the Jelal notebook were chosen as final submissions based on slightly stronger public scores. A Coleridge MLMv2 variant that was not submitted achieved a better private score of 0.228, compared with 0.196 for the reported submitted variant.

solution_title: 72nd Place: Training-only Site Bias and Image-reading LLM Labels
solution_summary: The final model used an ImageNet-pretrained 2.5D ConvNeXt-B with hierarchical per-finding attention over MRI windows and series. Label quality drove most improvements: source-specific out-of-fold teachers were combined with multimodal LLM image-and-report labels. A training-only site bias absorbed reporting differences and was removed at inference, improving private AUC by 0.007. The final single-seed model achieved 0.949 private AUC, outperforming the attempted ensembles.
compute: Image-label generation: 128 parallel calls, about 45 minutes, about 21k tokens per study; image training: 30 epochs.

solution_summary: The final solution equally blended two sensor sequence pipelines with substantially different architectures. One used modality-specific residual CNNs, cross-modal attention, a bidirectional LSTM, and auxiliary tasks; the other used gated sensor streams, attention pooling, and random sensor masking. Sensor alignment, motion features, and sequence augmentation helped standardize the small dataset. Combining the pipelines improved public performance from about 86.5 individually to 87.6, while manual upside-down corrections and leaking OOF distillation exposed weaknesses in validation.

The solution used seven weighted models based on a pretrained ResNet-50 FCN, varying image resolution, loss, folds, and test-time augmentation. All layers were fine-tuned with Adam, using restrained geometric augmentation and primarily binary cross-entropy minus log Dice loss. Geometric mask cleanup repaired antennas, filled selected holes and concavities, and removed stray contours. Post-processing increased the reported private score from 0.997010 to 0.997209.
compute: GTX1080Ti and GTX1080; GTX1070 for inference/TTA. GTX1080Ti used for 1918x1280 and 2010x1340.

solution_summary: The task was treated as direct multiclass classification using 15 QLoRA-fine-tuned Qwen models across three backbones and five folds. Data corrections and keeping near-duplicates together supported reliable validation, while focal and smoothed cross-entropy losses with delayed class weights addressed noisy, long-tailed labels. Inference used quantized models, including a GPTQ 32B base with a separate FP16 classifier head executed through vLLM. A weighted logit blend achieved private MAP@3 of 0.948.
compute: Single RTX 4090 for 8B models, four epochs; A800-40GB for the 32B model, three epochs.

solution_summary: The solution localized lungs with an EfficientNet-B0 detector trained on manually annotated boxes, then classified neighboring CT slices with SE-ResNeXt50 and SE-ResNeXt101 models. A second stage processed image embeddings and their neighboring differences with a bidirectional GRU to predict image-level and study-level labels. A single holdout of 1,000 studies guided tuning before models were retrained on the full training set. Final predictions were adjusted to satisfy label consistency constraints, producing a small local validation improvement.
compute: 576x576 localized inputs were the largest size that allowed the models to finish within 9 hours.

solution_summary: The solution represents each well as an image over candidate vertical depths and measured depth, with whole-well U-Nets predicting categorical depth distributions. Autoregressive tracking, a physics-guided HMM, segmented beam search, and posterior fusion provide complementary predictions. Seeded grouped cross-validation supports entropy-weighted test-time augmentation and a position-dependent nonnegative stack with disagreement calibration. The selected combination achieved 5.28 strict cross-validation RMSE and 6.251 private leaderboard RMSE.

The final solution ensembled two DeBERTa-v3-large models, including one with masked-language-model pretraining on FB2 data at a 0.4 masking probability. Adversarial weight perturbation and target-specific attention pooling had the strongest impact, with layer-wise learning-rate decay also helping. MLM slightly improved single-model CV while worsening leaderboard scores, but its inclusion appeared to improve the ensemble. The final ensemble achieved CV 0.44582 and public/private scores of 0.439025/0.435032; smooth-L1 loss, masking augmentation, and recurrent heads did not help.

The pipeline trained YOLOv5l on overlapping image tiles with balanced foreground/background sampling and strong augmentation, then detected objects on full images at higher resolution. Experiments included pseudo-label relabeling, scale and flip TTA, and fold-model fusion with WBF. Post-processing removed unreliable edge boxes and applied an online adaptation of Seq-NMS over the previous 20 frames. The strongest reported late submission used original labels and a five-fold ensemble, reaching 0.737 with Seq-NMS.
compute: Tesla T4 16GB on an EC2 g4dn.xlarge instance; training for 45–60 epochs.

solution_title: 6th Place Solution: Multi-view Multi-lateral Multi-stage Approach
solution_summary: The team used ConvNeXt-based mammography models with VOI-LUT processing, breast-region cropping, and extensive augmentation. YOLOX supplied training crops, while simpler rule-based cropping reduced inference time. Auxiliary prediction losses and weight averaging improved training stability, and the final approach combined models. A submission scoring 0.53 on the private leaderboard was left unselected because its validation and public scores were weaker.

solution_title: Silver medal solution: ViT-L/14 with test time augmentations
solution_summary: The solution used an OpenCLIP ViT-L/14 encoder pretrained on LAION-400M with aspect-ratio-preserving image resizing. A projection layer trained with ArcFace on Products-10k substantially improved the embeddings. Test-time augmentation combined predefined crops and masked pixel dropout. The final reported scores were 0.628 public and 0.631 private.

solution_title: 6th Place Solution for the NeurIPS 2023 - Machine Unlearning Competition
solution_summary: The team performed machine unlearning by resetting the original model's first and last layers, warming up through teacher-student distillation, and fine-tuning on retained data. Fine-tuning combined hard-label cross-entropy, soft cross-entropy, and KL divergence with cosine learning-rate scheduling. The method did not require the forget set and retained the starter notebook's preprocessing. Restricting warm-up to validation classes 0 and 1 achieved a private score of 0.07831, compared with 0.07219 using all validation classes.
