solution_summary: The approach optimized validated sentinel-post throughput using a live probe-and-select engine. Each model invocation measured template reward per second, selected the fastest sufficiently reliable template, and filled a replay-aware candidate budget. Unique destination domains preserved novelty credit, while short prompts and wrap-up phrasing reduced generation cost. solution_title: [15th place] A goal-based logic bot & code.

A space-time reservation table prevented friendly collisions while keeping planning practical for large armies. Independent goal assignment caused economic imbalance, and optimal conflict-based joint planning became too slow as unit counts increased. Incomplete attack and defense behaviors remained a substantial limitation.

Feature work included dimensionality reduction, genetic programming, large-scale feature search, interest-rate features, and meta features from application and bureau data. Blending methods included direct AUC optimization and adversarial validation, alongside prediction corrections and post-processing. Reported gains included a private-score improvement of 0.003 from meta features and 0.0002 from adversarial-validation-based blending.

The solution combines five-fold 2–2.5D segmentation models with an eca_nfnet_l2 backbone and a MONAI 3D U-Net. The 2–2.5D models start with BCE plus Dice loss and later switch to Dice alone, while randomly zeroing depth channels improved the score by about 0.01. The final predictions averaged the six checkpoints with the lowest validation losses and were clipped to 0–100; alternative sequence architectures and normalization layers did not improve results.

solution_summary: The author trained separate LightGBM models for each forecast horizon and UPDRS target using MAE. Relational knowledge distillation compressed 256-dimensional embeddings to 64 dimensions and outperformed adaptive average pooling. The image model used an EVA02-small backbone, GeM pooling, and an MLP for tabular inputs, concatenating image and tabular representations. An auxiliary cosine embedding loss targeted 1024-dimensional embeddings from multilingual-e5-large, while negative downsampling preserved examples with high false-positive rates. The combined image-model changes achieved a reported leaderboard score of 0.161. A single 3D U-Net predicted segmentation masks, and connected components converted them into localized detections. Seven-fold validation held out one sample at a time and evaluated all held-out predictions together. Larger patches, interior-only loss and prediction assignment, balanced patch sampling, and tailored augmentation improved validation. The reported CV score was 0.7781, with public and private scores of 0.72782 and 0.71783.

solution_title: 2nd Place - Weighted Box Fusion and Post Process

Post-processing improved cross-validation by approximately 0.008, while the fusion ensemble raised CV from roughly 0.700 for individual models to 0.741. solution_title: #60: Data augmentation explained: Generating more stars
solution_summary: The approach augmented stellar observations to simulate dimmer stars in the test distribution. It scaled signals downward and injected additional noise to preserve the expected relationship between brightness and shot-noise variance. The implementation supported downscaling only, which matched the stated test conditions. This augmentation helped tune predicted sigma values.

solution_title: 75th Place Solution for the DEFCON31 Competition
solution_summary: The author describes challenge-specific methods used to obtain 22 flags in an AI capture-the-flag competition. These included inspecting classification errors, clustering and visualizing hidden structure, counting image pixels, and constructing small white-box adversarial perturbations. Other challenges were solved through prompt injection, XML injection, iterative word guessing, image thresholding, and Python object-construction behavior. Several challenges remained unsolved, and matching the server's MobileNet weights was essential for the adversarial-image tasks.

The team combined CNNs trained on three CT image representations: multiple intensity windows, cropped windowed images, and cropped adjacent-slice RGB images. They removed patients shared between training and test data and used patient-level folds with balanced positive and negative patient sampling. A described training pipeline used AdamW, backbone freezing followed by full fine-tuning, geometric augmentation, and horizontal-flip inference. Metadata-based H2O post-processing improved most models, and the processed predictions were stacked.

solution_title: Provisional 8th Place Solution - Monai x EfficientNets x LGBM
solution_summary: The pipeline combines image-level EfficientNet predictions with exam-level volumetric predictions using tree-based stacking. Fold-specific probability calibration and LightGBM over neighboring slices substantially improve image-level predictions, reducing cross-validation log loss from 0.12 to 0.105. Exam-level models use positive exams and aggregate image probabilities into statistical features. Final postprocessing enforces prediction consistency and estimates the indeterminate target without a dedicated model.

The pipeline detected helmets with YOLOv5l, tracked detections bidirectionally, classified teams, and mapped helmets to player coordinates. Optical-flow prediction and interpolation reduced missed detections, while MobileNet-v2 features clustered helmets into two teams. A Hungarian assignment incorporated spatial distance and team mismatch penalties. XGBoost estimated frame-level mapping reliability, which was accumulated over tracks to assign player identities and resolve conflicts.

The solution ensembled multiple ARC solvers and applied filters targeting their recurring output errors, including redundant lines and incorrect shapes. It exploited stable task ordering across submissions to identify which tasks existing algorithms solved, then tested additional algorithms for complementary coverage. Binary search helped locate newly solved tasks so other tasks could remain assigned to the strongest solver. solution_title: Efficient Bird Species Detection Using Distilled Sound Event Detection Ensembles
solution_summary: The pipeline uses five publicly available distilled sound event detection models on overlapping audio windows. It combines clip logits with maximum-pooled frame logits, averages probabilities across folds, and smooths predictions over time. Maximum pooling across overlapping windows produces timestamp-level outputs. Validation studies and runtime measurements were still planned, so no numerical performance evidence was reported.

A reproducible solver factory promoted candidates only after correctness checks, generated holdouts, and strictly lower measured cost. Mining selected routes for kore per turn while avoiding enemy fleet paths, and expansion and spawning depended on resource surplus and relative fleet size.

compute: 4x RTX 3090: about two hours per fold; 2x T4 for parallel inference; reported 200% TensorRT speedup.

solution_summary: The solution used organ-specific segmentation models with a pvtv2-b4 backbone and convolutional or DAFormer decoders, trained at 768 × 768 resolution. Basic color and geometric augmentations were used throughout, with stain augmentation added for spleen and lung. Different organs used different fold ensembles and weighting schemes, while prostate used a single model because ensembling did not improve the public score. Final segmentation thresholds varied by organ and data source.

The solution used five-second log-mel spectrograms and an ensemble of 14 sound event detection models. Training combined clipwise and segmentwise binary cross-entropy losses, with softer targets for background birds and several audio augmentations. Validation relied on the provided training soundscapes, while inference used a lower threshold and file-level probability adjustments. A custom combination of geometric and root-mean-square ensemble averaging was among the reported improvements.
compute: 20–40 training epochs, reported as 24 hours on a GTX1060.

solution_summary: The solution combined eight B7 and B5 models in two inference branches with different tile overlaps. Pseudo labels were refined by manually adding missed targets, then used to train the B5 models. Because these labels could hurt predictions on another image, their influence was reduced through ensemble weighting and a guiding B7 model. Model-specific test-time augmentations and prediction averaging stabilized the output, while pseudo labeling reportedly improved the private score by about 0.003–0.004.

The solution ensembled 12 FT-Transformer models trained with different random seeds and used all five folds. Configurations were selected using MAE, with dimensions of 48–64, depths of 4–8, and eight heads. A high dropout rate of 0.4 was used, without augmentation or the shared blending resources.

The final solution blended a particle filter with three segment-level hidden Markov model variants, achieving CV 6.0904. Each model tracked a continuous geological path in a transformed depth coordinate, anchored at the last known sample and scored against calibrated gamma-ray references. Robust level-and-slope likelihoods, constrained drift-line searches, and evidence-based branch composition were central to the approach. The final weights were 0.50 for the particle filter, 0.25 and 0.05 for two tube-HMM transition variants, and 0.20 for a tube-HMM using mixed references.

The author generated five bitmap candidates per prompt with SDXL-Turbo using illustration-oriented prompt prefixes and suffixes. Each bitmap was converted to SVG through vtracer parameter searches, then optimized with scour to preserve quality within a roughly 10 KB size budget. SSIM guided selection of faithful vectorizations, and a subtle letter O was added to mitigate OCR hallucinations. PaliGemma2 and an aesthetic predictor selected the final SVG for prompt alignment and visual appeal.

The pipeline first predicted a missing-word position, generated candidate insertions, and selected a word using smoothed n-gram models up to length six. Logistic regression combined n-gram estimates, and a part-of-speech n-gram model helped locate the omission. Word-length-specific linear regressions estimated edit-distance gains, while another logistic regression estimated position confidence. Confidence gates selected between inserting a word, inserting a space, or leaving the sentence unchanged, and output words received their most common capitalization.

The solution used DeBERTa backbones pretrained on SQuAD v2, followed by bidirectional recurrent layers and token classification heads with auxiliary span-boundary supervision. Regularization included multiple dropout heads, hidden-state mixing, and masking patient-history tokens. One round of soft pseudo-labeling with a confidence-weighted loss was especially effective. Weighted probability ensembling and character-level boundary corrections produced a selected submission scoring 0.893 publicly and 0.894 privately.

The solution used LightGBM with more than 500 features derived primarily at the item-store level and trained only on 2017 data. Historical sales statistics, day-of-week patterns, promotion information, and product availability history were especially useful. Validation over July 26 through August 10 guided feature development. The final ensemble combined repeated runs from two teammates with different features and time windows, achieving 0.514 privately and 0.507 publicly.

solution_title: Home Depot Product Search Relevance, Winners' Interview: 1st Place | Alex, Andreas, & Nurlan
solution_summary: The team combined extensive text similarity and entity features with a large stacked ensemble of diverse regression models. Product clusters and query centroids were especially useful for handling noisy queries and measuring ambiguity. Validation averaged three grouped cross-validation runs to reflect unseen queries and products. The final pipeline contained more than 20 feature sets and roughly 300 first-layer models.
compute: Full feature extraction and training took several days; the best features and models finished in a few hours.

solution_title: Hybrid approach - ML and GOP (good old programming)
solution_summary: The author built a non-machine-learning baseline using OpenCV thresholding and contours to identify nuclei, then expanded their boundaries to approximate cells. Region masks and simple statistics supported label identification, while a graph represented neighboring cells. The submission used the standard CellSegmentator for RLE masks and the custom segmentator for other processing, scoring 0.053. A late addition of local binary pattern texture tests increased the score to 0.069.

The author applied a symbolic regression algorithm to construct three mathematical models. The final prediction averaged their outputs. Two discovered equations had the form tanh(f(x)), which the author describes as equivalent to a logistic function.
The post announces that the author has started publishing a summary of their solution. It links to the first part on a personal blog. No methods or results are described in the provided text.

The solution blended two XGBoost pipelines with LSTM, CNN, Transformer, and MLP models. The tree pipelines used extensive order-book features describing prices, spreads, volume, imbalance, temporal changes, and cross-stock ranks. Five XGBoost models trained with MAE loss and different seeds were combined by median prediction. The neural networks used raw inputs with timestamp normalization inside the network and logarithmic feature scaling.

solution_title: Train you very own deep convolutional network
solution_summary: The post provides a spatially sparse convolutional-network implementation and brief training instructions. It recommends LeNet-style architectures with many Network-In-Network layers and supports input canvases larger than 32×32 through sparsity. Training uses affine distortions and requires a reasonably fast CUDA-capable GPU. No detailed final architecture or quantitative results are reported.
compute: Requires a reasonably fast GPU supporting CUDA sm_20; runtime unspecified.

solution_title: 58th solution: SAINT+ based predicts user_answer and then answered_correctly
solution_summary: The solution first predicted a student's answer choice and then gathered the probability assigned to the correct answer inside the neural-network graph. This provided two backward signals and yielded a small leaderboard improvement. Time features were log-normalized, all tags were used, and continuous task-container identifiers supplied information about user expertise. Attention excluded interactions within the same container, while padding and lectures were excluded from the losses; static features went to the encoder and variable features to the decoder.

The team ensembled lenstool halo-location predictions generated from random subsets of galaxies. They merged estimates through partially informed clustering and applied 20–30 heuristic rules addressing unreliable detections, outliers, boundaries, and the competition metric. A second ensemble repeated merging and heuristic processing on different subsets of predictions 1,000 times, then took the median. The approach achieved public and private scores of 0.72590 and 0.72645.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution - Scaling Reinforcement Learning to the Stars
solution_summary: The solution trained a single 200-million-parameter transformer through 15 billion steps of pure self-play reinforcement learning for both two-player and four-player Orbit Wars. It combined entity-based observations with target-planet actions and continuous fleet sizing, relying on model scale to learn the game dynamics. Distributed PPO training and a parallel Rust simulator supported the large training workload. Quantization fit the model within submission limits, while a smaller fallback model handled tight CPU time budgets. The final model required approximately 2400 B200-hours, although late training emphasis on two-player games limited preparation for four-player matchmaking.
compute: 8x B200 for larger experiments; final training across four 8x B200 nodes with 8192 parallel environments; approximately 2400 B200-hours for the final 200M model.

solution_summary: The author developed NeXtVLAD to aggregate frame-level video features efficiently. It decomposes high-dimensional features into groups of lower-dimensional vectors, applies attention, and then performs NetVLAD aggregation over time. A single model with fewer than 80 million parameters achieved private GAP 0.87846, while a mixture of three models achieved 0.88722.

solution_title: My part of 8th place (Private LB) solution
solution_summary: The solution resized images to 224×224 and corrected brightness using each image's median. It combined several backbones with a U-Net-style decoder containing attention and hypercolumn features. Training used five-fold validation, hard example mining, a Lovasz hinge/BCE loss, and multiple learning-rate cycles. Averaged predictions with horizontal-flip augmentation performed best; puzzle-based post-processing improved the public score but left the private score unchanged.
compute: SeNet154 training and inference took about 6 days on one 1080 Ti GPU.

solution_summary: The solution used constant-Q audio representations with pretrained ResNeXt50 and MiT-B2 backbones, transformer sequence layers, and attention heads. Four training stages combined BirdCLEF 2021 and 2022 data, pseudo-label segmentation supervision, heavy noise, and frozen-backbone fine-tuning on 2022 classes. Weighted sampling addressed class imbalance, while waveform MixUp and focal loss supported training. Whole-file inference used sequence outputs, classwise attention rescaling, and low thresholds; the reported single-model and two-model score pairs have inconsistent public/private ordering across the post.

solution_title: MindsAI & Tufa Labs – ARC Prize 2025 Solution
solution_summary: The solution used a pruned 660M-parameter CodeT5-Large encoder–decoder trained on more than 100 million reasoning examples. Most performance came from extensive test-time training and augmented inference with reverse transformations and voting, which produced nearly additive gains. Additional improvements included richer augmentations, tokenizer dropout, span corruption, and a two-checkpoint ensemble. The reported private score was 15.42%.
compute: Google TPU training over many months, up to 2.5 years cumulative; final two-model inference on 4× L4 GPUs in approximately 11 hours.

solution_summary: The final approach matched Wi-Fi fingerprints to training points using cosine similarity and selected floors from the consistency of matches along each path. Accelerometer-derived step positions were combined with the Wi-Fi estimates through cost minimization. A population-based local search then refined paths using position, segment-length, heading, and corridor constraints. Snap-to-grid and leakage post-processing improved scores by roughly 0.3, and the author reported perfect floor predictions on both public and private data without a cross-validation framework.

The solution combined five LSTM angle-bin classifiers with five to seven DynEdge graph networks predicting XYZ vectors. LSTM classification worked better than direct vector regression, while graph networks benefited from longer pulse sequences. Separate ensemble weights for azimuth and zenith were selected on validation data. Combining the model families improved the private leaderboard score from 0.999 for the LSTM ensemble to 0.987.
compute: Around 30 minutes inference per graph network; around 2 hours for the LSTM ensemble.

solution_summary: The team manually authored and optimized Python solutions for all 400 grid tasks. Compact grid operations, recursive transformations, stateful comprehensions, and regular expressions supplied reusable patterns, while pysearch helped discover short formulas. Selected tasks used judge-specific shortcuts or hardcoded lookup tables. Compression was applied to 21 tasks, using specialized encoding and variable-name searches to reduce the final embedded script size.
compute: Average task required a few hours of manual optimization and review, with many revisits across 400 tasks and a five-person team.

solution_title: 17th Place Solution - How to Learn and Practice as a Beginner
solution_summary: The pipeline first segmented organs with a 2D UNet and refined spleen masks with a 3D UNet before cropping classification inputs. X3D_l classified liver, spleen, and kidney volumes, while bowel and extravasation used ConvNeXt features followed by LSTM and attention/max pooling. Pseudo-label pretraining, fine-mask refinement, and targeted crop augmentation supported the pipeline. Spleen refinement improved Dice from 0.880 to 0.943, and an end-to-end sequence model improved local validation but was not submitted.

The team normalized place text, engineered geographic and semantic features, and generated candidate pairs through several complementary matching rules. A lightweight five-fold LightGBM filtered candidates before a twenty-fold LightGBM evaluated more than 200 features. Final merging thresholds depended on the sizes of the groups being joined. The team also transferred known training matches to overlapping test records identified by cleaned names and rounded coordinates.
compute: Both LightGBM stages trained on the full 1.1-million-row training set outside Kaggle because of memory constraints; hardware unspecified.

solution_title: Kaggle 'Microsoft Malware Classification Challenge' 3rd place solution
solution_summary: The writeup provides reproduction scripts and notebooks for the malware classification submission, which scored 0.0040 on the private leaderboard. The workflow includes a main model, a separate 4-gram model, a semi-supervised step, and a final submission builder. Processing 4-grams was the largest memory bottleneck, while the other stages required at most 32 GB RAM. The text gives dependencies and hardware but little detail about model construction.
compute: 16 CPU cores and 120 GB RAM; stages other than 4-gram processing require no more than 32 GB RAM.

solution_summary: The solution used standard aggregate features and recomputed those features over records with positive transaction revenue. Training examples paired five months of history with a two-month target after a one-month gap. A later time period supplied validation. CatBoost regression with a small iteration count was sufficient to control overfitting.

The solution combines prompt exploits aimed at three distinct judge-score patterns. It uses a fixed pool of 50 LLM-generated generic essays and a public notebook word list, choosing the essay source separately for each exploit. Public leaderboard testing guided decisions because local judge simulations correlated weakly with public results. Reducing choices in a topic-selection exploit improved the score by about 3.27 points, while pairing the Japanese exploit with generic essays added about 1.56 points in the final submission.

The approach moved from whole-image models to single-cell models with progressively refined pseudo-labels. Cell labels were constrained by image-level ground truth and assigned using relative or absolute prediction thresholds over three iterations. Filtering nearly invisible segmented cells improved the leaderboard score by about 0.04. Manual review of mitotic spindle examples increased that class's score from 0.024 to 0.032.

solution_title: 7th place (public LB) solution : NN + Survival LGBM
solution_summary: The final solution blended a distilled neural network with a LightGBM survival model. The neural network learned pairwise player interactions, and its embeddings also supplied features to LightGBM. Survival modeling used a piecewise-constant hazard with a Poisson objective and converted predicted hazards into a yardage CDF. Projected positions, manual input scaling, augmentation, and output smoothing helped, while the authors acknowledged eventual overfitting to their validation split.
compute: LightGBM retraining took approximately one minute

solution_summary: The solution combined two public DeBERTa notebooks with a fine-tuned Mistral-Solar 10B model. An initial DeBERTa pass selected positive rows for subsequent inference, reducing false positives and limiting processing to fewer than 5,000 samples. The language model was trained on 945 PII-containing samples for five epochs, with JSON predictions converted into the competition format. The author reports that using only the first notebook and the Mistral model could achieve a private score of 96.3.
compute: Inference on two T4 GPUs; Mistral-Solar fine-tuning for 5 epochs.

solution_summary: The final approach stacked 60 XGBoost, CatBoost, and LightGBM models with a Ridge regression second level, using ten-fold out-of-fold predictions. Base-model selection searched CV RMSE cutoffs, with 572.6 giving the best stack. Ordinal quality features, aspect-ratio/carat features, and the original dataset provided the main gains. Duplicate-price overrides hurt private performance, while neural-network stackers overfit and blending performed worse than Ridge.

The solution trained classification decision trees separately for each patient and EEG channel, then averaged channel predictions. It used safe data files without preprocessing and extracted 73 real-valued features per channel from complete ten-minute recordings. Signal statistics, wavelet features, and cross-channel spectral correlations supplied the predictors. The model achieved 0.80396 public AUC and 0.79074 private AUC, while random validation overstated performance and testing on unseen subjects reduced AUC to about 0.6.
compute: Training and output generation took under one minute per patient.

solution_summary: The solution combines external essay datasets, duplicate removal, byte-pair tokenization, and TF-IDF features. Multinomial Naive Bayes and an SGD model are combined with tuned weights. Feature limits and removal of LightGBM and CatBoost reduced runtime, although the authors later judged removing those models to be a mistake for private performance. Changing TF-IDF n-grams did not help, and the best reported private score among the listed submissions was 0.898650.

The solution classified complete grapheme combinations and converted predictions back into the three required components. Separate EfficientNet-B7 models detected unseen classes and classified seen classes, while an unseen-class pipeline used font-synthetic training data and CycleGAN translation from handwriting to font-like images. A frozen font classifier supplied supervised guidance during CycleGAN training, and two font-specific models were ensembled for submission. The unseen-class model reached 0.8804 local recall in the reported experiment, although the author identified flaws in the random validation split.
compute: Each B7 stage: 1 Tesla V100 for 6 days; font classifier: 1 Tesla V100 for 4 hours; CycleGAN: 4 Tesla V100 GPUs for 2.5 days.

solution_summary: The solution averaged LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost predictions, with 25 seeds per model. Quake-based validation, fixed boosting rounds across folds, and feature filtering addressed unstable validation distributions. The team selected 15 features and trained models for both time to failure and time since failure. A reconstruction of the test failure distribution informed post-processing, producing public and private scores of 2.10809 and 2.40159.

The team combined YOLOv5m and YOLOv5s detectors trained at multiple large image resolutions. Video-based validation, recall-focused checkpoint selection, and tuned weighted boxes fusion guided the final pipeline. Mixup, mosaic, and strong HSV augmentation supported ten-epoch training with Adam. Enlarging inference images beyond their training resolution looked promising publicly but failed locally; the final submission scored 0.713 privately and 0.648 publicly.

The final pipeline used manually engineered light-curve features, passband-level prediction features, and separate galactic and extragalactic models with and without spectroscopic redshift. LightGBM and XGBoost multiclass predictions were combined with per-class binary classifiers through a LightGBM ensemble. Feature selection, frequency summaries, Bazin fitting, and redshift-adjusted flux features supported the models. Final CV was 0.3252 with spectroscopic redshift and 0.3842 without it, while a class-99 adjustment added a small leaderboard improvement.

The solution ensembled frequency-attention sound-event detection models trained on labeled audio and pseudo-labeled soundscapes, with OpenVINO inference. It combined two pseudo-label training strategies, averaged checkpoints, maintained EMA weights, and used frozen-backbone minority-class heads. No local validation was performed, and a second pseudo-label iteration reduced standalone scores but was retained for ensemble diversity. Temporal and file-level probability smoothing produced a large gain, with final scores of 0.904 public and 0.918 private.

solution_title: [Top 300] You can get a Bronze Medal without doing (m)anything!
solution_summary: The author equally blended predictions from two public notebooks. These were a GPU LightGBM baseline and a neural network using pairwise ranking loss. The blend achieved 0.686 cross-validation and 0.692 on the private leaderboard.

The team used LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost with substantial effort devoted to identifying transactions from the same user. Date-like quantities derived from TransactionDT and D features helped establish identities, while historical transaction counts and cumulative amounts helped verify them. User identities were incorporated as features, in postprocessing, and through pseudo-labeling. Validation trained on the first three months, excluded a one-month gap, and evaluated on the final two months; it tracked the public leaderboard better than the private set.

The author constructed customer–article candidate tables using the 10,000 most popular articles from the previous two weeks. RAPIDS cuDF and batches of 1,000 users made the large feature-generation pipeline practical. Purchase counts, purchase probabilities, and recency features fed ranking models trained with randomly sampled negatives. An ensemble spanning models, negative samples, and training periods scored approximately 0.0323 publicly and 0.0319 privately; binary-loss models, highly imbalanced training, and deep or sequential models did not work.
compute: cuDF candidate construction took minutes for all customers per week; intermediate datasets exceeded 1.5 TB on disk.

solution_summary: The solution averaged about 30 diverse RNN, DPCNN, and gradient boosting models. Neural networks used several pretrained word embeddings, including multilingual BPEmb embeddings. Translation-based training augmentation and test-time augmentation provided the main performance boost. Training used five-fold cross-validation on one GPU.
compute: 1 GPU

solution_summary: The solution first recovered leaked targets through sequential column patterns found with brute-force search and heuristics. For rows without recovered targets, it used boosted trees and recurrent neural networks with row statistics, temporal summaries, string-derived features, PCA, and clustering features. Leaked test labels were also used to evaluate models and choose ensemble weights. Fifteen models were stacked using neural network, LightGBM, and ExtraTrees second-level models, with additional averaging of public kernel predictions.
compute: Approximately one day to search for leak patterns.

solution_summary: The solution combines engineered product, medical-keyword, interaction, and missingness features with 13 predicted class and cumulative-probability features. Those probabilities come from XGBoost, random forest, and logistic regression models and feed a final linear regression. Robustness mattered more than added model complexity, as more elaborate regressors and ensembles did not improve the result. The final continuous predictions are converted to classes using optimized monotonic cutoffs.

The solution used a 2.5D pipeline with skull cropping, training-only vessel segmentation, frame classification, and sequence aggregation. CoAtNet and MaxViT classifiers benefited from position-aware modeling, carefully sampled neighboring frames, refined positive masks, and strong augmentation. Vessel segmentation supplied useful negatives, while a sequence model improved on simple maximum aggregation. A three-model ensemble achieved 0.895 CV and reported public and private scores of 0.84, with frame subsampling used to control inference time.
compute: A two-model pipeline was estimated to run in 7 hours.

solution_summary: The approach ensembles pretrained image classifiers with variation in architecture, image resolution, and training folds. Custom OpenCV augmentation supports arbitrary rotations and downscaling without fixed border artifacts, while dropout and flexible pooling help control overfitting and accommodate different resolutions. The code also supports test-time augmentation. A submission-handling bug affected private scores, and dense-sparse-dense training increased overfitting.
models_pretrained: ["Torchvision DenseNet and ResNet", "Inception-V4 and Inception-ResNet-V2", "Facebook ResNet-200", "Wide ResNet WRN-50-2 (excluded)", "Facebook ResNeXt-101-32x4d (excluded)"]

solution_summary: The pipeline generated about 1200 candidates per session from visited items, multiple covisitation matrices, and neural next-item predictors. LightGBM rankers reranked candidates using session-item interactions, neural similarities, item popularity, and session statistics. Feature selection and target-specific negative sampling kept training data manageable. Averaging nine rankers improved the leaderboard score from 0.604 to 0.605, and local validation closely tracked leaderboard changes.

The solution extended a public LightGBM baseline with target encoding, one-hot encoding, and aggregates over selected time windows. Feature importance helped prune the many generated features, while a bureau debt-to-credit ratio raised local CV from 798 to 799+ as reported by the author. The team also explored stacking diverse boosting models with LightGBM and ElasticNet meta-models, adding selected first-layer features to the LightGBM meta-model. Averaging 30 predictions across random seeds achieved their best private score, but that submission was not selected.

solution_title: Avito Winner's Interview: 2nd place, Changsheng Gu (aka Gzs_iceberg)
solution_summary: The solution combines field-aware factorization machines, factorization machines, and XGBoost for click prediction. Preprocessing uses feature hashing and negative downsampling, with substantial effort devoted to feature extraction and validation design. The author trained models with different feature sets to support ensembling. Hyperopt tuning produced little improvement.

The team split hierarchical sales forecasting into count-like product series and more continuous aggregate series. Negative-binomial DeepAR directly generated quantiles for product-level hierarchies, while higher aggregates used bottom-up LightGBM medians adjusted by Gaussian DeepAR quantile-to-median ratios. They validated on three recent 28-day windows and improved the final system with a second LightGBM model. The final submission achieved private WSPL of 0.16721.

solution_title: [7th Place Solution] HMM + UNet (agent is all you need)
solution_summary: The pipeline combined an HMM with learned emissions, two second-pass UNet refiners, and uncertainty-gated auxiliary corrections. Synthetic wells with realistic fabricated conditioning errors taught refiners when to distrust first-pass predictions before short real-data fine-tuning. Leak-free five-fold well-grouped validation supported every stage, while substantial inference engineering kept the selected version within the runtime limit. The selected version achieved 5.2025 pooled local error and 6.057 private error; later variants performed better privately despite weaker public scores.
compute: T4 inference stub: 5 minutes 54 seconds; approximately 50–65 seconds per hidden well, under a 9-hour runtime limit.

solution_summary: The solution treated disease grading as regression and linearly stacked EfficientNet-b0, b3, b4, and b5 models at image size 380. Models were pretrained on 2015 data and fine-tuned on 2019 data with five-fold cross-validation. Aspect-ratio-aware cropping aimed to prevent the models from exploiting black borders associated with class labels. Training augmentation and eight-way test-time augmentation supported a reported QWK of 0.930, with local CV QWK of 0.93456.
external_data: ["2015 retinal image training and public/private test data"]

solution_title: Solution to Duplicate Problem by Reverse Engineering (0.0005 Boost)
solution_summary: The author describes a next-click time feature grouped by IP, app, device, and operating system, together with a label-dependent ordering trick for duplicate clicks. They hypothesized that downloads were attributed to the latest matching click and used the target to order training clicks within the same second, while ordering test clicks by click ID. Combined with the matching time-delta feature, this ordering reportedly improved public leaderboard performance by 0.0005. Applying the ordering with other time-delta groupings did not work because it introduced incorrect information.

The author developed a WiFi localization model based on weighted nearest neighbors, with different neighbor counts for floor and coordinate predictions. RSSI values were converted to linear scale, filtered using timestamps, and compared with correlation or Bray–Curtis dissimilarity. Gaussian process regression reconstructed radio maps in areas with insufficient training coverage. Cost minimization and grid snapping improved the private score from 4.84857 for WiFi alone to 3.17900.

The team treated molecular image recognition as translation, using a ViT encoder and an original Transformer decoder. They pretrained on roughly 12 million molecular images synthesized from approved InChIs, then fine-tuned on 2.4 million original images at higher resolution. Expanding the encoder from 12 to 24 layers improved performance to 0.74 CV and 1.44 leaderboard score. Greedy decoding controlled inference cost, and RDKit normalization further improved the reported score to 1.37.
compute: Single A100 GPU on GCP and 8×RTX5000 GPUs; large-model inference at 384×384 took about 7 hours.

solution_summary: The solution combined single-stream and dual-stream DINOv3-Large regressors, followed by pseudo-label-based test-time training. Training used grouped, stratified five-fold validation, partial backbone freezing, and averaging of selected checkpoint weights. Post-processed ensemble predictions supplied pseudo-labels for adapting the best single-stream fold on the combined training and test sets. The final prediction blended Stage 1 and Stage 2 outputs with weights of 0.2 and 0.8, reporting public and private scores of 0.77 and 0.65.
compute: Two GPUs for parallel inference, with one processing five single-stream folds and the other five dual-stream folds; TTT lasted 12 epochs.

solution_summary: The team extended a public feature baseline with recording segments and information-theoretic features. They selected 60 features separately within each fold using CatBoost RecursiveByShap and ensembled CatBoost, LightGBM, ExcelFormer, and MLP models across folds and seeds. Neural models benefited from log-transformed inputs, Gaussian noise, and a softmax score-distribution output. ExcelFormer achieved the strongest listed individual CV score of 0.5916, and the team favored validation consistency over apparently stronger but potentially overfit configurations.

solution_title: Our solution, 4th place on the private LB
solution_summary: The final system connected two U-Nets: one predicted vector fields, and the other used these fields to predict masks, watershed energies, and nuclei centers. Reliable instance separation depended on center-seeded watershed and postprocessing that recovered missing instances, split merged nuclei, and removed unstable masks. The submission combined four grayscale models and two models using the H channel of HED stain decomposition, with flip and rotation augmentation at inference. Extra annotations and synthetic touching or overlapping nuclei supplemented training, while pretrained encoders and removing vector prediction did not improve results.
external_data: ["Unspecified external annotated datasets and additional histology annotations", "Synthetic touching and overlapping nuclei"]

solution_summary: The solution adjusted training time-to-failure targets using an inferred origin of the test data and an estimated optimal cycle maximum of 12.625. A search over candidate maximum values minimized segment-weighted absolute error across held-out earthquake cycles. LightGBM with many features was the main model, while a simple GRU with six features also performed well under the adjusted targets. The author reported MAE improving from 2.251 with default targets to 1.948 with modified targets.

The solution generated plausible TVT trajectories with HMMs and a particle filter, then added anchor-relative, delta-prediction, and direct correlation neural models. Sequential SoftMax gates combined five complementary candidates using geometry, GR observations, disagreement, and uncertainty. Leakage prevention covered well-grouped splits, fold-local preprocessing, and synchronized out-of-fold base and gate predictions. Averaging five folds across five split patterns achieved fold-safe local RMSE 5.2884 and private score 5.836.

The author built a Kumoko-inspired ensemble agent, integrating multiple algorithms through separate rewritten modules to isolate their state. Action selection sampled algorithms using nonnegative dllu scores as weights, and the implementation included mirrored agents. A score-history-based strategy increased randomness during poor performance, although its benefit was uncertain. An early neural-network attempt failed, and the strongest surviving submission was an older agent developed before RPS Geometry appeared.

solution_title: Forgot to shuffle the data while splitting & boom
solution_summary: The author built a basic kernel using an unshuffled train/validation split and observed strong sensitivity to the holdout size. Increasing the holdout fraction from 0.20 to 0.25 improved the reported public score from about 0.32 to 0.31120. Shuffling worsened the reported score to 0.5 or above, while a 0.24 holdout produced substantially worse public and private results than 0.25. The post reports this unexplained split sensitivity without describing the model or a complete final pipeline.

solution_title: 6th place solution つ ◕_◕ ༽つTAKE MY ENERGY ༼ つ ◕_◕ ༽つ
solution_summary: The agent combined 50 public bots with 50 anti-bots designed to exploit their deterministic behavior. It scored candidates over the last 40 rounds and sampled moves from a performance-weighted distribution. Move probabilities were converted to expected gains using win probability minus loss probability. When ahead by at least 60 points, the agent switched to random play to conceal its strategy. A probability-output variant and imitation of strong players' historical responses were also explored.
external_data: ["Public Rock Paper Scissors bot code", "Strong competitors' game histories"]

solution_title: Ensemble with Weighted MBR for Akkadian Translation
solution_summary: The system combined two independently trained ByT5 models with diverse candidate generation and weighted Minimum Bayes Risk decoding. Each model supplied beam-search outputs and samples at three temperatures, yielding 20 candidates before deduplication. Input normalization and rule-based output cleanup addressed inconsistent transliterations and formatting noise. Consensus scoring combined chrF++, BLEU, Jaccard similarity, and a length bonus to select more stable translations.

The solution averaged LSTM, BERT-base, and GPT2 models, although the listed model counts do not match the stated total of 33. Every model predicted 18 binary targets covering toxicity, toxicity types, and identities, which improved performance. The final prediction combined these outputs with explicit corrections intended to reduce identity bias and improve the competition metric. Character-count embeddings diversified the LSTMs, while length sorting and batch trimming accelerated BERT inference.
compute: Single base BERT inference accelerated to 3.5 minutes.

solution_title: [6th place code] Pseudo Labelling with single LGBM model.
solution_summary: The final approach used a single LightGBM model with pseudo-labeling. Pseudo-labeling improved the public leaderboard score from 0.84198 to 0.84185. Extensive ensembling offered little benefit and hardly improved public leaderboard performance. The chosen submission scored 0.84249 privately, while an unselected pseudo-labeled submission achieved 0.84245.

solution_title: 24th place solution: Couple more tricks, and how I kinda sorta cheated
solution_summary: The solution ensembled MLPs, DenseNets, and ResNets, with most weight assigned to MLPs. Classification targets used sigmoid-transformed returns to smooth labels dynamically across all five response targets, whose predictions were averaged. Internal validation used log-transformed trade weights to reduce the influence of extreme trades. Deployment routed high-weight observations through a large ensemble and low-weight observations through a single MLP to save runtime. Two submissions used opposite feature-dependent thresholds of 0.49 and 0.51 to hedge different market conditions.

solution_title: 1st place solution: everyone can be a winner!
solution_summary: The pipeline trains roughly 15 XGBoost models using three parameter configurations and selects about 90 prediction features for a neural network stacker. The stacker uses two sigmoid hidden layers, standardized inputs, Adam, and L1 regularization. Adding neural network predictions to the stacking features slightly improves the reported private score from about 1.73900 to 1.73890. The final step uses a weighted average.

The team combined several image-classification backbones and ensembled predictions across image sizes from 512 to 800. Pseudo labels, oversampling, class weights, and extensive augmentation addressed limited data and class imbalance. Training used focal loss and linear learning-rate decay with a ten-epoch warmup, and SE-ResNet performed particularly well. The author reports that the team's score was canceled over shared-code overlap.

The solution used a retrieval cascade followed by fine-tuned Qwen 14B, 32B, and 72B rankers operating on progressively smaller candidate sets. Carefully generated and filtered synthetic questions improved performance and generalization to unseen misconceptions. Claude-generated reasoning was distilled into smaller Qwen reasoners, while retrieval training emphasized candidate recall rather than ranking precision. Validation grouped questions by ConstructId, and final models were fitted on all available training data.
external_data: ["Eedi - Mining Misconceptions in Mathematics synthetic MCQs", "Eedi - CoT Dataset"]

solution_title: 64th Solution - A physics-guided particle filter for geosteering TVT prediction
solution_summary: The solution reconstructs structural elevation using 72 physics-based particle filters spanning noise settings, dip regimes, and seeds. Averaging particles within each filter before scoring hypotheses was central, with hybrid weights incorporating likelihood, smoothness, and gamma-ray correlation. A geometric nearest-well correction and a 1.05 excursion scaling further improved predictions. Honest out-of-fold evaluation reached about 7.39 ft RMSE, closely matching the private score of 7.338 ft.
compute: Multi-hour particle-filter run; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: A single tabular Transformer tokenizes numerical features with column embeddings and jointly predicts 424 targets. Historical targets shifted by four days provide the main temporal signal alongside the raw market features. Causal missing-value filling and training-only standardization support stable training and inference. Masked MSE, mixed precision, gradient clipping, warmup with cosine decay, and validation-based checkpoint selection complete the pipeline, which achieved a private score of 0.490.
compute: Approximately 12 minutes GPU training; submission notebook runtime approximately 12 minutes 21 seconds.

solution_summary: The final ensemble combined EfficientNetV2-M, EfficientNet-B6, and ConvNeXt-M with a hierarchical architecture that allocated more embedding capacity to individual identity than species. Switching from the detic dataset to the backfins dataset substantially improved the score. Training used subcenter CosFace with dynamic margins, alongside geometric and color augmentations, local grayscale transformation, and CLAHE at both training and inference. CosFace outperformed ArcFace in the author's experiments, while several triplet-loss approaches performed worse than CosFace.

The submission generated adversarial examples using the momentum iterative method. The authors observed limited transferability for targeted attacks across models. They attributed this difficulty to differing decision boundaries in the 1,000-class ImageNet setting. The post links to downloadable models and an implementation of the method in Cleverhans.

The solution first segmented individual cervical vertebrae in 3D, then classified fractures using cropped vertebrae and 2.5D CNN features aggregated by an LSTM. Each vertebra supplied 15 sampled positions with adjacent slices and a predicted segmentation mask as input channels. Separate classifiers learned individual vertebra labels and patient-level fracture labels, with several backbones and folds included in the final submission. Direct 3D CNN classification was unsatisfactory, while patient-level classification constrained backbone size because of memory use. Submission inference took 7.5 hours.
compute: More than half of models trained on a Z8G4 workstation with dual A6000 GPUs; submission inference took 7.5 hours.

solution_title: Mick Wagner on finishing second in the Ford Challenge
solution_summary: The author used an out-of-the-box SQL Server Analysis Services neural network to detect driver alertness. Holding out complete trials, rather than randomly selected records, had the largest reported impact on model accuracy. Training data was narrowed to the initial loss of alertness, and exploratory analysis supplied additional environmental and vehicle variables plus physiological variable P6. The neural network outperformed the tested decision tree.

solution_summary: The author's strongest model used pretrained deberta-v3-xsmall with multiple auxiliary prediction heads. Training used the full dataset and sample weights based on signal-to-noise ratio and read counts, although limited compute prevented completing all folds. Blending more of the best checkpoints consistently improved leaderboard performance. The team's final blend underperformed this individual model.
compute: One 1080TI GPU; small batches and long training prevented completing all five folds.

solution_summary: The author's contribution extended a public kernel with frequency encodings, Malaysian demographic data, and breed information. A LightGBM adversarial classifier identified training examples unlike the test set, and the most dissimilar 15% were removed. This filtering improved the leaderboard score by approximately 0.01; before the team merge, the approach scored 0.47 on the leaderboard and 0.48 in stratified cross-validation. Numerous alternative models and features did not help, while unstable QWK and kernel reproducibility complicated model selection.

The solution combined public training and inference code with confidence-filtered pseudo-labels and audio augmentation. The final ensemble contained five HGNet-B0 models with different spectrogram parameter configurations and achieved 0.936 public and 0.934 private scores. The author identified limited architectural diversity as a weakness and reported that vocal removal, larger models, larger input shapes, and a second pseudo-labeling round did not help.

The solution creates four training datasets named N1, N2, N3, and RND, plus 319 expert training sets. Separate scripts generate predictions from the main models and expert models, which are then blended into two final submissions. NumPy, pandas, and scikit-learn support feature processing, data handling, and training. The two blends reversed their relative performance between the public and private leaderboards.

solution_title: Otto Product Classification Winner's Interview: 2nd place, Alexander Guschin ¯\_(ツ)_/¯
solution_summary: The solution uses stacking with out-of-fold predictions as metafeatures, processing raw and TF-IDF-transformed data in parallel. KNN, random forest, and XGBoost supply first-level predictions, while neural networks and XGBoost serve as second-level classifiers. Diverse KNN metafeatures and second-level bagging were particularly useful. Combining the second-level neural network and XGBoost improved private leaderboard log loss from about 0.391 individually to 0.386.

solution_title: 35th Place Solution: Ensemble 10 Models with Hill Climbing
solution_summary: The solution combined survival-target gradient boosting models, LitNN models trained with pairwise ranking loss, and an unchanged public Yunbase pipeline. Boosting models used KM, NA, and Cox target transformations after separate power transformations within event and survival groups, and predictions were averaged across two seeds. Hill climbing with a 0.01 search step and negative weights improved the ensemble, while one strong standalone LitNN model was excluded because it reduced ensemble CV. Adding Yunbase increased CV from 0.6869 to 0.6876.

The pipeline first classified ship presence with a ResNet34 and ResNeXt50 ensemble, then segmented selected images with a DenseNet169 U-Net. Overlap-aware validation and contour labels helped address leakage and separation of nearby ships. Training combined binary cross-entropy and Dice loss with augmentation, cyclic learning rates, and test-time augmentation. Morphological postprocessing separated connected masks, while public-leaderboard threshold tuning overfit and probability averaging worked poorly.
compute: 6 Nvidia 1080Ti or equivalent GPUs and 2 smaller GPUs.

solution_summary: The author adapted a baseline sound-event detection model with a pretrained DenseNet121 backbone and a smaller attention block to reduce overfitting. Thirteen fold models combined mixup and non-mixup training, audio noise augmentation, and SpecAugmentation. Inference required agreement between clipwise and framewise predictions, used ten stochastic augmentation passes, and combined models with a four-vote threshold. Ensemble decisions mattered most because individual models were weak on the public leaderboard and local validation did not track it reliably.

The solution fine-tuned Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with QLoRA in two stages, first on general preference data and then on competition-like data. Character-count truncation markers, response swapping within batches, and auxiliary response-model classification improved accuracy. Settings were evaluated on one fold before retraining on all data. Inference distributed samples across two GPUs and selectively averaged swapped-response predictions for the most uncertain 40% of samples.
compute: Two GPUs for inference; response-swapping augmentation doubled training time.

solution_summary: The final solution used weighted rank averaging of Lasso, logistic regression, and a shared tuned SVM submission. Because cross-validation was unreliable, the author developed a submission-similarity ranker to screen candidates against previously scored public submissions. Feature selection, random seeds, and ensemble components were chosen with heavy dependence on public leaderboard feedback, which the author acknowledged introduced leakage. Adding the SVM supplied useful diversity and raised the public score to 0.881.

The approach trained CNNs on the last two weeks of data, using separate models for each forecast horizon to avoid recursive prediction drift. A cumulative sum over ReLU outputs enforced nonnegative predictions and ordered quantiles. Training used pinball loss with narrower quantiles initially before switching to the target quantiles. Five models per horizon were bagged, then daily predictions were smoothed and rounded to integers.

The solution combined two DeBERTa-v3-large models and an LSTM, with one transformer receiving the summary and prompt context while the other transformer and LSTM used only the summary. Validation grouped examples by prompt, and the selected approach included the unusual prompt 814d6b in evaluation. Training used SmoothL1 loss, AdamW, linear warmup and decay, and exponential moving averages. The final submission ensembled three seeds trained on all data, achieving a private score of 0.457.

The solution adapted a previous BirdCLEF approach using ResNet and EfficientNet backbones, with pseudo-labeling and temporal post-processing as the main changes. Pseudo-labeled segments received losses without aggregation, whereas competition data used max aggregation across segments. RMS-based audio sampling and cached 32 kHz resampling improved training effectiveness and speed. Weighted temporal smoothing plus a species-level global average improved both public and private scores by roughly 0.014–0.016. Since CV was unhelpful, model choices relied on limited public leaderboard checks.

The solution centered on transaction aggregation features, arithmetic interactions between historical and new transaction aggregates, and date features. Count-vector features were selected, while word2vec and neural-network out-of-fold predictions provided additional inputs. Out-of-fold predictions from about 70 LightGBM and neural-network models were stacked. The reported stacking scores were 3.627 in cross-validation, 3.669 on the public leaderboard, and 3.601 on the private leaderboard.

The team pretrained medium-sized image models on the 2015 competition data, then fine-tuned with five-fold validation on 2019 data combined with IDRID and MESSIDOR. They abandoned image preprocessing in favor of strong augmentation and jointly trained classification, ordinal regression, and regression heads with a learned linear combiner. Staged freezing and regression-label noise helped address uneven head training and overfitting. Their selected ensemble contained 20 models with ten-way test-time augmentation and a trimmed mean, chosen despite weaker holdout and leaderboard results in the hope of better generalization.
compute: FastGPU.net server with 4x V100 GPUs.

solution_summary: The team trained CNN embeddings with ArcFace and softmax, with ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-101 giving the best validation result. Inference assigned images to the nearest normalized class centroid by cosine distance and rejected non-landmarks using a softmax threshold. Ten-crop averaging and weighted voting across architectures and five folds improved predictions. The best single model achieved private GAP 0.205, while the ensemble reached 0.228; kNN brought no significant improvement.

The solution used LightGBM DART with temporal aggregates, differences, ratios, missingness statistics, and date features. Its most important addition was time-aggregated out-of-fold predictions from models trained on individual customer records before customer aggregation. Adversarial validation and shuffled-target importance guided feature removal, while three different feature sets supplied a weighted rank ensemble. The best submission scored 0.79922 locally, 0.80088 publicly, and 0.80852 privately, with distribution-shift-aware submission selection proving helpful.

The final solution averaged predictions from four EfficientNet-B5 classifiers trained with different image sizes and historical data combinations. Triple stratified splitting, image augmentation, and fresh majority-class subsampling each epoch supported training. All models used AdamW and a one-cycle learning-rate schedule for 20 epochs. The ensemble achieved public and private leaderboard scores of 0.9570 and 0.9403.

The author trained separate modified U-Net segmentation models for ten classes using 20-channel satellite imagery and 224-by-224 patches. Preprocessing aligned spectral channels at 3360-by-3360 resolution, normalized their values, and increased positive training examples with windows around labeled pixels. Class-specific, image-level stratified folds supplied multiple model weights, while grid search addressed unstable training. The final approach mostly used Adam, batch normalization, and rotation augmentation, with a Jaccard-based objective; the provided text ends before completing the validation discussion.
compute: NVIDIA GTX 980 8 GB running almost 24 hours daily during the competition; two additional TITAN 12GB GPUs after joining the team.

solution_summary: The solution linearly combined three EfficientNetB3 classifiers and five ResNet50 classifiers. EfficientNet inputs used polar unrolling at 300×768 resolution, with one model pretrained on 2015 data before fine-tuning on 2019 data. These models used cropping, Ben Graham preprocessing, zoom and flip augmentation, and geometric-mean flip TTA. The EfficientNet models reported scores of 0.788, 0.782, and 0.794; ResNet50 models used 300×300 images with gray-border cropping.

The author used heavily blended RoBERTa-base span-extraction models, with a small benefit from SQuAD2 pretraining. Removing special-character tokenizer merges let models select punctuation spans more precisely, while preserving spaces helped model annotation artifacts. The end-token head incorporated the predicted start-token representation, and sentiment-specific training handled neutral examples separately. Final submissions used either regular model blends or pseudo-label-compressed models and performed almost identically.

The pipeline detects lung nodules with a 3D Faster R-CNN based on U-Net, then classifies patients using features from sampled nodule proposals. Training combines LUNA16 with manually annotated competition scans and cleaned nodule labels. CT preprocessing standardizes voxel spacing and intensity and masks areas outside the lungs. Patient probabilities combine proposal probabilities with a trainable dummy-nodule probability, while alternating detection and classification training helps prevent overfitting.

solution_summary: The solution uses separate architectures for complete sensor sequences and IMU-only sequences, then combines roughly 20 diverse models with hill-climbing weight selection. Complete sequences use bidirectional Mamba branches with Transformer sensor fusion, while IMU-only sequences use an SE-Transformer. Handedness and device-orientation corrections, acceleration features for missing rotations, and staged hard-sample training improve robustness. Reported CV scores were 0.9027 for the full model and 0.8537 for IMU-only, with a private score of 0.861; gesture-count postprocessing added 0.003 on the public leaderboard.

solution_title: 4th place writeup - Instruct LLM is all you need
solution_summary: The solution used SALSA to classify rule violations directly from an instruction model's next-token probabilities over a small answer vocabulary. Training incorporated labeled few-shot examples, deduplicated comment–rule pairs with soft targets, AWQ models, and Generalized Cross-Entropy. A smaller model supplied approximately 8,000 uncertain test examples as soft pseudo-labels for a larger Qwen-3 14B model. Blending the two stages at 0.8:0.2 achieved public AUC 0.93382 and private AUC 0.9286.

solution_title: How on Earth did I win this competetion?
solution_summary: The solution used a DNN based on a Variable Selection Network, with an eight-neuron linear projection for every feature instead of conventional scaling. Heavy dropout and final probability reweighting were effective. Training used ten folds with repeated runs, retaining the two best models per fold because results were highly unstable. Fold construction considered both the target and a prediction-difficulty label, while gradient boosting and feature engineering overfit.

The final submission combined seven 2.5D segmentation models trained on all available data, varying slice inputs, training schedules, and encoder-decoder combinations. ConvNeXt backbones and class-specific mask thresholds were particularly effective. ACS convolution enabled experiments with ImageNet-pretrained backbones for volumetric segmentation. An alternative ensemble replacing two 2.5D models with 3D models scored higher, but was not selected.

solution_title: DeepZot on Dark Matter: How we won the Mapping Dark Matter challenge
solution_summary: The approach fit star and galaxy images using pixel-level maximum likelihood with galaxy and point spread function models. Residual distributions across images guided model and parameter assessment. A neural network then corrected ellipticity estimates using a selected subset of fitting outputs. Feature choice mattered: including galaxy centroid position worsened the correction.

The author achieved a score of about 0.24 using an NLP ensemble assembled from public kernels. The main components combined count and TF-IDF representations with multinomial Naive Bayes, Bernoulli Naive Bayes, and logistic regression. Additional features and parameter tuning came from community notebooks. GRU models were explored but were not integrated before time ran out.

The solution treated plates as domains and used plate-aware batches during training and domain-specific batch statistics during inference. CNN backbones fed shared and cell-specific classification heads trained with ArcFace losses. Fine-tuning with exemplar memory modules for HUVEC-05 and test experiments improved the reported leaderboard accuracy by approximately one percentage point. Predictions used cell-specific heads, averaged the two imaging sites, and applied linear assignment without test-time augmentation.

The author used deep learning and random forests on approximately 8% of the data. The post shares only this brief model overview. Further implementation details and results were deferred to a later update.

The solution combined several LoRA-trained embedding retrievers with two stages of Qwen reranking. Few-shot synthetic questions supported retrieval of unseen misconceptions, while validation gave equal importance to seen and unseen misconceptions. Reranker generalization improved by excluding test misconceptions from training and using self-distillation. Combining original and rephrased misconception logits and averaging both orderings of the top two candidates each helped refine the rankings.
compute: Synthetic generation: 2x A40 for 3 hours; retriever training: 1x RTX 3090 for 9 hours per model; reranker training: 1x A40 for 6 hours per model. Some A100 experiments; approximately $300 total.

solution_summary: The author used a target-stratified five-fold pipeline combining tree models and neural networks with basic feature engineering. FT-Transformer performed strongly on its own and contributed useful diversity, alongside factorization machines and DANet. A reused stacking implementation combined the models, while missing values received only basic model-dependent treatment. The main submission achieved 0.95069 in cross-validation and 0.95081 on the private leaderboard using Kaggle CPU and dual-T4 resources.

solution_summary: The authors trained Protenix on competition data combined with CASP16 pseudo-labels and date-filtered RNA PDB structures. Training retained unresolved residues through masking, incorporated multiple conformations, and used MMseqs2 alignments where available. Output selection retained the highest-pLDDT structure and then selected additional conformations for RMSD diversity. The reported single-model submission scored 0.46388, while experiments using RibonanzaNet or Nufold for longer sequences scored 0.478 and 0.479.

solution_summary: The solution combined a blend of two sequence-model architectures with a physics-based matching algorithm. A long-trained LSTM used only nine raw and categorical features, while a second architecture combined LSTMs with convolutional Transformer encoder layers and engineered features. The blend achieved a reported score slightly above 0.1107 before matching corrections. By reconstructing the data-generating PID controller and exploiting discrete pressure levels, the matcher recovered exact predictions for about 66% of the data, including additional matches obtained by modeling injected noise.

solution_summary: The final system used a nonlinear LightGBM stacker combining diverse base predictions with strong original features. The author's main contribution was a LightGBM model using roughly 800 tabular features and 100,000 TF-IDF features, scoring 0.2175 public and 0.2213 private RMSE. Relative price statistics over granular textual groups were central, supplemented by user-level text factors, behavioral aggregates, and image features. Cached aggregate tables, greedy feature selection, and single-fold evaluation accelerated experimentation.

The author repeatedly submitted a fixed set of nine essays, keeping the similarity score near 1/9 and below the 0.2 threshold. Testing combinations of three fixed essays made it easier to identify effective payloads than using fresh random text. Some essays repeated an override topic to reduce dependence on the actual judging topic, while others used grading instructions, arithmetic prompts or numbered summary choices to influence judges. The reported public and private scores were 29.303 and 29.811.

The team ensembled diverse transformer regressors with different pooling methods, sequence lengths, and fine-tuning configurations, alongside three embedding-based SVR models. Multilabel-stratified folds gave strong agreement between ensemble validation and leaderboard performance. Pseudo-labeling and averaging pseudo-labels with actual training labels helped, although training-data soft labels could cause severe overfitting. Target-specific ensemble weights were tuned with Optuna using out-of-fold predictions. The selected ensemble achieved CV 0.44096 and private score 0.433356.

solution_title: Kaggle IEEE's Signal Processing Society - Camera Model Identification
solution_summary: The system used a nine-model ensemble for camera model identification. External images from Yandex.Fotki and Flickr were essential and underwent filtering before training. Initial models generated pseudo-labels for test images, after which the same nine models were trained again using those labels. The supplied final weights include DenseNet161 and DPN92 models.
