solution_summary: The post describes a cropping method for removing black backgrounds from segmentation images. Median filtering before thresholding suppressed background noise, and zero padding improved behavior around gray corner pixels. All slices within a sequence were cropped at identical coordinates to preserve alignment. Aspect-ratio preservation was tested but omitted because cropping was mainly vertical.

solution_title: 6th simple solution, pre-training, single model private 0.66927
solution_summary: The author described a pretraining strategy for cloud segmentation using automatically generated cloud masks. Pixels above a threshold of 115 provided labels for pretraining on all 9,244 images, and those weights initialized a second training stage. This improved cross-validation scores by 0.005–0.01. Reported single models paired EfficientNet-B4 with U-Net or FPN, achieving private scores of 0.66927 and 0.66827 respectively.

solution_title: Rossmann Store Sales, Winner's Interview: 3rd place, Neokami Inc.
solution_summary: The solution used neural networks with learned entity embeddings to represent categorical features in continuous spaces. These embeddings addressed sparse categorical combinations and reportedly outperformed XGBoost with the same features. A small input dropout rate of 0.02 improved generalization. The final submission averaged ten networks, requiring about 3.5 hours of training on a GTX 980 GPU.
compute: Nvidia GTX 980 GPU; 20 minutes per network and about 3.5 hours for ten networks; prediction time was small.

solution_summary: The approach used predictions from a public LLM ensemble as soft labels to pretrain DeBERTa on selected unlabelled rule–body pairs. Claude-assisted subreddit screening reduced approximately 12 million possible pairs to 800K by excluding subreddits with very low estimated violation rates. The final submission combined DeBERTa-large with a triplet model using eight augmentations and an FP16 Llama 3B model. An earlier two-seed DeBERTa-base version improved the reported score from 0.912 to about 0.924.
compute: Two-seed DeBERTa-base submission took around 1 hour; current score attained in under 6 hours.

solution_title: First Place Write-Up: Or How I Won the Lottery
solution_summary: The final approach combined LightGBM, two XGBoost regressors, CatBoost, and ExtraTrees in a voted ensemble. It predicted the continuous PCIAT total score and converted predictions into sii labels. Robustness came from stratified validation, repeated tuning splits, careful cleaning, actigraph features, and Lasso-based imputation. Manual feature selection reduced the inputs to 39 features, while quantile binning helped handle noisy measurements.

solution_title: 149th Place Solution for the ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions Competition
solution_summary: The final solution averaged five CatBoost models and five LightGBM models trained with different seeds. It used 20-fold multilabel stratification based on the target and Greek metadata, with model selection guided by cross-validation despite substantial fold variability. Early stopping and regularization limited overfitting, and the final features were the original training columns excluding Id. Predicted Greek metadata features were rejected because they hurt generalization. The combined ensemble achieved CV 0.12087 and private leaderboard loss 0.39377.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution, ensemble of old and new methods
solution_summary: The solution began with an undisclosed detector-free transformer matcher that achieved private/public scores of 0.838/0.833. Ensembling it with QuadTree, LoFTR, and SuperGlue raised those scores to 0.862/0.859. Normalizing positional coordinates to the training resolution consistently improved transformer matchers, while aspect-ratio-dependent fixed input sizes controlled memory use. Fundamental matrices were estimated with OpenCV USAC_MAGSAC, without test-time augmentation or multi-resolution inference.

The solution started from a public submission because the author's neural networks did not improve beyond 7.7 CV. It corrected floor predictions using shared Wi-Fi and device-ID leakages, changing only three private-test paths. Coordinates were then postprocessed as a shortest-path problem using Dijkstra's algorithm over training and generated waypoints. Generated waypoints followed hallway and spacing constraints, while leakage-based endpoint corrections did not combine well with the shortest-path step.

solution_title: 18th place solution from 300-th at Public LB
solution_summary: The solution used a two-layer RNN with 96 units and five-fold training. Important details included semantic Bernoulli dropout on embeddings, preserving tokenizer characters, increasing batch size over epochs, and trimming sequences within each batch. Embedding weights were trained only in the final epoch. Local CV was approximately 0.696–0.698, while several more complex architectures and typo corrections were excluded.

solution_title: 43rd Place : Summary and What Worked Well
solution_summary: The solution combined dimensionality-reduced raw and binarized inputs with MLPs, TabNet, and boosted trees for CITE and multiome prediction. Selected models also used PCA features, day information, and highly correlated raw features for individual CITE targets. Donor-grouped validation received greater ensemble weight than ordinary KFold. Adding per-target boosted-tree models produced the best ensemble and raised the public score to 0.8142.

solution_title: Prompt Ensemble Diversification with Family-Weighted Voting on gpt-oss-120b
solution_summary: The solution used an unmodified gpt-oss-120b model with eight parallel, tool-assisted reasoning attempts spanning different prompt families. The final submission combined a mixed reasoning schedule, entropy-weighted answer selection, and strict early stopping requiring agreement across families and a low-temperature attempt. Persistent Python kernels, prefix caching, and adaptive problem budgets supported inference within the runtime limit. The reported public score was 42/50, compared with 38 for an earlier QLoRA attempt, while an ablation baseline reached 43/50.
compute: Single NVIDIA H100 80 GB; 17,400-second (~4.83-hour) inference budget for 50 problems; eight workers.

solution_summary: The author explored diverse architectures, including CNNs and DANets, alongside FLAML and AutoGluon. Out-of-fold and test predictions from standalone models became inputs to an AutoGluon ensemble. AutoGluon selected blending weights and stacking layers. The reported scores were 0.97043 for cross-validation, 0.97085 on the public leaderboard, and 0.97020 on the private leaderboard.

The solution stacks three shallow XGBoost models trained on different feature subsets using logistic regression. It replaces extreme calc and osmo values with missing values, then introduces additional missingness at rates based on the train-validation score gap and feature importance. Validation uses 10-fold repeated K-fold with 10 repeats, also supplying more predictions for the stacking model. The author reports a cross-validation score of 0.812 and a small benefit from the additional missingness.

The solution trains only on rows belonging to near-duplicate sequences and forces predictions for other rows to zero. Features describe time groups, elapsed production time, neighboring rows, and the size and position of duplicate sets. XGBoost and random forest predictions are combined with a weighted average. More elaborate ensembles vary feature subsets and algorithms, including one selected submission that requires at least 11 prior submissions to predict a positive.

solution_title: ARC Late Submission: 29 tasks, +38% from 1st Place
solution_summary: The author improved a late ARC submission by combining existing notebooks within the three-guesses-per-task limit. A sparse notebook supplied the base predictions, and another notebook filled unused slots. Removing duplicate guesses increased solved tasks from 24 to 28, and choosing the filler notebook's most confident guesses raised the total to 29 out of 100, with a reported score of 0.715. The main finding was that prediction diversity and efficient use of guess slots substantially improved the ensemble.
compute: The two source notebooks run in less than 9 CPU hours total.

solution_summary: The pipeline corrected image rotation, detected and segmented ECG leads, and digitized cropped signals using complementary MaxxViT and DINOv3 ViT architectures. Synthetic annotated images supported the localization stages, while competition data supported digitization. Segmentation-aware inputs helped with overlapping leads, and progressive resolution training supported the ViT models. An ArcFace-based out-of-distribution detector selectively suppressed specialized model predictions, improving public/private scores from 22.54/22.10 to 22.80/22.48.

The team combined text, image, categorical, and temporal features across a broad collection of tree, linear, and neural models. Dense RNN and sentence2vec features, pretrained word embeddings, and out-of-fold target features were useful components. Their ensemble retained all 154 first-level models, used LightGBM and Keras at the second level, and weighted averaging at the third level. Cross-entropy objectives and category-specific training increased diversity, while stacking improved the score by almost 0.004 over the best first-level models.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled 3D ResNet18 and ResNet34 models trained on overlapping papyrus tiles using 32 depth slices. Training combined binary cross-entropy, AdamW, warmup scheduling, and strong mosaic and Albumentations augmentation. Inference used larger overlapping tiles, discarded predictions near tile edges, and applied rotation and flip augmentation plus denoising. The reported scores were 0.804 public and 0.668 private.

The solution combined 42 CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost, TabM, and neural models, with target construction providing the main gains. Separate classification and event-time ranking models were combined through a risk formula, alongside models trained on shifted and reweighted Nelson–Aalen targets. Greedy ensemble selection reduced a much larger model library, while logit-space averaging and conservative post-processing improved the combined predictions. The full ensemble scored 0.69881 privately, while a four-model version achieved 0.69812.
compute: Final 42 models: about 6 GPU hours and 14 CPU hours; ensemble-selection inputs: about 75 hours total; submission inference about 45 minutes.

solution_title: 29th Place Solution for the BirdCLEF+ 2025 Competition
solution_summary: The solution trained several image backbones on standardized audio representations with varying segment lengths, focal loss, and time-frequency augmentation. Training used 10–30 second segments, while inference used five-second segments and averaged logits from the five best checkpoints per model. The stated final weighted blend combined EfficientNet, ResNeSt, and ConvNeXt, although NFNet was also listed among the backbones. Models were trained on all data for the final solution, with ONNX used for runtime performance; reported public and private scores were 0.902 and 0.906.

The post describes pruning a pool of more than 200 models using Optimal Brain Surgery on logistic-regression weighted log loss. About 25 diverse models were sufficient for logistic regression and MLP stackers, whereas tree stackers preferred nearly the entire pool. The author also found balanced accuracy extremely noisy, limiting confidence in small performance differences.

solution_title: [10th] Place Solution for the  Image Matching Challenge 2024 - Hexathlon
solution_summary: The pipeline corrected image orientation, selected image pairs, extracted and matched keypoints, and fused matches before reconstruction. It combined ALIKED with LightGlue and AffNet/HardNet with AdaLAM, using center crops to improve transparent-object matching. COLMAP's incremental mapper reconstructed scenes with nearly default settings. Runtime constraints limited the final submission to two-model fusion; alternative HardNet weights and image embeddings showed no meaningful local gains.

The author started from the highest-scoring public notebook and tuned its random seed, obtaining about 442773 with seed 5. A local search swapped vertical photos between paired vertical slides, improving the score to 442776. Reapplying the notebook's slide-swap and sequence-reversal search raised the final score to 442789.

The solution predicted a joint target combining gesture, orientation, and an initial behavior state. It blended heavily bagged CNN-attention and BERT-based architectures, including separate IMU-only and full-sensor variants. Subject-history post-processing exploited the constraint that each joint target occurred at most once per subject. Limited sensor feature engineering and phase-specific augmentations supported training, while random inference order caused substantial score variation across resubmissions.

The solution used a two-stage architecture with a 2D image classifier followed by a 1D classifier aggregating predictions across instances. Rather than cropping anatomical regions, it trained an auxiliary detector and used its heatmaps to weight feature extraction. This preserved image context and reduced sensitivity to uncertain detections. Self-supervised learning using coordinate-based multiview similarity slightly improved leaderboard scores, while manual relabeling was unsuccessful.

The solution combined extensive tabular feature engineering with a diverse pool of 330 models stacked using Ridge regression. TabM was the strongest individual model, while negative stacking weights helped remove redundancy between correlated predictions. Model diversity mattered more than small cross-validation improvements from similar models. The final ensemble achieved CV 8.5659 and LB 8.53642, with predictions clipped to the target range.

solution_title: 14th place solution: An attempt to reverse-engineer the dataset
solution_summary: The author traced training questions to source articles and used their categories to build a large retrieval and training corpus. GPT-3.5 generated about 750,000 segment-question-answer triplets, which supplied all model training data. Retrieval combined fine-tuned e5 and bge embeddings with TF-IDF similarities. The final ensemble contained three DeBERTa multiple-choice models, each evaluated with four different retrieved-context collections.
external_data: ["Adjacent by Category (AC) generated training dataset", "Grandparent (GP) dataset", "Natural Sciences (NS) dataset", "GP Plus 1 (GPP1) dataset", "AC-750 dataset"]

solution_summary: The author focused almost entirely on modeling rather than feature engineering. Time of day was the only added feature described in the text. The final submission combined four models trained with different sequence lengths, while further architecture details were supplied only as an image.

The author trained a SAINT+-style encoder-decoder transformer with two encoder layers, two decoder layers, 256-dimensional embeddings, and sequences of length 100. Encoder inputs combined question metadata, attempts, lag time, and a continuous harmonic-mean feature, while decoder inputs used shifted answer and timing information. Training used Adam for 25 epochs with a reduced learning rate for the final five epochs. Reported local training and validation AUCs were 0.804 and 0.806.
compute: GPU training took approximately 7–8 hours for 25 epochs; inference took 3–4 hours.

solution_summary: The solution improved teacher-generated reasoning traces through task-specific symbolic solvers and iterative dataset refinement. Bit-operation verification, cryptarithm fallbacks, and structural constraints on numeric operators increased solved-example accuracy from 87.7% to 89.4%. Cryptarithm data was rebalanced and expanded with synthetic tasks. The resulting dataset supported three stages of LoRA supervised fine-tuning, with deliberately aggressive fitting to reduce trace errors.
external_data: ["Open Progress Prize Publication dataset generation pipeline"]

solution_title: A brief introduction to the 1st place solution (codes released)
solution_summary: The final prediction blends bagged LightGBM models and neural networks with weights of 0.6 and 0.4. Feature engineering captures conditional listening probabilities, chronological position, matrix-factorization embeddings, and neighboring listening events. The neural networks separate user, song, and context fields and use regularized categorical embeddings and user-song dot products. Chronological validation avoids future information, and complementary model predictions raise the reported ensemble score above 0.7498.
compute: Single GTX 1080; neural-network predictions generated in several minutes

solution_summary: The solution paired a fine-tuned Bengali wav2vec2 model with a 5-gram KenLM language model. After screening numerous pretrained ASR models, the author selected shahruk10/wav2vec2-xls-r-300m-bengali-commonvoice and trained it first on filtered speech data using streaming, then on the competition examples folder. The second training stage with KenLM improved the reported score from about 0.424 to 0.404. Punctuation correction, Qwen-based typo correction, logit stacking, and Conformer-based punctuation integration did not work successfully.
compute: Approximately 20 hours for the first streaming training stage.

solution_title: 6th Place Solution: Trusting The OOF Plateau
solution_summary: The solution stacked out-of-fold probabilities from 92 public artifacts and locally trained models. The pool included neural tabular models, boosted trees, factorization-style models, and additional diverse learners evaluated with five-fold validation. Stable local OOF performance guided inclusion and final selection over more appealing public leaderboard variants. The stack reached 0.970718 OOF and 0.97054 private, a small improvement over its strongest individual public stacker.
external_data: ["Public OOF predictions and shared model artifacts"]

solution_title: [18th Place Solution + Lessons Learned from This Competition] (ISAKA's part)
solution_summary: The author explored several word-order search methods without reporting a successful final contribution. Optuna optimized per-word priorities and found the optimum for a ten-word case within hours, but scaled poorly. Fixing sentence prefixes and merging phrases reduced the search space while risking exclusion of the optimum. Alphabetically guided insertion and swapping were also explored, while reheating and temperature tuning failed to improve the best simulated-annealing score.
compute: The ten-word ID0 optimum was found within a few hours.

solution_summary: The solution used separate 18-layer transformers for 2A3 and DMS, combining sequence embeddings with per-base pairing probabilities from four RNA structure methods. Dynamic position bias helped generalization to longer sequences, while postnorm improved convergence and performance. Training weighted each base's loss using its reaction error and progressively included lower-quality sequences, with the DMS model initialized from the trained 2A3 model. A final epoch on fold 0 validation data improved the reported public and private scores to 0.14199 and 0.14458.

The author used the TabPFN-3 client with default model settings and five-fold stratified cross-validation. Feature engineering replaced sky coordinates with trigonometric transforms, inverted absolute redshift, and removed two unhelpful derived features. A brute-force search optimized class probability multipliers against balanced accuracy using pooled out-of-fold predictions. Applying these multipliers to a full-data model raised local balanced accuracy from 0.95745 to 0.96642 and produced a private score of 0.96657.
compute: Client-based five-fold cross-validation took approximately 30 minutes; resources provided by Prior Labs.

solution_title: Post mortem -- what worked for me
solution_summary: The solution used ordinal encoding for ordinal columns and sparse one-hot encoding for all remaining columns. A logistic regression model with the saga solver used a carefully tuned C of 0.1172 and 50 iterations. Cross-validation guided regularization tuning and generally tracked public leaderboard changes, although an earlier C value would have performed better on the private leaderboard. Other encodings were tested, but none surpassed one-hot encoding.

The post describes a language-specific post-processing method applied to existing test predictions. For each example, the authors averaged changes across consecutive submissions to estimate a prediction trend. They then pushed the best submission's prediction further in that direction using a weight typically set to 1 or 1.5. The improvement was small but significant relative to the other methods in their solution.

The solution stacked diverse boosted trees and tabular neural networks across two stages, followed by an XGBoost stacker using selected out-of-fold predictions. A consistent five-fold stratified split supported model comparison across multiple feature sets and training-data variants. The final ensemble used 78 weak learners, with CatBoost the strongest individual model and neural networks providing complementary signal. Target-reversal postprocessing based on duplicate relationships was retained in both final submissions.
compute: Interim experiments used 2× A6000, 2× A6000 Ada, A100, 2× A5000, RTX 4090, and a local RTX 3090.

solution_summary: Images were converted to three replicated green channels, resized with aspect ratio preserved, and center cropped. Fine-tuned pretrained CNNs on Cartesian images formed a weighted ensemble, with weights tuned on a holdout set. Polar transforms provided complementary representations that exposed radial structure and allowed peripheral background removal. An XGBoost model using flattened convolutional features from Cartesian and polar ResNets improved the private leaderboard score by about 0.07 when added to the ensemble.

solution_title: What Are Your Takeaways? & What Was Your Best Score?
solution_summary: The approach optimized feature clipping and row removal with Optuna, using a weighted RMSE score across the supplied data and original data. Most station 3–7 columns were zeroed, while forward selection retained station 1–2 features and BOD5_5. Several outlier detectors were tuned, and difficult examples identified by a random forest were duplicated to reach 3,500 submission rows. The reported best private score was 1.02648.

solution_title: 15th Place Solution : 6 kinds of AttentionPooling for each metric work well for us
solution_summary: The final submission combined 11 DeBERTa models with ensemble weights optimized separately for each scoring dimension, achieving private/public scores of 0.4346/0.4351 and local CV of 0.4431. Major improvements came from metric-specific attention pooling, adversarial weight perturbation, layer-wise learning-rate decay, and last-layer reinitialization. Some models also used sliding windows, 640-token limits, and normalization after pooling. Pseudo-labeling produced their strongest single model, but no pseudo-label-trained model was included in the best final ensemble.

The baseline approximated FiveThirtyEight matchup probabilities from team-rating differences and substituted its more precise first-round predictions. Two submissions then applied complementary probability overrides to uncertain matchups, setting predictions between 0.34 and 0.66 to either 0.36 or 0.64. This conservative submission-diversification strategy improved the best log loss from the baseline's 0.42217 to 0.38864. Thirteen scored close matches received these overrides, with a favorable 9:4 split in the better submission.

The approach fine-tuned BERT large on related intermediate tasks, then repeatedly fine-tuned each resulting model on GAP. For each task, the best half of models by validation loss were averaged, followed by averaging across task ensembles. Model instability across seeds made this heavy ensemble useful, reducing stage-one test loss from 0.33 to 0.296. Unrelated intermediate tasks and vanilla BERT large trained directly on GAP hurt the ensemble.

The approach combined public ensemble predictions with mutation effects derived from protein structure confidence and energy calculations. Confidence features used row-averaged PAE, logit transformations, averaged baseline estimates, and standard-deviation scaling to reduce noise in mutation deltas. Repeated Rosetta relaxation and FoldX repair improved the wild-type structural baseline for energy comparisons. The author also probed the public leaderboard split and optimized submissions against simulated public answers, while attempts to obtain useful training data remained unsuccessful.

The team optimized task-specific ONNX graphs through an LLM workflow centered on ChatGPT Web and later extended to Codex. A transferable rulebook and per-task bundles combined generator code, fixed examples, baseline networks, supported operators, and the official scoring harness. Optimizations exploited generator invariants and graph fusion to reduce intermediate memory and parameters while checking correctness on generated and fixed cases. The workflow exceeded 8,000 points, with periodic separate passes to improve the slowest tasks.

solution_title: 27th solution with luck and some questions from me
solution_summary: The author used a custom Keras RoBERTa architecture with unusual segment embeddings and masking behavior. The last four layers were concatenated and passed to linear output heads, with sample weighting and task loss weights adjusted to match development-set distributions. One epoch of RAdam training used a 0.05 warmup, and a single model performed inference with stride 128. Development-set threshold tuning suppressed low-confidence answers, yielding reported CV, public, and private scores of 0.523, 0.63, and 0.65.
compute: TPU training and GPU execution; one training epoch.

solution_summary: The solution blends extractive QA models within XLM-RoBERTa Large, MURIL Large, and RemBERT backbones, then votes on words across the three families. Its main training innovation is a single ordered data recipe combining multilingual QA datasets, negative sampling, and progressively longer sequences. Random context crops and token masking add diversity, while public leaderboard feedback guides selection and EM/F1 supports later early stopping. Both selected submissions scored 0.787 privately, and punctuation adjustments reduced private performance by 0.004.
compute: 1 RTX 3090 and Colab Pro; MT5-Large trained on Google Colab
external_data: ["TyDi English, Bengali, and Telugu", "English SQuAD", "Hindi MLQA and XQuAD", "Google Natural Questions", "Tamil SQuAD (tested, rejected)", "zacchaeus corrected chaii dataset (tested, rejected from ensemble)"]

solution_summary: The author experimented primarily with SE-ResNeXt50, while SE-ResNeXt101 and PNASNet-large delivered the highest accuracy. Training used Apex O2 mixed precision, weighted focal loss, gradient accumulation, and learning-rate scheduling intended to limit overfitting. Label cleaning and additions based on out-of-fold confidence helped substantially, and label-smoothed models contributed to the ensemble. The final augmentation recipe used replicated-border padding, modest geometric changes, cropping, flips, and intensity adjustments; several larger architectures and stronger transformations performed poorly.
compute: 1080 Ti used with Apex O2; distributed training on 4–8 GPUs was also discussed.

solution_summary: The author modified a public notebook to detect outliers using the entire dataframe rather than a small subset of correlated features. The approach used SVM and an isolation-based detector without clipping targets or features. It achieved a private score of 1.0185, although the isolation-based detector was inadvertently applied twice.

solution_title: 26th Place Solution: Trend Adjustment and Population Correction
solution_summary: The author recalculated historical microbusiness densities using a fixed 2021 population base. LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost used target lags, business-count differences, rolling means, and exogenous features, with a smaller CatBoost model stacking their results. Postprocessing identified larger counties with consistent recent growth using rolling medians and linear regression. Predictions for those counties were adjusted with heuristic factors checked through daily submissions.

The post congratulates participants after the Week 1 competition concluded. It praises OsciiArt's notebook as a useful benchmark across all four weeks. It reflects on the quality of work produced during a hectic first week without describing the author's own solution.

solution_title: Silver medal in very first competition!!! (A noob first Kaggle Experience)
solution_summary: The post reflects on the author's first months participating in Kaggle and learning through the MoA competition. It thanks teammates and community contributors for their support. It links a public notebook but provides no technical description of the solution.

solution_title: [11th place solution] I have survived in this storm
solution_summary: The solution used ResNeXt50 tile-pooling models with 128 intermediate-resolution tiles of size 128×128. Removing uncertain training examples using out-of-fold predictions was the most important improvement, adding approximately 0.01 or more to the private score. Kappa loss, progressive resizing, random tile removal, and offset-based tile selection augmented the pipeline, while training duration was limited to avoid learning annotation bias. The final majority-vote ensemble of eight models with six test-time augmentations scored 0.917 publicly and 0.930 privately.

The pipeline trained pretrained SENet154, PNasNet-5, and SE-ResNext101 models with five-fold multilabel stratification and cropping designed to preserve image-level labels. Successive stages removed noisy training examples, mined hard samples, added confident pseudo-labels, and fine-tuned tag-only models. A LightGBM second-level model used neural predictions, image statistics, and ImageNet class predictions, while postprocessing applied separate culture and tag thresholds and label-count limits. Training took approximately 10–15 days, and kernel runtime limits prevented submission of the complete ensemble to the private stage.
compute: 6x 1080 Ti, 36 CPU cores, 120 GB RAM; approximately 10–15 days training

solution_title: 1st Place Solution - CatBoost All The Way Down
solution_summary: The solution retained numerical columns alongside categorical copies and included the original dataset. XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost each averaged ten Optuna-tuned configurations, complemented by a neural network. Each of the four prediction streams was improved by a CatBoost model initialized with those predictions as its baseline, then a neural network stacked the improved outputs. All decisions followed cross-validation, and the final model achieved CV 0.97059 and private score 0.96938.

The approach distilled an ensemble of four teacher models into SE-ResNeXt101 and Inception-ResNet-v2 students to use the inference budget efficiently. Student targets combined teacher probabilities scaled by 0.7 with the original labels using an elementwise maximum, helping address missing annotations. Training began with the dense head alone before unfreezing all layers, and used crop, flip, and erasing augmentation. Averaging student outputs with seven test-time augmentations achieved a public leaderboard score of 0.664.
compute: Almost all models trained on Kaggle kernels; SE-ResNeXt101 training around 13 hours and SE-ResNeXt50 around 7 hours.

solution_summary: The solution combined stacking and weighted averaging using Ridge. Its model pool contained five AutoGluon models, three XGBoost models, four LightGBM models, one CatBoost model, and two histogram gradient boosting models. AutoGluon produced the best individual leaderboard score of 0.98518, while XGBoost had stronger out-of-fold scores than the other models. Limited available time constrained experimentation.

The solution used CosFace with various backbones on six-channel, 512×512 images, with CLAHE applied to some models. Models were trained in two stages using RAdam and a cyclic learning rate, with cross-validation in the second stage. Inference retained training mode, used eight test-time augmentations, and combined both sites and models. Plate-leak correction and Hungarian assignment refined predictions; mixup and a control-image subtraction model performed poorly.
compute: Cloud instances with V100 GPUs; count unspecified.

solution_title: 6th place solution. Higher resolution is all you need.
solution_summary: The solution used only competition training images, split into overlapping patches for training and inference. The final submission combined three HTC models with Res2Net101 and ResNeXt101 backbones, although ensembling offered little improvement in the author's experiments. Training used MMDetection with a default 1x schedule followed by SWA, and inference used three image scales. Class-specific score and area filtering, overlap removal, and DIoU-based weighted cluster NMS refined predictions, with inference taking two hours per model.
compute: 2 hours inference per model

solution_summary: The author's contribution combined two neural architectures using alternative sensor fluctuation feature sets. Features included lag differences, backward and forward rolling statistics, cyclical time, and cosine similarity to capture repeated patterns. Gaussian targets and binary cross-entropy supported event prediction, with grouped stratified validation. Combining the two model types reached 0.804 CV and 0.810 private leaderboard score using peak detection alone; augmentation and stacking did not work.

The solution used aggregate features and previous/next click intervals calculated across all data, including test_supplement. It also generated five-fold out-of-fold LIBFFM predictions and trained LightGBM while retaining all positive examples and half of the negatives. The final submission averaged several LightGBM models trained on different data and feature subsets. Column-wise binary storage supported fast loading, and training used 96GB of RAM.
compute: 96GB RAM

solution_summary: The solution used only patent titles and CPC information to create search candidates. Title TF-IDF supplied the initial candidates, with CPC TF-IDF and title word frequencies filling gaps when information was sparse. Candidate filtering removed short words and words contained in other word sets. The resulting candidates were optimized using simulated annealing adapted directly from two public notebooks.

solution_title: 32nd Place - Barely shaken up - It was all about diversity
solution_summary: The final system combined three branches: target regression, outlier classification, and regression with mean-replaced outliers. Each branch stacked LightGBM and XGBoost models, with individual models bagged over three seeds, and ridge/lasso regression combined the branches. Diversity came from hyperparameters, loss functions, and feature subsets. Neural networks failed, while some auxiliary classifiers were excluded from the final ensemble; the reported final CV score was 3.6253.

The solution adapted speech-recognition methods to landmark-based fingerspelling using a Conformer with intermediate CTC supervision. Inputs combined selected hand, pose, and lip xy coordinates with frame-to-frame motion. Hand flipping, sequence reversal, and concatenating videos with their phrases improved validation, while unmasked outputs and a large convolution kernel improved sequence modeling. Training ran for 300 epochs, with the final 100 using only the main training data; masking, distance features, and MLM pretraining did not work.

solution_title: Lessons learned from a 95 position drop (Public 11th place)...
solution_summary: The team selected two single LightGBM models as its final submissions. They had tested ensembles of diverse models and multiple LightGBM models but saw insufficient improvement in validation and public leaderboard results. Unselected ensembles ultimately performed better on the private dataset. The author attributes the selection difficulty to poor agreement between cross-validation and leaderboard results.

The solution learned denoising autoencoder representations using categorical embeddings for both noisy inputs and clean reconstruction targets. All categorical variables used five-dimensional embeddings, with fixed noise of 0.25 and 1,000 autoencoder training epochs. A two-layer MLP consumed the learned representation. Three autoencoder–MLP runs and one LightGBM model were stacked with XGBoost's linear model, reaching 0.9008564 CV and 0.90053 private score.

solution_title: My First Silver Medal: Solution Approach (Simple & Single model)
solution_summary: The author cleaned text and trained bert-base-uncased on the earlier Jigsaw toxic-comment classification dataset to predict class probabilities. Bayesian optimization selected class weights against the competition validation data. Inference combined the probabilities with those weights into a toxicity score, then ranked scores to eliminate duplicates. Multiple folds, additional datasets, and ensembles were suggested as future improvements.

The team used a two-stage recommendation pipeline with candidate generation followed by ranking. Candidates came from several models, including sequential recommenders built with RecBole, and the ranking stage stacked Re-Action aid and Related aid model outputs. Training used 4w labels with session-grouped validation and roughly 100 candidates and 100 features per session. The final ensemble combined six models with different candidate cutoffs and teammates' submissions.
compute: Google Colab Pro+

solution_summary: The final system used Google ByT5-Large trained in FP32 on roughly 510,000 filtered parallel pairs derived from host-provided materials. Extensive cleaning, particularly canonicalizing damage markers, supported a curriculum progressing from word-level adaptation to sentence training and increasingly augmented fine-tuning. Inference used beam top-1 selection, dynamic batching, and long-source chunking on two T4 GPUs, followed by gap and bracket cleanup. Reranking, retrieval-assisted decoding, and cross-model ensembles did not improve leaderboard performance.
compute: Final FP32 inference on dual T4 GPUs, with workload split round-robin.
external_data: ["Chicago Assyrian Dictionary (CAD), host-provided", "415 publications, host-provided", "Old Assyrian Lexicon (eBL), host-provided", "AKT batch, host-provided", "Hecker ICK4 letters, host-provided", "Kouwenberg grammars, host-provided", "Supplementary dictionaries and glossaries, host-provided"]

solution_summary: The author trained an LSTM on tokenized reconstructed essays and combined its hidden representations with engineered writing-process features. Five stratified folds produced additional hidden-layer features, which fed a LightAutoML regression stage. Including training-set hidden representations caused target leakage and an overly optimistic cross-validation score of 0.584. After the author fixed the leakage, the score worsened to approximately 0.6.

solution_title: 5th (Correction: now 7th) Place: A Rules-Based Bot Without Much Search
solution_summary: The final bot combined readable rules with exact planning for survival-critical decisions, without a general runtime policy search loop. Its strategy used one frontier scout, continuous mine revisits, coordinated wall carving, and an endgame escape planner. Exact spacetime reachability prevented premature digging, while a Dijkstra planner handled escape actions under scroll deadlines. Replay-based regression fixtures and deterministic tie handling improved reliability, while additional mines, a second early scout, and movement hysteresis reduced performance.

The solution extended a LightGBM baseline with chemically motivated SMILES features and synthetic data augmentation. Features captured radical-marker positions, RDKit conformer geometry, and aromatic and aliphatic ring properties. Target-specific quantile objectives emphasized higher Tg and Rg values while using median regression for the other properties. Public SMILES datasets expanded coverage, and functional-group substitutions generated additional examples with heuristic Rg adjustments and noise.
external_data: ["SMILES Extra Data by dmitryuarov", "Tc SMILES by minatoyukinaxlisa", "Tg of Polymer Dataset by akihiroorita"]

solution_summary: The solution fits parametric transit shapes and polynomial backgrounds to light curves, then uses small neural networks to correct the estimated spectra and uncertainties. Wavelet detection initializes transit regions, while GPU-parallel wavelength fitting reduces runtime. A separate baseline network supplies fallback predictions when fit diagnostics indicate unreliable results. Five-fold predictions are averaged, and repeated visits are combined using uncertainty weights. Fitting behaved worse in the competition environment than offline, potentially contributing to the validation-to-leaderboard gap.
compute: P100 GPU in Kaggle; preprocessing 12–15 seconds per transit, FGS fitting 2–3 seconds, AIRS fitting 6–7 seconds, neural networks 1.5–2 seconds; neural training 150k epochs.

solution_title: 16th place solution with detailed and readable code for beginner
solution_summary: The team trained noisy-student pretrained image classifiers on combined 2019 and 2020 data at 512-pixel resolution. They emphasized repeatedly balanced five-fold splits, SnapMix augmentation, bi-tempered loss with label smoothing, and Adam optimization. Training also used delayed backbone unfreezing, EMA and mixed precision, with five-view test-time augmentation. Their strongest reported combination of B3, B4 and ResNeXt50 achieved 0.9014 private accuracy; SAM improved local validation but was not retained as the final optimizer.
models_pretrained: ["Noisy-student B0, B3, B4 and ResNeXt50 models"]
compute: Up to 2×2080Ti and Colab Pro; split development took 4–5 days using Colab Pro with B0.

solution_title: 15th solution feature selection and trust your CV
solution_summary: The solution combined two teammates' groups of feature-based models using equal weights, with feature selection and trust in cross-validation guiding decisions. The author's pipeline selected compact subsets from public and custom features, including essay and event TF-IDF, a word_comma_cusor feature, and burst features. Feature5 and feature6 used LightGBM, CatBoost, XGBoost, and SVR with five-fold validation and Bayesian optimization of ensemble weights, while all four feature groups used five seeds. Feature selection improved CV by about 0.008 despite worsening public performance by 0.003; the author's ensemble achieved 0.579 on public and 0.568 on private evaluation.

The author modeled the competition as independent groups generated by make_classification and selected informative features using a standard-deviation threshold. Gaussian mixture models captured multiple Gaussian clusters per class, with clusters assigned to classes by their dominant training labels. Hyperparameters were tuned on synthetic datasets matching the inferred generation process, using random initializations and covariance regularization that increased with feature count. The resulting parameters achieved at least 0.99 AUC on the noise-free synthetic targets and were then applied to competition data.

The team developed feature-rich LightGBM and XGBoost models and combined them with public CatBoost code. The boosting ensemble scored 0.78 publicly and approximately 0.76 privately. Adjusting maximum sequence length to 720 and using 20 folds improved CV and leaderboard scores by about 0.01. Simple weighted integration and boosting feature engineering were considered the main gains, while attention changes did not significantly improve CV.
The post shares a YouTube link to a presentation. It provides no description of the competition approach, methods, or results.

solution_title: We just grew (really) lots of trees....
solution_summary: The solution represented each neuron pair with engineered connection features and used a tuned random forest for classification. Base indicators included correlation, igg, and ige with multiple burst-filtering thresholds. The largest gains came from topological features that measured indirect connections and normalized connection strength against other relationships. The reported score was 93.8%.

The team explored feature selection and multiple model families while monitoring cross-validation performance on noisy banking transaction data. The listed models were Elastic Net, XGBoost, random forest, ExtraTrees, linear SVM, and k-nearest neighbors. The writeup reports a maximum AUC of 0.82847. It does not explain the final combination of models or provide detailed feature engineering and validation procedures.

The author describes a single-model pipeline starting from the original 40 features. The main contributions were removing rows considered fake before generating leak predictions and using leaked values for data augmentation. Additional feature selection was used in the author's stronger single models. Those models achieved approximately 0.52 privately and 0.48 publicly, while the shared pipeline used improved private-leak parameters.

The author improved a WaveNet model by synthesizing signals for higher channel counts from single-channel sequences. Random sequences of length 4,000 were summed, and the resulting signals were adjusted to match the original data's mean and variance. Augmenting the five- and ten-channel cases improved CV from 0.9388 to 0.9423 and the leaderboard score from 0.941 to 0.945. Transfer learning from single-channel models had failed across HMM, random forest, and WaveNet.

The solution reconstructed row and column sequences and used them to infer client groups. Validation kept each client's rows together, and predictions were averaged across multiple cross-validation seeds. Nonzero sequence statistics and recent-window features produced about 3,500 features, reduced to roughly 1,000 through selection. The final model blended LightGBM, XGBoost, and random forest predictions; adding test leaks improved local validation but had uncertain leaderboard impact.

solution_title: [3rd Place] Single model scored 0.0975 w/o PID controller
solution_summary: The solution used Conv1d followed by stacked LSTMs, trained with MAE objectives for pressure and pressure differences. It combined original inputs with four engineered features and one-hot encoded resistance and compliance. Masking, local sequence shuffling, and especially mixup improved generalization. Median and seed ensembles, rounding, and two rounds of pseudo-labeling produced reported scores of 0.0942 public and 0.0970 private.

The post announces results from two versions of the author's public notebook and links to them for implementation details. Version 34 was selected and scored 0.76818 privately, while the unselected version 29 scored 0.77121. The author comments on leaderboard randomness and efforts to avoid overfitting but does not describe the solution pipeline in the post.

solution_title: 71st Place / Solo Silver: A Multi-Armed Bandit–Inspired Multi-Agent System
solution_summary: The solution optimized 400 independent ONNX programs using isolated GPT search episodes managed by a deterministic controller. An adaptive scheduler allocated exploration, while paper-cost gates and independent verification admitted only legal, exact, lower-cost rewrites. Search ran concurrently, but profiling, state updates, and releases were serialized with snapshots and rollback. Prompt refinements and targeted searches helped raise the score from 7166.77 to 7520.46, a gain of 353.69 points.
compute: M1 Pro MacBook; search episodes capped at 15 minutes, usually 10 concurrent workers.

solution_summary: The team built a purely rule-based agent from a public beta-competition solution, retaining a sequential structure for defense, capture, fleet attacks, expansion, and mining. Future-board simulation and more accurate route evaluation improved mining but consumed substantial computation. Simple expansion rules and immediate defensive reinforcement worked best, while many late strategic refinements produced similar scores around 1550–1600. Runtime optimization was essential under the three-second action limit, and coordinated attacks and abandoning doomed shipyards remained unimplemented.
compute: Three-second per-turn computation limit; Python implementation.

solution_title: 68th Place — How I Overfit Public LB...
solution_summary: The solution stacked 30 diverse base learners using a gated residual network trained on the original seven features and out-of-fold predictions. All learners shared a 15-fold split, and the final predictions averaged three meta-model seeds. The stack achieved 0.05919 CV and 0.05624 on the public leaderboard. Public leaderboard tuning and the absence of an independent holdout contributed to poor private generalization.

The solution ensembled AlbuNet, ResNet50-based, and SCSEUnet segmentation pipelines trained through repeated fine-tuning stages. A three-parameter inference rule first detected positive images using a high probability threshold and minimum area, then produced their masks with a lower threshold. Training combined BCE, Dice, and focal losses, progressively adjusted positive sampling, and generally moved from 512 to 1024 resolution. Despite a single model scoring better publicly, both final submissions were ensembles to reduce suspected overfitting, yielding private scores of 0.8679 and 0.8641.
compute: One, sometimes two, GTX 1080 Ti GPUs; batch size 2–4

solution_summary: The team trained a Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct preference classifier through external-data pretraining and distillation from five Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct teachers. Teacher predictions supplied soft labels across curated preference datasets and synthetic multilingual response pairs, with manual correction of suspicious annotations. The final classifier linearly merged two students trained on different data mixtures. Efficient unpadded inference supported a second response-swapped pass on the most uncertain third of samples.

solution_title: Private LB 13th Solution - so near yet so far :)
solution_summary: The team trained EfficientNet B0–B5 and RexNet variants in PyTorch, modifying the networks with convolution and squeeze-and-excitation heads and removing the last two blocks. Oversampling cover images to match the number of stego images improved both cross-validation and leaderboard scores. They trained more than 80 models, selected the top six by cross-validation in each fold, and combined predictions with an unweighted geometric mean while avoiding leaderboard feedback for selection. Their best single EfficientNet B5 achieved 0.927 on the private leaderboard and 0.928 on the public leaderboard.

The solution selected dataset mentions from Data Citation Corpus and original EUPMC mappings, retaining only identifiers present in article text. DOI types were predicted by six CatBoost models using article-dataset metadata similarities, while accession types used zero-shot Qwen2.5-Coder with local text context and additional BioSample metadata where appropriate. Source-family filtering, label-aware validation, and predicting accession IDs only for articles without DOI predictions were central decisions. The full pipeline achieved 0.890 public and 0.797 private F1, with a reported training-set runtime of 29 minutes including CatBoost training.
compute: Training-set runtime: DOI pipeline 13 minutes, accession pipeline 16 minutes, full solution 29 minutes; includes CatBoost training.

solution_title: #1 Solution: Exploiting the Flawed Random Generation
solution_summary: The author identified dependence between training and test samples caused by reusing random seeds with slightly different sampling probabilities. This produced exact duplicates and near-duplicate pairs that explained unusually strong ExtraTrees leaderboard performance. The final approach transformed decamer counts to expose these paired samples and used a radius-neighbor classifier to match them. For low-resolution samples, the transformation reconstructed lists of 100 decamers from 286 count features.

solution_title: Winning Solution 34th Solution (Possible 22nd Solution) LB Public: 0.954 LB Private: 0.92
solution_summary: The team extended a public TF-IDF approach with a weighted voting ensemble and an additional random forest to increase model diversity. The random forest received a relatively small weight. They also added the AI-Generated Abstracts dataset to improve training-data diversity and balance the label distribution. The selected submission scored 0.92 privately and 0.954 publicly; a similar unselected notebook achieved 0.929 privately.

The solution used NuSVC with features derived from cosine-kernel PCA, Gaussian mixture models, and agglomerative clustering. It replaced labels that disagreed sufficiently with model predictions, retrained, and applied pseudo-labeling across 512 cases at a stated ratio of 0.2. Partial prediction scaling with StandardScaler improved the leaderboard score by 0.002, and four seeds were ensembled. Reported public and private scores were 0.97513 and 0.97565.

The author contributed a dual-GRU model using anglez, hour, and a version of anglez masked at repeated data. One branch compressed the full sequence with a CNN, while the other used minute-level summary statistics. Their outputs were added to predict Gaussian event targets at minute resolution. Cross-validation guided peak selection, retaining secondary peaks and up to 35 predictions per day for each event type.

solution_title: [7th Place] My solution: only behavior cloning + two small rules
solution_summary: The final agent used an 8.2M-parameter entity Transformer trained by behavior cloning on public replays, with team, date and outcome conditioning. Recency-weighted training and a specialist fine-tune on the strongest team's newest versions mattered most. Autoregressive unit decoding coordinated actions, while NumPy inference took about 0.1 seconds per turn. Two inventory-preservation rules converted six losses into wins on 61 held-out forks; reinforcement-learning experiments were excluded from the final submissions.
compute: One RTX 5090 for training; Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus (24 cores) for evaluation. Training stages took 51, 7 and 3 minutes; inference approximately 0.1 seconds per turn on Kaggle CPU.
external_data: ["Kaggle public daily episode datasets", "Public replays of the target team's newest versions"]

solution_summary: The final agent adapts Ilia's multi-armed bandit approach to select from a pool containing roughly 20 strong RPS contest agents, anti-agents, and simpler strategies. It uses a Beta distribution to choose the agent most likely to win, with step size 4 and decay rate 1/1.05. The author manually explored many parameter combinations and also tested Dirichlet distributions to represent wins, losses, and ties. Although Dirichlet variants performed better on average, including an adaptive variant that chose parameters each round, the Beta agent ultimately performed best late in the competition.

The team developed a lumbar MRI classifier using EfficientNet encoders, YOLO-localized level crops, and attention-based multiple-instance learning. Adding adjacent slices as input channels and attending across longer modality-and-slice sequences improved the reported public score from 0.55% to 0.43%. Correcting slice sorting and duplicate modality metadata further improved the reported score to 0.42%. Regression localization, vertebral segmentation, and cascaded severity classifiers did not outperform the stronger pipeline.

The author replicated a Vowpal Wabbit setup described by another competitor and extended it with cross-validation and additional features. This provided a practical way to work with more data than the author had previously handled. The approach exceeded the author's expectations, and the implementation was shared publicly.

solution_title: Solving IMO Problems with Five Minds and a Confident Consensus
solution_summary: The pipeline ran 15 GPT-OSS-120B attempts across five reasoning prompt families, each using a multi-turn Python tool loop. Final answers were selected through frequency and inverse-entropy voting, with bonuses for agreement across families and penalties for suspect outputs. FP8 KV caching, reusable sandboxes, adaptive deadlines, and consensus stopping improved throughput within the available runtime. A repair fallback handled cases with no valid answer, and the reported final score was 40.5/50. Removing tools or replacing structured multi-turn interaction substantially reduced performance.
compute: 16 worker threads and 16 Python sandboxes; 17,400-second overall runtime budget, with 300–900 seconds per problem

solution_title: Some small findings from a part of 2nd place solution
solution_summary: This component of the team's solution reconstructed loan interest rates, predicting missing payment counts for current applications from previous applications. It estimated market rates using a timestamp proxy and standardized interest rates to reduce sensitivity to temporal differences between training and test data. Additional features encoded EXT_SOURCE_X rather than the target, and LightGBM models corrected neural-network residual errors. The author's model achieved CV 0.80742, public score 0.80779, and private score 0.80306.

The team stacked first-layer field-aware factorization machines and XGBoost models beneath a second-layer XGBoost model. Features captured page-view and impression counts, document and user confidence vectors, their similarities, and subsequent browsing behavior. Pairwise ranking objectives and separate models for present and future test samples were central modeling choices. Removing leak rows before FFM training and merging leak information afterward improved single-model performance; reported best public scores were 0.6974 for FFM and 0.6885 for XGBoost.

The solution used an ensemble of pretrained token classifiers followed by a LightGBM stage that selected candidate discourse spans. Low thresholds generated about three million training candidates at roughly 95% mean recall, and approximately 170 features supported sentence-level selection. Additional candidates retained the highest-probability 65% of selected spans, improving the score by about 0.008. Adversarial training and model diversity also helped. The second stage increased CV from 0.712 to 0.748 and leaderboard score from 0.706 to 0.742.
compute: Stage 1 took 7 hours online; stage 2 took 1.5 hours online.

solution_summary: The agent was entirely rules-based, combining economic valuation with constrained path optimization. It projected board state and military power over 30 turns, then valued ships, bases, defense, and attacks using discounted economic returns. Priority spawning protected threatened shipyards, while trial fleet sizes and specialized zombie routes balanced mining and combat objectives. Base expansion depended on economic value, resource geography, and the value of alternative flight plans.

The author built a linear baseline using zero-alpha Ridge on a single PCA component of fruitset, fruitmass, and seeds. LightGBM and CatBoost models then predicted residuals using several feature variants, while additional models predicted yield directly. Training combined synthetic and original data, with validation restricted to synthetic data. LAD regression without an intercept combined the model predictions.

The solution averaged three BERT-Large models and one BERT-Base model with custom pooling across multiple transformer layers. The base model added cleaned text and category/host embeddings, while the large models used separate question and answer inputs with target-specific routing. Weighted binary cross-entropy, staged encoder unfreezing, and layer-dependent learning rates supported training. Post-processing substantially improved scores, and the final ensemble achieved 0.42430 privately and 0.47259 publicly.

solution_title: 使用 gluon 实现狗品种分类
solution_summary: The initial pipeline extracted pretrained CNN features, concatenated them, and trained a two-layer neural network for dog-breed classification. A comparison of pretrained models led the author to retain InceptionV3 and ResNet152_v1 features, improving the test score from 0.28228 to 0.27143. DenseNet features were dropped after the comparison. The final update trained with Stanford Dogs Dataset features using InceptionV3 and ResNet152_v1 and reported a score of 0.00398.

The team averaged four configurations of tile-based multiple-instance CNNs using SE-ResNeXt and EfficientNet backbones with ordinal-regression heads. Online uncertainty sample mining and mixup addressed noisy labels, while repeated high-loss screening removed the most suspicious 10% of examples within each grade. Slide- and tile-level augmentation, four-way test-time augmentation, and QWK threshold optimization completed the pipeline. The authors prioritized public leaderboard feedback over CV because training labels were noisier, and reported final improvements of 0.018 public and 0.017 private over a referenced model without denoising.

The solution shifted the 11-class batches by 2.724 and removed the seventh training batch. Wiener and bandstop filtering improved simple probabilistic models, with GMM reaching 0.941 CV and Naive Bayes reaching 0.942 CV, but did not improve WaveNet directly. GMM weighted predictions and class probabilities were then supplied as neural-network features, alongside cleaning of 50 Hz noise. HMM sampling, blending/stacking, TCNN, and CRF did not help.

solution_title: Solo silver - minimum resources solution with heavy postprocessing
solution_summary: The solution trained EfficientNet-B7 models with ArcFace loss on 768-pixel images using public image datasets and a private dataset for species classification. It combined nearest-neighbor prediction tables from individual models instead of concatenating embeddings because folds and label encodings differed across datasets. Test images were divided into four categories using predicted species and body characteristics, with category-specific model selections, prediction averaging, agreement filtering, and new-individual thresholds. Training separately within species groups did not work.
compute: Kaggle TPU for model training, Kaggle GPU for embeddings and nearest-neighbor calculations, and mostly a home CPU for final postprocessing. Training and embedding calculation took five weeks.

solution_summary: The final submission averaged five models incorporating all four supplied embeddings and achieved local CV of 0.7028 and a private score of 0.69721. It combined recurrent models with a Keras sparse TF-IDF model and an RNN built on top of TF-IDF-to-Ridge predictions. Vocabulary matching used lemmatization and case changes, while concatenated embeddings improved convergence efficiency. Runtime constraints led to smaller RNNs, asynchronous CPU-side work, and rejection of CNN models.
compute: GPU execution for PyTorch models; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_title: RECOD.AI - LUC Scientific Image Forgery Detection - 29th Place Solution
solution_summary: The solution trained a DINOv2-based segmentation model on competition data and RSIID copy-move examples, including reconstructed authentic counterparts. Five-fold stratified grouped validation kept related authentic and forged images together, while partial encoder fine-tuning and augmented training supported adaptation. Inference averaged eight geometric transformations and used a conservative confidence gate before submitting one merged binary mask. Submission selection required positive lift over the authentic-only baseline in every dataset split; exact CV and public scores were unavailable.

solution_title: Simple simulated annealing and boundary optimization
solution_summary: The layout optimizer combined an annealing-inspired cubic step-size decay with Gaussian position and rotation perturbations, retaining legal moves that improved compactness. It periodically compressed the target bounding box and propagated improvements from larger layouts to smaller ones by removing boundary trees. Independent tree-count groups ran in separate CPU processes, with atomic saves and interruption handling preserving progress. Numerical margins and bounded coordinates supported geometric validity.
compute: CPU multiprocessing with configurable worker count MAX_WORKERS = TOTAL_CORES / x; exact hardware and elapsed runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution generated candidates from several co-visitation matrices, recent session items, and Word2Vec neighbors, then reranked them with XGBoost. Features described users, items, their interactions, and candidate provenance. Memory downcasting, session partitioning, negative undersampling, and chunked inference made most of the pipeline feasible on a 16 GB MacBook. Candidate recall reached 62.04% for clicks, 53.89% for carts, and 73.23% for orders; inference selected the top 20 predictions.
compute: Mostly a MacBook with 16 GB RAM; XGBoost training took approximately 20–30 minutes. All-event co-visitation computation used Kaggle notebooks.

solution_title: Solution: Public LB 8th place | Private LB 3rd place (updated 2026-04-28)
solution_summary: The final pipeline used pretrained SAM3 segmentation and classical feature matching without training a model. It normalized panel appearance, suppressed text and arrows, and matched SIFT descriptors with FLANN, Lowe's ratio test, and homography RANSAC. A second pass targeted biological objects and used deterministic fallback crops to improve coverage. Supplemental figure-based data revealed why neural models trained on individual synthetic images transferred poorly.
