solution_title: 3rd public/20th private solution-segmentation + simple tiles and multiheaded attention
solution_summary: The team classified whole-slide images using tile sets, ResNeXt50 backbones, attention across tile features, and multiple prediction heads. Strong augmentation and progressive resolution increases supported training, while segmentation-selected tiles added diversity to simple tile models. Their selected four-model submission scored 0.921 publicly and 0.927 privately; a simple-tile single-fold model also achieved 0.927 privately. An unselected five-model ensemble used the middle three predictions for averaging, while segmentation alone and attempted denoising showed less convincing benefits.

The final pipeline combined pretrained ResNets and DenseNets trained on JPG images with five-fold cross-validation and soft pseudo-labels from test data. XGBoost learned to combine test-time transformations, which the author identified as the most important improvement. The resulting models were combined with weighted voting based on public leaderboard F2 scores. The final ensemble scored 0.93340 on the public leaderboard and 0.93220 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Initially GTX1060; later GTX1080 Ti enabled five-fold cross-validation.

solution_summary: This reproduction guide describes a feature-based CatBoost pipeline with preprocessing, feature extraction, prediction, and postprocessing scripts. The provided artifacts include teammate features and submissions, class weights, and trained models, with postprocessing handling ensembling and class 99. Full reproduction is estimated to require a few months on the stated machine, while using extracted features and trained models takes about four hours. The short workflow is reported to score 0.680 publicly and 0.700 privately.
compute: Google Cloud Engine n1-standard-64, 64 CPUs and 240GB RAM, Ubuntu 16.04; full reproduction takes a few months, short reproduction about 4 hours.

solution_title: Public Silver → Private 0: A Portfolio Bet That Missed
solution_summary: The author reverse-engineered the evaluator and optimized public attack replay throughput using short clean URLs, suppressed reasoning, and a short termination phrase. For the hidden private guardrail, the final submission allocated 2,000 candidates across roughly 11 attack routes using confidence and expected reward per hop. This portfolio failed to transfer effectively because exfiltration was blocked and only the confused-deputy floor survived, producing a private score of 2.64. The postmortem identifies offline timing probes across submissions as the missed way to resolve guardrail uncertainty.
compute: Fixed replay budget of 9,000 seconds per model; termination prompt reduced measured response times to about 2.1 seconds.

solution_summary: The final solution used a custom C++ patent search engine to evaluate an ensemble of four query generators and choose the best query for each test row. Patent tokens were reformatted into an uncompressed binary store, and a search index covered all 13 million patents while excluding description terms. A greedy target-group optimizer supplied most queries, with frequent-pattern and best-effort generators providing alternatives. Moving from the original Python frequent-pattern pipeline to this system improved the public score from 0.53 to 0.76.
compute: Single-thread laptop benchmark on 200k patents: under 0.2 ms per query in memory and under 0.3 ms on disk.

solution_summary: The pipeline combined multilingual Transformer retrieval, character TF-IDF retrieval, and matches transferred from related training topics before LightGBM classification. Transformer embeddings used ArcFace training and normalized concatenation, while topic text included ancestor titles. Relative-probability postprocessing applied different rules to training and unseen contents and was particularly important. The main solution achieved 0.764 validation and private scores; the efficiency variant reached 0.740 private with about 20 minutes of CPU runtime.
compute: Efficiency solution: around 20 minutes CPU runtime

solution_summary: This post announces that the author published their solution under the competition guidelines. It links to a GitHub repository, a model summary, and presentation slides. A model structure image is embedded, but the provided text contains no substantive description of the approach.

The solution averaged six LightGBM regressors with different validation seeds and hyperparameters, then converted predictions into accuracy groups using fixed thresholds. Its central decision was to trust repeated truncated, installation-grouped validation over the small public leaderboard. Roughly 300 features were selected from thousands of candidates, including title-normalized accuracy, title-specific event statistics, and relative ratios. Neural and embedding approaches were omitted because they were unstable, slow, or failed to improve performance.

The solution combined pairwise toxicity ranking models trained on Ruddit with regression models trained on Toxic comments. RoBERTa models used linear or attention heads, while a TF-IDF Ridge model added complementary text and handcrafted features. Model development prioritized validation_data.csv, and Optuna selected ensemble members after min-max scaling their outputs. The final ensemble summed 13 models and achieved a validation score of 0.709 and a public leaderboard score of 0.819.

The solution applies five-class classification, including background, followed by four-class defect segmentation. Classification uses ResNet50, EfficientNet-B3, and SE-ResNeXt50, while segmentation uses U-Net, PSPNet, and FPN with ResNet encoders. Larger crops and combined BCE and Dice loss worked well. Smaller crops, pseudo-labeling, mixup, CutMix, larger encoders, and thresholds above 0.5 were unsuccessful.

The pipeline segmented the cervical spine, extracted individual vertebrae, and trained complementary 3D CNN and slice-based CNN-transformer classifiers. Class activation sequences from the 3D classifier supplied slice-level pseudolabels for the slice-based model. Three exam-level transformers consumed the two feature sequences separately and concatenated together. Their weighted ensemble formed the final prediction, with fused features achieving the strongest individual cross-validation result.

solution_title: 44th solution... Thank you for your questions and advices
solution_summary: The solution removed a rolling-mean trend from each signal and compressed it into statistical features over 250 segments. Two bidirectional LSTM architectures combined attention pooling with temporal max pooling, with one variant adding self-attention. The author trained two models separately for each of the three phases, producing six models overall. Final predictions used a weighted average of the two model variants, with Adam, binary cross-entropy, dropout, and a decaying learning rate used in training.

The solution modeled displacement from the last known depth and combined 13 predictors spanning engineered-feature trees, dilated CNNs, alignment searches, and guided re-decodes. Ensemble membership depended on both individual error and error correlation, with weights fitted greedily and then frozen. Nested well-grouped validation and per-well robustness checks controlled selection and calibration. Capped alignment corrections, an additional CNN, disagreement-based amplitude adjustment, and stratigraphic smoothing produced final public and private RMSE values of 5.888 and 7.341 feet without external data.

The approach encoded feature-value frequencies using all available data while excluding fake test rows. It then combined 200 LightGBM submodels through a Naive Bayes formulation, with each submodel using one original feature and its frequency. Frequency encoding first reached 0.901 public score, removing fake rows raised it to 0.913, and the final combination reached 0.922.

The solution used CenterNet with a DeepLabV3+ architecture and EfficientNetV2 backbones. It produced heatmaps at one-eighth input resolution with an additional regression head, training at 1280×720 and predicting at higher resolution. Blending two models achieved a private score of 0.712 at 1.4× inference resolution and 0.722 at 1.6×. An attempted overfitting strategy failed.

The solution tokenized questions with NLTK TweetTokenizer and used fixed embeddings formed by averaging GloVe and Paragram. Two bidirectional LSTM layers fed pooled and attention features into a small dense classifier. Length bucketing made training more than three times faster, enabling nine epochs for each of five folds. Checkpoint ensembling raised average validation performance from about 0.694 to 0.700, followed by averaging fold probabilities and thresholds.

This post compiles tips shared by other competitors and links to their solution discussions. It highlights frequency counts, per-feature LightGBM ensembles, handling unique values, synthetic samples, and additional folds. It does not describe the author's own competition solution.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution: The Solution Without Crop2
solution_summary: The author described a collection of challenge-specific CTF solutions and linked their source repository. Several challenges used hill climbing, while others relied on enumeration, image editing, model inspection, or manipulating outputs. The murderbots approach used LightGBM and assigned positive labels to the top ten samples. Other methods included concatenating argmax outputs, sorting inputs by standard deviation, and applying a two-dimensional Fourier transform.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution: AnchorCNN — Conditional Probabilistic Path Modeling
solution_summary: The solution used an anchor-grid CNN to predict conditional distributions of TVT changes, preserving multiple plausible interpretations of ambiguous gamma-ray matches. Physically consistent synthetic wells combined master typewell profiles, transformed real trajectories, and realistic residual noise, while trajectory-slope features constrained the geological structure. Dynamic programming computed the expected path exactly, and final predictions averaged folds, seeds, grid resolutions, and shifted inference grids. Robust model selection rejected gains driven by a few influential wells; the selected submission achieved an OOF score of 5.140 and a private score of 5.802.
compute: Training: 5 folds × 3 seeds in about 10 hours on one unspecified GPU. Ensemble inference: 200 hidden test wells in about 40 minutes on a Kaggle T4.

solution_summary: The solution reused features from a public notebook and added day and hour features derived from transaction time. It trained CatBoost, XGBoost, LightGBM, random forest, logistic regression, and a simple neural model. Hill climbing selected the ensemble weights, with XGBoost receiving the largest positive weight and CatBoost a negative weight. The post does not report validation or leaderboard scores.

The solution used a sliding-window approach with a deep neural network and features describing shopping timing, promotions, historical sales, and product-class substitution effects. Class-level sales and promotion features were considered the main advantage, although their individual impact was not measured. Training separate models for perishable and non-perishable goods improved the public score by about 0.001 over the combined model's 0.510. The final ensemble combined both variants with AhmetErdem's public kernel and reached 0.507, while extending temporal validation from 16 to 32 days helped guide perishable-goods training.

The author's contribution used a two-stage candidate generation and reranking pipeline, with about 180 candidates per session. Candidates combined revisits, several co-visitation variants, Word2Vec similarity, and frequent items from clusters of session embeddings. Type-specific LightGBM classifiers reranked candidates using 91 features; including ranks beyond the candidate extraction cutoffs significantly improved scores. Training used week 3, validation used week 4, and the final ensemble of experiments achieved public and private scores of 0.594.

The post links to a paper about efficient hierarchical object detection with imbalanced data. It provides the paper title and an arXiv URL. No implementation details or experimental results are described in the post itself.

solution_title: 【35th place solution】Score up by pseudo labeling
solution_summary: The solution averaged predictions from diverse feature sets and models to reduce the risk of overfitting a small training dataset. Two records with timing errors were removed, improving local cross-validation. Pseudo-labeling was effective locally, particularly for gradient-boosted decision trees. SVR, Lasso, and Ridge added useful prediction diversity and sometimes handled extreme scores better than the tree models.

The author's component used a two-stage pipeline that extracted image-based neural predictions and combined their temporal shifts with LightGBM. YOLO player crops included channels marking the target players' helmets and all players' helmet locations. Moving-average smoothing and threshold selection produced the final contact predictions, with three-fold validation grouped by game play. The team reported public and private scores of 0.786 and 0.783, although this post describes only the author's contribution.

The solution distilled diverse teacher models into efficient audio classifiers using pseudo-labels from unlabeled soundscapes. Training combined competition recordings, additional Xeno Canto data, and matching species from previous competitions, with class balancing and five-second log-mel inputs. The final ensemble contained 14 model weights, primarily EfficientViT-b0 and MNASNet-100, and scored 0.689970 private and 0.742124 public. Secondary-label loss masking and temporal smoothing helped, while unreliable validation and public-score-driven selection limited the final ensemble.

The neural networks differed in text representation, embedding training, image features, and regression losses, while a learned image-feature compressor improved the non-neural models. Nested validation accounted for prediction averaging, and the linear stack used adversarial-validation sample weights plus corrections for correlations between folds. solution_summary: The solution uses U-Net models with ResNet34d and ResNet50d backbones, trained on 2048-pixel tiles resized to 1024 pixels. Image-separated five-fold validation and full-resolution out-of-fold Dice guided selection, while an auxiliary boundary channel helped supervise mask edges. Training combined focal and Lovasz losses, MixUp, stochastic weight averaging, and geometric and color augmentation. Overlapping inference, flip TTA, and a 0.7:0.3 backbone ensemble achieved a reported private score of 0.947; pseudo-labeled models were rejected because their CV was worse.

solution_summary: The team assembled an ad hoc ensemble through repeated public-leaderboard feedback, combining XGBoost models, a shifted neural network, Extra Trees, and public-kernel predictions. Blending used several types of means alongside multiplicative adjustments, shifts, and compression of extreme predictions. A small component normalized prices by CPI and used time-weighted regression features, weighted XGBoost, and monthly macro adjustments. The author could not reconstruct all contributions, but reported that the late Extra Trees addition improved private-board performance.

solution_title: Silver Medal - LB=0.39 - Sliding Time Cross Validation!
solution_summary: The author developed sliding time-window validation to reflect temporal changes between training and test data, assigning random dates to training rows with missing dates. This approach achieved average local balanced log loss of 0.27, public score of 0.17, and private score of 0.39, with validation improvements tracking leaderboard improvements. Analysis across 25 OOF folds showed that prediction thresholding helped some periods but not others. The final submissions instead used leaderboard-probed pseudo labels, including a variant that zeroed predictions below 0.1; both choices hurt private performance.

The strongest single model used separate ResNet18 branches for RGB imagery and NIR-derived channels, concatenating their outputs before fully connected layers. Branch-specific learning rates, validation-loss scheduling, augmentation, and F2 threshold tuning supported training and inference. The ensemble combined DenseNets, mixed-channel models, WideResNets, and ResNet18 variants trained across multiple folds, with submission weights derived from holdout F2 scores. The best reported blended ensemble achieved public and private scores of 0.93015 and 0.93217.

solution_title: 23rd place solution: ensemble, rank passage and predict span
solution_summary: The solution used a BERT passage ranker to retain ten long-answer candidates per record, followed by an ensemble of four joint span-prediction models. The span models started from SQuAD-pretrained BERT or SpanBERT checkpoints and were trained for one epoch on either the full Natural Questions dataset or the ranker-selected subset. Candidate filtering achieved about 0.98 recall@10 and made inference faster while slightly improving validation performance. Averaging the span-model scores increased the private leaderboard score from 0.65 for a single model to 0.67.
compute: Public-test ranking took about 5 minutes; prediction took about 3 minutes per span model.

solution_title: 30 th Place Simple Solution & Eid Mubarak
solution_summary: The solution used public notebook pipelines, with DeBERTa-v1-base for experiments and DeBERTa-v3-large for the final models. Masked language modeling, adversarial weight perturbation, and varied classification heads supported training and diversity. Five-fold validation guided selection of different folds from different models for the final ensemble. Borrowed post-processing improved the leaderboard score by 0.003, while padding optimization allowed more models to fit into inference.
compute: Kaggle GPU; hardware model and training duration unspecified.

solution_summary: The team extracted faces with MTCNN, enlarged square crops by 1.2, and resized them to 224×224 for EfficientNet binary classifiers. They used extensive image augmentation, balanced sampling, Adam, a one-cycle learning-rate schedule, and FP16 training. Final submissions included an EfficientNet ensemble that failed private scoring and a mixed ensemble reported at 0.33552. Handcrafted features and temporal approaches offered limited gains, and generalization beyond face-swap deepfakes remained difficult.
compute: 4x 2080TI Lambda workstation; batch size 16 per GPU, 625 iterations per epoch, 12,500 total iterations

solution_summary: The solution stacked image-only EfficientNet-B0 predictions with tabular features in LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost models. Generalization strategies included repeated negative undersampling, patient-grouped validation across multiple seeds, fixed training lengths, and handling unseen categories as missing. Two augmentation patterns and two feature sets supplied diversity, with unweighted prediction averaging. The reported scores were 0.183 CV and 0.171 private leaderboard; a second submission limiting negatives per patient performed worse privately.

The pipeline emphasizes strong bounding-box detection before predicting masks for each detected cell. Detectors use strong feature extractors, 1536-pixel inputs, and LIVECell pretraining, while four UPerNets and two Mask R-CNNs predict masks from ensembled boxes. Accurate ROI cropping, mask interpolation, and probability averaging are central to the segmentation stage. Mask-based instance rescoring improves astro validation COCO mAP by 0.01, followed by thresholding, overlap removal, and small-instance filtering.
compute: Sponsored Z8G4 workstation with dual A6000 GPUs and ZBook with RTX5000 GPU

solution_summary: The solution aligned fragment volumes in depth using intensity-curve-based shifts and scaling, then trained five U-Net models with a pretrained MaxViT encoder. Each model processed six three-slice groups and combined their logits through a linear layer. Training used mask-aware random crops, extensive visual augmentation, weighted BCE, and validation F0.5 checkpoint selection. Overlapping inference patches, twelve-way test-time augmentation, and averaging across folds produced a private score of 0.641814 and public score of 0.723345.
compute: 1 x 3090, 1 x 3080Ti mobile; 64 training epochs

solution_title: NeuroGolf 2026: ONNX graph optimization and validation across 400 tasks
solution_summary: The workflow optimized 400 ONNX grid-transformation models individually, starting from community archives and retaining a known-good anchor. It reduced evaluator-measured tensor memory and parameter cost through graph simplification, sparse updates, factorization, and narrow arithmetic, while separately addressing runtime behavior. Structural checks, public examples, generated differential tests, profiling, and isolated submissions controlled integration. The archive records an improvement from 7269.47 to 7441.86, although the author could not establish that the best archived package was the final selected submission.

The solution used LightGBM predictions with effective removal of drifting 50 Hz interference. Cleaning averaged residuals over nearby cycles grouped by their position modulo 200, and signal shifts were also important. The team identified a correlated-signal leak limited to one private max10 set. They developed a Bayesian inference model but omitted it from the final solution because its performance was virtually identical to LightGBM after cleaning; its estimated transition probabilities also supported augmentation.

The solution combined DeBERTa models with LightGBM, using both a base model and a large model fine-tuned with LoRA. Blending results with LightGBM produced the best reported CV and private scores, listed as 492 and 482. GPT-style regression fine-tuning and supervised fine-tuning of Llama for direct target generation did not work. Additional data from ChatGPT and SFT Llama2 was also reported as unsuccessful.

solution_title: 64th Place - Elasticsearch to find them all
solution_summary: The solution retrieved Wikipedia context with Elasticsearch and combined five DeBERTa models trained on shared and privately generated data. Retrieval paired each question with individual answer options and expanded retrieved sentences with neighboring sentences. The full June 2023 Wikipedia dump improved article coverage, while different context configurations provided complementary predictions. A confidence-dependent ensemble improved both validation and leaderboard scores; a Mistral LoRA experiment could not be submitted because of engineering issues.
compute: Elasticsearch took 7 hours for 4,000 queries on T4 x2 nodes, 1 hour on P100 nodes, and 3 minutes on a local machine with a regular SSD.
external_data: ["Shared training datasets", "Privately generated training data", "JJ's wiki dataset", "Full Wikipedia June 2023 dump"]

solution_summary: The solution combined ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet models with sub-center ArcFace and tuned dynamic margins. Bounding-box mixing, multi-level GeM features, and a larger learning rate for the classification heads improved recognition. Predictions blended cosine-neighbor scores with margin-free logits, followed by unknown-individual thresholding. Two rounds of pseudo labeling improved results, and the final submission combined around 50 models.
compute: 2-8 NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs (32GB); batch sizes 16-32; 20 or 30 training epochs

solution_summary: The author used AutoGluon to train large ensembles of base and stacked models. Categorical values longer than one character were treated as noise and replaced with missing values. The final retraining excluded a particularly slow XGBoost model and produced 98 base models and 64 stacked models over five and a half days. Public performance improved marginally, while private performance remained around 0.98507, suggesting limited benefit from the increased complexity.
compute: Two Gold 5320 CPUs; intermediate run took three days, final retraining took five and a half days. Initial GPU attempt appeared unused.

solution_summary: The solution trained XGBoost models on synthetic data supplemented with stroke cases from the original dataset. It used stratified 10-fold validation scored only on synthetic observations to limit overfitting to the original distribution. Preprocessing included one-hot encoding, nearest-neighbor BMI imputation, clinical risk-factor features, and centering and scaling continuous variables. A 500-iteration randomized hyperparameter search produced five selected configurations whose 50 fold-level test predictions were averaged. Alternative model families, cross-family blends, and prediction ranking were explored but were not used in the final ensemble.

The team stacked a neural network, two LightGBM models, and XGBoost using three independently developed feature sets. Feature importance and adversarial validation helped select features, while validation grouped examples by rescuer. They converted predictions to ranks and optimized thresholds to produce the five discrete adoption classes. Duplicate-image matches were used to overwrite predictions, and a manually curated dictionary corrected text typos.

solution_title: 12th place solution: Simple features and LSTM.
solution_summary: The solution compressed recordings into fixed-length statistical sequences and ensembled four selected models separately for tDCS FOG and DeFOG. Models were mainly LSTMs, with CNN-head, multitask, percentile-feature, and longer-sequence variants, plus a transformer for DeFOG. Subject-grouped validation guided tDCS selection, while Notype data provided DeFOG validation so all labeled DeFOG data could be used for training. The final submission scored 0.444 publicly and 0.341 privately.

The solution combined heavily downsampled LightGBM models with a smaller neural-network contribution through rank-based weighted averaging. Features were computed on the full dataset and included categorical combinations, click counts, time gaps, historical attribution ratios, and latent categorical embeddings. Bagging across independently sampled negative examples enabled hundreds of features with short training times. The final ensemble achieved 0.98343 on the public leaderboard, while a five-bag LightGBM model achieved 0.98420 privately.
compute: LightGBM training under 30 minutes; reported model training memory under 100 GB; no GPU for neural-network work

solution_summary: The final solution blended bagged neural networks with LightGBM models that corrected their residual errors. The neural networks treated each coupling pair as a sample and described other atoms relative to that pair. Distances to intermediate atoms resolved positional ambiguity and substantially improved performance. An initial standalone LightGBM approach was superseded, but residual correction remained valuable and the final blend reached -3.032 on the leaderboard.

The team focused on teaching an LLM to reproduce an existing reasoner rather than substantially expanding its solving ability. They built a synthetic problem generator calibrated to training-data statistics and trained on synthetic samples before original samples at a 2.5:1 ratio. Character-level synthetic tokens for cryptarithms and gradient clipping improved learning stability. The reasoner solved 87.8% of the analyzed problems, while preference learning with SimPO and ORPO was excluded because it did not sufficiently improve accuracy.

The final model was a feedforward neural network with three 100-unit hidden layers, strong dropout, and categorical cross-entropy. Its most valuable features measured minimum distances from the ball carrier under projected player trajectories over two seconds at 0.2-second intervals. Physics features, ten-network bagging, augmentation, Nadam, and auxiliary prediction heads provided further gains, reaching a reported score of 0.01272. Model selection balanced a late-2018 holdout against a separate 34-fold weekly validation scheme.

The solution combined a fine-tuned global CNN retrieval model with a publicly available local Detect-to-Retrieval model. Global retrieval shortlisted training images, and local matching refined label scores. The largest improvement came from promoting test images that locally matched highly ranked landmark predictions, followed by interleaving two resulting prediction lists. The final private/public scores were 0.37601/0.32101; an additional shallow network improved the private score but was omitted because its public score declined.

The final solution used a single Protenix model augmented with representations from AIDO.RNA-650M. The RNA language model remained frozen while the augmented structure model was fine-tuned on the complete 2024-12-04 RNA3DB release. Inference used the EMA checkpoint from step 1600, with MSAs enabled despite their omission during training. The model achieved public and private leaderboard scores of 0.42849 and 0.49758; alternative ensembles, coordinate averaging, and a learned ranker did not improve the approach.

The author focused on custom weighting in a three-model audio blend. Out-of-fold probabilities were used to help control overfitting. They report that final evaluation scores usually exceeded public scores, but provide no model identities or numerical metrics. Musical and bioacoustic feature development and custom pretraining are described as future plans.

The solution detected helmets with YOLOv5 trained on supplemental photos at increased resolution. Two-stage color clustering identified teams, while CenterNet estimated player orientation and helmet-to-sensor offsets to improve matching distances. Field lines supplied geometric alignment, and candidate player subsets were matched through linear assignment. SORT-based tracking reused team features, and tracking consistency raised team-classification accuracy from 97% to 98%.

The post reports an efficient single model trained on the final competition day, with scores of .564 public and .562 private and eight minutes of inference. The model was not included in the team's submitted blends. A two-fold blend submitted after the deadline scored .560 on both leaderboards without tuning. Technical details are deferred to an external report and linked resources.
compute: 8 minutes inference for the single model

solution_title: 12th place solution - from public 281st to private 12th!
solution_summary: The solution trained a single ConvNeXt-Small on two million synthetic combinations of pure gravitational-wave signals and random noise backgrounds. Signal transformations and image augmentations provided variation during training, while four-way flip augmentation was used at inference. The single model achieved public and private leaderboard scores of 0.76 and 0.78, respectively. An ensemble of many models performed poorly, and ConvNeXt-Tiny achieved a similar private score.

solution_title: My journey + Constrained TSP to get from 2440 to 2430
solution_summary: The author first alternated constrained traveling salesman optimization with permutation rebalancing, reaching a score of 2440, then used wildcard dynamic programming to reach 2438. Their final improvement encoded wildcard selection as a single-vehicle asymmetric capacitated routing problem in LKH-3. Ordinary permutations had zero weight, wildcards had unit weight, and vehicle capacity two enforced the wildcard budget. Restricting wildcards to the first position of mandatory permutations produced a score of 2430 after several hours.
compute: NEOS attempt ran into memory issues; initial optimization ran for several days, final wildcard optimization for several hours.

solution_summary: The final approach stacked 17 base models: five LightGBM, four XGBoost, two CatBoost, and six Keras models. Logistic regression combined their predictions, while an XGBoost stacker performed poorly. The only retained engineered feature was the number of missing values per row, and Optuna supported tuning. Diversity mattered: a deep XGBoost component was weak alone but valuable to the stack, and Keras models contributed despite weaker standalone scores.

The solution combined several Wikipedia retrieval pipelines with fine-tuned DeBERTa and causal language models. Dense article retrieval, sentence-level TF-IDF, and paragraph-level sparse retrieval supplied complementary contexts. About 3000 ChatGPT-generated questions formed a validation set that guided ensemble selection and weights. Confidence-based staged inference reserved expensive models for harder questions, enabling eight DeBERTa model-context predictions and three LLM predictions within nine hours. The final weighted ensemble achieved private and public scores of 0.925 and 0.931.
compute: Staged ensemble inference within 9 hours.

solution_summary: The approach began with cross-validation predictions from quadratic discriminant analysis. Those predictions supplied test pseudo-labels and identified training labels to flip before Gaussian mixture modeling split each batch into six clusters. Cluster assignments were mapped to class labels, and the relabeling and clustering cycle was repeated once. With limited threshold tuning, the method achieved 0.9754 CV, 0.9744 public, and 0.97598 private scores.

solution_title: Congrats to winners! Sharing my interesting discoveries and tricks
solution_summary: The team used two-stage stacking with roughly 200 features and 50 neural features from varied LSTM models, followed by ensemble selection across XGBoost, LightGBM, and neural networks. Their best unadjusted single LightGBM model achieved 0.176 cross-validation log loss. Neighbor-intersection leakage guided probability adjustments, including a separate correction for question pairs with no shared neighbors. Retraining LSTM feature generators with leakage features improved the reported leaderboard score from 0.134 to 0.131, although ensemble overfitting remained unresolved.

The pipeline cleans non-ASCII characters in author records before identifying duplicate authors. It generates candidate duplicate IDs to improve recall, then applies precision-oriented identification and refinement. An optional preliminary model identifies confident duplicates across the full dataset to improve coauthor and covenue matrices. The writeup provides execution instructions but no evaluation metrics.
compute: PC with 16 GB RAM running Ubuntu 13.04 for all code except model 0; model 0 requires 32 GB RAM.

solution_summary: The solution extracted temporal, Fourier, cepstral, and spectral features from ten segments of each sensor signal. Missing feature values were replaced with -1, and feature extraction for train and test took about 90 minutes. An LSTM followed by three Conv1D layers and three dense layers was trained with Nadam and MAE loss. Predictions from eight models trained on subsets of the training data were averaged for the final submission.
compute: 90 minutes for train and test feature extraction; hardware unspecified.

solution_title: My solutions to all but crop2
solution_summary: The author linked a notebook containing solutions but described only experiments on the unfinished crop2 task. These experiments used backpropagation to modify network inputs rather than model parameters. The author also inspected and manipulated internal network quantities, but reported that this work did not help solve crop2.

The team trained bird classifiers on 30-second recordings divided into six 5-second segments, using both primary and secondary labels. Their most useful modification was resizing spectrograms to 256 × 512, improving both public and private scores by 0.01. They trained five folds across five backbone types and averaged all predictions, with the NFNet backbones producing the strongest individual results. Validation relied on validation loss and the public leaderboard, while several audio augmentations, attention heads, and SED models were unsuccessful.
compute: 2 A40 GPUs in the cloud

solution_summary: The author adapted Cfish to meet strict memory and binary-size limits using handcrafted evaluation instead of NNUE. Smaller tables, simplified history indexing, dead-code removal, and binary compression brought memory to about 4 MB and the executable below 64 KB. Search changes inspired by Stockfish16 and custom SPSA tuning each added roughly 30 Elo. O3 compilation improved search speed by about 8–9%, while NNUE training and time-control tuning were not retained.
compute: Single local machine with multithreaded SPSA tests; Kaggle single-core execution; approximately 4 MB engine memory and binary below 64 KB.

solution_summary: The final selected approach combined XGBoost, a neural network, and TabPFN with weights of 19:1:10 chosen by cross-validation grid search. Output post-processing tailored predictions to the competition metric, with the pp_prob method preferred over an analytical alternative. The selected ensemble scored 0.185 in cross-validation and 0.39 on the private leaderboard. A rejected ensemble of 20 XGBoost models used negative downsampling and label reversal, and later achieved a better private score of 0.34.

The final submission averaged three models with weights 0.58, 0.16, and 0.26. The two original models separated OwnerOccupier and Investment predictions and targeted price per square meter and total price respectively. Cleaning invalid floor areas was essential for the price-per-meter target, and averaging hundreds of XGBoost estimators compensated for unreliable cross-validation. The solution also used quarter scaling coefficients and an adapted public-kernel model.

The pipeline extracted DOI candidates from the DataCite portion of MDC Data Citation Corpus v4 and accession IDs from EuropePMC, with identifier-specific filters. DOI types were classified zero-shot by Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct-AWQ using surrounding context, citation statistics, dates, and publication metadata. Classification forced a Primary-versus-Secondary choice and compared logits. Accession IDs instead used rules based on biosample membership and elapsed time, because LLM classification did not work for them.

solution_title: Placed 194th of 4,186 - Open AI Agent Security Competition
solution_summary: The author audited guardrail and scoring code, then tested hypotheses against the actual GGUF target models. The final selections hedged between a public marker-exfiltration strategy and 2,000 benign confused-deputy email candidates intended to survive stricter private checks. Short notification prompts, minimal terminal replies, unique recipients, and success filtering improved replay efficiency and scoring coverage. Multi-post packing and combined attack messages were rejected after hosted evaluation exposed overhead and unreliable execution.

solution_title: 3 rd place solution - Directional Trends Over Volatile Noise
solution_summary: The author trained a separate model for each target, using only the assets specified in target_pairs.csv. Targets were recomputed from prices, and training used the full available history subject to forecast-horizon alignment rather than excluding the public leaderboard period. Features included positive and negative lags, rolling means and maxima, and differences, with forward and backward filling for missing values. The supplied text ends before the model details and complete evaluation procedure are described, and its claims of causal alignment coexist with the use of negative lags.

solution_title: Short summary for our approach (public 5th -> private 212th)
solution_summary: The approach used LightGBM gamma regression on 449 selected features from a public feature pipeline containing over 800 features. Validation used shuffled eight-fold cross-validation. Predictions from models trained for different numbers of boosting rounds were averaged because early stopping was unreliable. The best public score was 1.259, while the two selected submissions scored approximately 2.496 on the private leaderboard.

The efficiency solution used DeBERTa-v3-xsmall with six target-specific regression heads incorporating multi-head attention and mean pooling. Training combined labeled essays with ensemble-generated pseudo labels selected to match the training target distribution, improving cross-validation by about 0.003. Freezing the bottom six layers, reinitializing the top layer, adversarial weight perturbation, and EMA further improved generalization. Parallel inference with maximum length 448, dynamic padding, and batch size four achieved a runtime of 742 seconds. ONNX offered little speed benefit, dynamic quantization harmed performance, and Ray inference was slower.
compute: Inference runtime 742 seconds using four parallel test partitions, batch size 4, maximum length 448, and dynamic padding.

solution_summary: The final solution was a weighted ensemble of XGBoost, nearest-neighbor, and random-forest models, achieving a private score of 0.392898. The author varied XGBoost objectives and evaluation criteria, and explored neighbor counts and weighting schemes for nearest neighbors. Ensemble weights were assessed using public leaderboard performance. An alternative ensemble containing only three XGBoost models would have achieved 0.393273, while stacking and synthetic feature engineering were left unexplored.

solution_title: 18th place with only Kaggle and free Colab
solution_summary: The solution combined two DeBERTa-v3-large configurations and DeBERTa-large-MNLI using weighted character-level predictions. Useful changes included preserving line breaks, lowercasing, adding clinical shorthand tokens, masked-language-model pretraining, and pseudo-label fine-tuning. Ensemble weights were 0.4, 0.2, and 0.4, followed by whitespace correction. Experiments mostly used free Colab T4 GPUs, and GPU limits left one configuration with only two of five folds completed.
compute: Most experiments on free Colab T4 GPUs; one full fold trained and tested on Kaggle; one configuration stopped after two of five folds due to GPU time.

solution_summary: The model uses a network-in-network CNN to process individual players and their teammate and opponent pairs, pooling their interactions before combining them with ball features. Missing player states are replaced with dummy out-of-distribution values and accompanied by demolition indicators. Training uses symmetry-based permutations, while inference averages predictions over permutations, which the author reports substantially improved performance. Multiple scoring horizons provide additional supervision and yield a marginal improvement, with greater loss weight on the main ten-second target.

The solution blended global and local models with weights of 1:4. The global pipeline generated feature combinations, selected about 200 by correlation with sii, and imputed missing values using cluster means. It modeled three groups of questionnaire targets and combined five model families through stacking and seed averaging. The local component trained a separate predictor for each test point using approximately 100 nearby training observations, while further global optimization tended to overfit and worsen leaderboard performance.

The submission combined outputs from two public kernels. It retained leak-based values from one kernel and filled entries without leak values using predictions from the other. The post provides no further model or validation details and criticizes publishing strong kernels shortly before the competition deadline.

The solution blends LightGBM and a stock-wise Transformer with weights of 0.6 and 0.4 after averaging eight folds for each model. LightGBM uses roughly 400 engineered features, while the Transformer uses the 200 most important features and attends across stocks at each timestamp. Timestamp-wise rank Gaussian normalization and masked mixup support neural-network training. Centering and scaling predictions improve scores, while stacking and several alternative modeling strategies failed.

The team combined three mammography pipelines using standard image backbones, modified GMIC networks and multiview MVCCL models. VinDr BIRADS pretraining, external datasets and pseudo-labels supported several models, while another pipeline used ROI extraction and weighted training. Their selected submissions were a seven-model blend and a vote across the three pipelines. Both reached a private score of 0.48 despite CV scores of 0.555 and 0.547, showing a substantial validation-to-leaderboard gap.

solution_summary: The solution used multiple-instance learning to infer cell-level protein labels from weak image-level supervision. An initial stage pooled bags of 16 cells using attention, then generated missing labels to support a second stage using eight cells and Transformer-based cell pooling. The final ensemble combined three initial-stage models and two second-stage models with four test-time augmentations. It achieved private/public scores of 0.515/0.514, although the author reported a noticeable score loss when moving inference from Volta hardware to P100.

solution_title: 67th place solution - and good result in my own competition and challenge
solution_summary: The author trained a LightGBM regressor on 80 million steps from agents scoring at least 900. The regressor was combined with a public greedy algorithm and performed best among the approaches tried. Updating training data with games played in the final days helped the approach. The author also submitted extra copies of the best model to reduce the risk of an unfavorable evaluation outcome.

solution_summary: The solution separately estimated EFS probability with a CatBoost classifier and EFS time with a CatBoost regressor trained on EFS-positive samples. Both predictions were generated out of fold using ten folds. Optuna optimized coefficients of a ratio of cubic polynomials in the two predictions against the competition metric. The final prediction ensembled ten first-stage models with their corresponding optimized coefficients.

The final ensemble centered on Perch with ProtoSSM soundscape adaptation and sparse ResidualSSM/MLP corrections. BirdNET+ V3 supplied the largest visible improvement when restricted by class reliability, independent-branch agreement, and clipped corrections. Distilled SED predictions and a small class-restricted NFNet contribution added complementary signals, followed by mild taxonomy, site-prior, and sonotype adjustments. The displayed scores were 0.953 public and 0.948 private; later hedges preserved these scores without demonstrating additional gains.

solution_title: 9th solution(with github code): Laplace distribution noise likelihood optimization
solution_summary: The author adapted an LSTM starter by replacing L1 loss with a masked Laplace negative log-likelihood. The model predicted both pressure and a separate uncertainty scale at each time step, allowing errors to have different variances across the sequence. A 20-model ensemble reached 0.1095 on the public leaderboard, and test-data pseudo-labeling improved this to 0.1068. Later augmentation and leak-search experiments did not improve the score.

solution_title: Bronze Medal Solution: Two Families, Opposite Transfer
solution_summary: The author analyzed SDK control flow and an obtained private-guardrail wheel to determine which attack families could survive replay. This analysis favored clean confused-deputy email actions using fixture-approved recipient domains, while a separate exfiltration submission hedged against a different defense. Replay-budget tuning increased candidate throughput but saturated amid scoring variance. The deputy specialist scored 9.375 on both public and private evaluations, whereas the 91.620-public exfiltration specialist scored zero privately.

solution_summary: The final CatBoost model corrected a base trajectory assembled from particle filtering, GRU/WARP models, and nearby-well surface transfers. Predicting the smoother TVT-plus-Z surface and supplying candidate paths, typewell relationships, and multiscale gamma-ray features mattered more than changing model families. Validation grouped complete wells, excluded validation wells from labeled donor features, and checked gains through whole-well bootstrapping. The final system achieved 7.133 OOF RMSE and 7.900 private RMSE.

solution_title: [48th place] what worked and what did not work
solution_summary: The solution extended a public RoBERTa kernel with batch size 64, label smoothing, and a cross-entropy loss that penalized distance from the true span. Neutral tweets returned the full text, and offset correction addressed whitespace-related extraction errors, adding about 0.004 on the leaderboard. Fold-specific confident pseudo-labels added about 0.002 while avoiding validation leakage. Averaging logits across multiple seeds, five-fold models, and full-data models added about 0.001; text augmentation, positive/negative upsampling, and elaborate transformer heads did not help.

The detection pipeline used a hybrid 3D–2D–3D architecture with a MaxxViT encoder and a detection head predicting class scores and spatial offsets. External data, extensive volumetric augmentation, mixup, and fp16 mixed precision supported training, with four fold checkpoints in the final detection ensemble. Validation on half volumes better reflected the positive/negative balance of the leaderboard and guided blending choices. The final blend suppressed predictions that both solutions considered negative using separate Otsu thresholds, then selected coordinates by the highest normalized score rank. TensorRT and two T4 GPUs reduced detection inference to about five hours.
compute: Two T4 GPUs running parallel inference; detection runtime approximately five hours.

solution_summary: The writeup documents Python software for the seizure prediction competition and provides basic execution instructions. It reports public and private leaderboard AUCs of 0.79650 and 0.79458. It lists dependencies but does not describe the features, model architecture, training, or validation approach.

The solution used a single deep neural classification architecture adapted from an earlier competition solution. Missing values were iteratively imputed using both training and test data, while actigraphy ENMO features were grouped by weekday or weekend and time slot. Training used all available data and class-balanced loss weights. Predictions were averaged across ten random seeds.

The author compared rule-and-comment prompt templates across language models and smaller text classifiers. The strongest reported ensemble combined Qwen 4B, Llama 3B, Ettin 400M, and mmBERT Base, achieving 0.915 private and 0.918 public scores. Larger models used a safety-token prompt with labeled examples, while smaller models used a direct safety-classification format. The author concluded that increasing model size was more effective than combining many smaller models.

solution_summary: The author adapted their previous bird competition approach with two stated changes. Training first covered all bird species and then continued on 21 species. Each species received its own leaderboard-selected threshold. A single fold achieved a private score of 0.78.

The solution combined BERT and XLNet models, including twin encoders that processed questions and answers separately. Three twin-model heads used pooled representations, separate target heads, or an additional transformer, with outputs weighted 0.25, 0.25, and 0.5. Binary cross-entropy worked best among the tested losses. Final predictions were discretized with target-specific bins, and spelling scores were set to zero outside two English-language hosts.

solution_title: 33rd Solution Writeup and Discussion on GST
solution_summary: The solution used three-layer SAGEConv graph networks that fused node and configuration features before graph-context processing. Preprocessing added graph features, removed constant dimensions, encoded element types, and log-transformed large-valued features. Collection-specific layout models used Graph Segment Training with historical embeddings and stale embedding dropout to address memory limits. SAGEConv consistently beat alternative graph blocks, and the original segment weighting generalized better than a corrected version.

solution_title: BirdCLEF+2026 18th Place Solution: Ensemble is all we need
solution_summary: The best submission combined two mel-spectrogram SED branches with a Perch/ProtoSSM branch using equal-weight per-class rank averaging and TTA. Perch distillation, sequence modeling, and site/hour priors supplied complementary acoustic and contextual information. Pseudo-label MixUp was limited to a Perch single-model run, and temporal smoothing plus file-level scaling refined predictions. The three-model ensemble scored 0.957 privately, outperforming the four-model version with an added NFNet branch.
compute: CPU-friendly inference in batches of 128 soundscape files; specific hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The final submission combined 21 transformer model variants with ensemble weights determined by Nelder-Mead optimization. Important improvements included adding an LSTM after the transformer and freezing the transformer for the first two epochs. Target-specific models and negative weights for some weaker standalone models improved ensemble diversity. The resulting ensemble achieved a CV score of 0.4435.

The final submission combined LightGBM, CatBoost, several sequence-based neural networks, and a simple MLP using extensive writing-process and essay features. Models shared ten-fold cross-validation splits, with multiple seeds used for many models. Manually chosen weights allocated 65% to LGBM models and 35% to neural networks because CV-optimized ensemble weights did not transfer well to the public leaderboard. Selective rounding and clipping completed the pipeline, which achieved ensemble CV 0.5866, public LB 0.575, and private LB 0.561.

solution_title: You could have gotten 34th place using XingJian Lyu's public weights
solution_summary: The author submitted a blend using another participant's public weights while exploring their incorporation into an ensemble. Integration was unsuccessful because the GPU and CPU mel-spectrogram implementations could not be reconciled, even with matching parameters. The post recommends blending three of the shared weights and links a submission kernel, but gives little training detail.
compute: Submission inference used CPU for longer runtime.

solution_title: 43 place solution of 2 Experts and the farmer
solution_summary: The team primarily used LightGBM with approximately 500 molecular features and blended in a customized message-passing neural network for diversity. Extensive seed averaging was particularly useful. Features described atomic geometry, neighboring atom types, partial charges, substituents, and molecular structure. Chemical libraries supplied useful descriptors despite the team's limited initial domain knowledge.

The team fine-tuned a pretrained Indic wav2vec2 speech recognition model on an augmented subset of more than 100,000 competition samples. They selected cleaner samples using agreement between existing transcripts and MOS quality predictions, and removed audio shorter than one second. Audio augmentation included noise, background mixing, speed changes, SpecAug, and sampling-rate changes. Predictions were refined using pretrained Indic KenLM decoding, a fine-tuned XLM-RoBERTa punctuation restoration model, and Bengali spelling correction.

solution_title: 13th Place Solution - A Kaggle beginner's attempt
solution_summary: The solution generates images with quantized FLUX.1 Schnell and converts them to SVG using VTracer. Binary search maximizes bitmap resolution under the 10 kB SVG limit, while path compression permits larger source images. A small letter in the bottom-right corner reduces OCR hallucinations. Candidate selection uses one or two dummy VQA questions and linear regression to predict fidelity scores, favoring more generated candidates over more questions per candidate.
compute: Image evaluation takes <2 seconds per question; FLUX.1 Schnell generation takes approximately 1 second per image.

solution_summary: The solution generated candidates from item-pair matrices and Word2Vec similarities, then ranked them with CatBoost. Matrix aggregation emphasized both infrequent session items and recent interactions, producing about 200 distinct candidates per session. Additional inverse-distance and directional matrices improved the reported scores, while Word2Vec similarities also became ranking features. A final voting ensemble achieved a public score of 0.586 and a private score of 0.585.

The approach replaced chains of proper nouns with a shared PROPN token before training a simple token classifier. Predictions above a probability threshold identified candidate mentions, which were decoded back to their original strings. Frequency filtering then exploited the limited set of dataset names across the documents. The author reported that the approach could achieve approximately 0.4 on the private leaderboard and sometimes detected plausible mentions absent from annotations.

The solution combined five models with a DeBERTa-Large backbone and complementary language-model classifiers. More than 65,000 Reddit comments supplied domain-specific augmentation, with confidence-filtered pseudo-labels controlling training quality. Test-time pseudo-label fine-tuning adapted models to private rules, while multiple prompts improved prediction stability. Ensemble weights were chosen manually, and the reported private score was 0.921.
compute: Submission runtime optimized to under one hour; Reddit collection took one week.

solution_summary: The team combined extensive augmentation, staged loss training, and an ensemble of models trained at different image sizes. A dual-path SE-ResNet50 model captured both dependencies and independence among grapheme roots, vowel components, and consonant components to handle unseen combinations. Reduced focal loss improved cross-validation recall. Class-specific prediction adjustments, initialized from inverse class frequencies, had a substantial impact on the competition metric.

The author formulated family scheduling as mixed-integer optimization with an under-approximation of the accounting penalty. Convex penalty terms were replaced by maxima of affine functions, with randomized greedy slope selection keeping the formulation small. Repeated solver runs restricted occupancy around the incumbent and limited families to preferred days. An integrality-relaxation experiment identified regions needing wider occupancy bounds and helped improve the objective from 114958.43 to 114957.38.

The solution trained seven department-specific LightGBM models with a Poisson objective and early stopping. Features combined calendar and event proximity, relative price changes, historical sales lags and rolling means, and categorical item and store identifiers. Forecasts were generated recursively, using predictions to construct later lag features. Store-and-department correction multipliers estimated from the last validation week adjusted systematic forecast bias, and the private score stayed close to the public score.

The approach first adapted DeBERTa-v3-large with masked language modeling on the previous Feedback competition dataset, reaching approximately 4.5 perplexity. Essays were processed as token-classification inputs with discourse-specific boundary tokens and additional discourse-type embeddings. Effectiveness supervision was restricted to discourse start and end tokens, whose probabilities were averaged during inference. The final submission averaged variations of the five-fold model.

The author fine-tuned ImageNet-pretrained Inception-v3 models at image sizes ranging from 400×400 to 800×800. Five-fold cross-validation, flip and rotation augmentation, and pseudo-labeling helped address the small training set. The final submission averaged 19 predictions, most themselves averages over five folds. VGG16, ResNet50 and several additional augmentations were tested but excluded because they performed worse.

The solution combined image-model predictions with tabular features in CatBoost and blended models across five validation folds. Image approaches included ResNet18 and EfficientNetB0 with one-hot metadata, plus DreamSim embeddings classified by LinearSVC. Patient-level and patient-location aggregations delivered the largest tabular improvements, while top-k feature selection improved both validation and leaderboard performance. Handcrafted image features lost their benefit after neural-network out-of-fold predictions were added.

The solution extracted image and metadata features with noisy-student-pretrained EfficientNet-B3 through B7 models, then used patient-level transformers to classify images jointly. Both stages predicted eight diagnosis classes, with melanoma probability taken from the softmax output. ISIC 2019 data, patient-grouped validation, repeated splits, and extensive augmentation supported training. Final submissions combined base models and contextual transformers through averaging before softmax, while the authors reported weak agreement between CV and leaderboard results.
compute: Tesla V100 and Titan RTX in parallel; total training approximately 1.5 weeks on both GPUs, or 2.5 weeks on one Tesla.

solution_summary: The solution blended six XLM-RoBERTa-large models, including three initialized from masked-language-model adaptation to the test set. Adversarial validation selected translated training and validation examples resembling the test distribution. Diversity came from losses, hidden-layer combinations, learning rates, sequence lengths, and data composition. Training used TensorFlow and Keras on TPUs, with GPUs used for prediction and adversarial validation.
compute: TPUs for training; GPUs for predictions and adversarial validation.

solution_summary: The author corrected signal micro-drift by fitting Gaussian mixtures to 100,000-point batches and aligning component means to shared fixed signal levels. Mixture-derived channel probabilities also helped identify and remove 50 Hz interference and its harmonics using FFT. A plain WaveNet trained with cross-entropy on these probabilities and time-symmetric rolling features substantially improved over tree models. The final submission bagged five models with different seeds and learning rates; a single WaveNet achieved about 0.946 public and 0.945 private.

The system used a nine-layer CNN with 128-bin mel spectrograms and random four-second excerpts. Semi-supervised training combined curated samples with unlabeled noisy samples after warming up the backbone on the noisy set. Focal loss and a multilabel adaptation of ArcFace were paired with spectrogram augmentation and time reversal. Sliding-window averaging and augmentation on short clips produced a single-model stage-one lwlrap of 0.712.

The solution used a six-layer transformer with sequences of up to 3,500 investments and the original 300 features. It optimized Pearson correlation directly, training for 10 epochs on the training data followed by three epochs on supplemental data. Feature-level random zeroing and sequence-level random masking provided augmentation, while validation used the last 100, 200, or 300 periods. The final ensemble combined five seeds; the transformer outperformed the tested LightGBM, MLP, and 1D CNN models.

The solution combined an optimized mean prompt with predicted tags and a full prompt admitted by a learned gate. LoRA-tuned Mistral models benefited most from synthetic prompt variations and cluster-balanced training data. Cluster-specific templates were selected only when two cluster assignments agreed, otherwise falling back to the global template. The first four components scored 0.71, while cluster selection added about 0.005 locally.

The author's contribution combined text preprocessing, semantic representations, similarity features, and frequency and graph features. The repository covers boosted trees, a decomposable attention model, LSTM experiments, and MLP models. Ensembling included stacking and in-fold optimization of ensemble weights. The author cautions that some generated features were absent from the final model, so the precise final feature set is unspecified.

solution_title: Up 580 positions on lb and a bronze medal for a simple catboost solution
solution_summary: The final approach used CatBoost for the CITE and Multiome tasks, with feature selection and target-dependent training settings. Donors were one-hot encoded, while days were represented numerically after comparison with one-hot encoding. The author selected about 600 CITE inputs by feature importance and identified three especially useful Multiome inputs alongside SVD components. Model capacity was concentrated on stronger CITE target groups and early Multiome target components. Additional raw-data features did not help, and planned neural networks and second-level linear models were not pursued.

The solution combined thirteen transformer experiments using DeBERTa, patent-specific BERT, and RoBERTa encoders with several prediction heads and losses. Inputs included CPC section tokens, anchor and target phrases, and CPC context separated by a custom token. Out-of-fold predictions supported both Nelder–Mead weight optimization and BayesianRidge stacking. Both ensemble methods achieved a reported private score of 0.8638.
compute: Local machine: Core i7-12700, 64GB RAM, RTX 3090

solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B with supervised reasoning data, then used DPO to favor shorter correct responses. LMDeploy with 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV cache quantization improved inference efficiency. Inference combined direct reasoning and executable Python samples through self-consistency, with early stopping at both sample and question levels. Dynamic time budgeting balanced remaining questions, producing scores of 34/50 public and 31/50 private.
compute: Single 8x A800 machine: 11 hours for eight SFT epochs and 40 hours for four DPO epochs; online inference tests on 4x L4 and local tests on 2x A800.
