solution_summary: The team pretrained Gemma-2-9B on public reward data with binary preference labels, then fine-tuned on competition data and a separate 33k dataset. Reward pretraining improved both cross-validation and public leaderboard scores by up to 20 points. Their final ensemble combined two one-epoch runs with different response ordering and used swapped-order inference for one model, achieving about 0.873 on a local single fold. Length-aware batching, two-GPU data splitting, and INT8 inference supported a final 4k context limit.
compute: Two Kaggle T4 GPUs for concurrent inference; final context limit 4k.

solution_title: [112th Place] How I missed Rank 2 of M5-Accuracy by a factor!!!
solution_summary: The team used LightGBM with validation on 1.5 years of future data to choose hyperparameters. They then retrained on the entire dataset, favoring a standard approach to limit overfitting. After the competition, applying a scaling factor of 0.955 to their submission produced a reported private leaderboard score of 0.52123.

solution_title: my 10 day journey in this competition and solution sharing
solution_summary: The author combined LightGBM and neural networks trained on 2017 data with historical sales statistics, categorical information, promotion summaries, and category-level statistical features. A weekday-aligned 16-day validation period and filtering to recently active store-item combinations improved agreement with the public leaderboard. LightGBM importance reduced more than 2,300 features to approximately 400, while neural networks used one-hot categorical inputs. The final 0.54/0.46 weighted ensemble scored 0.503 publicly and 0.516 privately, although many feature improvements transferred poorly to the private period.

solution_title: 85th Place Solution for the AI Village Capture the Flag @ DEFCON31
solution_summary: The author solved 21 capture-the-flag tasks using task-specific searches, data inspection, and adversarial queries. Successful methods included brute force, clustering and geometric token traversal, image hill climbing, SQL injection, and prompt injection. Pixel frequency inspection and vocabulary searches also exposed hidden answers. Several other challenges remained unsolved despite optimization attempts.
external_data: ["MNIST", "English vocabulary book", "Google image search Granny Smith image"]

solution_summary: The final submissions equally blended public notebook-based models with modifications to cleaning, features, and prediction scaling. Manual inspection of individual building meters was considered the most important step, while grouped target encoding and model-specific feature removal also helped. Leaked test ground truths from five sites guided validation and experiments. Multiplicative prediction shrinkage improved the private score by about 0.004–0.005, while alternative models and stacking were excluded after disappointing validation results.
external_data: ["Leaked test ground-truth labels for sites 0, 1, 2, 4, and 15"]

solution_summary: The author's single model uses CatBoost ranking over ten weeks of training data with recency-dependent sample weights and popularity-based candidates. The ensemble takes the top 24 items from each of 13 models and reranks them using CatBoostRanker. Its features include first-stage predictions, customer-normalized scores and ranks, model-group aggregates, customer and article attributes, and purchase counts across time windows. The ensemble improved CV from 0.0365 to 0.0407 and private leaderboard performance from 0.03048 to 0.03294.

The solution combined per-frame gradient-boosted tree classifiers with dilated temporal convolutional networks trained on centered temporal windows. Body-normalized motion features supported both approaches, while strong spatial augmentations were especially valuable for the neural models. Greedy ensemble selection optimized nested F1 separately for action and lab combinations, with out-of-fold checks used to assess ensemble generalization. Strided inference, interpolation, and pairwise action threshold tournaments completed a pipeline that reached 0.516 privately.

The solution used a two-stage pipeline: UniXcoder generated cell embeddings, and a transformer predicted notebook cell order from those embeddings. Both stages used multiple training objectives, and the second stage accepted up to 512 code cells and 512 markdown cells. The final submission blended three models trained on different combinations of competition data and KGTorrent data. UniXcoder performed best among the tested first-stage pretrained models.

solution_title: A solution for efficient computation of optimal paths
solution_summary: The post describes a fast path optimizer rather than the complete game strategy. It expands path states with time, position, flight-plan length, and facing so that transitions form a directed acyclic graph. A forward dynamic-programming pass processes each edge once, with pruning and extra state flags improving practicality. The Cython implementation computes paths in about 0.05–0.15 seconds, although its compressed state cannot fully represent environmental changes caused by earlier actions.
compute: Approximately 0.05–0.15 seconds per path optimization

solution_summary: The solution calibrated sensor measurements using selected pixel regions and estimated wavelength-specific transit depths with polynomial fitting. Gradient-based transit boundaries and smoothing reduced noise, while zero-crossing and polynomial fluctuation features measured spectral dynamics. The final prediction combined a signal-weighted flat spectrum with scaled dynamic residuals, with Nelder–Mead optimizing residual weights and uncertainty. Additional depth scaling and uncertainty inflation improved robustness.

The team segmented abdominal organs and trained dedicated classifiers on cropped regions, while bowel and extravasation models used larger images with black borders removed. Organ classifiers combined 2.5D CNNs with recurrent models, and a separate two-stage pipeline converted image features into series predictions. Positive oversampling and iterative image-label refinement were particularly helpful. A four-layer MLP stacked predictions using the competition metric, improving the reported overall CV loss from 0.3827 to 0.3736; the final submission achieved 0.3686 CV.

solution_title: 2nd place solution --- Avoid leaks and overfitting
solution_summary: The final approach stacked six prediction streams from CatBoost and RealMLP using a neural network. Target statistics were calculated inside cross-validation, and only multi-seed averages were considered when selecting base predictions. Correlation filtering, forward selection, and backward elimination reduced the candidates before rank-transformed variants were added. The final submission achieved 0.95535 private AUC; a separate outside-CV encoding submission was nearly identical, while cross-validated hill climbing was rejected over suspected overfitting.
compute: Used a local PC and Kaggle compute; exhausted the weekly Kaggle GPU allocation.

solution_summary: The solution used a contrastively trained multilingual retriever followed by binary classification rankers. Same-language cosine retrieval supplied candidates and hard negatives, with a single MPNet retriever retained after retrieval ensembling failed to improve leaderboard results. Rankers benefited from SimCSE initialization, FGM, and EMA, and their outputs were blended using regression-derived weights. Threshold tuning and a top-four fallback completed the pipeline, with the best reported ensemble achieving 0.751 on the private leaderboard.

The author reports using stacking for motion prediction. They chose this approach because they found ensembling difficult. The remaining details appear only in embedded images, so the provided text does not establish the component models, training procedure, or numerical results.

The solution generated over 200 OOF prediction sets from diverse tabular models and feature representations using consistent stratified five-fold splits. It selected 100 strong, relatively diverse models using an AUC cutoff and greedy Spearman-correlation selection. A custom optimizer jointly learned ensemble weights and a power transform applied to ranked predictions, reaching OOF AUC 0.955785 with power 0.8. The final submission scored 0.95534 on the private leaderboard, while soft and hard pseudo-labeling offered no consistent gain.

The pipeline trains XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost with stratified cross-validation and domain-inspired features. It combines weighted ensembles, multi-seed bagging, and stacking across saved run bundles. Stacking base predictions from 12 bundles achieved the best public ROC-AUC of 0.69768, while a 90/10 stacker–bagging blend achieved the best internal OOF score of 0.729185. More elaborate encoded features and a class-weighted categorical LightGBM configuration degraded performance.

solution_title: Diagnosing Heart Diseases in the Data Science Bowl: 2nd place, Team kunsthart
solution_summary: The team combines classical ROI detection with VGG-inspired networks that predict cardiac volume distributions from SAX, 2Ch, and 4Ch MRI views. Physical-resolution normalization, extensive spatial and temporal augmentation, and test-time averaging improve robustness without manual labeling. Patient models aggregate predicted slice areas using fixed geometric volume calculations, avoiding the severe overfitting observed with recurrent aggregation. The best patient model achieved local CRPS of 0.0105, although outlier differences made this an optimistic estimate of leaderboard performance.

The solution combined heavily regularized Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and dense neural network models using historical market features. It converted 424 daily targets into one regression problem by adding target_id, with a chronological 80/20 validation split. Cross-market spreads, ratios, lagged values, rolling correlations, and technical indicators supplied the main signals. Feature clipping and convolution smoothing of blended predictions reduced volatility, producing a private leaderboard score of 0.445.
compute: Full ensemble: approximately 6–7 minutes training and 16 seconds per testing batch. Simplified model: 1–2 minutes training and 3–4 seconds prediction.

solution_title: Flavour of Physics Technical Write-Up: 1st place, Go Polar Bears
solution_summary: The solution reconstructed particle mass using physics equations and then learned corrections to that engineered feature. Small XGBoost models helped control mass correlation, while a much larger XGBoost model predicted reconstructed-mass error using multilevel cross-validation and bagging. Corrected mass features also fed a bagged neural network with a single eight-neuron dense layer. The final combination addressed discrimination, agreement testing, and mass correlation, while FlightDistance corrections and dropout did not improve results.

solution_title: 113th Place: [Working Note] Reverse-engineering the score surface of AI Agent Security: Multi-Step Tool Attacks
solution_summary: The author reverse-engineered scoring and guardrail code to identify reachable security predicates and throughput limits. The main attack repeated secret-bearing HTTP posts up to eight times, using clean URLs to bypass payload inspection and Harmony formatting to reduce gpt_oss reasoning latency. Static candidate emission improved throughput, while same-day paired submissions exposed frequent failures of offline improvements to transfer to production. The final exfiltration submission scored 95.130 publicly but zero privately, while an email-based hedge retained 21.465 on both.
compute: 9,000 seconds per model per phase; offline shot-completion measurements used a GPU.

solution_summary: The team ensembled BERT base, BERT large, XLNet, and RoBERTa with task-specific regression heads and additional features. Vanilla binary cross-entropy remained competitive with more elaborate losses, while an early BCE/MSE blend became ineffective after post-processing. The largest gains came from domain-based spelling rules and discretizing predictions according to inferred numbers of raters. Min-max scaling before rounding prevented small predictions from collapsing to zero and added roughly 0.02 after an initial rounding gain of about 0.03.

The solution builds a filtered, word-level SQLite database and generates patent search queries as single-word OR-chains. Neighbor publications supply word-occurrence features, and iterative selection rewards true matches while penalizing false positives. Misinterpreting mAP as precision weakened the submitted approach: the best submission scored 0.66, while a revised notebook targeting mAP achieved over 0.72.

solution_title: 303rd / Bronze writeup: sub-voxel localization, a learned coordinate head, and a lot of dead ends
solution_summary: The solution retained a public temporal-UNet3D detector and ILP tracker, improving coordinates with local soft-argmax sub-voxel refinement. Refinement along z contributed most of the gain, and feeding refined z coordinates into edge prediction helped beyond changing output coordinates alone. The author selected two submissions with different coordinate schemes, scoring 0.955 and 0.954 publicly, and tuned relinking bonuses and raw-edge overrides. A replay harness accelerated experimentation, but its in-sample bias made leaderboard checks essential and many promising offline changes failed to transfer.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution: 72 OOFs, a whole lotta Autogluon, and 31 scores of 0.98512 or above (on the private LB)
solution_summary: The solution combined 72 out-of-fold prediction arrays from diverse models using Ridge ensembles and AutoGluon stacking. A poisonous-probability feature derived from an exact solution to the original dataset improved some models and added ensemble diversity. Cross-validation and model diversity guided development, while blends with other submissions were less dependable. The strongest reported private score was 0.98517 from a blend that was not selected for the final submissions.
compute: Kaggle CPU/GPU runs constrained by GPU quota and 12-hour limits; an additional 3-hour run used 32 CPUs on Lightning.ai.

solution_summary: The final approach ensembled GRU and Transformer models using two weeks of known-feature lags rather than target lags. Inputs included categorical embeddings, baseball statistics, game and standings information, transactions, follower counts, and previous-month target aggregates. Both backbones fed convolutional processing and separate prediction heads for each target. Time-based validation, full-data training, multiple checkpoints, and seed ensembling supported the final submissions; the individual GRU and Transformer scored approximately 1.25 and 1.27.
external_data: ["Example roster, game, and box-score data dataset"]

solution_title: Deep CNN for Time Series Correlation Measurement
solution_summary: A deep convolutional neural network detected correlations from pairs of derivative activity recordings and achieved 93.96% AUC. Adding overall brain network activity as a third input row helped the network account for noise and activity-dependent behavior. Threshold-based frame filtering retained high-activity fragments and reduced recording length to roughly 1% of the original. Training used 1.2 million balanced positive and negative examples, while hidden-layer activation analysis with SVMs guided architecture refinement.
compute: Designed to run on a GPU; hardware model and runtime unspecified.

solution_title: How we did it: the winners of the IJCNN Social Network Challenge
solution_summary: The team combined graph de-anonymization against a fresh Flickr crawl with random-forest link prediction. Manually identified high-in-degree seeds supported iterative matching through cosine similarity of already mapped neighbors. De-anonymization covered about 80% of nodes but only about 60% of test edges, making the machine-learning fallback essential. The random forest used neighborhood and random-walk features, with an estimated, bias-adjusted AUC of 93.5–94% that was not verified by Kaggle. Final predictions prioritized available de-anonymization evidence, including unanimous votes across multiple identity candidates.
compute: Flickr crawler ran on a small cluster of 2–4 machines.

solution_summary: The solution modeled question histories with sequences of length 256, using engineered answer-pattern features and a custom GRU architecture. It calculated content similarities through 16 learned transformations and used a reverse GRU pass followed by a forward pass, alongside a two-layer MLP. Training used question interactions only, large batches, and a decreasing learning rate over 15 epochs. Seven seeds trained on the whole dataset formed the final ensemble, improving the reported leaderboard score from 0.813 for a single model to 0.815.
compute: 8 hours training on a 4-GPU machine

solution_summary: The solution combined listing attributes with count, ratio, text, geographic, and manager-level features. It created two stacking systems: one using five-fold out-of-fold predictions from diverse models, and another using repeated feature subsets for tree models. A weighted average of the two stacking outputs formed the final submission.

solution_title: 🥈24th Place Solution(A potential solution for achieving private 0.70)
solution_summary: The final submission ensembled 2D U-Nets with RegNetY-016 backbones, taking three consecutive slices as input at original image resolution. Tversky loss, resolution-related augmentation, channel reversal, and strong cutout were central to robustness. Enlarging images during inference consistently improved results, with a reported 0.1 private-score gain from 1.2× scaling. Reliable validation remained difficult, and the author associated the final model's weaker private performance with its smaller Tversky beta; 3D models and pseudo-labeling did not provide meaningful gains.

The solution fits Gaussian mixture models jointly to training and test data without supervision, then uses training labels to map clusters to classes. Its main modification rounds estimated cluster means to hypercube vertices to match the synthetic data generator. Selecting among different cluster counts, equalizing cluster probability mass, and increasing covariance regularization provided further improvements. Mean rounding alone with three clusters per class achieved a score above 0.974.

solution_title: 5th Place Solution : My First Competition and First Gold
solution_summary: The final ensemble combined eight LightGBM models, four CatBoost models, and one neural network. Training used in-season data and removed unusual engagement events such as retirement games. Features captured pitcher rotation, upcoming games, recent engagement targets, and batting and pitching contributions. Validation used July 2021 after training through June, and the author identified recursive target lags as a possible cause of weaker later-period performance.

The solution combines manually designed tree tilings, repeated spyrrow packing runs, and simulated annealing refinement. An interactive web interface supports visual comparison and removal of low-density subsets before repacking. A custom exact-outline tool lets a retained group of trees act as one shape, enabling dense tiling cores with individually packed peripheral trees. Separate machine queues continuously generate and refine candidates with different annealing settings.
compute: Laptop for interface and orchestration, two 128-thread machines for spyrrow, and one 24-thread machine managing simulated annealing.

solution_summary: The author generated 1,000 essays with an LLM using a prompt that asks for a review of an essay deserving a score of 9. The intended mechanism is for an LLM judge to accept the review and assign that score. If the judge rejects the review, the submission contains no actual essay to evaluate. The post links a solution notebook but reports no measured results.

The solution combined sensor-specific CNN branches with phase-aware attention and separate model variants for missing sensor configurations. Handedness normalization, subject corrections, engineered IMU signals, and phase-aligned mixup supported training. Online pseudo-label updates improved predictions during test inference. The largest gain came from predicting 102 composite classes and jointly assigning labels within each subject under a no-repeat constraint, raising private performance from 0.858 to 0.878 with pseudo-labeling enabled.

The solution combined extensive feature experiments with an ensemble of XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and histogram gradient boosting models. The most influential change removed training examples with ages above 21 or below 3 to better match the inferred test distribution. Approximately 200,000 synthetic examples supplemented roughly 74,000 competition training examples, making five-fold validation sets similar in size to the test set. Optuna selected model parameters, while an additional Gradient Boosting model was omitted because its small validation benefit did not justify the time cost.

The final stack combined Bi-LSTM, whole-word-masked BERT-Large-Uncased, and XLNet using an ExtraTreesClassifier meta-model. Neural networks also predicted toxicity subtypes and an inverse annotator-count target, with the latter improving five-fold cross-validation by 0.0003. Adding five selected subtype predictions to the stack improved its public leaderboard score from 0.9461 to 0.94671. PyTorch mixed precision and bucket sequencing helped accelerate experiments.

The post congratulates the winners and thanks the organizers. The author shares a link to a notebook titled evolutionary-algorithm. No implementation details or results are described in the post itself.

The pipeline segmented C1–C7 vertebrae with a 3D SwinUNETR and classified individual vertebra volumes using an ensemble of 3D EfficientNetB4 and DenseNet209 models. External spine datasets supported segmentation training, while the 87 competition masks served as a held-out test set with mean Dice around 0.90. Vertebra alignment, mask cleanup, removal of neighboring vertebrae, and horizontal-flip TTA improved the pipeline. Patient predictions used the three highest fracture probabilities, but rounding extreme probabilities was later identified as harmful.
compute: Segmentation and preprocessing: ~4.5 hours; ten classifiers: ~2.5 hours inference.

solution_summary: The solution averaged equally weighted logits from nine 3D U-Nets, eight of which were pretrained on simulated data before competition-data fine-tuning. Experiment-based holdout validation and Optuna searches guided model selection. Training combined segmentation losses with modest augmentation, while an accidentally randomized orientation objective contributed to four final models. Custom KL-based particle splitting and geometric centroid refinement improved the leaderboard score by about 0.015.
compute: KL postprocessing takes 90 minutes on a P100.

solution_summary: The author used ten-fold multilabel-stratified validation and kept preprocessing within the validation pipeline to control leakage. CatBoost encoding supported most models, while Gaussian Naive Bayes received an additional failure-indicator feature and distribution transformations. Logistic regression determined weights for a voting ensemble, which achieved a reported CV score of 0.98006 and was retrained on the full dataset. A later correction states that the best submission excluded Random Forest and LightGBM DART.

The final ensemble combined a model representing title plus body separately from the answer with metadata, and a BERT model concatenating title, body, and answer across ten folds. The ensemble scored 0.4003 on the leaderboard. GloVe and FastText embeddings offered insufficient accuracy, and hyperparameter tuning had little effect. Trimming, summarization, and a regression head with MSE did not yield reported improvements, while a LAMB optimizer attempt stopped with an error.

The solution used median-based traffic forecasts with a lower percentile replacing the median in a second aggregation stage. Validation comprised six consecutive 61-day test periods spanning roughly a year, with training-to-test gaps chosen to reflect the competition. Aggregating about eight or nine first-level medians using percentiles around 27.5–37.5 improved validation scores by approximately 0.2–1.0 across folds. Aggregate exploratory analysis suggested declining interest in event-related pages, and the author estimated a competition score improvement of roughly 0.4 or more, although other submission differences and limited testing made attribution uncertain.

solution_title: Orbit Wars — 🥈 Silver Medal Solution (#220 / 4,730 teams)
solution_summary: The agent used the public ProducerLite utilities with a vectorized heuristic planner for continuous interception, exact ship-flow scoring, attack selection, and redistribution. Its strongest improvements came from ETA-aware reinforcement risk, sparse candidate projection, and broad Optuna tuning across more than 3,500 trials. Separate endgame and four-player settings adapted behavior, while limited opponent modeling and weaker four-player performance remained constraints.

solution_summary: The team built ten model variants with extensive user-level and transaction feature engineering, including a LightGBM single model scoring 0.9588 on the public leaderboard. They combined stratified and time-series validation models using weighted blending. User-history post-processing replaced predictions with zero or one when matched training users had uniformly legitimate or fraudulent transactions. This improved public and private scores by 0.0007 and 0.0004, while neural networks and pseudo-labeling did not work for them.

The author blended their best existing solution with a leading public notebook. This last-day blend produced a surprisingly strong result. The post provides no model, feature, validation, or blend-weight details.

The solution analyzed guardrail rules and scoring predicates to focus on benign email actions that triggered the confused-deputy predicate. Repeated full-pipeline runs used elapsed time to infer that the hidden private guardrail blocked exfiltration attempts while allowing the chosen email candidates. Separate prompt templates and short runtime probes optimized reliability and throughput for GPT-OSS and Gemma. The final submission strategy emitted many prevalidated candidates with distinct recipient domains and skipped discovery to maximize the number replayed within the evaluation budget.

solution_summary: The solution combined Cascade Mask R-CNN models with diverse backbones, using both original tiles and tiles padded with neighboring tissue. A four-fold spatial validation scheme and stain transformations helped approximate generalization to an unseen whole-slide image. Models were trained in two stages, consolidated with stochastic weight averaging, and ensembled across fold and full-data models. Several mask filters removed unreliable instances; the ensemble without dilation achieved 0.588 on the private set, compared with 0.526 with dilation.

The retrieval pipeline combines global CNN descriptors, nearest-neighbor search, geometric reranking, and diffusion-based query expansion. An ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 was fine-tuned on Landmark Recognition Challenge data with GeM pooling and hard-in-batch triplet margin loss. Faiss retrieved candidates, and local image matching with RANSAC reranked the top 100 images. Diffusion supplied the final query-expansion stage.

The solution used a Qwen 32B retriever trained with a custom MultipleNegativesRankingLoss implementation in Transformers, followed by a Qwen2.5 32B-AWQ reranker. Retriever training used LoRA with rank 64 and alpha 128, a learning rate of 1e-4, batch size 64, and one hard negative. Validation splits were adjusted to contain approximately 60% unseen misconceptions, improving correlation between cross-validation and the leaderboard, although performance dropped on the private leaderboard.

The author's contribution combined EfficientNet classification models with YOLOv5x and EfficientDet opacity detectors, using 512×512 images throughout. Auxiliary segmentation loss improved classification, while pneumonia detection pretraining supported the detectors. Weighted boxes fusion and geometric box filtering refined detection predictions, and detection confidence adjusted the Negative and None classification scores. The final submission scored 0.623 in CV and 0.621 on the private leaderboard.

The author engineered categorical encodings, target statistics, numeric transformations, PCA components, and centroid distances. A diverse set of 28 first-level models supplied out-of-fold predictions for second- and third-level stacking. Model selection considered prediction correlations and MAE across target percentile ranges, using stratified ten-fold validation throughout. Two additive post-processing approaches were evaluated, but the final submission without post-processing performed better on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: [LB 125th Position - .795] Pure Feature Engineering .(3M pkl files) Comp & Solution
solution_summary: The solution combined gradient boosting models using roughly 39–41 features with an AKT neural network. Features captured user and content accuracy, recent answers, Elo estimates, lecture activity, and elapsed time between attempts on the same content. Lecture features improved both cross-validation and leaderboard performance, whose results closely tracked each other. Several alternatives, including TF-IDF over content histories and additional rolling-window features, did not help.

The team trained 12 variants derived from a public baseline and selected a six-model ensemble. They ranked candidates by out-of-fold AUC and explored several ensemble sizes and combinations of the strongest models. Selection considered average, rank, power, and Bayesian-optimized ensemble AUC, favoring consistently strong results with fewer models. The selected six-model ensemble achieved a private score of 0.9413.

The author solved multiple CTF tasks using exploratory data analysis, adversarial image attacks, injection exploits, and targeted prompts. Matching the image classifier locally enabled FGSM attacks, while differentiable JPEG processing made the compressed-image challenge solvable. Other successful approaches included PCA, greedy point traversal, pixel probing, and image thresholding. Several challenges remained unsolved despite experiments with evolutionary optimization, black-box attacks, and phrase manipulation.

The authors describe their approach as nested ensembles incorporating pseudo-labeling. The post provides only a one-line outline. It gives no architectures, training settings, validation details, or scores.

The final unlearning submission pruned the model and added small noise to its fully connected layer. A single warmup epoch began with retraining, interleaved forget batches with multiple retraining batches, and ended with retraining alone. The team explored numerous other unlearning strategies and tested approaches on a model trained from scratch on downsampled CIFAR. The author attributed the weak outcome partly to transferring a one-epoch schedule from CIFAR, where the model's overfitting made that schedule appear sufficient.

solution_title: 20th place solution - generate lots of code with a 32b model
solution_summary: The solution used an unfine-tuned 32B DeepSeek-R1-distilled Qwen model in 4-bit AWQ format, served through vLLM. Seven initial prompts branched into reasoning and repeated Python generation, yielding up to 108 programs and nine boxed answers per problem. A custom weighting algorithm combined executed-code and boxed answers while discounting correlated branches and applying agreement bonuses and penalties. Adaptive token budgeting and asynchronous code execution controlled runtime; the two submitted variants scored 27 and 25 privately.

The team built complementary 1D ConvNeXt, Transformer, U-Net, and LSTM models that represented atmospheric profiles as sequences of 60 heights. Large low-resolution training datasets, physically motivated features, and careful input and target normalization were central to the pipelines. Learning-rate scheduling and regularization substantially affected performance, while selected moisture tendencies were replaced with deterministic values after prediction. The strongest reported individual ConvNeXt achieved a private score of 0.78281.

solution_title: My stable solution to get a bronze medal
solution_summary: The author compared submission stability for standalone LSTM and LightGBM models against combinations of both. Single LSTM submissions tended to drop substantially on the private evaluation, whereas single LightGBM submissions tended to improve. Ensembling or stacking the two model types limited the reported score movement to approximately ±0.02.

The solution developed WaveNet-based 1D EEG models, 2D spectrogram models, and fused 1D+2D models. Training first used all samples and then restricted training to samples with at least ten votes. The 2D backbone was trained separately before attention-based fusion because the branches exhibited very different optimization behavior. Patient-grouped validation, EEG slicing, augmentation, and extensive test-time augmentation supported reported public scores around 0.26 for 1D and 0.25 for fused models.

The solution centered on per-column duplicate indicators and value counts, including row-level duplicate totals and statistics calculated over 300,000 rows. A particularly effective feature transformed raw values using min-max-scaled counts and the row mean. Earlier experiments masked raw values using duplicate indicators and replaced zeros with column means. Blending LightGBM and CatBoost with twofold and threefold training augmentation raised the reported score to approximately 0.923–0.924.

The solution relied on train-on-test training and an ensemble of language models, with safety moderation models improving the combined predictions. Combined training and test data were deduplicated, subreddit information was removed, and conflicting labels were resolved by majority vote with ties discarded. Models were trained with Unsloth and QLoRA, while a vLLM modification enabled Gemma2 inference in fp16. Local validation did not track leaderboard performance, so model decisions relied on leaderboard feedback.

Training uses purged temporal folds and early stopping on validation AUC, although the author notes possible encoder leakage. The stronger submission adds a public PyTorch architecture and combines last-fold weights with weights trained on filtered full data.

solution_summary: The solution handled accession identifiers and DOIs with separate extraction and classification pipelines. DOI processing used Qwen3-4B for noisy-window detection and larger language models for metadata extraction and classification using author overlap and context. Training used MDC corpus versions 3.0 and 4.1 with consensus-generated labels; planned DOI-specific Light-R1 fine-tuning was blocked by label issues.

The pipeline combines a leakage solution with predictions from Random Forest, XGBoost, SGDClassifier, and Naive Bayes models. The four classifiers are blended using a weighted average of predicted probabilities. The blended output is then stacked over the leakage solution; no performance score is reported.

Retrieval averaged embeddings from three fine-tuned Qwen2.5-14B models and SFR-Embedding-Mistral with weights 0.4, 0.5, 0.4, and 0.1. The suffix search eventually discovered the token lucrarea, while refining attacks around model predictions hurt performance. The short-prompt model scored 0.52 alone and 0.70 with a mean prompt, illustrating how strongly the metric rewarded its preferred word distribution.

The final approach used scaled features and L1-regularized logistic regression with the liblinear solver. Feature selection, UberImputer imputation, missingness indicators and a small adjustment to measurement_2 improved performance. A separate shallow LightGBM model for rows with missing loading was tested but omitted, despite later showing a private leaderboard benefit.

solution_title: Exploring the combination of search and learn for the ARC25 challenge
solution_summary: The strongest submitted approach made minor adaptations to the previous year's transduction method with test-time training. Most research instead explored deep-learning-guided program synthesis with hindsight relabeling in a search-and-learn loop. That experimental system outperformed pure search for an equal prediction budget, but remained incomplete and solved none of the private ARC-AGI-2 test tasks.

solution_title: "Single" LSTM model with Magic Features. 0.1093 LB.
solution_summary: The shared single model used four LSTM layers followed by dense and output layers with skip connections. Handcrafted aggregation features were the main ingredient, together with reversed sequence training that also exposed features from the original order. Additional transformations handled inspiratory u_in values and the sign of pressure targets. After standard postprocessing, the model scored 0.1093 publicly and 0.1133 privately.

The final agent used a rule-based evaluator and lightweight search with an original Mega Gardevoir deck. It mapped opposing archetypes onto six target board plans, scoring actions by progress toward the selected plan and switching when observations contradicted it. Improvements were screened through calibrated opponent bots, board-formation metrics, and real ladder comparisons, with replay diagnostics used to detect regressions. The final 1,000 ladder games produced a 57.1% win rate across 28 archetypes; endgame DFS and a learned self-play system were withdrawn after weaker results.

The team created 772 handcrafted features and retained 411 through manual and correlation-based selection, including removal of temporally unstable features. Ten diverse tree models were stacked with RidgeClassifier, calibrated, and averaged across five random seeds. Validation used five stratified group folds grouped by WEEK_NUM. A final year-dependent downward score correction used the maximum payment year, while the calibrated stack achieved a reported local CV AUC of 0.859322.

The final approach trained XGBoost with a custom multiclass-style MAP ranking objective using every row where a product was added. Key features included exponentially weighted product histories, relative income measures, calendar variables, and lagged customer information. Simple sums of model scores and a payroll-to-pension score rule provided additional gains. Using more training data drove major improvements, while attempted customer-record cleaning hurt performance and reliable local validation remained unresolved.

The final approach used EfficientNet-B4 with black-border cropping, heavy augmentation, and five-fold test-time augmentation. Sampling favored severe classes in the older data to counter the new dataset's class imbalance while retaining all new examples. The solution used soft-constraint simulated annealing, increasing overlap penalties while testing fixed container sizes. Dimer lattice potentials encouraged ordered configurations, and a variable-box polishing stage removed residual overlaps. Parallel tournament selection and repeated basin hopping refined candidates, including seeds obtained by adding or removing particles from neighboring configurations. Maintaining three seed lineages improved diversity, and incorporating public configurations further reduced the final score to 69.106266.

Waveform shifts, channel removal, and negative-example channel swaps provided augmentation, and ten parameter variants were ensembled. That ensemble reached 0.8803 private AUC; a broader ensemble reached 0.8816 but was not selected for the final submission.

Unlabeled audio intervals from example_test_audio and BIRDCLEF 2020 served as noise and as an additional nocall class. Three mel spectrograms with different window sizes were stacked to form the model's three input channels, although this choice was not compared against duplicated channels. Heavy microscopy-specific augmentation and cross-entropy plus soft Dice losses supported training on a small dataset. Averaged masks underwent watershed processing, followed by LightGBM models that selected candidate separations and removed poor instances using predicted IoU. External microscopy datasets and flip/rotation test-time augmentation were also included.

The solution extracted three-hop subgraphs around configurable nodes and removed duplicate configurations. Separate models for each subtype used three SAGEConv layers with normalization and residual additions from the initial node embedding. Listwise loss converged faster and performed better than pairwise loss in the author's experiments. Using the provided training and validation splits, the approach achieved public and private scores of 0.684 and 0.688.

The pipeline filtered and downsampled transit signals, smoothed across wavelengths, and extracted and flipped the transit portion. It optimized a baseline and molecular concentrations against the observed signal using molecular spectra from ExoMol. Post-processing blended the first wavelength prediction with the remaining wavelengths, while wavelength-specific uncertainty estimates came from training RMSE and were clipped around their mean.

solution_title: Entropy-Weighted Majority Voting with gpt-oss-120b for AIMO3

It does not describe a reproducible final pipeline. The author congratulates the winners and saves several public notebooks for future reference.

solution_title: Detoxify Baseline ended up in the silver zone!
solution_summary: The post reports a Detoxify model achieving a private leaderboard score of 0.80857. It links a notebook describing offline use of the model. No additional training, feature engineering, or ensemble details are provided.

The author combined frequency encoding, out-of-fold target encoding, and quantile binning with several tabular models. XGBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM, and RealMLP variants used different feature subsets to diversify predictions. Rank-based hill climbing selected blend weights from approximately 10–15 models. The final ensemble achieved 0.95574 CV and 0.95532 on the private leaderboard, with CV-to-leaderboard alignment identified as a major concern.

The solution extended two public BERT pipelines with large models, concatenated representations from the last eight layers, and combined cased and uncased embeddings. Ten-fold cross-validation and candidate–pronoun product features improved results, alongside tuning the neural prediction heads. Four architecture variants were combined using LightGBM and Lasso, with LightGBM achieving CV 0.3059 and leaderboard loss 0.2047. Fine-tuning, label correction, ELMo, and a Siamese network did not work in the author's experiments.

The solution ensembled NFNet/CaiT and EfficientNetV2m pipelines for study classification, with NIH pretraining improving validation and leaderboard performance. Diversity came from preprocessing, architectures, augmentations, and training with BCE or CE loss; a segmentation auxiliary head was used in the EfficientNet pipeline. Image-level none predictions combined three sources, while opacity detection ensembled YOLOv5, YOLOX, and EfficientDet D5. The final ensemble achieved 0.636 CV, 0.645 public leaderboard, and 0.634 private leaderboard scores.

solution_summary: The team's component used detected backfin images to train two EfficientNet-B7 embedding models at 512×512 resolution, one with ArcFace and the other with CurricularFace and a BN neck. Training covered three folds of a random ten-fold split and included test-set pseudo-labels from an ensemble. Individually normalized backfin and body embeddings were concatenated for nearest-neighbor retrieval, with Bayesian optimization used to tune embedding weights and new_id replacement applied afterward. The embedding ensemble achieved about 0.930 local cross-validation performance.

solution_title: 5th Place Solution | Imputation Without Any Imputers
solution_summary: The author imputed nearly all features except x_e_out using relationships found in the original dataset, with closest-value matching when synthetic noise prevented exact matches. Engineered features described cylinder geometry and combinations intended to cancel physical units. Models used different feature subsets and estimators, with ridge regression fitting ensemble weights including an intercept and negative coefficients. Original data supplemented training but was excluded from validation, while Optuna tuned gradient boosting models.

The solution trains a single CatBoost model on the competition training data combined with the original training data, removing duplicate rows and identifier columns. Product ID is retained as a categorical feature, which the author identifies as a major improvement. Optuna and Wandb support hyperparameter sweeps, and a fast 80/20 validation split determines the iteration count for full-data training. CPU training was more accurate than GPU training, and the final results were 0.98125 locally and 0.98426 on the private leaderboard.
compute: CPU training; hardware model and training time unspecified.

solution_title: Read the Scorer, Not the Model: Engineering for the Guardrail You Can't See
solution_summary: The solution analyzed the competition guardrails and focused on confused-deputy findings expected to survive both content and provenance defenses. A local harness using the competition models measured whether candidates fired and how much replay time they consumed. Incremental budget-aware filling and model-specific template selection raised the specialist's public score from 10.815 to 20.775. The author retained separate confused-deputy and exfiltration specialists; the former transferred unchanged to private evaluation, while every exfiltration submission scored zero.
compute: Measured gpt-oss candidate latency of 1.2 seconds with injection versus 4.3 seconds plain; Gemma measured 1.45 seconds plain versus 1.9 seconds injected.

solution_summary: The final ensemble combined EfficientNet, SE-ResNeXt, ResNeSt, and a GeM-equipped EfficientNet using hard voting. Training used sixteen 512×512 tiles from the middle resolution layer, with tissue distributed evenly across tiles and scale changes providing augmentation. Synchronized batch normalization was particularly important for larger models. O2U-Net noise filtering was excluded because it did not help the public leaderboard, although retrospective private results improved for Radboud data.

The team extended a public DeepSeek-math notebook with asynchronous vLLM inference to increase the number of sampled solutions. They generated both code and text answers, then asked the model to solve a multiple-choice question containing the five most frequent candidates and combined that result with original response counts. Parsing fixes and explicit code-error feedback improved robustness. AIME83-86 was chosen for validation, while a problem-type classifier and automatic code-formatting ideas were not adopted.

The selected submission uses L2-regularized logistic regression to stack clipped probability logits from 99 diverse base models, averaging test predictions over five seeds. Tree ensembles and MLPs supplied strong standalone predictions, while weaker sequence, graph, kernel, and factorization models contributed complementary rankings. Adding original F1-strategy data was the most reliable feature-development gain, and the final predictions received no post-processing. The stack achieved 0.95536 OOF AUC; a post-deadline rank blend of stronger candidates reached 0.95505 private AUC.

solution_title: rm -rf * Six Days Before Deadline — Then... Climbed Back to the Edge of Gold
solution_summary: The author built an automated search system in which coding agents competed to improve ONNX solutions across 400 tasks. Agents shared incumbent solutions and notes, while an advisor challenged premature claims of optimality with simple questions. Human-written task rules encouraged architectural rewrites, and validation gates screened indexing errors, duplicates, and runtime failures. The system generated 330,924 candidates over three weeks and achieved a final score of 7994.76, with additional validated improvements left unsubmitted.
compute: 21-day campaign; 64 concurrent coding agents at peak; remote compute VM with unspecified hardware.

solution_title: [3rd place] All Medalists Who BC'd on Our Records MUST Vote!
solution_summary: The solution used a 10.4M-parameter Transformer policy initialized through behavior cloning from strong teams' public replays and improved with self-play PPO. Stable learning required critic pre-warming, per-decision probability-ratio clipping, and a separate antisymmetric critic, with terminal win/loss as the reward. League training and promotion gates selected stronger generations, while paired games on verified fast engines guided decisions. Inference rules repaired ineffective actions and handled late-game melon purchases, increasing the reported gen70 win rate from 74.2% to 87.8%.
compute: Up to 23 A100s; 20.1B training positions across about 21M games and 1,883 generations; final run about 360M steps.

solution_title: 10th Place Solution for the Stanford Ribonanza RNA Folding Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined symmetric 1D convolution and transformer layers without positional encoding, training both sequence-only models and models with CapR and per-nucleotide BPP summaries. A custom uncertainty-aware MAE loss weighted prediction errors using a normal-distribution potential derived from measurement uncertainty, improving convergence and smoothness. Sigmoid output constraints and one-hot nucleotide inputs also helped. The final mixed ensemble favored sequence-only predictions with 5:3 weights to reduce dependence on structural features whose generalization the author distrusted.

solution_title: 27th solution, Swin transformer. Simple and Lucky.
solution_summary: The solution used a pretrained Swin Large model with 384-pixel inputs trained across ten folds. Image features were concatenated with a learned 256-dimensional representation of 12 auxiliary features before a linear prediction head. Training used four epochs per fold, AdamW, cosine scheduling, gradient clipping and BCEWithLogitsLoss. The reported scores were 16.98523 privately and 17.83676 publicly, and the author did not ensemble the model with a separately trained efficient model.

solution_title: LB 58th/PB 152th Place solution. Mainly about "Bert replication[SingleLB.847]"
solution_summary: The final submission used static weighted blending of four sensor-sequence models, including a BERT replication and several recurrent architectures. The strongest single model improved through IMU time stretching, copying gesture tails, and removing two subjects with abnormal device wearing. It used 10-fold stratified group validation and achieved an overall out-of-fold HF1 of about 0.8397 and a public leaderboard score of 0.847. The post focuses on these improvements rather than detailing every model in the ensemble.

The author trained RoBERTa and DeBERTa models on Jigsaw2018, Jigsaw2019, and Ruddit data. For the two Jigsaw datasets, their multi-label probabilities became inputs to linear severity models fitted on competition validation data, with weights optimized by genetic algorithms. Model selection emphasized validation performance because the public leaderboard appeared misleading. The final weighted rank average combined 15 models and achieved a private score of 0.8139.

The author shares a single XLM-R model trained with pseudo-labels and knowledge distillation. It scored 0.9475 on the leaderboard and 0.9487 after applying another competitor's hardcoded multipliers. The team struggled to ensemble effectively and felt that heavy reliance on pseudo-labels, compounded by distillation, made blending harder.

solution_title: Credit where credit's due: Joe Malicki on placing third in 'Give Me Some Credit'
solution_summary: The final solution averaged gradient boosted trees trained with a 50/50 class balance and random forests trained with a 10/90 balance. Domain knowledge drove features involving debt, disposable income, age, debt-to-income thresholds, and round income amounts. Unusual delinquency codes and debt-to-income values for missing-income records were important data observations. Logistic regression stacking on a small holdout underperformed selecting the best models, and private test results agreed more closely with local evaluations than with public scores.

solution_title: 7th Place Solution — Way Too Many Models, One Simple Stack
solution_summary: The primary solution combined 556 verified local and public prediction streams using six cross-fitted, regularized logistic regressions on rank-normalized predictions. Fixed ten-fold validation and outer-fold ensemble fitting guarded against optimistic blend evaluation. Exact-value target encoding captured synthetic-generator artifacts, while model diversity and negative residual corrections supplied smaller gains. The strict primary achieved 0.97087888 OOF AUC, while a separately selected Gaussian-copula hedge achieved the better private score of 0.97112.
compute: GPU used to refit the final clean 556-stream C-bag.

solution_summary: This repository overview identifies the author's landmark retrieval competition solution but provides little methodological detail in the text. Its download scripts are forked from anokas's image-downloader kernel. It also includes scripts for DELF extraction and verification. No training setup or quantitative retrieval results are described.

solution_title: Building an Automation factory with different AI models
solution_summary: The author used several AI assistants to understand transformation rules, implement experiments, and review failures. The main technical observation was that changing internal representations mattered more than reducing graph node counts. Public solutions served as starting points for further optimization, but the post provides no detailed final pipeline or numerical results.

The team selected an early AutoGluon submission that also succeeded in the AutoML Grand Prix portion of the competition. Their third submission tied their fourth submission on the private leaderboard while being substantially simpler. The selected approach avoided the post-hoc ensembling described in their original writeup. The post suggests that improving the best default configuration was difficult, potentially because the synthetic data was already largely solved apart from injected noise.

The team optimized a public TF-IDF ensemble for runtime using the DAIGT v2 training dataset. They removed LightGBM and multinomial naive Bayes, reduced n-grams from lengths 3–5 to 3–4, and cut CatBoost training to ten iterations with Bayesian parameter tuning. These changes reduced runtime from over two hours to eight minutes while retaining public AUC above 0.956. Adding an unsupervised clustering blend improved the public score by roughly 0.0015 but hurt the private score, and code cleanup saved another twenty seconds.
compute: Runtime reduced from over 2 hours to 8 minutes; clustering added 60 seconds and code cleanup saved roughly 20 seconds.

solution_summary: The post explains a scorecard for tracking leaderboard movement and comparing teams over time. It defines score differences, distance to the leader, movement indicators, and a simple extrapolation of future leaderboard scores. It also links to notebooks analyzing top submissions and daily predictions.

The pipeline combined template-based modeling, DRfold2 predictions for short RNA, and Protenix diffusion predictions. Sequence identity determined whether three of the five prediction slots were reserved for templates, while Kabsch RMSD and farthest point sampling selected structurally diverse alternatives. Long sequences were processed in overlapping chunks, aligned and blended before applying physical constraints. The best private and public scores were 0.447 and 0.433.

solution_summary: The final approach used Chemprop directed message-passing networks with selected external polymer data, standardized targets, and auxiliary RadonPy prediction tasks. Rare elements were mapped to more common analogues, and exhaustive dimerization was retained despite mixed validation results. Hyperparameter search and averaging nine models across data splits and weight initializations produced public/private scores of 0.062/0.088. Post-competition experiments corrected a training–inference cyclization mismatch and explored a Tg Fahrenheit transformation, yielding further improvements.

The final solution blended modified versions of three public kernels, with SchNet receiving by far the largest weight. The main SchNet changes were separate models for each coupling type and increased batch sizes, often using 16 samples. Under time constraints, the author stopped generating out-of-fold predictions and guided later blending decisions using leaderboard scores. The best individual SchNet scored -1.971, while the final blend scored -2.21819 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Eight SchNet models, each taking 6–8 hours for 60–90 epochs on Kaggle GPUs; 99% of computing used Kaggle Kernels.

solution_summary: The final approach ensembled large pretrained language models with an attention head and an SVR component. Ensemble-generated pseudo-labels on cleaned external summaries and Wikipedia abstracts provided the largest improvement. Selecting three useful pseudo-labeled datasets and adding model and fold diversity helped achieve a public score of 0.450. Iterative pseudo-labeling, classification, added noise, and interval mean matching did not improve the final approach.

solution_title: Unselected top scored simple Kmeans solution
solution_summary: The author describes a simple k-means clustering approach. Toxicity severity was scored using Euclidean distance from the non-toxic cluster centroid. The approach achieved 0.818 on the private leaderboard, with no further pipeline details provided.

The proposed pipeline encodes categorical variables, removes features with low mutual information, and denoises inputs with a denoising autoencoder. It then splits the data for validation, tunes gradient boosting models with Optuna, and combines them using VotingRegressor. The author suspects information leakage because preprocessing precedes the validation split and asks for feedback. No performance results are reported.

The best solution ensembled seven full-data-trained DeBERTa models to increase model diversity within the inference budget. Models varied in pretrained checkpoint, input construction, pooling, freezing, layerwise training settings, and auxiliary loss. Increasing inference sequence lengths improved cross-validation and public scores, though its private benefit was limited. A simple mean ensemble selected with hill climbing achieved CV 0.46394 and private score 0.45515, while GBDT postprocessing was excluded from the best submission.

solution_title: 5th place solution: Llama 2 70B meets Sparse & Dense Retrievals from Own parsed wikipedia dataset
solution_summary: The solution combined BM25 and two dense Wikipedia retrievers with fine-tuned Mistral 7B and Llama-2 70B models. Custom Wikipedia parsing preserved numeric and mathematical content, while held-out question sets guided development. Quantized layer-by-layer inference and shared-prefix choice-order augmentation made the large model practical within notebook limits. A confidence-based three-stage pipeline achieved 0.926 private and 0.928 public scores.
compute: Kaggle notebook inference used approximately 6GB GPU memory; Wikipedia indexing took several hours, and 200 multithreaded searches took approximately 2 minutes.

solution_summary: The final retrieval system concatenated 512-dimensional descriptors from four models into a 2048-dimensional representation. It combined three GeM CNN models with a DELG model, trained on the clean training set with strong image augmentation. CosFace, focal loss, label smoothing, and warm-up cosine scheduling supported training, while validation used global average precision on sampled index images. The ensemble achieved public and private scores of 0.36644 and 0.32878, with an inference kernel runtime of 8 hours 20 minutes.
compute: Inference kernel runtime: 8 hours 20 minutes

solution_title: 45th Place | What I have learnt through TPS- Sep 2021
solution_summary: The approach addressed missing values with mean imputation and standardized the features, saving the processed data to avoid repeated work. Stratified cross-validation worked best, with two folds used for quick screening and ten folds for stronger candidates. LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost predictions were ensembled using weighted averages and powered submissions. GPU availability and slow CPU runs influenced the experimentation workflow.

solution_summary: The solution handled TMA images with center cropping and used a thumbnail segmentation model to locate a cancerous region in each WSI. Sixteen classifiers from four architecture families predicted six sigmoid scores, including a non-cancerous class, and their outputs were combined by median averaging. Regenerating thumbnails for slides containing multiple adjacent slices significantly improved performance. A single classifier paired with the segmentation model scored 0.49 publicly and 0.55 privately, and no external data was used.
compute: 2x T4 GPUs, with models divided between GPUs for memory efficiency.

solution_title: [40th place] Boltzmann Ensemble: A solution from statistical thermodynamics
solution_summary: The author combined shared notebook predictions using exponentially decaying weights based on public leaderboard error. Each model received weight exp(b*(S-x)), so stronger models contributed more, with b as the single meaningful tuning parameter. The best value of b changed substantially during the competition. The approach offered simple weight tuning but did not account for model correlation or allow negative weights.

The submitted solution was a single U-Net with a timm-resnest26d backbone, using 512×512 ash-color images and only the target frame. It used five folds, included validation data in training, and applied a 0.3 output threshold. An ensemble-code mistake prevented the intended multi-model blend from being submitted; the single model scored 0.688 in CV and 0.66321 privately. A corrected ensemble would have scored 0.67366 privately, while nine-channel temporal inputs did not work.

solution_title: 1st place solution: Bayesian Inference, of course
solution_summary: The solution converted raw sensor frames into wavelength-dependent signals, then used an iterative Bayesian model to estimate transit depths and uncertainties. Its prior combined physical transit modeling, polynomial drift, Gaussian noise, and a transit-spectrum representation using both Gaussian processes and PCA. Grid search and BFGS initialized the nonlinear inference, with fallback fits for suspicious signals. A 12-parameter post-hoc calibration was essential, with removing it reducing the private score by 0.152.
compute: Final submission used 8 Bayesian solver iterations; released code uses 4 to fit training and inference within the 9-hour submission limit, costing 0.001 score.

solution_title: Metamorphic contract tests for authorization in tool-using agents
solution_summary: The author built a deterministic, model-free contract audit of the public guardrail and scoring predicates in SDK 3.1.2. Its 174 schema-valid cases test field selection, authorization semantics, provenance windows, and path normalization. The audit found 27 authorization-semantic false negatives, while distinguishing reachable failures from cases blocked before scoring. Pinned sources and canonical JSON support reproducible regression testing, but the study does not demonstrate improved attack-search performance.
compute: CPU-only, internet-disabled validation run; no model or tool handler invoked.

solution_summary: The author used a two-stage pipeline combining YOLO detection ensembles with EfficientNet-based U-Net segmentation. Dataset2 detection boxes were selectively replaced by larger predictions from models trained on dataset1 to address annotation-size differences. Detection combined ten models with sixteen test-time augmentations through weighted box fusion, while segmentation used four models without TTA. Two final submissions differed in box dilation and other settings; the version without dilation achieved a private score of 0.560.

solution_title: 113th place solution - some notes from the kaggle freshman
solution_summary: The solution used EfficientNet-B5 with 456 by 456 images and five-class classification. Preprocessing cropped gray borders, replicated the green channel, and applied CLAHE, followed by geometric and color augmentation. One model trained from scratch on 2019 data, while another pretrained on 2019 data plus non-normal 2015 examples before fine-tuning on 2019 data. Five-view test-time augmentation and averaging the two models improved the reported leaderboard score from 0.808 and 0.798 individually to 0.817.

The solution combined EfficientNet-b3 cell classifiers with an EfficientNet-b7 image classifier, HPA segmentation, and Gridify and Gapmask inference. Gaussian-noise label smoothing, mixup, public training data, and deep supervision substantially improved the cell models. Inference used eight-way test-time augmentation, prediction filtering, and a 0.7/0.3 blend of cell and image predictions, with blending adding about 0.04 mAP. The final configuration using the original HPA Segmentator achieved 0.5771 public and 0.5499 private scores.

The solution ensembled multilingual question-answering models with different tokenizers by mapping token logits to characters and averaging them equally. Several models benefited from SQuAD 2.0 fine-tuning before training on chaii, MLQA, and XQuAD. A non-zero Jaccard percentage criterion stabilized checkpoint selection, while punctuation and year-extraction rules corrected answer spans. The two final submissions scored 0.767 and 0.777 privately, and a subsequently identified combination scored 0.784.
compute: GPU resources provided by NYU Shanghai faculty; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution ensembles a custom-tokenizer TF-IDF approach with LightGBM using DeBERTa-v3-base predictions and handcrafted text features. It uses DAIGT-v2 data, with readability, sentence, paragraph, punctuation, part-of-speech, and vocabulary statistics. Test-only tokenizer training, a roughly 120,000-token vocabulary, spelling correction, log-loss optimization, and post-processing helped. Mean-pooled DeBERTa features and train-plus-test tokenizer training did not help, while LightAutoML frequently exceeded submission time limits.

The solution used drift-removed, Kalman-filtered signals and discarded approximately 4% of training data as excessively noisy. WaveNet models were trained with macro-F1 early stopping and rollback to earlier weights. A Monte Carlo-inspired ensemble normally rounded the median prediction. For the group with the highest average number of open channels, it instead selected the maximum prediction to compensate for systematic underprediction.

For the first three weeks, the author manually forecast daily log increments for each location and applied daily decay to reflect slowing growth. The final week used XGBoost to predict next-day log increments from lagged and difference features for cases and fatalities, plus continent. Training emphasized recent observations, excluded the earliest data, and rounded features, while validation used the last seven days. The final forecasts applied a smaller daily decay, and adjustments based on news about testing expansion had previously proved unhelpful.

solution_title: 288th / 4,020 (top 7%): what 22 leaderboard probes taught us about this metric
solution_summary: The final solution forked the public x138 cell-tracking pipeline and adjusted re-admission and detection or division-veto thresholds. Rebasing onto this stronger pipeline mattered more than extensive tuning of the older baseline, yielding a best private score of 0.921. Their own temporal 3D U-Net and Hungarian linker underperformed because detector precision was the bottleneck. Metric audits and experiments showed that train-movie validation was in-sample for the public models and that small public-score differences were unreliable guides to private performance.
compute: Shared GPU quota of 30 hours per week; GPU model unspecified.

solution_summary: The author trained diverse boosting and neural models using five preprocessing pipelines, adding the original dataset to training in three pipelines while validating only on competition data. AutoGluon ensembled out-of-fold predictions from 52 models and achieved 0.970887 CV, 0.97329 public, and 0.96900 private scores after 24 hours of training. Another submission matched the private score through ridge and logistic regression stacking followed by weighted averaging. Brute-force model selection outperformed RFECV for this alternative ensemble.

solution_summary: The final submission voted across three rexnet_200 models, one densenet161, and one resnest50d. The classifier pipeline converted five-second clips into three-channel log-mel inputs and used several audio augmentations, including modified mixup. Checkpoints were selected by soundscape F1, and largely unspecified post-processing improved the leaderboard score from 0.65 to 0.70. A separate ResNet18 sound-event detection approach with site-specific data and generated nocall examples was tried but excluded from the final submission.

solution_title: 96th Place Solution for the ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions Competition
solution_summary: The final approach used CatBoost with ten stratified folds and averaged predictions from one model per fold. It applied no postprocessing and did not use special splitting based on the Greek metadata. Small changes to a public baseline's splits and hyperparameters improved cross-validation and public scores slightly, but worsened the private score slightly. A separate neural network experiment optimized a custom implementation of the competition metric that the author believed was incorrect.

The solution used log-mel spectrograms with a previous year's architecture modified to use EfficientNet B0, B1, and B2 backbones. Its most stable training recipe pretrained on the first 15 seconds of earlier BirdCLEF recordings, excluding classes present in 2024, then trained the final models on the first 5 seconds of 2024 recordings. The pipeline included Mixup V2, while heavy augmentation improved cross-validation but hurt leaderboard performance. The best single B2 model scored 0.68 public and 0.67 private, and the final six-model ensemble scored 0.70 public and 0.67 private before postprocessing, which provided a slight further improvement.

solution_title: 2nd Place. Journey Down the Rabbit Hole of Pseudo Labels
solution_summary: The final ensemble combined two EfficientNetV2-S pipelines and one ECA-NFNet-L0 pipeline operating on five-second spectrogram segments. Large-scale Xeno-Canto pretraining and iterative soft pseudo-labeling of soundscapes delivered the largest improvements. Balanced sampling, minority-class upsampling, and author-grouped validation supported training, although small validation gains correlated poorly with public scores. File-level probability scaling improved predictions, and the final submission omitted overlapping-window TTA. The strongest individual model reached 0.917 public and 0.91 private AUC.

solution_summary: The main pipeline generated one Protenix structure per target and used it to condition RNAPro refinement with frozen RibonanzaNet2 embeddings. Alignment-based template modeling supplied backup structures, while final prediction slots were filled by RNAPro outputs first and Protenix/TBM fallbacks afterward. Restricting Protenix to one sample made refinement feasible within the runtime budget, improving the private score from 0.410 for standalone Protenix to 0.464. A second selected notebook used multi-seed Protenix predictions and consistency-based structural selection.

solution_title: From Production Optimization to Competitive Farming: My Kaggriculture Solution
solution_summary: The agent combined a replay-derived production schedule with bounded crop and livestock substitutions and forecast-guided selling. A small gradient-boosted model predicted rival sales, while rules preserved production reserves, feasible procurement, and worker execution. Optimizing terminal cash difference exposed market-timing gains that production totals alone missed. Livestock selection added 1,770 mean cash difference across 18 recorded-opponent scenarios, and an online snapshot reported 57.84% wins over 925 completed games.

The final solution averaged four neural models: two shallow MLP variants, a residual-style multihead network with cluster embeddings, and TabNet. Preprocessing combined quantile transforms, PCA, statistical features, clustering, and feature selection, with recursive selection based on MLP permutation importance providing a substantial CV improvement. Training used multilabel-stratified folds, seed and split bagging, label smoothing, and nonscored-target pretraining for one MLP. Pseudo-labeling gave a small improvement, while drug-group validation and several augmentation approaches were unsuccessful.

The final system retained an unchanged MXFP4 gpt-oss-120b model and the public-consensus inference recipe. Eight parallel Harmony rollouts used stateful Python kernels, stopped when four answers agreed, and selected answers through entropy-weighted voting. It scored 42/50 publicly and 39.5/50 privately. The main contribution was a reproducibility package and negative-results study: none of sixteen tested departures produced a detectable improvement.
models_pretrained: ["unsloth/gpt-oss-120b MXFP4", "huikang AIMO2 LoRA adapter", "EAGLE-3 draft head"]

solution_summary: The solution concentrated on retrieval, combining five routes over Wikipedia corpora with two DeBERTa models for multiple-choice answering. Sentence encoders trained with SimCSE were strengthened by mining incorrect high-ranking results as hard negatives. Dense retrieval was complemented by TF-IDF and article reranking with BM25 or LightGBM to handle long documents. Sharded indexes reduced FAISS memory requirements, and sentence-model improvements added reported leaderboard gains of 0.015 and a further 0.005. The authors suspected the answer models contributed to overfitting.

solution_summary: The women's model extended a logistic regression baseline with aggregate scoring features and achieved a Brier score of about 0.160. The men's approach combined XGBoost with external ratings, seasonal ranking changes, home/away statistics, and aggregate box scores. Ensembling XGBoost with logistic regression produced a more satisfactory prediction distribution than scaling or risk-oriented features, yielding a men's Brier score of about 0.195. Validation covered multiple seasons, although the final ensemble had a lower overall CV score than XGBoost alone.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution - How to properly utilise noisy annotations
solution_summary: The solution combined five MMDetection models spanning ViT-Adapter, CBNetV2, and DetectoRS architectures. Its strongest improvement came from training COCO-initialized models on noisy dataset 2 before fine-tuning on clean dataset 1 with stronger augmentation and larger images. Some final models also used dataset 3 pseudo labels, although these did not improve leaderboard scores. Flip and multiscale inference, weighted box fusion, and morphological mask cleanup completed the ensemble, with cleanup adding about 0.005.

solution_title: [22nd Place] Behavior Cloning and PPO with Diverse Opponents
solution_summary: The solution used separate opening and later-game Transformer policies initialized with behavior cloning, followed by PPO training for the strategic phase. Pre-generated day-12 states reduced rollout cost, while diverse opponents and evaluation gates limited specialization and regression. A parallel actor predicted compound actions, and a sequential executor enforced feasibility alongside deterministic purchase and endgame corrections. The final PPO-initialized policy fine-tuned on strong-player replays outperformed continued PPO training.

solution_title: 4th place solution - Llama3 🦙 70B is all you need
solution_summary: The main submission combined ten DeBERTa V3 Large models trained with focal loss and BiLSTM/GRU heads across two five-fold configurations. Whitespace replacement and Unicode normalization were especially important for consistent token alignment, while inference used substantially longer sequences than training. LLM-generated examples, particularly those from Llama 3 70B Instruct, and paraphrased false positives strengthened the training data. The team tuned ensemble weights and thresholds and retained simple name-filtering rules after more elaborate validators failed to help.
