solution_title: Silver - LB 0.770 - Two Lines of Code!
solution_summary: The solution improved a public CTC-based fingerspelling notebook by retaining half of the frames with missing hands during preprocessing and inference. It increased the frame length to 216 and trained for 200 epochs, with a larger batch size and proportionally increased learning rate for speed. Random temporal resizing helped the model handle different signing speeds and frame rates. Replacing predictions shorter than three characters with a constant baseline added another improvement, bringing the reported leaderboard score to about 0.770.

The post thanks the organizers and congratulates the winners. The author reports finding 18 flags and links to a notebook containing solutions and unsuccessful attempts. They ask how close their attempt at the Inversion flag was, but provide no methods in the post itself.

The solution stacked CatBoost models and SAINT-like Transformers with a CatBoost meta-model. Its 160 engineered features described question statistics, user performance histories, timing, Word2vec similarities, and question-transition graphs. The stacker used eight base-model predictions and the 75 most important engineered features, with nine-fold validation and three-seed averaging. Although the Transformers had weaker standalone validation results, they improved the stack, which achieved 0.810 CV and 0.809 on the private leaderboard.

The pipeline combined R preprocessing and conference-strength offsets with DataRobot time-aware feature engineering and AutoML, followed by probability smoothing in R. Separate men's and women's models predicted both win probabilities and point margins, with elastic net models performing well. Rolling rankings and possession-normalized box-score differentials captured season-long strength and recent form, while mirrored neutral-site games reduced home-away asymmetry. A generalized additive model used predicted margins to smooth win probabilities. The final private score was 0.17522, and an R replication produced outputs with correlation above 0.993 to the original submission.
compute: Published notebook pipeline designed to stay below the 30 GB RAM limit for non-paying accounts.

solution_summary: The team built a soft graph transformer that processed whole molecules, representing atoms, atom pairs, and higher-order structures as nodes. Distance-aware attention combined hierarchical chemical embeddings with Fourier-encoded physical quantities and specialized coupling heads. Small dropout and atom-removal cutout regularized training, while dihedral information and Coulomb-force features hurt generalization. A robust blend of 13 architecture variants achieved a private score of -3.245 without extra molecular datasets.
compute: Most models trained on 4x RTX2080 Ti systems; five such systems available during the month, plus six single V100s in the final week.

solution_title: First Kaggle Competition Experience (Team: rm-rf / | Private LB: 385)
solution_summary: The best submission blended a MobileNet from a public starter kernel with a ResNet-152 trained using fastai. Training progressively increased the fraction of data while decreasing image resolution, moving from 1% at 256 pixels to 20% at 64 pixels. Larger pretrained ResNets consistently improved performance in their experiments. The author identified experience with training and combining models as the main limitation.
compute: 20 Kaggle kernels, a GTX 1070-based laptop, and AWS p3 instances for experiments.

solution_summary: The final ensemble combined eight strong models, including LSTMs and two or three Transformers. Transformer models used a customized classification-regression loss with softmax class probabilities, while weighted sampling improved the LSTM models. An R/C-group median ensemble optimized through hill climbing improved over a simple median. Nearest-neighbor matching, LSTM stacking, and a Time2Vec front end did not yield usable improvements.
compute: TPU used for LSTM training.

solution_summary: The team modified EfficientNet-B4 with an intermediate attention mechanism and trained both end-to-end and Siamese variants. Five folder-based folds produced ten models in total. Training used single-face frames, appearance and compression augmentations, and Adam for at most 20,000 iterations. Inference sampled 72 frames per video, handled multiple faces using maximum scores, and averaged network and frame scores before applying sigmoid.

solution_title: 79th Place Solution: Distance Attention with Dijkstra's Algorithm
solution_summary: The solution combined distance attention and multihead attention with recurrent or WaveNet heads, alongside separate recurrent and graph convolutional models. Graph shortest paths, base-pair probabilities, alternate structures, and neighborhood aggregates supplied structural information. Signal-to-noise filtering and weighting controlled training quality, while five folds were assigned using ranked signal-to-noise values. An out-of-fold optimized weighted ensemble of all three model families achieved an updated final score of 0.35173.

solution_title: My Summary Notes on the 'ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions' Competition
solution_summary: The author presents strategic lessons about model selection under limited submissions, hidden test data, and substantial overfitting. They emphasize evaluating varied models and favoring approaches that generalize through regularization. For the final submissions, they selected one moderately performing approach and one more generalized approach, without identifying their model architectures. The observed public-to-private shakeup reinforced their conclusion that stronger generalization should have received more attention.

The post collects feature engineering ideas, XGBoost tuning guidance, and ensemble strategies without documenting a confirmed final pipeline. It emphasizes validation-driven feature selection and tuning gamma jointly with tree depth and other parameters. It also describes averaging powered predictions and discusses how model correlation affects that ensemble. A suggested XGBoost exercise targets a cross-validation score of at least 0.841, but no achieved final result is reported.

The author initially built a hill ensemble of over 200 models but did not submit it because of uncertainty about its leaderboard performance. During the final week, they switched to a single model whose architecture and training details are unspecified. That model scored 0.05697 on the public leaderboard and 0.05850 on the private leaderboard, close to the ensemble's private score of 0.05848.

The solution used LightGBM with five selected signal features and a target transformation motivated by the suspected test-distribution leak. Normalized time to failure was scaled by twice an estimated private-set mean, with two submissions using estimates of 6.3 and 5.9. Validation held out every pair of 15 complete earthquakes, excluding incomplete events. A separate experiment using a Siamese 1D CNN to model earthquake period and normalized time to failure did not succeed.

solution_title: [Chai Time] Sanyam explains top solutions from AI4Code
solution_summary: The post shares a YouTube video by init27 explaining published competition solutions. It recommends watching the video while waiting for the private leaderboard. The post itself provides no solution methodology or implementation details.

The team combined 15 custom 1D models with eight 2D models operating on CQT and CWT representations. Whitening with an average negative-sample PSD was crucial, and detector-specific branches with delayed feature fusion made the 1D models especially effective. Simulated-wave pretraining, soft pseudo-labeling, waveform mixup and extensive test-time augmentation improved performance. CMA-ES ensemble optimization with polynomial prediction features produced their best submission score of 0.8829.
compute: Best single 1D model trained in approximately 8 hours; some team members used JarvisLabs.ai GPU workstations.

solution_summary: The solution combined Mask R-CNN and Hybrid Task Cascade instance segmentation models trained at multiple image sizes. Predictions were matched through connected components of an IoU graph, then their masks and confidence scores were merged. Four-way test-time augmentation improved the metric by roughly 0.01–0.015, while a second-level mask-quality predictor added about 0.01. Dropping categories requiring unpredicted attributes produced a substantial gain; attempts to predict attributes did not improve results.
models_pretrained: ["Mask R-CNN X-101", "Hybrid Task Cascade X-101-64x4d-FPN with DCN"]

solution_summary: The author solved several capture-the-flag tasks using prior writeups, prompt injection, and semantic word search. Successful language-model attacks used multilingual requests, fabricated dialogue roles, and alternative wording to elicit flags. The semantle challenge was solved by narrowing the semantic topic and testing words from a Wikipedia page. Attempts involving adversarial images, IPv6 prompts, and pickle payloads did not obtain flags.
external_data: ["Wikipedia page for semantle word candidates", "Wikipedia granny image"]

solution_title: Winning Solution in 1 line of code !!
solution_summary: The post presents a training-free prediction rule that sorts test machines by AvSigVersion and assigns decreasing detection scores. It attributes the rule's effectiveness to a sharp decline in detection rates during the final days of the private test period, which the author says could not be inferred from training data. A diagnostic kernel either excludes those days from scoring or adjusts predictions to account for the decline. For one example submission, the reported private score rose from 0.636 to 0.758 with those days removed and to 0.749 with them adjusted.

solution_title: 3rd place solution of ALASKA2 Image Steganalysis
solution_summary: The solution combines CNNs operating on color images and DCT coefficients for image steganalysis. Its reproduction pipeline also trains an MLP using feature maps dumped from trained CNNs. JPEG quality and payload metadata are extracted during preparation. Training primarily used four NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs with 16GB memory each.
compute: Primarily four NVIDIA Tesla V100 16GB GPUs for training.

solution_summary: The pipeline detected helmets with YOLOv5x, estimated tracking-to-image homographies, and assigned player identities in two passes. Shape-context matching initialized the homography, while subsequent frames reused and refined earlier transforms with adaptive rejection of false detections. DeepSORT tracks then stabilized identities through voting and conflict resolution. Custom helmet detection improved the private score by 0.057 compared with replacing it with baseline detections.
compute: AWS SageMaker p3.8xlarge; detector trained for 20 epochs with batch size 16

solution_summary: The author used simulated annealing exclusively, emphasizing starting sentences, search control, and computational resources. For the fifth sample, randomly formed alphabetical blocks separated by repeated conjunctions enabled a perplexity of 28.5. The final neighborhood used word swaps and word relocation. Combining high-temperature exploration, reheating, and low-temperature refinement sustained progress.

solution_title: Awaiting private results. Results of the competition for me.
solution_summary: The author tried 2D, 2.5D, and 3D approaches but reported that predictions stayed near class frequencies. A later architecture compressed a 3D volume into a 2.5D representation before classification to reduce training time, using 256×256×256 inputs. Volumetric augmentation slowed training, and highlighting organ regions did not improve results. A subsequent segmentation-based pipeline encountered a submission scoring error, leaving the approach unsuccessful.
compute: TPU; augmentation substantially slowed processing.

solution_summary: The final efficient submission used a single-fold DeBERTa-v3-small model trained with pseudo labels and teacher distillation. Adversarial weight perturbation reduced overfitting, while an outlier-aware distillation loss and pretraining on pseudo-labeled FB1 data improved validation performance. ONNX optimization reduced inference time by about 30 seconds. The reported four-fold CV was approximately 0.449, with a private leaderboard score of 0.438798.
compute: ONNX optimization reduced runtime by around 30 seconds.

solution_summary: The final solution blends four LightGBM models and reports CV 0.41653, public score 0.85191, and private score 0.86777. Extensive light-curve features include grouped statistics, cross-passband color differences, rolling features, PCA, and out-of-fold redshift predictions. Optimizing class-dependent sample weights with GPyOpt reportedly improved the leaderboard score by 0.04. Classwise prediction scaling optimized with Nelder-Mead added a reported 0.03 improvement, with an additional rule boosting predictions above 0.76. Several alternatives, including neural time-series models, stacking, and Gaussian-process-derived features, did not improve results.

solution_title: #8 private 6 public approach- Simple ensemble and probing
solution_summary: The solution combined a heavily weighted GAM with a smaller blend of LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost models. Features captured calendar cycles, weekdays, holidays, GDP, and specific date windows. Tree models were tuned and blended with Optuna, with validation examined separately for January–March and April–December. Country-level adjustments, rounding, and adding one to selected submissions were guided by public leaderboard feedback.

The author explored adjacent-value differences, signal smoothing, and frequency-domain features before emphasizing links between training and test sequences. Linked training data supplied predictions for connected test sequences, while a random forest handled test groups without training links. The initial linking approach overfit the public data. Visual inspection and correction of links joining different surfaces improved reported public accuracy from 0.96 to 0.98 and private accuracy from 0.68 to 0.76.

The team combined four DeBERTa variants for discourse tagging, aligning predictions across different tokenizers through overlapping token groups. Topic-based validation and a held-out portion of out-of-fold predictions guided post-processing. Text boundary corrections, conservative optimization, stochastic weight averaging, and mean-teacher label filtering improved training. Final rules repaired tag sequences and extended extracted spans.
models_pretrained: ["DeBERTa v1 large and xlarge", "DeBERTa v2 xlarge", "DeBERTa v3 large"]

solution_summary: The solution combined string matching with two stages of spaCy 2 text classification. The first stage selected sentences mentioning datasets, while the second distinguished dataset names from organizations, locations, and other false positives. Training examples were expanded with dataset names and acronyms discovered through abbreviation detection and dataset-related keyword matching. The approach was designed for fast training and adaptation to unfamiliar publications, motivated by expected differences between public and private documents.

solution_title: 59th Place Solution (And My First Silver Medal)
solution_summary: The author combined XLM-RoBERTa variants, including a large model with additional masked language modeling, through a stacking pipeline. One submission averaged 12 prediction files comprising nine individual models and three blends. Blending that result with ExtraTrees predictions trained on validation data improved the private score from 0.9469 to 0.9471, while several experimental weighting schemes failed.
compute: Kaggle for MLM training; Google Colab TPU for XLM-RoBERTa training.

solution_summary: The answerer prioritized protocol rules and predefined keyword-question answers before falling back to Llama 3.1-8B-IT with retrieved Wikipedia context. The asker selected clear, independent questions using an expected candidate-reduction metric, while the guesser maintained soft keyword scores to tolerate inconsistent answers. Dataset construction produced 15,113 keywords and 521 questions, with tier-based priors and a separate Agent Alpha binary-search path. Wikipedia context improved the reported CV score from 17.1% to 31.4%.
external_data: ["Wikipedia context", "Discussion-shared keyword datasets", "Top participants' episode questions", "Offline Policy Questioner Agent shared datasets"]

solution_summary: The solution removed a fitted 50 Hz sine wave from each signal and aligned its phase before feeding all 800,000 samples into a 1D CNN. Twenty-five models trained on different 80/20 splits were combined using a small neural stacking model. Mean squared error and manually tuned class weights worked better than binary cross entropy. A final majority vote across the three signals in each measurement improved training MCC from about 0.70 to 0.72, and the final private leaderboard score was 0.65595.

solution_title: 24th Place Solution(detailed): multi-task Elastic Net ensemble & Optimized Post-Processing Approach
solution_summary: The team combined gradient boosting, AutoGluon, and pairwise ranking neural networks trained as regressors and classifiers. Feature engineering included score interactions, categorical combinations, clustering, race-specific features, and selected TF-IDF features. Regression predictions were stacked with multi-task Elastic Net, while classifier predictions guided race-specific post-processing optimized with Optuna. A weighted ensemble and selectively applied custom ranking networks produced a private score of 0.694, supporting their decision to prioritize cross-validation.

solution_title: [48th place solution] Multi-label K-Fold for CV Strategy
solution_summary: The solution combined engineered writing-process features with character TF-IDF and count features from reconstructed essays. Multilabel stratification used the score and selected correlated features to create more stable folds. Predictions from LightGBM trained across six seeds and ten folds were averaged, then blended with public Denselight predictions using weights of 0.65 and 0.35. The reported public and private scores were 0.576 and 0.567, while several neural models and feature-selection approaches did not work.

The post shares a script that blends submission CSV files from a directory. It independently min-max scales each submission's six toxicity prediction columns before averaging them. The active configuration uses equal weights, while an optional branch supports manually specified weights. The blended predictions are written to a new CSV, with no performance results reported.

The solution rendered each well's GR matching surface as an image and predicted the correct depth path. Expressing depth as residuals from a trajectory chord narrowed the prediction range and enabled finer vertical resolution, which was the largest improvement. Synthetic geology shifts and swaps with realistic noise diversified the small training set. A fixed-weight blend of four heatmap and detection models achieved 4.91 pooled five-fold CV and 6.411 private score.
compute: Two months of single-model development; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution combined finetuned transformer regressors with varied backbones, sequence lengths, and pooling methods. Repeated pseudo-labeling on previous Feedback competition data provided pretraining before finetuning on the competition labels. Experiments were compared using three-seed averages, followed by five-fold evaluation for promising changes. The final ensemble used target-specific, bounded weights optimized with Nelder–Mead; full-data models were blended with some fold models.
compute: Around two weeks working on the competition; approximately half spent on accuracy and half on efficiency.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled DeBERTa-v3-large token classifiers trained on competition data, public synthetic data, and newly generated PII examples. Generation used competition and mixed PII vocabularies with Qwen and Mistral models. A multilayer token classification architecture with weighted cross-entropy improved stability and reduced sensitivity to thresholds. The submitted result scored 0.96670, while a shared five-model ensemble reached 0.96816 without preprocessing, postprocessing, or threshold tuning.

The attacker adapts Carlini-Wagner-style optimization to generate transferable adversarial examples against an ensemble of six models. A hyperbolic-tangent parameterization keeps perturbations within the permitted epsilon interval without explicit clipping at each iteration. Nine iterations with a learning rate of 2.0 accommodate the competition's runtime limit, while experiments achieved roughly 95–100% attack success against included models. Median-filter-aware attacks were tested but excluded because they reduced speed and attack success within the available iterations.
compute: 11GB GPU memory, batch size 10 for six models; approximately 100s graph initialization and 50s checkpoint restoration on Google Compute Cloud; nine attack iterations within 300s.

solution_summary: The post announces a retrospective repository published more than six months after the competition. The author says they reviewed 481 training runs and 196 submissions and rebuilt the final solution as a package. It points readers to code and supporting tables covering validation, tiling, two heads, ensembling, and unsuccessful experiments, without explaining those methods in the post.

The author compared two rank-32 LoRA fine-tunes of a strong Kien adapter: preserving verified reasoning prefixes and training repairs, versus rewriting complete solutions. Solver-generated symbol-cipher traces were mixed with correct baseline replay traces and trained with completion-only loss. Neither method learned the missing digit-mapping search, but prefix preservation caused much less damage to the neighboring digit-operations task. The selected prefix-surgery model scored 0.85 privately despite weaker held-out performance than the baseline, so the author does not claim a reliable improvement.
compute: Trained on Modal; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The author shared a public repository for their Santander work. They reported trying amootone's feature management method, but provided no modeling or validation details in the post. The linked materials are in Japanese, and no scores or concrete findings are reported.

Two U-Net-style pipelines used ImageNet-pretrained SE-ResNeXt50 backbones, enhanced decoders, and deep supervision. Both used replication padding, SGD with cosine cycles, five-fold validation, and two selected snapshots per fold. Predictions were averaged and thresholded across the pipelines. Mosaic-based neighbor rules substantially improved the public leaderboard score but provided little private-score benefit, with one rule harming private performance.

The team generated Stable Diffusion training images from diverse external captions and a custom combinatorial prompt generator. Their strongest models used CLIP vision towers, with projection heads initialized by learning a mapping between CLIP text embeddings and the competition's MiniLM embeddings. Training generally used two epochs, layerwise learning-rate decay, minimal cropping augmentation, and gradient accumulation. The final ensemble combined several vision models with a small contribution from GIT image captioning; WiSE-FT improved individual models but did not help the ensemble.
external_data: ["Diffusion DB", "Conceptual Captions", "COCO image captions", "Flickr Image Captions", "jeinsong ChatGPT prompts"]

solution_summary: The pipeline first localized spinal findings with heatmap models, then classified coordinate-centered crops with a 2.5D CNN and recurrent architecture. Expanded Gaussian labels and external coordinate data improved localization, while modeling relationships among findings at the same spinal level improved classification. Training first without metric-specific weighting, then freezing the backbone and tuning the head with weighted and any loss, reduced overfitting. CutMix at probability 1.0 and an ensemble that propagated each detector's outputs separately through classification were particularly effective.

The solution combined roughly 1,300 NLP, question-frequency, and graph features in neural networks, LightGBM, and XGBoost models. About 15 base models were stacked with additional meta-features, improving cross-validation loss from approximately 0.185 for the best single model to 0.157. The final ensemble mixed stacked and base predictions with weights of 0.75 and 0.25, improving leaderboard performance despite hurting cross-validation. Predictions were also adjusted according to question frequency to address systematic differences between validation and leaderboard data.

The author built neural models using PCA-reduced inputs, selected original features, metadata, and neighborhood or donor/day aggregates. Validation explicitly tested generalization across days and donors, alongside a relaxed split that allowed more training data. Linear regression combined out-of-fold predictions after balancing donor/day groups, and the relaxed-split ensemble performed best among the selected submissions. PCA denoising and validation discipline mattered more than pseudo-labeling or transformer experiments, which were unsuccessful.
compute: Kaggle memory and disk constraints dominated implementation work; no hardware specified.

solution_title: Detecting Hard Problems by Answer Diversity
solution_summary: The solver ran gpt-oss-120B with parallel Python-enabled attempts and used answer diversity to detect difficult problems during inference. It selected answers by plurality on the default path and median-capped logprob weighting when more than four distinct answers appeared without a 40% vote share. A fine-tuned problem classifier supplied category-specific mathematical hints at confidence of at least 0.90. The public score increased from 36/50 to 39/50 after adding routed hints, although concurrent changes and missing paired ablations prevent clean attribution.
compute: Single NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU; 5-hour limit per notebook; classifier on CPU.

solution_summary: The solution generated patent-search token pairs from CPC codes, titles, abstracts, and detailed descriptions associated with each target row. It retained pairs that discriminated target patents from other test patents and the broader patent collection. Pairs sharing tokens were merged to reduce query token counts. Calculating all patent metadata resolved the author's validation difficulties, and the linked notebook reported a leaderboard score of 0.83.

The author's best submission used Sentence-BERT embeddings as inputs to an SVR model, achieving a leaderboard score of 0.612. A separate experiment augmented competition texts with CBT training data and fine-tuned forward and backward AWD-LSTM language models using ULMFiT. Regression heads from these models were ensembled to pseudo-label CBT texts, which supported another training iteration. Both approaches were considered robust, but time constraints prevented further pseudo-labeling cycles.

The team built transformer models with concatenated CLS embeddings and separate question and answer modeling. Host and category embeddings, statistical features, and text cleaning improved performance. Resetting predictions to 0 and 1 reportedly added at least 0.05 on the leaderboard. Combining models improved validation and leaderboard scores by about 0.02; an unselected weighted blend achieved a private score of 0.42787.

The solution combined neural networks with fixed and trainable frontends, with architecture choices providing the largest gains. Bandpass filtering and selected waveform augmentations helped, whereas whitening did not. Retraining with soft pseudo-labels improved AUC by about 0.001, with a further benefit from label smoothing. Cross-validated ridge stacking and greedy model selection produced a 20-model ensemble with 0.88283 CV AUC and 0.8829 private leaderboard AUC.

The final solution combined predictions from numerous public notebooks through a manually tuned cascade of weighted blends, including negative weights. Each stage was adjusted using public leaderboard feedback, with little original feature engineering or model development. Final predictions were scaled, shifted slightly toward zero, and clipped, achieving 0.41521 public and 0.42192 private scores. A separate stacking submission used five-fold grouped cross-validation and achieved 0.42711 privately, performing worse than the leaderboard-tuned cascade.

solution_title: Avito Duplicate Ads Detection, Winners' Interview: 1st Place Team, Devil Team | Stanislav Semenov & Dmitrii Tsybulevskii
solution_summary: The solution relied on extensive text, image, and metadata feature engineering with XGBoost as its only learning method. Text similarities, learned word embeddings, local image descriptors, and pretrained neural image features described each advertisement pair. The final predictions averaged XGBoost models trained with different random seeds. Feature extraction took three to four days and model training took one to two weeks.
compute: Feature extraction: 3–4 days; model training: 1–2 weeks.

solution_title: 8th place solution: matched filter and CNN
solution_summary: The team combined a PyFstat matched-filter search with CNNs trained for stationary and non-stationary noise. High-confidence matched-filter detections supplied approximately 1,700 positive pseudo-labels, while synthetic mixtures expanded the small training set. The final scoring rule placed matched-filter detections above the remaining samples, which were ordered using CNN scores. Matched filtering alone achieved AUC 0.8406 on 600 training samples but only 0.764 privately and 0.760 publicly, motivating the combination.

The solution combined pretrained EfficientNet-B7 Noisy Student and ViT Base16 models using only competition data. Five-fold stratified validation and out-of-fold accuracy guided selection, with bi-tempered logistic loss, label smoothing, and model-specific augmentation. Standard four-pass test-time augmentation stabilized predictions. An equally weighted blend outperformed the individual models and the tested weighted blend, reaching 0.901 CV accuracy and 0.900 private leaderboard accuracy.

solution_title: 135th place - Adding item amount check and Prefix Tree+Binning based text processing
solution_summary: The approach combined RAPIDS nearest-neighbor search on TF-IDF text features with an EfficientNet and NFNet image ensemble using ArcFace. Text processing repaired split words, normalized similar misspellings, and cleaned strings. Quantity detection helped reject products with matching names but different sizes or quantities. Identical titles or perceptual hashes added matches, while Jaccard filtering refined text matches.

The author's best solution used XGBoost. They tried several XGBoost configurations and found no improvement from adding other model libraries. The post links to the implementation but provides no further pipeline or validation details.

The solution used stratified cross-validation and an ensemble of nine tree-based classifiers and regressors. Its components included a decision tree, random forests, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost. Optuna optimized the coefficients used to blend predictions. Two notebook versions achieved private scores of 0.77044 and 0.77126, and the author reported selecting the wrong version.

The post describes a reproducible submission formed by averaging seven model checkpoints. That submission is reported to score 84.698 on the private evaluation, although it is not the team's best submission. The authors also provide their LOUPE TensorFlow toolbox implementing learnable pooling modules and gated variants. Further architectural details are deferred to the linked paper.

The author engineered 11,226 features and investigated predicting normalized earthquake-cycle position rather than time to failure directly. A CNN operating on binned waveform statistics estimated cycle position and helped infer the earthquake-interval distribution of the test data. Final LightGBM models excluded short-interval training segments and used selected segments to resemble the inferred test distribution. The four-segment submission achieved a private score of 2.41465.

solution_title: [22nd Place + Code] Margin Scheduling – First time on Kaggle :D
solution_summary: The recognition pipeline used ResNet152V2 with GeM pooling and EfficientNetB6 with global average pooling, both trained with ArcFace on Cleaned GLDv2. Gradually increasing the ArcFace margin alongside cosine learning-rate periods made training easier, while Data Echoing accelerated training by about 20%. Inference used index embeddings with KNN retrieval, object-detector-based non-landmark removal, and baseline DELG local descriptors with RANSAC re-ranking. Non-landmark removal improved the public leaderboard score by about 0.005, although time constraints prevented full training convergence.

solution_title: Thank you --and thoughts on the final ranking
solution_summary: The solution trained separate classical classifiers on TF-IDF representations of page text, URLs, and metatags, then combined their outputs with a linear classifier. Custom features came from parsing useful elements of raw pages. Cross-validation guided development because noisy labels made the public leaderboard unreliable. The final score closely matched cross-validation performance.

solution_title: Our 30th Solution: In which our heroes tried Quantum Gravity, Adaptive Noise and other cool stuff…

Diverse first-level models fed isotonic-transformed predictions into second-level models and a final linear regression. The submission blended that stack with the strongest multimodal RNN. Feature-diverse LightGBM models reached 0.2203 on the public leaderboard, while the multimodal neural model reached 0.2207; discretizing predictions did not help.

solution_title: 9th Place Solution – Logistic Regression - Meta Model
solution_summary: The final solution stacked out-of-fold predictions from primarily XGBoost and LightGBM models using logistic regression. Different hyperparameters and six-fold versus seven-fold training created diversity among the base models. XGBoost was strongest individually, while LightGBM with GOSS and handcrafted features contributed useful additional signal. Logistic-regression stacking outperformed simple averaging and achieved a final leaderboard score of 0.38393.

solution_title: 36th Place Solution - LLM-Based Sentence Alignment Strategy + MBR Model Ensembli
solution_summary: The author combined two ByT5-base models and one ByT5-large model through minimum Bayes risk ensembling. GPT-4o-assisted sentence alignment produced two different versions of the official training data, while filtering an external Hugging Face corpus supplied additional training examples. Diversity in data sources and alignment granularity mattered more than adding similar models. The ensemble achieved 38.1 on the private leaderboard, whereas no individual model exceeded 36.
compute: Each of the three models was trained locally using a single A100 GPU.

solution_summary: The final solution used a single Xception model following Puzzle-CAM to learn localization from image-level labels. Cell probabilities combined image-level predictions with normalized CAM logits, using sliding-window inference and flip-and-scale test-time augmentation. External data and larger input crops improved public scores in ablations, and Xception achieved public 0.527 and private 0.495. Detection models and classifiers trained on CAM-derived cell labels were unsuccessful, while model ensembling added too little benefit to retain.

The solution used a three-block neural architecture to model player interactions, individual players, and global play context with minimal feature engineering. Separate small transformers handled offense, defense, and the rusher, with geometric relationships providing the most important information. A yardline-dependent mask constrained the predicted cumulative distribution and improved the score by about 0.0003. The final submissions combined several architectures and retained two best epochs per model.
compute: Up to 12 epochs per model; parallel TimeDistributed processing reduced training time by about 40%.

solution_summary: The author explored interactive code generation and pairwise solution comparison with an unspecified LLM. Code was generated incrementally, executed with added instrumentation, and fed back with variable values inserted as comments. Multiple solutions were generated under a dynamically allocated per-problem time budget, then compared repeatedly with their order reversed. Limited experiments suggested better code generation for SymPy-heavy problems, while solution comparison rejected obvious errors but showed a preference for the second plausible answer.

The solution retrieved candidate duplicate products from multiple image, text and TF-IDF representations, then classified pairs with CatBoost using roughly 500 features. Triplet-loss fine-tuning improved image and text embeddings, while five-fold validation searched candidates against the full training collection. Modified agglomerative clustering over predicted pair similarities raised the score to about 0.79. Mixed precision, NVIDIA DALI and RAPIDS inference made the ensemble fit within the two-hour inference limit.
compute: Baseline inference approximately 30 minutes; optimized full pipeline within 2 hours.

solution_title: 8th Place Solution for the Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations Competition
solution_summary: The author trained a simple neural network using statistical features for cell types and compounds. Median features and random selection among statistical summaries improved model diversity and performance. Validation used cell-type-stratified folds with several split counts. A weighted blend of three augmentation variants achieved a leaderboard score of 0.547.

The solution ensembled 3D ConvNeXt-like segmentation models with U-Net-style decoders. The author used fastai tabular preprocessing, Optuna tuning, and 10-fold cross-validation while retaining the original features. Adding the original dataset substantially improved results. Adding KaggleX data to the stacking model further improved public performance but worsened private performance, suggesting overfitting.

solution_title: 33th Place Solution - 1D-Unet with GRU, Detect repeating signals
solution_summary: The solution extended a public event-detection baseline with ensembles across input durations and encoder architectures. It inserted bidirectional GRUs into the skip connections of a 1D U-Net to improve temporal predictions. Peak-detection tuning and correlation-based suppression of repeating daily signals reduced false positives. The reported leaderboard score increased from 0.707 for the baseline to 0.764 after these improvements.

This post announces the release of submission code and model documentation. It links to a repository, a precompiled Linux binary with dependency sources, and related blog posts. It provides no substantive description of the modeling approach.
compute: A CUDA-capable graphics card is required to run the released code.

solution_summary: The solution classifies discourse text with DeBERTa-v3-large, adding discourse types and text from the same essay as context. Capitalizing discourse types improved scores, and two of four models received masked-language-model pretraining on reformatted Feedback 2021 data. A LightGBM stack over the four models improved performance more than weighted averaging. Training used a 512-token limit, CLS embeddings, two epochs, and StratifiedGroupKFold; reported private scores were 0.589 and 0.590.

solution_title: [Working Note] What Survives an Unknown Defender
solution_summary: The author built a portfolio of tool attacks by evaluating 17 routes against 11 modeled guardrails and separately testing model compliance. The submission used a public-score prefix followed by email-based confused-deputy candidates that the private replay could reach more cheaply. Enumerated recipients and forged analysis turns enabled reliable multi-recipient email fan-out. A byte-identical resubmission produced a 16.4-point public-score difference, undermining small version comparisons; the selected v6 recorded 84.085 public and 13.405 private.

The solution ensembled feed-forward neural networks with a complementary annotation propagation pipeline. Neural networks used Prot-T5 and ESM2 embeddings, taxonomy features, and QuickGO annotations, with concatenated skip connections improving performance. Models predicting 2,000–3,500 common annotations were combined across targets and seeds using 10-fold validation. A separate SprofGO/QuickGO merge propagated child probabilities upward through the ontology; the best single neural model scored 0.605 publicly, while propagation alone reached 0.597.

The author added color normalization before running icecuber's solver to remove irrelevant differences in color representation. Combining this approach with the baseline raised the reported score from 26% to 28%. Graph-based attempts were unsuccessful, and neural cellular automata did not exceed 1%. The specific code version shown was not tested.

solution_title: 7th solution -  **Not great things but small things in a great way.**
solution_summary: The team engineered over 500 useful aggregation features, producing more than 1,200 total features. They trained 11 LightGBM models with different data representations and parameters, then added two neural networks for diversity. A linear-regression stack of all 13 models achieved 0.8062 CV, 0.80871 public, and 0.80396 private scores. Model decisions emphasized cross-validation rather than the public leaderboard.
compute: Approximately 10 days for feature engineering, 10 days for LightGBM work, and the last 4 days for neural networks.

solution_summary: The approach removes drift and periodic contamination, then predicts residual noise relative to a linear signal-target relationship. Five batch-specific models use lagged signals, rolling extrema, and features derived from an estimated signal, with LightGBM and small dense neural networks. Synthetic sums of m5 minibatches augment m10 training, whose final predictions come from a weighted four-model ensemble. The solution achieved 0.94443 cross-validation, 0.94685 public, and 0.94539 private scores.

The solution combined sequence models with subject-based models that used a Transformer to share information across a subject's sequences. Separate IMU-only and all-feature variants handled different levels of missing sensor data, while ensemble weights adapted to the available subject history. Subject-split five-fold validation scored 0.855 for IMU-only models and 0.898 for all-feature models. Subject context improved performance by about 0.02, but shuffled inference order caused submission variability.

The final submission used a 10-fold LightGBM model and scored 0.20018 on the public leaderboard. The approach emphasized cleaning, feature selection, additional time windows, winsorization, and removal of unusually large target-to-volatility ratios. DART training with manual early stopping helped control overfitting, while predicting the original target was preferred over predicting a volatility ratio. A public TabNet and neural-network ensemble achieved the author's best leaderboard score but was not selected for final scoring.

solution_title: Kaggle - Web Traffic Time Series Forecasting
solution_summary: The solution combines a Fibonacci-window median baseline with convolutional neural networks for page-traffic forecasting. Page-wise log transformation and standardization use the Fibonacci median as the center, and pages are divided into four traffic-scale groups. Low-traffic pages use the median baseline, while the other pages use a one-layer 1D CNN with median and standard-deviation inputs. Predictions are combined by taking the median across five training runs, and validation favors using the group-2 model for group-3 pages. The reported stage-2 private SMAPE is 37.919.

The solution combined essay statistics with features extracted from writing event logs. Essay features captured text structure, punctuation, and punctuation errors, while event features described counts, numerical distributions, pauses, and writing bursts. CatBoost, LightGBM, and XGBoost were tuned with Optuna under ten-fold stratified validation. Final predictions were ensembled with weights optimized on out-of-fold predictions.

solution_title: 27 Test Set Basic Stats in 8 minutes
solution_summary: The post provides a BigQuery SQL pipeline for extracting object-level features from astronomical time series. It computes summary statistics, flux-to-error-derived features, skewness measures, flux ranges, weighted flux means, and the duration between detected observations. It reproduces features from a linked kernel while excluding tsfresh features and avoids manually splitting series by object. The reported query completed in just under eight minutes and processed 16.9 GB; no predictive model or competition score was provided.

solution_summary: The solution trained a deep convolutional network with 3×3 kernels, pooling, dropout, and fully connected layers. Images were augmented with cropping, horizontal reflection, and scaling, then processed with z-score normalization and ZCA whitening. Averaging six runs with different seeds improved the reported score from 0.93320 to 0.94150. Network In Network alternatives performed less well.
compute: GTX760; 20 hours training and 2.5 hours prediction; developer environment listed 15GB RAM.

solution_title: 6th Place Solution March Machine Learning Mania 2026
solution_summary: The solution combined feature-based classifiers, Elo ratings, and alternative pipelines to produce calibrated matchup probabilities. Temporal validation and optimized ensemble weights were central to avoiding leakage and reducing variance. Small seed-based blends and prediction clipping helped control overconfidence, while manual overrides and ESPN bracket information hurt calibration. The final reported Brier score was 0.1181 across 126 games.

The post thanks the organizers and questions whether the evaluation sample represented the full shopper dataset. The author describes how an apparently worse submission on the test sample actually performed better on the full dataset. They argue that this misleading feedback discouraged further development, but provide no modeling or pipeline details.

The submission modified the Obsidian chess engine to meet strict executable-size and memory limits. Its central change was an NNUE architecture whose feature transformer shared weights between horizontally mirrored piece-square features. This retained more strength than an ordinary 64-wide transformer while using the same feature-transformer storage. The engine was compiled as a shared library loaded by Python.
compute: Compressed executable ~25 KB excluding the NNUE network; memory usage below 5 MB.

solution_summary: The agent used a C++ rule-based skeleton controlled by roughly 1,500 tunable parameters. Randomized games and custom statistical tools guided mostly correlation-based manual and automatic parameter updates, while neural-network and random-forest tuning proved unhelpful. Game telemetry shifted strategy toward unit-based power generation, and a custom replay viewer helped expose logic bugs. Precomputation and forward simulation supported efficient action queues, although combat and movement conflicts sometimes disrupted predictions.

The solution used pretrained ResNet20, DenseNet121, and DenseNet169 models adapted to grayscale digit images. ReLU activations were replaced with Mish, and the classification heads used concatenated pooling, batch normalization, and dropout. Training combined Over9000 with a one-cycle schedule without warm-up, gradient clipping, discriminative learning rates, and five-fold validation. ArcFace, initial backbone freezing, larger ResNets, and Dig-MNIST did not improve the approach.

solution_summary: The described game-playing solution uses OrbitNet, a roughly 1.2-million-parameter transformer with planet tokens, a global token, and pairwise geometry biases. Passive game rollouts encode fleet effects into bounded planet features, while pointer, continuous launch-fraction, and value heads produce actions and position estimates. Separate two-player and four-player agents train with self-play PPO and a league of past checkpoints; the former starts randomly and the latter starts from imitation learning. Candidate selection uses local win-rate evaluation on unseen boards, and one submission includes an inference-time strategy whose details are absent from the provided excerpt.
compute: Self-play PPO league training on a single GPU; GPU model and total runtime are unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution combined LightGBM, CatBoost, and neural networks using engineered customer identifiers, count encodings, and aggregated features. Monthly validation tracked customers seen in training separately from unseen customers, enabling distinct blends: LightGBM with CatBoost for overlapping customers and LightGBM with neural networks for non-overlapping customers. Predictions were consolidated per customer, usually using the 90th percentile, which improved both validation and leaderboard performance. The final submission rank-averaged several strong blends, while an alternative submission using customer-grouped validation for unseen customers scored slightly lower.

The final solution averaged a Vision Transformer with modified input layers, LightGBM, and CatBoost. Parquet measurements were aggregated per participant, categorical variables were one-hot encoded, missing values were filled using age-and-sex group means, and features were min-max scaled. Five-fold stratified validation and MAE guided learning, followed by threshold rounding of ensemble predictions. The reported private score was 0.476, while optimized ensemble weights, a quadratic-weighted-kappa metric, and an alternative target did not improve the final result.

The solution extracted spatial features from fMRI maps using channel-wise 3D convolutions with weights shared across channels to reduce overfitting. These features entered an Edge Update GNN together with FNC correlations. Averaged graph outputs were concatenated with sMRI loading features and passed through an MLP to predict age and the other targets.

The pipeline combined pretrained YOLOv5 helmet detectors, Hungarian assignment between detections and player tracking coordinates, and DeepSort tracking. Weighted box fusion and horizontal-flip augmentation improved detection, while digit, orientation, and movement classifiers adjusted assignment costs. Dynamic programming matched tracker boxes to detector boxes, followed by duplicate-label repair and heuristic cluster splitting. Detector quality was the main bottleneck, and a shorter-trained detector achieved a substantially better private score than the selected longer-trained version.
compute: GTX 1080 Ti GPUs mentioned; full submission pipeline took approximately 8+ hours.

solution_summary: The documented approach constructed a square tiling of trees, treated it as one object, and used Sparrow to place additional trees around it. Simulated annealing then compressed the configuration, with center-directed moves helping improve packing. This worked mainly for larger tree counts, while a teammate's undocumented approach improved smaller cases. Non-square tilings and more explicit optimization of surrounding trees were explored without successful implementation.

solution_title: 54th solution with a nice user_product purchase encoding
solution_summary: The solution's strongest feature encoded each user's product purchase history as a sum of inverse powers of two. A separate model predicted the None outcome using existing user features and aggregated predictions from the main model. These prediction-derived features were generated with cross-validation to avoid leakage, yielding an overall improvement of about 0.01. Most processing used Pandas, with groupby parallelism organized into a small number of chunks per core.

The final solution fine-tuned Qwen2.5-14b-it with LoRA in two stages using combined preference datasets. It removed duplicates, swapped answer positions, and truncated the middle of inputs to retain both beginnings and endings. Hard-label training produced probabilities for additional conversations, followed by training with smoothed labels and model-generated soft targets. Single-token vLLM inference extracted A/B logits, with post-processing for close decisions, and the reported final leaderboard score was 0.712.
compute: 6 A100 GPUs; approximately 12 hours for stage 1 and 16 hours for stage 2. T4 inference used CPU offloading.

solution_title: 104.98 Public, 8.705 Private: How an email.send Hedge Kept Us Alive
solution_summary: The team built two candidate portfolios combining a high-throughput public attack channel with a shared Confused Deputy email tail. A family-level UCB search optimized prompt templates, while verification and unique scoring-cell generation controlled portfolio quality. The private guardrail blocked the marker-bearing HTTP attacks, leaving the email hedge responsible for almost all of the 8.705 private score despite a best public score of 104.98. The central lesson was to diversify across guardrail failure hypotheses and explicitly preserve the hedge in final submission selection.

solution_title: 1st: A brief review of the competition experience (Detail solution is on the way)
solution_summary: The final submission used a four-fold DeBERTa v3 large model, with the main effort devoted to expanding topic diversity through LLM-generated data. Three rounds of meta pseudo-labeling connected generated topics and summaries to the annotated training data. Training first used pseudo-labeled examples and then the original training set, while incorporating prompt text into the inputs. Sorting inputs by length kept inference within the time limit.
compute: Estimated inference time of 7 hours after length sorting; otherwise more than 9 hours.

solution_summary: The post describes data handling and position sizing improvements without specifying the predictive model. The authors excluded the final 180 training days for fair evaluation and dropped early records with extensive missing values after identifying leakage from backfilling. They clipped and scaled predicted excess returns before applying tanh to obtain positions between zero and two. The reported Sharpe ratio was 2.19 on training data and 2.16 six months later, although performance remained sensitive to the S&P 500 trend.

solution_title: [2nd Public/90th Private] Solution for the SenNet + HOA - Hacking the Human Vasculature in 3D
solution_summary: The pipeline pretrained U-Net variants with strong augmentation and mixup, then fine-tuned on dense kidney annotations with EMA and weaker augmentation. Training used 1024×1024 images and Dice loss, with kidney2 held out for validation. Inference combined sliding windows, five test-time augmentations, multiple resolutions, and experiments with several model ensembles. Threshold choice strongly affected generalization: lower fixed thresholds worked better privately, while percentile thresholds were risky. The best private score reported in the table was 0.589, and the author suspected validation design and some augmentations contributed to the public/private mismatch.

The team built transformers that incorporated base-pair probabilities through attention injection, token mixing, convolutional matrix mixing, and a dual attention stream. Masked convolutions replaced transformer MLPs, while error-aware weighting, sequence flipping, and staged pseudo-label training improved learning from noisy targets. One model family also benefited from masked-language-model pretraining on competition data. The final combination of about 20 models scored 0.14189 on the private leaderboard, while additional BPP sources and external-data fine-tuning offered little private-test benefit.

The tracking-by-detection pipeline combined a 3D U-Net detector, a visual three-frame division and motion model, and a transformer linker followed by greedy lineage decoding. Detector training used masked reconstruction pretraining, manual masks, point-derived stamps, and filtered pseudo-labels. Visual occupancy maps provided strong linking and division evidence, while separate division-kind and child-selection heads reduced false divisions. Five-fold averaging and flip augmentation supported final inference, although detector pseudo-label generation made second-round validation optimistic.

The approach fine-tuned a pretrained EfficientNetB6 on whole-slide images using a TPU. Slides were processed with pyvips and resized to 512 × 512 RGB images without tiling. The classification head used 0.5 dropout, two output nodes, and class weights. Training ran for 12 epochs with a learning rate ramp-up and decay, plus random brightness, contrast, saturation, and hue augmentation.

solution_title: 45th solution, my journey and learnings, feeling grateful :)
solution_summary: The author adapts the public bert-joint pipeline using a newly trained model initialized from bert-large-uncased. Training proceeds for one epoch on SQuAD followed by one epoch on Natural Questions at a learning rate of 3e-5. Extensive inspection of Natural Questions development predictions guides manually selected post-processing thresholds. A bi-LSTM intended to learn those rules was explored but abandoned because of time constraints.

solution_title: Stacked Boosting Ensemble with Ridge Blending
solution_summary: The solution combined extensively engineered categorical and numerical features with boosting models and OOF stacking. Twenty-fold stratified validation and inner-fold feature statistics controlled leakage, while scikit-learn target encoding outperformed the tested GPU implementation. Optuna selected 20 OOF prediction features for a Ridge meta-model, which achieved 0.91973 CV. Final isotonic calibration slightly reduced the leaderboard score from 0.91734 to 0.91733.
compute: Kaggle notebooks and cloud clusters; one feature-rich XGBoost model took around 16 hours.

solution_summary: The author trained a customized Xception network on one-second audio converted into normalized log-mel spectrograms. Training used balanced batches, user-separated validation, and three output tasks covering silence detection, standard labels, and expanded labels. Manual review of out-of-fold predictions removed about 1.7% of mislabeled training audio and increased cross-validation scores from 0.967 to 0.987, with clean-data experiments reaching about 0.99. Generalization remained weaker because the test set included unfamiliar words that closely resembled target words; phoneme-based augmentation was proposed afterward.
The post shares a dataset link containing nine samples for different indices that pass crop1. It identifies index 8 as the hardest case. It provides no explanation of how the samples were produced.

solution_title: 5th Place Solution Sharing: A Learnable Pooling Approach
solution_summary: The solution aggregates intermediate backbone feature maps with NeXtVLAD, concatenates the resulting vectors, and projects them into a 512-dimensional embedding trained with ArcFace and a dynamic margin. Training alternates frozen-backbone pooling optimization with full-model fine-tuning across V2X, V2C, and V2Full, increasing image resolution only in the last frozen-backbone stage. Nonlandmark examples from the 2019 test set improved training, while using all of V2Full as the inference index was important. The final ensemble combines three Swin variants, ResNeSt101, and EfficientNetV2-M; local validation accuracy reached approximately 95–96%.
compute: Initially 1× RTX 3090, later supplemented with 2× V100; training Swin-base-224 took approximately 3 days on one 3090.

solution_title: 2nd place solution with code and data
solution_summary: The author first trained a general human-versus-AI classifier using roughly half a million paired examples generated from SlimPajama with diverse LLMs. Language models were then fine-tuned on student essays to generate more realistic prompt-domain text, including citations and typos, for further classifier adaptation. The final ensemble combined DeBERTa models adapted on this generated data with versions additionally fine-tuned on DAIGT-V4, reaching public/private scores of 0.967/0.983. Blending with a TF-IDF kernel improved the public score but reduced private performance.
compute: Several days to generate about half a million human/AI pairs.

solution_summary: The team trained LightGBM and XGBoost multiclass log-loss models with varied features, weights, and parameters. Features included up to five months of lags and summary statistics over those lags. A greedy ensemble selected additional predictions by lowest Pearson correlation and slightly outperformed broadly merging many predictions. The shared code produced a public score of 0.0306377, while missing-month imputation, historical backfilling, and older lags did not help.

The team combined five absolute-position predictors and three motion-delta predictors using weighted averages and uncertainty-aware cost minimization. Validation used 548 training paths selected to match seven observed test-set conditions. Corrected maps supported iterative corridor snapping, followed by discrete optimization over nearby grids with penalties for position, motion, and path plausibility. Discrete optimization was the decisive improvement, producing final CV and leaderboard scores of 2.523 and 1.392 without using leakage.

The solution used a two-stage virtual-geosteering pipeline combining physics trackers, spatial geometry, and learned tracker-confidence estimates. A LightGBM classifier produced five error-bin probabilities that informed an ensemble of 24 LightGBM variants and three deep sequence models. Target and loss diversification, optimized blending, and stratified well-level validation addressed heterogeneous trajectories. Robust polynomial refinement and an uncertainty-dependent fallback to particle-filter predictions constrained implausible outputs.

The solution combined XLM-RoBERTa, RemBERT, and MuRIL question-answering models trained with competition data, MLQA, and SQuAD. Models shared a document stride of 135 and maximum length of 400, with selected fold models used for inference. A staged voting system first compared top answers, then expanded to the top two answers per architecture and used Levenshtein similarity to resolve remaining ties. This voting pipeline increased the public score from 0.792 to 0.811.

solution_summary: The solution used a two-stage pipeline that detected objects and then segmented each cropped instance. Detection used an FPN with a deformable ResNeXt152 backbone, while segmentation used ResNet152-C4 with upsampling and U-Net-like skip connections. Class-balanced sampling and ImageNet initialization supported training without additional datasets. Averaging two segmentation models with horizontal-flip inference improved the private score from 0.4740 to 0.4796.

solution_title: 🎅 Generating a 2428 solution in 100 lines of code
solution_summary: The post thanks the organizers and community and congratulates participants. It links to a notebook describing the team's journey to a 2428 solution. The post itself provides no implementation details.

The solution combined four XGBoost models and two GRU models sharing roughly 600 features. It used capacity-normalized targets, including a residual relative to a two-day lag, and validated on a chronological holdout after the first 500 days. Monthly retraining incorporated newly available observations and improved test performance. The combined models achieved a reported test score of 52.3090 with three updates, while neural models contributed about 0.9 improvement.

The pipeline first segmented sagittal images to assign vertebral levels, then segmented axial slices to crop bone regions. A 2.5D EfficientNet-B5 classified fractures using slice labels inferred from bounding-box annotations and fracture-free patients. Pseudo-labeling raised slice-level AUC from 0.916 to above 0.94. A bidirectional GRU with attention and convolution combined extracted slice features into study-level predictions, while ensembles did not improve leaderboard results.

solution_title: Part of 8th Place Solution - Macro DSL
solution_summary: The team's overall submission combined three approaches, and this post explains the author's domain-specific-language contribution. The DSL used larger macro-like commands to make program composition manageable with a simple search. Its initial split-filter-combine operations targeted tasks where panels or objects are selected or combined into a smaller output. The author subsequently extended the approach to other task types, accepting reduced generality to obtain a feasible competition solution.

The post announces a paper written by the author and teammate Ross Wightman about their adversarial attack. It links to the paper and asks whether it merits inclusion on arXiv or in the competition book. The provided post contains no technical description of the attack.

The team trained 25 model configurations across four folds, producing 100 neural networks using several CNN architectures and a weather-only AC-GAN. Eight-way test-time augmentation generated activation summaries that fed per-label XGBoost stacking models. Label-specific thresholds were optimized per fold with smoothing, and fold votes determined label inclusion. The final submission averaged second-level soft predictions and achieved 0.9345 CV and 0.93206 private score.

solution_summary: The agent combined behavior cloning from strong public players with PPO refinement of the later game. A small transformer consumed game-state tokens, recent history, and a fixed reference action tape, then emitted atomic unit commands and market orders. The submitted agent used a frozen imitation policy through day 11 and switched to PPO on day 12, with greedy inference throughout. Cached openings, GPU simulation, and accelerated distributed training made learning practical, while league-based greedy evaluation selected checkpoints.

solution_summary: The team built its approach around ConvNeXt and CaFormer backbones, drawing heavily on shared community work. Models were fine-tuned for 80–120 epochs. Final predictions used both weighted-mean and median ensemble strategies. The author reported almost no difference between public and private leaderboard results.

The author developed a diverse Ridge ensemble and a second submission based on a neural network augmented with model predictions. The better final submission added SVR, LightGBM, CatBoost outlier-classifier and XGBoost predictions as numerical neural-network features. Fold-specific median target encoding and leakage-controlled cross-validation supported the modeling pipeline. The neural ensemble scored 72468 in cross-validation and performed better on the leaderboard than the Ridge ensemble despite the latter's stronger validation score.

The author trained NASNetLarge from scratch on 224×224 images using only two training archives. Labels appearing fewer than 50 times were removed, leaving 3,862 categories. Albumentations transformations and four-way test-time augmentation supported training and inference, while tuning the prediction threshold to 0.049 raised validation F2 to 0.68. Blending NASNet, Xception, and VGG-16 helped stage 1, but the stage 2 solution used NASNet alone.

The post announces an external writeup about the author's experience in the competition. It provides a link and invites questions or requests for clarification. The supplied text contains no technical solution details.

The authors trained a small transformer and a bidirectional GRU to predict three-dimensional unit direction vectors, optimizing mean angular error directly. Memory-mapped training data and an iterable dataset enabled fast loading. The transformer scored 0.983 on both public and private evaluations, while the GRU scored 0.987 despite training on a single GTX 1080.

solution_title: 23 flags with elegant solutions especially to Cluster 3 and Semantle
solution_summary: The post outlines methods for two capture-the-flag challenges and links a notebook containing additional solutions. For Cluster 3, tuned t-SNE parameters automatically recovered the ordering of scattered tokens. For Semantle, gradient descent with buffer replay searched for words and reportedly completed the challenge in roughly a dozen or more guesses. The post does not describe the remaining challenge pipelines.

The shared experiment used a U-Net with an EfficientNet-B4 encoder initialized with noisy-student weights. Training used label smoothing without pseudo-labeling. The author shared training, inference, and tile-generation code, and reported that an older experiment scored 0.912 publicly and 0.948 privately but was missed in submission selection.

The approach uses five-fold EfficientNetV2 predictions to soften positive labels that receive low model confidence. Multilabel CutMix and mosaic combine disease labels by union, with healthy tissue contributing no disease label. ResNet50 and ResNeXt50 models use extensive augmentation, test-time flips and center crops, and late class balancing. Training also uses label smoothing, warmup, cosine annealing, and AdamW; a proposed LeafGAN extension remained unfinished.

solution_title: 27th Place Solution - Listening to the Pantanal
solution_summary: The solution combined four CNN sound-event-detection streams with a Perch/ProtoSSM branch, prioritizing complementary predictions under a CPU runtime limit. Students learned from hard labels, Perch embedding targets, and frozen CNN teacher outputs, with selective pseudo-labeling used only in one branch. All labeled soundscapes were included in training, while focal-audio folds guided checkpoint selection. OpenVINO and ONNX deployment, shared audio preprocessing, temporal smoothing, and weighted percentile-rank fusion enabled the ensemble to fit nearly within the full 90-minute budget.
compute: CPU inference with 13 SED checkpoints and one Perch/ProtoSSM branch; nearly 90 minutes.

solution_summary: The author developed diverse forecasting models using reservation-derived expected visitors, rolling averages, competitor counts, and holiday indicators. Experiments used both expanding chronological validation and random five-fold validation, with some models predicting residuals relative to rolling averages. A one-hidden-layer neural network combined models, but the ultimately successful submission averaged the SurpriseMe! submission with the best single public-leaderboard model. That single model used random five-fold validation and features calculated from all training data, including future observations.

solution_title: 29th LB And  LB 0.94376 for single Bert-Base
solution_summary: The solution combined six LSTMs, three GPT-2 models, and three BERT models, assigning 80% of the ensemble weight to BERT and reporting a score of 0.94599. BERT-base was trained for two epochs with learning rates of 2e-5 and 1e-5. Training used identity-aware sample weights and a loss combining weighted binary cross-entropy for the main target with unweighted binary cross-entropy for additional outputs. The author also mentioned length-matched batching, tensor trimming, and head-and-tail handling of long comments, although the displayed tokenization code only retains the beginning.

The author focused LLM reasoning on compact graph representations, then used Codex to implement Python builds and lower them to ONNX. Compressed history packets, a knowledge base, specialized agents, and an automated harness supported parallel candidate exploration. Candidates had to run within 30 seconds, and a local dashboard helped inspect solutions. Late experiments exposed architecture-dependent floating-point behavior, including a Task262 exceptional-float representation that removed ten charged parameters but behaved differently on ARM and x86.
compute: Day-job MacBook, one Pro account, six Codex CLI instances; additional testing on an old Linux box.

solution_summary: The solution trained nine SE-ResNeXt classifiers with different input sizes and aspect ratios to accommodate varied image shapes. Training used broad image augmentation, focal loss, and SGD with Nesterov momentum, followed by separate thresholds for culture and tag attributes. Ensemble experiments progressed from averaging to shared class-wise MLP stacking and then graph-based stacking across classes. Adding image-size metadata to the graph stack produced the best reported result, with CV 0.6487 and public score 0.657.

solution_title: just for fun - half of a general solution
solution_summary: The author proposes recovering hidden target values by probing the competition's average absolute error score. Changing one prediction between its minimum and maximum possible values isolates that target's contribution, allowing its value to be calculated from the score difference. Reusing the previous score and deriving the last target from the remaining error reduces the proposed requirement to N score evaluations for N targets. The post does not explain how to recover all 10,000 targets within the stated limit of 5,000 submissions or report an implemented result.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution (convert the COVID affected 2020 week8-week32's emission)
solution_summary: The author identified weeks 8–32 of 2020 as COVID-related emission outliers using monthly year-over-year comparisons. They rescaled emissions in that period using ratios of weekly averages from affected and unaffected data. Training used only weeks up to 48 and the three complete features latitude, longitude, and week number. The solution trained 280 LightGBM models, with a separate model for each store and forecast day. Features included sales lags, time-ordered target encodings, binary sales predictions, and distances from event dates, while recursive features were excluded. Final models used all days through 1941, trained for 300 rounds without early stopping, and ensembled predictions from iterations 100, 200, and 300.

solution_title: 8th Place: Last hours top and late to be higher
solution_summary: The solution combined UniverseNet, Faster R-CNN, and YOLOv5 detectors with ResNet34 classifiers for filtering and adjusting box probabilities. Pseudo-labeling 31,000 NIH images added a small ensemble gain, while custom box voting accounted for confidence, overlap, and distinct supporting models. The solution used logistic regression over four meta learners, each built by stacking gradient boosting models. More than 30 GBMs were explored, with categorical handling and hyperparameters tuned across XGBoost, CatBoost, and LightGBM. Several columns retained both categorical and numerical representations, and the original dataset was used only for training. Four repetitions with different random seeds and OOF predictions were used to assess robustness.

Four-fold weight averaging and CTranslate2 beam-search inference produce a single inference model. The full ablation reaches 40.8 private score, while reranking and stronger-model decoding ensembles provided no useful gains.

solution_summary: The author started from Dominic Breuker's solution and repeatedly replaced groups of bags with randomly constructed bags of the same type, retaining changes that improved the leaderboard score. solution_title: 85th Place - Physics-Aware LightGBM with Test-Time Calibration
solution_summary: The solution generated multiple geological TVT trajectory candidates and trained LightGBM to combine them with engineered well, GR, typewell and spatial features. Candidate agreement and uncertainty helped the model assess which physical hypotheses to trust, while validation grouped samples by well. Structural post-processing reduced noise and unrealistic drift, and masked-prefix calibration estimated conservative well-specific bias corrections at inference. A robust physics consensus provided an additional constraint; geological features and priors contributed more than extensive model tuning.

The final solution ensembled 18 transformer models across DeBERTa, Longformer, and Funnel variants with a maximum sequence length of 1600. Training used Fast Gradient Method for robustness and exponential moving averages to smooth training. Post-processing merged selected discourse spans, filtered Lead and Concluding predictions, extended span boundaries, and scaled token probabilities using factors found by genetic search. Optuna tuned post-processing hyperparameters, and DeBERTa-xlarge achieved the strongest reported individual CV score of 0.7092.

solution_title: 8th place private solution - a single SMILES-based transformer model is all we need. And a proper benchmarking
solution_summary: The final solution used SMILES-only multitarget transformers, with separate training and averaging for shared and unseen building blocks. Fine-tuned MolFormer and a compact custom RoBERTa were the strongest models. For unseen blocks, similarity-aware and block-exclusive five-fold splits supported validation, while balanced training sampling retained a realistic class imbalance in validation. Shared-block models trained on nearly all 98 million molecules, and extensive experiments favored SMILES transformers over graph models and descriptor-based alternatives.

The pipeline used candidate blocking, transformer pair matching, and custom cluster merging. Blocking combined geographic coordinates, character TF-IDF names, category embeddings, and exact attribute matches to obtain about 12 candidates per record. A single mDeBERTa-v3-base model was fine-tuned on all training data with distance and country tokens and FGM adversarial training. Average-linkage-style post-processing requested missing pair predictions as needed and used raw logits, with an expected improvement of roughly 0.025 over predictions without post-processing.

solution_summary: The model combined three pointwise convolution layers with four pre-layer-normalized transformer encoders and dense layers. It used 17 features, emphasizing player geometry relative to the rusher's movement direction; polar-angle features improved the score by about 0.0003.
