Additional techniques included noise and positional augmentation, 20-pass test-time augmentation, snapshot ensembling, and downsampling 2017 data.

The final submission was a weighted average of two CatBoost models, two PerpetualBooster models, and one LightGBM model. Ensemble weights were found by hill climbing on out-of-fold predictions from non-stratified 10-fold cross-validation. Feature treatments included categorical representations of continuous values, binning, count encoding, target encoding, and a rounding transformer that mapped unseen values to the nearest observed value. A fastai neural network received no ensemble weight, while attempts to use k-nearest neighbors for continuous target encoding produced substantially worse results.

The approach extracted ORB descriptors from every image across the FLAIR, T1w, T1Gd, and T2 modalities and pooled them by patient. MiniBatchKMeans built a visual vocabulary from the training descriptors, and each patient was represented by a normalized visual-word histogram. A default SVC with probability estimation learned from these histograms and generated test predictions. Predictions were weakly separated, with private leaderboard scores around 0.60 and later submissions scoring 0.58 and 0.59.

solution_summary: The post thanks the organizers, participants, and sponsor. It links to a GitHub repository containing code and documentation. The provided text contains no technical solution details.

The author used agents derived from Rps-dojo and a multi-armed-bandit approach against deterministic agents, with only marginal modifications. The central strategy was persistent submission of successful variants, reaching nearly 400 submissions. Early submissions used random Nash-equilibrium play until a scoring change reduced their effectiveness. The method adapted a two-stage training approach from A Closer Look at Few-Shot Classification. It used an SE-ResNeXt50 backbone and 448×448 images for both training and testing, with half-crop augmentation. Cosine distance was omitted because it converged slowly and produced low precision. Class 23079 was removed from training and testing.

The solution trains a ResNet50-FPN Faster R-CNN detector on all training data for 480,000 iterations with batches of eight, treating all 500 classes independently of their hierarchy. It then continues training for 230,000 iterations after downsampling classes appearing in at least 5,000 images to improve rare-class learning. Inference uses original and horizontally flipped images, and predicted labels are expanded according to the class hierarchy. Non-maximum suppression combines the expanded predictions.

solution_title: Dato Winners' Interview: 1st place, Mad Professors

solution_summary: The solution calibrated observations on GPU and extracted signals from the brightest pixels. It fit a polynomial-times-step transit model with nonlinear least squares to identify transit boundaries, remove background trends, and estimate wavelength-specific depths. Taylor-weighted spectral smoothing used a smaller window when predicted spectra had high variation, improving the leaderboard score by 0.03 over the initial 0.611. solution_title: 59th place solution - there is nothing special

solution_title: #120 Solution - Simple with huge jump in LB

solution_summary: The approach combined public-notebook feature engineering with tabular models and several image architectures. Additional features improved individual models but reduced ensemble cross-validation performance.

solution_title: 78th Place Solution: Neural Stochastic Path Generator
solution_summary: A neural stochastic controlled differential equation generated candidate TVT paths using observed feature changes, correlated noise, and a frozen per-well offset network. A separate nested ridge corrector adjusted the candidate mean using estimator disagreements projected into an anchored quarter-sine basis. Joint generator-corrector training, EMA, and uniform averaging across three seeds improved stability and correction quality. Robust surface smoothing and sequential multiscale dip correction reduced CV RMSE to 7.3534, while selecting by CV rather than public leaderboard performance proved crucial.

solution_title: 6th place solution. A YOLO-like text span detector.
solution_summary: The author formulated discourse extraction as YOLO-like text span detection with objectness, boundary regression, and discourse classification outputs. RoIAlign aggregated token logits into word-level outputs, enabling straightforward decoding and averaging across tokenizers. Training used positive-word assignment inspired by YOLOX, random token masking, and one-cycle scheduling with late-epoch weight averaging. The final DeBERTa-large and DeBERTa-xlarge ensemble used non-maximum suppression and achieved a private score of 0.732.

solution_summary: The team constructed prompt attacks that made the three judges disagree, targeting score patterns of 099, 909, and 990. Carefully designed leaderboard probes revealed public index counts, enabling a balanced assignment of attack types. The solution emphasized CutMix augmentation, confidence-selected pseudo-labeling, and cross-validation-driven post-processing. solution_title: Home Depot Product Search Relevance, Winners' Interview: 3rd Place, Team Turing Test | Igor, Kostia, & Chenglong
solution_summary: The team combined extensive text preprocessing with roughly 500 engineered features measuring query-product similarity, brand and material agreement, and semantic relationships. Their features included character-aware intersections, position-weighted ngrams, TF-IDF, SVD representations, Word2Vec, and WordNet similarities. A custom validation splitter modeled train/test overlap in queries and products, producing a consistent local-to-public score gap of about 0.001–0.002. solution_summary: The solution averaged the last five runs of a field-aware factorization machine trained with libffm defaults, including k=4. solution_title: 114th Place Solution: standard_error Works as a Feature
solution_summary: The solution combined eight transformer regressors with LightGBM through weighted stacking. Its central idea was to predict standard error with LightGBM and use that estimate alongside transformer predictions for readability prediction. Diversity came from RoBERTa, ELECTRA, XLNet, and Funnel models with attention, convolutional, and mean-pooling heads. The combined stack achieved 0.452 CV and 0.458 private score, with some overfitting; no external datasets were used.

The solution trained and ensembled QLoRA language models during the testing phase, prioritizing efficient use of two T4 GPUs. The two final submissions combined Qwen3-14B and Llama2-13B with either bge-base-en-v1.5 or Llama3.1-8B models. Data deduplication, additional negative examples, length-aware training and inference, and global rank ensembling supported the approach. Model changes were evaluated through leaderboard feedback without cross-validation; the final submissions achieved public/private scores of 0.933/0.927 and 0.932/0.926.

solution_summary: The author encoded version variables using their relative ranks within months and weeks, with AvSigVersion serving as a timestamp. They also dropped values whose distributions differed between training and private test data and used time-based validation. Relative ranking improved cross-validation and public leaderboard performance, while rolling ranking could not be implemented efficiently. The final submission was chosen using cross-validation and public leaderboard results.

solution_title: 7th place - EfficientNet, Transformer and a 2nd opinion [edited]
solution_summary: The pipeline extracted image features with EfficientNet B5/B3 and passed each series through a four-layer transformer to predict image and series labels. Trainable CT windows, positional embeddings, and competition-weighted losses supported the two-stage model. Selectively running additional models on uncertain series improved the leaderboard score from 0.162 to 0.157 while limiting repeated inference. Final predictions were minimally adjusted to satisfy label consistency requirements.

The solution used 3D nnUNet models trained with several patch sizes after removing two incorrectly labeled cases. Larger-patch models were initialized from the smaller-patch model, and training on all available data used the final saved checkpoint. Test-time augmentation improved the reported scores. The final six-model ensemble included cross-validation models and achieved 0.886 public and 0.879 private scores.

solution_summary: The solution combined ResNeSt 101 and deformable ResNeXt 101 detectors with FPN necks and ATSS heads. Training used extensive augmentation, smaller anchors, COCO initialization, and quality focal plus DIOU losses. Five-view test-time augmentation and both model outputs were merged with weighted boxes fusion, with two successive pseudo-labeling rounds applied only to ResNeSt. The reported public and private scores were 0.7672 and 0.7125.

solution_title: 65th Place Solution — a CONFUSED_DEPUTY hedge against the private guardrail
solution_summary: The author analyzed the competition evaluator and public guardrail to determine which attack predicates were reachable in the offline fixture sandbox. They selected two different final builds as a portfolio: a high-scoring public exfiltration approach and a clean confused-deputy approach. The latter used secret-free email calls with varied fixture recipients and avoided reads that would taint subsequent actions. All submitted exfiltration builds failed on private evaluation, while the selected confused-deputy build preserved its 24.87 score.

The author describes a bird-song classification solution based on EfficientNet and Mel spectral features. Audio sampling was limited to 32 kHz, and the author emphasizes sensitivity to hyperparameter settings. The post references KerasCV training and inference starter notebooks but supplies few implementation details. Higher sampling rates, voice activity detection, and GPU use are proposed as future directions.

The solution trains ArcFace EfficientNet models on externally provided backfin and fullbody crops, including a fullbody model specialized for belugas. It concatenates embeddings for nearest-neighbor retrieval and combines model target confidences by summation. Crop-specific augmentation and species-dependent thresholds support identification of known and new individuals. Pseudo-labeling failed, while inference augmentation was limited to horizontal flips; reported public and private scores were 0.829 and 0.792.

The post links to a solution notebook and points readers to an attached text file of generated features. It notes that the features include manual inputs. The post itself does not describe the modeling pipeline or results.

solution_title: Solution Sharing:  I got to #23 with xgb/rf/knn
solution_summary: The solution trained k-nearest neighbors, random forest, and XGBoost models on two spatial and temporal feature sets. Cyclic time encodings and added temporal probabilities helped the strongest kNN model reach about 0.585, with the probability adjustment improving its leaderboard score by 0.005. Model combinations were evaluated using a chronological 70/30 split and predictions generated cell by cell on a 100×100 grid. The final ensemble combined weighted votes with reciprocal weights for each model's first, second, and third predictions.

The author used AutoGluon and included the original data in training while excluding it from cross-validation. Five-fold validation was stratified by three price-per-square-meter groups. This approach produced the author's best local validation results, while a single model did not achieve comparable performance. Multiclass group prediction, feature engineering, oversampling, and undersampling did not improve local validation.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution — A Pure Global Feature Approach
solution_summary: The solution learned global image embeddings using Sub-center ArcFace with class-size-dependent dynamic margins. Models were pretrained on the full GLDv2 dataset and fine-tuned on images from the competition's landmark classes with progressively larger resolutions. Inference combined powered cosine similarities from five nearest neighbors with powered ArcFace-head scores. Ensembles concatenated model embeddings and averaged head logits, reaching a private score of 0.6344 with nine models.

The solution minimized perplexity through local permutation search using word relocation, phrase relocation, and phrase swaps, with neighborhood sizes adapted to each problem. Search history and recorded local minima supported backtracking, while scrambling and other kicks moved the search into new basins. Pinning the last word helped problem 3 improve from 197.5 to 191.5, and combining solutions from related problems helped escape a plateau on problem 5 before a custom kick reached 28.5. Simulated annealing, phrase-based decomposition, branch and bound, and random-permutation bandit approaches were unsuccessful.
compute: RTX A6000 used for local neighborhood search.

solution_summary: The team combined EEG waveform, learned wavegram, and spectrogram models using recurrent, WaveNet, and image backbones. Training generally progressed from examples with at least four votes to fine-tuning on examples with at least ten votes, with some models subsequently using pseudo-labels for lower-vote data. Contrastive learning, auxiliary tasks, multiple temporal windows, and varied channel montages supported model quality and ensemble diversity. L-BFGS-B optimized ensemble weights over roughly 150 candidates, with iterative pruning typically retaining 20–30 models and yielding a reported CV score of 0.2023 on examples with at least ten votes.

The solution used the supplied features plus leaked data, with missing leaked values estimated through two-stage modeling. Other targets served as predictors during imputation, and five gradient boosted tree models with different seeds supplied averaged predictions. Additional engineered features and modeling discrepancies between original and leaked targets did not improve results. The final output was averaged with Alexander Ryzhkov's LightAutoML predictions.

The team combined public signal features with additional MFCC features, producing roughly 8,000 candidates. Statistical selection and permutation importance reduced the feature set to 189. A deep neural network provided features for a CatBoost model, improving leaderboard performance. Averaging the pipeline across five random seeds achieved public/private scores of 3730808/3830808.

solution_title: 1st place solution - external data, teacher/student and sentence transformers
solution_summary: The author retrieved external text snippets similar to each training excerpt using sentence embeddings, then pseudo-labeled and filtered them using the original excerpts' standard errors. Large pretrained language models first trained on this selected data and then on the original training set. Six-fold models, bootstrap models and a full-data ALBERT model were combined through ridge regression ensembles and weighted averaging. Repeated pseudo-labeling improved cross-validation but hurt leaderboard performance, while a separate sentence-embedding regression approach also produced competitive results.

The solution combined 56 networks using finding-specific probability weights, with 2.5D whole-study models and anatomically targeted crop models. DICOM-derived acquisition attributes guided series selection and supplied model inputs, while femur segmentation provided landmarks for compartment crops. Training targets mixed LLM readings with out-of-fold image-model predictions, with confidence-weighted losses. Structural isolation of knee compartments and models with different anatomical views mattered more than small backbone changes. The final submission scored 0.965 public and 0.954 private.
compute: Inference on 2×T4 within 9 hours for 56 networks.

solution_summary: The final submission blended MLP, TabNet, and ResNet predictions with weights of 0.5, 0.3, and 0.2. solution_summary: The author built a basic tabular classification pipeline comparing XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and an MLP. solution_summary: The final model was HistGradientBoostingClassifier trained on 13 raw features and 39 multiclass target-encoding features. Exact numeric values were treated as categories for encoding while retaining their original numeric representations. Nested five-fold cross-fitting prevented label leakage, and test probabilities were averaged across the five outer models. Class-balanced training and a fixed 90 boosting iterations produced public and private scores of 0.95017 and 0.95035.

PlantHydra combined direct trait regression, species classification and soft classification into a three-head model. DINOv2 vision backbones and plant-domain pretraining supplied image features, while structured self-attention integrated environmental metadata. Training combined trait accuracy, trait-vector consistency and long-tail classification objectives with different learning-rate schedules for heads and backbones. The final submission manually weighted heads from multiple models, with soft classification providing a useful balance between regression and hard species assignment.

solution_summary: The solution used a single DeBERTa-v3-small model to rank markdown cells against segments of ordered code cells. Each segment contained 16 code cells, with a maximum input length of 384, balancing context retention against sequence length. Separate heads predicted segment membership and within-segment position, while a third head learned cell continuity. Adaptive cell truncation retained more information within the token budget.

The final CPU pipeline combined frozen Perch v2 features with logistic regression, spatial Mamba, spatial attention, and temporal SSM heads, plus a pseudo-trained ConvNeXtV2 spectrogram model. Shared Perch inference and fold-safe pseudo-label generation were central to efficiency and validation discipline. solution_summary: The final system was a weighted blend of sparse text classifiers, LightGBM, readability rankings, DeBERTa-v3-large, and a QLoRA-trained Mistral model. Sparse models used TF-IDF with test tokenization and spelling correction, while LightGBM selected its top 10,000 features in a two-stage pipeline. Training drew from several versions of essay datasets, with source-weighted sampling for LightGBM. Several alternative reward, ranking, token-level, and probability-based methods failed or were removed, and reliable CV-to-leaderboard correlation remained unresolved.

The solution combined topography-guided ConvNeXt regression, U-Net and Squeezeformer predictions, and particle-filter tracking through ridge-fitted ensemble weights. The strongest component rendered gamma-ray residuals and topographic uncertainty as images, then predicted control-point corrections to an initial physical TVT path. Large-scale staged synthetic pretraining, multi-trajectory prediction, and real-well fine-tuning were central to its accuracy. Vertical-flip inference and quarter-point re-anchoring improved validation, and the full ensemble reached an OOF RMSE of 4.998 despite uneven private-set generalization across components.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled two sound event detection models and a simple 2D CNN operating on mel spectrograms, combining their logits. solution_summary: The solution combined a detection model covering all six targets with specialist models for opacity, none, and study-level predictions. EfficientDet-D5 represented each study-level label with a full-image bounding box, while the none score was computed from the top three opacity box scores. The best configuration used 36 tiles of 256×256 pixels and an EfficientNet B2 model. Transpose and vertical and horizontal flips worked best at both tile and assembled-image levels, and the same transformations were used for test-time augmentation. solution_title: Rank 120 approach - simplicity is the name of the game!
solution_summary: The solution blended boosted trees and neural networks, with boosted-tree stacking using original features and out-of-fold predictions. Feature engineering was minimal, while survival-target transformations, event-dependent target separation, and shuffled 10-fold validation were central choices. The author manually tuned ensemble weights, including negative weights, and submitted versions with and without classifier-based prediction masking. The unmasked final blend scored 0.693 on the private leaderboard, slightly above the masked version's 0.692.

solution_summary: The pipeline used separate ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet B4 models for image and exam predictions, followed by models that incorporated neighboring slices. Metric analysis enabled image-model training on positive exams only, while the exam model focused on central slices. A random forest refined image predictions, and GRU and 1D CNN models predicted exam targets from sequences of pooled CNN embeddings. These stages improved the leaderboard loss from 0.215 to 0.183 and cross-validation loss from 0.235 to 0.203. Adding location information from class activation maps did not improve results.

solution_title: #19 Solution | AutoGluon + TF + LightGBM + XGBoost + Calibration
solution_summary: The author trained AutoGluon, LightGBM, XGBoost, and TensorFlow models, comparing three preprocessing options with 10-fold cross-validation. The final ensemble combined the best AutoGluon model with an AutoGluon combination of the other model ensembles, reaching 0.98527 CV. The team generated weekly recommendation candidates using popularity, purchase history, collaborative filtering, and color alternatives, then ranked them with LightGBM. Customer, article, and collaborative filtering features were especially important for late improvements. Training used selected candidate examples and a forward weekly validation split. Cold-start and sales-channel post-processing preceded a six-model blend that improved the leaderboard score by about 0.001.

The notebook blends precomputed predictions from several supplied submission files. It first averages neural-network and SVM predictions by identifier, then sequentially blends three more submissions with fixed weights. Finally, predictions whose identifiers contain age are increased by one percent before export. The text does not describe base-model training, validation, or a resulting score.

The final solution stacked 28 models with logistic regression, transforming their predictions into logits before fitting the combiner. An earlier submission combined nine diverse models, while a broader experiment combined 32 models from accumulated OOF predictions. Removing models with identical fold scores slightly improved CV and public leaderboard scores, although the unfiltered ensemble performed best privately. Threshold tuning improved CV and public scores but did not improve the private score.

solution_title: 5th-Place writeup (with Better Compression Algorithm and Seed Cracking)
solution_summary: The team built handwritten Python solutions and reduced their size through intensive code golf and custom compression tooling. Their strongest compression improvements combined dynamic programming for Huffman code lengths, automatic variable renaming, and genetic optimization of source names and deflate payloads. They also recovered test-generation seeds and used regeneration for one particularly difficult task. Their compressor improved the score by about 700 points over native zlib, while early AI-generated and DSL-based solutions were ultimately replaced.

The solution used Feature Pyramid Network detectors with ResNeXt backbones, including variants with modulated deformable convolutions. Class-balanced image sampling and long single-GPU training were central to the pipeline. Parent-class boxes were added after inference, and eight models were combined with carefully tuned class-wise NMS and overlap-based score addition. Ensembling improved the private score from 0.56369 to 0.60231.
compute: Single V100 GPU training; 3 million baseline iterations; K80 GPU validation every 200,000 iterations.

solution_summary: The solution combined repeated-trip matching with supervised driver signature models built from GPS-derived telematics features. Trip matching ensembled Douglas–Peucker runs at different sensitivities, while the telematics stream combined six models using random forests, gradient boosting, and logistic regression across three feature sets. Model choices were guided by leaderboard performance, and ensemble weights were chosen manually with individual performance in mind. Combining trip matching with telematics improved private AUC from 0.91375 to 0.97398.

The team stacked many base models built from diverse feature sets contributed by different members. A consistent cross-validation approach was central, with model decisions guided by agreement between validation and public leaderboard scores. They removed Scirpus’ features because their validation gains did not carry over to the leaderboard. Recurrent models on the time-series data were considered but never run.

solution_title: Place 347: No difference between submitting once and submitting 100 times
solution_summary: The author used a feature-engineered TabM model and combined predictions from several models through linear regression. The ensemble inputs included LightGBM, CatBoost, RealMLP, and TabM. The single TabM achieved CV 0.05592 and leaderboard score 0.05546. Observed agreement between other contestants' CV and leaderboard scores motivated focusing on CV optimization, while full-data retraining was not attempted because selecting iteration counts was uncertain.

The author trained a ResNet18 sound event detection model through spectrogram adaptation, supervised relabeling, and pseudo-label training. Loss was restricted to explicitly labeled classes and windows, with ensemble-generated positive pseudo-labels receiving half weight. Overlapping spectrogram windows and framewise predictions supported inference across full recordings. The individual model achieved public and private LWLRAP scores of 0.949 and 0.951.
compute: Google Colab; 50 epochs in stage 1 and 5 epochs each in stages 2 and 3.

solution_title: [3rd place solution] Trust CV is all you need.
solution_summary: The author trained a DeBERTa-base regressor on reconstructed essays with anonymous characters and extracted its 128-dimensional penultimate-layer representation. These context features were concatenated with public-notebook features selected using importance scores from three tree models. LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost, and several neural models were trained across multiple seeds and stratified folds, then combined with weights loosely based on cross-validation. Neural models achieved approximately 0.580–0.590 CV, and final predictions were clipped to the score range of 0.5–6.0.

Correlation, covariance and related connectivity matrices fed linear regressors and SVR, whose predictions were stacked and blended across roughly 70 base models. Atlas diversity, including atlases derived across sites and from unrelated experiments, was central to controlling site-specific overfitting. The reported private scores were 0.15714 with leave-one-network-out features and 0.15689 without them; 3D CNNs and autoencoders did not improve the approach.

solution_title: Simple rule-based bot for Halite IV [4th place solution]
solution_summary: The final Halite bot used hand-written rules with more than one hundred manually chosen parameters. Its strategy built triangular shipyard plantations, let halite regenerate, and coordinated mining, hunting and guarding through scoring functions and linear sum assignments. Cargo-aware safety and dominance maps guided territorial defense, attacks and shipyard expansion. Evolutionary tuning was abandoned because of overfitting and symmetry, and a late critical bug weakened the final bots.

The author built a LightGBM classifier for three-class irrigation-need prediction. Categorical inputs and target labels were label encoded, with consistent input mappings used for training and test data. A stratified 80/20 holdout measured Balanced Accuracy. The trained classifier and target encoder were saved for inference, and predictions were converted back to original class labels.

The solution combined intermediate BERT representations with a pointwise convolution, attentive span extraction, and a fully connected classifier incorporating manual distance features. External datasets improved initialization when used to train only the classifier head, while joint external-data fine-tuning made results worse. Using Winobias for validation and subsequently fine-tuning a single BERT layer with the head frozen brought the reported score to roughly 0.33–0.34. The final submission averaged four models and clipped predictions at 0.01.

The solution combined XGBoost and CatBoost using historical target statistics, categorical counts, temporal listening features, and LightFM matrix-factorization features. Non-target features used all available data, including future listening behavior, while target-derived features used historical records. Training used the last 35% of records and a second shifted window; six windows improved validation by 0.005, but only two were used for test predictions. The final blend combined eight predictions from both model families, both windows, and variants with and without matrix-factorization features.

The author trained an MLP to imitate WeKick agents from scraped episode replays and sampled actions stochastically. Player-centered spatial features and extensive rules helped the policy handle states poorly covered by demonstrations. Rules governed sprinting, special game modes, boundaries, and distant-ball defense, while doubling logits sharpened action probabilities. Two agents reached approximately 1,300 scores on the final day, with hard built-in AI replacing easy AI for local evaluation.

solution_title: [0.67] 742nd Place Solution - Single Transformers Model Comparison Between Data Aggregation and None
solution_summary: The author compared a Llama sequence model with a Gated Tab Transformer using aggregated session features. The sequence approach grouped event rows by session, encoded categorical values as integers, and filled missing numerical values with zero. Despite five-fold stratified validation and experiments with alternative classifiers, the sequence model achieved only 0.621 privately. The Gated Tab Transformer performed substantially better, reaching a private score of 0.67; shorter sequences also worked better in submission experiments.

The solution extended an autoencoder-pretrained graph neural network with LSTM, GRU, and WaveNet layers for ensemble diversity. Training and inference used original sequences, reversed sequences, Arnie-generated structures, and reversed augmented samples. Additional base-pair probability features, graph adjacency matrices, and predicted 3D atomic distances improved predictions. Limited early pseudo-labeling accelerated convergence, and the final approach blended more than 20 models, although the author reported substantial sensitivity to evaluation conditions.

The solution combined silence-trimmed log mel-spectrograms with PCA-reduced spectral and temporal statistics. A modified MobileNetV2 extracted spectrogram features, which were joined with the additional features before dense classification layers. Ten stratified folds used staged training, variable-length inputs, random erasing, and mixup. Geometric averaging across folds and repeated crops at six lengths produced a MAP@3 score of 0.943289.

The solution blended slightly modified CNN14 audio models using standardized spectrograms with 128 mel bins. Recordings were resampled to 32 kHz, divided into 10-second chunks, and augmented by adding bird recordings, noise, and animal sounds. Four-fold validation attempted to separate recordings by author and creation information, with checkpoints selected using XC and BirdCLEF validation. The initial blend achieved 0.649 on the private leaderboard; later species-specific threshold adjustments improved public results without changing the private score.

solution_title: 97th Place Solution for the RSNA 2023 Abdominal Trauma Detection
solution_summary: The final model combined a 2.5D ResNet with a single-layer LSTM containing 128 hidden units. It used volumes of shape 128 × 64 × 64, with a window step of two and width of three. Binary injury outputs used sigmoid activation, while the other targets used softmax.

The approach combined two SeResNext101 models and two EfficientNet B5 models with different preprocessing and training schedules. Training incorporated the previous competition's data while validation used stratified folds of the current dataset. Both soft-label retraining and hard-label fine-tuning on test predictions improved performance and diversified the ensemble. A later SeResNext101 experiment using pseudo labels from both architectures achieved a private score of 0.931, exceeding the final submission.

The solution ensembled nine TResNet-M and TResNet-L models trained from ImageNet and iNaturalist 2018 pretraining at different resolutions. A compact bottleneck head enabled larger batches, supporting cross-entropy with label smoothing and a hard-mined soft-triplet loss. Late-stage class balancing, specialized augmentation, and high-resolution fine-tuning improved the classifiers. Post-processing exploited the guarantee that every class appears in the test set, bringing the ensemble's public score to 0.86310.
compute: A single V100 16GB supported batch size 128 for TResNet-M at 448×448; best single model used 100 initial epochs plus 10 fine-tuning epochs.

solution_title: Worst place writeup (15th solution) with code

Training used smoothed cross-entropy, AdamW, five epochs, best-checkpoint selection, and seed restarts for poorly performing large-model runs. Hill climbing selected complementary predictions rather than simply prioritizing the strongest individual cross-validation scores. Post-processing was applied both within cross-validation splits and after blending the split predictions.

solution_title: How a Last-Week Deputy Hedge Won Gold #15
solution_summary: The team built an automated search, verification, and submission pipeline for adversarial prompts against two victim models. Their public-board approach minimized generated tokens per successful single-call candidate, while a separate confused-deputy submission diversified against different private guardrails. Calibration on the actual grader and filtering unsuccessful variants were central because local timing and behavior did not transfer reliably. The exfiltration submission scored 118.25 publicly but zero privately, while the hedge achieved 29.52 privately.

solution_summary: The solution used item-based collaborative filtering for candidate recall, followed by a five-fold LightGBM LambdaRank model. Popularity weighting improved recall, while ranking features emphasized customer–item interactions, purchase timing, and category statistics. The recall stage scored about 0.028 on the leaderboard, and ranking increased this to 0.031. The author attributed limited ranking gains to a last-week validation dataset covering relatively few customers; deepMatch and neural ranking alternatives did not improve the approach.

The solution combined efficient CT preprocessing with small, single-stage multi-task models, without using the supplied image labels or segmentation masks. It ensembled two MIL-like models and two recurrent models using EfficientNet and DenseNet backbones. Patient-grouped stratified validation supported target-specific ensemble weights and prediction scaling, with strong agreement between out-of-fold and leaderboard scores. The final ensemble scored 0.3859.
compute: Training DICOM-to-PNG export took approximately 20 minutes.

solution_summary: The approach began with a Conformer and CTC loss, then improved through a transition to SqueezeFormer and a revised landmark encoder. Further changes included Mish activations, temporal reduction, and a shared-parameter training path that omitted temporal reduction and received an additional CTC loss. Augmentation concatenated random examples and synthesized frames for noisy samples using character-to-frame alignments from another trained model. The author reported improvements but did not retain experiment logs to quantify individual contributions.

The solution separated organ, bowel, and extravasation prediction according to the available label types. A 3D segmentation model generated organ crops, which were classified using 2.5D CNN and LSTM models with study labels and, for bowel, image labels. Extravasation used a two-stage CNN feature extractor and GRU sequence model, improved by an auxiliary segmentation head trained from bounding-box annotations. Validation used five patient-grouped folds, while direct detection and separate organ models did not work well.

solution_title: Efficiency 3rd Place : Public Model + Simple Post Processing
solution_summary: The approach used a publicly shared embedding model to retrieve the top 25 misconceptions by cosine similarity to concatenated question metadata and answer text. Its main contribution was adjusting similarities with precomputed associations between constructs and misconceptions, using separate bonuses for safe and potential matches. Misconception embeddings were computed ahead of inference to improve efficiency. The adjustment parameters were not cross-validated, and the handling of unseen constructs could disadvantage misconceptions already present in training.

The author combined fine-tuned Qwen and Llama models with DeBERTaV3 and a bge-base-en nearest-neighbor classifier. Training data incorporated labeled positive and negative examples, with duplicate rule/body pairs removed. Models used test-time training, and cross-validation guided ensemble weights. Two submissions prioritized either CV or leaderboard performance; the best leaderboard ensemble included Qwen2.5-7B, Llama3.2-1B, bge-base-en, and seed-ensembled DeBERTaV3.

The author develops player evaluation metrics from tracking data while excluding ball information to reduce dependence on quarterback accuracy. Receiver scores combine separation, endpoint execution, route efficiency and consistency, while defender scores combine coverage tightness, pursuit angle, discipline and consistency. Experiments with artificial ball-location noise showed substantially greater degradation for the ball-dependent model. The analysis covers 14,108 plays and reports that player execution retained 76% of its level on wild throws.

The team trained separate survival-related regressors and classifiers using boosted trees, AutoGluon and PRL neural networks. Regressors targeting eight outcomes were combined through multi-task Elastic Net, while classifier probabilities drove race-specific prediction adjustments optimized with Optuna. Custom PRL networks were blended selectively for high efs probability cases and weaker-performing races. Selecting the stronger cross-validation solution yielded a private score of 0.694.

The solution combined spatiotemporal graph convolutions and Transformers to jointly classify all 16 mouse agent-target pairs. Videos were standardized to 30 FPS and lab-normalized coordinates, with motion and inter-mouse features as inputs. Training transitioned from mixed cross-entropy and macro soft F1 to pure soft F1, with invalid behavior combinations masked. The final ensemble averaged probabilities from pairwise and non-pairwise models using different keypoints and sequence lengths, with horizontal-flip inference augmentation.

The submission used a simple Gaussian process classifier. Leave-one-out cross-validation suggested promising performance. Its public score of 0.70536 discouraged further tuning, but the model ultimately performed well on the private leaderboard.

The final solution averages XGBoost and LightGBM predictions across 20 seeds per model. Its main improvement came from frequency-based features computed on training data combined with non-fake test rows, replacing values with NaN according to frequency thresholds. The best single model used 601 features, including original columns, two transformed feature sets, and a null count. Five-fold stratified validation, positive-row duplication, and augmentation supported a final public score of 0.924.

The SmallData team announces that its competition code repository is public on GitHub. The post notes that the repository preserves commit history from the competition. It also announces a planned paper describing the method, but provides no technical solution details.

The solution treated behavior detection as lab-specific action classification using geometric, motion, body-part-distance, and temporal features. It combined XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, PyBoost, and TabM with ensemble weights fitted on out-of-fold predictions. Video-level five-fold validation supported negative sampling, calibration, and action-specific threshold fitting. Final processing restricted predictions to valid combinations, smoothed them over action-dependent windows, selected one action per frame, and merged consecutive frames into intervals.

A neural stacker fed a YDF model alongside original features, and their predictions were blended equally. solution_title: Homesite Quote Conversion, Winners' Write-Up, 1st Place: KazAnova | Faron | clobber
solution_summary: The team built a three-meta-layer ensemble using approximately 125 selected models from a pool of about 500. Diverse categorical representations, date features, engineered interactions, and feature subset selection drove both model strength and diversity. Neural networks were the strongest stackers, alongside XGBoost and logistic regression. Careful stratified cross-validation and checks across fold seeds helped control overfitting, yielding a private AUC of 0.97024.

The final approach used EfficientDet5 and EfficientDet7 trained on 512×512 and 1024×1024 images. Training combined bounding-box cleaning, extensive online augmentation, stratified five-fold splits, and source-based splits for some fine-tuning. The team manually adjusted training, used early stopping, and changed augmentation distributions over time. Earlier Faster R-CNN and YOLOv5 experiments were superseded, with YOLOv5 removed after it was prohibited.

solution_title: 2nd place solution - pure Bayesian Inference, no deep learning
solution_summary: The solution uses Bayesian inference with Gaussian process priors to separate transit depth, stellar spectrum, drift, and detector noise. A custom iterative solver estimates posterior transit depths and uncertainties, with KISS-GP reducing the cost of spectral drift modeling. A rough fit across test planets supplies one uncentered PCA component for a second fitting pass. Invalid-pixel interpolation and adaptive temporal binning support preprocessing, while final depth and uncertainty scaling correct systematic errors.

Subject-grouped nested validation, local attention bias, waveform augmentation, and frequency filtering helped handle noisy data. Class-specific ensemble weights were optimized with GP_minimize while accounting for an outlier subject.

solution_title: Public 531st -> Private 10th: The Complete Solution Code
solution_summary: The approach forecasts county-level microbusiness density with CatBoost and five separate models for different future horizons. Features combine technical indicators with external economic and demographic data, using only three months of history. Optuna minimizes SMAPE, and cross-validation is used to assess generalization.

The team combined a two-class classifier with an ensemble of several object detectors. The detector set included multi-head VFNetX, YOLOv5l, CenterNet2 DLA, and PAA with NFNet. Training used oversampling, light augmentation, and insertion of cropped abnormality boxes into healthy backgrounds. Weighted boxes fusion with IoU 0.3 prepared boxes, while a modified version handled post-processing.

The author engineered two datasets and trained a separate stacking ensemble on each. Both stacks used out-of-fold predictions and logistic regression as the second-level model. Their final prediction averaged the two stacks. The author attributed the main advantage to feature engineering and prioritized 10-fold cross-validation over public leaderboard feedback.

The solution ensembles U-Net segmentation models with four timm backbones and tunes each model's threshold on out-of-fold validation predictions. Training used no image augmentation, while the MaxViT models used stochastic weight averaging over their final five epochs. Experiments initially used small models and images before scaling up during the final week. Several alternative losses, architectures, and postprocessing approaches offered insufficient gains or were too expensive to pursue.

The final ensemble combined 29 token classifiers across six model families, including four DeBERTa variants, Funnel Transformer, and ELECTRA. Training used masked language modeling, with different losses and adversarial training methods for different backbones; DeBERTa models also used limited pseudo-labeling. Cross-validation guided ensemble weights, while selected clinical features received separate thresholds. Span-boundary postprocessing and threshold tuning improved the predictions.

solution_summary: The team built a two-level stack using LightGBM, XGBoost, and random forests across five feature datasets. Twelve first-level predictions fed second-level XGBoost and random forest models, blended with weights of 30% and 70%. Extensive order, manufacturing-path, timestamp, duplicate, and numeric features drove performance, with five-fold validation used to monitor stability. Scaling the cross-validated classification threshold by 0.92 produced 0.50888 private MCC, slightly below the 0.50954 obtained without scaling.

solution_summary: The pipeline combined multilingual text embeddings with geographic coordinates to retrieve candidate location matches, then classified candidates using separate XGBoost models for each neighbor rank. Missing text was filled from nearby locations, and embeddings from multiple language models were concatenated and refined with weighted DBA/QE. Graph postprocessing using Dijkstra distances expanded match sets and reduced false negatives. Training the embedding models on all available training data improved results but contaminated downstream validation; the reported score progressed from 0.922 to 0.947.

solution_summary: The team stacked CT windows into three-channel images and trained models using patient-based and study-based splits. Their two-stage 2D pipeline combined CNN backbones with a second CNN operating on predictions from five neighboring slices. An additional end-to-end sequence model used a bidirectional LSTM to incorporate study context. They stacked model predictions with a multilayer perceptron and averaged the outputs from the two split strategies.

solution_title: 40th Place Solution - Improving prediction with FFT-based data cleaning
solution_summary: The solution cleaned timestamps and event boundaries, then generated FFT-cleaned sensor features at several thresholds. Seven models combined different feature extractors with a UNet and a one-dimensional decoder, using five-fold grouped validation. Increasing recurrent feature dimensions from 64 to 128 helped more consistently than FFT cleaning on the private leaderboard. A two-stage optimized ensemble achieved 0.79049 CV and 0.802 private score.

solution_title: Study Log: Reflecting on the Differences Between Top Solutions and My Approach
solution_summary: The author reflects on their prompt recovery approach and compares it with stronger solutions. They constructed a validation dataset by applying extraction rules to public data, obtaining reasonably good correlation with the leaderboard. They identify insufficient attention to mean prompts and the T5 metric as weaknesses. The post provides validation insights but does not describe a complete final modeling pipeline.

The solution used XGBoost with iterative feature engineering and forward feature selection. V columns were grouped by missing-value counts, then reduced using correlations and unique-value counts. Additional features included frequency encodings, user-level aggregations, and transaction-day offsets derived from D columns. Similar reduction of C and M columns hurt AUC and was rejected. Reported scores were 0.951265 for local cross-validation, 0.928873 on the private leaderboard, and 0.954825 on the public leaderboard.

solution_title: [8th Public / 18th Private] - Full Wikipedia Passage-level Retrieval
solution_summary: The pipeline retrieved passages directly from full-text Wikipedia, reranked sentence chunks, and supplied the resulting context to DeBERTa answer models. A compressed full-Wikipedia index was complemented by a more precise science-specific index. Training used diverse synthetic questions and deliberately weaker retrieved contexts, which improved leaderboard performance. The full retrieval index alone achieved 0.891 with a public model, while learned tree-based rerankers performed worse than embedding scores.

solution_title: 7th Place Solution for the Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations
solution_summary: The author first learned cell-type, compound, and gene embeddings using a deep tensor-factorization approach trained on long-form competition targets. A second three-layer fully connected network used these embeddings to predict the target, with batch normalization and dropout. Four-fold validation held out selected compounds within each cell type, and final predictions averaged the fold models. Features from prior biological knowledge and other large models did not help, so the final approach relied on the learned embeddings.

solution_title: 6th solution: Node-level Instance Norm + Residual  SageConv on 5-hop-neighbour Subgraph
solution_summary: The solution uses separate graph neural network approaches for layout and tile runtime prediction. For layout, it reduces large graphs to five-hop neighborhoods around configuration nodes and trains a four-layer residual SAGE model with pairwise ranking loss. Graph instance normalization and gradient accumulation make training manageable in GPU memory. For tile prediction, GAT performs better than SAGE, and listMLE better targets the top-five ranking objective.

solution_summary: The team combined TF-IDF logistic regression, recurrent neural networks, attention models, and models using engineered text statistics. Word and character models used varied normalization and embeddings, including GloVe and fastText, while seed averaging and ten-fold stacking added diversity. The final blend assigned 60% to the strongest stacked and blended solutions and approximately 20% each to two individual blends. Setting predictions for 1,240 non-English comments to zero provided a small improvement, yielding scores of 0.9881 publicly and 0.9880 privately.

The submitted solution ensembled EfficientNet B7, B5, and B4 initialized with noisy-student weights. Training ran for 30 epochs using only the supplied competition data. solution_title: TEAM HITHERTO — From Productive-Region Localisation to Transfer Failure
solution_summary: Team Hitherto developed a controlled search process for locating productive tool-agent attack configurations using aggregate public scores. They varied prompt representations, candidate generators, ordering, traversal, pacing, allocation, and portfolio composition, then attempted configuration-level reproduction. Several productive public regions were reacquired, although candidate-level and predicate-level attribution remained unavailable. The team reported zero private yield, with the exact selected configuration unverified.

solution_title: A brief overview of 13th-place LB solution
solution_summary: The solution trained ontology-specific MLPs on normalized ESM2 embeddings, using both the original training annotations and updates from UniProt and QuickGO. Target terms were selected by frequency, and predictions were averaged across cross-validation folds and six MLPs. Post-processing applied taxonomic constraints, propagated child scores to parent terms, and filtered low-confidence rare terms. The final predictions were averaged with eligible external GO annotations.

solution_title: 181th Place Solution | ChatGPT please rest now
solution_summary: The solution used a repeatable task-specific loop to generate, optimize, validate, and merge compact ONNX graphs. Direct-output Einsum representations, quantized intermediate tensors, and removal or sharing of constants produced substantial cost reductions. Candidates had to pass cached examples, fresh ARC-GEN tests, static checks, runtime checks, and the exact pinned inference runtime. About 150 tasks received the full optimization loop, and the final score was 7440.82.

solution_title: 116th: six weeks with LLM coding agents, and why replays mattered more than RL
solution_summary: The final bot directly replayed ShunkiKyoya's recorded games, selecting compatible tapes through a prefix trie and a simulation-tuned routing table keyed by shop sequences. Order prioritization and a weed guard improved execution without changing the underlying farming plan. On fresh worlds against seven opponents, it achieved 1044 wins out of 1120 games, compared with 974.5 for the plain replay trie. Earlier boosted models, bandits, and behavior cloning followed by PPO failed to compete with strong public bots.
compute: Routing simulations: 73.7k games on two 112-core nodes; bot loads in under 0.7 seconds and moves in under 1 ms.

solution_summary: The author trained separate models for each scoring target to reduce the high correlation observed across baseline predictions. The final ensemble combined four separate-model configurations with five joint models that used separate output heads. Class-specific ensemble weights were optimized with scikit-optimize, producing CV 0.4422 and private score 0.434121. Separate models improved accuracy but made inference slow, while external-data pretraining, pseudolabeling, random masking, and tree-based stacking did not help.

solution_title: 29th Place Solution for the AI Village Capture the Flag @ DEFCON31 Competition
solution_summary: The writeup describes methods used to solve several AI capture-the-flag challenges. Clustering tasks used KMeans inertia and two-dimensional t-SNE visualization, while semantic guessing tasks relied on searching common English words and arranging high-scoring terms. Other challenges were solved through unsafe pickle handling, OCR-mediated XML injection, prompt injection, and task-specific prompts. The account covers selected tasks and omits complete executable solutions because the endpoints were unavailable.

The solution followed a compact training-data approach, sampling customers across months to approximate the June 2015 product distribution and adjusting it for popularity trends. It used random-split cross-validation, product-history features, customer-level aggregates, and one-hot encoded categorical values. A post-processing rule enforced the relationship between pension and payroll products, while older product history informed customer scores. Two team members' solutions were combined, and attempts to exploit household relationships or unrestricted historical features did not improve results.

The approach used T2-weighted MRI images with blank slices removed, slice cropping, depth-64 SIZ processing, normalization, and zero centering. A 3D ResNet50 was trained with batch size 16, an initial learning rate of 0.01, and a learning-rate scheduler. Using a single validation fold, the author selected five models from each training cycle for the submission ensemble. The author reported that the model did not generalize.

The solution emphasized engineered rental-listing features and diverse encodings of manager identity. Nested cross-validation supported target-dependent statistics and a large stack built with XGB and StackNet. A final XGB stage used recursive feature elimination, followed by averaging five selected models and predictions across validation folds. Stacking improved the reported leaderboard loss from roughly 0.515 for the strongest single model to 0.50068.
compute: Laptop; about two full days to train all models.

solution_summary: The agent used four LightGBM predictors trained on the latest 50 matches to predict either player's next move from two or three recent matches. Each predictor supported winning, drawing, and losing responses, yielding 12 strategies whose weights changed after each match. Confidence thresholds triggered random play for uncertain predictions, while a safety rule favored moves with low loss probability. The author repeatedly adjusted thresholds, weight updates, training history length, and LightGBM parameters.

The author combined ideas from public notebooks into a tabular modeling pipeline with interaction features, noise, hyperparameter tuning, and model ensembling. They used stratified cross-validation, progressively reduced regularization, and selected the best model in each fold. One submission achieved a private score of 0.84248 despite a less favorable public score of 0.84195. The writeup emphasizes uncertainty about which additions actually improved generalization.

solution_title: 11th Place Writeup - Transformers and Pseudo Label
solution_summary: The solution blended a hybrid regression network with a Conformer-based discrete-pressure classifier. The regression network combined convolutions, time-aware disentangled attention, and LSTMs, while the classifier added relative time distances to attention. Fine-tuning for individual resistance/compliance combinations and separate outputs for real and pseudo labels improved the models. Ensemble-generated test pseudo labels and a final blend of old and retrained models improved the public score from 0.1112 to 0.1074.

The team used a two-stage 2D pipeline that first segmented tumors and then classified MRI sequences using the original images and two predicted tumor masks. A UNet++ with a DenseNet121 backbone supplied masks to a bidirectional LSTM with an Eca NFNet L0 feature extractor. Tumor-based filtering, overlapping 35-slice chunks, patient-level prediction averaging, and zoom test-time augmentation helped stabilize predictions. The classifier achieved 0.685 validation AUC and 0.60696 private leaderboard AUC, while 3D models and external-data self-supervision did not improve results.

solution_summary: The final approach used a logistic regression stacker built from the author's own out-of-fold predictions, followed by cross-fitted QSO/STAR residual correction. A 5% stellar-locus model contribution added diversity, and constrained Optuna blending preserved at least 88% of this strong anchor. Five-fold stratified validation, fold stability, prediction differences, and submission audits guided selection. solution_title: #1 Solution - Experimenting with the data generation model
solution_summary: The selected ensemble simply averaged models developed through several approaches, with CatBoost consistently providing strong results. An alternative ensemble used Optuna to optimize weights against out-of-fold predictions but achieved a slightly worse MAE of 1.33566. Generating additional training rows and recovering targets through the data generator's imputation or sampling functions did not help sufficiently. solution_summary: The solution retrieved candidate content using four transformer embedding models trained with ArcFace, then reranked candidates with CatBoost and XGBoost. Topic texts incorporated ancestor titles, while reranking features captured embedding similarity, TF-IDF similarity, and topic-tree relationships. Embeddings were concatenated for retrieval, and reranker predictions were averaged before channel-specific thresholding and correlation-based post-processing. The published submission achieved 0.7152 CV F2 and 0.707 on the public leaderboard.

solution_title: Loss function and a short report (LB: 5)
solution_summary: The solution combined ten LSTM models, five BERT-Base models, and three GPT2 models using a shared sample-weighted loss. Sample weights summed each example's estimated influence across overall, subgroup, BPSN, and BNSP AUC terms. Inverse class-frequency contributions helped balance positive and negative examples within each metric component, although overlapping subgroups prevented exact balance. The overall reported score was approximately 0.94725.

solution_title: Brief summary of 13th place solution (hide the pain Harold)
solution_summary: The final solution combined one DistilBERT, two ALBERT-large models, and one BERT-large WWM model using a LightGBM candidate classifier. Model scores were supplemented with answer length and document-position features, while DistilBERT prescoring reduced inference work for the other models. Improvements included smoothing logits across neighboring windows, jointly scoring answer start/end pairs, and stochastic weight averaging. Validation used the official Natural Questions development set, where the best blend reached about 0.67, compared with about 0.68 on the leaderboard.

The solution blends two LightGBM models trained on closely related wavelet-derived feature sets. Its central post-processing step rescales predictions to a test-target mean estimated as 6.51 from a paper. Repeated nested validation guided feature selection and conservative, strongly regularized model settings. Statistical features were removed, while target normalization improved validation but hurt private leaderboard performance. The submitted models inadvertently used only about 60% of the training data.

solution_title: From nothing to something... a 103 LB jump!
solution_summary: The solution combined Wikipedia retrieval with a single fine-tuned DeBERTa model trained on shared examples and custom GPT-3.5-generated data. Retrieval used a modified public notebook, expanded TF-IDF fitting, and a custom FAISS index built from page titles and two paragraphs. Predictions from parsed and cohere contexts were used when their ensemble confidence exceeded 0.41; otherwise, the same model's prediction using the custom six-million-page Wikipedia embeddings was selected. A more complex dynamic voting ensemble across four models and three contexts was tried but was not successfully developed further.

solution_summary: The author trained multiple pretrained language-model backbones with hidden-layer pooling and attention pooling for readability regression. The author used Seresnet and ResNet34D networks with several pooling methods and dilated CNNs for ink detection. Training included extensive image augmentation and a combined BCE, Dice, and Tversky loss. Predictions underwent mask post-processing and rotational test-time augmentation. The post points readers to a GitHub repository containing the author's solution. It describes this as the author's first medal. No approach, implementation details, or results are provided in the post itself.

solution_title: Melbourne University AES/MathWorks/NIH Seizure Prediction 2016: 5-th place
solution_summary: The team split EEG recordings into unfiltered 30-second epochs and extracted kernel-derived, spectral-energy, and channel-spectrum correlation features. Patient-specific tree ensembles predicted each epoch, and their probabilities were averaged for each recording. Six-fold stratified validation without shuffling was essential to avoid leakage between neighboring epochs. A weighted ensemble of seven models achieved public/private AUCs of 0.81423/0.79363, although missing random seeds limited reproducibility.

The author tested a pure one-dimensional convolutional network after the competition by converting SE-ResNeXt50 from 2D to 1D operations. Inputs were normalized drawing sequences containing x, y, time, and pen-state channels, interpolated and clipped to length 224. Training for slightly more than a day achieved private/public scores of 0.939/0.940. The main benefit was speed, with 1,700–1,800 training samples per second on two 1080 Ti GPUs and over 3,000 inference samples per second on one GPU.

solution_title: 3rd solution - single TRANSFORMER model, link to kernel
solution_summary: The solution aggregated event logs into game sessions and fed session sequences into a single transformer without positional embeddings. Separate categorical embeddings and log-transformed continuous features formed each session representation. The model jointly predicted accuracy group and correct/incorrect counts, combining direct and count-derived predictions at inference. Pretraining with 41,194 additional game-session labels and sequence-removal augmentation supported a best private score of 0.564.

solution_title: March Mania 2026: Top 8% (304th Place) – Bronze Medal Solution
solution_summary: The solution predicted point margins using a 60% GLM, 30% TabPFN, and 10% XGBoost ensemble built on 13 relative team features. Feature selection emphasized stable coefficients across seasons, with walk-forward validation providing realistic historical backtests. Separate modified sigmoid calibrations and probability clipping converted margins into men's and women's win probabilities. The submission achieved a Brier score of 0.1271382, prioritizing stability and interpretability over a larger feature space.

The solution used a single XGBoost classifier for men's and women's basketball win probabilities. Its central emphasis was possession-level efficiency features, including shooting, turnovers, rebounds, and corresponding opponent statistics. MinMax scaling and shuffled 10-fold cross-validation performed best among the tested preprocessing and validation choices. It used only competition data, made no manual prediction overrides, and reported a private score of 0.17619.

solution_title: 51st Place Solution - And Some of my Explorations and Learning
solution_summary: The final submission ensembled CatBoost, LightGBM, and a gradient boosted regressor using calendar, holiday, GDP, spline, and periodic features. Optuna tuning, stacking, and more elaborate ensembles produced strong validation scores, but the simpler ensemble performed better in leaderboard probing. Time series cross-validation did not fully track leaderboard performance. Deep learning was too slow, while Google Trends and additional spline or trigonometric features did not improve results.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution  -  tmp's part ( code updated )
solution_summary: The solution blended complementary approaches, with the described CITEseq pipeline combining MLP and LightGBM models. Preprocessing combined count transformations, normalization, standardization, and day-based batch correction. Multiple decomposition features and features with stable target correlations across donor-day groups improved performance. Random five-fold validation tracked leaderboard results, while day-based splits provided an additional robustness check; the described Multiome feature experiments were excluded from the selected submission.

The solution combined six DeBERTa-v3-large models trained on the full dataset with different sequence lengths and slightly varied hyperparameters. It tokenized the supplied substrings, averaged subtoken probabilities, and reduced BIO targets to seven classes before restoring the format afterward. Generated training data was included at half weight. Name propagation, address newline corrections, and downscaling the O-class probability were important post-processing steps; augmentations did not improve the final submission.

solution_title: 10th Place Solution: Hierarchical Bayesian Model with 5 features
solution_summary: The solution used a hierarchical Bayesian regression model with five features to predict PCIAT total scores. It modeled age-category random effects and respected the target's lower bound of zero, while imputing missing features with training medians. Posterior means were converted to SII using thresholds optimized for training QWK. Seven-fold stratified validation and averaged, rounded test predictions produced reported scores of 0.441 CV, 0.447 public, and 0.473 private.

The solution used a modular library of rule-based strategies for factory placement, factory operation, and robot behavior. The latest placement strategy scored ice and ore separately and considered nearby rubble. Robot control combined spatial state matrices, environmental monitoring, and task allocation to manage mining, clearing, combat, charging, and collision avoidance. Searching for paths within cropped map windows proved unexpectedly useful.

solution_title: When the Public Score Lies: Guardrail Divergence & the Deputy Survivor
solution_summary: The team reverse-engineered replay scoring and measured real victim models to optimize scoring events per generation-second. Public performance reached 89.020 through output minimization, fixed-count candidate emission, and GPT-OSS-specific eight-hop posting, but exfiltration scored zero privately. A deliberately retained benign confused-deputy email portfolio produced the surviving private score of 18.375. The main missed opportunity was failing to apply the same throughput optimization effort to that surviving primitive.

solution_summary: The pipeline refined an existing grid-detection stage and focused on digitizing four cropped long ECG leads. ConvNeXt Large, an SNR-aware loss, and iterative grid alignment improved signal quality. Training and inference used three image resolutions and multiple model architectures. Extensive data generation, CycleGAN style transfer, and algebraic lead corrections did not help.

The solution modeled missing values separately for F1, F3, and F4 using an average of a TensorFlow neural network and a LightGBM/XGBoost regression combination. The number of missing values per row was a crucial feature, with its addition and other changes improving the reported score from 1.04555 to 0.94694. Public-test probing suggested that the public score mostly reflected F4, so model combinations were selected on that feature group before being applied to the others. Modeling every group slightly outperformed an alternative that mean-imputed F1 and F3.

The pipeline combined diverse image models with metadata, then fed their predictions into gradient-boosted tree stacks. Patient-aware validation balanced positives while limiting the influence of patients with many negative samples. Patient-and-location aggregate features and removal of zero-importance features improved performance, while restricting each stack to at most two CNN predictions worked best. An optimized weighted average of three stacking models, a metadata-only tree model, and a standalone CNN achieved CV 0.1793 and private leaderboard score 0.171.

solution_title: A simple post-processing for your solution
solution_summary: The authors apply selective rounding to model predictions as a post-processing step. Predictions within 0.2 of an integer are rounded, while other values remain unchanged; a tolerance of 0.3 is also suggested. They report that this adjustment helped improve their competition standing, without providing numerical scores or details of the underlying models.

solution_title: [8th Place Solution] Understanding Data Before Designing Methods
solution_summary: The solution processed TMA and WSI images separately while aligning their physical magnification scales. Mask-derived patches trained TMA classifiers and ArcFace retrieval models, with a classification ensemble resolving uncertain retrieval results. WSI predictions used multiresolution feature extractors followed by DTFD-MIL, with synthetic Other slides supporting outlier detection. TMA-trained features greatly accelerated MIL convergence, while PLIP validation results were poor and an additional high-resolution branch crashed.

The solution ensembles RoBERTa-large, DeBERTa-large, and ELECTRA-large architectures. A trained RoBERTa-large model generates pseudo-labels for 20,000 Wikipedia texts, which are used to train the different models before full fine-tuning on the competition training set. Differential learning rates are applied across transformer layers, while alternative hidden-state selections and pooling methods perform similarly. The ensemble reports private scores of 449–450; larger Wikipedia samples reduce performance, and feature engineering and reinitialization do not help.

solution_title: Label Denoising with Large Ensembles of Heterogeneous Neural Networks
solution_summary: The pipeline trained heterogeneous first-level neural networks using video-level and frame-level data. Their predictions were averaged across folds and merged into features for a second-level LightGBM model. LightGBM outputs supplied soft labels for subsequent TensorFlow ensemble models. Out-of-fold predictions from those models trained the final ensemble.
The post links to the team's model report hosted on GitHub. It invites comments and questions about that report. The provided post contains no technical description of the solution.

The solution blended LightGBM, XGBoost, and two neural networks, largely reusing the author's previous month's approach with parameter changes and categorical-feature handling. Optuna optimized blend weights using cross-validation out-of-fold predictions. The blend achieved 0.84228 private and 0.84157 public scores, improving on every individual model. Experiments with a denoising autoencoder were unsuccessful.

The solution combined XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost variants with target-specific categorical encoding and outlier removal. Optuna was used to optimize weighted ensembling, and the submitted blending approach used an arithmetic weighted mean. A geometric mean of five results achieved 0.88951 and handled outlier predictions better, but was not the selected approach. Neural networks generally performed poorly except on Other Faults.

The solution ensembles fine-tuned language models with support vector regression using pretrained embeddings. Embedding extraction varies pooling strategies and maximum input lengths across several transformer checkpoints. A very low layer-wise learning-rate decay factor combined with a high learning rate improved cross-validation and public leaderboard performance. The reported DeBERTa-v3-base example used AWP and achieved CV 0.44912, public score 0.436664, and private score 0.440466.

The team broke the ciphers and reconstructed preprocessing to match decoded text to possible classes. They narrowed ambiguous assignments using class occurrence counts, sampling without replacement, known training observations, and document difficulty consistency. Public submission scores and their ordering supplied constraints for evaluating candidate solutions locally. After manual reductions and an optimized C++ exhaustive search, they fixed a pipeline bug and obtained a perfect score.

solution_summary: The author trained protein classifiers with a custom F1 loss and combined them with teammates' BCE-trained models. Training used 512-by-512 RGBY images, HPA v18 external data, rare-class oversampling, and augmentation weighted by class frequency. The loss added BCE for classes absent from a batch and clamped negative-target probabilities to emphasize hard examples. A uniform threshold of 0.205 and replacement of poor-quality test images with similar better-quality images completed the approach; the latter improved the score by about 0.002. A five-fold SE-ResNeXt50 ensemble achieved private score 0.562 but was excluded from the final submission because of its weaker public score.

solution_title: 5th Place Solution - An ensemble of 53 OOFs
solution_summary: The author built a diverse ensemble dominated by XGBoost and LightGBM, with additional tree models, neural networks, and logistic regression. Diversity came from hyperparameter changes, different fold counts, and augmenting training with one to six copies of the original dataset. Treating numerical features as categorical, sometimes alongside their numerical representations or after binning, improved results. The selected submission scored 0.38502 on the private leaderboard, while the highest-CV alternative scored 0.38509.

The author improved a public notebook approach with stricter answer parsing, explicit time management, and sequential sampling. Rejecting malformed or invalid answers increased the public score from 14 to 19 without other changes. Sequential selection was more stable than Thompson sampling, and the final approach reached public scores around 19–20. The submission failed on the private evaluation.

solution_title: Prudential Life Insurance Assessment, Winner's Interview: 2nd place, Bogdan Zhurakovskyi
solution_summary: Linear regression gave the author's best results, with extensively tuned XGBoost achieving similar performance. The models were compared using kappa scores across 200 random train/test splits with a 30% test fraction. The main insight was that simple linear models can match or outperform more complex algorithms on this dataset. The writeup does not describe additional features or a final ensemble.

The solution stacked out-of-fold predictions from 35 models drawn from public notebooks and the author's own training runs. Its strength came from model diversity, since no individual model exceeded 0.97 on either leaderboard. The final submissions used single-level and two-level stacking, with a public GPU logistic regression stacker playing a key role. A ridge stacker augmented with three original features achieved the best retrospective private score of 0.97045, but was not selected.

Character inference depended on flipped images and retaining progressively better candidates, while another challenge was solved by brute-forcing an API. solution_summary: The solution convexly blended two independent pipelines built around particle filtering and multi-scale typewell matching, with LightGBM, CatBoost, and Ridge above them. Fold-safe development was the central safeguard against public leaderboard overfitting. The final scores were 7.764 public and 9.064 private, while oracle analysis suggested that further gains were limited by an inability to infer the direction of far-tail errors.

solution_summary: The author trained separate transformer agents from scratch with PPO self-play in a JAX recreation of the game. Timing-focused observations, an analytic shot planner, auxiliary future-state prediction, and early episode termination improved learning. Candidate targets were restricted to four high-logit targets plus four random targets to reduce planner cost. Historical opponent sampling rescued four-player training, while the two-player agent overfit to its own playstyle despite strong local evaluations.

solution_title: 3rd place solution: VQA/AES=0.81/0.64 Diffusion model + differentiable SVG optimization
solution_summary: The pipeline generated eight FLUX bitmap candidates per description, vectorized them with vtracer, and selected promising SVGs using SigLIP and short aesthetic optimization. A differentiable approximation of evaluation preprocessing helped align refinement with the scoring process. Compression, size searches, and optional path pruning kept the final SVG within the 10KB limit.
