VizWiz captions were particularly important for leaderboard generalization, alongside regenerated SD2 images from Diffusion DB and smaller COCO and Lexica datasets. Linear probing before fine-tuning, EMA, and layer-wise learning-rate decay helped preserve pretrained representations. solution_title: Congratulations, thanks and what worked (and what didn't) for me.
solution_summary: The final solution combined XGBoost and Keras neural networks through blending and stacking. Strong XGBoost results came from lower learning rates, much longer early stopping patience, and a fair objective constant of 0.4. Blending R and Python XGBoost predictions achieved a reported leaderboard score of 1103.5. Stacking used proper out-of-fold predictions, but the author attributed the final setback to insufficient attention to leakage during blend optimization.

solution_summary: The approach fine-tuned a Nemotron model with LoRA on carefully structured reasoning traces from original and synthetic problems. Trace design emphasized explicit local computation, consistent references, and uniform rules, with generation differences guiding repeated revisions. A bit-manipulation solver reduced complex cases to five templates and two anchor tables, achieving 99.4% exact match before model training. Category-specific operation priors and a rebalanced training mix provided additional gains, while final training reportedly reached 99% bit-manipulation solve rate after about eleven hours.
compute: RTX 6000 Pro through Colab Pro G4 and Kaggle compute; approximately $120 total spend and 11 hours for final training.

solution_summary: The team extended a popular Swin image model with supplied metadata and image dimensions, aspect ratios, and file size. These features improved cross-validation by about 0.3 and the leaderboard score by about 0.2, and the final submission used ten folds. They also used SVR ensemble heads with a search over the C parameter. A dual-output BCE and RMSE objective improved validation but was abandoned after weaker leaderboard results, despite later showing promise on the private leaderboard.

The model represented each assessment using its preceding 80 game sessions and up to 100 events per session. A hierarchical network used shared fully connected event layers followed by a session-level transformer, with tied accuracy-group embeddings improving QWK. Explicit blank categories worked better than transformer masking. Blending out-of-fold predictions with training targets improved the private score from 0.550 to 0.554, although it complicated validation and encouraged overfitting.

solution_title: 3rd place solution + my first Kaggle competition! 🎉
solution_summary: The author built an agent configuration that trained LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost, and a logistic regression baseline. Out-of-fold validation determined whether to use the best single model or a blend. The workflow submitted an early baseline and iterated on features within a 60-minute session budget. Local configuration validation helped address failed submissions caused by schema errors.

solution_title: part of 4th place solution: GAPNet & dual loss ResNet
solution_summary: The team emphasized diversity and combined around 25 models using different architectures and validation schemes. The author's GAPNet variants used a pretrained ResNet18 backbone, multiscale pooling, SE blocks, and external HPA images. A second contribution used ResNet34 with an auxiliary segmentation loss derived from the green channel to regularize classification. Combining these contributions improved the reported public score from 0.609 for the GAPNet ensemble to 0.618.

solution_title: 24th Place Solution 🏅 - My second ever Kaggle competition 🔥
solution_summary: The solution ensembled XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost using ten-fold training. Geographic features included distances to large California cities and the coastline, PCA coordinates, rotated coordinates, and polar coordinates. Optuna was used for light tuning of XGBoost. Model decisions relied on a local 80/20 validation split that excluded the original dataset, which the author reports generalized well to the private leaderboard.

The team trained XLM-RoBERTa Large, MuRIL Large, and RemBERT on several QA datasets while oversampling the competition data. Five-fold validation used only original competition validation examples, with early stopping based on Jaccard score. A custom softmax normalized start and end logits across all context splits, making scores more comparable across models and raising the public score from 0.809 to 0.821. Custom punctuation handling and Tamil stemming provided additional improvements.

solution_summary: The pipeline first trained an EfficientNet-B4 segmentation model on partial annotations to locate four tube types and background. Its out-of-fold predictions supplied five additional channels to image classifiers trained at resolution 640. Patient-level validation, multihead classification, and shared pretrained starting points improved cross-validation performance. Simple averaging of four classifiers reached 0.968 CV, 0.971 public, and 0.973 private. A segmentation variant predicting all 11 labels plus background did not work.

The team experimented with YOLO versions, image resolutions, random seeds, and repeated training/validation splits. Training used mosaic, mixup, perspective, shear, and automatic augmentation. Their final ensemble combined self-trained YOLO v8 and v10 models with public YOLO v10 and v11 models, giving their strongest leaderboard results.

Elapsed-time features, previous-group prediction probabilities, and prior-group features were central to the approach. Click aggregates and selected recap features helped, while neural-network blends and several spatial or embedding features did not. solution_title: 81st Place Solution for the Stanford Ribonanza RNA Folding Competition
solution_summary: The author replaced an initial 12-layer Transformer with repeated groups of three Conv1D blocks followed by a Transformer block. Training data were filtered to reads of at least 100, and selected unreliable reactivity targets were set to NaN and excluded from loss calculations. A final ensemble improved the public score to 0.14381 but worsened the private score to 0.18093 because it included a seed variant with poor generalization across sequence lengths. The author identified missing validation on test-like lengths as a major weakness.

The authors generated 20-question game demonstrations with GPT-4o and fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B on successful games. Their guesser received a concise hint summarizing prior rounds, while the answerer answered each question without game history. On 108 held-out keywords, behavior cloning increased Llama's success rate from 5.56% to 24.07%, compared with GPT-4o's 23.15%. The resulting guesser remained sensitive to incorrect answers, and the answerer sometimes mishandled alphabetical questions.

solution_summary: The solution combined tabular regressors, voxel-based neural networks, and models trained on brain-parcellation signals. LightGBM and XGBoost used tabular inputs, voxel statistics, and selected neural hidden features. Prediction distributions were screened for train-test discrepancies, and cross-domain interactions fed linear SVM and LightGBM stacking models whose predictions were blended. Model diversity and removing noisy predictions mattered most, while several alternative stacking methods and pseudo-labeling failed.

The solution combined CNN, LSTM and GRU forecasts with LightGBM models. Validation reproduced the forecast horizon and weekly boundary while excluding future information across all series, then models were retrained on the latest data. Averaging ten random initializations and predictions from every epoch improved robustness. Adjusted promotion information improved the public score but performed poorly on the private leaderboard.

The author trained separate IMU-only and full-sensor classifiers using multibranch CNNs, phase-specific GRUs, and attention, mean, and max pooling. The full model additionally extracted spatial TOF features with a 2D CNN and fused TOF and THM sensors with a Performer. Physical sensor corrections, quaternion cleanup, model-specific augmentation, and ten-fold subject-grouped validation were central to the pipeline. Fold logits were averaged at inference, yielding CV scores of 0.842 for IMU-only and 0.898 for full data, with a private leaderboard score of 0.845.

solution_summary: The Tile pipeline used a four-block relational graph convolutional network with node opcodes defining relations and ListMLE as its ranking objective. For Layout datasets, the team used three GATv2 blocks and repeatedly concatenated configuration features so that information from the relatively few configured nodes would survive message passing. Configuration embeddings and one-hot vectors, together with a virtual node for graph representation, were central to this approach. Reported Layout Kendall-Tau CV scores ranged from approximately 0.3 to 0.94 across the four datasets.

The solution ensembled four Cascade Mask R-CNN models with ConvNeXt Tiny and ConvNeXt V2 Base backbones. Training used only the blood-vessel class, image augmentation, and two validation folds separated by whole-slide image. Inference combined six image scales, weighted boxes fusion, and hard voting over masks. The ensemble achieved a private score of 0.541 without dilation, while clipping masks to fused boxes was tested but omitted from the final submission.

The author created two small datasets covering rewrite-prompt recovery and original-text type classification. Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 was supervised fine-tuned for each task, and combining rewrite-prompt predictions from three models produced a small improvement. Experiments with expanded text types, Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1, and PPO did not work well. The post also acknowledges a shared mean prompt scoring 0.63 that the author could not improve.

The main solution equally averages one LightGBM model on raw features and five neural networks trained on denoising-autoencoder representations. It removes calc features, one-hot encodes categorical features, and applies RankGauss normalization for neural networks. Autoencoders learn from train and test features using swap noise, with hidden activations supplying supervised inputs. Five-fold validation guides modeling, and a second selected blend adds 32-bag variants and a lightly weighted public script for a small score increase from 0.2965 to 0.2969.
compute: GTX 1080 Ti for neural networks; models can run with 32 GB RAM using data swapping

solution_summary: The post describes signal-offset correction rather than a complete modeling pipeline. Class-conditional signal averages exposed anomalous offsets in training batches 4 and 9, which were corrected with batch-specific additive shifts. For test data, KDE comparisons against corrected training data revealed a similar misalignment in group 4, addressed by adding 2.750 to its signal. The author identified this preprocessing idea as the most useful of their experiments but did not quantify its score improvement.

The approach scores candidate answers using positional distances between question and answer words in a corpus. For each word pair, it takes the 20th percentile of minimum within-document distances and converts it to an inverse square-root score. It aggregates pair scores by their median and selects the highest-scoring answer. Performance began to converge around 0.38–0.40 with more than 2,500 corpus pages, while memory usage was approximately 2–3 GB.
compute: Approximately 2–3 GB memory

solution_title: 69th solution of this competition without hacking metrics
solution_summary: The team ensembled LightGBM and CatBoost using 610 and 535 selected features respectively. Retaining highly sparse features, converting dates to day offsets, and reducing high-cardinality string values improved performance. Main complexity parameters were set manually, with Optuna tuning the remaining parameters. The reported best private score was 0.524 without a date hack and 0.591 with it; the adopted similarity-based date inference did not deliver the expected improvement.

The solution generated recommendation candidates with four recall models and ranked them with LightGBM LambdaRank. A gated two-tower mixture-of-experts model supplied candidates, embedding similarities, and demographic-based recommendations for users without purchase history. Text and image clusters provided additional product features, including for cold-start items. The final submission combined earlier submissions; the best reported local CV and leaderboard scores were 0.039 and 0.0349.

solution_summary: The solution used a modified Fastai tabular model with several submodules and pitch-control features evaluated at 224 locations ahead of the rusher. Its outputs passed through softplus, were normalized into probabilities, and were cumulatively summed for direct CRPS optimization. Plays were standardized so rushers moved toward increasing Y, producing an additional reported leaderboard improvement of 0.00010. Pitch control contributed an estimated improvement between 0.00010 and 0.00030, while the author regretted leaving inconsistencies in speed and acceleration uncleaned.

solution_summary: The solution used a two-stage pipeline with CenterNet detection followed by ResNet-based character classification, developed on Google Colab without pretrained models. Validation grouped examples by book title, and the classifier concatenated object aspect ratio and size at its fully connected layer. Both stages used augmentation, test-time augmentation, and ensembles, while pseudo-labeling was more useful than attempted domain adaptation. The shallow detector achieved approximately 0.90 IoU, 0.98 F1 at IoU above 0.5, and 0.99 center-based F1.

solution_title: [24th Place Solution] A Population-Based Reinforcement Learning Ecosystem
solution_summary: The solution bootstrapped a small Transformer policy from LightGBM imitation teachers and then improved it with population-based PPO and GAE. Teachers trained on a small replay collection generated tens of thousands of games for policy and value distillation. A roughly one-million-parameter Transformer represented board state and legal actions as tokens, supporting sequential choices through a pointer head. Fast C++ inference enabled extensive match collection and evaluation, while matchup-specific experts and human feedback guided policy and deck development.

solution_summary: The solution removed 13 bad images, resized inputs to 320 by 512, and trained augmented U-Net segmentation models. Seven model variants used different encoders, CBAM attention, and either hypercolumns or feature pyramid attention, with five folds per variant. Training combined BCE and Lovasz hinge losses with deep supervision, Adam, and cosine warm restarts. Averaging 35 models, flip-based test-time augmentation, and cross-validated mask thresholds produced public and private scores of 0.67698 and 0.66713.

The pipeline corrects image orientation, retrieves candidate pairs with DINOv2, and extracts ALIKE features from cropped image patches. LightGlue matching and tuned RANSAC filtering provide correspondences for COLMAP reconstruction with a Simple-Radial camera model. Geometric consistency and keypoint refinement are the main improvements over public baselines. Across the listed validation datasets, average score, mAA, and clusterness were 48.55%, 42.07%, and 85.08%.

solution_summary: The author trained several MMDetection detector families using five folds, primarily at 1024×1024 resolution. The central strategy was to pretrain on all data and then fine-tune on rare radiologists while preserving fold assignments and retaining a controlled number of empty images. Augmentation, mixed precision where supported, and cosine annealing with warm-up supported training. Higher-resolution GFL variants and class-balanced sampling were explored, with sampling providing no improvement and the 2048-resolution variants scoring worse privately than their 1024 counterparts.

The author built 135 sets of out-of-fold and test predictions using XGBoost and LightGBM. The final prediction averaged logistic-regression stacking with a hill-climbing ensemble of those predictions. Treating every feature as categorical and adding the original data improved performance, along with selected XGBoost settings. CatBoost was excluded, feature engineering was unhelpful, and additional predictions sometimes worsened hill-climbing performance.

solution_summary: The approach modifies CenterNet to detect helmet impacts from sequences of 15 consecutive video frames, using an EfficientB5 feature extractor and separate detection heads for individual frames. Training emphasizes impact-containing frames and combines independently computed losses for impact and non-impact helmets with a weighted sum. Video augmentation supports the temporal input pipeline. Post-processing links nearby detections with IOU-Tracker, retains the middle box of each trajectory, and applies a confidence threshold that varies over the course of the video.

The author used a single XGBoost model after disappointing results from ensembles in previous competitions. Validation followed a community-proposed cross-validation approach, whose details were not included. Most engineered features based on V1–V28 were unhelpful, while one linked feature slightly improved cross-validation.

The solution combined five XLM-RoBERTa-large, five MuRIL, and four RemBERT question-answering models through hard voting. SQuAD2 fine-tuning preceded competition training, with seed diversity for XLM-RoBERTa and fold diversity for the other architectures. Linear warm-up and early stopping supported training, while additional Tamil datasets and hyperparameter tuning improved the public score. The final reported public/private scores were 0.808/0.770, and several alternative ensemble and augmentation approaches did not help.

solution_title: 1st Place Winning Solution - Hungry for Gold
solution_summary: The final solution was a weighted blend of seven models spanning multistage neural stacking, TabNet, simple neural networks, a residual network, and DeepInsight CNNs. Blend weights reflected leaderboard performance and prediction diversity, while an alternative blend optimized out-of-fold weights with Optuna and SLSQP. Feature engineering included dimensionality reduction, quantile transforms, clustering, and gene and cell summary statistics; label smoothing and multiple seeds helped regularization and stability. DeepInsight CNNs added useful diversity and improved private log loss by about 0.00008, with the final blend reaching 0.01599.

The author reduced the arm configuration problem to a point-space traveling salesman problem by restricting the arm's degrees of freedom. They modified the standard configuration near the start and return paths and computed transition costs between configurations for LKH. The resulting tour was rotated to the desired starting point, converted back into configurations, and cleaned of duplicates. The restrictions simplified optimization but limited efficient movement between quadrants.

The solution used a two-stage U-Net teacher–student pipeline to combine catheter segmentation with classification. A teacher learned five-channel masks and eleven classification targets from annotated images, then supplied soft masks for student training on the full labeled dataset. Validation used five-fold GroupKFold separately for annotated and unannotated images. A hillclimb ensemble with identity and horizontal-flip inference achieved 0.968 public and 0.972 private scores.

solution_summary: The solution averaged two DeBERTa-v3-large configurations, each trained on four prompt-grouped folds, for eight inference checkpoints. The configurations differed in input formatting and pooling, using summary-only mean pooling or GeM pooling over the question and summary. Restricting pooling to the relevant text was the largest source of improvement, and individual model CV scores were 0.482 and 0.492. Cross-attention variants, separate backbone passes, layer changes, longer inputs, and ensembles with other backbones did not yield significant improvements.

The solution stacked logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost predictions using a calibrated ridge meta-model. Each base model used five stratified folds and three random seeds, with local cross-validation guiding decisions. All original features were retained, using sparse one-hot encoding for logistic regression and ordinal encoding for trees. Probability clipping produced final public and private scores of 1.08564 and 1.08763.

solution_title: [8th] Place Solution for the [Predict Calorie Expenditure] Competition
solution_summary: The final solution blended predictions from three TensorFlow models, one CatBoost model, and one XGBoost model. Hill climbing selected additions and optimized their blending weights, starting from the CatBoost prediction. The author's private TensorFlow models supplied diversity alongside unchanged public tree-model notebooks. The reported ensemble RMSE improved from 0.058812503 to 0.05846814.

The solution used a simple activity-level XGBoost model augmented with strong group-and-date leakage features. Confidence-ordered heuristic scores captured matching dates, surrounding outcomes, extrapolation, and unseen groups, and training scores were generated by excluding each person in turn. Additional predictors included person-excluded target means for char_10 and continuous group_1 values. Postprocessing combined the most extreme prediction within each group with individual activity predictions at 90/10 weights and applied rule-based overrides.

solution_title: 14th Place Gold - Image Text Decision Boundary
solution_summary: The solution combined RAPIDS TF-IDF features, EfficientNet image embeddings, and multilingual XLM-RoBERTa text embeddings. A cross-validation-derived piecewise linear boundary jointly considered image and text cosine distances, improving the reported score from 0.730 to 0.750. Graph-based match corrections, product-specific boundary adjustments, and unit consistency checks further raised the reported score to 0.770.

The team combined public-notebook features with counts, LDA topics, t-SNE representations, and classifier-derived probabilities and expectations. TabPFN, MLPClassifier, and MultinomialNB used 100 PCA components, and their outputs augmented an ensemble of XGBoost and six linear regressors. Repeated LOFO selection reduced roughly 1,400 features to about 350, and linear regression determined ensemble weights. Five-fold stratified validation guided selection alongside public leaderboard improvements; reported scores were approximately 0.592 CV, 0.570 public, and 0.566 private.

The final approach trained EVA, ConvNeXt, and Swin models on millions of Stable Diffusion 2 images generated from external image and video captions. Caption filtering, similarity deduplication, and multiple generated images per caption helped shape the training data. Models used mixed precision, horizontal flips, and a revised cosine-plus-MSE objective during retraining. Fourteen models were combined with equal weights and resolution-based test-time augmentation, while captioning pipelines were abandoned because inference was too slow.

solution_title: 43rd Position - Blending with Quasi-MC AND TPE
solution_summary: The solution combined extensive astronomical feature engineering and feature selection with a diverse pool of tree models, neural tabular models, and a stacking model. Features included color differences, redshift interactions, spatial coordinates, category statistics, and frequency counts, with retention guided by cross-validation. Optuna optimized ensemble weights against out-of-fold balanced accuracy using Sobol exploration followed by TPE refinement. The final blend achieved OOF balanced accuracy of 0.97030 and a private score of 0.97025, while MLflow supported reproducible experiment tracking.

solution_title: 54th place solution [No lottery - just a baseline]
solution_summary: The solution blended a LightGBM Tweedie model and a WaveNet model with a GRU component using weights of 0.8 and 0.2. Validation used three temporal windows, including a prior-year window chosen to resemble the final evaluation season. Median absolute deviation identified spikes, which were replaced with values from seven days earlier, and LightGBM predicted demand differences relative to 28 days earlier. Rolling mean-to-median ratios helped, while several custom losses, encodings, and stock or hierarchy corrections did not work.

solution_title: 2nd place - NNs sometimes work better than GBMs
solution_summary: The solution built a diverse 75-model ensemble dominated by 60 TabM models, with neural networks accounting for all but seven members. Diversity came from combinations of roughly 170–700 engineered features, about six tuned hyperparameter sets, and models predicting residuals from linear formulas. Genetic programming contributed 14 features intended to approximate the original data-generating formula. TabM was the strongest individual model, achieving 8.59254 private RMSE, and reliable CV–LB correlations supported selection of two final ensembles.

The author used probit generalized linear models driven primarily by opponent-adjusted offensive and defensive efficiency. The final prediction weighted approaches based on efficiency, box-score statistics, and gambling-related features, with an ad hoc spread/data weighting. Validation held out each of 16 seasons in turn, and some probabilities were manually adjusted. The reported private leaderboard score was 0.43148, with model execution taking roughly 30 seconds after historical statistics were prepared.

Localization combined 3D ConvNeXt slice predictors with 2D ConvNeXt and EfficientNet coordinate regressors, including domain-specific pretraining. Severity models used bidirectional LSTMs and attention-based multiple-instance learning with auxiliary losses. Perturbing slice indices during training improved robustness to localization errors, and the architecture changes and ensembling improved the reported public score from about 0.37 to 0.33.

solution_summary: The solution fused FLAIR, T1w, T1wCE, and T2w MRI sequences into four-channel images at ten uniformly sampled positions per patient. A convolution mapped these inputs to three channels for a pretrained EfficientNet B0, whose frame embeddings fed two LSTM layers and a binary prediction head. Training used normalized 256-by-256 images, simple consistent augmentations, binary cross-entropy, and Adam for 15 epochs. Predictions were averaged across five stratified folds; the author reported public scores of 0.65–0.67 and cautioned that the results were not clinically useful.

solution_title: [12th solution] Full, reproducible solution with code
solution_summary: The solution used a CTC encoder combining transformer and convolution layers, with positional encoding added before the first transformer layer. Inputs comprised selected facial, hand, and pose landmarks using X/Y coordinates and temporal differences at offsets of one and two frames. Circular-window augmentation and two-stage sample filtering supported training a roughly 15.5-million-parameter model for 1,500 epochs, achieving public and private scores of 0.794 and 0.779. Submission constraints required 16-bit quantization and reducing the maximum input length to 320 frames, with negligible reported score loss from quantization.
compute: Most training on Colab TPU; final model trained for 1,500 epochs.

solution_title: 22nd Place Solution - Z3 Constraint Satisfaction Solver
solution_summary: The author explored constraint solving, shape lookup, segmentation, neural networks, and tree models for reversing Game of Life. Z3 produced the best reported score of 0.08410, but required extensive distributed notebook execution. A much faster segmentation solver separated independent shapes and matched their histories using symmetry-invariant hashes, scoring 0.08631. Neural networks solved forward simulation reliably but performed poorly on reversal, while pixelwise tree experiments exceeded execution limits.
compute: Approximately 5000 hours on 4 CPUs for Z3, using nine notebook forks; GPU experiments also reported.

solution_summary: The final solution averaged three ResNet200d models with different preprocessing, including two pretrained on ChestX and one on ImageNet. Large image cutouts and motion blur reduced overfitting, while CLAHE slightly improved cross-validation for one model. Validation used stratified group folds for two models and stratified folds for the third. Increasing inference resolution by 100 pixels provided a small leaderboard improvement.

solution_summary: The solution trained a CNN on sampled cells using image-level labels through pooled cell features. During inference, removing the pooling across cells allowed the same classifier to produce individual cell predictions. The most useful post-processing reduced predictions for border cells, followed by cell-level fine-tuning using out-of-fold predictions. Blending each cell prediction with the image's average cell prediction provided an additional improvement.

The team moved from ResNet50 to Inception models in Keras and trained using one iteratively stratified 85/15 split. Helpful methods included class balancing, weighted losses, cosine warm restarts, standard image augmentation, and occasional removal of the green channel and labels. External data was limited to rare classes, with duplicates removed. Their best private result was 0.505 from six SE-BNInception models with fixed thresholds, but this candidate was not selected because its validation and public scores were worse.
compute: Primarily one 1080Ti with 64GB RAM; occasionally 1060 workstations with 8–16GB RAM. A ramdisk with swap provided approximately 3x loading speedup.

solution_summary: The final submission stacked 60 models by transforming their predictions into logits and fitting cuML logistic regression. The base ensemble mainly contained XGBoost and tabular neural networks, supplemented by linear models, public-model ports, and specialized models. A shared five-fold split enabled consistent comparison, with ensemble diversity and cross-validation guiding selection. The final reported CV AUC was 0.94697 and private AUC was 0.94602, without pseudo-labeling.

solution_summary: The solution centered on GPT-OSS-120B with Python tools, efficient vLLM serving, and multiple reasoning attempts. Cleaned mathematical benchmarks supported model selection and inference experiments, while speculative decoding and sampling optimization improved throughput. Judge-corrected answer selection was the most promising improvement over majority voting, although the provided excerpt does not fully specify the submitted scaffold. Pruning, distillation, and reinforcement learning did not produce reliable gains, and the reported private score was 26.5.

solution_summary: The solution uniformly averaged probabilities from DeBERTa QA-style models trained with pseudo-labeled instances. Pseudo-labels were retained when all cross-validation models agreed, removing roughly one third of instances and improving the leaderboard score by 0.001–0.002, although validation scores were inflated by leakage. Confidence-based filtering performed worse, while pseudo-labels from ensemble outputs performed similarly but were not selected. Training used RAdam, a fixed learning rate, gradient clipping, and carefully initialized output weights. Both reported final ensembles achieved 0.893 on the public leaderboard and 0.892 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: We killed 33 of our 35 experiments. The other two won us bronze. [496/5375]
solution_summary: The final pipeline combined a likelihood-weighted particle filter with a GBDT and physics stack, then added trajectory corrections, a nearby-well donor shift, a bidirectional GRU, and global recalibration. Frozen multi-axis validation gates governed component acceptance, with no tuning against the public leaderboard. The GRU supplied the largest individual gain and improved isolated wells that the spatial donor approach could not address. Deployment fixes restored silently disabled donor and GRU components, and the selected submission scored 8.983 privately against approximately 8.71 OOF.
compute: Three-week development period; GRU trained for 150 epochs with hidden size 192 and two seeds.

solution_summary: The solution used an XGBoost multiclass classifier with shuffled four-fold stratified cross-validation. Feature engineering combined symptom clusters with more than 6,000 pairwise AND, OR, and XOR features derived from binary inputs. Starting from the original features, the author selected additional features according to MAP@3 performance. SelectKBest and Boruta-SHAP performed worse than this model-driven selection procedure.

The final solution blended six 2D EfficientNets with three 1D CNNs, including two ResNets with Transformer heads. Bandpass filtering, CQT inputs, and waveform augmentation were central to performance. The team stabilized early training through InstanceNorm replacement or a two-epoch warm-up that trained BatchNorm and the linear head while freezing other encoder layers. Fine-tuning at a small learning rate without augmentation pushed performance above 0.88 on the public leaderboard, while adding 1D models consistently improved blends.

The team first trained SE-ResNeXt-101 and EfficientNet-B6 on individual CT slices represented by three windowed channels. Out-of-fold predictions were then assembled into patient-level sequences and used to train a small convolutional model over neighboring slices and labels. Both stages used weighted log loss and Adam, with cross-validation supplying the second-stage training data. Incorporating sequential information improved the private score from 0.05425 to 0.04793.

solution_title: 86th place solution, with full source code of keras-yolo3
solution_summary: The author used a Keras implementation of YOLOv3 for object detection and converted Open Images annotations to its required format. Training included learning-rate range finding, a cyclic learning-rate scheduler, and gradient accumulation through SGDAccum. The shared pipeline also covered model verification and submission generation. Limited time and GPU resources constrained experimentation, and the final private score was 0.16889.

The author used a random forest with out-of-fold predictions and no hyperparameter tuning. The main customization was constructing cross-validation folds using PCA to minimize differences between folds and selecting the number of folds. The writeup emphasizes trusting cross-validation because public leaderboard performance was misleading.

The author used order-one Fourier features to represent the dataset's strong seasonality. Hybrid models were tuned with grid search and then ensembled. GDP per capita improved the public score during experimentation but was excluded after ordinary GDP showed slightly higher correlation with the target. The post provides selected methodological details and refers readers to a full notebook.

The post consists solely of a link to a GitHub repository for the Favorita competition. It provides no description of the approach, experiments, or results. No solution details can be extracted from the supplied text.

The author used an RTKLIB baseline with a lower elevation mask and base station values accounting for tectonic plate movement. Postprocessing detected implausible position jumps, interpolated outliers and applied several position shift variants, which delivered much of the improvement. A public stopping correction algorithm provided little cross-validation benefit, while LightGBM velocity prediction did not work well. A uniform pipeline enabled Bayesian hyperparameter optimization against ground truth after excluding problematic paths.

The agents used distributed IMPALA with staged training against easy and hard bots, followed by self-play. Relative, grouped vector features and fully connected networks supported CPU-based training. Checkpoint rewards established basic attacking skills before self-play switched to scoring rewards alone. Action masking accelerated learning but restricted passing tactics, and a model trained without masks achieved the author's highest submitted score.
compute: Initially 80 CPU cores (~190k episodes/week); 1000 CPU cores per competition experiment at 20k+ fps; maximum 2500 CPU cores in the last two weeks. GPUs were unnecessary.

solution_summary: The author center-cropped and downsampled images to 84×84, then divided each heart's images into three anatomical regions. A neural network directly predicted both CDFs from randomly sampled regional images and odd or even time steps, with translations and flips for augmentation. Inference combined many sampled and augmented views, with inverse-CDF averaging performing slightly better than direct CDF averaging. Deeper networks and higher resolutions caused severe overfitting.
compute: Could run overnight on a three-year-old MacBook Pro.

solution_title: #8 solution: Ensemble of 15 same NN models
solution_summary: The solution feeds 120 engineered interaction features into a four-layer transformer encoder with a fully connected classifier, using sequences of length 128. User history, content difficulty, user–content differences, timing, and answer-choice behavior supply the main predictive signals. Robust normalization clips feature outliers before centering and scaling, while validation combines unseen users with time-split histories of shared users. An ensemble of five folds and three snapshots per fold achieved reported public/private scores of 0.814/0.816, with online inference taking less than four hours.
compute: Online inference for 15 neural models took less than 4 hours; each model file was approximately 7 MB. Hardware was not stated.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution - JAPE: Just Another Proper Ensemble
solution_summary: The final submission used AutoGluon to ensemble 136 out-of-fold prediction sets from a diverse collection of models. Diversity came from model families, feature engineering, hyperparameters, fold choices, and inclusion or exclusion of the original dataset. A prediction-flipping adjustment improved the selected submission to a private score of 0.97801. Late baseline-initialized boosting experiments were not selected, while a faster neural-network and hill-climbing ensemble tested after the deadline exceeded the AutoGluon results.
compute: AutoGluon ran on CPU for close to 12 hours per run; the post-deadline neural ensembler took nearly one GPU-hour and the alternative ensemble under 1.5 hours overall.

solution_title: 39th place solution, submission errors and memory leakage
solution_summary: The solution blended dedicated BERT models for questions, answers, and their combination, using title-grouped validation and weighted binary cross-entropy. Higher loss weights emphasized sparse target columns. Column-specific mapping of extreme predictions to zero or one produced the stronger private result, scoring 0.40901. Optimized target quantization showed public gains but reduced private performance, while Keras memory leakage limited ensemble size.

The team expanded the image dataset using private and Flickr images filtered by camera metadata, editing history and licensing. Separate ensembles handled unaltered and manipulated images, averaging CNN scores across architectures and patch sizes. Small-patch training followed by larger-patch fine-tuning and dedicated detectors for difficult manipulation classes improved performance. A compact pair of Xception models achieved public and private scores of 0.986666 and 0.981309.
compute: NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPU with 16GB RAM

solution_title: Kagengers: How to fall from top (2nd public/very low private)
solution_summary: The team combined LSTM and BERT predictions through a LightGBM stacker augmented with text statistics. Vocabulary-aware cleaning, a weighted multitarget binary loss, and splitting long comments into shorter BERT segments were useful components. Cross-validation predictions supplied stacking features, and group weight adjustments improved the combined AUC objective. A configuration with three LSTMs and two small BERT variants achieved 0.94639 publicly, but late model rebuilding introduced fold leakage, errors, and an unstable final mix.
compute: Training on Kaggle kernels; reported achievable configuration inference approximately 3600 seconds.

solution_summary: The author explores pairwise excerpt comparison as an alternative to direct readability regression, explicitly separate from the team's final solution. Random excerpt pairs receive probability targets derived from their Bradley–Terry scores, and a binary classification model learns these comparisons. At inference, a test excerpt is compared with a training excerpt whose known target anchors a log-odds conversion back to a readability score. A RoBERTa-Base starter notebook achieved private and public leaderboard scores of 0.477 and 0.500, respectively.

The final approach used a LightGBM stacker trained on three-class OOF probabilities from a diverse pool of tree, neural, and linear models. Diversity of errors mattered more than small improvements in individual model scores, with logistic regression providing especially valuable complementary predictions. Features included reciprocal conductivity, cyclic transformations, discretization, interactions, and categorical embeddings. The ensemble reached a reported public score near 0.98201, while hill climbing and blended meta-models underperformed the single LightGBM stacker. YDF and GraphSAGE were excluded after degrading ensemble results.
compute: CPU and GPU random forest training; a single SVM could take more than two hours

solution_summary: The solution used a DINOv3 large vision transformer with two-patch and eight-patch image inputs, LocalMambaBlock feature fusion, and a five-target regression head. Validation grouped rows by image and stratified by species after pooling rare species into an Other category. Training used competition-weighted MSE, EMA, mixup, and geometric augmentation. The submitted approaches were a single model and a two-patch/eight-patch ensemble with balance post-processing, achieving local CV scores of 0.8610 and 0.8660 and private leaderboard scores of 0.63. TTA, broader model ensembles, and additional appearance augmentations did not help.

The solution first detected helmets with Faster R-CNN and then classified impacts using temporal SlowFast networks. The strongest classifier processed 20-frame crops with RGB plus two helmet-center heatmap channels. Temporal label expansion, impact oversampling, and an IoU tracker helped train the models and suppress duplicate detections. Horizontal-flip test-time augmentation improved the private score to 0.6341, and adding a full-frame action detector increased it to 0.6355.
compute: Extracted video frames were stored on SSD; training hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution trained product-specific XGBoost models for each historical target month, using all available product ownership lags and purchase/drop history. Product-specific weighted averages combined the monthly models, with the largest weight generally assigned to June 2015. Post-processing adjusted prediction confidence, calibrated product totals, and incorporated dependencies between salary-related products to improve expected MAP. Two final ensembles combined selected submissions using weights informed by prediction correlations and public leaderboard feedback; stacking and bootstrapping performed worse.

The team manually implemented and optimized solutions for all 400 tasks. They first prioritized correctness, then studied short public solutions and repeatedly reduced code length. A custom dashboard prioritized tasks by score gaps, code-length gaps, and update history, supporting iterative improvements across teammates. The effort exceeded 1,000 hours over three months and drew on AI assistance and public code-golf resources.
compute: Over 1,000 hours of team effort across three months; hardware unspecified

solution_summary: The solution generated three sentiment-span candidates with multi-head BERT, RoBERTa and ELECTRA models, then reranked them with an additional ELECTRA scorer. Auxiliary token and tweet sentiment tasks supplemented start/end prediction, while smoothed targets and stochastic weight averaging supported training. Fold ensembles combined candidate scores across model families, and whitespace-aware preprocessing and postprocessing corrected character offsets. Cross-validation was around 0.732 over a broad range of weights, although the final weighting was sensitive and difficult to select reliably.

solution_title: MITSUI&CO. Commodity Prediction Challenge - 15th Place Solution Writeup
solution_summary: The solution combined attention, residual, and autoencoder networks with retraining every seven newly labeled test days. It engineered 2,658 financial features and selected 800 using mutual information, although selection considered only the first target. Purged cross-validation, a hybrid MSE–Spearman loss, and performance- and recency-based ensemble weights supported adaptation to changing markets. The final approach scored 0.445 in Round 3; a target-specific alternative scored better initially but failed to complete that round.

The team separated pneumothorax classification from segmentation and combined multiple networks for each task. A rule-based ensemble used classification probabilities, maximum pixel probabilities, and agreement between segmentation networks to decide whether to emit a mask. Hyperopt optimized ensemble composition, while a genetic-algorithm-like search selected per-image segmentation thresholds. Networks generally trained for 15–20 epochs with Adam and BCE or BCE plus Dice; joint classification-segmentation training and external data were unsuccessful.
compute: Main training used 2x2080 Ti and 2x1080 Ti machines; experiments also used P100 and V100. Lyan used 2080 Ti and P100 cards. Most networks trained for 15–20 epochs with batches of 1–2 per GPU.

solution_title: [102nd place] Rush Hour on the LB
solution_summary: The final submission blended two public models with a separately developed wins, draws, and losses regression approach, using approximately 64%, 33%, and 3% weights. The WDL component predicted proportions and used 236 features selected through iterative CV and leaderboard experiments. Clipping predictions and multiplying by 1.1 consistently gave a small public-score improvement. A separate DeepTables neural-network submission covered the possibility of a larger distribution shift.

The author trained one BERT-like attention network with eight outputs covering all coupling types, supervising only the relevant output for each example. Atom sequences, a learned classification token, pooled attention representations, and engineered molecular features fed residual and feed-forward layers. Training directly optimized the evaluation metric with Adam and a cyclic learning rate. A single model reached -2.607 after about 30 hours on a V100, with subsequent type-specific fine-tuning providing roughly another -0.015.
compute: GCP V100 GPU, around 30 hours, batch size 2048; initial Kaggle training ran for 9 hours with batch size 1024.

solution_summary: The solution split bird species by training-set size and combined CNN and sound event detection models trained with different losses. Common species used BCE-trained CNN and SED models, while rare species used focal-loss SED models with pseudo-label-guided cropping and manually expanded training examples. Noise mixing and other augmentations improved robustness, with mixup especially valuable for CNN training. Species-specific thresholds were critical, and the best-public submission scored 0.8750 publicly and 0.8126 privately.

solution_summary: The final submission used a LightGBM model with 1,200 features derived from the 200 original variables. The approach emphasized independent per-variable transformations, including count encoding, masking singleton values, and count-scaled normalized values. Identifying real test samples informed count encoding and experiments with adding test data to training. Stacking and test-data inclusion yielded larger cross-validation gains than leaderboard gains, while feature selection and pooling similar features were unsuccessful.

solution_title: 222th Place Solution: Correlation CV vs Public LB 0.16, vs Private LB 0.73
solution_summary: The solution combined ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet models with and without metadata and ResNeSt models without metadata. It used five-fold leak-free stratified validation, external melanoma training images, extensive augmentation, and 16-way test-time augmentation. Models were selected using out-of-fold scores and combined through weighted prediction ranks, with weights optimized by Optuna. The ensemble achieved 0.9534 CV and 0.9391 private AUC, and individual-model CV correlated much better with private than public scores. Oversampling, label smoothing, and a longer StepLR training schedule did not work well.

solution_summary: The strongest pipeline combined five YOLO models with a Cascade R-CNN using weighted boxes fusion, accepting R-CNN boxes only when they overlapped YOLO detections. A manually selected sequence validation set guided model selection and correlated strongly with private leaderboard performance. Adding missing annotations, including background images, and tracking each model's detections before fusion improved results. Optical flow helped reset trackers and reduce false positives, and the best pipeline achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.720.

solution_summary: The solution used a two-stage pipeline with a temporal convolutional base model and boosted-tree stackers trained on out-of-fold probabilities plus engineered features. Categorical embeddings were scaled using elapsed-time differences before three temporal convolution layers, skip connections, and readout. Validation used five-fold stratification by session correctness with five seeds, and additional fielddaylab data was included. Blending three stackers pushed local CV slightly above 0.7, but the author attributed weaker private performance to late over-tuning.

solution_title: 16th place solution (all you need to know)
solution_summary: The team averaged provider-specific ResNet34 and EfficientNet-B0/B1 models, adding an EfficientNet-B1 U-Net classifier for Radboud. Their preprocessing combined two tiling strategies, favored 25 tiles of 256 by 256 pixels, and replaced nearly white tiles with other tiles. Augmentation and removal or isolation of duplicates and noisy images improved validation. Radboud U-Nets used segmentation supervision and random-density tile selection, which brought a reported 0.01 improvement and helped stabilize the ensemble; segmentation was unsuccessful for Karolinska.
compute: Random-density Radboud U-Net training required around 128 epochs.

solution_title: 2nd Private LB/ 3rd Public LB Solution - Transformer
solution_summary: The solution corrected year-specific measurement differences and engineered 36 player and spatial features. A transformer with two encoder and two decoder layers relied on many attention heads. Validation always trained on 2017 data and held out week-grouped portions of 2018. Alternating learning rates and snapshot ensembling improved performance within the CPU training limit.
compute: Four-hour CPU training allowance; final full-data training repeated for 11000 seconds and 9000 seconds in safe mode.

solution_summary: The solution stacked diverse neural networks and LightGBM models, then equally blended LightGBM and XGBoost stackers. Its neural network combined categorical embeddings, numerical features, character TF-IDF, and recurrent-convolutional text features. Public-kernel features, image descriptors, user duplicate counts, and consecutive-item price differences helped. More folds and seed bagging improved performance; the best individual neural network and LightGBM scored 0.2194 and 0.2196.

Every categorical feature was count-encoded using combined training and test data. LightGBM models were trained with five-fold cross-validation, and their predictions were averaged. The submission achieved public and private scores of 0.68406 and 0.66474, respectively. The author reported no special submission-selection validation strategy and estimated about ten hours for the complete pipeline.
compute: About 10 hours for data processing, training, and prediction

solution_summary: The team emphasized fewer models and greater variation in data. They trained using a referenced 60k dataset, set maximum sequence length to 640, and froze embeddings and 18 layers. Attempts to improve document retrieval through Sentence Transformer changes or BM25 were unsuccessful, as were additional answer-prediction data and paid custom data. Expanding retrieval sources was constrained by a stated requirement for more than 200GB RAM.

solution_summary: The final approach predicted each UPDRS score using an optimized month trend adjusted by protein-dependent constant shifts. A protein was selected using its average correlation with the four targets, and separate shifts were optimized within protein quantile ranges. Missing values were forward-filled, predictions were rounded, and validation grouped patients to avoid leakage. The final reported score was 69.7, compared with 69.8 for an earlier Random Forest and trend hybrid.

The author built two LightGBM classifiers per question using complementary summaries of gameplay events. One feature set captured elapsed time by room and level, while the other measured relative frequencies of fqid groups. Question-specific ensemble weights were selected using a small portion of the training data, with an emphasis on efficient execution. The selected submissions achieved a highest private score of 0.689 with roughly half a minute of code execution and four to six minutes of scoring; an unselected submission reached 0.693 in about nine minutes overall.
compute: About 30 seconds of code execution and 4–6 minutes of scoring; another submission took about 9 minutes total.

solution_summary: The team extracted DOI candidates with regular expressions and validated them against the competition corpus and dataset prefixes derived from DataCite metadata. An LLM re-extracted uncertain DOI candidates from their original context, while DOI classification used semantics in the main text and author overlap in references. Accession IDs passed through regex extraction and contextual rules before LLM classification. The authors suspected these rules caused overfitting and regretted rejecting a simpler pure-LLM alternative.

solution_title: how a newbie got to public 19th place
solution_summary: The author extended a shared neural-network baseline with separate branches for game context, players, wind, and ranked spatial features. Direction normalization, mirrored training examples, and mirrored test prediction averaging improved robustness. Dropout, batch normalization, early stopping, and greater weight on 2018 data controlled overfitting and season differences. The safe submission trained on 2017–2018 data and reached a reported score of 0.01200 after the fourth rerun, while the aggressive submission deteriorated and was suspected to have fallen back to prior predictions.

The described 2.5D pipeline first classified whether targets were present and then controlled segmentation with those predictions. It stacked three slices at stride two and used U-Net segmentation with EfficientNet B4-B7 backbones. Classification learned from empty and positive images, while segmentation trained only on images containing masks with a weighted BCE-Dice loss. Model fusion and horizontal-flip inference augmentation brought the pure 2.5D approach to approximately 0.889 on the public leaderboard.

The solution combined an optimized constant prompt with output from Mistral 7B Instruct using a fixed response prefix. The constant prompt was built by greedily appending tokenizer vocabulary items that improved mean embedding similarity, with repeated uses of the Romanian word “lucrarea” proving useful. Validation subsets were selected to reproduce observed leaderboard scores, and differences between Torch and KerasHub ST5 implementations informed prompt length choices. Constant prompts alone achieved scores around 0.69, while Mistral performed slightly better than Gemma 1.1 in validation.
compute: P100 GPU job mentioned for greedy prompt search; no runtime stated.

solution_summary: The team used pre-release AutoGluon with an experimental 2024 zeroshot hyperparameter portfolio. Second-level stackers received only model predictions, while numeric target values were used to stratify cross-validation folds and reduce outlier-driven distribution shifts. Additional data and text feature generation were excluded after validation showed no convincing benefit. Extensive cross-validation supported selecting their first submission despite its weak public score of 72221.55.

The team built a five-stage instance segmentation pipeline centered on ResNeSt200 Mask R-CNN models. Cleaned LIVECell SH-SY5Y data, higher image resolution, and backbone fine-tuning strengthened the initial models. Two rounds of pseudo labeling used mask-overlap clustering and pixel voting, followed by an ensemble of models from both rounds. A CatBoost false-positive filter using 130 instance features raised the reported leaderboard score to 0.341.
compute: Training batch size of 2; hardware and runtime unstated.

solution_summary: The solution used MMDetection Mask R-CNN models with Hybrid Task Cascade, with the final submission combining r101 and x101 models. Training began at lower resolutions and continued from checkpoints at 1024 × 1600, using SGD and learning-rate reductions. The best submission used the last two checkpoints from each model with three-scale and mirror test-time augmentation. Frozen batch normalization performed better than an attempted SyncBN setup, and accidental inclusion of validation data in training led the author to use leaderboard feedback for validation.
compute: Initially two machines with 3×1080Ti each; two additional devboxes became available for the weekend. r101 trained for 18 epochs and x101 for 9 epochs.

solution_title: Score! Xavier Conort on coming second in 'Give Me Some Credit'
solution_summary: The solution combined diverse models, with the best ensemble excluding SVMs. Its most important engineered feature estimated the likelihood of delinquency exceeding 90 days. A weighted GBM was the strongest individual model, scoring 0.86877 on the private set. Adding weaker but complementary models improved the overall result.

The solution combines three supervised feature sets with structure, sequence, and protein-interaction kNN label transfer. Each supervised set blends a hierarchy-aware neural network, logistic regression, and PyBoost using protein-language-model embeddings, taxonomy, non-experimental annotations, and optionally literature embeddings. Validation balances multilabel distributions while keeping identical sequences together. A NaN-aware weighted ensemble and GO hierarchy, taxonomic, known-label, and score filters produce the final predictions.

solution_summary: The final system averages two EfficientNetV2-S variants and a MaxViT model, with auxiliary supervision used in two models. Large mammograms, rule-based ROI extraction, VOI LUT, strong regularization and controlled class proportions in each batch were central to performance. Patient-grouped cross-validation selected thresholds, while inference used models trained on all data and averaged the top three predictions per prediction ID. The ensemble achieved local pF1 of 0.482 and private pF1 of 0.49.

The author investigated lower bounds for unrestricted wildcards using symmetric traveling-salesman formulations solved with Concorde and QSopt. An approximately 8,000-node model reached a bound of 2425.21, with a target of proving 2428. A smaller model was inadequate because it could not preserve the 2440 non-wildcard solution, while a larger model was proposed as a costly fallback. The post also describes earlier use of S5 subgroup structure and vertex-cover software to construct a 2428 solution, and proposes symmetry-aware cuts.

solution_summary: The solution combined pretrained QuadTreeAttention LoFTR and SuperPoint/SuperGlue without competition-specific training or fine-tuning. Three inference scales per model substantially improved matching, and the combined result reached 0.845 on the private leaderboard. Scale-specific confidence thresholds, aspect-preserving padding, and removal of out-of-image correspondences controlled match quality. FP16 reduced memory use, while standard MAGSAC++ was retained for accuracy after faster alternatives and a two-stage variant were tested.

solution_summary: The author reports using L1-regularized logistic regression, with a best single-model score of 0.38. They also report best scores of 0.40 for k-nearest neighbors and 0.41 for an SVM. The post provides no feature, validation, or ensemble details and asks others to share their methods.

The solution averages predictions from two nodule-based pipelines trained using LUNA data. One uses U-Nets in three anatomical directions, extracts measurements from the largest detected nodules, and classifies them with XGBoost. The other trains a 3D VGG derivative on nodule cubes and aggregates convolutional features across overlapping scan chunks for another XGBoost classifier. Using eleven-slice inputs improved the U-Net Dice score from 0.50 to 0.75, while strong LUNA performance did not always transfer to the competition data.

solution_summary: The author improved a shared baseline by switching from EfficientNet B3 to B4, using rectangular CutMix, and gradually decreasing the learning rate. Predictions were adjusted by inverse class frequencies, with the weights raised to the power of 1.2 for the final adjustment. The final approach trained on all available training data and blended two runs with different seeds. Learning-rate changes and class-frequency adjustment each added about 0.007 on the public leaderboard, within a budget of 60 TPU hours.

solution_summary: The solution centered on value-frequency features computed jointly over training data and genuine test rows. Identifying and excluding artificial test rows from these calculations stabilized validation and leaderboard performance, with additional frequency thresholds and mean-centered features bringing a single model to about 0.923. The final submission combined models trained on shared ten-fold splits using logistic-regression stacking and simple blending, selected by cross-validation.

solution_title: The last 2 hours: a solo bronze from a two-tier agent swarm
solution_summary: The author reduced the cost of already-correct ONNX networks using an autonomous agent swarm operating on a corpus seeded from a public solution. Read-only theorist agents identified optimization opportunities, while task-specific workers applied shared compilation tricks and redesigned expensive networks. Candidates were banked only after exactness, fresh-input generalization, independent-runtime scoring, and submission-safety checks. The final two-hour surge increased the public score from 7394 to 7430.00, banking 163 improvements with no reported regressions.
compute: One Mac Studio with 16 cores; approximately 1,000 concurrent agent sessions and 2,056 processes at peak; final surge lasted about two hours; approximately $220 in account costs.

solution_summary: The author built 24 models with varied feature sets, emphasizing prediction diversity and deliberate column removal. Ensemble construction used ROC AUC rather than leaderboard scores. A hill-climbing procedure selected positive and negative model weights, including small contributions from weak standalone models. The reported ensemble ROC AUC reached 0.92821, compared with 0.92781 for the best individual model.

The solution improved public approaches by smoothing the input signals with sliding-window averages and smoothing the estimated transit depths across wavelength bands. Savitzky–Golay filtering reduced fluctuations in the bandwise depth predictions. A linear regression model predicted uncertainty using the relationship between planetary uncertainty and variation across band depths. The reported correlation supporting this relationship was approximately 0.701.

The code fits a separate six-component Gaussian mixture for each of 512 magic-value groups, using combined training and test data. It selects high-variance features and appends a heavily weighted target coordinate, with test targets initialized to 0.5. Five perturbed initializations are tried, and the model with the highest lower bound supplies clusters that are labeled by training-class majority. Submission predictions depend on a per-group positive-count check, with small random noise added when that check passes.

The solution generated candidates using co-visitation matrices and reranked them with LightGBM, adding CatBoost for orders. Features combined session recency, interaction counts, viewing duration, item popularity, conversion rates, co-visitation weights, and Word2Vec similarities. Orders predictions were averaged across models trained on separately truncated session datasets, but this improved little over a single LightGBM model, and expanding the candidate pool from 50 to 75 brought little benefit. Final cross-validation scores were 54.54% for clicks, 42.08% for carts, and 65.80% for orders.
compute: Ran entirely on Kaggle using multiple notebooks; some notebooks took 4–6 hours.

solution_summary: The final system ensembled 65 CNN models covering 13 model configurations and five folds. Architecture diversity improved local and leaderboard scores, and models were selected using local inference results. Training used primary and secondary bird labels, BCEWithLogits loss, mixup, and cosine annealing. Six-second inference clips and a fixed prediction threshold of 0.2 were selected, while clip-length ensembles and several conventional augmentations did not improve results.

The solution combined five EfficientNet and EfficientNetV2 models using weights learned through ridge regression. Models used stratified five-fold validation, mixup, extensive augmentation, and flip-based test-time augmentation. Three-channel inputs and larger image sizes were particularly useful, with a six-channel model retained for ensemble diversity. Several alternatives were unsuccessful, including classifier stacking, logistic-regression weighting, and pseudo-labeling, which overfit.

The team used nnU-Net with a custom 3D encoder and 2D decoder, weighting depth features with squeeze-and-excitation blocks before aggregation. Fragment-specific normalization and intensity-based selection of 32 slices supported large training patches. They combined selected folds from two training configurations and used eight-way test-time augmentation. Both submitted post-processing approaches improved public results but did not generalize, with threshold and component filtering reducing final Dice by 0.002.

solution_title: 74th place: knee-centred views, LLM labels, and OAI-trained readers
solution_summary: The pipeline retained all slices from five MRI series and combined full-field images with detector-positioned local views in a multiple-instance reader. Report-derived labels were refined using rank-preserving OOF pseudo-labels, selected multimodal LLM reads and independent OAI image models. ConvNeXt-S and EfficientNetV2-S members were averaged, with one final submission additionally incorporating OAI readers at inference. Independent validation sets guided member selection, and the best private submission achieved 0.949 AUC.
