solution_summary: The solution predicts continuous ECG trace coordinates from individual row crops rather than segmenting trace masks. Training relies primarily on synthetic ECGs with precise pixel labels, mixed with competition data for adaptation. A cross-row refinement model and a BiLSTM model provide complementary predictions, combined with weights of 0.6 and 0.4 respectively. Metric-aware losses and signal post-processing support an ensemble public score of approximately 19.75 dB.
compute: Multi-GPU training via DistributedDataParallel; hardware and duration unspecified.
external_data: ["Synthetic ECGs with pixel-perfect ground truth", "ImageNet-22k pretraining data"]

solution_summary: The final pipeline ensembled five YOLOv5x detection folds and used a separate binary classifier to filter normal images. Annotation preparation fused boxes, removed suspicious annotations, and corrected some calcification boxes using RetinaNet predictions. The classifier used four EfficientNet-B5 noisy-student folds, followed by removal of highly inconsistent examples and retraining. Switching from RetinaNet to YOLOv5 substantially improved detection, while label smoothing, VFNet, and EfficientDet were unsuccessful. The custom classifier improved the private score from 0.271 to 0.272.

solution_title: 6th place:  Micro-inputs, Lots of Data + Distance Order to Ensemble!
solution_summary: The author's contribution used ResNeSt50 models with compact 128- and 196-pixel rasters and five condensed input channels. Training on multiple chopped versions of the full dataset, promoting scene diversity, and undersampling crowded scenes were central to improving data coverage and performance. The two models reached scores of 11.9 and 11.15 after 68.8 million and 71.4 million samples, respectively. The ensemble aligned trajectory modes by distance traveled before averaging, with validation-optimized weights incorporating distance and confidence.

The post provides incomplete code for an MLP and its graph-data loading pipeline. The loader joins node features and opcodes along graph edges and associates them with configuration features. It constructs normalized rank targets from the labels. Missing code tokens prevent reconstruction of the full architecture, and no validation results are reported.

solution_title: A kaggle newbie's 🥈23rd solution:  Just follow-up excellent public works & ideas
solution_summary: The solution used two external essay datasets with selected prompts excluded, supplemented by pseudo-labeled test examples. A tokenizer trained on test text produced TF-IDF features capped at five million, which fed a diverse ensemble of linear, probabilistic, and boosting classifiers. The final pipeline also included test-text correction and a referenced postprocessing method. Adding DistilRoBERTa increased the public score from 0.962 to 0.965; a submission without correction achieved 0.923 on the private leaderboard.
external_data: ["DAIGT v2 train dataset", "Mistral-7B instruct texts dataset"]

solution_title: My best solution only using manager_id
solution_summary: The author combined four XGBoost models linearly. Features included listing metadata, description length, creation times, room counts, and grouped property statistics. Manager-level statistics captured class rates and class-specific averages of price, bedrooms, and bathrooms. The author considered feature engineering a limitation and did not report a numerical score.

The solution trained a shared model for both defog and tdcs data. DeBERTa or vision transformer encoders fed an LSTM or GRU, typically with two to four encoder layers and one recurrent layer. Inputs used patches of size 7–13 and sequences of 192–384 patches. Heavy sequence augmentation was a central part of training.

solution_title: 317th Place Solution for the LLM Science Exam
solution_summary: The final system used Platypus2-70B-Instruct with Wikipedia retrieval and layer-by-layer weight loading. Questions and answer options were embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 to retrieve five similar Wikipedia texts, which were included in the prompt. Answer probabilities were ranked to produce three options, achieving reported accuracy of 0.888. Earlier experiments included fine-tuned BERT, DeBERTa with sentence retrieval, and Longformer with paragraph retrieval.
compute: Final inference: 200 questions in 3 hours on 2 GPUs described as T5; Longformer inference: approximately 40 minutes on the same stated GPU configuration.
external_data: ["Wikipedia texts and embeddings", "6,500 extra training examples, source unspecified"]

solution_summary: The solution ensembled five 1D U-Net variants combining WaveNet, bidirectional GRU, and a small ViT component. Subject-wise scaling and overlapping daily sequences supplied sensor values, differences, and cyclic time features, with five-fold GroupKFold validation. Joint segmentation and event detection used segmentation outputs to inform the event head, with negative downsampling and extensive skip connections. Weighted probability averaging, smoothing, peak detection, and time-of-day filtering produced a private score of 0.786.

solution_title: 52nd Place Solution — Physics Bank + Typed Crossformer
solution_summary: The solution generated a bank of 65 candidate trajectories and context channels using physics, alignment, surface, and geometry methods. A Typed Crossformer distinguished candidate families, contextual evidence, and protected trajectory anchors to predict changes from the last known TVT. Frequency-aware fusion and bounded physical corrections produced a stable parent prediction, followed by a 10% residual correction between two differently regularized Typed models. Well-level cross-validation and conservative corrections were central to reliable transfer, with the final model achieving 6.1150 OOF RMSE and 7.087 private RMSE.
compute: Training performed in FP32; approximately 1.89M parameters per fold model.

solution_summary: The solution combined many tabular models and ensembles, with LAMA DenseLight working best as the ensembler. Strong individual models included tuned CatBoost and XGBoost, xLearn FFM, and Keras FM. Thirteen genetic-programming features improved scores by 0.0025–0.003 when added to raw data and still added about 0.0001 after count and target encoding. Adding more models eventually improved CV slightly without improving the public leaderboard.

The team trained ImageNet-pretrained SE-ResNeXt50, DPN-92, and SE-ResNeXt101 models using both simplified and raw drawings. Strokes were stored in individual binary files to accelerate random access and experimentation. Larger image resolutions improved results, while three-channel stroke timing and stroke-count encodings raised the public score to about 0.951. Batch sizes increased across snapshots to as many as 10,000; the post leaves details of the final 0.953 phase to a teammate.
compute: About 400 GB of SSD storage for drawing files; limited GPU resources constrained 256-pixel training.

solution_summary: The solution equally blended a public tabular model with a MaxViT image model, emphasizing prevention of overfitting under extreme class imbalance. Its most effective method was training first on historical ISIC data and then on ISIC2024 alone. The image pipeline used patient-grouped stratified validation, extensive augmentation, post-augmentation standardization, and six-channel RGB plus HSV input. Test-time augmentation improved the private result despite little change in local or public scores, while oversampling and auxiliary loss did not work.
compute: RTX4070 Ti Super throughout the competition; also tried vast.ai and runpod.io near the end.

solution_summary: The team combined spectrogram-based 2D models, raw-EEG 1D models, and hybrid models using a geometric mean of predictions; the detailed writeup covers the Japanese team's components. These components used CWT spectrograms with EfficientNet and hybrid networks that converted raw EEG into image-shaped CNN features. Two-stage training, pseudo labels for sparsely annotated samples, and adjustments to the Other class improved leaderboard scores. The best Japanese spectrogram-only single model scored 0.264 publicly and 0.313 privately, while the best hybrid scored 0.266 and 0.331.

The team treated ion-channel prediction as a parameter-optimization problem using a single highly customized hidden Markov model. They corrected drift and signal scale, removed periodic noise, and decomposed higher-channel categories into combinations of lower-channel processes. Modified forward-backward passes exchanged information and were blended across several preprocessing variants. Batch-specific unsupervised thresholding matched estimated label distributions, and the optimized model reached 0.94584 on the private leaderboard.

The pipeline pretrained models on identities expanded through horizontal and vertical flips, then trained branches for seen graphemes, unseen graphemes, and ArcFace embeddings. Encoder heads used GeM or average pooling, normalization, and fully connected layers, with a separate convolutional stacking head. Training combined CutMix and geometric augmentation with pc-softmax, negative log-likelihood, SGD, cosine annealing, and stochastic weight averaging. ArcFace inference compared train and test embeddings using cosine similarity and a threshold derived from validation embeddings.

The solution mainly used EfficientNet B0–B5 image models, including models that concatenated patient metadata with CNN features. Effective choices included BCEWithLogitsLoss, progressive learning, warmup, AutoAugment, CutMix, random resized crops, and snapshot ensembles. Predictions were combined through several ensemble strategies, with weights searched on cross-validation. Models trained at resolution 384 also performed better when evaluated at 456 and 512, and combining these predictions improved results.
compute: Used public TPU notebooks.

solution_summary: The solution stacked more than 30 EfficientNet models trained with different image sizes using an ExtraTreesClassifier. Five-fold validation used logloss because it was more stable than AUC, and EfficientNet B5 at 512 pixels was the strongest model-size combination. External-data pretraining followed by fine-tuning on 2020 data, checkpoint averaging, and extensive test-time augmentation improved performance. Statistics across repeated predictions supplied stacking features, producing a reported validation AUC of 0.9536 and leaderboard AUC of 0.9457.
compute: Most models trained on TPUs in Colab or Kaggle; each fold used 150 inferences from five checkpoints and 30 augmentations.
external_data: ["2018 data and unspecified external data with 30K samples"]

solution_summary: The author used CatBoost with handcrafted text features for the efficiency track, emphasizing writing errors, readability, prompt overlap, and early-summary characteristics. Optuna tuned separate content and wording models, while GroupKFold with five seeds supported validation and the public leaderboard sometimes informed feature decisions. Regex, word lists, and NumPy vectorization reduced feature extraction overhead. Reported CV, public, and private scores were 0.52, 0.452, and 0.504; inference compilation alternatives were rejected because compilation costs outweighed their speed gains.

solution_title: Godday's Solution that didn't Appear in Public Notebooks.
solution_summary: The team used a GRU to forecast trends and XGBoost to predict residual information, adding both outputs for the final forecast. GRU validation used five rolling windows, while XGBoost used three group-based validation runs. They also shifted forecast origins to test longer horizons against the January leaderboard. The residual model improved both local and leaderboard results, with the fifth-month leaderboard score decreasing from 3.4 to 2.5.

The solution adapted Agentless into a pipeline that localized relevant files, generated reproduction tests, created patches, and verified them before submission. Qwen2.5-Coder-32B served through vLLM provided structured outputs, with execution feedback driving test and patch retries. Carefully selected few-shot test examples and selective skipping of uncertain patches were central to performance. Evaluation used SWE-Bench-Verified, while exhaustive unit testing and extra tests generated after patching were discarded because they hurt efficiency or reliability.
compute: Two RTX 3090 GPUs rented on vast.ai for local evaluation; most issues took 5–7 minutes.

solution_title: 26th Solution - 3D UNet + CCL with Morphological Post Processing + Custom Loss Function
solution_summary: The solution used MONAI 3D UNets trained on small spherical particle labels and reconstructed predictions from overlapping volumes. Tversky-loss variants, rotation and flip augmentation, and model/TTA aggregation formed the core ensemble. Thresholding and morphological dilation before connected-component labeling improved detection, with Optuna tuning particle-specific settings. Validation used one held-out tomogram, and a custom object-recall loss model was retained for ensemble diversity despite no clear standalone leaderboard gain.

The author focused on events with hits confined to a single detector string, typically involving three or four sensors. Their modeling attempts performed worse than a copied EDA+PCA notebook baseline. The post reports an unsuccessful exploration and asks whether others found effective methods for these events.

The team combined a five-fold 3D EfficientNet approach with an end-to-end 2D model containing four different CNN branches. Training used volumetric or Keras augmentation, while the 2D pipeline randomly exchanged MRI modalities between branches. Bayesian optimization selected linear ensemble weights, and test-time augmentation improved the reported component scores. The final ensemble scored 0.68340 publicly and 0.52730 privately, reflecting a substantial generalization gap.
compute: TPU referenced in the 2D model code; configuration and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: Across four competition weeks, the team used a custom growth model with a growth rate reduced by an accelerating decay. Earlier fatality forecasts combined lagged case predictions with country-specific fatality rates, while the final week modeled fatality curves directly. The final submissions blended their model with public solutions using different weights, generally favoring their own forecasts and using them exclusively for Chinese locations. More optimistic assumptions performed better overall, while short-term growth tuning produced overly pessimistic forecasts in the second week.
external_data: ["Public predictions from osciiart, rohanrao, and david1013", "Public predictions from cpmpml and team, gaborfodor, and osciiart", "Worldometer data for retrospective comparison"]

solution_title: Top #3 score solution writeup - Predict the Introverts from the Extroverts
solution_summary: The final submission blended tree-based models, an MLP, and logistic regression with weights of 50%, 45%, and 5%. Predictions were converted to labels using a 40% probability threshold. The author spent only a few hours and made four submissions, relying on a shared notebook.
compute: A few hours of work; four submissions.

solution_summary: This post announces uploaded solution files required by the competition rules. It describes a PDF containing model documentation and an archive containing MATLAB training scripts. It invites questions but provides no substantive pipeline details in the supplied text.

solution_title: 14th place solution (GCN from scratch in Kaggle kernel)
solution_summary: The author built a Keras graph convolutional network using atom identities, bond information, distances, angles, and dihedral features. Six graph convolution layers updated atom representations before transferring information to edges for coupling prediction. Auxiliary predictions of charges and shielding eigenvalues fed back into the network, while predicted magnetic contributions were summed for the final target. A single run scored about -2.6 after 27 hours, and averaging roughly ten runs produced a final score of -2.9.
compute: About 27 hours per script run, split into three 9-hour sessions with saved weights; approximately ten runs averaged.

solution_summary: The final solution equally averaged four models: two EfficientNet-B5 models, a Vision Transformer, and an SE-ResNeXt50. Different training pipelines provided useful diversity, with eight-way test-time augmentation applied to all models except SE-ResNeXt50. The author's models used combined 2019 and 2020 data, duplicate removal, stratified five-fold validation, extensive augmentation, and bi-tempered loss. Pseudo-labeling and self-distillation improved validation but hurt leaderboard performance and were excluded from the author's final models. The final ensemble achieved 0.910 on the public leaderboard and approximately 0.901–0.902 on the private leaderboard.
compute: TPU used for one teammate's B5 training; final ensemble submission inference took almost 8 hours.

solution_title: From 0.290 to 40.410 Public, Then 0.000 Private: Agent-Security Overfitting
solution_summary: The author used controlled experiments to refine an SDK GoExplore search around a productive HTTP seed, then pivoted to direct static candidate generation. Seed ablation and moderate search geometry improved adaptive search, while mixed portfolios and post-search cloning did not beat the clean specialist. The selected finals were a 700-candidate static generator and a clean adaptive-search submission, scoring 40.410 and 18.315 publicly. Both targeted the same HTTP/sentinel behavior, and the final private score was zero.

The solution combined BERT-base-cased, BERT-base-uncased, and XLNet-base models with customized heads using weights of 2:4:4. Training used ten grouped folds, three epochs, AdamW with OneCycleLR, and a combined BCE and label-frequency-weighted MSE loss. Adding a category token improved CV by a reported 0.05, and predictions were discretized through optimized binning. Several alternatives, including pseudo-labeling, multisample dropout, SWA, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, did not work for the author.

solution_title: A boring solution: Gemma-7b / Mistral SFT + Metric learning & Retrieval [0.66]
solution_summary: The author generated synthetic rewrite pairs after identifying recurring text types in organizer data and leaderboard tests. A fine-tuned T5-base encoder retrieved rewrite prompts from public prompt collections, while Mistral and Gemma-7b were separately fine-tuned for generation. Concatenating the generative and retrieval outputs improved the score to 0.66. Text-type prefixes added about 0.01, and a later appended phrase raised the reported score to 0.71.

The solution generated many sub-agents from Markov predictors, 22 rps_contest bots, a sklearn-compatible agent, and Iocaine. Variants changed the player perspective, probability normalization, move delays, and cyclic action shifts. A MultiArmedAgent scored sub-agents over a recent window using rewards and streak bonuses or penalties, then generated actions from the highest-scoring candidates. Conditional random play and a fixed 25% random-action probability helped obscure the strategy, while nesting the meta-agent inside another ensemble proved unsuccessful.

solution_title: 22nd solution: base model, training, and post-processing
solution_summary: The team fine-tuned a preference classifier based on princeton-nlp/gemma-2-9b-it-SimPO, which outperformed the standard instruction-tuned base in their experiments. Adding 33,000 arena conversations and swapping response order helped, whereas the 55,000-example preference dataset, model-based relabeling, and label smoothing did not. Temperature scaling improved results by 0.001–0.002, and replacing predictions for truncated long examples with less confident length-based probabilities added about 0.001. A text-generation regularization model was excluded based on public results despite later showing stronger private performance.

The team solved the original round of the gift-matching competition to optimality with mixed integer linear programming. They implemented one formulation in SAS PROC OPTMODEL and another through COIN's C++ APIs. SAS/OR took about one hour to build and solve the model, while Cbc 2.6.2 took about 40 hours.
compute: About 1 hour to build and solve with SAS/OR; about 40 hours with COIN/CBC.

solution_summary: The solution combined FFT features covering 1–47 Hz with correlation coefficients and their eigenvalues. Correlation features were computed from both frequency-domain output and the original time-domain data. Separate random forest classifiers with 3,000 trees were trained for each patient.

The team blended diverse neural text classifiers and sparse-feature models using several pretrained word embeddings. Most neural models used bidirectional GRUs with max and attention pooling, complemented by hierarchical attention, CapsuleNet, DeepMoji, Bi-LSTM, and DPCNN models. Byte-pair decomposition, embedding-based spelling correction, and language translation reduced out-of-vocabulary words and improved the blend. Simple and geometric averaging produced a final reported cross-validation score of 0.99294, while nonlinear stacking was unsuccessful.

The solution stacked a couple of LightGBM models with a neural network, using about 30 engineered features. Time-based entropy, historical-period counts and lead times were useful. They approximated sub-second timestamps from click order and click counts within each second, which provided a substantial early gain. Removing device 3032 improved the score by about 0.0004, while stacking added roughly 0.0003.

The approach represented taxi trajectories using roughly 100-meter geographic grid cells paired with four velocity directions. Training trajectories were selected by a threshold on shared features and weighted by their overlap with the test trajectory. Destination prediction minimized the weighted sum of distances, while extra weight on the final feature and truncation after prolonged stops improved matching. Validation reproduced the test sampling process by cutting trips active at a chosen time, providing useful relative comparisons between approaches.

The solution generated Boolean patent queries by finding selective subqueries and combining them through beam search. A custom C++ searcher and probabilistic approximation of the competition metric made evaluation over approximately 13 million patents practical. Validation filtering improved agreement with leaderboard scores, and shared query tokens were factored out to conserve the token budget. About 6% of generated queries matched exactly the 50 target patents.

The post shares a link to an unselected submission and congratulates other competitors. It also links to a teammate's analysis and test-set simulation notebook. No substantive modeling or training details are provided.

The solution marked summary spans copied from the prompt by matching n-grams of length at least three, then supplied the marked summary, question, and title to DeBERTa-v3-large. This compact input enabled an ensemble of 44 models spanning four folds, different layer-freezing settings, and separate or joint target prediction. The submitted ensemble achieved 0.4659 CV, 0.427 public, and 0.465 private. A late LightGBM residual correction improved these to 0.4643, 0.425, and 0.464 respectively, but finished after the competition deadline.

The solution fine-tuned a Qwen-32B classifier with LoRA, a global misconception head, and 15 question-specific local heads. Restricting local-head gradients into the backbone helped control overfitting, while correctness labels were assigned afterward using rules. Five-fold stratified validation guided learning rates, input formats, and question-specific model weights despite inconsistent validation and leaderboard behavior. The final ensemble combined weighted probabilities, top-three consensus, and maximum confidence, slightly improving the public score over simple weighted averaging.

The team grouped stocks by 33SectorName and trained a separate LightGBM regressor for each sector, assuming within-sector stock behavior was correlated. Models predicted the provided change-ratio target, and submissions ranked those predictions. They tuned four hyperparameters on a single model covering all stocks, then reused those settings for every sector model. Training used available features from stock_price and stock_list.

The author trained YOLOv3 with spatial pyramid pooling, initialized with ImageNet-pretrained Darknet53 weights, following the creators' COCO architecture and training regime. Training used class-balanced subsets that expanded from approximately 320,000 to 430,000 images. Rare-label images were retained while common-label images were limited, and training ran for just over 500,000 batches. The author considered training-set composition important but did not verify that claim experimentally.
compute: GCP preemptible instance with 16 vCPUs and 4 P100 GPUs; approximately 50,000 batches per 24 hours, with just over 500,000 batches total.

solution_title: Santander Value Prediction Challenge: Open Solution
solution_summary: The authors present an open collection of LightGBM pipelines with shared code and experiments. Variants explore binarized inputs, row aggregations, and dimensionality reduction, with five-fold cross-validation documented for the baseline. The latest listed approach uses bucketed row aggregations and reports CV 1.333 and leaderboard score 1.38, compared with baseline scores of 1.39 and 1.43.

The approach focused on making validation reliable when additional images contained other frames from the same patients as the training set. Color histograms and k-means clustering grouped similar images, and 20 of 100 clusters were reserved for validation. The authors manually removed roughly 15% of additional images and gave the remaining additional data less weight. Validation scores of 0.75–0.8 were close to their final result.

solution_title: 3rd place solution - two stage flip augmentation stacking with code
solution_summary: The solution blended LightGBM and CatBoost with three-seed averaging and a two-stage prediction-feature pipeline. Swapping agent order with corresponding target and advantage transformations was central to augmentation. Validation grouped game rulesets, while English-rule TF-IDF/SVD features, null-importance selection, and Optuna tuning supported modeling. Multiplying predictions by 1.12 improved the leaderboard score by 0.002.

solution_title: 4th place solution: using PCA (least shakeuped solution)
solution_summary: The solution applies six-component PCA separately to each input column, predicts the components with XGBoost, and reconstructs emissions through inverse PCA. Validation holds out each available year in turn, followed by training on all available data to forecast 2022. Using all columns outperformed the emissions-only and SARIMA alternatives on both local validation and the private leaderboard. Multiplicative postprocessing hurt the selected final submission, and the author reports that unscaled predictions would have performed better.

The team combined XGBoost and a Keras neural network with data cleaning, engineered features and macroeconomic adjustments for falling housing prices. One approach transformed the training target using macro indicators, removed samples with large relative prediction errors, and added a specialized Ownership model. The other used GDP-based prediction adjustment, a four-layer neural network, and separate XGBoost models for earlier and later years. Predictions were combined with manually selected weights; one teammate reported pre-merger scores of 0.30891 public and 0.31246 private.

The pipeline converted DICOM images to PNG, cropped breast regions, and trained ConvNeXt v1 Small models at 1536×768 using patient-grouped validation. Positive-class sampling, extensive augmentation, model selection, and postprocessing were central to performance. Three models using average or trainable GeM pooling were combined with weighted horizontal-flip TTA and either probability aggregation or confidence voting, followed by thresholding around 0.5. Probability aggregation reached 0.63 publicly and 0.47 privately, while the voting submission reached 0.62 publicly and 0.50 privately.
compute: Training on cloud: 1–2× A6000 or A100 GPU-80GB.

solution_summary: The solution integrated predictions from four small image models into tabular gradient-boosted models. Two image models used broader positive labels to produce complementary signals. Shared patient-grouped stratified folds and balanced image training supported reliable validation. The final combination used LightGBM with and without image features, CatBoost, and XGBoost, reaching a CV score of 0.183099.

The post points readers to the author's GitHub repository of competition code. It contains no description of the modeling approach. No techniques, validation details, or results are provided in the text.

The final submission ensembled eight models and discretized selected output columns to values observed in training, choosing those columns through out-of-fold comparisons. The strongest single model was a two-part RoBERTa base model that separated question-label inputs from answer-label inputs. Modified pooling over multiple hidden states and differential learning rates improved validation performance and convergence. Basic text augmentation and back-translation were also used, while T5, extra tokens, and larger models did not help.

The post thanks participants and administrators and credits a teammate with solving and proving the problem. It links to a GitHub repository and a proof PDF. No methods or implementation details are described in the provided text.

solution_title: [16th place solution] Features Diversity and Ensemble
solution_summary: The solution emphasized customer-history features and diversity across LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost, two neural network architectures, and TabNet. Hull moving averages, differences, and last observations were combined differently for each model family. Using all difference features caused leakage and poor CV-to-leaderboard agreement for some models. The final rank ensemble used Optuna-selected weights, manual weights for public models without out-of-fold predictions, and multiple random seeds.

solution_title: 201st Place Solution for the Google - Fast or Slow? Predict AI Model Runtime
solution_summary: The author copied a public runtime prediction notebook using a modified BERT model. Preprocessing used an adjacency matrix and a virtual first node, with a train/validation split. The modification supplied the public notebook's output as input and copied it to the output. The reported public and private scores were 0.39199 and 0.27376, with no private-score improvement from the modification.

The solution used a modified U-Net with stacked dilated convolutions in its bottleneck, trained at 1536×1024 and 1920×1280 resolution. Pseudo-labeling was a major source of improvement, alongside a combined binary cross-entropy and Dice loss. The final prediction combined fold ensembles at both resolutions using leaderboard-based weights and horizontal-flip test-time augmentation. A single model scored 0.997193, increasing to 0.997222 with flip averaging, while threshold tuning provided only a tiny additional gain.
compute: Around 2 days of training per single model; batch size 1.

solution_title: 13th Place Solution — Frozen DINOv3-7B + Stacked Ridge
solution_summary: The solution froze DINOv3 ViT-7B and trained lightweight stacked Ridge regressors on multi-scale, multi-depth image representations. Left-right views and four pooling statistics captured local evidence, with intermediate layers and pooling providing the largest gains. Separate raw-target and log-target stacks were blended, then predictions were averaged across fold settings and constrained by biomass identities. The base pipeline scored 0.75696 publicly and 0.64833 privately; stacked XGBoost did not improve performance.

A single neural network jointly modeled approximately 145,000 Wikipedia traffic series. Its WaveNet-like architecture used stacked dilated causal convolutions. Separate encoder and decoder parameters and training unrolled over the full 64-day horizon helped the decoder cope with accumulating prediction errors.
compute: 12 GB GPU recommended; actual hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_title: 12th Place Solution: Stacked Ensemble with Ordered Target Encoding
solution_summary: The final system stacked 41 models from six algorithm families using a LightGBM meta-model trained on aligned out-of-fold class probabilities. Ordered target encoding with four shuffled training copies was the main improvement, while a separate interaction-based feature pipeline supplied complementary models. Individually weak classifiers improved the learned stacker despite hurting greedy ensembles. OOF-tuned log-probability shifts addressed class imbalance and helped reach 0.98082 private balanced accuracy.
compute: AWS SageMaker c5.9xlarge for boosters and g4dn.xlarge for cuML/neural models; Kaggle T4 jobs.

solution_summary: The solution extracted structural, count, and hash features from assembly and byte files, then greedily reduced roughly 2,000 candidates to 25 features. It averaged ten random forests of 1,500 trees each, changing hash seeds between forests. Its most influential step sharpened and renormalized predicted probabilities using class-specific powers tuned by cross-validation. Calibration reduced CV log loss from about 0.02 to 0.005, with public and private leaderboard losses of about 0.004 and 0.006.

The author trained a LightGBM classifier on customer–article pairs from four recent purchase windows, sampling 30 negative articles per customer. Features included purchase counts for customers and articles. Validation used the following week, and inference scored a shared pool of 15,000 popular articles for every customer. The large candidate pool improved scores substantially but made inference expensive.
compute: Google Colab Pro+, 1 GPU; approximately 15 hours training, 7 hours validation inference, and 100 hours test inference; multiple sessions doubled speed.

solution_title: 38th place - 41 Models, Custom Features, and Hill Climbing
solution_summary: The author generated out-of-fold predictions from 41 models trained with varied feature sets. A hill-climbing ensemble selected 16 models spanning CatBoost, Extra Trees, XGBoost, MLP, and Ridge regression, producing the best final CV score. Feature experiments included aggregates, clustering, time-series-inspired features, binning, transformations, and PCA. Kernel issues limited tuning, and the author identified excessive reliance on the public leaderboard as a submission-selection weakness.

The author compared factorization machines, random forests, gradient boosting, and XGBoost. XGBoost achieved the highest reported private score at 0.39498. Ensembling the models did not improve performance.

The solution used a small SMILES transformer trained from scratch with four encoder layers, eight attention heads, and 32-dimensional representations. Nearly character-level tokenization worked better than more elaborate schemes. Pretraining combined masked-token prediction with chirality-aware ECFP prediction, followed by supervised training on competition and external binding data with masked losses. Validation held out building blocks, while larger models, fingerprint inputs, and ZINC pretraining did not improve the approach.
compute: A100 on Google Colab; MLM training approximately 100 epochs of 10K steps with 2028 samples per batch.
external_data: ["Building Block-Based Binding Predictions for DNA-Encoded Libraries", "ZINC (unsuccessful pretraining experiment)"]

solution_summary: The solution estimates a smooth formation-elevation curve using geometric constraints and exact HMM forward–backward inference rather than neural networks. Its strongest single-model components were correlated-residual whitening, restricted dynamics, sparse template corrections, and tempered averaging across depth basins. An equal-weight ensemble of five deliberately diverse configurations improved pooled CV RMSE to 5.976 and achieved 7.444 private RMSE. Extensive experiments identified ambiguous repeating rock layers and unavailable reference-curve detail as the main limitations.

solution_title: [Private 58th] TabM, AutoencoderMLP with online training & GBDT offline models
solution_summary: The final ensemble combined online-updated TabM and AutoencoderMLP networks with offline LightGBM, XGBoost, and ridge models, reaching a leaderboard score of 0.0092. TabM used categorical one-hot encoding, standardized continuous inputs, lag and periodic features, and an auxiliary responder target. Validation held out the last 120 dates, while training windows excluded earlier data with extensive missing values. Daily neural-network updates mixed the latest labeled date with sampled historical data and improved both neural models; online GBDT updates and sequence-model experiments were unsuccessful.

The author fine-tuned Perch v2 end-to-end with a sound-event detection head, retaining mean and learnable GeM frequency-pooling variants. Seven-fold grouped multilabel validation, checkpoint and fold weight soups, masked asymmetric loss, and waveform MixUp supported training. A second training run incorporated soundscape pseudo-labels and additional secondary labels. Dense overlapping inference and temporal smoothing fed a final rank blend with a public pipeline, reaching approximately 0.962 public and 0.954 private AUC.
compute: Inference takes about 20 minutes.

solution_summary: The author built CNN and GNN models with independent blocks for multiple RNA structural adjacency representations. Validation grouped sequences by edit-distance clusters and reserved all 206-length samples in one fold to monitor longer-sequence performance. Training combined signal-to-noise-weighted MAE and MSE, and test-set pseudo labels improved the best single model's private score from 0.14299 to 0.14186. Blending all models improved CV and public scores but produced a worse private score than the best pseudo-labeled single model.

solution_title: Ensembling a RF, GBM, and NN to reach 91st Position — with fastai and Scikit Learn
solution_summary: The author ensembled a random forest, a gradient boosting machine, and a neural network. Some engineered features were included, but feature importance analysis suggested they contributed little. The submission experienced a favorable shift between the public and private leaderboards.

The solution trained LightGBM forecasts at hierarchy levels 1–10 and 12. Level 12 used recursive Poisson forecasting, while higher levels predicted sales value day by day with RMSE or Tweedie objectives. Higher-level predictions were allocated to individual series using level-12 value shares, then combined with extra weight on levels 8 and 9. Combining hierarchy levels consistently improved WRMSSE over the standalone level-12 model across the reported evaluation windows.

solution_title: 29th Place Solution: FT-Transformer + Exact-Value Target Encoding
solution_summary: The best final submission was a single FT-Transformer with exact-value target encoding fitted separately inside each outer training fold. It used PLR-lite numeric embeddings, a fixed 16-epoch training budget, and class-prior correction, achieving a private score of 0.95070. Nested cross-validation selected both final submissions in advance, including a separate four-family stacked ensemble, without relying on public leaderboard movement. Exact-value encoding mattered most, while extra ensemble members and several attempts to add diversity or features failed to improve the validated solution.
compute: Kaggle GPU runtime; discusses P100 compatibility and pinning a Tesla T4 for API pushes.

solution_title: s3 class postprocessing (+0.008 on private LB)
solution_summary: The team multiplied positive predictions for class s3 by 1.5 as a final ensemble postprocessing step. They observed that s3 appeared unusually frequently in out-of-fold and test predictions despite roughly balanced true-positive label counts. They reasoned that incomplete labeling made the model too conservative about this common co-occurring class. Scaling improved the private leaderboard score from 0.933 to 0.941, while similar adjustments were not useful for other classes.

solution_title: 28th Place Solution (Silver) - Multi Stage Decision Tree + 66% Defensive Randomness
solution_summary: The best agent used a two-stage decision tree to predict opponents from a rolling history of both players' actions. Predictions from the first tree became additional history inputs for the next tree, allowing the agent to model reactions to its own predictions. Playing randomly 66% of the time reduced predictability while providing observations of opponent behavior. The winning configuration used a nine-move window and ten-turn warmup, scoring 971.0 and recording more wins than losses despite frequent draws.

The solution combined 58 tree and neural models trained on multiple feature representations using shared stratified folds. Clipped logit predictions became 174 inputs to a regularized GPU CatBoost stacker, averaged over five seeds and five folds. Custom RealMLP supplied the strongest standalone predictions and useful diversity. Nelder-Mead optimization of class multipliers increased OOF balanced accuracy from 0.950788 to 0.950868, with a private score of 0.95067.
compute: GPU CatBoost meta-learner; 25 fold fits across five seeds and five folds.

solution_summary: The solution predicted discourse effectiveness from whole essays using both token classification and span-based classification with DeBERTa models. CLS and SEP markers identified target texts, and combining model variants improved validation despite weaker individual DeBERTa-V2-xlarge results. Bayesian optimization selected ensemble weights using out-of-fold validation predictions. A subsequent LightGBM model incorporated neighboring discourse effectiveness and location features, reaching CV 0.578 and private leaderboard loss 0.573.

The author's strongest submission stacked four LightGBM models using another LightGBM model. Data preparation ideas came from public notebooks after initial experiments with several model families underperformed strong public solutions. A separate selected submission blended public solutions and scored 0.952 publicly and 1.286 privately. The LightGBM stack improved the private score to 1.25001, with a public score of 0.959.

The main approach performed kNN recognition using global descriptors from three ResNeSt models trained with CosFace and label smoothing. GeM pooling, extensive augmentation, larger-image refinement, and in-place knowledge distillation supported descriptor training. Similarity to the GLDv2 test set filtered non-landmark images, while 600 historical non-landmark test images were added to training. A global-only submission achieved a private score of 0.5983; a global-plus-HOW similarity blend improved the public score but slightly reduced the private score.
external_data: ["GLDv2 test set", "Previous year's recognition competition test set", "GLDv2clean (tested replacement)"]

solution_title: 1st place: genetic algorithm and GPU relaxation
solution_summary: The solution combines an island-based genetic algorithm with batched GPU relaxation to pack trees into progressively smaller squares. Rotational symmetry and crystal-based initialization reduce the search space, while diversity-aware selection and island resets prevent premature convergence. Precomputed separation distances make local optimization fast enough to evaluate many candidate layouts. A final legalization step removes residual overlap.
compute: 1000 RTX 5090 GPU-hours on vast.ai for about $250; roughly half for final search and half for development. Relaxation throughput: 30,000 runs/second for 100 trees.

solution_summary: The final system combined temporal residual 3D U-Net detectors with learned candidate selection, temporal linking, and division scoring. Synthetic faint-cell tracks and preservation of weak original-view detections helped retain evidence that could become convincing over time. Auxiliary detector banks contributed supported tracks and graph agreement, while final recovery checked unused candidate paths against original images without rerunning detection. The final pipeline achieved 0.970 private and 0.968 public scores, with CV improving from 0.951217 to 0.953024 after faint-track recovery and border trimming.
models_pretrained: ["Unspecified models pretrained on external microscopy data"]
external_data: ["Unspecified external microscopy data used for experimental pretrained models"]

solution_summary: The author trained LightGBM on the full training set using next-click times, counts, entropy statistics, session summaries, and categorical interaction features. Memory-efficient NumPy feature storage made full-data training feasible on a 32 GB machine. Validation used the latter half of the final training day, with additional AUC checks by hour. Removing timezone-based daily count features improved agreement between validation and leaderboard results. The final submission rank-averaged two own models with Dirk's predictions, achieving private AUC 0.9828279.
compute: 32 GB RAM machine; 1.5–2 hours per validation run and 3 hours per full model build; 13 iterations. Additional feature exploration on an 8 GB MacBook.

solution_summary: This post describes retrieval postprocessing that connects test and index images through labeled training images when direct nearest-neighbor matching misses relationships. It combines landmark-based bridged distances with direct distances computed after database augmentation. Cubed direct and bridged confidences are added to rerank the top 100 index images. The postprocessing reportedly improved public and private scores by 0.075–0.09, with hyperparameters optimized on the 2019 index and test dataset.
compute: Google TPU Research Program supported training bigger models in the final few days.

solution_title: Public LB Top 10, Private LB Top 26 Solution (Single Bert - 0.94560)
solution_summary: The team combined four BERT models, one LSTM, and one GPT-2 using a squared power ensemble. Their main focus was a weighted multi-output binary cross-entropy loss emphasizing non-toxic examples mentioning selected identities. Text preprocessing refined contraction handling, and the LSTM used combined GloVe and FastText embeddings. Reported scores included 0.94560 for tuned BERT, while additional BERT pretraining and dynamic layer-wise decay did not work.

The team generated impact candidates with EfficientDet and rescored expanded helmet crops using binary classifiers on nine stacked grayscale frames. Detector and classifier positive-label windows differed to exploit the evaluation tolerance while keeping classification targets precise. Multi-view threshold adjustment and temporal suppression removed inconsistent or duplicate detections. An ensemble of seven detectors and 18 classifiers achieved local, public and private scores of 0.64, 0.66 and 0.69.
compute: Z8G4 workstation with dual RTX6000 GPUs and ZBook with RTX5000 GPU.

solution_summary: The solution stacked hundreds of diverse CNNs with XGBoost models using prediction statistics, radar-image statistics, and incident-angle features. Fixed incident-angle-based folds helped control validation leakage, while CNN diversity came from random configurations and image augmentation. Final XGBoost training used conservative settings to reduce cross-validation overfitting. The submission combined a 95% average of angle-aware models with a 5% average of models excluding incident angle, and explicit post-processing was rejected.
compute: Rented EC2 spot p2.xlarge machines with K80 GPUs at $0.37/hour; individual models trained in minutes

solution_summary: The answerer first applied 22 regex functions to recognizable linguistic questions, then used Mistral-7B with majority voting across three few-shot prompts for remaining questions. Prompts and models were evaluated on roughly 1,300 questions, with the best individual prompt reaching 91% accuracy. The final questioner used Agent Alpha-style alphabetic bisection over a keyword list with estimated probabilities and guessed the most probable remaining candidate. Keyword probabilities came from repeated LLM generation within a detailed category hierarchy, supplemented with common nouns and geographic names. A probabilistic semantic question tree was abandoned because other bots answered its questions unreliably.
compute: Mistral inference took approximately 15 seconds per response; hardware unspecified.
external_data: ["Wikipedia articles (tested, rejected)", "Popular English nouns", "Countries and cities"]

solution_summary: The post shares training and inference links and outlines the team's common validation procedure. Labels were aggregated by EEG identifier and normalized, and EEG recordings were cropped to their middle 10,000 frames. Evaluation used five-fold Group K-fold with a vote threshold of at least ten. Individual modeling approaches are linked elsewhere and are not described in the supplied text.

solution_title: Best Pre-trained models - private score(80.4) - 69th place
solution_summary: The solution combined embeddings from four sentence encoders as features for a ridge regression model. Transformer outputs used attention-mask-aware mean pooling. A second ridge model used TF-IDF features, and the final predictions ensembled the two regressors. The author suspected that several encoders had already seen Ruddit during pretraining, but did not establish this.

The solution combined Inception-v3, Inception-v4, and Xception models trained on official PNG/TIFF images and external data. Four-channel inputs, class-balanced sampling, multilabel-stratified splits, and multiple image scales supported training. ImageNet-initialized models were first trained at size 512 and then refined at larger sizes, with checkpoints selected by validation loss. The final ensemble combined architectures, scales, and folds, with per-class thresholds optimized for F1; test-time augmentation and several alternative models did not help.

The selected solution used a fixed prompt bank and budgeted bandit to maximize verified single-post exfiltration findings per replay second. It probed templates, tracked firing and effective cost, and used backup switching and bounded top-ups. The selected variants reached 91.845 and 91.440 publicly but both scored zero privately. Separate confused-deputy kernels showed better transfer, including 17.600 public and 15.560 private, but were not selected.
compute: Approximately eight seconds per live candidate, with a 9,000-second replay cap.

solution_summary: The author constructs a training subset intended to resemble the private test set's inter-earthquake timing. CatBoost is trained on heavily overlapping random chunks using 32 statistical, peak, trend, and spectral features. Feature definitions reduce sensitivity to the drifting signal mean. All sampled chunks are used for training without providing a cross-validation set to the regressor. An attempt to combine time-since-failure and time-to-failure predictions was unsuccessful.

solution_title: Solution for Recruit Restaurant Visitor Forecasting Competition
solution_summary: The pipeline preprocesses competition data and generates visitor, reservation and weather features. It trains LightGBM and Keras models and combines their predictions with a weighted average. The blend achieved a private score of 0.505, improving on the individual models' scores of 0.509 and 0.513.

solution_title: Open-sourcing the code of Missed 5th place :)
solution_summary: The author shared an unselected submission that cleans the dataset by removing observations with unusually large prediction errors. A random forest regressor generates out-of-sample predictions through leave-one-out cross-validation. The method ranks observations by absolute residual and removes the ten largest. The cleaned dataset is submitted after dropping the residual column.

Detector signals were calibrated, masked, inpainted, spatially summed, and temporally filtered before entering a six-block residual convolutional model. The model combined normalized light curves with population-standardized wavelength statistics and normalized planet features, predicting transit depth and log uncertainty through separate heads. Training used MSE plus the competition's Gaussian log-likelihood error and several temporal, trend, and parameter-noise augmentations. Simple averaging across observations, offsets, and models worked best, while random folds were preferred over feature-based stratification.

The final system used three ByT5 models trained on selected data mixtures, with a Gemini-driven pipeline for sentence alignment, normalization, and corpus expansion. Improving heterogeneous document, OCR, and PDF data mattered more than increasing model size. Inference pooled and deduplicated candidates from beam search and multi-temperature sampling across models. Optuna-tuned weighted MBR reranking combined chrF++, BLEU, and Jaccard agreement, producing results comparable to or better than beam search and voting.

The team's main strategy was to ensemble more models, including a DeepTables neural network. Local cross-validation appeared unreliable, so the author relied partly on leaderboard feedback. Public and private scores ultimately differed little. A submission failure was traced to repeatedly loading the DeepTables model inside predict; loading it once outside the function resolved disk exhaustion.
compute: Online inference batch size 100, with 600 model loads before the fix; maximum disk capacity 57.6 GB.

solution_summary: The authors combined 34 variations of a neural network through weighted prediction averaging. Networks expected to perform well received higher weights, while weak networks were discarded. Their best included single network achieved 0.97147 on the private leaderboard. Subsequent reconstruction showed that longer training and an improved validation setup helped, while incomplete parameter records limited reproducibility.
compute: Training 34 networks and generating a solution takes several days on a machine with two high-powered GPUs.

solution_summary: The author built separate player-player and player-ground contact pipelines, each using an XGBoost candidate extractor, a small 2.5D CNN, and a final XGBoost classifier. Helmet and tracking data supplied 1,031 tabular features, while candidate pruning substantially reduced the image-processing workload at 0.992 recall. Helmet-scaled crops, player markers, and temporal shifts supported image learning, and the final classifier combined both camera-view scores with the original tabular features. The reported final private leaderboard score was 0.767, and an update attributed the validation discrepancy to folds with excessive player overlap.
compute: NVIDIA RTX 3090 Ti; approximately one hour to train all five folds of three-channel 2.5D CNNs for five epochs each. Polars feature extraction took 17–18 seconds.
external_data: ["Previous NFL competition data (NFL-2), attempted for pseudo-labeling"]

solution_summary: The solution generated images with SDXL and a custom LoRA trained on simplified synthetic images selected for aesthetics and prompt alignment. Basic VQA questions ranked candidate images, while frames, gradient backgrounds, and small visual modifications improved aesthetic scores. Training used color quantization, filtering, and offset noise to encourage suitable compositions and strong contrast. The custom LoRA outperformed the tested model and prompting combinations, while Qwen-generated VQA questions provided no improvement.

solution_title: Caterpillar Winners' Interview: 3rd place, Team Shift Workers
solution_summary: The team built a diverse weighted ensemble dominated by XGBoost, with one ExtraTrees model also retained. Feature engineering, variation in feature sets and parameters, and reliable local cross-validation drove improvements. Prediction-based meta-features from several algorithms added useful diversity despite weaker individual performance. Earlier large-scale XGBoost bagging gave way to cross-validation-guided blending, and component features resembling TF-IDF were effective.
compute: Early bagging experiments ran 100 or more XGBoost models overnight.

solution_summary: The approach centered on LoRA fine-tuning Gemma-2-9B-it for response preference classification. Key improvements included adapting o_proj and gate_proj, increasing training length to 3072, using adapters across all layers, adding 21k external examples, and increasing LoRA rank to 64. A replacement classification head and test-time augmentation also helped, with the experimental table reporting a TTA leaderboard score of 0.892. The author additionally explored DeBERTa and Llama3.1-8B-it, while identifying convergence and distillation as unresolved issues.
compute: A100-40G and A100-80G GPUs used in experiments

solution_summary: The post contains only a link to a Kaggle notebook about feature engineering for tabular and image data. It provides no approach description in the supplied text. No methods, implementation details, or results can be extracted from the post itself.

The author selected two ensembles containing 21 and 24 models and evaluated them with five-fold cross-validation. They used the original dataset and added engineered features to a few models to increase diversity. Treating all features as categorical was highlighted as a valuable approach that contributed to ensemble diversity. The selected submissions scored 0.97217 and 0.97335 on the reported leaderboard, while the author's highest leaderboard submission was not selected.

solution_title: Gilles Vandewiele's A "better" but useless solution: Private 0.97266
solution_summary: The author modified a published leak-exploiting kernel by replacing its cleaned data with ragnar123's clean_kalman dataset. This substitution achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.97266 despite very low cross-validation and public leaderboard scores. The post presents this result as evidence of a data problem and describes the approach as practically useless.

solution_title: 11th Place Solution for the LEAP - Atmospheric Physics using AI (ClimSim) Competition
solution_summary: The final submission ensembled six residual neural networks spanning bidirectional LSTM, GRU, RNN, and 1D-CNN architectures. Inputs combined standardized raw values and standardized log-absolute values with carefully initialized embeddings, while validation used a later year than training. Outlier-driven instability was addressed through staged training, either starting with clipped values or progressively expanding the training time span. Large-batch, low-learning-rate finishing improved some models, and hill-climbing ensemble weights produced CV 0.73472.

The solution blended a weighted heuristic predictor with a two-headed CNN that estimated the spectrum and its average uncertainty. Gaussian and Savitzky–Golay smoothing supported noise reduction, transit boundary detection, and prediction smoothing. Polynomial transit fitting and selected frequency intervals supplied the main features, while a 21-frequency CNN window helped control overfitting. Blend weights selected by training RMSE produced a reported public score of 0.692; predicting gas compositions and combining gas spectra did not work on public data.

The solution used two stages of DeBERTa training, with an ensemble generating soft pseudo-labels for unlabeled patient notes before new models were trained on labeled and pseudo-labeled data. Blending character-level probabilities transferred knowledge from larger teachers, including a model too expensive for final inference. The final submission combined four models with three folds each, and a common five-fold split agreed well with leaderboard results. Simple span cleanup helped, while alternative backbones and stackers did not improve the blend.

The author extended an existing Kore Beta rule-based agent with additional tactical and economic rules. A 20-turn board projection supported defense, fleet interception, and shipyard attacks based on expected reinforcements and spawning capacity. Expansion, ship transfers, and spawning rules coordinated resources across shipyards. Mining fleet sizes and trip durations depended on distances to friendly and opposing shipyards.

The authors trained breast-level LSTM models on sequences of four mammogram images, repeating images for shorter sequences and truncating longer ones. Final models used convnext_tiny and tf_efficientnetv2_s backbones with 1280 × 800 images, four external datasets, and extensive augmentation. Training lasted 20 epochs, and the best single model achieved a cross-validation F1 of 0.504. These models complemented teammates' image-level models; LSTM inference used YOLOX-cropped images saved to disk because the fully GPU-based DALI pipeline could not accommodate its varying image inputs.
compute: GPU-based DICOM decoding, YOLOX cropping, and CNN inference in teammates' DALI pipeline; hardware model and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution combined a pretrained Faster R-CNN Inception-ResNet-v2 base detector with ResNet-101 detectors trained on six class-frequency subsets. Splitting the imbalanced dataset improved performance substantially over a single model. Pseudo-labeling and overlap-based sample weighting addressed missing annotations, while class-specific validation performance guided model selection and confidence rescoring. Hierarchical class expansion and Soft-NMS completed the detection pipeline.

The team combined noisy-student EfficientNet B3/B4/B5, Inception V4, and SEResNeXt50 backbones. EfficientNet models joined multilevel local attention features with global ArcFace and BNNeck representations, averaging three classifier logits at inference. Training first covered the 5,000 most frequent categories, then expanded to all categories using weight imprinting and balanced sampling. A convolutional stacking network combined models, and species-count post-processing raised the final private score to 0.84484.

The solution optimized a universal mean prompt on a public prompt dataset, starting with beam search and refining it through word insertion and pruning. The authors then selected a training subset whose evaluation scores better matched leaderboard behavior, improving the public score from 0.68 to 0.70. Prompts exceeding 128 tokens required extra pruning because they scored poorly. Appending Mistral 7B output to the optimized mean prompt added approximately 0.005.

solution_title: Approach: ML-drifted-random-walks (Brownian particle in "ML"-field) and call for collaboration
solution_summary: The author describes repeated random walks guided by a model that estimates the distance from a puzzle state to its solution. At each step, possible moves are ranked by predicted distance and one of the top candidates is sampled, with unsuccessful walks restarted. A brute-force neighborhood around the solved state can provide an easier stopping target followed by a short completion path. The approach solved smaller globe puzzles, but larger puzzles required stronger guidance than the author achieved.

The team adapted the architecture from the linked paper to predict outputs on connections between atoms. They first trained separate networks for j_1, j_2, and j_3 couplings, then specialized them into individual coupling types. Their main training trick was to initially provide Mulliken charges as features and remove them later in training. No numerical results or additional implementation details are reported.

The model represents each question by taking the elementwise maximum over pretrained GloVe word embeddings and predicts duplication through a fully connected network with sigmoid output. It uses four hidden layers of 200 dimensions, batch normalization, binary cross-entropy, and Adam. Max pooling slightly outperformed mean, sum, bidirectional LSTM, and GRU representations, while dropout reduced accuracy. Selecting the checkpoint with the highest validation accuracy produced a held-out test accuracy of 0.8291.
compute: AWS EC2 p2-xlarge GPU instance; approximately 120 seconds per epoch for 25 epochs.

solution_title: TFLite beam search with char ngram rescoring (59th place)
solution_summary: The author implemented beam search using TensorFlow operations under the competition's TFLite restrictions. Beam search improved both public and private leaderboard scores by 0.005 across their models. Larger search widths improved validation results but exceeded inference time limits. A character bigram language model trained from training phrases provided no score improvement.

The solution searched for a broadly effective mean prompt by predicting leaderboard scores from scores on several datasets. A lasso regression predictor achieved R² of 0.97, enabling component-wise optimization of a target embedding. GPT-3.5 prompt variations and a token-level genetic algorithm then searched for text close to that target, reaching 0.66 against an estimated maximum of 0.68. Appending the resulting mean prompt to a teammate's tuned model output produced a score in the high 0.68 range.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution | Hill Climbing + Ridge Ensemble
solution_summary: The solution used hill climbing to select complementary tree and neural models, then applied Ridge stacking to their rank-transformed predictions. Base-model diversity came from feature engineering, hyperparameters, seeds, and inclusion of existing ensembles. The selected stack used 36 models and alpha 10, trading a slightly weaker post-cutoff CV score for better leaderboard generalization. It achieved post-cutoff CV 0.70860 and public score 0.70739.

The team detected cars with three Faster R-CNN models and regressed their translation and quaternion rotation using a separate Q-Net. Detector training used dimension-adjusted boxes derived from supplied car models, preceded by BDD100k fine-tuning. Q-Net combined crop features with numerical box features, and ten-fold predictions were averaged. Fusion with a teammate's CenterNet predictions raised scores from 0.124 to 0.131 publicly and from 0.116 to 0.123 privately.
models_pretrained: ["DenseNet121", "Faster R-CNN X-101-32x8d-FPN", "Faster R-CNN R-101-FPN", "Faster R-CNN R-50-FPN", "CenterNet"]

solution_summary: The solution adapted a public CenterNet baseline with a ResNet152 backbone and larger input images. It simplified prediction by dropping several pose outputs and converting row, column, and depth directly to spatial coordinates. Five-fold ensembling, adjusted thresholds, and test masks improved detection, while three-scale ensembling offered little clear benefit. Combining the team's models achieved public and private scores of 0.129 and 0.119.

The post shares a prediction post-processing pipeline without describing the underlying models. Each target is independently min-max scaled and then rounded downward to a grid determined by its number of raters. Spelling predictions are forced to zero outside two English-language Stack Exchange hosts. Targets with 18 or 30 raters receive minimum predictions of one-third or one-fifth, respectively.

The author used XGBoost and converted class probabilities into expected wine-quality values. Optimizing thresholds for quadratic weighted kappa provided the largest improvement, followed by manual hyperparameter tuning. Two-fold stratified cross-validation produced the selected model, while training on all data performed worse. Outlier removal and weighting predictions to match training class frequencies both reduced performance.

The strongest single model was depth-four XGBoost with about 140 features and a private leaderboard score of 0.50460. Regularized Bayesian target ratings provided the largest improvement, alongside listing metadata, image metadata, geographic clusters, grouped statistics and image-time leakage features. Around 15 first-level models included continuous-target and one-versus-all formulations, feeding XGBoost and LightGBM second-level models. Their geometric mean, followed by prior correction, formed the final submission.

solution_title: The Monkeytyping Solution to the Youtube-8M Video Understanding Challenge
solution_summary: The repository describes a pipeline that trains individual models, selects their best checkpoints, and generates intermediate predictions. A trained stacking model combines those predictions into the submission. Separate data paths support base-model training and ensemble training and validation. Bagging, boosting, distillation, and cascade model scripts are also provided, but their architectures and contributions are not explained.
compute: Training a model may take 3–5 days; hardware is not specified.

solution_summary: The solution trained Mask R-CNN with a Swin Transformer backbone and HTC RoI head using a two-stage pseudo-labeling pipeline. Models trained on dataset 1 produced pseudo labels for datasets 2 and 3, followed by five-fold training on all three datasets. Inference combined multiscale and flip augmentation, proposal and RoI ensembling, and mask filtering. Dilation remained beneficial on both leaderboards, although its advantage shrank from 0.1 to 0.02 after improving dataset 2 supervision.
models_pretrained: ["Mask R-CNN with Swin Transformer backbone and HTC RoI head", "YOLOv8"]

solution_summary: The author described a Transformer model trained and validated with TensorFlow on a Google Colab TPU, while noting that it differed from the version responsible for their private leaderboard score. Elapsed-time and lag-time features improved leaderboard performance, and an auxiliary objective predicting the actual user response allowed longer training without overfitting. Historical counts and correctness ratios by part, answer, and user–question pair further improved cross-validation performance to 0.813. An epoch over one million sequences of length 128 took five to six minutes.

solution_summary: The solution used single-cell ResNet50 and EfficientNet B4 models alongside image-level SE-ResNeXt50 and EfficientNet B7 models. External data and downsampling balanced label counts to about 10,000 per label, improving the leaderboard score by roughly 0.01. Filtering cell crops by average pixel intensity addressed weak labels and some protruding nuclei, contributing another 0.03–0.04. Single-cell models used 128-pixel inputs and test-time augmentation, while image-level models used 640-pixel green-channel inputs.

The team generated candidate location pairs with geographic and fine-tuned SentenceBERT nearest neighbors, then classified pairs using seven LightGBM models. Two-stage contrastive fine-tuning supplied harder negatives and improved candidate recall to 0.986. Embedding similarities, transliterated character TF-IDF similarities, categorical encodings, and geographic aggregates enriched the classifier. Training on more locations substantially improved results, and RAPIDS reduced inference time by a factor of 40.
compute: Single GPU on Google Colab for embedding models; Google Colab Pro+ for classifier training.

solution_summary: The solution used small recurrent neural networks with stock attention to learn from minimally engineered market sequences across all stocks in a time bucket. A stronger variant incorporated neighboring time buckets identified through recovered prices, and final submissions ensembled either ten stock-attention models or six neighbor-aware models. Per-stock standardization, log transforms, normalization across stocks and features, and limiting model size were particularly useful. The author hypothesized that stock-split-related volume shifts caused private performance degradation, supported by a scaling experiment that worsened the score from 0.198 to 0.22.
compute: Single-fold training: 3D model 20 minutes for 30 epochs; 4D model 4 hours for 30 epochs; 5D model 24 hours for 20 epochs.

solution_title: [Private 24th, Public 30th solution] Prompt injection with random words
solution_summary: The solution mixed three selected attacks: Cut-off Date, Base64 Understanding, and Divisor Counting. The author collected around 100 submission results and trained a simple neural network to optimize their proportions. The reported rounded-down proportions were 0.297, 0.407, and 0.296, respectively. The remaining search focused on the random seed, with seed 5 selected.

solution_title: Imitation Learning by Semantic Segmentation for Halite IV Competition (8th Gold solution)
solution_summary: The bot used centralized imitation learning to predict immediate ship actions from board states collected from strong opponents' replays. It treated the board as a multichannel image and action prediction as semantic segmentation. Handcrafted spatial and historical features supported the learned policy, while tuned rules overrode actions for spawning, conversion, and base protection. The writeup also describes extensive manual assignment and attack strategies that informed the approach.

The team settled on Cfish after trying Stockfish versions under RAM constraints. Evaluation relied entirely on a custom NNUE network combining convolutional and weight-sharing dense features. The network targeted a small binary, but its computational cost was excessive relative to its accuracy. Training mixed Leela-generated and Stockfish-generated data, while small hash tables, compiler settings, and feature removal reduced resource use.
The post links to the author's external explanation of their competition approach. It provides no methodological details in the supplied text. It also thanks Kaggle for organizing the competition.

solution_title: The Most Important Thing... (50th Public LB Solution)
solution_summary: The team used multilayer perceptrons with quantile-transformed features, softplus activations, AdamW, warm restarts, and a combined classification and MAE objective. Permutation-importance feature removal provided the largest reported improvement, reducing the leaderboard score from 0.01330 to 0.01320. They submitted a ten-fold model and a separate model bagged ten times on all data, stopping the latter at a categorical cross-entropy loss of 2.52. Many alternative architectures, embeddings, distributional outputs, and post-processing schemes failed to improve results.
compute: CPU-only; no GPU available.

solution_summary: The team combined image classifiers and tabular boosting models, with separate variants trained with and without historical ISIC data. Patient-grouped stratified validation kept image and table splits consistent, while public leaderboard checks assessed unknown hospital attribution. Extensive grouped and age-shifted metadata features, image out-of-fold predictions, and attribution-dependent model selection strengthened the tabular component. Optuna-tuned weighted averaging produced a reported CV score of 0.1839 and private score of 0.172.

The solution combined an autoencoder/GNN framework with an added GRU layer and RNA pairing and distance features. It retained more training measurements by masking unreliable individual targets and weighting sequences by cluster size and similarity to private data. Pseudo-labeling used reliable positions from the private set and randomly generated sequences, with uncertainty masking, target perturbation, and validation-based rollback of harmful training sections. Model diversity and correlation-based blending were important, while pseudo-labeling reportedly improved the score by at least 80 basis points.

The solution combined image models, temporal CNNs, and XGBoost in four stages. Two camera views produced player-level contact and ground predictions, which a temporal CNN smoothed before XGBoost associated player pairs. A second temporal CNN then smoothed pairwise contact predictions. Stratified grouped validation by game play tracked leaderboard performance closely, with final CV 0.77174 and private leaderboard 0.77004.

The team combined two independently developed ensembles built from extensive text features and diverse learners. Feature subsets were selected manually and by correlation, while cross-validation guided parameter optimization and generated predictions for stacking. Keeping text-processing variants with and without spelling correction added diversity. The final blend used different weights across ID ranges, and both submitted blends achieved private RMSE 0.43271.
compute: Feature generation could take 1–2 days, depending on computational power.
