solution_summary: The solution addresses the domain gap between relatively clean training audio and noisy inference soundscapes through a staged sound-event detection pipeline. It starts with a v2s backbone, removes human speech, cleans training data, and replaces raw-audio mixup with sumix. Pseudo-labeled five-second clips are randomly sampled into training audio, giving a reported public-score gain of 0.03–0.04. The final ensemble adds seresnext26t, v2_b3, and rare-species subset models, with additional postprocessing reported to improve results.

This post announces released notebooks, GitHub repositories and pretrained models for the team's ventilator pressure solution. It links resources for LSTM/CNN/Transformer modeling, PID controller matching and an LSTM on raw data. It also announces forthcoming notebooks and a more detailed blog post.

The model combined three transformer encoder blocks for questions, interactions, and cross-attention over questions, responses, and interactions. Historical user statistics initialized sequences, while temporal and task-container encodings represented event timing and order. Online question difficulty and a heuristic knowledge proxy enriched response embeddings. Training used overlapping sequence windows, a held-out set of users, and a Noam learning-rate schedule, converging in roughly 20–30 epochs.
compute: Kaggle GPUs initially, then TPUs; batch size 1024; 4–6 minutes per epoch; at most 4 hours training.

solution_summary: The author ensembled 20 transformer models diversified across tasks, backbones, pooling heads, and preprocessing, tuning their weights with Optuna. Regression used MSE, while classification used cross-entropy and converted class probabilities to similarity scores. DeBERTa-v3-large was the strongest individual backbone, and diversity improved the ensemble even when individual experiments did not improve cross-validation. The ensemble scored 0.8535 CV, 0.8514 public, and 0.8655 private; pseudo-labeling and masked-language-model pretraining did not help.

solution_title: Surrogate loss for modified Laplace log likelihood (79th solution)
solution_summary: The author shared a PyTorch loss for jointly predicting FVC and confidence from tabular data. It approximated the competition's Laplace log-likelihood using Smooth L1 prediction error. A leaky activation softened the confidence floor of 70 to preserve gradients during training, with an optional hard-clamped path. The best private score was -6.8383, although that model version was not selected for the final submission.

solution_title: Private 0.458 with 3 single cell classifiers (37th place solution) - a data centric approach
solution_summary: The solution focused on cell-level classification using a curated dataset of roughly 250,000 cell images with about 144 label combinations. Class-specific heuristics based on segmentation masks and fluorescence intensities removed noisy labels, while rare classes also received manual labeling. An ensemble of Inception v3, MobileNet, and DenseNet121 trained on resized images with rotations and flips achieved 0.458 private and 0.464 public scores. Combining image-level predictions offered little benefit and was excluded from the reported final approach.

solution_title: 18th place - Ensemble of 3 matchers + bonus crazy ideas that didn't work
solution_summary: The final pipeline combined correspondences from vanilla LoFTR, DKM, and PDCNet_plus. LoFTR used three image-scale combinations, while the dense matchers supplied overlap-dependent random samples. All matches were rescaled to original coordinates and pooled for MAGSAC fundamental-matrix estimation, with parameters selected using the public leaderboard. Additional matchers and more complex geometric refinement strategies did not improve the ensemble.
compute: Attempted local-feature refinement took over approximately 5 seconds for thousands of matches.

solution_summary: For CITE-seq, the author retained input variables whose standard deviation exceeded GAPDH's rather than applying PCA. An MLP used 0.75 dropout in its first layer to encourage automatic variable selection, while separate CatBoost models predicted the 140 targets. CatBoost outperformed LightGBM without hyperparameter tuning. For the multiome task, inputs were compressed separately by chromosome using SVD, and targets were converted to int8 to reduce storage and potentially round measurement noise.

solution_title: 41st Place Solution for the CAFA 6 Protein Function Prediction Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined ESM2 protein embeddings and learned taxonomy embeddings in a shared Conv1D backbone with separate BP, MF, and CC prediction heads. Training used positive-weighted binary cross-entropy with normalized Information Accretion weights, while validation used a holdout split and Micro-F1. Predictions were propagated upward through the GO hierarchy and blended with BLAST homology predictions and propagated GOA annotations. Hierarchical consistency and external biological evidence delivered the largest gains, with GOA contributing most and ESM2-3B outperforming the other tested embedding models.

solution_title: (Public 28) More Distillation and things that didn't work
solution_summary: The author selected a 14B Deepseek model with AWQ quantization and used majority voting with adaptive stopping to allocate more inference time to difficult problems. Local evaluation combined reference problems with 40 hard OpenR1-Math-220k examples and measured per-sequence correctness and completion. Additional distillation on hard problems increased per-sequence correctness from 0.29 to 0.35. Length-based preference optimization, TokenSkip compression, and merging models trained on separate mathematical subtasks did not improve results.

The author found inference faster on a P100 than on two NVIDIA T4 GPUs. They set the repetition count to 27 and used the resulting submission as their final entry, achieving a public score of 23. Other settings, including temperature, were left unchanged.

solution_title: Artem777 in MITSUI&CO. Commodity Prediction Challenge
solution_summary: The solution trained an LSTM to forecast all 424 commodity features and recursively extended those predictions over five days. It then derived target log returns and spreads mathematically from the forecast features. Mean imputation, standardization, and 50-day input windows supported training with a chronological validation holdout. Blending predictions with recent label-lag averages was the strongest improvement, and the reported private score was 0.514.
compute: Training took approximately 2–3 minutes on a standard CPU or under 1 minute on a P100 GPU; prediction took under 500 ms per batch.

solution_summary: The solution used a three-stage fracture-detection pipeline, beginning with vertebra-aware frame sampling and available fracture boxes. A second model processed five frames in 2.5D with an LSTM head. Study-level RNN or 1D-CNN models combined slice probabilities with the most confident YOLOv5-l fracture-box probability. Study-level aggregation extracted useful signal despite imperfect fracture detection, and correcting the evaluation metric helped substantially.

solution_title: 4th Place Solution - Optimizing a Simple email.send Attack
solution_summary: The solution repeatedly induced empty email tool calls that the guardrail permitted but the evaluator classified as unauthorized. Unique recipients obtained separate scoring cells, making reliable execution throughput more valuable than attack diversity. Model-specific prompts minimized output and maximized shared-prefix cache reuse, with ordinary quotation marks notably improving Gemma throughput. Small probes, staged benchmarks, and parallel reproducibility checks supported a final reported score of 41.325.
compute: Three Colab A100 instances used for parallel reproducibility validation.

solution_summary: The solution combined fine-tuned Protenix and RNAPro with conventional and motif-based template modeling. Motif-based modeling assembled structures using a constructed motif and loop library and SPOTRNA secondary-structure predictions, while RNAPro refined template-derived predictions. Protenix generated diversity through inference with and without MSA and through weights from different training steps, and an internal score selected five submission structures. GPU memory limited fine-tuning to shorter sequences. Clustering-based automatic selection and a multimer-specific model were tested but excluded from the final submission.
compute: GPU memory limitations restricted training to relatively short sequences.

solution_title: 19th place (solo gold): a behaviour clone of the 1st, 3rd and 7th place teams
solution_summary: The final agent cloned three strategically compatible teachers using twelve small residual CNNs trained on replay actions. It averaged probabilities across three model families, applied legality-aware unit decoding and error-diffusion purchase decoding, and added three rules for overflow and endgame selling. Training from scratch and retaining the final epoch outperformed fine-tuning and validation-loss checkpoint selection. The final score was 5,210.3; paired local tests supported model selection but missed free-play states where imitation errors accumulated.
external_data: ["M & M & P & Q, DSM, and DECEM teacher replays", "Older M & M & P & Q submission replays", "Boey replays"]

solution_summary: The final submission combined three ViT models with weighted averaging and five test-time augmentations. One model processed 384×384 images directly, while two variants split 448×448 images into four patches and combined their features using attention weights. Training used five stratified folds, 2019 and 2020 data, simple spatial augmentation, and a decaying learning rate. Larger-image CNN alternatives were discarded over concerns about overfitting; the ensemble achieved public and private scores of 0.9075 and 0.9028.

The solution combines models trained on selected months to match the expected June product distribution and seasonality. Its main blend weights December–January and June–December–January models by 0.3 and 0.7, with specialized predictions for taxes, existing customers holding no products, and e-accounts. Features capture product history, recent holdings, product combination frequencies, and customer attributes. Missing values and pension payment anomalies are repaired, deposit additions are suppressed, and pension and payroll recommendation order is adjusted.

The final solution combined LightGBM, a message-passing graph model, and a neural network using median stacking followed by Lasso regression to smooth predictions. Molecular geometry, bond properties, atom neighborhoods, and substituent counts were central features. The final individual models achieved reported leaderboard scores of -2.103, -2.24, and -2.11, respectively. SchNet was limited by training time and initialization sensitivity, while equation-based coupling features suffered from unreliable calculated angles.

solution_summary: The main submission combined 19 transformer-based models, including RoBERTa embeddings followed by SVR and ridge regression. Ensemble weights were optimized with Nelder–Mead and adjusted using cross-validation and public leaderboard feedback, with negative weights allowed. Most models were trained with dropout disabled, and only one RoBERTa model received masked-language-model pretraining. Piecewise multiplicative post-processing improved the score by approximately 0.001–0.002, and the described submission achieved 0.446 on the private leaderboard.
compute: A100 and V100 GPUs on GCP; P100 GPUs on Kaggle.

solution_summary: The solution routed tokens into custom regex-based categories and used separate character-level sequence-to-sequence models for categories requiring learned normalization. Punctuation and a corpus-derived set of clean words were copied unchanged, while electronic tokens used rules. Neighboring tokens supplied context to the neural models, with input length restricted to keep training manageable. Reported category validation accuracies ranged from 79.23% for electronic tokens to 100% for punctuation, and grouping similar tokens accelerated training.
compute: 5–6 days developing the approach and training models; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution combined EfficientNet study classifiers with DetectoRS and UniverseNet image-level detectors. Five-fold iterative stratification balanced study classes and box counts, while classifier diversity came from auxiliary branches, resolutions, and folds. Detection used pseudo labels, non-maximum weighted ensembling, and flip or multiscale test-time augmentation. The study-level ensemble achieved approximately 41.5–41.6 mAP on the leaderboard.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution (Part of data processing and Image-level model)
solution_summary: The pipeline extracted fixed-aspect-ratio breast regions with YOLOX and classified them with image-level CNNs and multi-view CNN–LSTM models. Four external mammography datasets improved validation performance and training stability, while encoded machine, site, and view metadata supplemented CNN features. Predictions were combined conservatively using fold-dependent weights and thresholds selected from out-of-fold data. The LSTM-focused submission achieved CV 0.554 and a private score of 0.53, with more stable thresholds than image-level models.

The solution combined CNN14, ResNet38, and EfficientNet models with direct five-second classification inference. Its most important improvement was training sound event detection models on longer clips to reduce label noise, alongside model-derived clipping probabilities and label smoothing for secondary labels. A small validation set with controlled nocall proportions supported sample-averaged F1 evaluation and threshold selection. Background and spectral augmentations addressed domain shift, while optimized resampling allowed all models to run in about 20 minutes.
compute: All-model inference took 20 minutes with kaiser_fast resampling and around one hour with kaiser_best; hardware unspecified.
external_data: ["Background audio from the external data thread", "Six shared recordings and two example audios for validation"]

solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned a DINOv3 Huge backbone with LoRA and treated biomass prediction as density estimation. Images at 1024×2048 resolution were split into non-overlapping 512×512 tiles to preserve local texture. A shared attention gate weighted token-level densities, and five target-specific heads predicted three quantiles each before aggregation across tokens and tiles. Training used pinball loss on log-transformed targets, AdamW, early stopping, and bfloat16 precision. A custom toroidal roll augmentation encouraged the model to focus on texture density rather than absolute position.
compute: Single NVIDIA A100 (40GB); 10 hours training; gradient accumulation steps=4.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution for the Predict Student Performance from Game Play Competition
solution_summary: The solution blended XGBoost models with lightweight convolutional neural networks, with event duration driving both approaches. XGBoost used aggregated durations and event counts, while the neural network multiplied learned duration representations by summed categorical event embeddings. Supplemental game logs improved cross-validation by about 0.002, and repeated validation guided feature and architecture choices. A single global prediction threshold favored robustness, and TensorFlow Lite accelerated the lightweight neural network.
compute: Initial Transformer experiments took approximately 2 hours per fold; the initial Conv1D model was about 10 times faster.

solution_summary: The agent used two LightGBM models trained on logs from 3,000 games to estimate each bandit's initial threshold at every step. One model emphasized exploitation, while the other transformed the target to favor exploration through a greater penalty for underestimation. Their predictions were combined with weights that shifted toward exploitation over time, adjusted for decay, and used to select the highest-valued bandit. Candidate agents were evaluated through about 1,000 games against the author's strongest existing agent, while attempts to withhold information from opponents failed.

The author searched word permutations using a priority queue ordered by perplexity, exploring local neighborhoods and allowing limited worsening moves. Restarts, larger perturbations, and exchanging solutions between teammates' different algorithms helped escape local minima. Cached scores reduced repeated evaluations, and final neighborhoods were checked using the Kaggle metric on T4 GPUs. The search repeatedly recovered a 298.9 solution for id2, while branch-and-bound, large random searches, loss-based heuristics, and frozen phrases were unsuccessful.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution Writeup for Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations
solution_summary: The solution combined ChemBERTa embeddings of molecular SMILES with one-hot identifiers and target statistics grouped by cell type and molecule. LSTM, GRU, and one-dimensional CNN models were trained across five folds and multiple feature representations. A weighted combination of four losses and augmentation that zeroed random input entries improved predictive performance. Later experiments found GRU and CNN stronger individually than LSTM, and removing ChemBERTa padding improved the private score to 0.719.
external_data: ["Wikipedia descriptions of cell types and molecules"]

solution_title: 1st place solution: Metric learning and GPT
solution_summary: The author used a GPT causal language model for dataset-name span extraction, predicting starts and conditioning end predictions on the selected start. Replacing 95% of training mentions with random dataset names helped prevent memorization. Beam search generated candidate spans, followed by probability and corpus-frequency filtering. The selected submission scored 0.565 privately; adding abbreviation-detector predictions reduced performance, and the teammates submitted their models separately because their ensemble was unstable.

solution_title: 3217th -> 17th place simple LSTM model with custom loss function
solution_summary: The author trained a small LSTM on short chunks of time-series observations, using seven time points in the submitted model. A custom loss rewarded returns while penalizing squared returns, with a tunable coefficient controlling the risk penalty. The model had a final public score of about 4000 and performed unexpectedly well on reruns. The author hypothesized that penalizing risky trades helped as rerun data moved further from the training regime.

The solution used the original data alongside a stacked ensemble. CatBoost, XGBoost, and random forest formed the first level, with LightGBM as the metamodel. Validation used five splits repeated ten times. Permutation importance was applied separately to each model.
external_data: ["Original data referenced in the linked competition discussion"]

solution_summary: The solution averaged predictions from two mixture-of-experts models, an LSTM, and a two-hidden-layer neural network. The mixture-of-experts models used 24 and 16 mixtures and trained for about 10 epochs each. The LSTM trained for only half an epoch but added nearly 0.01 GAP to the ensemble, which the author attributed to complementary frame-level information. The final ensemble achieved a private leaderboard GAP of 0.81390.
compute: Google Cloud Platform ML Engine using free trial credits; MoE models trained for approximately 10 epochs each and LSTM for approximately half an epoch.

solution_summary: The solution trained five ImageNet-pretrained CNN architectures on 256×256 image patches, including patches from an additional dataset. Training augmentation simulated JPEG compression, resizing, and gamma changes, while validation kept original images separate between splits. At inference, model probabilities were averaged over augmented patches and models, followed by majority voting across patch labels. Additional checkpoints improved the private score from 0.983 to 0.986.

The solution used ordinary least squares regression to predict point spreads from three differences in team efficiency ratings. These measured scoring efficiency margin with greater weight on recent games, draw-foul efficiency, and three-point efficiency. Opponent- and tempo-adjusted ratings were computed through regression on one-hot team identifiers, and candidate features were compared with leave-one-out cross-validation. A logistic regression converted predicted spreads and an interaction with scoring-efficiency residual variance into win probabilities.

solution_title: [143th place] single model trained with cross entropy / contrastive loss using fastai
solution_summary: The submission was based on an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 trained with a combined cross-entropy and contrastive objective. Training used one-cycle scheduling, progressive image resizing, gradual unfreezing, discriminative learning rates, and Adam. The model learned from extracted bounding boxes with moderate augmentation and progressively harder datasets with some class balancing. Predictions used Euclidean similarity between feature vectors, without cleaning the training data.

The solution ensembled five-fold U-Net and U-Net++ models with pretrained EfficientNet-B7 and MiT-B5 encoders. Organ-specific resolution adjustment, strong augmentation, histogram matching, and two rounds of pseudo-labeling on external HPA and GTEX images helped address differences in scale and staining. Inference combined checkpoint weight averaging, fold prediction averaging, flip augmentation, and small-region removal. The selected ensemble scored 0.83266 on private evaluation, while an unselected ensemble containing an additional MiT-B3 model achieved 0.83419.

solution_summary: The author trained five EfficientNet models on the full GLDV2 dataset using CurricularFace loss, Adam, and gradient accumulation, then concatenated their embeddings for retrieval. The main improvement came from assigning soft landmark scores to both test and index images using their five nearest GLDV2 images. Retrieval ranked index images by the dot product of these landmark-score vectors, then appended missing embedding-based nearest neighbors. This post-processing improved private leaderboard performance by 0.075 to 0.464, with a final public score of 0.448.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled two sets of five-fold segmentation models with ResNeXt50 and ResNeXt101 backbones. Inference expanded each tile in every direction and retained only its central predictions to suppress edge artifacts. A fixed threshold of 0.5 was chosen to limit bias from training labels.

solution_title: Innovative Approach to Predictive Modeling: Ensemble Learning with LightGBM and XGBoost - 7th place solution
solution_summary: The solution combined LightGBM and XGBoost classifiers through soft voting. Categorical variables were label-encoded, and additional diagnosis-date and disease features were created from existing data. The author used a stratified split and Optuna to tune both models against negative log loss. Final probability predictions were averaged and evaluated with log loss.

The author solved several AI security challenges by adapting strategies from earlier CTF competitions. They identified poorly classified demographic groups, counted pixel intensities, and optimized images against a MobileNetV2 model while matching submission preprocessing. Other challenges used carefully rendered text, inverted model probability selection, and pixel-value changes to expose hidden messages. Iterative experimentation with image formatting and learning rates was central to several solutions.

The team blended LightGBM cross-entropy and multiclass models, CatBoost multiclass models, and a three-layer one-vs-rest MLP. Time-decayed behavioral features and aggressive importance-based feature selection were central to the pipeline. Validation mimicked test truncation, and sampled out-of-fold predictions guided blending and threshold optimization. One final submission achieved a truncated score of 0.5818 and a private score of 0.557.

The solution used SENet154 with a separate binary classification task for each whale identity, allowing new_whale images to participate in training. Inputs combined RGB images and masks, and training progressed from identities with many examples to all samples with most layers frozen. Treating flipped known whales as separate identities, adding confident pseudo-labels, and applying class balance postprocessing improved performance. Four-fold cross-validation with these refinements achieved 0.973, while ensembles with other architectures provided no improvement.

solution_title: Thanks . We all did Best. Solution Outline (Public LB 9th place)
solution_summary: The team extended a public baseline with a noise and mixup setup adapted from a previous competition solution. They trained diverse CNN and sound event detection models, downweighted secondary labels, and experimented with recording-quality-based label strength. Ensembling and post-processing were crucial, with the reported public score improving from about 0.72 to 0.78. Class-specific thresholds produced their best private score of 0.66, but that variant was not selected because its public performance suggested overfitting.

The team stacked EfficientNet-B5, ResNeXt-101, ViT-B16 and an embedding-based KNN using a 1,500-tree CatBoost model. Training combined 2019 and 2020 data, with stratified five-fold validation restricted to 2020 examples. A three-stage training schedule moved from balanced data to the natural class distribution and finally augmentation-free fine-tuning. Three-crop inference and fold averaging supported a final reported CV score of 0.904 and private score of 0.899.

solution_title: 7th Place Solution for the BirdCLEF 2024 Competition
solution_summary: The final ensemble combined two sound event detection models and one CNN, including a specialist model for 66 rare species. Extra xeno-canto audio, soundscape clips extracted with bird classifiers, and knowledge distillation improved the baseline from 0.65 to 0.70. Training species subsets separately was the most important design choice, although a broader three-subset ensemble was withheld because of overfitting concerns. INT8 quantization of SED encoders reduced one model's inference time from 100 to 80 minutes, while CNN quantization hurt accuracy.

solution_summary: The solution combined three BERT variants and three RNN models through weighted averaging. Ensemble weights were optimized with SciPy Nelder-Mead against cross-validation performance. RNN diversity came from translation augmentation and data from an earlier toxicity competition. Missing identity annotations were estimated by a separate RNN trained on fully annotated examples, reflecting that missing annotations do not imply absent identities.

solution_title: 46th place with classification and barely using external data.
solution_summary: The solution combined five-fold EfficientNet B3, EfficientNet B5, and SE-ResNeXt101 classifiers trained with fastai. Training used image augmentation, label-smoothed cross-entropy, Adam, and a one-cycle learning rate schedule, with limited external data added only to training folds. The author favored models with prediction correlations below 0.9 and selected horizontal-flip inference ensembles. Combining all architectures with horizontal flips achieved a private score of 0.926.

solution_summary: The solution used a residual 1D CNN on 122-dimensional hand and lip coordinates, with Self Conditional CTC and greedy decoding. Randomly dropping hand landmarks across consecutive frames helped control overfitting. Self Conditional CTC substantially improved performance without increasing computation. The PyTorch model was converted to a 16-bit quantized TFLite model using onnx2tf; stochastic weight averaging and a Levenshtein OCR decoder did not help.

The solution combined dense neural networks with engineered numerical features, a user identifier, and user-level aggregates. Numerical inputs received log transformation, standardization, mean imputation, and missingness indicators, while categorical inputs generally used reduced-cardinality one-hot encoding. A four-dimensional user embedding and a regularized factorization-machine branch handled selected categorical information. Blending networks trained with different losses and adding denoising-autoencoder representations brought the reported leaderboard AUC to 0.9564, with 0.9548 unshuffled cross-validation AUC.

solution_title: [Private LB0.63] FewShot Prompt & Chain of Thought (CoT) Approach (No Mean Prompt or Model Training)
solution_summary: The author recovered rewrite prompts using few-shot prompting and chain-of-thought reasoning without training a model. A filtered public dataset containing Gemma-7B-IT generations supported evaluation, with UMAP used to assess diversity and visual inspection providing a final check. The adopted pipeline passed a first-stage prediction into a second stage, retaining natural text or refining it when needed. This approach produced relatively strong, correlated CV and leaderboard scores, while mean prompts and model training were rejected because of mismatches between their evaluation results.

solution_title: 7th  Place Solution for the AIMO3 Competition
solution_summary: The solution used GPT-OSS 120B without additional training, running up to eight parallel mathematical reasoning attempts per problem with Python tool access. A concise olympiad-style prompt enforced the answer range and boxed output format. Valid answers were combined using inverse mean-token-entropy weights, with conservative repetition-based stopping and dynamic time allocation. Longer prompts and more elaborate entropy metrics did not consistently improve results; the simpler configuration achieved public scores of 36–40.

Diverse base learners included TF-IDF linear models, LightGBM, a factorization machine, a ridge classifier, and GRU networks with pretrained word embeddings. Rank transformation and automatic blend-weight optimization improved cross-validation, yielding 0.99231 five-fold CV and 0.9872 on the private leaderboard, although the final blend did not outperform the XGBoost stacker at the reported leaderboard precision.

solution_summary: The author developed an anchor-relative particle-filter, spatial projection, and LightGBM pipeline, then separately extended an ablated public pipeline with a pretrained full-well residual ensemble. They sought second-stage coverage using the previous Quora competition and questions scraped from users with many insincere posts. solution_title: A Big Data Alternative Approach using PySpark ML
solution_summary: The author presents an alternative approach using Apache Spark and PySpark ML. The approach uses competition data to tell a story and demonstrate the workflow in a video. The provided text does not specify features, models, validation, or results.

The final agent was a deterministic greedy fleet planner that simulated candidate launches and scored their effect on net ship advantage over opponents. Its selected modification relaxed launch acceptance, expanded target coverage, and increased simultaneous waves during the first 50 turns. Replay diagnosis motivated this opening change, while reinforcement margins, safe source draining, exact interception, and regrouping remained intact. solution_title: 5th place solution - 3D interpolation is all you need (updated with code)
solution_summary: The author trained U-Net ensembles using kidney-level holdouts and progressively added soft pseudo-labels from another kidney and an external spleen scan. Boundary-weighted cross-entropy combined with Dice or Tversky and focal loss addressed missed vessels, while input upscaling improved small-vessel detection. Inference used overlapping windows across all three axes and rescaled private volumes to the training voxel resolution before restoring predictions. The stronger final submission reported 0.923 validation Surface Dice and 0.691 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: 128th place solution - Don't trust the public leaderboard!
solution_summary: The selected solution fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3-large on competition data combined with the nbroad dataset. Training used batch size 2, two epochs, a learning rate of 3e-5, and maximum sequence length 1024. Inference increased the maximum sequence length to 1792 and used a stride of 384. The selected model scored 0.960 publicly and 0.958 privately, while an unselected alternative achieved 0.959 privately despite its lower public score.

The pipeline combined ResNeSt50 slice features with separate transformers for slice-level and exam-level pulmonary embolism predictions. An additional end-to-end CNN-transformer model focused on slices selected using out-of-fold PE scores. A manually supervised heart detector localized inputs for a pretrained 3D RV/LV network, whose features were combined with PE predictions in a linear model. Multiple models and label-consistency postprocessing produced a reported public score of 0.150, with full-test inference taking seven to eight hours.

solution_title: 67th Place Solution but Just ElasticNet performed way better!
solution_summary: The solution combined EfficientNet B5, quantile regression with a modified loss, and ElasticNet in an ensemble. EfficientNet B5 used 520×520 inputs to predict coefficients for linear decay, with cross-validation assessed using the competition metric. Quantile regression used an asymmetric loss with quantiles 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8. ElasticNet used 10-fold GroupKFold validation and ultimately performed better alone than the submitted ensemble.

The solution pretrained ByT5-large on multilingual translation pairs extracted from supplied publications, then fine-tuned on refined competition training pairs. LLM processing extracted translations, segmented documents into sentence-like examples, and repaired suspicious translation pairs. Three separately fine-tuned models supplied candidates for minimum Bayes risk decoding using the competition metric as utility. solution_title: 1st Place Submission - Another victory for raddars code
solution_summary: The submission adapted an existing Python XGBoost pipeline to the current tournament data with only minor changes. Features included regular-season team and opponent averages, recent win ratios, team quality, and tournament seeds. The author removed exponentiation from the team-quality calculation to avoid infinite values and disabled seed-based matchup overrides. Validation used shuffled five-fold cross-validation repeated three times.

The author used user and session data, excluding training users absent from the session table. Session information became three feature views: binary indicators, seconds counts, and seconds shares across actions and devices. The final prediction averaged neural-network and tree ensembles with two stackers trained on a diverse collection of base-model predictions. The work took four days, split equally between data preparation and modeling.

solution_summary: The team used a two-stage retrieval and classification pipeline with channel-level five-fold validation. MPNet similarity models and a RoBERTa ArcFace model generated candidate neighbors. Contrastively trained second-stage models, a longer-context reranker, and LightGBM progressively improved results. LightGBM combined probability rankings and metadata, producing CV around 0.74 and private leaderboard 0.721.

solution_title: 22nd place solution: I asked ChatGPT for feature transformation ideas
solution_summary: The author combined original features with physiological transformations suggested by ChatGPT. Five-fold validation stratified examples using 100 quantile bins of LocalOutlierFactor scores, which reduced variation in fold RMSE. XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost were tuned with Optuna and combined through RidgeCV ensembles. The best submission achieved 0.05873 cross-validation RMSE and 0.05851 private leaderboard RMSE.

The pipeline retrieved candidates using repeat actions, next actions, and weighted item collaborative filtering. Ranking used session and item aggregates, temporal features, collaborative filtering scores, and embedding similarities, with separate feature sets for clicks and carts/orders. CatBoost ranking improved over the initial LightGBM approach, and blending both models with teammates' predictions reached a reported leaderboard score of 0.604. A chronological holdout tracked leaderboard performance well, while Polars and accelerated inference substantially reduced processing costs.
compute: CatBoost GPU inference reported as 30 times faster than LightGBM CPU inference; hardware models unspecified.

solution_summary: The final system combined eight EfficientNet-B0 models with six test-time augmentations each. It used conventional tiles and a mixed-size tile composite that aimed to preserve tissue shape while reducing blank space. GeM pooling, binary cross-entropy, and smoothed ordinal-style labels formed the core model setup. Larger backbones and regression losses did not improve public results, and the final ensemble achieved public and private scores of 0.894 and 0.932.

The solution ensembles eight transformer configurations using DeBERTa-v3-large, BERT for patents, and Funnel Transformer. Inputs combine anchor, target, context code, and context text, with different separators and attention or CLS heads providing diversity. Validation groups examples by anchor and stratifies by score; moving from four to eight folds improved CV and private leaderboard performance. Label smoothing and Mixout helped, and Nelder–Mead optimized the ensemble weights. The final ensemble achieved 0.8490 publicly and 0.8633 privately.

The author converted each sky into a grid and trained a gradient boosting classifier on aggregated tangential and cross ellipticity features. Predicted probability maps were searched for squares with high mean probability, excluding a neighborhood after each halo detection. The method achieved an average training distance of 740 and a training metric of 0.82, but angle control remained difficult. Manual interpretation of the maps produced the author's best submission, suggesting room to improve automated localization.

solution_title: 20th Place Solution: GPT-2 Income Tokens, a Generator-Aware LR and Residual GBDT
solution_summary: The solution blended gradient-boosted trees, generator-aware ridge logistic regression, and RealMLP using rank-space hill climbing. Income features derived from GPT-2 token boundaries and cross-fitted target encodings supplied important gains. Residual boosters initialized with leakage-safe logistic-regression logits further improved individual models. Shared stratified folds and nested validation guided model selection and blend weights, producing 0.94672 nested-CV AUC and 0.94570 private AUC.
compute: Kaggle notebooks; T4 GPU for XGBoost and RealMLP, CPU for LightGBM and CatBoost.

solution_summary: The solution addressed the mixture of seen and unseen drugs by blending models trained under two validation schemes. Metric learning with L2 Softmax and cosine similarity estimated whether a drug resembled known training drugs and controlled the blend. Shallow ResNet-like neural networks and TabNet used raw measurements, transformed features, and summary statistics. The final reported private score was 0.01602.

The solution combined almost 200 handcrafted statistical and NLP features with out-of-fold predictions from four neural networks with different architectures. A final LightGBM model used stratified K-fold cross-validation, early stopping, and a very small learning rate. The preprocessing pipeline included tokenization, spellchecking, unique-question extraction, and FastText embedding preparation. The reported private leaderboard log loss was 0.13497.

solution_title: 9th place solution desription: A rule based hybrid IL model
solution_summary: The agent combined a mostly stateless rule engine with a neural policy trained by imitation learning on recorded game episodes. A decision engine used turn number, enemy distance, and resource density to switch between the approaches, with weighted output combination also described. Efficient pathfinding and limited persistence of previous plans supported unit coordination. Backtesting combinations of engine versions was central to selecting competitive releases.

solution_title: Silver medal solution and approaches we tried on the way
solution_summary: The final approach used a frozen CLIP ViT-H/14 encoder with a trained linear, normalized projector supervised by an ArcMargin classification objective. Cached image embeddings enabled inexpensive projector experiments, with Gaussian feature noise and dropout reducing overfitting. Carefully selected, mostly instance-oriented datasets and dataset-specific weights were central to performance. Switching to the larger pretrained CLIP encoder and an improved dataset mix reached a score of 0.646 without backbone fine-tuning.

solution_title: 15th place solution: single stage object tracking
solution_summary: The solution used a single-stage FairMOT helmet tracker with additional impact and team-feature branches and an HRNet32 backbone. Cross-view identity supervision and team clustering supplied information for extensive opponent-pair postprocessing. View-specific threshold optimization produced about 0.45 overall cross-validation and public/private scores. solution_title: 37th place solution - TabPFN with only comp. data and basic FE.
solution_summary: The final solution used TabPFN with basic feature engineering on only the competition's synthetic data. The author avoided adding features to limit overfitting on the very small dataset and avoided original data to preserve the generated train/test distribution. This configuration achieved their best private score. XGBoost with the additional original data was their next-best approach, while combining the two models was only suggested afterward.
The post links to a blog describing the team's approach. It also provides a download link for source code and some trained models. The supplied text contains no technical description of the solution.

solution_title: Representation Anatomy, Basin-Seeded Blending, and Priced Claims
solution_summary: The final solution blended community predictions and in-house GBDT variants, using a greedy selector over probability, rank, and rank-logit views. Injecting an independently constructed rank-average ensemble as a meta-member escaped a local optimum and produced an honest OOF AUC of 0.946459 and private AUC of 0.94544. Representation analysis supported exact-income target encoding, multiple smoothing strengths, and low-order digit features. Fold-contained reproduction, held-out selection-bias checks, and paired bootstrap testing governed admission of new components, including rejection of a reproduced model that added no blend gain.

solution_title: 69th Place Solution for the Improve a Fixed Model the Data-Centric Way! Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined cleanlab-based removal of low-quality rows with feature selection guided by RandomForestRegressor importance and cross-validation. It removed 472 rows and zeroed all but seven features, achieving a score of 1.02390. Standard-deviation and Tukey-fence outlier removal were less effective, and a manual cleanlab quality threshold outperformed automated label-error detection. Feature selection alone looked strongest locally but performed poorly in submission, while combining cleaning with selection was more robust.

The solution combines one neural network, one LightGBM and four XGBoost models, followed by question-specific MLP and logistic regression stacking. Aggregate timing features and information from previous level groups strengthen the base models. Averaging the two stacking outputs and optimizing each question's threshold with Powell improved CV by 0.008. The final scores were 0.70573 CV and 0.702 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: Self-playing Transformer based solution proof of concept
solution_summary: The author describes an initial Rock Paper Scissors agent built around a transformer that consumes the previous n moves. It learns by playing against itself and other custom agents. The approach was submitted, but limited development time left further tuning and improvements unexplored.

The solution retrieved 25 misconception candidates with Qwen-14b-awq and used a LoRA-fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32b-awq to select among nine candidates at a time. Training examples combined the correct misconception with retrieved negatives and misconceptions absent from the labeled training set. This augmentation improved the private score from 0.514 to 0.531, although the public score decreased. A pointwise Yes/No scoring alternative performed poorly.

solution_title: 8th place solution | From multilabel to multiclass
solution_summary: The solution recast 206 binary targets as 328 observed target-combination classes to capture target correlations. Softmax predictions were mapped back to the original targets through a fixed correspondence matrix. The final submission equally averaged multiclass and multilabel versions of TabNet and neural networks, with quantile transformation, PCA, and row statistics. Diversity from the multiclass formulation was particularly useful for blending, and the selected submission scored 0.01603 on the private leaderboard.

The author combined four distilled models trained with different spectrogram settings, architectures, and augmentations. ECA NFNet teachers transferred predictions to EfficientNet students using focal loss plus multi-label knowledge distillation. Multi-label distillation improved the reported results relative to the compared alternatives, and configuration diversity helped the ensemble remain robust.

Training examples paired varied source texts with rewrites produced from procedural, public, and LLM-generated prompts, expanded through GPT-3.5 mutations. solution_title: Took a gamble.  Didn't pay off.  1122th place.  😕
solution_summary: The author trained independent XGBoost models for each protein using fingerprint representations, emphasizing 2D pharmacophores to improve generalization to unfamiliar chemistry. Validation included stratified random splits and splits with no building blocks shared between training and validation; the latter performed worse but still appeared promising. A 1145-bit building-block presence fingerprint improved both public and private leaderboard performance when its predictions were used only for shared building blocks. The author also explored per-building-block pharmacophores and concatenated similarity vectors, but the overall competition outcome was disappointing despite encouraging cross-validation.

The final submission combined LightGBM with a neural network and trained on all available data. Validation used the last three months of training data, and useful features included time-of-day indicators, month-boundary indicators, and wind magnitude. Although the neural network scored worse individually, it substantially improved the ensemble. The team modeled both the target and its difference from the value 48 hours earlier, retained a submission without refitting, and found capacity-normalized targets ineffective.

The team averaged 12 fold models across three architectures using equal weights. They used multilabel-stratified folds and image sizes of 128×128, original resolution, and 300×300. Training combined CutMix, Mixup or Cutout, label smoothing, Adam, and plateau-based learning-rate reduction over 100 or 150 epochs. The first architecture produced 186 outputs split into three softmax groups. The reported score changed from 0.9784 on public evaluation to 0.9507 on private evaluation.

The team combined several language-model pipelines trained to classify misconceptions through assigned answer-token logits. Synthetic explanations, filtered misconception candidates, and additional prompt context improved selected models, while distillation and label smoothing addressed label noise. Correct-answer status was identified separately and added during post-processing. The pipelines used Gemma, Qwen, and a distilled DeepSeek model, with one two-model ensemble reaching 0.948 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: How to take the ArcFace Baseline from private lb: 0.470 (public: 0.522) to 0.804 (public: 0.834)

The model combined concatenated average and maximum pooling with species classification and a metric head using multi-sample dropout and Elastic Margin Loss. Training used the entire dataset without validation, 12,157 pseudo labels, diverse crop sources, and image augmentations. Inference averaged embeddings across crops and horizontal flips before KNN retrieval.

solution_summary: The solution trained multiple U-Nets, mainly with MobileNet encoders, using different RGB composites and image scales. Augmentation and staged training with BCE/Dice followed by Lovasz loss were important. A second U-Net stacked the first-stage probabilities and improved the score by 0.006 over simple averaging. Threshold tuning, tiny-mask removal, and hole filling completed the pipeline.

The solution binned each signal to 187 points and normalized each wavelength by its mean before averaging wavelengths. A five-segment, degree-two fit estimated transit breakpoints and mean transit depth. Uncertainty came from the standard deviation of 100 estimates using random subsets of 50 wavelengths. A deep feedforward network predicted the spectrum relative to its mean, increasing the score from 0.62 to 0.65, although mean estimation remained the main limitation.

The team created roughly 500k samples using several LLMs and publicly available source texts. RoBERTa models predicted T5 prompt embeddings, enabling cosine-similarity retrieval, while Mistral generated additional candidate prompts. They improved outputs by evaluating permutations of concatenated candidates against the predicted embedding. Experiments with end-token suffixes led to the replacement token “lucrarea,” while deliberate overfitting to the public prompts was rejected.

solution_title: Knowing Is Not Enough: We Predicted the Private Board, Optimized the Wrong One
solution_summary: The selected final generated simple sentinel-post candidates and tuned their count to maximize public replay throughput. A compliant mock agent, controlled ablations, and simulated stricter guardrails helped characterize scoring and transfer. The authors correctly predicted that payload inspection would block their exfiltration channel, but still selected it over a transferable email-deputy probe. The selected submission scored 56.96 publicly and zero privately.

The solution used robust weighted least squares, Kalman smoothing, and RTKLIB for GNSS position estimation. Routes were manually labeled Highway, Tree, or Downtown using Google Earth Pro, and Optuna tuned satellite-selection criteria separately for each environment. For non-highway routes moving below one meter per second, position covariance was tripled before Kalman smoothing, improving the reported private score from 1.904 to 1.863. After the competition, annotation-independent post-processing achieved a private score of 1.784.

The solution started with an LKH tour and refined it using a custom penalty-aware Lin–Kernighan search. Cumulative sums accelerated penalty calculations, while non-sequential moves, restricted candidate sets, and relaxed gain constraints enabled increasingly high-order moves. Localized tour kicks followed by reoptimization and GPX2 recombination provided further gains. The reported score improved from 1516321 after the initial TSP stage to 1514014 after the final stage.

solution_summary: The final blend combined a Transformer, TabNet, and neural networks using different feature sets. Handcrafted book and trade features replaced a slow RNN feature extractor with almost no performance loss, while the Transformer captured relationships across stocks. Nearest-neighbor time buckets supplied averaged stock features, improving reported CV from 0.211 to approximately 0.198 and public leaderboard performance from approximately 0.200 to 0.189. The solution ensembled five submissions using preprocessing from two public kernels. Two models used three GRU layers with 400 or 410 units, while two others used three dense layers with 500 or 400 units; context features were concatenated between layers. These networks produced nine linear outputs and trained with quantile losses, Adam, dropout, and plateau-based learning-rate reduction. A public quantile-regression baseline supplied the fifth model.

The solution combines several transformer regressors using ridge regression and LightGBM, with manual features contributing through LightGBM. Five-fold validation without shuffling was chosen to approximate generalization across text sources. Dropout remained active during inference, and predictions were averaged across random seeds. Averaging the ridge and LightGBM outputs achieved a private score of 0.448, although the author questioned the improvement because the public score worsened.

solution_summary: The solution used Qwen3.5-35B-A3B in a Python-driven, multi-turn tool-integrated reasoning pipeline without fine-tuning. Dynamic time allocation, context summarization, syntax repair, and role-specific sampling helped manage limited compute. solution_summary: The author used the challenge dataset and trained models through MLJAR's automatic training workflow. The post links to project results and a video showing how the project was created. It provides no model, feature, validation, or ensemble details.

It combined robust Huber regression, custom-objective XGBoost, and a feedforward neural network using median-based traffic features. An XGBoost residual stack incorporated out-of-fold Huber and neural predictions, reaching a stage 1 public score of 41.4 versus 41.8 for the neural network alone. solution_title: [93th place solution] BPP as embedding layer
solution_summary: The solution constructed contextual nucleotide embeddings from base-pair probabilities, distance-derived matrices, and an identity matrix. A learned convolution combined five relationship channels, and the resulting scores mixed nucleotide embeddings before positional encoding and a transformer. This aimed to capture information associated with pseudoknots without representing them explicitly. Across four fold models, learned weights consistently favored base-pair probabilities and self-identity while penalizing distance; an earlier custom self-attention approach failed.

The solution used a DSL-like collection of Python converters and mergers to transform grids through object representations. More than 100 converters and ten mergers handled operations such as object identification, recoloring, rotation, movement, and composition. A shared context carried information inferred from training examples, including output-only colors and output shape. An earlier CNN image-generation approach failed because training data were too scarce.

The authors provide an extensible end-to-end toxic comment classification starter with fastText–GRU and GloVe–LSTM pipelines. Their ensemble workflow tunes a second-level model using held-out validation predictions and then applies it to test predictions. solution_title: Quick 3rd place solution (no pp) + source code
solution_summary: The solution combined a character-level GRU-head model with a token model using a beam-search-like span decoder. Its model mix included RoBERTa base, RoBERTa large, and BART large, with diversity emphasized. The token decoder conditioned end predictions on three candidate start states and ranked the resulting nine spans by probability products. Fuzzy label matching and freeze-unfreeze training supported the pipeline; each main approach scored about 0.728 on the public leaderboard.

The solution used a diverse ensemble of LightGBM, GradientBoostingRegressor, random forests, and linear regression. Model and ensemble decisions were driven by ordinary KFold cross-validation rather than the small public leaderboard. Nonlinear feature engineering and iterative feature removal were especially important for linear regression. Target encoding AgeInDays also helped some tree models, while LightGBM hyperparameters were tuned manually after Optuna results proved sensitive to fold seeds.

The solution combined EfficientNet-b5 classifiers operating on RGB, YUV, and Lab images with a modified EfficientNet-b2 processing engineered DCT coefficients. Training used flips, right-angle rotations, CutMix for color models, and SGD with cosine annealing. An MLP fused normalized pooled features because simple averaging did not combine the weaker DCT model effectively. A final LightGBM stacker used MLP predictions and t-SNE CNN features, reaching 0.9405 validation and 0.931 private scores.

solution_summary: The pipeline standardized DICOM volumes, located a coarse vessel ROI, and refined vessel masks with two complementary nnU-Net models. A vessel-pretrained classifier used region-masked pooling and a location-aware transformer to predict anatomical labels and overall aneurysm presence. Backbone pretraining and heavily weighted auxiliary aneurysm localization were central to performance. Four-fold averaging and flip augmentation produced a reported full-resolution score of 0.916.

solution_summary: The solution divided the spatial domain into grids and trained local models on the resulting subsets. It augmented grid borders and periodic time boundaries, then explored feature subsets and grid resolutions. The final version blended KNN, XGBoost, and random-forest probabilities with tuned mixture weights. The author reported a score around 0.60078 for the improved pipeline.

The final approach regressed sea lion counts from whole images using a fully connected network and averaged the two best models. An earlier Tiramisu segmentation model predicted six classes around annotated dots but was biased toward background. Larger segmentation masks with Dice loss detected plausible regions of interest, although the subsequent regression overfit. TensorFlow object detection and U-Net segmentation remained unimplemented ideas.

The team ensembled BERT, DistilBERT, and XLNet models trained separately on questions and answers. They used five-fold GroupKFold validation and concatenated hidden states for prediction. Rank averaging improved the score by 0.002, followed by threshold adjustments for highly imbalanced targets. Several alternatives failed to help, including BART/T5 encoders, stochastic weight averaging, separate head training, statistical features, BERT with USE, GloVe, and LSTM.

The post compares differing predictions across nine submission files sharing a public score of 0.976518. It lists thirteen row IDs with assigned Extrovert or Introvert labels. A private score as high as 0.970850 is reported, but no training pipeline or rule for selecting the listed labels is explained.

solution_title: 41st Place Solution for the Child Mind Institute - Detect Sleep States Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined ten U-Net models using five backbones and two training-validation splits. Inference used overlapping windows with half-window hops to reduce false detections near segment edges, followed by non-maximum suppression. A custom ensemble inspired by Weighted Boxes Fusion combined predictions within each fold and then across folds, and predictions in periodic padding intervals were removed. The full pipeline achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.802, with ablations showing benefits from overlapping inference and padding removal.

The team combined Qwen3 sequence classifiers with Qwen2.5 causal language models fine-tuned using LoRA. Prompts included all answer choices, and question-specific misconception hints or restricted candidate labels improved accuracy. Multi-task learning, R-Drop, adversarial weight perturbation, and exponential moving averages improved classifier generalization. Confidence-based staged inference reserved larger models for difficult samples, while float16 inference and reduced padding enabled a larger ensemble within the time limit.
compute: Kaggle T4 inference environment; 9-hour inference limit. Full-test 72B inference took about 3 hours, reduced to about 1 hour through selective inference and CPU offloading.

solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned a LAION-2B-pretrained CLIP visual encoder for 22 epochs on a custom mixture of landmark, product, food, car, furniture, and storefront datasets. A single 64-dimensional fully connected projection layer was trained using ArcFaceMarginLayer and outperformed deeper projection heads. Increasing inference image size from 224 to 240 improved the score by approximately 0.003–0.004. Strong augmentation, contrastive learning, alternative pooling and margin layers, and several dataset expansions were unsuccessful.

solution_summary: The solution stacked predictions from RoBERTa, ELECTRA, MPNet, and Longformer models together with sentence embeddings. A notebook-level transformer predicted cell ranks alongside auxiliary ordering targets. Training used L1 loss on ranks scaled by notebook length, giving longer notebooks greater influence. solution_summary: The solution combined four-class study classifiers, binary opacity classifiers, and YOLOv5 detectors. Classification models used auxiliary segmentation heads, diverse image sizes, and horizontal-flip inference augmentation; some also used padding removal and percentile clipping. Classification predictions were combined using power ensembling, while binary predictions lightly calibrated detection scores. One submission scored 0.619, and several external-data and pseudo-labeling experiments failed to improve the overall blend.

solution_summary: The team trained diverse audio classifiers on overlapping three-second chunks represented as mel-spectrograms. Manually collected labels were the main improvement, followed by pseudo-labeling that raised the reported score from about 0.950 to 0.96x. Training used waveform and spectrogram augmentation, four folds, and validation-based checkpoint selection. The final ensemble contained more than 80 models.

The approach adapted a BirdCLEF 2018 sound event detection model by replacing its predictor with a pretrained PANN CNN. Training used 30-second snippets from the official data plus xeno-canto crawls, with binary cross-entropy covering foreground and background species. Augmentation randomized stereo downmixing and added bird-free noise from two external datasets. Inference first selected recording-level species using 20-second windows, then localized those species in 5-second windows with a lower threshold.

solution_summary: The author extracted features with a pretrained ResNet50 and trained XGBoost on those features, reporting a score of 0.95030. solution_summary: The approach clustered each class before Gaussian mixture modeling, using three clusters per class. StandardScaler stabilized covariance calculations, while two-fold training supplied regularization by fitting each model on half the available samples. The author combined 42 models of the same type to improve robustness and retained default regularization parameters. Model-specific tuning was unsuccessful, and comparisons between rank and probability averaging gave mixed results.

The solution used feature trimming based on a randomly generated dummy feature. Features whose importance fell below that dummy feature were removed. The author reported little improvement after three attempts and did not implement the more advanced methods considered.

The solution combined image-retrieval shortlists, MASt3R matching, and COLMAP reconstruction. It supplemented MASt3R semi-dense correspondences with ALIKED and SuperPoint keypoints, improving matching coverage and scores. Engineering optimizations and parallel execution across two T4 GPUs allowed more image pairs within the runtime budget. The best submission scored 52.64 publicly and 56.00 privately, while pre-clustering was omitted from the final pipeline.

solution_summary: The solution used LightGBM with 19 calendar, building, weather, and aggregate features. Validation followed chronological splits, while leaked test-period data supported training, evaluation, fusion tuning, and submitted results. Feature engineering included group counts, energy aggregates, cosine wind direction, and log transformations. Memory reduction and aggressive filtering of unreliable sites and anomalous readings were central practical measures, although removing zero readings increased overfitting.

The author trained toxicity models using data from the first Jigsaw competition and selected models against a filtered version of the competition validation data. Filtering removed pairs with close toxicity scores, low toxicity scores, or similar meanings, reducing the evaluation set to roughly half its original size. The final ensemble combined RoBERTa and TF-IDF with ridge regression at weights of 0.892 and 0.108. Training used five folds and ten epochs without learning-rate changes or a scheduler.

The final pipeline fed predictions from eight bagged LightGBM models into an FTRL model. It used 38 engineered features across roughly 100 million records, with chunked construction and manual array conversion to fit memory limits. Bagging increased cross-validation from 0.791 to 0.792, while standalone FTRL was weak. Adding LightGBM predictions to FTRL improved the leaderboard score from 0.792 to 0.793.

solution_summary: The author trained AutoGluon with best_quality presets separately on each training split of a manual 20-fold cross-validation loop. Test predictions were averaged across the resulting models, and final submissions were selected using average validation scores. This added an outer ensemble around AutoGluon's internal ensembling and stacking and reportedly improved cross-validation performance. Training took approximately 20 hours.

solution_summary: The approach perturbed convolutional weights around their original values, then trained on the retain set for four epochs to restore useful knowledge. Training used SGD and a custom cross-entropy-based loss that heavily favored class 0, with another light weight perturbation before the final epoch. An earlier research approach worked in the starting kit but encountered compilation problems in the competition. solution_summary: The solution used a transformer embedding retriever followed by a transformer sentence-pair classification ranker, with XGBoost for ranker stacking. Retriever pretraining combined masked language modeling and supervised SimCSE contrastive learning over three rounds, refreshing hard negatives from earlier checkpoints. Five pretrained models generated mean-pooled embeddings for cosine-similarity retrieval of the top 100 contents per topic. Validation used five stratified group folds by topic ID, and the final ensemble used eight models across two folds, achieving public and private scores of 0.717 and 0.745.

The author developed two image-matching pipelines based on previous prize-eligible solutions and validated them on diverse historical datasets. The AffNetHardNet8 and AdaLAM pipeline combined several detectors at different image resolutions and benefited from higher RANSAC thresholds. The best-scoring pipeline used ALIKED, DISK, and SIFT alongside LightGlue, NetVLAD retrieval, PixSfM, and rotation matching, with ALIKED detection and resizing settings tuned through validation. Scene-specific combinations were tested but were not selected because their behavior on unknown private scenes was uncertain.

The submission supplied two template-based structures, two Protenix predictions, and one RNAPro prediction for every target. A LightGBM model ranked templates using RNA, description, protein, DNA, ligand, and chain-composition similarities. Neural inference incorporated associated molecules while limiting their size, MSA depth, and diffusion work to meet runtime constraints. Long sequences were split into overlapping chains and chunks, then reconstructed with Kabsch alignment. RNAPro and Protenix ran concurrently on two T4 GPUs.

solution_summary: The solution used a three-layer ensemble built from over 200 diverse out-of-fold prediction sets generated with AutoGluon and custom models. Four second-layer models combined XGBoost and neural networks with confident test pseudo-labels, either appended as training rows or converted into nearest-neighbor features. Feature interactions, target and frequency encoding, and averaging across folds and seeds supported the base-model diversity. A hill-climb weighted blend of the four second-layer models achieved CV 0.977594 and private leaderboard score 0.97790.

solution_title: 72nd place solution(ensemble of LightGBM and Sequential NN)
solution_summary: The solution combined LightGBM DART models using customer-level aggregates with GRU and transformer sequence models. Tree features included aggregate combinations and recent differences, while neural inputs used one-hot categories, missingness indicators, and linear interpolation. Although neural models scored below the tree models individually, combining them improved the public score from 0.799 to 0.800. Logistic regression or MLP stacking performed particularly well, and the final submission scored 0.80011 locally and 0.80780 on the private leaderboard.

The author trained two groups of heterogeneous language models in Kaggle kernels and distilled them into BERT students. A five-fold group including BERT, XLNet, GPT2, and LSTM was compressed into BERT large cased, while a four-fold transformer group was compressed into BERT large uncased. Final inference averaged folds and blended the two student groups across nine runs. The resulting blend achieved approximately 0.946 on the leaderboard.

solution_title: [Private 47th / Public 55th] Stable local cv & public leaderboard using stacking with linear models and forward selection
solution_summary: The team stacked diverse transformer predictions with readability measurements using Ridge regression, linear SVR, and ElasticNet, then blended the three outputs. Five-fold validation stratified on binned targets guided model selection and produced out-of-fold features. Readability features, attention heads, learning-rate scheduling, and target perturbation helped handle the small dataset and noisy labels. Forward feature selection improved ensemble diversity and performance, while additional pretraining did not help.

The final system combines four Helsinki translation pipelines and four byT5 pipelines, using extracted external translations and gold-quality data. Each model generates four beam-search candidates, and weighted Minimum Bayes Risk decoding selects a translation from the pooled candidates after normalization and deduplication. solution_summary: The team combined complementary candidate generators with LightGBM ranking models. One pipeline filtered roughly 600 popular items to 130 candidates before adding purchase history, while the other generated diverse candidates using grouped popularity, image similarity, co-occurrence, and graph walks. Rich customer, article, interaction, repurchase, and similarity features supported the ranking stage. Combining candidates improved the reported score from 0.0355 to 0.0362, and the ensemble reached 0.0368.

A Siamese CNN learned image labels and consistent activation maps, with external data and balanced sampling supporting training. solution_summary: The author built a chart-reading pipeline combining chart classification, text detection and recognition, object detection, and segmentation. Geometric filtering and label-to-tick matching converted detected chart elements into numerical values, with specialized handling for each chart type. Training used only competition data, reserving half of the extracted data for validation before retraining on all data. The reported best validation score was 0.871, while the best public and private scores were 0.86 and 0.69.

The solution used UNet with a ResNet34 backbone and an auxiliary branch for empty-mask classification. Training combined mask BCE, Dice loss, and empty-mask BCE, while gradually reducing the proportion of non-empty samples to match the dataset. It trained on random 512×512 crops and inferred at 768×768, with validation-selected rules suppressing empty or small predicted masks. The final ensemble averaged four selected checkpoints across eight folds and used horizontal-flip test-time augmentation.

solution_title: Why does postprocessing work? 2nd place magic
solution_summary: The team inspected most buildings individually and removed anomalous readings, particularly zeros, making data cleaning central to its approach. Removing these readings raised the mean prediction, and downward multiplicative correction improved results. A controlled experiment introduced artificial zero readings into an otherwise clean building to examine the interaction between cleaning and prediction scaling. Removing the artificial training outliers improved CV from 1.16 to 0.17, while subsequent scaling by 0.92 improved the experimental leaderboard score from 1.19 to 1.14.

The solution combined feature-engineered CatBoost and XGBoost classifiers with multi-label transformer–LSTM sequence models. Validation used five-fold GroupKFold by session, and 11,343 additional complete sessions extracted from raw data particularly benefited neural models. Game-specific timing, movement, task, and previous-prediction features supported tree models, with null-importance feature selection for level-group and combined classifiers. Separate logistic regression stacks for tree and neural models were blended at a 6:4 ratio, producing CV 0.7046 and a private score of 0.704.

The solution used a fixed validation set of 663 images drawn from usask_1 and portions of other sources. Its main described contribution was a custom augmentation pipeline with cropping, padding, resizing, color transfer, background-image Mixup, and rotation with pseudo-labels. Standard flips and right-angle rotations supplemented these augmentations. For the SPIKE dataset, weighted boxes fusion combined pseudo-labels with supplied ground-truth boxes; the text does not specify the detector architecture or numerical results.

The solution combined three models implemented in R and Python, mainly using LightGBM and XGBoost with different features. One component was a stacking regressor containing ten regression models. Models were tuned and validated using the current dataset and previous competitions. Submission variants used different amounts of extreme-probability clipping, and one shifted predictions toward models ranked more highly by historical validation.

solution_title: Solution Arhitecture Pipeline for Bronze Medal
solution_summary: The pipeline began with tuned EfficientNet B2, B3, and B4 models using ImageNet or noisy-student initialization. Weighted out-of-fold predictions with eight test-time augmentations identified noisy training labels and reliable examples from the previous year's competition. Models trained on original, cleaned, and extended datasets then supplied twelve predictions to a bagged, two-layer stacking system. Bagging generalized better on the leaderboard than boosting despite boosting's stronger validation accuracy.

Diversity and robustness mattered because both the public leaderboard and four-prompt cross-validation were considered uncertain. solution_title: Surviving Hidden Private Guardrails via Confused Deputy Chaining
solution_summary: The author developed a confused-deputy attack that used a static payload marker without reading secret files, aiming to avoid provenance tracking. Unique recipients increased diversity rewards, while latency probes selected model-specific prompt formats and a timer bounded candidate generation. The author reports a verified private score of 19.650 and stable local runs, but did not select this approach for the final submission.

solution_title: Model Capability Dominates: Why Prompt Diversity Fails
solution_summary: The baseline used quantized GPT-OSS-120B with eight samples, temperature 1.0, and entropy-weighted voting. Repeated experiments found that prompt diversity and smaller alternative models did not reliably improve this baseline, whose public mean was 39.3/50 across 21 runs. The final submission added a code re-execution verifier and scored 41/50 publicly and 40.5/50 privately, although external testing found no robust benefit from any tested verifier. The main diagnosed limitation was selection loss: correct generated candidates often lost the vote by a single agreeing attempt.

solution_title: 3rd place - Ridge and CV are all you need
solution_summary: The author built a diverse ensemble of more than 60 tabular models and combined their out-of-fold predictions with multi-target Ridge regression. Ridge scaled more reliably than hill climbing or genetic algorithms as the ensemble grew. Additional diversity came from neural networks, boosted trees, and classification models trained as one-hot target regression. Accidentally label-encoding product features improved cross-validation by 0.0001.

solution_summary: The team modeled filtered raw gravitational-wave signals with multi-kernel Conv1D networks, later using separate encoders for each detector and ResNet34 to fuse their features. Synthetic pretraining followed by brief fine-tuning on the original data mattered more than mixing synthetic and real samples. Predicting signal parameters during pretraining added a small improvement, while augmentation hurt the strongest synthetic-pretrained models. The strongest described model reached 0.8858 public leaderboard score; segmentation, denoising autoencoders and hard-example mining did not improve the approach.

solution_title: 178th of 4,251: one human, one agent, and a bet against the public board
solution_summary: The campaign used a persistent experiment ledger and a CPU replica of the scorer to optimize attack success per replay second. Its public approach combined validated marker attacks, model-specific message forms, and latency budgeting, reaching 88.695. For final scoring, it selected two complementary submissions: real-secret read-and-post chains followed by confused-deputy attacks, and a pure confused-deputy submission. These choices prioritized coverage of restrictive hidden guardrails despite low public scores.
