solution_summary: The final detector combined five YOLOv5 models, one Faster R-CNN model, and six VFNet models. Weighted boxes fusion merged the training annotations and combined predictions, with model weights determined by validation mAP50 and class-specific IoU thresholds. Classification predictions filtered most detectors, while three YOLOv5 models remained unfiltered to compensate for classification errors. Smaller seven-model ensembles achieved private scores of 0.3–0.304, but the author selected the larger ensemble expecting better generalization.

solution_title: BirdCLEF+ 2026 Bronze: EoS, OOF Gating and PCEN Sidecars
solution_summary: The selected solution used an EoS ensemble with OOF-gated PCEN corrections, supported by comparisons against BirdNET, sidecar, taxonomy, and replay variants. Recording-grouped validation on five-second soundscape windows tracked macro AUC and weak species separately. Rank-based post-processing and strict audits of offline artifacts, CPU runtime, and submission shape guided candidate selection. The selected submission scored 0.95095 publicly and 0.94141 privately.

solution_summary: The team built diverse LightGBM models around customer-level financial aggregates, recent repayment behavior, debt ratios and derived interest-rate features. They predicted missing external scores and loan terms, and blended a cash-loan-specific model with the broader model. Feature selection and out-of-fold weighted blending were followed by a simple tree stacker added to the final blend. Their selected stack-plus-blend submission achieved CV 0.807420 and private score 0.80354, with a substantial gap between validation and private performance.

The final system blended three Perch-v2-based audio classifiers, with nearly all weight assigned to the strongest Perch MLP model. Cubing predictions before weighted blending limited weaker models' influence to confident predictions. Genus- and class-level smoothing then shared information among related species. The final score was 0.951 macro ROC-AUC, with the power blend reported to improve on naive blending by 0.002.

solution_summary: The team removed suspected noisy columns and one-hot encoded the remaining data into 207 features. They trained XGBoost, five-fold LightGBM models, and a neural network with separate reg, car, and ind input groups. Harmonic averaging combined the models, with final family weights of 0.4, 0.4, and 0.2 respectively. Stacking was unsuccessful, while the final blend achieved a private score of 0.29187.

The pipeline rectifies ECG images and predicts all leads directly using ten models with several backbone and output-head designs. High-resolution remapping, grayscale inputs with coordinate features, and robust synthetic augmentation support signal recovery. Predictions undergo Fourier-domain resampling and conditional corrections based on ECG lead relationships. Test-time augmentation improved performance by 0.07, and lead correction added another 0.06.

solution_summary: The solution combined models trained on backfin, full-body, and SOD crops, including full-body crops produced by a YOLOv5 detector trained on aggregated manual annotations. Names were normalized and split into surnames, full given names, and initials. Duplicate candidates required identical surnames and compatible subsets of given names, comparing initials with the first letters of full names. Keyword clustering was explored, but the best result retained all name-based candidates without filtering by keyword similarity.

Within each image, model predictions and relative ranks or median thresholds identify positive and negative cell labels. Ambiguous labels remain missing, and cells with missing values are removed, while originally absent classes stay negative. The solution ensembled EfficientNet B3–B7, SE-ResNeXt101, and ResNeSt101 models with varied image sizes and optional metadata. Training and validation combined 2018, 2019, and 2020 data to stabilize evaluation despite scarce positive examples. Nine-class diagnosis prediction with cross-entropy improved performance over binary melanoma classification, and inference used the melanoma softmax probability. Five-fold evaluation, eight-way test-time augmentation, and ranking predictions before ensembling produced a final private score of 0.9490 for the ensemble optimized on all-year validation.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution - From Embeddings to Matches
solution_summary: The solution trained separate image and text encoders with ArcFace and combined their normalized embeddings for product matching. Its main improvement came from three-stage Iterative Neighborhood Blending, which refined embeddings using similarity-weighted neighbors before searching for matches again. Final predictions united refined combined matches with image-only and text-only matches, using tuned distance thresholds and a relaxed rule for the second match. Embedding retrieval and refinement mattered more than further encoder improvements, and the reported public leaderboard score reached 0.793.

The solution combined ResNet50, InceptionV3, and InceptionResNetV2 trained from scratch at different image resolutions. Diversity came from architecture, image size, and augmentation schedules, while tuning on the tuning set addressed differences in label distributions. Predictions on original and mirrored test images were combined using a weighted average. Tuning substantially improved all three models, with the strongest reported Stage 1 score reaching 0.550.

solution_summary: The solution averaged predictions from two complementary 2.5D YOLO detectors, an EfficientNetV2-S-based 3D CenterNet, and three boosted-tree meta-classifiers. Adjacent slices formed YOLO inputs, while the CenterNet combined slice-wise features with a shallow 3D head and auxiliary vessel supervision. Meta-classifiers used all base-model predictions plus age and sex, with the parallel configuration outperforming the series configuration in cross-validation. The final submission averaged two folds and achieved a private score of 0.8230 because submission issues prevented using all five folds.

solution_summary: The team initialized a tour with LKH, then improved the prime-adjusted objective using several local-search moves and gradually increasing penalties. A cumulative-sum scoring trick made move evaluation dramatically faster and enabled extensive optimization in pure Python under PyPy3. Further gains came from perturbing and reoptimizing tours, EAX-based kicks, and shuffling segments of up to 200 cities with lower-bound estimates. Team members repeatedly exchanged improved tours through a shared folder, reaching a final score of 1514438.

solution_summary: The overall solution ensembles a simple 3D ResNet18 classifier with MONAI object detectors, while this post details the classifier. Volumes are rescaled to a fixed voxel size, and a 76-class head predicts motor location on a coarse spatial grid or the absence of a motor. Strong augmentation, constrained MixUp and positive-crop oversampling support training from scratch. Sliding-window inference, quantile-based thresholds and accelerated model exports enable efficient deployment; the classifier alone scored 0.875 on the public leaderboard.

solution_title: 25th Solution - Custom MIL with timm backbones
solution_summary: The solution precomputed 16 RGB tiles per image and trained multiple-instance learning models that concatenated instance feature maps along the channel dimension. Patient-disjoint, label-stratified five-fold validation guided training and model selection. The efficiency-focused notebook included BM25 and TextBlob features, although their contribution was uncertain. Keyword matching, important-sentence comparisons, and several text similarity metrics failed to improve scores. A short-input DeBERTa experiment with frozen layers and fold-specific GRU heads showed a large validation-to-public-score gap. solution_title: Fine-Tuning of TransPolymer for Polymer Property Prediction
solution_summary: The author fine-tuned TransPolymer with LoRA to predict five polymer properties from augmented SMILES strings. Each target had a separate dataset and model, with a 10% holdout and early stopping. Converting Tg to Kelvin and dividing by the maximum value across training and holdout data substantially improved predictions; z-normalization was less satisfactory despite slightly higher correlation. The reported public and private scores were 0.068 and 0.087.

The author started from a publicly shared submission and concentrated computation on IDs 3, 4, and 5. All improvements used simulated annealing, with insertion-based neighborhoods playing the central role. Fixing the first word helped escape a local optimum for ID 3, while distance-biased insertion quickly improved ID 4. For ID 5, mixed neighborhoods, alphabetical-block initialization, and variable-length insertion progressively reduced the score to 28.52.

solution_summary: The solution uses a transformer with linear embeddings for pose, lips and eyes, alongside linear and spatiotemporal graph representations of the dominant hand. Preprocessing selects and aligns the target hand, resizes sequences to 16 frames and normalizes coordinates using face landmarks. LightGlue matched learned features, while nearest-neighbor ratio matching handled SIFT; combining complementary matches delivered the largest improvement. Reconstruction used COLMAP with conditional shared intrinsics, rotation-aware PixSfM refinement, and localization of otherwise unregistered images. The final submission scored 0.523 privately, while stronger SuperPoint configurations were excluded because of licensing concerns.

solution_title: #4 solution | Beating a dead horse: blending works, but "blending" doesn't
solution_summary: The author submitted two hill-climbing ensembles containing 32 models each, using out-of-fold predictions to support blending. The stronger ensemble used only the author's models, while the other also incorporated public notebook predictions. Diversity came from factorization machines, Lasso, CatBoost, neural networks, and several tree families, with categorical treatment of all features working particularly well. AutoGluon-generated encodings gave a small gain, and adding original used-car data improved the ensembles by about 20 RMSE points. Additional feature engineering was discarded because its cross-validation gains did not transfer to the leaderboard.

The author reformulated prediction as individual cell-type, small-molecule, and gene tuples rather than predicting entire rows. The neural architecture combined molecular descriptors, 10-dimensional gene PCA features, and cell representations enriched by a graph convolution over six fully connected cell nodes. Attention layers and random noise in cell features supported representation learning and generalization, and a larger model incorporated three copies of the base architecture. Training used MSE, AdamW, and five-fold cross-validation.

solution_title: 5th place Approach and Solution Walkthrough and Live Discussion
solution_summary: The post announces a live presentation by two participants about their competition approach and solution. It schedules the presentation for 12 November 2021 at 18:30 IST (13:30 GMT). It provides a YouTube link but contains no technical solution details.

The final solution used weighted ensembles of SE-ResNeXt50 and Res2Net trained on 256×256 images. Removing image cropping and using CutMix alone were the most useful changes reported. Training used 80/20 splits and a step learning-rate schedule, with the strongest public ensemble combining two Res2Net splits and one SE-ResNeXt split. That ensemble scored 0.9884 publicly and 0.9290 privately, while a three-checkpoint DenseNet121 ensemble achieved a better private score of 0.9381. Local validation scores did not reliably predict either leaderboard.

The author evaluated two approaches derived from another participant's shared methods. The first used gradient boosting for feature selection followed by linear regression with L1 loss. The second used a custom autoregressive-style weighted linear formula with a defined cost and gradient, running in minutes and achieving the better private score. Public/private scores were 0.41820/0.42668 for the first approach and 0.41833/0.42532 for the second.

solution_title: My single-(ok, 1.5-)model solution and source code [19th place]
solution_summary: The solution first classified images with a fine-tuned Xception network using sigmoid outputs and generalized mean pooling. Training included landmark and non-landmark images and a slightly reweighted loss whose benefit was uncertain. Google DELF features then rescored each prediction by matching against up to 32 images from its proposed category. A weighted combination of neural-network and DELF confidence improved public/private GAP from 0.145/0.149 to 0.211/0.192.

The team built six segmentation models with varied residual encoders, enhanced decoders, and deep supervision using Lovasz softmax. Training used SGD, ten folds, and cosine annealing over seven cycles per fold, followed by voting across snapshots. Jigsaw-based handcrafted postprocessing improved public results much more than private results. Pseudo-labeling added a reported 0.002 on both leaderboards, while the object-context module did not work for the team.

The final solution rank-blended XGBoost and LightGBM models using target encoding with CatBoost, then applied heuristic post-processing. Feature engineering centered on proxy cardholder identities, shifts and arithmetic relationships in anonymized columns, categorical combinations, and transaction-amount aggregations. CatBoost performed particularly well on existing cardholders, while LightGBM and XGBoost complemented it on new users. A simple holdout supported validation, and post-processing raised the reported public leaderboard score from about 0.9662 to 0.9672 despite concerns about leaderboard-driven overfitting.

solution_title: [87th Place] 🧽🛁 Everybody wants clean data, but nobody wants to clean the data.

Class-weighted cross entropy corrected residual imbalance and reduced the weight of the non-PII class to favor recall. The final ensemble used per-class model weights selected on a separate validation set, and the best individual models scored around 0.96 on the public leaderboard.

solution_title: How I won the  Predict HIV Progression data mining competition
solution_summary: The author addressed distribution differences by identifying five patient groups and matching training controls to the main prediction group. Group-specific models were replaced with adjustments that aligned predictions to estimated group response means. Recursive feature elimination reduced more than 600 candidate features, and the final models used fewer than the 120 variables selected as optimal. Random forests generated predictions, with caret providing tuning and validation support.

The solution ensembled a dilated sequence-to-sequence LSTM and an attention-based sequence-to-sequence LSTM. Inputs combined calendar encodings, event and series-ID embeddings, previous-day sales, and selling prices, with sales and prices normalized by their input-window means. Models predicted 28 days from 364 days of history and were trained with SPL loss, RMSProp, learning-rate reduction, and early stopping. Predictions from three time-series validation folds were averaged for submission; added lag, rolling, and noise features produced little validation improvement, and the models performed better in uncertainty forecasting than accuracy forecasting.

A residual convolutional network combined spatial and economic features, with sequential attention-based worker decisions constrained by legal actions and shared resources. The planner replayed opening history into its trackers, then combined tile production schedules using market values, labor costs, and capital requirements. Daily production planning and hourly revisions coordinated work, purchases, delivery, and sales; the best submission achieved a competition rating of 5111.2.

The final submission blended eight recurrent models across four architectures, using a GRU classifier and three LSTM variants. Models consumed nine sensor and pulse features, with architecture-specific scaling and either cross-entropy or von Mises–Fisher loss. The solution used ten-fold RoBERTa span extraction, supplemented by models trained on cleaned target spans and models that restored character-level label noise. Majority voting combined the pseudo-labeled, cleaned, and noise-restored predictions, achieving a private Jaccard score of 0.718. The author interpreted the eight API outputs as character-position classes and probed the model with single-pixel perturbations. Recognizing that repeated or visually similar characters could cause class preference resolved the ambiguity. Overlaying the clear character images onto the unresolved positions revealed the static key, "letmeout".

solution_title: Private score 0.81148. What could've been the 5th place solution (Single model)
solution_summary: The author fine-tuned BERTweet Large for pointwise toxicity-ranking regression, achieving a private leaderboard score of 0.81148. Training used the original Jigsaw competition data, retaining toxic examples and sampling non-toxic examples, with inverse-frequency weighting of the six toxicity labels. Validation pairs were converted into regression targets using a Bradley–Terry model. Text cleaning removed IP addresses, converted emojis and Unicode, and limited repeated characters or words.

The best agent used imitation learning with a U-Net trained on roughly 1,000 winning episodes from a strong team. Training explicitly included idle center actions, limited sampling to four actions per turn, and undersampled the dominant idle class. Test-time augmentation was retained for robustness, and ONNX Runtime accelerated inference. PPO reinforcement learning and value-guided MCTS were explored extensively but did not outperform the imitation-learning solution.

The recovered prompt concatenated an optimized generic mean prompt, a Mistral-generated component, and a rule-based component. The mean prompt was searched token by token against a mean embedding, using competition scoring and random candidates for diversity. Mistral used few-shot prompting and chain-of-thought, while rules extracted dialogue participants and style keywords from rewritten text. The mean prompt scored about 0.67 privately, and the two additional components each reportedly added roughly 0.005–0.01.

solution_summary: The solution combined eight segmentation models and eight classification models, using several backbones and input resolutions. Models were trained on random 80% subsets with strong augmentation and mask-dependent segmentation losses. Predictions were averaged with flip-based test-time augmentation, then filtered using classification thresholds, segmentation thresholds, and minimum mask sizes. More complex blending hurt performance, and an alternative set of class-specific thresholds overfit the public leaderboard.

The pipeline cleaned and transformed the data, engineered features, and trained multiple random forests to predict product G. It selected forests using training accuracy and combined their predictions by majority vote, with cross-validation used to report performance. State rules corrected the resulting product predictions before submission. The default configuration scored 0.53705 on the private leaderboard, while combining it with Breakfast Pirate's ABCEDF predictions achieved 0.53715.

solution_summary: The approach estimated camera poses by combining correspondences from five feature detection and matching models. It calculated a fundamental matrix from the merged matches and passed it directly to PyColmap reconstruction, bypassing exhaustive matching. The reported public and private scores were 0.164598 and 0.173382.

The final solution combined logistic regression, LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost models using gradient-descent ensembling and ranked predictions. It relied on ten-fold stratified cross-validation, adding the original stroke dataset while restricting validation to synthetic samples. Category replacements, recursive feature elimination, and selected interaction features improved the models. The tuned XGBoost was the strongest individual model, while alternative encoders and forward selection were unsuccessful.

The approach combined CatBoost, LightGBM, and a LightAutoML Denselight network using aggregated tabular features. Stratified grouped validation helped assess feature changes, although small CV improvements and parameter tuning correlated weakly with leaderboard performance. CatBoost performed best, while simpler neural modeling outperformed attempted transformer alternatives. The author submitted both the best unmodified model and a version with date-derived metric adjustments, choosing DEVIDE=1/2 and REDUCE=0.03; the model pool without those adjustments reached approximately 0.53 private score.

The solution forecasts microbusiness density with simple multiplicative trends estimated for counties, states, and groups defined by active-business quantiles. Recent six-month performance determines clipped growth factors for one- and two-month horizons. Forecasts start from the best public submission and cover optimistic and pessimistic trend scenarios, with a May seasonal adjustment. Validation favors different persistence or trend rules for counties with low active-business counts and finds complex gradient boosting less stable.

solution_title: fast.ai, a viable time series solution
solution_summary: The author used a simple implementation of fast.ai's tabular library for earthquake prediction. They reported a decent result despite expecting deep learning to perform poorly on this type of problem. The post links to the implementation but provides no feature, validation, or training details.

The efficiency solution used one DeBERTa-v3-xsmall model to predict both content and wording scores. It marked text sequences shared with the original passage using braces around overlaps of at least three tokens, supplying copying information with little added sequence length. Whitespace cleanup, frozen embeddings and the first layer, and Ray multiprocessing supported efficient prediction. The final configuration achieved a private score of 0.491 with about 25 minutes of inference, while quantization and model-weight averaging were unsuccessful.
compute: 4 CPU cores; approximately 20 minutes plus 4 minutes of additional steps; final inference reported as 25 minutes.

solution_summary: The solution used a large multilayer ensemble with minimal feature engineering and base models trained on different target transformations. A repository of 98 models supplied diverse tree, neural-network, and AutoML predictions. Ridge regression, hill climbing, and AutoGluon formed the second layer, with model selection performed separately for each method. Their out-of-fold predictions were combined by weighting, followed by an LGBM classifier and a masking trick.

solution_title: 21st Place Solution -> Binary Classification with a Bank Dataset Competition
solution_summary: The solution used a large stacking classifier built from roughly seventy models, including neural networks, boosted trees, decision trees, and logistic regression. A Keras neural network extracted features for downstream models and substantially improved cross-validation scores. Additional engineered features helped particular model families. Careful validation that avoided preprocessing leakage guided submission selection, and the submission with the highest validation score performed best privately.

The solution trained XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost regressors on four feature subsets and stacked their out-of-fold predictions with RidgeCV. Features described essay structure, writing bursts, key presses, word lengths, stylistic errors, punctuation, and tokenizer n-grams. Stratified five-fold validation and averaging across three random seeds supported the final ensemble of 12 models. Optimized essay reconstruction, Polars and Pandas processing, and multiprocessing reduced feature preparation to about 43 seconds and model inference to about 8 seconds.

solution_summary: The approach extracted and cached 256-pixel tissue tiles from fourfold downsampled slides, then sampled 26 crops per image. A shared-weight siamese network used a semi-weakly pretrained ResNet18 and averaged crop outputs before a binned prediction head. Random crop selection, flips, rotations, and rectangular occlusion helped generalization, while color augmentation offered little benefit. A single 70/30 split yielded a validation score of 0.8504, with reported public and private scores of 0.8503 and 0.8966.

solution_title: Kaggle Otto Group Product Classification Challenge
solution_summary: The final solution ensembled neural networks, XGBoost, random forests, and support vector machines. Regularized Greedy Forest and a linear model were also listed, but were excluded from the final ensemble. The post provides no details about preprocessing, validation, or ensemble weighting and links to a blog for further information.

The efficiency-track solution used linear regression with 13 features. The wording model additionally took the content score as an input. Feature engineering and modeling ran in the multithreaded datatable package, with grouped k-fold validation and quasi-random shuffling. Predictions were clipped to the original score range, and both training and inference took only a couple of seconds.

solution_summary: The final approach averaged five-fold DeiT-base-384 and EfficientNet-B4 models, including models trained with additional 2019 cassava data. Handling label noise was central: the author removed a small fraction of confidently identified noisy samples, used a modified OUSM loss, and applied strong augmentation with mixup and CutMix. Flip and zoom test-time augmentation consistently improved CV and public scores by 0.001–0.002. The three-model ensemble achieved 0.9017 on the private leaderboard, while knowledge distillation was excluded despite producing a single-model CV score above 0.91.

solution_title: The Great Shakeup: 92.2 public to 0.0 private, and why my hedge survived
solution_summary: The author selected two specialist submissions to hedge against changes in the private guardrail: pure marker exfiltration and nearly pure confused-deputy attacks. Marker exfiltration fell from 92.245 public to 0.000 private, while the confused-deputy submission retained 9.820 private from 10.445 public. The best-of-two scoring rule made diversification across submissions central to the strategy. Restricting the confused-deputy engine to whitelisted domains proved overly cautious, since a broader variant scored 10.755 privately.

The solution trained LightGBM on categorical identifiers, calendar features, cyclical encodings, and a binary year-parity feature. Training excluded February through June 2020, and an explicit adjustment removed Argentina's declining annual sales trend. Predictions were multiplied by coefficients borrowed from a community notebook. A second submission stopped applying those coefficients after May, but performed poorly on private data despite a much better public score.

The team treated temporal localization as classification of five-frame video segments. Transformer and bidirectional GRU sequence models used whole-video context, while NeXtVLAD models used only the segment frames. An EM-like pretraining process generated segment labels from video-labeled training data, retrained models on those labels, and fine-tuned on segment annotations. Two EM iterations were run, and tested multiple-instance learning approaches did not outperform this process.

The solution combined fine-tuned language models, models further trained with pseudo-labeled Feedback Prize 1 essays, and RAPIDS SVR models on language-model embeddings. Fold-specific pseudo-labeling and duplicate removal controlled leakage, and pseudo-labeling produced a substantial improvement. Target-specific ensemble weights were optimized with Nelder–Mead and shared across folds, yielding local CV of 0.4436. Final predictions averaged the five-fold models with models trained on all data; the author reported good CV–leaderboard correlation despite a validation implementation bug.

solution_title: 59th Place Solution for the Home Credit - Credit Risk Model Stability Competition
solution_summary: The final solution combined six models: the author's CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost, and LightAutoML components, plus a teammate's CatBoost and LightGBM. The two contributors engineered features independently, and one final ensemble gave CatBoost the largest weight. Counting category occurrences in previous-application data improved the leaderboard score by 0.013. Additional features used riskassesment_302T and the number of months associated with previous loans, with the former adding 0.001.

The author describes a solution based on gradient-boosted decision trees and links to a separate notebook. The post says no special techniques were used beyond GBDTs. It provides no model configurations, validation details, or numerical results.

solution_title: Delta x,y CNN + MLP network from 5th place solution
solution_summary: The solution predicts waypoint-to-waypoint displacement using a CNN over IMU signals combined with a large neural network for contextual path features. Inputs include site and floor embeddings, device calibration information, movement timing, nearby waypoints, and wall geometry. Gaussian noise, alternating losses and optimizers, site-specific fine-tuning, and averaging roughly a dozen networks improved accuracy. The multisite model achieved below 1.0 m MAE averaged across displacement coordinates, with some fine-tuned sites reaching 0.6–0.7 m.

The pipeline extracted slice features with EfficientNet B0 and B2, then classified exams and slices using a sequence-level 1D CNN. Trainable CT windows and metric-weighted binary cross-entropy adapted training to the competition, while mixed precision reduced resource use. Predictions were averaged across five folds and both backbones, followed by minimal corrections for label consistency. The combined submission scored 0.156 privately, and the reported total cross-validation BCE was 0.201473.

solution_summary: The team optimized tree packings using Spyrrow/Sparrow initialization, simulated annealing, and a memetic algorithm. For large configurations, they represented a dense lattice block as a single concave-hull polygon so Spyrrow could arrange free trees around it before restoring the lattice. Aspect-ratio perturbations helped escape local minima, and adding or removing trees transferred strong layouts between neighboring problem sizes. Their two best layouts achieved scores of 0.328x.

The author divided the location task into spatial cells and tuned models on a small geographic subset using a temporal holdout. The final ensemble summed probabilities from 13 models spanning nearest neighbors, tree ensembles, naive Bayes, and several kernel density implementations. Diversity across model families and cell configurations, followed by greedy ensemble selection, was central to the approach. Optimizing ensemble weights produced only negligible improvement, so the final combination was unweighted.
compute: Evaluating one model on the tuning subset took within 20 minutes.

solution_summary: The team trained four-layer bidirectional LSTMs using a small set of unnormalized raw, cumulative, logarithmic, and difference features. They improved learning by adding similar training breaths and their known pressures as input features, together with auxiliary regression and classification targets. Inference ensembled predictions from five neighbor choices, and the final training used full data with more than 30 seeds. Pseudo-label training with 14 models slightly improved the reported leaderboard score from 0.0999 to 0.0998.

The solution detected scientific panels before looking for reused content between blot or microscopy panels within a figure. Class and geometry filters plus ResNet-50 retrieval shortlisted pairs for RootSIFT matching with horizontal-flip checks and MAGSAC++ verification. Matched regions were grouped, projected into original image coordinates, filtered, and encoded as instance masks. Figures without multiple relevant panels were submitted as authentic because intra-panel detection was unfinished.

solution_summary: The author ensembled five pretrained language-model configurations using separate question and answer branches, with categorical embeddings in some models. Simple text cleanup and last-hidden-state CLS representations supported the models, while validation Spearman correlation guided early stopping. Mapping predictions to percentiles of unique training-label values produced the largest reported improvement. The final ensemble reached 0.438232 local CV and 0.41208 on the private leaderboard.

The author pooled data across subjects, which substantially improved leaderboard performance over subject-specific models despite their strong cross-validation results. Signals were resampled to 500 samples per second, and short windows from three segment positions were converted into log band-power features. Channels were selected and ordered by ictal-versus-interictal d-prime discrimination, yielding 192 features per segment. RBF SVMs with gamma 1.58 produced the required predictions, with one SVM per prediction task.

The solution computed engineered features and trained XGBoost to predict duplicate questions. Most features came from public competition kernels and discussions, with additional contributions from teammates. Some supplied feature CSVs were unavailable in the shared material, limiting reproducibility. The reported private leaderboard score was 0.14137.

The solution detected characters with a two-stage CenterNet pipeline using HourglassNet backbones, then classified cropped characters with three ResNet-based models. The second detection stage removed image margins using first-stage boxes, and both stages' boxes were ensembled. Classification incorporated bounding-box aspect ratio, horizontal-shift test-time augmentation, and a pseudo-labeled third model. Augmentation was essential for avoiding overfitting, and the final private leaderboard score was 0.900.
compute: All models trained on one GTX 1080 on a home server.

solution_summary: The final pipeline used a single ByT5-large model pretrained on external Akkadian-English material and fine-tuned on organizer data. Cleaning parallel pairs, normalizing both languages, and repairing corrupted test transliterations reduced data noise and distribution mismatch. Beam and temperature-sampled translations were reranked with chrF++ Minimum Bayes Risk decoding. Data and decoding quality mattered more than model scaling, with representative single-model private scores around 39.6.

solution_title: 2nd place solution to Facebook V competition on Kaggle
solution_summary: The approach combined online learning from test predictions with Gaussian mixture estimates of location likelihoods. A multipass version repeated learning from predictions for 20 iterations and scored 0.62036, close to the actual final submission's 0.62170. Validation slices monitored convergence and estimated prediction correctness probabilities used to adjust learning weights. Processing was split into parallel slices, and the author acknowledged leakage in the validation GMM setup.

solution_summary: The solution fitted transit depths with polynomial regression without deep learning. Transit boundaries were initialized from smoothed signal derivatives and refined against the fitted baseline. Mean transit estimates combined polynomial degrees, while wavelength-specific predictions used noise-adaptive smoothing and mean alignment. Missing-value handling improved leaderboard results, and uncertainty estimates incorporated residual noise and spectral flatness.

The solution fine-tuned BERT-large with a small custom output head and no additional statistical features. Offset-aware tokenization and truncation located the pronoun and candidate names, whose embeddings were combined through element-wise interactions and shared trainable projections. Truncation choices strongly affected performance. Averaging six models improved the corrected stage-one score to 0.275.

solution_title: Efficiency 18th Solution (most fast in Efficiency LB)
solution_summary: The student uses the first four layers of DeBERTa-v3-xsmall with weighted layer pooling, mean pooling, and no dropout. It learns regression predictions from an averaged teacher ensemble using competition data and FB1 data. A custom clipped MSE loss changes its treatment of small and large errors during cosine learning-rate decay. The efficiency submission reported a private score of 0.448837 and scoring time of 345, with teacher quality identified as a limitation.

solution_summary: The approach combined multiple models with class-specific blending weights optimized for log loss. CutMix was the most effective tested augmentation, particularly with a larger alpha and retained control samples. Seed-fold predictions were weighted by each class's positive training count to reduce the influence of folds with no positives. Model combinations were evaluated by CV, with early stopping and label smoothing used to limit overfitting.

solution_title: Kaggle: Quick, Draw! Doodle Recognition - 8th Place Solution

solution_title: [327th Place Solution]  Ensemble & C++ SAT Optimization
solution_summary: The author modified a Sparrow nesting engine to favor tight square bounds and added simulated annealing to improve placements. solution_title: 1st place solution with very simple code
solution_summary: The final approach used a small 3D ResNet10 with binary cross-entropy and Adam, without model ensembling. Repeated five-fold experiments ranked ideas by average out-of-fold performance because individual runs were highly unstable. MRI volumes were centered on the slice showing the largest brain cross-section, improving local validation by roughly 0.01–0.02. Training lasted 15 epochs with a learning-rate reduction after epoch 10.

solution_summary: The final notebook combined three prompt attacks adapted from public notebooks and forum ideas without filtering. They exploited model sensitivity to option positions, direct instructions to award a grade of nine, and model-specific wording in an adapted add-it-up attack. Adding step-by-step reasoning and simplifying the model wording both reduced scores. Filtering also overfit, reducing the reported private score from 28.494 to 27.853.

solution_title: (16th place) Improve your imitation agent with rules
solution_summary: The team adapted sazuma's imitation agent by training a center action and removing its nighttime movement restriction. They added rules for city production, movement ordering, evacuation, transfers, and returning units to resources or cities. These rules achieved roughly a 90% win rate against the modified vanilla imitation agent with identical model parameters when no time limit was imposed. Frequent time-limit violations remained an unresolved weakness of the final bots.
This post asks the administrators when final placements will be announced. It contains no modeling approach or solution details.

The final approach used a frozen CLIP backbone with an ArcFace head to learn 64-dimensional image embeddings. Restricting training to 4,000 classes from Products10k and GLR worked best. Validation across multiple retrieval datasets had weak leaderboard correlation, although a Stanford Online Products furniture subset was relatively useful. Text-image contrastive training, UMAP, separate category spaces, CLIP fine-tuning, other pretrained backbones, and extra transformer layers did not improve the approach.
The post thanks the organizers and participants and congratulates the winners. It links to the author's report and code on GitHub. No solution methods are described in the supplied text.

solution_title: Rank 93 Solution: Or how you can still win a medal without any model fine-tuning
solution_summary: The team used a model without fine-tuning because of limited time, skills, and resources. They made roughly 90 submissions and emphasized persistence in obtaining their result. The post links to a kernel but provides no substantive architecture, training, or inference details.

The final solution ensembled five-fold BERT Base models with separate question and answer models, a sequence model with statistical features, and DistilBERT embedding sequence and LSTM models. Statistical features and prediction post-processing provided major gains, including quantile mapping and optimized thresholds that pushed extreme predictions to zero or one. The team discarded its TensorFlow models after post-processing substantially improved the PyTorch models. A GPT-2 alternative achieved a slightly better private score but was not selected for the final submission.

The solution exploited target ordering leaked through killPlace within equal-kill player groups. It combined these constraints transitively in a directed acyclic graph for each match, using XGBoost group predictions to resolve otherwise unknown ordering. Group travel distance features were especially useful for the regression model. Missing groups were inserted at evenly spaced ranks before converting group ranks to player winPlacePerc predictions; graph sorting took seven minutes for roughly 20,000 test games.
compute: Per-game graph construction and sorting took seven minutes for approximately 20,000 test games.

solution_summary: The author used an Elo rating model similar to FiveThirtyEight's rankings, with parameters informed by a reusable tuning notebook. Aggressive manual adjustments raised UConn's rating by 175 points and assigned seeds 1–3 an almost certain first-round win. Two submissions covered opposite outcomes for the evenly matched Nebraska–Gonzaga game. The author attributed the strong result to these higher-volatility adjustments and submission strategy.

The author built LightGBM forecasting models in R using data.table and 21 features, calculating lagged rolling means directly from wide sales tables. Including the day number helped public performance, while a learning rate around 0.01 hurt it. Three similar models differed in randomly selected validation rows, with days 1914–1941 held out consistently for final validation. Combining the models produced a public score of about 0.59 and a private score of 0.63026, with plots and distribution checks used to verify the submission.

The solution used a neural network with two hidden layers after permutation-based feature removal and batch normalization. It added a feature indicating whether a stock appeared in the preceding time step, restricted training to later intervals, and weighted newer observations more heavily. Targets were standardized separately within each time step, and each epoch contained two passes with different losses, batch sizes, and learning rates. Predictions from epochs 11, 16, and 21 were averaged; adding LightGBM was explored but not completed because of memory issues.

The author attributes their best unselected submission to an active learning approach. That submission scored 1.0088 on the private leaderboard and 1.4094 on the public leaderboard. The post links the submission file and promises code later, but provides no implementation details.

The solution customized nnU-Net v2 into a two-stage 3D segmentation cascade, using full-resolution predictions as priors for cascade refinement. Models trained on all available labeled data with 128-sized patches, while inference used 192-sized patches, customized rotation and mirror TTA, and probability-map ensembles. Connectivity was encouraged through clDice and refined through distance transforms, Hessian ridge detection, and morphological pruning. Pseudo-labeling was not retained, and the best reported private submission used 8,000 epochs each for low-resolution and cascade training.
compute: Multi-GPU inference; best reported model trained lowres for 8,000 epochs and cascade for another 8,000 epochs.

solution_summary: The author modified Sparrow's packing search, focusing on groups with fewer than 100 trees. Increased sampling and rotation-range pruning improved exploration efficiency. A mixture of trees with two fixed orientations and trees with unrestricted orientations encouraged lattice structures while allowing corner adjustments. Groups were selected and configured manually, and the results were blended with public kernels.

solution_title: [7th place solution] Essays predictions as features
solution_summary: The solution combined selected action features with punctuation counts, word and paragraph bags of words, and predictions from essay-based models. A custom BPE tokenizer produced count and TF-IDF features for LightGBM classification and regression models, whose outputs became additional features. LightGBM, Denselight, and TabNet were tuned with Optuna and combined using Nelder–Mead optimized weights. Five-fold GroupKFold validation correlated well with leaderboard performance, with final CV of 0.568 and private score of 0.562.

solution_title: 110th Place,  Did Not Work: Splitting Thin/Thick Vessels Approach
solution_summary: The author combined a 2D U-Net operating on three orthogonal planes with a 3D U-Net, expecting them to capture larger and smaller vessels respectively. Training used all data for pretraining, followed by fine-tuning on dense kidney1 and kidney3 annotations with spatial and contrast augmentations. A thickness-based mask split used skeletons and distance transforms, but the author reported that this approach overfit cross-validation. Inference combined predictions with logical OR, using thresholds adjusted on kidney2.

The author solved a broad collection of adversarial ML and security challenges using model matching, input probing, brute force, and injection attacks. Matching the deployed MobileNetV2 and sentiment model enabled local searches for adversarial images and score-matching passphrases. solution_title: 195th Place Solution for the AI Agent Security - Multi-Step Tool Attacks Competi
solution_summary: The submission returned prevalidated libraries of single-message candidates, optimizing replayed scoring events per second. One final portfolio used marker-bearing HTTP posts to distinct clean hosts, while the other used notification emails as a hedge against stricter private checks. Token instrumentation and leaderboard calibration guided throughput decisions, while chains, multiple posts, and GPU submission settings failed to improve results. The marker portfolio fell from 52.710 public to 0.600 private, whereas the email hedge transferred from 14.835 public to 15.075 private.

solution_summary: The author released a trained neural network solution for diabetic retinopathy detection. The implementation used Lasagne and Theano, with the included model depending on cuDNN. solution_title: [Working Note] 66th place What Didn't Work, and What Was Left
solution_summary: The author selected attack candidates through offline replay on both competition models and a cascade of proxy guardrails. Both final submissions used a benign-form unauthorized email action, with one adding a special-token suffix intended to reduce replay latency. These variants transferred to private evaluation with scores of 13.125 and 24.855, while high-scoring public marker approaches scored zero privately. solution_summary: The authors released code for their Doodle challenge solution. Their approach combined diverse models, encoding methods, and input sizes. A carefully constructed ensemble stabilized the score, while detailed methods and numerical results were deferred to a future journal.

The solution used three Qwen-based stages without additional model tuning by the authors. An open-sourced Qwen2.5 14B model was followed by reranking 25 candidates with Qwen2.5 32B AWQ and then seven candidates with a QWQ 32B reasoning model. The final stage could generate up to 1,500 tokens per task, although incomplete and incorrectly formatted responses sometimes occurred. Adding QWQ improved public and private scores from 0.500 and 0.457 to 0.519 and 0.497, respectively.

The pipeline extracted signal-containing audio segments to reduce mislabeled training crops. It mixed log-mel inputs in the power domain and used the union of their labels. A separate ResNet18 call detector complemented a multitask model with primary and background label heads. Training progressed from primary labels to background supervision and then soft pseudo-labels, with the last stage improving public and private scores by 0.004 and 0.006.

This excerpt describes preprocessing and candidate features for an EEG seizure prediction solution. Recordings were divided into unfiltered 30-second epochs, which performed better than 15- or 60-second epochs. The authors explored existing feature extractors, channel correlations, spectral correlations, and several spectral-energy representations, but the excerpt does not identify the final feature subset or models. The reported public/private AUCs were 0.81423/0.79363.

The solution averaged soft predictions from 27 models across folds and seeds, using FPN, PANet, and EMANet decoders with modified ResNet encoders. Models were trained at roughly 768×768 resolution with AdamW, using either BCE alone or a weighted BCE and Dice loss. Horizontal-flip augmentation at inference was used for FPN models, while the other models used multiple image scales. Separate thresholds of 0.2 for segmentation and 0.72 for classifying non-pneumothorax images completed the pipeline. Reducing PANet channels preserved performance, and replacing EMANet's direct upsampling with gradual upsampling improved performance.

solution_title: Predicting March Madness: 1st Place Winner, Zach Bradshaw

solution_title: #4 Solution | So close yet so far (thank you and congratulations to all!)
solution_summary: The final submission combined nine locally trained AutoGluon models by taking the mode of their predictions. Experiments progressively incorporated feature engineering and ideas prototyped with Optuna, cross-validation, and manual ensembles. Adding deduplicated examples from the original mushroom dataset provided a small improvement. The selected submission scored 0.98530 on the public leaderboard and 0.98509 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Intel 13700K + RTX4090; individual AutoGluon experiments ran for 6, 12, 24, 30, or 36 hours.

solution_summary: The solution fits a differentiable physical transit simulator with explicit limb darkening, initialized by Kalman smoothing. It models wavelength-dependent gain drift and smooths the resulting spectrum before using linear regression to estimate transit depths. Separate small neural networks predict uncertainty, while a distance threshold determines whether PCA-derived spectral features are included. Averaging models across seeds improves stability, and the physical model supplies strong depth estimates with limited downstream modeling.
compute: Local RTX 5090: preprocessing 17 minutes, initialization 1 minute, physical depth fitting 3 hours 35 minutes, model training 11 minutes. Kaggle P100 runtime was about twice as long; calculations generally used 64-bit precision.

solution_summary: The approach inferred matchup win probabilities from FiveThirtyEight’s March Madness projections, then generated 1,200 linear transformations concentrated near that baseline. It simulated 25,000 tournaments using the baseline probabilities and selected the transformation that most frequently finished among the top five candidates. The selected transformation amplified probabilities above 0.93 and became contrarian between 0.36 and 0.64. It went 10–3 on contrarian games and improved overall log loss by 0.036; two similar runs scored 0.39429 and 0.39662.

The team generated recommendation candidates with several complementary strategies and ranked them using LightGBM LambdaRank. Ranking features combined candidate-generation scores and flags with weekly customer and article statistics. They trained models for five target weeks, validated against subsequent transactions, and ensembled the five models at inference. Useful candidate sources included age-bin popularity, co-purchases, t-SNE neighbors, ALBERT neighbors, and compressed sequence Word2Vec representations. The learning-rate 0.1 submission achieved private MAP@12 of 0.02813, while several neural and image-based candidate strategies were excluded.
compute: Initially MacBook Air (M1, 2020), 8-core CPU, 16 GB RAM, no deep-learning GPU; final two weeks used GCP instances with 48-core CPU and 384 GB RAM.

solution_summary: The final solution combined six video models: a GRU, three nonlocal NetVLAD variants, and two Soft-DBoF variants. Linear averaging of multiple checkpoints improved the individual models. The models were converted from float32 to bfloat16 to reduce their size, then combined into a final inference graph by adding prediction results. The implementation used TensorFlow 1.9.0 and a machine with four GTX 1080 Ti GPUs.
compute: 4× NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 Ti; 2× Intel Xeon E5-2630 v4 CPUs, 20 cores total; 128GB RAM.

solution_summary: The final approach instruction-tuned Qwen2.5 14B as a causal language model using competition data, LMSYS, and DPO 40k. Inputs combined the prompt, both responses, and the winner, with middle truncation for long sequences. An earlier Gemma2 9B classification model blended with LightGBM achieved 0.685 on the private leaderboard, while the Qwen approach improved this to 0.712627. The authors used simple instruction tuning without distillation or chain-of-thought training data.

The final translation model was ByT5-XL trained for three epochs on approximately 36,000 samples. The author expanded the original training data about fourfold using Turkish-to-English translations, material extracted from additional PDFs and pseudolabeled text segments. Larger ByT5 variants performed better, while causal language models and other T5 variants were weaker. Manual sentence alignment required substantial effort but had limited impact.
external_data: ["Shared non-English AKTs", "Innaya_v2.pdf", "A Historical Geography of Ancient Anatolia in the Assyrian Colony Period", "Agents, Archives, and Risk", "published_texts.csv"]

solution_title: 3rd place solution: a single xgb model
solution_summary: The approach trains an XGBoost model using the competition training data and the original dataset. The original dataset appears twice in the stated training mixture. Multiclass log loss is the evaluation metric.

The final ink-detection solution ensembled two architectures across two folds. One architecture was ResNet34d-U-Net with 256-pixel crops and 32 depth slices, and the other was PVTv2-B3-DaFormer with 384-pixel crops and 16 depth slices. Validation used fragment-1 and fragment-2aa.

solution_title: 2nd place solution explained: the power of original dataset
solution_summary: The final model ensembled LightGBM and XGBoost, with most effort devoted to improving missing-value imputation. The author used relationships in the original dataset, especially author-specific feature pairs and triplets, to recover missing competition values. Baselines used author-grouped mean imputation, and several MICE approaches were explored for remaining gaps. Rounding imputed values to original-data values worsened CV, while an experimental blend incorporating oversampled original data was not selected because its CV gain was uncertain.

solution_title: (88th place, 9th on public LB) Pure LLM Solution Team (AI)kinator
solution_summary: The solution combined a shallow deterministic question tree with a fine-tuned Mistral Nemo 12b-instruct model for subsequent play. Monte Carlo simulations optimized the early question order using public keywords and GPT-generated similar keywords. Roughly 300 GPT-4o self-play games supplied QLoRA training data, with rank 32 and three epochs chosen to limit inappropriate imitation. GPT-4o won about 35% of generated games, while fine-tuned Nemo achieved nearly 20% on unseen keywords in self-play; guessing and answering remained weaker components.

The solution combined five bird-audio models using different CNN backbones and two mel-spectrogram configurations. Masking time and frequency bands was particularly effective, while several waveform and noise augmentation experiments failed. Predictions were smoothed across shifted audio windows and adjusted using confidence elsewhere in the same soundscape. The final ensemble used a percentile threshold of 0.78, although 0.75 performed slightly better on the private evaluation.

The author treated the task as classification and built diverse tabular models using competition data, original data, and additional engineered features. One pipeline used shuffled 10-fold stratified validation and positive-weight hill-climbing blending, achieving 0.90620 CV and 0.89766 private score. Another held out two years and combined models with ridge regression, achieving 0.89355 CV and 0.90190 private score. Engineered features often reduced individual model performance but still contributed useful diversity to blends. The author emphasized simple models, limited tuning, and approximately three hours of overall effort.
compute: Kaggle CPU kernels; approximately three hours of total effort and 15–20 submissions.

solution_title: Small steps: Gareth Campbell on placing fourth in Wikipedia's Participation Challenge
solution_summary: The approach centered on users' edit counts over the preceding few months. Reversions, article types, and comments offered little predictive value compared with recent activity. The author used Stata and emphasized that many small experiments cumulatively improved predictions.

The final ensemble combined five-fold EfficientNet-B6 and B7 models with a B6 model retrained using soft test-set pseudolabels. Training used three diagnostic classes, additional 2019 images, and sevenfold oversampling of 2020 melanomas. Large batches, RandAugment, square-crop inference, and validation-based checkpoint selection supported the image-only models. Pseudolabeling was particularly valuable, and its standalone model achieved the author's highest private score although the ensemble was selected.
compute: 4x NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti 11GB and 4x Quadro RTX 6000 24GB; larger final models trained on the Quadro setup.
external_data: ["2019 melanoma data", "Chris Deotte triple-stratified data splits"]

solution_title: 5th place solution: one-stage I3D with additional 2D model for bbox centers
solution_summary: The solution combined four I3D video models for helmet box sizes and impact detection with two FPN-ResNet34 image models for helmet centers. Training used eight-frame patches, hard negative mining, and a second stage that trained the video models' FPN heads on full images with frozen backbones. Replacing point targets for helmet centers with fading circular targets raised local validation performance from 0.48 to 0.58. Averaged predictions, multiscale inference, spatial and temporal suppression, and cross-view filtering produced the final detections.

The solution combined five PyTorch models built around stacked LSTM-GRU networks with different hidden sizes, embeddings, and preprocessing choices. Models used FastText or GloVe plus Paragram embeddings, with attention and capsule components in one architecture and Gaussian noise in some models. Each network trained for five to six epochs without folds, and predictions were combined using linear regression coefficients. Pseudo-labeling, broader preprocessing changes, and frozen recurrent-weight reuse did not provide enough benefit; total runtime was 6352.2 seconds.
compute: Runtime: 6352.2 seconds

solution_title: 6th Place Solution - Lightgbm with Target flattened
solution_summary: The solution used XGBoost with the forecast horizon as an input to predict a geometric monthly growth rate directly across one to five future months. It combined smoothing of anomalous observations with lag, difference, rolling-statistic, and state-cluster features. Training targets were scaled according to the active business base and transformed back during prediction. Validation covered the last 12 months and considered how many months improved, while final forecasts received a small upward adjustment.

The approach trained a ResNet101 global image descriptor with GeM pooling and contrastive learning on the landmark recognition training set. Multi-scale descriptors were normalized and transformed with PCA whitening with shrinkage learned on the retrieval index. Retrieval used diffusion over a reciprocal nearest-neighbor graph. Concatenating the descriptor with an externally trained R-MAC descriptor improved the final submission to 59.1 publicly and 57.6 privately.
models_pretrained: ["ResNet101 pretrained on ImageNet", "R-MAC trained on an external dataset"]
compute: Search machine: Intel Xeon E5-2630 v2 @ 2.60GHz, 256 GB RAM, 12 threads, one Tesla P100 16 GB. Descriptor extraction: 170 ms/image on GPU; query: 12 ms CPU search plus 150 ms GPU diffusion.
external_data: ["ImageNet", "Google Landmark Recognition Challenge training set", "Unspecified external dataset for R-MAC"]

solution_title: AIMO3: Inference-Time Reasoning, Optional RAG, and Dynamic Deadline Allocation
solution_summary: The final pipeline uses base gpt-oss-120b served through vLLM, with a short computation-focused prompt and stateful Python tools. Parallel stochastic attempts are combined through consensus and inverse-entropy weighting, while three-stage deadlines extend computation only when agreement remains insufficient. Tool-output truncation and a final boxed-answer recovery prompt help preserve usable answers within the available budget. Hybrid retrieval, alternative backbones, and merged supervised fine-tuning were discarded; the final submission scored 40/50 publicly and 41/50 privately.
compute: A representative inference run used eight parallel attempts, with completion times of about 292–557 seconds.

solution_summary: The author trained an XGBoost model to predict margin of victory and tuned hyperparameters using cross-validation measured by mean absolute error. Historical win rates by final point spread converted predicted margins into win probabilities. Aggressive probability overrides increased confidence in strong favorites and selected high seeds in early rounds. UConn's championship run exposed a weakness because the model favored NC State and Stanford in those matchups.

The post describes a label-noise pattern associated with consecutive spaces in tweets. The authors hypothesized that annotation removed repeated spaces, causing mismatches when selected text was recovered from the original tweet. Their models accidentally incorporated behavior that captured this pattern, and correcting it reduced performance, so they retained it. The full implementation is not disclosed, and the author explicitly says the final solution used no post-processing.

The solution blended four LightGBM and neural network models, including separate models for each forecast day and models covering all 16 days. Training used only 2017 data, with extensive windowed sales and promotion statistics across item and store groupings. Missing or negative promotion and target values were replaced with zero. A weighted linear blend outperformed stacking and achieved public and private scores of 0.504 and 0.509.

The solution used Gaussian process regression to model multiband lightcurves and extract about 200 features for a single LightGBM classifier. Physically motivated degradation expanded the training data to roughly 270,000 objects that better resembled the test set. Five-fold validation kept all degraded versions of each source object together. Leaderboard probing informed a weighted combination of known-class predictions for class 99, improving the public score from 0.726 to 0.670.
compute: Gaussian process fitting: approximately 10 fits per second and around 3 days total.

solution_summary: The author combined 21 transformer models using target-specific ridge regression and the Netflix ensemble method. Model diversity produced the largest improvement, including contributions from models weaker than DeBERTa individually. Two rounds of pseudo-labeling on earlier student-writing competition data provided a smaller additional gain, with pseudo-data restricted by fold. Training primarily used mean pooling, AdamW, and SmoothL1Loss, with multi-label stratified validation across different fold counts and seeds.

solution_title: Diabetic Retinopathy Winner's Interview: 1st place, Ben Graham
solution_summary: Images were scaled to a consistent retinal radius and normalized by subtracting local average color before CNN processing. A random forest converted network predictions into integer labels while combining information from both eyes. Increasing image radius beyond 270 pixels offered no apparent benefit, and multiple views or network ensembles improved accuracy very little. SparseConvNet supported experiments with fractional max-pooling, while image sparsification remained unsuccessful because of time constraints.

solution_title: A Single Write-up on CIBMTR from a Kaggle Newbie
solution_summary: The reported final approach combined XGBoost and a Survival Transformer through weighted averaging to balance survival prediction accuracy and racial-group fairness. Preprocessing included numerical and categorical imputation, categorical encodings, standardized numerical features, and SMOTE for smaller racial subgroups. Several other tree and neural models were evaluated, with Optuna tuning for XGBoost and Adam with cyclical learning rates for deep learning. The author reported a 3.8% improvement in stratified C-index and a fairness score above 0.72, although blend weights and tuning values were omitted.

The solution combined sparse text features, image metadata, self-trained word embeddings, and ad activity features with custom title-cluster aggregates. Clustering titles within narrow subcategories enabled price comparisons, with within-cluster price rank providing a substantial improvement. Neural networks supplied image and text representations, although text embeddings trained directly on the target overfit LightGBM and were replaced by embeddings trained to predict other ad attributes. The final system used three stacking layers of LightGBM, neural networks, and ridge regression, followed by a linear average.

The approach used simulated annealing across all ids, primarily changing parameter settings between instances. Neighborhood moves inserted either individual words or consecutive blocks, while swap moves were discarded. Observations of promising permutations guided partial fixing of words and further annealing, reaching 28.5 on id5. Parallel searches, batched scoring, and cached evaluations improved search efficiency.

solution_title: Trust CV can beat blind blending
solution_summary: The author improved LightGBM and XGBoost with ordered target encoding and implemented RealMLP with categorical representations selected by cardinality. Direct one-hot encoding for small categories improved generalization compared with embedding every category. A five-model ensemble drew most of its strength from CatBoost, RealMLP, and TabM, with smaller contributions from XGBoost and LightGBM. The selected submission scored 0.91700 publicly and 0.91813 privately; an alternative using a strong open-source TabM scored slightly higher but was not selected.

The pipeline detects characters with Hybrid Task Cascade, groups detections into lines, and recognizes cropped lines with a CRNN. Joint CTC-attention training improves character positioning, while a six-gram language model supports beam-search decoding. Augmentation, dropout, cutout, early stopping, and SGD fine-tuning improve recognition. Snapping predicted centers to nearby strokes and removing duplicate outputs bring the reported public score to 0.938, without model ensembling.
compute: Detection: 8x M40 for 5 days; recognition: 8x 2080 Ti for one week.

solution_summary: The solution generated raster images with FLUX.1-schnell Q6_K through stable-diffusion-cpp-python and converted them into compliant SVGs with VTracer and Scour. Binary search and SSIM comparisons tuned conversion parameters within the time limit. Generation latency and unresolved CUDA issues limited optimization, while a heuristic vector-style prompt, OCR decoys, and a fine-tuned CLIP model were used with limited testing. Scores varied substantially across seeds.
compute: T4 x2 GPUs attempted; first image generation took over 55 seconds.

solution_summary: The solution represented each play as a defense-by-offense tensor of relative player locations and velocities and processed it with a two-dimensional CNN. Convolutions and mixed average/max pooling captured player interactions without imposing an arbitrary player order, while training directly optimized CRPS. Game-grouped cross-validation scored only 2018 plays, and mirrored-coordinate augmentation, test-time averaging, and seed bagging improved robustness. The final submissions trained eight models within 8,500 seconds and achieved public scores of 0.01205 and 0.01201.
compute: Kaggle CPU runtime with four concurrent model fits; eight models per submission, below 8,500 seconds total.

solution_title: 179th place / top 5% (not submitted) solution - first competition
solution_summary: The author's best unsubmitted solution combined basic features from a public kernel with roughly 800 time-series features generated using tsfresh. Correlation filtering, feature ranking including RFECV, and manual choices reduced the inputs to 50 features. TPOT optimized a pipeline with ElasticNetCV and LassoLarsCV stacking stages, sequential L2 and L1 normalization, and a final LinearSVR. It achieved an average CV score of 2.04663 and a private score of 2.48755; the author did not submit it because they distrusted their CV, and an augmentation experiment did not work.

The solution used a custom CNN and MLP-Mixer hybrid to model both neighboring atmospheric levels and global interactions. It concatenated individual and group-normalized features, applied tanh squashing to stabilize outliers, and scaled targets to unit RMS. Training mixed low-resolution and aqua-planet ClimSim data, and predictions were averaged across eight models with different seeds and depths. Physical target reconstruction and output clipping complemented the ensemble, whose individual private leaderboard scores ranged from 0.778 to 0.781.
compute: RTX 4090; approximately 27 hours for 3 epochs on 161,464,320 examples at batch size 256; about 1TB storage available.

solution_summary: The post shares a GitHub repository for seizure prediction code. The author says final testing is still underway and the code is largely ready. They acknowledge incomplete documentation and offer to answer questions, but provide no methodological details.

solution_title: 36th place - deberta-large-1024/longformer-large-1536 ensemble with thresholding + code
solution_summary: The final ensemble contained two DeBERTa-large configurations, two DeBERTa-v3-large configurations, and one Longformer-large configuration, each trained on five folds. Predictions were aligned to text characters and averaged before extracting discourse spans. DeBERTa-large performed best individually, while model diversity added roughly 0.004 to the score. Tuning class-specific probability and length thresholds on out-of-fold predictions added another roughly 0.004, with final public and private scores of 0.707 and 0.719.
compute: 15GB GPU for training; inference across 25 fold models took a little over 8 hours in a Kaggle kernel.

solution_summary: The pipeline first propagated IP information across cookies sharing a handle and generated device-cookie candidates using shared IP rarity rules. It trained eight bagged XGBoost classifiers on device, cookie, and relational aggregate features. Confident test predictions updated training features before retraining. Postprocessing expanded weak candidate sets, propagated matches across shared handles, and applied thresholds conditioned on candidate and handle information.
compute: HP DL160 G6 server, 48 GB RAM, two Intel Xeon X5675 processors with six cores each and hyperthreading; Gentoo Linux. The author says 32 GB RAM should suffice.

solution_summary: The final solution used two EfficientNet-B0 models based on a public training notebook. Predictions were rounded before averaging, producing scores of 0.880 on the public leaderboard and 0.934 on the private leaderboard. Experiments with different networks, custom tile cropping, and strong augmentations did not outperform the simple approach.

The team combined translated training data, soft pseudo-labels, and multiple stages of transformer fine-tuning. Freezing embedding layers reduced memory use and enabled larger batches, while translation-based test-time augmentation improved predictions across six languages. They further blended models trained with unsupervised data augmentation and language-specific models for Spanish, Italian, and Turkish. Their best submission reached a public leaderboard score of 0.9504 and was also their best submission on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: [242nd Place] A Particle-Filter Baseline with TabM Residual Learning
solution_summary: The pipeline constructed a smooth physical TVT baseline with a bootstrap particle filter, then used TabM to learn its residual errors. Features captured trajectory, GR correspondence, filter uncertainty, known-section backtests, virtual observation widths, neighboring formations, and azimuth. Leakage-safe five-fold validation grouped all rows by well and excluded validation wells from spatial lookups. The best unselected submission blended direction-specific TabM experts with an azimuth model, achieving OOF RMSE 7.8648 and private RMSE 7.974; the selected submissions achieved private RMSE 8.370.

solution_summary: The final ensemble averaged two multimodal neural networks and a random forest. The neural models combined pretrained ResNet34 or MobileNetV3 image branches with fully connected branches for environmental and geographic features. The random forest used those tabular features plus image-channel percentiles, while five-view test-time augmentation improved neural predictions. Adding validation data to final training helped slightly; label aggregation and several alternative backbone configurations performed worse.

Public pseudolabels and prior-year pretrained checkpoints supplied the largest gains. The six models were averaged equally, converted with OpenVINO, and blended equally with a public Perch/ProtoSSM pipeline. The final blend scored 0.955 privately, while a subsequently evaluated 0.6–0.4 blend scored 0.957.

solution_title: This was not the way  (public 18th private 83rd solution)
solution_summary: The team developed two default-prediction pipelines using hundreds of aggregation features and ensembles dominated by LightGBM and CatBoost. One pipeline also included XGBoost trained on only 50,000 samples, and missing birth dates were filled from related columns. Model diversity came from varying tree depths, learning rates, and leaf counts, while blending and selection balanced local validation with leaderboard results. A week-number regression strategy was abandoned in favor of a public metric-hacking notebook, although retrospective results suggested their original strategy could have performed better.

solution_summary: The solution generated recommendation candidates, constructed article and customer–article features, and ranked them with LGBMRanker. Candidate sources included repeat purchases, matching product codes, user-based collaborative filtering, and several popularity lists. Seven weekly validation folds used three preceding weeks for training, and predictions from the fold models were combined with weights. Customer-only features did not help, while article identifiers and product codes were excluded because they overfit.

solution_title: BirdCLEF 2026 — A TabPFN-Inspired ICL / Retrieval-Based Pipeline
solution_summary: This prototype framed multilabel bird recognition as in-context prediction over pretrained Perch embeddings. A transformer processed labeled support examples, learnable thinking tokens, and unlabeled queries. Predictions combined a parametric classifier with attention-based transfer of support labels through a learned gate. The approach targeted rare and underrepresented classes, but validation, support construction, calibration, and metadata integration remained unfinished.

The pipeline detected animals with YOLOv5 and classified expanded crops using Dynamic Margin ArcFace with DOLG CNN backbones and separate identity and species heads. ConvNeXt performed best, with other CNN families included for diversity. Three rounds of pseudo-labeling improved average single-model public scores from 0.855 to 0.865, and the final ensemble concatenated features from 12 models. Species-specific new-individual thresholds increased the public score to 0.888.

solution_title: 285st Place Solution for The 2026 NeuroGolf Championship
solution_summary: The solution optimized 400 task-specific ONNX programs for correctness, parameter cost, and inference memory rather than training a conventional model. A per-task selection between existing and public models established a stronger baseline, followed by small graph rewrites and direct ARC-rule implementations. Independent rules, exhaustive or synthetic inputs, backend comparisons, and immutable artifact audits controlled adoption. The final score was 7396.89, an audited improvement of 128.90 points, despite several locally successful compression candidates failing on hidden cases.

solution_summary: The pipeline corrected image orientation, cropped the paper, detected grid keypoints, and rectified ECG images through triangulated warping. U-Net models with DINOv3 ConvNeXt backbones detected keypoints and extracted signals through jointly trained segmentation, learned warping, regression, and resampling modules. Iterative manual annotation and pseudo-label refinement improved keypoints, while adjacent-lead features helped recover signals extending beyond their nominal regions. A weighted ensemble of three signal models with rotation TTA achieved 21.86 public and 21.57 private using only competition data.

solution_title: 60th place solution : A* algorithm for pathfinding
solution_summary: The author used A* pathfinding for all main functions of their competition agent. They link a GitHub repository containing the code and explanations. The post provides no further implementation details or quantitative results.

The team developed an SED model and a separate Tropic model without manual labeling. They improved the SED baseline with mixup, intelligent cropping, and a better training schedule, reaching 0.91760 public and 0.92270 private scores. Experiments with diverse TIMM backbones showed that model diversity improved ensemble performance. Substantial GPU resources allowed rapid experimentation.
