solution_summary: The author used VGG16 without its original top, adding a 1,024-unit fully connected layer and five linear outputs for count regression. Training used SGD and mean squared error. Additional post-processing improved the regression predictions, although its details were not provided.

The solution averaged six models combining EfficientNetV2-S classifiers with sound event detection models on compact mel spectrograms. Geographic coordinates provided additional classifier inputs, while audio augmentation and region-of-interest sampling supported training. A weighted multitask binary cross-entropy loss predicted both species and bird families, and external recordings supplied additional audio and bird-free background noise. Secondary labels, a smaller backbone, and temporal probability adjustments did not improve the approach.

solution_summary: The solution blended two stacked ensembles built around LightGBM and neural networks, using standard five-fold validation and a time-based validation scheme with a four-day gap. Text representations, image features, user aggregates, and categorical interaction statistics supplied complementary information, while the strongest neural network used stacked bidirectional GRUs. Time-aware target encoding and diverse feature-channel models helped the ensembles. A final blend of 35% time-series stack and 65% five-fold stack achieved a public score of 0.2136.

solution_title: 21 Public/56 Private Solution - Data Augmentation and Feature Engineering
solution_summary: The solution ensembled four decoder LLM classifiers trained with LoRA to predict 37 misconception classes. Prompts included reconstructed answer options and option letters, while known question information fixed the True/False component of the target. Text perturbations and random removal of optional prompt tags improved robustness, and length-sorted dynamic padding nearly doubled inference speed. Final submissions combined model probabilities, optionally incorporating rank averaging and question-specific class filtering, with exact training matches promoted to the first prediction.
compute: Most training used 4× RTX 3090 GPUs with DDP; some runs used one A100 80 GB. Each model trained for 3 epochs.

solution_title: #9 Solution with CODE - Team BIG HEAD: Training model bonanza, TTA and L2 stacking.
solution_summary: The team trained about 50 models using three consecutive CT slices as input and predicting six labels for each slice. Fastai v1 models used standard windowing, while fastai v2 variants used a subdural window and a loss emphasizing subdural hemorrhage. Means and standard deviations from ten test-time augmentations supplied central and neighboring slice features to XGBoost and CatBoost stackers. The two stackers were averaged, allowing individually modest models to contribute to the final ensemble.

The team built a scheduling pipeline that conserved small toys for increasing elf productivity before larger jobs. Four integer linear programs generated productivity runs, allocated remaining small toys, and optimized scheduling offsets, while hill climbing improved medium-toy oscillations. An Euler tour construction divided the work among 900 elves, followed by local swaps that brought their finishing times within one day. The final pipeline also reduced waiting losses by swapping items within runs.
compute: Early solution: around 5 seconds on a Dell 6420 laptop; hardest final ILP: about 3 hours to find a reasonable solution.

solution_summary: The team first ran simulated annealing across three machines for about five days. They then combined an approach abbreviated BS with simulated annealing for another 21 hours across three machines. Merging the resulting solutions improved the objective from 12384669985 in the first phase to a final 12384507107.
compute: First phase: three machines, 20 threads on a 24-core machine, approximately five days. Second phase: three machines, 21 hours.

solution_summary: The solution combined two Bayesian latent team-strength models, a possession-statistics logistic regression, and an XGBoost model using only Kaggle box scores. Adjusting spreads for home advantage and compressing extreme margins addressed overconfident predictions. A constrained logistic stack combined model logits, with tuning and ensemble fitting based on temporally valid out-of-sample predictions. The ensemble scored 0.4102, improved to 0.3998 by applying a binary prediction strategy to one first-round game, while the best individual model scored 0.4050.

The team reformulated permutation ordering within each of three strings as asymmetric traveling salesperson problems and developed assignments based on 2-cycles. Splitting these cycles into blocks produced a score of 2440 without wildcards, which they verified was optimal under that restriction. Their final construction paired cycles differing by a swap of the last two letters and exchanged their final block permutations across strings. Using each wildcard as three characters reduced the score to 2428, whose optimality remained unproven.

The final approach used BigGAN with a smaller generator, a stronger discriminator, shared class embeddings, and hierarchical noise injection. Image preparation emphasized retaining recognizable dog content through padding and geometric transformations. Sharper resizing followed by denoising worked better than smooth resizing, while brightness and contrast changes hurt the metric. The solution retained the original exponential moving average after several architecture and training alternatives failed to improve results consistently.

solution_title: The reason of the fall from the first place of the public LB.
solution_summary: The author used leaderboard feedback for validation, particularly when selecting features. They also describe using an ensemble of LightGBM models. The post provides no feature definitions, ensemble construction details, or quantitative results.

The policy is initialized by behavior cloning from a strong player's replays, then improved with asynchronous IMPALA-style reinforcement learning using terminal win/loss rewards. Historical opponents and a delayed moving teacher maintain strategic diversity and stabilize learning. A structured attention network explicitly represents planets, fleet arrivals, and directed edges with legal-action masking. Optimized simulation and mixed-precision execution support large-scale training, while separate two-player and four-player artifacts run on CPU at submission time.
compute: Approximately one week of training on one NVIDIA RTX 5090; CPU submission inference.

solution_summary: The solution progressively developed a stride-one QuartzNet/Jasper-style model using CTC loss, initializing each experiment from the preceding best checkpoint. Architectural additions included SE blocks, hypercolumns, masked convolutions, a depthwise CNN layer, and an LSTM, with the final listed experiment reaching CV 0.8301. Training used temporal augmentation, LookAheadAdamW, a Onecycle schedule, and all supplemental data. Validation used 20 random folds grouped by sequence length rather than user, while pseudo-label experiments and Conformer variants provided limited or inferior results.

The team blended character probabilities from multiple five-fold DeBERTa-xlarge and DeBERTa-v3-large models. In-task masked-language pretraining on patient notes, fold-specific hard pseudo-labels, and span-boundary corrections improved performance. FGM helped DeBERTa-v3-large slightly but did not help xlarge. The final ensemble scored 0.893 on both public and private leaderboards, using a threshold of 0.44.

solution_title: JED Working Note — Reverse Engineering the Replay Wall
solution_summary: The post consists solely of a link to another Kaggle writeup. The linked title concerns reverse engineering replay behavior in the JED benchmark. The supplied text contains no solution description or experimental results.

The submission generated confused-deputy candidates and optimized how many successful replays fit within the grading time budget. Live latency probes selected efficient phrasing, while conservative cost estimates, fallback behavior, and reserve margins controlled submission size. Local scoring checked attack success against both target models, although grader runs were still needed to validate timing. The reported effective private score was roughly 20, while a separate exfiltration approach reached 86.4 publicly but transferred poorly.
compute: Grader target models used quantized llama.cpp inference on 2x T4 GPUs, with roughly 9,000 seconds of replay budget; local hardware was unspecified.

solution_summary: The pipeline separated classification from segmentation and combined several larger models. Classification used SE-ResNeXt101 and SENet154, with model selection based on F0.5 to reflect the greater scoring benefit of correctly identifying negative images. U-Net segmentation models were trained through four stages, increasing resolution and introducing soft pseudo-labels before a final symmetric Lovasz stage. Aggressive augmentation, gradient accumulation, snapshots, and test-time augmentation supported both branches.

The team combined diverse credit-history feature sets with boosted trees, linear models, and denoising-autoencoder neural networks. Aggregations, temporal slices, ratios, and feature selection were central, with final feature supersets containing roughly 1,800–2,000 variables. All base models used five-fold stratified validation, and more than 90 base predictions fed a multilevel stacking pipeline. The final output equally blended three upper-level predictions; neural networks contributed useful diversity despite weaker standalone AUC.
compute: Most XGBoost models used GPU gpu_hist; LightGBM used CPUs. A complete five-fold DAE+NN run took about one day on a GTX1080Ti.

solution_summary: The solution combined XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost models using three target formulations described as Nelson, Kaplan, and Cox loss, without feature engineering. It also incorporated the public PRL neural network notebook. Both components used 10-fold validation and multiple-seed ensembling. Version 17 was selected for submission, although version 4 performed best on the private leaderboard.

The author used BERT with USE features and Crawl embeddings, training separate models for questions and answers. USE features improved performance substantially, while Crawl embeddings contributed little. RoBERTa performed close to BERT on the public leaderboard despite receiving less development time and lacking USE features. The pipeline used head-and-tail tokenization, a custom loss, and post-processing from a public kernel, implemented in PyTorch.

The solution trained multilingual and English sentence embedding models, retrieved language-matched content candidates, and classified candidate pairs with LightGBM. Rich topic context and distance-space features were central to the pipeline, alongside preferential sampling of harder non-source examples. Topic-wise probability scaling enabled a shared decision threshold, and five models were combined by majority vote. A single-model inference example achieved 0.705 public and 0.741 private scores, while long embedding training limited the number of completed folds.
compute: About 40 hours per fold for 250 epochs; RTX 4090 purchased. Completed three of five long-training folds plus an all-data model.

solution_title: 17th Solution [3d part] and Kaggle Issue Report
solution_summary: The author's contribution used nnUNet for 3D segmentation, training one model on all data and five cross-validation models. Training used batch size 4, 1,500 epochs, and learning-rate adjustments. Combining the six models reached 0.887 on the public leaderboard, while the five-fold ensemble reached 0.885 without test-time augmentation or post-processing. The team's final ensemble took the union of 2.5D and 3D predictions.
compute: A modified submission was expected to finish in about 8 hours 20 minutes but timed out under the 9-hour limit.

solution_summary: The solution stacked embeddings from four EfficientNet models trained with different rasterization settings, using a dropout and linear ensemble head. Custom L5Kit optimizations accelerated rasterization by more than fourfold and enabled efficient training on the full dataset with multiple GPUs. ImageNet initialization and lower-resolution pretraining were important, while chopped validation and bootstrap analysis guided model selection and excluded unstable larger backbones. The final B3/B5/B6/B6 ensemble achieved a private score of 8.579, compared with 9.070 for the best single model.
compute: Mostly 8x V100 nodes; a full pass over 191,177,863+ samples took within two days with medium-sized models.

solution_summary: The author trained an RNN on user-product purchase sequences, predicting purchases at every order using simple order features and learned product, aisle, and department embeddings. Loss masking restricted training to reorder events, while sampling or weighting users prevented prolific shoppers from dominating training. Final submissions blended the RNN with a gradient boosting model and optimized expected F1. Around 10,000 users were held out, and submitted models remained trained only on the training fold.

The solution used organizer-provided cell segmentation and a two-stage training pipeline to turn image labels into cell-level supervision. Six EfficientNet-B0 models trained with different seeds generated cell pseudo-labels, which were constrained by known image-level negative labels. Additional HPA images targeted weaker classes and supplied 1,123 negative images, while channel-intensity augmentation and weight decay supported cell-model training. The best submission scored 0.50626 private and 0.50738 public.
compute: Stage-two training: over 500,000 examples; one epoch took 6 minutes on an unspecified latest-generation GPU.
external_data: ["Organizer-provided extra public HPA dataset", "1,123 negative HPA images"]

solution_summary: The solution used a two-stage segmentation pipeline with U-Net models and EfficientNet-b0 backbones. A coarse model covered entire images at reduced resolution and emphasized avoiding false negatives, while a second model examined regions around potential glomeruli at higher resolution. Training-image selection mattered more than changing backbones. Model selection used spatially held-out portions of each tile, and late experiments incorporated visually checked pseudo-labels from test tiles.

The final solution ensembled eight sequence models, including convolutional Transformer-GRU hybrids, recurrent CNNs, a 1D U-Net, and SqueezeFormer variants. Ensemble coefficients were optimized with Nelder-Mead on external validation data withheld from all training. Standardization, additional low-resolution data, target-specific fine-tuning, and physical postprocessing contributed to performance. The ensemble achieved 0.78116375 CV and 0.77477 private score, while fitting separate coefficients per output column generalized worse.
compute: Approximately 24 hours on an A100 to train SqueezeFormer on 16M samples.
external_data: ["External validation data", "All low-resolution data", "6M additional samples extracted from Hugging Face"]

solution_summary: The solution combined attention-equipped 1D ResNet U-Nets with sequence vision transformers across five subject-grouped folds. Training used randomly sampled 8192-step windows and strong augmentation, with cutmix particularly helpful. The final ensemble assigned 0.4 weight to convolutional models and 0.6 to transformers. Transformers performed better locally and publicly, but convolutional models performed better on private evaluation, suggesting validation missed transformer overfitting. Pseudo-labeling was tested but excluded because it did not improve CV or public scores.

The solution combined XGBoost and LightGBM classifiers wrapped for multi-output prediction. Preprocessing removed the identifier, split mixed_desc, and generated groupby features from categorical and numerical columns. Repeated multilabel-stratified cross-validation evaluated the models using ROC AUC. Final test predictions were the average of the two classifiers.

The solution combined LightGBM, CatBoost, and a neural network with weights of 0.3, 0.3, and 0.4. Manual feature engineering captured assessment distributions, experience, accuracy, and learning speed, followed by feature selection that reduced roughly 150 features to 51. All models used 20-fold bagging, with neural network predictions additionally averaged across three seeds, and test-set assessments supplied extra training samples. Validation randomly selected one assessment per child to mirror the test structure, producing a truncated CV score of 0.575 and public and private leaderboard scores of 0.559.

The author used a basic LightGBM model with stock-return, amplitude, volatility, and moving-average features. Local walk-forward cross-validation guided model development. Aggregate features received sensible defaults until their values became available. The author stopped development partway through because of time constraints.

The solution trained SE-ResNeXt50 models on 512- and 1024-pixel RGBY images, alongside lower-capacity ResNet34 models at 512 pixels. It used rotation and flipping augmentation, focal loss with gamma values of 2 and 2.5, and five-fold cross-validation. The final ensemble weighted 24 models, giving greater weight to gamma-2.5 models, and achieved a private score of 0.547. An alternative union of labels from two individual models achieved a slightly higher private score of 0.550 despite weaker public scores.

The solution used a two-stage pipeline: a multitask FPN with a ResNet34 encoder removed empty masks, followed by separate binary U-Net segmenters for each class. The first stage used five folds, while each class had two U-Nets trained only on images containing that class. Training combined binary cross-entropy and Dice losses, with flip and brightness augmentation. Checkpoint weight averaging improved validation by 0.005–0.01, and stage predictions were averaged with flip test-time augmentation.

The approach used YOLOv5 to create separate body and fin crop datasets sharing individual identities, with full frames used when detection failed. Large-image embedding models were trained on all training identities using separate body and fin AM-Softmax losses, and their features were averaged at inference. A diverse ensemble and confident pseudo labels provided substantial gains, with the author's best ensemble scoring 0.863. Final post-processing used separate new-individual thresholds for whales and dolphins.

The team built a teacher ensemble combining regressors on pooled DeBERTa embeddings with publicly shared fine-tuned DeBERTa models. They used it to pseudo-label 15,000 essays from earlier Feedback Prize competitions, then fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3-xsmall on those essays and 4,000 labeled competition essays. MLP and RBF Kernel Ridge heads worked better than SVM, while scaling embeddings hurt performance. The efficient student achieved a private score of 0.442 with a reported runtime of 1,336 seconds.
compute: Efficiency submission runtime: 1,336 seconds.

solution_summary: The author reused code from a previous competition with no major adjustments. The post highlights using Optuna to find weights. It links a notebook but provides no model details or numerical results.

The solution averaged predictions from ELECTRA-small-discriminator and LightGBM regressors. It distilled ELECTRA-base into ELECTRA-small, used pseudo-labeled FB1 essays, and supplied n-grams, statistical text features, and transformer predictions to LightGBM. Adding transformer predictions as features delivered the largest improvement, with prediction features and ensembling improving scores by about 1%–1.5%. The final efficiency-focused version used only the syntax and phraseology ELECTRA-small models and achieved a private score of 0.452429.

solution_title: congrats to Guanshuo Xu! and [14th place] solution
solution_summary: The solution used four EfficientNet models: B3 and B4 trained on an 80% split, plus counterparts trained on all the data. Training changes were guided by a stratified 20% holdout, with progressively stronger augmentation and adjustments when validation performance stalled. Multiple checkpoint predictions and flip-based test-time augmentation fed a stacking pipeline whose test inputs mixed partial-data and full-data predictions at 25% and 75%. A two-hidden-layer neural network was the strongest stacker, achieving 0.936 CV, while stacking improved the leaderboard score by about 0.003–0.004.

The final solution averaged six time-based components without using the supplied auxiliary features. Department-level pooling across stores used reduced-rank SVD or averaging of correlated, standardized series to suppress noise. Forecasts combined STL decomposition, exponential smoothing, ARIMA, Fourier regressors, and simple seasonal baselines. Adjusting Christmas sales for calendar shifts was especially important; the reproduced ensemble scored 2303, while the strongest single model scored 2348.

The final submissions combined 30 models using two ensemble strategies. The best submission used a ridge ensemble and achieved five-fold CV of 0.05884 and a private leaderboard score of 0.05846. A hill climbing ensemble had slightly better CV but a slightly worse private score of 0.05848. A shared single-model XGBoost notebook contributed useful diversity to the ensemble.

The solution averaged predictions from CatBoost, LightGBM, and XGBoost, with each framework also ensembled across five cross-validation folds. Hyperparameter tuning was moderate, while adding the rdMol feature delivered a notable improvement. Feature importance from full-feature models guided retraining with 800, 1000, 1200, or 1400 features. The best configuration was selected using cross-validation MAE.

The author optimized word permutations using parallel local searches with a threshold-based simulated annealing variant. Candidate moves included segment permutations, remove-and-insert operations, and graph-based ATSP moves, with crossover used to revive weaker search paths. GPU batching and a global score cache supported efficient evaluation, while position-normalized discounted perplexity encouraged changes near the beginning of sequences. The method frequently recovered the best scores on most samples, although one sample benefited from a teammate's word grouping; differentiable and reinforcement-learning alternatives were less successful.
compute: A100 GPU; batch size 104 for sample 5; reported average GPU utilization of 98%.

solution_title: How I did it: Diogo Ferreira on 4th place in Elo chess ratings competition
solution_summary: The author developed a probabilistic chess-rating approach in which each player's rating lay between zero and one. Ratings represented the probability of one player defeating another, and the author later recognized the connection to the Bradley–Terry model. The approach underwent extensive parameter tuning and repeated competition submissions over 15 weeks. A Python 2.6 implementation was shared through a linked project page, but the post provides few algorithmic details.
compute: 2.4GHz dual-core laptop; parameter tuning ran for days at a time.

solution_summary: The solution used a single geometry-aware transformer adapted from the PoinTr paper. Its blocks combined radius-graph queries with multi-head attention, and radius-based edges performed significantly better than KNN-based edges. The final model had four transformer blocks and an embedding dimension of 256. Limited training time constrained exploration of larger models, and the author suspected that the edge-convolution structure scaled less effectively than self-attention alone.

solution_title: #25th Solution by finally_overfitting (Say No to Gradient Boosting)
solution_summary: The team used five-fold validation stratified jointly by target class and adversarial estimates of how test-like each sample was. Their models included LightGBM, neural networks with entity embeddings, and FTRL models, with frequency encodings and parsed version fields supporting the tree models. They submitted an aggressive weighted ensemble and a defensive stack containing only neural networks and FTRL models, based on the latter models' perceived resistance to overfitting. The aggressive submission scored 0.704 publicly and 0.64729 privately, while the defensive stack was the successful final choice.
compute: Neural network training took approximately 30 minutes per fold; memory limits constrained experiments.

solution_summary: The pipeline combined a retrained temporal 3D U-Net detector, learned coordinate refinement, and geometric edge scoring followed by global optimization. Training the detector on both embryos and building the edge training table with the same predictions and refined coordinates used at inference were central choices. Detection recovery, smoothing, and geometric division attachment completed the tracks. The final submission scored 0.950 Public and 0.940 Private, although a discarded two-seed detector average performed best on Private.

solution_title: [43rd place] Our CV strategy (+77 positions in private)
solution_summary: The authors describe their validation strategy for multilabel image segmentation. They grouped cases across folds and stratified slices by their combinations of labeled organs. They also reverse-engineered the competition metric to improve validation fidelity. Their CV score tracked the leaderboard closely, with a reported difference of approximately 0.002.

The solution combined 14 image-only models, mainly Swin Transformers, with Bayesian ridge stacking. Duplicate-aware validation and image similarity matching connected current images to roughly 70,000 images from a previous competition. For sufficiently similar matches, five adoption-speed-specific Bayesian ridge models used out-of-fold predictions and previous competition metadata for post-processing. Direct metadata use, YOLOv5 crops, image statistics, and CNN augmentation were reported as unsuccessful.
external_data: ["Previous competition training and test images and metadata"]

solution_summary: The author trained a recurrent self-play agent using separate actor and privileged critic networks in a fully JAX-based pipeline. ConvNeXt and MLP encoders fed a Transformer state encoder and an xLSTM memory core, with a Transformer decoder predicting unit actions sequentially. A smaller agent supplied a teacher for the larger model, followed by extensive PPO training with shaped rewards and a mixture of recent and historical opponents. The final actor contained approximately two million parameters and selected actions greedily under validity masks.
compute: Started training at home on an 8GB GPU and also used university/institute compute resources; final training used 1,024 parallel environments.

solution_title: My take on the data leak
solution_summary: The author exploited the tendency for images sharing an incidence angle to share a label. They compared grouped statistics from handmade labels with grouped statistics from ConvNet predictions. Results were similar, and the final choice used prediction statistics because it handled training and test images consistently and avoided additional manual labeling.

solution_title: Fast Matlab code to get a score of .93985
solution_summary: The approach applies signal processing before inverse covariance estimation. The author credits the winning team with prompting closer attention to this preprocessing. The complete run takes 13 minutes on a laptop, with most time spent reading data and writing the submission.
compute: 13 minutes total on a laptop, mostly data reading and submission writing

solution_summary: The solution trained a MONAI 3D U-Net with class-aware crops and extensive spatial and intensity augmentation. Its configuration used channels of 64, 128, 256, and 256, strides of 2, 2, and 1, and one residual unit. Ensembling with YOLO improved the private score from 0.726 to 0.755. A cluster filter rejected detections whose coordinate spread exceeded a particle-radius-based threshold.
compute: L4 GPU

solution_title: [34th Place Solution using single EfficientDet + Pseudo Labeling]
solution_summary: The solution trained a single EfficientDet D5 on the full dataset for 40 epochs at 512×512 resolution without cross-validation. It then used pseudo labeling for another 10 epochs with the same extensive augmentations. Final predictions used test-time augmentation and weighted boxes fusion. Larger models, longer training, mixup, and several alternative detector configurations did not work well.

The solution combined embedding retrieval with classification models and non-landmark distractor penalties. Concatenated 512-dimensional model features retrieved seven training images, whose cosine scores were adjusted with averaged classification logits and precomputed distractor scores. EfficientNet B5 and B6 classifiers were trained on the full landmark label space, while retrieval training favored the cleaned three-million-image subset. Final landmark scores aggregated the adjusted retrieval matches together with the classifiers' top prediction.

The solution used protein measurements and visit_month while excluding peptide data. Separate CatBoost models were trained for each combination of UPDRS target other than UPDRS_4, visit month, and forecast horizon, with Optuna tuning each model. A public linear trend model handled UPDRS_4 with a clip month of 54 and replaced CatBoost predictions at the training-range boundaries. GroupKFold validation favored this hybrid over standalone CatBoost, and MAE performed better than MSE as the CatBoost objective.

The final solution stacked 33 CNN and vision transformer models plus two auxiliary classifiers using a LightGBM meta-model trained on out-of-fold predictions. Stratified five-fold validation, additional 2019 data, pseudo-labeling, duplicate removal, and label-noise correction supported training. Diverse augmentations and four-view test-time averaging improved robustness, while transformer models added useful ensemble diversity. Stacking reached 0.9067 CV and 0.9016 private leaderboard accuracy, with single-fold base-model inference taking eight hours.
compute: PyTorch GPU/TPU pipeline; final inference took 8 hours using one fold per base model.
external_data: ["2019 labeled cassava data", "2019 unlabeled cassava data", "PlantVillage", "ImageNet"]

solution_summary: The solution ensembled three small LLaMa-inspired models using selected 2D hand, face, and pose keypoints. Inputs were centered on the head, with missing values replaced by zero, and supported sequences up to 512 frames. Keypoint selection, mixup, RMSNorm, Lion optimization, and weight EMA drove the main gains. The three-model ensemble achieved private/public scores of 0.8584568/0.7725324, while larger models faced inference timeouts and external data did not help.

The solution emphasized training-month selection, combining June 2015 with several other months and ensembling the resulting models. Each run blended an XGBoost model with a Keras neural network using a weighted average, with lagged product ownership as core features. Sampling across months also contributed to the final ensemble despite weaker standalone performance. Product-specific prediction adjustments produced a large boost, and the author submitted variants with different amounts of post-processing without knowing which performed best privately.

solution_title: A general walk through my solution with trick 55th
solution_summary: The final architecture used separate pretrained RoBERTa base models for title–body and title–answer pairs, predicting question and answer targets separately. It pooled the last three output layers and combined the embeddings with URL/category encodings and Universal Sentence Encoder features. Predictions were averaged across six model pairs, with grouped validation, best-checkpoint selection, warm-up scheduling, Adam, and mixed precision. Mapping predictions to plausible discrete target values raised the public score from about 0.415 to over 0.450; additional manual column tuning was less reliable, and the submission without that extra tuning performed better.

The author tried a simple Keras neural network on 27 input features. It used batch normalization, two ReLU hidden layers with 32 and 16 units, and dropout of 0.1 after each hidden layer. Seven sigmoid outputs produced the predictions. The post reports a positive impression but provides no numerical results or validation details.

The efficiency-focused solution used DeBERTa-v3-xsmall trained with pseudo-labels from a seven-model ensemble on previous Feedback Prize data. Fold-matched pseudo-label generation reduced leakage, while blending ground-truth targets with ensemble out-of-fold predictions improved scores. Training used sequences up to 1845 tokens, whereas inference used 512 tokens and unpadded batches of one for better speed and accuracy. The final submission used the best validation fold instead of an inference ensemble and achieved a private score of 0.438556.
compute: Reported scoring time: 928 (unit unspecified).

solution_summary: The final submission used a single pretrained DELG model without additional training, focusing on geometric verification and parameter tuning. Its RANSAC settings included a reprojection threshold of 13, 5,000 iterations, confidence of 0.99, and max distance of 0.85. Additional RANSAC options did not improve results. Separately trained EfficientNets were not included in the final submission; the best reported variant scored 0.4924 public and 0.4721 private.
compute: Training constrained by Kaggle TPU access of 40 hours/week and Colab TPU access of 6 hours/day.

solution_summary: The solution combined fine-tuned BirdCLEF 2025 SED models with a Perch-distilled model, diversifying backbones, spectrograms, and training recipes. The three model groups received weights 0.4, 0.2, and 0.4, with the largest benefit coming from combining the two distinct families. Carefully tuned sampling addressed rare species, recording-domain imbalance, and site bias. OpenVINO inference used selected window-shift augmentation, prior fusion, and confidence-dependent file and temporal refinement.

The solution added categorical copies of ten selected variables and an integer remainder feature from ST depression. AutoGluon ran with the best_quality preset and log loss, with dynamic stacking and additional stack levels disabled. Its final weighted ensemble combined CatBoost, LightGBM, and neural networks, with CatBoost receiving most of the weight. The ensemble achieved validation log loss of approximately 0.26675 after an 11-hour Kaggle CPU run.
compute: Kaggle CPU for 11 hours; ensemble fitting used 4 CPUs and no GPUs.

solution_title: 21st Place Solution: Final Blend Selection with Ridge and Nelder-Mead
solution_summary: The author built roughly 50–70 models and selected Ridge and Nelder-Mead blends for the final submissions. Strong XGB, RealMLP, and CAT variants formed the core, while weaker models with different errors contributed through negative blend weights. Expanding the Nelder-Mead blend to 12 models increased CV AUC to 0.919810. Model selection emphasized improvement within the ensemble rather than isolated model scores; Hill Climbing and alternative meta-models were not selected.
compute: Limited GPU resources restricted hyperparameter tuning to a small number of models.

solution_summary: The solution combined a 3D CNN, a hybrid 2.5D/3D CNN and LightGBM, with separate ensemble weights for ground and player contact. Video models learned from sideline, endzone and concatenated features, while LightGBM used roughly 1,100 tracking and helmet features. Bounding-box rendering, contact-type colors and aspect-preserving crops improved image inputs. The 3D CNN, hybrid CNN and LightGBM achieved cross-validation scores of 0.770, 0.768 and 0.740, respectively.

The solution focused on extensive sensor feature engineering and stacking XGBoost and nearest-neighbor models with two models from public notebooks. Features came from original and transformed signals, PCA-derived signals, aggregated sensors, and public TSFresh and STFT datasets. Sensor clustering and cross-validated cluster encodings reportedly reduced MAE by about 400,000. Robustness came from fold-based validation and averaging XGBoost predictions across seven seeds, while nearest-neighbor models used leave-one-out validation.

solution_title: 47th place solution - no training, no dataset label string matching
solution_summary: The solution first selected sentences using string matching for dataset-related words, then extracted dataset names with a pretrained ELECTRA question-answering model. Extraction required the model probability to exceed a threshold. Trained DistilBERT, RoBERTa, and fastText sentence classifiers performed worse than the regex filter. The final pipeline required no competition-specific model training.

solution_title: 1st Place: By the skin of my teeth
solution_summary: The final submission equally blends AutoGluon and logistic-regression-on-logits ensembles built from a large, diverse prediction pool. Extensive feature engineering and variants that excluded Driver or the original dataset added useful diversity. The pool contained 186 out-of-fold predictions, including four second-level predictions whose inclusion carried acknowledged leakage risk. The final blend achieved public and private scores of 0.95488 and 0.95503.
compute: AutoFeat experiment timed out after 12 hours.

solution_title: Public #2, Private 0: Throughput Engine That Optimized Its Own Extinction
solution_summary: The team optimized synthetic exfiltration attacks for scoring output per decoded token, using model-specific prompt framing to minimize tool-call overhead. Its two final submissions instead attempted web-preceded combinations of exfiltration or unauthorized email actions, and both scored zero. The analysis attributes this failure to a shared read-before-action taint rule and a private payload scanner. A payload-free unauthorized email action without a preceding read was identified as transferable, but the team declined to reserve a final slot for it.

The authors share their work on a custom loss called StableRocAucLoss. They link a notebook containing the approach and invite discussion of methods for addressing stability. The post gives no loss formula, model configuration, validation details, or results.

The submitted notebook used vLLM to generate 60 solutions per problem with the dsl-math-rl default prompt and selected answers by majority vote, achieving 18 points. A separate approach generated 64 solutions for each of 8,000 curated math problems and used known answers to label solutions for reward-model training. That approach scored generated solutions with a reward model and voted among high-scoring candidates, with dynamic time management intended to allow roughly 30 generations per test problem. It missed the submission deadline, so its private score is unknown.

solution_title: How Far Can Verified Synthetic Data Go?
solution_summary: The author trained a rank-32 LoRA adapter for NVIDIA Nemotron using synthetic reasoning traces generated by deterministic puzzle solvers and checked against ground truth. Long, explicit traces were more effective than concise explanations, while selective adapter placement slightly improved performance and reduced overfitting. The final submissions were a selectively placed LoRA adapter and a TIES-style checkpoint merge, both reaching a private score of 0.86. Data quality, curriculum balancing, and error analysis mattered more than architectural changes.

The author initialized every family on its most preferred day, producing zero preference cost but violating attendance constraints. They attempted to restore feasibility by greedily moving families from overcrowded days to undercrowded days, including chains of two moves. Early improvements were inexpensive, but costs rose sharply as cheap moves disappeared. They abandoned the approach after preference cost exceeded 75,000 while day 1 still had more than 300 people, and wondered whether longer move chains would help.

solution_title: 17th Place Solution: GPT-2 Income Tokens and a 3-Model Logit-Rank Blend
solution_summary: The core solution blended XGBoost, a generator-aware ridge logistic regression, and an LR-to-XGBoost stack. Its strongest features modeled repeated income values and GPT-2 token-prefix biases through cross-fitted target statistics and hierarchical shrinkage. Shared stratified folds and repeated OOF half-split comparisons guided decisions, with deterministic rules applied after blending. The three-model blend achieved 0.946672 OOF AUC, while the submitted pipeline also included public predictions and reached 0.94571 private AUC.
compute: Public three-model notebook: Kaggle T4 GPU, 3.3 hours, using 20 folds instead of the final core's 40.

solution_summary: The solution used CNN models to generate initial predictions. A genetic algorithm then refined those predictions. The brief post provides no training, validation, or numerical performance details.

The solution combined pooled RNNs and K-max text CNNs trained on several preprocessing variants, with both word-level and character-level inputs. Dropout and batch normalization reduced overfitting, while pretrained embeddings and an auxiliary bad-comment label increased diversity. A single LightGBM stacking layer combined out-of-fold predictions from neural models, LightGBM, and NBSVM with text metadata. Bagging character-level and word-level RNNs exceeded 0.9869 private AUC, and additional metadata improved local AUC from 0.9920 to 0.9928.
compute: Character-level models usually converged after 60–70 epochs, about five times the word-level models.

solution_summary: The author treated the task as regression and built 505 selected features, including misses, rounds, and custom counters. The final ensemble used 15 LightGBM models trained with randomized grouped cross-validation and labeled test samples. Each model had independently optimized rounding thresholds, and voting combined validation scores with prediction confidence. Avoiding test-feature distribution adjustments and train-distribution-based threshold tuning was considered important for generalization.

The solution uses Qwen3-32B to create one paraphrase of each training body with rule-specific prompts. Phi-4, Qwen-2.5-14B-Instruct, and Qwen3-14B are then trained with QLoRA to predict Yes or No from a body and rule. Training uses Unsloth and Distributed Data Parallel, with all processes executed during the notebook test run. Pseudo-labeling, the Muon optimizer, and few-shot generation of additional training data did not work well.
compute: Multi-GPU training with DDP; GPU models and count unspecified.

solution_title: Quick reflection - a tale of diminishing returns [#3 place]
solution_summary: The author describes a final ensemble containing 38 models and emphasizes its diminishing returns. Improvements were already limited to the fifth decimal after about ten models and the sixth decimal after about fifteen. Roughly twenty additional models improved the ensemble's cross-validation score by only about 0.00003, while model identities and combination details are not provided.

The solution combined four ImageNet-initialized EfficientNets trained on original 512×512 RGB images with flip augmentation. Reduced early strides, multisample dropout, and concatenated global max and average pooling defined the models. Training used cross-entropy and AdamW with cosine decay, with a separate staged schedule for B4. The ensemble improved public/private scores from 0.930/0.921 for the best single model to 0.936/0.928, while local validation suffered from a weighted-AUC implementation issue.
compute: 4× Quadro RTX 6000 24GB; B8/B5 trained on 8× V100 32GB; batch size around 32–40

solution_summary: The solution used a RadImageNet-initialized 2.5D ConvNeXt-Small with series-level slice transformers and finding-query attention across the study. Local Qwen and MedGemma report labels were progressively adapted toward radiologist image definitions through out-of-fold teacher–student training and gold-set fine-tuning. Interpolating trained trunks back toward their RadImageNet initialization provided a consistent gain. The final rank ensemble included student families, OAI-trained synovitis specialists, and scanner-specific synovitis correction, scoring 0.963 public and 0.948 private AUC.
compute: Two T4 GPUs for inference with a 6-hour budget and at least 30 checkpoint passes; approximately 13.6 minutes per checkpoint on one T4 for roughly 1,300 studies.
external_data: ["RadImageNet knee MRI slices", "OAI MOAKS image labels", "Pseudo-labelled OAI studies"]

solution_summary: The author's solution was based on Mask R-CNN. The post emphasizes higher image resolution as beneficial but provides no specific resolution or experimental results. Source code and a model are linked in a GitHub repository.

solution_title: 3rd Place Part III - Pesudo Astronomer's Feature Engineering
solution_summary: The author engineered astronomical light-curve features, with sncosmo template-fitting parameters and chi-square values providing the largest gains. Eight template variants were retained for the extragalactic model, and seven of the ten most important LightGBM features came from these fits. Additional features described luminosity, observation timing, estimated spectroscopic redshift, and periodicity. Class90-only pseudo-labeling improved early experiments, whereas pseudo-labeling all classes did not work.
models_pretrained: ["Supernova templates: salt-2, salt-2-extended, nugent-sn1bc, nugent-sn2, snana, sako"]
compute: Template extraction ran at 1–2 lines/sec across 30 preemptible instances, completing each run within one day; repeated about 15 times.

solution_summary: The solution used four levels of ensembling built from diverse XGBoost, LightGBM, and neural network models. Base-model diversity came from varying original-data inclusion, numerical feature treatment, and regularization, retaining models that improved the ensemble. Higher layers used ridge regression and HC, while neural network and XGBoost stackers were discarded. The author trusted cross-validation for final selection, and the last submission achieved a private score of 0.38486.

The final agent extended the public orbit_lite planner with a rule-based greedy strategy implemented using PyTorch tensors. It projected future trajectories and garrisons, solved moving-target intercepts, and greedily selected fleet waves by net ship-flow advantage. The decisive adjustment increased the ETA-aware reinforcement-risk term so attacks accounted for enemy reinforcements arriving during flight. Evaluation used thousands of competitive replay maps, with a direct 120-map comparison confirming a win-rate increase from 25% to 36%. Learned policies and phase-dependent configuration switching did not outperform the tuned planner.

The solution combined extensive feature engineering and XGBoost models with an L2/L3 ensemble. A major signal came from duplicated consecutive records, which supported chunk statistics and features from neighboring records. Time-based production activity, failure proximity, and numeric transformations supplied additional features. Four-fold validation balanced duplication patterns, while three training seeds and selective negative downsampling supported model averaging; the final ensemble's validation standard deviation was below 0.004.
compute: Initial desktop machine with 16 GB RAM; total training time unspecified.

solution_summary: The final predictor blended an online TabM neural network at 70% with a static LightGBM ensemble at 30%. TabM adapted daily using a rolling three-to-four-day window, a small learning rate, and older data to limit forgetting. LightGBM supplied stable historical patterns using base features and previous-day responder lags. Validation held out the last 100 days, although leaderboard correlation was weak, and a local API simulator checked the full retraining and inference pipeline.

solution_title: LB15: Extension to @huikang's progress prize solution
solution_summary: The author extended a public baseline by improving bit-manipulation and cryptarithm reference solvers, then fine-tuned an LLM on their execution traces and synthetic exercises. Truth-table reconstruction raised bit-manipulation reference accuracy to 92.1%, with model inference reaching 93.3% on the training set. The cryptarithm solver combined memorized multiplication candidates with backtracking, but inference accuracy lagged its 28% reference accuracy. Training used extensive operation drills and roughly 2000 steps, producing 89.5% overall training-set accuracy with acknowledged development leakage and a smaller private-set gain.

The author trained separate XGBoost and CatBoost models for each lab using a filtered subset of the competition training data. Ego-centric coordinates, feature pruning, and bidirectional EMA smoothing formed the core pipeline. Predictions were averaged across models, with threshold-relative Z-scores resolving competing classes. Gap filling, spike removal, and left-right augmentation did not improve the final approach.

The solution ensembled two U-Nets with MaxViT encoders, using standard ash-color inputs and soft targets averaged from individual masks. Correcting a half-pixel label offset enabled effective rotation augmentation and eight-way test-time augmentation, followed by a learned convolution restoring the original alignment. One model used a single time point, while the other packed four time points into a spatial panel. Validation-tuned averaging and a threshold near 0.45 produced a private score of 0.724.
compute: 35 or 40 training epochs per model; batch size 4 with gradient accumulation 2

solution_title: 83rd solusion and this is my firstintroduction of solution !
solution_summary: The approach converted whole-slide images into TMA-like training images and fine-tuned pretrained MaxViT-Tiny and ConvNeXt-Base models with added multihead attention. Weighted cross-entropy, strong augmentation, label smoothing, mixup, and manual removal of invalid-looking examples supported training. Validation used five-fold StratifiedGroupKFold incorporating labels and TMA status, and predictions below 0.3 probability were assigned to Others. Tumor-mask preprocessing and flip test-time augmentation did not help; a 0.4 Others threshold performed better but was not submitted.

The authors implemented a simple mixup approach that mixed mel-spectrograms for speech recognition. They shared a repository containing the implementation. VGG reached 0.89839 with this augmentation, and other models reportedly reached at least the stated 0.90% figure.

solution_title: 403rd Place Solution for the Stanford Ribonanza RNA Folding Competition
solution_summary: The author trained a TensorFlow/Keras sequence model described as an RNN with six attention layers and eight heads to predict DMS and 2A3 reactivities. Training used quality-filtered data, five dataset repetitions, sinusoidal encoding, dropout, and Gaussian noise. A custom loss and exponentially decaying learning rate were used with KFold validation, and predictions were clipped to the interval from zero to one. The reported public and private scores were 0.15803 and 0.24428.

The author combined LightGBM, logistic regression, CatBoost and XGBoost with equal weights. Features came from Raddar's public notebook, with separate variants including and excluding Team Quality features. An SVM was dropped because training was too slow. Seed-based probability overrides used conservative values, including 95% for seed 1 and 90% for seed 2.

The team extracted features from the full dataset but trained on data retaining only 5% of negative examples to reduce memory and training costs. Count, cumulative-count, time-delta, unique-count, and IP association features supported LightGBM and neural-network models. The final ensemble weighted three LightGBM and three neural-network predictions using public leaderboard scores. The best single LightGBM scored 0.9837 privately, versus 0.9834 for the best neural network, and offline cross-validation proved more representative than the public leaderboard.
compute: Reported RAM capacities of 128 GB, 64 GB, and 32 GB across teammates, with an additional 16 GB purchased. Training one fold with about 200 features took approximately half an hour on an Intel i7.

solution_title: RedTeam: Cost-Effective Exfiltration Search for Tool-Using Agents
solution_summary: The author built a budget-aware search over sandbox attack templates targeting a known public guardrail's marker-exfiltration weakness. The system raced templates separately for each model, admitted multi-event forms only when their measured yield justified their cost, and retained verified candidates within a replay-cost ledger. Adaptive fallback, candidate ordering, and budget top-up improved throughput and robustness, while email-based forms were removed after poor results. The reported public scores were 93.445 for v44 and 92.375 for v33, with evaluator changes and uncertain private-policy transfer limiting the comparison.
compute: 9,000-second attack budget per model row; 80 submissions reported.

solution_summary: The author ensembled tuned tree models, mainly XGBoost and CatBoost with a smaller LightGBM contribution, using different target transformations. Optuna tuned the separation between event-status groups and the weights of event-positive samples, with most models scoring about 0.676–0.682 in five-fold stratified validation. Refitting on all training data and weighting predictions using out-of-fold results particularly helped a pairwise ranking neural network. The final submission combined public solutions with some of the author's models and achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.69328.

solution_title: 14th Place Solution for the Optiver - Trading at the Close Competition
solution_summary: The solution averaged the latest LightGBM and CatBoost predictions while periodically refitting both models with revealed targets. Important features included target lags, signed imbalance size, refreshed global features, and corrected technical indicators. Chronological streaming validation improved agreement with the public leaderboard after leakage fixes. Two final submissions used 170 features without postprocessing and 193 features with zero-sum postprocessing, achieving private scores of 5.4457 and 5.4458.

solution_title: 10th Place Solution - ~350 oofs => 9 hillclimbing versions => Final Autogluon ensemble
solution_summary: The solution generated about 350 out-of-fold predictions from boosted trees, neural networks, and logistic regression using fixed six-fold stratified validation. Model diversity drove hill-climbing ensembles, and AutoGluon combined the nine best ensembles for the final submission. Original-data weighting and targeted weight increases for near-miss class rankings improved individual models. The final ensemble achieved CV 0.383918 and private leaderboard score 0.38472, while extensive feature engineering failed to improve the single-model baseline.

The author trained DenseNet161 and ResNet152 models with custom fully connected classification heads on original-image and cervix-cropped inputs. Manual quality filtering left approximately 5,000 training images from the training and additional datasets. Validation used 10% of the original training data, without ensuring patient separation. The final prediction blended the models, and stage 1 test data was excluded from training.

The author tuned sparse LightGBM and NFFM baseline models, emphasizing features conditioned on Windows SKU edition. Important features included edition ratios for geographic and organizational groups, relative software release dates, and differences between antivirus and OS dates. Hardware clusters and a blend of models trained on early and late data also helped. The author suspected that date features could overfit and reported disappointing private leaderboard generalization.

The post describes a feature-generation approach that models individual previous applications using the applicant's current default target. Supporting credit-card, POS cash, and installment records are aggregated by previous-application identifier before fitting this model. Predictions are then aggregated by current applicant and merged into the main training data as additional features, with the same idea applied to bureau records. These features improved cross-validation performance from 0.798 to approximately 0.801.

The author built a multimodal feature pipeline combining image classifier outputs, image quality measurements, text representations, and structured group statistics. Ten models each of LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost formed the first layer of a two-layer stack. A second LightGBM learned from the first-layer outputs and improved the public score to 0.2192 and the private score to 0.2230. Five-fold validation maintained a stable gap from the public leaderboard.

The solution used a modified Keras RetinaNet detector with a ResNet101 backbone. The main changes were dataset-adapted anchor ratios, augmentation including random noise, and dropout. The reproduction commands train for 40 epochs with batch size 14 and 1,250 steps per epoch, then filter detections with a 0.2 score threshold and 0.1 non-maximum suppression threshold. The writeup provides separate training and inference procedures for both competition stages.
compute: 1 NVIDIA Tesla V100 32GB; 5117 14-core 2.00GHz processor; 256GB DDR4 RAM; 40 epochs, batch size 14, 1,250 steps per epoch.

solution_title: Code to ensemble boxes for object detection
solution_summary: The author describes using Weighted Boxes Fusion to ensemble object-detection boxes in the 2018 and 2019 competitions. WBF replaced non-maximum suppression in their approach. The post releases a Python package containing WBF and several alternative suppression or fusion methods, without describing the underlying detectors or training pipeline.

The pipeline first detected candidate helmet impacts with a 2D DetectoRS model and then classified temporal crops using 3D video models. Helmet-detection warm-up and expanded temporal labels supported detector training, while several video architectures improved classification. Full five-fold validation across 120 videos guided thresholds and post-processing, including temporal clustering and cross-view filtering. The submission selected by CV achieved 0.5125 CV and 0.5153 on the private leaderboard.

The solution trained exclusively on the competition's synthetic data and used 15-fold stratified validation. Six arithmetic features were added only after they improved two separate models, while all original features were retained. Observations were removed following another competitor's proposal. The final ensemble combined seven XGBoost models with different parameters and stratified-fold seeds; several alternative model families did not help.

The solution combined YOLOv5, EfficientDet-D2, and Detectron2 ResNet detectors through a staged ensemble with varying degrees of local validation. Its main innovation was modified weighted boxes fusion that summed detection confidences and normalized them to favor agreement across models, approximating radiologist consensus. Public leaderboard feedback guided the final ensemble, but excessive weight on models without local validation caused overfitting: the selected submission scored 0.354 public and 0.314 private, while an unselected lower-weight alternative achieved 0.330 and 0.321. Classifier-based filtering, NIH pretraining, and class-specific detectors did not improve the final approach.
compute: 4x Quadro GV100, 4x GeForce GTX 1080, 4x Titan X, Ryzen 9 3950x, Nvidia RTX 3080, Quadro RTX 6000; reported reproducible with one GPU.

solution_summary: The team blended DeBERTa models with different input arrangements, sequence lengths, and backbones. Adding prompt text and freezing layers produced the largest reported validation improvements, while input diversity also helped. They validated by grouping on prompt_id, trained submission models on all prompts, and averaged two seeds for most models. The selected blend achieved reported PB/LB scores of 0.456/0.427; an alternative containing LightGBM achieved 0.453/0.428 but was not selected.

The solution used an end-to-end transformer encoder to predict spectral means and uncertainties from calibrated, clipped, and normalized signals. An intermediate transit head learned from signal-derived labels and symmetry constraints, and its outputs informed the final prediction head. Training optimized Gaussian negative log-likelihood with signal and transit augmentations. Flip test-time augmentation and inverse-variance weighting combined three models, while a single model could reach 0.552.

The team ensembled a 3D U-Net with several 2.5D U-Net, FPN, and UPerNet segmentation models. Inputs used three or five channels, with normalization based on either five-channel maxima or case-day maxima. EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, and ResNet backbones supplied model diversity, alongside different losses and augmentation pipelines. Lowering segmentation thresholds was the main postprocessing adjustment, with small-bowel predictions particularly sensitive to the threshold.
compute: TPU used with TensorFlow; hardware count and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The author identified 93 groups of 40 columns and exploited target leaks in the data. A LightGBM model was trained on the original training set plus leaked, non-fake test rows. Features included means, quantiles, and exponential moving averages based on column order within each group. Differences between successive nonzero values did not improve cross-validation, while the model without leak overrides scored approximately 1.07 publicly and 1.06 privately.

The post critiques the supplied bird-call segmentation system using counts of recordings with labels and detected segments. The author estimates that many calls may be missed and suggests that minimum region-size filtering could discard split or deformed syllables. It argues that these false negatives undermine downstream classification and may explain the importance of location information.

The authors developed vedaseg while experimenting with semantic segmentation for steel defect detection. The PyTorch library followed a modular design inspired by mmdetection and supported architectures including FPN, U-Net and DeepLab variants. The post describes the experimentation framework but does not identify the final competition model, training procedure or ensemble.

The competition solution directly optimized trajectory positions and time offsets as TensorFlow model weights using pseudoranges and delta measurements. Its objective combined satellite-distance errors, delta-change errors, and an acceleration penalty to reduce trajectory wobble. Delta measurements were filtered by satellite consistency, and ground-truth positions were not used in the submitted approach. After the competition, base-station pseudorange corrections and ground-truth-relative offset corrections improved the reported private and public scores to 1.39533 and 2.59287.

The approach trained separate support vector regression models for the five soil targets. It used only part of the spectral input, applying a Savitzky–Golay first derivative with polynomial order 3 and window size 21. Model parameters were tuned separately for each target through cross-validation. Both cross-validation and public leaderboard scores were close to 0.40, while the author reported that late tuning hurt private leaderboard performance.

The author built an efficiency-focused logistic regression pipeline using datatable LinearModel. Session aggregates and selected categorical features formed a small, interpretable feature set, with different features chosen for different level groups. Thread tuning and reduced notebook startup overhead improved runtime. The selected submission scored 0.687, trained in under one minute, and took around 2–3 minutes for scoring, with identical public and private scores.
compute: 2 CPUs, 2 threads; training under one minute; scoring around 2–3 minutes

solution_title: 17th Place Solution – The Unluckiest Near-Gold Finish!
solution_summary: The final submission combined 16 models, primarily CatBoost and neural networks, with an additional XGBoost classifier. The author explored four target transformations and applied a 0.1 shift associated with efs==1 that improved both CV and leaderboard results. Optuna optimized the ensemble weights. A stable gap of approximately 0.005 between CV and leaderboard scores supported confidence in validation.

The solution combined nine CNN segmentation models with EfficientNet-B5 and ConvNeXt-base encoders and a modified U-Net decoder. Strong augmentation and training on both whole images and random tiles were central to the approach. Inference combined whole-image transformations and size-dependent crops through thresholded voting with organ-specific thresholds. The best single model achieved 0.810 on the private evaluation, and increasing image brightness slightly improved scores.
compute: Training exclusively in Kaggle kernels; best single model trained for 65 epochs.

solution_summary: The main solution stacked 25 tuned boosting models with ridge regression and converted continuous predictions into classes using optimized thresholds. Training combined competition and original data, while cross-validation metrics used only competition samples. Minimal correlation-based features involving acidity and density improved performance. Conservative predictions worked better under quadratic weighted kappa, while a separate neural network submission explored predicting rare extreme classes.
compute: Built 1,466 models.

solution_summary: The pipeline normalized location text, generated candidate matches with text and embedding similarity, and classified pairs using heavily regularized LightGBM. Five SBERT models supplied similarity features, while concatenated embeddings from two models achieved candidate coverage above 99% maximum IoU. Local validation reached about 94.3, and cuML accelerated inference. Count features improved validation further but were not submitted.
compute: GPU inference with cuML; hardware unspecified.

solution_title: A solution to texture tasks and open-sourcing some utilities
solution_summary: The author built Java grid and mask utilities, invariant shape hashes, and an object-oriented DSL with an interactive editor for ARC tasks. Their texture reconstruction method detects strong translation symmetries and combines shifted images through strength-weighted color voting. A related procedure detects folding symmetries and votes across promising axes. They report apparent success on all training translation tasks without extensive validation, and roughly 80% success on folding tasks.

The final solution ensembled four folds of DeBERTa-v3-large using paired summary and prompt inputs with a maximum length of 1,600 tokens. Training used four epochs, AdamW and a cosine learning-rate schedule, with no frozen layers or extra pooling. Longer input lengths helped, while masked-language-model pretraining and pseudo-scored extended data were excluded after disappointing generalization. The final public and private scores were 0.429 and 0.458.
external_data: ["Previous CommonLit competition datasets", "CommonLit website texts and questions", "GPT-4-generated student-style summaries"]

solution_summary: This post describes the agent workflows and token-efficiency practices used to optimize task-specific ONNX models, while leaving other solution details for later. Single-task exploration alternates with multi-task transfer of newly discovered optimization tricks. Concrete improvement targets, persistent task notes, reusable builder utilities and a shared cookbook reduce repeated work. Candidates are validated against competition examples, ARC-GEN pairs and selected randomized variations.
external_data: ["ARC-GEN generated input-output pairs", "Human solutions to similar ARC-AGI problems"]

solution_title: 31th Place Solution | Using NLP for tabular data!
solution_summary: The author converted tabular symptom rows into natural-language descriptions and trained BERT with the Bio_ClinicalBERT backbone. The approach used raw data without additional preprocessing. It achieved a best public score of 0.40728, with notebook results varying by random state. Small-data overfitting remained a concern, while synthetic data, ensembling, and sentence-pair classification were suggested as future extensions.

The author constructed patent search queries from rare individual words and adjacent word pairs joined by OR. Corpus-wide token frequencies identified both distinctive patents and small groups sharing uncommon terms. Validation used 2,000 patents with 100 nearest neighbors from embedding data retrieved through BigQuery and closely matched leaderboard behavior. Adding adjacent pairs from titles, abstracts, and claims that covered at least two target patents and appeared fewer than eight times in the corpus improved the reported score from 0.77 to 0.81.

The team combined DeBERTa and Longformer token classifiers trained with either 13 BIO labels or eight entity classes. They merged BIO probabilities into eight classes and performed weighted averaging at spaCy-token level before reconstructing BIO labels. Class weighting, external datasets, newline tokens, and negative-example selection produced complementary precision and recall profiles. Document-level name averaging, probability adjustment, and entity-specific rules were important postprocessing steps, while padding and batch-size changes more than doubled inference speed.
compute: DeBERTa-v3-large inference reduced from about 1 hour to about 30 minutes.

solution_summary: The solution used a five-fold EfficientNet-B3 slice classifier followed by a five-fold MLP and bidirectional LSTM operating on extracted slice features. The second stage jointly predicted image and exam labels while directly optimizing the competition metric. Sampling only 30 slices per patient per epoch and using preconverted 256×256 JPEGs made training feasible on the author's hardware. Multi-sample dropout, weight averaging, and rule-enforcing clipping completed the pipeline, whose validation scores were close to the public score of 0.179.
compute: 1x RTX 21080Ti (as written); sampled CNN training took approximately 9 hours for 20 epochs; sequential-model epochs took approximately one minute.

solution_summary: The final solution used Ridge regression without an intercept or nonnegative coefficient constraints to combine diverse GBMs and AutoGluon predictions. Feature engineering emphasized row aggregates, sorted feature values, threshold counts, and target-derived statistics while removing unhelpful original and redundant features. Three repeated K-fold runs provided robust OOF predictions for ensemble selection. The final ensemble achieved a reported public score of 0.86943, with reliable CV limiting the need for submissions.
compute: Used Kaggle GPU quota for Optuna optimization, with a maximum timeout of 5400 seconds.

solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned Gemma and Llama preference classifiers initialized from previously trained competition models, using proportional middle truncation of the prompt and responses. An initial three-model teacher ensemble produced soft pseudo-labels, followed by an expanded multilingual synthetic-response dataset and confidence filtering. The final classifiers were pretrained on 95k pseudo-labeled examples and fine-tuned on all competition data in English-first, multilingual-second epochs. Inference combined original and swapped response orders with a 2.5:1 weighting and selectively ran the Llama model on uncertain examples. The expanded pipeline improved the private score from 0.708 to 0.716 while retaining a public score of 0.709.

The author trained CatBoost, XGBoost, LightGBM, and Lasso models using five-fold stratified cross-validation and blended their predictions. Among the tested submissions, the best blend gave CatBoost twice the weight of each other model. Small per-fold grid searches added parameter diversity and improved private scores by about 0.0002. Ordinal encoding of smoking status slightly improved CV, while a risk-factor-count feature was excluded after failing to help.

solution_title: Ensembling approach, Reservations, Outliers and Golden Week flag
solution_summary: The final submission blended two LightGBM models with an LSTM encoder–LightGBM decoder and an LSTM encoder–LSTM decoder. The author filtered recent reservations, added a Golden Week indicator, removed outliers, and introduced a model trained only on 2017 data with year-earlier lag values. Final weights were 60%, 30%, 5%, and 5%, respectively, producing 0.516 private and 0.478 public scores. Earlier comparisons suggested harmonic or arithmetic averaging could outperform subjective blend weights.

The solution stacked about 30 LightGBM, RNN, MLP, and ridge models with a LightGBM meta-model. Diversity across model families mattered more than isolated improvements to individual models. Smoothed relative-price features, group statistics, text representations, and image features strengthened the base models. Validation progressed from a holdout of recent days to five-fold time splits, and an alternative MLP stack was too correlated to improve the ensemble.
compute: RNN development used a MacBook GPU; five-fold RNN training with two bags and 256-wide embeddings took about 36 hours on AWS P2.

solution_title: 1st place: One vs Rest + Multiclass Models
solution_summary: The solution combined 61 out-of-fold prediction sets from public notebooks and the author's own models. It exploited the rarity of Low–High confusion through a two-stage binary classification scheme, first separating Low from the rest and then Medium from High. Five-fold logistic regression blended logit-transformed predictions using the same two-stage structure. Greedy threshold searches optimized balanced accuracy, producing ensemble cross-validation of 0.98155.

solution_title: Public → private shakeup on our end. Any chance of getting the private dataset
solution_summary: This post asks organizers for information to explain a large public-to-private performance collapse. The authors hypothesize that private payload inspection blocked their plaintext sentinel exfiltration submissions, while explicitly treating this explanation as unconfirmed. They request released fixtures and guardrails, submission diagnostics, or confirmation of the mechanism, and invite other teams to share which attack families transferred.

The solution predicted whether pairs of hits belonged to the same track, then reconstructed tracks from those probabilities. Its network used 27 inputs, including spatial coordinates and hit directions derived from cells, and five large hidden layers. Prediction-based reconstruction achieved about 0.8, while fitting circles in the xy plane raised the score to about 0.9. A further z-axis constraint based on dr/dz improved the score by 0.003.

The writeup presents a malware classification solution with a reported minimum private leaderboard log loss of 0.005335339. Its requirements include Python 2.7, NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, and XGBoost. It provides a script invocation but does not explain feature construction, model configuration, or validation.

The team fine-tuned Nemotron-3-Nano-30B with rank-32 LoRA adapters using carefully revised reasoning traces derived from Tong Kang's shared artifacts. Improving trace structure and manually checking reasoning, together with choosing an appropriate training duration, mattered most. A custom 1,200-problem validation set combined unseen synthetic look-alikes and unsolved problems to better track leaderboard performance. Final selections included the strongest single adapter and a conservative consensus-based adapter merge, both reported at 0.87 public and 0.86 private scores.
external_data: ["Tong Kang's shared artifacts and traces", "nemotron2026privateadaptermergev1 adapter dataset"]

solution_summary: The author trained three recommender approaches: modified cosine similarity, hybrid matrix factorization, and regression based on user views and purchases. Predictions were combined through a weighted arithmetic mean. Hyperopt tuned the blending weights using held-out training weeks.

solution_title: 12th Place Solution - top of the silver...
solution_summary: The solution combined XLM-RoBERTa, MuRIL, and language-specific WECHSEL RoBERTa models trained with five-fold validation and external question-answering data. Token probabilities were mapped to character positions so models with different tokenizers could be ensembled. Language-specific postprocessing normalized Hindi numerals and cleaned answer punctuation and suffixes. The selected three-model ensemble scored 0.792 publicly and 0.760 privately, while the postprocessed two-model ensemble achieved a slightly better private score of 0.761.
compute: Colab Pro+ and Kaggle notebook

solution_summary: The final submission distilled a DeBERTa-v3-small model using ensemble pseudo labels for previous-competition texts and out-of-fold pseudo labels for current training texts. The student first trained entirely on pseudo labels, then continued fine-tuning on actual labels at a low learning rate. Optimized ONNX inference with pre-tokenized, dynamically padded inputs ran in about 18 minutes and scored 0.437961. An unselected xsmall model was faster and scored better, while quantization and alternative ONNX tooling did not help.
compute: Final small-model inference: around 18 minutes; unselected xsmall model: approximately 12 minutes.

solution_summary: The pipeline processed individual long-answer candidates and fine-tuned RoBERTa-large with answerability and short-span heads. TF-IDF-guided negative sampling reduced the training set while rotating negative subsets across epochs. End-span prediction was conditioned on the predicted start token, and answer thresholds were tuned on the official development set. A three-model logit ensemble required restricting candidate counts to meet runtime limits; both the individual models and ensemble scored 0.68 on the private test set.
compute: Single V100 GPU, approximately 4 hours per epoch for 312k examples using mixed precision.

solution_summary: The solution combined DeiT tiny, small, and base encoders with a transformer decoder that primarily generated SMILES. Training progressed from randomized-SMILES decoder pretraining to synthetic-image training and then higher-resolution fine-tuning on hard training examples and test pseudo-labels. Adversarial validation motivated separate models for two test subsets, with subset-dependent ensemble weights. Rotation augmentation and per-token logit averaging were used at inference, with InChI predictions providing a fallback for invalid SMILES, yielding a reported leaderboard score of 0.64.

The author trained an XGBoost classifier in BigQuery ML, which allowed training on all available data.
