Features combined content-level aggregates, cumulative question and lecture tag statistics, recent interaction windows, and timestamp lags. The final prediction averaged XGBoost with two SAKT models at weights of 3:1:1, reaching a public leaderboard score of 0.787. Leave-one-out validation guided evaluation, while iteration and fold ensembles of XGBoost did not improve over the single model.

solution_title: Top 6% in my first Kaggle competition: a hand-written planner with lookups
solution_summary: The final agent was a handwritten planner and executor using public replay-derived openings, farm targets, layouts, and crop counts. Daily worker routes combined angular sweeps, value-aware job selection, supply planning, and opportunistic reassignment. Exact last-day simulated annealing and morning large-neighborhood route search converted unused time-bank capacity into substantial gains. Builds were selected using both head-to-head tests and recorded-opponent replays with towns held fixed.
compute: Game budget: 1 second per turn plus a 60-second bank. Final agent used about 4 seconds loading tables, about 1.3 seconds for morning search, and about 25/13 seconds for the first two last-day searches.
external_data: ["Vadim Vasilenko public game replays", "DSM public game replays"]

solution_title: 2nd solution of CAFA 6: py-boost, GCN, and articles data
solution_summary: The solution combined multilabel gradient boosting, logistic regression, and neural networks using pretrained protein embeddings, taxon features, and supplementary biological information. Article TF-IDF embeddings provided the most important new improvement, while additional training data and cross-ontology features mainly improved robustness. A graph convolutional stacker combined 11 predictors per ontology with electronic GO annotation features and learned term embeddings. Conditional-probability modeling and graph-based postprocessing extended predictions across the ontology and improved their consistency.
compute: Single V100 32GB GPU; approximately 2 hours per fold for a 4,500-output PyBoost model.
external_data: ["CAFA 5 proteins", "UniProt", "PubMed article titles and abstracts", "GOA releases 226 and 228"]

solution_summary: The approach smoothed anomalous sales from March through December 2020 and added calendar, holiday, and cyclical seasonality features. Models trained on 2017–2020 data and were evaluated on April–December 2021 SMAPE. Predictions received multiplicative postprocessing, and the final blend combined a CatBoost submission with two public notebook submissions. solution_title: A Hybrid Physics–Machine Learning Framework for Polymer Property Prediction
solution_summary: The solution predicted polymer properties hierarchically, first building stable FFV and Tc ensembles and then using those predictions for other targets. Blending machine learning with mathematical expressions from a physics model was particularly important for sparse Tg data. Structural features, molecular descriptors, cleaning, and scaling supported the models. Grouped cross-validation and out-of-fold predictions guided tuning, while output adjustments improved stability without increasing scores.

The solution combined four instance segmentation models with YOLOv6m to improve detection recall. Training used both datasets, followed by fine-tuning on dataset1, with validation restricted to dataset1 to match the test distribution. Removing duplicate annotations and glomerulus labels, using light multiscale augmentation, and improving optimization helped training. Equal-weight box fusion, averaged masks, small-instance removal, and mask-based score refinement completed the pipeline.

This post describes the matching-classification and leakage postprocessing portions of a larger solution. XGBoost and LightGBM used string, geographic, categorical, and TF-IDF similarity features, while an XLM-RoBERTa model combined paired text with geographic distance. The models were ensembled, and validation deliberately allowed shared-record leakage to reflect overlap between training and test data. Matching test records to copied training records enabled prediction overrides, raising the reported leaderboard score from 0.949 to 0.971.

The final submission averaged ten single-image EfficientNet models covering five folds and two backbones. YOLOX localized breast regions before high-resolution cropping, and multi-task pretraining on VinDR preceded fine-tuning on competition data plus DDSM. Deep supervision, balanced batches, augmentation, and plain binary cross-entropy were important for the imbalanced task. Multi-image architectures and second-stage models using probabilities and image embeddings did not work well.

solution_title: Saving 10 places using Wildcards… by Hand  (and Goodbye!)
solution_summary: The author manually improved three strings by concentrating wildcard changes around expensive permutation transitions. Each string was split at transitions costing six or seven, then matching four-digit patterns were sought near substring ends and earlier positions. Applying the pattern operation twice per string produced the reported savings. The final score improved from 2442 to 2432.

The solution selected the 16 darkest image tiles and combined Swin Large with coat_lite_medium. Attention pooling replaced average pooling, and the competition metric was implemented as both the training loss and evaluation metric. Patient-grouped stratified validation guided improvements in both mean performance and stability, with MoCo-v3 pretraining reducing fold variability. The author fine-tuned four pretrained sequence-classification models with LoRA and combined their predictions with public-notebook models using simple averaging. The main strategy was to expand model and subset diversity rather than extensively tune individual models. The ensemble reached approximately 0.944–0.945 CV and 0.945/0.949 private/public scores.

The agent searched cached pseudorandom sequences to infer an opponent's RNG seed, falling back to an irrational Nash-equilibrium agent when no match was found. Its best version cached 666,666 seeds from three RNG implementations and scored 875.0. A later vectorized rewrite searched two million seeds but performed worse. The author could not establish whether the apparent advantage reflected exploitable sequence matches or statistical noise.

Images were cropped and resized to 3384 by 720, and an object detection threshold of 0.25 gave the best leaderboard score. Adding lower-resolution predictions covering the full image did not improve performance.

solution_summary: The author developed two submissions to address differences between original and synthesized data. One used mixed data, while the other used only synthesized data. The mixed-data submission scored better publicly, but the synthesized-only submission achieved a private score of 51.535 despite weaker public and cross-validation results. The post links a final notebook but provides no model architecture or ensemble details.

The author used a universal transformer-based approach that predicts the next puzzle move one step ahead. It solved every Wreath puzzle, all Globe puzzles except 8_25, and Cube puzzles of sizes 3 through 6. The linked cube_6/6/6 example used 739 moves, while time constraints prevented completing all puzzles.

solution_title: From public kernels to silver in a few days (52nd place before and after rescore)
solution_summary: The author adapted a public PyTorch transformer pipeline with warmup and linear learning-rate scheduling, augmentation, test-time augmentation, and group k-fold validation. They blended transformers with varied hyperparameters, explored a small RNN contribution, and applied a linear prediction correction. Pseudo-labeling targeted robustness to longer molecules and improved individual models, although its initial ensemble gains were small. After the rerun, the best submission used only pseudo-labeled models and scored 0.35092 privately and 0.23679 publicly.

solution_title: 11th Place: In the midst of entrance exams
solution_summary: The solution built roughly 250 diverse out-of-fold predictions across five to six feature sets and many tabular model families. Feature engineering included target encoding, polynomial and categorical interactions, notebook-derived meta features, and removal of the Driver column. GPU hill climbing, Ridge blending, and multilevel stacking were central to ensemble construction. The final ensemble also blended RealMLP and TabM outputs projected through the final OOF sample space.
compute: GPU-based hill climber; hardware model and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The team built seven distinct engineered datasets and trained one model per dataset to create diversity. Six boosting models and one neural network were combined using logistic and linear stackers. Bayesian hyperparameter searches tuned the boosting models, while the neural network used PReLU, batch normalization, and high dropout. Feature diversity worked better than varying models on one large feature set, with the linear stack reaching 0.805 CV and 0.807 on the leaderboard.

The solution combined DeBERTa v3 large with LightGBM using optimized weighted averaging. DeBERTa consumed the summary, question, title, and prompt text with a maximum length of 1536, frozen embeddings and early layers, and joint prediction of content and wording. Validation grouped examples by prompt, and the ensemble improved the CV score from 0.4816 for DeBERTa to 0.4748. LLM-generated training examples, LightGBM stacking, and several input modifications did not help.

The solution ensembles YOLOv8m segmentation models trained at input sizes of 512, 640, and 1024. Models first learned from unknown and glomerulus annotations treated as vessels, then were retrained using only correct vessel labels. Rotation and flip augmentation, mask fusion, dilation, DBSCAN-guided cropping, and SAM refinement supported the predictions. Scaling augmentation failed, while stain normalization hurt the public score but improved the private score; the reported best private score was 0.561 with a two-model ensemble and no dilation.

The author describes one ResNet50 model initialized with ImageNet weights that achieved a leaderboard score of 0.111. Images were resized to 256×256 and randomly cropped to 224×224, with horizontal flipping and normalization. Training used batches of 32 for up to eight epochs, starting at a learning rate of 0.0001 and halving it at epochs five and seven. One eighth of the training images were held out for validation, and inference used center crops.

The author progressively improved a scheduling solution using mixed-integer linear programming and local heuristics. An initial CBC-based iterative approach supplied a warm start for CPLEX, followed by reduced and fuller Xpress formulations. Pruning variables by accounting cost and occupancy bounds made the optimization more manageable. Good starting solutions and commercial solvers were central to reaching a final objective of 68888.04.
compute: CPLEX: two hours in Watson Studio cloud; Xpress: eight hours for each of two successive optimization stages.

solution_title: 43d Place Solution for the Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations
solution_summary: The final submission equally blended a Pyboost model and a neural network. Drug categories were the main addition to the public Pyboost baseline, alongside quantile-encoded cell and drug identifiers and SVD-compressed targets. The neural network used SMILES and cell type, with MAE for training and Mrrmse for validation. Cross-validation stability guided submission selection over stronger public scores from more complicated blends.

The solution used an encoder-only SAKT-like attention model with LSTM-encoded inputs, a sequence length of 400, 512-dimensional representations, and four attention heads. Precise task-container indexing and attention masks prevented leakage, while 90 handcrafted history and lecture features supplemented the sequence model through an MLP. Validation combined two million user-split rows with one million time-series-split rows to approximate the expected test population. A weighted average of six similar models achieved 0.817 public and 0.818 private scores, compared with 0.814 and 0.816 for a single model.

solution_title: Public 8th / Private 24th Solution (Miss a gold solution)
solution_summary: The final solution combined one Qwen3-reranker-8b causal language model with four sequence classifiers trained on the original 65 classes. Prompts included question context and structured information such as answer options, correct answers, and possible targets. Efficient LoRA training supported experimentation, and the ensemble used entmax probabilities with agreement and confidence adjustments. Rare-class probability boosts and constraints based on question–answer mappings and answer correctness refined the final predictions.
compute: Single A100; Unsloth reportedly doubled experimentation speed.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution for the CAFA 5 Protein Function Prediction
solution_summary: The solution used neural networks combining protein language model embeddings with taxonomy and non-experimental annotation features. Sequence embeddings came from T5, ESM2t36, ESM2t48, and combinations of these models. Non-experimental GO annotations were encoded by evidence type and processed with a kernel-size-one convolution. Validation simulated future annotation discovery using newer experimental annotations while excluding sub-ontology data already annotated in training.

solution_summary: The solution retrieved Wikipedia paragraphs directly and used a pretrained Xwin 70B model to evaluate candidate answers. Retrieval combined question embeddings with averaged answer embeddings, with e5-large-v2 used in the best submission. Prompt refinement improved results, while a logistic regression classifier trained on the model's last hidden state produced the best reported private score of 0.908. Memory and runtime constraints required limiting inputs to 1024 tokens, and the best submission took 8 hours 58 minutes.
compute: Best submission inference: 8h58 with 1024-token maximum; retrieval approximately 25 minutes over 140 GB of embeddings. Alternative DeBERTa inference used FP16 and PyTorch DDP on T4.

solution_title: 2nd place solution will be published June 16th/17th
solution_summary: The team describes an approach based on nnU-Net for processing 3D images. A 3D U-Net predicts blobs through pixel-wise regression. The post provides this brief outline while announcing that a fuller solution writeup will follow, without reporting training details or numerical results.

The final system combined seven neural networks and two weaker LightGBM models through a shallow LightGBM stacker. Neural networks supplied most of the predictive strength, while the tree models added diversity. Predicted host galaxy spectroscopic redshift helped both model families, and flux-related features improved the tree models. A heuristic adjustment for Class_99 provided a modest gain, and the final reported leaderboard score was 0.694 with a cross-validation score of 0.264.

The pipeline standardized image orientation, retrieved candidate image pairs with NetVLAD, and matched SuperPoint features using SuperGlue with MagSac filtering before incremental COLMAP reconstruction. Retrieval improvements included flipped-image descriptors, iterative reranking, image-size augmentation, and graph-based pair selection that maintained connectivity. Single-threaded COLMAP modifications made reconstruction deterministic, and one selected solution corrected EXIF orientation handling. The reported public and private scores were 0.485 and 0.514; several refinement and image-registration alternatives failed to improve leaderboard results.
compute: One CPU thread for deterministic COLMAP reconstruction.

solution_title: Super simple and super effective trick - 13th place
solution_summary: The author trained an MLP to correct movement vectors calculated with organizer-provided functions. Building and floor one-hot vectors were combined with the raw movement calculations, reducing average error from 2.67 m to 1.86 m. The corrected vectors improved cost minimization, followed by fitting paths into hallways.

The solution trained on both FGVC7 and FGVC8 data and averaged predictions from pretrained ResNet50 and SE-ResNeXt50 models. It addressed noisy labels by updating training targets after each epoch with a mixture of predictions and existing labels. Automated hyperparameter tuning included choosing the label-update mixing coefficient. Healthy leaves were inferred from the absence of predicted diseases, with disease probabilities scaled upward to reduce excessive healthy predictions.

solution_title: Silver Medal in My First Kaggle Competition
solution_summary: The post celebrates the author's first Kaggle competition and thanks community members for their help. It acknowledges baseline notebooks, feature-engineering discussions, and an encouraging hint from another competitor. It does not describe the author's competition pipeline or provide technical results beyond the competition outcome.

The solution directly regressed sentence-transformer prompt embeddings from images using EVA02, two ConvNeXt models, and a ViT. Training used roughly five million generated image–prompt pairs, similarity-grouped validation, frozen-backbone warmup, and subsequent fine-tuning on the expanded dataset. The final ensemble combined 18 model instances and learned separate combination weights for each embedding dimension. Dimension-specific weights added only 0.0002 over model-level weighting, while caption generation and several alternative losses or pooling methods were less effective.

solution_summary: The team built a retriever-reader pipeline around a custom STEM Wikipedia corpus and synthetic multiple-choice questions. Fine-tuned embedding retrievers supplied candidates to a DeBERTa cross-encoder, which selected two to four context chunks for an ensemble of readers. Readers combined DeBERTa variants with a LoRA-tuned Mistral model, while low-confidence questions were routed to zero-shot 70B models. Cross-option modeling and selective large-model inference were central, and attempts to fine-tune a 70B model with QLoRA failed.

The author reused a public model notebook and added token-level post-processing for PII detection. The rules applied thresholds, removed honorifics, repaired BIO sequence boundaries, and filled isolated outside-label gaps. These adjustments helped on the public leaderboard but transferred poorly to the private evaluation. The author presents the approach as an overfitting failure case.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution for the Google - Fast or Slow? Predict AI Model Runtime Competition
solution_summary: The team predicted runtimes with a graph network using SAGEConv, self-channel attention, cross-configuration attention, and pairwise hinge loss. Graph pruning, configuration deduplication, and compact configuration storage made training substantially more efficient. Standardized numerical features and shared embeddings for consistently padded layout features improved optimization, while cross-configuration attention helped the model compare configurations directly. Configuration-permutation test-time augmentation and model averaging improved predictions; the best reported ensemble scored 0.736 privately and 0.757 publicly, although that submission was not selected.

solution_title: Teaching a Model to Read the Sky
solution_summary: The final classifier blended LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost using engineered filter-color differences and redshift transformations. Rare-class training weights and final class-weight adjustments targeted balanced accuracy, while averaging across more splits and seeds improved stability. Cross-validation guided model selection and reached approximately 0.9669, close to the public score. Real survey data, pseudo-labeling, neural networks, and TabPFN did not improve the tree ensemble.
compute: Free Kaggle GPU; earlier work on a laptop

solution_title: Really Simple Approach to Get 39th Place
solution_summary: The solution separated wavelength prediction from uncertainty prediction. It extended Sergei's method to multiple wavelengths by smoothing AIRS signals along the wavelength axis, and combined FGS1 and AIRS light curves for wl_1. A random forest predicted wavelength-specific uncertainty from signal and prediction statistics, improving the leaderboard score from 0.572 to 0.607. Five-fold stratified validation was used, while a CNN approach failed to outperform the simpler method.

solution_title: How I did it: Martin Reichert on 3rd place in Elo comp
solution_summary: The author developed a chess rating approach inspired by Chessmetrics after evaluating established rating systems. Performance, opponent quality, activity, weighting, and consistency over time guided the rating design. Parameters and algorithms were iteratively adjusted against cross-validation data. Submission 23 ultimately performed better on the final evaluation than submission 50, which had the author's best public score.

solution_title: Recruit Coupon Purchase Winner's Interview: 2nd place, Halla Yang
solution_summary: The solution used an XGBoost classifier to estimate purchase probabilities for user–coupon pairs and recommend each user's ten highest-scoring coupons. Training examples came from 24 weekly periods, with the last week held out for parameter tuning before retraining on all weeks. Important features captured direct coupon views before display dates, repeated purchase preferences, demographic peer behavior, and the full geographic coverage of coupons. Logistic regression, random forests, SVMs, and deep neural networks were explored, but gradient boosting performed best.

The solution used a four-fold U-Net with a SE-ResNeXt101 encoder, CBAM attention, hypercolumns, and deep supervision. Training balanced tiles by mask presence and masked area, with patient-grouped validation and pseudo-labels from competition and external images. Inference retained only the central 512×512 region of each original 1024×1024 tile to reduce edge artifacts. The reported public and private Dice scores were 0.936 and 0.951.
compute: Center-only tile inference required four times the inference time.

solution_summary: The solution used NFNet-backed sound event detection models with clipwise outputs and emphasized clean labels and post-processing. Human verification of high-confidence training predictions produced 2,000 clean examples, which were mixed with unscored-species data and weighted pseudo-labels. Ten models were combined by voting, with shifted-window inference and species-specific threshold adjustments. The full post-processing pipeline raised public performance from 0.79 to 0.84 and private performance from 0.76 to 0.80.
compute: About 14 hours for 30 epochs in Colaboratory

solution_summary: The solution ensembled five sequence models combining WaveNet-style blocks, bidirectional LSTM or GRU layers, and optionally Transformer encoders or dense recurrent connections. Auxiliary prediction of first and second pressure differences stabilized training and materially improved performance. Pseudo-labeling, 15-fold validation stratified by R and C, and loss restricted to u_out equal to zero also helped. Optuna-tuned weights and a spread-dependent mean-or-median ensemble produced CV 0.096600, public LB 0.1131, and private score 0.1171, with the unusually low CV attributed to pseudo-label training.

The post announces released submission code and public datasets while briefly describing the ensemble. The author's individual component scored 0.782 on the public leaderboard, and combining it with a teammate's GCN and LGB models reached 0.792. The linked resources contain the fuller solution, while this text provides only a short account of its components.

The solution combines two neural text models with a sparse-feature regression pipeline. One neural model aggregates FastText-initialized word embeddings before an MLP, while the other applies convolutions to Word2Vec-initialized embeddings. The sparse pipeline stacks LightGBM predictions into Ridge and averages Ridge with FastFM. Final predictions combine the three branches in log1p space with weights of 0.25, 0.30, and 0.45, while multiprocessing and chunked reading reduce resource usage.

The author generated roughly 4.4 million images from diverse prompt sources, matched the organizer's generation settings, and removed near-duplicates. Pretrained EVA and ViT image encoders were fine-tuned with a linear embedding head and negative cosine similarity loss. Validation grouped samples by embedding clusters, and learned linear coefficients combined model predictions. The best submission retained only EVA models, dropping the weaker ViTs.
compute: Mostly RTX 3090 GPUs; approximately 215 GPU-days for 25 models plus 85 GPU-days for failed, suboptimal, or interrupted runs; individual runs lasted up to 9 days.

solution_title: 218th place: trust the private guardrail, not the public score
solution_summary: The author analyzed evaluator code and modeled stricter private defenses to distinguish fragile marker-exfiltration attacks from transferable confused-deputy attacks. The final selection paired a clean unsolicited-email build with a high-public-score marker build as a hedge. The selected deputy build scored 14.625 privately while the marker build scored zero; an unselected repetitive deputy build reached 20.610, showing that isolated-candidate throughput mattered more than template diversity.

solution_title: 9th Place Solution: Human-Auditable CoT Target Engineering
solution_summary: The solution refined public reasoning traces and used one epoch of LoRA supervised fine-tuning without expanding the synthetic problem set. Task-specific changes made arithmetic traces consistent, cipher reasoning shorter, and Bit and Equation rule searches more deterministic. Training emphasized Bit, Cipher, and Equation through oversampling, while held-out fold validation guided trace revisions. Validation was nearly perfect on several simpler categories, but Cryptarithm remained weak because the model did not reliably learn multiplication patterns.

The author modified a deepfake challenge video by placing an emoji over the boss's face. This yielded a flag on the first attempt. Based on public notebooks, the author suspected that any ten-second video other than the original might also have succeeded.

The solution combined ArcFace-based image models with TF-IDF and SBERT text representations. EfficientNet and NFNet variants supplied complementary image embeddings, while title preprocessing removed noise and standardized words and units. The largest improvement came from nearest-neighbor post-processing that repaired self-only matches and propagated reliable links. A B3 model plus TF-IDF reached 0.763, and adding other models raised the public score to 0.771.

solution_title: 17th Place Solution for the Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations (ADEFR)
solution_summary: The solution blended four gradient-boosting regression variants and then equally mixed their output with a public solution. Shared features included gene-level PCA, mean single-cell expression, raw differential expression, and smoothed expression features. DGE-derived PCA contributed nearly half the measured feature importance, and ridge smoothing slightly outperformed nearest-neighbor smoothing. Validation held out cell types, while training weights reflected the number of cells supporting each target.

The solution retrieved candidates from session history and task-specific item collaborative filtering, then ranked them with LightGBM and CatBoost binary classifiers. Ranking features combined session and item statistics, interaction recency, Word2Vec similarities, collaborative filtering scores, and temporal counts and ratios. Training used three weeks of data and five seeds for session cutoffs, improving local validation by 0.001. The authors also reported gains from combining task probabilities and pooling carts and orders training data. Combining the two classifiers scored 0.600 on the leaderboard, and voting with teammates' predictions increased this to 0.602.

solution_title: Analyzing private vs public leader board ranks by approach
solution_summary: The author briefly reports using LightGBM with domain-based feature engineering. No feature definitions, training settings, or validation details are supplied. Most of the post requests participants' approaches and leaderboard data for a comparative analysis.

The solution combined dense Wikipedia sentence retrieval with TF-IDF paragraph retrieval to supply contexts to fine-tuned DeBERTaV3 Large and LongFormer Large models. Dense retrieval used two embedding models and two query formulations, while training used a public 60k dataset and a generated 39k STEM dataset with iterative relabeling. Predictions were combined through checkpoint-specific blends and a confidence-triggered DeBERTa/LongFormer backup for TF-IDF contexts. Context limits and composition choices were tuned on 500 public examples, yielding 0.928 public and 0.916 private leaderboard scores. The best submission took 8:52:43 to run.

solution_summary: The final pipeline first used a U-Net with an SE-ResNeXt50 backbone to identify pneumothorax through a 2,000-pixel threshold. Balanced batches accelerated this detection stage, and unanimous positive predictions from earlier classifiers recovered additional cases. A separate U-Net trained only on positive images then segmented cases accepted by the detection stage. Both stages used folds stratified by pneumothorax area, while the segmentation stage combined binary cross-entropy and Dice losses at 768- and 928-pixel resolutions.

The team optimized ONNX solutions across 400 tasks through repeated, human-guided ChatGPT conversations focused on one task at a time. Prompts included the current model, solver, official scorer, task interpretation, numerical improvement targets, and constraints distilled from earlier failures. Compact representations and transferring successful ideas between tasks helped reduce model costs. A dashboard supported task selection and progress tracking, and repeated passes brought the score to about 8,000.

solution_title: Biohub Cell Lineage Story -🥉bronze medal solution
solution_summary: The pipeline combined a 3D U-Net cell detector, a transformer edge scorer, and an integer linear programming solver to construct lineage graphs. Two edge-scoring seeds were fused using harmonic probabilities, followed by motion relinking, gap closing, and conservative division handling. Linking was the main bottleneck: approximately 83% of missed edges already had both cells detected. Reported results reached 0.954 public and 0.922 private, while the author emphasized embryo-held-out validation because public films duplicated training data.

The solution fine-tuned GloVe and Paragram embeddings with Word2Vec CBOW on competition training and test text. It randomly selected 400 of 600 embedding dimensions for each fold to reduce computation and diversify models, improving the public score despite worse local validation. A two-layer bidirectional LSTM with max pooling incorporated word and sentence statistics. Predictions were averaged across five folds.

The team ensembled 20 models spanning 2D and 2.5D architectures. The described component used EfficientNet-B7 U-Net, EfficientNet-B7 U-Net++, and MiT-B5 U-Net models, with averaged annotator labels and image resolutions of at least 512 pixels identified as especially valuable. Training used AdamW, cosine scheduling with warm-up, and soft binary cross-entropy. Ensemble weights were optimized with Nelder–Mead at a fixed threshold because validation splits produced inconsistent preferred thresholds.

solution_title: Caterpillar Winners' Interview: 1st place, Gilberto | Josef | Leustagos | Mario
solution_summary: The team combined diverse models through stacking and blending, with XGBoost, Regularized Greedy Forests and factorization machines among the learners. Feature engineering captured physical tube properties, aggregated statistics and quantity-dependent pricing. Predictive tube identifiers and other soft leaks were especially valuable, while transformed cost targets improved model performance. Out-of-fold predictions supported the final ensemble; neural networks were tried but underperformed XGBoost.
compute: Mario: about 2h30m per model and 20h for stacking/test predictions; Josef: up to 15h for out-of-fold/test predictions; Lucas: minutes to 10h per model; bagged XGBoost: 3–4h per model on an 8-core CPU.

solution_summary: The solution used EfficientNet-b0 through b3 with joint classification and regression training, retaining regression predictions at inference. Images were cropped to remove black backgrounds, resized to 384×384, and augmented geometrically. Training combined 2015 and 2019 data with five-fold validation and high-confidence pseudo-labels from the 2019 public data. Pseudo-labeling was identified as the most important improvement and helped both local MSE and quadratic weighted kappa.

The approach combined five SE-ResNet50 models trained identically on different training subsets. Splitting by whole-slide image, resizing inputs to 196×196, and increasing test-time augmentation to 16 variants improved performance. A simple ensemble achieved 0.9810 on the private leaderboard, outperforming a more elaborate weighted ensemble despite its lower public score. ReduceLROnPlateau was also used, although its benefit was uncertain.

The final ensemble combined XGBoost, a small feed-forward neural network, and ANNOY nearest-neighbor models trained on two engineered datasets, yielding six base models. One dataset combined competition and original data with 314 features, while the other had 467 features and incorporated target encoding learned from the original data. A forest of XGBoost stumps combined their predictions, with validation performance close to the leaderboard score. Supervised neural encodings, triple interactions, and predictions from original-data models were abandoned because they did not materially improve validation.

solution_title: 2nd place solution overview: detection + full-page classification
solution_summary: The pipeline separated class-agnostic character detection from classification using large contextual crops and fixed predicted boxes. Five book-based folds supplied out-of-fold detection boxes, while ResNet152 and ResNeXt classifiers learned both character classes and a false-positive class. Confident test predictions supported pseudo-label training, and a LightGBM/XGBoost second level selected candidate classes from classifier outputs. The final second-level blend achieved a public score of 0.949.

solution_summary: The author reconstructed public-test targets through leaderboard probing and trained ensembles using protein stability predictions and structural properties as features. The two selected submissions used hill climbing with positive-only or signed weights, but unselected random forests generalized better by capturing feature interactions. Relative solvent-accessible surface area was particularly useful, and deletion mutations were assigned the worst predicted stability at their residue position. A later update reported private scores of 0.525 for corrected hill climbing and 0.560 for random forest, highlighting both preprocessing errors and difficult model selection.

solution_summary: The solution combined diverse boosted-tree models, field-aware factorization machines, and neural networks. Five-fold stratified validation used a seed selected for similar fold statistics, with three model seeds averaged within each fold. LightGBM importance and shuffling guided feature selection, while grouped embedding networks carried substantial ensemble weight. Two-stage logistic-regression stacking selected complementary predictions using their correlations and validation improvements.

The final submission averaged independently developed LightGBM models and then overrode selected confidently identified fraudulent users. User identification, extensive group aggregates, and behavioral history features were central to performance. Labels inferred through user matching and leaderboard probing also guided feature selection and ensemble-weight experiments. Monthly grouped validation and a stacked model trained on single-transaction users supported a final private AUC of 0.942453.

The solution used RTKLIB position estimates followed by generic and phone-specific directional bias corrections. RTKLIB provided the largest improvement, while constrained corrections for individual phone models further reduced error. The selected submission scored 2.508 publicly and 2.094 privately. Stop averaging and outlier correction did not improve the best submissions, while an unselected tectonic correction would have slightly improved the private score.

solution_title: 7th place solution, single model, no supplemental data used

The model used more than 900 selected features from a larger undisclosed feature pool and standard time-series cross-validation. A control model using only the original 300 features scored 0.112, highlighting the importance of the undisclosed feature work.

solution_title: Silver medal for a First timer, Thank you for your inputs
solution_summary: The author combined XGBoost predictions for Class with TabPFN predictions for Gamma after exploring Greek metadata as alternative targets. Preprocessing included label encoding, median imputation, outlier removal, and random oversampling. XGBoost hyperparameters were tuned with five-fold cross-validation, while TabPFN used a single split. Reported accuracies were 0.931 for XGBoost and 0.965 for TabPFN on Gamma; an earlier ensemble of conventional classifiers was less successful.

The author combined LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost using 10-fold stratified cross-validation and Optuna-optimized weighted averaging. Feature engineering included arithmetic combinations and logarithmic transformations, although the supplied formulas omit feature names. Modifying the ensemble-weight objective to emphasize errors at higher ages reportedly improved the score by almost 0.006, and predictions above 18 received a small upward adjustment. Attempts to repair inconsistent measurements and convert the target to classification did not improve the approach.

The team blended an encoder-only Transformer, a SAINT+ encoder-decoder Transformer, and LightGBM models to obtain 0.814 public and 0.816 private scores. Transformer training used task-aware leakage controls, while LightGBM relied on 264 question and user-history features. On-demand HDF5 history loading reduced RAM consumption by 97%, and Treelite compilation accelerated LightGBM inference threefold. Time limits prevented using beneficial SAINT+ test-time augmentation, and the team explicitly declined private-score probing.
compute: HDF I/O overhead approximately 45 minutes; compiled LightGBM inference approximately 10 ms/batch and 10 minutes total

solution_summary: Audio was converted into log-mel spectrograms and processed with sliding-window CNN predictions. Temporal predictions fed both an RNN and a Rakeld plus ExtraTrees branch, whose outputs were averaged. A curated-only model generated pseudo labels for noisy data, blended with the original labels at a 0.75 to 0.25 ratio before retraining on all data. DenseNet121 training used spectrogram augmentation, mixup, cyclical learning rates, stochastic weight averaging, and snapshot ensembling; ICT-style semi-supervised learning did not work.

solution_title: 30th Place 827 Private LB with image size 840
solution_summary: The team developed separate image-matching ensembles optimized for validation and leaderboard performance. The best leaderboard submission combined SuperPoint with two SuperGlue passes, LoFTR, reversed MatchFormer, and MatchFormer Light, with a classifier deciding whether to add DKM. Padding masks, depth or segmentation masks, reversed image order, and flips improved matching diversity. The validation-oriented submission scored 0.813 public and 0.816 private, while alternative geometric estimators and several additional matching strategies failed to improve results.

The author adapted an existing greedy scheduling notebook by modifying its shipment scoring function. Two distance-based factors favored shipments near the initial position early in scheduling, with that preference fading over time. The author also tuned the branching factor and a root-count test parameter. The post attributes most of the underlying solution to the original notebook author.

The selected submission used a fine-tuned Lumina-Image-2.0 model to generate flat raster images, followed by iterative vectorization and SVG optimization. It generated ten candidates per prompt across two GPUs and selected an output using prompt alignment and aesthetic scores. Adapting training to smaller image sizes made generation practical, while an OCR decoy was included in the final pipeline. Direct SVG generation with Qwen fine-tuning failed, and several alternative diffusion models and scoring adjustments did not improve the selected approach.
compute: Inference on 2 GPUs, generating 5 images per GPU at 320x320; nearly 2 weeks spent attempting Qwen fine-tuning.

solution_summary: The pipeline extracted reduced-resolution odd video frames, selected candidate events using an EfficientNetV2 classifier and temporal score peaks, and localized event regions with a U-Net. Manually annotated event centers enabled ROI extraction, which the author found essential for competitive performance. A 3D Channel-Separated Network classified 16-frame ROI clips, with background examples periodically downsampled during training. Combining its scores with candidate classifier scores improved performance by approximately 0.01, and the full pipeline took about 80 minutes per video.
compute: Approximately 80 minutes per video in a Kaggle kernel: extraction 15 min, candidate selection 20 min, area detection 15 min, classification 30 min; manual annotation took several weeks.

solution_summary: The team trained SE-ResNeXt50/101 and Inceptionv3/v4 on 512×512 RGB or RGBY images, adding external images to the training portion of every fold. Deep supervision supplied classification heads at multiple spatial resolutions, with equally weighted training losses and averaged head predictions at inference. The final submission combined four models by weighted averaging and used class-dependent thresholds. Focal loss underperformed, while stacking improved local F1 by 5% but performed poorly on both leaderboards and was excluded.

solution_title: 21st Place Solution: Deep Transformers 1400->21 and the String-Matching repulsion
solution_summary: The pipeline expanded dataset-name labels with external sources and added 5,000 publications before training transformer NER models. Keyword-based sentence selection reduced false positives and made inference roughly ten times faster. A weighted six-model NER vote fed candidate mentions into sequence classifiers, followed by removal of short acronyms. Conservative fine-tuning and dropout aimed to limit overfitting despite an imperfect thematic validation split, and the ensemble exceeded 0.5 on the public leaderboard.

solution_summary: The solution stacked seed-averaged Ridge, MLP and LightGBM models using a Bayesian Ridge second stage. Features combined loading and functional connectivity inputs with interactions, image correlations, and image histogram and statistical summaries. Statistics computed over smaller image cubes were more effective than whole-image summaries. Adversarial validation guided removal of site-discriminating features, and the final stack achieved local CV of 0.15674 and a private score of 0.15786.

solution_title: 1199 positions gain in the private ranking solution
solution_summary: The solution combined LightGBM regressors trained with different seeds using weighted voting and averaged predictions across selected feature sets. Preprocessing included constant missing-value imputation, MinMax scaling, and label encoding. Feature selection and Nelson-Aalen target transformation were emphasized, alongside additional survival-derived features. K-fold validation used the stratified concordance index, and the reported private score was 0.692 versus 0.684 publicly.

solution_title: [Solution]: LB 11.8 RMSE 🚀 RAPIDS +  WarpGBM 0.1.23 w/ Eval
solution_summary: The post presents a competition-tested WarpGBM notebook alongside a software release. Its pipeline combines GPU histogram-based training with categorical encoding, high-order interactions, group means, and numerical transformations. Validation includes holdout RMSE and early stopping, while target encoding is performed within cross-validation. The described setup reportedly achieved approximately 11.8 private leaderboard RMSE.

solution_title: 4th Solution (Team Durrett): IL from multiple agents
solution_summary: The final agent used imitation learning from seven leading agents with a shared CNN and a separate fully connected head for each teacher. At inference, only the head trained on the strongest teacher was used, and a single forward pass produced actions for every unit and city tile. Greater network capacity, FReLU, squeeze-and-excitation layers, a transformer encoder, and prolonged training improved performance. Rules resolved conflicting moves and prioritized worker construction, with thousands of self-play games used to evaluate them; reinforcement learning attempts were unsuccessful.
compute: About one week to train the final model; average inference about 1.5 seconds per turn except the first turn.
external_data: ["Lux AI replay dataset from seven leading agents"]

solution_summary: The solution trained EfficientNetV2 B0 and B3 models on single-channel spectrograms through three stages. It began with 2021–2024 data, then focused training on the competition targets, and finally incorporated pseudo-labeled 2024 audio. Unlabeled recordings were split into five-second segments, with low-entropy examples retained and weak class probabilities zeroed. Mixing these soft-labeled segments with labeled audio improved the leaderboard score by approximately 0.04.

The final submission blended 18 diverse models with weights determined by ridge regression. Different feature subsets supplied additional diversity, while grouping duplicate training rows sharply reduced development time. Adding the original data improved performance, and models learned log1p(cost) before predictions were inverted with expm1. The ensemble included random forests, extra-trees, a neural network, and gradient boosting models.

The solution retrieved candidate dataset DOIs and accession identifiers from DCC4 and Europe PMC, then verified their presence in article PDF text or XML. Matching handled DOI version suffixes, Zenodo URLs, and identifier-specific source restrictions. Ordered heuristics classified references as primary or secondary using dates, reference-section placement, author overlap, repository identity, and contextual phrases. Final submissions varied selected database exclusions and SAMN rules, while article-ID casing triggered additional exclusions learned from training data.

The solution combined misconception reasoning, embedding-based recall, and a teammate-provided reranker. Expanding misconception descriptions helped distinguish semantically similar labels and improved the leaderboard score by 0.017. Qwen-32B-Instruct provided the strongest recall, with single-model recall scoring 0.534 LB and 0.489 PB. Query-side error reasoning and the author's reranking experiments were less effective, while synthetic data improved local validation more clearly than leaderboard results.

solution_title: 84th place solution and consideration on the use of validation data
solution_summary: The submitted unlearning method trains on softened forget-set labels and ensembles the resulting model with the original model. Validation predictions from the original model are sorted into five intervals, whose means define replacement targets for corresponding forget-set intervals. Training minimizes L2 distance to these targets to make forget-set outputs resemble validation outputs. The author reports that this worked well on CIFAR10 and used the original-model ensemble to preserve retain-set information without additional retain-set training.

The solution combined known rock-paper-scissors bots using an iterated version of the iocaine meta-predictor. The final ensemble applied three levels of iocaine to predictors from several existing bots and tree-based methods, weighting their contributions according to historical performance. Every other move was random to disrupt opponents. Moderate iteration depths worked well against meta-strategies, while an experiment with 500 levels failed.

The team rank-averaged seven diverse causal language, classification, and retrieval models, achieving 0.92657 on the private leaderboard. Most models trained on test.csv, with synthetic data supporting DeBERTa and Qwen2.5-7B. Compliance-focused few-shot prompting improved Qwen3-4B, while expanded LoRA modules made Gemma2-2B an effective classifier. Model selection emphasized diversity and runtime within the 12-hour limit, using public leaderboard feedback.
compute: 12-hour training and inference limit; Gemma2-2B completed in 90 minutes.

solution_summary: The main model classified ordinary spectrogram crops whose frequency range and duration were fixed separately for each class, with an added frequency-coordinate channel. Training used 26 song classes, masked focal loss, a custom label-aware mixing and balancing procedure, time jitter, and white noise. External Xeno Canto recordings supplied weak negatives, while out-of-fold pseudo-labeling mined additional positives from unlabeled training regions. The final rank ensemble weighted this architecture at 97% and SED models at 3%; a single five-fold model scored 0.961 private and 0.956 public.
compute: Ideas and implementation completed in approximately seven days.

solution_summary: The solution combined single-encoder and dual-encoder BERT and XLNet models with independent heads for each target. Rank-based min-max scaling of targets improved CV by about 0.01, while validating only on questions appearing once made validation more representative of test performance. A weighted ensemble reached 0.404 CV before greedy prediction discretization, which improved CV and leaderboard scores by roughly 0.03. A spelling classifier using retrieved Stack Exchange tags performed worse than the neural predictions with post-processing.

The solution used behavior cloning with a small Transformer, first learning from winning games of leading teams and then fine-tuning on a carefully selected teacher. Selecting submissions with a consistent strategy mattered more than model architecture or adding more teachers. The final policy averaged action probabilities across three seeds, each using averaged late checkpoints. Head-to-head games showed that validation loss could favor weaker policies and misleading extra features.

The solution used DINOv3 patch features to predict nonnegative local biomass densities and summed them into five image-level targets. Gradual unfreezing preserved pretrained representations, while splitting images and labels in half expanded training data. High resolution, consistency constraints between targets, and stratified grouped validation were central to performance. The final ensemble combined six model configurations across two seeds, with inference optimized for the time limit.
compute: Huge+ at 864px: 20 hours for 5 folds on Colab A100 80GB, 76GB VRAM at batch size 8; parallel FP16 inference on two T4 GPUs within a 9-hour limit.

solution_summary: The pipeline ensembled three retrievers and passed their candidates through a cascade of Qwen rerankers at 14B, 32B, and 72B sizes. Dynamic retrieval selected 32–64 candidates, which the rerankers reduced to eight, then five, before final listwise ranking. Models were fine-tuned on approximately 1,800 competition examples plus 10,000 synthetic examples. Claude-generated reasoning, misconception demonstrations, abundant training negatives, and teacher-generated pseudo-labels were key to performance and generalization.

solution_title: my solution to the MSD challenge..
solution_summary: The solution used item-based collaborative filtering with a newly designed parametric similarity between songs or users. Calibrating recommendation scores for ranking increased the reported leaderboard score from 0.16665 to 0.17712. Aggregating rankings with a user-similarity predictor further raised the score to roughly 0.178. The author identified the similarity function and calibration as the crucial improvements.

The author describes the CosFace component of a team solution using SE-ResNeXt101 and bounding-box annotations shared by another participant. CosFace with a margin of 0.6 and LayerNorm before L2 normalization performed best among the tested loss and normalization choices. Final models used grayscale and RGB images at two resolutions, trained with AdamW for approximately 30 epochs. New-whale examples were excluded from training, and the submission targeted roughly 27% new-whale predictions; several augmentation and alternative unknown-class treatments failed.
external_data: ["Bounding-box annotations from @radek, including updated v2 annotations"]

solution_summary: The team trained football agents through reinforcement learning and self-play using dense layers and an LSTM. Multi-head value estimation, engineered relative-position features, and dense reward shaping supported training. They learned additional playing styles from opponents' replays through GAIL and built a diverse league of opponents. A final agent trained against that league gained roughly 100 internal Elo over their earlier candidate, while a local Elo evaluation pool enabled faster model comparison.

The solution ensembled six SegFormer models trained through customized MMSegmentation with binary segmentation and group normalization. Hand-labeled lung data, external images, stain variants, and pseudo labels expanded the training set. Training used a combined cross-entropy and Lovasz loss, while inference combined flips and multiple scales with organ-specific thresholds. The ensemble achieved 0.83562 privately, compared with 0.82821 for the best single model.
compute: Google Colaboratory; limited GPU resources; batch size 1; 45,000 training steps.
external_data: ["HPA images and H&E/PAS stain variants", "External spleen images", "External lung images"]

solution_title: 23rd Place Silver - Balanced Stochastic Data Loader
solution_summary: The solution trained FPN segmentation models with EfficientNetB2 and EfficientNetB0 encoders using ImageNet weights. A balanced loader sampled the same number of label-containing crops from every training image, after downsampling at three scales and applying augmentation. Six models trained on all available training data were ensembled, achieving public 0.920 and private 0.947. A separate five-fold check averaged 0.945 on 14 images, with a much weaker result on one unusually light image.
compute: 4 NVIDIA V100 32GB; 50 epochs, batch size 24 at 768x768; a few minutes per epoch.

solution_summary: The solution predicted ground and nearby-player contacts jointly for each player over a time interval using an end-to-end video and tracking model. Video encoders supplied spatial activations, while alternating transformer layers combined tracking information with video evidence and interactions across players and time. Overlapping temporal predictions and predictions from both player directions were averaged. A weighted ensemble of seven models achieved a private score of 0.7956, with substantial variation in model behavior across validation folds.

solution_summary: The solution used ArcMargin embedding models to retrieve candidate location pairs and LightGBM to determine matches. Inputs combined sparse text representations, categorical and binary attributes, and sinusoidal geographic encodings. Matching features included embedding, geographic, and string distances. A text-only XLM-RoBERTa candidate model and additional neighbor-ranking features raised the reported public score to 0.923.

This component of the team solution modeled each whole well as a continuous geological alignment path using a distributional 2D U-Net over candidate TVT states and sampled well positions. Synthetic geological paths supported pretraining before real-data fine-tuning, and a diverse core ensemble was followed by a bounded residual refiner. Structural particle trajectories and cross-well surface candidates supplied conservative corrections gated by small tree-based utility routers. Nested whole-well validation protected model and routing choices from held-out targets, and the final system improved pooled OOF RMSE from 6.1895 to 6.0665 and private RMSE from 6.985 to 6.729.
compute: Two T4 GPUs for neural ensemble inference.

solution_summary: The author adapted shonenkov's public training and inference baseline. They used a B7 model and adjusted the batch size to fit their hardware. The post gives no further training, validation, or performance details.

The pipeline heuristically extracted DOI and accession candidates from PDF text and combined PDF references with full XML text. Candidates were enriched with context, abstracts, and author names, then filtered for data-related keywords. Qwen2.5-32B-instruct-awq classified candidates using four source-specific prompts, followed by a publisher-prefix filter. The final submission was selected using local CV; larger models, ensembling, fine-tuning, and several extraction and prompt refinements did not improve the score.

The solution emphasized diversity across datasets, model families, seeds, and folds to improve robustness. About 50 tree and neural models were blended using log10 odds, with weights optimized on out-of-fold predictions. Neural networks improved the ensemble despite weaker individual validation scores. The final ensemble achieved 0.8009 CV and 0.8075 private leaderboard scores, while hard pseudo-labeling and deeper neural networks did not help.

The approach concatenated notebook cells into one transformer sequence, placing markdown before code and adding cell-type separators. DeBERTa-v3-large encoded the sequence, with mean pooling and a linear layer producing one score per cell. Pairwise margin ranking loss trained the scores, which were sorted at inference to recover cell order. Cell compression and longer inference sequences helped, while T5-style sequence-to-sequence and multilingual models did not.

The solution stacked predictions from six pretrained image models and three models trained on sensor-pattern features using an XGBoost meta-model. High-confidence pseudo-labels added 1,116 unaltered test images to first-layer training, and test-time augmentation improved the strongest DenseNet201. Approximately 3,000 linear-pattern and noise-pattern features supplied complementary predictions. The selected stack excluded pseudo-labeled examples from second-layer training and scored 0.9847 on the private leaderboard; a stack including them scored 0.9866.
compute: About one week available for model training; limited GPU resources, with no hardware specified.

solution_summary: The solution uses only historical revenue and averages two complementary models. The first forecasts aggregate revenue from previously paying users with Prophet, then allocates it according to historical payment shares. The second estimates transaction-state transition probabilities and conditional spending from separate yearly windows. Its yearly forecasts are combined with weights of 0.3 and 0.7 before averaging with the first model.

The solution used neural networks with an input shape of (200, 2) and within-class shuffle augmentation. A single model achieved public/private scores of 0.9239/0.9232. The final ensemble varied the positive-to-negative ratios used in augmentation and improved these scores to 0.92502/0.92421. LightGBM experiments remained below 0.922 and were not included in the stated final ensemble.

The solution handled non-is relationships and attribute-like is relationships separately. For non-is relationships, Cascade R-CNN detected 57 object classes, then geometric features supported LightGBM relationship classifiers after merging 287 triplet classes into 90 groups. A separate Cascade R-CNN directly detected 42 attributed-object classes for is relationships. Combining the two submission sets achieved public and private scores of 0.38469 and 0.30781, while undersampling traded detection accuracy for shorter training.

The solution combined RTKLIB positioning with weighted least-squares estimates and a custom nine-state Kalman smoother modeling position, velocity, and acceleration. Additional estimates came from RTKLIB observation data, providing coverage where device GNSS fields were missing. Four solutions were merged using pointwise inverse-variance weights, with outlier removal and a small final latitude/longitude bias correction that improved the score by about 0.04. Parameter selection relied on training data rather than leaderboard feedback; RTKLIB atmospheric corrections and attempts to improve point positioning from base positions did not help.

The solution averaged four nf-regnetb1 and HRNet18 classifiers trained on spatially stacked cadence frames with a second channel identifying on-target and off-target observations. Higher resolution, customized MixUp and CutMix, and focal loss drove the main improvements. Training used mixed precision, exponential moving averages, and warmup followed by cosine decay, while inference included test-time augmentation. The ensemble reached about 0.800 on the leaderboard; extensive pseudo-labeling, normalization, and unsupervised experiments did not improve results.
compute: 4x V100; approximately 7 hours for nf-regnetb1 and 24 hours for HRNet

solution_summary: The team combined a ship/no-ship classifier with an ensemble of four U-Net segmentation models using shallow and deep encoders. Reliable validation and suppressing false positives mattered more than improving segmentation alone. Carefully chosen 256-pixel crops supported training, while full-image fine-tuning improved local validation from 0.490 to 0.520. Their best individual validation model used a ResNet34 encoder trained for more than 300 epochs.

The approach clustered each class separately and used GMM models with either four or three clusters per label. The ensemble combined these models with pseudo-labeled variants using probability thresholds of 0.9 and 0.1. Four clusters per label performed better on the leaderboard despite three clusters giving stronger cross-validation results, making ensembling central to handling the validation mismatch. The author reports a submission scoring 0.97488 with 0.968 cross-validation.

The team used CNN ensembles with complementary image resizing strategies that preserved or distorted aspect ratio. Combining those strategies improved scores by about 0.1–0.15, potentially because stretching retained more usable detail for thin plankton. They also trained networks on four levels of hierarchical labels and combined predictions through conditional probabilities and consistency constraints. Hierarchical ensembles yielded another reported improvement of about 0.1–0.15, while unknown and miscellaneous classes remained challenging.

The post identifies the SZU_N606 entry as an instance-segmentation solution for the video segmentation challenge. It names separate training and testing scripts. It provides no architecture, training configuration, validation method, or numerical results.

solution_title: 36th place solution: agentic workflow and chatGPT is all you need
solution_summary: The submission contained 400 task-specific static-shape ONNX programs, optimized by replacing bulky grid-processing pipelines with compact symbolic representations. Narrow data types, low-rank factors, final-node Einsum contractions, and native geometry operators reduced counted parameters and intermediate memory. A strict runtime-matched harness checked exact outputs, stress cases, shapes, operator legality, and graph artifacts before accepting changes. The final submission scored 7629.26, with all 400 tasks passing the local gate and a total modeled cost of 567,746.

The pipeline combined multiple 2D CNN classifiers with sequence models to incorporate information across CT slices. CNN inputs used different combinations of adjacent slices and brain, subdural, and bone windows. An MLP plus LSTM consumed embeddings from multiple models, followed by a 1D CNN plus LSTM using CNN logits, first-stage sequence logits, and position metadata. The author identified sequence modeling as the key component and reported stable performance without a shakeup.

The final solution averaged EncNet and U-Net-style segmentation models with diverse backbones and image resolutions. Models were averaged across four folds, with EncNet additionally combining 512- and 1024-pixel variants. Crop, rotation, and distortion augmentation, Dice-based losses, and model-specific test-time augmentation supported performance. Classification and segmentation thresholds plus removal of small predicted regions completed the pipeline; focal loss and lower image resolutions performed poorly.

The author formulated trajectory prediction as classification by clustering validation trajectories into target classes. Classification candidates were reduced to three trajectories through a distance-based merge with probability-weighted coordinates and summed probabilities. The final blend combined three regression models with classification models using 500, 1,000 and 5,000 classes. This improved the public leaderboard score from 15 to 12.8.

solution_title: 35th Place Solution - Basic MPNN & First Medal
solution_summary: Each scalar coupling was represented by its own molecular graph and modeled with a message-passing neural network. Connectivity depended on coupling type, adding edges to the target atoms and relevant shortest-path atoms while expressing geometry relative to those atoms. Fully bidirectional graphs were particularly valuable, and small amounts of dropout and batch normalization improved the initial transformation. The author trained one model per coupling type, eight models total, without ensembling.

The solution classified football events using EfficientNet-B1 on 11 channels of absolute differences between grayscale video frames. Larger images, temporally varying affine augmentation, and Gaussian event labels were central to the approach. Five models trained with different CV splits were ensembled, and additional manual annotations improved the reported score to 0.792. CPU video preprocessing and GPU difference and batch construction made inference fit within the time limit.
compute: CPU preprocessing and GPU batch construction; six models fit the inference time limit, with five submitted.

solution_summary: The solution used DeBERTa-v3 models on essays assembled from ordered discourses marked with discourse types and special tokens. Diverse preprocessing, auxiliary ranking and topic targets, and different discourse heads contributed complementary predictions. Pretraining on earlier Feedback Prize essays and one round of soft pseudo-labeling supported the neural models. Averaged second-level predictions and essay metadata were passed to a discourse-level LightGBM stacker without further postprocessing.

The solution generates adversarial examples using the basic iterative method. Its central modification is to blur gradients by convolving them with a Gaussian filter. The author describes this as regularization that improves transferability, allowing attacks to affect many types of models simultaneously.

The post links to a submission notebook and reports its private leaderboard performance. It says the linked approach can be pickled and deployed for live predictions. No modeling or training details are provided in the post itself.

The solution averaged six weekly time-series models with equal weights and then adjusted Christmas forecasts for shifts in the holiday's weekday. Models forecast each department across stores, reflecting the observation that seasonal patterns were primarily department-specific. Including the fourier.arima component improved the reported final score from about 2320 to around 2300. That component added roughly two hours to the 30–40 minute runtime of the remaining models.
compute: Best single model: ~5 minutes; ensemble without fourier.arima: 30–40 minutes; including it adds ~2 hours.

Additional agents contribute feature-engineering ideas and modeling insights through shared knowledge and packaged research tasks. Reported single-model results reached CV 0.97070 and leaderboard 0.97174 for RealMLP, and CV 0.97020 and leaderboard 0.97030 for XGBoost. The post emphasizes the agent workflow without detailing the final ensemble configuration or specific new features.

solution_summary: The solution used a four-output ResNet34 classifier to route images to separate defect-specific FPN segmentation models with EfficientNet-B2 encoders. Each segmenter's training set combined all positive examples with classifier-selected candidates, reducing class imbalance. Training progressed from binary cross-entropy to Lovasz hinge loss and cycled through several crop sizes within each epoch. Class-specific classification and pixel thresholds, together with minimum mask size filtering, controlled false positives.
compute: Initially borrowed a GTX 1080, then trained locally on an RTX 2070; final training ran 24 hours per day after October 18.

solution_summary: The author built a fully convolutional sequence-to-sequence model using FAIR's toolkit and its English–French architecture. Training used about five million examples from eight Russian data files, retaining all non-self tokens and 10% of self tokens. A 20K source BPE vocabulary excluding digits and an approximately 2K target vocabulary gave the best results. The Russian model scored 0.9928 without output post-processing, despite training ending before full convergence.
compute: Single Tesla V100 on AWS p3.2xlarge; 17 hours, 13 epochs

solution_title: Homesite Quote Conversion, Winners' Interview: 3rd place, Team New Model Army | CAD & QuY
solution_summary: The authors built a multistage stacked ensemble using many dataset transformations and model families. Integer encodings, response-rate encodings and differences between correlated numeric variables were combined to strengthen individual models. They retained even weak first-level predictors to provide diversity and abandoned feature selection after finding nearly all variables relevant. Bayesian optimization tuned the pipeline, and cross-validation showed that fold variability was substantial relative to differences among strong ensemble mixers.
compute: Multithreaded XGBoost ensemble training took under an hour; a 10-bag ran overnight on a 16GB/i7 Macbook Pro.

solution_summary: The author cleaned the validation data and trained transformer models with ranking loss across five folds. Additional experiments trained on JTCC toxicity labels, with the toxic category proving more useful than separately combining category predictions. Retraining JTCC-pretrained models on cleaned ranking data slightly improved cross-validation. The final ensemble combined base transformer models with seven-fold TF-IDF and FastText models, while public leaderboard scores were considered poorly correlated with validation.

solution_title: private LB: above 0.94568, public LB: 0.947 solution
solution_summary: The solution used cleaned signals and added synthetic training samples by summing two five-channel signal segments. Two LightGBM regression models with different feature sets supplied additional inputs to modified WaveNet models. Dropout, slower learning-rate reductions, sequence reversal augmentation, and alternative class weighting helped train diverse models with different precision and recall behavior. The final predictions ensembled several WaveNet outputs, while poor predictions near sequence boundaries remained a limitation.

solution_title: 31st place silver medal solution - My first competition medal
solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned ai4bharat/indicwav2vec_v1_bengali with filtered competition audio and additional speech datasets. Selecting audio with MOS at least 2 and randomly repartitioning the supplied training and validation audio improved the leaderboard score to 0.430. Training used reverberation, speed and volume perturbations, and background noise, alongside a 5-gram language model built from competition and external text. Punctuation restoration and speech enhancement attempts were unsuccessful.

The solution used an ImageNet-pretrained WiderResnet38 U-Net with reflection padding from 101×101 to 128×128 and several geometric and intensity augmentations. Training proceeded through 500 epochs with Adam and BCE, another 500 epochs with a lower learning rate and Lovasz loss, and an SGD phase with cosine scheduling. Long training and selecting checkpoints using the leaderboard metric mattered more than validation-loss early stopping. Horizontal-flip inference and snapshot ensembling were combined with mask averaging across four folds, yielding a reported private score of 0.881. Wrapping reflected borders back into predictions helped one standalone submission substantially but slightly reduced the final ensemble score.
compute: 1080 Ti GPU; approximately 9 hours for 500 epochs

solution_summary: The solution ensembled self-attention neural networks with LightGBM models adapted from public kernels. The neural model encoded session history with a Transformer encoder and joined average- and max-pooled history representations with current assessment features. Features included per-session event counts and durations, plus prior correct and incorrect counts for the queried assessment. The network used mean absolute error, and optimized rounding thresholds converted continuous predictions into accuracy groups by maximizing quadratic weighted kappa.

The team retained a public notebook's detections and link probabilities and added small 3D CNNs to verify divisions and cell links using original-resolution crops. Their pipeline recovered confident discarded detections, relinked tracks with motion information and a committee, filled gaps, and added or vetoed divisions. Averaging multiple judges and recovery improved both leaderboards, but public-score-based component selection transferred poorly to the private embryo. The safe final submission scored 0.92921 privately, while a later submission that restored a rejected component reached 0.93517.
models_pretrained: ["Biohub 0.947 LB public notebook detection and linking models", "biohub-x138 coordinate refinement head"]

solution_summary: The solution trained a residual-encoder 3D U-Net from scratch to predict multichannel aneurysm blobs. It cropped a central superior ROI, standardized image orientation and spacing, and optimized binary cross-entropy over the hardest 20% of voxels. Inference used a single model with maximum aggregation across voxels and patches. Successful submissions used a 1500-epoch checkpoint and achieved 0.83 on both leaderboards; later checkpoints and more elaborate inference encountered timeouts.

external_data: ["ADAM", "Large IA Segmentation dataset", "INSTED", "Lausanne TOF-MRA Aneurysm Cohort", "Royal Brisbane TOFMRA Intracranial Aneurysm Database", "Jianxiaokuang aneurysm dataset"]

solution_summary: The final solution blended store-specific and global LightGBM regressors with Keras and fastai tabular neural networks. Features included prices, calendar information, sales lags, rolling statistics, and category-level sales encodings. Three carefully chosen temporal validation windows guided model and blend selection, while model diversity reduced variability across windows. A weighted geometric blend excluded the Keras prediction on the final forecast day because of an anomalous spike. Local validation was 0.549 and the private score was 0.552.

solution_title: 6th Place Solution: A Tracker That Teaches Itself
solution_summary: The solution jointly detected cells and predicted parent links from three native-resolution frames using six models across two architectures. Each model rescored shared candidate links with its own LightGBM model, and averaged probabilities fed a global ILP for tracks and divisions. Sparse-label training combined masked unknown regions, a cell-count prior, and repeated whole-pipeline teacher–student pseudo-labeling. Test-time augmentation and drift correction were especially valuable, and the final submission scored 0.953 privately, with another checkpoint selection reaching 0.955.
compute: T4 inference used fp16 for a 3.5× speedup over emulated bf16, allowing six models within 12 hours.

solution_summary: The solution combined information from frames t, t-5, and t-10, using 1×1 convolutions to reduce computation. Training and prediction were restricted to the first 105 frames. Post-processing required detections to appear in both camera views and removed nearby duplicate detections through repeated temporal filtering.

The solution combined LoFTR and DKM matches, using LoFTR on full images and both models on promising cropped regions. K-means selected crop centers, and bidirectional homography warping produced additional correspondences. Radius NMS reduced redundant points, while tuned VSAC estimated the fundamental matrix faster without reducing the final score. Inference used a longest image side of 1080 pixels; several additional crop, filtering, and augmentation ideas were not retained.

The solution used a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-14B retrieval model followed by a fine-tuned Qwen-72B option-scoring stage. Retrieval training used SFR-Embedding-2_R as a seed model to obtain 100 negative instances and ran for 20 epochs. The larger model was fine-tuned with QLoRA, quantized with GPTQ, and used option log probabilities to sort candidates within groups. Synthetic data improved recall but was excluded because it did not improve the overall score.

The solution combined DenseNet121 and ResNet101 metric-learning descriptors into a weighted, normalized 2560-dimensional representation. solution_summary: The solution emphasizes feature engineering for malware classification. The author constructed approximately 28,000 features organized into nine feature sets.
