solution_summary: The solution used a single Whisper medium model with beam size four. Training data was cleaned using host-provided metadata, and roughly 80% of the dataset was presented as paired audio combinations to accelerate training and reduce annotation noise effects. SpecAugment, SpecAugment++, and CutOut provided augmentation. Correctly handling audio longer than 30 seconds and sentences longer than 448 tokens improved the leaderboard score from 0.43 to 0.38.

The author describes an ensemble of more than ten XGBoost models, more than ten LightGBM models, and approximately twenty neural networks. Ten-fold out-of-fold predictions were used with Ridge as the second-level model. The best individual XGBoost scored 1115.89595 on the private leaderboard, while the best neural network scored 1122.06610. The post asks why the combined solution underperformed despite competitive individual models.

solution_title: 76th Private/11th Public - CSIRO Biomass Prediction Pipeline
solution_summary: The pipeline combined two S5-based multiple-instance models with an attention-based uncertainty model using DINOv3 embeddings. Multiscale crops, vegetation indices, and SigLIP semantic similarities supplied complementary information. Grouped cross-validation, fold-specific scaling, and test-time augmentation supported the individual models. Per-target ensemble weights and physical constraints improved weighted R² from 0.7865 for simple averaging to 0.7901.

The final solution equally averaged Qwen3-1.7B-base, a triplet-trained BGE encoder, and three DeBERTa-v3 models, all using online learning. Qwen benefited from prompt refinement and LoRA pretraining on roughly 6,000 synthetic examples checked by a second language model. Hard negative mining improved BGE, while cross-rule negative augmentation improved the smaller DeBERTa models. Local validation correlated poorly with leaderboard results, and slower embedding models and a LightGBM stack were discarded.

The solution extended a public baseline with 89 matchup features describing seeds, Elo, GLM team quality, and possession-based team efficiency. A conservative XGBoost regressor predicted score margins, with overtime statistics normalized before season summaries were built. Leave-one-season-out predictions supported separate men's and women's isotonic calibration and light tail sharpening. Seasonal model margins were averaged for submission, achieving reported out-of-fold margin MAE of 9.2418 and calibrated Brier score of 0.16272.

solution_title: [22nd] place solution: Only Wifi Models + Public Post Processing + Pseudo labels
solution_summary: The solution used only Wi-Fi BSSID and RSSI features, with a sequential RNN as its strongest model. Site-specific LSTMs and an MLP added diversity to the ensemble, which scored about 4.8–4.9 before post-processing. Public post-processing methods with optimized cost minimization improved the score to 3.57. Retraining with post-processed test predictions as pseudo-labels and adding those models to the ensemble yielded a final reported score of 3.43.

The team blended predictions from several public notebook pipelines using fixed weights. They identified extreme essay scores as disproportionately important under RMSE and trained a separate LightGBM classifier to detect essays scoring 6.0. Predictions with high classifier confidence were replaced with 5.5, improving the ensemble; the classifier achieved approximately 0.90 ROC AUC.

solution_title: 1st Place solution of category "BigQuery ML Models built in SQL"
solution_summary: The author built a SQL-only solution using BigQuery's basic machine-learning capabilities. Features represented turns, intersection clusters, and population by ZIP code. Separate detailed and general linear-regression models were trained per target, with the general models handling unknown intersections. No cross-validation or grid search was used, and sandbox quotas limited experimentation.
compute: BigQuery sandbox quotas restricted training to a few models per week.

solution_summary: The author used ten repeats of stratified ten-fold validation to guide feature engineering and model selection. Useful features included kidney-failure, sums of pain-related features, and selected polynomial feature pairs. Variance filtering at 0.1 was applied to five classifiers, which were combined in an unweighted ensemble. The final public and private scores were 0.37089 and 0.52302; clustering did not improve validation.

The solution used separate PCA and SVD transformations for cell and gene features, Gaussian rank scaling, and importance-selected raw feature subsets. Two neural models used ResNet and highway fully connected architectures, trained with Adam, label smoothing, and OneCycleLR. Predictions were averaged across two models, three seeds per model, and five folds, producing a reported score of 0.01609. TabNet, convolutional approaches, non-scored-target pretraining, clustering, DeepFM, and autoencoders did not help.

The author log-transformed all input features and combined six tree-based models through hill-climbing ensembling. Adding a Nyström logistic regression model and then a neural network increased diversity and produced incremental leaderboard gains to 0.79101. The selected submission was another ensemble with a slightly higher public score, whose exact composition was not specified. PCA, t-SNE, clustering, and cluster target encoding did not improve performance.

The team used Network Deconvolution to distinguish direct dependencies in inferred networks. They report that it improved almost every adjacency matrix they tried. The author also published a Python implementation alongside the original authors' MATLAB version. The full submission pipeline is deferred to a separate post.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution for the CAFA 6 Protein Function Prediction
solution_summary: GOAlpha combined seven predictors spanning protein sequence, interaction networks, structure, domains, and biomedical literature. An XGBoost learning-to-rank model integrated their scores with GO term frequency and species features. Model selection used 1,000 held-out experimentally annotated proteins sampled to match the test species distribution. Sequence predictors were strongest individually, while structural and literature evidence added complementary signals; the final private score was 0.52430.
compute: Modern GPU servers; component training under one day, inference within one day, final learning-to-rank integration a few hours.
external_data: ["SwissProt, GOA, and GO functional annotations", "Protein-protein interaction network", "Biomedical literature"]

solution_summary: The solution accelerated candidate scoring through batch evaluation, threshold-based individual rescoring, and a persistent cache. Batched simulated annealing searched word permutations with several neighborhood operations, multiple retained candidates, and partial shuffling. For example 4, beam search supplied strong initial sequences for annealing. Combining complementary sequences from two teammates and refining them reduced the example 5 score from roughly 31.2–31.4 to around 30.0.

The solution combined EfficientNetV2-S and HGUNet sound-event detectors with a ProtoSSM branch built on Perch embeddings. Pretraining on birds and non-birds substantially improved coverage, while carefully selected soft pseudo labels improved training further. Rank blending, temporal and contextual gates, and taxonomic smoothing combined the branches. The selected configuration reported a public score of 0.960, with CPU inference taking approximately 60 minutes.
compute: NVIDIA A100; approximately 8 hours per fold across 4 folds; Kaggle CPU inference approximately 60 minutes.

solution_summary: The author selected two separate notebooks representing marker-based exfiltration and a one-step email confused-deputy attack. The competition took the maximum score of the selected notebooks rather than blending them. Marker-based exfiltration collapsed to zero privately, whereas the confused-deputy notebook transferred from 29.730 publicly to 29.670 privately. Hybrid attack families failed on both evaluations, making separate notebook selection decisive.

solution_title: 2nd Place - Stacking Transformer and Linear Regression
solution_summary: The final approach stacked a transformer on a linear regression model by training it to predict the regression residuals and summing their predictions. The regression used sinusoidal calendar features and effects for GDP, store, product, country, and holidays. The author also described a standalone transformer improved with two rounds of pseudo-labeling and median aggregation across five seeds. Choosing the future annual trend multiplier was particularly consequential; the final submission choices used a constant 1.06 multiplier and a mildly increasing linear multiplier. The stacked model achieved a private score of 0.04498.

The solution combined log-mel spectrograms, temporal waveform statistics, and clip length with a nine-layer CNN. Axis-specific pooling treated time and frequency differently, and some models included squeeze-and-excitation blocks and highway connections. Training used noisy-data pretraining, label smoothing, mixup, random five-second crops, and padding, followed by three-way test-time augmentation. A neural stacker learned class-specific ensemble weights and label correlations, improving CV from 0.89763 for a single model to 0.9108.

The solution ensembles modified RNAdegformer models, a convolutional model with residual base-pair-probability attention and bidirectional LSTMs, and a Transformer with BPP attention bias. RNA sequences and EternaFold BPP matrices provide the main inputs, with ContraFold used in some variants. Training first uses a lower signal-to-noise threshold and then fine-tunes on cleaner examples; predicted reactivity errors also guide pseudo-label selection. Five-fold validation gives the best individual model a CV score of 0.11976 and a private score of 0.14124.

The team ensembled segmentation networks with classification predictions to suppress false positives. Segmentation models used EfficientNet and SE backbones with FPN, LinkNet, and U-Net architectures, while classification was handled through a segmentation network with an additional fully connected head. Classification thresholds and class-specific mask-size filtering produced approximately 0.670 out-of-fold Dice and 0.6783 public leaderboard score. Restoring masks for otherwise empty predictions and taking mask unions increased the public score to 0.6800. An abandoned ensemble variant ultimately achieved their best reported private score of 0.67254 but was not selected.

The solution used a modified DeepAR LSTM network trained with Tweedie loss and recursive 28-day forecasts during training. Inputs combined sales lags and moving averages with calendar, event, price, category, SNAP, and zero-sales features. Checkpoints were selected by their mean WRMSSE across 14 historical periods because scores varied substantially across time. Final predictions combined 43 models, including models trained with and without dropout; alternative architectures, losses, and forecast reconciliation did not improve the approach.

The solution blended separate study classifiers and image detectors using only competition data in its final pipeline. Nine study models across five folds used cross-entropy classification with auxiliary U-Net segmentation, while EfficientDet and YOLO provided bounding boxes. Detection outputs were fused with weighted boxes fusion, and the none score combined box confidence with negative and atypical study probabilities. Study-grouped validation and auxiliary tasks supported generalization; unified classification-detection models were competitive but slightly weaker than separate models.

The author trained LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost regressors using ideas from public notebooks. They then averaged five models, including contributions from public GAM approaches, reaching a public score of 6.58 and a private score of 7.44. Rounding predictions and adding one to every prediction further improved the public score to 5.596 and the private score to 6.47.

The system converted silence-trimmed audio into normalized mel-spectrograms and combined a custom CNN with VGG16 batch normalization. Its four-stage warm-up pipeline moved from noisy data to curated data and then selectively reincorporated reliable noisy samples. SpecMix replaced time and frequency regions between samples, with targets weighted by the contributed pixels. Predictions were averaged across training stages, architectures, and overlapping audio windows; the supplied notebooks achieved public lwlrap of 0.738.
compute: Nvidia RTX 2080 ti, Intel Core i7 4790k, 24 GB RAM; public-test inference under 1000 seconds

solution_summary: The solution combined a raw-waveform HGNetB0 model, a mel-spectrogram EfficientNetB0 model, and a model concatenating both feature streams. Training used random five-second clips, mixup, and binary cross entropy, with spectrum cutout augmentation. A weighted ensemble achieved 0.743960 public and 0.687173 private scores, and inference used OpenVINO.

The solution used an iteratively annotated YOLOv5 detector to crop salient whale bodies before training identity embedding models. ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet and NFNet backbones used GeM pooling, BNNeck, and ArcFace or AdaFace, with texture-focused augmentation and mixup to reduce overfitting. Iterative pseudo-labeling progressively expanded training data and incorporated body and part models. Concatenated embeddings and cross-fold submission merging produced an ensemble, with reported leaderboard performance reaching 0.886 during pseudo-label iterations.

The solution generated extensive synthetic seismic data by forward modeling blended velocity maps and trained a modified EVA02 Vision Transformer. Its architecture separated early intra-channel processing from later shared processing and decoded spatial predictions with pixel shuffle. Muon with auxiliary AdamW improved optimization, followed by three training stages with increasing resolution and final training on validation data. A weighted blend of stage models used clipping and rounding; correcting an inference preprocessing mismatch yielded public/private scores of 7.96/7.99.
compute: More than 13 TB storage and approximately 5.5 days on 4× A100 SXM 80G.

solution_summary: The post thanks the organizers and expresses appreciation for the Santa competition format. It links to a GitHub repository containing code and an English/Japanese solution explanation. The provided text contains no technical description of the approach.

The solution centered on recovering leaked targets through ordered row and column relationships. The author identified 100 useful column sets of length 40, yielding 7,841 leaky test rows. For the machine-learning component, they used Emmanuel Perry's public kernel reported at 1.37 on the leaderboard. Other modeling experiments and additional column sets were not retained or offered little benefit.

The author describes their detector, image-level prediction, and post-processing contribution to a team solution. Pseudo-labels from the public test set, BIMCV, and RICORD improved the reported YOLOv5x opacity cross-validation score to 0.53870. Data cleaning removed side-view images and validation-related duplicates, while post-processing fused boxes and adjusted confidence using image-level probabilities. The final submission combined Yolotrs-384, Yolov5x-640, and a pseudo-label-trained Yolov5x-512, all with test-time augmentation.

solution_title: My engineering approach to the problem. #49
solution_summary: The author uses a baseline model after abandoning attempts to train their own. Training-set embeddings are precomputed and stored in SQLite to accelerate evaluation. Embeddings from an Open Images subset act as a non-landmark filter, reducing the remaining dataset by about tenfold. The approach scored around 0.6 in tests on 2019 competition data, but transferred less successfully to this contest, and SIFT local scoring offered little benefit.

solution_title: 21st - A Bag of Words is All You Need
solution_summary: The model represented each notebook cell as a single token, disregarding sentence grammar. Cell embeddings came from sparse-dense multiplication of TF-IDF matrices and word or word-ngram embeddings, enabling global attention across every cell in a document. The BERT-like architecture optionally biased attention using an identity matrix or character-ngram similarity. Training took about 20 minutes per epoch, and the highest-scoring notebook used no external data.
compute: About 20 minutes per training epoch; hardware unspecified.

solution_title: 3rd place, team Dmitry&Leustagos, members: Lucas Silva, Dmitry Efimov
solution_summary: The solution trains several model families, including gradient boosting, random forests, logistic regression, glmnet models, and libFM factorization machines. Training scripts indicate multiple feature variants, including frequency and occurrence representations. Models are trained in two successive groups and then combined by a final ensembling script to produce test predictions. The post mainly documents the software environment and execution sequence, without reporting evaluation scores or ensemble details.
compute: Windows 7 Professional x64 or Ubuntu 12.04; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_title: We were late for seconds, please accept our writeup
Throughput and Survival: A Source-Verified Model of the JED Attack Benchmark
solution_summary: The author inspected the shipped evaluator and selected attacks using a locally constructed battery of plausible hidden guardrails. The final entry paired a confused-deputy submission with a marker-exfiltration hedge, prioritizing transfer across defenses over public scores. Model-specific prompts minimized generated output so more independent candidates could be replayed within the evaluation budget. The selected deputy scored 24.99 publicly and 25.02 privately, while marker submissions scoring above 90 publicly collapsed to zero privately.

The author built two compact 1D CNN variants with residual connections and dilated and standard convolutions. Training used mixup, while preprocessing diversity came from two bandpass frequency ranges. Averaging the CNN variants and preprocessing variants improved performance, and training on the whole dataset raised the public score further. Stacking with a public-notebook CQT model produced a reported public score of 0.8836.

The final submission averaged several variations of a stacked prediction pipeline. The second-level model was ridge regression, using both out-of-fold predictions and predictions on training examples. Gaussian noise reduced overfitting in this blending stage, while Optuna optimized ridge regularization and feature scales. The final submission scored 0.15665 publicly and 0.15741 privately.

solution_title: 6th place solution - with a visualization of our Jaccard scores over time
solution_summary: The team emphasized architecture diversity and public leaderboard feedback because local cross-validation appeared unreliable. They mapped model logits to character positions so models with different tokenizers could be combined, and normalized logits to account for scale differences. The final weighted ensemble combined Roberta Large, Muril Large, Rembert Large, Xlm Info Large, and Wechsel models. This progression improved the public score from 0.785 for the initial XLM Roberta Large approach to 0.821.

solution_summary: The solution predicted sentence discourse types using Persuade 2.0 annotations and inserted those labels into essays before training neural scoring models. This structural information improved individual models by approximately 0.005–0.006 on both cross-validation and the leaderboard. DeBERTa and Longformer models with varied pooling supplied out-of-fold predictions to a LightGBM stacker alongside essay statistics, spelling-error counts, and features from a previous competition model. Validation balanced scores and topics across four folds, and three LightGBM seeds were blended for stability. The reported stack achieved 0.85891 CV and 0.835 private score, although later analysis suggested stronger performance on Persuade-derived data than on Kaggle-only data.

solution_summary: The final solution ensembled XGBoost, LightGBM, a neural network, a field-aware factorization machine, a regularized greedy forest, and public models. Predictions were combined using a geometric mean. The author reported component scores between 280 and 284 and found feature engineering difficult to improve.

solution_title: My solution for the RSNA 2024 Lumbar Spine Degenerative Classification, using only the competition data
solution_summary: The pipeline used YOLO to locate lumbar spine levels and guide condition-specific cropping. Spinal canal coordinates identified the three closest axial slices and established left and right directions in sagittal images. Dedicated EfficientNetB0 backbones processed spinal canal, neural foraminal, and subarticular image groups, with a dense network predicting severity for five categories. The shared pretrained model was then fine-tuned separately for each lumbar spine level.

solution_title: Getting to Rank 25 by Teaching LLMs to Golf
solution_summary: The author used Claude, GPT-5, and Gemini agents to develop and shorten Python solutions for ARC tasks. The final workflow combined task descriptions based on Anchors, Clues, and Transforms with an expanding checklist of code-golf tricks, structured design reviews, and iterative testing. A grammar of grid transformations further constrained solution search toward reusable compact patterns. Approximately 370 problems were primarily golfed by agents, and solutions for at least three problems beat the leaderboard best during the final week.
frameworks_libraries: ["Claude Code", "Gemini Canvas", "GPT5 Codex", "Codex on the Web"]

solution_summary: The solution ensembled seven image-to-sequence models with EfficientNet encoders and LSTM decoders. Training incorporated millions of RDKit-rendered extra molecules, image morphology augmentations, small rotations, and border cropping. Beam search generated candidate strings, which were normalized with RDKit before majority voting and validity-based fallback. The final submission scored 1.32 on the public leaderboard and 1.31 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Local machine with a Quadro RTX 6000 GPU.

solution_summary: The solution uses a flat classifier that first retrieves candidate classes by cosine similarity to class centroids, then applies a separate logistic regression classifier to each candidate. Training examples are assigned to nearby candidate classes to construct the binary classifiers' datasets. Text features use a modified TF-IDF weighting followed by L2 normalization. The combined classifier achieved LBMaF 0.33025, compared with 0.28931 for the nearest-centroid baseline and 0.23088 for k-NN.
compute: 32GB RAM required; prefetch may exceed 15 hours. Reported NCC+BC training time is 15 hours and prediction time is 2 hours.

solution_summary: The author links code for their competition algorithm but gives little detail about the method. They report using the small-image version of the dataset because they started late. They expect better results at the original image size, but provide no supporting experiment or score.

The author shares a notebook about searching for blending weights with Optuna. The post identifies automated blend-weight tuning as its approach. It provides no details about the component models, validation, or achieved results.

The solution combined an ensemble predicting unsafe outcomes with another ensemble ranking event cases, using a probability formula to combine them. The author defined the unsafe target using an event-time cutoff and trained the ranking models on logit-transformed ranks. Logit adjustments and scaling improved the final scores, alongside many AutoGluon models and additional target ensembles. Feature changes were limited to HLA sum recalculation, preserving an unusually informative original column, and rounding age features.

The selected submission combined ResNeXt50, EfficientNet-B3, and ViT models trained with five folds and additional 2019 data. Training used image augmentation, Adam, and cosine annealing after warmup, while heavier test-time augmentation worked best for this submission. It scored 0.8984 on the private leaderboard. An unselected, lighter ResNeXt50 and EfficientNet-B1 submission with light test-time augmentation scored 0.8993; SnapMix, CutMix, and pseudo-labeling did not help.

The author identifies XGBoost with a linear booster as the best single model. Code for reproducing the competition solution is linked on GitHub. The detailed approach is deferred to a PDF, so the supplied text provides no further pipeline or evaluation details.

The pipeline used 3D organ segmentation followed by organ-specific classification pipelines. Liver, kidney, and spleen shared a sequence model, while bowel and extravasation used two-stage training with image-level supervision and frozen feature extractors. Series selection based on aortic attenuation, segmentation-guided crops, and metric-weighted losses were important design choices. Multiplicative post-processing tuned on out-of-fold predictions improved mean CV loss from 0.3994 to 0.3889.

solution_title: What is the secret of getting 0.9363015?
solution_summary: The team optimized gift assignments with Google OR-Tools min-cost max-flow over roughly 100 gift types per run to fit memory. A repeated repair procedure fixed twins and triplets assigned different gifts by reserving their chosen gifts and rerunning flow for the remaining children. Larger optimization blocks made that repair unstable or nonterminating. They also tried mixed-integer programming over about 40 gift types per run, but improvement stopped at 0.9356.
compute: Approximately 16 GB memory; including all unhappy edges exceeded available memory.

solution_summary: The author formulated gift matching as an integer program resembling a transportation model. Assignment variables were restricted to twin-related pairs and pairs appearing in child or gift preference lists to keep the model manageable. Penalized slack variables represented assignments outside those preference lists, and objective coefficients were scaled to integers. The implementation used C++ with Gurobi, with an MPS export supplied for compatibility with other solvers.

solution_title: Solution from Dawnbreaker on steroids in top-40
solution_summary: The solution ensembled ResNet50, DenseNet121, DenseNet169, and SE-ResNext models trained with random crops and horizontal flips. A separate ResNet50 classifier detected non-landmarks using manually labeled examples. The four-network ensemble scored 0.159 on the public leaderboard, compared with 0.139 for three networks. A late distance-based penalty for recognition classes added about 0.002 to the score.

solution_title: 14th Place Solution : pretrained with pseudo labels
solution_summary: The final solution averaged four DeBERTa and ELECTRA model configurations with equal weights using character-level predictions. Its main improvement came from pseudo-labels, used both for intermediate pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning and for expanding each fold's training data. Training included mixup, random masking, multi-sample dropout, and memory-saving optimization techniques. The selected submission achieved a private score of 0.892; the authors acknowledged some residual pseudo-label leakage in the final CV score of 0.898527.

solution_title: Creatures of Habit:  Neil Schneider on placing second in the dunnhumby Shopper Challenge
solution_summary: The approach modeled customer spending separately by weekday to capture habitual differences in shopping behavior. Spend predictions targeted the highest-density spending ranges rather than conventional regression estimates. SAS handled data manipulation and range construction, while R's gbm package supplied boosted regression models. Inventory-control time series methods and ordinary regression performed poorly.

The solution extended a shared baseline with improved answer parsing and repeated-generation voting. It stopped iterations early when the leading answer had sufficient support, transferring saved effort to later problems. Experiments supported allocating about 20–21 iterations to half the problems and 10–11 to the rest. Student–teacher validation, early difficulty identification, and multiple-choice follow-up rounds were explored but did not produce stable validation and public leaderboard results.

The final submission combined EfficientNetV2-M and EfficientNet-B3 classifiers with YOLO-M and YOLO-X detectors for model diversity. Tuning data augmentation was the main breakthrough in controlling overfitting after a prolonged period of unsuccessful experiments. The four-model ensemble matched the reported LB 6.29 and PB 6.15 scores of the EfficientNetV2-M plus YOLO-X configuration with test-time augmentation. Classification augmentation and YOLO-X hyperparameters remained incompletely tuned.

The author modified an existing ensemble pipeline by replacing stratified folds with multilabel stratified folds. This improved individual model performance but reduced ensemble performance on both public and private scores. They suggested that greater randomness in validation splits might provide more useful ensemble diversity.

solution_title: [5th solution]: Ensemble of CNN1d, Transformer, Mamba models
solution_summary: The solution treated molecular strings as character sequences and ensembled CNN1D, transformer, and Mamba models for three-target multilabel prediction. A small convolution learned character combinations, while tuned batch normalization was particularly important for the large-batch CNN. Different architectures used different folds to improve ensemble diversity within the training budget. Post-competition comparisons suggested that the transformer was the most robust architecture.
compute: HP Z8 Fury-G5 workstation; per-fold training took 7 hours for CNN1D, 28 hours for transformer, and 36 hours for Mamba.

solution_summary: The solution retrieved candidates using a co-visitation matrix and weighted bidirectional item similarities for click-to-click and click-to-cart interactions. A LightGBM binary classifier ranked candidates using session, item, session–item, similarity, and word2vec embedding features. Validation followed Radek’s CV strategy, and online training combined train_v1, train_v2, and valid. The single model achieved a weighted local recall@20 of 0.5915 and a leaderboard score of 0.60335; blending probabilities with a previously submitted model increased the score to 0.60341.

solution_title: Open sourcing my solution [2D Model, PyTorch]
solution_summary: The team combined 2D images with DICOM metadata to help identify the vertebrae present in each slice. They engineered slice-position features and used geometric, brightness, and distortion augmentations. Training used a cosine schedule with warmup and restarts, and the best submission used six epochs. Segmentation, region-of-interest cropping, and 2.5D modeling were suggested as future improvements.
compute: Kaggle GPUs and notebooks; roughly 10 hours per epoch; best submission trained for 6 epochs.

solution_summary: The author evaluated several text-to-image models and selected DMD2 and SDXL Flash for final submissions. DMD2's model-card demo provided a strong starting point, with simple parameter adjustments adding approximately 0.02 and showing good stability. SDXL Flash reached 0.67 on the public leaderboard with demo code and improved through basic tuning, but repeated submissions varied substantially. Earlier experiments included SDXL Base, Turbo, Hyper, and SANA 1.5.

solution_title: Sparrow for square packing | 108th Place Solution
solution_summary: The solution selected packing strategies by configuration size, using unrestricted angle optimization for N ≤ 100, CMA-ES optimization of two orientations for N between 120 and 130, and public baselines elsewhere. Modified Sparrow and jagua-rs supported square packing by minimizing the larger dimension, first expanding the smaller dimension and then shrinking both uniformly. A custom C++ simulated annealing implementation further refined small configurations. The final submission improved 67 of 200 configurations and reported a 0.175% improvement over the public baseline.

The author built a hill-climbing ensemble of public notebook approaches, averaged across five seeds and ten-fold cross-validation. Essay reconstruction and word-, sentence-, and paragraph-level length and frequency aggregates improved validation and leaderboard performance. Classification models, synthetic augmentation, oversampling, and several activity-based features did not help. The approach achieved approximately 0.594 CV but suffered a private leaderboard shakeup.

The solution combined a 384×384 Swin Transformer with a larger patchwise TNT model trained on roughly 13 million images, including synthetic renderings of approved extra InChIs. Eight models were ensembled at each decoding step, balancing total weights equally between the two architectures. Beam search with width 16 improved the reported leaderboard score from 0.63 to 0.60, with expensive decoding restricted to about 20,000 images where models disagreed. RDKit validation postprocessing provided a small additional benefit.

solution_title: 419th: Tensorflow and additionally ( Vienna RNA, Scikit Learn and XG Boost)
solution_summary: The post describes RNA reactivity modeling notebooks using TensorFlow with TPU support and XGBoost regressors. Preprocessing integrates competition data with RMDB and separates experiment types. XGBoost variants use RNA folding features or simpler sequence length and experiment type encodings. Validation uses MAE, but the post does not identify a definitive final model or report numerical results.

solution_summary: The solution identified invasive hydrangea in images. Its best submission averaged 19 predictions in a bagged ensemble and achieved 0.99770 ROC-AUC. The writeup lists software dependencies but does not describe the underlying models or training procedure.

The solution combined GNN, Transformer, LSTM, and SAKT models for neutrino direction prediction. LSTM and SAKT training used a custom cross-entropy objective with nearby-area penalties, AdamW, and staged cosine learning-rate schedules. Events were grouped using line-fit predictions and metadata so each group could receive different ensemble weights. Expanding from six to thirteen groups improved the reported leaderboard score to 0.974, with a private score of 0.975.

The solution averaged class probabilities from a default LightGBM, a small neural network, and an autoencoder-based classifier. All input features were standardized without feature engineering. The autoencoder's encoder was frozen before adding classification layers, and the final predictions selected the three highest averaged probabilities. The ensemble achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.53179, outperforming its individual models.

solution_title: Transformer-based Solution & What was missing to top spots?
solution_summary: The author trained a pretrained SS-Former-S segmentation model using three neighboring slices as 2.5D input. The final prediction averaged five models trained with case-grouped stratified folds and horizontal-flip test-time augmentation. Training used 640×640 images, rotation, crop and dropout augmentations, a polynomial learning-rate schedule, and equally weighted Dice and binary cross-entropy losses. The ensemble scored 0.869 privately and 0.883 publicly; an EfficientNet-based U-Net and an ensemble with an older SSFormer version were evaluated but excluded.

Cross-validation predictions are used to optimize the ensemble, and an ANN using PCA and windowed correlation features is identified as the best standalone model. solution_title: 345th Place Solution for the NVIDIA Nemotron Model Reasoning Challenge
solution_summary: The team fine-tuned Nemotron LoRA adapters through supervised learning, emphasizing trace consistency, balanced batches, and repeated adaptation. Stratified and length-aware batching improved stability, while additional passes helped recover categories harmed by new operation examples. They normalized reasoning traces and generated targeted arithmetic examples, filtering subtraction puzzles with a rule-based solver. Category-level validation guided adapter selection, and their final reported revision reached 0.860 private accuracy.

The team combined CNN classifiers and sound-event detection models trained on expanded and cleaned bird audio data. Validation used a held-out portion of BirdCLEF 2023 while all BirdCLEF 2025 data supported training. Random audio sampling, audio mixing, focal BCE, checkpoint averaging, and pseudo-labeled soundscapes supported robustness. A 20-model ensemble reached a private score of 0.927, while the best result used six CNN and six SED models with rank-aware post-processing and ONNX inference.

solution_title: SQL feature engineering + XGBoost (.4026 private LB, 1/2 of #100 solution)
solution_summary: The author used a basic model with features largely based on Sh1ng's kernel. Additional features treated departments as if they were products, with only marginal benefit. The main contribution was SQL-based feature engineering in Postgres, adopted because the workflow needed arrays and aggregate functions beyond the initial SQLite setup. The post does not specify the model type or provide quantitative performance results.

solution_title: Late Submission Request - Writeup Published Minutes After Deadline
1st Place Solution for the Regression with an Abalone Dataset Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined OpenFE feature generation, model-specific feature selection and extensive GBDT ensembling. Models were tuned with Bayesian optimization and trained with 10-fold cross-validation, adding the original Abalone data only to training folds. A 49-model ensemble used OOF-optimized coefficients, including negative weights, followed by a 17% blend with one public ANN submission. The ensemble obtained CV RMSLE 0.14514, and a submission excluding the public notebook achieved public/private scores of 0.14372/0.14379.

solution_title: 2nd place solution - Squeezeformer + BPP Conv2D Attention
solution_summary: The solution used a modified Squeezeformer encoder with a GRU head and ALiBi positional encoding. Its most important component processed the provided base-pair probability matrix with a shallow 2D CNN and injected the result into attention as a bias. Training used signal-to-noise-weighted MAE over 200 epochs, and auxiliary structural features supplied only small gains. Seed ensembling improved public and private scores to 0.135 and 0.140, while self-supervised learning, larger models, and pseudo-labeling were not adopted.

solution_title: Public #3, Private #40 - No ensemble small enough
solution_summary: The author submitted two ensembles: a 26-OOF ensemble selected for public leaderboard performance and a 122-OOF ensemble selected for cross-validation performance. Their private scores were 0.05853 and 0.05855, respectively, despite substantially different public scores. Pruning additions using both CV and public results encouraged public leaderboard overfitting. Positive-weight hill climbing produced smaller ensembles with better private results, but those alternatives were not selected.

The solution trained a Swin Large 224 model using clean training data, metadata, and image dimensions. Training used ten folds, image augmentation, and a frozen-then-unfrozen schedule with checkpoints selected by the competition metric. Extracted embeddings fed a stacked regression model using SVR, Ridge, and linear regression. Inference used YOLOv5-derived dog/cat features and 15 augmentations, with greater ensemble weight on stacked regression and the worst out-of-fold models removed.
compute: Stronger GPUs were used to test the largest models; hardware unspecified.

solution_title: José P. González-Brenes and Matías Cortés on winning the RTA challenge
solution_summary: The final approach uses random forests trained only on the more recent dataset. Features describe time, date, weekday, neighboring routes' latest observations, and optionally recent travel-time trends. Two feature configurations are assigned to different route segments according to which worked better. Linear regression, recency-weighted regression, and autoregression were explored before settling on this approach.

The author generated approximately 6,000 features and selected several subsets using validation-set permutation importance. XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost models varied in preprocessing, features, hyperparameters, and seeds, and about 40 models were averaged. XGBoost was the strongest individual model, with single-model five-fold AMEX scores around 0.797. Feature engineering and selection consumed most of the effort, while several neural approaches, distillation, and stacking features did not help.

The solution used a compact DeepFinder-inspired volumetric network trained on randomly sampled 128-cubed patches from all seven volumes. Percentile-based normalization, spherical training labels, spatial and intensity augmentation, and regularized training supported the small architecture. Inference combined four seeds, overlapping patches, and flip and rotation augmentation, followed by connected-component filtering. It achieved public and private scores of 0.7798 and 0.7825; larger models overfit and a multicascade network did not improve results.

The author explored several WaveNet-based architectures for sensor-sequence classification and found that temporal 1D CNNs performed better than WaveNet. Experiments included multi-kernel dilated inception convolutions, a WaveNet–Transformer hybrid, and WaveNet combined with xLSTM and attention pooling. Another architecture split each sequence into equal transition and gesture segments, processing them with WaveNet and a temporal CNN respectively. The post describes architectural experiments without identifying the final submitted configuration or reporting numerical scores.

solution_title: [22nd place] From 325th in Public LB to 22nd in Private LB
solution_summary: The solution combined structured pet attributes with metadata, sentiment, text embeddings, image embeddings, and extensive aggregate features. Breed information was normalized, supplemented with predicted dog breeds, and enriched using external breed datasets. XGBoost and LightGBM regressors used this feature set, including frequency-encoded categorical variables. Final predictions averaged both regression outputs and fold-averaged optimized rounding coefficients.

solution_summary: The author built a Bayesian linear regression model in pymc3 to estimate team scoring and matchup spreads. Team-level posterior distributions modeled field-goal attempts and percentages, with a league-level error term absorbing additional variance. Win probabilities came from 5000 posterior simulations per potential matchup. Overrides for high-seed versus low-seed tournament games helped the final score.

The solution combined five biomass regression pipelines built on DinoV3 and DinoV2 representations. It varied spatial coverage through patch grids, dense sliding windows, larger patches, and a multiple instance learning transformer. Frozen embeddings, robust regression loss, seed averaging, and removal of two noisy samples helped address limited training data. The weighted ensemble achieved a public R2 of 0.779, while conventional fine-tuning and aggressive test-time augmentation caused overfitting.
compute: Feature extraction distributed across dual GPU nodes

solution_summary: The solution first trained EfficientNet-B5 on labeled data, then repeatedly fine-tuned it on test data with pseudo-labels. Limited augmentation, strong stochastic depth and dropout, and mixup with logical-OR targets helped retain sensitivity to weak signals. Images were merged along time and resized to 512×512, with vertical-flip augmentation at inference. Repeated pseudo-label training raised Public LB from 0.800 to 0.813, and the final submission averaged five high-scoring submissions.

solution_title: Avito Duplicate Ads Detection, Winners' Interview: 2nd Place, Team TheQuants | Mikel, Peter, Marios, & Sonny
solution_summary: The team engineered 587 features describing text, images, location, prices, attributes, and connected groups of ad pairs. They trained diverse base models, including bagged XGBoost and neural networks, and combined 14 predictions through random forest and XGBoost meta-models with weighted rank averaging. Temporal feature screening helped control overfitting, although their final chronological holdout became unreliable during meta-modelling. Cluster-size features were particularly useful, and the final rank average achieved a reported leaderboard score of 0.95294.

The team trained sentence-level named entity recognition models with a joint objective for dataset presence and entity boundaries. They ensembled RoBERTa with SciBERT, Conll, and BioBERT pipelines, filtering test sentences with regular expressions to fit inference limits. Limiting publications per dataset stabilized validation. Postprocessing and dataset-name string matching improved public results but hurt private performance; the unselected ensemble achieved about 0.414 privately.

The author shared an agent-swapping augmentation for predicting game-playing strength. Agent1 and agent2 were swapped during both training and inference. A simple CatBoost model with five-fold cross-validation and almost no feature engineering achieved public and private scores of 0.427 and 0.432.

The pipeline generated SN_filter predictions and pseudo labels, following the author's earlier TReNDS methodology. XGBoost stacking combined model outputs, but pseudo-label-model out-of-fold predictions made stacking prone to overfitting. Adding Gaussian noise to both out-of-fold and test predictions resolved this issue. Cross-validation and leaderboard scores were reported to be strongly correlated, allowing relatively few submissions.

The solution combined four Swin Large models with SVR and Gaussian process regressors trained on normalized 1536-dimensional image embeddings. Selected neural models used focal loss and mixup, and all models used five-pass test-time augmentation for cross-validation. Ridge and CatBoost stacking incorporated metadata and YOLOv5 animal features, with their outputs blended at weights of 0.8 and 0.2. The author also reported that an earlier Swin Large 384 submission achieved a private score of 16.975.

The final submissions blended seven strong, diverse models. One blend optimized cross-validation performance, while the other selected weights using model correlations and leaderboard scores. CNN models contributed useful diversity and improved the blend. The team retained its existing validation scheme rather than adopting a drug_id split because of time constraints.

The team combined global and finding-specific local features from densely cached multiview MRI windows using CoAtNet and CAFormer models. Training targets blended multiple report-label sources, image-first Astra assessments, and calibrated OOF predictions through two self-distillation rounds. Their models used hierarchical attention or contextual window-logit aggregation, followed by frozen-backbone fine-tuning on larger bags with reset heads. Two selected ensembles achieved 0.957 private AUC, while an unselected combination reached 0.958.

The solution fine-tunes a pretrained 1.1-billion-parameter DINOv3 backbone on paired image halves, fusing their features with two local gated convolution blocks. It predicts Green, Dead, and Clover biomass directly and derives the remaining targets through mass balance. A SigLIP semantic-feature tree ensemble contributes 25% of most final predictions, while Clover uses only DINO. Regularization, grouped cross-validation, log-space Huber loss, and target-specific calibration supported a mean CV R2 of 0.83 and a private leaderboard score of 0.74.

solution_title: A Self supervised approach for detecting gravitational waves
solution_summary: The author explored Barlow Twins training with two 1D CNNs operating directly on gravitational-wave waveforms. Signals from different detectors served as alternative views of the same underlying event, with one network handling Hanford/Livingston and the other handling Virgo. After representation learning, the frozen networks produced embeddings from all three detectors, which were concatenated for a fully connected classifier trained on 10% of the training data. The experiment scored 0.851 on the leaderboard.

The author built and submitted a vision transformer for 3D medical images. The experiment aimed to compare this architecture with Efficient3D. The post shares a linked notebook but provides no training, validation, or quantitative comparison details.

solution_title: 17th place solution summary - there is nothing special
solution_summary: The solution combined LightGBM and CatBoost predictions using a weighted geometric mean. A chronological holdout covering the final 20% of training data provided reliable model selection, while test predictions used stratified five-fold training with iteration counts estimated across three seeds. Features included frequency encodings, combined identifiers, user-level aggregates, and missingness patterns, with covariate-shift filtering and removal of raw V features. The ensemble achieved validation AUC 0.95541 and private leaderboard AUC 0.940934.

solution_title: Modular Autonomous Agent for General-Purpose Tabular Prediction
solution_summary: The solution used a modular autonomous tabular-ML workflow with a main orchestration agent and a separate exploratory-analysis agent. Reusable prompts guided baseline modeling, automatic feature generation, evaluation, and multiple candidate submissions while respecting execution time. Cross-validation informed model evaluation, but final submission selection remained a separate responsibility of the main agent. The reported public and private scores were 0.826 and 0.779.

The post describes a notebook-based Russian text-normalization pipeline using competition files, an additional Russian dataset, and downloadable supporting files. Preparatory notebook sections build frequency dictionaries saved as pickle files. With those artifacts available, running the imports and main-loop sections produces the final result. The text provides no model architecture, evaluation score, or substantive description of the normalization logic.

solution_summary: The approach combined high-resolution breast crops with an EfficientNet encoder and U-Net++ decoder for joint classification, segmentation, and auxiliary prediction. External mammography datasets supplied pretraining, while heavy augmentation and mixup helped control overfitting. A CatBoost meta-classifier combined predictions and per-breast statistics with age, site, and laterality, typically improving scores by about 0.02. The author selected submissions using leaderboard and cross-validation performance; a completed relabeling and retraining pipeline achieved a private score of 0.51 but was not selected.

The solution used sound-event-detection models with attention pooling and EfficientNet backbones. Both clipwise and maximum segmentwise outputs received BCEWithLogitsLoss, despite the clipwise output already passing through sigmoid. Iterative pseudo-labeling of training soundscapes began with a single model's clipwise predictions and then switched to ensemble segmentwise predictions. The final two models achieved public and private scores of 0.928 and 0.923.

The team trained several CNN architectures using external HPA images, initially in 512-pixel grayscale format and later in a changed format. Training used image augmentation, binary cross-entropy, and NAdam with layer-specific learning rates, with 12-way test-time augmentation for prediction. Threshold search was unsuccessful, so they selected a fixed threshold of 0.205. The best five-fold single-model result was 0.597 public, while combining models from the first two stages was expected to exceed 0.62.

solution_summary: The pipeline first detected vessel regions with YOLO and then classified cropped 3D regions using ResNet-18 models. Higher-resolution feature maps and spatial classification heads substantially improved performance, with top-N aggregation converting spatial scores into case predictions. Eleven models with varied crop sizes, resolutions, and strides formed the ensemble. An EfficientNet-based voxel-spacing fallback handled missing DICOM metadata and improved the private score from 0.84 to 0.85.

solution_title: 548th Place Solution for the RSNA 2023 Abdominal Trauma Detection Competition
solution_summary: The final approach combined an EfficientNet-B4 DICOM image model with a weighted baseline using organ-specific ensemble weights. An initially planned NII branch was removed because its contribution was negligible, while organ-specific image crops failed because of overlap and occlusion. The image model used binary cross-entropy, Adam, and three training epochs, with additional regularization and batch-normalization adjustments. Evaluation used an 80:20 holdout and an additional in-sample check, reporting out-of-sample F1 of 0.73 and accuracy of 67%.

The pipeline trained pairwise Huber regressors, LightGBM models, and shallow Extra Trees on technical indicators and engineered features. It retained seven experts according to how frequently each achieved the smallest training residual, then learned per-row expert probabilities with Extra Trees and Gaussian naive Bayes classifiers. Missingness indicators, temporal differences, and predictions from small linear regressions expanded the features. Final predictions combined the experts using the selector probabilities and were clipped to a fixed range.
compute: Four concurrent processes for Huber fitting; LightGBM configured with four threads.

solution_title: Rank 4 approach - lots of features, lots of simple models and a ridge blend!
solution_summary: The solution combines extensive interaction feature engineering with a large collection of boosted-tree and AutoGluon models. Shuffled ten-fold cross-validation tracked leaderboard performance closely, and LightGBM produced the strongest individual models. Standardized predictions from 382 models were combined using ridge regression. Rounding predictions to the nearest target value gave a negligible validation improvement, with the final ensemble achieving a private leaderboard score of 11.54182.

solution_summary: The solution combined PointPillars-based LIDAR detectors with an image-assisted Frustum ConvNet pipeline. Voxel resolution, point-cloud coverage, and voxel capacity mattered most for the LIDAR models, while image proposals added complementary detections, particularly for pedestrians and bicycles. Flip test-time augmentation and class-specific rotated soft-NMS merged predictions across both pipelines. The combined system reached private/public scores of 0.202/0.205, exceeding the saturated LIDAR-only ensemble.

solution_title: Optiver Trading at the Close Analysis with LSTM and ConvNet
solution_summary: The post describes two standalone neural models for stock return prediction. An LSTM uses raw features and lagged targets, achieving a public leaderboard score of 5.3508. A ConvNet combines raw inputs with imbalance features and scores 5.3439, with its residual component credited for much of the performance. Global stock mapping is suggested as a potential improvement rather than a demonstrated component.

The author sampled plausible latent sky configurations using MCMC on a simplified generative model. They then optimized predicted locations against the Dark Worlds metric averaged over those posterior samples. Prediction optimization consumed more time than hypothesis sampling, while extensive additional runs changed little about final test performance. The post also proposes evaluating predictions against multiple plausible explanations of each observed sky to reduce evaluation variance.

solution_title: Bronze solution but an interesting insight [Genetic Programming]
solution_summary: The author moved away from deep learning and explored genetic programming inspired by a public simulated annealing approach. A tree-based representation appeared most promising and produced good results. Its resource demands exceeded those of annealing, limiting further work.

The solution used two U-Nets: one localized sea lion centers and the other segmented sea lions by type using manually refined masks. Morphological operations combined the center predictions and outlines to separate touching animals and count them. Predictions at different scales were ensembled, particularly for pups, but image scale variation remained unresolved. The best ensemble scored 13.03/14.03 on private/public data, only slightly better than the best single model.

The solution used only AIRS-CH0 and derived critical preprocessing and fitting choices from the simulation code. It disabled hot-pixel processing, subtracted wavelength-dependent foreground and jointly fitted transit dips with a separable gain-drift model. Bootstrap uncertainty estimates supported Gaussian-process smoothing, which was blended with autoencoder and NMF reconstructions at weights 6:2:2. A separate uncertainty blend completed the predictions, yielding public/private scores of 0.7330321/0.7420624.

The solution inverted the ventilator's proportional–integral controller to recover pressure directly from u_in. It enumerated discrete controller parameters and candidate pressures, solved for the initial integral, and reconstructed the pressure sequence using an exponentially decaying integral. A strict discreteness check recovered exact pressure for about 30% of inspiratory observations, while piecewise-linear inputs and clipping prevented broader recovery. An earlier recurrent physics model scored around 0.5, and the author lacked a strong model for the remaining observations.
compute: C++ brute-force search took about 5 minutes for all test data; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The final approach used regularized linear regression to predict changes in a log-transformed target, with a separate model for each forecast horizon. Features captured current density and population, changes in density and active businesses, and three- and six-month summary statistics. Expanding-window walk-forward validation guided modeling, while counties where the model could not beat the last-value baseline received that baseline instead. Multiplicative postprocessing improved validation and leaderboard performance, whereas nonlinear models and numerous external data sources did not help.

solution_title: Picture Perfect: Bo Yang on winning the Photo Quality Prediction competition
solution_summary: The final approach mixed random forests, GBM, and two forms of logistic regression using different combinations of raw and derived variables. The most useful features were smoothed word-level good-album averages, calculated separately across text fields and aggregated for albums and locations. Geographic and socioeconomic external data provided small gains, while word pairs yielded no useful signal.

It combined Moore and Talisman Red ratings with weights of 60% and 40%. Manual adjustments boosted UConn because season-long injuries had depressed its ratings. Avoiding 100% win probabilities for heavy favorites was especially valuable when Baylor and Iowa lost.

solution_title: 492nd Place Solution: 2 Steps Learning, BC then RL
solution_summary: The author trained a deck-specific Entity Transformer through behavioral cloning followed by PPO, finishing with a Crustle and Mega Kangaskhan ex deck scoring 890.4. Lexical card-effect features helped generalize to cards poorly represented in replays. Fast Rust-based episode collection and a diverse pool of locally trained opponents were central to effective reinforcement learning. Prioritized opponent sampling and replay-weighted local validation helped approximate the changing competition environment.

solution_summary: The described approach used predictions from six timm image models as features for tabular classifiers. LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost used resampling and ugly-duckling features, with image-derived features excluded from LightGBM because of overfitting. HBOS anomaly features added approximately 0.001 to the leaderboard score. The author described a leakage-free alternative to the selected submission and relied heavily on leaderboard feedback because CV correlation was weak.

The solution used greedy hill climbing to combine 138 models across tree and neural architectures, reaching 0.91974 out-of-fold AUC. Diversity came from training models on different subsets of more than 800 engineered features. Original IBM data supplied categorical numeric aggregates and class-conditional distribution features, while joint frequencies, clustering, and periodic encodings added complementary signals. Several heavily weighted models avoided in-fold target encoding, and overly large individual feature sets, complex distance features, and high-threshold pseudo-labeling offered little benefit.

The author concentrated training on a large vision transformer with 384-by-384 inputs and added a ResNeSt200-backed LSTM attention model for diversity. Training used all supplied data, additional synthetic molecular images each epoch, and some pseudo-labeled test data. The final ensemble combined seven transformer checkpoints and two LSTM checkpoints, each evaluated on original and horizontally flipped images. Predictions were filtered by InChI normalization quality and then voted on, with model preference breaking ties. The best transformer checkpoint scored 0.67 on the leaderboard, while the ensembled transformer checkpoints reached 0.63.

solution_title: 301st-place solution: a bounded native-link guard (0.957 public)
solution_summary: The author added a conservative native-link restoration rule to an existing pretrained 3D detection and tracking pipeline. The inference pipeline combined UNet/Transformer predictions, spatial test-time views, and a DeepCenter 3D gate for selected tracking decisions. Restoration considered only strong, short native one-to-one links displaced by motion relinking, with strict exclusions, a small restoration budget, and graph repair. Paired development replay showed a positive metric change, while the selected notebook achieved public score 0.957 without a separately verified private score.

solution_summary: The solution focused on temporal distribution shift between training, public test, and private test data. Estimated sampling dates supported month-based validation, removal of original version features, and development of more stable features with split-normalized counts and ranks. A three-stage training pipeline blended models trained on each month and the full dataset using weighted geometric averaging. The final ensemble combined about ten LightGBM models and four Keras neural networks through a ranked geometric weighted average.

The solution ensembled five DeBERTa models with mean pooling and linear or LSTM heads. Restricting mean pooling to student-answer tokens produced the largest improvement. LLM-generated question variants and auxiliary writing-quality targets provided further gains. Pseudo-label training enabled longer sequences and effective training of the base model, improving CV from 0.4581 to 0.4476.

The final RPS agent selected among 32 strategies derived from modified RPSContest bots, including counterparts that modeled its own action history. Several performance scorers nominated strategies, and a further scorer chose between their outputs. Mathematical constant sequences supplied exploratory moves, while Dirichlet sampling and score-dependent switching varied the agent's behavior. Extensive experimentation with strategy combinations and selectors shaped the final system.

solution_title: 9th Place Solution - shu421 part (1D WaveNet + Transformer + GRU)
solution_summary: The author described sequence models with WaveNet feature extraction, convolutional downsampling, residual bidirectional GRUs, and an MLP decoder, with a transformer in one variant. Inputs combined scaled sensor values and differences, cyclical hour features, and a repeated-wave indicator. Training used Gaussian event targets, strongly weighted event losses, AdamW, and cosine annealing. The two variants achieved private scores of 0.805 and 0.811, while overlap inference and several augmentation, pretraining, and stacking approaches did not help.

The solution first separated known and unseen graphemes using distances to class feature centers learned by ArcFace models. Known graphemes were classified as whole graphemes and then mapped to their components, while unseen graphemes were handled by separate component classifiers. ArcFace models used resized 320×320 images, cutout, and 90 training epochs. The component models used mixup and only 10 epochs because longer training hurt performance on unseen graphemes.

solution_title: Hybrid RAG + Multi-Attempt Tool Use for AIMO Progress Prize 3
solution_summary: The pipeline served gpt-oss-120b through vLLM and retrieved solved mathematical problems from a cleaned corpus of roughly 120,000 examples. Hybrid semantic and keyword retrieval supplied five reference solutions, while eight seeded reasoning attempts used persistent Python sandboxes for calculation and verification. Final answers were chosen by inverse-entropy weighted voting, with early stopping and adaptive time budgets. The public score remained approximately 40 out of 50, offering no improvement over simpler baselines; private results were still pending.
compute: Global notebook timeout of 17,400 seconds; adaptive 300–900 seconds per problem

solution_summary: The solution used DeBERTa-v3-large with a custom mean-pooling layer restricted to the summary tokens. Inputs combined the summary with all prompt text fields, separated by special tokens. Training used a maximum length of 1,500, while inference used 2,048 and benefited from averaging multiple checkpoints per epoch. It achieved CV 0.474 and private score 0.469, with approximately 8.5 hours of inference.

solution_summary: The pipeline detected and cropped the main image region, classified slices for organ presence, and retained segmentation predictions only for positive classifications. It used 2.5D U-Nets with EfficientNet backbones, with separate segmentation models trained on positive samples. Detector cropping reduced training resource requirements, while EMA, SWA, mixup, and cutmix helped training. Adding dedicated segmentation models improved the reported public score from 0.886 to 0.890, although that result was not submitted.

solution_title: Predicting Problematic Internet Use in Children and Adolescents
solution_summary: The solution predicts problematic internet usage from physical activity data using an ensemble of XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost. It includes preprocessing and feature engineering, although specific transformations are not described. Evaluation uses stratified k-fold cross-validation, with custom optimization targeting quadratic weighted kappa. Threshold optimization is applied to improve the final predictions.

The team used ResNet50, DenseNet121, InceptionResNetV2, and EfficientNet-B7 with noisy-student weights, with image sizes of 812 and 1024. EfficientNet performed relatively well on multiple diseases, and larger images improved scores. Training used geometric augmentation, categorical cross entropy plus focal loss, pseudo-labeling, stochastic weight averaging, label smoothing, and oversampling, with test-time augmentation benefiting several backbones. CycleGAN-generated disease images reduced the score and were excluded, while several other augmentation methods also failed to help.

The team combined roughly 40 image classifiers with LSTM models and a LightGBM second layer. The booster learned candidate-label correctness from top-ten class probabilities and raw stroke timing features. Enforcing equal test-set class counts improved individual models by about 0.7%, and reciprocal-rank weighted voting further improved the blend. The best individual model scored 0.946, while the blended submissions reached approximately 0.957.

The author estimated offensive and defensive power ratings at multiple expectiles using convex optimization, capturing variation in team scoring performance. Selected score-related features fed an ensemble of four LightGBM models. Training used historical tournament and non-tournament games, treated each team-season separately, and emphasized recent seasons and tournament games. Two submissions hedged the first-round matchup with the greatest model disagreement through opposing manual overrides.

Random-walk positional encodings, additional points sampled around detections, and similarity-and-distance-based labels improved the graph model. Combining k-NN and Delaunay edges gave the strongest graph results, and the selected submission combined predictions by maximum. solution_title: #81: First Top 10% but It Could've Been Better...
solution_summary: The solution stacked XGBoost and CatBoost with RidgeCV as the final estimator. Correlation analysis guided the creation of child-related and facilities features, while tree feature importances guided feature removal. Bayesian optimization tuned model parameters. Target encoding hurt private performance, and the author's best submission omitted both target encoding and the original dataset, scoring 0.29329.

The solution separated image-space tour optimization from lifting the tour into valid arm configurations. A custom TSP solver gradually penalized violations of liftability conditions, while a randomized lifting algorithm used adaptive backtracking, directional drift, and local repairs. Merging previously generated tours with IPT and a limited genetic algorithm produced a final score of approximately 74075.706541. Careful integer scaling of color and movement costs improved optimization precision.

solution_summary: The solution used single-image classification with three ConvNeXt V2 nano configurations and one EfficientNet V2 small configuration, followed by maximum aggregation. Training used rotation and flip augmentation, Adam, and OneCycleLR for 33 epochs. Removing positive-labeled images with confidently negative OOF predictions improved CV by about 0.03–0.04. A percentile-based threshold improved the leaderboard score by roughly 0.015 and was retained in one final submission, while inference was optimized for two T4 GPUs.

solution_title: It’s SFT all the way down
solution_summary: The author trained autoregressive game policies through supervised imitation of winning players, generating each turn's commands sequentially. solution_title: #7 Private LB and #2 Public LB solution
solution_summary: The approach began with Optuna-tuned XGBoost and then added pseudo-labeling. Derived features, particularly interactions involving hemoglobin and other biological measurements, improved the public score further. The final submission also combined predictions from shared notebooks using weighting. Changing the seed from 42 to 43 raised the public score to 0.88136, and the reported final private score was 0.87926.

The solution trained exclusively on the curated data subset. Random shifts and noise produced four augmented spectrogram versions per sample, followed by further image-style augmentation. A convolutional network with skip connections and two fully connected layers was trained using fast.ai. Inference blended 24 models trained on different random subsets and used 30-fold test-time augmentation.

The final submission combined two LightGBM models and one CatBoost model by weighted averaging, using about 130 features. The strongest features summarized how unusual a user's answer choices were, followed by correctness-aware Word2Vec similarities and TrueSkill estimates. Historical accuracy, target encodings, and timing features also contributed, producing a private score of 0.802. A transformer model remained unfinished, while tag and lecture features did not help.

solution_title: A 0.45 tree-based solution and a few thoughts
solution_summary: The author developed the substantive approach after the competition, reaching approximately 0.45 with frozen DeBERTa representations and engineered essay features. Mean-pooled last-layer embeddings were combined with TF-IDF, essay structure, punctuation errors, and language detection scores through scikit-learn pipelines. LightGBM, XGBoost, and a simple PyTorch model produced similar results on these features. Batched embedding inference addressed GPU memory issues without fine-tuning DeBERTa.
compute: GPU inference; batched processing was needed after out-of-memory issues.

solution_summary: The solution retrieved candidate educational content with sentence-transformer embeddings and reranked it with a cross-encoder initialized from the first-stage model. Inputs included topic ancestry, text fields, language, and content-kind markers. Validation grouped by topic and stratified by language, and the final classification threshold maximized validation F2. Topics with no accepted predictions received their highest-scoring content.

The team used an EfficientDet-D5 ensemble trained across two folds and evaluated it with source-separated cross-validation using original weightings. Their main strategy was source-separated pseudo-labeling to address the expected dominance of UTokyo images in the test set. Predictions from the best cross-validation model divided test images into groups with fewer than 39 detected wheat heads and at least 39 heads. Separate models were trained on the original training data plus each group's pseudo-labels, then applied to their corresponding test groups.

The solution calibrated the instrument signals, removed temporal outliers, and extracted transit-phase statistics alongside CNN features. These features fed a 36-member rational quadratic neural ensemble that directly predicted both the target and uncertainty. Gradient-based phase detection and frequency-chunk features improved validation, while soft rational quadratic grouping provided a substantial gain. Training emphasized ensemble members with above-median losses, and a simple 80/20 split tracked leaderboard behavior closely.
compute: Reprocessing all calibration data took over one hour, even with joblib.

solution_summary: The team trained Qwen2.5-14B on verified long chain-of-thought solutions, then refined it on a heavily filtered tool-integrated reasoning dataset. A linear merge of the CoT and TIR checkpoints improved accuracy while reducing response length and code executions. FP8 TensorRT-LLM inference, ReDrafter speculative decoding, asynchronous generations, and adaptive time budgets made the model practical under competition limits. The merged model achieved 69.1 maj@16 on their 256-problem benchmark, and private evaluation aligned better with cross-validation than public results.
compute: CoT training: 512 H100 GPUs for 48 hours.
external_data: ["AoPS forum mathematics problems", "nvidia/OpenMathReasoning", "AIME 2024 and 2025; HMMT 2024 and 2025"]

solution_summary: The team reused public nucleus detection and linking weights, then concentrated on graph repairs and division handling. Their main submission added divergence-gated second daughters and removed false divisions using daughter separation rules and a trained 3D mitosis classifier. Local replay and metric-aware acceptance criteria guided changes, though validation overlapped the public models' training data. The main submission achieved 0.92042 private score and narrowly beat their alternative public-notebook stack.
models_pretrained: ["pilkwang public detection and linking weights", "anvithpothula centroid-refinement head", "DeepCenter", "ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18"]
