solution_title: 3rd Place Solution — March Machine Learning Mania 2026
solution_summary: Separate men's and women's logistic regression models used team differential features, custom ratings, and selected interactions. Careful feature pruning improved generalization on the small tournament training sets, while boosted trees performed poorly on unseen games. Predictions were blended with ESPN BPI, Vegas, and Kalshi probabilities through round-dependent tiers. The final combined cross-validation Brier score was 0.12352, and the submission scored 0.1160374.
compute: No GPU required; full pipeline runs in under 30 seconds on a modern machine.
external_data: ["Barttorvik", "Massey Ordinals", "nishaanamin/march-madness-data", "WNCAA NET Rankings", "ESPN BPI", "Vegas moneylines", "Kalshi championship futures"]

solution_summary: The solution ensembled eight U-Net models using mit-b2 and pvt-v2-b2 encoders, with four rotation variants during inference. It grouped selected scan channels along the batch dimension and split fragment2 to support four-fold validation. Encoder features passed through SK attention and additional feature-processing modules. Training used SoftBCELoss, AdamW, and warmup followed by cosine annealing; the reported single PVT model outperformed the ensemble on both leaderboards.

The author developed an auxiliary-classifier relativistic least-squares DCGAN and a BigGAN-like model for dog image generation. Both used head-oriented square crops with extra context, resized to 80×80 and randomly cropped to 64×64 during training. Auxiliary classification and a compiled TensorFlow training loop improved the first model, which achieved a reported leaderboard score of 52. The BigGAN-like model initially scored 47 and improved to 42 after changes to batch size, Adam settings, channel widths, and learning-rate decay.
compute: TensorFlow training-loop compilation reportedly doubled training speed; updated BigGAN trained for 40,000 iterations.

solution_summary: The solution primarily used LightGBM with a separate model for predicting no purchases and F1 optimization. User-level aggregates of features and out-of-fold predictions helped restore grouping information missing from individual user-product rows. Temporal repurchase features and order-distribution statistics were important inputs. A learning rate of 0.01 and averaging models with different feature orderings improved results, while several more elaborate feature ideas added little.

The submission primarily extracted dataset names using exact string matching and regular expressions. A small, manually selected collection of dataset names found through Google substantially improved public scores. Regular expressions classified token types, identified candidate phrases, and filtered them using dataset-related indicators. BERT contributed little, and public leaderboard probing caused overfitting despite reaching a maximum public score of 0.410.
external_data: ["Manually selected dataset names found through Google, about 2 KB"]

solution_summary: The solution blended two public-notebook-based predictors using ECA-NFNet-L0 and SEResNeXt26t architectures. Predictions were smoothed across adjacent five-second audio chunks, and a power adjustment boosted classes outside the most confident top-k predictions. The final blend used weights of 0.85 and 0.3, with the author stating that SEResNeXt received more weight. Outputs were rounded to four decimal places.
compute: GPUs; no hardware model or runtime specified.

solution_summary: The author reflects on overfitting and feature-selection experiments without describing a final submission pipeline. Recursive feature elimination produced training cross-validation AUCs of 0.997–0.999 across several random seeds, yet the selected variables did not exceed 0.9 AUC on the test set. The main lesson was that strong internal cross-validation results could still give misleading evidence about generalization.

The author adapted raddar's Vilnius NCAA baseline and applied goto_conversion to make more aggressive predictions. The approach performed well in a tournament with relatively few surprising outcomes, although the selected winning team was eliminated earlier than expected. Another submission combined AutoGluon with goto_conversion and scored 0.12480.

The model jointly encoded concatenated markdown and code cells with DeBERTa-large, mean-pooled cell representations, and used a GRU to predict markdown positions relative to code cells. Notebook statistics and code-cell absolute positions supplemented the learned representations, while MAE supervised the resulting absolute-position predictions. Training included MLM pretraining and progressively larger cell counts and sequence lengths. Three inference cycles with shuffled markdown cells improved the reported score from 0.9067 to 0.9100.

solution_title: Top 4% Solution: Model Diversity, FE & Systematic Experimentation
solution_summary: The solution developed a diverse seven-model blend through systematic experiments tracked in MLflow and evaluated with five-fold out-of-fold metrics. Handcrafted indicators, categorical combinations, digit features, and target encoding supported strong tabular models, while ResNet added useful diversity despite weaker standalone accuracy. Optuna optimized blending weights and class-wise probability thresholds for balanced accuracy, producing a blend with local CV 0.98089 and private score 0.98048. The final system applied heuristic hard voting to that blend, individual models, and two shared submissions, achieving a private score of 0.98151.
compute: ResNet configured to use CUDA and 12 threads; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_title: It seems supervised learning always got better scores.
solution_summary: The author used unsupervised methods including user-based collaborative filtering, item-based collaborative filtering, and local PageRank. A single local PageRank method achieved 0.71644. The post also raises an unresolved question about constructing representative positive and negative samples for supervised learning.

The solution ensembles six image classification architectures for a 128-class furniture recognition task. The documented training interface includes mixup augmentation and its alpha parameter. Predictions use horizontal flips at test time, and a separate statistics script calculates weights for fine-tuned models before submission generation.

The solution used a two-stage retriever and reranker built with sentence-transformers and an XLM-R distilled RoBERTa paraphrase backbone. Topic inputs incorporated metadata, hierarchical context and child titles, while validation separated known and unknown channels. Retriever training used MultipleNegativesRankingLoss, and its weights initialized a reranker trained with OnlineContrastiveLoss. Contrastive reranking improved CV F2 from 0.4565 to 0.5414 and the leaderboard score from 0.553 to 0.619; ensembling hurt leaderboard performance.

The team focused on processing sensor signals separately within behavior phases, reasoning that phase affects how behaviors appear. They applied the ATAR algorithm from spkit and reported improvements in cross-validation and leaderboard performance. They also tried retrieving similar signals with Faiss during inference, but noted that they missed incorporating subject information. The post leaves the broader model pipeline and numerical results unspecified.

solution_title: How I got my run time down from 10 hours to 10 minutes
solution_summary: The author accelerated a toy-scheduling implementation by replacing individual toy records with a histogram indexed by duration. This reduced processing from ten million records to roughly 25,000 distinct durations, followed by substitution of actual toys into the resulting schedule. Ignoring relative arrival times and starting all toys in 2015 simplified implementation. Although runtime fell from hours to minutes, the approach was abandoned for a teammate's slower implementation that produced better solutions and supported further improvements.
compute: Original Python implementation: 10–12 hours; histogram processing: a couple of minutes plus several minutes for back substitution.

solution_title: 57th place solution, SoftTripletLoss, 256x512 image size, fastai v1
solution_summary: The author trained an ImageNet-initialized DenseNet121 embedding model with soft-margin triplet loss, batch-hard mining, and distance regularization. An epoch-level mining procedure built difficult batches using hard positives and negatives, while the custom head pooled the left and right image regions separately. Training used bounding-box crops, color jitter, cutout, staged unfreezing, and one-cycle schedules. The best single model with test-time augmentation scored 0.904 publicly, and an ensemble of 13 submissions reached approximately 0.93.
compute: One NVIDIA 1080; approximately 3.5 hours at 64×128, 6 hours at 128×256, and 15 hours at 256×512.

solution_summary: The team combined 21 models spanning bidirectional LSTMs, BERT, GPT-2, and TF-IDF classifiers. A test-sized holdout stratified by identity annotation count guided checkpoint selection and blending. Their custom iterative weight search allowed negative coefficients and outperformed stacking and alternative blend formulas. The final blend achieved a validation score of 0.94379378.

solution_summary: The solution used stacked transformer encoder layers with shared weights to model players and predict rushing-yard outcomes. Concatenating the runner's raw inputs onto every player's inputs was the most useful feature change. Alternating two shared parameter sets performed slightly better than sharing a single set, while position and season embeddings and sine/cosine orientation features supplied additional inputs. The best submission scored 0.01190 in random five-fold CV and 0.01295 on the public leaderboard, with unresolved validation issues linked to overlooked 2017 data problems.
compute: Competition constraint of four hours of CPU time.

solution_summary: The competition solution combined a bert-base-uncased model with metadata features and target-specific output adjustments. Host information and answer length provided particularly strong gains, while clipping predictions using out-of-fold grid search improved Spearman correlation. A later experiment added whitespace-cleaned RoBERTa predictions, increasing ensemble CV from 0.392 to 0.412 and leaderboard score by 0.015.

The solution stacked DeBERTa v3 base with LightGBM and added handcrafted language features. Freezing the first four encoder layers and using the CLS representation improved regression performance. Features from the referenced FB3 competition, readability statistics, and prompt-summary embedding similarity helped, while removing length_ratio also gave a small improvement. Joint prediction of content and wording worked better than separate target models, and alternative encoders and pooling methods did not improve results.

The pipeline tracked MTCNN face detections across time and extracted face-region videos for an ensemble dominated by 3D CNNs. Seven 3D models covered four architectures and two resolutions, with one SE-ResNeXt50 image model added to the ensemble. Pixel augmentation, random cropping, and 3D CutMix supported training, while simple pooling outperformed learned fusion. Ensembling improved the reported public score from 0.341 for I3D alone to 0.253.
compute: PNG frame conversion experiment took almost a week and produced over 500 GB of data.

solution_summary: The author trains SchNet and an edge-updating SchNet separately for each of eight coupling types, yielding sixteen models. Both architectures jointly predict coupling constants, coupling contributions, and atomwise magnetic-shielding values, with multitask learning providing effective regularization. The second architecture incorporates geometric edge features and predictions for other coupling types from the first architecture. Final predictions average the two architectures, and training uses Log L1 loss. Dropout and other noise-based regularization produced poor results.
The post links to a separate notebook containing the authors' unselected solution. It says their best private solution was not chosen. No methods are described in the post itself.

The author's contribution used a ConvNeXt Large U-Net adapted from Berthly's model, with interpolated image resizing. After initial OpenFWI training, predicted test velocity maps were passed through a forward model to construct additional training pairs, followed by three fine-tuning cycles. Test predictions were further optimized through the forward model using backpropagation on reconstruction L1 loss. The reported leaderboard error improved from 27.2 initially to 17.2 after fine-tuning and 13.5 after post-processing, before blending with teammate contributions.

The solution updates the author's public encoder-decoder notebook with longer input sequences and a smaller model. Input length increased from 128 to 288 frames, while batch size increased from 64 to 512. Encoder units decreased from 384 to 288 and decoder units from 256 to 128. The author attributes the performance improvement mainly to reduced overfitting from lower capacity and larger batches, with TPU execution enabling faster experimentation.
compute: TPU

solution_summary: The solution trained seven image neural networks with repeated cross-validation and combined their predictions through XGBoost stacking. A separate XGBoost spatial model used nearest-neighbor features from incidence angle, exploiting strong label relationships among nearby angles. Image and spatial predictions were fused with a formula for independent probabilities. The final pipeline retrained five image networks and the spatial model using pseudo-labeling; an unselected mixing variant achieved a private score of 0.0853.

The solution emphasized engineering survival targets and sample weights using event indicators and survival times. Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards estimates were scaled using out-of-fold event predictions from CatBoost and LightGBM. The final ensemble combined CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost, and TabM through multiple stacking layers and five-seed averaging. It achieved CV of 0.695 and public and private scores of 0.694.

The final solution ensembled two distilled MLP-encoder and frame-Transformer models using sequence lengths of 25 and 80. Landmark normalization, type-specific MLPs, convolutional smoothing, and an efficient DeBERTa attention implementation formed the core architecture. Extensive augmentation, high-loss sample exclusion, mean-teacher distillation, and checkpoint soup improved training. Patient-grouped stratified validation correlated well with leaderboard results, and the best model reported CV 0.749, public 0.795, and private 0.877.
compute: 8 GPUs; 1403 hours of experiment monitoring in April; Nobuco reduced inference from 45 to 38 ms/iteration.

solution_summary: The agent learned actions from replay data using a U-Net with engineered spatial maps and broadcast scalar features. Training first used Frog Parade replays, then fine-tuned on Flat Neurons replays with masked weighted BCE and diagonal-flip augmentation. Two models with different feature sets were equally ensembled and evaluated through head-to-head matches. The models were converted to ONNX and deployed inside a C# agent with additional post-processing.
compute: Two models, each trained for about one day; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The submission retrieved similar historical taxi trajectories using starting and cutoff locations, extending a benchmark that used only one point. Training rows were restricted to relevant calendar and time contexts, with timestamp and polyline as the main inputs. Similarity incorporated distance, overall bearing, and last bearing, and predictions used similarity-weighted averages of coordinates and log trajectory length. Thresholds were selected intuitively from a few examples, without formal cross-validation or ensembling.

The solution classified tokens into roughly 40 operation-specific classes, then applied deterministic transformations or dictionary replacements. An attention-based LSTM encoder-decoder used token embeddings, sub-token types and lengths, and word2vec embeddings to resolve ambiguous cases. Valid-class restrictions and a two-model combination addressed impossible outputs and class imbalance. Training used Adam and cross entropy, with a 20% validation holdout before full-data training; public GitHub data improved replacement dictionaries.
compute: GTX1060 GPU; about 6 hours to train two models

solution_title: 9th place solution: Optimize diversity when representation is limited
solution_summary: The pipeline filled five RNA structure prediction slots using template-based modeling, Protenix, Boltz2, and a de novo fallback, then refined eligible targets with RNAPro. Its central strategy was selecting structurally diverse candidates while adapting the template/model balance to sequence length. Protenix combined MSA and no-MSA predictions and handled long sequences through overlapping chunks. More elaborate template searches improved local validation but did not help when combined with deep models on the leaderboard.
compute: 2× T4 GPUs, with work distributed across both GPUs in every phase.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution for the AIMO3 Competition
solution_summary: The solution adapted a public baseline using unmodified gpt-oss-120b with Python execution, eight parallel solvers, and majority voting. Its main contribution was prompt refinement informed by qualitative analysis of 1,120 generated answers on reference and external math problems. Prompts emphasized explicit constraints, mathematical reductions, bounded search, and verification. Japanese prompting, forced self-correction, consistency-inspired prompts, and increasing the solver pool to sixteen did not improve results.

The solution combined diverse pretrained transformers with an attention head over their final sequence representations and two readability features. Binned, stratified five-fold validation and averaging across multiple seeds supported model comparisons on the small, noisy dataset. Models used AdamW, MSE loss, frequent validation, and stochastic weight averaging after epoch three. Backward ensemble selection produced roughly 38-model submissions within a three-hour runtime, with RidgeCV and Bayesian ridge chosen as the final ensemble methods. The RidgeCV submission scored 0.447, while the unselected Netflix weighting method scored 0.446.
compute: Approximately 38 models per final ensemble within a 3-hour submission runtime; GPU hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution built a diverse stack of 115 base models using varied preprocessing, engineered features, and model settings. Base learners included boosted trees, TabNet, and generalized additive models, with Optuna used to tune several tree models. Elastic Net performed best among the tested linear meta-models, and its initial output was fed through Elastic Net again for the final predictions. Careful basic preprocessing and a reliable cross-validation pipeline were central to the approach.
compute: CPU and/or GPU used for XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost training; hardware models unspecified.

solution_summary: The method averaged 10 fully convolutional networks to segment the left ventricle in individual MRI images, using Sunnybrook data and roughly 200 manually added images. Localization, alignment, augmentation, batch normalization, and a modified Dice objective supported segmentation quality. Segmented areas were integrated into volumes and corrected with a nonlinear fitted function. A three-model fallback handled difficult cases, while data cleanup mattered more than the modest ensemble gain.
compute: NVIDIA GTX 970 and 980Ti; about 4 days to train and evaluate using both GPUs.

solution_summary: The author used the Munkres/Hungarian method in their competition solution. They report that this was necessary to achieve a score of 1.0. The post links the project source code but provides no further pipeline details.

The solution used a pretrained ResNet34 with Heng's decoder in PyTorch, trained across five folds using Peter's recipe. A second variant added spatial squeeze-and-excitation only in the decoder because of an implementation mistake, yet still improved the public score slightly. The final prediction blended the original and modified models with approximate weights of 0.43 and 0.57 and used horizontal-flip test-time augmentation. The initial model reached 0.841 on the public leaderboard.
compute: Most training used a virtual machine configured with 4 Tesla K80 GPUs.

solution_title: 585th Place Solution for the ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions Competition
solution_summary: The primary solution used LightGBM with manually chosen hyperparameters and averaged predictions over ten stratified folds and five random seeds. Preprocessing combined three-neighbor imputation, removal of EJ, and robust scaling. Depth limits and feature sampling by tree were useful regularizers, while several alternative models and feature elimination approaches did not help. A second submission stacked LightGBM, TabPFN, and CatBoost with an ElasticNet meta-model, scoring 0.473 privately.

The solution combined three ECA-NFNet image models with SBERT and TF-IDF text representations. Image embeddings were concatenated, and image and text cosine similarities supplied a quadratic feature expansion for logistic regression stacking. Training pairs included all same-group matches and an equal number of hard negatives selected using combined similarity. Base models and the stacker were initially trained on separate halves of the data, after which the base models were retrained on all data while retaining the stacker.

Separate GRU ensembles handled tDCS FOG and DeFog using acceleration features and per-record scaling. Training on short sequences and predicting on much longer sequences was the most consequential choice. DeFog benefited substantially from iterative pseudo-labeling of notype data constrained by the Event column, while tDCS models varied their target loss weights. The combined system scored 0.548 in cross-validation, 0.530 publicly, and 0.450 privately.

solution_title: Silver Medal Solution[29th]: ByT5-XL Custom CPT with Dictionary Data + KL-Anchored LoRA
solution_summary: The author adapted ByT5-XL using Akkadian continued pretraining, followed by fine-tuning on original and synthetic translation pairs. Inference used BF16, lightweight minimum Bayes risk decoding, and minimal text cleanup. Model scale mattered most, while fine-tuning improved cross-validation but reduced leaderboard performance because of a suspected distribution mismatch. The reported pipeline scored 37.6, KL-anchored LoRA reached 37.1, and the unmodified base model remained strongest at 38.0.
compute: CPT took approximately 27 minutes on RTX PRO 6000 (96GB); BF16 inference ran on T4 16GB using approximately 7.5GB VRAM.

solution_summary: The author added the original diamond dataset and encoded ordered categorical attributes as integers. Two training variants increased diversity, including one that reordered x and y by their minimum and maximum. Several model families were tuned with Optuna to produce out-of-fold predictions. A linear stacking model combined those predictions, with recursive feature elimination reducing 22 candidate prediction files to 15 for the final submission.

solution_title: First silver zone, Some ideas sharing, Congrats to everyone!
solution_summary: The solution aggregated authorized historical and new transactions, grouped new transactions by month lag, and applied log1p normalization after merging. It defined outliers as targets with absolute values of at least 10 and trained LightGBM and neural network models on all data, non-outlier data, and outlier detection. LightGBM feature importance guided feature selection, and Ridge regression stacked the models. Five-fold stratified validation produced a score around 3.63, while the final score was better.

The solution blended 29 EfficientNet and EfficientNet V2 models with sound event detection heads trained on log-mel spectrograms. Training used 5- or 20-second chunks, noise and volume augmentation, equally weighted primary and secondary labels, and pseudo-label-based loss masking for some models. Inference used overlapping 40-second chunks, with blending weights and thresholds tuned together. Separate call and nocall thresholds, site-specific species masking, and validation weighted to match the public nocall ratio completed the pipeline.

solution_title: # 35 Place - Time for a write up
solution_summary: The final solution combined TabM, target-encoded XGBoost, and three CatBoost variants using different categorical feature representations. Hill climbing selected five contributing models from 17 candidates, with the remaining models receiving zero weight. The ensemble achieved 0.95574 CV and 0.95533 on the private leaderboard. Sequential Keras networks failed to outperform logistic regression.

The team built a compact CFish fork with a custom neural evaluation function under strict binary and memory limits. Extensive code removal, compiler tuning, compression, and reduced tables made room for roughly 48 KB of network weights. Search improvements were tested through OpenBench, while SPSA tuned search, time management, and selected neural weights. The evaluator used compact piece-square features and two-stage training on privately generated chess games, with each stage taking about eight hours on an RTX 3090.
compute: RTX 3090 for network training, about eight hours per stage; engine testing used approximately 144 + 32 + 384 CPU threads, with another 256 Google Cloud threads in the final days.
external_data: ["Private Ethereal-generated chess games", "Leela Chess Zero datasets (tested without improvement)"]

solution_title: 24th place - mixing all I can - BERT+XLNET+GPT2+LGB
solution_summary: The solution combined base BERT, XLNet and GPT-2 models with LightGBM models trained on engineered text features. Separate transformer inputs and models handled question-only targets and targets involving answers. Training used three folds drawn from a ten-fold grouped split, with one-cycle scheduling and early stopping on Spearman correlation. Predictions were weighted using softmax-transformed validation scores, then rounded using a separately selected policy for each target.

The solution combined independently trained embedding, cross-encoder, and LoRA-tuned LLM systems. Bi-encoders learned rule/comment relationships with triplet loss, while cross-encoders used rule-comment pairs and cross-rule hard negatives. A quantized Qwen model supplied continuous violation scores from constrained Yes/No inference, and the pipeline also used labeled examples provided in test columns. The full ensemble reported ROC-AUC 0.929 in 11 hours; a later pipeline, whose details are not provided, reached 0.933 in 7 hours.
compute: LLM training distributed across two GPUs using DeepSpeed ZeRO-2; full ensemble runtime 11 hours; later optimized pipeline 7 hours.

solution_summary: The final solution combined three U-Net-like segmentation models using DPN or WiderResNet38 encoders with the teammate's models. WiderResNet variants used SCSE decoder blocks, image and vertical-coordinate input channels, and auxiliary salt-presence prediction; one also included object context and an intermediate regularization loss. Training used five folds stratified by salt area, staged Adam optimization, and cosine-restart fine-tuning. Inference averaged checkpoints, folds, and horizontal flips, then suppressed masks classified as empty and filled holes. Threshold tuning and auxiliary supervision helped, while several alternative architectures, augmentations, and postprocessing methods failed.
compute: 4x1080Ti rig; hundreds of experiments

solution_summary: The pipeline jointly detected cells and scored temporal links using six networks from two 3D encoder–decoder architectures. Iterative teacher–student training expanded sparse annotations into millions of pseudo-labelled cells and links. Shared detections, member-specific LightGBM re-scorers, and averaged link probabilities fed a global integer linear program, followed by drift-compensated position smoothing. Rotation augmentation and drift correction were particularly valuable, and the submitted pipeline scored 0.953 privately.
compute: Training used RTX 3090/4090 with bf16 mixed precision; inference ran within 12 hours on two T4 GPUs using fp16.

solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned a COCO-pretrained Hybrid Task Cascade model with a ResNeXt-101-64x4d-FPN backbone using light augmentation and multiscale training. Validation-based threshold tuning produced the largest reported improvement, raising the leaderboard metric from 0.21913 to 0.30011. Multiscale and horizontal-flip inference plus an ensemble of three checkpoints improved it further. Class filtering, suppression of overlapping same-class masks, and removal of tiny objects completed the pipeline, reaching 0.33621.
compute: 8 Tesla V100 GPUs, batch size 16; approximately 3 days training

solution_summary: The author's component uses LightGBM with 74 selected features, including grouped counts, next-click information, target encodings, and summary statistics. The final temporal split uses day 7 for target encoding, days 8 and 9 for training, and the last 2.5 million training rows as a holdout. NumPy memory mapping makes the data manageable, while Bayesian optimization tunes model parameters. Seven selected models are blended using SciPy-optimized weights with a softmax constraint, then combined with teammates' predictions.
compute: Machine with 64 GB RAM; an additional teammate-provided computer was also used.

solution_summary: The pipeline first fixed floor predictions using WiFi CNNs, public RNN models, and a small amount of device/timestamp leakage. WiFi models estimated approximate positions while sensor CNNs predicted displacement for individual path legs, with site-specific fine-tuning improving validation performance. Extensive geometric post-processing aligned the resulting path shapes with floorplans and waypoints, and splitting longer test paths improved predictions. Final outputs combined multiple processed ensembles, although post-processing lacked reliable cross-validation.

The solution used two conformer-like encoders combining transformers, CBAM-equipped 1D convolutions, and bidirectional LSTMs, trained with CTC and intermediate CTC losses. Inputs combined normalized landmark coordinates, frame differences, and hand joint distances into 582 features. Training first used supplemental and competition data, then continued on competition data alone. INT8 quantization reduced the model to about 16 MB, while masking augmentations and an autoregressive decoder did not help.

The solution trained separate LightGBM ensembles for energy production and consumption, using 75 and 85 features respectively. Feature selection and parameter tuning relied on custom evolutionary search, chronological validation, and extensive experimentation. Lagged target statistics, weather deviations, calendar features, and separate target normalization formulas were central to the pipeline. Each ensemble combined three estimators and was retrained every nine scoring days using newly revealed data.
compute: About 20 minutes on an unspecified GPU to train both ensembles; approximately 10 retrainings during evaluation.

solution_summary: The authors describe code slightly modified from their team's best official submission. With only 137 training rows and an outlier-sensitive RMSE metric, their strategy emphasized simple preprocessing and modeling to limit overfitting. They also determined that only 321 of the nominal 100,000 test rows were real. The text does not identify the specific model or preprocessing operations.

The final submission averaged a single CatBoost model configuration across 20 folds. Correctly encoding CustomerId and Surname as high-cardinality categorical variables was important. The author emphasized CatBoost parameter tuning and categorical encoding choices, while noting that the solution could still be improved.

The team used Codex to semi-automate Python code shortening across 400 ARC-style tasks, generating multiple candidates and selecting short correct programs. Prompts incorporated general golfing knowledge, lessons extracted from successful solutions, and per-task experiment histories. Core implementation techniques included recursive grid transformations, regular expressions, and Chinese-remainder-based grid traversal. For longer programs, zopfli compression, Latin-1 embedding, and variable-name searches reduced final byte counts, with renaming saving roughly 2–12 bytes on applicable tasks.

solution_title: 38th place — a wellbore problem from two physicists' points of view
solution_summary: The solution blended a geometric geology prior with gamma-ray correction, a deterministic geosteering search, and two boosted-tree stacks. The prior borrowed neighboring wells' dip information through five complementary estimators, then used a pairwise LightGBM tournament to combine their paths. A variational gamma-ray correction and a diverse piecewise-linear beam search supplied complementary physical interpretations. The fixed blend achieved 6.842 private RMSE, while visible-prefix calibration was excluded because it consistently hurt offline evaluation.

The solution used only AIRS data, applying standard corrections, normalization, Gaussian denoising, transit-phase detection, and polynomial detrending. Features described the full signal and wavelength groups of 6, 10, and 25, including transit-depth estimates and in-transit statistics. An ensemble of 500 Ridge and 500 PLSRegression models used randomized settings and training subsets, with the lowest and highest 30% of predictions removed before averaging. Prediction dispersion supplied uncertainty estimates scaled using leaderboard feedback, and the selected variant achieved a private score of 0.6293136.

solution_title: [76th place] Another fork of "Building a Basic Rule Based Agent in Python"
solution_summary: The solution extended a public rule-based agent with predefined factory behavior and robots that reacted dynamically to opponents. Factories built a small fleet, conserved resources, and began growing lichen late in the game when water reserves permitted. Robots used shortest-path routing, local collision avoidance, and action-queue reuse to conserve power. Restricting rubble clearing encouraged robots to assist other factories and attack enemy lichen, producing the final score improvement.

The author fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium with Flow-GRPO to optimize the competition metric directly. Gemini-generated descriptions and question-answer pairs supplied training and local evaluation data, while the harmonic mean of VQA and aesthetic scores served as the reward. Generated images were converted to SVG with vtracer and simplified, then PaliGemma filtered three candidates per prompt at inference. Local scores peaked near 0.77 after 500 steps, with VQA improving from 0.82 to 0.91, although the optimal checkpoint was not submitted.
compute: 4 H800 GPUs; 512x512 images; 8 images per GPU per step and 16 images per description; local peak after 500 training steps

solution_summary: The approach combined t-SNE representations with meta bagging and reported a public score of 0.41599. The author emphasized meta bagging and representing the data through multiple transformations. A proposed update would use meta-bagged neural networks with first-stage predictions averaged across an RBF SVM, random forest, and gradient boosting model.

The solution ensembled three offline LightGBM models, four XGBoost models, and one online LightGBM model retrained every five days on a 60-day window. Features included revealed targets, historical stock embeddings, sector-relative performance, and auction-price estimates. Date-based cross-validation used five-day gaps, while Optuna and manual adjustments selected hyperparameters. Online learning, index-weighted target centering, and hyperparameter tuning produced the largest public leaderboard gains.

The released agent used a single 22.4-million-parameter network trained by behavior cloning from game replays to predict worker commands, quantities, and ordered market instructions. A residual CNN encoded spatial information, daily GRU memory tracked ongoing jobs, and attention coordinated workers within each turn. Structured decoding enforced local feasibility and shared seed quotas, while auxiliary objectives and history erasure supported training. Deployment used one fixed style, greedy CPU inference, and a final-turn liquidation rule; the writeup emphasized complete-game evaluation without reporting a numerical win rate.
compute: Runtime uses greedy decoding on CPU; training recipe specifies CUDA bfloat16 and supports multi-GPU training. Hardware counts and training duration are unspecified.

solution_title: Private LB 36th place/Public LB 1138th place [Silver medal] solution
solution_summary: The final solution ensembled EfficientNet-B7, EfficientNet-B3a, and SE-ResNeXt50 using 512×512 images and five-fold validation. The B3a pipeline first trained the head with a frozen backbone, then fine-tuned the full model with Ranger, CutMix, and label smoothing. Test-time augmentation was applied to the models, and the selected ensemble scored 0.900 privately. An unselected ensemble using stochastic weight averaging reached 0.901, while noise-handling experiments gave no improvement or failed.

The team blended two complementary pipelines: stacked classifiers built on ImageNet features and ROI-based VGG networks trained from scratch. The feature pipeline used five pretrained architectures, eight flip/rotation variants, six first-level learners, and three second-level models. Suspected patient overlap across validation folds undermined weighted blending, so the stacked models were combined with an unweighted arithmetic mean. The two teammates' best predictions were then averaged using Stage 1 leaderboard feedback.
models_pretrained: ["ImageNet-pretrained VGG16, VGG19, ResNet50, Xception, Inception V3"]
compute: First-stage training took about 50 hours.

solution_title: 36th Place - Trust Your CV - Optimize PP
solution_summary: The author adapted public XLM-RoBERTa notebooks and tuned hyperparameters, learning rates, and schedules. The best submission used a probability-product span score with extra emphasis on the start position. This postprocessing improved CV, public, and private scores, with the final model reaching CV 0.700 and private score 0.744. A separate public-score-driven weighted ensemble generalized poorly, reinforcing selection by local validation.
external_data: ["TyDiQA (post-competition mention)", "MLQA and XQuAD (referenced training notebook)", "Extra Tamil data (referenced training notebook)"]

solution_title: 7th Place Gold - CNN Transformer with Invariant Features
solution_summary: The author trained temporal CNN Transformers jointly across labs using invariant tracking features and losses that masked unannotated actions. Diverse feature families, temporal windows, and augmentations enabled transfer across different recording setups. The final system blended a ten-network ensemble with per-lab, per-action XGBoost models trained on neural out-of-fold predictions and public-baseline features. It achieved CV 0.559, public score 0.562, and private score 0.523.

The solution normalizes handedness and device orientation before modeling fixed 96-step sensor sequences. WaveNet, ResNet, U-Net, and SqueezeFormer models use temporal and quaternion-derived features, weighted training, augmentation, and EMA parameters. Subject-grouped stratified validation supports experimentation, while the final ensemble uses 20-fold bagging. Four modality and accelerometer variants allow inference routing around missing rotation features, which improved the private score by 0.0015.

The final pipeline allocated two predictions to template-based modeling, one to Protenix, and two to RNAPro. Template coordinates were adapted to the query, perturbed for diversity, and geometrically smoothed, while RNAPro refined the template-derived structures. Overlapping chunk inference improved Protenix predictions for long sequences. Validation and public leaderboard tracking guided the ensemble, with the two selected submissions differing in whether Protenix used RNA MSA.

The author extended a shared LightGBM pipeline with roughly 100 temporal and item/store categorical features. Training covered 19 weeks starting March 15, 2017, with the latest possible week reserved for validation. Older training weeks received lower weights so the model emphasized recent customer behavior. The solution reached a public score of 0.513, and the author attributed its stronger private performance to the larger training set and recency weighting.

solution_title: [54th solution] Baseline inference optimization with TTA (No additional training)
solution_summary: The team reused the public baseline's trained models and concentrated on inference optimization because they lacked resources to retrain the first stage. Moving model loading outside loops, changing image resizing, and many smaller changes reduced inference from nine hours to 2.5 hours. They then added three-way test-time augmentation selected through public leaderboard experiments. The final augmented solution scored 0.221 on the public leaderboard and 0.216 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Optimized inference: 2.5 hours versus 9 hours originally; three-way TTA fit within 9 hours.

solution_summary: The author reused a segmentation pipeline from Severstal and ensembled 20 models trained across five folds. The models combined U-Net with EfficientNet-B0/B3 encoders and FPN with ResNet34 at moderate image resolutions. BCE plus Dice loss, heavy augmentation including mixup, and cosine annealing worked well. Final masks used label, mask, and minimum-component thresholds; PSPNet, larger images, plain BCE, and pseudo-labeling were unsuccessful.

The solution blended CNNs trained on mel spectrograms with either time-localized labels or recording-level weak labels. Masked losses ignored unannotated segments, while scaled pseudo-labels and partial manual annotations supported additional training stages. A large weak-label ensemble introduced diversity through backbones, seeds, augmentations, and randomly selected teacher predictions. Species-specific probability scaling corrected label-distribution differences, and public leaderboard feedback guided selection because local validation did not correlate reliably.
compute: GPU spectrogram processing and augmentations; close to 2,000 experiments.
external_data: ["Hosts' research paper on test label distribution"]

solution_summary: The approach compared face embeddings using three complementary pairwise metrics and combined average and maximum pooling. Progressive layer freezing, Adam with a starting learning rate of 1e-5, and 224-pixel images gave the best results. Flipping, blurring, and rotation helped, while minimum pooling, SENet, and random grayscale augmentation did not. Focal loss improved the public score but slightly worsened private performance.

solution_title: 763rd Place Solution for the BirdCLEF 2023 Competition
solution_summary: The system segments bird recordings, extracts audio features, and stores them as two-dimensional grayscale images with 8-bit quantization. A simple sequential convolutional network classifies birds, with separate notebooks handling exploration, dataset conversion, longer training, and submission. Its main contribution is an interpretability workflow that reconstructs approximate audio from intermediate activations or a selected bird output. Accuracy is described as satisfactory for demonstrating the system, but no numerical result is provided.

The solution combined extensive feature engineering with LightGBM, two XGBoost configurations, and CatBoost. Features included mapped-attribute distances, categorical interactions with weight capacity, external price statistics, target encoding, missingness indicators, and supervised autoencoder representations. Ten-fold out-of-fold predictions fed a BayesianRidge stacker, and the best submission was blended with public submissions. An early prediction adjustment lost its benefit as the models improved, while automatic feature selection optimization was unsuccessful.
compute: Vast majority of computations used free Kaggle resources.

solution_summary: The solution treated discourse identification as named entity recognition and combined five transformer models with weighted averaging over selected folds. Class-specific expansion of short predicted spans improved public/private scores by 0.007/0.005. Additional post-processing corrected span linking, extended it to other discourse types, optimized thresholds, and removed inappropriate capitalized endings. Topic-based multitask training, concatenated final layers, alternative losses, and large batches did not work well.
compute: Colab Pro+ mainly using V100, and GCE preemptible A100 instances.

solution_summary: Gradient boosting models separately estimated event probability and survival time conditional on an event. A TabM network directly optimized a sigmoid-smoothed version of the competition metric. All models used 20-fold cross-validation with five random seeds. A linear neural stacking layer combined TabM risk with second-order combinations of the boosting predictions using the same metric-oriented loss.

solution_title: 9th: From Reinforcement Learning to a Final BC Agent
solution_summary: The final agent uses an 18.4-million-parameter Transformer and farm CNN trained by behavior cloning from strong replays. Reconstructing executed actions, maintaining within-turn resource dependencies, and adding multiscale market history were central to the pipeline. Training combines action imitation with economic and forecasting objectives, using a replay mixture emphasizing MMPQ trajectories. A single EMA checkpoint runs with deterministic argmax decoding and ahead-of-time CPU compilation; local complete-game comparisons favored it over historical BC opponents.
compute: PPO experiments used four GPUs with 512 games per rollout wave; final inference targeted Broadwell CPUs.
external_data: ["Competition replay corpus, including MMPQ and other submissions"]

solution_summary: The solution combined iterated local search with repeated simulated annealing to optimize word order for perplexity. It evaluated batches of insertion, swap, and shuffle neighbors, using adaptive perturbations to escape local optima. Compact score caching and a dynamically updated bigram distance matrix reduced expensive model evaluations. The author reported roughly 100-fold search-efficiency improvement from pruning and a final perplexity of 28.5.

The team combined several candidate generators using rank-based weights to select 150 items per session, achieving an overall candidate recall of 0.6854. Ranking used item, session, user-item, and candidate-generation features, with separate models for clicks, carts, and orders in one teammate's pipeline. The final submission ensembled probabilities from XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost, producing a small improvement within the 0.602 leaderboard score range. Stacking performed well in validation but did not translate to leaderboard gains.

The algorithm initializes two tours with Concorde's linkern and constructs a candidate edge set from their edges and nearby neighbors. It repairs shared-edge conflicts by repeatedly optimizing tours with increasing conflict penalties, eventually forbidding new conflicts. A custom Double-Lin-Kernighan search alternates tour balancing and feasibility objectives before another repair pass. Repair typically yields a worst tour around 6542000, while further improvement mainly narrows the gap between tours and eventually stalls; the final paths are formed by removing each tour's longest edge.

solution_title: 10th MaskRCNN without ensemble and TTA solution.
solution_summary: The pipeline combined a Unet101 at 384×384 resolution with Mask R-CNN, with the final reported score of 0.851 obtained without TTA or ensembling. Effective changes included online hard-example mining, random multiscale training, stronger augmentation, and larger mask crops trained with Dice and binary cross-entropy losses. Mask-overlap soft NMS handled instance rescoring without relying on rotated boxes. TTA and checkpoint ensembles hurt public scores but improved private results, while smaller FPN anchors and Cascade R-CNN did not improve the solution.

solution_title: How to improve Sh1ng solution without Arboretum
solution_summary: The author combined four LightGBM models with shared arboretum predictions using weights based on public leaderboard scores. Improvements included averaging three-fold predictions, treating None as a product during F1 optimization, and adding users' last prior orders as training examples with those orders excluded from feature computation. The reported result exceeded 0.4059 on the public leaderboard and 0.4041 on the private leaderboard. Inverse order-frequency weighting initially helped publicly, but the author later attributed the public/private gap to that choice.

The solution used XGBoost with 62 engineered features selected for validation performance, public test performance, and execution efficiency. Ten-fold stratified cross-validation and early stopping determined the iteration count before training on all available data. Predictions were averaged across 50 seeds. R's stringi functions helped keep preprocessing and feature creation fast.
compute: Kaggle notebook CPU; approximately 15 seconds importing/preprocessing, 40 seconds feature creation/essay reconstruction, and 85 seconds training 50 seeds.

solution_summary: The useful pipeline combined preprocessing, pseudo-labeling, and custom span postprocessing, while the final base architecture was not specified. Preprocessing raised the reported score from 0.712 to 0.717, and pseudo-labeling with labels voted on by three models increased it to 0.720. Pseudo-labeled training used a learning rate of 4e-5 instead of the base model's 2e-5. Rules handling whitespace, punctuation, and alignment to the original tweet raised the score to 0.729; the planned final model ensemble was abandoned because uploading weights was too slow.

The solution embedded RNA node features and processed them with paired-node concatenation, bidirectional GRUs, and residual convolution blocks. Larger convolution kernels, signal-to-noise sample weighting, and a cubic prediction transformation improved performance. Cluster-based GroupKFold supported model selection, while bagged models were blended with a model using base-pair probability information. Pseudo-labeling was abandoned after public-score degradation despite improved validation and later-observed private results.

solution_title: 4th place solution, CSN is all you need for 3D
solution_summary: The pipeline first segmented vertebrae in 3D and then classified vertebra-centered crops with video-pretrained CSN networks. A UNet-style segmentor used an ir-CSN-50 encoder, while four-fold classification used ir/ip-CSN-152 models. Video pretraining worked better than the explored inflated 2D and sequence-head alternatives. Subsampling, segmentation-mask inputs, visibility-adjusted labels, and consistent slice augmentations supported the classification pipeline.

The solution pretrained bird-audio models on XCM and earlier BirdCLEF datasets before training on the 2024 competition data. It selected approximately 21,000 unlabeled frames using agreement between evaluation-mode predictions and eight noisy dropout predictions. Training then combined these pseudo-labeled frames with competition data and noise from nocall audio and ESC-50. An eca_nfnet_l0 and effnet_b0 ensemble improved public/private scores from approximately 0.66/0.63 to 0.702/0.666, with leaderboard scores guiding decisions because of domain shift.

solution_title: 9th Place Solution for the "ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions" Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined diverse models and preprocessing pipelines to reduce overfitting on the small dataset. The first component ensembled two XGBoost and two TabPFN classifiers with oversampling, constant imputation, and the Greek Epsilon feature. A second component used scaled data, 40 selected features, and XGBoost and LightGBM models with 15-fold prediction averaging. The final blend weighted the first ensemble three times as heavily as each of the other two models.

The solution classified TF-IDF features with multiple classifiers, retaining LightGBM and adding ComplementNB and LinearSVC. Removing Cat substantially reduced runtime, from roughly two hours to 15 minutes. Separate pipelines trained on DAIGT-V2 and additional external training data were blended at a 6:4 ratio, with min-max normalization applied to predictions before integration. External data was the main contributor to performance; mixing the datasets directly achieved a higher private score but was rejected because of its lower public score.
compute: Runtime reduced from approximately 2 hours to about 15 minutes after removing Cat.

solution_title: Solo 60th Place Solution - Forward Ensembling & Pseudo Labeling External Data
solution_summary: The solution combined ResNet200D and SEResNet152D models trained at different image resolutions through annotation-based teacher–student training. Selected models received an additional NIH pseudo-label training stage before supervised fine-tuning, ending with augmentation-free epochs. Forward selection built separate ensembles for two validation folds, whose predictions were blended with public five-fold ResNet200D models. Both selected submissions scored 0.971 privately, although incomplete cross-validation and possible external-data duplicates limited confidence in validation.
compute: Z8 workstation for main experiments and ZBook Studio laptop for smaller experiments; RTX Quadro 8000 and RTX Quadro 5000 mobile GPUs.

solution_title: A simple method to get 0.009 booster in private
solution_summary: The post describes a holiday-aware weekday recoding trick for restaurant visitor forecasting. Holidays are treated as Saturdays, while adjacent weekdays are mapped to Friday before a holiday and Monday after it. The author reports that the rule helped across Golden Week and other holidays and attributes the finding to exploratory analysis and cross-validation.

The author adapted a shared RaLSGAN kernel to generate dog images. Increasing discriminator capacity, adding generator normalization, and introducing breed-label auxiliary supervision progressively improved the score. ResNet blocks in both networks and conditional batch normalization in the generator brought the final reported score to 44.69. BigGAN was considered but was not implemented.

The solution ensembled eight LSTMs, four BERT base models, two BERT large models, one GPT2, and one XLNet with varied seeds and sequence lengths. Every model combined pooled text representations with 11 statistical text features and used a loss combining weighted binary prediction with auxiliary targets. Transformer models ultimately trained on all available data, while BERT layer selection and an accidental gradient-accumulation implementation improved results. Adding XLNet raised the reported ensemble score to 0.94646, and BERT input trimming helped keep total inference near 5,500 seconds.
compute: Approximately 5,500 seconds total inference.

solution_summary: The solution trained image masking models with ResNet50 and MobileNet encoders using TensorFlow-backed Keras. Five-fold validation kept all 16 images of each car together to prevent related views crossing folds. Folds were constructed by sorting mask sizes, accounting for variation among cars.
compute: Prediction command specifies GPU indices 0, 1, and 2.

solution_summary: The team averaged several diverse blends built around MLPs, skip-connected MLPs, TabNet, and public baseline models. Preprocessing included RankGauss normalization, PCA features, and variance-threshold feature selection. Transfer learning, learning-rate scheduling, multiple folds and seeds, and soft pseudo-labeling contributed to the ensemble. The final blend achieved public loss 0.01822, while drug-based probability correction showed uncertain value and several feature and stacking experiments failed.
compute: HP Z8 with Intel Xeon Gold 6234 CPU @ 3.30GHz × 32; reported eight times faster than a Kaggle kernel.

solution_summary: The post announces that the author has published code and documentation. It links to the HiggsML GitHub repository. The provided text contains no description of the solution methods or results.

solution_title: 136th place solution for AI Village Capture the Flag @ DEFCON31 competition
solution_summary: The author solved 20 CTF challenges through a mixture of visualization, brute-force search, embedding similarity, and security exploits. Successful methods included isolating a misclassified demographic subgroup, decoding text with t-SNE, and searching pretrained Word2Vec embeddings. Prompt injection and role impersonation unlocked several LLM challenges, while XML injection and a pickle payload solved other tasks. Several image and model attacks remained unsuccessful.

solution_title: 16th Place Solution - Kalman Filters and Boosted Trees
solution_summary: The team combined a custom Kalman-filter forecasting component with a boosted-tree solution from public notebooks. The custom component used the R package KFAS and a relatively simple pipeline built from scratch. Weak performance on sparse series motivated a loess-based choice between the two forecasting approaches for each series. The resulting approach functioned as a mixture of experts.

The authors share an open ship detection solution with a runnable U-Net training and inference pipeline. Preprocessing prepares metadata and overlaid target masks once for reuse in experiments. Five listed versions improve the leaderboard score from 0.573 to 0.725, with the latest version reporting CV 0.719.
compute: Cloud training commands specify an m-2p100 worker.

solution_title: 14th place solution multitask LSTM - Team "no pressure"
solution_summary: The team trained four-layer and five-layer bidirectional LSTMs in Keras and PyTorch, using robust scaling and raw or log-transformed u_in inputs. Predicting pressure together with pressure differences improved performance, with MAE loss and linear output activation supporting these targets. Their median ensemble of 15 models scored 0.1107 privately, while a stacking variant scored 0.1111. Numerous alternatives failed to help, and pseudo-labeling delivered only a marginal improvement.

The solution separated ordinary target prediction from outlier detection using two models. A regression model was trained without outliers, while a binary model predicted whether an example was an outlier. Final predictions added the regression output to negative 33 times the binary output. The author reported a best public score of 3.677.

The solution used an MXNet U-Net-like network with separate input branches for A, M, and P channels. An adaptive crop sampler was updated each epoch using the network's performance on different classes. Supporting scripts handled augmentation and conversion between polygon and raster representations.

The submission adapted an existing ARChitects-derived baseline using quantized Nemo Mini with LoRA fine-tuning. It combined grid augmentations, task-specific retraining, Turbo DFS beam search, and augmented candidate scoring across four GPUs. The author's principal change was empirically selecting random seed 19920627. Reported scores varied from 3.33% to 6.67% across seed configurations, illustrating sensitivity on the small evaluation set.
compute: 4 GPUs for parallel training and inference.

solution_summary: The solution combined 13 speech recognition models using MFCC and audio spectrogram features. Architectures included convolutional LSTM, LSTM-L, C-RNN, GRU-L, and ResNet, with background noise and time-shift augmentation. Each model was retrained using the training set plus test examples pseudo-labeled at confidence above 95%, without external data. Weighted averaging performed better than linear-regression stacking on the private leaderboard.

The author focused on feature engineering, reporting improvements from DCA, Magic, TruncatedSVD, FA, and LDA. The ensemble selected neural networks, LightGBM, CatBoost, XGBoost, and kernel ridge, with ridge used for CITE-seq. Validation split the data by batch, although the author questioned how well this reflected private performance. The neural network was the strongest single model, while some final plans remained unfinished and unsubmitted.

The solution used cased BERT base and large models with progressively narrowing classification heads and selected intermediate BERT outputs. Training used corrected labels, six folds, dropout, BertAdam, learning-rate reduction, and early stopping. A LightGBM second-stage model combined both BERT models with distance, URL, text statistics, and encoded-pronoun features, with hyperopt used for parameter search. An additional BERT fine-tuning experiment and a cosine-scheduling/RMSprop experiment failed to improve scores.

The solution combined fine-tuned image-model features with tabular features in a soft-voting ensemble of LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost. Image training preserved lesion aspect ratios and addressed class imbalance with resampling, heavy augmentation, and MixUp. Five image backbones were retained, and consistent validation folds connected image and tabular training. Permutation importance removed roughly 190 tabular features, improving CV from 0.179 to 0.183.
compute: Parallel inference on two T4 GPUs in half precision, batch size 512.

solution_summary: The solution combined pretrained LoFTR, SuperGlue, and DKM matching results without fine-tuning. Initial multi-resolution matches defined covisibility crops through DBSCAN clustering, followed by another matching stage on those crops. Original and cropped-image keypoints were concatenated before USAC_MAGSAC estimated the fundamental matrix. The selected configuration took approximately nine hours and achieved a private score of 0.86343.
compute: Approximately 9 hours for the selected inference configuration.

solution_summary: The team fine-tuned Nemotron-3-Nano-30B using LoRA and synthetic problems paired with rule-based solver traces. Their central design separated information the model should memorize from consistency checks it should perform within its reasoning trace. Cryptarithm traces recalled a precomputed signature catalog and applied constrained depth-first search, while bit-manipulation traces compressed strings into hexadecimal and repaired candidate rule sequences. Main training used 220,000 samples, followed by a lower-learning-rate continuation emphasizing bit manipulation; the reported private score reached 0.908.
compute: Main training about 119 hours; additional training about 51 hours.

solution_summary: The team combined object detection and classification models in an ensemble. Its detectors included SSD trained with extra ImageNet data and Faster R-CNN implementations across several frameworks. Classification models operated on image crops using VGG, ResNet, Xception, and Inception architectures. The post gives only a brief technical overview, with much of the discussion devoted to competition outcomes.

The solution ensembled two models and credited Google's MuRIL BERT model. One model was first fine-tuned on SQuAD v2.0, while the other was first fine-tuned on translated SQuAD. Both were then fine-tuned on CHAII, MLQA, and XQUAD. The author reported that an unselected best model could have achieved a 0.745 private leaderboard score.

The solution used Elo ratings adjusted by seed, rebounding, and field-goal percentage differences to predict basketball matchups. Separate normal and logistic link functions converted adjusted rating differences into men's and women's probabilities. Grid search evaluated parameters by replaying seasons from 2010, while simulated tournament paths updated ratings before later-round predictions. Recent-form sensitivity was useful, and a manual Princeton rating adjustment added a speculative component; the reported private score was 0.17557.
compute: MacBook running grid search all day.

solution_summary: The solution combined CatBoost, LightGBM and XGBoost with image-derived features from EVA02-small and EdgeNeXt models. Patient-relative lesion features, Local Outlier Factor scores and standardized image-model predictions improved the tabular pipeline, with noise added to image-derived training features. Repeated stratified group cross-validation guided most changes, while ranked predictions were averaged across a large seeded ensemble. An externally trained three-class image model provided useful additional features, but synthetic-image models were excluded because they did not improve the final ensemble.
compute: GBDT models trained on GPU; the 150-model tabular ensemble took under 20 minutes to train.

solution_summary: The solution used three U-Net models with EfficientNet, RegNet and SE-ResNeXt encoders on 512-pixel ash-color images. Averaging individual annotations into soft targets substantially improved validation and leaderboard performance. Validation used five chronological folds and a separate holdout, although fold scores correlated poorly with leaderboard scores. Easy negative images were filtered to reduce training time, and final predictions combined weighted models with fold-specific thresholds and a final threshold on averaged binary masks.

solution_title: 14th place solution [6th if resized the boxes]
solution_summary: The final system combined a U-Net style segmentation network with one Mask R-CNN, two Faster R-CNN models, and one RetinaNet. Segmentation learned from both positive and negative images, while the described detector training used positive samples on different splits. Intersecting segmentation and detection outputs filtered false positives and produced the largest improvement. The system achieved leaderboard scores of 0.220 and 0.222 in the two stages; later box-shrinking experiments reached 0.236 but were not included in the submission.
compute: Single 1060 GPU; segmentation training ~20 hours; detector training reported as ~5 hours.

solution_summary: The team trained a small tabular neural network with two 32-node hidden layers to predict FVC and its uncertainty directly. They increased the emphasis on absolute error in the competition loss and validated with five patient-grouped folds using every pair of measurements where the target occurred later. Gaussian noise augmentation coupled the input and target FVC changes, adjusted Percent consistently, and was followed by input normalization. Final predictions averaged FVC across folds and combined uncertainty estimates using their quadratic mean; trusting cross-validation paid off despite misleading public leaderboard feedback.

The code reads the competition's sample submission with pandas. It writes that table unchanged to submission.csv without an index. This provides a submission-format baseline with no model training, feature engineering, or evaluation shown.

The solution trained EfficientNet-L2 recognition models on full-body crops with adaptive-margin ArcFace, RandAugment, and SGD. Repeated pseudo-labeling with a confidence threshold of 0.8 was the main source of improvement, with each round initialized from ImageNet weights. Some models were fine-tuned on YOLOX crops, and the final ensemble combined four models with different pseudo-label rounds and image configurations. Cosine-similarity retrieval with a fixed new-individual threshold produced public 0.897 and private 0.872.
compute: Batch size 16 on a single RTX 3090 with checkpointing and mixed precision; also reported sponsored dual-A6000 Z8G4 workstation and RTX5000 ZBook.

solution_title: (Rank 39 Upto 250 points added) Why there is so significant difference between private and public scores???
solution_summary: The post celebrates an improvement in the author's competition result and links to a solution notebook. It asks why public and private scores differed enough to produce the change. No modeling, preprocessing, or validation details are provided in the text.

The approach combined community bag-packing optimization with leaderboard submissions that revealed gift weights. Early submissions probed coal to build bags with known high weights, but this became too slow to remain competitive. The final variation modified 300 bags by replacing a train with a bike, detected bags that exceeded the weight limit, and restored those bags to their original contents. The author reports that this added approximately 1,000 points.

The author built a Rust simulator with compact flight-plan encoding, precomputed trajectories, and persistent collision events. Restricted pseudo-rollouts evaluated future positions after existing fleets resolved without launching new fleets. A heuristic-guided MCTS approach underperformed a rule-based baseline, so the submitted agent selected among heuristic candidate actions using simulations and pseudo-rollouts. The initial Rust simulator measured about 0.08 ms per step versus 12.9 ms for Python, while the final agent took roughly 5–1000 ms per decision.
compute: Final agent: 50–100 simulation steps plus pseudo-rollouts, taking 5–1000 ms per decision; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The author presents a competition solution created as a quick code sample. Training is launched through the src/train.py script, with an example that redirects output to a results file. The text does not describe the model, features, or validation procedure.

solution_title: Silver Medal - 243rd Place - Create Labels from Reports and Images
solution_summary: The approach combined hybrid image-and-report LLM annotations with an upgraded 2.5D CoAtNet architecture. Compact canonical MRI mosaics improved multimodal labeling, while the image model retained spatial quadrants and MRI sequence hierarchy instead of relying on global pooling alone. Cached-feature head training and a short late-backbone fine-tuning stage enabled inexpensive upgrades across seven streams. The standalone model reached 0.954 public AUC, and its rank blend with a public notebook reached 0.959.

solution_title: 59th Place Solution for the Detect and Classify Traumatic Abdominal Injuries Competition
solution_summary: The pipeline converted CT scans to PNG and trained a U-Net using annotations generated by Total Segmentator to locate abdominal organs. It sampled 32 evenly spaced slices per scan, extracted EfficientNet features, and combined the sequence with an LSTM. TensorFlow augmentations expanded the training data, while organ-specific losses focused supervision on relevant slices and assigned greater weight to injuries.
compute: TPU training; hardware details and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The team combined symbolic regression, modified multiclass neural networks, XGBoost/LightGBM ensembles, and CatBoost models using nested cross-validation. Feature engineering emphasized chemical ratios, interactions, and aggregate acidity measures. The two selected submissions used different blends of these model families. An unselected blend of symbolic regression, CatBoost, and XGBoost/LightGBM achieved the best reported private score of 0.59656, reinforcing the value of validation and model diversity.

solution_title: 40th Place Summary - In Chris and CV we trust
solution_summary: The author used weighted ensembles of EfficientNet B4–B7 models, mostly initialized with Noisy Student weights. Models used images at 384, 512, and 768 pixels, five validation folds, and 15-way test-time augmentation. Larger networks and images generally performed better, while previous competition data added ensemble diversity. Metadata was incorporated at roughly a 90/10 image-to-metadata split; the reported 18-model submission with metadata achieved 0.9434 private AUC.

The solution blended ResNeSt200 Mask R-CNN models initialized from LIVECell pretraining with Cellpose. It used both three-class and class-specific models, five-fold training, multiple image sizes and extensive inference augmentation. Class-specific inference combined weighted boxes fusion, non-maximum suppression and mask averaging. Two final ensembles, one including pseudo-label-trained models and one without them, both achieved 0.354 on the private leaderboard.
compute: Ensemble inference constrained by the allowed nine-hour runtime.

solution_title: 4th place solution for the GWI competition
solution_summary: The author generated more than 10 million synthetic samples and trained a roughly 100-million-parameter hybrid vision transformer and 2D convolution model for about three weeks. Improving the synthetic data generation and using physically accurate flipped samples were central to the approach. The final ensemble combined two orientation-specific models with a Style-focused model, using family-specific weights and several checkpoints per model. Family-aware clipping, rounding, and grouping of predicted velocities provided a small additional improvement.
compute: Kaggle and Colab T4 GPUs for generation (~13k samples/hour); TPU training for ~3 weeks; about $400 in Colab credits.

solution_summary: The approach restricted predictions to names, addresses, emails, URLs, and IDs. Names were detected with spaCy models, while the remaining four types used regular expressions. The author trained multiple spaCy models and selected better-performing ones, without providing validation details or scores.

solution_title: 36th solution : Cheap Transformers that can run on gaming laptops and does not require a BPP matrix
solution_summary: The author developed a lightweight transformer that predicts RNA reactivity from short sequence cuts without a base-pair probability matrix. Predictions from multiple cuts were combined for each nucleotide, improving cross-validation by approximately 0.005. The final ensemble varied transformer settings and cut lengths of 64, 96, and 128, achieving a private score of 0.15346. Short inputs reduced memory and training costs, while pseudo-labeling provided little leaderboard benefit.
compute: Runs on a gaming laptop GPU; hardware model and runtime were not specified.

solution_summary: The author trained a separate LightGBM model for each cryptocurrency using only Close prices and a common feature definition. Features described logarithmic price changes, market-wide averages, and each currency's deviation from the market. Seven-fold embargo validation was used, and training began only when enough currencies were present, with limited forward filling for gaps. Inference finished within nine hours, but its cost prevented further ensembling.
compute: Inference completed within nine hours; hardware unspecified.

solution_title: 79th place - beginner tutorial in applying a previous solution with minimal changes and training time
solution_summary: The pipeline adapted an earlier cervical-spine solution into organ segmentation followed by four organ-specific injury classifiers. A segmentation model processed 128-cubed volumes, and its masks guided construction of 15 six-channel 2.5D inputs per organ. Left and right kidneys were concatenated for a shared kidney classifier, while extravasation used an optimized constant. Training for 15 classifier epochs scored 0.615 privately using about 30 Kaggle GPU hours; extending to 45 epochs improved the score to 0.548 with roughly 30 additional hours.
compute: About 30 Kaggle GPU hours initially; roughly 30 additional GPU hours to extend classifiers from 15 to 45 epochs.

solution_title: 1st place solution: Correct Data is All You Need
solution_summary: The final system ensembled three sound event detection models with NFNet and ConvNeXt backbones. Expanded, deduplicated bird audio and selective pretraining mattered alongside class-dependent sampling and carefully chosen augmentations. Five-fold stratified validation guided experiments, followed by full-data retraining for the ensemble. ONNX improved deployment, and power-mean aggregation plus a blend of attention and timewise predictions provided small gains. The reported best private score was 0.76392.
compute: A100 GPUs; 294 experiments, approximately half with five folds and half with full-data training
