solution_title: Tentative 3rd Place Solution (6th in Public) - life is volatile
solution_summary: The final solution stacked LightGBM and neural-network models, with feature design providing the main improvements. Nearest-neighbor features identified time IDs with similar market conditions and included relative neighbor distances. Predicting volatility relative to observed 600-second volatility improved robustness. Auxiliary models learned short-horizon volatility from combined train and test observations and estimated market-wide average volatility, supplying additional main-model features.

solution_title: Silver Medal via Universal-Survival CD Strategy
solution_summary: The author selected a confused-deputy email attack for its expected robustness to a stronger hidden guardrail. Short prompts used semantic alternatives to monitored sharing keywords, rotated recipients for novelty credit, and applied model-specific formatting to improve throughput. Candidates were replayed against the public guardrail and retained only when the intended predicate fired. The email attack retained 21.255 privately from 22.500 publicly, whereas the stronger public exfiltration exploit and destructive-write and untrusted-action alternatives scored zero privately.

solution_title: Images disappeared from Writeup? Anyone else effected?

solution_summary: The approach trained separate segmentation networks for individual feature classes, with separate methods for water prediction. Prediction used cropping and test-time augmentation, followed by merging class outputs and cleaning overlapping classes. Competition predictions used selected epoch/model combinations for classes with unstable training results. A subsequent reimplementation improved performance by up to 20% for some classes, while sparse training data made others difficult to reproduce.
compute: Titan X Pascal 12GB and GTX 1080 8GB; approximately 7 hours per 50-epoch training stage and 5 hours per class for prediction on Titan X.

solution_summary: The solution combined absolute positions from Wi-Fi and beacon bidirectional LSTMs with relative displacements from a sensor-based 1D CNN. Interpolating training waypoints every second was the largest reported improvement to the absolute model. A corridor-constrained probabilistic path sampler fused absolute and relative predictions and incorporated the device ID leak, followed by snapping positions to a grid. The final reported public/private errors were 2.64846/3.07282.

The solution emphasized generalization through question-order-invariant engineered features and a shared LSTM. The LSTM outputs were combined using squared differences and sums so swapping questions preserved the representation. Bounded feature values, rare-word replacement, dropout, and Gaussian noise reduced opportunities to overfit. The final predictions ensembled multiple neural networks.

solution_title: Potential 6th place solution with a single model ! [all about layers]
solution_summary: The authors used a single pretrained SEResNeXt50 with three output heads, trained on cropped 128×128 images. Training ran for 30 epochs with shift, scale, rotation, Mixup, a OneCycle learning-rate policy, and the Over9000 optimizer. Their improved model replaced adaptive pooling with GeM, replaced batch normalization with group normalization, standardized convolution weights, and removed dropout and weight decay. Together with referenced post-processing, the reported approach achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.9557 and a public score of 0.9703.

The solution retrieved candidates from user history, three co-visitation matrices, a small BERT masked language model, and matrix factorization, then ranked them with separate CatBoost models for each target. Session segmentation and exponential time weighting were the most consequential retrieval improvements, while around 200 user, item, and interaction features supported ranking. Transformer and matrix-factorization scores were strong ranking features, although their leaderboard gains were limited. The final approach reached about 0.601 on the public leaderboard without useful gains from ensembling.
compute: A100 GPU: BERT training took 7 hours for 3 epochs; matrix factorization took 7 hours for 20 epochs; CatBoost took 2–4 minutes per fold for 5,000 iterations. Ranker inference took 1–1.5 hours.

solution_summary: The team built 587 features capturing similarities between ad texts, images, locations, prices, and JSON attributes, with feature engineering driving most of the gains. Connected ad-pair cluster sizes improved the score by 0.003–0.004, while a meta-model added roughly 0.0015 over their best XGBoost. They screened features for temporal instability and validated on the last third of training data, although that holdout became unreliable near the end. TF-IDF, word2vec, advanced cluster statistics, and several alternative base models were discarded because of overfitting or weak gains.

solution_title: How to win Santa's Workshop Tour
solution_summary: The author linearized the accounting objective by enumerating consecutive-day occupancy combinations and solved mixed integer programs with Gurobi. Preference-cost lower bounds and incumbent upper bounds eliminated expensive variables, producing a solution of at most 70134 in roughly 70 minutes. A MIP large neighbourhood search then improved the incumbent by restricting daily occupancies around an existing solution. Finally, the bounded original formulation proved optimality in about a day.
compute: Reduced MIP: roughly 70 minutes; final optimality proof: about a day.

solution_summary: The solution combined embedding retrieval with a multiclass reranker. More than 10,000 synthetic examples improved single-fold recall from 0.430 to 0.470, while three concatenated embedding models provided retrieval diversity. Both stages used Qwen models with averaged five-fold LoRA weights, including variants augmented with inferred error reasons. A weighted ensemble of three rerankers improved the private score from 0.485 for retrieval to 0.564.

The solution trained separate transformer actor-critic policies for two-player and four-player OrbitWars through PPO self-play. A custom C++ engine handled launch calculations, while structured invariant features and factored action heads supported tactical decisions in one forward pass. Auxiliary launch-success prediction, a no-op probability anchor, and adaptive surrender improved training efficiency. Prioritized fictitious self-play substantially strengthened the four-player agent, while CPU simulation throughput limited compute utilization.
compute: Hardware ranged from RTX 3090 with 16-core Ryzen 9 to a rented 8x5090, 384-core machine; larger machines achieved 15k–20k steps/s. Final two-player and four-player models trained for approximately 4B and 2B steps.

solution_summary: The solution ranked products using naive Bayes models based on query text, time, and user click history. Item priors were smoothed within category and 12-day periods, while separate unigram and unordered bigram models were combined linearly. Query preprocessing used lemmatization, stopword removal, and splitting joined words and numbers. The final ranking demoted products the user had already clicked for the same query and returned the five highest-ranked items.

solution_title: 250th Place Saved by Public Single Model
solution_summary: The author slightly adjusted public ensembles for one final submission and selected a public single-model solution as a backup. Small datasets and substantial missing test data motivated the more conservative second choice. The backup used a five-fold model and held up on the private leaderboard, while the first blend deteriorated.

The post announces the author's open-source tsboost forecasting package and links its GitHub repository. It promises a future release of the full competition solution and possible support for confidence intervals. It also discusses the competition's evaluation methodology, without explaining a concrete solution pipeline.

solution_title: Building a Top-Scoring Orbit Wars Agent: From Random Fleets to a GPU-Simulated
solution_summary: The agent used a PyTorch tensor simulator that reproduced fleet movement, production, and combat to forecast planet states and evaluate candidate launches. Sparse recalculation of only affected planets enabled thousands of candidates to be scored by their effect on the relative ship balance. A constrained greedy planner coordinated attacks and reinforcements, with phase-dependent thresholds and deterministic selection among twenty tuned profiles. The reported score was 1091.1; the experimental MCTS and risk engines did not contribute to live decisions.

The solution used a borrowed CNN architecture trained with RMSProp, ReduceLROnPlateau, and geometric augmentation. Three initial models trained for different durations and holdout sizes supplied ensemble predictions for pseudo labeling. Two further models used ordinary and class-adjusted pseudo labels. The stronger submission combined these models and reduced selected class probabilities, reporting scores of 0.9936/0.9952.

The solution learned features directly from raw stroke segments with a dilated 1D CNN, then rasterized the learned point features into a grid for an ImageNet-pretrained convolutional backbone. This trainable frontend replaced conventional RGB rasterization and the backbone's initial convolution and pooling layers, preserving temporal and stroke connectivity information. Training used half precision, initial backbone freezing, Adam, and gradient accumulation. The final ensemble combined six models using validation-loss-based probability weights, achieving local MAP@3 of 0.9101 and a private leaderboard score of 0.95101.
compute: A 1080Ti and a Titan; models typically converged in about 2.5–3 days.

solution_title: 34th place solution - Using CT Scans (+ Code)
solution_summary: The solution blended three ResNet50 models trained on windowed CT images with selected metadata. CT volumes were converted to Hounsfield units, cropped, reshaped to 50 slices, and represented using three windows. Patient-grouped five-fold validation, random informative-slice sampling, and a combined quantile and metric loss defined training. Final FVC and confidence predictions were averaged, while brightness and saturation augmentation helped one particularly strong model.

The author's contribution combined LightGBM and CatBoost models built from six independently engineered data pipelines. Features included financial ratios, applicant and related-person summaries, contract aggregations over multiple time windows, and categorical diversity statistics, with forward selection and null importances used for selection. Validation used five sequential week-based folds and omitted the metric's slope term. Recovering dates from credit-bureau refresh dates enabled metric manipulation that improved private scores to 0.560–0.617, compared with roughly 0.520 without it.

The solution trains a 3D U-Net on 128×128×32 volumes with binary focal loss and random spatial augmentation. Training uses sparse labeled data, AdamW, and cosine learning-rate decay, followed by tiled prediction. Thresholds are chosen using the expected vessel volume ratio, and depth-first connected-component filtering removes small isolated predictions. A large-vessel-component variant reports a private score of 0.756793 despite a public score of zero.

The solution averages four segmentation models using EfficientNet-B0 or SE-ResNeXt50 encoders with U-Net, Link, and FPN architectures. Tiles are resized to 256×256, with pseudo labels and d48_handlabel used during preparation. Each model uses five folds and a combined BCE–Dice loss with BCE weight 0.75. Extensive image augmentation and horizontal/vertical flip test-time augmentation support the final ensemble.

The author used a ten-layer neural network with stacked autoencoders followed by Maxout and rectified-linear layers. Hundreds of these networks were combined with SVMs, random forests, and other models in a large ensemble. Unsupervised learning substantially helped the downstream network but also contributed to overfitting. The complex ensemble generalized poorly compared with its public leaderboard performance.

The solution combined engineered metadata, patient context, frozen DINOv2 embeddings, and EfficientNet B0 melanoma scores in LightGBM classifiers. Within-patient lesion ranks provided the largest improvement, complemented by anchor comparisons, clustering, and metadata and image similarity features. Four binary and multiclass model variants were trained across five folds and five seeds, with validation grouped by patient. Weighted blends achieved approximately 0.169 private score, and the author attributed the weaker generalization to distribution shift.

The team stacked neural networks and boosted-tree models using five-fold predictions and a LightGBM stacker. Auxiliary price models trained on active listings were a major contributor, including neural networks and category-specific XGBoost models using extracted text attributes. Neural models varied their text embeddings and attention architectures, embedded log-transformed prices, and averaged predictions across epochs. Alternative-target classifiers and their prediction entropy also supported the stack, while user-ID models were excluded because their CV-to-leaderboard relationship was unstable.

This writeup describes the signal-processing and synthetic-data portion of a 1D neural-network solution. It used high-pass and notch filtering and generated noise from an estimated power spectral density. The team reproduced merger signals with PyCBC/LALSuite, iteratively refined physical parameter distributions using auxiliary regression, and created synthetic pretraining data. Initial simulations with guessed parameter distributions transferred poorly, while refined distributions and an additional SNR target proved more useful.

The author built a LightGBM model, starting with a small feature subset and exploring feature combinations and parameters. Experiments included factorized categorical encoding, count encoding, and cross-validation. The post gives a broad account of the approach without specifying the final configuration or validation scores.

solution_title: Blending best public submissions - 17th | Simple approach - ~70th
solution_summary: The final submission averaged selected public notebook predictions, motivated by a suspected data construction error and leaderboard probing. The author's original pipeline corrected the COVID sales disruption, engineered calendar features, and trained a regularized LightGBM regressor on a logarithmic target. Optuna tuned regularization, and probing supplied prediction multipliers. That original approach achieved 6.08955 on the public leaderboard and 7.21200 on the private leaderboard.

The solution used four-layer bidirectional LSTMs trained on the inhalation phase, with engineered features and auxiliary pressure-derivative targets. Interpolation-based augmentation, ensemble-based pseudo-label pretraining, and small perturbations at inference improved predictions. Increasing from six to sixteen folds generally improved scores by about 0.003. The final ensemble combined heavily regularized ridge predictions for low-spread samples with a median across model folds for high-spread samples.
compute: Sixteen-fold models took approximately 14 hours to train for 350 epochs.

solution_title: 18th Place with no Neural Nets - LGB and FM - 0.40604
solution_summary: The solution combined a Wordbatch factorization machine with a custom LightGBM through weighted averaging, reaching approximately 0.406. LightGBM used categorical features, selected Wordbatch vectors, handcrafted text features, target encodings, and out-of-fold predictions from Ridge and multinomial Naive Bayes models. Naive Bayes predictions and selection of individual Wordbatch vectors each improved the score by roughly 0.003. Stage 2 preparation reduced performance, but both batched and unbatched inference submissions completed.

The inference pipeline decoded video with OpenCV, transferred frames to GPU, and extracted faces using a modified MTCNN implementation. Gamma correction, generous face margins, and centroid-based tracking supported face detection and artifact removal. An ensemble of EfficientNet models processed up to 100 frames per video, with hold-out ridge regression applied to model outputs. Switching from average to maximum probability when enough frames appeared fake improved the reported score from about 0.29 to 0.27.
compute: GPU processing for frames, gamma correction, and face extraction; hardware model unspecified

solution_summary: The solution combined six BERT variants, thirteen RNN models, and GPT-2 in a weighted ensemble dominated by BERT. Several BERT variants received additional pretraining on competition data, while training a cased model on uncased text added diversity. Training used a custom multitask binary cross-entropy loss, layer-dependent learning rates, gradient accumulation, and head-and-tail truncation to 220 tokens. GPT-2 underperformed expectations individually but still improved the ensemble.
compute: Single V100 GPU; approximately 2 hours per BERT-base training epoch.

solution_summary: The post thanks Nestlogic and its CEO for support. It also acknowledges Martin Piotte's kernels and tips and Andrew Ng's Deep Learning Specialization. No competition approach, pipeline, or results are described.

The solution averaged LightGBM and categorical-embedding neural networks trained with both shared-horizon and separate-horizon formulations. Rolling sales averages, weekday averages, and promotion features supplied most of the predictive value, with additional grouped statistics contributing relatively little. Validation used a single chronological 16-day holdout, and longer training histories improved validation but could hurt private performance. Averaging diverse models made results more consistent, with final blends scoring 0.513–0.516 on the private leaderboard.

The team combined credit-scoring features and block-specific prediction features with statistical aggregates. Feature selection relied on local cross-validation, and exchanging useful features improved both members' models. The final submission averaged four second-level stackers trained on first-level predictions and selected raw features, achieving 0.80511 private LB and 0.80855 CV.

The team blended ViT-B/16, EfficientNetB4, ResNeSt101e, and SE-ResNeXt50 models using averaged fold predictions and test-time augmentation. They increased augmentation repetitions for the small ViT input and retained flips after stronger brightness and contrast changes failed to improve results. A Conv2d-plus-MLP stacker used blended predictions as pseudo labels and Gaussian feature noise, increasing the public score from 0.905 to 0.907. Simple averaging was more robust on noisy test data, while confusion-matrix-guided blending worsened private performance.

The author trained separate NFNet-F0 image and Indonesian DistilBERT text embedding models using multi-similarity loss. Five-fold embedding concatenation, alpha query expansion, and relaxed thresholds for sparse matches improved retrieval. GeM pooling and cross-batch memory were particularly useful for image training, while text augmentation helped the language model. Combined image/text validation F1 increased from 0.88777 to 0.91179 with query expansion, but lowering the final matching threshold worsened private leaderboard performance.

solution_title: A technique that worked for me (~0.001-0.002 improvement) that none of the posted (so far) solution used
solution_summary: The post describes batch construction that mixes high- and low-SNR examples, reserving 30% of each batch for low-SNR samples. Since SNR metadata was unavailable, a model with at least 0.87 AUC supplied a proxy based on absolute prediction error and a 0.5 cutoff. The method improved the reported 1D and B0 models but degraded B3. Training examples in decreasing SNR order caused severe overfitting within the first epoch.

The solution classified filtered MegaDetector animal crops using a single EfficientNetB4 initialized with ImageNet noisy-student weights. It combined iNaturalist data, extensive augmentation, and a custom classifier head incorporating cyclic time features and crop metadata. Predictions were averaged across test-time augmentations, crops, and images grouped by time and location. Training took two hours, and the selected submission scored 0.930 on the public leaderboard and 0.903 on the private leaderboard.
compute: 2 hours of training for 7 epochs

solution_summary: The team built 442 features from all tables and ensembled LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost classifiers. They used mean, maximum, and minimum aggregations, retaining closed-contract columns from bureau_a_1. Drift-prone columns were removed, and selected features received arithmetic, robust-scaling, or quantile transformations. Training on the first 10 weeks and validating on the remaining 80 weeks provided only limited leaderboard correlation.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution for the March Machine Learning Mania 2026 Competition
solution_summary: The final predictor blended XGBoost at 60% and logistic regression at 40%, using combined historical men's and women's tournament data. Matchup features summarized relative team strength through season statistics, efficiency, Elo, seeds, ranking consensus, schedule strength, and recent form. Logistic regression used standardized inputs while XGBoost used raw features, and final probabilities were clipped to reduce extreme errors. Ten-fold Brier-score validation favored logistic regression individually, while the final competition Brier score was 0.1149886.
compute: Approximately 4 GB RAM and 5 minutes runtime.

solution_title: 12th Place Solution - Overview with code files
solution_summary: The solution blended public EfficientNet models with locally trained EfficientNet B0/B1/B2 and DenseNet121 models operating on collections of 256×256 tiles. Initial B0 models used five-fold stratified validation and scalar regression, while later models used the full dataset with ordinal regression. Diversity came from architectures, tile counts, two padding-based tile extractions, and several test-time augmentation schemes. The selected weighted ensemble scored 0.92960 privately, with stochastic TTA causing small differences on reruns.

solution_summary: The solution combined roughly 100 models built from multiple transformations of rental listing data. Its strongest features described duplicate listing groups through temporal price changes, group statistics, and ranks, with additional gains from repairing building identifiers and normalizing addresses. Numerical binning, interactions, and cross-validated feature selection supported a diverse model pool. An equally weighted combination of gradient boosting, neural, and linear stackers achieved 0.497X, although the linear component was later found to overfit.

solution_title: Rust Solution, the Good Bits: MCTS, Game Representation, Rust/ONNX Submission
solution_summary: Ferrihelion combined precomputed geometric tables, a small graph-aware transformer, and single-turn autoregressive MCTS in a Rust game engine. The policy and value network learned from self-play against current and historical agents plus scripted opponents. Cached geometry, subtree reuse, and a batched inference backend made the search practical, while a Rust and ONNX submission stack handled CPU deployment. Long-horizon strategy did not emerge reliably, and expensive per-turn search limited self-play throughput.
compute: Submission ran on a slow CPU with 1 second per turn and 60 seconds of overage; batched self-play inference used GPUs near full utilization.

solution_summary: The task was represented as an offset-versus-position image and solved with CNNs predicting distributions over geological offsets. The final ensemble combined three CNN lineages with a particle filter and weighted members using posterior entropy. Synthetic geology pretraining followed by fine-tuning against label-conditioned posterior targets produced the largest improvement, reducing one engine's public score from 7.931 to 5.747. Distance-dependent priors and piecewise-linear smoothing refined the trajectories, while transferred geological-boundary features added no value.

solution_title: Code from a record breaking 903 place drop
solution_summary: The team combined diverse PyTorch image classifiers trained with different architectures, hyperparameters and input resolutions. Most models used 256×256 images, substantial augmentation, cross-validation and test-time augmentation. F2 threshold optimization and manual ensemble thresholds converted predictions into labels, although submission selection overfit the public leaderboard somewhat. A filename-ordering bug corrupted private-set predictions; corrected submissions included private scores of 0.93202.

solution_title: EcoBangBang's Approach - Yet Another RL Solution
solution_summary: The final agent used a shared convolutional ResNet policy with spatial feature maps, unit energy and action masking. Training used V-trace, teacher KL loss and self-play with a zero-sum baseline output, progressing from match rewards to game rewards. Removing the disproportionately large UPGO policy-gradient loss restarted improvement and helped the agent exceed a 1900 rating score. Hidden-state inference and temporal map features supported the policy, while an intermediate rule-based agent helped uncover feature-map bugs.

The solution uses a cascade that first selects candidate PII tokens and then scores the retained spans with more expensive models. A fast recurrent model feeds a miniature attention and GRU model, followed by an eight-layer DeBERTa-v3-xsmall model. All stages learn through distillation from a diverse DeBERTa ensemble, with out-of-fold filtering probabilities used to train the filtered stages. Span separators and preserved original positional indices support filtered inference, and the final stage reports approximately 0.965 CV.
compute: Reported stage runtimes: about 2 minutes for stage 1, under 1 minute for stage 2, and 2–3 minutes for stage 3; hardware unspecified.

solution_title: Jeremy Howard on winning the Predict Grant Applications Competition
solution_summary: The author explored application success rates with Excel pivot tables, then built grant-level and person-level features in C#. Useful signals included processing dates, missing values, applicant qualifications, publication records and application-level aggregates. A generalized random forest modeled these features. Preprocessing grouped rare categorical levels and represented missing continuous values with a missingness indicator plus median imputation.

The solution fused eight image-classification backbones using weights based on public scores. Single-model improvements included taxonomic classification losses, dynamic-margin subcenter ArcFace, an additional cross-entropy head, stronger augmentation, and multi-scale center-crop inference. ImageNet22k initialization, staged layer freezing, and mixed precision supported training, with an additional post-processing step contributing about 0.001. The complete fusion achieved a private score of 0.87662.
compute: 100 training epochs; batch size 512, or 256 for large models.

solution_summary: The author submitted two similar image-generation kernels based on BigGAN. The model used shared breed-label embeddings, hierarchical latent noise, projection, and an auxiliary classifier, trained with RaLS and weighted auxiliary classification loss. Generator weight averaging and uniform noise on real images were additional components. Loosely truncated latent sampling favored diversity despite weak visual quality, and the linked kernel reported a public score of 15.81605.

The solution used three DeBERTa variants, including a model with layer drop and multisample dropout and a larger model adapted with LoRA. Predictions from different tokenizers were aligned through character positions before conversion to spaCy tokens. Training combined synthetic essays with manually corrected competition labels and replaced names every epoch. Extensive rules corrected entity boundaries, propagated name labels within documents, and filtered or reassigned predictions.

The final solution averaged probabilities from five Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct variants distilled from larger Qwen models. Distillation delivered the largest reported gain, while EMA stabilized full-data training. A prompt-based explanation score was used to redesign cross-validation after generated samples failed to improve CV. Different distillation-loss weights supplied ensemble diversity, and torch.compile enabled inference with all five merged models.

The solution combined EfficientNet and DOLG models trained on full-body crops and horizontally concatenated views containing backfins or original images. Each model jointly predicted species and individual identity, using softmax and CurricularFace losses, and was trained with pseudo-labels from the team's best ensemble. A second stage used nearest-neighbor candidates and engineered distance, species, rank, and out-of-fold features to train XGBoost and LightGBM confidence models. The final predictions used weighted voting with weights optimized on five-fold out-of-fold predictions, plus horizontal-flip test-time augmentation.
compute: All models trained on TPUs; Google TPU Research Program supplied V3 TPUs on GCP for larger models near the competition's end.

solution_title: 69th Place Solution for the LLM Science Exam Competition
solution_summary: The solution used Wikipedia context retrieval with an ensemble of three DeBERTa models and one zero-shot Longformer. Two DeBERTa models came from public releases, while the team's own model used an all-mpnet_base_v2 Wikipedia index and 27,000 selected training questions. The final ensemble weights were manually set to 0.5, 0.25, 0.15, and 0.1. Larger ensembles had stronger cross-validation results but timed out, and Longformer fine-tuning was unsuccessful.

The solution constructed patent retrieval queries using a whitespace-free AND syntax that bypassed a competition query constraint. A custom C++ inverted index supported efficient generation of subqueries covering individual targets and target pairs while excluding non-targets. Greedy coverage selection, slightly improved with beam search, assembled the final query, with negative subqueries removing unwanted matches. The approach achieved 0.99872 on the private leaderboard, and 91% of evaluated rows retrieved all 50 targets.
compute: C++ implementation used about 25 GB RAM; approximately 5 times faster and 3 times more memory efficient than Python

solution_summary: The solution emphasized self-doubt in prompts to encourage repeated checking of mathematical answers. Repeating “Be skeptical of your answers.” three times was the most effective prompt variation on the leaderboard. Generation temperature was set to 0.7 for stability. A dynamic time budget reserved additional time for difficult problems while keeping inference within the competition limit.

After comparing seven baseline models, they tuned three selected models with Optuna. The final classifier combined LightGBM, random forest, and XGBoost through equally weighted soft voting. solution_summary: The post investigates rerunning a publicly shared 2018 women's basketball solution for the 2022 men's competition. The author found that selecting 2022 season statistics produced a score of 0.66334, while retaining the original 2018 setting reproduced 0.51577. The discrepancy came from which season's team statistics were merged before XGBoost scoring. This explained unusual team preferences in the reproduced bracket.

The final submission blended four DeBERTa token classifiers at the character-probability level. Models used masked-language-model pretraining, fine-tuning with SmoothFocalLoss, text augmentation, and pseudo labeling. Case-specific thresholds and detailed span-boundary corrections refined predictions. A character classifier with a GRU head improved the best private submission when ensembled with token models, but that ensemble was not selected for the final submission.

solution_title: 207th Place Solution for the Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations.  Late submission 0.576 private LB.
solution_summary: The author describes a late submission assembled from other competitors' predictions, selecting models separately for compounds and cell types. A weighted combination of ten models scored 0.718, while compound-specific model selection scored 0.657. Multiplicative post-processing further reduced the reported score to 0.576, with the detailed late submission labeled 0.577. The author leaves open how to explain or reliably choose the best model for each compound.

Training examples came from four nonoverlapping 168-day observation windows, each paired with a 62-day target window after a 46-day gap. Features included encoded categories, session timing, and user-level pageview and hit statistics. The solution separately predicted customer return probability and transaction amount conditional on returning, multiplying the two predictions. This decomposition was crucial, improving on direct regression, with a reported leaderboard score of 0.88140.

The final agent used Claude Sonnet 4.6 to write and execute its own training pipeline within the competition's session budget. It handled mixed feature types with ordinal suffix extraction, leakage-controlled target encoding, label encoding, median imputation, and missingness flags. Predictions averaged 45 LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost models across three seeds and five folds. Reliable autonomous orchestration mattered more than further model tuning, producing public and private scores of 0.816 and 0.779.

solution_summary: The author explored recurrent neural networks for EEG event detection and shared their Torch implementation. They also linked a blog post explaining LSTM implementation details. They missed the first submission deadline, so the post reports no final competition score.

The team trained separate study classifiers, none-class predictors, and opacity detectors using deduplicated competition data and stratified group cross-validation. EfficientNet classification ensembles used auxiliary segmentation losses, attention-based heads, noisy student training, and horizontal-flip inference. Detection combined EfficientDet, YOLOv5, and RetinaNet experiments with public-test pseudo-labeling and weighted boxes fusion. Final post-processing power-blended detection confidence and none probabilities, with classification models providing a major contribution.

The solution used a frozen ViT-H-14 backbone pretrained on LAION2B with two separately trained 64-dimensional embedding heads. Both heads were trained with ArcFace, with dropout applied only to the first head. The heads used different combinations of external image datasets, and their normalized outputs were added together. solution_title: The Hedge That Held: Predicting Private-Guardrail Transfer Offline
solution_summary: The authors submitted a high-throughput exfiltration engine and a separate Confused-Deputy portfolio selected for robustness to stricter guardrails. Their offline proxy harness identified payload inspection as fatal to the public exfiltration strategy and favored benign-looking email actions instead. Adaptive template measurements optimized replay throughput separately for each target model. The exfiltration submission fell from 88.890 publicly to zero privately, while the hedge retained its 15.555 score.
compute: Local GPU for proxy evaluation; each target model had an independent 18,000-second evaluation budget.

solution_summary: The pipeline averaged particle probability volumes from ten diverse 2.5D and 3D segmentation models, then extracted connected-component centroids using particle-specific thresholds. Simulated-data pretraining brought the 3D models closer to the 2.5D models in accuracy. FocalTversky++ loss produced confidence maps better suited to averaging than the overly binary outputs obtained with Dice and Tversky losses. Sliding-window inference, border removal and TensorRT execution across two T4 GPUs supported efficient prediction.
compute: Parallel inference with two T4 GPUs

solution_summary: The system retrieved overlapping Wikipedia chunks, reranked them with a teacher-trained DeBERTa model, and answered questions with DeBERTa and Mistral multiple-choice models. A specialized masked language model handled long answer options differing in only a few words. XGBRanker fused retrieval scores, model logits, and a flag for cross-referencing options such as None of the above. The full system achieved private/public scores of 0.931489/0.931543, with Mistral handling half of the test questions.

solution_summary: The team trained RoBERTa base and BERT base uncased on competition text with competition labels and additional dataset labels. They intersected the models' predictions and removed short predictions except for a small whitelist. The described pipeline also added string matches against training and shared labels, while the author reports that the best private submission omitted string matching. Public leaderboard changes guided decisions about which extra labels to include, and the team lacked a proper validation strategy.

The main model paired a spatiotemporal Transformer encoder with a TXP-CNN decoder to predict one player's future trajectory from all-player context. A confidence head predicted coordinate uncertainty and used Gaussian negative log likelihood, which outperformed the tested alternative losses. Passer-relative coordinates, consistent play direction, and auxiliary pre-pass trajectory tasks supported training. The final approach also used architectural ensembling, player-permutation augmentation, and test-time training with a marginal reported improvement.

The team trained more than 20 CNNs on RGBY images at three resolutions, initializing the yellow-channel convolution weights from the red channel. The approach used weighted BCE, horizontal and vertical flips, and class-specific thresholds. Ensembling provided the largest gains, but selecting ensembles and thresholds by public leaderboard performance generalized poorly. A more evenly balanced ensemble achieved a private score of 0.554.

solution_title: An efficient solution to Lung function decline prediction
solution_summary: The post links to a notebook described as an efficient competition solution. It provides no modeling, training, or validation details in the text. It closes with a brief thank-you.

Custom heads concatenated several pooling outputs, while Chinese back-translation followed by pseudo-labeling expanded training data. A weighted content and wording loss and ridge-derived ensemble weights improved performance. solution_title: 5th Place Solution — msa and protenix and TBM
solution_summary: The solution combined template-based RNA modeling with Protenix diffusion predictions using length-dependent allocation of five output slots. Template candidates received geometry-aware gap filling, structural perturbations, refinement, and diversity selection. Protenix primarily used MSAs with depth at least 700, with independent diffusion samples and a full-MSA diversity hedge for short sequences. Long-sequence predictions used aligned overlapping chunks with smooth blending, and deterministic inference settings supported reproducible ablations.

solution_summary: The team built a preprocessing pipeline that rendered field lines, player and ball detections, team assignments, and nearby player skeletons on a black background. They also tried crops centered on the ball to suppress irrelevant video content. Despite extensive optimization and experiments with general action recognition, soccer-specific, and custom temporal models, they did not obtain reasonable results. solution_summary: The solution blended tuned RTK positioning with a modified public carrier-smoothing and Kalman-smoothing baseline, giving RTK a final weight of 0.8. Phone-specific performance motivated the stronger RTK weight. Post-processing replaced anomalous RTK points with baseline predictions and softened stationary-position averaging by blending stop means with original coordinates.

solution_title: 20th place solution (how I spent lots of time on things that didn't work)
solution_summary: The author generated synthetic gravitational-wave signals and noise using test-derived timing, gaps, and noise statistics, producing about 200,000 training samples. Preprocessing removed line and spot noise, filled gaps with surrounding noise levels, and reduced magnitude and cross-detector features to 360×360 inputs. EfficientNet-B5 models trained across five folds with mixup, Adam, and cosine scheduling, while inference varied the random noise used to fill gaps. The final blend weighted the author's predictions equally with a public notebook's predictions; validation tracked the public leaderboard well, while several alternative architectures and denoising approaches failed.

solution_title: Silver Medal Solution[29th]: ByT5-XL Custom CPT with Dictionary Data + KL-Anchor
solution_summary: The reported pipeline adapted ByT5-XL through Akkadian continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning with original and synthetic translation pairs, reaching an LB score of 37.6. BF16 precision, model scale, domain lexical resources, and minimal output cleanup were central findings. Inference used a small candidate pool with chrF++ consensus minimum Bayes risk decoding. Fine-tuning improved cross-validation while degrading leaderboard performance; KL-anchored LoRA partly reduced this degradation, but the unmodified base model still scored best at 38.0.

solution_title: 18th Place Solution - Careful Ensembling + Resampling Diversity
solution_summary: The final solution stacked 16 base models with regularized logistic regression, prioritizing diversity over extensive tuning. It combined LightGBM, XGBoost, an entity embedding neural network, Regularized Greedy Forest, and field-aware factorization models with different encodings and resampling strategies. Sandwich downsampling was especially valuable, and model selection used five-fold validation scores and Spearman correlations between test predictions. Additional aggressive positive-class upsampling improved mean validation from 0.2920 to 0.2924 but hurt the private score.

solution_title: Santander Product Recommendation competition on Kaggle
solution_summary: The writeup outlines a code pipeline that imports raw data, creates features, trains a model, and generates test predictions. The solution combined seven global descriptor models trained with ArcFace loss on GLDv2 clean data. GeM pooling and a 512-dimensional neck produced embeddings for nearest-neighbor classification against an expanded reference set. Non-landmark similarities penalized noisy references and test predictions, while quantile transformation stabilized similarity scores. solution_title: Best graduation gift(#24 solution to consider magic)

Features combined counts with values, suppressed singleton values as noise, and added standardized and nonlinear count transformations. Feature selection produced a LightGBM model with 0.9247 cross-validation AUC, while a neural network reached 0.9218. solution_title: 6th Place - A lot of features, a lot of ensembling
solution_summary: The final ensemble contained 231 models, drawing heavily on many XGBoost feature experiments and selected public notebook predictions. Linear-regression predictions were valuable features, with triply nested cross-validation used to prevent leakage during target encoding and feature generation. Classifier-based gating at the target boundaries provided small individual improvements and useful ensemble diversity. Additional meta models used class probabilities and regression predictions, although the final linear post-processing could make cross-validation optimistic when model folds differed.

The solution first localized the external cervical OS using a custom CNN trained on three manually annotated points. Distances between the predicted points controlled image zoom and cropping before classification. Reduced-filter architectures resembling Inception, ResNet, and Xception addressed overfitting, and approximately ten model predictions were averaged. Training used separate train-only and train-plus-additional-data splits, although localization accuracy and limited validation folds remained concerns.

solution_title: [20th] Place Solution for the [Optiver - Trading at the Close] Competition
solution_summary: The author used a single LightGBM model with 145 engineered features and retrained it from scratch every 22 scored days. Feature selection relied on local validation, which correlated well with the public leaderboard, and validation used the earliest training dates to preserve recent data for fitting. Features covered imbalances, lags, grouped statistics, previous-day targets, and rolling or expanding statistics. To limit submission memory and runtime risks, the author restricted the feature set and removed the first 100 training dates, then centered predictions by subtracting their mean.

The author used frozen BERT large uncased embeddings, concatenating its final nine layers into 9,216-dimensional vectors. These embeddings were combined with pronoun and candidate position, length, and distance features in a fully connected neural network. Separate candidate scores were converted into three-class probabilities using softmax with a fixed zero score for the neither class. The model used corrected labels, strong regularization, Adam, and ten-fold cross-validation over all GAP data, with final predictions blended across the ten models.

solution_title: 5th solution: prompt is all you need
solution_summary: The author reformulated phrase similarity prediction as a cloze prompt and used the logit of the label word YES to estimate similarity. Binary cross-entropy trained this output against the similarity target. Adding the other targets associated with the same anchor supplied additional context. The prompt model achieved 0.8535 CV and 0.8570 leaderboard scores, outperforming the attention-pooling baseline.

The submission dispatched between a teacher-conditioned behavioral clone for two-player games and a smaller single-teacher clone for four-player games. The two-player attention network shared knowledge across leading players while conditioning on teacher identity and replay recency, then fixed a selected teacher personality at inference. Winner-only replay selection and full-game evaluation were more useful than imitation metrics alone. Two-player performance remained competitive, but weak four-player play limited the final result, and self-play experiments did not provide a reliable ladder improvement.

solution_title: Private Leaderboard 3442 - A Beginner's Simple Solution and Key Takeaways

Predictions from LightGBM with 300 estimators and default-parameter CatBoost were averaged. XGBoost and a simple neural network performed worse, and removing columns with many nulls was less effective than retaining them.

solution_title: 2nd place solution & private LB 0.577 QUICK OVERVIEW
solution_summary: The solution combined several unspecified methods in an ensemble and applied a subtractive smoothing step. Adding the ML models with positive weights reduced performance, so their ensemble predictions were instead subtracted from the main ensemble. solution_title: 37th Place Solution for the MITSUI&CO. Commodity Prediction Challenge
solution_summary: The final approach used CatBoost multi-output regression with a loss that supports missing targets. It used all target and volume features without feature engineering. The solution trained a denoising autoencoder on both training and test data to produce representations for heavily regularized MLPs. Multiple DAE–MLP configurations were combined with LightGBM models using ridge stacking and averaging. DAE training and validation received most of the development effort. solution_title: 13th Place Solution for the "ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions" Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined two LightGBM classifiers and one CatBoost classifier. Preprocessing added missing-value indicators, mean imputation, EJ label encoding, and statistics grouped by EJ. Training used downsampling, class weights, ten-fold stratified validation, and seed averaging. The final weighted blend achieved public and private scores of 0.22 and 0.36.

The solution used XGBoost and LightGBM classification and regression models with a custom stacking pipeline, ultimately submitting an XGBoost stacker. Passing even a single LightGBM model's predictions through the stacker substantially improved its score, from 0.51072 to 0.50678 on the private leaderboard. Additional inputs included TF-IDF features, a fair-value prediction model trained on medium-interest listings, shared StackNet predictions, shared features, and leaked data. Out-of-fold validation for stacking was implemented late, limiting tuning, and growing overfitting suggested that greater feature diversity could have helped.

The pipeline first classified nocall audio from mel spectrograms using freefield1010. Those predictions weighted noisy labels when training bird classifiers on short recordings, with ten models used in the final submission. A LightGBM stage evaluated five candidate birds using classifier outputs and metadata, while training soundscapes served as validation. Ternary search selected thresholds, and preserving the original nocall proportion performed better than reducing it to 54%.
compute: Three teammates primarily used Colab Pro.

solution_summary: The solution used separate regional pipelines with an image classifier feeding its prediction vector and metadata into a detection-crop classifier. Both stages used ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet B3 with 400×400 inputs, and MegaDetector V4 supplied the detections. Emphasizing single-detection images helped reduce weak-label ambiguity, while sampling and borrowing species examples across regions addressed class imbalance. Five-fold ensembles and species-specific detection thresholds completed the pipeline; iterative pseudo-labeling and satellite-based location clustering remained experimental.
compute: Google Colab for MegaDetector V4 inference on all images.

solution_summary: The pipeline generated event candidates with activity and fake-data heuristics, corrected their positions with LightGBM regression, and scored them with separate onset and wakeup models. Extensive window statistics, time features, and candidate relationships supported both modeling stages. Nested validation grouped by series prevented leakage between step correction and scoring, while training weights reduced the influence of distant targets and unreliable labels. Candidate suppression and daily score normalization produced scores of 0.825 in cross-validation, 0.783 public, and 0.844 private.

solution_title: 49th place (silver, solo): whole-study 2.5D reader + report labels + rank blend
solution_summary: The author trained a whole-study 2.5D ConvNeXt reader with a Transformer and finding-specific cross-attention, using scanner-grouped folds and complete-study inference. Soft report labels were repeatedly blended with out-of-fold image teachers while remaining anchored to the original text targets. The final system combined the author's models with complementary public models through percentile-rank blending and applied clinical post-processing rules. Label refinement accounted for most of the model gains, and the final submission scored 0.962 public and 0.951 private.

solution_title: EoS9 + V68 NFNet Add-on: AI-Assisted BirdCLEF+ 2026 Experiments

Group ten-fold validation replaced ordinary K-fold, although only folds 4 and 7 were used to train four models with two hidden sizes. solution_title: [CPU Only]６th Place Solution for "Linking Writing Processes to Writing Quality"

solution_title: Virtual LB 130th: Mel spectrogram feature + class balance simple solution

solution_title: Place 70 solution  trust CV is all you need
solution_summary: The author emphasizes trusting cross-validation when selecting submissions for this synthetic Playground dataset. Their reasoning is that training and test distributions should be consistent because the data are machine generated. They report achieving 0.918 but submitting a result of 0.916, expecting the choice to generalize better to the private leaderboard. No model architecture or feature pipeline is described.

A modified ResNet10-based 3D CNN initialized predictions around target medians and achieved 0.1695 cross-validation without additional features. Its out-of-fold predictions were combined with loading and functional connectivity features in LightGBM, MLP, SVM, and ridge models. Feature-specific regularization and aggressive loading-feature duplication supported the second-stage models. Adversarial validation predictions supplied sample weights, narrowing the validation-to-leaderboard gap to 0.1562 versus 0.1566, although the author believed this adjustment mattered less on the private test set.

The solution combined image-level classifiers that assigned cell predictions through class activation maps with classifiers operating on individual cell crops. Two rounds of soft pseudo-label training, D4 test-time augmentation, and simple averaging linked these complementary approaches. Training used competition and public HPA data, while model selection relied heavily on public leaderboard feedback because local metrics correlated poorly. Area-based confidence scaling improved the final public score from 0.580 to 0.594, with a private score of 0.540.

solution_title: 5th place solution, maskrcnn, pseudo label and cellpose
solution_summary: The solution combined Mask R-CNN and Cellpose through staged training on LIVECell and competition data. Mask R-CNN generated pseudo-labels for the semi-supervised dataset, and its predictions were converted into flow and semantic segmentation representations. Cellpose was pretrained on LIVECell excluding shsy5y cells, then fine-tuned with additional channels and used for final prediction and post-processing with diameter set to 19. Deep Watershed variants and OmniPose did not work.

The author explored detecting the Other class using soft thresholding and anomaly detection on latent features from a subtype classifier. One-Class SVM and Isolation Forest experiments did not improve results. A convolutional autoencoder was also attempted to identify unfamiliar tissue through reconstruction error, but the approach was not finished or optimized. Evaluation remained a major difficulty, and the post asks others for successful ideas.

The author trained a graph convolutional network to classify compiler configurations by their runtime order. Node features and edges contributed to a handcrafted runtime estimate used to normalize configuration runtimes and construct ordered classes. The model produced configuration-by-class probabilities, and the top five classes were returned for the tiles dataset. Cross-config attention was identified afterward as a possible improvement.

The solution resized and padded images for an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet34 encoder with FPA attention and a convolution-plus-GAU decoder. Training used Lovasz loss, SGD, cosine annealing and extensive geometric and brightness augmentation. Depth channels and a revised stratification method improved the pipeline, with the latter reportedly adding 0.03. A transferred five-fold average ensemble reached 0.883 privately using a 0.45 threshold.

The author built separate men’s and women’s tournament models using competition data and engineered team ratings and summary statistics. Bidirectional stepwise regression selected variables, including multiple weight-of-evidence transformations of a relatively small set of underlying characteristics. Out-of-time evaluation guided development, while normalization appeared to add little for the women’s model. A simpler alternative without weight-of-evidence fields performed substantially worse.
compute: Moved execution from a local machine to Kaggle; hardware and runtime were not specified.

solution_title: 49 place solution - meh models, +0.04-0.05 private LB postprocessing
solution_summary: The author averaged six five-fold model configurations using EfficientNet-B2 and RexNet200 on PCEN and mel spectrograms. Normalizing prediction scales and using overlapping inference windows improved ensemble behavior and temporal coverage. Species-specific false-positive suppression and smooth geographic and temporal adjustments provided substantial additional gains. Conservative threshold selection worked well on private data, and the best submission scored 0.63/0.68 with postprocessing versus 0.59/0.62 without it.
compute: RTX 2060 Super; at most one five-fold training run per day with mixed precision; cached spectrograms approximately 150 GB each.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution ➡️ Distill is all you need🔥🔥🔥
solution_summary: The solution adapted Llama 3 70B, Qwen2 72B, and Gemma2 9B using LoRA or QLoRA after an initial training stage on UT data. Five-fold teacher predictions from the larger models supplied distillation targets for Gemma2 9B, which the author identified as the most important component. The fold-specific LoRA weights were averaged, and the resulting model was quantized to 8 bits with GPTQ. Submission inference used test-time augmentation with a sequence length of 2000, improving the reported leaderboard score from 0.882 to 0.876.

The author used a linked updated GOTO conversion solution as the basis of their submission. They added subjective tournament expectations favoring Duke, Florida, Auburn, and Houston for the Final Four, with Duke reaching the final. They also favored Connecticut and South Carolina reaching the final. The post attributes the result to these six gambles and luck, while linking a notebook for implementation details.

The post announces a packaged team solution available through a GitHub repository and a Docker image for prediction. It also links a downloadable example output for interactive browser viewing. It provides no substantive description of the modeling pipeline.

The solution used BERT question-answering models with unchanged text and experiments on negative sampling rates. Whole-word-masking BERT Large Uncased performed best, and its weights were combined with ordinary BERT Large before classifier-only fine-tuning and teacher-to-student distillation. Knowledge distillation was described as the key contribution, with further classifier-only tuning of the student. The student scored about 0.7118 on the development set and 0.7 on both public and private leaderboards; the attempted augmentation methods did not help.

solution_title: 1151 Place Solution for the Linking Writing Processes to Writing Quality Competition [275 efficiency leaderboard]
solution_summary: The author focused on engineered writing-process features and selected LightGBM and CatBoost for tuning after comparing four baseline regressors. Features described activity streaks, text structure, production rates, writing and revision time, and intervals between keystrokes, with selection based on correlation with essay scores. Optuna tuned hyperparameters, and shuffled 10-fold cross-validation guided model comparison. The reported public and private scores were 0.607 and 0.589; removing the lowest-scored essays and oversampling low scores did not help.

solution_title: 40th place solution | MLPs, ResNet, TabNet & Clustering
solution_summary: The final ensemble combined four MLPs, one ResNet, and one TabNet with weights of 0.5, 0.1, and 0.4 respectively. Training used multilabel-stratified ten-fold validation, five seeds per fold, label smoothing, low weight decay, and OneCycleLR. Changes were generally retained only when both CV and public leaderboard performance improved. One final submission additionally blended predictions with known drug labels using nearby t-SNE clusters, improving private loss from 0.01611 to 0.01609.

The team built a multi-stage state-space model with active and inactive states and Negative Binomial emissions for discrete demand. They simulated demand at level 12 and aggregated independent store trajectories through level 10, while modeling levels 1–9 individually. Hand-crafted seasonality and store-department event coefficients incorporated supply-chain knowledge. The approach produced explainable demand distributions and stable scores across years and periods, but did not model pricing effects or new SKUs.

The solution prioritized candidate recall, combining 21 retrieval methods with article embeddings and similarity search. Image, text, TF-IDF, and word2vec embeddings supported candidate generation and cosine-similarity features. A single LightGBM ranker used windowed article, customer, and interaction statistics, with reusable features cached to accelerate inference. Word2vec trained on all transactions improved both validation and leaderboard scores, but future information inflated local validation: MAP@12 was 0.0441 locally versus 0.0350 on the leaderboard.

solution_title: 9th Place Solution (Forget set-free Approach, 3rd on Public LB)
solution_summary: The approach alternated stochastic layer re-initialization with knowledge-preserving training using only the retain set. Two final variants each trained for five epochs, distributed over three or four forgetting-and-remembering cycles. Layer-wise selection, excluding fully connected and projection-shortcut layers, was more effective than element-wise selection. MSE performed best among the tested losses, and repeated cycles improved unlearning more effectively than increasing the re-initialization ratio.
compute: Submission constraint: 512 independent unlearning runs within 8 hours; each final algorithm uses 5 epochs.

solution_title: 28th place, A 0.0006x boosting trend feature and non-overfitting target encoding (attributed rates)
solution_summary: The post describes feature experiments that were omitted from the final submission after misleading public leaderboard feedback. Day-excluded target encoding reduced overfitting, and combining smoothed and unsmoothed encodings gave a small additional gain. Ratios of downloads on the previous two days captured trends and improved the private score from 0.9821 to nearly 0.9828. The author also reported useful count-ratio features and emphasized trusting local validation.

solution_title: 22th place solution / for English edition and 中文版本
solution_summary: The solution used Mask R-CNN with a Swin Transformer backbone and category-specific anchor sizes and aspect ratios. Models were pretrained using external data supplied by the competition. Training combined image augmentation, cosine annealing, and stochastic weight averaging, while inference used test-time augmentation. Four models handled classification and segmentation, followed by confidence and minimum-area filtering and index-ordered overlap removal.

The solution averaged predictions from WaveNet–GRU variants trained on overlapping time-series windows with subject-grouped validation. One variant initialized its convolutional backbone through next-value prediction on unlabeled sequences, while variants differed in validation filtering and checkpoint selection. Final inference used long segments, resampled tdcsfog signals, and converted models for CPU execution. A post-competition investigation found that the pretrained variant helped GPU inference despite hurting the submitted converted ensemble; a two-variant GPU ensemble scored 0.437 on the private leaderboard.
compute: RTX 3090: approximately 1–1.5 hours per pretraining epoch; final converted-model inference ran on CPU.

solution_title: 69th Place Solution for the AI Village Capture the Flag @ DEFCON31 Competition (22 Flags)
solution_summary: The author solved a collection of AI capture-the-flag tasks using data analysis, adversarial images, and iterative prompts. Pivot tables identified misclassified populations, while KMeans and manifold dimensionality reduction recovered clues from embeddings. Square Attack produced adversarial images, and pixel counting and intensity filtering solved image-based tasks. Other flags came from OCR XML injection, prompt refinement, unsafe pickle deserialization, and natural-language DNS updates.

solution_title: 3rd place solution - beam search and character head
solution_summary: The solution combined two diverse span extraction pipelines using RoBERTa-base, RoBERTa-large, and BART-large backbones, each trained with five seeds. One pipeline used refined tokenization and a conditional start/end decoder, while the other expanded token representations into character representations and applied GRU layers to predict character spans. Handling shifted labels caused by consecutive spaces was central to performance. Tweets with consecutive spaces used only the character model ensemble, while other tweets used substring search to maximize agreement with model predictions under Jaccard similarity. The combined ensemble achieved a private score of 0.733.

The solution used separate preprocessing and ensembles for Citeseq and Multiome. Citeseq combined four MLP models with two LightGBM models, using alternative preprocessing pipelines and out-of-fold predictions to select weights. Multiome used TF-IDF, log transformation, normalization, and PCA before ensembling four MLPs with different activation functions. Donor-based validation reached 0.896 for Citeseq and 0.670 for Multiome, while the combined submission scored 0.814 publicly and 0.772 privately.

The selected submission used IsolationForest to identify and remove anomalous rows, retaining 3,325 of 3,500 rows and achieving a private score of 1.01699. An alternative applied outlier detection separately to each column and then dropped rows containing missing values. That unselected submission retained 2,687 rows and achieved a better private score of 1.01535.

The solution jointly optimized GNSS observations and trajectory smoothing through a custom constrained solver implemented in TensorFlow. It combined pseudorange, Doppler, and ADR residuals with a piecewise-constant-jerk trajectory model, robust observation constraints, and uncertainty weighting. External base-station and satellite products supported relative positioning and atmospheric corrections, while an optimized timing offset addressed velocity discrepancies. The final submission took the median of multiple base-station solutions, with all optimization performed in double precision on CPU.
compute: CPU optimization using double-precision floating point; convergence described as slow.

solution_summary: The author adapted their small-dataset approach by computing nearest neighbors from similar queries within the same category and omitting category-specific normalization. When fewer than five items were available, they filled the recommendation list using category, query, and global popularity. A 10% validation holdout tracked leaderboard performance well, and the author reported no overfitting problems. The last submission scored 0.57142, and the final Python script ran in 21.5 minutes on a laptop.
compute: Final Python submission script: 21.5 minutes on a laptop.

solution_title: Non-technical write-up & on the importance of the Kaggle community
solution_summary: The team combined transformer outputs with a character-level LSTM for sentiment span extraction. Preserving spaces in this pipeline substantially improved performance, and the team later recognized that this exploited a pattern in the labels. They also used smoothed cross-entropy loss and selected ensembles that scored 0.734 on the public leaderboard. Later work improved cross-validation performance and robustness without surpassing their earlier public score of 0.735.

The author trained several ResNet, ResNeSt, and ResNeXt models and selected checkpoints and ensembles using F1 on train_soundscapes. Adding secondary labels with probability 0.3 helped, while other augmentation produced gains below 0.01 and EfficientNet B0–B5 did not work. Two ensemble candidates were chosen: one optimized for local F1 and another incorporating some randomness in model selection. Predictions were filtered using season and location, with H3 geographic segments derived from training metadata providing a reported 0.01 improvement.

The solution used false-color images and UNet models with strong backbones, training on all individual annotations. The central finding was a suspected half-pixel image-mask misalignment that made ordinary flips and rotations ineffective. Shifting images by half a pixel during training and inference corrected alignment and allowed normal augmentation. A custom mask-flipping alternative also worked, while other bands and 2.5D inputs were abandoned and successful small-model pseudo-labeling was not extended to larger models.

solution_title: My creativity paid off in this challenge, but nevertheless DAE is the goal and key.
solution_summary: The author fine-tuned a DAE implementation shared by another participant. Its predictions were ensembled with predictions from XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and an Octopus machine learning model. Combining these model scores was credited with improving the final result, although no ensemble weights, validation details, or numerical scores were provided.

The pipeline generated recommendation candidates through repurchases, related products, popularity, collaborative filtering, and tag-vector similarity. CatBoost YetiRank reranked candidates using static attributes, transaction aggregates, recency, interaction counts, similarity scores, and LightFM user embeddings. Four models trained with different history lengths and parameters were ensembled. The best single model achieved CV 0.03589 and private score 0.03391, although changing training duration sometimes reversed the validation and leaderboard trend.
compute: 224-core machine; up to 20 hours to train one model.

solution_summary: The solution built diverse customer-level datasets using pairwise feature differences, sequence aggregates, temporal changes, missingness features, and sequential encodings. It combined LightGBM DART, CatBoost, XGBoost, neural tabular models, and a public transformer model. Training TabNet on out-of-fold SHAP values from LightGBM made it useful for the ensemble and achieved a leaderboard score of 0.797. Five-fold validation, multiple seeds, and forward selection of ensemble weights supported the final blend; ordinary feature selection, sequential models, and alternative losses did not help.
compute: 12 GB GPU; NODE used batch size 64.

solution_summary: The solution uses U-Net segmentation models trained with Adam, adding batch normalization and ReLU to convolution blocks. Multiple pipelines vary image resolution, spectral channels, patch size, and class coverage, including a three-input network that combines imagery at different resolutions. Hard-negative mining supplies roughly one third of each epoch's samples, while flips and rotations augment training. Selected predictions are combined across epochs and pipelines, with morphological processing and water-class subtraction used for some masks. The author's solo public score was 0.50165, and further results came from combining predictions with ZFTurbo.

The approach combined diverse 3D ResNet, SEResNet, and DenseNet models with other team predictions through stacking. Individual 3D models were relatively weak, but their complementary predictions improved ensembles, including a weighted blend that achieved 0.1582 on the public leaderboard. Resizing volumes and normalizing them using site-specific statistics improved diversity and leaderboard performance. Float16 data accelerated experimentation, while selected important models used float32 for accuracy.
compute: One float16-data model took about 5–10 hours for five folds with ten epochs each; float32 took 2–3 times longer.

solution_summary: The solution blended several LSTM neural networks and XGBoost models trained with slightly different settings. Feature engineering supplied about 60 motion, geometry, and metadata features, while five shared body parts enabled joint training across laboratories. Lab embeddings and allowed-action masking supported the neural model, and XGBoost used feature selection, F1-based early stopping, and probability smoothing. Lab- and action-specific thresholds were tuned on out-of-fold predictions, with conflicting actions resolved by probability-to-threshold ratios.

The author built deep-supervised and multiclass segmentation models across seven random train-validation splits, using pretrained ResNet34 with scSE encoders. Model-specific padding or bilinear resizing produced 128×128 inputs, followed by varied geometric and photometric augmentation. Training used cosine learning-rate restarts, with object-context modules added to some folds. The final ensemble averaged sigmoid predictions from selected cycles and horizontal-flip inference, then applied a 0.5 pixel threshold. Larger encoders and alternative ensemble methods did not improve on this approach, while directly averaging raw Lovasz-trained outputs performed poorly.
compute: GTX 980m; Neptune.ml and Google Cloud Platform also used; fold training schedules ranged from 210 to 295 epochs.

solution_title: 86th - Bronze Medal - with Silver Gold Magic Explained
solution_summary: The competition submission combined EfficientNet models with a learned image-resizing module, larger input sizes, and five-fold ensembling. A final correction increased predictions for test images identified by a model trained on disagreements between two approaches, improving the leaderboard score to 0.779. Several attempts to exploit off-cadence images or test pseudo labels reduced performance. Post-competition experiments showed that strong mixup with a large EfficientNetB4 improved generalization, reaching public and private scores of 0.786 and 0.781.
compute: 4 NVIDIA V100 GPUs, running constantly for several days.

solution_summary: The repository describes a default-risk prediction pipeline using LightGBM with Gradient-based One-Side Sampling. This model contributed to a larger ensemble of 13 models combined through linear regression. The standalone model achieved a private ROC AUC of 0.8044, and the repository lists its dependencies and tested Python environments.

solution_title: 35th Place Solution- Magic PP - Site 2 correction
solution_summary: The team used tabular data and blended a public kernel with two three-level stacking ensembles. They adjusted features between acquisition sites using mean shifts and estimated site membership with an ensemble of classifiers. Ranked classifier outputs were converted into site probabilities to blend predictions under alternative site assumptions. Each main component scored 0.1585 on the public leaderboard, while the final blend reached 0.1584.

The team used coding agents and manual orchestration to optimize task-specific ONNX programs, merging independently developed candidates by verified score and then speed. Shared recipes, compact memory and per-task histories helped agents reuse discoveries and avoid repeated failures. The strongest improvements came from algebraic representations that minimized charged intermediate memory, often ending directly in Einsum. Runtime screening became essential: the locally best set scored 8041.20 but exceeded the time limit, while the submitted set scored 8038.62.

The final ensemble combined 14 two-stage XGBoost models with seven online models. The key choice was using the second half of training data for base learners and the first half for the meta learner. Base predictions came from random forests, SGDClassifier, online logistic regression, and XGBoost, with XGBoost providing the meta classifier. The best single model scored 0.0043835 publicly and 0.0044595 privately; several additional ensemble and structured prediction ideas did not help.
compute: 8-core server with 32 GB RAM for most submissions

solution_title: 🏅 37st Place Solution: Self Prompt Tuning with DINOv3
solution_summary: The final model kept DINOv3 frozen and trained task tokens, prompt tokens, and target-specific regression heads using token embeddings plus pooled patch statistics. Target-informed initialization, Gram Schmidt orthogonalization, and an orthogonality loss maintained distinct token representations. Random multi-crop training averaged independent predictions, and full-data training used cross-validation training loss to determine duration. Inference combined tiled crops, geometric flip augmentation, and multiple checkpoints from one training run; reported leaderboard scores reached approximately 0.75.

The author pursued computational efficiency with an LSTM model operating on raw game events without manual feature engineering. Two LSTMs separately processed user interactions and conversations, using categorical embeddings and elapsed-time differences between consecutive actions. Optimizations improved five-fold cross-validation from 0.698 to 0.700 and the public leaderboard score from 0.701 to 0.703. All private leaderboard submissions scored below 0.69, an unexplained generalization drop.

The solution used a WaveNet-based neural network with random-forest probabilities as additional inputs. Signal cleaning and augmentation mattered more than model tuning, with signal flipping and random shifts improving generalization. Models trained on different synthetic datasets were compared using out-of-fold scores on the same original, non-synthetic data. One submission blended two models and achieved 0.94529 private, while another modified the seventh test batch using a separate reduced-signal model and channel restoration.

The solution combined three neural networks, XGBoost, yunbase version 21, and a collection of XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost models through weighted integration. Feature engineering and parameter tuning improved the neural network, while weighting difficult samples helped address challenging cases. The author reported neural network scores of 0.6837 CV, 0.688 public LB, and 0.691 private LB in the prose. Embeddings, attention, GNN modifications, and alternative losses did not improve performance, and additional combination features were ineffective for the tree models.

The pipeline combined a pretrained Bengali speech recognition model, a six-gram KenLM language model, and a punctuation restoration model. ASR training used several speech datasets, stronger augmentation for read speech, and removal of samples with the highest fitted word error rates. Chunked inference handled long recordings, while external Bengali text corpora supported language modeling. Punctuation restoration used an IndicBERTv2 backbone with an LSTM head and an ensemble of three models.
