solution_summary: The solution used seven ImageNet-pretrained CNN regressors to predict multimodal trajectories and their confidences from rasterized scenes. Long training on the full dataset, suitable optimization parameters, and extensive raster caching mattered more than more elaborate prediction architectures. A Set Transformer combined candidate trajectories into three outputs by optimizing a confidence-weighted ensemble loss directly on validation or test predictions. Predictions from a 16-mode model contributed to this loss but were excluded from transformer inputs. Rasterization and caching improvements reduced CPU load by roughly sixfold, while the transformer ensemble improved loss by about 0.2 over numerical optimization.
compute: Each CNN trained about 5–7 days on one GPU: 2080 Ti or 3090 for larger models; cached full-dataset samples occupied around 1.3 TB.

solution_summary: The solution normalizes signals and averages over time to form 360 by 360 inputs, improving CV and leaderboard scores by about 0.02 over power spectrograms. Generating balanced synthetic samples with signal depth uniformly distributed between 10 and 100 was the most important improvement, supporting a single-model leaderboard score of 0.761. The ensemble primarily uses ConvNeXt-XLarge, with NFNet and EfficientNet variants, strong augmentation, and leaderboard-based weights. Validation keeps corresponding noise and signal pairs together, while segmentation-based alternatives were abandoned because training was unstable.

The solution emphasized cleaner training labels, manually selecting and relabeling ten-second segments from recordings with secondary labels. Its final rank ensemble combined four sound-event-detection models with a separately trained ProtoSSM plus MLP model. Perch v2 and BirdSet-based distillation, tuned mel spectrograms, checkpoint soups, and sampled pseudo-label data supported the neural models. Nighttime-aware mixup and rare-class oversampling addressed data distribution issues, and the additional ProtoSSM model reportedly improved the score by about 0.005.

The solution first constructed strong horizontal-photo subsequences and joined them using vertical photos. Remaining vertical photos were paired using a modified, vectorized method with penalties for selected slide sizes, adding about 60 points. The resulting slides were inserted and rearranged using the same subsequence-building procedure, followed by segment reversals to improve the score. The final score was 443363 against an estimated theoretical maximum of about 443400, with a runtime of roughly 40 minutes.
compute: Runtime approximately 40 minutes.

solution_title: 2nd place solution: SED + CNN with 7 models ensemble
solution_summary: The solution ensembled seven SED and CNN models trained on current and historical competition recordings plus additional xeno-canto data. Training combined extensive audio augmentation, label-based sampling weights, and pretraining on 834 species before fine-tuning on the 264 target species. Cross-entropy training generally preceded binary cross-entropy training, with varied clip lengths and mixup rates providing diversity. OpenVINO reduced inference time by about 40%, enabling the seven-model ensemble. Weighted raw-logit averaging achieved public/private scores of 0.84/0.76, outperforming the rank-based alternative.
external_data: ["BirdCLEF 2020/2021/2022 competition data", "2020 additional competition data", "xeno-canto", "Rainforest and environment background sounds", "freefield1010", "warblrb", "birdvox"]

solution_summary: The author selected two submissions to hedge between public-score throughput and survival against an unknown guardrail. The surviving submission used marker-free CONFUSED_DEPUTY candidates with two messages, exact email argument keys, and a clean final continuation request. Static SDK analysis and local checks guided predicate eligibility, message ordering, recipient choices, and scoring behavior. The public-optimized submission scored 136.250 publicly but zero privately, while the hedge scored 24.360 privately. Keeping a fixed recipient sacrificed distinct-cell bonuses, which the author identifies as a mistake.

solution_summary: The final approach fine-tuned LLaDA-8B for ARC and recursively refined grid predictions through soft masking and continuous token embeddings. It replaced one-dimensional positional encoding with a two-dimensional scheme and used a separate model to predict output shape. An earlier autoregressive approach used task-specific adaptation, speculative decoding, and augmentation-based candidate scoring before being superseded. The selected diffusion submission scored 21.67% publicly and 16.53% privately; another hyperparameter selection achieved 19.17% on both.

solution_summary: The final pipeline combined attention-head embeddings from nine fine-tuned transformers and trained a Gaussian process regressor on their concatenated out-of-fold representations. The regressor reduced overconfident predictions in the small-data setting and achieved public and private scores of 0.448. Transformer training used stratified five-fold validation, masked-language-model pretraining for selected models, stochastic weight averaging, and selective removal of transformer dropout. Pseudo-labeling improved an alternative submission to a private score of 0.446, but those models were excluded because their public scores were worse.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution — Feature Engineering and Logistic Regression Stacking
solution_summary: The final solution stacked 115 prediction columns with L2-regularized logistic regression on clipped logit predictions. Diverse tree and neural models benefited from cross-fitted target encodings, income rounding, original-data statistics, and soft pseudo-labels. Income tokenizer groups and features from a source-trained DistilGPT-2 added useful diversity. The ensemble achieved 0.946717 CV and 0.94584 private AUC, although later stacking experiments reused historical OOF predictions and were not fully nested.

solution_summary: The pipeline reconstructed PDF text using font sizes, then extracted DOI links and accession identifiers from PDF structures and regular expressions. It filtered ambiguous identifiers with Qwen and DOI prefixes using metadata obtained through the DOI API. Classification contexts incorporated mention frequency, table references, and extracted author names. Separate Qwen models handled DOI and accession classification, while several context expansions, verifiers, and ensemble approaches were rejected after reducing public scores.

solution_title: 1st place solution [segmentation with partly U-NET and ensembling part]
solution_summary: The solution combined 3D segmentation networks with MONAI object detectors, training from scratch without external or simulated data. The segmentation approach used a partial U-Net with single-pixel targets on its penultimate feature map and strongly weighted cross-entropy. Seven experiment-based folds supported threshold calibration, while rank-based distribution matching made segmentation and detection feature maps compatible for blending. JIT or TensorRT export accelerated inference enough to support a larger ensemble.

solution_title: Linear Regression Is All you Need (9th solution week 4)
solution_summary: The submitted solution blended simple linear models for cases and fatalities, using log-space relationships to capture epidemic trends. Cases combined an autoregressive model with a model designed to capture curve flattening, with weights adapted to historical case counts. Fatalities combined regressions on lagged cases, past log fatalities, and past log cases. Time-based validation guided the approach, and a post-deadline change using more recent case information achieved a private score of 0.41840.

solution_title: 10th Place Solution: A Compass, Not a Map
solution_summary: The solution generated geological trajectory candidates using structural priors, particle filtering, and HMM inference, then combined them with neural stratigraphic-position estimates through a learned selector. A TCN and an additional U-Net corrected the resulting trajectory, with disagreement-dependent blending and a heel-anchored gain providing final improvements. Paired OOF evaluation across 773 wells supported a final CV score of 5.7189, while the selected submission scored 6.269 privately. A strong local gain from nearby-well anchoring was rejected after evidence of poor public transfer, although that rejected variant later scored better privately.

solution_title: 12th Place Solution: Linear Regression + XGBoost for Residuals
solution_summary: The solution modeled sales trends with linear regression and learned residual effects with XGBoost. Product-specific sine and cosine features captured annual cycles for most products and two-year cycles for Kaggle and Kaggle Tiers, with a logarithmic target transformation supporting the regression formulation. The model also represented relative GDP, store effects, weekends, and holidays. Imputing missing Kenya Holographic Goose sales was a major improvement, while inaccurate forecasts for 2018 and 2019 hurt private evaluation performance.

The team ensembled sound event detection models using SE-ResNeXt and EfficientNet backbones, with five folds per backbone and 30 epochs per run. Both primary and secondary labels were used, while the backbones saw different five-second audio segments and used different seeds. Audio and image augmentations, CutMix, Mixup, and cosine learning-rate schedules supported training. Focal loss with alpha 0.75 and gamma 5 delivered a major improvement and better validation-to-leaderboard agreement; the ensemble threshold was 0.25.
compute: Trained in Google Colab notebooks; five folds per backbone and 30 epochs per run.

solution_summary: The core pipeline used YOLOv9 to locate key points and extract patches, followed by a Siamese network for severity classification. Random patch pairs supplied similarity labels, and a custom cosine similarity loss trained the embeddings. Inference compared each patch against diverse reference images, averaged similarities by class, and normalized the scores into probabilities. The author also used an ensemble containing single-stage multitask models and a sagittal T2 volume approach.

The team ensembled RoBERTa and ELECTRA models with varied pooling heads, pretraining choices, and layer reinitialization. Differential learning rates, gradient accumulation, and reinitializing the last five layers helped fine-tuning. One submission used forward selection on out-of-fold predictions to combine 14 models, while another used leaderboard-based weights. Both achieved a private score of 0.458; external-data pretraining and embedding-based stacking were unsuccessful.
compute: Kaggle Kernels and Google Colab using seven accounts for experiments.

solution_summary: The solution combines a 1D U-Net with a GRU, using raw enmo, absolute angle changes, and contextual time and sensor flags. Event targets mix broad and narrow Gaussian heatmaps to balance training stability with accuracy at different tolerances. Training uses random 12-hour samples, binary cross entropy, AdamW, and stochastic weight averaging, while inference processes entire series. A 120-model ensemble feeds smoothing and candidate extraction designed to retain multiple possible events per night.
compute: Approximately 18 minutes for full test processing, including 45 seconds of model inference; 120-model ensemble completed within 120 minutes.

solution_summary: The solution filtered prediction features by their value ranges and Spearman correlation with the target. It applied isotonic calibration and trained with AutoGluon. Feature removal based on expected calibration error and experiments with FLAML did not work. The author emphasized trusting local cross-validation and the usefulness of calibration and stacking.

solution_title: 246th Place (Silver): Report Labels Are Not Expert Labels
solution_summary: The final pipeline rank-blended public Raptor, R6 and S6fall models with per-finding weights and flip augmentation. Its main original contribution subtracted cross-compartment OA ranks to reduce excessive coupling inherited from report-derived labels. Independent OAI expert reads supported the correction before submission, while leaderboard feedback guided its strength. Both final submissions achieved 0.944 private AUC, and none of the team's own trained models remained in the final blend.

solution_title: 13th Place Solution: Using Positive Examples from Other Rules as Negative Exampl
solution_summary: The approach trained on positive and negative examples from the public test set and augmented 30% of examples by assigning different rules and negative labels. The ensemble combined quantized Qwen3 models with DeBERTa models, withholding additional data from DeBERTa-small because it hurt ensemble performance. Qwen3-8B achieved a private score of 0.923. Experiments also explored reinforcement learning and synthetic rule-specific examples, with mixed results.
compute: Reported training times: Qwen3-8B 8h; Qwen3-1.7B 1.5h; DeBERTa-base 1h; DeBERTa-small 0.5h.

solution_summary: This post outlines the neural-network component of a broader solution containing four neural networks and several XGBoost models. Denoising autoencoders learned interactions among numerical, categorical, text, and image features using both training and test data. The learned encoder was then reused with a classification head, with image features also supplied directly to that head. Input-feature dropout helped control overfitting and encouraged reconstruction of missing information from other modalities.

The solution combined a full-data regression model with two specialist regressors trained on subsets defined by predicted outlier probability. A binary classifier split cards at probability 0.015, and its predictions together with full-regression predictions were central features for the high-probability model. Feature selection reduced thousands of candidates to about one hundred, including two-stage target encodings aggregated from transactions to cards with less weight on earlier month lags. The final prediction blended the specialist outputs with the full regression, while model decisions relied on local cross-validation.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution for the Vesuvius Challenge - Surface Detection Competition
solution_summary: The solution used weighted four-model nnU-Net ensembles trained with different patch sizes and fine-tuning schedules. It fused post-softmax probabilities and applied extensive geometric mask repair to remove small components, close holes, patch sheet gaps, and fill cavities. Post-processing raised the best ensemble's private score from 0.596 to 0.627. The authors also found that public-score-driven choices of probability fusion and thresholds were inferior on the private evaluation, while touching sheets remained unresolved.

The solution trained separate LightGBM models for pitchers, batters, and players without 2021 playing time, using role-specific performance features. Training and validation were restricted to in-season data and excluded 2020. Features described daily league activity, game popularity, season progress, and player performance at daily, season, and previous-season scales. Two chronological validation schemes supplied parameter sets for retraining, and final submissions blended their predictions with reciprocal 0.7/0.3 weights. Target lags were omitted because they reduced validation accuracy for pitcher and batter models.

The tracker combined flow-based 3D nucleus detection, pseudo-label refinement, learned linking and division models, and global integer linear programming. Biology-derived features and a learned per-node division cost produced the largest individual improvement, adding 0.035. Out-of-fold training and cross-embryo validation supported the stacked models, while track verification, smoothing, and gap bridging cleaned the output. The final public/private scores were 0.969/0.962, with the full pipeline running in about 30 minutes on two T4 GPUs.
compute: 2 × T4; approximately 30 minutes for four visible movies; gradient-boosted models run on CPU.
external_data: ["Ultrack zebrafish_embryo light-sheet volume, Royer Lab/CZ Biohub"]

solution_title: Guardrail Archaeology: Reconstructing a Hidden Defense from Code and Commits
solution_summary: The author used public implementation details, release history, and controlled proxy tests to predict which attacks would transfer to the hidden guardrail. The selected attacks targeted conditional draft authorization and a mismatch between action-time authorization and final-turn evaluation. They scored 21.230 and 18.915 privately, closely matching their public results. Literal-marker exfiltration attacks scored much higher publicly but all failed privately, supporting the decision to prioritize authorization failures.
external_data: ["Public release tags and PyPI wheels", "Public guardrail design and repository history"]

solution_summary: The author ultimately used a random forest with engineered features and selection focused on reducing overfitting. Insights from a disclosed train-test relationship led to removing earthquakes 5 and 6 because their split reflected a different stress threshold. The author also reduced the training weight of short earthquakes to account for a train-test distribution mismatch. Extensive RNN experimentation was abandoned, and computationally expensive Matrix Profile statistics offered little benefit.

The author adapted a public multi-model image matching baseline by tuning ALIKED and LightGlue parameters. The final configuration used 8192 features, a detection threshold of 0.005, at least 100 matches, and resizing to 1500. Image pair shortlisting used a similarity threshold of 0.08. These changes improved the public score by 0.01 and private score by 0.0018; the tested TTA alternative did not outperform 8192 features.

The author submitted a PolyBERT regression model and an ensemble combining PolyBERT with ChemBERTa. The approach used official and competition-shared data, runtime molecular augmentation, separate scaling for each target, and pooled transformer outputs feeding a regression head. Training used mean squared error with missing labels masked, while predictions were clipped to physically or mathematically valid ranges. Attempts at label balancing, learned target scaling, pseudo-labeling, and tabular modeling did not improve sufficiently to enter the final approach.

The author described solutions to several capture-the-flag challenges using model probing, serialization behavior, OCR-mediated XML injection, and adversarial attacks. Single-pixel probes exposed class activation patterns, while matching MobileNetV2 weights enabled accurate reproduction of a challenge model. For the passphrase challenge, a sentiment-score search combined a carefully chosen initialization with equal-length words and an NLTK vocabulary sweep. The author reported reaching 24 challenges, while Hush, CIFAR, and Granny 3 remained unsolved.

The described portion combined whole-video predictions, three five-frame models, and a label-conditioned localization network. The five-frame models comprised one DBoF and two VLAD networks pretrained on the previous year's sequences and fine-tuned on current annotated fragments. An LSTM localization model processed frame sequences concatenated with target-label embeddings while masking unannotated frames. Weighted geometric combination produced fragment scores, and the team's final submission used a ranked-sum ensemble with the teammate's contribution.

The solution generated search queries from CPC codes and title words using document frequencies. Tokens were scored by their frequency among neighboring patents divided by their global document frequency, and the top 25 were joined with OR. Experiments with code pairs yielded only a small score improvement, with final inclusion unspecified. Applying the same approach to claims, abstracts, and descriptions failed, possibly because it ignored repeated occurrences within documents.

solution_title: From Soundtracks & Signatures to Stars & Galaxies: Ali Hassaïne and Eu Jin Lok on finishing third on the Mapping Dark Matter Challenge
solution_summary: The team predicted galaxy ellipticity with a linear fit over a large collection of diverse image features. Morphological operations used structuring elements derived from star images, followed by quadrupole moment measurements. Geometrical descriptors inspired by handwriting and signature analysis added further signals from thresholded galaxy and star images. The implementation used C++ and OpenCV.

The solution combined 29 models into four local ensembles and averaged those ensembles equally. All models used 512-pixel inputs, with diversity supplied by architectures, training losses, augmentation, and ensemble construction. The author's FastAI models used staged unfreezing, while the PyTorch models used extra training data, bi-tempered loss, and mixed augmentation techniques. Public pretrained competition models and test-time augmentation further expanded the ensemble.

solution_title: General Intelligence - Open source framework for structural pattern learning (my ARC approach)
solution_summary: The author describes an unfinished ARC reasoning approach released after missing the competition deadline. The General Intelligence framework uses active, self-organizing knowledge for structural pattern learning. It is described as interpretable, compositional, and able to work with tiny datasets, but no measured competition results are provided.

solution_title: A ConvNet for Kaggle Statoil/C-CORE Iceberg Classifier Challenge
solution_summary: The solution uses a ConvNet with separate metadata and two-channel radar image inputs. Its augmentation pipeline supports HH and HV images directly and applies flips, rotations, shifts, and zooms. The author reports scores around 0.194–0.205+ and suggests further training and optimizer tuning as possible improvements.

The team combined improved GPS baseline positions and inter-point displacements with post-processing and averaging. The baseline work filtered poor pseudoranges, smoothed them with carrier-phase measurements, and used Doppler measurements to bridge short carrier-phase interruptions. Satellite uncertainty adjustments and removal of suspected multipath measurements helped, particularly in downtown areas. Reference-based differential positioning failed, while self-relative positioning and satellite coordinate corrections did not provide the hoped-for gains.

The solution combined diverse recurrent and convolutional text networks with LightGBM and XGBoost models using extensive engineered features. Frozen pretrained embeddings and a locally trained FastText embedding supplied complementary text representations, with FastText also imputing missing embeddings. Eight-fold out-of-fold predictions supported fold-specific HillClimb weighting and nonlinear XGBoost stacking. The final blend weighted HillClimb and the stacker 4:1, with neural networks contributing 54% and boosted trees 46%.
external_data: ["Twitter GloVe embeddings", "Common Crawl GloVe embeddings", "Common Crawl FastText embeddings"]

solution_summary: The solution uses XGBoost with varied feature combinations and 10-fold training predictions. Features include row statistics, manifold representations, and class-specific distance distribution percentiles. Previous model predictions are also reused as features, and a genetic algorithm selects an ensemble with replacement. The author monitors new submissions against the best existing submission as a proxy for overfitting and reports a leaderboard score of 0.40327.

The team treated landmark recognition as instance search because classes had limited internal variation and were numerous. A kNN classifier combined global CNN descriptors with geometric matching of local features. They learned GeM descriptors on the competition training set and used DELF features with ASMK indexing for geometric verification.

solution_title: 3rd solution - supplement to the post-processing section
solution_summary: The post describes retrieval post-processing experiments rather than a complete training pipeline. Re-ranking, database-side augmentation or neighbor blending, and graph-based re-ranking were unsuccessful. The author also explored feature dimension processing and Bayesian weight search. Weight search helped before a score of 0.875, but at 0.880 it performed similarly to concatenation.
compute: GPU acceleration mentioned for an unsuccessful re-ranking experiment; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The approach reranks the base model's top-five text-span candidates with a model that predicts each candidate's Jaccard score. A RoBERTa-base model takes sentiment, tweet, and candidate text as input and is trained with mean squared error against measured Jaccard scores. The final ranking score adds the predicted Jaccard score to the average of the base model's softmax start and end scores. Reranking improved cross-validation and private leaderboard scores by 0.003–0.005, with public leaderboard gains of 0.001–0.003.

solution_title: 20th Place Solution; XLM-Rs, xtune, hacky postprocessing
solution_summary: The solution ensembled nine XLM-RoBERTa-large question-answering models built using five training recipes. Diversity came from alternative prediction heads, multilingual external QA datasets, additional MLM pretraining, and staged fine-tuning. Five-fold language-stratified validation supported early stopping and seed selection. Postprocessing converted eligible Hindi numerals to Arabic digits, favored earlier answer spans, and penalized spans near chunk boundaries. The ensemble scored 0.811 on the public leaderboard and 0.755 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: 98th place: Cell tracking with a LightGBM division classifier
solution_summary: The solution extended a public temporal 3D U-Net detector, transformer link scorer, and ILP tracking pipeline with coordinate refinement and learned division detection. A small neural head predicted bounded coordinate shifts from local decoder features, and its output was averaged equally with a second head. A LightGBM classifier replaced fixed division rules using 19 geometric, tracking, and network-derived features. The coordinate ensemble raised the private score to 0.921, and the division classifier at threshold 0.01 raised it to 0.929; several locally promising changes failed to transfer.
models_pretrained: ["Public temporal 3D U-Net detector", "Public U-Net, transformer and ILP stack", "Division veto U-Net"]

solution_summary: The final prediction averaged four similar Keras networks combining Dense and bidirectional GRU processing with WaveNet and Dense classification layers. Inputs included Gaussian-mixture signal encodings, segment-group features, and stacked predictions from random forest and histogram gradient boosting classifiers. Automatic sinusoidal drift removal and exclusion of outliers in training batch 8 supported the pipeline. Training used Adam, stochastic weight averaging, and a one-cycle schedule, with checkpoints selected by validation F1. Five-fold validation balanced batches and used a seed chosen for similar target distributions across folds.
compute: Single GTX 1080Ti

solution_summary: The final system combined eight U-Net and FPN segmentation models with EfficientNet-B5, SE-ResNeXt50, and InceptionV4 encoders. Single-channel adaptation of pretrained weights, larger batches, and carefully sampled ensemble pseudo-labels helped training. Predictions used horizontal-flip TTA, minimum defect-area thresholds, and per-pixel conflict resolution. RMS averaging improved the public score but reduced the final private score to 0.90274; rerunning the ensemble with arithmetic averaging scored 0.90975. An abandoned classifier-based threshold adjustment produced the author's best private score of 0.91023.
compute: Home RTX 2080 Ti (11GB), then rented cloud Tesla V100 GPUs (16GB); typically 150–200 epochs.

solution_summary: The solution used only the main tabular data, removing rows without targets and columns exceeding a tuned missingness threshold. A shared preprocessing pipeline retained 21 features, used iterative numerical imputation and MinMax scaling, and fed DeepTables, CatBoost, and LightGBM models. Global threshold optimization converted predictions to ordinal labels, followed by majority voting across the three models. The ensemble achieved reported public/private scores of 0.458/0.469.

The solution averaged predictions from CatBoost, XGBoost, and TabPFN, with decisions guided by cross-validation. It added a time feature, assigned test samples a time beyond the training maximum, removed rows missing time, and filled other missing values with -100. UMAP followed by k-means provided cluster features, while manual permutation-based selection removed features that hurt validation. LightGBM reduced validation performance, and Optuna, stacking, and attempts to extend TabPFN did not produce useful gains.

solution_title: 22nd place journey : a completely different motion prediction approach
solution_summary: The team modeled raw agent histories with PointNet rather than rasterizing scenes through L5kit. Their best network combined four PointNet branches viewing 10, 5, 3, and 1 historical frames, projected and concatenated their embeddings, and predicted through a fully connected head. A custom loss ignored agents after they left the scene, and training used Adam with a step learning-rate scheduler. The approximately 40-million-parameter model scored 13.353 publicly and 12.912 privately, with fast training and inference despite lacking road-lane information.
compute: Single Colab Tesla V100; full-data training took 30 minutes for a light PointNet and 90 minutes for four branches; inference took 14 to under 30 minutes.

solution_summary: The final submission equally blended a particle-filter selector ensemble with a corrected spatial U-Net ensemble. The particle-filter branch scored 20 candidate trajectories using supervised selectors and converted their scores into smoothly interpolated blending weights. The U-Net branch represented each well as an image and used physically constrained synthetic geology, first for pretraining and then throughout mixed real-and-synthetic training. Spatial validation diversity, fold-local statistics, and decisions based on cross-validation were central to robustness.
compute: CPU-inference PF bank; the author's solution took 6.5 hours to score before merging. U-Net training used 200 synthetic-only epochs followed by 50 mixed epochs.

solution_summary: The author averaged four point-forecast models, including three using time-series cross-validation with different losses and one using rolling prediction. A weekend feature, zeroing of tiny predictions, and a multiplier close to one were applied to the accuracy forecasts. For uncertainty prediction, the final point forecast was converted using a public notebook and averaged with a separate quantile-regression notebook submission. Negative uncertainty predictions were clipped to zero.

The approach used two candidate ensembles pairing EfficientNet B5 at image size 456 with B4 at image size 328, with standard augmentations and test-time augmentation. Gaussian blur with a value of 20 gave slightly better results, and training used only the current competition data. Fixed QWK cutoffs avoided tuning to the public test set, while local QWK, validation loss, early stopping, and the train–validation loss gap guided model selection. Green CLHE preprocessing did not improve results and was excluded; the validation strategy translated into better relative performance on the private leaderboard.

The author's contribution centered on LightGBM models using handcrafted light-curve statistics and fitted-curve parameters, combined with teammates' neural models through stacking. Class-frequency-adjusted sample weights matched the evaluation metric, while Gaussian flux-noise augmentation expanded the small training set. Removing continuous host-galaxy photo-redshift reduced harmful training bias, and scaled class-99 probabilities handled the unseen class. Cross-validation was unreliable, and a late Gaussian-process interpolation experiment remained slightly worse than the best submission.

solution_title: Silver Medal (80th place) after 6 years of procrastination
solution_summary: The post thanks Kaggle, its operations team, and community contributors for the competition. It mentions ArcFace and Meta Embeddings as favorite shared ideas without explaining the author's own pipeline. It also links to the author's kernel.

solution_title: Summary: how we found the optimal (?) solution
solution_summary: The team formulated family assignments and attendance constraints as a mixed-integer program solved with Gurobi. They linearized the nonlinear accounting penalty using binary attendance indicators and pairwise product variables. To make the larger revenge problem tractable, they initialized a smooth attendance schedule and repeatedly optimized restricted neighborhoods within 20 people of the current daily attendance. This produced their best known submitted solution and a deep local optimum, without a proof of global optimality.

solution_title: Post-mortem for HuiUnited's Halite IV bot (26th rank)
solution_summary: The bot used hand-built rules for collecting halite, navigating, depositing, and later hunting enemy ships. Ships selected nearby rich cells with distance weighting and avoided duplicating neighboring ships' targets, while risk-based move ordering helped ships escape crowded situations. Switching empty ships to opportunistic hunting around step 70 raised the reported score from roughly 1100 to 1200 and helped preserve the fleet for later collection. Further improvements came from opening targets, shipyard placement, opponent-responsive creation rules, and an all-out endgame deposit strategy.

The team normalized detector signals with a running mean spectral estimate and used windowing and bandpass preprocessing. They trained diverse CNN approaches using detector permutations, CQT/CWT representations, and parallel backbones under stratified five-fold training. Random channel shuffling and time shifts supplied augmentation. Stacking roughly 50 models with an MLP classifier improved on weighted averaging, reaching 0.8830 public and 0.88133 private scores.
compute: GPU resources provided by Solvers Club; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The submission combined fine-tuned Protenix models modified to accept RNA multiple sequence alignments. Training used date-filtered competition sequences, curricula progressing from shorter to longer sequences, and representative sequences selected through clustering. Length-specialized models were combined with a strong model using a 2:3 weighted ensemble. Local validation did not correlate with public leaderboard performance, and the team could not reliably select the best predicted structure.

The solution combined EfficientNet B5, B6, and B7 models with ImageNet and noisy-student weights, trained across three folds on 384×384 images. Training included 2018 and 2019 data and brightness and contrast augmentation. Model predictions were combined using power averaging with exponent 2, then blended by weighted averaging with an ensemble of four public leaderboard solutions. The resulting submission scored 0.9644 on the public leaderboard and 0.9458 on the private leaderboard.
models_pretrained: ["EfficientNet B5, B6, and B7 with ImageNet and noisy-student weights"]

solution_summary: The solution trained separate solo-action and pair-action temporal models using body-part distances, velocities, accelerations, and metadata. It combined multi-scale CNNs with Bi-GRU or Transformer layers and also used SqueezeFormer variants. Training used lab-stratified five-fold validation, binary cross-entropy, EMA, augmentation, and validation-optimized lab-action thresholds. Sliding-window averaging and flip augmentation supported inference, while a frame-rate correction for AdaptableSnail increased the private score from 0.521 to 0.530.

The solution uses BlueCast AutoML to build an ensemble of five XGBoost models following a multiclass strategy. It does not add engineered features. Hyperparameters are tuned with simple train-test splits, which worked slightly better for the author than cross-validation. The reported score is 0.887.

The approach used a slightly tuned fastai tabular neural network for time-series prediction. Inputs included calendar features and target values lagged by seven and fourteen days. TimeSeriesSplit evaluated performance, and the network trained for eight epochs with two hidden layers and a batch size of 256.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution about k_features and LGBM2
solution_summary: This post describes one teammate's feature-engineering contribution rather than the complete modeling pipeline. Useful text features included five-dimensional TF-IDF/SVD representations and summary statistics of description doc2vec vectors. The approach also used 256-dimensional first-image DenseNet121 features, rescuer-level aggregates and age-derived indicators. Alternative text reductions, image extraction changes and cute-pet features were unsuccessful, and a PyTorch data-loader experiment ran out of memory.

The solution combined LightGBM and a neural network using weights optimized for AUC. Augmentation improved the LightGBM component, while the neural network was essential to the combined result. Features captured value frequencies, products and ratios between raw values and counts, and rank and z-score transformations within frequency groups. The initial LightGBM achieved approximately 0.9215 CV and 0.92033 private leaderboard AUC.

The solution ensembled 21 models spanning gradient-boosted trees, Transformers, a 2D CNN, and a GRU. Features included horizontally pivoted histories and meta features that improved both tree models and Transformers. LightGBM used ten stratified folds, while CatBoost ran on GPU with default parameters. Ensemble weights were selected using the public leaderboard because CV-based weighting performed worse; the best public submission scored 0.80199 publicly and 0.80881 privately.
compute: GPU used for CatBoost; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_title: Rank 46 Solution - keep the CV discipline
solution_summary: The solution used a single 2D U-Net with a maxvit_small_384 backbone and 384×384 tiles. Training ran for 15 epochs with volume normalization, light augmentation, and resizing-based augmentation to handle resolution changes. The team validated on kidney_3 dense, preferred final-epoch weights, and used a prediction threshold of 0.1. Although 2.5D and 3D approaches performed better locally, concerns about test-time depth resolution favored 2D; their best submission scored 0.615.

The solution adapted earlier ARC solvers using domain-specific programs searched over a DAG, decision trees, and CNNs. Extra memory and runtime enabled deeper searches, longer training, and larger ensembles. Predictions were combined using majority voting, manual priority rules, and probabilistic model selection. Augmentations included diagonal flips, color changes, and symmetry transformations.
compute: Kaggle Kernels with 30 GB RAM and a 12-hour runtime allowance.

solution_summary: The solution used EfficientNet B7 and Swin Transformer on constant-Q representations, EfficientNet B3 on continuous wavelet representations, and a modified 1D CNN. Each model used five-fold validation, with attention modules and horizontal spectrogram shifts applied to the image models. Observatory-specific normalization, channel-axis spectrogram alignment, and SAM optimization helped. EfficientNet B7 achieved the strongest reported individual scores, while mixup, VQT, and SETI pretraining did not work.

solution_title: [3rd Place Solution] AlphaFold Style Twin Tower Architecture + Squeezeformer
solution_summary: The final solution blended a BPP-aware Squeezeformer with an independently trained AlphaFold-inspired twin-tower model. The twin-tower model learned sequence and pair representations from clean sequence data, while Squeezeformer used BPP matrices and additional noisy examples improved by blending labels with model predictions. Relative position encodings and communication between sequence and pair representations were central architectural choices. Longer twin-tower training improved its score, and the two models provided complementary predictions.
compute: Twin-tower training: 2x RTX 4090 GPUs, 30 hours; initially 60 epochs. Squeezeformer: 200 epochs.

solution_summary: The solution built cumulative gameplay features and trained diverse neural network and tree models using repeated five-fold predictions with Optuna tuning. A three-level ensemble stacked base predictions with engineered features, then combined second-level outputs using weights optimized by gradient descent. The neural network used Yeo-Johnson preprocessing, dropout, and activation followed by batch normalization. OptimizedRounder converted predictions into classes, while game-world clustering and test-mean adjustment were rejected. The selected ensemble achieved validation QWK of 0.61606 and a private score of 0.548.
compute: 9-hour execution budget; reported cumulative fit times included 2 h 1 min for Keras and 1 h 18 min for XGBoost.

solution_summary: The pipeline used YOLOv5 to select tumor-containing axial T1wCE slices for EfficientNet B3 classification. Predictions used four-way test-time augmentation with squared-probability aggregation, while studies without usable detections fell back to a 3D classifier adapted from ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet B1. The best reported validation AUCs were 0.6829 for 2D classification and 0.6936 for 3D classification. The authors cautioned that the small dataset and unstable results suggested learning noise or unrelated features, limiting clinical usefulness.
models_pretrained: ["ImageNet-pretrained models adapted for 3D classification; EfficientNet B1 selected"]
compute: RTX 3090, Google Colab Pro and Kaggle.

solution_summary: The author moved from a single LightGBM model to ensembles after feature and hyperparameter selection proved insufficient. Combining CatBoost and LightGBM benefited from differences between their predictions. A voting ensemble of two LightGBM models with different boosting types provided the final improvement. The author also explored a metric hack but emphasized restraint to avoid overfitting to the public leaderboard.

The team combined stochastic optimization, incremental local search, and SAT solving to recover predecessor boards. A shared service measured improvement per hour and routed processing power toward the most productive algorithms. Iterative SAT solving favored sparse predecessors, used backtracking and increasing timeouts, and eventually benefited substantially from Kissat on difficult cases. Partial center solutions and fast pixel-flip search complemented the exact solvers.
compute: Distributed work across available cores; solver timeouts increased from 1 minute to 10 minutes, 1 hour, and finally 2 hours.

solution_summary: This writeup describes the graph-network component of a broader team solution that also included neural networks, LightGBM, feature engineering, and stacking. The successful graph architecture updated node and edge information together and used a separate MLP for each coupling type. Joint training across coupling types was more stable than training them separately. NNConv, SchNet, and subsequent per-type fine-tuning were unsuccessful or produced worse results.

The solution dropped bin_0, ordinal-encoded ordinal features, and one-hot-encoded the remaining features. It used logistic regression with the liblinear solver and tuned the regularization parameter C with Optuna. The final model was trained on all data without K-fold training, yielding a reported score of 0.80850.

solution_title: Efficiency solution: Private 0.918, Public(4th) 0.935, in 5min for spaCy ner
solution_summary: The solution ensembled three spaCy NER models initialized from en_core_web_lg and trained on public and external data. Sentence filtering reduced average text length from about 3,800 characters to fewer than 500, while preserving useful name-bearing headers. Specialized input windows, batched processing and extensive rules handled names and other PII categories. Reported leaderboard inference time was approximately five minutes.
compute: About 5 minutes leaderboard inference time.

solution_title: 21st Place Solution [ Representation is all you need]
solution_summary: The approach used fully connected network representations of protein sequences as inputs to XGBoost. Predictions were exponentiated and quantile-filtered to reduce ranking ties. The final ensemble combined this approach with ThermoNet and a notebook using difference features derived from published PDBs. It achieved public and private scores of 0.59749 and 0.52441.

The solution processes sixteen scanner views with a pretrained ResNet-50 and applies attention to its feature maps. Convolutional pyramid pooling and average pooling feed an attention-equipped LSTM, followed by a layer predicting probabilities for seventeen threat zones. It learns zone associations from binary labels without segmentation or additional data. Training takes roughly 12–16 hours on one GTX 1080 ti, and longer training improved test results.
compute: Single GTX 1080 ti, 32 GB system RAM; roughly 12–16 hours of training.

solution_summary: A unified model jointly handled labs, trackers, self-actions, and interactions using motion features, actor-relative coordinates, and metadata embeddings. Grouped processing kept input streams separate before mixing their information, with convolutional, GRU, and ModernBERT backbone variants. Masked keypoint pretraining supplied ensemble diversity, while annotation-aware cross-entropy avoided penalizing unannotated actions. A 45-model ensemble, overlapping inference, and lab-action threshold optimization achieved 0.5430 CV; the broader team ensemble reached 0.5702 CV and 0.525 private leaderboard score.

solution_title: My first medal. 75th place with the help of genetic algorithms.
solution_summary: The agent mapped the opponent's last ten moves to responses through a dictionary of 59,049 entries. A genetic algorithm evolved populations of 64 agents, selecting the best two through single-elimination tournaments and recombining their dictionaries. Random mutation counts between 1 and 60 produced the biggest improvement. The submitted agent came from generation 150; performance deteriorated after roughly 300 generations.

solution_title: Enhancing Kidney Microvascular Structure Segmentation with Morphological Operations - Private LB .451
solution_summary: The author modified a public segmentation notebook and refined its predicted binary masks using morphological operations. Morphological gradients enhanced boundaries, while iterative erosion, opening, and closing removed noise and smoothed structures. The approach also increased the prediction score assigned to the glomerulus class. It achieved a private score of 0.451, but the author did not select this model for the final submission.

solution_title: Fair Cell Activation Network and Swin Transformer, the 1st place solution
solution_summary: The author developed a Fair Cell Activation Network based on Puzzle-CAM to improve cell-level recall under image-level supervision. Its predictions supplied rule-based, five-level labels for a pretrained Swin Transformer trained on individual cell crops. Weighted averaging combined the two models, and a separate completeness predictor reduced confidence for incomplete border cells. The two-model approach scored 0.555 privately, while a six-model ensemble reached 0.566; border processing added about 0.007–0.01.

solution_title: Solution to Kaggle's Mercari Price Suggestion Challenge
solution_summary: The solution ensembled a factorization machine trained with FTRL and a neural network. The factorization machine used n-gram features. The neural network used word embeddings, providing a second representation for the ensemble.

solution_title: 135th Place Solution - My First Full Competition
solution_summary: The final solution blended probabilities from an external RealMLP, histogram gradient boosting, LightGBM, and a custom RealMLP-style neural network. Target encoding of repeated numeric values and LightGBM prior correction were useful components. Blend weights were selected through OOF evaluation with grid and random searches, yielding 0.950723 balanced accuracy. Additional weaker models and logistic-regression stacking did not improve on the four-model probability blend.

The solution combined ResNet34 at 512×512 with InceptionV3 and SE-ResNeXt50 at 1024×1024 using weighted prediction averaging. Official and external images were split with duplicate awareness, and larger inputs used per-image normalization and learned spatial pooling. Training used focal loss, Adam, gradient accumulation, and stopping based on the common class rather than overall macro F1. Checkpoint averaging, eight-way test-time augmentation, and prevalence-matching thresholds completed the pipeline, although unstable validation limited confidence in individual improvements.

The solution used sound-event-detection models with EfficientNet backbones, pretrained on earlier BirdCLEF data and fine-tuned on the current competition. It combined waveform mixing and noise augmentation with spectrogram masking, rating-weighted loss, and some pseudo-label fine-tuning. Final inference averaged probabilities from 15 model instances and used ONNX Runtime with concurrent execution. The best individual model achieved private/public scores of 0.72714/0.81836 with a ten-minute submission time.

solution_summary: The author combined YOLOv5 and Detectron2 predictions using weighted boxes fusion. Adding a public prediction result to this ensemble produced the strongest submission. The final three-source weights were [2, 1, 3], yielding 0.294 public and 0.282 private scores. Five-fold training and test-time augmentation were attempted but abandoned because of other work.

The final pipelines used only BirdCLEF 2024 audio, combining cleaned training recordings with pseudo-labeled soundscapes. ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet-B0 and RegNetY-008 classified 10-second mel spectrograms, trained with cross-entropy, random segments, masking, and horizontal CutMix. Important improvements came from classifier-based label cleaning, soundscape pseudo-labeling, longer input context, and sigmoid inference with chunk averaging and minimum-reduction ensembles. The selected six-model configurations achieved private scores around 0.689–0.690, while OpenVINO made CPU inference feasible.

solution_summary: The author describes a small adjustment that incorporates a Bayesian prior approximated from the training-set distribution. They report that this helped in the rental-listing competition when further model improvements were difficult. Most features came from variations of public kernels, and the post provides no detailed model or validation pipeline.

The approach paired the 200 original variables with frequency-count features computed from training data and real test rows, excluding fake test data. Column-shuffling augmentation preserved each original variable together with its count feature, and diverse models were ensembled and stacked to reach a reported CV score of 0.923. The best single CatBoost model used stratified 21-fold validation and achieved a public score of 0.92275. A complementary ensemble trained 200 separate variable-level models and combined them through logistic regression.
compute: Best single CatBoost model completes in 2 hours; hardware unspecified.

solution_title: [Silver Medal] Simple and Interpretable Hybrid Agent Using CatBoost and Rules
solution_summary: The agent combined an improved Lucario rule-based policy with CatBoost imitation learning from strong players' winning replays. Each legal candidate action became a row with 740 interpretable state and action features, and the classifier ranked candidates within each decision. Context gating and automatic rule fallback stabilized decisions outside the learner's scope. CPU-only final training took 22 minutes and 10 seconds, and local evaluation achieved a 68.30% win rate over 2,000 games.
compute: 4-vCPU machine, no GPU; final training 22 minutes 10 seconds; inference approximately 1.09 ms per candidate.

solution_summary: The solution blended XGBoost, LightGBM, and several DAE–MLP variants using weights optimized on out-of-fold predictions. DAE training used decreasing learning rates and progressively decaying swap noise, with three DAE runs retained for inference. Diversity came from categorical binning, passing noisy inputs through the DAE during MLP training, and including reconstruction and mask predictions as features. Ten-fold stratified validation outperformed five folds, and the strongest individual model scored 0.89964 privately.
compute: Around 27 DAE runs of 600 epochs each; retained runs generally extended to 1200–1800 epochs, with one reaching 2400.

solution_summary: The approach estimated transit losses directly from smoothed signals without a predictive model for the spectra. Time-shifted signal differences located transit phases, while local linear fits corrected remaining trends. Individual wavelength estimates borrowed information from nearby wavelengths through Gaussian weights that became more uniform for noisier signals, followed by a small correction for each star. A customized random forest estimated uncertainty by aggregating predicted absolute errors with RMSE, reportedly improving the score by about 0.03.

The solution blended ResNet34, ResNet50, EfficientNet-b4, and EfficientNet-b5 models across several input resolutions and preprocessing variants. Removing black borders and subtracting Gaussian-blurred images was central to reducing image-source cues and improving generalization. Manually chosen ensemble weights worked better than hyperopt, and some models benefited from test-time augmentation. The best single EfficientNet-b5 model scored 0.814 publicly and 0.927 privately, while confidence-thresholded pseudo-labeling gave a modest improvement.

The solution combined a large ensemble of 1108-class image classifiers with different architectures, channel selections, and cross-validation models. Images were processed at 512×512 resolution with rotation and clipping augmentation. Predictions were normalized and passed through linear sum assignment to enforce the groups-of-277 plate restriction. Pseudo-labels were then used to retrain selected models, including EfficientNet.

The solution classified overlapping audio windows using MFCC features and a random forest with 87 binary outputs, then averaged window probabilities into clip predictions. Simplifying window features, shortening windows, and enlarging the forest mattered most. The authors later replaced MFCC averaging with PCA and reached a reported private AUC of 0.915. They optimized mainly against 10-fold cross-validation, which measured 0.943 ± 0.010, and excluded a tested neighboring-clip leakage adjustment.
compute: Borrowed 16 GB RAM to increase the forest from 25 to 250 trees.

solution_title: 24th place solution | Logistic model on top of Ensemble (XGB + Catboost + LGBM)
solution_summary: The solution stacked XGBoost, CatBoost, and LightGBM base models. Their out-of-fold predictions formed the training data for a logistic regression meta-learner. Ten stratified folds were used to improve validation reliability and model robustness.

The solution predicts player trajectories with a spatio-temporal GRU and gated neighbor attention. A hierarchical decoder establishes a coarse global path before refining it to full resolution. Training combines robust Cauchy position loss with weak velocity regularization based on random smoothing kernels. A genetic algorithm searches model subsets and ensemble weights using out-of-fold predictions and validation RMSE.

The author reports reusing raddar's 2018 women's competition solution. No modifications or implementation details are described. The post provides a link to the earlier solution but does not explain its methods.

The solution constructed an initial robot path and represented route optimization as an asymmetric traveling salesman problem. Eight-neighbor movement made the arm configuration cost equivalent to geometric distance, combined with color cost using a scale factor of 2550. LKH 3.0.7 optimized the route with a virtual endpoint and tuned patching and kick parameters. A two-step jump connected the origin to the initial route point.

The solution used a pretrained RoBERTa-large Siamese bi-encoder with CLS pooling and sigmoid-transformed question-answer dot products. Preprocessing replaced code and LaTeX with special tokens and preserved both ends of sequences within a 450-token limit. Seven GroupKFold models were averaged, followed by target-specific prediction binning tuned on out-of-fold predictions. Additional data, categorical features, alternative pooling, freezing, and crop-based test-time augmentation did not improve results.
external_data: ["Unspecified additional data for flawed targets, tested without improvement"]

solution_summary: The solution combined extensive data cleaning and imputation with diverse regression models trained across six validation regimes. Features included location information, suspicious-price classification probabilities, floor-space-related targets, and lagged macroeconomic indicators. Base models were stacked across regimes, with linear stacking performing best, and robust stacks were blended for the final submission. A slight downward prediction adjustment compensated for an unreliable time component, while tree stacking and feature-weighted linear stacking were unsuccessful.

The selected submission ensembled two three-channel 2.5D U-Nets with ConvNeXt-Tiny backbones, trained on all provided data including kidney_1_voi. Whole slices from multiple axes were processed at 1536x1536, with strong spatial augmentations and random 3D slice rotations in one model. Training combined focal, Dice, boundary, and custom losses, while inference used three axes, eight-way TTA, high resolution, and a 0.4 threshold. The selected dynamic-resolution ensemble scored about 0.774 privately, but an unselected single model trained with 3D rotations achieved about 0.835.

solution_title: [29th Place Notes] how to train a single deberta model of 0.972 on public LB
solution_summary: The final submission combined three DeBERTa-v3-large models trained on manually balanced folds. The most important change was collapsing BIO labels into eight classes during training and restoring prefixes in post-processing, which improved public scores and CV agreement. Training also downsampled essays without PII and reduced the weight of the outside class. Inference used a 0.9 threshold, several targeted corrections, and the maximum positive prediction when multiple subtokens mapped to one token.

The pipeline classified cropped faces from sampled video frames using ImageNet-pretrained ResNeXt and DenseNet models. BlazeFace with additional overlapping detection windows improved face detection coverage, while augmentation provided the largest generalization gains. Final predictions averaged face predictions across 100 frames per video and across several models. External FaceForensics data, recurrent temporal modeling, and a learned prediction aggregator were explored but excluded from the final pipeline.
compute: Parallelized frame extraction, face detection, and inference at 25 frames per second in the Kaggle environment.

solution_title: 14th Place Solution for the Bengali.AI Speech Recognition Competition
solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned Bengali Wav2vec2CTC on selected competition audio and decoded it with KenLM. Filtering easy and hard examples helped the model adapt to diverse speakers, while punctuation restoration supplied the largest inference improvement. White-noise augmentation, unigram vocabulary support, and a wider decoding beam provided smaller gains. The final reported scores were 0.380 public and 0.458 private WER, with validation based on the leaderboard because of domain shift.

The final system served unmodified gpt-oss-120b with a short system prompt and eight parallel, Python-assisted reasoning attempts. It selected answers using inverse confidence weights derived from a five-component entropy measure, with agreement-based cancellation and adaptive time limits. Nine identical submissions averaged 40.78 publicly, while the private score was 41.5/50. More elaborate prompts, arbitration pipelines, increased attempt counts, and GRPO fine-tuning provided no reliable improvement or caused substantial failures. Repeated-run evaluation exposed substantial score variance, limiting causal conclusions about individual changes.
compute: Approximately 5 hours of H100 GPU time per submission; final notebook budget 17,400 seconds. GRPO experiments cost approximately $300 in B200 GPU time.

solution_title: 27th Place Solution (8th in Public):  1DCNN for share and ChemBERTa for non-share
solution_summary: The solution treated shared and nonshared targets separately. Nonshared predictions used protein-specific ChemBERTa fine-tuning, building-block validation, external sEH data, and frozen early layers. Shared predictions used a larger 1D CNN with attention, shortcut connections, batch normalization, and a five-fold average ensemble. CV-based ensemble weights raised to the fifth power worked best publicly for most nonshared models, while graph models and stacking were unsuccessful.

The agent generated predictions from recent matches in game history, partial matches, and rotated interpretations of its own and its opponent's behavior. It selected predictions using decayed performance scores, a recent-error gate, and voting among strong candidates. Its main defensive mechanism randomly rotated half of its chosen actions toward a draw to confuse opponents. Periodically disabling that defense created short opportunities to gain points before opponents adapted.

The solution combined LightGBM LambdaRank rerankers with graph neural networks using distinct candidate-generation pipelines. LightGBM used recency-weighted co-visitation candidates and 344 engineered features, while eight-layer GNNs processed session subgraphs with node and edge features. Increasing GNN inference candidates and combining four GNN models improved performance. Calibrating LambdaRank scores onto the GNN probability scale enabled weighted averaging, reaching a private score of 0.60313.
compute: GNN inference with 1024 candidates took several days.

solution_summary: The pipeline retrieved 35 candidate misconceptions with a shared Qwen-14B embedder and reranked them with Qwen-32B-instruct-AWQ using six LoRA variants. A self-trained retriever reduced performance and was removed. Leaderboard probing suggested that unseen misconceptions dominated the test set, motivating a probability multiplier calibrated so they represented 75% of top predictions. This adjustment and randomized reranker candidate ordering increased the private score from 0.564 to 0.602.

The solution combined an SVR trained on pretrained image embeddings with an ensemble of image regression models. Embeddings from multiple timm and CLIP models were concatenated, with forward selection choosing which models supplied features. The image branch combined vision transformers and CNNs, with beit_large_patch16_224 the strongest individual model. Combining both branches achieved CV 16.818 and private leaderboard score 16.8225.

The solution combined five image classifiers with a shared multilayer classification head and SoftTriple metric learning. Training used ordinary cross-entropy for 30 epochs followed by balanced-softmax cross-entropy for five epochs, alongside strong augmentation, exponential moving averages, and mixed precision. Five-pass test-time augmentation and soft voting were followed by rules that swapped the two highest-scoring classes based on confidence and predicted class frequency. The final ensemble achieved public and private scores of 0.77625 and 0.73534, while computation limits restricted experimentation and convergence.

The final submission combined Conv1d, a FastText-style neural network and FM+FTRL. Five-fold cross-validation and Hyperopt supported offline model selection and parameter tuning. Conv1d and FastText scored 0.413 and 0.414 individually on the public leaderboard, with their ensemble reaching 0.405; FM+FTRL achieved 0.407 alone. GRU was abandoned for lower accuracy and higher runtime, while several linear and boosted-tree alternatives were also uncompetitive.

The solution exploited similarity between consecutive driving images by finding nearest neighbors and incorporating their predictions. Four selected CNNs used original images or synthetic RGB channels formed from averages or differences of neighboring images. A second-level optimizer combined each image's prediction with predictions from its 20 neighbors, followed by a weighted geometric blend across models. The final cross-validation score was about 0.116 with 96.4% class accuracy; zeroing tiny probabilities improved validation but was omitted from the final submission.

The solution used a weighted ensemble of XGBoost and LightGBM without adding new features. Numerical inputs were standardized, while categorical inputs used M-estimate encoding for XGBoost and one-hot encoding for LightGBM. Validation used ten-fold stratified cross-validation, and tuning ensemble weights was the main driver of leaderboard improvement. Additional features, CatBoost, alternative preprocessing, and dataset pruning did not help.

The author combined six transformer model variants, each trained across five folds, and used 612,000 hard pseudo-labels in subsequent training. The ensemble reached 0.8942 cross-validation and 0.89067 private leaderboard scores, with limited leaderboard benefit from model diversity. Restoring missing initial characters in predicted spans improved the score by 0.002. Minimizing input sequence length enabled inference over 30 models in about 480 minutes, while biomedical model variants did not improve results.
compute: Inference for 30 models took about 480 minutes.

solution_summary: The final pipeline averaged U-Net models with pretrained ResNet34 and ResNet50 encoders, scSE modules, hypercolumns, and depth channels. It used four folds from a random ten-fold split, edge padding to 128×128, augmentation, and horizontal-flip test-time augmentation. Training progressed from models without depth channels to depth-aware fine-tuning and finally pseudo-label fine-tuning, using Lovasz loss and SGD with learning-rate scheduling. The reported final scores were 0.866 public and 0.887 private; CRF processing and replacing padding with resizing did not help.

The writeup provides execution instructions for a whale-detection code pipeline. It specifies generating training and test metrics, running an ordering script, and then generating a submission. It lists required Python packages and directory setup but does not describe the modeling method or report results.

The solution combines a DINO v3 visual pathway with SigLIP semantic features to capture complementary aspects of pasture composition. Each image is split into two halves, encoded with the same DINO backbone, and fused using Local Mamba blocks. Training uses three-fold stratified group validation, differential learning rates, and a weighted Huber loss on log-transformed targets. Post-processing enforces nonnegative predictions and the component relationships between biomass targets; mean validation R² was 0.844.

The author provides a runnable version of their competition solution but delegates architectural details to an interview and diagram. Model selection uses a five-fold cross-validation score above 0.833600. The submitted model scored 0.88209 publicly and 0.88682 privately, with reproduction differences attributed to random seeds.

The author treated the task as cell-tile classification and combined predictions with HPA Cell Segmentator instances. Tiles centered on nucleus bounding boxes and sized by the cell bounding box's shorter side improved performance. A two-stage training pipeline used pseudo-labels, thresholding, and sampling, with image-grouped multilabel stratified validation. Green image-level label predictions were also incorporated, while several alternative tile constructions and imbalance treatments reduced scores.
compute: Kaggle Notebooks; TPU training and GPU inference; 1–2 hours per model for five epochs.

solution_summary: The author built an image-matching pipeline from previous competition solutions using ALIKED and AffNet keypoints with fusion. Increasing the ALIKED keypoint count and the minimum-match threshold helped. Adding AffNet also improved the solution through model fusion. Image rotation and AdaLAM parameter adjustments did not provide useful gains.

The solution combined eight ImageNet-initialized CNNs trained on five-second mel-spectrogram inputs with varied transformations, resolutions, and model heads. Silence removal and extensive noise and image augmentation helped bridge the gap between training recordings and test soundscapes. Training beyond the local validation optimum improved leaderboard performance, and final models used all training data with binary cross-entropy loss. ONNX conversion enabled the ensemble to meet runtime limits, while root-mean-square prediction aggregation outperformed ordinary averaging.

solution_title: One trick that can give you a bronze medal or above
solution_summary: This post describes audio-level threshold post-processing rather than the team's complete modeling pipeline. A confident detection in any clip lowered the threshold for the same species throughout the recording, with thresholds optimized against cross-validation using Optuna. Applying this processing to a public inference notebook improved its private score from 0.55 to 0.62. Location- and month-based threshold adjustments were tested but excluded from the submission because they hurt the public score, despite producing a private score of 0.68.

solution_title: 29th public - Am I the only one that approach this with regression?
solution_summary: The author trained a neural network to predict 300 yardage quantiles, inspired by distributional reinforcement learning. Quantile loss replaced quantile Huber loss, and the outputs were converted into yardage class probabilities. Features included projected player trajectories, distances to defenders, and defender counts around and ahead of the rusher. The approach reached a reported score of 0.01305.

The author modeled EC1 and EC2 as separate classification problems after removing redundant columns, erroneous records, and duplicate rows. For EC1, an Optuna-tuned CatBoost, LightGBM, and XGBoost ensemble achieved 0.71205 local OOF CV and was blended with two public notebook predictions. EC2 ensembles were rejected in favor of predictions from one public notebook because of its relatively strong CV performance. The final submission scored 0.66095.

solution_title: 27th place simple solution (0.932 public, 0.940 private) - dl_pipeline
solution_summary: The best single model used DenseNet121 features with a fastai classification head and cross-entropy loss on mel spectrograms. Training used long crops around true-positive events, waveform distortion and pitch shifting, mixup, and strong dropout. Inference on much narrower crops followed by per-class maximum pooling and averaging across three crop widths improved public performance from 0.925 to 0.928. The final ensemble of modified training runs scored 0.932 on the public leaderboard and 0.940 on the private leaderboard.
compute: GTX 1080; approximately one minute per training epoch; 30 epochs, batch size 32.

solution_title: Optimizing scored harm per model turn in multi-step tool-agent red-teaming
solution_summary: The submission used archive search over user-message chains, confirming successful mechanisms through live replay and expanding them across distinct scoring targets. A runtime governor limited candidate volume, while a family allocator balanced attack classes under uncertainty about the private guardrail. The selected submissions included a pure exfiltration line and a mixed line incorporating value-level authorization confused-deputy cases; only the latter retained private score, reaching 2.665. Packing multiple actions, suppressing reasoning, and quality-diversity search failed to improve the relevant hosted or controlled results. A separately calibrated replay-cost oracle served as a retrospective risk analysis rather than the shipped candidate-count selector.
compute: Hosted replay budget of 9,000 seconds per phase; submission probes took approximately 11 hours.

solution_summary: The author tested 18 prompts across nine local LLMs using approximately 150 synthetic topics. They searched all three-model combinations for correlation with public leaderboard scores, including scores from public notebooks. Selected combinations evaluated about 50 attacks, seeking strongly divergent judge scores such as 909, 099, or 990. The author concluded that this validation approach was unreliable because of prompt sensitivity and unknown judges; their best submission was a small modification of a public submission.
compute: Used the weekly 30-hour Kaggle notebook allowance during two weeks of experimentation.
external_data: ["Approximately 150 synthetic topics", "Public notebook submissions and scores", "Public notebook and ChatGPT-generated attacks"]

solution_summary: The solution used one pretrained XLM-RoBERTa architecture trained across multiple data mixtures and folds. Competition data were supplemented with MLQA, XQUAD, Tamil-translated SQuAD, and Google-translated SQuAD2.0. Soft voting across 12 folds achieved a private score of 0.740, exceeding the 0.727 from a publicly stronger five-fold ensemble. The final selections were 12-fold and 17-fold ensembles, while hard voting consistently performed worse.

The solution improved a transformer token-labeling baseline by correcting label construction, tokenizer offsets, and character-span extraction. Fourteen diverse models generated fold-separated pseudo-labels for approximately 110,000 unlabeled examples, followed by one epoch of additional training and two extra-large DeBERTa models. Character-level logits were ensembled with optimized weights, and five-fold GroupKFold guided model selection. The stronger final submission achieved CV 0.8967 and private score 0.892, despite weakening CV–leaderboard correlation above 0.89.
compute: A 24GB memory limit is mentioned; extra-large models used batch size 2. GPU resources were provided by Prof. Ross at NYU Shanghai.

solution_summary: The solution combines ten pretrained image classifiers trained and evaluated in PyTorch. Each model uses twelve test-time views, and predictions are combined with a geometric mean and probability calibration for the expected test class balance. Most models achieved 85–87% validation accuracy, while NASNet reached 84%. Model-specific ensemble weights were removed from the final submission to reduce public leaderboard overfitting.

The pipeline detected western blot and microscopy panels, retrieved suspicious pairs with specialized embedding models, and localized duplications with keypoint matching and geometric verification. A manually corrected validation set and large deduplicated biomedical image collection supported reliable model development. Matching individual western blot lanes was the largest breakthrough, increasing the public score from about 0.375 to 0.431. Stronger microscopy embeddings, augmentation, ensembling, threshold tuning, and a masked public segmentation fallback added further gains, with the post reporting a best private score of 0.55.
compute: Local RTX 4090 and cloud A100 or RTX 6000; trained blot matching reduced inference from roughly 2.5 hours to 20 minutes.
external_data: ["PubMed Central biomedical papers", "BioFors", "Organizers' panel detector dataset"]

solution_summary: The best submission was generated by benchmark_2299.R and scored 2299.60492 on the public evaluation and 2394.70198 on the private evaluation. A separate safety submission used week alignment, week blending, and trends at the store and department levels. That submission scored 2360.39811 publicly and 2432.86274 privately, while the best submission's methodology is not described.

solution_title: Silver Write-up: Improving “The Producer V2” Without RL
solution_summary: The solution extended the public Producer V2 agent with deterministic, projection-based planning and hand-tuned heuristics. Its main improvements were production-aware source selection, pooled attacks from multiple planets, and rejection of launches arriving too late. Higher ROI and launch-size thresholds, conservative reinforcement estimates, and a separate four-player configuration reduced wasteful attacks. An optional opponent launch predictor was implemented but disabled in the submitted configuration.

solution_title: Lb 8.33 with ARChitects Approach and a 0.5B model (Private Runtime ~5 hours)
solution_summary: The team adapted the ARChitects' previous winning approach to Qwen2.5-0.5B and fine-tuned it using ARC 2 tasks. Single-task test-time training used 560 augmented samples per task, with embedding and output layers frozen. Greedy inference used 16 augmented samples, keeping the pipeline simple. The notebook achieved a leaderboard score of 8.33 and finished the private test set in about five hours.
compute: 4 GPUs; approximately 5 hours total on the private test set, including an estimated 1.5 hours of inference; lambda.ai compute credit.

solution_summary: The churn classifier relied on extensive feature engineering, diverse tabular models, and a three-stage ensemble. A feature store of more than 600 candidates supported model-specific subsets, with target-encoded interactions, arithmetic combinations, grouped aggregations, counts, and rounded features providing useful signal. XGBoost was the strongest single model, complemented by LightGBM, CatBoost, TabM, RealMLP, and other architectures under shuffled 15-fold stratified validation. AutoGluon stacking, hill-climbing blending, and final averaging achieved a reported CV AUC of 0.9197980 and leaderboard AUC of 0.91735, although many blends failed to improve on strong single models.
compute: L4 Colab, A100 Colab/A100 (80GB), and A6000Ada (48GB); about 220 single models and more than 330 models in the full pipeline.
