solution_summary: The solution constructed a 24-word OR query from individual title words and CPC terms. It shortlisted title words using the top 100 TF-IDF features, evaluated candidate queries using AP@50 and document coverage, and greedily assembled the final query. Alternative experiments included T5 title-to-query generation, linear programming, abstract text, and beam search, with beam search blocked by submission scoring errors.

solution_title: 3rd place solution: Ensembles of deep (49 layer) MLPs
solution_summary: The final system averaged 15 deep MLPs trained with different seeds, with five response outputs per model and a decision threshold of 0.5. Data preparation removed the first 85 days, retained zero-weight rows, and filled missing values using medians conditioned on f0. The networks combined logarithmic feature extensions, batch normalization, dropout, skip connections, and a mixture of smoothed BCE and a utility-like loss. A chronological holdout guided development, public leaderboard submissions guided the final training duration, and TensorFlow Lite conversion made inference practical.

The solution combined five pretrained image architectures trained at different input resolutions using five-fold cross-validation. Rotation, flip, and occasional zoom augmentation supported the base models, whose out-of-fold predictions fed per-label boosted-tree classifiers. The author attributed stability to using different image resolutions and reported substantial gains from optimizing F1 separately for each model and class. A voting ensemble of the second-level classifiers achieved 0.93288 public and 0.93201 private scores.
compute: ResNet50 required almost 35 hours for five folds; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution applied a sequence of specialized solvers ordered by their assumed reliability. These included finite differences, variable-spacing differences, pattern matching, recurrence relations, and fits using previous terms, with held-out last terms used to assess some predictions. Publicly shared predictions replaced roughly 4,000 unreliable estimates and improved the submission by about one percent. A sequence-mode fallback handled unsolved cases, while false positives and nonlinear overfitting were major limitations.

The team combined genetic search and simulated annealing to optimize tree packings, using dense patterned seeds, corner mutations, and fine local moves. Soft-wall rotations and hard-wall collision resolution supported complementary search behavior, while temperature-dependent moves shifted from global exploration toward compaction. They also transferred layouts from larger instances by removing boundary-biased trees and generated dense tessellated candidates through grid optimization and cropping. GPU/SIMD acceleration enabled larger searches, but increasing population size had limited returns and late tessellation candidates rarely surpassed heavily optimized incumbents.
compute: GPU/SIMD parallel processing; hardware model and runtime unspecified.

solution_title: [ Public 11th / Private 45th] We found the leak but it was too late
solution_summary: The team ensembled several image models trained with different augmentations, achieving a public leaderboard score of 17.77. They then identified approximately 1,700 training images shared with the earlier PetFinder.my Adoption Prediction competition. Using these duplicates, they trained LightGBM with AdoptionSpeed and other features from that competition. Replacing ensemble predictions for detected private-test duplicates with LightGBM predictions improved their reported score to 17.66.
compute: Z8 workstation

solution_title: Stable gold medal solution 29.303 public / 29.395 private
solution_summary: The team searched extensively for three prompt attack templates and tuned their random English words to satisfy language and similarity constraints. They reduced the submission to ten distinct essays, repeated roughly 100 times each, to reduce grading variance. Random subset simulations and permutation seed changes helped identify topic-sensitive attacks and select a stable 4/3/3 template allocation. The final submission scored 29.395 privately and 29.303 publicly.

The team trained CLIP L image embedding models with a linear neck and ArcFace loss on external datasets spanning seven image domains. Domain sample counts followed the published domain proportions, with uniform sampling over identities and disjoint identities for training and validation. Training first froze the backbone and then fine-tuned it, using cosine annealing with warmup in both phases. The 336-resolution model achieved 0.8074 CV and 0.614 private leaderboard score; Swin–CLIP fusion and saliency-based cropping did not help.

solution_title: (Best private 0.602) 297th Place Solution for the HuBMAP - Hacking the Human Vasculature Competition. How I lost the gold medal.
solution_summary: The final ensemble combined 13 MaskDINO, YOLOv7-seg, and Cascade Mask R-CNN models using weighted mask fusion and multiple inference resolutions. Validation held out one whole-slide image at a time, and larger images helped detect small masks. EMA and memory-efficient mask handling supported the pipeline. Dilation and threshold choices damaged the selected submissions, which scored 0.334 and 0.394 privately; removing dilation from one submission later achieved 0.602.

solution_title: Unsupervised Geometric Approach (Score: 0.148) - No Training Data
solution_summary: The author proposes a training-free method based on a geometric density invariant. Amino acid sequences are mapped to a geometric resonance score derived from hydrophobicity density. The method reportedly achieves a private Spearman score of 0.148 and outperforms many trained baselines. Implementation details are linked in a GitHub repository but are not described in the post.

The final submission combined a Perch-based branch with EfficientNetV2-S and NFNet sound-event detection branches in class-wise rank space, followed by hierarchical taxonomy smoothing. The Perch branch used frozen embeddings, state-space models, MLP probes, mapped-class distillation, and a pairwise-ranking objective. The SED branches added multi-seed diversity, pseudo-labeling, source-weighted losses, and complementary acoustic representations. The final configuration achieved public and private scores of 0.95586 and 0.95482.
compute: Perch v2 executed on CPU using ONNX

solution_summary: The solution combined EfficientNet B0, B1, B2, and V2S runs using a geometric mean. Inputs stacked all six observations in time and represented raw intensity, frequency-normalized intensity, and ON/OFF target status as three channels. Untied mixup and several signal-aware augmentations were explored, including shifting observations by one position and assigning a negative target. Including OFF observations helped leaderboard performance, and the shift augmentation with SpecAug enabled detection of a new test-data class. Alternative normalization schemes and confident pseudo-labeling provided little benefit.

The submitted approach trained a LightGBM regressor with approximately 500 features and optimized its outputs using Nelder–Mead. Features were filtered using adversarial scores, although later submissions convinced the author that this filtering was unhelpful. The author emphasized validation conditions matching evaluation and using more features until cross-validation performance saturated.

The solution used a pretrained DINOv3 ViT backbone with left-half, right-half, and full-image streams and mixture-of-experts regression heads. Timestamp removal, staged augmentation, auxiliary objectives, and Gaussian negative log-likelihood losses incorporating biomass identities supported training on the small dataset. Final predictions combined five weighted biomass predictors with a separate state predictor, flip-based test-time averaging, and state-specific corrections. The final results section reports public/private scores of 0.76/0.66, despite a conflicting private score in the introduction.
compute: Two GPUs for parallel inference; GPU types unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution combined four-layer MLPs and CatBoost models separately for multiome and CITE, using CV-based weighted averaging. Multiome preprocessing used Okapi BM25 and 64-component LSI, supplemented by binary, word2vec, cluster-average, and connectivity features. CITE used per-cell normalization and logarithmic transformation, with selected important genes handled separately. Validation used the 10% of training examples most similar to public-test data according to a binary classifier, and the best CV submission also achieved the best public score.

The author describes a five-fold RoBERTa-base model that jointly predicted span boundaries and a token-level span mask. Training used the penultimate hidden layer, a bias-free output head, one-cycle scheduling and label smoothing after removing noisy examples. Inference summed fold logits and cleaned extracted text, falling back to the full tweet for empty predictions. This model achieved 0.720 privately but was not the selected submission.
compute: GPU training; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_title: What a ride! Parts of 6th place solution
solution_summary: The author fine-tuned image-level DenseNet and Inceptionv3 models initialized from HPA 2018 solutions and adapted them for cell-level inference. GAPMASK restricted pooling or attention to individual cell masks, while GRIDIFY assembled cell-centered crops at a resolution consistent with training. Validation grouped similar images to reduce plate-related leakage, and negative-class suppression provided a small improvement. These contributions reached a 0.549 public score and improved the combined team blend by about 0.02.

solution_summary: The post exploits label continuity across images sorted by patient ID and image position. It proposes patient-level categorical encodings, aggregation statistics, and temporal features such as lags and differences. The author reports that stacking with these features worked well, while patient-ID overlap observed in stage 1 did not carry over to stage 2.

The author combined template-based RNA modeling with DRfold2, focusing on inference optimization rather than training or fine-tuning. Templates supplied coordinates through sequence alignment, geometric gap reconstruction, and confidence-dependent refinement. DRfold2 improvements targeted more reliable structure ranking and faster differentiable optimization, with Boltz-1 integration in a second notebook submission. Short sequences, exhausted time budgets, and DRfold2 failures used the template pipeline.
compute: No GPUs available for local training; inference and optimization ran on Kaggle GPUs. Method refined over 90 days.

solution_summary: The writeup lists an image-classification pipeline and marks the options that worked. DenseNet and Inception variants were successful, alongside rotation and flip augmentation. The pipeline included five-fold cross-validation, 16-way test-time augmentation, and threshold search. Test-time prediction averaging, majority voting, soft F1 loss, and binary cross-entropy were identified as working methods.

solution_title: 6th place solution (CV: 0.7069 / Public LB: 0.706 / Private LB: 0.713)
solution_summary: The solution used classification to screen images before segmentation, combining models trained on positive images with models trained on all images. Its ensemble combined temporal 2.5D networks using five or seven frames with 2D U-Nets using eleven spectral channels. Both hard labels and soft labels derived from individual annotations were used, alongside exponential moving averages. Long training made the eleven-channel input effective, while validation-optimized percentile thresholds outperformed fixed thresholds.

solution_summary: The approach combines pretrained image-matching models without fine-tuning. Matches are extracted at multiple image scales, mapped back to original coordinates, and pooled before MAGSAC estimates the fundamental matrix. The selected final submission ensembles LoFTR, QuadTree, SuperGlue, and DKM and achieved a private score of 0.852. Alternative ensembles achieved 0.853 with LoFTR, SuperGlue, and DKM and 0.843 when SuperGlue was excluded.

solution_title: [50th Place - Silver] Summary of our journey
solution_summary: The team solved a colored traveling salesman formulation with LKH3, adapting it to support asymmetric distances and a MINMAX objective. Tour augmentation helped improve the non-wildcard score to 2440. They then heuristically selected mandatory permutations and replaced their symbol 1 with wildcards, reducing the final score to 2430. A Gurobi MILP alternative solved smaller instances but exhausted available memory on the full problem.
compute: Personal computers and small Azure machines from student accounts; ran out of RAM for n=7.

solution_title: 12st Place Solution for the  SenNet + HOA - Hacking the Human Vasculature in 3D
solution_summary: The solution trained a nearly classical 2D U-Net from scratch in TensorFlow, using all available training data except the kidney_3_dense labels. Statistical ROI extraction removed empty margins before resizing images and masks to 1024x704 and storing them in TFRecords. Training used weighted binary cross-entropy, Adam, cosine decay with warmup, and checkpoints selected by minimum validation loss over 60 epochs. Increasing image resolution improved the reported score to 0.636, and public and private results differed by 0.012 points; overlapping tiles and an additional decoder extension were unsuccessful.

The author tuned Linear Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost with GridSearchCV and submitted both averaged and stacked ensembles. XGBoost without engineered features delivered the best reported performance, and using more training data helped. Manually engineered features reduced performance, while proposed feature-removal experiments were not completed. Limited laptop resources forced data reduction and caused repeated crashes.
compute: Laptop with unspecified hardware; repeated crashes due to computational demands.

solution_title: 13th place solution: 10 times the work to finish 13th instead of 4th
solution_summary: The author built diverse out-of-fold predictions and used AutoGluon to ensemble 79 OOF sets in the strongest selected submission. A second selected submission combined 11 OOF sets from CatBoost, XGBoost, LightGBM, and an MLP. The larger ensemble achieved CV accuracy of 0.94192 and private accuracy of 0.94151. Diverse CatBoost settings and neural networks helped complement boosted trees, but strong CV/public correspondence did not reliably identify the best private submissions.

The solution averaged three-channel InceptionV3, one-channel InceptionV3, and a custom audio CNN. Offline audio augmentation and crops biased toward louder regions improved robustness, with strength-adaptive cropping adding about 0.01 to cross-validation and 0.004–0.005 to the leaderboard score. Models were warmed up on noisy data and fine-tuned on curated data, with Inception models receiving an additional stage without random resized cropping. Validation used test-time augmentation for stable checkpoint selection, and the final ensemble achieved a private score of 0.75302.

solution_title: My incredibly lucky 6th place solution w code
solution_summary: The author combined an eight-fold e3nn model with a public notebook ensemble, assigning them weights of 0.2 and 0.8 respectively. The e3nn model used atom coordinates and local molecular features around the mutated residue, adapting the ThermoNet data pipeline. Inference averaged predictions from AlphaFold structures and Rosetta-relaxed structures. The standalone e3nn scored 0.362 on private and 0.346 on public evaluation, underperforming ThermoNet.

solution_summary: The author ensembled XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost models using basic feature engineering. No feature definitions, validation design, or ensemble weights were provided. The author emphasized stopping work when a metric hack was declared legal, without claiming to use that hack.

The solution used three stages, beginning with eleven CNN models trained on windowed CT images with patient-based five-fold validation. Adjacent slices and smoothed labels provided context around hemorrhage boundaries. Image predictions were converted into study-level aggregate and moving-average features for LightGBM, MLP, and CNN stacking. A final LightGBM stacking stage used the same feature construction and clipped output probabilities.

The author tuned random forest, XGBoost, and logistic regression models with Optuna using RSKfold validation. Feature importance guided removal of unimportant features, with cross-validation checking whether removal helped. An additional KNN model joined these models in a soft voting ensemble that scored approximately 0.817 in cross-validation. Predictions from both the ensemble and a standalone random forest were submitted because the forest had slightly better validation performance.

The author's contribution used DeBERTa variants with pseudo-labeling and two rounds of knowledge distillation on Feedback Prize 1 data. Rounded pseudo-predictions determined frequency-ratio sample weights to address label-distribution differences, while original Feedback Prize 3 labels were retained to limit confirmation bias. Some initial models used ordinal regression, and later distilled models used simple dense regression heads. The final blend combined four author models with a teammate model using Huber-regression weights, and cross-validation ultimately guided ensemble and submission selection.

The author implemented Oriented SSD for ship detection and shared the code. The model constrains predicted shapes to rectangles. The author described its leaderboard performance as modest but highlighted this geometric property as interesting.

solution_title: 6th place solution, Factorial HMM with a shared factor
solution_summary: The solution modeled ion channels with a factorial hidden Markov model, using four hidden states per channel and shared transition probabilities. Expectation-maximization learned transitions from training labels, then fitted Gaussian emission parameters to test signals and produced posterior MAP predictions. The signal scale was fixed near 1.234 because estimation failed in low-activity sections. Repeated short-time Fourier filtering and prediction cycles removed spectral noise, although the author expressed reservations about this cleaning procedure.

The final solution used a RoBERTa multitask model trained jointly on discourse boundary detection, discourse effectiveness classification, and essay scoring from three Feedback Prize competitions. It achieved public and private scores of 0.457696 and 0.458945, respectively. Experiments showed benefits from a convolutional layer, prior discourse-boundary fine-tuning, and hyperparameter search, while frozen essay embeddings performed substantially worse. Balancing task losses remained difficult: the final balance improved essay scoring while degrading discourse detection.

The solution separates material attributes from interactions between object pairs and uses RetinaNet models for both branches. One model detects 42 object–attribute combinations, while another predicts enclosing rectangles for nine relationship types. Object detections from the Object Detection Track are matched to relationship boxes using overlap and allowed class combinations, with confidence weights tuned through SciPy and a paired-box NMS step. The best submission scored 0.20109 on the leaderboard; an attribute-only detector and a LightGBM validity filter did not improve the final approach.

solution_summary: The author trained AutoGluon models using ECFP molecular fingerprints and preprocessing adapted from a public notebook. The optimize_for_deployment preset was selected to accelerate training. The final ensemble combined a 1024-bit fingerprint model using 1,500,000 × 2 examples and a 2048-bit fingerprint model using 960,000 × 2 examples.

The solution used separate sales, customer, and month-ahead models with different feature subsets, plus an all-features model. Feature engineering combined store attributes, calendar and promotion variables, competition information, holidays, weather, and historical sales and customer statistics. Historical summaries were grouped by store and combinations of day, promotion, and school holiday status. Seasonal models also included distance from the start of summer holidays, while relative weather features contributed little.

solution_title: Silver with Two Specialists: Public Throughput, Private Transfer
solution_summary: The author selected two separate attack families to cover different hidden guardrail policies. V43 maximized public replay throughput with short, model-specific marker requests, while V37 used screened, marker-free status notifications to synthetic recipients. Distinct destinations and recipients increased scoring-cell coverage, and replay cost constrained candidate construction. V43 achieved 92.655 public but zero private, whereas V37 transferred from 15.990 public to 15.975 private.
compute: Notebooks ran with internet disabled.

solution_summary: The author extended a public notebook with borrowed feature engineering and nine additional models. Logistic regression blended or stacked their predictions, with more than a dozen random seeds used across cross-validation and the stacking model. The final submission was manually selected despite weak validation and public leaderboard results, motivated by discussion of noisy data. The reported comparison included ridge, ROC, gradient, and XGBoost classifier level-one entries.

solution_title: Dual-Head Model with 4-stage Training, 2nd Place Solution
solution_summary: The team trained dual-head U-Nets with classification and segmentation outputs, using annotation-derived masks as supervision rather than classifier inputs. Successive mask-generation stages produced pseudo masks for the full training set, followed by classifier training with ResNet200d and EfficientNet-B5/B7 backbones. The best individual configuration used EfficientNet-B7 at 768 resolution, and model ensembles improved results further. Inference used classification heads, horizontal-flip augmentation, and a ChestX image-retrieval shortcut; the reported final Private LB was 0.97641.
compute: Inference notebook finished in about 8 hours and 50 minutes.

solution_summary: The author built matching men's and women's basketball pipelines using regression-derived team ratings followed by two stages of XGBoost predictions. A GLM converted predicted score differences into win probabilities, which drove 100,000 tournament simulations. Team ratings were the most important features. The final submission manually forced UConn to win every possible men's matchup, substantially improving the result over the unaltered probabilities.
compute: Initial execution of the complete modeling framework takes multiple days.

solution_summary: The solution combined 2.5D and 3D segmentation models with a separate model that predicted where annotation truncation began. Training excluded slices with apparently truncated labels so segmentation models could learn complete masks without misleading negative targets. Postprocessing removed masks below the predicted truncation depth and removed the top and bottom two pixels, while low-intensity cropping accelerated prediction.

The solution emphasized reliable triple-stratified cross-validation and used images without metadata. Its best single model was EfficientNet-B5 at 512×512, first trained for eight-class classification on 2019 data and then fine-tuned on 2020 plus 2018/2017 data. This training sequence improved CV by 0.01 and private leaderboard performance by 0.005. The single model achieved 0.944 CV before test-time augmentation, and ensembles reached private scores between 0.9452 and 0.9492, although many constituent models overfit.

solution_summary: The pipeline combined a seven-class 2.5D CNN with XGBoost using tracking data and CNN predictions. The CNN processed nearby frames from both camera views, with helmet-dependent crops and helmet boxes drawn onto the images. XGBoost added temporal tracking and prediction features, image availability, and normalized helmet-distance differences. The CNN achieved a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.59, while the full pipeline scored 0.740 in cross-validation and 0.742 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: 514th Place Solution for the RSNA 2023 Abdominal Trauma Detection Competition
solution_summary: The author selected twenty 256×256 PNG images per CT series and standardized unusual DICOM files. A nearest-neighbors model trained using segmentation information filtered images for target organs, and nearest neighbors also predicted injuries using roughly one-third of the data. Final predictions covered liver, spleen, and kidneys for limited patients, with average values filling unpredicted cases. Private results were better when kidney predictions were omitted, and bowel predictions were unsuccessful.
compute: Nearest-neighbors approach could run without a GPU; actual hardware and runtime were not specified.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled Kinetics-pretrained 3D ResNet152, ResNet200, and ResNeXt101 encoders with U-Net-like decoders. Its strongest augmentation randomly cropped depth layers, pasted them at different depth positions, and zeroed a few layers to improve generalization between fragments. Checkpoint selection favored high validation scores with low false positives, while label smoothing, CutMix, and intensity clipping provided additional gains. Four-fold local validation guided the final selection, and the stronger reported ensemble achieved a private score of 0.674544.

solution_title: 19th Place Solution: 108 OOFs blending with RidgeCV
solution_summary: The solution blended 108 diverse models with weights learned through RidgeCV. Gradient boosting models supplied the strongest individual predictions, while neural networks contributed complementary errors. Diversity came from engineered feature sets, multiple target encodings, hyperparameters, seeds, and data splits. The preferred submission excluded a linear regression component and achieved 0.977242 CV and 0.97744 private leaderboard scores.

solution_title: 6th Place Solution for the CAFA 5 Protein Function Prediction Challenge
solution_summary: InterlabelGO combined feedforward neural networks using ESM embeddings with sequence alignment against UniProt-GOA. The neural component averaged five models per GO aspect and multiplied an information-accretion-weighted soft F1 objective by a ranking loss designed to capture label correlations. Alignment scores used bitscore and sequence identity to weight search hits, and validation determined the linear blending weight. The weighted soft F1 loss substantially improved performance over BCE, and the reported private score was 0.56076.
compute: RTX 4090 and i9 13900K on Ubuntu 23.10; approximately 3 minutes per neural model and around 60 minutes for all 15 models. For 2,000 proteins, neural inference takes under 10 minutes and DIAMOND under 2 minutes.

solution_summary: The selected final submission generated a fixed collection of Confused Deputy candidates requesting short email actions with non-secret content. It alternated GPT and Gemma layouts by call order and did not run evaluator trials during generation. This submission scored 24.37000 publicly and 24.65500 privately. A separate exfiltration selector optimized scoring events per unit time and achieved a much larger public score but zero privately, illustrating the weakness of that selection criterion.

The team started from an open-source implementation, tuned bbox3 parameters, and modified the sa_v8 execution flow. Layout analysis shifted their attention toward global tree arrangements and small-N instances, including 180-degree rotational symmetry for even N. Near the deadline, they incorporated ideas from another public solution and used repeated bbox3 scans and local adjustments for incremental improvements. A Python translation of Sparrow components was explored, while several additional structural strategies were studied only after the competition.

solution_title: 16th Place Solution Writeup for the Open Problems – Single-Cell Perturbations (Los Rodriguez)
solution_summary: The team trained a deterministic neural network using drug and cell median response features together with pseudobulk log-fold changes from selected variable genes. Cell features entered both the encoder and decoder, and leave-one-drug-out validation on NK cells produced 146 models whose predictions were aggregated by median. A second ensemble focused on 256 variable genes and 60 variable drugs, with enhanced predictions blended at 80% weight into the corresponding base predictions. This refinement consistently improved performance, while conditional VAEs and ATAC-seq features offered no benefit.

solution_title: 41st place: post-processing, a fine-tuned detector, and a flipped public LB
solution_summary: The author extended the public x138 cell-tracking pipeline while preserving its transformer and ILP linker. The main improvement came from a CNN3D and ConvNeXt division ensemble that attached only unparented second daughters, alongside a minimum track length of eight. Detector fine-tuning used intensity augmentation and a two-seed weight soup, with rotation restricted to the secondary detector. Local per-video and cross-embryo validation guided final selection despite opposing public leaderboard trends; the selected fine-tuned submission scored 0.936 privately.
models_pretrained: ["DeepCenter / TemporalUNet3D public weights", "convnext_nano.in12k_ft_in1k", "DINOv2-small", "Public primary and secondary 400-epoch detector checkpoints"]

solution_summary: The solution combined image-model predictions with engineered tabular features in LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost. Image models learned five related labels, with some additionally trained on segmentation masks generated by models fitted to ISIC 2018. External skin-lesion datasets, diverse image architectures, and EMA checkpoints supported the image pipeline. The ten-model image ensemble achieved OOF 0.17458, and tabular models using its features reached a geometric-mean pAUC of 0.18703. Final submissions blended metadata-only predictions with image-enhanced predictions at weights of 0.2 and 0.8.

The team estimated GNSS positions using robust least squares and corrected their errors with LightGBM. They then applied outlier rejection, Kalman smoothing, cross-phone trajectory averaging, and stop detection. Tree areas used snap-to-grid, while downtown trajectories used a Dynamic Time Warping variant. The authors attributed weaker private performance partly to emphasizing downtown and tree areas over highways.

solution_title: The Perfect Storm: Meet the Winners of 'Give Me Some Credit'
solution_summary: The team combined classification and regression variants of random forests and tree boosting with a neural network. Only methods that improved cross-validation results were retained in the ensemble. Two particularly predictive engineered features were total late days and the difference between income and expense. Neural networks added useful performance beyond the bagging and boosting methods.

solution_title: Generalizing Agent Attacks to the Unseen Private Guardrail
solution_summary: The documented algorithm targeted marker-free confused-deputy email calls to improve transfer to an unseen stricter guardrail. It generated deterministic notification requests with unique recipients, retaining only live-verified tool firings. One-hop probes reduced search cost, while latency measurements and replay-cost accounting sized the returned candidate list. The documented variant deliberately disabled control-token forging and served as a robustness complement to a public-focused submission; no final private score is reported.
compute: Approximately 9,000 seconds of replay per model/guardrail combination; model-load warmup 75–150 seconds.

solution_summary: The system extended 6D-VNet using a three-stage Hybrid Task Cascade detector, an ImageNet-pretrained HRNet backbone, and separate rotation/classification and translation heads. Additional ApolloScape training images and geometric mask–mesh alignment substantially improved results. Neural Mesh Renderer refinement, confidence filtering, and ignore-mask filtering further improved predictions. The final six-model weighted ensemble achieved 0.140 private and 0.151 public mAP, despite a substantial gap between local validation and leaderboard scores.

solution_title: AI Village Capture the Flag @ DEFCON31 - 22 Points
solution_summary: The author reports solving 22 capture-the-flag questions, including the test, using a range of challenge-specific techniques. Clustering, visualization, and manual pixel inspection helped identify hidden data patterns. Image attacks depended on matching the model's preprocessing and applying PGD, with BPDA and iterative JPEG compression for a defended model. Other challenges were solved through translation, prompt manipulation, score-guided word searches, and exploiting exposed request formats.

The final submission used an Optuna-weighted ensemble of seven XLM-RoBERTa variants trained on all available training data for two epochs. Diversity came from alternative answer-span labels, label filtering, negative undersampling, and training-set pseudo-labeling. Validation grouped contexts by their first 20 characters to keep near duplicates together. The pipeline also used cumax and numeric answer postprocessing, while character-level ensembling and two-stage passage selection were excluded.

The post describes trajectory postprocessing combined with Akio-pp, improving the public score from 3.515 to 3.191. A nearest-neighbor altitude model and surrounding relative-coordinate features supported outlier detection. Outliers were reconstructed through forward and reverse relative-position accumulation at ten thresholds, with the resulting 20 trajectories combined using inverse-threshold weights. Stop prediction was also retained, while several earlier smoothing methods and experimental corrections were excluded or unsuccessful.

solution_title: Congrats to the winners and insights sharing
solution_summary: The post congratulates competitors and thanks the organizers and teammates. It reports submission-based observations suggesting that the final 20,000 test records belonged entirely to the private leaderboard, while other records were split randomly. The author speculates that this split contributed to leaderboard movement but does not describe a competition solution.

The author describes resolving a persistent notebook exception shortly before the submission deadline. The shown change builds inference row names by iterating over conditions and spinal levels. This allowed the notebook to submit successfully and receive a score, but no modeling or training details are provided.

The solution combined two ways of incorporating the original dataset. LightGBM and CatBoost were trained after appending original observations as training rows, achieving CV 0.97523. A TabM model instead used original-data-derived column features with target encoding and reached CV 0.9744. Ensembling these approaches increased CV to 0.97634.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution: Sparse + Dense matching, confidence-based merge, SfM, and then iterative refinement
solution_summary: The team built a coarse-to-fine structure-from-motion pipeline combining sparse and detector-free image matching. Rotation and overlap detection improved matching, while confidence-guided merging reduced multi-view inconsistency before COLMAP reconstruction. Iterative transformer-based feature-track refinement and geometric optimization then improved camera poses and point clouds. The final variant used SuperPoint–SuperGlue with LoFTR, replacing LoFTR with DKM on Haiper, and reported a private score of 0.594.
compute: Evaluation machine with 2 CPU cores and 1 GPU; submission runtime constrained

solution_title: The 2nd Solutions(Single fold and single model)
solution_summary: The final submission used Pnasnet5large with images resized to 545×545. The approach used a single fold and pseudo-labels with confidence of at least 0.95, alongside geometric, image-filtering, and random-erasing augmentation. Training used cross-entropy loss with a cosine learning-rate schedule and warmup over 30 epochs. Pnasnet5large achieved 0.98182 on the private leaderboard and 0.98189 on the public leaderboard; ResneSt101 was also evaluated.

The solution treated proteins shared with the CAFA 5 test set separately from newly added CAFA 6 proteins. It combined three historical submissions for the former and used Diamond predictions for the latter, then added GOA UniProt All and GAF predictions across both subsets. Standard Diamond sensitivity scored 0.39019, outperforming the more sensitive variant. A retrospective ablation showed that removing Diamond entirely would have improved the score to 0.39693, while combining historical submissions was better than relying on only one.

solution_title: A view from the Midfield (14 flags)
solution_summary: The author solved CTF challenges using targeted prompts, manual semantic searches, clustering, and direct inspection of data. For clustering tasks, they used score queries with binary partitioning to identify a demographic rule, and KMeans followed by per-cluster multidimensional scaling to reveal text. Other solutions counted MNIST pixel values and isolated an exact pixel value to expose a hidden image. Several language-model challenges were solved with translation, role-play, or simple requests, while numerous challenges remained unsolved.
external_data: ["Combined MNIST training and test sets", "Internet translation-bot prompt"]

solution_title: Public 7th and Private 15th solution (Nothing but just multiplied a factor of 1.2)
solution_summary: The solution combined two public notebook submissions with a small contribution from the author's own Conv1D, LSTM, MLP, and LightGBM models. Neural models used standardized targets, while inputs included one-hot cell and compound identifiers and character-level TF-IDF representations of SMILES. The public submissions were blended with different weights for the first 128 rows and the remaining rows, then postprocessed using a linked notebook. The final blend assigned 95% weight to the processed public blend and 5% to the author's predictions, and multiplied predictions by 1.2, selected through public leaderboard probing amid substantial disagreement with cross-validation.

The final solution ensembled nine segmentation models with DenseNet201, EfficientNet-B5, ResNet34, and SE-ResNeXt50 encoders using FPN or U-Net decoders. Joint segmentation and classification heads enabled soft gating of segmentation predictions, with grayscale inputs and focal-based losses proving useful. Inference averaged logits with three-flip augmentation, then thresholded masks at 0.55 and removed masks smaller than 256 pixels. Model selection used Dice scores excluding empty masks, while architecture, seed, and fold diversity strengthened the ensemble.
compute: FastGPU.net servers with 8×V100 and 4×V100; final public+private inference approximately 30 minutes. Rejected full-resolution HRNetV2 experiment took 22 hours on 8×V100.

solution_title: 7th Place Solution - A good CV is all you need
solution_summary: The final submission weighted CatBoost, XGBoost, LightGBM, and a neural network trained on tabular data. Tree models combined metadata, engineered group statistics, and out-of-fold CNN predictions. CNNs used an auxiliary lesion identifier head and pretraining on earlier ISIC data. A hospital-aware validation design simulated unseen hospitals and correlated strongly with leaderboard results, guiding final submission selection.

The solution built on a shared select-patch-verify starter and focused on avoiding high-risk bugs. Keyword filtering provided only marginal improvements. The final strategy selected predictions from a particular model weight configuration that processed fewer cases but had a favorable correct-to-wrong ratio among successful attempts. Both submissions using this selection logic earned gold medals.

The author explored adding seven prompt features to an existing essay scoring pipeline. Known prompts received one-hot features, while a trained model supplied prompt predictions for essays with unknown prompts. An ANOVA test supported the association between prompts and scores, and the approach improved 15-fold cross-validation. The author did not select this notebook for submission because of its low leaderboard performance.

The author built a mostly stateless rules-based agent that secured tree clusters, transported resources by cart, and extracted protected wood through chain transfers. Units selected actions through multiple scoring passes with conflict resolution, supported by weighted A* and cached Dijkstra distance approximations. Limited persistence reduced unstable movement, while replay analysis against other players exposed problems that self-play often concealed. Attempts to add reinforcement-learning biases failed, and the author judged the cluster-centered strategy weaker than expansion near coal and uranium.

solution_summary: The final system combined six DeBERTa-v3-large model configurations, training content and wording targets separately across four folds. solution_title: Robust Multispecies Audio Classification for BirdCLEF+2026 Wetland Biodiversity
solution_summary: The solution combined a Perch embedding and temporal-model branch with a distilled spectrogram-based sound-event detector. Spatiotemporal priors, class-specific MLP probes, bidirectional state-space modeling, and residual correction refined predictions across each recording's twelve windows. Rank fusion combined the two branches, and a dominant main model received small contributions from two supplementary models before taxonomy smoothing. It achieved public and private scores of 0.95288 and 0.94295, with the author identifying reliance on public-board tuning as a limitation.

The author implemented a U-Net segmentation pipeline in Keras with an empty-mask classifier and supervised side outputs. Training began with an image-adaptive focal loss and finished with Lovasz loss, while fold predictions were averaged. Robustness measures included excluding vertical and tiny masks from training and applying flips plus vertical dilation at inference. A logistic regression ensemble of four models recalibrated their logits and improved the leaderboard score by 0.005 over the best individual model.

The final solution blended a neural network, TabNet, and LightGBM with weights of 0.4, 0.4, and 0.2. Features came from public notebooks plus original-price features, with zero or mean imputation chosen per feature. Validation grouped by stock ID, using a KNN-based grouping approach for the neural network and standard GroupKFold for TabNet and LightGBM. The neural network combined stock embeddings with numerical inputs, bidirectional LSTM and GRU layers, pooling, and dense layers; the team also retained features it believed were affected by leakage despite weak public leaderboard results.

The author built a LightGBM model from tsfresh features and matching features derived from subject-normalized values. Recursive feature elimination reduced roughly 9,000 generated features before training. The final blend assigned about 0.4 weight to LightGBM, 0.2 to the author's LSTM, and the remaining 0.4 to shared notebook predictions. The individual LightGBM and LSTM models achieved private scores of 0.97816 and 0.98259, respectively.

The final submission blended four paired-input transformer models with a USE and engineered-feature model. Separating question and answer inputs, adding category features to a deeper regression head, and transforming targets improved validation performance. Shared rounding parameters applied before and after weighted blending were especially important, jointly improving cross-validation by about 0.05. Training used two stages, with the transformer frozen during final regression-head tuning.

solution_title: Solution Writeup: Deterministic Solvers, Trace Design, and Runtime Evaluation
solution_summary: The submission used supervised fine-tuning with category-specific deterministic solvers, verified reasoning traces, and rank-32 LoRA. Diagnostic probing found that most examined failures diverged when naming operators and operands. Reordering traces to compute before declaring improved local bit-manipulation accuracy from 33.3% to 53.6%, but reduced the public score. The author also observed substantial accuracy differences between inference environments despite identical weights, and reported a private score of 0.604.

The solution aggregated spatial signals, binned time, and combined normalized frequencies using inverse-variance weights to estimate transit timing and depth. A custom neural model combined polynomial-fit residuals, fitted curves, variances, and initial depths while restricting nonlinear processing to scale-invariant features. Convolutions and an LSTM refined global and frequency-specific depths and uncertainties, with a depth-profile uncertainty estimate contributing a substantial score gain. Direct negative-log-likelihood optimization achieved about 0.64 in two-fold CV and 0.658 on the private leaderboard for a single model.

The author searched feature subsets separately for six tree-based classifiers. These models were combined through a VotingClassifier weighted according to their validation scores, followed by another feature-subset search for the ensemble. The two final submissions were selected solely by CV, scoring 0.8227 and 0.8225 with four and five features respectively. This selection also identified their two highest private scores despite other submissions having stronger public scores.

The author adapted Martin's approach, first training the encoder as a classifier to reduce training time. Embeddings were L2-normalized and scaled by a learned, regularized parameter, with a larger matching head. The final ensemble combined two SEResNet34 models at 512×512 and two SEResNet50 models at 384×384, achieving 0.922 privately versus 0.904 for the best individual model. Heavy augmentation, progressive resizing, BCE loss, SGD warm restarts, and threshold selection were useful, and all models were trained without local validation.

YOLOv5x6 and EfficientDet D3 undergo multiple training rounds on Livecell and the train-semi-supervised dataset before fine-tuning on competition data. It matched all unique image pairs, corrected image orientation, cached intermediate features and matches, and explicitly selected the reconstruction's initial image. Repeated geometric matching retained stable matches, while repeated reconstructions with different match thresholds reduced randomness and selected stronger scenes. The final multi-run step improved public/private scores from 0.497/0.542 to 0.506/0.562.

Ensemble approaches included optimized weighted averaging and LightGBM stacking of retrieval similarities and reranker logits, followed by threshold and fallback top-k tuning. solution_title: 2nd Place Solution: MST-Aided SfM & Transparent Scene Solution [Prize Eligible]
solution_summary: The team used separate pipelines for conventional scenes and transparent or reflective scenes. Conventional scenes combined a point-and-patch global descriptor, three local matching systems, and two-stage MST-guided structure from motion. Transparent scenes instead recovered image capture order from global similarities and arranged cameras around a closed loop, improving scores by about 0.06. PixSfM refinement and relocalization of unregistered images provided additional gains.

The author describes their contribution to a team pipeline combining LightGBM anomaly and speed estimates, Kalman smoothing, and carrier-phase-derived relative movement. Forward and backward Hatch filters were particularly effective, with missing measurements borrowed from other phones. Group-based validation tuned filter parameters and phone averaging weights, followed by downtown grid snapping and stationary-point averaging. The author's parameter ensemble scored about 2.149 in CV, while the combined team pipeline reached CV 2.0569 and LB 2.285.

The solution combined assessment-order indicators, normalized event counts, and activity aggregates with boosted trees and a GRU-attention neural network. Five-fold grouped validation with truncation evaluated models using RMSE, and an ElasticNet second level combined their predictions. Threshold selection used out-of-fold predictions and repeated sampling by installation ID, producing two final thresholding strategies. Test data extended training folds but were excluded from validation and threshold determination; the reported ensemble scores were 0.538 public and 0.556 private.

solution_title: 31st place solution and some points about the competition
solution_summary: The post reports experiments and practical observations without specifying a complete final pipeline. EfficientNet_b0, eva02_small_patch14, and edgenext_base had manageable memory requirements, while larger alternatives exhausted memory and SelecSLS and NextViT overfit. The author recommends ensembles and multiple voters, observing that removing low-importance features did not reliably improve validation. solution_title: [5th place solution] Vanilla Transformer, Data2vec Pretraining, CutMix, and KD
solution_summary: The solution processed dominant-hand, pose, and lip landmarks in 3D using aspect-ratio correction and strong spatial and temporal augmentation. A convolution-stem transformer with rotary position embeddings was pretrained using Data2vec 2.0 and fine-tuned with CTC loss. CTC-derived character alignments enabled temporal CutMix, which improved performance by about 0.02 and made supplemental competition data beneficial. A large teacher was distilled into a 24-layer, 256-dimensional student with separate CTC and distillation heads, while a simple 5% holdout tracked leaderboard improvements better than participant-grouped validation.

The solution used a three-stage pipeline combining GPU sensor calibration, hierarchical physical transit fitting, and cross-validated spectral post-processing. Global transit fits constrained shared orbital parameters before instrumental drift correction and wavelength-specific depth estimation. Final spectra blended PCA-regularized and Savitzky-Golay-smoothed predictions, while an empirical uncertainty model was optimized directly against the competition score. Ten-fold validation grouped by planet supported wavelength-dependent uncertainty calibration and averaging of fold predictions. The pipeline ran in under 1.5 hours on a Kaggle P100 instance and around five minutes on a machine with 100 CPU cores and four L40s GPUs.

RMS-based sampling, high-resolution mel spectrograms, and max aggregation over three five-second segments were important in the first stage. The second stage trained four CNNs on selected audio segments and pseudo-labels, followed by seven epochs of pseudo-label-only fine-tuning. The reported second-stage public and private scores were 0.909 and 0.908.

The solution combined LightGBM, generalized additive models, nearest neighbors, and a teammate's neural network through LightGBM stacking. Nested cross-validation provided a more dependable estimate of submission performance than ordinary validation. MFCC and signal-variance features supported both time-to-failure regression and a binary detector for the interval between acoustic peaks and target resets. Distribution-based sample weights and fixed predictions for selected segments further improved the submissions.

The final solution stacked roughly 100 XGBoost and Keras base models using a one-hidden-layer Keras network bagged 20 times. Diversity came mainly from alternative feature representations, target transformations, and objectives rather than extensive single-model tuning. Five-fold unstratified cross-validation used identical folds at both levels. The neural stacker corrected systematic base-model errors, making further prediction post-processing unnecessary.

solution_title: 6th Place Solution for the HMS - Harmful Brain Activity Classification Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined Kaggle spectrograms, derived EEG spectrograms, global raw EEG images, and local raw EEG images using four separate DINOv2 vision transformer backbones. Patient-grouped validation and two-stage training on low-vote then high-vote examples structured the experiments. Mixup was the most useful augmentation, while global and local EEG representations captured complementary information. A five-model ensemble with temporal test-time augmentation achieved public and private scores of 0.22600 and 0.283302.

solution_summary: The solution combined image-only neural networks with a LightGBM model using their predictions and incidence-angle information. Neural networks shared a five-fold split, and a subset was selected by the cross-validation score of its mean predictions. Incidence-angle group statistics computed across training and test data, plus KNN regression outputs, supplied the final model's features. Final probabilities were clipped, and an unselected submission achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.0854.

The team combined eight transformer dual-encoder retrievers with pointwise and listwise rerankers. Retrieval-oriented pretraining and language- and channel-aware negative sampling supported candidate retrieval, while enriched topic representations and ancestor auxiliary labels strengthened reranker supervision. Retriever similarities and reranker probabilities were blended, then filtered with a constant threshold and adjusted with fallback and hidden-content rules. Threshold tuning used only a small validation subset and was identified as a limitation; a promising QA reranker was not incorporated.

solution_summary: The solution used sparse n-gram features and weighted blends of Multinomial Naive Bayes, SGD, LightGBM, CatBoost, and Random Forest models. Naive Bayes and SGD used a combined external dataset with a minimum document frequency of two, while CatBoost and LightGBM used the original DAIGT V2 dataset. The two selected blends achieved public scores of 0.970 and 0.966 and private scores of 0.907 and 0.908. Post-deadline blends with greater CatBoost weight achieved better private scores, while feature reduction and newly generated GPT-3.5 training data did not help.

solution_title: 33rd Place Solution Using Embedding Imputation (0.9872 private, 0.9876 public)
solution_summary: The solution combined CapsuleNet, two RNN variants, a two-layer CNN, and NB-SVM through prediction averaging and LightGBM stacking. Its main contribution was handling missing embedding vectors using fastText OOV prediction and similarity-based imputation for GloVe and LexVec. A custom neural-network wrapper supported AUC-based early stopping, out-of-fold prediction generation, and random hyperparameter search. Averaging multiple stacking seeds produced scores of 0.9872 private and 0.9876 public after more than 1000 neural networks were trained within one week on two 1080 Ti GPUs.

solution_summary: The pipeline centered on a cleaned signal dataset, synthetic ten-channel augmentation, and consistent grouped validation. Random forest, LightGBM regression, and MLP regression supplied out-of-fold predictions to a tuned WaveNet model. Training and inference used sequence flips, macro-F1 checkpoint selection, and sliding-window prediction. An XGBoost classifier refined WaveNet predictions using signal and residual noise features; it helped the public score, while private performance was similar, with the best reported private submission scoring 0.94568.

Models generated pseudo labels for the semi-supervised training images and were then fine-tuned again with the expanded data. At inference, weighted boxes fusion combined Cascade Mask R-CNN and YOLOv5x detections, and weighted masks fusion combined masks across folds.

solution_title: LB=0.65 Solution (Simple ensemble: Mistral-7B + Phi2-7B + T5-base + mean prompt) for the Kaggle - LLM Prompt Recovery

These were few-shot Mistral inference, a LoRA-tuned Phi2 model followed by PPO, and a fully fine-tuned T5-base model. Training data preparation emphasized unique prompts, deduplicated source texts, balanced sources, and synthetic prompts generated with GPT-4. The combined approach scored 0.65 on both public and private leaderboards, despite persistent disagreement between cross-validation and leaderboard results.

solution_title: 168th Place Solution 18 flags for the AI Village Capture the Flag @ DEFCON31 Competition
solution_summary: The author solved challenges using brute-force search, visual inspection, targeted prompts, and iterative synonym search. Datamuse synonyms enabled automated progress on Semantle, while t-SNE exposed clusters useful for another flag. Other successful approaches included editing suspicious image pixels and submitting a pickle containing a callable reference. Several attempts remained unsuccessful, including black-box adversarial optimization, Optuna-based pixel changes, and OCR-oriented image manipulations.

solution_title: 281 place solution making me Kaggle Expert
solution_summary: The solution combined bbox3 with simulated annealing and boundary refinement. The author ran 14 instances with different random seeds to explore alternative packings. solution_summary: The author submitted two patent-query approaches, reporting scores of 0.98 and 0.91. The stronger approach exploited query syntax that avoided counting explicit AND tokens, pairing target patents and joining shared rare tokens. Candidate clauses were checked against the test index to exclude unintended patent matches. The conventional approach optimized CPC-based Boolean queries with simulated annealing and an approximate expected mAP objective. Large preprocessing workloads used compressed tokenized files and sharded LevelDB indexes.

solution_summary: The author trained EfficientNet-B7 embedding models on all available training data without folds, using SGD, cosine learning-rate annealing, and AMSoftmax. The central idea was to place multiple representations of each image in one embedding space by treating body, fin, full-frame, and Detic-box crops as additional images. Three original models were combined with three models retrained using ensemble-generated pseudo-labels, reaching a reported leaderboard score of 0.862, while the final team ensemble reached 0.884. A fixed 19% threshold handled new individuals.

This post describes the object-detection component of a product-matching solution. A pretrained YOLOv5m model supplied object categories, confidence scores, and bounding boxes, with a low confidence threshold retaining more candidate objects. Bounding-box area and distance from the image center guided selection of the main product, favoring central objects. Cropping that object reduced background distractions, although the post provides no quantitative evaluation of its contribution.

The agent scored each ship's possible actions using local heuristics combined with a global game state. Its central component iteratively predicted enemy movement probabilities, with remembered local situations adjusting predictions during play. Resource potentials, yard distances, geometric escape options, coordinated attack targets, and mining thresholds shaped decisions. Removing an obsolete enemy-avoidance factor improved the reported leaderboard score from about 1100 to 1200, while parameter tuning and the elimination mode remained underdeveloped.

The final system combined a diverse transformer ensemble using ridge stacking and prediction-bin post-processing optimized with Nelder–Mead. The post describes 26 models initially and later a final ensemble of 27 models, dominated by DeBERTa variants. Knowledge distillation, pseudo labeling, paragraph tokens, adversarial weight perturbation, and varying sequence lengths improved individual models. Five-fold validation supported model selection, while masked language modeling and tuned weighted averaging did not improve the final approach.

solution_summary: The solution combined XGBoost, LightGBM, and a tabular neural network using a second neural network as the stacker. Piecewise linear encoding of continuous variables substantially improved the base neural network, while categorical features used embeddings. The stacker learned separate weights for each class probability using all three models' predictions jointly. This architecture improved the score by about 0.004 over simple averaging, while adding the base neural network contributed about 0.001.

solution_title: Brief overview of the 7th place solution
solution_summary: The solution trained LightGBM after repeating the Kaggle-only examples that were absent from Persuade 2.0. It used stratified folds and removed duplicates between training and validation to prevent leakage. Repeating those examples five times brought cross-validation and public scores closer, but the repetition count was overfit to the public leaderboard. A notebook using three repetitions achieved the author's highest private score of 0.838.

The solution ensembles U-Net segmentation models with large convolutional and transformer encoders at resolutions of 512 and 768. Its main improvement comes from two rounds of fold-based pseudo-label generation, followed by training with equal proportions of original samples and soft pseudo-labels. Training combines cross-entropy, Dice and focal losses with EMA and post-training SWA. Validation uses the organizers’ split and the same four-way test-time augmentation used for inference.
compute: 4x A6000, about one week of training; most time spent creating pseudo-labels.

solution_title: 16th place solution - Team : Deimon Devil Bats
solution_summary: The solution stacked video and tracking neural-network predictions into a CatBoost contact detector. Four 2.5D CNN models covered two camera views and joint versus separate contact outputs, while a transformer-LSTM supplied additional tracking predictions. Temporal transformations of these predictions and tracking features improved the second-stage model, raising CV from 0.7030 for tabular features alone to 0.7683. CNN embeddings, homography-based helmet interpolation, and batch player detection approaches did not help.

The solution blended pretrained EfficientNet-B4 and EfficientNet-B5 models using grayscale images resized to 25% of their original size. Filtering overexposed image regions produced a large accuracy improvement. Training first froze the encoders for 10 epochs, then fine-tuned the full models for another 10 epochs at a lower learning rate, with horizontal and vertical flips. Postprocessing used the 95th percentile of class probabilities to estimate class presence and conditional Dice, choosing between empty and nonempty predictions by expected Dice score.

The solution averaged six U-Net models using 2.5D encoders that processed groups of three slices and pooled features along the depth axis. Models used several CNN backbones, with ConvNeXt-small reported as best. Training used five folds, mixed precision, BCE plus Dice loss, and masked invalid regions. Inference used overlapping windows, a 0.5 threshold, and exclusion of empty image regions; 3D encoders, SegFormer, mixup, and additional slices did not help.

The author's contribution used candidate retrieval followed by a LightGBM LambdaRank model. Candidates combined popularity, purchase history, color alternatives, co-purchases, user attributes, and word2vec similarity, achieving 31% recall. The ranker used 118 features and three weekly training windows weighted 7:2:1, with the following week held out for validation. It scored 0.03353 locally and 0.03045 privately; a relational GNN attempt produced poor results and was abandoned.

solution_title: [18th place] Our approach - Pure greedy Lightgbm
solution_summary: The agent used a single LightGBM model to estimate a threshold for each bandit and select actions greedily. Training data came from more than 25,000 scraped matches, represented from the perspective of top agents or qualifying match winners. The model trained on more than 250 million rows with 15 features, weighting examples by agent score. Updating every bandit's prediction each round improved local performance, while alternative exploration strategies, ensembles, LSTM, and XGBoost did not improve the approach.

The solution fine-tuned IndicWav2Vec and a larger XLS-R backbone after filtering noisy audio and annotation pairs. Filtering restored agreement between local WER and leaderboard performance. The ensemble concatenated frozen ASR embeddings and trained a transformer encoder with a CTC head. A pruned KenLM language model and punctuation restoration further improved recognition, while separating logit generation from decoding controlled memory usage.

solution_title: 3rd place solution: How far can deep learning go?
solution_summary: The solution combined diverse spectrogram classifiers and matched-filter-like models trained on synthetic gravitational-wave signals and noise. Online noise generation matched test-sample statistics and injected frequency-matched signals, reducing background overfitting. Hierarchical ridge stacking and a repeated-split linear ensemble were combined by rank averaging. Matching overlapping real-noise bins across test samples enabled subtraction-based denoising of approximately 1,100 samples, improving private AUC from 0.801 to 0.826.

solution_title: 7th place solution: T5 decoding, iterative mean refinement, LLMs and a gold medal mean string
solution_summary: The solution combined an offline optimized constant prompt with predictions from two untuned 7B language models, Mistral and OpenChat 3.5. It estimated the target mean in T5 embedding space from leaderboard feedback and optimized strings through greedy random token edits. At inference, agreement between the two model predictions determined their weights relative to the mean prompt, after averaging prefix variants to reduce wording sensitivity. The resulting embedding was decoded through further token-edit search; the optimized constant prompt alone scored approximately 0.693.
compute: GPU evaluation; about 3 hours for two-model predictions and 5–6 hours for final string optimization, using 200 epochs and batch size 16.

solution_summary: The solution combined XGBoost, Keras neural networks, SVR, and factorization machines trained on the same ten folds. Multiple target transformations, pairwise feature interactions, and neural network bagging supplied diverse predictions. Nelder–Mead optimization selected weights to minimize MAE, both globally and within prediction ranges. Blending these two weighting schemes achieved a final cross-validation MAE of 1115.80, with some private leaderboard overfitting.

solution_title: When Specialized Guardrails Disagree with the Benchmark
solution_summary: The author evaluated 66 attack candidates by comparing packaged and family-specific guardrails through live execution and repeated local validation. Analysis separated authorization correctness, guardrail decisions, successful tool effects, and benchmark predicates using ordered turn logs. The final comparison found 12 genuine catches, three security regressions, five false positives, five reference denials, and two fixture artifacts. These final experiments were conducted after submission and scoring, and did not establish cross-model generalization or successful real-secret exfiltration.

solution_title: NeverGiveUp: Majority-First Tool-Augmented Reasoning for AIMO3
solution_summary: The solver used gpt-oss-120b without fine-tuning, with eight parallel reasoning attempts and stateful Python tools. Majority voting selected answers, with mean token entropy breaking ties. Deterministic seeds, streaming answer extraction, agreement-based early stopping, and per-problem time budgets made inference more reliable under runtime limits. Both public and private scores were 42/50.

solution_summary: The team combined models developed independently by its constituent teams and members. Ensembling these contributions formed the stated prediction approach. The team built recommendation pipelines that generated candidates from session history and co-visitation relationships, then ranked them with LightGBM and CatBoost. Important features included recent interactions, co-visitation probabilities, Word2Vec distances, BPR scores, and normalized next-action bigrams. Session-grouped validation, negative downsampling, and predictions from other action models supported training. The final ensemble stacked prediction scores and ranks with LightGBM and CatBoost, averaged their outputs, and supplemented recommendations with popular items. Neural alternatives did not improve the final blend, while the LightGBM stack reached a reported score of 0.604.

solution_summary: The final agent used a single 4.3M-parameter network combining a residual 1D CNN and ModernBERT for both two-player and four-player games. It encoded ten body-level features across a simulated future horizon and restricted decisions to doing nothing or launching all ships toward a nearby reachable target. Training used PPO self-play from scratch for 10 billion steps, which outperformed initialization from imitation learning. Rotation and opponent-permutation augmentation, action masks, and inference-time prediction averaging supported the final submissions.

Both models were trained from scratch with reduced epoch counts, and all Percent-related features were removed. Fixing the EfficientNet quantile at 0.5 replaced an expensive selection procedure and reduced total inference time to three minutes. solution_summary: The solution combined study-level classification with image-level detection. EfficientNet V2 and Swin classifiers predicted five classes including 'none', using sigmoid binary cross-entropy, auxiliary segmentation, and pseudo labels. Patient-grouped validation and a change in augmentation were important to classification performance. YOLO and MMDetection detectors were combined with weighted boxes fusion, and detection confidence was adjusted using the predicted 'none' probability. The best detector achieved a private score of 0.096, increasing to 0.101 with the detection ensemble.

solution_summary: The solution combined DeBERTa-v3-large with LightGBM and trained target-specific models. It reinitialized the last two layers and replaced paragraph separators with a dedicated token. Optuna supported tuning, while Nelder–Mead optimized ensemble weights. Rule-based adjustments to content and wording predictions had only a very small reported private-score effect, and alternative backbones, pooling changes, and layer freezing did not help.

The solution trained EfficientNet sound-event detectors on high-resolution log mel-spectrograms. Nearly square spectrograms and temporal moving-average smoothing were major improvements, with smoothing suppressing short false-positive events. A teacher-student stage progressively incorporated model predictions to recover missing labels, particularly for strong-label training. Averaging first-stage and second-stage models achieved a public score of 0.924.

solution_summary: The post shares links to a competition code repository, notes, and an internal leaderboard wiki. It mentions a Makefile-based competition framework and links to its introduction and repositories from earlier competitions. The provided text does not describe the competition's modeling pipeline.

The author trained several ResNet-family models with 160-pixel inputs, finding ResNeXt-101 strongest. Training progressed from the fully connected layers to the full network, using Adam initially and SGD with manual learning-rate reductions afterward. Randomly sampling one image per item with hard negatives worked best, and predictions used ten-way test-time augmentation. solution_summary: The solution converted three detector signals into CQT or CWT images, stacked them along the frequency axis, and classified them with EfficientNet V2 models. Signal-to-noise analysis guided frequency selection and border cropping, while division by average negative-sample images and log scaling improved the inputs. Mixed precision, Adam, OneCycleLR, repeated training cycles, and random time shifts supported training. Second-level models combined out-of-fold predictions, improving public performance from 0.8826 for the best single model to 0.8832. Pseudo-labeling provided a small gain, while ResNet34, briefly tested 1D models, and synthetic positive samples did not deliver the desired improvements.

solution_title: Approximation solution for LAP, 30th place solution
solution_summary: The team adapted Martin's solution by replacing exact linear assignment with a randomized greedy approximation. Searching rows in random order and removing matched rows and columns reduced assignment complexity to O(n²), making that step take only seconds. Bootstrapping produced a single-model public score of 0.915, and ensembling raised it to 0.944. The authors observed that voting ensembles overfit public results more readily than ensembles based on output scores.

solution_summary: The post announces that the author's competition solution is available. It provides links to an arXiv report and a GitHub code repository. It invites comments but contains no technical description of the approach.

The author combined seven models: logistic regression, a neural network, XGBoost, LightGBM, and three CatBoost variants. Extensive categorical encoding, including discretized numerical and SVD-derived features, was the main contributor to performance. Original data preceded competition data for order-sensitive CatBoost encoding, and preprocessing stayed inside model pipelines to limit cross-validation leakage. Ridge Classifier determined ensemble weights, while final training used 30 folds and leakage-related postprocessing.

solution_title: How to gain +1839 places during shakeup - complete code!
solution_summary: The author submitted a modified version of Andrew Lukyanenko's regression notebook. The main change replaced some full-history grouped feature means with expanding means within each installation, aiming to reduce leakage. The author also removed hard-coded QWK thresholds.
