solution_title: 9th place solution with code: single model
solution_summary: The team moved from SE-ResNeXt50 to SENet154 and incorporated hypercolumns and deep supervision. The final approach used one model architecture across ten folds with reflective padding and resizing, reporting scores of 0.890/0.875. AdamW with a Noam scheduler, cutout and stochastic weight averaging worked well. A symmetric Lovasz loss produced a particularly strong improvement, while SGD, mixup, additional ensembling and decoder variations did not help.

The solution combined a WaveNet branch with a branch containing two bidirectional GRUs, followed by concatenation and a fully connected layer. Stride-one max pooling before the wave block increased the receptive field and improved validation and leaderboard scores. Training used categorical cross-entropy, focal loss, and Tversky loss together. Predictions were averaged across seven group batch sizes.

solution_title: 162nd Place (Silver): Three AI-Agent Lineages, a Frozen-Score Mystery, and Trust
solution_summary: The final pipeline combined a fold-pure geometric dip backbone with GR-to-typewell matching corrections, CNN Readers, and an anchored Ridge residual. Prefix calibration and a larger cosine Reader improved pooled grouped cross-validation to 7.3812 across 773 wells. Model selection relied on nested or leave-fold-out evaluation and pooled statistical gates rather than public scores. The deployed solution scored 7.328 publicly and 8.009 privately, and the authors documented hidden-test correction failures through byte-level submission comparisons.

The solution ensembled YOLOv8l-seg and YOLOv8m-seg models trained at image sizes 640 and 1024, combining predictions through weighted mask fusion. WSI-based validation, balanced sampling, and pseudo-labeling were central to training. Unlabeled-data pseudo-labeling improved local mask mAP50 by about 0.04, and retraining on hidden-test pseudo-labels during submission added about 0.005 to public and private scores. All submissions applied a small dilation, and the best reported private score was 0.544.

The team trained EfficientDet-D5 on 1024×1024 images with manually cleaned bounding boxes and stratified five-fold splitting. Mixed precision enabled a batch size of two at that resolution. Two rounds of pseudo-labeling incorporated test images, with weighted boxes fusion configured differently for pseudo-label generation and final prediction. The final submission scored 0.7666 publicly and 0.6916 privately.

The final system blended 2.5D U-Net++ predictions with 3D MONAI U-Net predictions at weights of 0.7 and 0.3. The 2.5D branch used ImageNet-initialized RegNet, neighboring slices, random crops, mixed precision, and MixUp. The 3D branch used volumetric crops and overlapping sliding-window inference. Anatomical slice filtering, missing-slice filling, and cluster filtering improved the leaderboard score by about 0.004, with a similar additional gain from combining the branches.
compute: RTX 5000; around 12 hours per fold for the 2.5D pipeline

solution_summary: The solution ensembled FPN, U-Net, and custom attention U-Net models with several encoder sizes. Progressive training increased image size from 256×256 to full resolution, initially freezing the encoder except for batch normalization layers. Augmentation used flips and brightness, gamma, and contrast changes. Triple thresholding and flip test-time augmentation completed the pipeline.

The approach optimized pre-partitioned permutation groups with the LKH traveling-salesman solver using string-overlap costs. Wildcard patterns replaced the permutations they represented, and a modified distance function allowed LKH to optimize their placement. Experiments favored wildcards replacing the first character of mandatory permutations, with individual wildcards saving five points. Combining compatible wildcard pairs produced strings of length 2430, while longer wildcard patterns did not achieve the hoped-for 2428 result.
compute: Approximately 3–4 minutes per LKH group optimization; longer verification runs took hours. Hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution estimated transit depths with ordinary least squares after polynomial detrending and precise phase boundary detection. Quantile regression identified residual outliers, while a second model denoised wavelength signals using SNR-weighted SVD and smoothing. Predictions were averaged across shifted bins and refined with covariance-aware reconstruction, bias correction, and conditional blending. Prediction uncertainties were expanded using disagreements between models and nearby wavelengths.

The post states that the author used only a kernel during the competition. It links to that kernel and invites interested readers to ask questions. No approach or pipeline is described in the post itself.
compute: Used only a Kaggle kernel.

solution_summary: The approach used bidirectional breadth-first search or simple beam search for wreaths and small cubes. Large cubes and globes were handled by first fixing special structures and then applying beam search over parity-preserving moves. Carefully enumerated commutators, including three-cycle moves and compositions, expanded the move pool while limiting disruption of solved pieces. Public group-theory optimization and hill-climbing notebooks further shortened solutions, and stronger public solutions were adopted where applicable.

The solution combined three XGBoost recommendation models with end-to-end neural models and LightGBM stacking. The tree models separately handled repeat purchases, popular recent items, and alternate colors of previously purchased products. Neural models learned article similarities using metadata, compressed image features, and graph embeddings, then classified candidates using similar transaction items. Optuna optimized the final blend directly for MAP@12, producing CV 0.04047 and private score 0.03394.

The selected submissions used TabM over residuals with prediction averaging across random seeds. One variant trained on the full dataset plus pseudo data and averaged 20 seeds. Multiple fold configurations produced similar private scores around 0.05564. An unselected ensemble combining TabM and a neural-network stack achieved a slightly better private score of 0.05563, despite the individual models having nearly identical CV scores.

The final system stacked LightGBM models using temporal, accuracy-history, and quiz-history features. A first model trained on half the data supplied predictions and previous prediction errors to second-level models trained on the other half. Averaging second-level models with 256 and 500 leaves achieved 0.799 public and 0.8000 private leaderboard scores. Memory constraints shaped the retained quiz-history features and prevented adding another ensemble model.
compute: Notebook used almost all 16GB of memory; limited GPU resources.

solution_title: Airbnb Kaggle Competition: New User Bookings
solution_summary: The repository contains the author's Python 2.7 competition code for predicting a new Airbnb user's first booking country. It requires user records and web session data from the competition. The reported prediction score is around 0.88670. The main ideas section is unfinished, so the text does not establish the modeling pipeline or which listed packages contributed to the final predictions.

The solution combined two DynUNets, a larger UNet, and MSNet in a weighted ensemble for volumetric segmentation. All models trained on the full dataset using BCE plus Dice loss, with more than 1,000 initial epochs followed by more than 100 tuning epochs. Strong intensity augmentations compensated for ineffective DynUNet dropout, and hole filling refined predictions. The ensemble achieved 0.882 publicly and 0.876 privately.

The team corrected acoustic signal drift, selected distributionally stable features, and restricted training to earthquake cycles whose feature distributions resembled test data. They used shuffled three-fold validation and blended LightGBM, SVR, and a multitask neural network. Auxiliary neural-network targets captured imminent failure and time since failure, improving predictions near earthquake endings. The ensemble achieved approximately 1.83 cross-validation MAE, although a LightGBM and neural-network blend would have achieved a better private score of 2.25909.

solution_title: Road to Deterministic & Efficient Inference and Contamination Free Evaluation
solution_summary: The system used GPT-OSS 120B for tool-integrated mathematical reasoning under a strict inference budget. Static per-question budgets and a self-healing Python execution environment reduced score fluctuations and execution failures. Speculative decoding and FP8 KV-cache quantization reportedly doubled token throughput, enabling more reasoning attempts. The authors also built a 68-problem evaluation set using publication-date restrictions, integer-answer reformulation, and empirical difficulty filtering.
compute: Single NVIDIA H100, 80GB VRAM; strict 5-hour execution window.

solution_summary: The solution combined Py-boost, ExtraTrees, and ridge and nearest-neighbor recommender models for cross-cell-type expression prediction. It transformed log10pvalues to t-scores before modeling and converted predictions back afterward. Noisy target encoding and synthetic compound mixtures supported generalization, while custom validation restricted the compounds available for each held-out cell type. Py-boost performed worst in cross-validation but best on the leaderboards, scoring 0.572 public and 0.748 private. The analysis identified substantial cell-count and Limma artifacts, motivating the decision against external biological data.

The team normalized categorical values, imputed missing data, and engineered clustering, date, and group-count features using combined train and test data. LightGBM models used shallow trees and short early stopping settings to limit overfitting. They ensembled models from random cross-validation with several split counts and ultimately removed version columns. The selected submission achieved approximately 0.662 private AUC, while an unselected submission achieved approximately 0.664.
external_data: ["Dates shared by Chris Deotte in Discussions"]

solution_summary: The final solution blended a deletion-specific baseline, a simple local hydrogen-bond-donor descriptor, ranked Rosetta energy terms, and RASP predictions. Architecture experiments revealed that averaging a local molecular descriptor captured much of the useful signal from a more complex 3D network. Rosetta scores across the molecule and hydrogen-bond-donor values near mutations were the central predictive signals. The submitted blend scored 0.532 privately, while an unselected equal-weight Rosetta–AVGP3 blend scored 0.540.

solution_title: Private LB 0.083 | GNN Embeddings + Stacking Ensemble
solution_summary: The solution trained a GINEConv graph network and combined its embeddings and predictions with molecular descriptors, compressed fingerprints, and graph features. Target-specific gradient boosting models were stacked using a random forest meta-model. GNN embeddings dominated the reported feature importances, and the selected graph architecture scored 0.069 on the public leaderboard. Multiple global nodes, descriptor injection into the GNN, and contrastive subgraph pretraining did not help.

The solution retained baseline image-pair selection and combined ALIKED keypoint detection with LightGlue matching. It classified datasets as transparent or non-transparent using normalized image correlation, then selected different image sizes and matching thresholds for each category. Images were split into four regions, and matching tested four rotations before choosing the orientation with the most matches. These division, resizing, rotation, and threshold choices were tuned against both cross-validation and leaderboard performance.

The solution combined LightGBM and a neural network in an ensemble. Feature engineering included text character and word counts, predictions from ridge models, regional attributes, and geographic coordinates. The neural network dependencies included trained word2vec, DenseNet161, and features from AVA. The writeup is an incomplete repository outline and does not report validation details or quantitative model results.

The model combined transformers, CNNs, and recurrent layers, with a bidirectional LSTM before and after the transformer stack. It incorporated positional encoding and attention based on base-pair probabilities. More than 30 model variants and some public models were combined using ridge stacking with backward elimination. The author attributed the leaderboard drop to poor generalization to longer sequences, where predictions for positions 68–91 differed from earlier positions.

The solution fine-tuned one ByT5-base model in three stages, progressing from 81K mixed-quality sentence pairs to human-labelled data and finally competition-only LoRA adaptation. NotebookLM supported extraction from scanned publications, transliteration matching, and pseudo-labelling, while formula-based synthetic examples added diversity. The first two stages improved local BLEU by 2–3 points over human-only training, and the final adaptation reached an approximately 39 submission score. Dataset refinement and selected publication-derived examples were central to overcoming a prolonged plateau.

The solution trained sound event detection models with EfficientNetV2 backbones on ten-second clips, expanding training to 316 categories using previous competitions. Cross-entropy substantially improved results over binary cross-entropy, and entropy filtering selected pseudo-labels whose training loss was downweighted. Five B3 models and one S model were ensembled, followed by temporal smoothing and mean blending. The reported public and private scores were 0.920 and 0.919, while the intended local validation strategy was ineffective.

The final solution blended rule-specific embedding classifiers, DeBERTa NLI models, retrieval components, and several language models trained or adapted at test time. Preprocessing removed subreddit information and exact duplicates, while embedding classifiers down-weighted near-duplicate examples. The language models used moderation prompts with constrained Yes/No outputs, and Qwen-32B selected examples asymmetrically by similarity. Per-rule rank normalization and incremental weighted blending combined the diverse components, with public leaderboard feedback guiding overall evaluation.

solution_summary: The solution used a weighted ensemble of six CNNs, including two DenseNet201 models and four other architectures. Images were resized to 224×224, with random stain normalization applied to one DenseNet and excessively white images removed for stain normalization. Training combined a short SGD one-cycle schedule, image augmentation, and test-set pseudo-labeling for every model. Four-way test-time augmentation supported inference, and all work used Keras on Kaggle Kernels without external data.
compute: Kaggle Kernels; one-cycle training over 6–7 epochs

solution_title: 43rd Place Solution for the Predict Calorie Expenditure Competition
solution_summary: The final solution combined five forest models, including four boosted models and one random forest, with two neural networks using weighted voting. Forest parameters were tuned by grid search, while Optuna optimized voting weights separately by sex. Validation used four folds and scored pooled out-of-fold predictions, with a reported best CV score around 0.5918. Neural network predictions were clipped to the target range, and increasing tree counts by one third produced almost the same private score as the original counts.

solution_title: 10th Place Solution | A 90% coverage keyword list is ALL you need
solution_summary: The agents used alphanumerical bisection over large keyword lists, prioritizing likely guesses through keyword tiers. Iteratively generated keywords were combined with Wikipedia unigrams and bigrams, producing a two-million-entry list covering roughly 90% of the private keywords. Carefully structured prompts supported a Phi-3-medium answerer, while regex matching and function calling handled common question patterns. The final stronger agent skipped the alpha handshake, and local comparison-question accuracy was approximately 80–90%.
compute: Answerer ran on a single GPU in the Kaggle environment; GPU model unspecified.
external_data: ["Wikipedia dump", "Public keywords from keywords.py and scraped public keywords", "llm20-evaluation-games-collected private-keyword evaluation dataset"]

solution_summary: The approach combined roughly 1,000 engineered features with XGBoost and bagging, including assembly structure, instruction counts, file sizes, system calls, functions, and selected n-grams. TF-IDF followed by nonnegative matrix factorization worked well for system-call and function features. A semi-supervised procedure sampled test labels from predicted probabilities and averaged several runs, improving single-model private leaderboard loss from about 0.0055 to 0.0045. Adding 14 selected 10-gram features targeting poorly predicted training examples reduced that loss further to about 0.0041.

The pipeline separated keypoint extraction and matching, followed by structure from motion and pose recovery. It used KeyNetAffNetHardNet with more keypoints, multiple image resolutions, and geometric filtering that combined fundamental-matrix and homography results. Reconstruction tried different minimum matching requirements and selected the result covering the most images, with early termination when sufficient coverage was reached. Images left unregistered by COLMAP were estimated with solvePnPRansac.

solution_title: How I did it: Ming-Hen Tsai on finishing third in the R competition
solution_summary: The final approach used L2 logistic regression with categorical expansion, scaling, and explicit second-degree polynomial features. Cross-validation guided penalty tuning, while averages of package attributes supplied valuable user-level features. Labels were directly assigned to test instances that also appeared in training. Random subspaces failed, AdaBoost offered only slight gains, and preferential attachment improved cross-validation without improving the submission.

solution_title: 12th place solution NN part with code
solution_summary: The writeup describes the neural-network component of a broader solution, using SAINT-based and AKT-based knowledge-tracing models without lectures. Both models used TUPE-style positional embeddings and lag-time-scaled attention, with simultaneous interactions handled specially. Sliding windows created training sequences, while the AKT variant added decoder self-attention layers and masked simultaneous samples. Lag-time attention scaling reportedly improved the score by about 0.01.
The post congratulates Sander and collaborators. It links to an external blog post about plankton classification. The provided text contains no solution details.

The code fits separate Gaussian mixture models for each of the 512 values of wheezy-copper-turtle-magic. Each group uses variance-based feature selection and standardization, followed by six-component mixtures initialized from three clusters per target class. Several initialization variants use Graphical Lasso precision estimates, and the mixtures are fitted jointly on training and test features. The submission averages eight prediction variants; the reported AUC calculation uses training predictions rather than the commented-out cross-validation loop, and no numeric score is provided.

solution_title: 126th Place Solution - EfficientNet-B0 SED + Perch Distillation
solution_summary: The author trained EfficientNet-B0 sound-event detectors with Perch-v2 embedding distillation and inserted the resulting ONNX models into a public ProtoSSM and MLP-probe inference pipeline. The backbone learned only from distillation, while a detached SED branch learned classification with attention and generalized mean frequency pooling. Multiple pseudo-labeling rounds transferred complementary ConvNeXt predictions back into B0, and the best B0 checkpoint for each fold formed the final SED ensemble. The final pipeline scored 0.949; ConvNeXt inference exceeded CPU time limits, and further SED changes did not improve the overall score.
compute: Colab NVMe waveform cache; CUDA distillation; hybrid four-fold CPU inference took 87 minutes, while five-fold hybrid inference timed out at roughly five hours.

solution_summary: The solution generated precise Boolean query candidates from corpus-wide term counts and words shared by pairs of target patents. An integer linear programming solver selected up to 25 candidates to combine with OR, maximizing target coverage while penalizing false positives within the token budget. A query-construction trick reduced AND clauses and phrases to one counted token without changing their parsed meaning. The published validation index guided development, and the solver improved the score by about 0.01 over a greedy approach; without the token trick, the approach achieved a leaderboard score of 0.85.

The agent estimated hidden machine thresholds using supervised learning on game histories whose true thresholds were available through the Kaggle API. LightGBM quantile regression performed best, with the percentile controlling exploration versus exploitation and the best reported score reaching 1449.4. Its 32 features described game progress, both players' choices, reward histories, and posterior threshold statistics; the round number and opponent behavior were especially important. Log-space posterior calculations and an LRU cache improved numerical stability and runtime, while an omitted rounding step was identified as a remaining modeling error.
external_data: ["Game histories downloaded through the Kaggle API"]

solution_summary: The approach used a one-dimensional convolutional neural network with raw accelerometer and gyroscope measurements, orientation-derived differences, and FFT features. Orientation measurements were converted to Euler angles before taking first differences to capture surface vibrations. Three-fold GroupKFold produced validation scores around 0.65–0.70, while separable convolutions performed slightly better than standard convolutions. The standalone model was reported to score about 0.87 on the private leaderboard, and chaining test samples increased the leaderboard score to 0.99.

The author extended a public word-frequency approach with frozen roberta-large-openai-detector predictions and pseudo-labeling. Predictions from the first and last 512 tokens became features for independently trained LightGBM and XGBoost models, which were ensembled with the public notebook's predictions. Confident pseudo-labels were selected separately by prompt to reduce topic bias, using different selection proportions for generated and human text. The reported ensemble achieved 0.965 publicly and 0.930 privately; detector fine-tuning was abandoned because of overfitting.

The team developed Transformer, LSTM, CNN-LSTM, and LSTM-GRU models, then combined 200 prediction sets using a median ensemble with optimized weights for a 72-model subset. Auxiliary pressure difference and cumulative-pressure targets and cosine schedules improved individual models. The final submission came from CNN-LSTM models trained on all training data plus ensemble-generated test pseudo labels, achieving LB 0.110. This final stage used CutMix and a causal CNN that generated time-step features before the LSTM.

solution_title: 18th Place Solution - Homemade Vectorizer + ImageReward + NLTK
solution_summary: The pipeline generated several raster images with quantized Flux.1 Schnell, converted them to SVG, and selected candidates using ImageReward and aesthetic scores. Custom vectorization combined color clustering, segmentation, contour extraction, and polygon simplification, with four parameter settings satisfying the SVG size limit. NLTK supported noun-based sub-prompt scoring and definition-expanded generation prompts. ImageReward was a better proxy for the competition score than CLIP or SigLIP in the author's tests.
compute: Kaggle-provided GPU resources; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned two CLIP architectures with sub-center ArcFace and adaptive margins using landmark and product images. Nine runs with different augmentations were merged into two architecture-specific model soups. Their two 512-dimensional descriptors were concatenated and reduced from 1024 to 64 dimensions with PCA. ObjectNet was used only for offline validation.

The pipeline routed scatter plots through Donut axis-label extraction and two EfficientDet detectors for data points and chart boundaries. Pixel positions were converted into numerical values using the detected chart limits, while Matcha handled the remaining chart types. Matcha benefited from generated training images, ten training epochs, 1024 patches, and using all extracted images for final training. The resulting pipeline reached a public score of 0.74.
compute: Google Colab Pro+ A100 GPUs with 40 GB VRAM; more than 30 models trained.

solution_title: Competitive Olympiad Reasoning Under Kaggle Constraints
solution_summary: The final system used GPT-OSS-120B without fine-tuning, generating eight parallel reasoning trajectories with persistent Python tool access. Majority voting over boxed integer answers was combined with restrained reflection, deadline-aware stopping, and runtime cache reuse. The submission scored 39/50 publicly and 40.5/50 privately. Exploratory fine-tuning was not adopted, and repeated confident failures on IMO 2025 Problem 6 demonstrated that tool use and consensus could not reliably repair flawed problem understanding.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution To the 2017 National Data Science Bowl
solution_summary: The post documents the author's contribution to a team solution and links to a separate technical report. Neural networks were trained exclusively on LUNA16, using enhanced annotations containing LIDC radiologist labels. A separate non-neural diagnosis model was trained using competition stage 1 data. The repository provides training and scoring code, with reproduction caveats involving missing model uploads, absolute paths, local Keras modifications, and OpenCV compatibility.

The pipeline localized spinal levels, cropped sagittal and axial MRI volumes, and classified conditions with multi-view 2.5D models. SpineNetV2 sagittal crops were corrected with keypoint predictions, while a manually annotated YOLOv10 detector supported axial cropping and anatomical cross-plane alignment. Multiple backbones were combined through symptom-specific weighted probability averaging, achieving a best CV score of 0.3758. The team found that 3D models, pseudo-labeling, external-data pretraining, and external-data segmentation did not work.

solution_summary: A small neural policy combined convolutional board processing with a separate pathway for scalar game state. Behavioral cloning from daily competition datasets initialized the policy before PPO self-play training in a fast JAX simulator. Simple outcome-based rewards with light energy shaping and extensive checkpoint evaluation were central to training. The resulting agent excelled at survival and energy accumulation, but a homogeneous opponent pool left weaknesses in direct combat.

The solution centered on eca_nfnet_l0 models with a compact bottleneck and a contrastive adversarial domain objective added to binary cross-entropy. Model settings were selected using the public leaderboard, with mixup and CutMix as the principal augmentations. Averaging predictions across neighboring time windows added a small improvement. The selected ensemble also included EfficientNetV2 and ReXNet, although an unselected ensemble of two NFNet models achieved a private score of 0.68.

solution_title: My first time-series competition: From potentially #15 to eventually #232
solution_summary: The author selected a modified public forecasting model that replaced a fixed 1.06 multiplier with the ratio of current-year to previous-year GDP, alongside a strong public-score blend. The GDP change slightly improved the public score but worsened the private score from 0.04840 to 0.06370, while the blend also deteriorated privately. A late GAM experiment with the 1.06 multiplier was not selected, despite subsequently showing closely aligned public, private, and internal-validation scores. The main lesson was the risk of selecting on a public period that differed from the private forecast years.

The solution averaged the top six predicted probabilities from XGBoost and KNN models, improving public leaderboard performance from 0.592 and 0.585 individually to 0.603 together. Both models used spatial grids, while XGBoost used basic time features and gave more weight to recent observations. The KNN approach averaged models with shifted hour features to address time cyclicity. Estimated test-versus-train place frequencies were also used to reweight predictions, yielding about a 0.004 public leaderboard improvement.
compute: XGBoost model: 4 days on a dual-core MacBook Pro.

solution_title: San Francisco. August 8. Meetup. Team ods.ai 7th place solution.
solution_summary: This post announces a meetup presentation about the author's competition solution. The event was scheduled for August 8 in San Francisco. It invites readers to attend and provides a meetup link, but contains no technical solution details.

solution_title: The way to the 18th place, just for rookies.
solution_summary: The team developed a strong LightGBM through parameter tuning and extensive feature engineering, reaching 0.2184 with five-fold averaging. Features included text and categorical hashes, segmented price and item sequence values, character-level TF-IDF, target encodings, external income and population data, and basic image features. Combining LightGBM with neural networks and a teammate's diverse models improved the public score further. The final stacking effort covered approximately 40 models and reached 0.2156 on the public leaderboard.
compute: 20-core server; approximately 3 hours per LightGBM fold.

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution Vesuvius Challenge – A postprocessing win
solution_summary: The team trained two nnUNet ResEncTrainer models with 128³ and 160³ patches and combined their logits with weights of 40% and 60%. Mirroring and rotation augmentation at inference preceded morphological cleanup and segmentations at several thresholds. Their central postprocessing method detected tunnels using Euler numbers and repaired sheet components through PCA-based interpolation, escalating thresholds when sheets remained merged. The local interpolation submission scored 0.622, while a global interpolation variant reached 0.631 on the private leaderboard. Alternative topology-oriented losses were unsuccessful or reduced surface Dice.
compute: Postprocessing optimized from about 3 minutes to about 1 minute per volume.

solution_title: 14th place solution. Custom Mask and LSTM encoder/decoder
solution_summary: The solution used custom sampling masks to reduce redundant adjacent frames and downsample easy examples with target displacement below six meters. A CNN combined with LSTM encoding and decoding processed 300×300 images and ten history steps, predicting positions and yaw represented by sine and cosine. Training first used distance-balanced sampling, then continued with unbalanced sampling and a log10-scaled loss to stabilize fluctuations. About two days of training produced a public score below 13 and a private score around 12; heavier temporal models and several sequence-based alternatives offered little benefit.
compute: About two days of model training; roughly 80,000 iterations with batch size 64.

solution_summary: The solution used EfficientNetB2 classifiers on MegaDetector crops, combining undersampling and oversampling to address species imbalance. Location-independent validation, CLAHE preprocessing, and exponential moving averages supported training. Country-specific experts handled geographically implausible predictions, while a full-image classifier contributed a small weighted prior. Counting used conservative confidence filtering and a maximum-based estimate with a final mean absolute difference adjustment.

The final agent used a zero-shot Llama-3.1 SauerKrautLM 8B Instruct model with 4-bit quantization. Outlines and Pydantic schemas constrained questions, answers, and guesses, with internal reasoning generated before the response. Model selection emphasized instruction following and reasoning benchmarks. Self-play achieved a 12% success rate, while conditional prompting and Monte Carlo Tree Search were unsuccessful.
compute: Competition environment: single T4 GPU, 15GB GPU RAM, 60 seconds per response.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution - Significantly Reduced the Fluctuations caused by Randomness!
solution_summary: The final pipeline exhaustively matched image pairs with SP/SG, selected the best of four image rotations, and used geometric verification before COLMAP reconstruction. Resizing large images and adjusting keypoint extraction settings substantially improved matching, including a scene-level mAA increase from 0.1 to 0.6. EXIF-derived focal lengths and shared camera settings reduced submission variability to at most 0.004 on the public leaderboard. The final exhaustive pipeline scored 0.507 and took nearly nine hours; faster retrieval-based pairing and several refinement methods were explored but not retained.
compute: Final exhaustive pipeline: nearly 9 hours; DINOv2 pair selection variant: 7 hours.

solution_summary: The solution used separate Endzone and Sideline detectors to generate high-recall impact candidates, followed by ResNet3D classifiers on helmet crops spanning nearby frames. Temporal NMS and cross-view filtering reduced candidate duplicates and unsupported detections. Eight classifiers with horizontal-flip TTA were combined, with adaptive thresholds limiting each video's prediction count. The final validation F1 was 0.47, and both detector and classifier training used single-fold models.

solution_title: I thought for sure this approach would work! But it didn't.......
solution_summary: The author tried selecting the best question context from passages retrieved through different methods and corpora. They used bge-large-en-v1.5 embeddings and cosine distance to choose a context for each question. The leaderboard result was disappointing, and the approach was abandoned late in the competition so the author could focus on better-performing attempts.

solution_title: Quick 1st place solution overview before the night
solution_summary: The pipeline used transformers to predict token-level start and end probabilities, then mapped these probabilities back to the input text using offsets. Character-level models consumed the mapped probabilities to refine span extraction. The two selected submissions each used four character-level models and diverse transformers, without post-processing. They achieved private scores of 0.735 and 0.736.

The solution distilled DeBERTa base and large models into a DeBERTa-v3-small student with a maximum sequence length of 384. Student training mixed original labels and out-of-fold pseudo targets in a 0.1-to-0.9 ratio. It disabled attention and hidden dropout while using heavy sentence and paragraph dropout, multi-sample dropout, layer averaging, and mean pooling. Reported runtime was 22 minutes with a +0.008 change in MCRMSE.
compute: 22 minutes runtime

solution_summary: The approach combined additional synthetic samples with original data and engineered physical ratios and size-related features. Several tree-based regressors were trained on different feature subsets using a shared stratified five-fold out-of-fold structure, with validation restricted to competition data. Optuna and LAD regression were used to tune ensemble predictions, and rounding predictions to the nearest integer substantially improved validation and leaderboard scores. Several alternative model families and attempts to overlay training-data predictions were unsuccessful, while the author observed that a better-CV submission would have generalized better than the public-leaderboard-selected submission.

solution_title: 95th Place Solution for the CZII - CryoET Object Identification Competition
solution_summary: The solution ensembled seven MONAI 3D U-Nets and improved performance primarily through training patches, augmentation, and post-processing. Training used small particle-center masks, Tversky loss, and patches wider in XY than Z. Sliding-window inference fed GPU watershed processing with particle-size filters that removed many false positives. The author reported improving the public score from 0.58 to 0.729, while heatmap models, synthetic data, deeper networks, and a 2D detection filter did not yield useful improvements.
compute: Used Google Colab and Kaggle Kernels; moving watershed operations to GPU reduced computation time by approximately 70–80%.

solution_summary: The pipeline selected candidate image pairs with DINOv2, then pre-matched them using ALIKED and LightGlue with rotation retries. Valid pairs were matched across four image quadrants and a half-sized original, producing 25 combinations that improved robustness to scale and perspective changes. Cached features, RANSAC filtering, and careful reconstruction registration supported efficient and reliable pose estimation. Parameter tuning mattered substantially, and the reported private score was 49.05; SIFT replacement and scene clustering alternatives did not improve the final approach.
compute: 2x T4 GPUs for parallel processing.

solution_summary: The author selected two final submissions, one exploiting data leakage and one using a neural network without leakage. The leakage approach followed ideas from a shared kernel and fell from a reported 0.82 to 0.60 on the private set. The neural network achieved 0.71 on the public set, demonstrating useful performance on the small dataset, although the post does not clearly report its private score.

solution_title: Some useful and useless ideas(Part of rule, planning and evaluating, 25th)
solution_summary: The author describes rule-based components supporting a teammate's learned Lux agent. Unit production prioritized resource blocks with fewer friendly units relative to resources, while a defensive rule assigned units to threatened cells using maximum-weight bipartite matching. A modified Dijkstra algorithm computed arrival times while accounting for cooldown, resource collection, consumption, and survival. Symmetric evaluation inputs, seeds, and ordering reduced variance and made debugging easier.
compute: Modified Dijkstra optimized to 0.004 seconds per unit on a 32×32 map.

solution_title: 3rd place solution (0.447 private - 3 models simple average)
solution_summary: The selected solution used a simple average of RoBERTa-large and DeBERTa-large models trained through repeated fold-specific pseudo-labeling cycles. Attention heads, weighted hidden-layer averaging, multi-sample dropout, differentiated learning rates, and staged learning-rate schedules supported training on the small, noisy dataset. External texts supplied pseudo-labeled training examples, with fold-specific labeling avoiding the leakage seen in an earlier variant. The best selected submission scored 0.442 publicly and 0.447 privately; an unselected variant reached 0.446 privately.
compute: 1080 Ti initially; RTX 3090 when switching to large models.

solution_title: Swedish Institute of Computer Science solution
solution_summary: The authors release their competition code and briefly identify two contributions. Custom cross-validation rules split segments in a way intended to reduce overfitting. Parallel data input and output supported the pipeline, but the post does not describe models or features.

The author built an ensemble dominated by CatBoost models, with four models retained from early AutoGluon experiments. Inputs received minimal processing beyond integer encoding of Sex, and most models omitted the original dataset because it added little value. Ridge was selected for the final ensemble after comparisons with Lasso, AutoGluon, and hill climbing. Hill climbing had the strongest CV, while an unselected AutoGluon ensemble later proved competitive on the private leaderboard.

The solution combined tabular models whose feature spaces, losses, and class decompositions produced complementary errors. Balanced class weights gave the largest initial improvement, while target-encoded XGBoost, a logit-adjusted RealMLP, and a binary CatBoost cascade lifted the stack beyond conventional GBDTs. The final selection used more heavily vetted blends of meta-models, prioritizing cross-validation evidence over a slightly better public score. The selected submissions scored 0.97041 private, while additional tree tuning and several specialized feature approaches brought no useful stack improvement.

The final submission ensembled roughly 40 mostly original models with some public models and scored 0.251 on the private leaderboard. A forgotten variation of a public 1D CNN notebook performed substantially better, reaching 0.310 private and 0.386 public. The team generated candidates using weighted covisitation matrices, FastText neighbors, session history, and popular items. XGBoost and LightGBM ranked candidates using extensive item, session, interaction, and co-occurrence statistics. Training used session-grouped folds and negative sampling, while final predictions were scaled and combined with weights based on out-of-fold scores. Several embedding and collaborative-filtering approaches were limited by performance or inference cost.

solution_summary: The solution treated fraud detection as identifying fraudulent clients and generalizing to clients absent from training. Client identities were reconstructed using card, address, and relative transaction-day information. Rather than feed these identities directly into the model, the team created client-level aggregate features and removed identifiers and other columns likely to cause memorization. This post explains the central feature-engineering insight while deferring model, validation, and ensemble details to another post.

The author identifies the team's public writing-quality fusion notebook as its best notebook. They report small improvements from integrating additional notebooks, but provide no model, feature, validation, or weighting details. solution_title: Simple XGB with hyperparameter tuning with optuna
solution_summary: The author first tried LightGBM but found it ineffective. They then switched to XGBoost and tuned its parameters. The reported public and private leaderboard scores were 98.114 and 98.037, respectively.

The author used VGG11 with 40 × 98 log mel spectrogram inputs and ensembled models using log mel and MFCC features. Mixup with alpha set to 2 improved performance, and ensembling reached a best private score of 0.90908. Knowledge distillation produced a smaller, fast model scoring about 0.90. The selected final submission scored 0.90790.

The author added the original data after distribution comparisons suggested it was closer to the test set than the provided training data. Features were removed separately for each model using permutation importance with correlation considerations, and duplicate records were dropped. Optuna selected the ensemble weight proportions. solution_title: Open Problems | My solution and ideas
solution_summary: The solution combined dimensionality reduction, selected features, tree models, and neural networks for Multiome and CITEseq prediction. Multiome used SVD on inputs and targets, while CITEseq also benefited from correlation-selected features with negatively correlated features flipped. Models included single-target boosting regressors, ridge regression with pseudo-labeling, and several dense and convolutional neural networks. Normalized averaging weighted by each target's out-of-fold correlation performed best among the blending approaches.

solution_title: Trying to reproduce the winning solution
solution_summary: The author attempted to reproduce a winning approach using dataset preparation, a denoising autoencoder, and a final neural network. RMSprop replaced SGD for faster autoencoder convergence, but the original 4500-1000-1000 final network stalled at a loss near 0.6. Training used reduced-radius labels, Dice and focal losses, extensive augmentation, and regularization, with all training data used for the final submission. Two-stage processing, larger encoders, and simulated data did not work.

The solution blended three LightGBM models trained with different seeds with predictions from three public kernels, assigning 66% of the weight to the author's models. Feature development used two month-based folds and leaked readings from four sites, which were excluded from final training. Data cleanup, selective feature retention, categorical typing, and log1p transformations formed the preprocessing pipeline. Excluding the four sites improved the private score from 1.266 to 1.262, while a single model without late manual cleaning achieved 1.25, suggesting that some cleanup hurt performance.

Its main predictors were grouped expanding and rolling congestion means, all lagged by seven days to prevent leakage. Training used only workdays, and predictions were rounded to integers. solution_title: 13th Place Solution - 2.5D YOLO Ensemble with DBSCAN
solution_summary: The solution combined six 2.5D YOLO detectors and clustered their 3D detections with DBSCAN. Horizontal and vertical flip inference augmented detections, while different models processed alternating slices. The best individual models scored above 0.83.

solution_summary: The team focused on likelihood encoding of feature interactions after observing strong improvements early in the competition. They developed multiple representations and levels of interactions, then combined models through stacking and ensembling. Additional teammate features helped later in the competition, although their construction is unspecified. Regularized greedy forests performed almost as well as XGBoost but were slow, and training experiments remained unfinished.

The solution used two-stage factor graph optimization, first estimating velocity from Doppler and then estimating position and receiver clock from corrected pseudorange, ADR differences, and velocity constraints. Separating the stages enabled velocity cleanup, interpolation, and stop detection before position optimization. Robust Huber estimation, base-station corrections, and phone-specific observation handling were central to accuracy. Processing the complete test set took about 30 minutes, and a post-competition base-station coordinate correction produced public and private scores of 1.372 and 1.197.

solution_summary: The pipeline upscaled images and ran LoFTR, adding reversed-order SE2-LoFTR matches only when fewer than 2,000 matches were available. Difficult pairs received DKM-based region proposals, followed by SE2-LoFTR on corresponding crops. Keypoints were rescaled before fundamental matrix estimation with USAC_MAGSAC. Upscaling to a longest side of 1176 was the most important improvement, while conditional use of additional matchers saved computation.

solution_title: My solution, and yet another magic multiplier story..
solution_summary: The solution trained a separate LightGBM model for each forecast horizon day, sharing each model across all stores and other data slices. It used rolling and seasonal sales statistics, holiday proximity features, target encodings, and price features, with model settings selected through seven 28-day backtests. Seasonal gap imputation hurt validation, while removing out-of-stock gaps helped only moderately. A final per-item trend multiplier substantially harmed the submitted private score: the postprocessed version scored 0.72667, compared with 0.58797 for a later submission without that adjustment.

The solution combined a DenseNet169 U-Net and an EfficientNet-B4 FPN, both with classification heads, into an eight-model average. Training used extensive image augmentation and a joint loss dominated by segmentation BCE and Dice, with a smaller classification contribution. Flip-based test-time augmentation and CV-based threshold optimization completed inference. The author reported public and private scores of 0.67376 and 0.66765 using one RTX2080Ti.

solution_title: 46th Place Solution — Hedging the Hidden Guardrail
solution_summary: The team optimized candidate throughput in an offline agent-security benchmark and manually selected two complementary submissions. Its main portfolio targeted confused-deputy email actions, while a marker-exfiltration engine hedged against a weaker hidden guardrail. Model-specific prompting, live predicate validation, and single-call candidates improved throughput and reliability. solution_summary: The pipeline combined ensemble cell-center detection, dense motion estimation, learned matching, division identification, and joint lineage graph optimization. Sparse annotations were handled by masking uncertain detector background and separately calibrating whether graph candidates would be evaluated and correct. Gap filling, short-component removal, and affine coordinate refinement improved the resulting tracks. The final solution achieved 0.977801 CV and 0.967 private score, with private Division Jaccard of 0.47; video-level validation allowed overlapping crops from the same embryo across folds.

solution_summary: The author's higher-scoring selected submission stacked 74 out-of-fold predictions with Ridge regression. A retrospective comparison showed that an 11-model ensemble using positive-only hill-climbing weights achieved a higher private leaderboard score. That ensemble mixed AutoGluon, CatBoost, LightGBM, linear regression, ResMLP, and LNN models with varied feature sets. A distinctive component combined binned-target classifier probabilities with original features, then fitted another CatBoost to residuals.

The solution combined EfficientNet-B6 Noisy Student image embeddings and multilingual BERT text embeddings, both trained with ArcFace heads. It averaged snapshot and text augmentation embeddings, normalized them, and retrieved matches with cosine KNN separately on image, text, and concatenated representations before taking their union. Training used staged backbone unfreezing, frozen image-backbone batch normalization, and two-fold grouped validation, with changes accepted only when both CV and public leaderboard scores improved. Jaccard-based merging with majority voting added a small gain, bringing the final private score to 0.740.

The author trained a neural network with one hidden layer that scored 0.799. They describe averaging runs with different random seeds and hidden-layer widths as a way to exceed 0.8. XGBoost and nearest-neighbor experiments performed poorly, and stacking the nearest-neighbor model with the neural network did not help.

The author selected models using cross-validation and found 384×384 to be the best tested image resolution. Ensembling considered how much candidate models changed existing predictions, excluding candidates with very large differences. The successful submission combined a CV-considered model with a model other than the highest public-scoring one. The author attributed the outcome partly to avoiding public-score overfitting and examining sensitivity and prediction differences across models.

The solution combined AlphaZero-style learning and Monte Carlo tree search with a sparse NNUE-style policy/value network. A four-layer MLP consumed about 2,400 binary features and predicted policies and values for all players together. Training used roughly 200,000 self-play games, with pairwise cross-entropy defining the value loss. C++ inference with AVX2 vectorization supported about 100,000 search nodes per second locally, and using average action values reduced sudden deaths against weaker opponents.

solution_summary: The solution combined a two-stage normal/abnormal classifier and 14-class detector with a separate 15-class detector. EfficientNet and ResNet classifiers accompanied EfficientDet detectors, with five-fold stratified validation. Consistent NMS annotation fusion and normal-case thresholds were central to the pipeline. solution_summary: The final predictor is a sigmoid classification hyperplane using 15 features. Its coefficients were estimated through leaderboard probes and L1-penalized logistic regression using the training data together with the 2,225 public-test observations. The author adjusted coefficients using training data and zeroed those with magnitude below 0.04 to limit overfitting. The reported scores were 0.914 CV, 0.890 public leaderboard, and 0.869 private, with only 50 coefficients probed before the competition ended.

solution_summary: The solution used a graph transformer with directional bond edges and additional edges linking atoms two or three graph steps apart. Chemical attributes and geometric distances and angles replaced explicit coordinates, preserving rotation and translation invariance. Its attention updated edge embeddings from atom-edge triplets and aggregated edges into atom representations, with predictions averaged across both edge directions. Training combined a modified LAMB optimizer, one-cycle scheduling, coupling-specific fine-tuning, stochastic weight averaging, and averaging predictions from two train/evaluation splits.

The solution separated dataset-reference retrieval from Primary/Secondary classification and handled DOIs and accession identifiers independently. Retrieval relied on external citation and text-mining corpora, followed by repository exclusions, document-presence checks, and rules matching labeling conventions. Classification combined metadata heuristics, a LoRA-adapted MedGemma DOI model, and specialized BiomedBERT models with carefully constructed contexts. Large batches, identifier replacement, and multi-seed out-of-fold averaging improved classifier stability, while accession retrieval reached 0.98 F1 before type classification.

Training alternated imitation learning, HandyRL self-training, and renewed imitation learning, with player shuffling and flips for augmentation. Search used decoupled UCT with UCB1, ten-turn playouts, shaped rewards, and a public agent policy for first visits. A C++ implementation increased playouts from 600 to 4000, while TorchScript accelerated model inference; quantization and several search variants were unsuccessful.

solution_title: Bronze Scissors or long path to the 115th place

Most of the writeup describes unsuccessful alternatives, especially behavior cloning with LSTMs and Transformers trained on game replays. Sliding history windows and inputs containing both players' actions could reproduce moderately complex deterministic strategies, but could not compete with ensemble agents. Attempts to exploit fluctuations in random opponents failed because successive random actions are independent.

solution_summary: The agent combined simple move strategies, each with two counter-strategies, and tracked match history using an n-gram tree. A separate n-gram search examined each strategy's past success following similar sequences of wins and losses. Weighted collections of rolling windows scored strategies, and repeatedly layering this mechanism helped adapt to opponents while introducing instability. Historical-episode replay selected useful windows from a larger collection that was too slow for competition use.

The solution predicted player displacements from 20 pre-pass frames using temporal convolutions, static features, and a transformer for interactions among players. Gaussian negative log-likelihood losses modeled trajectory uncertainty, with auxiliary velocity and acceleration losses stabilizing training. Rotation, earlier prediction starts, and vertical flips improved generalization using only competition data. The final prediction averaged more than 100 models with differing features and game-grouped validation splits.

The solution used a three-channel EfficientNetV2-XL model trained with the timm training framework and strong augmentation. Training used 592×592 inputs, while inference used 624×624 inputs with a 0.95 center crop from video frames initially resized to 712. Much of the effort focused on video memory use and inference speed, with a time-limit safeguard that filled unfinished portions with default submission values. The reported public and private leaderboard scores were 0.611522 and 0.602592.

The solution pretrains a 3D encoder with InkClassifier3DCNN, then transfers it into a segmentation model with depth attention pooling and a 2D FPN decoder. Training samples ink-containing and ink-free regions at a 1:8 ratio and uses extensive image augmentation. A U-Net denoiser predicts noise that is subtracted from the segmentation output. Pretraining improved cross-validation by 0.03–0.06; reported scores were 0.685 on CV, 0.69 on the public leaderboard, and 0.65 on the private leaderboard.

The final solution combined generator-aware numerical features, fold-local target statistics, ridge logistic priors, and residual boosted trees. A regularized logistic stack combined logits and percentile ranks from 54 prediction streams, reaching private ROC-AUC 0.94575. Representation improvements and complementary residual models drove the gains, while late validation remained conditional on an existing OOF library rather than a fully nested pipeline.

solution_summary: The unlearning strategy used only the retrain set in three stages. It reset the fully connected layer and fine-tuned the whole model, then injected additive noise into randomly selected layers and fine-tuned those layers. A final whole-network fine-tuning stage restored accuracy, while randomized perturbations promoted diversity against membership inference attacks. Class weighting, multiplicative noise, gradient-informed perturbations, label smoothing, and focal loss did not improve the approach.

The solution trained LightGBM models separately for each meter after removing long constant-target streaks and zero electricity readings. A temporal holdout determined building-specific prediction tree counts, although this helped the public score more than the private score. They expanded the available word and block transformations and adapted operation weights according to the scores those operations produced. solution_summary: The final pipeline used RMSE loss and about 20 features covering calendar information, events, SNAP, and rolling target means. Confidence or energy scores ranked candidate structures, and Arena refined DRFold2 outputs. Protenix fine-tuning suffered from overfitting, and adding Boltz reduced ensemble performance.

Feature values were clipped at the 95th or 99th percentile to reduce the impact of outliers. Explicit missing-value embeddings improved convergence and generalization for both tabular and sequential networks.

solution_summary: The solution used information from neighboring properties, including roughly three million properties without associated sales. Constraints on model fitting helped produce more robust results. Stacking was the other major component of the final pipeline.

The solution used Qwen2.5-14B for both misconception retrieval and reranking, trained with modified FlagEmbedding code. Training data included about 2000 deduplicated synthetic examples generated by Qwen2-72B for misconceptions absent from the training set. The retriever used contrastive QLoRA fine-tuning to return 25 candidates, while a LoRA reranker scored the generated answer "Yes" for the top five. Reranking improved the final leaderboard score from 0.418 to 0.463. Validation split by question ID was acknowledged as inadequate, and faster vLLM inference remained an unfinished idea.

Feature masks were selected using cross-validation ROC AUC, but their benefit varied by subject and they were omitted for subjects with fewer than 500 training samples. It combined two temporal models, spatial test-time augmentation, bidirectional harmonic link fusion, and constrained graph selection with conservative repairs. solution_summary: The solution trained TabNet with pinball loss on tabular variables and engineered CT lung features. Training examples were augmented by treating each available FVC measurement as the patient's first visit and recomputing related features. Segmented and rescaled lung volumes supplied geometric, HU distribution, and histogram features, which improved cross-validation. Training used five stratified folds, SGD, and a one-cycle schedule for 350 epochs. solution_title: Stacked Gradient Boosting Ensemble for Pit Stop Prediction
solution_summary: The solution stacked LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost using a meta-model trained on out-of-fold predictions. Engineered features described race length, relative tyre age, degradation per lap, and driver-race interactions. Categorical variables received ordinal encoding, with unseen categories mapped to -1. Five-fold prediction averaging and stacking provided improvements, with feature engineering and ensemble design contributing more than extensive tuning.

solution_title: 18th place solution - You really don't need big models
solution_summary: The strongest described model combination used NFNet-L0, NFNet-L1, BERT-large, and TF-IDF, with ArcFace fine-tuning for learned embeddings. Full cosine similarity matrices were combined multiplicatively and reranked using neighboring predictions. The biggest improvement came from constructing groups to match the training group-size distribution, raising the score from .739 to .759. A lightweight ResNet18, BERT, and TF-IDF variant scored .749, and a later neighborhood-blending update reported .762/.772.

solution_summary: The solution combined pretrained LoFTR with QuadTreeAttention and MatchFormer without additional training. Shared image preprocessing, carefully tuned matching thresholds, and robust resizing fallbacks made the two matchers work together. Their keypoints were scaled back to original coordinates and concatenated before estimating the fundamental matrix with OpenCV MAGSAC. The combined system outperformed either matcher alone, while alternative estimators and a third matcher were not retained.

The solution trained a hybrid depthwise 1D CNN and Transformer from scratch using only competition landmarks, then ensembled four seeds. Correct variable-length masking, nose-referenced normalization, and lagged motion features supported efficient inference and consistent training behavior. Strong regularization and temporal and spatial augmentation were essential during 400-epoch training. The final single model achieved about 0.80 participant-split CV and 0.88 private score, while the seed ensemble achieved a reported LB score of 0.81.

solution_title: [Working Note] Throughput Races and Confused Deputies
solution_summary: The solution used a clean confused-deputy email action that survived the private guardrail, rather than relying on public-only secret exfiltration. It probed a small template pool on each target model and selected the template with the highest measured scoring throughput, varying recipients to earn distinct scoring cells. A deterministic guardrail-transform estimator predicted approximately 18.4 private score, closely matching the observed 18.39. Packing multiple actions into candidates reduced performance because it sacrificed diversity bonuses.
compute: CPU-bound replay; environment rebuilt and reparsed a 19,679-page corpus per candidate.

solution_summary: The pipeline screened defect-free images with an ensemble of EfficientNet-B1 and ResNet34 classifiers before running a larger segmentation ensemble. Segmentation combined EfficientNet-B3 U-Net and FPN models with additional public U-Net models, using weighted BCE and BCE–Dice training. Crop training, flips, brightness and contrast augmentation, defect blackout, and flip-based inference supported generalization. Two rounds of agreement-filtered pseudo-labeling added 1,135 images, while mask-size and connected-component filtering removed small predictions; pseudo-labels and public models increased the reported private score from 0.90663 to 0.90883.

The team blended five DeBERTa variants using character probabilities. Training included masked language modeling, size-dependent learning rates, multi-sample dropout, FGM, and selective pseudo-labeling. Pseudo-labeling and adding the largest model improved public results but were less reliable on the private leaderboard. Final spans used whitespace adjustments and thresholds tailored to cases and features.

The author adapted public image-matching pipelines from the 2023 and 2024 competitions. They tuned parameters and applied contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization to every image. The post provides code but no quantitative results or further implementation details.

solution_title: [LB Pub 29 Pvt 28] Enhancing the efficiency of a reasoner using SFT and GRPO [Fast-Math-R1-14B]
solution_summary: The team fully fine-tuned DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B on 7,900 difficult math examples, then applied GRPO to reduce reasoning length while preserving accuracy. Format, cosine, and length rewards improved efficiency, with early checkpoints avoiding later training collapse. Submission inference used 4-bit AWQ quantization and a ModernBERT difficulty predictor to allocate output tokens dynamically. The final model scored 29 publicly and 28 privately.
compute: 8× H200 GPUs; approximately 10 hours each for SFT and GRPO.

solution_summary: The solution combined EEG features from multiple epoch lengths and trained general models using data from all three subjects. Features included frequency-band power, channel summary statistics, temporal and frequency correlations, and averages across channels. Training incorporated leaked preictal examples, while grouped cross-validation kept consecutive files together to reduce overly optimistic estimates. Averaging quadratic SVM and RUS boosted tree predictions consistently improved over either model alone, producing public scores around 0.775–0.815. Subject-specific models performed poorly on the revised test set despite competitive local validation scores.

The main pipeline shortlisted image pairs with EfficientNet-B8 at a similarity threshold of 0.6, then detected and matched features with KeyNetAffNetHardNet and AdaLAM. Combining matches from resolutions 1696 and 1536 improved performance over single-resolution processing, with reported public and private scores of 0.451 and 0.471. Additional experiments used a ConvNeXt shortlist model, scene-dependent resolutions, and less frequent global bundle adjustment to address runtime constraints. The author reports selecting the wrong submission and notes a stronger ConvNeXt-based variant with mAA of 0.504.
compute: Kaggle-provided GPU; model and runtime unspecified.

solution_title: 11th Place Solution - Simplicity (Luck) Is All You Need
solution_summary: The solution used a CatBoost regressor to stack LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost models, following a public notebook. The author emphasized extensive hyperparameter tuning and feature variations while validating on the last five months. A weighted blend of three or four strong public submissions slightly outperformed the best cross-validation model on the private leaderboard.

The pipeline combined single-frame 2D CNNs with a 1D CNN processing tracking and helmet-position sequences. Three image variants covered zoomed-out, zoomed-in, and masked views, with the same model handling Endzone and Sideline inputs. Predictions and learned features were stacked together with tabular features, followed by moving-average postprocessing. Grouped validation by game_play achieved 0.740, while the private score was 0.7302.

The solution blended six DeBERTa configurations using out-of-fold predictions from five of ten stratified group folds, with additional full-data training. Masked language model pretraining, adversarial weight perturbation, and soft pseudo-labeling were important improvements. Sentence deletion and auxiliary span-boundary targets added diversity, while whitespace trimming cleaned predicted spans. Runtime limits required selecting only some fold checkpoints for the final submission.

The pipeline first trained a VGG-based U-Net to segment tumors from Task 1 FLAIR scans. It then resampled Task 2 scans, selected 154 slices centered on the largest tumor area, and extracted 58 radiomics features from predicted masks. An XGBoost classifier used these features to predict MGMT status. Segmentation achieved about 0.92 CV, while experiments using true Task 1 masks achieved classification CV above 0.64.

The final solution combined ten models across two data preparation approaches. One approach treated the task as a conventional time series problem with lags, expanding and moving statistics, and graph statistics. The other used tsflex, with XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Random Forest, and AdaBoost trained for each representation.

solution_title: 4th Place Solution Brief Summary : Magic of 1D CNN
solution_summary: The main model was a custom deep residual 1D CNN with an LSTM head, operating on horizontally concatenated and bandpass-filtered detector signals. This single architecture achieved 0.8838 public and 0.8823 private leaderboard scores. The final ensemble also included 2D models based on constant-Q and continuous wavelet transforms. Windowing, channel-specific normalization, colored noise and signal shifts strengthened the 2D models, while alternative sequence heads did not outperform LSTM.
compute: All models trained on JarvisLabs.ai GPU instances; GPU types and training time unspecified.

solution_title: 48th place solution, Ensemble + Oversampling outliers + Weighted loss + U connections
solution_summary: The author moved from an MLP to a U-ViT transformer with U-Net-like connections for atmospheric sequence prediction. Oversampling high-error rows and inversely weighting their MSE contributions reduced training from about 150 epochs to five. Selected q0002 variables were handled with closed-form predictions and zeroed in network inputs and targets. An ensemble of six models with different shuffle seeds improved the score from 0.741 to 0.757.

The solution combined extensive user-history and ad-interaction features with diverse first-level models and stacked ensembles. A fast custom field-aware factorization machine enabled rapid experimentation and became the strongest single model, scoring 0.70053 on the private leaderboard. Validation used roughly six million rows sampled to resemble the test set's mixture of common and future days. The final submission used a geometric mean blend of a teammate's meta-stack, bagged XGBoost, and bagged Keras models, with manually selected weights.

solution_title: 16th Place - So Close to Gold Medal 😀
solution_summary: The solution fine-tuned Gemma2-9B-IT with LoRA, using broad module coverage and carefully tuned rank and alpha settings. External deduplicated data, longer contexts, test-time augmentation with two Gemma2 models, and retaining the end of long conversations improved performance. The final approach trained in fp16 and used 8-bit inference to accommodate longer inputs, reaching a reported public score of 0.885. Attempts to generate additional training examples or labels with Llama3.1-405B did not help, while the published best single model achieved CV 0.878 and public LB 0.888.
compute: Training used NVIDIA 8x V100 32GB GPUs and sometimes 4x A100 80GB GPUs.

solution_summary: The author describes an unselected approach using RegNetY-32GF with 512×512 images. Training used extensive image augmentation, focal loss, momentum SGD, and cosine annealing. The pipeline also included pseudo labeling and single-fold inference without test-time augmentation. The author explicitly says this was not the chosen solution and provides no performance results.

The solution trained models for Alpha, Beta, Gamma, and Delta and used their predicted probabilities as stacked features. A basic CatBoost model was evaluated with five-fold stratification repeated five times. LightGBM imputers were created for every feature, although removing them did not change the score. Later feature engineering and alternative models did not improve the public score, so the original submission was retained.

solution_title: [30th place solution] Weird TTA trick? Detect by quadrant provided a great boost!
solution_summary: The author used an EfficientDetB5 detector trained at 640×640 with random resized crops drawn from crop sizes between 640 and 1024. At inference, predictions from four overlapping 640×640 quadrants were stitched together and combined with predictions from the full image resized to 640×640 using weighted boxes fusion. Boxes near quadrant edges were discarded, while full-image predictions helped recover missed detections. This inference approach improved the public score from about 0.72 to 0.7535; mosaic augmentation did not help.

solution_title: 3rd place solution - GRU, UNET and LGB!
solution_summary: The team combined GRU, U-Net, and LightGBM predictions for sleep onset and wakeup detection. Daily sequences were downsampled to 30-second intervals and represented by seven features covering signal variability, repeated-value noise, and event timing frequencies. Sequence reversal and expanded event targets improved neural-network training, with the best single GRU reaching 0.835 local validation. The reported weighted ensemble achieved about 0.840 CV and 0.848 private score, with peak-spacing post-processing producing the final events.
compute: Inference took approximately 1.5 hours.

solution_summary: The author trained separate models for each coupling type and optimized MAE. Averaging the type-specific validation scores tracked leaderboard results, with reported differences within approximately 0.05. Features came from public kernels, and memory constraints led to processing kernels separately and tuning their models. Distance, angle, and graph-based approaches were researched but were not understood or used effectively.

The author developed one submission from an earlier winning pipeline, modifying feature engineering and sampling validation by year. A second submission used Silver's probabilities sharpened through goto conversion and ultimately scored better. Tournament seed transitions mapped valid matchups, and efficient simulation generated the full 10,000 brackets. Probability clipping was rejected after backtesting showed little benefit.

The agent combined fixed semantic questions with initial-letter questions selected using dictionary letter frequencies. Its guesser shuffled and rephrased the question-answer history into keyword descriptions, then retried guesses that contradicted fixed answers or repeated earlier keywords. Gemma generation used temperature 0.99, and the answerer voted over ten generated answers with an initial-letter hint. Reported results were 11 wins and 2 losses as questioner and 6 wins and 10 losses as answerer, suggesting the answerer was the weaker component.

The team optimized ONNX programs using a large parallel fleet of LLM sessions, algorithmic searches, and a shared Git repository. Its most important component was a validation gate combining CPU scoring, static and runtime checks, and sparse Kaggle probes that identified hidden-set failures while conserving submissions. Major program optimizations included collapsing transformations into Einsum operations, exploiting convolution behavior, using float32 underflow for selection, and reordering Einsum operands. A second pipeline combined ChatGPT Pro proposals with iterative Codex optimization and version tracking; the final banked bundle scored 8048.80.
compute: Approximately 330 concurrent chat workers across about 11 enabled accounts; CPU scoring and GPU correctness screening. Sparse probes took about 90 seconds versus about 1500 seconds for a full bundle.
