solution_summary: The author built an ensemble from publicly shared notebooks after starting the competition ten days before the deadline. Limited time constrained the development of original models. The post links the resulting solution notebook and credits the public notebook authors, but provides no model or ensemble implementation details.

The final detector used YOLOv3 after an initial R-CNN experiment proved too slow. Training data was balanced by excluding images containing only very common objects, leaving 200,000 images. The learning rate decreased linearly but was raised slightly when loss plateaued. Predictions used a 0.01 confidence threshold and class hierarchy expansion, without ensembling.
compute: 1080 Ti; initial R-CNN training about 600 ms/image; YOLOv3 about 4 hours/epoch.

solution_summary: The solution used RegNetY-16.0GF with 960×960 crops from 1024-resolution images and only the current competition's data. Higher resolution produced the largest reported improvement, raising the private score from 84.1 to 91.9. Iterative pseudo-labeling, dropout, and an ensemble of models trained with different settings further improved performance. AutoAugment, random cropping, horizontal flips, and test-time augmentation were also used, with the final ensemble achieving public and private scores of 96.2 and 95.9.

solution_title: Rossmann Store Sales, Winner's Interview: 2nd place, Nima Shahbazi
solution_summary: The solution combined 15 models using XGBoost and extensive sales feature engineering. Zero-sales days were retained to derive features describing unusual sales around consecutive store closures, alongside expanded holiday and promotion features. Sales and customer moving averages over different windows, grouped by store, weekday, and promotion, produced a complementary model for blending. Building models and generating predictions took more than 25 hours.
compute: 8-core CPU and 16GB RAM; models run in parallel on a laptop and desktop; more than 25 hours to build and predict with 15 models.

solution_summary: The final submission combined 16 transformer models with ensemble weights optimized by Nelder–Mead. Training generally used binary cross-entropy, adversarial weight perturbation, layer-wise learning-rate decay, partial layer freezing, and half precision. Adversarial weight perturbation produced the largest CV improvement, while models trained without it added ensemble diversity because its public leaderboard effect was unfavorable. FGM, last-layer reinitialization, and LightGBM stacking did not work.

The agent used imitation learning with separate U-Net models for unit actions and sap targets, trained on selected winning Frog Parade replays. Spatial features combined observations, exploration estimates, symmetry, and previous unit positions, while global features entered the U-Net bottleneck. Models switched once a hidden sap parameter became estimable, and inference combined eight augmented predictions with probability filtering and overlap-aware action selection. Fine-tuning on the strongest teacher submission helped, while long-term temporal architectures and reinforcement learning were unsuccessful.

solution_title: 322 place solution for the "ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions" competition
solution_summary: The author standardized numerical features, label-encoded categorical features, dropped missing values, and retained outliers. Optuna Bayesian optimization selected hyperparameters for XGBoost, which was then trained across five folds. The final predictions came from the single fold model with the best F1 score. Balanced class weights were tried but did not improve results.

solution_title: 14th place solution NN (surviving the big shakeup)
solution_summary: The solution uses a multilayer perceptron with batch normalization and dropout between linear layers. Feature engineering includes products, ratios, a logarithmic transformation, and a grouped transformation, although the column names and some operations are missing from the supplied code. Training uses weighted cross-entropy with different weights for the six classes and sum reduction. The incomplete configuration prevents recovery of most training settings.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution - An Ensemble of 100 OOFs
solution_summary: The solution combined 100 out-of-fold prediction files from the author's models and adapted public notebooks. Model and feature diversity mattered more than optimizing a single learner, with RealMLP variants among the strongest individual models. A simple linear regression stack outperformed hill climbing on both public and private leaderboards. Models were added incrementally while monitoring cross-validation and leaderboard agreement, although inconsistent folds and seeds likely widened the validation gap.
compute: Local mobile RTX 4060 and Kaggle notebooks; some models exceeded local GPU capacity.

solution_title: 84th Solution: Based on Transformer, the GraphTPU model
solution_summary: The approach modified the open-source Google GraphTPU code by replacing its MLP with a Transformer. The author reports that this improved prediction accuracy. Preprocessing also contributed, but the post provides no details about those operations, validation, or numerical results.

The author built a combinatorial tracker that constructs short tracklets and extends them through detector layers using local helices. Repeated searches used different detector regions and constraints, selecting tracks and removing their hits after each round. A fitted magnetic-field model adjusted helix extrapolation, while manually chosen cuts controlled hit acceptance. The implementation worked but was extremely slow, and its seeding strategy remained underdeveloped.

The solution combined SuperPoint/SuperGlue, KeyNet/AffNet/HardNet with Adalam, and SOSNet with Adalam for local feature matching. NetVLAD retrieved image pairs, while hloc organized the pipeline and Colmap performed reconstruction and localization. Merging matches and applying geometric verification improved reconstruction efficiency within the nine-hour limit. Rotation compensation helped some individual matchers but added no benefit to the final ensemble, and several alternative matchers were too slow or less accurate.
compute: Final matching ensemble selected to fit a 9-hour time limit.

solution_title: [late sub 0.9828771]How Boosting from 0.9671 to 0.9823 my first competition on kaggle
solution_summary: The author trained LightGBM on the full training data with about 40 features covering grouped counts, conversion rates, and click timing. Time-delta features produced the largest gains, and validation restricted to selected hours closely matched the private score. The post reports a public score of 0.9816 after blending several models, while describing the final model as a single LightGBM. A later update reordered duplicate clicks and added next-second and next-third click deltas, reaching 0.9828771 privately.

The main submission generated single-call exfiltration candidates exploiting the public guardrail's inspection of URLs but not request bodies. Live verification, latency-aware budgeting, analysis-channel control tokens, and oversized candidate lists maximized replay throughput. The selected finals paired this public approach with a benign-email hedge. The best public score was 91.080, but both selected submissions failed privately because of content inspection and an incorrect recipient domain.

The solution trained separate LightGBM models for each forecast day, recalculating lagged features for each prediction horizon. It used RMSE rather than a custom competition metric because the author considered the latter noisy and prone to overfitting. Three years of history supported feature calculation, while training used one year with December excluded and rows before a product's first store sale removed. Features combined calendar and price information with holiday effects and sales statistics at three aggregation levels.

solution_title: 5th place solution. Higher Resolution and Dataset1 is all you need.
solution_summary: The final submission used a single-fold HTC-DB-B model trained only on dataset1 with COCO pretraining. Training combined a standard schedule with stochastic weight averaging and scale, flip, and rotation augmentation. Inference used multiple scales and both flip directions, with weighted cluster NMS using DIoU. Fold ensembles and a larger backbone were excluded based on local and public results, although both later performed better on the private evaluation.

The author developed a stateless, rule-based Halite bot. It scores each ship's possible destinations using weighted intentions and jointly assigns actions to maximize satisfied intentions. A separate assignment procedure allocates ships to mining, combat, rescue, and shipyard-related targets under availability constraints. Special endgame rules prioritize returning halite to shipyards.

solution_title: [1st place solution] Improved Squeezeformer + TransformerDecoder + Clever augmentations
solution_summary: The solution combined landmark-specific convolutional feature extraction, a modified Squeezeformer encoder, and a two-layer transformer decoder. Strong temporal and landmark augmentations supported deeper models, while rotary attention and caching reduced runtime and model size. A confidence head identified corrupted inputs for replacement with a fixed phrase. The final submission averaged decoding logits from two full-data model seeds and used manually ported FP16 TensorFlow Lite inference.
compute: Training runs used an A100 card and Kaggle kernels; 400 training epochs; two final FP16 models totaled 39988 KB.

solution_title: 5th place: 100 OOFs, laziness, and a blunder or two
solution_summary: The author collected approximately 100 diverse out-of-fold prediction sets, predominantly from gradient-boosted trees, and combined them through ensemble methods including Ridge and AutoGluon. Target and pair encoding, feature variations, and 30-fold cross-validation strengthened individual models; the strongest standalone XGBoost model used median encoding and achieved private RMSE 11.67004. An AutoGluon ensemble OOF was also included among the inputs to the final ensemble. Clipping was critical: an unclipped submission with strong public performance deteriorated to private RMSE 177.25179, while the other selected submission avoided that failure.
compute: Used Kaggle GPUs only; encountered GPU quota, 12-hour runtime, and memory limits.

solution_title: How I drop from 0.9805 Private LB to 0.974 (113rd Solution)
solution_summary: The solution used a modified SEResNeXt50 with 128×128 inputs, combined max and average pooling, and a multilayer classifier. Five-fold and snapshot ensembles, extensive augmentation, SGD, and soft pseudo-labeling supported the approach, followed by weighted blending with NasNet and DenseNet models. The stronger ensemble achieved a private score of 0.9805. A final rule forcing white central patches to negative labels reduced the private score to roughly 0.974 because apparently empty patches could still belong to tumor regions.

solution_title: 4th solution: Multitask Learning, Semi-supervised Learning and Ensemble
solution_summary: The solution combined ResNet34 models on log-mel spectrograms with EnvNet-v2 models on waveforms. Separate classification heads for curated and noisy labels enabled shared feature learning without treating both label sources identically. Offline sharpened soft pseudo labels improved validation performance and added useful ensemble diversity, while ordinary pseudo labeling, Mean Teacher, and MixMatch were unsuccessful. The final weighted ensemble mixed time-window lengths and used full-audio inference with padding augmentation, reaching 0.896 CV lwlrap and 0.75787 on the private leaderboard.
compute: All model training ran on Kaggle kernels.

solution_title: 5'th place : simultaneous span segmentation and classification + WBF
solution_summary: The team combined DeBERTa Large and xLarge models using both pure named entity recognition and a multitask entity and span segmentation setup. Models used five folds, 1,024-token inputs, and strided inference, with stable multilabel stratified validation. Weighted boxes fusion was the main driver of the late improvement, alongside token-count and score filtering. Question answering approaches and simple averaging of word scores were unsuccessful.

The solution uses two CaFormer stages to estimate a sound speed field and then correct its residual error. A forward simulation from the first prediction supplies signal discrepancies to the second stage, alongside the original signal and predicted field. Five-fold out-of-fold predictions provide realistic second-stage training inputs, and physically simulated flips preserve source positions. The second stage reduced local error from about 27 to 13 for a single prediction and 11 using five first-stage outputs, with a public score of 13.
compute: First stage trained for 120 epochs; second stage for 125 epochs.

solution_summary: The solution built two feature sets around categorical group statistics, particularly rich representations of manager_id, with a second set incorporating leaky target encodings. A three-layer stack combined LightGBM, XGBoost, neural networks, and additional StackNet outputs, ending with a weighted average across ensembles from both feature sets. Grouped numeric statistics contributed most to the strongest single model, while image CNN experiments and categorical-to-categorical encodings were abandoned. The two feature sets achieved public leaderboard scores of 0.507 and 0.511 with XGBoost.

solution_title: 8th Place Solution: 2-Stage Fine-tuning + High Quality Data Extraction
solution_summary: The solution fine-tunes ByT5-XL in two stages: broad supervised training on roughly 350,000 noisy pairs, followed by exactly one epoch on about 65,000 curated pairs. Host publications and PDFs supply the data, with layout-specific OCR and language-model extraction addressing page-boundary alignment and merged columns. Byte-level modeling and the noisy-to-clean training sequence were the main contributors to exceeding 40 on the leaderboard. Longer clean-data training, several augmentation and reinforcement-learning approaches, and LLM post-processing failed to help, while local validation remained unreliable for model selection.
compute: Pipeline stated to be replicable on a single A100 instance or two RTX 6000 GPUs; first-stage training used two devices.

solution_summary: The author extended raddar’s 2018 solution with an XGBoost model and additional compound team evaluation features. More than 100 candidate features were reduced to about 20 using SHAP importance and manual selection guided by cross-validation loss. Selected early-round game predictions were manually overridden, with overrides differing between submissions. From the Elite Eight onward, predictions came directly from the model, which incurred substantial losses on UConn games.

The approach froze an openCLIP ViT-H-14 backbone pretrained on LAION-2B and trained a linear embedding head without batch normalization or dropout. Self-supervised contrastive training used 130,000 images with paired original and augmented batches. Training ran for 30 epochs with Adam and a total batch size of 512, followed by test-time augmentation using square zero padding and direct resizing. The author reported a private leaderboard score of 6.37.

solution_title: Key of the 10th solution? : Where sSE Block looks
solution_summary: The author examines spatial squeeze-and-excitation blocks through a visualization notebook. They identify sSE blocks and RandomErasing as potentially important parts of their solution. The visualizations suggest similar squeezed features across components but behavior different from global average pooling. The contribution of that difference is presented as a hypothesis.

The team trained diverse segmentation networks on full-resolution images using five shared folds. Their ensemble included a custom U-Net, LinkNet variants with Inception-v3 and DenseNet encoders, and modified PSPNet models. The LinkNet variants produced the team's best models, with Adam and scheduled learning-rate drops used for their training. A planned second-level model was not trained because of time constraints, and the team used over 40 GPUs in total.
compute: Over 40 GPUs used in total across the team.

solution_summary: The solution combined four image models through a learnable fusion layer and passed the resulting feature to an ensemble of XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost models with tabular features. Image training combined positive examples from ISIC2020 and ISIC2024 with equally sampled ISIC2024 negatives, using patient-grouped five-fold validation and 160×160 images. Patient-level and patient-by-location normalization features, along with ensembles across random seeds, strengthened the tabular pipeline. The image-feature submission achieved a private leaderboard score of 0.16941, compared with 0.16217 for the tabular-only submission, although the authors cautioned that detected leakage made their CV reference unreliable.

The solution combined four fine-tuned language models adapted from public Kaggle notebooks. It replaced probability-based voting with weighted logit averaging and reranked predictions using the IsCorrect flag to favor structurally valid labels. Memory-management changes enabled the ensemble to run reliably, and Qwen3-4B replaced Qwen3-8B. The reported private score improved from 0.945 to 0.946, with the author attributing the main gains to logit averaging and domain-aware reranking.
compute: Configured memory limits: 12 GiB on each of two GPU devices and 48 GiB CPU memory; hardware models and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution arranged four consecutive 256px slice patches into a 512px image to preserve inter-slice context for a 2D segmentation model. A U-Net with a MaxViT backbone was trained on overlapping patches from three kidney-volume orientations. Whole-kidney percentile normalization and simple geometric and appearance augmentations supported training, while scaling augmentations did not work. Inference averaged rotated and repeated patch predictions, merged patches using a maximum operation, and processed all three anatomical planes.

The solution encoded notebook cells individually with CodeBERT or a combination of CodeBERT and multilingual MPNet, then modeled cell interactions with parallel transformer decoders. Binary ordering predictions placed markdown cells between code cells and ordered markdown cells within each bin. Larger-notebook sampling, gradient clipping, and loss adjustments helped end-to-end training. The final ensemble averaged outputs across four folds, two model families, and additional second-level encoder variants; external notebooks improved individual encoders but contributed little to the ensemble.

The final solution ensembled two Gemma2-9B-IT models trained with opposite response orders and a Llama3-8B pair-preference model. Training incorporated competition data, an additional 33k dataset, and approximately 45k pseudo-labeled examples constructed from filtered LMSYS-Chat-1M conversations. LoRA adaptation, 8-bit inference, merged adapters, and length-dependent batching supported the pipeline. Llama inference was restricted to selected sequence lengths to meet notebook limits, and its addition improved the reported private score from 0.9859 to 0.9828.

solution_title: We will post the winning solution here
solution_summary: The authors outlined three complementary approaches focused on offer similarity, customers' underlying purchase propensity, and relationships shared across offers. Offer-based validation helped select features and interactions despite differences between training and test offers. They treated within-offer discrimination and overall AUC as separate objectives and combined several approaches, but deferred the detailed solution.

The final submission used logistic regression over 27 stackers and 60 base models. Model selection relied on cross-validation with weighted log loss rather than the noisy public leaderboard or balanced accuracy. Learners supporting sample weights used inverse-prior weighting, while RealMLP and TabPFN outputs were divided by class priors and renormalized. Hill climbing in logit space performed worse than logistic regression.

The solution used shared 1D convolutional encoders with kernel sizes from one to six and global average pooling for each question. Absolute differences and elementwise products of the question representations were combined with engineered features in a dense classifier. Class weighting and additional similarity features substantially improved performance. Geometric averaging of 15 CNNs achieved a public leaderboard score of 0.133.
compute: 1050 GPU; approximately 130 seconds per CNN epoch versus 400 seconds for a 250-unit LSTM.

solution_summary: The team replaced train.csv with 14.5K curated translation pairs extracted from source documents and held out AKT 6d as a 392-sample validation set. They standardized transliteration conventions and trained mT5 and ByT5 variants, including a higher-dropout model and checkpoint averaging. Four configurations generated ten beam-search candidates per input, and chrF++ consensus selected the final translation through minimum Bayes risk decoding. Additional model-generated, Gemini-corrected data was prepared near the deadline but could not be used for training because of compute limits.

solution_summary: Two U-Nets produced bounding boxes used to guide random crops for a diverse ensemble of CNN classifiers. Five-fold out-of-fold predictions fed an XGBoost blender, with the final output averaged across 500 randomized runs. Extensive augmentation was central, and the author compared submissions with and without additional-folder images, which contained test leakage. Final training included train and test_stg1 images; private scores were 0.88856 with additional images and 0.83209 without them.

The approach fine-tuned ImageNet-initialized VGG, InceptionV3, and ResNet50 models and combined them in an ensemble. VGG received an additional stage of fine-tuning across all layers. Further training used class weights to address imbalance while monitoring AUC each epoch. The best submission achieved a reported leaderboard score of 0.99553.

solution_summary: The team combined three XGBoost models, one LightGBM model, and one CatBoost model in a weighted ensemble. The author's XGBoost pipeline used five-fold stratified validation, a log-transformed target, backward feature elimination to eight features, and manual hyperparameter tuning. Adding original data to training substantially improved CV, while validation excluded original samples. Ensemble weights were selected from out-of-fold predictions, and the submission with the best private result had a CV score of 0.292843.

The solution combined diverse models and preprocessing variants through 10-fold stacking. Its strongest individual XGBoost model used categorical interactions selected partly by mutual information, a fair objective, and a transformed target. The first layer contained 81 models, followed by one XGBoost model and two neural networks. The final predictions used nonlinear weighted combinations and conditional adjustments, with weights optimized by Nelder-Mead across folds. The best second-level model achieved 1114.645 cross-validation error and 1097.87 on the public leaderboard.

solution_title: 49th silver, 2.5DCNN solution, public0.736, private0.722 (shakedown from 39 to 49)
solution_summary: The solution adapted a public 2.5D CNN baseline using EfficientNet B0 and B1 trained from scratch, temporal shift modules, and multitask contact classification. It combined helmet-centered image sequences from two camera views with metadata, filtered candidates by distance, and oversampled contact events. Validation used one game-play-grouped fold, and the final predictions came from a simple two-model ensemble. Multitask learning stabilized training and improved CV to 0.755 and the private score to 0.722. Removing ffmpeg from the submission notebook reduced estimated runtime from 7.5 to 2.5 hours.
compute: Estimated submission runtime reduced from 7.5 hours to 2.5 hours by removing ffmpeg.

solution_title: 26th Place Gold | Macro BC + Day Compiler
solution_summary: The agent separated daily strategic decisions from exact operational planning. A behavior-cloned network learned macro intents from expert games, while a deterministic C++ compiler handled placement, routing, hiring, funding, and sales. A causal transformer forecast opponent sales, enabling a dynamic program to optimize selling times and overnight inventory. Paired game evaluations, multiple seed sets, and detailed failure analysis drove selection, with the opponent forecaster providing a particularly large benefit.
compute: Day compiler: about 1–2 seconds, worst 3.5 seconds on Kaggle CPU

solution_summary: The solution trains ByT5-base on a mixed corpus expanded to approximately 64,000 samples through alignment cleanup, splitting, publication extraction, and pseudo-labeling. Gemini-3.0-flash-preview supports this data engineering, with lexicon-based proper-noun corrections reducing translation noise. Training uses FP32, AdamW, gradient accumulation, and length grouping, while inference chunks long inputs at spaces according to token counts. Four models are combined into weighted pairs and decoded with minimum Bayes risk using chrF++ similarity; increasing data volume was the most reliable improvement.
compute: Single RTX 4090; training approximately 10–12 hours with group_by_length enabled.

solution_summary: The agent learned a deck-specific policy through behavioral cloning on 1,377 replay matches containing 75,849 decision states. Separate state and chain Transformers scored short action chains using option pooling, cross-attention, and an auxiliary value objective. Official-engine verification supplied features and overrode the policy for guaranteed wins or safe attacks in stalled games. Test accuracy reached 82.81% Top-1 and 95.56% Top-3, while 1,000 evaluation matches produced a 57.4% win rate excluding draws; the planned reinforcement-learning stage remained unfinished.

The pipeline extracted candidate DOIs and accession identifiers with regular expressions, then filtered them against reference corpora. DOI types were classified with a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct model using abstracts, data sections, and local context. Accession classification used the same model family with additional table information and nearby rows. Fine-tuning improved DOI results, while prompt engineering improved accession results.

The pipeline used 3D organ segmentation to extract enlarged organ cubes, followed by diverse 2.5D plus 3D classification models. Liver masking, organ-specific batch sampling, and two crop sizes contributed most to accuracy. Models shared information across injury targets, and some were initialized using image-level bowel and extravasation training. Target-specific weighted averaging and further prediction weighting achieved a final CV score of 0.3316, while metric-optimized stacking performed worse due to overfitting.

solution_title: 7th Place Solution - Cascade RCNN+Tracking ( Public LB is not all you need.)
solution_summary: The team built a single customized Cascade R-CNN detector with stronger backbone components, an enhanced feature pyramid, double detection heads, and IoU-based loss. Extensive weak and strong augmentation and multiscale training and testing supported robustness. Norfair tracking improved detections as a postprocessing step. Model design was initially selected using a video-based train-validation split, followed by full-data training and public leaderboard comparisons; the approach ultimately performed robustly on the private leaderboard despite poor public results.

solution_title: How i get the  Top 5 solution  :Give me Some Credit !!
solution_summary: The author presents a credit scoring project intended to predict financial distress over the next two years. The described pipeline combines preprocessing and modeling under a CRISP-DM methodology, without specifying the model architecture or preprocessing operations. Evaluation includes F-beta, ROC AUC, and average precision, with a reported private ROC AUC of 0.86914.

The team trained EfficientNetB4 and EfficientNetB5 models for both classification and regression, using 256×256 and 328×328 inputs respectively. Images were cropped, normalized, and augmented with color changes, affine transformations, and flips. Training used Adam, task-specific losses, and stepwise learning-rate decay, while inference used ten stochastic augmentations. The final submission combined the two regression outputs and achieved public and private scores of 0.835 and 0.925.

The solution combined two neural networks with two hidden layers and an XGBoost classifier. XGBoost also selected features for the neural networks, and predictions from 50 models were averaged for each classifier variant. The final blend assigned 60% weight to the two neural network averages and 40% to the XGBoost average. Stratified four-fold cross-validation guided parameter tuning, and the final ensemble achieved public and private scores of 0.52832 and 0.52625.

solution_title: 20th Place: Bilinear CNN with FL + LS
solution_summary: The author explored bilinear CNNs with different CNN backbones, including EfficientNet variants B0 through B7. Experiments varied image resolution, focal loss, label smoothing, augmentation, and stopping schedules. The final submission ensembled solutions that each exceeded 0.970 on the public leaderboard. The post does not specify exactly which experimental settings survived into those models.

The author developed a global linear multiplier with coefficients optimized for SMAPE by split month and forecast horizon, alongside an SVR approach. Models predicted active microbusiness counts because density can be calculated from active counts and county population. Validation used the last 12 months and tracked gains against a last-value baseline separately for each horizon. SVR outperformed the other tested algorithms, and RAPIDS reduced notebook runtime from 4607 to 136 seconds.
compute: Notebook runtime: sklearn SVR 4607 seconds; RAPIDS SVR 136 seconds, reported 34x faster.

solution_title: Entropy-Weighted Self-Consistency for Olympiad-Level Mathematical Reasoning
solution_summary: The solution uses GPT-OSS-120B with MXFP4 quantization through vLLM and combines eight parallel reasoning attempts using inverse-entropy-weighted answer voting. Each attempt has an isolated, persistent Jupyter kernel for symbolic and numerical computation. The best configuration used temperature 1.0 and flat time allocation, answering 44 of 50 public problems correctly. More attempts reduced completion rates under the runtime limit, while geometric budgeting and SFT or GRPO fine-tuning did not improve the baseline.
compute: Single NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80GB GPU, 2 CPU cores, approximately 29 GB RAM; 17,000–17,400 seconds allocated within a five-hour limit.
external_data: ["IMO shortlist problems, Putnam solutions, and AIME problems"]

solution_summary: The solution added a weekend feature and combined four forecasting models. Three models used three-fold time-series validation with RMSE, Poisson, or a custom loss, while the fourth used rolling prediction. Their predictions were averaged, very small values were set to zero, and a multiplier close to one was applied.

solution_title: 655th Place / Bronze — From Replay Cloning to an 18-Agent PPO League
solution_summary: The team initialized deck-specific policies through behavior cloning from strong public replays, then refined a diverse population through PPO self-play. A compact entity-based Transformer scored legal actions, while a separate privileged critic was used only during training. Terminal game outcomes replaced misleading shaped rewards, and conservative guards vetoed only actions provably harmful from public information. The submitted agent reached a rating of 857.3, with teacher quality and deployment reliability emerging as major practical constraints.

solution_title: Words of Wisdom From Ben Hamner, Our Newest Recruit
solution_summary: The approach exploited weekly shopping patterns and the greater relevance of recent visits. Simple predictors used a recency-weighted weekday mode for visit dates and the mode of a weighted kernel density estimate for spending, with more complex methods incorporating these predictors. Optimization proceeded first for dates and then for spending conditional on the predicted date. Matching the competition metrics mattered substantially, while gradient-based approaches performed poorly and joint date-spend optimization remained unfinished.

The solution combined sensor statistics from the time and frequency domains with MFCCs, rolling statistics, and tsfresh features. Shuffled five-fold validation guided forward selection down to roughly 100 features per model. LightGBM, XGBoost, and neural networks supplied out-of-fold predictions for two LightGBM stacking models. Averaging those stacks reduced the reported error from approximately 4.5M to 4.38M.

The final solution combined seven image models using ridge-derived ensemble weights. Image features were fused with embedded categorical features, and two models used SVR on extracted features. Training combined a custom RMRSE loss with SmoothL1, small learning rates, frequent validation, and early stopping. The ensemble achieved CV 17.16897 and private score 17.05251; a separate ridge stacking experiment performed better but was not submitted.

The final submission simply averaged BERT-base-uncased, BERT-large-uncased, GPT2, and XLNET predictions. The most effective change converted continuous targets into multiple thresholded binary labels, with their predicted probabilities averaged at inference. All models used sample-weighted binary cross-entropy and multi-sample dropout, which modestly improved leaderboard performance and stabilized training. An auxiliary toxicity-score target improved BERT-base and GPT2, while text preprocessing showed no clear benefit.

The solution extends a public notebook with three-dimensional polynomial fitting that includes the frequency direction. Each frequency is normalized separately, while mean-frequency transit timing and depth guide signal adjustment and subsequent depth estimation. Uncertainty is estimated separately for each planet. A linear regression approach using frequency indices 180–186 achieved a strong local result but failed on test data.

The author trained two retrieval models, one using raw images and another using DELF inputs. Their output vectors were concatenated for indexing. Query expansion and geometric verification supplemented retrieval, but the post provides no numerical results or training details.

The final pipeline averaged nine diverse U-Net and FPN segmentation models with EfficientNet and SE-ResNeXt encoders. Models used focal loss, Adam, plateau-based learning-rate reduction, weighted sampling, and image augmentation; some incorporated pseudo-labels, SCSE layers, or Mish. Training used 256×800 images and inference used 256×1600 images, with no test-time augmentation. Class-specific label thresholds and a common pixel threshold produced the masks, with a reported private score of 0.90765 for the selected submission.

The approach converted temporal information into five frequency channels and processed cropped horizontal slices with a CNN. Each slice contributed a predicted volume, and contributions from the same study were summed during both training and inference. The CNN also predicted uncertainty and was trained using the negative log likelihood of a normal distribution.

The approach trained XLM-R large with staged adaptation across toxicity datasets, subtitle data, and the competition validation data. Three-stage training produced better private scores than the other schedules examined. Replacing binary training labels with probabilities from a strong existing model improved validation AUC by about 0.003 and enabled useful training on combined datasets. A model trained with 790,000 examples achieved 0.9464 public and 0.9445 private scores.
external_data: ["Toxic Comment Classification dataset", "Unintended Bias in Toxicity dataset", "Open subtitle dataset"]

solution_summary: The solution emphasized combining diverse tabular models with little feature engineering. Its model collection included XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, TabM, RealMLP, and LNN. A final Ridge ensemble achieved 8.57299 CV and 8.57775 on the private leaderboard. CatBoost received less tuning and was reported to run slowly.

The final solution ensembles a custom approach with the public MCTS Starter and MCTS: DeepTables NN notebooks. The custom component estimates the likely outcome between two random MCTS agents to improve on AdvantageP1. It trains DeBERTa on LudRules text and uses LightGBM to refine the predictions. Data augmentation was identified as a missed opportunity and was not used.

solution_title: Code and Documentation for Winning Solution
solution_summary: The post announces attached documentation and links to a code repository. It provides no methodological details in the supplied text. The author closes with thanks.

solution_title: 139th Place Solution for the Predict Podcast Listening Time Competition
solution_summary: The solution used a single XGBoost model with 15-fold validation. Its main contribution was extensive categorical interaction engineering motivated by changes in the relationship between episode length and listening time across other attributes. Combining categorical columns produced 480 additional features, which were target encoded. Ensembling and more extensive tuning were suggested as future improvements rather than reported components of the submission.

The team trained frame-level models on the regular video training set, then fine-tuned them briefly on validation segments with labels, gaining about 0.04. Their strongest approach used gated attention and multiple attention networks to pool frames for different video topics, reaching a public leaderboard score of 0.772 for one model. They increased loss weights for the 1,000 classes represented in the test segments and combined 12 models spanning attention, DBoF, CNN, netVLAD, and LSTM architectures. Selecting predicted training segments and pseudo-labeling test segments did not improve results.

The author submitted three independent approaches to address uncertainty about evaluation and test distribution. A conservative feature-based approach improved shared features with LightGBM and CatBoost tuning, while punctuation and mouse-event features failed. A larger blend of tuned LightGBM, XGBoost, and neural networks achieved public/private scores of 0.577/0.570. A simple blend of two public notebooks performed best privately, scoring 0.578/0.568.

solution_title: N-gram works. Even for non-Russian Kagglers
solution_summary: The team used an n-gram approach for Russian text normalization. All team members were non-Russian speakers, and the post presents n-grams as their entire approach. It links their implementation and states that the code applies only to the Russian competition, without providing training details or numerical results.

solution_title: #43 Explainable model almost without machine learning
solution_summary: The author compared grouped and ordinary cross-validation to distinguish unseen house sizes from repeated sizes. The final model included the original dataset and used only squareMeters, made, and cityCode. It first predicted the mean price for exact three-feature matches, then used two-feature matches ignoring cityCode. Houses without either match were handled by linear regression.

The solution separates the target distribution into four components informed by X0 and tunes predictors for the components independently. Three components use XGBoost models fitted on the full training set with different parameters and feature subsets, while the smallest, hardest component receives its cluster mean. Repeated five-fold cross-validation and paired significance tests guide model selection. A second validation framework removes the 1% largest out-of-fold errors, exposing outlier-driven overfitting and leading to revised parameters and features for the final submission.

The team addressed early overfitting with additional regularization and semi-supervised learning using external essays. They collected synthetic T5 essays, back-translations, scraped essays, and previous Feedback Prize data, then cleaned and selected the examples. Selecting neighbors by pseudo-label distance worked better than embedding similarity and predominantly selected synthetic data; scraped essays were excluded from the final solution. External data was split into folds before pseudo-labeling to prevent leakage.
external_data: ["Previous Feedback Prize competition data", "StudentShare essays, excluded from final solution", "IvyPanda essays, excluded from final solution", "EssayForum essays from HuggingFace datasets, excluded from final solution"]

solution_summary: The solution used a two-stage pipeline: a ConvNeXt Base DINOv3 image classifier extracted features, and a Transformer classified complete image sequences. Neighboring slices formed RGB inputs with two different slice spacings, and negative sampling emphasized earlier false positives. Training included spatial augmentation and left-right flips with corresponding label changes. The final ensemble used four ConvNeXt Base models, with long sequences subsampled to meet inference runtime constraints.
compute: Kaggle inference runtime varied from less than 8 hours to exceeding the 12-hour limit.

solution_summary: The final solution blended LightGBM, neural networks, and several stacking models. Strong improvements came from passband ratio features, a modified Bazin light-curve fit, predicted hostgal_specz features, and combining raw and log-transformed inputs in the neural network. Sample weighting based on hostgal_photoz and ddf improved the score by about 0.02, while logistic-regression stacking improved it by about 0.04. Averaging log predictions worked better than ordinary averaging; autoencoder features and test-set pseudo-label augmentation did not help.

The solution used a three-stage pipeline consisting of modified YOLO detection, InceptionResNetV2 relationship classification, and LightGBM score prediction. YOLO's loss was changed to handle incomplete labels, parent-child classes, and class imbalance. Relationship training examples were constructed from annotated boxes, with unmatched relationships assigned a None target and image crops combined with class and geometric features. LightGBM then estimated whether each predicted relationship was correct using detector and relationship-model outputs.

The solution extended a public rule-based baseline with action planning, concentrated offensive forces, and revised expansion and defense rules. It compared current actions against future opportunities and gathered ships at a main shipyard for attacks. Faster expansion and more flexible defensive reinforcements improved performance, while safer mining heuristics made results worse. Repeated small attacks that disrupted opponents' expansion increased the agent's rating by about 150 points.

The solution converted signals into 256×256 mel spectrograms and trained several ResNet-family CNNs. A weighted ensemble combined these predictions with tree-model predictions from shared tabular pipelines, assigning about half the weight to ResNeXt101. Using enough models improved prediction stability, including stability on the private leaderboard. EfficientNets underperformed ResNets, while TabNet and MLP experiments were unsuccessful.

The solution combined six ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNetV2B0 classifiers with added dense classification heads. Categories with fewer than ten images were merged into an unknown class, and two-stage fine-tuning used label smoothing to address noisy labels. Category predictions were averaged and filtered at a probability threshold of 0.4. The out-of-sample score combined average classifier uncertainty with five times the average standard deviation of category predictions.

The team combined LightGBM and XGBoost models with extensive handcrafted tabular, text, and image features. They expanded JSON parsing and used all available image, sentiment, and metadata files. Rescuer and state aggregates, website-inspired ranking features, and image quality measurements were important parts of the pipeline. Different validation strategies and model variability supported ensembling, with double cross-validation used to check reliability.

The final submission combined four PANNs and four PaSST models using GeM aggregation with p=3. Validation split the scored species into three folds grouped by recording author, while all unscored species remained in training. PANNs used ResNet-34, and PaSST learned from both original labels and PANNs pseudo-labels. Group-specific quantile thresholds were tuned on the public leaderboard. A late experiment improved the score from 0.7626 to 0.7645 by removing PaSST.

The post provides a runnable code workflow for learning entity embeddings of categorical variables on Rossmann sales data. It describes preparing features, training models, and examining the learned embeddings, while directing readers to a separate branch for the original competition code. A visualization of German state embeddings reportedly resembles their geographic arrangement, but the text gives no predictive scores or detailed final model configuration.

solution_title: 9th place: SWIN/VIT/CAIT + Heng decoder with code: tugstugi's part (updated)
solution_summary: The author developed image-to-InChI models using transformer encoders and progressively deeper decoders, with a Swin encoder and a 12-layer, 16-head decoder reaching a single-model leaderboard score of 0.74. Fine-tuning on teammates' pseudo-labels substantially improved an earlier model. Stochastic weight averaging, cropping and rotation augmentation, and corresponding test-time augmentation each helped, while CaIT contributed diversity to the ensemble. Additional ResNet classifiers addressed m0/m1 errors, and decoder-step ensembling failed.

solution_summary: The author reconstructed standard UPCs by calculating missing checksums and padding short codes with leading zeros. Company identifiers were derived primarily from the first six digits, and missing UPCs received a sentinel value. Corrected UPCs successfully retrieved product information through Walmart's API, and the author reported a modest improvement from this work.

solution_title: 13-th place solution summary 0.44091 (65-th on public LB: 0.459~0.467)
solution_summary: The solution averaged 50 models spanning XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, field-aware factorization machines, and xDeepFM. Features combined tabular information, detected language, TF-IDF/SVD text representations, GloVe embeddings, and aggregated DenseNet image embeddings. Validation grouped examples by RescuerID, with ten folds used for final training to reflect the separation of rescuers between train and test. The ensemble achieved validation RMSE 1.038 and QWK 0.457; aligning the final prediction histogram with training labels achieved a private score of 0.44091, outperforming the alternative tuned toward the public leaderboard.
compute: GPU used for XGBoost training; hardware model and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled 3D ResNet34 models selected from three fragment-based validation folds, using 192×192×16 inputs. Preserving image resolution helped retain spatial-frequency information, while blur augmentation improved validation performance by roughly 1–2%. Inference used test-time augmentation and a fixed threshold of 0.50. Larger inputs, label erosion, and alternative losses did not help.
compute: Google Colab Pro+, three concurrent fold sessions; A100 took 30 minutes per epoch at batch size 16.

solution_title: Top 25th place with TabM only and nothing else
solution_summary: The author trained a single modified TabM in one 10-fold cross-validation loop for event classification and survival-time regression. Separate output heads split TabM's submodels between the tasks, with event flags supplied only to the regression head near the end of the forward pass. Regression used all observations, with survival times normalized separately for censored and non-censored groups and classification loss scaled against regression loss. Without changing hyperparameters, the private score improved from 0.69320 to 0.69435.

The solution reconstructed transit signals through classical fitting rather than a learned model. It masked the transit phase and fitted a quadratic baseline before modeling ingress and egress with two oppositely signed error functions. Fit uncertainties were scaled to provide approximately 99% confidence coverage. A statistical comparison selected either predictions from groups of 15 wavelengths or a single wavelength-inclusive estimate when spectral sensitivity was low.

The author adapted a public Gemma 2 training and inference baseline using a quantized Gemma 2 9B instruction model with LoRA sequence-classification adapters. Inference used a simple test-time augmentation method. Longer input lengths generally improved leaderboard scores but caused unstable runtimes and occasional timeouts.

The author's contribution used a two-branch network combining stacked bidirectional GRUs and attention with a fully connected metadata branch. Timestamp inputs included flux, flux error, passband encoding, and time differences, while Gaussian noise and spatial dropout reduced overfitting. Out-of-fold RNN predictions helped teammates build LightGBM models, and incorporating teammate-provided features improved the reported private score from 0.93560 to 0.85371. Autoencoder-based features, autoencoder pretraining, CNNs, and adversarial sample weighting did not help.

The final submission used a single embedding neural network with relatively little feature engineering. The author improved it by adding projected player positions at future time offsets and removing unhelpful features. A regression output was added alongside softmax classification, although its benefit varied across folds. Earlier experiments used separate LightGBM yard models and season-specific speed and acceleration adjustments; post-competition experiments suggested that a different season adjustment could have substantially improved performance.

The author describes three unsuccessful speech-recognition experiments without presenting a final working pipeline. Converting audio to spectrograms and applying image algorithms did not work. Noise reduction during inference worsened the score despite adding little overhead. A preliminary linear-probe implementation also failed to deliver the hoped-for out-of-distribution improvement before time ran out.

The solution emphasized Wikipedia retrieval and ensembled four DeBERTa-based open-book models. It replaced the Wikipedia dump, tuned overlapping text chunks, and selected gte-base and e5-base retrieval encoders using leaderboard feedback. Inference used four different retrieved-context sets, with scores combined through their maximum and mean. Retrieval evaluation reached 0.94 recall@1 and 1.0 recall@30 on a restricted synthetic evaluation set, but local validation did not reliably track leaderboard performance.

solution_title: 37th Place (Silver, Solo) — The improvement loop, not the graph tricks
solution_summary: The solution optimized one ONNX graph per ARC task through an iterative fleet of Claude and Codex coding agents. Shared global guidance and detailed per-task histories let successive attempts reuse discoveries and avoid repeated failures, while a priority scheduler directed effort toward promising tasks. Graph optimization emphasized small intermediate representations and terminal operations that wrote directly to the uncharged output tensor. Every adopted candidate was checked through real submissions, with batch splitting used to isolate regressions; the final reported score was 7621.91.
models_pretrained: ["Claude Opus 4.8", "Claude Fable 5", "Codex 5.5", "Codex 5.6-sol", "GPT-5.5 Pro", "Public ONNX model bundles"]
compute: Initially one laptop, later two laptops running coding-agent fleets; second laptop added July 2; Claude Max ×2 and ChatGPT Pro & Plus.

solution_summary: The solution split survival prediction into event classification and conditional event-time regression, motivated by the synthetic data generation process. XGBoost and HistGBM regressors used event status as a feature, with that feature set to one during validation and test inference. A CV-weighted classifier ensemble supplied event probabilities, which were multiplied by a sigmoid transformation of predicted time to produce risk. A neural network optimized an approximation of the competition metric with an auxiliary classification loss, and its predictions were rank-ensembled with the main pipeline.

solution_title: Make the most of all available resources
solution_summary: The author experimented with ByT5 for Old Assyrian-to-English translation using a fixed validation subset from the original training data. Adding expert translations extracted from academic publications improved the score by about 0.6 over a roughly 33.1 baseline, while sentence recombination and Claude-generated translations reduced performance. Data quality, byte-length limits, numerical artifacts, and language consistency were central concerns. Several cleaned corpora and revised extraction rules remained untested or incompletely used, so the proposed combined training dataset was not established as a completed final pipeline.
compute: Experiments relied on free resources, including Kaggle's free online GPUs; no specific GPU model or runtime stated.

solution_title: 63rd place solution - Single Cascade R-CNN + Norfair
solution_summary: The solution used Cascade R-CNN with a Res2Net-101 backbone at 2560×1440 resolution. Norfair supplied tracking. The shared notebook trained on videos 0 and 1 scored 0.694, while the submitted version trained on videos 0, 1, and 2 scored 0.685. The author attributed the weaker submitted result to insufficient hyperparameter tuning.

The solution combined diverse tabular models and public notebook predictions through hierarchical stacking, with cuML logistic regression as the final meta-model. Reusable out-of-fold predictions enabled rapid experimentation with ensemble architectures and validation of every ensemble decision. Frequency encodings, target encodings, and interaction features provided incremental gains. The selected 129-model ensemble generalized better than the 221-model ensemble despite its lower cross-validation AUC.

Keyboard typo augmentation of AI-generated DAIGT V2 texts produced a submission scoring 0.935 privately and 0.929 publicly, but the team did not select it for final scoring. The authors lacked a reliable local validation scheme to identify this submission's strength. Synonym replacement scored 0.914 privately, while spelling correction on both DAIGT V2 and the competition test set scored 0.903 privately despite a public score of 0.966.

solution_title: 3rd Place Solution - Madtown Machine Learning Madness
solution_summary: The team extended Bradley–Terry logistic regression by sharing team-strength parameters with a linear model of scoring margins. The final model used team identity and regular-season winning margins, outperforming their more elaborate feature and ensemble experiments. For uncertain matchups, two submissions assigned opposing 64% predictions using team IDs to choose sides. This deliberately randomized submission strategy benefited from a favorable outcome split and reduced reported log loss from about 0.473 to 0.427.

The solution combined a sound event detection model with a mel-spectrogram classifier, achieving a private score of 0.79 versus 0.76 and 0.77 individually. The SED model used an EfficientNet backbone, five-second inputs, and extensive augmentation, while the classifier used ResNeSt and seven-second random crops. A second classifier training round revised crop targets using out-of-fold predictions and ground-truth labels. Final predictions multiplied the two models' probabilities and marked the highest-confidence third of test predictions as positive.

solution_title: Unlocking Polymer Secrets: Our Approach to NeurIPS 2025 Open Polymer Prediction
solution_summary: The team transformed polymer SMILES into molecular descriptors, fingerprints, and graph statistics, then reduced redundancy with PCA and scaling. They trained separate models for each property, primarily using gradient boosting and random forests, and tested a graph neural network for Rg. Scaffold-based cross-validation, random hyperparameter search, and early stopping guided model development using weighted MAE. The final approach ensembled multiple models per property, and the team submitted its two strongest solutions.

The author trained cell-level EfficientNet models and combined them with teammates' image-level models. The final cell models learned from blended out-of-fold predictions, using mean squared error to reduce the effects of weak image-level labels; both multichannel and green-channel-only variants entered the final ensemble. Manually labeling mitotic spindle cells enabled a dedicated binary classifier that improved public score by about 0.008 and private score by about 0.014. The out-of-fold-target models scored around 0.528 publicly, with similar private performance.

The solution uses a streaming weighted ensemble of ElasticNet, XGBoost, and LightGBM to predict winsorised excess returns. It retrains on an 800-row sliding window and periodically updates hyperparameters with a narrow search. Position sizing, volatility estimation, regime multipliers, and smoothing are designed around the metric's volatility and underperformance penalties. Fixed ensemble weights outperformed Ridge stacking, while excess-return targets provided substantially more stable positions than raw returns.

The author first filled missing values with CatBoost, then obtained better scores using a large PyTorch neural network with batch normalization. Its excessive runtime motivated a smaller deep network implemented in Keras. The final described recipe used swish activations, AdamW, 70 epochs, and a batch size of 16,384, without callbacks. Runtime constraints drove the design: RAdam was more accurate but too slow, while mish performed worse than swish.
compute: 36,000-second runtime limit; personal AMD GPU mentioned

solution_title: Fast and light ensemble model (37th after 2nd rerun)
solution_summary: The post links to a GitHub repository containing a description and source code. It also embeds three images from that repository. The provided text contains no substantive explanation of the approach or results.

The solution used parallel tempering over simulated annealing instances with separate tabu lists and random seeds. Temperatures were distributed along a ladder and exchanged through odd-even swaps, while re-insertions were most useful when restricted to global-best improvements. Random swaps, rotations, local rotations, sort moves, and fixing positions supported the search, although progress eventually plateaued. Genetic algorithm experiments failed, and the author identified premature stopping, insufficiently tailored moves, and debugging issues as key lessons.

solution_title: Iterative Pseudo-Labeling with Multi-Architecture Ensemble LB 0.09 (0.067)
solution_summary: The solution combined a molecular GNN, a character-level 1D CNN, and a regression head on frozen PolyBERT embeddings. Five-fold validation stratified by SMILES length supported three rounds of ensemble pseudo-labeling, with fold-specific labels and agreement-based confidence weights. Final submissions combined models from all four training rounds using either per-target optimized weights or simple averaging. The optimized 12-model ensemble achieved a cross-validation weighted MAE of 0.044167, although the author questioned leaderboard reliability.

The agent combined a diverse library of Rock, Paper, Scissors policies through several adaptive selection layers. It expanded base policies with deterministic, cyclically shifted, and opponent-countering variants, then combined the three best policies by decayed performance. A further selector chose among scoring configurations using Dirichlet-sampled weights, while defensive rules switched to random play when confidence or performance was insufficient. Online LSTM scoring adapted well locally but performed worse on the leaderboard.

The team generated 64 images with SSD-1B, converted them into compact SVGs, and selected the candidate with the highest processed aesthetic score. Their approach exploited differences between OCR and scoring preprocessing by adding an OCR decoy, hidden prompt text, and searched aesthetic artifacts. Lightweight generation components and contour-based vectorization kept the pipeline within runtime and SVG size limits. Their selected SVGs averaged approximately 0.563 aesthetic score and 0.88 VQA score on validation.
compute: Two T4 GPUs, 32 images each; reliable single-threaded generation took about 30 seconds for 64 images, with about 2.5 seconds for SVG conversion.

solution_summary: The final solution combined the original and synthetic datasets and ensembled LightGBM regressors with rounding. Mutual information guided feature removal, alongside added engineered features. Optuna mainly searched model random seeds and the number of stratified folds, with limited additional parameter tuning. LightGBM and CatBoost classifiers were dropped, while t-SNE features and feature scaling did not improve results.

The author explored cell classification with Negative-Unlabeled labels and an ensemble of ten ResNet34 models. A symmetric AUC objective sought to reduce bias from falsely assigned cell labels without requiring class priors. Validation aligned better with leaderboard performance than BCE, but sigmoid optimization and separating cells from image bags limited improvements. solution_title: 11th place solution (with updated code on github)

solution_title: 8th place solution - a densely connected GNN

solution_summary: The solution ensembled three MixNet models predicting either three or six possible future trajectories. solution_summary: The solution combined target-specific spectral preprocessing with small neural networks. The solution adapted the Center-Resnet starter with mask and position inputs, focal-loss heatmaps, and revised regression targets. It predicted image-plane offsets and log depth, and doubled regression loss weights to improve balance with heatmap learning. Position jitter, Gaussian noise, and brightness and contrast augmentation supported training, while masks suppressed invalid predictions. The final submission scored 0.086 on the private leaderboard; several changes failed to improve results, and a locally promising head modification was discarded based on its public score.

The final submission combined EfficientNet-B7 with an average of EfficientNet-B6 and Inception-ResNet-v2, giving B7 half the total weight. Larger images, Noisy Student weights, training without a validation holdout, and horizontal and vertical flips were the main successful choices. Preprocessing and hyperparameter optimization were implemented as separate reusable components, with predictions saved for later blending. Cross-validation metrics guided the blend optimization.

The final pipeline used 36 tiles of 256×256 pixels per slide, with transpose and flip augmentation applied both to individual tiles and concatenated inputs. EfficientNet B0 and B1 models were trained with Adam, gradual warmup, and cosine annealing. Inference combined 32 test-time augmentations across two tile-generation modes and ensembled B0 fold 0 with B1 folds 0 and 1. Tile resolution, test-time augmentation, and fold selection based on agreement between cross-validation and leaderboard scores mattered most; removing white space reduced training loss without improving quadratic weighted kappa.

solution_summary: The solution converted forecasting into regression using one LightGBM model per store and three Keras networks with categorical embeddings. Their point predictions were combined by a weighted geometric mean, with LightGBM alone used for an anomalous final day and exponential smoothing applied across the forecast horizon. Hierarchical aggregation and tuned normal or skew-normal multipliers converted these predictions into quantiles. Blending multiplier-based estimates with historical daily and weekly sales quantiles was especially important at the lowest aggregation level. Recurrent models were explored but excluded from the final blend.

A RetinaNet treated the 42 distinct “is” triplets as detection classes, while another detector found objects for other relationships. LightGBM estimated relationship coefficients from object labels and box geometry, which were combined with detection confidences to score box pairs. solution_title: 11th Place Solution: AutoGluon with Two-Feature-Set Blending

solution_title: Kernel Density at the checkout: D'yakonov Alexander on winning the dunnhumby Shopper Challenge

solution_summary: The solution focused on identifying related transaction sequences, treating fraud as a pattern across similar samples. Grouping keys used V307, device and identity information, card identifiers with adjusted D features, and amount with day and address. A two-stage modeling pipeline improved the score by about 0.001. Grouping the card-and-D key across training and test data together, followed by rule-based result processing, provided a substantial further gain, reaching a reported leaderboard score range of 0.9600–0.9630.

The author extended a public ECG digitization pipeline with high-resolution homography, refined grid detection, and rectification. Two cascaded heatmap CNNs refined grid points using manually labeled examples, with a reported validation localization error of 0.146 pixels for the second network. Signal extraction used doubled image width, subpixel soft labels, coordinate features, and a ten-seed ensemble. Final signals combined overlapping lead-II estimates and applied Einthoven error correction.

The solution fed LightGBM classifier probabilities into a LightGBM regressor to improve prediction diversity and essay scoring. Word and character count n-grams were combined with engineered quotation, spelling-error, and sentence vocabulary features. Feature-importance filtering and modest hyperparameter tuning supported consistent private scores around 0.823, with the selected solution scoring 0.82397. TF-IDF and a Bayesian-regression extension were explored but not retained for the main solution.
compute: Approximately 96 seconds for submission predictions; final leaderboard reported 114 seconds. Classifier inference took 9–10 seconds and regressor inference about 2 seconds.

solution_title: 1st Place Solution for the AIMO3 Competition
solution_summary: This research-based account describes an inference pipeline for GPT-OSS-120B on a single H100 using memory optimizations and coordinated reasoning. It combines shared-prefix caching, 8-bit KV caches, and entropy-weighted aggregation of parallel generations. Persistent Jupyter kernels execute generated code and return verification feedback, while adaptive scheduling manages the notebook deadline. The author emphasizes prompt quality and inference engineering but provides no quantitative competition result.
compute: Single NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU

solution_summary: The final approach used an EfficientNet B3 initialized with Noisy Student weights and three classification heads on original 137×236 images. Switching from cropped to uncropped images was a major improvement, followed by aggressive Mixup and Cutmix. Training used weighted cross-entropy, AdamW, a one-cycle schedule, and three final epochs without augmentation. The author trained five folds and reported a score of 0.985 with a small validation-to-leaderboard gap.

The pipeline retrieved 160 misconception candidates per question-answer pair and reranked them to select 25. It fine-tuned an SFR-Embedding-2_R retriever and a quantized Qwen 32B reranker with LoRA, using question-grouped cross-validation and downsampled negatives. The reranker scored candidates through forced Yes/No token probabilities, with vLLM prefix caching accelerating repeated prompts. Hard-example mining improved validation but not leaderboard results, while several alternative input and quantization approaches did not work.

The solution used gradient boosting on mostly raw forecast features without preprocessing. Each station received all 75 forecasts from its four nearest mesos, supplemented by month, distance, and latitude differences. Eleven models were trained, one per forecast member, and averaged to optimize MAE. Validation used three contiguous blocks of years.

The solution combined 2D CNNs that used neighboring CT slices as channels or combined their feature maps to classify the middle slice. Preprocessing corrected gantry tilt and applied a manually designed nonlinear HU transform, which outperformed alternative windowing schemes. Models used patient-separated five-fold training, RAdam, spatial augmentation, fold ensembling, and test-time augmentation. A second-level linear model combined predictions from neighboring slices, giving a small gain over averaging; a segmentation-trained model was retained for diversity despite little log-loss benefit.

The solution prioritized simplicity and stability with a four-layer dense neural network. It trained on later training periods plus supplemental training data, transformed the target logarithmically, and removed 127 target outliers. Features were processed with a quantile transformer without additional feature engineering. Training used Adam and mean squared error with custom 20-fold validation and a 10-time-ID purge.

The solution combined EfficientNet study and opacity classifiers with three YOLOv5 detection models. NIH chest X-ray pretraining, soft-label self-distillation, pseudo-labeling, and heavy augmentation improved performance, while an auxiliary segmentation head contributed to the ensemble. Detection predictions were fused with weighted boxes fusion and combined with a blended None-class prediction. The final total score was 0.644 public and 0.617 private; the study ensemble improved cross-validation and public results but underperformed the best single model privately.

The solution combined HandyRL self-training with Monte Carlo Tree Search. Training for 5,000 epochs with a large minibatch produced a best score of 1112, while ensembling models from several epochs scored around 1100. The author found extended training and MCTS important, whereas larger models, parameter changes, player-centered inputs, and ensembling without MCTS did not work.

solution_title: [4th Place Solution] Conformer Encoder-Decoder Ensemble with beam search and edit_dist optimization
solution_summary: The solution ensembles two encoder-decoder models with adapted 12-layer Conformer encoders and small two-layer Transformer decoders. Normalized landmark coordinates and temporal differences were combined with extensive spatial, temporal, and token augmentation. Training used cross entropy followed by minimum error rate fine-tuning to better match character edit distance. Cached beam search improved the final ensemble by about 0.005, and replacing predictions for severely corrupted samples with a fixed string yielded another 0.005.
compute: Local RTX 3090; about two days per full 12-layer encoder training run; most experiments used shallower models on approximately 20% of the data.

solution_title: 137th place solution, ProtoSSM + 3 SED models ensemble(Private 0.94386)
solution_summary: The team blended diverse sound-event detection models with a ProtoSSM pipeline built on Perch embeddings. The SED models used EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, and MobileNet backbones with attention pooling over spectrogram features. Official-data overlays, Xeno-canto recordings, and pseudo-label mixup expanded training diversity, with pseudo-labeled models helping the ensemble even when their individual scores were weaker. Final combinations were selected using public scores because local validation correlated poorly, and the ensemble achieved 0.955 public and 0.944 private.

The solution relied on translated training data and an ensemble of models trained on different data variants. Adding XQuAD and MLQA helped, while translating Natural Questions provided further gains. The author compared logit averaging with span-score voting that supports different tokenizers. Models trained with iterative HardEM denoising and negative sampling remained useful for ensemble diversity despite weak standalone results. Several alternative pretrained models, architectures, translation models, and ensemble methods were tried without improving results.

The solution used a single 39 MB sequence model trained with intermediate CTC loss, without ensembling. Inputs included three-dimensional coordinates from both hands, eyes, lips, and pose landmarks, with pose and z coordinates improving the score. The network combined a dense layer, four Conv1D layers, and six Branchformer layers with relative multi-head attention and stochastic depth. Training ran for 150 epochs using Adam with Lookahead, cosine decay with warmup, and adversarial weight perturbation.

The team combined several ResNet variants, a multi-head model, staged models, and an ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet B7 using image sizes of 512, 640, and 736 pixels. EfficientNet B7 was trained with different losses and used four folds from a ten-fold split. They applied a referenced post-processing trick and compared ensemble weights based on leaderboard scores versus cross-validation scores. Both weighting approaches achieved a private score of 0.972, with the final submission scoring 0.969 publicly.

The team fine-tuned a Bengali wav2vec CTC model after filtering noisy competition samples using transcription error rates. A five-gram language model trained on external Bengali text improved decoding. Inference used length-based batching and selectively applied Demucs denoising according to preliminary transcript token counts. XLM-RoBERTa punctuation models provided the largest stated improvement, exceeding 0.030 on the leaderboard.
external_data: ["indicCorp v2", "Common Voice transcripts", "FLEURS transcripts", "OpenSLR transcripts", "OpenSLR37 transcripts", "OSCAR text"]

solution_summary: The solution used only text, combining parsed HTML with supplied and independently extracted boilerplate. More than 100 tag-weighted text sets were transformed into over 300 representations and modeled with logistic regression before ensembling. Writing-style metadata scored reasonably alone but added no useful ensemble improvement. The selected submission achieved a private score of 0.88817, while an unselected candidate achieved 0.88915.

solution_title: My best single model and solution
solution_summary: The solution emphasized feature engineering by separating listing attributes into manager and building groups, then linking and comparing them. It incorporated the published image-time leak and trained diverse classification and regression models across four feature datasets. Multiple stacking levels combined cross-validated predictions, with a weighted geometric blend of XGBoost and neural networks mixed with Extra Trees, followed by averaging two final stacks. The best single model scored 0.50379 publicly and 0.50500 privately; a description-source feature helped publicly but hurt privately, while prior correction contributed only a tiny gain.
compute: About four hours to generate four expensive features; a precomputed timeout.csv was provided.

solution_summary: The solution used DenseNet121 to classify 1,108 categories from 512×512 images. Training included geometric and brightness/contrast augmentation, normalization, Adam, and a decreasing learning rate. The authors averaged predictions and reported using plate leakage, controls, and several classification losses.

solution_title: 13th Place (Final) 1st Place (6 Weeks In) Final Solution
solution_summary: The solution combined LightGBM and Keras neural networks using 17 features built from lagged market statistics, timestamp averages, and asset identity. Its central improvement was reconstructing two targets and switching between their models according to whether missing asset observations forced the beta component to zero. Expanding temporal validation across different market regimes guided model selection, while additional Binance currencies provided small consistent gains. The best ensemble scored 0.0565 on the original test period and 0.0475 on the supplemental period.
compute: Submission inference completes in roughly 7 hours.
external_data: ["Public exchange API data from Binance, FTX, Coinbase, and Kucoin", "Additional Binance currencies including XRP and ZEC"]

solution_summary: The solution converted the expression matrix into long format and ensembled tabular neural networks, random forests, XGBoost models, and fine-tuned transformers. PCA denoising improved the tabular networks, while their learned categorical embeddings provided stronger tree features than directly added biological information. Transformer regressors used different input wording for DeBERTa and TinyBioBert, and multiple seeds diversified the ensemble. The final ensemble scored 0.553 on the public leaderboard and 0.753 on the private leaderboard.
compute: SaturnCloud A10 GPU; DeBERTa 20–25 epochs took 48–60 hours, and TinyBioBert 20–30 epochs took 24–30 hours, both with batch size 256.
external_data: ["ENSEMBL", "Wikipedia", "PubMed", "British Society for Immunology website", "OP2 Additional Features Dataset", "OP2 TabMod NN Embeddings Dataset"]

solution_summary: The team fully fine-tuned Gemma 2 and ArmoRM-Llama3 classifiers using prompt-grouped validation and additional deduplicated training data. Training both response orders together improved performance, and a teacher ensemble generated 240,000 pseudo-labeled examples for a second training stage. Final supervised fine-tuning produced a two-model ensemble with a 2:1 ratio and an old-leaderboard score of 0.868. Padding-free sequence packing and optimized attention kernels accelerated training and inference.
compute: 4× A100 80 GB for experiments during the final 10 days; inference on 2× T4 in FP16.
external_data: ["Deduplicated 33k dataset, 21k examples used", "lmsys-1m, 110k examples", "Other unnamed datasets, 130k examples"]

solution_summary: The solution combined pretrained MatchFormer, QuadTreeAttention, two scales of SuperPoint plus SuperGlue, and Patch2Pix. Match caps balanced the contributions of the matchers and reduced runtime, while MAGSAC estimated the fundamental matrix. Fixed-seed validation on 80 and 800 images guided implementation checks, although its correlation with leaderboard scores was weak. Patch2Pix provided only a slight improvement, and several refinement and filtering approaches failed to help.
