The team emphasized signal preprocessing: aligning the test distribution with training through cross-correlation and removing 50 Hz sine noise. Their ensemble contained six WaveNet variants, two CNN2d-WaveNet hybrids, one CNN2d, and one LightGBM model. The strongest models used either a CNN2d-WaveNet hybrid or WaveNet with cleaned signal, signal differences, and rolling minimum and maximum features. They excluded a noisy portion of the eighth training batch and blended fold predictions, with EMA decay providing a substantial benefit.

The solution averaged three small CNNs trained on normalized images with either white-region removal or duplicate-region removal. Short training, label smoothing, and class-balanced binary cross-entropy helped limit overconfidence in a low-signal task. Four-flip test-time augmentation was followed by probability rescaling and clipping. This calibration improved the reported CV loss from 0.655 to 0.640, with a private leaderboard loss of 0.666.

The final solution averaged ECA-NFNet-L1 and EfficientNet-B2/B6/B7 predictions across several input resolutions, using original and horizontally flipped inputs. All six cadence tiles were stacked and resized through a nearest-neighbor enlargement followed by area downsampling, which was important for benefiting from larger inputs. Training used LAMB, warm restarts, lightly weighted cross-entropy, MixUp, and horizontal flips. Normalized data from the earlier competition version and soft pseudo-labels for the new test set improved performance; the best single model achieved 0.79648 private AUC.
compute: Local RTX 3070, later RTX 3080 Ti; Kaggle TPUs for EfficientNet-B6/B7; seven training epochs with warm restarts.

solution_title: 11th place solution: Transformer with MFE distance embeddings (with code)
solution_summary: The solution modified Hugging Face BERT with RNA structure features, BPP attention injection, interleaved one-dimensional CNNs, and relative distance embeddings. Eternafold supplied the most useful folding features, while CapR accelerated convergence and bpRNA had uncertain benefit. Most final models shared a two-dimensional CNN within each transformer block to balance accuracy and training time. A single model scored approximately 0.1432 publicly, and averaging slightly different models brought the score below 0.14.

solution_title: 63rd Place Solution for the RSNA 2023 Abdominal Trauma Detection
solution_summary: The solution ensembled a single-stage CT-Net architecture covering all organs with a multi-stage pipeline for the kidneys, liver, and spleen. The multi-stage pipeline used EfficientNet-v1b0 to predict sub-volumes before applying CT-Net. The single-stage model alone achieved a leaderboard score of 0.61 without tuning. The author describes the final architecture as only partially finished.

The approach used JAN BRE's Baskfins and Fullbody datasets with EfficientNet models trained using ArcFace loss at 768-pixel resolution. Embeddings from nine models were combined, and cosine distance between training and test images supported identification; weaker ConvNeXt and water-removed-data models also contributed to the ensemble. Training ran for 30–50 epochs with five warm-up epochs followed by cosine learning-rate decay. A single validation fold achieved 0.72 without new_individual and 0.86 with a 0.6 threshold, after which models were retrained on all training data and the test threshold was increased to 0.65.
compute: TPU; limited available training time.
external_data: ["Baskfins and Fullbody datasets by JAN BRE"]

solution_summary: The author first trained a simple neural network and used its out-of-fold predictions to relabel the top 5% of suspected mislabeled examples. Retraining on corrected labels improved the reported leaderboard score from about 0.749 to 0.75010. A further round using pseudo-labels for 5% of the data reached about 0.75070, before blending with a shared post-processing kernel. Predictions were converted to percentile ranks before blending to reconcile differing model probability scales for AUC.

The submission combined 19 models spanning multiple architectures and fold strategies. Most models split images into left and right streams and fused pretrained backbone features through Mamba blocks before predicting three biomass components and deriving aggregate targets. Heavy augmentation, reduced backbone learning rates, and output scaling supported performance, while metadata supervision and test-time augmentation were dropped. Individual model sets generally exceeded 0.64, with the final three-backbone set reaching 0.67.

The solution ensembles LightGBM with XGBoost, combining Tweedie regression and classification predictions. Important components included pseudo-labeling samples without sii labels and percentile-based threshold optimization fitted within each training fold. Features included sequential statistics and dual categorical/numeric representations, with fold-specific median imputation. Evaluation and submission used five stratified folds across ten seeds, with per-seed Optuna tuning and voting to reduce seed sensitivity.

solution_title: Multi-Attempt Tool-Augmented LLM for Olympiad-Level Math Reasoning
solution_summary: The solution used an unnamed large language model served through vLLM to explore multiple mathematical reasoning trajectories. Each attempt could execute Python in a persistent Jupyter sandbox for symbolic computation and numerical verification. Final answers were extracted and range-checked, then combined through inverse-entropy weighted voting with early stopping on agreement. Dynamic time allocation, cached prefixes, and reusable sandbox kernels supported budget-aware parallel inference; no numerical evaluation result was reported.
compute: Tensor-parallel GPU inference with GPU memory utilization configured to 0.96; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The pipeline converts fluorescence recordings into spike trains using MATLAB and oopsi, then constructs pairwise correlation features under multiple spike and row filtering thresholds. Each correlation matrix is also transformed with the ND algorithm, retaining both original and transformed features. Features are Z-normalized before training random forest and gradient boosting models separately on normal-1 and normal-2 data. The four trained models feed a submission-generation script, although the writeup does not explain how their outputs are combined.
compute: Feature generation requires more than 32GB RAM and takes approximately 24–48 hours.

solution_title: [7th solution, my part] Single Stage Model Wins!
solution_summary: The solution combined a two-stage crop-and-classify model with a one-stage model intended to capture whole-image context and correlations across spinal levels. The one-stage model predicted level-point heatmaps and pixelwise grades, then pooled grades using the heatmaps to obtain levelwise predictions. Training exposed competition between localization and grading objectives, which the author associated partly with imprecise point labels and L5/S1 confusion. The final blend weighted the two-stage model at 0.75 and the one-stage model at 0.25, improving on the two-stage model despite implementation and training bugs.
compute: HP Z8 Fury-G5 Data Science Workstation

solution_title: 4th Place Solution for the Regression with an Abalone Dataset
solution_summary: The author adapted an existing notebook using OpenFE and a logarithmic target transformation. AutoGluon trained only tree-based models with a custom RMSLE metric. The final prediction was an equal-weight average of the adapted solution and the original notebook's output.

The solution combined LightGBM models trained on several target transformations using weighted averaging. Production and consumption were modeled separately, with residual targets based on historical values and an installed-capacity-normalized production target. Validation used a single February–May 2023 holdout, and historical-weather-derived features were excluded. The models were retrained once at the end of January 2024.

The author trained Keras CNN, LightGBM, and CatBoost models across multiple cleaned datasets and feature configurations. Removing simultaneous zero readings across meters at a site appeared more valuable than most feature engineering, while neural and tree models provided complementary predictions. One selected submission averaged over 30 experiments after correlation-based selection. The best private result instead used LightGBM to stack roughly ten leak-free predictions with meter identity, training the stacker on leaked target rows despite a worse public score.
compute: Zero-reading cleaning script ran for a few hours.

solution_title: 19th place solution: Loosen up, add a tree, and let the sparrows explore
solution_summary: The author built larger tree packings by slightly expanding an existing packing, inserting one overlapping tree, and using sparrow to resolve the overlap. Multiple random seeds and expansion factors produced candidates, with unsuccessful starts discarded early. The best candidates were compressed with sa_fast_v2 and eazy, yielding the author's best packings for most tree counts above 60.
compute: One illustrated sparrow overlap-resolution run took 70 seconds.

solution_title: 18th Place Solution: LGM with the mean of 3 months as targets
solution_summary: The solution used LightGBM regression with about 20 features derived from historical targets. Lagged values and rolling-window calculations captured temporal patterns at different offsets and window sizes. Predicting the mean of the three future months worked better than forecasting each month separately. The same predicted value was submitted for every forecast month within each county.

The solution combined three-fold, five-second SED models using three backbones with online Perch v2 embedding distillation and pseudo-labeled soundscapes. GRU, LSTM, LightGBM, and XGBoost stackers incorporated soundscape context, site/hour priors, and temporal features, with separate strategies for sonotype labels. Temporal smoothing and maximum-score propagation within related sonotype groups completed the pipeline. The final public and private scores were 0.94751 and 0.95675, with distillation, pseudo-labeling, and stacking each improving results.
compute: CPU inference for OpenVINO SED backbones; PyTorch heads and stackers.

solution_title: 326th Place Solution: AI Agent Security - Multi-Step Tool Attacks
solution_summary: The team reverse-engineered the deployed scoring predicates and tested attack recipes against real target models and reconstructed guardrails. A forged analysis-channel framing increased public-score throughput, but its exfiltration submission scored zero privately as anticipated. Their second final submission allocated roughly 80% to destructive writes and 20% to obliquely requested email actions, achieving 8.01 privately. Only the email component survived, exposing a costly allocation error despite their correct prediction of public/private divergence.
compute: Evaluator live-exploration budget: 9,000 seconds per model; targets run as quantized GGUFs.

solution_summary: The solution forecast monthly density multipliers with a small TensorFlow GRU rather than directly predicting density values. It first adjusted historical densities to a common census population basis and constructed overlapping county sequences. Training used the largest 90% of counties with county-grouped validation, while smaller counties received last-value predictions before adjustment. Public leaderboard probing supplied multiplier corrections that substantially improved the forecasts; a linear model with the same postprocessing was also submitted.

solution_title: RL PPO Light Layer on Base Layer; Final Rank 1231/10148 (4362.2 Final Score)
solution_summary: The solution added a small policy to the public Pipe-16 agent to choose among eight strategy options at four game stages. Exact simulator branching evaluated counterfactual actions on the same game state, removing seed noise that prevented ordinary PPO and GRPO from learning reliably. Search distillation followed by VinePPO improved close mirror matches, although wheat carry strategies remained vulnerable against an older opponent. The final agent performed better in 14 paired games and worse in seven against the previous best, and settled about 100 rating points higher live.

The team combined one-stage and two-stage solutions, with the described two-stage branch locating spinal keypoints before classifying cropped regions. One classifier fused sagittal and axial features, while another used single-view 3D regions centered on predicted coordinates. Multiple backbones and view-specific flip augmentation contributed to the ensemble. The described branch reported CV 0.373, public LB 0.35, and private score 0.40.

solution_title: FLG's Approach - Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Focus on Performance - 4th place
solution_summary: The agent used a custom DoubleCone convolutional network trained through self-play reinforcement learning, with imitation-learning experiments guiding architecture selection. Its observations combined current board features with three turns of history, while collision prevention and randomized communication costs made learning more practical. Training progressed from resource-focused shaped rewards to mostly outcome-focused zero-sum rewards, using Vtrace and a delayed teacher. CPU inference constraints led to a smaller final model, supplemented by a tiny transferred model and pattern matching to build longer action queues.
compute: Competition inference used CPU-only VMs, mostly appearing single-core; the imitation-learning dataset was around 300 GB.

solution_summary: The author averaged a single CatBoost model with predictions from two public notebooks. Feature engineering emphasized polar coordinates between P_2 and other features, together with statistics and interactions for groups sharing similar means or high correlations. Target encoding, PCA, binning, and lagged-data aggregations supplemented these features, while null importance reduced roughly 2,200 features to 1,200. The standalone model achieved mean CV and public leaderboard scores of 0.795; averaging improved the public score to 0.799 and the private score to 0.807.

The final submission ensembled five models each from Qwen3-8B, gemma-2-9b-it, and Hunyuan-7B-Instruct, including merged LoRA adapters. Concatenating adapter bottlenecks reduced causal-language-model inference cost while retaining much of the benefit of seed ensembles. Labels were reduced to 37 classes, prompts listed question-specific candidates, and affine output alignment supported combining causal and classification models. Shared frozen classification heads mitigated severe classification-model merging degradation, although gains remained inconsistent, and vLLM was excluded after slow T4 inference.
compute: T4x2 instance used for vLLM inference experiments

solution_summary: The post asks whether others are eagerly awaiting writeups from the leading competitors. It expresses interest in learning their approaches. It provides no solution methods or implementation details.

The approach used CenterNet-style detection with heatmap, offset, depth, and trigonometric pose heads, plus an auxiliary width-height task. ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18 and KITTI 3DOP-pretrained DLA34 backbones with FPNs benefited strongly from increased input resolution. Five-fold models were trained with geometric and color augmentation, RAdam, and cosine learning-rate annealing, then ensembled by averaging raw output maps. Mask filtering, distance-based suppression, duplicate-image ensembling, and score filtering completed inference; the ensemble achieved validation mAP 0.2736 and a private score of 0.115.
models_pretrained: ["ResNet18 pretrained on ImageNet", "DLA34 pretrained on KITTI 3DOP"]

solution_summary: The solution averaged six EfficientNet experiments, pairing larger networks with lower-resolution inputs to reduce overfitting. Images were cropped from gray borders, transformed into a common image type during training, and heavily augmented. Models were pretrained on the full 2015 dataset before five-fold training on the 2019 data, with eight-way dihedral augmentation at inference. The more diverse final ensemble replaced two models with variants trained using Ben's preprocessing and achieved a private score of 0.933.
compute: Approximately 10 minutes for 40 prediction passes over 1,928 images; six-model ensemble took 50 minutes for committing and 6 hours for submitting.
external_data: ["2015 diabetic retinopathy dataset, train and test"]

solution_summary: The solution trained Faster R-CNN and Cascade R-CNN detectors through MMDetection, with ImageNet-pretrained ResNeXt101 in the best single model. Fine-tuning on six class-frequency subsets addressed imbalance and improved the public score by approximately 0.05. Horizontal flips, multi-scale inference, parent-class expansion, and weighted ensembling produced a final public score of 0.608. Increasing the per-image detection limit to 600 also formed part of the final submission.
compute: Approximately 20 days to train Faster R-CNN + ResNeXt101 for 24 epochs; hardware unspecified.

solution_title: 45th place with XGBoost in first Kaggle competition
solution_summary: The solution used XGBoost throughout a two-stage pipeline, with AUC guiding optimization and tuning. Statement histories were summarized using 16 aggregations per numerical feature, including Hull and exponential moving averages. First-stage models generated out-of-fold predictions for two next-month delinquency outcomes, which were aggregated and added to roughly 3,000 features for the final XGBoost Pyramid model. The final training used the full dataset with round counts informed by CV early stopping, and the submitted standalone model scored 0.80798 on the private leaderboard.
compute: GPU used; GPU resources and remaining time were limited, with about 48 hours left for first-stage OOF prediction.

solution_summary: The pipeline corrected image orientation, pruned candidate image pairs with a trained scene classifier, and supplemented retrieval using NetVLAD. It extracted RDD features at two resolutions, matched them with LightGlue, and merged the matches. Pair pruning mainly saved runtime, enabling multiscale matching that raised the reported public/private scores to 48.02/47.88. Alternative pair classifiers and mixing other keypoint detectors with RDD descriptors did not work.

The author built regression models with holiday indicators and log relative GDP features, eventually selecting Extra Trees. Setting relative GDP to 0.4 for every country in 2022 produced the largest improvement, reducing public MAPE to about 7.5. Integer conversion and subtracting one further improved the author's predictions to about 6.13 public MAPE. The final solution combined these predictions with an adjusted public submission using weights of 0.175 and 0.825, then rounded the result, achieving about 5.93 private MAPE and 5.00 public MAPE.

The solution uses a fairly simple neural network classifier. It achieved approximately 81.818% classification accuracy. TF-IDF, spelling normalization, and neural network hyperparameter optimization were suggested as future improvements rather than reported experiments.
compute: GeForce GT 755M; Python 2.7 under Ubuntu 14.04

solution_summary: The final submission blended four models with different validation strategies and training-data partitions. The models used time-series or grouped cross-validation and were split by week, by category, or left unsplit. Grouping by year and month worked on both leaderboard splits, while the blend scored 0.56715 in cross-validation and 0.60101 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: Bronze Solution: Robust LoRA Adapter Selection and Packaging
solution_summary: The final submission packaged a public LoRA adapter for the official Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16 model, prioritizing compatibility and reproducibility. The pipeline discovered candidate adapters, normalized their formats, checked module and rank constraints, and produced the required submission archive. Because vLLM was unavailable in the final environment, it selected the preferred huikang_tinker adapter without validation-backed candidate selection. Additional supervised fine-tuning remained disabled because small runs could improve some task families while degrading others.
models_pretrained: ["Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16", "huikang_tinker adapter", "huikang_v27 adapter", "huikang_v20 adapter", "kienngx_submit adapter", "kienngx_v13 adapter", "kienngx_v4_small adapter", "llkh0a_unsloth adapter"]

solution_summary: The pipeline combined signal calibration and noise reduction with transit modeling and neural networks. Temporal binning, smoothing, normalization, and subtracting dark current before nonlinearity correction improved signal preparation. Pairing signals with all calibration files expanded training diversity. Modeling used a CNN with filter kernels and a projection layer alongside transit and tree-model stacking, although robust postprocessing remained unresolved.

The post describes cleaning and feature engineering for trip classification without specifying a final model. The author removed NULL-description rows when other descriptions were available within a visit and aggregated scan counts by visit and UPC to reconcile reversed scans. They inferred day and within-day visit features from the combined train and test sequence. UPC processing, count vectorization, and aggregate counts and sums completed the described approach.

The final submissions used diverse nine-model ensembles of fine-tuned language models with Nelder-Mead weighting. Custom heads combined hidden-layer averaging, an LSTM, vocabulary-level dense features, and handcrafted text statistics. Reinitializing upper transformer layers, removing dropout, and clipping gradients improved validation performance. Both selected ensembles achieved a private score of 0.452.
compute: 1× GeForce RTX3090

solution_summary: The solution identified 7,820 leaked test targets using 34 feature sets. Its machine-learning component stacked three XGBoost models: a tuned version of a shared kernel, a selected-column model, and a principal-component model. Feature engineering emphasized time-series structure in sorted column sets. The tuned shared-kernel component reportedly achieved 1.37.
The post links to the author's code and prompts in a Kaggle notebook. It requests feedback and explanations of MNIST hints. No solution methods or results are described in the provided text.

The final approach used a regularized Random Forest trained on the competition data and an additional obesity risk dataset. It retained all original features and added BMI and BMI prime multiplied by physical activity frequency; BMI was particularly important. The author tuned parameters with 300 Optuna trials using five-fold stratified group cross-validation, taking approximately four hours on CPU. The overview reports a CV score of 0.8892 and a private leaderboard score of 0.8825, although subsequent experiment tables report slightly different scores.
compute: CPU only; approximately 4 hours for training with 300 Optuna trials.

solution_summary: The project classifies crime descriptions into 39 category labels using a hybrid TextCNN and GRU network. It implements training and prediction with TensorFlow 2.x Keras and exports a model, vocabulary, label mapping, and training parameters. Prediction primarily loads the best validation checkpoint. No evaluation scores or comparison with alternative approaches are reported.

solution_title: How to drop more than 500 places!
solution_summary: The author adapted a shared benchmark into R and tuned radial-kernel support vector machines using repeated five-fold cross-validation. Most targets achieved RMSE between 0.3 and 0.4, while phosphorus remained substantially harder. Adding untransformed satellite data slightly improved pH and sand predictions, which were combined with the original predictions for one final submission. A second final submission ensembled the phosphorus SVM with a random forest, but leaderboard results were disappointing despite the validation estimates.

The solution used a single-stage video event model combining a mostly 2.5D EfficientNetV2 backbone with late 3D convolutions. Grayscale frame stacks provided temporal context across 15 frames while enabling efficient cached inference. SoccerNet pretraining improved the score by roughly 0.02, and fixed-video validation reached 0.857 with strong leaderboard correlation. The final system retrained on all available data and blended two models on alternating frames, taking about five hours to run.
compute: Inference used both CPU cores with threading; 2.5 hours per model, 25 minutes per video, approximately 5 hours for the final two-model solution.

solution_summary: The author used a single T5 generative model to map topics directly to lists of document identifiers. Training combined document-to-identifier memorization with topic-to-document recommendation, with memorization needed before recommendation could work. An additional task predicting a topic's position in the topic tree did not improve results. The approach achieved a public leaderboard score of 0.25 and was described as computationally demanding and highly sensitive to hyperparameters.

The solution ensembled DeBERTa-v3-large and DeBERTa-v3-base models trained with target-specific prediction heads, combining full-data and fold-trained models. Back-translation pretraining, Feedback Prize 2 pretraining, and pseudo-labeling improved performance, with particularly strong vocabulary gains from back-translation. Pearson and ranking losses helped harder targets, while target-specific ensemble weights balanced differences between models. The selected pseudo-labeling and Optuna ensemble achieved a reported private score of 0.43363, although tuning on all training OOF predictions made validation optimistic and a manually weighted alternative performed slightly better.
compute: Inference took 2 hours 20 minutes on 2 NVIDIA T4 GPUs for 23 full-training models and 23 fold models.

solution_summary: The team built a CatBoost-centered ensemble with DeepTables neural networks, combining augmented and non-augmented models through CV-based hill climbing. Validation used StratifiedGroupKFold grouped by the first letter of the game ruleset name and repeated three times. Agent-swapping augmentation, target transformation, one-hot encoding, and restrained feature engineering and selection contributed to the approach. Prediction scaling and sign-dependent blending with quantile models gave similar improvements of about 0.004–0.005, while discrepancies between CV and leaderboard performance complicated model selection.

The solution uses hierarchical Bayesian linear regression with Student-t observation noise and only daily-return inputs. It predicts the next two daily returns while setting minute-return predictions to zero. The Stan implementation places normal priors on regression coefficients and inverse-gamma priors on variance parameters, with Student-t degrees of freedom specified as 2.6. The author reports relatively consistent performance across cross-validation and leaderboard evaluations.

The solution used a publicly shared BERT masked language model as its foundation. External datasets from @mlconsult substantially improved the public score without hurting private performance. The two final submissions, with and without these datasets, scored almost identically at 0.372 and 0.373. The nine-hour kernel training limit constrained further training and model development.
compute: 9-hour kernel training time limit

solution_summary: The solution ensembled four EfficientNetV2 models across three image resolutions, including two large models trained with different seeds at 768 pixels. Geometric augmentation, geometric test-time augmentation, dropout, stochastic depth, focal loss, and pseudo labels for time steps 3 and 5 were useful. The ensemble scored 0.6936 on the validation folder, compared with roughly 0.690–0.692 for its first three individual models. Additional pseudo-label rounds, broader appearance augmentation, and several temporal 2.5D or 3D architectures did not help.

The author used brute-force computation to estimate whether each starting cell was alive or dead from a centered 7×7 block of stopping cells. The algorithm incorporated quarter-turn rotational symmetry and inversion symmetry. Computation ran across a 376-core Xeon cluster using OpenMP and MPI. An SSE implementation was left unfinished, and a GPU implementation was suggested but not attempted.
compute: 376-core cluster with E5420 Intel Xeon 2.5GHz processors

solution_summary: The post links to an external article explaining the features used in the team's final model. The author describes this as the team's first NLP problem and Kaggle competition. The post itself provides no concrete features, models, or implementation details and thanks the community.

solution_title: Temporal Modeling Approaches for Large-scale Youtube-8M Video Understanding
solution_summary: The authors provide data providers and model configurations for temporal video understanding approaches used in the competition. They evaluate temporal CNNs, two-stream recurrent networks, and fast-forward recurrent networks. The seven-layer fast-forward LSTM achieves the highest reported GAP@20 of 0.82750, while the two-stream GRU reaches 0.82366. Training and testing commands use PaddlePaddle with GPU execution enabled.

solution_title: 13th Place Solution for the UBC-OCEAN Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined separate WSI and TMA models, using pathology SSL feature extractors with multiple-instance learning and additional Transformer/CNN classifiers for TMA images. WSI processing used 10x magnification and tissue tiles, while synthetic TMA samples were generated from WSI tumor regions and augmented using stain references. Stratified group cross-validation and exponential moving averages helped manage overfitting, and embedding-distance and probability thresholds identified outliers. Inference took roughly 11 hours 15–30 minutes; manually screened synthetic TMA samples achieved a private score of 0.58, but that submission was not selected as final.
compute: Multiprocess CPU image loading and tiling took around 5.5–6 hours; total inference took approximately 11 hours 15–30 minutes, with at most 350 tiles per image.

solution_summary: The solution extended a public imitation-learning bot with a policy operating at individual-unit level. It added squeeze-and-excitation blocks, wider hidden layers, a center action, and learned city actions. Training used roughly 2,300 episodes and included demonstrations from second-place bots. The author reported improvements over the original baseline, while proposed U-Net ensembling and rule-based safeguards remained unimplemented.

The solution built XGBoost models on group-level activity aggregates and combined their predictions in a second-level model. Representative people-based cross-validation required removing a dominant all-negative group and deduplicating large groups. The second level incorporated leakage-derived information and temporal features, with additional manual overrides inferred through public leaderboard probes. The final submission averaged the best leaderboard and cross-validation models, which produced a substantial improvement.

solution_title: Some useful and useless ideas(maybe silver solution- 25th place)
solution_summary: The team combined imitation learning, rules, and reinforcement learning, with this account focusing on imitation learning experiments. Spatial and global features supported independent agent predictions using a multiscale residual architecture. Rotation and flip augmentation, time-aware test-time augmentation, stage-dependent sampling, and episode filtering were explored, although the author does not specify which all survived into the final submission. A U-Net approach underperformed independent agents and was not fully implemented, while final rule improvements covered defense, offense, unit allocation, and city strategy.
compute: TTA was disabled when estimated total execution time exceeded 3 seconds.

solution_title: 9th place solution + Pseudo label + IterativeImputer + Multi AutoGluon
solution_summary: The author trained five AutoGluon pipelines with different treatments of missing data and pseudo labels. Missing targets were first labeled using an ensemble of public solutions, then refined using trained AutoGluon models. Iterative imputation with a decision tree provided an alternative feature representation, alongside an untouched training pipeline and FTTransformer models. The five solutions were combined using performance-based weights.
compute: Only a few hours available for the competition.

solution_title: #2nd Place Solution(Team Peaky Blenders): Blends Of Blends.
solution_summary: The solution combined 56 models, excluding AutoGluon, with engineered features drawn from public contributions and tuned XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost models. Linear regression combined out-of-fold predictions, including additional weighted combinations of model and feature subsets, followed by forward feature selection. The final prediction blended this ensemble at weight 0.6 with a teammate's ensemble at weight 0.4, incorporating PyBoost and two public AutoGluon solutions. The blend scored 0.86943 publicly and 0.86902 on the private leaderboard; AutoGluon out-of-fold predictions were unavailable because of time constraints and model-loading errors.

solution_title: 213th Place: Two Coordinate Heads, One Better Step
solution_summary: The team retained a public cell-detection and tracking pipeline and focused its improvements on correcting detected coordinates before linking. Their new bounded MLP head used frozen UNet features, directional differences, and local detector logits, and was blended with the public coordinate head. Scaling the blended displacement by 1.15 counteracted vector shrinkage and produced scores of 0.957 public and 0.923 private. Most other changes provided little benefit, while writing floating-point centroids reduced performance despite preserving the tracking graph.
models_pretrained: ["Public temporal UNet3D and edge transformer", "Public V1284 coordinate head", "DeepCenter"]
compute: 2×T4; about 14 minutes on visible test, within 12 hours on hidden test; 7.5-hour repair deadline.

solution_summary: The solution used aggregate, peak-focused, detection-focused, luminosity, and light-curve fitting features with LightGBM, XGBoost, and MLP models. Training used both weighted multiclass log loss and standard multiclass log loss. Predictions from the weighted-loss models received class-specific weights optimized by gradient descent. The reported public and private scores were 0.838 and 0.851; autoencoders and augmentation did not work.

solution_title: My model architecture with code | part of the 11th place solution
solution_summary: The author built a modified U-Net with a SE-ResNeXt-50 backbone selected for its balance of accuracy and training time. The architecture adds multiple hypercolumns, deep supervision for empty-mask classification and intermediate masks, an OC block, dropout, and dilated convolutions. It achieved private and public scores of 0.881 and 0.865, respectively. Training could be fragile, with some random runs becoming stuck in local minima.

solution_title: How about that, my imitation learning / resnet model is my best sub
solution_summary: The best-performing model was an imitation-learning policy with a ResNet-like architecture and swish activations. It trained for 16 epochs on approximately four million games or replays filtered with a cutoff around 1100. Reinforcement-learning models trained for three to five days initially performed best, but the earlier imitation model became stronger near the end of the competition. The imitation model trained in hours and had approximately 96 MB of weights, barely fitting the size limit.
compute: RL training took 3–5 days; imitation training took hours. Hardware was unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution used LightGBM with separate feature processing for tile and layout data. Tile features summarized graph sizes and node/configuration attributes, while layout features flattened configuration arrays and removed constant and duplicate columns. Matching test graphs to structurally similar training graphs was the key layout strategy, based on the idea that they represented the same models at different batch sizes. Targets were min-max scaled and trained with cross-entropy loss using fixed boosting rounds without validation.

solution_title: 15th Place Solution Meta features ,FE, DART, CAT, XG , Tabnet , MLP , ensemble 😊
solution_summary: The final solution combined LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost, TabNet, MLP, and AutoML models using Optuna-derived weights in log-odds space. Flattened customer meta features and engineered statement aggregates were central, with temporal differences, percentage changes, and selected statement snapshots providing additional signal. Neural models benefited from Gaussian scaling, while hybrid meta and aggregate features required lower learning rates. The selected submission scored 0.80838 on the private leaderboard; another submission reached 0.80852.
compute: CatBoost configured for GPU devices 0 and 1.

solution_summary: The solution trained EfficientNetB5 on RGB images resized to 512, with flips, rotations, FiveCrop, and ImageNet normalization. Five stratified folds were trained for 10 epochs each using cross-entropy, Adam, and cosine learning-rate scheduling, retaining each fold's lowest-loss checkpoint. Inference averaged predictions from the five models.

The final pipeline concatenates embeddings from three public retrieval models and reranks candidates with an unfine-tuned Qwen 32B AWQ model through vLLM. It presents nine numbered candidates and reorders them using logits, then appends sixteen retrieval candidates to produce twenty-five outputs. Attempts to fine-tune retrieval models on generated data performed worse than available public models. The final solution therefore required no author-performed fine-tuning.
compute: Multi-GPU training was explored; hardware unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution combined public open-book science exam pipelines with a DeBERTa v3 large model. Removing duplicates and missing entries reduced a 60,000-example dataset to roughly 40,000 training examples. Using a search pipeline with 270,000 articles improved the reported leaderboard score from 0.846 to 0.901, with the first model supplying backup predictions. Final answers were the three options with the highest probabilities across the two prediction sources.
external_data: ["60k dataset from the public open-book baseline", "270k article dataset"]

solution_summary: The final solution averaged predictions from LightGBM, XGBoost, and logistic regression. Feature selection used tree-model importance and logistic-regression significance, because adding more variables increased log loss. AdaBoost, random forest, SVM, and ridge performed poorly on the previous year's results. Capping extreme probabilities and reversing near-even predictions also did not work.

The post announces that the final submission is available on GitHub in a solution folder. It acknowledges pysearch, a public solution by gary moss, and the code golf community. It provides no substantive description of the solution pipeline or results.

The team combined 23 regression models spanning convolutional transformers, U-Nets, and LSTMs with different training conditions. Most models trained on years 1–7 of low-resolution data and validated on a subsample of year 8, with some incorporating high-resolution data or pseudo-labeled test data. Climate-invariant features, uncertainty-aware loss, and extra hard examples improved individual models. Target-specific stacking and manually weighted ensemble combinations produced a submitted private score of 0.78503; later experiments showed further gains from full-data climate-invariant features.
compute: One member used 1x RTX 4090 and subsampled training data; a post-competition full-data lightweight CNN took approximately one day on RTX 4090.

solution_summary: The solution preserved subtle steganographic signals by reconstructing RGB images without JPEG rounding or truncation and predicting 10 cover/quality-factor/algorithm targets. Validation stratified images by JPEG quality and binned insertion amount, using one selected fold as a holdout. Pixel-preserving augmentations, especially grid shuffling, helped models focus on fine stego information. EfficientNet and ResNeXt models used eight-way TTA and ensembling, with the ensemble reporting public/private scores of 944/929.

The solution combined EfficientNet-B6 with Noisy Student, ResNeSt50, and a base patch-16 Vision Transformer, using stratified five-fold validation on the 2020 data. Training explored several augmentations and losses, with CutMix plus FMix improving validation and label smoothing giving the best loss performance. Inference used eight transpose/flip augmentations and simple prediction averaging. EfficientNet-B6 was the strongest single model, achieving 0.903 on the public leaderboard and 0.8946 on the private leaderboard.
models_pretrained: ["EfficientNet B6 with Noisy Student", "ResNeSt50", "Vision Transformer base patch16"]

solution_summary: The team combined transformer models with different architectural changes and training pipelines. Strong contributors included Eterna base-pair probabilities, relative positional bias, ResiDual with RMS normalization, and recurrent layers within encoder blocks. Signal-to-noise-weighted sampling allowed lower-quality samples to contribute, while filtered multi-stage pseudo-label training improved performance. Flip test-time augmentation and diverse model combinations contributed to the final ensemble.
compute: Final pseudo-label pipeline stage: under 2 hours per fold on a single RTX 4090.

solution_title: Reachability, Robustness, and Measurement in a Multi-Step Tool-Attack Benchmark
solution_summary: The authors constructed exfiltration candidates that exploited the public guardrail's inspection of destinations while leaving payloads unchecked. They increased score through repeated tool hops and unique candidate URLs, reporting near-eight-hop behavior for GPT-OSS and five hops for Gemma, with qualifications about those measurements. Source inspection and repeated submissions showed that replay throughput and runtime variability strongly affected public scores. The submitted approach scored 112.375 publicly but zero privately, overturning their earlier belief that public performance predicted transfer to the held-out guardrail.
compute: Benchmark targets ran as GGUF on T4-class GPUs; each replay phase had an 8750-second wall-clock budget.

solution_summary: The author used XGBoost with extensive feature engineering, generating roughly 100,000 candidate features. Feature importance filtering selected different feature sets for each question and improved CV from about 0.695 to 0.701. Adding predicted probabilities for earlier questions increased CV to 0.7032, with public and private scores of 0.701 and 0.702.

The final pipeline combined image-level and cell-level DenseNet121 classifiers using four-channel 768×768 images and pretrained weights from the previous HPA competition. HPA segmentation supplied masked cell crops, with heuristics removing problematic edge cells. Two cell classifiers were weighted together, then multiplied by image predictions; Negative predictions used a maximum rule and suppressed other classes. Extensive test augmentation and mixed precision were important, and the final submission scored 0.547 public and 0.530 private.
compute: Quadro RTX 5000 and RTX 2080S; cell-classifier epoch took 12–13 hours with mixed precision versus about 20 hours at full precision; 9-hour Kaggle inference limit.

solution_summary: The author built a two-scale neural network that localizes fish, refines spatial masks, and applies soft attention before classification. Five supervised masks describe the full fish region and its directional parts, with three additional masks reconstructed during refinement. Balanced pixel weights and constrained mask targets helped address the tendency to predict background everywhere. Localization appeared successful on roughly 70–90% of images by informal inspection, including multiple fish in unseen images, but the classification component failed to learn.

solution_title: 56th place solution: multimodal, treat montage as 2D image, channel swapping
solution_summary: The solution ensembled spectrogram, EEG-image, and multimodal models, mostly using EfficientNet backbones. Eleven downsampled EEG montages were stacked as a two-dimensional image, and symmetrical channel swapping substantially improved validation. Multimodal models combined separate spectrogram and EEG backbones, outperforming either modality alone. Training used all data first and then a subset described as having KL loss above 5.5. SLSQP-optimized ensemble weights yielded CV 0.2768 and private score 0.335807.

The author aligned the imagery to RGB resolution and concatenated it into 20-channel inputs for two U-Net-like segmentation networks. One network handled land and water classes, while the other handled large and small vehicles. Autoencoder initialization, staged encoder freezing, rotational patches, and vehicle-focused sampling supported training. Inference combined central patch predictions across offsets and rotations, with CCCI and shape-based rules refining the water classes.

The solution combined cased and uncased large BERT embeddings with 69 handcrafted linguistic and coreference features. A dense classification head combined two embedding MLPs, two Siamese models, and a feature MLP. Entity-substitution augmentation produced easier examples and overconfident predictions, while stacking and BERT fine-tuning did not deliver the expected gains. Final predictions were clipped at 0.01, although the authors later found that removing clipping was better.

The solution centered on numeric-value counts computed across training data and real test samples. Raw values were paired with versions masked according to whether their values repeated, then modeled with upsampled LightGBM. Additional count features, stricter rarity filters, and target-conditioned features provided small improvements. Linear blending of LightGBM and XGBoost variants reached a public score of 0.925.

solution_title: 67th Place Solution for the Kaggle - LLM Science Exam Competition
solution_summary: The team used an open-book multiple-choice pipeline with TF-IDF retrieval over cleaned articles and an ensemble of two fine-tuned DeBERTa large models. One model used all 60,000 training records with a maximum length of 256, while the other used 30,000 records with a maximum length of 512. Scoring answer options separately allowed larger inference contexts, and a revised input format gave a small improvement. Dense retrieval experiments consistently underperformed TF-IDF.
compute: Kaggle TPU; approximately 8.5 hours for two epochs on 30,000 records at maximum length 512.

solution_summary: The pipeline extracted image-level features with 2D CNNs and exam-level features with a 3D CNN, saving both to disk. A sequence model combined slice embeddings from multiple 2D models with the 3D exam embeddings. The 2D models were EfficientNet-B3, B4, and B5 trained with several geometric and intensity augmentations. The sequence model used the RSNA metric as its loss.

solution_title: My 7 day journey in this competition and solution sharing
solution_summary: The solution combined XGBoost and neural-network predictions with weights of 0.7 and 0.3. Its strongest features were more than 300 visitor-history features, including lags, differences, weighted moving averages, and rolling statistics. Separate features and models were built for each of the 39 forecast horizons, excluding visitor and reservation information unavailable at prediction time. Validation used a 39-day period starting March 12, 2017, and the ensemble scored 0.515 on the private leaderboard. A later Golden Week adjustment improved the single XGBoost model's private score from 0.516 to 0.508.

The author's contribution combined site-specific CNNs for Wi-Fi floor and absolute-position prediction with LSTM and GRU models for relative sensor motion. Wi-Fi inputs summarized RSSI over five temporal sections and included iBeacon signals, while validation grouped paths and stratified floors. Ensemble variance supplied uncertainty estimates for a cost-minimization smoother, followed by heuristics moving predictions toward grid points. Device-leak-based scale and rotation calibration improved the leaderboard error by 0.03 meters, while adding uncalibrated data did not help.

The author used a pooled model across subjects, particularly a RUS boosted tree ensemble, because it generalized better than their subject-specific implementation. Predictions from roughly 100-second windows were averaged into segment predictions, and training-group class proportions gave the best priors. The general model scored about 0.73 in local cross-validation and 0.74 on the leaderboard, while subject-specific models scored about 0.74 locally and 0.63 on the leaderboard. Explicit subject identifiers reduced performance.

solution_title: 90th Place Solution for the Bengali.AI Speech Recognition
solution_summary: The author fine-tuned a pretrained Bengali speech recognition model using a shared training notebook. The feature extractor and feature encoder were frozen, and training covered 10% of the training data for three epochs. Increasing decoder beam width to 2048 improved both public and private scores by 0.003. Fine-tuning took 16 hours on an unspecified GPU, while inference took about eight hours.
compute: 16 hours fine-tuning on an unspecified GPU; approximately 8 hours inference.

solution_summary: The solution combined label cleanup, RoBERTa span extraction, candidate reranking, and whitespace-aware postprocessing. Eight base models combined base and large variants, different output architectures, and two random seeds, with sentiment-balanced batches and stochastic weight averaging improving stability. A RoBERTa reranker predicted candidate Jaccard scores and combined them with base-model scores to select the final span, improving private scores by approximately 0.003–0.005. Sequence bucketing doubled inference speed, while postprocessing delivered a reported private improvement of 0.012.
models_pretrained: ["RoBERTa Base and Large pretrained on SQuAD2"]
compute: Sequence bucketing reportedly doubled inference speed; hardware and absolute runtime were not specified.

solution_summary: The author developed and compared multiple tool-attack submissions using AI coding assistants, with the best version scoring 0.615. Its key improvement was low-overhead environment snapshot restoration, which enabled more than 1,000 candidates within the time budget. Simple multi-turn prompts outperformed elaborate obfuscation, combined malicious requests, and large YAML payloads. Interface mistakes and failure to execute candidates through the environment explained several errors and zero-score submissions.
models_pretrained: ["Gemini 3.7 flash", "Gemini 3.8 flash", "Gemini 3.1 Pro", "Claude Sonnet 4.6 (thinking)", "GPT-OSS120B", "GPT-OSS (evaluation target)", "Gemma 4 (evaluation target)"]

solution_title: 2nd Place Solution for the ARC Prize 2024 Competition: Omni-ARC approach
solution_summary: The author fine-tuned Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on ARC datasets to predict outputs and generate new inputs, encouraging a shared representation of puzzle structure. LoRA adaptation was followed by separate test-time fine-tuning for every private test problem. Inference generated 96 augmented predictions per problem, reversed the transformations, and selected outputs by voting. Taking one attempt from this system and one from a public 2020 solution produced a leaderboard score of 40; test-time fine-tuning increased solved problems from 11 to 33 in one experiment.
compute: Main training: 2x A6000 GPUs, 200,000 steps; experiments used 48GB A6000s and final larger models used 80GB A100s. Test-time adaptation: approximately 300 steps per problem.
external_data: ["Michael Hodel's RE-ARC dataset", "Simon Strandgaard's PQA dataset", "Simon Strandgaard's Tama dataset", "Mini-ARC", "nosound's hand crafted ARC tasks", "Andy Penrose's tasks", "BARC datasets (tested without significant improvement)"]

solution_summary: The final solution blended an offline-trained graph neural network with an MLP trained inside the submission kernel. The GNN modeled player interactions using node, edge, and simulated future-position features, while the MLP used roughly a hundred selected positional features. Pseudo-labeled public test plays supplied some 2019 data for offline training, with acknowledged stage-one overfitting. Bagging and constraints on the predicted cumulative yardage distribution completed the pipeline.

The final approach ensembled LightGBM and CatBoost using event and assessment features, including eligible samples extracted from test data. Validation used stratified group folds and the median score over thousands of truncated samples, with thresholds optimized for that same objective. Fifteen bags of ten folds combined weighted rank averaging with final majority voting. An earlier sequence CNN reached about 0.520 publicly but was abandoned because adapting its memory-heavy implementation would take too much time.

solution_title: 2nd place solution write-up,Team "Under a penny", ebouteillon part 🔥
solution_summary: The author implemented a GPU genetic algorithm in PyTorch and explored exact SAT and constraint solvers for reversing Game of Life. Kissat solved 9,532 delta-one puzzles in 25 minutes, but higher deltas and difficult puzzles could take much longer. A notebook approach combined the GPU genetic algorithm with iterative OR-Tools solving on CPU, scoring 0.05353 in two hours. Team solutions were combined by selecting the lowest-scoring candidate separately for each puzzle.
compute: Notebook approach used 1 GPU and 2 CPUs; reported two-hour and nine-hour runs. SAT solving handled 9,532 delta-one puzzles in 25 minutes.

solution_summary: The author trained ten models using ResNet, SENet, DenseNet, and VGG architectures on MFCC, mel, and raw audio inputs. A weighted ensemble supplied pseudo-labels for two semi-supervised training procedures. One mixed selected test examples into training each epoch; the other pretrained on all pseudo-labeled test data before a single epoch of training-data fine-tuning. These procedures provided the main improvement beyond the initial ensemble, and an uploaded private submission scored 0.91084.

The solution combined modality-specific 1D-CNN branches with MLP layers and gesture-aware pooling driven by a separate U-Net. Correcting left-handed sensor coordinates and upside-down devices was particularly important, with test-time device correction improving the private score by 0.013. Training used auxiliary orientation and branch-specific classification losses, and inference selected IMU-only predictions when TOF data was mostly missing. The final ensemble averaged 100 networks trained on the full dataset with different seeds and used no post-processing.

The author built a rule-based agent centered on a modified Dijkstra algorithm for movement planning. Search regions were restricted, a one-turn stay action was added, and time-dependent collision penalties accounted for friendly and enemy positions. Reinforcement learning failed to learn, while the Python rule-based implementation completed self-play matches in 1–3 minutes.
compute: Python implementation; 1–3 minutes per self-play match.

solution_summary: The pipeline generated raster images with Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, fine-tuned through DRaFT-LV LoRA using preference and competition-specific rewards. It converted images into rough SVGs and refined path geometry and colors through differentiable rendering. Fine-tuning improved aesthetic scores by about 10%, VQA by about 5%, and the leaderboard score by roughly 0.03. Inference generated several candidates within about a minute and selected the best VQA-scoring SVG with an OCR safeguard.
compute: Approximately 60 seconds per prompt, typically generating 5–6 SVG candidates.

solution_summary: The solution constructed random-word essays with English and Japanese prompt injections that induced different grades across judge models. Extensive local testing against generated system prompts identified three complementary exploit patterns, while specialized wordlists helped preserve language and similarity scores. Repeating a small essay batch and probing public-split membership enabled more balanced exploit allocation. A stable batch of 26 essays achieved 30.050 repeatedly in public testing, although private results were slightly less consistent.

The author obtained better results with classification than regression and combined logistic regression with a custom Java SGD classifier. Confidence scores supplied stochastic training labels, with predictions averaged across 12 label draws for the Python models. The final submission averaged predictions from both implementations with varied text preprocessing. Bigrams, trigrams, and temperature rounding supplied text features, while the Java approach worked for S and W targets but not K targets.

The approach used Optuna-tuned LightGBM models and ensembled variants with different feature sets and player-position specializations. Historical target statistics older than 31 days improved predictions, followed by log-scale target modeling with endpoint values omitted. Manual corrections addressed no-hitters and Shohei Ohtani, although the author suspected the latter could overfit. The reported public score improved from 1.3490 to 1.3019, while the actual final result was unknown.
compute: GCP used because of insufficient memory; hardware unspecified

solution_summary: The post combines field analysis with the author's benchmark attack pipeline, optimizing validated candidate throughput against the public sandbox guardrail. The pipeline used a payload-inspection blind spot, model-specific prompt injection, successive-halving selection, and replay-aware candidate filling. Public results were strong but transferred poorly to private replay, with the author's reported private median falling to 0.07. The analysis attributes this gap to guardrail differences and insufficient portfolio diversity, while acknowledging substantial hosted variance and limitations of local mocks.
compute: Kaggle T4x2; 8,750-second generation envelope. CPU-only local validation averaged 9.05 seconds.

solution_summary: The author explored converting hand landmarks into video clips with TensorFlow preprocessing layers and adapting a streaming MoViNet classifier to 59 characters. The proposal uses pretrained video weights and conversion through SavedModel to TensorFlow Lite. Frame-level predictions and duplicate-aware post-processing were suggested as possibilities. The approach was not completed for the competition.

The post shares links to a speech-recognition paper and its code repository. The authors report testing their models on this competition's data and the later V2 release. It provides no model architecture, training procedure, or competition solution details.

The author used a linear regression with 29 coefficients and a bias to predict log sales normalized by GDP. Features represented country, store, product, weekday, annual product seasonality, and country-specific holiday effects. The small model avoided overfitting but treated all years equally without extrapolating trends into 2019. Reported SMAPE was 4.29899 on training, 4.13522 on the public leaderboard, and 4.66955 on the private leaderboard.
external_data: ["GDP data shared by Carl McBride Ellis", "Official holiday dates"]

solution_summary: The solution used multiplication-based feature generation and an SVC model. The author deliberately avoided using the Greek data. Keeping the approach free of complex ensembles was another explicit goal.

The pipeline extracted relevant text and standardized it using part of speech tags and lemmatization. It used GloVe 6B embeddings for transfer learning in a network combining embeddings, CNN, and LSTM components. Per-label decision cutoffs were selected using Hamming loss.

The solution combined several CNN architectures initialized with ImageNet weights and trained on small random image crops. It used competition-defined image manipulations for augmentation, 11-way test-time augmentation with geometric aggregation, and 40,000 additional Flickr images filtered by resolution. Prediction postprocessing added about three percentage points of accuracy, and the final submission used a mode blend of models. Individual models achieved reported private scores between 0.975 and 0.982, with each epoch taking eight minutes.
models_pretrained: ["ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 and ResNet101", "ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet121 and DenseNet201", "ImageNet-pretrained Xception", "ImageNet-pretrained ResNeXt101"]
compute: 8 minutes per epoch

solution_summary: The solution used the integer dataset supplied by raddar and engineered customer-level aggregates, temporal differences, ratios, and holiday indicators. Its base ensemble contained three LightGBM models, six XGBoost models, and four neural networks with varied representations and parameters. These 13 models were stacked using ten-fold cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, and early stopping. The reported selected result scored 0.80868 privately, while the best submission reached 0.80875.

solution_title: 8th Place Solution for the "ICR - Identifying Age-Related Conditions" Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined XGBoost and TabPFN ensembles trained separately for Class and the three condition-specific Alpha labels. Missing values were predicted with XGBoost, and feature subsets were selected through importance-based removal. Condition probabilities were combined using maxima for positives and minima for negatives, then averaged with the Class predictions and balanced. The submission scored 0.19 publicly and 0.34 privately; hyperparameter tuning and aggressive probability post-processing worsened performance.

The solution first optimizes a constrained traveling salesman tour using Concorde and a genetic algorithm, then converts the tour into arm configurations. Feasibility checks reject tours that violate longest-arm constraints or contain problematic early movements and boundary paths. Concorde repeatedly improves subsets of roughly 2,400 vertices to construct the initial population, and edge assembly crossover evolves the tours. A beam search that preserves diverse longest-arm states converts the optimized tour into configurations, achieving a reported score of 74075.7065416901.

The solution combined EfficientNet B2–B7 models with diverse pooling and attention heads, image sizes, seeds, and training datasets. Most model groups were blended with CV-guided weights, while Bayesian optimization selected out-of-fold ensemble weights for the B6 group. The final blend added a public metadata submission with weight 0.1 and predictions from models trained on the full 2020 dataset, followed by rank ensembling. It achieved public and private leaderboard scores of 0.9554 and 0.9383.

The solution distilled a two-stage DeBERTa-v3-large model into four-fold CatBoost models for faster inference. Each fold combined 15 handcrafted features with 32 SVD-reduced TF-IDF features, then trained sequentially on Kaggle-Persuade and Kaggle-Only soft targets. Out-of-fold predictions from the corresponding stage models were concatenated for threshold optimization, and training used MSE. Parallel feature generation and prediction reduced submission runtime to about 80 seconds.
compute: Four processes; submission runtime reduced from around 109 seconds to 80 seconds.

solution_summary: The final submission combined tuned LightGBM and XGBoost models through voting. Each model was bagged with 100 estimators, and predictions came from full-data fits. This reused the author's AutoML GrandPrix submission and scored 0.83699 publicly and 0.83905 privately.

The final ensemble combined three custom LightGBM models trained over different historical periods with two models adapted from public scripts. The best-scoring submission gave all five models equal weights, while a performance-weighted blend had better validation results. The custom models relied on carefully reconstructed zero-sales rows, filtered training periods, smoothed group sales statistics, promotion and holiday effects, and rolling sales averages. Model selection emphasized the last ten days of a fifteen-day validation window, and simple fixed rolling averages outperformed more elaborate forecasting variants.
compute: Used AWS EC2 late in the competition because a laptop could not handle two years of training data.

solution_summary: The author uses a single Matterport Mask R-CNN with a ResNet-101 backbone initialized from COCO. Only horizontal and vertical flips survived augmentation experiments, while additional H&E data and ensembling did not improve performance. Training uses Adam, checkpoint selection, lower learning rates, and early stopping, followed by binary dilation of predicted masks. Reported leaderboard scores were 0.489 in Stage 1 and 0.590 in Stage 2.

solution_title: Sharing my approach, 20th place solution -- Local 0.0487, Public 0.0498, Private 0.0582
solution_summary: The approach used a single XGBoost model with 350 engineered materials features. These described crystal geometry, elemental properties, bonds, forces, energies, statistical distributions, and a linear estimate. Heavy column and row subsampling improved performance despite substantial feature correlation. The reported error was 0.0487 in cross-validation, 0.0498 on the public leaderboard, and approximately 0.058 on the private leaderboard.

solution_title: 80th Place Solution: Two-Stage ALIKED+LightGlue Pipeline and Adaptive OmniGlue-Enhancement Pipeline
solution_summary: The authors used DINOv2 retrieval followed by ALIKED and LightGlue matching, with a second crop-matching stage and image rotation. An alternative submitted pipeline selectively added OmniGlue when initial matches had poor geometric distribution, subject to a 20% budget. Moving OmniGlue's DINO feature extraction to GPU reduced processing from 10 seconds to 1–2 seconds per image pair. The core pipeline achieved 34.18 private and 34.86 public scores, while OmniGlue showed better local results but greater leaderboard variability.
compute: GPU DINO feature extraction; image-pair processing reduced from 10 seconds to 1–2 seconds.

solution_summary: The final selected submission voted across five models, with DeBERTa-v3-large backbones described for several components. All models received ten epochs of masked-language-model pretraining and two-stage supervised training, first on Kaggle-Persuade and then on Kaggle-Only to match the test text distribution. Model diversity included ordinal regression, prompt-based scoring, CoPE, text cleaning, and hierarchical pooling. Threshold optimization on the full training set, including an extra search for the boundary between scores 5 and 6, improved validation and leaderboard results.

The solution combined boosted trees, tabular neural networks, AutoML models, and public-notebook approaches through strongly regularized ridge stacking. Around 150 engineered features included original-data target probabilities, nearest-neighbor churn statistics, clustering features, numeric transformations, and categorical interactions. Consistent ten-fold stratified splits aligned all out-of-fold predictions, and ridge-based feature elimination selected complementary models. Ridge generalized better than hill climbing, achieving CV 0.91968 and private ROC-AUC 0.91831.

solution_title: 7th Place: Global Task Optimization (Hungarian Matcher) + Time-A
solution_summary: The agent combined global objective assignment with symmetry-based map inference and coordinated path planning. Each unit received a distinct target, while prioritized space-time reservations prevented route collisions and jump-aware planning enabled wall crossings. Bottleneck-clearing rules and selective teammate crushing maintained forward movement. Near the end of a match, units abandoned resource collection and moved north to escape the elimination wall.

The team developed three independent approaches and ensembled them. This author's contribution used XGBoost, CatBoost, and LightGBM with a selected subset of eight features. Additional group-mean features were created for CatBoost using concatenated training, holdout, and test data. Manual hyperparameter tuning and robust cross-validation were the main priorities.

solution_title: Boosting Complex Solution with New Image Solution  -  266th Place Bronze Medalist
solution_summary: The author combined a DenseNet-169 image booster with strong published ensemble predictions through optimized mixing formulas. Image training used earlier ISIC cancer cases, replication of 2024 cancer cases, minority augmentation, and majority undersampling. Mixing parameters were evaluated using repeated stratified cross-validation on predictions for the entire 2024 training set. The selected submissions used a serendipitous houseblend parameter set and recalculated rep14 parameters, while other optimized houseblend variants later achieved private scores of 0.16953 and 0.16942. Public scores did not reliably identify the strongest private-score variants.

solution_title: 96th Place Solution: validation of noisy data improve ~0.02 LB score
solution_summary: The solution used five-fold VGG16 models on two-second audio clips with 180 mel channels. A curated-only model validated selected noisy examples before training on the combined dataset, adding about 0.02 to the score. A compact classifier head, reordered batch normalization and dropout, and strong dropout improved performance. SpecAugment and mixup were used during training, while inference averaged predictions across frames without TTA.
compute: All computation ran on Kaggle kernels; no local GPU server.

solution_title: The Leakage (and how it was fixed)
solution_summary: The author describes a leakage-only approach to the original dataset rather than an audio detection pipeline for the restarted competition. Logistic regression used file sizes, filename milliseconds, and chronological correlations without reading audio content. These features achieved 0.9973 AUC on the original release, including 0.945 from a single timestamp indicator. After the organizers corrected the dataset, the same approach achieved only 0.59 AUC.

The post announces the team's working notes and source code for BirdCLEF 2024. It says the notes cover architectures, data augmentation, domain shift, possible remedies, and an ablation study. The post itself provides no concrete implementation details or results.

The author combined the 2015 and 2019 retinal datasets for joint training to improve generalization and align local validation with public scores. Preprocessing removed black borders while preserving aspect ratios, and duplicates and confusing labels were removed. EfficientNet-B5 and B4 regression models used extensive augmentation, progressive image resizing, one-cycle training, and five-fold stratified validation. Averaged test predictions supplied pseudo labels for three more training epochs, and the final model average achieved 0.931 on the private board and 0.830 on the public board.

solution_title: How I Vibe-Coded my way to almost Top 10 position but then fell to 36th
solution_summary: The author directed Claude Opus 4.8 to inspect the competition SDK, implement sandbox attacks, and run experiments, consulting other models when progress stalled. Most development optimized public-score throughput by shortening generated tool calls and exploiting a mismatch between guardrail inspection and scoring. Demonstration-based formatting and shorter URL representations improved throughput, while Gemma candidates remained single-hop because of parsing problems and latency. The author ultimately selected a weaker alternative build after misjudging how the undistributed private guardrail would behave.

The solution combined modified 1D WaveNet features, trainable STFT features, and attention-pooled competition spectrogram features in a multimodal model. Spatial restacking of WaveNet outputs and STFTs helped image backbones capture relationships between EEG channels. Training emphasized reliable, high-vote examples and used brain augmentations, weighted KL divergence, and occasional noisy student labels. Different backbones and architecture configurations diversified the ensemble, with brain flipping also used during inference.

solution_summary: The selected solution used a single LightGBM model with more than 170 features and Faron's F1 optimization code. Features described purchase frequency, interactions, recency, streaks, order similarity, and diversity, supplemented by product-name statistics and word2vec-based clusters. A voting ensemble improved public scores by roughly 0.0005–0.001 when submissions were diverse. The strongest public ensemble overfit, so selecting the single model as well was beneficial.

solution_title: Simple model for April TPS (RESNET with CONV2D)
solution_summary: The post links to the author's notebook for the April Tabular Playground Series. It describes the linked model as simple. The post itself provides no pipeline details or results.

The solution improved baseline pseudoranges with a stacked XGBoost ensemble, then combined velocity estimation, outlier removal, device fusion, Kalman filtering, and averaging during stops. ADR relative positions were obtained through Android GPS tools after a custom implementation failed. Uncertainty-weighted alignment to ADR shapes and subsequent snapping to ground truth produced further gains. The best reported public and private scores were 3.159 and 1.801.
