solution_summary: The solution combined EfficientNet-b4 classifiers with several U-Net segmentation models, emphasizing model diversity for robustness. Classification used full images, while segmentation included both full-image and cropped EfficientNet-b3 U-Nets plus three models from a shared inference kernel. Training used crop, flip, and photometric augmentation, with a weighted BCE–Dice segmentation loss. Inference used horizontal-flip augmentation and classwise thresholds of 0.5.

solution_title: ... & I'd like to thank Kaggle, the challenge host, and everyone who made their notebooks public.
solution_summary: The solution expanded the two original categorical features with target-specific average responses grouped by cell type and drug. It also added roughly 500 binary SMILES fragment features and 2,000 binary Morgan fingerprint features shared across targets. The final predictions combined LinearSVR, neural network, NLP, and PYBOOST outputs with separate ensemble coefficients for each target column based on correlation values. The reported correlations for the example target were 0.24 for cell-type averages and 0.62 for drug averages.

The solution averaged six Conv1D neural networks trained jointly on tdcsfog and defog, excluding notype and unlabeled data. It combined raw acceleration with magnitude, normalized time, a dataset flag, and rolling-window features, using both short-window and long-window architectures. Validation used five folds grouped by subject, with the split seed adjusted to improve balance. A 500-step moving average improved predictions slightly, and the ensemble achieved public and private scores of 0.411 and 0.324.

The team combined LSTM, MLP, and LightGBM predictions with weights of 5:1:1. The main LSTM consumed six days of features and jointly predicted all four targets, while the other models used forecast-day features. Validation used nearby in-season months, and 232 features included prior-month player target statistics and joins across nearly all supplied tables. The ensemble improved the public score to 1.26, and inference robustness was checked with dummy future data and an API emulator.

The post shares links to presentations about the author's solution without describing its methods. It includes a recorded NeurIPS 2018 presentation, a Russian-language Moscow ML Trainings talk with automatic English subtitles, and a PDF presentation. The author also invites questions.

The author selected XGBoost after comparing several model families. Ten-fold validation scored only synthetic samples while adding the entire original dataset to every fold's training set. Preprocessing capped two extreme values, ordinally encoded BusinessTravel, one-hot encoded six categorical features, and standardized continuous variables. Simplifying JobRole categories and dropping features did not improve results.

The solution trained ReXNet200 image classifiers, extracted their embeddings, and modeled each study with two bidirectional LSTMs. Full-resolution windowed JPEGs, image augmentation, and separate BCE- and focal-loss backbone training supported the first stage. The sequence model jointly predicted image and exam labels, using attention aggregation for exam-level outputs and masking padded positions during training. The six-model average achieved public/private losses of 0.159/0.152, while the three-model BCE-only ensemble achieved 0.158/0.153.

The author focused on neural networks after observing a strong effect on the public score. A KMeans-based modification improved a referenced neural-network approach from 0.85424 to 0.85503. The post links the KMeans neural-network implementation and the final ensemble, but provides few implementation details.

The final approach averaged a LightGBM classifier and a feed-forward neural network trained on clinical and supplementary visit metadata. Blood protein and peptide measurements were excluded because they did not reliably improve validation. LightGBM predicted a target distribution that was converted into the integer minimizing expected SMAPE+1, while the neural network optimized SMAPE+1 directly. Leave-one-patient-out validation guided selection, and non-annual visit indicators were especially influential.

This unselected entry predicted outcomes using group means rather than a fitted predictive model. It grouped the latest four weeks of training data by city and a three-level source category, computed means in log space, and transformed predictions back to raw space. The approach achieved a private score of 0.31499. Its implementation used Python and pandas grouping and merging.

The solution stacked DeBERTa predictions and engineered text features into LightGBM models, then combined their outputs with selected raw Transformer predictions. Roughly 80 features described lexical overlap, semantic similarity, readability, and neighboring summaries. Seed averaging stabilized LightGBM evaluation and predictions. Ensemble weights were optimized with Nelder-Mead and adjusted by input length to favor LightGBM when prompts risked Transformer truncation.

The author built a compact model with roughly 30 features, emphasizing next-click and IP distinct-count features extracted separately for each day. Five-seed averaging improved this model, which scored 0.9828 privately and contributed diversity to the team ensemble. Pseudo-labeling and overlapping-window data augmentation failed to improve performance. A neural-network blender combined team models and neural networks to reach 0.9840.

solution_summary: The final submission stacked 59 diverse models using CatBoost. The author prioritized diversity across model families and gradually added out-of-fold predictions to the ensemble. The best feature set combined target and count encodings of feature pairs, numerical pairwise products, and cyclical features. TabM was the strongest individual model, while the CatBoost ensemble achieved CV 0.977432 and private leaderboard score 0.97796.

The author ensembled LightGBM, XGBoost, and a lightly tuned denoising autoencoder, using different feature sets to increase diversity. All models shared stratified ten-fold splits, and test predictions were averaged across folds. Hill climbing on out-of-fold predictions determined ensemble weights, producing a private score of 0.89890. A second final submission blended this ensemble with high-scoring notebooks and achieved a private score of 0.89934.

solution_title: 39th place solution: Ensemble Approach Using GBDT
solution_summary: The solution combined LightGBM and XGBoost models with a dual-head 1D CNN–LSTM trained for IMU-only and all-sensor prediction. Tree models used windowed signal features aggregated over full sequences and their latter halves, while the neural model used several augmentations and random sensor masking. Predictions were routed according to TOF availability and combined through weighted probability sums. Group-aware stratified five-fold validation reached 0.821 for IMU and 0.881 for all sensors; group-based post-processing added about 0.001, with public and private scores of 0.863 and 0.844.

The team merged two DSL solvers, public kernels, and a cellular-automata recurrent CNN into a combined ARC solver. Brute-force object extraction and symmetry transformations solved crop tasks, while frequency-based color encoding made the cellular-automata approach useful on the leaderboard. Voting added another solved task, and rotating training pairs into a common alignment improved a DSL solver. GPU execution optimizations helped fit the combined system within submission limits, while ordinary CNN solving, prediction averaging, and cellular-automata augmentation failed.
compute: Object-crop solver: 3 minutes in Python; cellular-automata execution accelerated approximately 2x on GPU.

solution_title: CNN can Visualize Contact (4th place K_mat part)
solution_summary: The author describes a contact-prediction component using a 2D U-Net to produce masks for individual players. Pairwise contact scores come from multiplying masks in the players' overlapping region and taking the maximum value. An ensemble variant processes the whole image and crops player representations in feature space. Predictions feed a second-stage model, and inference scales with the number of players; the emergent contact-localization masks provided limited benefit during the competition.

The final system blended five LightGBM models and one XGBoost model trained on the same set of more than 1,000 features. Models varied in objectives, boosting configuration, and target transformations. Features combined historical target aggregates, the previous 20 days or games of player statistics, and baseball-specific engagement signals. Validation used the last month of data before retraining on the full dataset.

The solution combined a lightweight Transformer with XGBoost and CatBoost, trained across five folds and three seeds. Training included additional raw sessions, while validation used only competition data. Event differences and flattened sequence features were important, and per-question linear regression combined predictions from multiple questions. The ensemble achieved 0.7044 CV and 0.703 private score, with threshold selection materially affecting results.

The solution predicted well trajectories with a UNet operating on depth-versus-position matching images, supplemented by particle filters and gradient-boosted trees. Its most effective late improvement was to build a reference log from each well's known section and use it both as a UNet input and as the particle filter reference. Independently trained networks and complementary model families were blended with well-specific weights, then smoothed. Well-level GroupKFold validation scored 5.66 across 773 wells, while the selected submission scored 6.299 on the private leaderboard.

The solution selects 54 features using model importance, permutation importance, and SHAP, then trains a diverse collection of boosting, linear, and neural models. It adds approximately 92,804 test-set pseudo-labels selected using residual-based thresholds and trains residual models to reduce bias. The final prediction assigns half its weight to the author's model and half to the geometric mean of three public submissions. The author reports that this blend stabilized predictions and slightly improved the leaderboard score.

The author reduced the label space using known answer correctness and question-specific candidate targets, then trained pointwise Qwen rerankers. Knowledge distillation from Qwen2.5-Math-72B-Instruct and target-specific few-shot examples improved the Qwen3-Reranker-8B model. Final selections included the strongest reranker and an ensemble with Qwen3-32B-AWQ; the ensemble achieved 0.94835 privately and did not surpass the best single model. Listwise ranking, chain-of-thought prompting, and retrieved explanation examples did not improve the final approach.
compute: T4 GPU used for online inference; final ensemble inference reported as 6.5 hours.

solution_summary: The solution combined DeBERTa out-of-fold predictions with a LightGBM model, text vectorizers, and linguistic features. Validation emphasized Kaggle-only essays from five expected test topics, weighted to their estimated test proportions, while training used all records with a Persuade source flag. The author fitted vectorizers on the test set, extended DeBERTa inference length to 1536, transformed its predictions into a CDF, and adjusted suspicious training labels. CV and leaderboard scores correlated weakly, so submission selection gave equal weight to both; the chosen solution scored 0.836.

The team blended XGBoost, sparse neural networks, logistic regression, and elastic net models, with specialized handling for devices with and without events. Features captured phone identity, app and category usage, event timing and location, TF-IDF representations, and brand/model frequencies. Out-of-fold predictions supported optimized blending, while fold and seed averaging improved stability. Their final leak-based submission added normalized row information for devices without events and matched training and test IDs, achieving public and private scores of 2.14223 and 2.14949.

solution_summary: The author submitted a heavily augmented ensemble without label correction and a second ensemble blending distilled students with their teachers. solution_title: 16 Public 61 Private LB Solution | Silver Medal Solution
solution_summary: The final approach used a structured chemical-feature pipeline with similarity filtering, noise augmentation, and variance-based feature selection. Chemical descriptors and polymer fingerprints supplied the main predictive signal, with K-Fold validation restricted to organizer-provided validation data. Predictions were clipped to each property's observed range. Complex ensembles, scaffold splits, external datasets, and heavy AutoML were less reliable than the feature-based approach.

solution_summary: The solution stacked eight out-of-fold prediction sets and used LAD for the final combination. Its main advantage came from matching fruitset and fruitmass values across the original, training, and test datasets, then replacing selected predictions with original-dataset yields. Corrections were expanded using progressively less restrictive match-count thresholds, stopping at the author's chosen risk level. This postprocessing produced much larger improvements than changes to model blending, while an exhaustive yield search improved out-of-fold results but transferred poorly to the leaderboard.

The author describes two separate question-answering approaches. The first uses pretrained Wikipedia GloVe embeddings to calculate cosine similarity between questions and answers, scoring around 0.31875. The second retrieves CK12 topics, collects corresponding Wikipedia pages, and ranks documents for question-answer pairs, scoring around 0.35375.

The solution ensembled five folds of a modified SE-ResNeXt50, replacing strided convolutions with convolution and maxblur pooling and changing the stem between training phases. It jointly classified root, vowel, and consonant labels while learning an auxiliary multilabel task over 61 decomposed grapheme parts. Training used Adam, plateau-based learning-rate reduction, basic augmentation, and DropBlock, with two folds fine-tuned using online hard example mining. Final predictions adjusted class probabilities by class frequency to improve macro recall, which the author considered especially important.

solution_title: 4th Place Solution — LightGBM with SMILES-Derived Features
solution_summary: The solution extended a public LightGBM baseline with chemically informed descriptors and external polymer datasets. Features captured radical-marker relationships, aromatic and aliphatic rings, and three-dimensional geometry from RDKit conformations. Target-specific quantile objectives used 0.85 for Tg and Rg and 0.5 for the other properties. Controlled SMILES substitutions around difficult cases expanded structural diversity, with heuristic Rg adjustments and noise providing synthetic targets.

solution_summary: The team abandoned machine learning because noisy evaluation made model quality difficult to judge. They submitted two opposite rankings based on one-day adjusted closing-price returns, placing stocks with positive expected dividends at the bottom in both. The descending-return version scored 0.347 privately, while the ascending version scored -0.196. The dividend rule reflected the expected price decline around ex-dividend dates, and the opposite rankings hedged the direction of the return signal.

The author reports improving a shared submission using results from several public notebooks. The post gives little detail about how those predictions were combined or adjusted. It reports a private score of 0.69470 and a public score of 0.69548, with the private score closer to the author's expectations.

The solution regenerated churn labels using both Scala code and the author's Python script, assigning different label versions to different models. Features combined payment and membership information, previous churn outcomes, transaction counts, demographics, and aggregated listening activity. Listening logs were taken from the month preceding membership expiration. XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost predictions were combined by simple averaging.

solution_title: 🥈 Quick overview of the 26th place solution [LB 0.24838]
solution_summary: The team used concatenated intermediate BERT-large embeddings and public-kernel linguistic features as inputs to a four-layer neural network. Training used ten folds and augmentation that swapped the A and B candidate columns. Blending models trained on corrected and original data improved public scores to about 0.33, with corrected/original weights of 0.6/0.4 achieving a private score of 0.24838. BERT fine-tuning was unsuccessful, and more complex classifier architectures offered no improvement.

The solution combined CNN spectrogram feature extractors with either 1D U-Net or LSTM decoders, plus a PaNNs feature extractor with an LSTM decoder. More than 20 models with different seeds and hyperparameters were ensembled, retaining models with CV scores of at least 0.753. Unnormalized angle and movement differences and sigma=12 helped, while a Transformer decoder and normalization of movement differences did not. The final public and private scores were 0.751 and 0.775.

The solution ensembled 12 DeBERTa-v3-large models trained with different external datasets and independently randomized splits. Validation stratified documents by label-presence patterns and used a 50/50 training-validation ratio. Adding newline token support, disabling truncation, removing documents containing only O labels, and adjusting O predictions improved leaderboard performance. BIO corrections and invalid-pattern filtering refined outputs, while ONNX allowed two additional models within submission limits.

solution_title: 16th Place Solution (Association x UserCF x NN-based x Matrix Factorization x Covisit x LightGBM)
solution_summary: The solution generated roughly 100 candidates per session using revisits, covisitation structures, collaborative filtering, and GRU4Rec, reaching validation candidate recall of 0.6396. A LightGBM ranker then used 291 features spanning interactions, aggregate statistics, association rules, embeddings, matrix factorization, and neural recommenders. Many feature families contributed small gains, while neural features were comparatively expensive. The final ensemble combined five candidate and model configurations, and the best single model scored 0.6017 on the private leaderboard.

The team built a three-stage cascade: multilabel classification, multilabel segmentation used to reject false positives, and class-specific binary segmentation. SENet154 classifiers filtered nearly half the images, while intermediate PSPNet and FPN ensembles further reduced false positives. Final localization used U-Net and FPN models trained on nonempty masks with Dice and focal losses. Pseudo-labels, classifier-initialized segmentation backbones, and checkpoint weight averaging improved the pipeline, with weight averaging adding approximately 0.3–0.5 percentage points.

The author describes an image chronology solution built from ImageJ feature engineering, data augmentation, and extreme gradient boosting, while referring readers elsewhere for full details. Neural architectures tested in Caffe failed to perform better than random predictions. Cross-validation supported selecting submissions despite low public scores. solution_summary: The solution extended a public neural-network baseline with player-wise global average pooling, Mish activation, RAdam, binary classification loss, and mixup. The strongest features projected future player positions from motion variables and measured distances and distance-to-speed ratios between players over time. Team and nearby-player aggregation features also helped, while permutation-based recursive feature elimination and Bayesian parameter optimization refined the model. The reported leaderboard score improved from 0.01385 to 0.01261.

Candidates were accepted through correctness and cost checks, with online score differences used to isolate hidden-input regressions. The strongest graph rewrites minimized charged intermediate memory through direct-output operators, recomputation, and reusable algebraic bases; all 400 tasks eventually passed.

Validation used a time-based split, and the extended convolutional model processed numerical values, categorical embeddings, and temporal differences through separate convolutional branches.

The final model used LightGBM predictions from individual proteins and peptides to adjust a public median progression baseline. solution_title: Rank 4 approach - thoughtful model choices and effective ensembles
solution_summary: The solution combined boosted trees and neural networks with a neural-network stack, selecting models through a shared stratified 10-fold validation scheme. Three compact feature sets were retained from five candidates, and original data was included throughout. Simple features and CatBoost with string-valued inputs were stronger than large collections of secondary features. The submission incorporating public models achieved 0.97002 CV and 0.96902 private leaderboard accuracy, slightly above the fully independent alternative. AutoGluon, private XGBoost models, and several classical models were unsuccessful.

The team built three complementary pipelines that localized individual discs before classifying severity from MRI crops. CoAtNet and EfficientNet models combined slice information with recurrent heads or modified 2.5D convolutions, while some models integrated axial and sagittal views. An MLP stacked model logits while directly accounting for the competition metric. Four-fold validation guided decisions, and the final ensemble achieved 0.382 CV loss and 0.401 private leaderboard loss.

The solution blended five XLM-RoBERTa large models, one XLM-RoBERTa base model, and one mBART large model using weighted rank percentiles. Training progressively specialized models from seven languages to three and then to individual languages, with different stages used for different test languages. Length-sorted dynamic padding and negative downsampling accelerated training, while a six-fold validation scheme represented both known and unseen languages. Language-specific prediction multipliers, derived using leaderboard probes, corrected differences in prediction distributions and substantially improved the public leaderboard result.
compute: V100 GPU; approximately 17 minutes per XLM-RoBERTa large epoch on the first training set.

solution_summary: The solution used bi-encoder retrieval followed by cross-encoder reranking, with multilingual pretrained models in both stages. Topic inputs included curriculum hierarchy information, while content inputs combined title, description, text, and kind. Retrieval selected candidates using cosine similarity, and rerankers used binary cross-entropy with FGM adversarial training. A 1:1:3 ensemble of three rerankers reached a private score of 67.8; graph link prediction and LightGBM attempts did not work.

The post thanks the organizers and reflects on the author's first experience solving AI riddles. It links to a notebook containing solutions for eleven flags and names the challenges covered. The post itself provides no methods or implementation details.

The final system fine-tuned a LAION-2B pretrained ViT-H to produce 64-dimensional retrieval embeddings using ArcFace and multiple external image datasets. Training first optimized the projection head, then adapted the backbone with a lower learning rate, frozen final classifier, and dropout to limit overfitting. Products-10K was reserved for final specialization, and the training sequence was repeated at higher resolution with fewer epochs and a lower learning rate. A single model with 290-pixel inputs and four-pixel overlapping patches achieved public and private scores of 0.732 and 0.728.

solution_title: My approach of single model with 2.234 public LB (without leak)
solution_summary: The approach split devices into groups with and without event records. Devices without events used a weighted blend of a neural network and XGBoost on phone brand and model, while devices with events used app, time, location, and phone features. The best event model was a two-hidden-layer sigmoid network with strong dropout, achieving 1.918 five-fold CV loss for that subset and 2.23390 public leaderboard loss after combining subsets. Averaging ten seeds improved the public score to 2.23210, while stacking feature variants and models reached 2.227.
compute: About 2 hours on a GTX 980 Ti for ten seeded runs.

solution_title: Blog post on how to get second place apparently
solution_summary: The post congratulates the winners and links to two blog posts describing the team's approach. It initially promises code and documentation for reproducing the solution. An edit adds a GitHub repository, but the provided text contains no methodological details.

The team assembled a positioning pipeline from public notebooks after joining shortly before the deadline. They obtained RTK and robust weighted least-squares estimates, applied separate Kalman filtering variants, and corrected phone-specific biases. Positions were shifted using median errors measured against training ground truth, then combined through medians and weighted averaging. Some submissions performed better than the ones ultimately selected.

The solution processes left and right image views with a shared DINOv3 backbone, fuses their features with self-attention, and predicts biomass through five regression heads. Auxiliary classification into seven biomass intervals improved both reported leaderboard scores by about 0.03. Training freezes the backbone first and then fine-tunes the full model, with larger input images proving more useful than larger backbones. The final pipeline iteratively pseudo-labels the test set, uses SWA, blends DINO-Large and DINO-Base predictions, and applies biomass-specific corrections. The submitted model scored 0.77 on LB and 0.67 on PB.

The final solution weighted three neural-model families: a feature-rich text network, a Conv1D network, and a simpler fastText-style network. The main model used average-pooled unigram and bigram embeddings plus explicit categorical interactions, with four bagged networks and target transformations for diversity. Direct bigram embeddings offered similar accuracy to CNN n-gram extraction at lower runtime. The main model achieved about 0.400x on the public leaderboard in 2500 seconds, while the two faster families together ran in under 20 minutes.
compute: 4 CPU cores for concurrent neural-network bagging; main model 2500 seconds; other two model families combined under 20 minutes.

solution_title: 13th Place Solution Summary - CVSSP & forecom.ai (0.527 LB)
solution_summary: The pipeline improved cell segmentation and used a trained classifier to detect mis-segmented cells near image borders. It ensembled four or seven cell-level models, including EfficientB4, ECA-NFNet-L1, and Swin Transformer, with fourfold test-time augmentation. An image-level Swin Transformer supplied additional predictions that were blended with cell-level decisions using class-dependent weights. Training included rare-class augmentation, focal and hybrid losses, AI-based label boosting, and manual labeling of some rare-class examples.

The solution extended a public WaveNet with 24 base convolution filters and three LSTMs. It used drift-corrected data and 42 features, including lags, signal powers, gradients, filtered signals, and shifted random-forest probabilities. Training combined normalization, Gaussian noise, flips, and a second optimization stage with L2 regularization and a smaller learning rate. Prediction averaging across augmentations and 13 sequence lengths produced a final OOF CV of 0.942421.

The solution combined CNN and graph-based models, including GRU variants and modified public architectures, through ridge stacking. EternaFold structures and pairing probabilities provided a substantial improvement, while additional folding predictions diversified attention inputs. Validation grouped similar sequences, and training retained all data with signal-dependent weights. Final predictions were clipped to the stated target range; pretraining had uncertain benefits and GRU gains on the public leaderboard did not carry through consistently.

The agent combined jump-aware breadth-first search with a tunable score function, mining-based energy accumulation, and worker-assisted survival. Its main advantage was actively seeking factory collisions with an energy lead rather than waiting for a late-game tiebreak. Scouts located opponents, while carefully placed miners supplied a large energy boost immediately before impact. Friendly collision avoidance and short-horizon miner survival checks improved reliability, although a similar combat-focused opponent exposed weaknesses in timing and mine departure decisions.

The author adapted a previous Tabular Playground solution notebook based on similarities between the datasets. Mean imputation was used for the F_1 and F_3 feature groups. For F_4, complete rows trained separate regressors tailored to each missingness pattern, jointly predicting missing columns from the remaining columns. This required substantially more than 80 regressors and reached about 0.8358.

The author shared findings on synthetic data generation, large-scale pretraining, and waveform-based refinement rather than a complete pipeline. Reverse-engineering revealed corrections to the published generation formulas and parameter distributions. Pretraining with 100 times the official data reportedly improved cross-validation by about four points at a cost of about $64. Per-sample ADFWI refinement improved the leaderboard score from 22.1 to 17.0, and arranging sensors in the last dimension worked better for envelope and correlation losses.
compute: Pretraining on 100 times the official data cost about $64.

solution_summary: The final system combined two teams' candidate-retrieval pipelines, feature sets, validation splits, and rerankers. XGBoost binary classifiers and CatBoost rankers used statistical interaction features and embedding-based scores from several recommendation models. The teams exchanged important features and combined predictions through both raw-score averaging and weighted rank-based fusion. Some retrieval and feature details remain unspecified in the writeup.

The solution trained ByT5 and Qwen3 translation models on competition examples, approximately 31,000 extracted PDF pairs, and Gemma-generated pseudo-labels. Data quality was the main driver: complementary OCR passes, LLM alignment, extensive text cleaning, and source quality assessment produced better training data. A distilled ByT5 model added diversity by learning from both original translations and downweighted Gemma translations. The final submission combined five ByT5 models and three Qwen models through minimum Bayes risk decoding with a character-based metric and ran for almost nine hours.
compute: Final submission inference: almost 9 hours

solution_summary: The solution repeatedly removed gifts from nearby trips and greedily reinserted them at their lowest-cost positions, retaining improvements. A custom geographic distance metric selected local groups, while trip splitting, cross-splicing, trip rebuilding, and global gift relocation broadened the search. Simulated annealing delivered the largest subsequent score reductions, with the author crediting the broader greedy searches for preparing useful configurations. The initial search reduced the objective from 29.121 billion to 12.423 billion in about four hours, followed by increasingly slow improvements.
compute: Initial search: about 4 hours, single thread on a 2.9 GHz Intel Core i7 laptop; annealing: around 30 minutes per trip group.

solution_title: A Bronze Medal Solution with fast.ai
solution_summary: The solution used an EfficientNet backbone with a U-Net decoder for segmentation. The author built the pipeline using fastai, segmentation_models_pytorch, and albumentations. The accompanying notebook explains how to construct segmentation models for images with arbitrary channel counts.

The solution retrieved Wikipedia contexts and scored each answer independently with fine-tuned decoder-only language models. Retrieval diversity across embeddings, Wikipedia dumps, and chunking strategies mattered more than extensive model tuning. LoRA-trained binary heads used vocabulary logits, with some heads also receiving averaged logits from the other answers. The six-model blend achieved 0.933 private performance, while a single model reached 0.932, within a nine-hour inference budget.
compute: Similarity search on two GPUs in parallel; final pipeline used 2.5 TB of inputs and nine hours of runtime.

solution_summary: The solution combined spatially sparse convolutional networks that exploited the predominantly white image backgrounds and allowed wide input fields for augmentation. Real-time geometric transformations, restrained scale variation, custom intensity encoding, and gradually increasing dropout supported training. The final ensemble contained roughly 15 networks and counted Graham's best model twice; five networks already achieved 99.8% of the best ensemble score. The author's encoding caused substantial overprediction of two classes, while Graham's best single network achieved a score of 0.599.

The solution stacked capacity-normalized production estimates from separate forecast-weather and historical-weather models into partition-specific XGBoost models. It predicted a ratio relative to a lag-based baseline, using multiple seeds and sample weighting schemes. Recent mean prediction errors supplied a correction term, and models were retrained every eight days. An 80/20 blend with the best public kernel improved the public score from 61.32 to 59.97, while standalone three-fold CV was 35.73.
compute: GPU training; retraining every 8 days.

solution_summary: The final ensemble combined gradient boosting, neural networks, and linear models trained with two categorical-feature configurations. Original-data target encoding was the only feature engineering reported to help, while shallow boosting trees performed particularly well. Ranked OOF predictions were combined using GPU-accelerated hill climbing, with model choices guided by CV and prediction correlations. The final CV score was 0.955803, with RealMLP the strongest individual model at 0.95576.
compute: GPU-accelerated hill climbing; GPU model unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution used two five-fold XLM-RoBERTa-large configurations, one with the final CLS token and another with concatenated average and maximum pooling plus eight-sample dropout. Training used sampled negatives, cleaned uppercase text, integer toxicity labels, and exponential learning-rate decay with warm-up. Each model was subsequently trained on validation data and pseudo-labeled test data, and inference covered head, tail, and mixed token selections. TensorFlow and TPU hardware supported training.
compute: TPU

solution_title: [22nd] CPT, GRPO and Extensive Work on the Data (No SFT)
solution_summary: The final translator adapted Qwen3-8B through domain continued pretraining followed directly by GRPO, omitting supervised fine-tuning. Extensive external corpus collection, LLM-assisted cleaning, and normalization produced about one million sentence pairs for pretraining, with roughly 30,000 high-quality Old Assyrian–English pairs retained for GRPO. The reward combined the competition's BLEU/chrF++ metric with output-format penalties. Inference generated candidates with vLLM and selected by length-normalized average log probability, followed by consistency safeguards. SFT variants and alternative decoding methods did not improve the final pipeline, while GPU compatibility and inference crashes prevented deployment of some promising alternatives.
compute: Kaggle GPUs were used for submission inference; GPU compatibility issues prevented use of Qwen3.5-9B. Hardware type and training runtime were not specified.

solution_title: 47th Place Solution: A Novel Transparent Scene Trick!
solution_summary: The authors focused on reconstructing camera relationships in transparent glass scenes. They treated image ordering as a closed-loop graph problem, using matching feature counts as evidence of image proximity. Their method combined a minimum spanning tree with depth-first search to impose loop constraints. It improved public and private scores by 0.03 and 0.02 respectively, while their handling of other categories suffered from public leaderboard overfitting.

solution_title: Learning log from the competition 🥈 -  draft to be updated
solution_summary: The retrospective describes TF-IDF models, transformer experiments, and ensembles, although the exact selected final composition is unclear. CatBoost helped balance overfitting from SGD and multinomial naive Bayes under prompt-held-out validation, and an unselected candidate achieved roughly 0.919–0.92 privately. Log-odds ensembling also produced a strong unselected submission, while the tuned DistilBERT model scored 0.887 privately and Mistral performed poorly. Pseudo-label stacking improved results but was not pursued, partly because CatBoost was slow.

solution_summary: The team emphasized anomaly removal, temperature interpolation, timezone correction, and diverse target transformations before training CatBoost, LightGBM, and MLP models on different data partitions. Features included categorical interactions, calendar information, frequencies, temperature lags and derivatives, cyclic encodings, and Bayesian target encoding. They used consecutive-month validation schemes and cleaned leak data to tune ensemble behavior. Log-space and generalized weighted means supported blending, and the final submission averaged four selected submissions; area-normalized targets improved the score by about 0.002.

solution_title: Very quick 1st summary of julian's part of 2nd place solution.
solution_summary: The pipeline used doctor-assigned LIDC malignancy labels and LUNA16 negatives to train a 3D CNN that jointly detected nodules and estimated malignancy. Training included non-lung negatives, mined false positives, manually annotated competition scans, and heavy augmentation. Multiscale scan predictions supplied maximum malignancy and location features to XGBoost, alongside abnormal-tissue estimates from a U-Net. Predictions were averaged with a complementary two-stage ResNet-like pipeline, while local cross-validation guided decisions despite inconsistent leaderboard feedback.

solution_title: 4th place solution for the NeurIPS-Ariel-24 competition
solution_summary: The solution estimated transit boundaries with piecewise quadratic fits and predicted spectra by fitting ingress and egress separately. Ingress estimates received more weight, while polynomial uncertainty estimation and adaptive wavelength smoothing improved robustness. Two additional TensorFlow models jointly fitted transit depths and polynomial drift across time and wavelength. The final ensemble combined three spectrum estimates equally and used separate uncertainty weights, reaching reported public/private scores of 0.703/0.715.
compute: Kaggle CPU/GPU notebooks; vectorized regression processed 256 planets concurrently on GPU.

solution_summary: The pipeline emphasized accurate image-pair selection before standard feature matching and reconstruction. DINOv2 patch features guided dataset-dependent top-k selection, while a KeyNet-AdaLAM score ranked candidate neighbors. ALIKED-LightGlue matches from full images and DBSCAN-derived crops were combined, filtered with MAGSAC++, and reconstructed using pycolmap. Strict pairing helped visually repetitive scenes, but stairs and opposite-view connections remained difficult; VGGT experiments were not integrated.
compute: Two T4 GPUs for parallel processing.

solution_summary: The solution used an Optuna-tuned LGBMRegressor with a target defined as the difference from its value 48 hours earlier. Validation used a single period from February through May 2023. Features summarized target histories over 8 and 15 days using linear regression slopes, intercepts, and squared residual errors, calculated directly with NumPy. LightGBM consistently outperformed CatBoost in the author's experiments, and retraining occurred once at the end of January 2024.

The solution combined bioinformatics descriptors in a hybrid of multilinear regression and ensembling, largely bypassing the provided training data. Relative solvent accessibility supplied a strong positional baseline and divided residues into core and surface groups for different treatment. Molecular dynamics RMSD, AlphaFold2 confidence, substitution preferences, and several stability predictors added complementary information. Public leaderboard tuning proved unreliable, and the more conservative final variant performed better privately; an unselected experimental submission scored 0.536.

solution_summary: The system retrieved 100 candidates per session from historical items, item-to-item expansion, and popularity fallback, then reranked them with LightGBM. Candidate scoring emphasized nearby interactions and normalized item similarities to reduce popularity bias. The ranker used 182 session, item, interaction, retrieval, and embedding features, with temporal validation on the following week. Five rankers trained with different negative-sampling and training seeds reached 0.601 on both public and private leaderboards. Cross-target prediction features helped locally but failed on the leaderboard, while embedding-neighbor retrieval did not improve hit rate.

solution_title: 7th Place Solution : My First Gold And I am in Tears
solution_summary: The final sequence-generation ensemble used two ViT encoders and one Swin encoder, each paired with a transformer decoder, averaging logits at every decoding step. Progressive resolution training, label smoothing, cutout, and random scaling improved robustness after validation analysis exposed failures on noisy images and long molecules. RDKit normalized predicted InChIs and supported replacement of invalid outputs with predictions from auxiliary models, followed by hard voting for remaining invalid cases. The logit ensemble scored 0.66 on the public leaderboard and 0.71 locally, improving to 0.60 and 0.66 after RDKit processing.

solution_summary: The solution stacked predictions from eleven models using an XGBoost meta-model. Recursive feature elimination with cross-validation was applied to the base-model predictions. The short writeup links to a notebook but does not specify the base models or report numerical scores.

solution_title: Curse of Overfitting (From Place 14th to Place 2484th)
solution_summary: The post shares a link to a competition script. It states that the script would have achieved a score of 0.828063. No modeling approach, validation procedure, or implementation details are provided in the post itself.

The pipeline combined boosted trees, MLPs, and TABM models trained with different feature sets and original data added as rows or columns. Features included categorical interactions and fold-local mean and count encodings, with additional counts calculated jointly on train and test. AutoGluon stacking provided a substantial improvement, followed by hill-climbing and logistic-regression ensembles combined equally. The best reported ensemble CV was 0.97746, and an AutoGluon ensemble with 320 candidates was also selected as an alternative submission.
compute: Seven AutoGluon runs with 16-hour runtime; AutoGluon and hill climbs on Colab L4; XGB on A6000 Ada/A6000/A5000/4090; LGBM on 4090; CatBoost on L4/A100; MLP and TABM on 2× T4.

solution_title: How to reduce the size of the MIP
solution_summary: The author improved an initial assignment with local search before applying a series of heuristically reduced mixed-integer programs. Most of the writeup describes an unsuccessful attempt to prove optimality through tractable linear relaxations and variable fixing. Convex-hull approximations, repeated domain reduction, cuts and reduced-cost fixing substantially reduced the formulation. The remaining program still contained millions of variables, and slow solver progress led the author to stop.
compute: The final Gurobi initial relaxation took several hours; the reduced MIP retained 2–3 million variables.

solution_title: 8th Place Solution: Regression models for binary classification
solution_summary: The author built a diverse ensemble of boosted trees, neural networks, linear models, forests, and GAM predictions. Features were standardized, and the original dataset was excluded after consistently hurting performance. Second-degree polynomial features improved logistic regression, while most other interaction experiments did not help. Calibration benefited selected model families, and ordinary KFold replaced stratified validation after improving CV; XGBRegressor was the strongest listed individual model at 0.03049.

The solution used invariant per-mouse and inter-mouse features with a TransformerConv graph network, a Squeezeformer temporal encoder, and pairwise or relation-network classification heads. Processing each mouse's temporal trajectory separately after social interaction modeling was a major improvement. Action-rich sampling, weighted focal loss, and high dropout supported learning from imbalanced data and generalization across labs. The final ensemble contained 23 models, mostly four-fold averages, with overlapping-window probability averaging and minimal segment filtering.
compute: About 15 minutes inference per model on one T4 GPU; 23 models in the final submission.

solution_summary: The solution extended a public kernel with XGBoost classifiers and class-specific normalization rules. One classifier predicted token classes, while an additional model distinguished four-digit dates from cardinal numbers. Customized functions handled six structured classes with reported accuracies of 98.9%–99.7%, although rare formats remained difficult. Another XGBoost classifier resolved ambiguous punctuation with about 98% precision and 99.3% recall.

The author links their own approach in a public notebook. The linked URL identifies a Mask R-CNN approach using torchvision, but the post provides no pipeline details. The author reports that the approach can achieve a score above 0.17 despite disappointing overall results.

The approach combined CatBoost and LightGBM with extensive arithmetic feature generation and sequential feature selection. A FailureID indicator derived from failures in the original dataset improved cross-validation, although the suspected direct ID leakage was not confirmed. Repeated multilabel stratified validation guided feature selection, tuning, and bagging with majority-class subsampling. The author reported a best CV score of 0.9809, but the selected submissions generalized less well to the private leaderboard.

The final system blended DeBERTa-v3-large and LightGBM predictions with weights of 7:3, tuned using out-of-fold predictions. Including the full prompt text improved local validation, and supporting sequences of length 5000 was crucial for the long test prompts. DeBERTa used a CLS-token head with 18 layers frozen, while LightGBM used 141 text-statistics features and separate models for content and wording. Validation grouped four folds by prompt, but inference used only two DeBERTa folds because four timed out; the ensemble achieved a private score of 0.461.
compute: Four-fold DeBERTa inference timed out; final inference used two folds with batch size 1.

solution_summary: The solution blended non-leaked models and then replaced predictions wherever an unambiguous label leak was available. Recovering feature groups and customer histories enabled stronger features and validation that avoided sharing customer information across folds. Artificial-looking test rows were removed, and ambiguous leak candidates were excluded. Feature engineering improved the non-leak public score from about 1.36 to 1.24.

The post describes a speed optimization for clustering-based particle tracking. Each candidate track receives an identifier computed by hashing the unordered set of its hit IDs, allowing identical tracks to be removed in linear time. In one DBSCAN stage for tracks with at least 14 hits, deduplication reduced 68,960 candidates to 4,737. This substantially reduced subsequent curve-fitting, outlier-removal, and merging work.

The solution combined 2D representations of raw EEG, STFT spectrograms, and multitaper spectrograms using ConvNeXt Base and MaxViT Tiny models. All models used 18 bipolar EEG signal differences, with several combinations of temporal windows. STFT spectrogram models achieved the best cross-validation scores and received the largest ensemble weight. The final submission blended raw EEG, STFT, and multitaper predictions with weights of 0.2, 0.65, and 0.15, respectively.

The solution ensembled large image classifiers, including EfficientNet B6 and B7, across resolutions from 1024 to 1408 pixels. It added three device-presence classes and intermediate supervised heads to improve learning. Deeper outputs also taught shallower blocks through self-distillation, while repeated training cycles used out-of-fold soft labels. The author identifies this noisy-student procedure as a major contributor, improving local CV and leaderboard scores by roughly 0.004–0.005.

solution_title: 9th Place Solution: Various Augmentations + A lot of Modeling tricks
solution_summary: The final ensemble combined CatBoost, two LightGBM DART models, and a transformed AdvantageP1 baseline. Eight-fold GroupKFold provided the most stable validation, while training used only original samples and agent swapping was retained for inference. Residual target prediction and optimized affine ensemble weights and clipping improved results. Training augmentations often improved cross-validation but hurt leaderboard performance.

The solution used a CNN and an FTRL-FM model based on a shared approach. Extensive text normalization improved both models and was particularly important for making the CNN effective. Network structure and training batch size were adjusted for slow CPU execution, with reported scores of 0.400 for the CNN and 0.415 for FTRL-FM.
compute: CPU execution; CNN described as very slow.

solution_summary: The model classifies ten driver actions using a pretrained VGG-16 convolutional backbone with three dense layers added on top. It fine-tunes the last seven convolutional layers and applies aggressive Eigenvalue Decay regularization to the dense layers. Training augmentation includes shear, zoom, and rotation. The reported model trained for 80 epochs, and the author suggests that longer training could improve performance.
compute: 80 training epochs

solution_summary: The final submission ensembled EfficientNet B1–B4 backbones with a triplet attention layer and GeM pooling. Training used only the new training data and ON channels, with five-fold stratified validation and resized inputs. A preliminary B4 model generated high-confidence pseudo-labels, followed by training all four architectures and a short refinement stage with lighter augmentation. The ensemble achieved 0.9100 CV and 0.80475 private leaderboard score, using four-way flip augmentation at inference.
compute: Stages 0 and 1: 60 epochs each with DDP and AMP; stage 2: 10 epochs with DDP and AMP. Hardware and elapsed time were not stated.

solution_summary: The solution averaged approximately 20 model folds across two complementary pipelines to obtain cell-level predictions. One pipeline trained on full images and predicted individual cells by masking other cells, with an additional variant centering the retained cell. The other trained a CNN on randomly sampled cell crops resized to 128×128, supervising each cell with its source image's labels. Final predictions used individual cell outputs without image-level predictions.
compute: Sponsored Z8G4 workstation with dual RTX6000 GPUs and a ZBook with RTX5000 GPU.

solution_summary: The solution combined EfficientNet-B2 classifiers trained on full images and MegaDetector bounding-box crops. Balanced Group Softmax addressed long-tailed class frequencies, and weighted image predictions were averaged across nonempty frames to classify each sequence. Models were trained progressively at higher resolution and validated using held-out camera locations. Animal counts came from the maximum number of confident detections in any sequence frame; geographic priors and DeepSORT tracking did not improve the final approach.

solution_title: 429th Place Solution for Evaluate Student Summaries Competition
solution_summary: The final pipeline combines fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3-base with separate LightGBM models for content and wording scores. Text preprocessing corrects spelling and extracts length, error, overlap, and entity features, while LightGBM also receives transformer predictions. Training uses four-fold GroupKFold, and final predictions average the transformer and LightGBM outputs. The author reported a score of 0.488 with 3.8 hours of training on a P100 GPU.
compute: P100 GPU, 3.8 hours training

solution_title: 494th Solution - Lessons Learned from submitting an Overfitted Model
solution_summary: The author submitted an XGBoost regressor with default hyperparameters under time constraints. Training used 538 games spanning five seasons, and the author later identified overfitting from the learning curve and the model's estimated 6,400 parameters. The solution also split predictions when normalized point differences fell below a chosen threshold, although the precise procedure was not described. The reported final score was 0.10149, and the model correctly predicted UConn as champion.

The solution used four stages: background removal exploiting information leakage, several neural and boosted-tree models, XGBoost ensembling, and a second leakage-based adjustment on the text. Contrast constraints helped preserve faded text in heavily stained areas. Shallow dense neural networks performed best, while the CNN was weaker, which the author attributed to its lack of fully connected layers. The final text leakage step reportedly halved the score.

solution_title: 2d-CNN for sparse heatmap images and MLP (1st stage 45th, 2nd stage 42nd place)
solution_summary: The solution combined a spatial CNN over sparse player heatmaps with an MLP over tabular features. Its 18 heatmap channels represented three player groups, three motion variables, and two snapshots, with convolutions preserving the field direction associated with gained yards. The network learned residual probabilities relative to the 2018 yard distribution, followed by goal-line constraints, normalization, and cumulative summation. Training used only 2018 data, small spatial shifts, Adam, and a linear cyclical learning-rate schedule. Graph-derived features, feature scaling, and lateral flips did not help.
The author used a deep convolutional neural network for document denoising. The implementation used Torch 7. The post links to a GitHub repository but provides no architecture or training details.

The team built an ensemble of two similar three-stage pipelines. Vertebra visibility and segmentation models generated slice-level fracture pseudo-labels and study-level crop regions. Lightweight EfficientNetV2 models combined neighboring slices with 3D convolutions, then a feed-forward model aggregated study-level prediction statistics. A 30–70 blend of maximum slice predictions and learned aggregation improved leaderboard scores by a reported 2–3 points.

The team hashed text into a 2^24-dimensional space, combining name n-grams, category–name interactions, and separately prefixed description and brand text. Five-fold out-of-fold Ridge and LinearSVR predictions became inputs to two LightGBM models alongside hashed names and numerical features. The final prediction was a weighted blend of the LightGBM outputs. Multiprocessing and parallel linear-model fitting enabled the pipeline to meet a one-hour time limit.
compute: Pipeline constrained to a one-hour time frame; multiprocessing and parallel Ridge/LinearSVR fitting used.

solution_summary: The solution retrieved content directly using cosine similarity between multilingual topic and content embeddings, without a reranking stage. Symmetric InfoNCE training relied on carefully constructed batches that avoided conflicting positives, oversampled missed matches, and included mined hard negatives. Translation-based language switching and a dynamic retrieval threshold improved scores. The leaderboard submission combined five models, while the efficiency submission used distillation, selective dynamic quantization, and a smaller ensemble.
compute: Five-model leaderboard inference took 9 minutes on a P100; two-model efficiency inference took 23 minutes.

solution_summary: The final model was XGBoost with about 600 features, including roughly 25 out-of-fold model predictions or likelihoods. Training used oversampling to a prior of about 0.13, while out-of-fold predictions came from five stratified folds on the original data. Text features combined multiple preprocessing variants, token bags, and longest common subsequences. Graph statistics and features weighted by out-of-fold predictions delivered significant gains; train-test appearance information was predictive but prone to overfitting. Markov-chain feature reweighting was also explored, although its benefit was unclear.

The post announces that the solution code is ready and functional. It says code review uncovered problems and that a revised v1.0 is available on a GitHub branch. It links to the repository, report, and README without describing the approach.

solution_title: [20th Place] Learning to Play Pokémon TCG
solution_summary: The final agent used a 25-million-parameter Transformer policy with a Hydrapple-Meganium deck. Action-dynamics contrastive pretraining preceded general PPO, deck-cluster specialist training, and focused Hydrapple PPO against self-play and specialist opponents. Structured state, legal-action, and recent-memory tokens supported policy and value prediction. An LLM agent optimized the final deck through mutations and measured gameplay outcomes.

solution_title: 45th Place solutions , learnings , trials and what could have been | 0.919/0.917 submitted too late :D
solution_summary: The solution trained DeBERTa models on 60k science questions with retrieved context, including interleaved context variants that improved generalization. Retrieval combined Openbook MiniLM with TF-IDF over science Wikipedia and Cohere data. A separate 500-question validation dataset enabled reliable model selection and averaging or Optuna-weighted ensembling of the top three models. The selected submission scored 0.905 publicly and 0.909 privately; stronger late experiments missed the submission deadline.

solution_summary: The author trained a CNN from scratch on the provided competition dataset. The solution used a single model without transfer learning, external data, or complex training techniques. Development took place within a one-week time constraint, and the post links a training and prediction notebook without providing architectural details or numerical results.
compute: One week available to develop the solution and make a submission; training hardware and runtime were not specified.

solution_summary: The authors started from a public generative model and increased its parameter count, improving their score from about 60 to 55. Measuring FID every few epochs guided model comparisons, cyclic learning rates, and small hyperparameter adjustments that brought the score to roughly 50. A broader weight initialization distribution produced the next major improvement to around 46, followed by smaller changes that reached about 43.

The author's sleep/awake indicator model was excluded from the team's final submission because it was difficult to combine with event-prediction models. The post describes timestamp adjustments that move predictions away from exact minute and half-minute boundaries to improve matching under the evaluation tolerances. A second adjustment shifts events according to their empirical 15-minute timing pattern, and this simple rule was retained in the final submission.

solution_title: Philipp Weidmann (5th in the Elo comp) on chess ratings and numerical optimization
solution_summary: The author describes an experimental chess rating system that jointly optimizes player ratings and predicts outcomes from rating differences plus the average white score. Pairwise fitting errors were weighted by the number of games, and a truncated Newton solver made optimization practical. The initial formulation produced poor predictions because indirectly connected players could acquire extreme rating differences; weak penalties between players who had never met improved results. The author ultimately abandoned this method for a better-performing approach that did not require optimization.
frameworks_libraries: ["Stephen Nash truncated Newton implementation in Fortran 90"]
compute: Rating optimization converged in less than 3 minutes on the author's notebook.

solution_summary: The post collects links to solution discussions for the HPA Single Cell Image Classification competition. It labels many links by their authors' placements. It does not describe an original approach or provide technical details about the linked solutions.

solution_title: Second Place Solution: The raddar Prophecy Strikes Again...
solution_summary: The successful submission used goto's starter notebook and goto_conversion as a foundation, with manual Florida overrides. The choice emphasized roster experience and continuity, analytics-driven coaching, and perceived undervaluation rather than consensus expectations. This concentrated gamble outperformed the author's other, more extensively prepared submission. The post does not specify the exact override probabilities or provide the full underlying modeling pipeline.

The solution combined seven VoxelNet models using FHD and PointPillars variants with diverse voxel sizes and feature extractors. Four flip-based test-time views and custom 3D box fusion were the main improvements. Fusion averaged box centers and sizes while interpolating doubled yaw angles to handle 180-degree ambiguity. The ensemble scored 0.220, while a slower post-competition Weighted Boxes Fusion experiment reached 0.222 on the public leaderboard.

The author fine-tuned Llama 3 and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct models on synthetic 20 Questions games generated by GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini. Training combined ordinary simulations, keyword-assisted simulations, and complete winning game snapshots, with some weights frozen and two stages differing in instruction masking. The final agent made one direct LLM call per phase without reasoning or ensembling. Fine-tuning raised nearly zero initial win rates to 31.2% on easy evaluation keywords and 13% across all evaluation keywords, but incorrect answers from other agents reduced real-game performance.
compute: Nvidia A100 GPU for training; competition resources limited usable models to approximately 8B parameters.

solution_summary: The code reconstructs lagged row relationships and column groups to recover leaked target values. It augments training with filtered leak-labeled test rows and builds group means and log means after treating zeros as missing. Ten XGBoost models predict log-transformed targets, and their predictions are averaged before inverse transformation. Available leaked targets override the model predictions in the submission; no validation score is reported.
compute: XGBoost configured with 4 threads.

solution_summary: The author prioritized stability by retaining every feature and removing observations only when four anomaly detectors agreed. The detectors were an autoencoder, Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor, and SGDOneClassSVM, and their consensus removed approximately 250 observations. Cross-validation served only as a rough strategy check, with the two observations whose targets exceeded 30 kept exclusively in training. Alternative submissions using cleanlab or removing only those two high-target observations performed better than the final submission.

The solution used LightGBM to stack five models: a tabular model, two Swin Large models, EfficientNet B0, and an SVR using headless Swin Large features. The tabular model combined provided metadata with inferred animal type and breed labels. Validation used ten stratified folds over binned targets, and the author trusted CV because leaderboard scores correlated poorly with it. The stack achieved 17.1585 CV and 16.9833 on the private leaderboard.

The final solution weighted Paul's predictions by two thirds and Ben's by one third. Paul combined roughly 15 models with varied algorithms and categorical feature sets, emphasizing cross-tabulation counts and stability across repeated validation splits. His stacking model also used category-frequency meta-features to adjust trust in individual models. Ben combined logistic regression with random forests, gradient boosting, and extremely randomized trees. The complete blend achieved a private score of 0.92360.
compute: Approximately 30 minutes per fold for Paul's models; stacking takes considerably longer; cache can grow to a couple of gigabytes.

solution_summary: The author submitted a rule-based game agent. They describe it as an ordinary approach with a few additional quirks already discussed in other solutions. The post links the implementation but provides no further algorithmic details or quantitative results.

The author used a linear model throughout the competition with separate TF-IDF representations for summary and description text. Additional features captured issue timing, tags, source, and four geographic regions. Direct optimization of RMSLE was important for competitive performance. The author discovered overfitting late in the competition and found early stopping useful.

solution_title: 25th Place Solution for the Google Research Identify Contrails to Reduce Global Warming Competition
solution_summary: The solution extracted per-frame 2D features and temporally modulated only the deepest feature map before a U-Net decoder. Its final ensemble combined EfficientNet-B3 and two PVTv2 backbones at different resolutions, four seeds, and horizontal-flip inference. False-color images were stored as uint8, and gradient checkpointing plus FP16 enabled higher resolutions on one RTX 3090 Ti. Validation and private scores were 0.692 and 0.700; separate late experiments found additional gains from alignment correction and soft labels.
compute: 1x RTX 3090 Ti

solution_summary: The solution modeled each feature independently, exploiting conditional feature independence and the predictive signal in repeated values. Frequency counts were computed jointly over training and genuine test rows, excluding synthetic test rows. Each column combined two shallow LightGBM models with a locally fitted logistic-regression smoother. Final predictions aggregated column outputs using the mean of their logits, and training plus prediction took about 3.5 hours.
compute: Training and prediction took around 3.5 hours.

solution_summary: The team blended 10 image classifiers trained with different crops, augmentations, and test-time augmentation. External Flickr images and confident pseudo-labels supported iterative training, including a second stage with a reset learning rate. One VGG-16 model trained exclusively on pseudo-labels in its second stage achieved 0.985 on the private leaderboard. Final class balancing helped publicly but was later judged to overfit; a late blend of three models scored 0.989 privately.

The author generated millions of Stable Diffusion images from diverse prompt sources and trained pretrained vision models to predict sentence embeddings. Prompt diversity came from DiffusionDB, COCO captions, chained BLIP-2 captions of Open Images, and ChatGPT-generated prompts. Linear probing followed by full fine-tuning and higher-resolution training improved performance. Frozen-backbone Q-formers added modest gains, and the final four-model ensemble used validation-optimized weighted averaging.

solution_title: 155th Place (Silver) Solution — EXFILTRATION=0 Privately, CD Survives
solution_summary: The team developed separate submissions targeting two independently reachable benchmark predicates and retained both as final submissions to hedge against private guardrail changes. Their main optimization was a live candidate-generation loop that retained successful attacks while estimating generation and replay budgets from observed latency. They used repeated same-day paired comparisons to distinguish variant improvements from infrastructure variability and allocated submission slots using estimated probabilities of exceeding their best score. All exfiltration variants scored zero privately, while confused-deputy variants transferred almost exactly from public evaluation.

The solution combined diverse models through a neural network ensembler fitted on out-of-fold predictions. XGBoost and dropout-regularized neural networks were the strongest individual learners, while weaker models still contributed useful differences. Neural networks benefited from logarithmic input transformation, standardization, and repeated training cycles that removed confidently predicted rows. The boosted neural network achieved a leaderboard log loss of 0.433, and model usefulness in the ensemble mattered more than individual scores.

The post thanks the organizers and participants and acknowledges other competitors' contributions. It announces that the author's solution has been published in a linked notebook. No technical description of the approach is included in the post itself.

The solution stacked out-of-fold class probabilities after clipping and transforming them to logits, using a small PyTorch logistic regression model. Predictions were averaged across five folds and five seeds, with class weights tuned for balanced accuracy. Adding Chris Deotte's published out-of-fold predictions improved the score by about 0.003 over the authors' roughly 30-model stack. Additional engineered features, boosted trees, and an FT-Transformer received zero ensemble weight.
compute: Kaggle P100 used to train the experimental FT-Transformer

solution_summary: The post links to a notebook presented as the author's competition solution. It reflects on an alternative submission that performed better than the selected final submission. The author says its low public leaderboard score discouraged selection, but provides no methodological description in the post itself.

The authors generated candidate inputs with EternaFold, RNAsoft, RNAstructure, and other tools, with EternaFold performing best. They tried stacking but found a Nelder–Mead blending approach more effective. Pseudo-labeling provided a substantial gain. The text does not specify the underlying model architecture or detailed training pipeline.

The final predictor averaged eight Inception and SE-ResNeXt models trained with SmoothL1 loss, extensive augmentation, and generalized mean pooling. Training combined the 2015 and 2019 datasets, with model decisions guided by the public leaderboard after an initial validation scheme proved unreliable. A second stage added soft pseudo-labels and adjusted labels from IDRiD and Messidor before ten more epochs of training. Changing the first ordinal threshold from 0.5 to 0.7 brought the reported private score to 0.936.

The team built a folded single-model segmentation baseline using ResNet152 and a modified decoder with hypercolumns, dropout, and squeeze-excitation. Training combined segmentation and heavily weighted boundary losses, switching the segmentation term from binary cross entropy to Lovasz hinge after 30 epochs. Strong augmentation helped, followed by ten final epochs using horizontal flips alone. Checkpoints were selected from averaged ordinary and augmented validation scores; the reported baseline scores were 0.869 and 0.887, without ensembling or post-processing.

The solution combined Xception models at resolutions 256 and 512 with a single-fold NASNet model at resolution 256. Training used flips and 90-degree rotations, BCE and focal losses, and Adam with learning-rate finding and triangular2 cyclical learning rates. Model blending was particularly valuable despite relatively weak individual models. The authors identified conservative augmentation and ineffective use of pooled compute as limitations.
compute: All but one final-submission model trained on a machine with 2x GTX 1080 Ti GPUs.

solution_title: [2nd] place solution (for the C in MYRCJ)
solution_summary: The author built per-building MLPs for RSSI-based absolute positioning and ordinal floor classification, plus a sliding-window LSTM for relative displacement from IMU data. RSSI training positions were improved by interpolation between waypoints. Post-processing alternated corridor geometry corrections with cost minimization before a final snap-to-grid step. The original pipeline achieved a public score of 3.256, and its relative-position model and post-processing were incorporated into the final team submission.

solution_title: My part of the 3rd place solution
solution_summary: The author's contribution used a domain-specific language with abstractions for colors, extracted image blocks, and binary masks. Predictors enumerated transformations, retained those consistent with every training pair, and applied the survivors to test inputs. Mosaic restoration predictors worked best on the test set. Before teaming up, the approach solved five tasks plus two from public kernels, and it also solved 138 training and 96 validation samples. Multiprocessing and block caching helped manage computation and memory.
