solution_summary: The author explored three mel-spectrogram feature formats for audio tagging. Experiments included background subtraction and frequency-envelope transfer to reduce differences between curated and noisy audio. The approach also included soft relabeling based on label co-occurrence and ensemble averaging with separate weights for each class and model. The post does not report scores and leaves the benefit of background subtraction uncertain.

solution_title: Two "Different" Finals, One Failure Mode: A Private-Transfer Post-Mortem
solution_summary: The selected approach maximized replayable single-post exfiltration events by exploiting a public guardrail that inspected the URL but overlooked the payload. Unique domains supplied diversity bonuses, and live latency measurements controlled candidate count within replay limits. Reasoning-collapse and wrap-up-collapse prompts raised the reported public score from 64.44 to 91.40. Both final submissions scored zero privately, while a separately developed confused-deputy hedge was not selected.
compute: Two target models evaluated sequentially; 18,000-second budget per model, with 9,000 seconds of replay per guardrail.

solution_summary: The solution stacked about 60 diverse base models using a two-layer Keras neural network. Extensive feature engineering supplied group statistics, smoothed target likelihoods, temporal features, geographic clusters, text signals, and XGBoost text predictions. Nested cross-validation protected likelihood features from leakage, and stratified five-fold splits supported base-model training. Grid-search bagging improved the strongest LightGBM model, while the better final meta-model used early stopping and 35 bags per fold, achieving a reported private loss of 0.49302.

The approach used LightGBM regression on visitor-level data. The target focused on second purchases, assigning zero to first-time purchasers who did not make a subsequent purchase. Existing features were aggregated with sums or means, and purchase history features captured whether a previous visit converted and its purchase amount.

The pipeline segmented ECG traces from rectified images and then reconstructed waveforms through post-processing. ResNet-18 and ResNet-34d encoders were trained with complementary full-image and half-width crops, and their predictions were combined. Corrected image warping and extensive geometric, photometric, and occlusion augmentation improved alignment and robustness. Missing waveform regions were repaired using beat-phase alignment and a temporal refinement model while preserving observed points.

solution_title: 2055th -> 158th Place Solution — Physics PF + Decorrelated Full-Well Decoders
solution_summary: The solution combined a physics-informed tabular ensemble with three full-well neural decoders designed to make different errors. It modeled smooth surface trends using known trajectory measurements, neighboring wells, and a momentum particle filter with weak gamma-ray likelihood. Frozen blending weights, row-wise winsorisation, and robust polynomial projection produced the final predictions. Strict grouped validation across 773 wells guided selection despite conflicting public feedback, yielding grouped CV of 7.5803 and a private score of 7.989.

The author used ten-fold cross-validation grouped by installation_id to account for correlated assessments. To approximate the test distribution, each assessment received weight inversely proportional to the number of assessment trials for its installation, and QWK was calculated on the weighted out-of-fold predictions. Reported CV was around 56, versus approximately 54 on both public and private leaderboards, which still helped avoid public leaderboard overfitting. Repeating fold generation across seeds and averaging results was suggested as a possible improvement.

The author trained CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost, a neural network, and logistic regression using both competition and original data. Categorical mappings and borrowed interaction features improved validation and public scores despite concerns about leakage. Log-transformed out-of-fold predictions fed a stacking classifier with its default logistic regression estimator. A final insurance-matrix correction improved the score by approximately 0.0006.

solution_title: Part of the 18th place solution (Naoism's model)
solution_summary: The solution trained ResNeSt50d on recordings no longer than 60 seconds, using biased five-second crops to reduce weak-label noise. Manual annotation identified nocall intervals and removable human speech, while noise augmentation and modified mixup addressed domain mismatch. Secondary-label losses were masked during mixup, and predictions were combined with power averaging and shifted-sequence inference. Recording-level probability boosts provided additional postprocessing; the best single five-fold model scored 0.6206 private and 0.7471 public.
external_data: ["Cornell Birdcall Identification 2020 example_test_audio nocall portions", "Rainforest Connection Species Audio Detection audio"]

solution_summary: The pipeline first trained a U-Net on LUNA/LIDC nodule annotations and averaged predictions from three orthogonal CT views. Iterative thresholding and clustering extracted plausible nodule candidates, retaining the top 20 by segmentation probability mass. A shared 3D ResNet processed each candidate using both CT intensities and segmentation probabilities. Maximum pooling across candidate probabilities produced a permutation-invariant patient cancer prediction and outperformed the other tested reduction functions.
compute: Ubuntu 14.04 machines; hardware and runtime unspecified

solution_title: 7th Place Solution: Ensemble of Two Protenix Models
solution_summary: The solution ensembled fine-tuned Protenix models with and without multiple sequence alignments. Two training strategies emphasized either CASP16 VFold predictions or host-provided structural data, with the latter producing the stronger private result. Each model generated five candidate structures, and k-medoids selected five structures from the combined ten. Endpoint padding and diversity-based selection improved local or public scores but brought little benefit on the private set; the stronger final submission scored 0.48511 privately.
compute: RTX 5090 or RTX 4090 for training.

solution_summary: The solution combines rank regression and pairwise similarity models in a two-phase pipeline for ordering markdown cells. The first phase estimates approximate positions, while independently trained models refine predictions within a 20-cell neighborhood, with temperature-based softmax ensembling. Offset sampling of code cells tripled the training data and improved CV from 0.8436 to 0.8506. Training initially with KGTorrent and competition data, then continuing on competition data alone, added another 0.002–0.004 CV.

solution_summary: The post explains how to extend flower-classification training with external datasets supplied as TFRecords with aligned labels. Adding the five sources produces 66,758 training images, with example training times for EfficientNetB7 and DenseNet201. It also describes saving weights to continue training across notebook sessions. solution_summary: The solution combines a text CNN with a factorization machine using weights of 0.6 and 0.4. The CNN uses Twitter GloVe embeddings, embedded categorical features, and a dense prediction head. The most important improvement was fine-tuning the CNN separately on each category, reducing validation RMSLE to about 0.408 and improving stability. The final ensemble achieved validation RMSLE of 0.399x–0.400x and leaderboard RMSLE of 0.401.

solution_title: Silver Medal - 104th Rank Solution in ISIC 2024 Challenge
solution_summary: The final approach ensembled LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost using engineered features and one-hot encoded categorical variables. Feature pruning, oversampling, undersampling, and hyperparameter tuning supported training, with stratified group cross-validation preserving patient splits. The team emphasized partial AUC, used early stopping, and reported threshold adjustment and output calibration. Prediction noise was explored, but its adoption and benefit were not specified.
compute: GPU acceleration; hardware and runtime unspecified.

solution_summary: The author used a single neural network with three 300-unit GRU layers, concatenation operations, dropout, and a final nine-output linear dense layer. Version 8 trained for 200 epochs and required about six hours on a GPU. Extending training to 400 epochs lowered training loss but performed poorly on the private leaderboard. An unselected submission scored 0.16959 after being passed over because of its weaker public score.
compute: GPU, approximately 6 hours for 200 epochs in version 8.

solution_summary: The solution used adversarial essay prompts to induce consistent disagreement among LLM judges and reports achieving a perfect score. Nonsense text built from random words addressed language-confidence and similarity constraints, while several prompt variants targeted conflicting instructions, code interpretation, and judge identities. Carefully designed submissions verified each attack's judge-specific outputs and inferred how samples were distributed across the public split. Repeating a small set of verified samples reduced the number of submissions needed for validation.

The team developed a Cfish-based chess engine optimized for the competition's binary size, memory, and short time controls. It combined specialized search and time-management changes with a compact NNUE evaluator trained progressively and quantized for deployment. Distributed testing used roughly 20 million games, with SPRT evaluating changes and SPSA tuning parameters. Compiler and code-size optimizations helped retain the evaluator within the size budget, and an additional 80,000-game test produced no crashes or time losses.
compute: Distributed compute resources used for around 20 million games; local testing used 1 thread, 1 MB hash, and speed-scaled 10 seconds per move.

solution_summary: The solution trained a DCGAN in PyTorch with latent dimension 64 and batch size 32. It used cropped images filtered by a stated ratio criterion, with horizontal flips and random crops for augmentation. Training stopped at the best FID, and the author selected the best randomly generated images.

The team combined SAINT++ sequence models with LightGBM for answer correctness prediction. SAINT++ used exercise, interaction, and prior-response embeddings, with added skip connections and dropout. Longer sequences improved performance, and the best reported configuration used sequence length 320, embedding dimension 224, and two encoder and two decoder layers. Combining two SAINT++ models with LightGBM achieved public and private scores of 0.808 and 0.810.

The pipeline started with continual self-supervised pretraining of ByT5-base on Akkadian text, followed by two-stage supervised fine-tuning within three grouped folds. Text normalization standardized gaps, fractions, and transliteration conventions, while overlap checks protected validation targets when adding external data. The three fold checkpoints were averaged into one model for efficient inference. Length-based batching, BF16, adaptive beam sizes, and minimum Bayes risk decoding with modified CHRF++ scoring balanced translation quality and inference cost.

solution_title: Guardrail-Dependent Failure Modes in Tool-Using Agents
solution_summary: The approach generated sandbox attack candidates under replay-time limits and retained candidates verified to trigger scored predicates. A parser-safe hop-chain respected the one-tool-call-per-generation constraint, but did not outperform single-post validation-fill in the real evaluation. Final submissions hedged a high-scoring public exfiltration family with a confused-deputy email family, whose score remained 20.095 privately. The study also mapped guardrail-dependent failures and reported a matched provenance defense that blocked its attacks without benign false positives.
compute: GPU-free mechanism reproduction: 16 checks, approximately 4 minutes; evaluation budget of 8750 seconds per phase.

solution_summary: The solution used only tabular data, with baseline lung-function measurements, age, elapsed weeks, sex, and smoking status as features. Final FVC predictions averaged nine different regressors. Confidence targets were derived from absolute FVC prediction errors, then modeled using the same regressor families. A binary classifier predicting whether confidence was at most 100 was used to post-process confidence predictions; image-based approaches and linear tabular augmentation did not work.

solution_title: 7th place solution - aka the first of the losers 😄
solution_summary: Separate production and consumption models predicted residuals after target normalization and an autoregressive baseline. The approach used 192 features covering target lags, weather, prices, calendar effects, and customer characteristics. Five-fold sliding-window validation guided Optuna tuning and selection of LightGBM and XGBoost models. The final ensemble averaged multiple parameter configurations and seeds, with ten models trained once at the start of February.

The team identified a seven-layer fast-forward LSTM as the central component of its solution. This model achieved 82.75% GAP@20 on the public test set. The post links a paper, code, and pretrained models but provides no further pipeline details.

The post announces that the author's competition solution is available on GitHub. It provides a repository link without describing the approach. The author offers to add further information or comments if readers are interested.

The solution created multiple text variants and a pool of over 1,400 statistical, linguistic, and graph features. Deep learning, XGBoost, LightGBM, and logistic regression models fed a multilayer stack comprising over 140 model outputs. Stacking improved the public score by about 0.007 over individual models scoring around 0.122–0.124. Rescaling predictions within clique size groups addressed train–test distribution differences and added about 0.001 improvement.

The author probed all 300 variables individually on the public leaderboard and converted their AUCs into linear coefficients. Training and public AUCs were combined with weights of 0.11 and 0.89, then centered at 0.5. Synthetic datasets calibrated to the observed AUC behavior supported learning a smooth coefficient shrinkage equation with Eureqa Desktop. The final linear prediction using the shrunken coefficients achieved private AUC 0.886 and public AUC 0.923.

The final submission combined eight models spanning LightGBM, tabular neural networks, Ridge regression, and NLP models on reconstructed essays. Shared stratified folds supported ensemble weighting, while extensive timing, pause, sentence, paragraph, and character-pattern features drove the tabular models. Particularly useful additions were character TF-IDF, fixed-time-window statistics, KNN predictions, and predictions from models trained on externally scored essays with letters replaced by q. The submission reported private/public scores of 0.557/0.575, while custom small-vocabulary language-model pretraining and alternative neural architectures did not help.
compute: NLP model: single RTX 3090, 27 minutes per epoch; eight models trained for 10 epochs on all essays.

solution_summary: The solution ensembled four segmentation models: U-Net with b2 and b4, U-Net++ with b2, and MANet with b4. Inference used 1024-pixel windows, overlap of 100, and a stated size of 512. YOLOv5 detected cells, and bounding-box area was compared with segmentation area to decide whether masks needed filling. The author reported LB 0.933 and PB 0.946.

The team optimized task-specific ONNX graphs by searching for representations with minimal stored parameters and charged intermediate memory. Common solutions used Einsum, analytic coordinates, compact convolutional operators, and small intermediate data types. An iterative prompting workflow retained only verified score improvements or equal-score runtime improvements. Every promoted graph passed structural checks, exact public examples, and 1,000 fresh generated examples.

The final submission used a bagged ensemble of LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost, and an additional LightGBM model without image features. The image features came from two MobileNetV3 CNN configurations, alongside engineered tabular features. The selected ensemble contained 40 models and achieved CV, public, and private scores of 0.182, 0.184, and 0.168 respectively. Extensive CNN experiments explored auxiliary targets, external datasets, partial-AUC loss, and test-time augmentation before the author combined image information with tree models.
external_data: ["2018, 2019, and 2020 datasets", "External datasets linked in ISIC discussion 515356"]

solution_summary: The model used eight variables expressed as differences between the two teams, although the model family was not specified. Features combined KenPom efficiency and schedule metrics, final Massey ratings, defensive rebounding, recent variability measures, and seed differences. The author noted that historical KenPom metrics incorporated tournament data, introducing some bias. The existing model was submitted once without adjustments or game-theoretic changes.

solution_title: 10th place solution: CNN with pseudo labels
solution_summary: The solution uses an EfficientNet-B5 CNN with separate heads for signal detection and frequency classification. PyFstat-generated training data, robust amplitude normalization, and soft pseudo-labels were central to the approach. Detector timestamps are aligned and temporally averaged into two-channel images, with clipping and standardization to handle noise differences. Five-fold stratified training, extensive augmentation, flip-based inference augmentation, and rank averaging complete the pipeline.

The final submission used a weighted ensemble of 21 models, with some predictions blended with SVR or ridge regression fitted to model embeddings. Indicator-specific tokens, layer-wise learning-rate decay, selective adversarial weight perturbation, and a classification model improved the ensemble. Only one pseudo-labeled model was retained despite broad CV gains from pseudo-labeling. The final ensemble achieved CV 0.4407 and a private leaderboard score of 0.434983; an alternative pseudo-label ensemble scored better privately.

The solution combined a modified 1D U-Net approach with a Spec2DCNN approach adapted from public code. Focal loss was the common training criterion. The author changed the 1D model's dataset, features, and architecture, while adding focal loss to the Spec2DCNN implementation. The submission scored 0.751 publicly and 0.786 privately.

The author trained pretrained ResNet and DenseNet classifiers through fastai using only competition data. Images were downscaled, augmented with reflection padding, and trained with QHAdam, a OneCycle schedule, and mixed precision. The detailed inference description averages six models equally with four-way test-time augmentation, achieving a private score of 0.6164 versus 0.5748 for the best individual model. ArcFace and several alternative architectures or auxiliary modeling ideas did not succeed.
compute: Five models trained at home using an RTX2070S and 4 CPUs; a sixth trained on Kaggle. Listed model durations range from 80 to 670 minutes.

solution_summary: The solution trained an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 entirely on Kaggle Kernels using a download-train-discard pipeline for dataset shards. It classified roughly 55,000 landmarks with at least 20 images, using 192×192 inputs, global max pooling, and a softmax output. Adam training lasted one full dataset epoch, with periodic learning-rate reductions, before overfitting appeared. Larger architectures, smaller inputs, and test-time augmentation performed worse.
compute: Entirely on Kaggle Kernels; ~30 seconds per tar download and 100–110 seconds per ~7,000-image mini-epoch; 500 mini-epochs.

solution_summary: The team identified an annotation-offset bug and built a pipeline that recovered intended spans before training and projected predictions back into the buggy annotation format. They trained RoBERTa and BERTweet using only the supplied training CSV and ensembled all five members' models at character level. Correcting the annotation mapping raised the score from 0.713 to 0.721, and further model, ensemble, and mapping improvements reached 0.731. They evaluated preprocessing and postprocessing under a perfect-token-model assumption to isolate mapping errors.

The solution focused on transaction features computed across historical/new data, time ranges, authorization flags, and categorical subsets. Dense temporal ranks and representative transaction categories improved performance, while only a few merchant-table aggregates helped. The author selected 93 features and ultimately contributed LightGBM models to the team ensemble, using both direct prediction and an outlier-handling approach. Reported scores were 3.621 CV, 3.666 public, and 3.601 private.

The solution recalculated a slightly better baseline from raw data and fed it through community post-processing and ensemble pipelines. Clustering the trajectories enabled highway-specific hyperparameter improvements after global tuning failed to help. The final custom step snapped SJC predictions to provided ground-truth points without interpolation. This snapping improved the private leaderboard metric by about 0.1, and public and private improvements tracked together.

The solution imputed F4 with a denoising autoencoder conditioned on missingness masks, mean-imputed F1 and F3, and ignored F2. Feature and mask embeddings were added before a seven-layer residual MLP, with masked reconstruction and loss calculations focusing learning on imputable values. Averaging repeated PyTorch and TensorFlow runs worked best, although TensorFlow runs were stronger individually. Conditionally combining single-attribute models for rows with exactly one missing F4 value improved the private score from 0.83351 to 0.83343.

The author shared an individual LSTM approach while withholding the full team solution. Adding self-attention and other modifications improved the notebook, which achieved a public score of 6.060. The team used snapping predictions to a grid, and the author explored corrections for implausible snapped paths. Those corrections were excluded because they hurt the public leaderboard, although private results later suggested a benefit.

The pipeline extracted faces with BlazeFace from one random frame per video for base-model training and ten random frames per video for stacking. ImageNet- and Noisy Student-initialized EfficientNets were trained with compression and downscaling augmentation, with class balancing adjusted between training stages. Base models were stacked, and the five best stacked models were combined through a frame-wise ensemble weighted by validation scores. Validation used data chunks 40–49, while stronger augmentation, alternative architectures, and stacking stacked models were unsuccessful.
compute: About 3–5 training epochs per model before overfitting

solution_summary: The solution combined ArcFace image embeddings, Indonesian BERT title models, and TF-IDF features for product matching. Similarity-based label cleanup and normalized alpha query expansion were important improvements. A LightGBM pairwise metamodel used similarity features, with cuML ForestInference accelerating prediction. Multiple predictions were combined and thresholds tuned on the public leaderboard; discriminative query expansion provided little benefit.

The author selected versions of public tabular notebooks using cross-validation and leaderboard performance. Memory limitations narrowed the first submission to two notebook versions. The second submission combined an image-based notebook with the same tabular starter for stability. That blend did not help the public leaderboard but improved private performance.
compute: Memory limitations constrained notebook selection; hardware and runtime were not specified.

solution_title: Single 5 fold deberta v3 large to obtain silver medal
solution_summary: The linked training notebook identifies the model as DeBERTa-v3-large. The author concatenated the final four layers, added an LSTM on top, and used adversarial weight perturbation. Concatenating the layers was reported to substantially stabilize training. The model achieved a cross-validation score of 0.4447 and a private leaderboard score of 0.436405.

solution_title: 82th Place Solution for the Kaggle - LLM Science Exam Competition
solution_summary: The solution combined a custom Wikipedia corpus, embedding-based similarity search, and a DeBERTa ensemble. The author rendered Wikipedia articles through a private MediaWiki service to preserve content lost by conventional dump processing. Among the tested embedding models, BAAI/bge-large-en achieved the highest reported training MAP@100 at 0.727. Half-precision storage and dual-T4 inference supported the large retrieval pipeline, while Longformer and Wikipedia masked-language-model fine-tuning were unsuccessful.
compute: 64 cores and 256GB RAM for corpus preparation; about 3 days uploading and 3 days downloading; 2x T4 for DeBERTa inference and similarity search.

solution_summary: The author reports using hypercolumns in the competition. They link a blog post describing the approach. The provided text gives no further pipeline details or results.

The solution used the Matterport Mask R-CNN implementation with a ResNet101 backbone and a RetinaNet classifier because the original classifier performed poorly. Detection training used only positive samples, with 5,093 training images and 566 validation images. Raising the RPN NMS threshold to 0.9 and using horizontal flips helped leaderboard performance, while backbone modifications gave only modest training-loss improvements. The reported scores were 0.236 for Stage 1 and 0.217 for Stage 2.
compute: 1 GPU, 8 images per GPU; approximately one week available for fine-tuning

solution_title: 33rd place solution - Polynomials, CNN and Ridge regression
solution_summary: The solution separated prediction into mean transit depth, atmospheric spectral shape, and uncertainty estimation. Smoothed and detrended lightcurves supplied the mean depth, while a small regularized CNN predicted relative spectral coefficients from wavelength-window depth estimates. Ridge regression further reduced reported RMSE from 64 to 58 PPM. The final uncertainty estimate used twice the standard deviation of each planet's predictions, while learned residual models failed to transfer local gains to the leaderboard.

The submission combined four DeBERTa-v3-large models with a TF-IDF ensemble containing MultinomialNB, SGDClassifier, and LightGBM classifiers. The TF-IDF branch received weight 0.65 and the DeBERTa branch 0.35. Training used diverse human and AI text, including DAIGT-V3 and self-generated ChatGPT data, with AI texts containing more than ten spelling errors removed. DeBERTa trained for five to six epochs with shorter training sequences and a 512-token inference limit, using stratified validation.

solution_title: A Dual-Stream DINOv3 + Gated Depthwise Convolutions + Auxiliary Metadata
solution_summary: The final system combined three DualGatedEncoder and TwinStreamMetaNet models using a DINOv3 vision transformer backbone. Images were split into left and right halves, whose tokens were fused through gated depthwise convolutions. Metadata prediction heads, metadata dropout, and mass-balance consistency gates helped the models rely on visual evidence while respecting biomass relationships. Four-way test-time augmentation and target-specific blending completed the pipeline, with the best single model scoring 0.75 on the public leaderboard.

The solution enriched each phrase pair with related targets sharing its anchor or anchor and context. A second stage included first-stage out-of-fold and test predictions as numeric tokens alongside those targets. DeBERTa and patent BERT models benefited from adversarial training, exponential moving averages, and limited knowledge distillation. Anchor-grouped cross-validation supported linear regression ensemble weighting, with strong agreement between validation and leaderboard scores.

The team combined the 2019 and 2020 datasets, removed duplicates using image embeddings and DBSCAN, and manually reviewed selected suspicious labels. They trained EfficientNet B4, ViT, Inception, and Xception with light augmentation and several label-smoothed losses. Training at 384 pixels followed by restricted fine-tuning at 512 pixels improved speed and performance, with 2019 data used only for training. Averaging model probabilities with five random-crop test-time augmentations achieved reported public and private scores of 90.2 and 90.1.

The solution is dominated by a three-layer feedforward neural network with store and item-class embeddings and a promotion-aware convolutional output, supported by LightGBM. Weekday-aligned training windows, recent sales aggregates, and sales from 364 days earlier capture seasonality. Carefully structured validation and early stopping mattered more than public leaderboard feedback. The main neural model scored 0.515 private and 0.508 public; a potentially better blend and promotion-aware postprocessing were not fully combined before the deadline.

The author uses a two-stage approach that first detects the driver's body and then classifies a cropped image. The method does not use semi-supervised learning. The post links to code and a conceptual diagram but gives no model architecture or numerical results.

The solution improved GNSS least-squares positioning by filtering low-elevation satellites and smoothing pseudoranges with valid accumulated delta ranges. Doppler-derived vehicle velocities provided accurate relative positions, with LightGBM and IMU features filling gaps. Several outlier filters and trajectory post-processing steps refined absolute coordinates. Phone-model-weighted averaging and area-specific processing completed the pipeline.

The pipeline combined object detection, Norfair tracking, and classification of cropped detections. Four detector types were combined with weighted boxes fusion, while tracking improved recall but introduced false positives. EfficientNetB7 and Eca NFNet L0 classifiers trained across five folds focused on difficult detector errors and incorporated additional Internet COTS images. Geometric blending of classification and detection confidence was estimated to improve the final private score by about 6%, reaching 0.706.
external_data: ["Internet COTS data with Creative Commons licenses"]

solution_summary: The post links to solution code but provides only limited technical details locally. It identifies a dataset construction vulnerability that makes invariant mass a perfect discriminator between signal and background. The author reports calculating the mother particle's mass despite missing azimuthal angles. The post also warns that exposing agreement and correlation datasets allows participants to overuse those tests, without describing the final model or ensemble.

solution_title: Lessons Learned - The Good and the Bad!
solution_summary: The solution trained segmentation models on balanced defect crops and transferred their weights to models that predicted full-width images. Its segmentation components were U-Net with ResNet34 and FPN models with InceptionV3 or ResNet34, supported by Xception and EfficientNet-B4 classifiers. Pre-classification reduced false positives, while a sliding crop classifier removed mask regions with low defect probability. The author also described skipping public test images to save inference time. A model achieved 0.905 private Dice, but the selected submissions favored public leaderboard performance and generalized worse.
compute: One-hour inference time limit.

solution_summary: The solution reversed the purchase-amount normalization and applied log1p, with derived aggregates reportedly improving the score by 0.04. Features included customer lifetime value statistics, regression features, transaction ratios, percentage changes, and separate authorized and unauthorized aggregates. Null-importance selection reduced the feature set before LightGBM and XGBoost regression on non-outliers. A LightGBM classifier routed suspected outliers to Ridge regression, and combining the results produced a reported best private score of 3.611.

The solution stacked diverse LightGBM models and an MLP with embeddings derived from continuous features. Diversity came from plain-feature models, threshold-based two-stage models, and training augmentation using a denoising autoencoder. Linear regression combined out-of-fold predictions, with nonlinear interactions between stacking features providing small further gains. The neural model achieved approximately 0.700X on both cross-validation and the leaderboard and improved the final stack.

The defense combined seven models and used a separate Inception v3 model as an adversarial-image detector. The ensemble's leading label was retained when it differed from Inception's prediction or received a majority of votes; otherwise, the second-best ensemble label was returned. Models ran sequentially and wrote temporary prediction files to avoid out-of-memory errors.

The approach used specialized covariance matrix features, Riemannian geometry, channel selection and an ElasticNet classifier. Models trained on random subsets of subjects were combined by averaging predictions. The team submitted independently tuned versions with and without leakage information. The online-compatible version scored 0.84585 on the private leaderboard, while the leakage-based version scored 0.87224.

solution_title: 24th Place Solution — 2-Phase SDF U-Net, PF/GBDT Legs, and a Disagreement-Tiered
solution_summary: The solution formulates well alignment as image-based signed-distance-field regression, combining GR matching, trajectory geometry, particle-filter densities and a supervised prefix inside each image. Synthetic-heavy pretraining and real-only refinement use anchor shifts, constrained jitter and donor-log replacement. Particle-filter, boosted-tree and geometric predictions join a disagreement-trimmed blend and fold-safe Ridge stack, followed by smoothing in TVT-plus-depth space. Grouped validation guided selection to a private score of 6.576, while the authors identified limited base-model quality, coarse vertical resolution and inability to represent multimodal alignments as major constraints.
compute: 2× V100 GPUs over three weeks.

solution_summary: The author benchmarked multiple quantile-forecasting approaches across hierarchy levels and combined predictions through stacking. Features included rolling sales statistics, historical quantiles, prices, hierarchical seasonal encodings, and event effects. Training used horizon augmentation for non-item series, random downsampling for item-level data, and sales-based normalization for time-series models. The author identified several reliability issues, including random splits for stacking, quantile fitting on validation data, and an event-feature leakage bug; a post-competition 0.97 adjustment substantially improved the submitted score.

The solution used three stacking levels built from diverse models, feature representations, and target transformations. Roughly 70 first-level models were dominated by bagged XGBoost and Keras neural networks, while about 50 second-level models were grouped and averaged into ten final features. A bagged quantile regression formed the third level, with power corrections and submission averaging providing additional refinement. The best individual XGBoost model achieved CV MAE of 1122.64977 and private leaderboard MAE of 1116.74215.

solution_title: Never Trust a Zebrafish You Have Not Met: 5th on Public 💪, 52nd on Private 🫠
solution_summary: The final pipeline kept public nucleus detectors fixed and improved detection fusion, tracking, division decisions, and graph cleanup. Its main learned addition was DivNet, a small 3D CNN trained across embryos and averaged over three seeds. Most settings were selected on the public leaderboard, which represented a different embryo from the private set and encouraged choices that did not transfer. The official submission scored 0.97290 public and 0.93485 private, while a post-deadline experiment using embryo-specific settings reached 0.95607 private without retraining.
models_pretrained: ["pilkwang public detector weights, 50-epoch support pack", "V1284 coordinate-refinement head"]
compute: DivNet trained on Kaggle T4 GPUs in about two hours; one rented A100 at about $0.70/hour ran the full pipeline over 199 training videos in about two hours.

solution_title: That was a surprise! Here is the 1st place solution....
solution_summary: The solution used AutoGluon Tabular with feature engineering taken from a public notebook. It combined common model families trained with eight folds, including boosted trees, random forests, and neural networks. Bootstrap aggregation, three stacking levels, and a weighted ensemble formed the final pipeline. The reported local cross-validation score was 0.5006.

The final pipeline trained 3D DenseNet121 and DenseNet169 classifiers separately for four MRI modalities across five stratified folds, producing 40 models. MRI volumes were cropped to remove empty slices, resized to 144³, standardized, and augmented with rotations and elastic deformations. Repeated training runs with cosine annealing were used to obtain sufficiently low validation loss, and equal averaging of the diverse models achieved an OOF ROC AUC of 0.692443. Segmentation-derived features and mask channels did not improve classification, while weighted blending also failed to outperform equal averaging.

solution_title: [Working Note] When a Strong Public Score Transfers to Zero
solution_summary: This controlled replication used a public baseline that searched seven single-message sandbox exfiltration templates. It selected forms by observed reward per second and minimum success rate, then packed candidates using conservative replay-latency estimates. The single formal submission scored 89.010 public and 0.000 private, showing complete failure to transfer to the hidden guardrail. The author attributes this outcome to correlated dependence on one public-policy gap and proposes broader policy validation as future work.

solution_title: 4th place solution: Stain Normalization is all you need
solution_summary: The solution used separate segmentation streams for lung images and other organs to reduce harmful cross-organ transfer. Its final ensemble combined CoaT-lite-medium, MiT/SegFormer, and MPViT encoders with daformer+unet decoders. Random Reinhard and Vahadane stain normalization during training helped bridge HPA and HuBMAP appearance differences. At inference, images were normalized toward organ-specific HPA references and predictions were averaged, without pseudo-labels or external data.

The solution combined ArcFace image embeddings with TF-IDF text embeddings. EfficientNet B1 and B5 outputs were concatenated before a softmax layer, and a separate single-fold EfficientNet B6 was also used. Cosine-distance KNN identified similar products. An image-specific distance threshold was relaxed when it returned at most one match.

The author contributed a BST transformer binary reranker using inputs from teammates' models and additional personal features. The implementation was ported from TensorFlow to PyTorch. Although gradient-boosted trees performed better individually, the transformer added diversity to the final ensemble. An iterative session stratification procedure avoided the memory requirements of stratifying all ground-truth items together.

solution_title: My brief summary,a mainly NN based solution(3th)
solution_summary: The solution combined neural networks and LightGBM using 23 categorical, click-timing, aggregate, and target-mean features. Careful imputation, logarithmic transformations, and standardization made the neural networks competitive, while GRU-based gating and architectural variations added diversity. Weighted averaging was followed by second-level neural networks using predictions and additional grouped features. The reported ensemble reached 0.9833 public AUC and 0.9840 private AUC, although the author observed sensitivity to distribution differences.
compute: Training and prediction for one fold took 2.x hours on a 1080i GPU.

solution_summary: The post describes feature engineering and overfitting control for fraud detection without specifying the full modeling pipeline in text. An inferred card-opening day combined transaction day with D1, while UID encodings helped identify previously observed entities. Time-window counts of transactions and product types helped with new UIDs. Rare UIDs appearing only in training were replaced with missing values so that additional UID encodings could be used with less overfitting.

The final ensemble combined three segmentation models with classification heads and nine segmentation-only models using four-view TTA. Segmentation-only models trained on positive labels, while classification predictions filtered negative outputs. Averaging the top 17,500 pixel probabilities supplied additional class scores, and the most probable class was forced positive for every image. EMA replaced averaging the last five checkpoints, and the final ensemble achieved 0.67175 on the private leaderboard.

The solution ensembled a CatBoost regressor trained on a Kaplan–Meier target with a PRL neural network, applying classifier-based event masking to both. Cross-validation stratified jointly by race group and binned target, using ten folds across thirty seeds for each model variant. Event masking used CatBoost, XGBoost, and LightGBM classifiers and improved the Kaplan–Meier CatBoost CV score from about 0.6781 to 0.6865. The final approach reported CV of 0.690, public leaderboard score of 0.689, and private score of 0.693.

The final ensemble combined EfficientNet B1, B2, and B4 models, with B4 providing the main contribution. The largest improvement came from retraining existing weights twice, lowering the learning rate, extending training, and adding JPEG compression augmentation. Models used different random train-validation splits, and blend weights were selected using leaderboard performance because consistent ensemble validation was unavailable. The strongest B4 model scored 0.930 locally and 0.925 on the private leaderboard.
compute: V100 GPU; approximately 2.5 hours per epoch; training extended to 50 epochs.

solution_summary: The solution combined extensive geographic, temporal, and route features with a two-layer stack. Correlated aggregate features were split into four datasets, each used to train five different base models. Route-distance and traffic-frequency representations were compressed with SVD, while rotated coordinates captured travel along Manhattan's street grid. A tuned XGBoost model combined the 20 base models.

The solution treated sensor sequences as images, with feature channels as image height and time as width, and used a DINO patch-8 XCiT model for multimodal inputs. Orientation multitask learning, MixUp, CutMix, and training with soft labels were major contributors. Sequences were cropped and resampled to 192 steps, with subject-specific sensor corrections and engineered motion features. Subject-grouped validation showed an improvement from 0.875 to 0.895 with soft labels, and the final ensemble scored 0.874 publicly and 0.849 privately.
compute: Vision model: 22 epochs at about 40 seconds per epoch; IMU-only 1DCNN + GRU: 120 epochs at about 110 seconds per epoch.

solution_summary: The final solution blended variants of a two-branch neural network implemented using the Advanced Keras notebook as a base. Feature interactions identified with Xgbfir formed a graph with two connected components, which determined the feature groups assigned to each branch. Restricting interactions to these groups was the central idea for reducing noise. A similarly constrained LightGBM model reached a leaderboard score of 0.99778 but was excluded from the blend.

solution_title: 75th Place Solution - Bronze - My First Competition Medal
solution_summary: The solution transcribed Bengali audio using a Hugging Face Wav2Vec2 CTC model with language model assisted decoding. Audio was preprocessed with librosa and processed in batches. Beam decoding produced transcriptions that were normalized and formatted with Bengali punctuation before submission. The writeup reports no quantitative evaluation.

The author describes their contribution using a RoBERTa-large readability regressor initialized through pairwise binary pretraining on competition excerpts. Training used standard-error-weighted MSE, strong Mixout with BERT-layer dropout disabled, and separate regression heads for hidden layers combined through learned weights. Random token insertion and a maximum sequence length of 300 were also used. The implementation achieved CV 0.4723 and leaderboard score 0.460, and the author subsequently trained additional models using pseudo-labeled external data.

The author trained an XGBoost regressor using 29 selected features describing seeds, average team statistics, Elo ratings, and team quality. Feature selection and further parameter tuning reduced the Brier score. The final predictions were adjusted upward, with additional manual overrides for several early men's tournament games based on seeds and expert opinions.

The team combined Swin Large, ViT Large, and CaiT image models trained in TensorFlow and PyTorch. TensorFlow models used binary cross-entropy and included three differently parameterized SVR heads, while PyTorch models used cross-entropy. A knowledge-distilled Swin variant improved individual-model CV, and a second-stage linear regression combined predictions from models trained on common folds. The final ensemble reached a CV score of 17.0275, with local CV tracking private leaderboard performance.

solution_title: #58 solution: CV = 0.475, Public LB = 0.43, Private LB = 0.492
solution_summary: The author represented symptoms through their frequencies across 11 diseases and standardized those frequencies with z-scores. KMeans grouped symptoms into three clusters, which supplied three symptom-count features and 33 disease-specific score features. Only these 36 engineered features were retained, and the original dataset was excluded. Reported scores were 0.475 CV, 0.43 public, and 0.492 private; the predictive model was not specified.

solution_title: 53th place solution: Fast or Slow with Data Prunning and Pretraining
solution_summary: The solution merged random and default layout datasets separately for NLP and XLA pretraining, then fine-tuned models for individual subsets. Fixed normalization statistics and removal of zero-valued feature dimensions reduced preprocessing inconsistency and training cost. Layout training used concatenated global pooling, increasing loss margins, Adam, cosine learning-rate scheduling, and gradient clipping for XLA.RANDOM. Reported layout Kendall tau scores ranged from 29.6% to 85.2%, while the separately trained TILE model achieved 90.82% validation OPA. A GENConv and Transformer hybrid and architecture-design experiments did not improve results.

The team trained furniture classifiers using 192,171 training images and 6,309 validation images. Initial Caffe experiments overfit, prompting a switch to PyTorch and broader model experimentation. They used TenCrop inference and generated three successive sets of test pseudo labels, with intermediate public scores reaching 0.12656. The final submission averaged models trained on all three pseudo-label sets, excluding two specified checkpoints.

The team used a SAINT+-like encoder-decoder Transformer with question, response, part, explanation, elapsed-time, and lag-time inputs. Splitting lag times into seconds, minutes, and days and distinguishing real zeros from padding each improved the score by about 0.003. Categorical time embeddings performed better than continuous embeddings. Blending Transformers with LightGBM and, in one configuration, CatBoost raised the public score to 0.804, compared with 0.799 for the Transformer and 0.794 for LightGBM.

solution_title: Explainable Models with Polymer Knowledge Features
solution_summary: The writeup focuses on interpretable polymer feature engineering used with AutoGluon and ensembling. Sanitized monomers were expanded into short polymer chains before extracting RDKit descriptors and empirical group-contribution estimates for polymer properties. Backbone length, rigidity, bond composition, and rotational features complemented literature-derived estimates of Tg, density, FFV, and Rg. The author reported improved cross-validation wMAE without retaining exact comparisons, and tree-based feature elimination highlighted several proposed descriptors.
external_data: ["Van Krevelen 1970 polymer group-contribution factors", "Albert Wu et al. 2021 paper"]

solution_summary: The solution combined a TF-IDF classifier pipeline with two DeBERTa-v3-large models and one RoBERTa model. Diverse datasets covered different prompts, generation settings, model sizes, and human text sources. Reverse-engineered spelling correction and similarity-based postprocessing supplemented the classifiers. The strongest single transformer classifier scored 0.96 public and 0.915 private.
external_data: ["LLM-generated text", "Student essays and open-source web text"]

solution_title: 19th Place Solution - First Time With NFNets
solution_summary: The team used 640-pixel images with NFNet F3 and ResNet200d models initialized from ImageNet weights. Training combined Ranger optimization followed by SAM fine-tuning, and pseudo-labeling the NIH dataset substantially improved cross-validation. The final ensemble weighted models according to validation performance, with NFNet contributing most. Selecting the highest-CV ensemble also identified their best private submission, while border removal and distribution-based post-processing did not help.

solution_title: 17th Place Solution| AutoML + Unicorn's pollen + Lack of sleep
solution_summary: The final submission combines a three-level AutoGluon stack with averages of previous models and public notebook predictions. OpenFE generated 470 features, which BorutaSHAP and RFECV reduced to 103. CleanLab and relabeling were also reported as useful components of the data-centric approach. The selected averaged submission achieved a private score of 0.90106, while PCA/ICA, standalone boosting, TabPFN, surname features, and the original dataset did not help.

The solution trained ResNeSt and RegNet models on randomly cropped log-mel spectrograms, combining models across folds and input resolutions. Mixing recordings without secondary labels created multilabel examples, while SED-derived pseudo labels corrected recordings with secondary labels. Record-wise validation and longer training were important for stable performance. Shifted test-time augmentation brought no improvement, and mixup and simulated nocall classification were unsuccessful.

The solution documents a scripted R and Python pipeline for cleaning text, constructing relevance features, and training diverse models. Feature scripts indicate Word2vec, Okapi, n-gram matching, TF-IDF, and product-name extraction. Five-fold cross-validation supports first-layer nearest-neighbor, random-forest, neural-network, XGBoost, SVM, and H2O models. Their outputs feed second-layer stacking and a final ensemble, although scores and combination weights are not provided.
The post links to the team's technical report on arXiv. It contains no description of the competition pipeline or methods. It also includes a hiring link.

solution_title: From 12th Public to 95th Private: Our Biohub Cell Tracking Solution
solution_summary: The team extended a public cell-tracking pipeline with additional detection and edge models, then refined the resulting lineage graph. Masking likely unannotated cells from detection loss reduced false-negative supervision and substantially accelerated training. The final system combined multiple checkpoints, constrained graph optimization, division checks, coordinate refinement, and duplicate-frame cleanup. It scored 0.971 public and 0.928 private, although validation comparisons were limited by embryo overlap and later training exposure to some validation videos.
compute: Pseudo-unlabeling reduced training time to roughly one tenth; hardware and absolute runtime were not stated.

solution_summary: The team used a classic simulated annealing algorithm. The post provides a source code repository for the solution. It does not describe the search moves, optimization settings, or measured results.

The team reused a sub-center ArcFace pipeline with dynamic margins, adding newer CNN and transformer architectures. Recognition used an 11-model ensemble containing three transformers, three new CNNs and five fine-tuned models from the previous year. Progressive image resizing, cosine learning schedules and Adam or AdamW formed the training recipe. Post-processing combined embedding similarity with classification probabilities and penalized non-landmark matches and frequent index classes; transformers were particularly strong for retrieval.
compute: Multi-GPU training with DistributedDataParallel; hardware types unspecified.

solution_summary: The solution used the LP 67xyz formulation. A consistency constraint linked adjacent days' transition sums and strengthened the linear program. Introducing a separate variable for each incoming transition sum made cutting and branching easier. An alternative formulation with 175 variables per day and many constraints was less successful despite convex-hull and lazy-constraint techniques.

solution_title: My first bronze medal(128th place solution)
solution_summary: The post celebrates the team's first competition medal and thanks teammates and supporters. It recounts a late improvement shortly before the final submission deadline and emphasizes perseverance. It links to a solution notebook but provides no methodological explanation in the post itself.

solution_title: The  needle in a haystack (12th place solution)
solution_summary: The author expanded training data into overlapping observation and target windows beginning every 15 days, producing roughly ten million observations. Each user could appear repeatedly with window-dependent targets and customer-lifetime-value features. A single random forest was chosen for stability without hyperparameter tuning. Boosting proved unstable, and stacking was discarded because reliable tuning data was too limited.

solution_title: 5th Place Solution: GNN with Invariant Dimension Features
solution_summary: The solution used a three-layer GraphSAGE network with separate weights for both edge directions and concatenated outputs. Training combined within-graph and batch-wide pairwise hinge losses on whole graphs. A transformer encoded dimension-wise features before summation, substantially helping tile prediction, while the final layout submission combined flattened-feature and transformer models. Feature handling, DropEdge, oversampling, and memory-mapped data loading supported the pipeline.

The solution classified chart types with a fine-tuned ResNet18d and routed scatter plots to a detection, OCR, and template-matching pipeline. Scatter reconstruction used detected point templates and a robust median-based regression method to reduce sensitivity to outliers. Other chart types were processed by a Pix2Struct model initialized from MatCha-base, using xyxy labels and rounded numerical targets. Chart classification achieved 0.995 accuracy on extracted data, while the scatter pipeline scored 0.51.

solution_title: Efficiency track 18th place (25th public): length of test dataframe, groupby, mean
solution_summary: The solution predicts correctness from question-level averages conditioned on discretized gameplay row counts. It fits separate length discretizers for level groups, computes mean correctness for question-bin combinations, and chooses a classification threshold by F1 score. This inexpensive baseline improved over using question averages alone. Reported scores were 0.671 public and 0.675 private.

The solution used second-stage stacking followed by optimization of ensemble weights. SVM and linear models performed well on tabular inputs, while tree models were less effective than KNN. A 3D ResNet18 was the strongest tested CNN, outperforming deeper ResNet and ResNeXt alternatives. Splitting fMRI volumes into three to six pieces improved performance, whereas eight pieces did not help.

The solution combines retrieved contexts with three open-book DeBERTa models and three models that answer without retrieved context. Retrieval repeats the question for weighting, reverses context order, and limits an added retrieval source to fifteen sentences. Context predictions are blended 4:4:2, while the final model blend gives ninety percent weight to open-book models. The described blend achieved a reported private score of 0.906.

The authors explored multiple pretrained RNA structure predictors and built a final ensemble, although its exact composition is absent from the provided text. Protenix, DRFold2, Boltz-1, and trRosettaRNA produced the strongest standalone results and received additional experimentation. Attempts to fine-tune Protenix on newer PDB structures were constrained by GPU access, while an altered AF3 implementation was unfinished. Both overlapping sequence chunking and chunking based on secondary structure failed to improve long-sequence predictions.
compute: Limited GPU access and compute/storage constraints prevented full fine-tuning experiments; hardware unspecified.

solution_title: My one trick for feature selection/data augmentation (183rd place)
solution_summary: The authors augmented each 150,000-point segment with six overlapping 140,000-point windows at different offsets. At inference, predictions from the six windows were averaged. This improved cross-validation by about 0.003 and reduced the importance of many potentially spurious features. Their best submission was a single LightGBM model trained with this scheme.

The solution trained sound-event detection and CNN models using only the competition's 2025 audio and soundscapes. RMS sampling, partial human-voice removal, extensive augmentation, and EMA supported first-stage training, followed by sparse soft pseudo-label training. Final predictions combined EfficientNetV2-B3 and SE-ResNeXt models across seeds with windowed TTA and temporal smoothing. The selected ensemble scored 0.913 publicly and 0.921 privately; a four-model ensemble timed out during the competition but reached 0.924 privately afterward with single-thread inference.
compute: Four-model inference took about 1 minute 20 seconds on ten 60-second soundscapes in a trial; the competition submission timed out.

solution_summary: The final approach adapted tubo's CNN/U-Net and LSTM pipelines and combined four architecture and input-length configurations. Inputs included motion measurements, temporal features, and a flag for repeated sensor values, while training predicted Gaussian event targets and an auxiliary sleep flag. Inference averaged overlapping windows, trimmed CNN window edges, and localized events through peak detection and score-weighted refinement. An earlier two-stage chunk-classification and event-regression approach scored 0.677 on the leaderboard but suffered from fixed chunk boundaries and limited model exploration.

The final solution used a single DeBERTa large model with token classification and weighted layer pooling. An auxiliary discourse-type classification task stabilized training and improved effectiveness prediction. The author also found that increasing the scheduler's epoch setting helped. The reported scores were 0.589 on the public leaderboard and 0.590 on the private leaderboard.

The solution blended BERT, OpenGPT/GPT-2, and XLNet models without text preprocessing, using a maximum sequence length of 256. BERT received additional language-model fine-tuning on competition data with modified segment IDs. Toxicity was represented as an 11-class distribution and trained alongside identity prediction with subgroup-aware sample weights. Final predictions used a weighted power blend with exponent 3.5.

solution_title: RSNA Intracranial Aneurysm Detection — My Approach (Top 5%/ 57th)
solution_summary: The solution used a three-stage 3D pipeline that localized the brain, refined arterial regions, and classified aneurysms within those regions. MedNeXt-S segmentation and anatomical priors reduced irrelevant background before downstream modeling. Transformer models and CNN–RNN models with attention supplied complementary predictions for a weighted ensemble. The reported final mean weighted AUC-ROC was 0.70.

Dense neural networks predicted SVD-compressed gene targets, which were reconstructed into the original gene space. Inputs combined cell identity, molecular fingerprints, drug properties, and optional aggregated SVD features. Model diversity came from skip connections, cell-based sample weighting, error-driven oversampling, and three regression heads encouraged to produce different hypotheses. The final submissions combined the best 16 and 80 submissions using weights derived from leaderboard RWRMSE.

The solution combined diverse CNN classifiers with nearest-neighbor retrieval from hidden-layer features. Separate ResNet50 classifiers reduced confidence for retrieval-challenge images and images without landmarks. Local-crop retrieval supplied additional high-confidence predictions, while merging combined model agreement and confidence scores. A filename-based heuristic further reduced low-confidence predictions for certain test images, although treating all such filenames as non-landmarks worsened the score.

The final approach combined LightGBM, XGBoost and CatBoost using continuous regression outputs, which substantially outperformed hard classification outputs. Feature preparation included memory-efficient dtypes, categorical treatment of two integer columns, splitting the string feature into ten positions, and borrowed interaction features. LightGBM predictions were clipped to the valid probability range, and evaluation was corrected from RMSE to ROC AUC. The regression ensemble achieved reported scores of 0.97952 / 0.97982, while PyCaret failed with out-of-memory errors and logistic regression ensembling performed poorly.
compute: LightGBM was run in CPU and GPU modes; GPU model and training duration were unspecified.

solution_title: 184th Place Solution ESM2 (2 models) using RMDB + QUICK_START datasets
solution_summary: The author fine-tuned ESM2 to predict RNA sequence reactivity using RMDB and QUICK_START data. Two separate models handled the two experiment types. Base-pair probability files were not explored, which the author identified as a potential improvement.

The solution uses three ensemble levels, beginning with about 50 subject-specific models built from filtered EEG signals and frequency-band covariance features. About 30 global second-level models combine their predictions, with recurrent networks exploiting event sequences and eight seconds of prediction history. A final AUC-optimized weighted average sharpens predictions around event-window edges. Model diversity and cross-validation stability guided the two final submissions, with reported score pairs of 0.98128/0.98109 and 0.98108/0.98095.
compute: Up to one week to generate final results.

solution_summary: The author used greedy local search to improve gift delivery trips. Moves included relocating or swapping gifts across trips and extending those operations to multiple gifts. Within trips, the method exhaustively tested permutations of sliding windows of five gifts, while another move tested permutations of six gifts from different trips. The reported objective value was 12425651858.70720.

The final solution blended 20 XGBoost models with 50 Keras models from three model variants. Pseudolabeling, label smoothing, and cosine learning rate decay were applied to some or all of the models. Optimizing batch size and learning rate was another important lesson from the competition. The final performance improvement came from relabeling 40,000 training samples that the models misclassified with the highest confidence.

solution_title: The Winning Solution I didn't submit!
solution_summary: The author mapped version variables to timestamps and centered their distributions by subtracting the median to address a consistent train–test time offset. A two-stage approach combined initial predictions with cluster-level prediction means for time-related variables. The standalone submission achieved 0.74 CV, 0.68967 public, and 0.68308 private scores. The automatically selected submissions were blends with public kernels, and the author could not verify that the attached notebook exactly reproduced the standalone submission.

solution_title: Congrats to the winners (88th place solution)
solution_summary: The author used a single EfficientNetB3 regressor pretrained on the 2015 competition data and fine-tuned on the 2019 dataset. Predictions were constrained to the range zero to four with a capped rectified output. Images were resized to 300×300, processed by cropping black bars and subtracting local means, and augmented with zooms, rotations, and horizontal flips. A validation run selected the training duration before retraining on all 2019 data; TTA, optimized rounding, and ensembles did not improve results.

The author replaced candidate names with standard single-token names and created a second version with the names swapped. BERT activations for the two candidates and pronoun were averaged across these versions and concatenated across all 12 layers. PCA reduced the resulting features to 600 dimensions before a small dense network with dropout was trained using five folds. The approach worked well without BERT fine-tuning, while autoencoding lacked sufficient data.

The solution combined three adapted approaches from previous NCAA competitions with an original stacking regressor containing ten regressors. Models were validated and tuned using the current dataset and previous competitions. Predictions were combined through a validation-guided weighted adjustment that moved outputs toward those of better-performing models. No manual prediction changes were made, and the model predicted Baylor as champion.

The solution combined spectrum models, raw EEG models, and a joint EEG-spectrum model in a weighted six-model ensemble. EEG preprocessing used a double banana montage, 0.5–20 Hz filtering, and clipping to ±1024, with STFT spectra feeding an X3D-L 3D CNN or an EfficientNet-B5 image model. Raw EEG was reshaped into an image for EfficientNet-B5 and HGNet-B5, with different filters providing diversity. Two-stage training changed voter-based loss weights and restricted the second stage to higher-vote samples. The final ensemble improved the private score from roughly 0.28 to 0.27, and the author considered raw EEG especially important.

The best model used prior averages for prospectid, zip5, and packageid with linear regression. Separate models predicted donation amount and response probability, which were combined by raising predicted gift to 1.15 and multiplying by predicted response rate. Most data preparation was performed in SQL Server because the dataset was difficult to handle in R. Demographic features proved difficult to incorporate because of geographic-key duplication and slow processing.

The author used a single XGBoost model with corrected targets from the original dataset and iteratively validated engineered features. Useful features included a balance-to-estimated-salary ratio, original-data overlap indicators, CustomerID–Surname combinations, and surname initials. High-cardinality variables used the author's described CatBoost frequency encoding, while low-cardinality variables used one-hot encoding. Optuna and early stopping improved tuning, whereas imbalance treatments did not help.

The author developed a physics-driven transit-fitting contribution that was combined with two other team solutions. After sensor calibration and temporal binning, two alternative lightcurve functions were fitted with Nelder–Mead optimization, with the lower-RMSE fit selected. Shared transit parameters enabled efficient wavelength-wise depth estimation, followed by five-component NMF smoothing and bucket-specific linear regression to correct for limb darkening. Duplicate observations were averaged, wavelength biases were corrected, and separate FGS and AIRS uncertainty formulas were optimized against the competition score.

solution_title: My solution without time series assumption
solution_summary: The solution averaged LightGBM models using raw song, user, and context features alongside recommendation-oriented features. These included SVD latent factors and interaction scores, neighborhood collaborative-filtering scores, user-specific similarities and category rates, and metadata embeddings. Validation used ten random splits, without accounting for the dataset's temporal ordering. The best single model achieved a public leaderboard score of 0.726.

The team trained ByT5-XL translators on carefully extracted book pairs, LLM-labeled untranslated tablets, and synthetic examples, discarding the official train.csv. Their strongest ensemble combined 11 models trained on different data mixtures and selected translations through weighted minimum Bayes risk decoding over beam and sampled candidates. CTranslate2 compilation and int8-float32 quantization enabled the ensemble to fit nearly within the nine-hour inference budget. The strongest unselected submission scored 43.2 privately, while selected variants scored 42.8 with repeated n-gram cleanup and 42.4 using a conservative four-checkpoint ensemble.

solution_title: automl pipeline: featurewiz, multilabel k-fold and optuna
solution_summary: The solution combined automatically generated features with correlation-based feature selection. Iterative multilabel stratification over the target and age bins improved the stability of cross-validation under imbalance. Optuna optimized ensemble weights and thresholds. The author reported a 0.02 improvement on both cross-validation and the leaderboard from feature engineering.

The solution used a single Whole-Word-Masking BERT Large model adapted from BERT Joint and trained in TensorFlow 2.1 on a TPU. Training included substantially more unanswered examples and ran for one epoch with batch size 128 and learning rate 5e-5. Postprocessing interpreted answer-type logits and used an HTML-based heuristic to select some non-top-level long answers. A linear regression verifier combined nine logits to assess answers.

solution_title: [8th place solution] : SpecMix and warm-up pipeline
solution_summary: The solution used a staged pipeline that first trained on noisy audio, fine-tuned on curated data, and then reused noisy data in a semi-supervised stage. Its SpecMix augmentation replaced frequency and time regions while combining targets with weighted averages. Final inference ensembled a simple CNN and VGG16 across ten cross-validation folds.

solution_title: NN as part of 13th place solution (late joiners view)
solution_summary: The author developed the neural-network portion of a team solution using count-encoded features paired with the original variables. Five architectures processed each variable separately until a final layer combined information across variables. Extensive bagging improved the neural ensemble, which achieved a reported leaderboard score of 0.923. The final submission blended neural and gradient-boosting ensembles with weights of 70% and 30%, selected through leaderboard probing.

solution_title: 5th Place - AI for large scale experimentation - s6e4
solution_summary: The final solution stacked class probabilities from 119 diverse base models using a multiclass LightGBM model. Strong boosted trees were complemented by tabular neural networks, grouped-feature CNNs, graph models, and specialist models. Important features included leakage-safe target encodings, numeric digit patterns, original-data distribution signals, and features derived from the original dataset's exact rule. Agreement-based pruning and five-seed stacking addressed noisy model comparisons, producing approximately 0.98178 CV balanced accuracy and 0.98133 on the private leaderboard.

The solution ensembles modified transformers that treat detector pulses as tokens. Models use two prediction heads: XYZ vector regression with MSE and classification over Fibonacci-sphere locations with smoothed binary cross-entropy. Training has a main stage followed by fine-tuning on longer sequences. Cross-validation and leaderboard scores correlated well, with the best single model scoring about 0.967/0.968 and taking about 30 minutes for the full test set.

solution_summary: The team combined seven models in a stacking ensemble. Weighted averaging was used for some highly correlated models, while preprocessing remained simple. The linked report emphasizes model architectures and NLP feature engineering, with attention-layer experiments conducted after the competition.

solution_title: 224th Place: Out-of-Sample Validation and What Did Not Transfer
solution_summary: The team adapted a public UNet detector and transformer linker pipeline with ILP linking and extensive post-processing. Their strongest improvement was refitting a small coordinate-refinement MLP on captured detector features, improving private performance from 0.91780 to 0.92312. Final selections also included track-end trimming and a lower detection-readmission threshold, although trimming reduced private performance. Embryo-held-out validation and exact replay checks exposed many nontransferring post-processing gains and weak agreement between public and private scores.

solution_summary: The solution paired sentence-level Wikipedia retrieval with DeBERTa v3 Large answer models. Elasticsearch retrieved candidates using both questions and answer options, and three context variants ranked them by search score, edit distance, or semantic similarity. Training used public 60k and 40k datasets, with longer inputs and context filling the available token budget improving accuracy. Averaging predictions from the three context variants improved performance over using one retrieval method.

solution_title: #51 Silver — the gate reads payloads, not provenance
solution_summary: The submission investigates attacks on tool-using agents by testing whether defenses track value provenance or inspect textual proxies. The author reports that text-based gates could be inverted with token or paraphrase changes that preserved the executed action, and studies forged turn boundaries and action ordering. A read-less exfiltration approach failed on the private evaluation, while a hedged confused-deputy approach preserved a nonzero result. The accompanying notebook checks numerical claims against archived measurements or named sources, with all 843 numeric literals resolving.

The author obtained 0.991099 using a single UGradientBoostingClassifier from hep_ml. The implementation combined R and Python 2.7. A new feature divided FlightDistance by LifeTime, and selected rows were removed from the evaluation file to obtain evaluation results closer to the leaderboard.
